en: The New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll One, composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan.
Now, as for the fundamental nature of sentient beings, it relies upon the ocean of wisdom as its source; the stream of all conscious beings is, in its entirety, [rooted therein].
The Dharma-body constitutes its essence.

It is only because emotions arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because perceptions shift that the essence appears diverse; yet when one realizes the source, emotions vanish, and when one knows the mind, the essence is unified.

This present *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Great Vaipulya Buddha-Flower Adornment, clarifies the primordial limit of sentient beings and reveals the fountainhead of the fruition of all Buddhas; it is the very foundation.
It cannot be accomplished through merit, for it is the source;
it cannot be attained through practice, for when merit perishes, the root returns, and when practice is exhausted, the source is perfected.
The source and root are inherently without merit; one who is able to act with spontaneous freedom according to conditions is none other than this Vairocana.
Taking intrinsic nature as light, wisdom responds according to the faculties [of beings], and great compassion rescues all things; thus he is so named.
Relying on this fundamental nature, he establishes his teachings and grace, which flow profusely throughout the Dharma-realm to nourish all living beings.

Thereupon, he takes up residence in the four heavens and manifests the eight stages of birth, finally achieving enlightenment within the site of awakening by manifesting the forest hermitage (*araṇya*).

In the Hall of Universal Radiance, the great mansion of the Reward Body, the eldest son Samantabhadra displays the fruits of realization within his treasury-body, while the youngest son Mañjuśrī first awakens the mind of enlightenment at the Golden [Mountain].
Through the Samādhi of the Ocean Seal, he descends as a spirit pervading the Dharma-realm; by means of the Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye, he reveals oceans of lands within a single mote of dust.
The two retributions of the primary and secondary bodies and their lands interpenetrate; the two gates of cause and effect mutually penetrate in essence and function.
Thus, the precious nets of the celestial realm cast shadows of the ten lands in ever-receding layers, and the stainless maṇi-jewels reveal the ten bodies in profound clarity.
Within the boundless realms of the lands, self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth, and the ten periods of past and present are contained within a single instant.
From beginning to end, it does not deviate from the present moment.
In its vastness, it takes empty space as its measure;
in its minuteness, it dwells within the infinitesimal atom without leaving a trace.
The ten directions are not contracted, yet they do not diminish within the smallest of forms;
a single speck of dust is not expanded, yet it contains the ten directions without obstruction.
Constantly dwelling in the ocean of wisdom, one distributes the fruits of virtue through the gates of the five stages.
He dwells eternally in the Hall of Dharma, manifesting his progress and cultivation atop the Nine Heavens.
As it is in this realm, so it is in the ten lands;
the assembly of sages is like clouds, merging within the ocean-like gathering.
Wisdom is universally unobstructed, its form like many mirrors that receive myriad shapes;
self and other do not hinder one another, like a thousand lamps sharing a single room.
This sutra contains, in total, forty chapters of sublime scriptures, which profoundly open the Dharma-gates of the fruition of virtue.
A hundred trillion wondrous words all extol the ocean-like conduct of the Buddha’s flowers.
Through the ten bodies and ten assemblies, he expounds the dharma-gates of ten times ten;
throughout the ten locations and ten directions, he opens the ten penetrations and unfolds the ten eloquences.
Within the "Chapter on Manifestation," cause and effect are revealed to conclude the beginning and end;
at Jetavana, the welfare of humans and devas is served to clarify the Dharma-realm.
Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra were separated from the Buddha's presence by their own sight and hearing.
Six thousand bhikṣus set forth on the road to inquire about the Ten Clarities.

At the eastern outskirts of the City of Awakening, the five assemblies all arrived; before the temple of the Ancient Buddha, they collectively ascended to the Ten Wisdoms. With Sudhana as the leader who illuminated the Way, he manifested the brilliance of the multitude who had gathered together in harmony.

Furthermore, he perfected the five stages of the Dharma-gate and possessed its full virtues; by practicing its regulations, he enabled beginners to easily attain understanding and resolve all doubts regarding practice, thereby leading them to place their faith first before Mañjuśrī and to realize the ultimate truth at the summit of Wutai Shan.
Passing through the five assemblies, he perfected one hundred and ten dharma-gates;
reaching the garden of Maitreya, he finalized the fruition of Buddhahood attained in a single lifetime.
Returning to show his former friend Mañjuśrī, he clarified that the fruit is identical to the cause.
Subsequently, one enters the body of Samantabhadra, manifesting the perfect culmination of essence and function. As for the title of this scripture, *The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

"Great" (Mahā) takes omnipresence as its meaning; "Vaipulya" (Broad) takes the integration of principle and wisdom as its merit; "Avataṃsaka" (Flower) signifies that even a single hair-pore contains all lands, while "Buddha" denotes the non-action of essence and function. "Flower" is a metaphor for the gates of practice that are delightful and capable of unfolding the merits of both phenomenon and principle; "Adornment" refers to the adornment of the environment and the inhabitants; and "Sūtra" means to thread together and stitch.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Lords" (*Lokendra-vyuha-parivarta*): Bodhisattvas manifest birth as world lords for the sake of all beings, and because they together reach the ocean-like assembly, it is called "Sublime Array.
As for a "chapter" (*parivarta*), it is so designated because similar gatherings share a common flow and distinct dharma-gates are equally demarcated.
This sutra consists of forty chapters in total; as this chapter stands at the beginning, it is called the first. Therefore, it is titled:
The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Chapter One: The Sublime Array of the World Rulers.

This single section of the sutra will be analyzed through ten general gates: First, clarifying the classification of schools based on the teachings; Second, clarifying the distinctions between schools based on their doctrines; Third, clarifying the differences in doctrinal meaning;

Fourth, clarifying the similarities and differences regarding the attainment of Buddhahood; Fifth, clarifying the distinctions in the vision of the Buddha; Sixth, clarifying the timing of the delivery of the teachings; Seventh, clarifying the provisional and ultimate nature of the Pure Land; Eighth, clarifying the scope of those gathered and transformed; Ninth, clarifying the duration of cause and effect; Tenth, clarifying the beginning and end of the assembly of the teachings. First, regarding the classification of schools based on the teachings: Now, when the Tathāgata attained the Way, his essence corresponded to the true source. Within the two gates of principle and phenomena, the one and the many penetrate each other; in the perfect stillness of wisdom and its objects, what dharma is not encompassed?

It is solely because vessels differ in their capacities and ritual protocols vary; because the gradual and sudden approaches from beginning to end accord with differing faculties; because the established teachings are appropriately distinct as Great or Small Vehicles; because the timing of cause and effect differs in its duration; because the manifested Buddhas and the original bodies differ in the means they employ for expression; because the lands differ in purity, impurity, increase, or decrease; and because the stages and causes and effects naturally correspond to one's own affinity.

Those who follow the school of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* are not yet familiar with the traces of the teachings; clinging to the provisional *Satyasiddhi*, they remain deluded and fail to advance in their practice.
If one does not comprehensively raise up the various schools to categorize their respective benefits and harms, there will be no way to resolve such delusions and stagnations.

Now, I shall briefly divide these into ten dharmas to elucidate the profound meaning, so that students may know the fundamental principle, transition from the provisional to the real without hindering their practice, and swiftly realize Bodhi.
The first, the Sūtra on the Śrāvaka Precepts, takes the existence of phenomena as its tenet.
The second, the Bodhisattva Precepts, takes both the existence of phenomena and reality as its tenet.
The third, the Prajñāpāramitā teachings, takes the exposition of emptiness to reveal reality as its tenet.
The fourth, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, takes as its tenet that [phenomena] are neither empty nor existent.
The fifth, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, takes as its tenets the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two forms of selflessness.
The sixth is the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, which takes as its central tenet the manifestation of the inconceivable through the harmonious integration of the two views of defilement and purity.
The seventh is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which takes as its central tenet the convergence of provisional means toward ultimate reality.
The eighth is the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, which takes the protection of the True Dharma as its central theme.
The ninth is the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which clarifies Buddha-nature as its central theme.

The tenth is the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Extensive Teachings*. This sūtra takes as its central tenet the fundamental wisdom and compassion of all Buddhas—the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*) in which cause and fruit are perfected, the one and the many mutually penetrate, and the phenomena and principle of the dharma-realm arise through dependent origination with sovereign non-obstruction.
The above classification of schools all inherits the fundamental tenets established by former masters.
Although there may be minor differences in increase or decrease due to individual perspectives, their major principles and terminology are largely similar.
As the various masters of the Western Regions and this land have each established their own religious traditions, these shall be further clarified later.

First, regarding those who hold that the precepts of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) are based on conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-satya*): when the Tathāgata first established them for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) engaged in the creation of karma, he declared what should be done and what should not be done, teaching the distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Establishing the teaching in this manner does not mean that [the phenomena] truly exist.
Such teachings are provisionally established based on the false perceptions of ordinary beings; they are used to restrain various evils and cause people to be reborn among humans and devas.
Therefore, the Preface to the Precepts states: "Those who wish to be reborn in the heavens or among human beings should always protect the feet of the precepts and not allow them to be impaired."

The conditioned activities performed by sentient beings are illusory and not real; as they have not yet attained the dharma-body or the wisdom-body, these do not constitute a doctrine of ultimate reality, but rather a doctrine based on conventional perception.
In the Hīnayāna, this serves as the standard for maintaining the teachings.
However, in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the maintenance of precepts is not treated in this way; as the sūtra asks: "Is the body itself the brahma-conduct?"

Are the four modes of deportment of bodily action, or even the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, the ten classes of precepts, the seven prohibitions, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*), and the head of the ordination platform (*maṇḍala*) the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
One who thus carefully contemplates in search of the holy life finds it utterly unobtainable.

Therefore, they are called those who practice the pure Brahma-faring; as stated in the "Chapter on the Brahma-faring": "One who practices such purity is said to uphold the precepts of the Buddha-nature, because they attain the Dharma-body of the Buddha."

Even at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening; because one upholds the precepts of the Buddha-nature, one becomes equal in essence to the Buddha. With principle and phenomena in equilibrium, one merges with the true Dharma-realm. Upholding the precepts in this manner, one does not perceive a self that can uphold the precepts, nor does one perceive another who breaks them. This is neither the conduct of ordinary beings nor the conduct of sages; one does not perceive a self that generates the bodhicitta, nor does one perceive the Buddhas attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.
"If there is any dharma, whether good or evil, that can be apprehended, it cannot be called pure conduct.

One should know that this nature-precept (*prakṛti-śīla*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the Dharma-body is the wisdom of the Tathāgata; the wisdom of the Tathāgata is right awakening (*samyaksambodhi*). Therefore, it differs from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), which involves acceptance and rejection.

Second, regarding the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Bodhisattva Precepts, which take as their primary tenet the simultaneous demonstration of both the provisional and the ultimate: for those among ordinary beings who possess the great resolve, delight in practicing compassion, and aspire to the fruit of Buddhahood, the Tathāgata declares that Vairocana Buddha is the original body and the thousands of billions of Buddhas are the transformation bodies, thereby causing them to suddenly recognize the derivative and return to the source.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "In this manner, thousands of billions [of beings], each leading hosts as numerous as motes of dust, have all come together to my presence.

It further says: "If a person receives the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas; having attained a rank equal to that of Great Enlightenment, they are truly the children of all Buddhas."
Since this is the precept of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-śīla*), it is therefore the True Vehicle.

This is the sudden revelation of the *dharmakāya*’s precept of intrinsic nature for sentient beings of great capacity; those of inferior capacity attain it gradually. Thus, a single teaching responds to two types of faculties.

In this manner, thousands of billions of beings, each accompanied by a multitude as numerous as motes of dust, have all come to my presence; this clearly demonstrates the relinquishing of provisional means to attain the ultimate reality, which constitutes the teaching of true existence.

Within this teaching, the provisional and the ultimate are revealed simultaneously; thus, it differs from the Hīnayāna, which holds that things were impermanent in the past and will be impermanent in the future, as that [Hīnayāna] merely aims at rebirth in the realms of humans and devas.
Although it establishes the doctrine of substantial existence, it differs from what is taught by Vairocana in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This sūtra still follows the emanations of the nirmāṇakāya before arriving at the fundamental body itself.

The fundamental tenet of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is that, from the very outset, it instantaneously reveals the Dharmadhātu and the Great Wisdom Reward-body (Bao-shen) as one's own original nature, wherein cause and effect, principle and phenomena, are manifested simultaneously.

Furthermore, the dimensions of the worlds described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* differ from those of the lotus-shaped world-system in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*; their breadth and narrowness are entirely distinct, as will be explained in detail below.

Regarding the third point—that the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā takes the elucidation of emptiness as its primary principle to reveal reality: when the Tathāgata first taught the vehicles of the two vehicles for the sake of ordinary beings among humans and devas, they were bound by and attached to both phenomena and principle as being real, and thus were unable to leave behind hindrances.

To teach the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) for the purpose of destroying what is grasped and clung to, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* explain eighteen kinds of phenomena: the worldly Three Jewels, the Four Noble Truths, the three periods of time, and so forth—all are empty, and even emptiness itself is empty, as explained at length in the sūtras.

This refers to the emptying of ignorance, various hindrances, and karmic actions; when ignorance is completely exhausted and hindrances and karma are all absent, self-nature nirvāṇa manifests spontaneously. This is the true existence, the school known as "Non-Empty."
Although it is indeed real, the doctrinal gates it expounds largely involve arising and ceasing; therefore, it cannot yet be considered perfect.
For example, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* fully possesses the marks and signs of the true recompense, being able to be both empty and substantial.
Within this section and within this chapter, the ten bodhisattvas and others are interwoven from top to bottom; the principles of emptiness and existence do not proceed in isolation.

Furthermore, Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī intersect one another; principle and phenomena penetrate each other and mutually reflect. Within this single scripture, each chapter penetrates the others and every sentence interweaves with the rest, such that the forty chapters of the sutra are all contained within a single word.

The ten thousand verses of the *Sārdhadvisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* are equal in their manifestation: when one is perfected, all are perfected; when one is destroyed, all are destroyed. This is because they are collectively equal in nature and equal in time.
As with these various forms of equality, the teaching of the Dharma is likewise equal.

Because they are thus equal—just as the present Buddha attains enlightenment simultaneously with the Buddhas of the three periods of time, because there are no three periods, and because there is no time—the causes and effects do not have a sequence of before and after as they do in this teaching, where the formation and destruction of worlds occur at distinct times.

Regarding the fourth, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, which takes "neither non-empty nor existent" as its tenet: after the Tathāgata had taught the doctrine of existence and the doctrine of emptiness, he taught this single section of scripture to harmonize the two views of existence and non-existence as the teaching of "neither non-empty nor existent."

The nine consciousnesses are said to be pure and undefiled consciousnesses, just as violent water gives rise to many waves; for just as all waves depend upon water as their basis, so too do the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses all depend upon the ādāna-vijñāna.
As the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "It is like a clean mirror surface: if the conditions for the arising of a single reflection appear before it, only one reflection arises;
if the conditions for the arising of two or many reflections appear, many reflections arise."
"It is not that this mirror-surface transforms into reflections, nor is there any cessation of experience to be found.
This clarifies the locus of the ninth pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*), which serves as the support for the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses.
Furthermore, it says: "In this way, although the bodhisattva relies upon and establishes himself through the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena (dharmasthiti-jñāna).

The intent of this sutra is to clarify that within the sphere of consciousness (vijñānāyatana), the essence of consciousness is fundamentally never separate from true wisdom (tathatā-jñāna); it is like waves arising from a torrential stream that are not separate from the substance of water.

Furthermore, just as a bright mirror, relying on its pure substance, contains many reflected images without any discrimination—because it is not obstructed by their existence yet is eternally non-existent—so too, the marks of consciousness perceived by one's own mind do not depart from the fundamental substance of non-active, pure wisdom.
The images thus manifested are entirely devoid of attachment to self or other, internal or external; they function in accordance with wisdom, free from all discrimination.

Because it severs the two bonds of existence and non-existence, it is neither empty nor existent; thus, a verse in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "The ādāna-vijñāna is profound and subtle; all seeds are like a turbulent torrent."
"I do not reveal this to the ignorant and foolish, for fear that they would conceptually grasp it as a self.

As for the statement that the *ādāna-vijñāna* is "profound and subtle," it leads those ordinary beings toward the transformation of consciousness into wisdom (*vijñapti-parāvṛtti*). It is not like the emptiness established through the negation of characteristics by the Two Vehicles or by Bodhisattvas at the initial stages of their training; nor is it like the substantial existence of the fetters held by ordinary beings. Because it is unlike either of these, it is neither empty nor existent.
What dharma is not empty?
It is wisdom, for it can accord with conditions to illuminate the capacities of beings and benefit them.
What dharma does not exist?

Because when wisdom correctly follows conditions, it is devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics, and lacks arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, it is for this reason called "neither empty nor existent.

Although this sutra thus brings about the knowledge that emptiness and existence are non-dual within the sphere of mind and consciousness, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not like this; rather, it takes the fundamental wisdom of the single reality of the Dharma-realm—the essence and function of the Buddha—as its basis. It merges the ocean of true nature, characteristics, Dharma-body, and Reward-body, directly revealing the Buddha-fruit virtue and the fundamental wisdom of the single reality Dharma-realm for those of superior faculties as a gateway for opening, showing, awakening, and entering, without regard for the consciousnesses that arise following delusion.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* appears in the world to reveal and awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s wisdom so that they may attain purity; therefore, it does not belong to any other vehicle, whether the second or the third.
Furthermore, regarding the dharma of the characteristics of the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata does not permit those of the three vehicles to understand it through their own wisdom.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "The meanings of the various natures and characteristics—only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know these matters."

Śāriputra, the pratyekabuddhas, and the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas are all unable to know this, because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* brings together those who studied the provisional teachings of the three vehicles to return to the true dharma-realm of the Buddha-vehicle.

The three vehicles before the gate merely receive provisional mounts, whereas the white ox in the open field alone clarifies true virtue; for this reason, there is a partial sense within [this teaching] that accords with and supports the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The vehicle upon which the dragon girl rides is precisely the white ox-vehicle; furthermore, she attains the same realization as Sudhana.

Therefore, the teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* directly reveals the fundamental essence, employing the gate of the Buddha-fruit of the Dharma-realm to directly transmit it to those of superior faculties among ordinary beings, enabling them to awaken and enter.
This differs from the provisional gateways established in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* regarding the five, six, seven, eight, or nine consciousnesses.

For instance, when the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* provisionally posits a ninth ādāna-consciousness, its underlying intention follows a different path: it is intended for those of the two vehicles who have long been weary of birth and death, and who cultivate emptiness and extinguish consciousness to directly proceed toward empty quiescence.

Furthermore, during the second period, when the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā was expounded, it was intended for those of the two vehicles and for bodhisattvas training gradually; it negated existence through the principle of emptiness and took the six pāramitās as the practice and vehicle.

Within this, although those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) have partially turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] and those who gradually study as bodhisattvas increasingly delight in emptiness, these are provisional teachings for bodhisattvas of the three vehicles as an initial door of counteraction. They are largely similar to the initial doors of counteraction of the small vehicle (hīnayāna), differing only in that they possess a partial increase in compassion. However, they have not yet realized the principles of the dharmakāya, the Buddha-nature, or the fundamental wisdom; they take the gate of emptiness as their vehicle and the six pāramitās as their practice. Their initial doors of counteraction are identical to those of the two vehicles: they enter the contemplation of emptiness only after first practicing the contemplations of impermanence, impurity, the white bone, and subtle atoms, whereas the two vehicles proceed toward cessation (nirvāṇa).

When a Bodhisattva remains in birth, they employ the contemplations of emptiness, selflessness, and so forth to subdue and restrain the notions of self and phenomena, preventing them from increasing; yet this is fundamentally not the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya Buddha-nature, for because their vision is not yet true, they take pleasure in emptiness and allow it to increase further.

For this reason, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* skillfully establishes a ninth consciousness as the purely immaculate consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*), stating that the eight consciousnesses take this pure consciousness as their support.

If he had wished to directly explain that the eighth seed-consciousness is the Tathāgatagarbha, he did so because his disciples feared suffering and its accumulation; furthermore, because they would find it difficult to believe and would be terrified by the notion that karmic seeds are eternally true, he provisionally established the ninth Ādāna-vijñāna as the pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*), desiring to cause the nature of non-extinguishing consciousness to grow into great Bodhi.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "As long as one has not yet perfected the Buddha-dharmas, one does not realize awakening by extinguishing sensation.
Since sensation is not extinguished, so too are perception and consciousness.

As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, for those whose faculties are mature, it is taught that the karmic seeds of the eighth consciousness constitute the Tathāgatagarbha; this will be further clarified in the subsequent text.

The *Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra* says, "The density of afflictions is the seed of the Tathāgata," and so forth. Among those who cultivate the path, there are diverse categories and approaches, with differences in understanding and practice that branch out in a thousand ways and myriad variations.
Aside from the two vehicles, there are four distinct categories of Bodhisattva vehicles: first, Bodhisattvas who cultivate emptiness and non-self;

second, Bodhisattvas who gradually perceive the Buddha-nature; third, Bodhisattvas who suddenly perceive the Buddha-nature; and fourth, those who [perceive it] through the Tathāgata’s intrinsic pure wisdom.

By means of the five stages of preparatory practice, one gives rise to differentiated wisdom; fulfilling the conduct of Samantabhadra and becoming a Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, one ultimately does not depart from the limit of a single kṣaṇa, yet fills the gates of the Buddha-fruit throughout the ten directions.
This provides a brief indication of the terminology, which will be explained in detail below.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "There is a class of bodhisattvas who, having practiced the six pāramitās for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, do not give birth into the family of the Buddha; they are still called 'bodhisattvas by designation.'"
The detailed exposition follows in the text below.
Although one may perceive the Buddha-nature, if one is unaware of karmic obstructions, one is still termed a "provisional bodhisattva.

As for the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which takes the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness as its core tenets, this sutra was preached on Mount Laṅkā in the Southern Sea.

As the Tathāgata passed by this mountain, Rāvaṇa, the Yakṣa King, together with the Bodhisattva Maticitra, arrived riding in a transformed celestial palace and invited the Buddha, the Tathāgata, to preach the Dharma upon this mountain.

The mountain is lofty and steep; looking down from below, one beholds the great ocean, and it has no gates or entrances. Only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are able to ascend; this signifies that the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground can only be ascended by those who are without mind and without realization.

Looking down upon the great ocean symbolizes that the ocean of the mind is fundamentally pure from the beginning; yet, driven by the winds of external objects, the waves of consciousness surge and fluctuate. To clarify that when one penetrates the nature of objects as being empty, the ocean of the mind becomes naturally still—where both mind and objects are quiescent, there is nothing that is not illuminated.
It is like the great ocean when there is no wind, where the sun, moon, and constellations shine with brilliant clarity.

The intent of this sutra is specifically for Bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature, teaching that the seed-consciousness and karmic consciousness are, in their immediacy, the Tathāgatagarbha; it is distinct from those of the two vehicles who seek quiescence by extinguishing consciousness.

Furthermore, because it differs from those who cultivate emptiness through the perfection of wisdom, it directly clarifies that the intrinsic nature of the substance of consciousness is entirely true; thus, it clarifies that the substance of consciousness immediately constitutes the functional activity of wisdom.

Just as when there is no wind over that great ocean, the reflections of objects become even clearer, so too it is with the ocean of the mind and the Dharma-gate: upon realizing the truth, consciousness becomes wisdom.

This sutra differs from the meaning of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* in that it separately establishes nine consciousnesses to guide those of initial capacity, gradually causing them to retain delusions in order to grow their Great Bodhi; thus it does not cause the mind to plant seeds in emptiness, nor does it allow the mind to be like a rotten seed.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* is the initial gateway for entering into delusion, while the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Vimalakīrti* directly reveal the fundamental reality of delusion.
The *Laṅkāvatāra* clarifies that the eight consciousnesses are the Tathāgatagarbha; the *Vimalakīrti* contemplates the true mark of the body, and the same applies to contemplating the Buddha.
The *Vimalakīrti* and the *Laṅkāvatāra* are identical, whereas the text of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* differs slightly from these two works.
It is not so in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, for the Buddha’s body, his realm, and the characteristics of his dharma-gates are inherently and mysteriously distinct.

It is taught that the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was spoken by a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya); its realm is a defiled land where [the Buddha] dwells upon a mountain peak; and regarding the dharma-gates, it teaches that the realm of consciousness is the truth. In its dialogues, Mahāmati Bodhisattva serves as the primary interlocutor. While the teachings clarified by the transformation body are provisional (upāya), Mahāmati primarily engages in debate and discernment.

According to the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Buddha-body is itself the fundamental true Dharma-recompense; the realm is the dwelling place of the Flower Treasury World; the Dharma-gates are the gates of the Buddha-fruit Dharma-realm; and the questions and answers are the wondrous functions of the wisdom of principle and phenomena of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. The aspects of the five stages of practice interpenetrate cause and effect, and the ten lands and ten bodies are thoroughly realized as mutually entering one another.

Regarding the discussion of similarities and differences, it cannot yet be fully stated; one must wait for the subsequent sections where they will be extensively distinguished according to their respective positions.

As for the sixth [treatise], the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, which takes the inconceivable as its central theme: the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* share ten points of difference and one point of similarity.

The ten kinds of distinctions are: first, the distinction of the adornments of the pure land; second, the distinction between the retributive and transformational aspects of the Buddha’s body and its various marks; third, the distinction of inconceivable virtues and supernormal powers; fourth, the distinction of the dharma-gates established according to the faculties [of beings]; fifth, the distinction of the assemblies who come to hear the Dharma; sixth, the distinction of the dharma-gates established through the teaching of the doctrine; seventh, the distinction of the practices established by the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti; eighth, the distinction of the locations where the dharma-gates are expounded; ninth, the distinction of the assembly that constantly follows the Buddha; and tenth, the distinction of the entrustment of the Dharma-treasury for its circulation. In one respect, the expedient means for entering the Path are the same.

First, regarding the distinction in the adornments of the pure lands: as described in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, when the Tathāgata pressed the earth with his toe, the trichiliocosm was immediately adorned with hundreds of thousands of various precious jewels, becoming like the land of the Buddha Ratnavyūha, adorned with the infinite merits of that Buddha. The entire great assembly marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, and each saw themselves sitting upon a precious lotus flower; yet it did not mention matters such as the adornments of inexhaustible buddha-fields being contained within a single hair-tip.

As explained in detail in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the realm of the ten Buddhas Vairocana consists of ten lotus-flower treasury world-oceans; within each of these world-oceans there are inexhaustible world-oceans, which fully encompass the realms of the Buddhas and the realms of sentient beings throughout the ten directions. These realms interpenetrate one another without mutual obstruction, adorned with myriad jewels like light and shadow, as extensively described in the sūtra.
It is not merely a matter of speaking of the adornment and purification of a single trichiliocosm.

Regarding the distinction between the various marks of the Buddha-body as retribution and as transformation: it is taught that this *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* was spoken by a transformation Buddha endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

In the preaching of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Buddha manifests the marks of ninety-seven great men, as well as the marks of as many great men as there are atoms in ten Flower Treasury World-Oceans; this is what is spoken by the Tathāgata of True Reward.

Regarding the distinction between the three inconceivable virtues and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), as described in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* concerning the supernormal powers of Bodhisattvas: they can place Mount Sumeru, in all its height and breadth, within a mustard seed; they can take the waters of the four great oceans and place them within a single pore; furthermore, within a small room, they can accommodate thirty-two thousand lion thrones, each eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in height.

Eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas, and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans were taken by Vimalakīrti; placing them upon the palm of his right hand, he lifted this great assembly and proceeded to the Āmra grove.
Furthermore, with his hand he grasped the Land of Wondrous Joy in the eastern direction, brought it here to show it to the great assembly, and then returned it to its original place.
Such supernatural transformations were manifested for the sake of those training in the provisional vehicles—the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas of the three vehicles—to display such matters to them.

Why is this? Because for those who follow the provisional teachings—such as śrāvakas and bodhisattvas—their vision of the Path is not yet ultimate, and they have not yet transcended the distinction between self and other; thus, the supernatural transformations they manifest depend on what is perceived by their own faculties, and all possess boundaries, limits, and spatial constraints.

Furthermore, at one time, it was by the Sage’s intention that, through the power of his spiritual transformations, he caused those of lesser faculties to gradually progress; this was not due to the inherent power of the Dharma itself.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, by the power of the Dharma and because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one is able to contain all Buddha-fields and sentient beings' fields of the ten directions within a single atom; yet the world does not become smaller, nor does the minute atom become larger. This is likewise true for every single atom throughout all the worlds of the ten directions.

As stated in the sutras, a bodhisattva attains equal and perfect enlightenment within the body of a single small sentient being and extensively delivers all beings, yet that small sentient being neither knows nor perceives it.
One should know that because the Buddha employs provisional teachings to guide those of inferior faculties, he appears outside the body to manifest supernatural powers and thus seems to come and go;

however, within the ultimate teaching, one awakens to one's own original mind through one's own fundamental awakening, such that the nature and characteristics of one's own body and mind are no different from those of the Buddha, and there are no views of internal or external, coming or going.

Therefore, while Vairocana Buddha does not move from his original place, his body sits pervasively in all places of practice (bodhimaṇḍa); likewise, the multitudes coming from the ten directions do not move from their original places, yet they follow the transformation and arrive. There is, in truth, no coming or going, nor is it brought about by supernatural power; thus the Sūtra says, "Because the Dharma is such."

Whenever the sutras state, "By the Buddha’s spiritual power, because such is the nature of the Dharma," they employ the Buddha’s spiritual power to extol the Buddha as supreme; yet, by stating "because such is the nature of the Dharma," they extol its fundamental virtue as being entirely devoid of transformation.

The physical forms, minds, natures, and characteristics of each individual land and realm, because they rely upon the fundamental source and do not follow delusion, manifest as all phenomena—whether large or small—as light and shadows; they reflect and penetrate one another, pervading the ten directions, entirely without coming or going, and entirely without boundaries.

That is to say, within every single sentient being, there are pores that pervade the ten directions; this differs from the provisional teachings which, by means of their supernatural powers, have limited comings and goings—lifting beings up and sending them away—which results in such false perceptions that they contravene the fundamental Dharma-body and obstruct the true Bodhi, the wisdom of original enlightenment.

Therefore, after the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti had manifested these supernatural transformations, he proceeded to expound the teaching of ultimate reality. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way."
"As I contemplate the Tathāgata, he does not come from the past, he does not go to the future, and he does not abide in the present.
This is explained in detail in the "Akṣobhyavyūha" chapter.

Therefore, for those with provisional faculties and limited views who delight in the extraordinary, the Bodhisattva provides a coarse introduction according to their capacity, causing them to develop a desire to learn before imparting the gateway of ultimate reality.
One cannot grasp at transformation to realize the True; thus one remains perpetually deluded regarding the realm of wisdom.
By recognizing the provisional as leading toward the Real, one migrates into the gateway of the Dharma-realm.

Phenomena involving effortful action are difficult to perfect because they follow conditions; non-action is easily accomplished. Those who act labor in vain and achieve nothing, whereas those who do not act find that things spontaneously accord with conditions.
The merit of non-merit is such that its merit is not in vain;
the merit of merit is such that all its merit is impermanent.

Cultivation accumulated over many kalpas ultimately ends in decay and ruin; it is not as good as the single thought-moment of the non-arising of dependent origination, which transcends the provisional views of the three vehicles.

Regarding the fourth point, the differentiation of the established Dharma-gates according to faculties: this *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* is directed toward those with the faculties of the two vehicles, causing them to turn toward the bodhi of a bodhisattva and enter the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna, for the sake of those bodhisattvas who have become stagnant in their purity and whose compassion and wisdom are not yet perfected, it causes them to advance in their practice.

This is just as when the assembly of bodhisattvas from the World of Universal Fragrance, desiring to return to their own land, requested the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to grant them a minor teaching.

The Tathāgata, observing the faculties of those bodhisattvas and seeing that they were lingering in the pure lands with inferior compassion and wisdom, then preached the Dharma for them, causing them to study the gate of liberation of the finite and the infinite.

The subsequent text states: "Without departing from great kindness, great equanimity, and great compassion, one deeply resolves upon the mind of omniscience and never forgets it; one teaches and transforms sentient beings without ever becoming weary or disheartened; one constantly recollects and practices the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); one regards all meditative concentrations as if they were hell, views the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) as if it were a pleasure garden, and perceives those who come to seek help as if they were virtuous teachers."
This is explained in detail as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

Since the compassion and wisdom of these followers of the Two Vehicles and Three Vehicles are not yet perfected, this sutra causes them to gradually cultivate and increase their compassion and wisdom; it does not immediately and abruptly reveal the Buddha-gate, nor does it immediately state that one attains perfect enlightenment at the initial mind of the Ten Abodes, nor does it immediately demonstrate its vast and wondrous matters, for all of these have their respective limits.

Fifth, regarding the various assemblies that come and hear the Dharma separately: as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, among all those who have come, with the exception of the great bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī and Maitreya, and the "echo" śrāvakas such as Śāriputra, the remaining external assemblies are all members of the provisional vehicles within the Three Vehicles.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas among them who are born into the various realms of existence together with those of similar kind; they all desire to bring the provisional teachings of the three vehicles to fulfillment and gradually cause them to progress, yet have not yet spoken of the complete, fundamental vehicle of the Buddhas.

As it is said in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, all those in the assembled multitude are those who have mounted the Tathāgata-vehicle; they possess the fruit-virtue of Buddha-wisdom as the very essence of the Dharma-body, and are endowed with the practices of Samantabhadra. They manifest as shadows throughout the oceans of lands and all places of practice in the ten directions, yet they return to constitute the original Dharma upon which the Tathāgatas ride; there is not a single individual among them whose faculties belong to the three vehicles.

Suppose there are those with the necessary faculties who are like the blind or the deaf—neither knowing nor perceiving; they are like a blind person facing the sun and moon, like a deaf person hearing the music of the heavens, like a pauper of karma encountering a celestial treasure trove, like one of great merit dwelling in hell, or like a hungry ghost standing on the shore of the great ocean.

Those whose capacities for the Three Vehicles have not yet exhausted their power of the Path and who have not yet turned their minds [toward the One Vehicle] constantly dwell within the ocean of the Dharma-realm, the realm of all Buddhas; though they share the same virtues and the same bodies as the Buddhas, they are ultimately unable to believe or know this, and so seek instead to see the Buddha through other means.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated and accumulated various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). Yet, if they have not heard this Dharma-gate of the inconceivable merits of the Tathāgata, or even if they have heard it at some time..."
"One who does not have faith, does not understand, does not comply, and does not enter cannot be called a true Bodhisattva, because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata.

One should know that among the assembly hearing the Dharma, this is entirely distinct from the assembly in the Sahā world described in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, where the two realms have not yet merged and the defilement and purity of the various followers of the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyuha) remain fully distinct.

It should be understood that such individuals have not yet attained true insight; though they maintain the purity of a single realm and are called "bodhisattvas," their realization of the Path has not yet reached perfection.

Such followers do not fully comprehend the Buddha’s intent; although they possess the aspiration to seek bodhi, their minds remain stagnant in the pursuit of a pure land, thereby remaining profoundly separated from the Dharmakāya and Jñānakāya.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Even bodhisattvas who have attained non-retrogression, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are likewise unable to know [this].

This is just as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* describes: one’s own body is no different from the Buddha-body, and one’s own wisdom is no distinct from the Buddha-wisdom; nature and characteristics contain and embrace one another, and the one and the many share both identity and difference. Dwelling in the waters of wisdom within the ocean of the Dharma-realm, they manifest as fish and dragons;
residing in the great mansion of nirvāṇa, they appear in the forms of yin and yang to transform sentient beings.

The principal and the attendant are sovereignly interwoven and mutually reflected; master and disciple are harmoniously fused, such that cause and effect penetrate one another—all such as this assembly.

Sixth, regarding the distinct establishment of the teaching and the dharma-gates: this *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* employs the householder Vimalakīrti to manifest a small measure of inconceivable transformation and adaptability, thereby causing those of the Two Vehicles to turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].
Furthermore, while abiding within birth and death, he manifested physical illness to demonstrate that defilement and purity are non-dual.

Moreover, he manifested illness to represent the great compassion of the Bodhisattva, fully expounding the gateway of non-duality, establishing the contemplative wisdom of concentration and insight, thereby manifesting the most essential nature of the Dharma of non-seeking.
Therefore, it is said: "One who seeks the Dharma should have no seeking toward any phenomena.

However, this does not yet seem to fully set forth the dharma-gates concerning the characteristics, causes, effects, similarities, and differences of the five stages—the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten bhūmis, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment—along with the sixth stage, as detailed in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Regarding the seven purities, the Bodhisattva manifests distinct practices: "purity" signifies the manifestation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), whereby he enters into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to manifest the practice of illness.

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Vairocana manifests entry into birth-and-death through great compassion to accomplish the practice of attaining perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), thereby demonstrating that great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*) can transcend the world.

Regarding the distinction between the eight locations where the Dharma-gates were expounded: the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* was taught in the Āmra Garden in the city of Vaiśālī, as well as in the chamber of Vimalakīrti.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was preached in the Bodhimaṇḍa of the kingdom of Magadha, as well as in all worlds and within all atoms.

Regarding the distinction of the nine groups of followers who constantly attend the Buddha: when the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* was preached, the śrāvakas served as the assembly of those constantly attending the Buddha, numbering only five hundred.

When the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was preached, the assembly of great Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle served as the constant retinue of the Buddha; this entire multitude, numbering as many as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, was entirely composed of those who embody the essence and function of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī.

Regarding the specific transmission and circulation of the Dharma-treasury entrusted [to the Bodhisattvas], it is stated in the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) of this *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: 'Maitreya!'"
"I now entrust to you this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which I have accumulated over immeasurable billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Thus, he immediately entrusted that sutra to those who had already become bodhisattvas and were born into the family of the Buddhas.

In the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata" (*Tathāgatotpattisambhavanirdeśa*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the entrustment for circulation is made precisely to ordinary beings at the stage of the initial resolve, who are first able to see the Way and be born into the family of the Buddha.
Why is this so? This sutra is difficult to enter; it permits only those capable of realization to realize it for themselves, and only upon such self-realization can one truly preach it.

It reveals that the three vehicles are provisional expedients, because the methods of cultivation and realization urged by the sages have not yet reached the ultimate reality, and thus all who preach these teachings likewise do not yet possess the ultimate reality.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "This jewel of a sūtra does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for the true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King—those who are born into the family of the Tathāgata and have planted the various roots of goodness that constitute the marks of a Tathāgata."
"O Son of the Buddha!
If there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate would soon perish and vanish. He asked:
If one grants that the true sons of the Buddha are as inexhaustible and boundless as the worlds of the ten directions—
wherein the number of world-microdusts cannot be known— then why worry that this sutra will perish and vanish for lack of true sons?
The answer is:

The meaning of this sutra is to entrust ordinary beings with the task of awakening them to enter this Dharma-gate, thereby causing them to be born into the family of the Buddhas; it causes them to teach others in turn so that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed, and thus enables ordinary beings to enter the realm of reality.
If this were entrusted to the great bodhisattvas, ordinary beings would have no connection to it, while the noble ones would naturally understand it for themselves.
If there were no ordinary beings who practice and study it, the Buddha-seed within the path of ordinary beings would be severed, and this sutra would perish and disappear.
For this reason, it is entrusted to ordinary beings for them to practice, rather than to those great bodhisattvas of the past who have already realized the path of seeing.

Since the expedient means for entering the path are identical for both, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "One who seeks the Dharma should have no seeking regarding any phenomena," and "Contemplate the true reality of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way."

"When I contemplate the Tathāgata, he does not come from the past, he does not go to the future, and he does not abide in the present"—such passages as these are roughly identical to the initial gate of contemplative wisdom.
The characteristics of entering the path, the gateways, the sequence, and the rules are entirely distinct, as explained in detail below.

Regarding the seventh [treatise], which takes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as its primary tenet for bringing the provisional into the real: this scripture leads those of the three vehicles to return to the true teaching of the One Vehicle.

It leads the various streams back to the great ocean and gathers the three vehicles to return to the single source. The teachings of the former great virtuous masters, such as Master Zang and others, constitute the "Common Teaching" (*sādhāraṇa-naya*), because the One Vehicle is heard together with the three vehicles;
the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* constitutes the "Distinct Teaching" (*asādhāraṇa-naya*), because the One Vehicle is not heard together with the three vehicles.

Contemplating this principle and synthesizing these two gates: the *Lotus Sūtra* employs provisional capacities to lead them back to the truth, while the *Avataṃsaka* allows those of sudden, great faculties to receive the teaching directly.

Although the name "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna) implies a convergence where the essential principles and practices are largely the same, when one examines their specific rules and models, there are many differences.

Now, wishing to provide a comprehensive account, the subject matter is so vast that it is difficult to cover exhaustively; therefore, I shall briefly present ten categories to serve as a guide to the general framework.

The ten sections are: first, the distinction of the Teacher; second, the distinction of the emission of light; third, the distinction of the buddha-field; fourth, the distinction of the principal requester of the Dharma; fifth, the distinction between the real and the manifested adornments of the great assembly; sixth, the distinction among those listed in the assembly during the introductory section; seventh, the distinction of the dragon girl’s transformation into a Buddha; eighth, the distinction of the buddha-field where the dragon girl’s Buddhahood resides; ninth, the distinction of the resolve for enlightenment made by the six thousand members of the assembly; and tenth, the distinction of the bestowing of distant predictions upon the śrāvakas.

First, regarding the distinction of the teacher: it is said that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached by the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha; furthermore, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who entered parinirvāṇa in the past, has come to testify to and authenticate this sutra, such that the Buddhas of the three periods of time all proclaim it together.

It is not so in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, for its teaching lord is Vairocana; as such, he is the True Body (dharmakāya) of reality, wisdom, and principle, adorned with the infinite ocean of marks and merits. All Buddhas of the three periods of time are of one and the same limit and a single moment within the dharma-realm; their retributive marks are layered and manifold, without any obstruction.

The beginning and end of time are one and the same, for they do not consist of the three periods; the Buddhas of the past are not of the past, and the Buddhas of the present have not newly emerged, because the nature and characteristics of fundamental wisdom are equal and principle and phenomena are not different.

Thus, this was spoken by the Original Buddha because [the audience] received the great root [of enlightenment] instantaneously; it is not a teaching of a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha), unlike the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna—who had entered parinirvāṇa long ago—appears, and the present Buddha emerges in the world to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
For this reason, it is said that the teachers are distinct.

Second, regarding the distinction in the emission of light: although the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* emits the resultant light from the tuft of hair between the eyebrows, the realms it illuminates are described as only eighteen thousand lands all becoming golden in color; thus, it still possesses limitations and does not accord with the boundless, immeasurable, and inexhaustible. Consequently, it merely manifests the resultant dharma and does not manifest the causal stage.

The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, as a single scripture, encompasses the teachings, practices, causes, and fruits; its manifestation of the Dharma-light is complete from beginning to end with the ten [stages], which shall be further clarified later.

Regarding the distinctions among the three lands: when preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he transformed the world three times to make it a pure land, relocated the devas and humans to other lands, and subsequently established the assembly gathered from other directions, transforming this defiled realm into a pure field.
When the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is taught, this very Sahā world is itself the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmakośa-lokadhātu*), with each and every world mutually containing one another.

As the Sūtra says: "Each and every world fills the ten directions, and the ten directions enter into one without remainder; the worlds neither increase nor decrease, for such is the nature of incomparable merit."

It is further said: "When the Buddhas attain enlightenment, they transform immeasurable multitudes within the body of a single small sentient being, yet that small sentient being remains unaware and unconscious of it."

This is simply because ordinary beings and sages share the same essence and possess no characteristic of shifting or changing; within even a speck of dust, self and other are of one body. This does not mean that, as in the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, one must shift from the realms of humans and devas before a pure land can be revealed; rather, this [teaching] was established for those with provisional faculties whose views remain stuck in the duality of self and other.
Therefore, we now clarify that the lands are distinct.

Fourth, regarding the distinction of the requester of the Dharma: at the time of preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the requester of the Dharma was Śāriputra, who served as the foremost among those who exhorted [the Buddha].

When preaching the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra—the Bodhisattvas corresponding to each respective stage—to each speak the Dharma-gates of their own stages as the opening of the teaching.

The Buddha represents the dharma of fruition; taking the fruition as the cause, the practice of great compassion perfects fundamental wisdom, whereby the essence of fruition is spontaneously realized. Thus, there is nothing that is not spoken.

Because the practice of great compassion arises from the root wisdom of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra represent the causal stage that can be described; they expound the dharmas of the Buddha-fruit to instruct and awaken sentient beings.

In the "Chapter on Incalculable Numbers" (*Asaṃkhyeya-varga*), the numerical laws of the world are so vast and immeasurable that only a Buddha can fully comprehend them. Because they do not pertain to the gates of cause and effect within the five stages, they are internal dharmas of the Buddha’s own stage, and thus are spoken by the Buddha himself.

The "Chapter on the Merits of the Minor Marks and Radiance" concerns the causes and fruits realized by the Tathāgata himself; it is the subsequent Buddha’s own exposition of the power of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), a dharma-gate of the constant radiance of merit and wisdom. Because it demonstrates that these are not included within the causal characteristics of the five stages, the Buddha also expounded it himself.
This clarifies that there are no two types of delusion regarding the fruit of Buddhahood.

Apart from these two chapters of the sutra, the remaining thirty-eight chapters are all dharma-gates concerning the characteristics of practice within the five stages; therefore, the Buddha did not speak them himself, but instead had the bodhisattvas within their respective stages—such as those of the ten faiths, ten abidings, and ten practices—speak for themselves, while the Buddha merely emitted light to signify them.
The manifestation of the light emitted therein represents the characteristics of the Dharma, which shall be explained in detail later.

When the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was preached, there were no śrāvakas or lesser bodhisattvas serving as the masters who requested the teaching; rather, it was entirely composed of great bodhisattvas within the stage of Buddhahood, who engaged in mutual dialogue to establish the modes of practice for the dharma-gates of the Buddha-fruit. This was for the sake of those with great faculties, so that they might directly take the fruit of Buddhahood as the cause through sudden realization.
Thus, the cause takes the effect as its cause, and the effect takes the cause as its effect, as is the case with various seeds and the like.
This can be seen by contemplating it through the power of concentration and wisdom.
Therefore, what is said here regarding the distinction between the Dharma Master and the others refers to the five great assemblies.

As for the distinction between the true and the manifested adornments of these great assemblies: as in the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the trichiliocosm is made pure and adorned, and all the manifested congregations fill it completely; yet all the Buddhas who come are said to be manifestations.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not like that; it contains ten locations and ten assemblies, all of which fill the ten directions without shifting from their original places while pervading the Dharma-realm. Within each individual physical form and every pore, world-systems are layered upon one another, and the bodies of Bodhisattvas and Buddhas mutually penetrate one another. Sentient beings of various kinds are likewise entirely unimpeded; body and land interpenetrate like shadows containing one another.

The assembly that has gathered does not destroy the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) while following its marks and signs; for the Dharma-body and its marks and signs are of one limit and without distinction—thus, the marks are entirely true and there is no transformation.
This differs from other teachings which speak of the transformation body and the true body as being intermingled; therefore, the present statement refers to a distinct great assembly.

Within the six introductory sections, regarding the listing of the distinct assemblies, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly, the assembly of śrāvakas is first listed, numbering twelve thousand people together.
Next in line was the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī together with her retinue of six thousand; she was his maternal aunt.
Next in line was the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā; she was the wife of the Buddha when he was a crown prince.
When the Buddha was a crown prince, he had three consorts:
the first was named Gopī, the second Yaśodharā, and the third Manuṣā.

Gopī is the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of the youth Sudhana at the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā). She symbolizes the joy of the Dharma of the tenth stage and its capacity for compassion; thus, she brings benefit to sentient beings through the Dharma.
"Delighting the body and mind through the Dharma" constitutes the meaning of "his wife.
Next, eighty thousand bodhisattvas are listed together; next, the various devas, nāgas, ghosts, and so forth are listed.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not like this: it first lists the principal bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds, without mentioning their attendants.

Next, following the assembly of Vajrapāṇi deities, there are fifty-five categories of various classes of gods, nāgas, devas, and others. Each category has its own distinct followers, and each group of followers consists of as many beings as there are atoms in a Buddha-world; in some cases, their followers are simply described as being "immeasurable."

Furthermore, regarding the first assembly, there are fifty-five groups of beings including those at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); the assemblies of the subsequent ten assemblies shall be clarified further below.

To discuss the great meaning: the ocean-like assembly of the Buddha’s bodies within the boundless *dharmadhātu* contains each and every body in a layered, infinite manner; a single body takes the *dharmadhātu* as its measure, such that the realms of self and other do not perish within the *dharmadhātu*, and thus one's own body is all-pervasive, severing all dualistic sentiments of subject and object.
To discuss this in brief: the arrangement of the assemblies and their members across these ten sessions shall be further clarified later.

From the first through the seventh session, the name "śrāvaka" is not heard at all; it is only within the eighth session that the assembly of bhikṣus first appears, and it is there that their specific characteristics are clearly elucidated.

Regarding the specific case of the seven dragon girls transforming their bodies to become Buddhas, as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in a single kṣaṇa, these dragon girls transformed their female bodies, perfected the practices of a bodhisattva, and attained Buddhahood in the southern direction.

It is not so in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; rather, simply by ensuring that one is free from biased views, great wisdom becomes ever more luminous, such that the essence of all phenomena is true and devoid of any characteristic of transformation.
As it is said in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, Śāriputra asked the goddess,
"For what reason do you not transform this female body?
The goddess replied to Śāriputra:
"For twelve years I have sought the mark of a woman and have been unable to find it at all.
What, then, could there be to transform?
Thus did the woman Āmrapālī speak to Śāriputra.
"A boy has fathered me, a girl;
one should know that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is suchness—what is there to transform?

As stated in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, among the fifty-three spiritual friends of the youth Sudhana—such as Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, elders, youths, upāsikās, maidens, sages, and non-Buddhists—each possesses their own bodhisattva practice and their own Buddha-dharma. Depending on the perceptions of sentient beings, these manifestations appear differently, yet it is never said that there is any transformation.
If one observes with the Dharma-eye, there is nothing mundane that is not true;
if one observes with the worldly physical eye, there is nothing true that is not mundane.

By means of the *Lotus Sūtra*, for those of the three capacities who have not yet exhausted their views regarding provisional teachings, it causes them to establish the seeds of faith. Furthermore, by swiftly transforming the female form into Buddhahood, it inspires a sense of wonder, whereby they finally resolve their minds to advance toward true insight. Thus, though they may not yet be capable of the fundamental teaching, they are led to give rise to roots of goodness.
This clarifies that the three provisional means are now led back to the single reality.

Furthermore, it refutes the fixed attachment to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* regarding time and eons, causing one to realize that within a single *kṣaṇa*, the nature of the three periods of time is fundamentally a single limit—beginningless and endless, equal to the Dharma. It tears apart the net of views of the three vehicles, dismantles the grass huts of the bodhisattvas, leads them to the gate of the *dharmadhātu*, and causes entry into the true abode of the Buddha; for this reason, the dragon girl was made to attain Buddhahood.
It is clear that this is not the result of long-term cultivation from the past, as her age is only eight years.

Furthermore, it is manifest that this is not the fruit of prior study; the transformation of her female state did not exceed a single kṣaṇa, and she has fully realized the fruits of Buddhahood without a hair’s breadth of deficiency.

The Dharma is fundamentally thus: its own substance is timeless. Yet those who study through provisional means have their vision obstructed by their respective three faculties; being deluded about the true Dharma, they conversely call it a transformation. Unaware that their own affairs are such as this, they remain entirely within the house, still harboring lingering views.
What is meant by "mysteriously pointing to the *Saṃghāṭa* outside the realm"?
This vision is not to be abandoned; otherwise, one will certainly stray for eternal kalpas.
Only when the mind turns back and this vision fades away will one finally return to one's original dwelling.
Why is it that at this time one must extinguish the karma of all views, only to labor in vain through the causes of suffering for many kalpas before turning back?

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s gateway of the dharmadhātu dependent origination clarifies that ordinary beings and sages share a single reality; yet as long as the barrier of views remains, one is an ordinary being when views persist, and a Buddha when deluded attachments cease.

In accordance with the nature of reality, every movement—whether looking up or down, advancing or retreating, or bowing the body in humility and reverence—is the practice of a Bodhisattva. There is not a single dharma that possesses a characteristic subject to transformation, nor one that undergoes arising, abiding, or ceasing; therefore, this is not the same as the Dragon Girl’s transformation of her body to become a Buddha.
Regarding the specific land where the eight dragon maidens attained Buddhahood, it is said to be the World Without Stain (Vimalā) in the southern direction, not this Sahā world.
The commentary explains:
because their minds have attained arhatship (āryasatya), it is called "Without Stain."
Because it is correctly aligned with original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya), it is designated as the South; this is because South and North constitute the axis of correctness.
Furthermore, the South represents illumination and emptiness; the South corresponds to the trigram Li, and within Li there is emptiness.
Regarding the *Li* method within the Eight Trigrams (*Bagua*), because the mind is fundamentally void and non-existent, it is nevertheless represented by means of the conventional Eight Trigrams.
Although the name "Eight Trigrams" does not exist in other directions, the method itself is one and the same.
Therefore, although the principle is thus, since there is a principle, there must also be a phenomenon; consequently, there must still be a land to which all may turn for refuge.

If one were to dwell separately in the South, self and other, this and that, would remain separated. This is because such a state merely accords with the three vehicles, using distinctions to guide those of provisional capacity to generate faith and understanding, thereby leading them toward the Buddha-vehicle. Thus, it is difficult to destroy the lingering influence of the remaining attachments to the three vehicles.
Furthermore, there is a partial turning of the mind in which the distinction between self and other has not yet been severed.

This is unlike the sudden realization of the essence of the Dharma-realm in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, wherein self and other are mutually penetrating, and within each and every atom one dwells in the gateway of Indra’s net.
Therefore, it is now said that the lands where they dwell are distinct.

Regarding the distinction in the resolve of the nine thousand and six thousand followers, as the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "When the dragon girl attained Buddhahood, all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of the Sahā world saw from afar the dragon girl’s attainment of Buddhahood, as she universally preached the Dharma for the assembly of devas and humans."
Their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all paid homage from afar.

Furthermore, in the passage below, it is said that three thousand beings in the Sahā world dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, and three thousand beings attained the bodhicitta and received their predictions of enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly accepted this in silence with faith.

Although the Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa and Śāriputra were wise men, they remained within the current of delusion; for the sake of benefiting those who are still in the dark, he was dispatched to provide instruction and practice to aid ordinary learners, thereby establishing a standard for them to follow.

The multitude of this Sahā world having already paid remote homage, these six thousand who have resolved their minds have not yet transcended the duality of self and other; they all follow the provisional teachings of the three vehicles regarding conditioned bodhi, and have not yet attained the fundamental awakening of the universal gate Dharma-realm, wherein self and others are of one essence.
For this reason, there is remote veneration. This is not the case in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

rather, through the Dharma-gate of the Universal Door Dharmadhātu and the vision of all phenomena, and the realm of the Tathāgata-garbha-body Samādhi—the Indrāla-net Adornment Dharma-gate—one simultaneously attains the revolving ocean of worlds and the successive layers of wondrous wisdom. This is because one realization is the realization of all, and one severance is the severance of all.

Within one's own body, there are the adornments of the oceans of Buddha-fields of the ten directions; within the body of the Buddha is the realm of one's own self, appearing and vanishing in successive layers.

The nature of phenomena throughout the worlds of the ten directions is likewise: it is like the many streams flowing toward the great ocean; though they have not yet entered the sea, their moistening nature does not differ, yet once they enter the great ocean, they all share the same salty taste.
All sentient beings are likewise so: although there is a distinction between delusion and awakening, they have never originally departed from the fundamental ocean of Buddhas.
Why, then, do the multitudes in this Sahā world in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* offer respectful salutations from afar?
The ritual procedures and rules for this matter differ entirely from those in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
For instance, within the "Dharmadhātu Chapter," the assembly of six thousand attained further clarity of their ten eyes in a single kṣaṇa;
five hundred young boys all realized ten bodies in one lifetime, and it was the same for all the other members of the assembly.

When Sudhana traveled south to seek his spiritual friends, the compassionate root of the Buddha-fruit was already perfected; he further entered the body of Samantabhadra, wherein all Dharma-gates were fully prepared, principle and phenomena were co-extensive, and there was no dharma that was not manifested.
Since the Dharma-realm already dwells within the midst of sensory objects, how could there be such a thing as a distant prostration?
Therefore, it is said here that the assembly of six thousand individuals has developed their resolve separately.

Regarding the tenfold bestowal of predictions upon the śrāvakas from afar: this is because, within the *Lotus Sūtra*, although the Dragon Girl suddenly realized the gate of the timeless Dharma-realm and fully manifested the fruit of Buddhahood.

Those of the three vehicles who study through provisional means possess a mind of faith and compliance; as the lingering influence of their former habits has not yet been extinguished, they are unable to realize sudden enlightenment and must ascend [to the goal] only after distant eons, and thus receive a prediction of future attainment at a remote time.
This differs from the *Avataṃsaka*, which holds that one is an ordinary person when deluded and a Buddha when awakened;
if residual habits remain, they are to be remedied by means of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Lacking the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they achieve only temporary subjugation; they cannot enter the swift current of the Buddha’s stream, but must pass through further distant kalpas before they can do so.

Because the roots of faith of those at the initial stage of the three vehicles are inferior, they are unable to free themselves from bondage; their fetters are numerous and heavy, and they take pleasure in attachment to birth and death.
Although they seek transcendence of the world, their faculties are inferior, causing them to stagnate and regress.
