Thereupon, the Tathāgata causes them to contemplate through such observations as birth, old age, sickness, and death; impermanence and impurity; momentary destruction; and the non-abiding of every thought-moment. By doing so, he causes them to give rise to weary detachment (*nirveda*). Once the mind of weary detachment is established, the mind abides amidst both the pure and the defiled.

Within the teachings of transformation, for the sake of those with such faculties, although the Tathāgata exhorts them to cultivate compassion and wisdom to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, he nevertheless refers to the Pure Land as being located in another direction.

Because those of the three vehicles have not yet eliminated their subjective discrimination (*dṛṣṭi-bhāga*), they perceive this Sahā world as perpetually defiled; therefore, by explaining cause and effect, [the Buddha] shatters their doubts and temporarily transforms it into purity. Once he withdraws his supernormal power (*ṛddhi-bala*), they again see it as defiled as before.
The teachings of the Three Vehicles already contain explicit clarifications on this point:

because of the habitual nature of the wisdom of the contemplation of impermanence, which is difficult to turn back, even though the Dragon Girl was suddenly shown the Buddha Vehicle, although she believed it, she could not immediately realize it.
For this reason, those who receive their predictions within the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* all do so after many kalpas.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* gradually leads them back [to the truth], whereas the *Avataṃsaka* bestows the teaching directly at all times, for it holds that one becomes a Buddha immediately upon generating the aspiration for enlightenment.
For this reason, the practices and faculties differ.
Within the same gate, there are two types:
first, those of the Tathāgata Vehicle who proceed directly to the site of enlightenment.
The vehicle of the Tathāgata is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

As stated in the "Bhadrapāla Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "Among all the various classes of sentient beings in the world, those who seek the Śrāvaka vehicle are few; those who seek the Pratyekabuddha vehicle are even fewer still; those who seek the Mahāyāna are extremely rare. While seeking the Mahāyāna may yet be considered easy, being able to have faith in this Dharma is exceedingly difficult."
Furthermore, a sutra states: "If there are sentient beings whose minds are weary and submerged, for them I preach the path of the śrāvaka, so that they may be freed from all sufferings.

If there are further sentient beings whose minds possess a slight degree of clarity and sharpness, for them I preach the Dharma of dependent origination, so that they may attain the state of a pratyekabuddha."

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who delight in learning the mind of loving-kindness and compassion, and who extensively benefit other beings, for them I shall preach the path of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who resolutely delight in the Great Matter, for them I shall manifest the Buddha-body and turn the inexhaustible Dharma of the Buddhas.
This refers to the division of the four vehicles (*catur-yāna*) within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

As in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the three carriages before the gate merely demonstrate provisional teachings (*upāya*), whereas the white ox in the open space clarifies the true doctrine (*saddharma*).
There is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third.
The provisional teachings outside the gates of the second and third vehicles serve to clarify the true teaching of the open ground.
While the four vehicles accord with one another and the two teachings share commonality, their established methods of transformation each possess distinct differences.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Only this one reality is true; the other two are not real.
Based on this single passage, it appears that the three vehicles (triyāna) are established.
Regarding their convergence, they again constitute four dharmas.
"Only this one reality" refers to the reality of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).
"The other two" refer to the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna; these two also include the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, as they are similar to the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas in their aversion to suffering.
This serves as a sufficient mirror and can be clearly reflected upon.
Within a single kṣaṇa, the two dragon maidens seal the nature of the three periods of time.

Furthermore, from the state of an ordinary person, one is immediately a sage without shifting by even a hair’s breadth; this is roughly identical to the dharma-gate of entering the Way through understanding and practice as exemplified by the youth Sudhana.

As for Sudhana attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime, it does not depart from the momentary limit (*kṣaṇa*) wherein one realizes the nature of the three periods of time as being entirely equal throughout past and present; thus, it is identical to the Dragon Girl’s instantaneous transformation of her body, the fulfillment of all practices, and the simultaneous completion of Buddhahood—all of which accord with the fundamental Dharma, for such is the nature of the Dharma.
The "time-intervals of establishment" refer to the mental objects and sensory dusts of sentient beings; when Sudhana realizes this, it is called "one birth.
Once the time-intervals of the three periods of existence are exhausted, what further birth could there be?
Therefore, it is called "one birth.
As for the other ten different designations, they have already been discussed previously.

Regarding the transformation of the dragon girl’s body and Sudhana’s lack of transformation, there is a distinction because while one involves a transformation, there is actually nothing to be transformed.
New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll One;
New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan.
The eighth, the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, takes the protection of the True Dharma as its primary theme;
for this sutra establishes a "Jewel Monastery" (*ratnavyūha*) above the desire realm and below the form realm, gathering all humans and devas therein.

The devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās of the two realms above and below, as well as the eight classes of spirits, including nāgas, and the bodhisattvas from other directions, all gathered at the Jewel Monastery.

Among the various spirits who did not go, the Four Heavenly Kings released glowing iron wheels that compelled them to proceed to the Buddha’s presence; the Tathāgata then commanded them all to protect the True Dharma.
Among all the māra kings, there was only one who did not obey the Buddha’s command, saying: "I shall only resolve upon bodhicitta when all sentient beings have become Buddhas."
The ninth [treatise], which takes the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as its primary doctrine regarding Buddha-nature, differs from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in ten ways and agrees in one.

The ten differences are: first, the difference in the location where the Dharma is preached; second, the difference in the adornment of the realm; third, the difference in the assembly of those who come to the great gathering; fourth, the difference in the principal and attendant dharmas of the wheel of Dharma established; fifth, the difference in the hearing of the Dharma by the assembled multitude; sixth, the difference in the purity or defilement of the land of retribution; seventh, the difference in the provisional or ultimate nature of the Buddha-body; eighth, the difference in the manifestation of birth, nirvana, and signs; ninth, the difference in the manner of teaching and practice; and tenth, the difference in the initial role as a friend and model.

Regarding the first type of sameness: it is like the grass found on the Snowy Mountains called "Fatty"; if a cow eats it, she produces only pure *sarpis* (ghee), which possesses no colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, or black.

First, regarding the distinction of the places where the Dharma was taught: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was taught at the place between the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River in the kingdom of Kuśinagara; the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was taught in the Bodhimaṇḍa within the kingdom of Magadha, beneath the precious Bodhi tree. Therefore, it is said that there is a distinction in the places where the Dharma was taught.

Second, regarding the distinction of the adornment of the environment: as it is said, when this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* was being taught, the auspicious and blessed site of the twin śāla trees was thirty-two yojanas in length and breadth, and the great assembly filled its entirety without any empty space remaining.

At that time, the Bodhisattvas of Boundless Body from the four directions, together with their retinues, occupied seats as small as the point of a needle or the tip of an awl; meanwhile, great Bodhisattvas from Buddha-worlds as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions, equal in number to those atoms, all assembled there.

Furthermore, the text states: "At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the ground of this trichiliocosm became entirely soft and supple; it was devoid of mounds, ravines, sand, soil, gravel, thorns, or poisonous weeds, and was adorned with various jewels, just like the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha Amitāyus in the western quarter."

At that time, the great assembly all beheld the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, just as one observes one's own body in a clear mirror; their observation of the various Buddha-lands was likewise so.
Furthermore, in the passage below, the twin śāla trees suddenly turn white, as described in detail in the sutra. As it says regarding the preaching of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

there are ten lotus-receptacle world-oceans, each with twenty tiers from top to bottom. Within the lowest tier, to speak briefly, there are vast lands numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-fields surrounding [the central one]; each such land has as many minor lands as the atoms in ten buddha-fields as its retinue, doubling at each successive level above.

Thus, within these ten Padma-garbha worlds, the ground is composed of vajra; the trees, terraces, pavilions, halls, palaces, ponds, and oceans are all adorned with various jewels, as described in the sutra: "Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment in the forest hermitage where he first attained perfect awakening. That ground was firm and composed of vajra, adorned above with exquisite jewel wheels, various precious flowers, and pure mani-gems, wherein infinite oceans of forms and appearances were manifest."
"In this manner, down to all the inconceivable eons of adornment in every buddha-field, they are all entirely contained and manifested.
The preceding two pages of the sutra consist of praises for all the adornments of the Buddha’s realm.

Furthermore, the detailed exposition of such adornments in the subsequent "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World" (*Huazang Shijie Pin*) constitutes the adornment of the Tathāgata’s own true retribution-body (*vipākakāya*); it is not, as in this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, a temporary transformation into purity for the sake of sentient beings through the Buddha's supernatural power.

Why is this so? It is because the assembly gathered for this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* consists of a diverse multitude of roots belonging to the three vehicles; were it not for the sustaining power of the Buddha’s spiritual authority (*buddhādhiṣṭhāna*), they would not be able to perceive it spontaneously and without effort.
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the assembly of the One Vehicle, the roots are pure and there are no mixed groups.
Because the śrāvakas have distinct roots, they were originally not seen within that assembly.
Although the sutra also mentions "by the Buddha's supernatural power" (*ṛddhi*), the subsequent text states it is "because such is the nature of dharmas" (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, regarding the term "Buddha's supernatural power," "supernatural" (*shen*) refers to the state of being a *arhat* (one who has attained truth); it is not the same as the reality of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). It is called "supernatural" because the Buddha’s power causes them to see [the truth] momentarily.

One should know that the Adornment of the Flower Treasury (Huazang zhuangyan) is the true retribution of fundamental clarity, whereas the supernatural power of nirvana is merely a temporary expedient manifestation.

Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* deduces that the Buddha’s pure land lies to the west, beyond lands as numerous as the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers, and is not located here; thus, it is clearly known to be a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) and not the ultimate reality.

Regarding the distinction between the assemblies gathered at the three great meetings: it is said that all those present at this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* are of the lineage of humans and devas; the multitudes of the Three Vehicles are all mindful of the Tathāgata, their eyes filled with tears as they carry and honor the fragrant firewood, lamenting in sorrow and grieving as they long for and follow the Buddha-sun.
Such assemblies as these are those fit to hear of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
with the exception of those bodhisattvas of the single vehicle who have entered the Buddha’s wisdom and others like them, all remaining cases are to be understood accordingly.

The assembly that has gathered for the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* consists entirely of bodhisattvas within the stage of Buddhahood in the ocean of nature and wisdom; it is purely of the One Vehicle, with no other categories whatsoever.
The hosts of humans, devas, and gods all share the same roots; they enter the stream of the Buddha’s wisdom and are endowed with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Within the first assembly, the multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds, are all born from the ocean of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness.

The ocean of roots of goodness is the ocean of wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; it is produced by great wisdom, and all Buddhas are born from that which takes the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body as its root.
Were it otherwise, all gateways of practice would belong entirely to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

This multitude, from their initial aspiration until their entry into the ocean of Buddha-wisdom, rely upon the cultivation of the six stages—namely, the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten grounds, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment; thus, the characteristics of their practices differ according to their varying degrees of depth.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, those of the three vehicles are equally subsumed, and the seeds of goodness among humans and devas alike come together at the assembly.
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, however, the multitudes of the three vehicles do not partake in its assembly; even if they were within the assembly, they would be like the deaf who hear nothing.

One should know that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* brings together the three vehicles—the assembly of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, humans, and devas—which differs from the *Avataṃsaka*. This [latter] is the assembly of bodhisattvas within the stage of the One Vehicle; those in the initial stage of generating the resolve for enlightenment rank equal to the Buddha’s own stage, enter the flow of the Buddha’s wisdom, and share the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby becoming true sons of the Buddha.

Regarding the distinction between the primary and attendant figures among those who established the Wheel of Dharma: at the beginning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the foremost of those who made the request were Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Siṃhanāda Bodhisattva, Śāriputra, and others; they were the leaders of the request for the sake of the Dharma’s standard and measure.
The Māra Pāpīyān exhorted the Tathāgata to enter *parinirvāṇa*.

As stated at the beginning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, this refers to the great bodhisattvas within the stage of Buddhahood—namely Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Bodhiśiras, Dharmamati, Guṇakara, Vajradhvaja, Vajragarbha, and so forth—including these ten heads, ten wisdoms, ten forests, ten banners, and ten treasuries. This is because they establish the dharma-gates of the five stages of the practices leading to the fruit of Buddhahood, as each of these stages clearly contains the state of Buddhahood.

Therefore, as established in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, all the bodhisattvas who engage in dialogue regarding the Dharma principles are the assemblies of bodhisattvas from the ten directions and this very land. They have all thoroughly penetrated the true source and their wisdom is equal to the Dharma-realm. They manifest throughout the ten directions, arriving without coming and reaching without going; they are the manifestations of the Dharma-nature, not brought about by physical movement. Within a single speck of dust there are infinite clouds of bodies, and within a single hair-tip the inconceivable ocean of marks appears; it is thus throughout the entire Dharma-realm of the ten directions.
In all places they suddenly appear, yet they come from nowhere;
they suddenly vanish, yet they go nowhere.

At all times and in all places—within the bodies and appearances of sentient beings, within the realms of mountains, rivers, great oceans, and the ten directions of empty space—they manifest forms and images with sovereign mastery over existence and non-existence, inexhaustible and infinitely layered; all are such great assemblies of Bodhisattvas.

Therefore, this is not the same as the case in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa and the Śrāvaka Śāriputra—having been born into human families and manifesting the status of ordinary beings to lead those of the three vehicles—beheld the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and were moved by grief; their tears flowed down to fill their eyes as they came together for the assembly.

Regarding the five groups of beings who have come to hear the Dharma, this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is intended for those śrāvakas, followers of the two vehicles, and provisional-vehicle bodhisattvas who, while practicing various contemplative exercises, have not yet abandoned their attachments and hindrances; who delight in and cling to all conditioned activities, grasping at the characteristics of those activities; and who are deluded regarding these very characteristics concerning the unconditioned Dharma-body, which is fundamentally self-existent, beyond proof, and beyond cultivation.
Through the cultivation of practice, this cultivation is manifested and established, whereby bodhi and nirvāṇa are realized as both subject and object.

For the sake of those with such faculties, the Tathāgata, in this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, has taught that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and are subject to arising and ceasing; once arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss.

Because the wholesome practices one performs and the bodhi one is able to realize are phenomena subject to arising, and the nirvāṇa realized is a phenomenon subject to cessation, as long as the mind retains the duality of subject and object, arising and ceasing will never cease.
Because arising and ceasing do not cease, one becomes obstructed by the True Principle.

Now, within this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is therefore taught that both the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the two—the awakening (*bodhi*) that realizes and the nirvana that is realized—must both be extinguished before one accords with the True Principle. Thus, the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena is a law of arising and ceasing; once arising and ceasing have been extinguished, quiescent extinction is bliss.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata conceals his body so that it does not appear, and all subject and object of the mind are exhausted, this is called Great Nirvāṇa.

The nirvāṇa of the two vehicles involves subject and object, as well as cultivation and realization; for this reason, it is termed conditioned and untainted (*anāsrava*). Consequently, the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is devoid of subject and object.
Therefore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Cunda said to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"Do not say that the Tathāgata is the same as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Is it spoken with knowledge or without knowledge when one says that the Tathāgata is identical to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)?
If one were to say that the Tathāgata is identical to all conditioned phenomena, then one could not say that he is the Sovereign Dharma King among humans and devas within the triple world.

Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* causes those of the three vehicles to know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), awakening (*bodhi*), the capacity to realize, and the nirvana to be realized are all impermanent. That which has never existed from the beginning is what is born; not realizing any cessation, and being without practice or cultivation, is called Great Nirvana—this is termed "Perfect Quiescence" (*parinirvāṇa*).

Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* causes those practitioners of the three vehicles who delight in attachment to practice to abandon practice and abandon cultivation; it causes those who have something realized to practice non-realization and non-cultivation.

As in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, all those from other lands who come to this realm, as well as the humans and devas of this land who take their places in the assembly, attain mastery over both principle and phenomena, and the non-obstruction between principle and practice, from the very moment they first resolve their minds toward enlightenment.
The principle of Mañjuśrī and the practice of Samantabhadra are stamped all at once, like a seal pressed into clay.
Being stamped all at once, there is no priority, sequence, or interval; all are in accordance with the fundamental Dharma, for it is naturally so.

If one maintains notions of beginning and end, cause and effect, or priority and sequence, these are all mundane sentiments and all subject to birth and extinction; they involve formation and destruction, and merely serve to sever attachments according to one's faculties, rather than opening the way to the orthodox lineage of attaining Buddhahood.
All gateways through which the various teachings lead one forth ultimately enter the ocean of fruition—the principle and wisdom of the Avataṃsaka; only then will they be truly in accord with reality.

The teachings are clearly manifest and serve as perfect mirrors; you should thoroughly examine the scriptural texts and let your wisdom illuminate them accordingly, so that you may achieve sudden and profound awakening.

When the sun of wisdom breaks through the clouds, one suddenly ascends the wondrous peak; in an instant, one climbs the ocean of gnosis. The dualistic views of ordinary beings and sages are washed away by the water of meditative concentration, while the two gates of compassion and wisdom are finally manifested through the Dharma-body.

This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is taught directly for those of the most supreme great mind; it is like bestowing a precious throne directly upon an ordinary person, or like dreaming of a thousand years at night which vanish as soon as one awakens.

As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called 'Fatty' (*meda*); if a cow eats it, she produces only ghee (*sarpis*), which has no blue, yellow, red, white, or black color."
The one of the supreme great mind is likewise so: they suddenly perceive the Buddha-nature and immediately achieve perfect enlightenment, rather than arriving gradually from a lower stage.

Therefore, what is said here regarding the distinction between the assembly that comes and the hearing of the Dharma is based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which subordinates the derivative to the essence; it does not yet discuss the unimpeded simultaneous application of wisdom and compassion, or the ultimate and conventional truths.

Regarding the distinction between the pure and impure abodes of the six lands of retribution, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* indicates that the Buddha’s land of retribution is located in the west. Beyond thirty-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Buddha-lands, there is the land of Śākyamuni’s retribution. Because those of the three vehicles who follow provisional teachings have not yet eliminated their defilements and purity, they perceive this Sahā world as foul, evil, and impure; thus, the Tathāgata provisionally points to his land of retribution as being in the west.

According to the teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* on ultimate reality, this Sahā world is pure and stainless, and the worlds of the ten directions are pure and without blemish; for in the case of Bodhisattvas of the ultimate teaching, both defilement and purity have been exhausted, and thus their realm is purely immaculate.
Because the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings produce defilement within the inherently stainless and pure realm, the *saṃbhogakāya* land is pointed out as being in the West.

Regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real aspects of the seven Buddhas' bodies: as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Tathāgata endowed with the thirty-two marks is the provisional aspect, while the true principle of *nirvāṇa*—perfect quiescence—is the real aspect; this is because all the immeasurable adornments of the retributive marks exist in dependence upon the truth.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, for Vairocana Buddha, principle and phenomena are non-dual; without impairing the Dharma-body, he manifests an ocean of forms that is immeasurable and inexhaustible. Thus, form is identical to nature, and fruition is identical to principle, like light and its shadow, sovereign and unimpeded.
Furthermore, I shall briefly clarify the provisional and the ultimate, while leaving the details for later sections.

Regarding the distinction between the manifestation of the eight phases of birth and parinirvāṇa: this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* establishes for the various humans, devas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—the followers of the two vehicles—the descent from Tuṣita Heaven, the taking of birth, and the entry into nirvāṇa as the eight phases of attaining the Way. It also speaks for the sake of the Mahāyāna bodhisattvas that there is no descent from Tuṣita Heaven into the mother’s womb, and it teaches permanence, bliss, self, and purity, being without beginning or end, and neither arising nor ceasing.

Nevertheless, he remains hidden and does not manifest, yet he still designates his land of retribution as being in the West; beyond thirty-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* buddha-fields from here, there is the land of retribution of Śākyamuni.

Thus, this Sahā world is a transformed land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*) and a defiled realm; because such distinctions exist, it separately attracts those with provisional faculties. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not like this:

it directly reveals the original body and the fundamental dharma, transcending emotional views. It is without beginning or end, its temporal phases of the three periods are severed, and it is the Dharma-gate of the ocean of fruition—spontaneous, free, and unimpeded in nature and characteristics—a single, perfect true retribution that is neither born nor extinguished, neither permanent nor discontinuous. It is intended for those of the highest, superior faculties who receive it directly.
The operational mode of the teaching and its dynamic influence are thus.
This is not like the provisional teachings, which are accomplished gradually according to a sequential order.
It is just as when one has ascended nine fathoms of a mountain peak; one cannot suddenly sever one's tracks.
One who ascends the ten-tiered steps cannot lose their footprints.
When one first attains the rank of the first grade of officialdom, they consider themselves merely a minister.

Yet, when one hears that an ancient scholar suddenly ascended to the Nine Palaces, the bright pearl was instantly illuminated, its light pervading all directions; its bounty drenched the great ocean, every single drop filling it to the brim.

The emptiness of a single atom and the dharma-realm are without differentiation; yet sentient beings, due to their various categories, forcibly give rise to attachments and remain bound within them. As their faculties and capacities are unequal, the provisional and the ultimate differ accordingly, such that these teaching gates manifest in a thousand variations and ten thousand distinctions.

One must know that while provisional and ultimate teachings exist, one should recognize the provisional and cultivate the real; one must not remain long stuck in the provisional school and become deluded regarding its ultimate teaching.
Ninth, as for the distinction between the characteristics of teaching and practice, this is as explained by the Ten Ground Bodhisattvas in the "Tathāgatagarbha" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Even when a Bodhisattva has ascended to the stage of the ten bhūmis, they still do not clearly perceive or see the Buddha-nature.

Rather, from the stage of the ten abodes following the ten levels of ordinary faith, one perceives the nature of the Tathāgata in small measure. One establishes the successive stages of the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten bhūmis, cultivating them gradually; it is only at the stage of Equal Enlightenment that the perfection of causal practice becomes manifest, and only at the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment is one truly a Tathāgata.

It is also said that on the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called "Fatty" (*meda*); if a cow eats it, it produces only pure *sarpis* (clarified butter), which has no colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, or black.
Likewise, it speaks of the teaching of sudden realization.
It should be understood that this sutra further contains the dharma-gates and spiritual dispositions of five vehicles, six vehicles, and seven, eight, nine, or ten vehicles.

Moreover, within this sutra, besides the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, there are three types of Bodhisattva Vehicles; when these are combined with those two vehicles, they constitute the five vehicles.
Furthermore, by incorporating the five precepts and ten wholesome actions of humans and devas, these constitute the six vehicles and seven vehicles.
Moreover, when those of the three vehicles hear this together and each attains their respective teachings, with these mutually integrated, there are nine vehicles.
What are the characteristics of these three types of bodhisattva-vehicle practices?
First, the vehicle that cultivates the dharma-gate of non-self;
second, the vehicle that gradually perceives the Buddha-nature from the ten abodes through the ten stages.

Third, it is like the lush, fatty grass of the Snowy Mountains: if a cow eats it, it produces only the purest *sarpis* (clarified butter), without having to pass through the gradual stages of milk, curd, cream, and so forth.
In the "Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature," it is said: "Once the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have perceived this nature, they all speak thus:
'How extraordinary, World-Honored One!'"
"We have wandered through immeasurable births and deaths, constantly deluded by the notion of non-self.
This refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, it is said: "There are bodhisattvas who, having practiced the six pāramitās for immeasurable kalpas and attained the six supernatural powers, and having recited and mastered the eighty-four thousand dharma-treasuries, still do not believe in this profound sūtra."
This is an example of that.
The supernormal powers they attain do not arise from their innate nature; rather, through the cultivation of various virtues and the contemplation of non-self, they receive rebirth as superior devas.

Furthermore, there was once a man from Northern Yue who, in his previous life, also practiced the contemplation of non-self (anātman). As a result of that karma, he was reborn in that country with a lifespan of a thousand years; food and clothing appeared spontaneously. There, seven-inch grains of non-glutinous rice were cooked by fire-jewels, and wherever the fragrance reached, people would all come together to eat.

There is no absence of the Buddha-dharma, nor is there a failure to attain liberation; rather, all these faults arise from errors in past conduct and understanding, which cause what has been attained to never be lost.

This *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that although there are distinctions among humans, devas, non-Buddhists, and the three vehicles, they ultimately all return to the Buddha-nature, the nirvāṇa of perfect stillness, the truth of non-substantiality. It does not manifest a retributive form with distinctions of self and other; rather, it perfectly encompasses both principle and phenomena, and its wisdom and function are unimpeded, layered upon one another. Yet, it still establishes distinctions such as self and other, or purity and defilement; therefore, it is said that Śākyamuni’s retributive land lies beyond lands as numerous as the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers to the west.
Because their faculties are not yet fully capable of receiving instruction, the teaching is presented according to those faculties.

For those belonging to the three vehicles who are still bound by fetters, the teaching directly reveals the gate of the principle of Buddha-nature, perfect quiescence, and true suchness; it does not yet demonstrate the successive layers of the retributive marks. If they encounter these, they will become obstructed by various views, giving rise to delusion and attachment, which in turn blocks the Dharmakāya.

As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit following the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is precisely what is perceived at the initial moment of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. It is like the grass on the Snowy Mountains called "fatty": if a cow eats it, she produces only pure *ghṛta* (clarified butter), which possesses no colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, or black.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when a Bodhisattva at the first stage of the Ten Abodes attains the vision of the Way, they suddenly perceive that themselves and others are, from time immemorial and without end, without past and without present, fundamentally Buddhas; their physical and mental natures and characteristics are fundamentally the birth of the Buddha.
Taking this Buddha-gate as liberation, they ride the Tathāgata-vehicle straight to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Sudhana, ten thousand dragons, six thousand bhikṣus, five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, five hundred boys, and five hundred girls suddenly manifest the five stages; collectively they align with the gate of the principle and wisdom of the Buddha-fruit. Thus, the first dwelling is the tenth stage; the first dwelling is itself the rank of Buddhahood.

If one abiding in the first stage does not immediately attain the rank of Buddhahood, it is like a minister of state who, from the first of the nine grades up until reaching the first rank, is called only a "minister" and not a "king."

One should know that the provisional teachings establish a sequence of five stages and ten grounds, which are ascended one by one until the completion of three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; yet, during this time, one is merely called a bodhisattva and not a Buddha, nor is one said to have mounted the Tathāgata-vehicle and reached the site of enlightenment directly.
It is only because they cultivate the contemplation of non-self and their compassion surpasses that of the Two Vehicles, yet they do not perceive the Buddha-nature, that they are called Bodhisattvas.

If even those who have a slight perception of the nature attain the Buddha Vehicle, it is like a single hair-tip drop or many drops within the great ocean—within each and every drop, one attains the great ocean itself.

Thus, within the five stages of the bodhisattva, each of the ten abodes and ten grounds contains the fruit of Buddhahood. Just as a single drop of water from the great ocean does not exist apart from the nature of the ocean, so too do these practices proceed without departing from the Buddha-nature; it is by virtue of that Buddha-nature that one advances and cultivates.

As in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Tathāgata directly reveals his complete fruition—the ten wisdoms such as the Immovable Wisdom—to ordinary beings for their faith and cultivation; it is like an ordinary person suddenly ascending to the precious throne, personally holding the royal position and comprehensively knowing the affairs of all ministers, encompassing and containing every category of being without exception.

The characteristics of the bodhisattva practices within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* are likewise thus: from the very beginning of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) upon first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one suddenly perceives such a Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, Buddha-nature, and the fruit of non-effortful wisdom; one universally practices all the myriad deeds of Samantabhadra, following conditions without obstruction, all of which are entirely without effort.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Buddha-nature is not something produced; it is merely covered by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).

Now, from the initial stage of the Ten Abidings onward, through the self-substance of the non-productive samādhi (*anabhisaṃskāra-samādhi*) which accords with reality, the adventitious afflictions are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
Only the true essence and function are free from greed, anger, and ignorance; in their spontaneous operation, one is immediately a Buddha.

Therefore, when one thought-moment accords with reality, one becomes a Buddha in that very thought-moment; when one day accords with reality, one becomes a Buddha in that very day. Why wait for eons to cultivate gradually?

Having accumulated practice over many kalpas and reached the fruit after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, why would the obstacles to vision cease even as the mind takes the duration of those kalpas as its object?
The Dharma-gates of the Buddhas are fundamentally not subsumed within time; calculating time to establish kalpas is not the Buddha-vehicle.

Tenth, regarding the distinction between the initial friend and the preceptor, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "A youth on the Snowy Mountains encountered a rākṣasa and resolved his mind [on awakening]; he valued half a verse more than his own life."
"I have heard that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing; when arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.
It is said that Buddha-nature and nirvana cannot be cultivated through conditioned practices, nor can they be realized by the mind.
It cannot be cultivated through practice, for practice is conditioned and impermanent.
It cannot be realized by the mind, for there would then be subject and object.
Therefore, one cannot cultivate its nature through practice, nor can one realize its principle with the mind; for as for the mind, its nature is fundamentally devoid of subject and object.
Therefore, Cunda said: "Do not say that the Tathāgata is identical to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

This is according to the model established by the youth Sudhana in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, who, from his initial generation of the bodhicitta under Mañjuśrī until his final encounter with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, states for each of the fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*):
"I have resolved my mind toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
How should you instruct me to study the bodhisattva path and practice the bodhisattva conduct?
He did not speak of such matters as the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena.

Why is this? Because this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* elucidates the gateway of the dharma-realm of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as the non-duality of principle and phenomena; there is no condition that is not quiescent, and no phenomenon that is not true.

The great ocean of the single true nature throughout the worlds of the ten directions is the perfect circumference of great wisdom; it constitutes the realm of the land as a whole, being the ocean of nature and the single true Dharma-realm, for it is not a matter of sentient or insentient beings as described according to their karma.

Because the purely true realm within the *Avataṃsaka* is, in its entirety, wisdom, the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes take insight (*prajñā*) as their realm; the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices take knowledge (*jñāna*) as their realm; and those of the Ten Dedications and the Ten Stages take the wondrous as their realm, without speaking of the distinction between the two views of the sentient and the non-sentient.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is taken as the manifestation of the fundamental Dharma because it differs from the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles.
It pertains to both the insentient and the sentient, and thus involves arising and ceasing.

Therefore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, regarding the youth of the Snowy Mountains who spoke of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-anityatā*), it is because the faculties, lineages, and practices of the three vehicles are inferior; the Buddha caused him to discipline his conduct until it was supple and to subdue his coarseness and evil, only then becoming fit to enter the Path.
Consequently, by calculating that what has been taught constitutes established reality, one obstructs the nature of non-action and abandons the realization of ultimate truth.
For this reason, it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, and both the subject and object of realization are likewise dharmas subject to arising and ceasing.

Unlike Sudhana, who at the single thought of generating the aspiration for enlightenment suddenly transcends subject and object, realizing the nature of the three periods of time as being beyond past and present, and awakening to his own mind as inherently Buddha—neither achieving perfect enlightenment nor realizing bodhi.
Regarding the nature and characteristics of body and mind, there is neither realization nor cultivation; they are neither formed nor destroyed, being thus from the very beginning.

Whether moving or still according to conditions, existence and non-existence are not impaired; all practices performed arise solely from wisdom. Therefore, it is not said that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
Regarding the single type of sameness: it is like the analogy of the lush, fatty grass on the Snowy Mountains in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Furthermore, as stated in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva King of Universal Radiance and Noble Virtue": "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; there is no distinction between the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha."
"The nature and characteristics of the Triple Gem are eternal, blissful, self, and pure; all Buddhas never ultimately enter into parinirvāṇa.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvāṇa."

As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha rebukes the biased views of the two vehicles, asserting that [their claim that] the Buddha descended from the Tuṣita Heaven to enter the womb, and that his manifestation of the eight phases of enlightenment, were all instances of such biased views.

This is just as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where wisdom enters the three periods of time without coming or going; the Buddhas of the ten directions realize great bodhi through the nature that is devoid of past and present.

In a single thought-moment one perceives the Way; the views of past and present are exhausted, and both the new and the old are entirely non-existent. This is identical to the Buddhas of the past—those of billions of kalpas and those of unspeakable kalpas—who all attained Buddhahood simultaneously, and it is also identical to the Buddhas of the future who will attain Buddhahood simultaneously throughout unspeakable kalpas.
Because one realizes for oneself that the three periods of time have no temporal duration, and because there is no temporal duration, there is neither coming nor going.

Even if sentient beings do not personally perceive and know that their own body and mind are originally and perfectly awakened, the perfect virtue of the original awakening of their own body and mind is fundamentally without cessation.

If there are sentient beings who, through self-inspection, know that their own body and mind have been fundamentally and perfectly awakened—because this fundamental perfect awakening has from the beginning been unborn and is inherently thus, and because from the beginning there has been neither a subject that awakens nor an object to be awakened.
If there is one who awakens, they awaken in this very manner, because fundamentally there is neither an awakener nor that which is awakened.

Such fundamental awakening is the realm of the Buddha: it is without ordinary person or sage, without stability or distraction; it is neither cultivated nor realized, neither wise nor foolish, and neither arising nor ceasing.
The provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles were expounded for those of inferior capacity to lead them here to this *Avataṃsaka*’s true teaching, wherein they may suddenly enter the Buddha-gate.

Although the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explains that the principle of the Buddha-nature and Dharma-body is identical to that of the *Avataṃsaka*, its explanations regarding the reward land (*saṃbhogakāya-kṣetra*), the Buddha-body, and the marks, wisdom, and functions are entirely distinct, as can be understood from the ten preceding sections.

As for the teachings of the two scriptures, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, although they were manifested by the Transformation Buddha, both intend to cause those of the Two Vehicles, as well as the classes of humans and devas, to achieve the Dharma of the One Vehicle.
Therefore, because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* breaks the distant bonds of the three vehicles, it enables the dragon girl to attain bodhi through her own fundamental nature in a single kṣaṇa.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* refutes the icchantikas' lack of Buddha-nature, thereby enabling the butcher Pūrṇamukha to attain perfect enlightenment within the Bhadrakalpa.

Furthermore, if a cow eats the fatty grass of the Snowy Mountains, it produces only ghee; it does not first become milk or cream before becoming a wondrous medicine. In a single stroke, it is directly and instantaneously realized, its essence remaining unchanging, just like the fruit attained by that dragon girl.

The teachings of these two sutras, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa*, share the same essential intent: they cause those of the three vehicles to relinquish provisional means and enter the ultimate reality, thereby perfecting the single true gateway of the Dharma-realm.
All other teachings are provisional explanations; even if they discuss the principles and phenomena, they do so only partially, and within them the ritual procedures cannot be fully complete.

This is exclusively the fundamental gateway of the Buddha Vairocana within the Dharmadhātu of the *Avataṃsaka*, wherein principle and phenomena, nature and characteristics, are perfectly complete and mutually integrated; all other gradual teachings ultimately converge herein.

At that time, those practitioners who followed the various paths and became mired in provisional teachings would take many kalpas before their spiritual lineage could be redirected; those of inferior intelligence created hardships for themselves of their own accord, which was not due to the intent of the Sage, yet resulted in such a state.

Question: As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the butcher Wide-Forehead (Pṛthuvyañjana) shall attain perfect enlightenment within this Bhadrakalpa. According to what the Buddha has taught, one thousand Buddhas appear in this Bhadrakalpa; the fixed number among them is clearly set forth in the scriptures.
Furthermore, there are more than a thousand individuals with broad foreheads; how could it be that some among this number attain Buddhahood repeatedly?
The answer is:
for those who study the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles and whose fetters have not yet been extinguished, repeated attainment of Buddhahood is impossible.

Reaching its essence throughout the three periods of time and all kalpas, the Buddhas all collectively and simultaneously attain perfect enlightenment; fundamentally there is no sequence of before or after and no obstruction, because the fundamental nature of the Dharma has no temporal duration.

Ordinary sentiments are perversely bound and give rise to delusions; within the net of false views, one perceives the appearance of Buddhas in the world, yet in reality, the Buddhas—the true and authentic ones—conform to the fundamental nature and are neither born nor extinguished.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Buddhas do not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvāṇa.

This is because the Buddhas are merely the manifestation of the physical body in accordance with the nature, being the true reality of their own essence, spontaneously quiescent, and arising through conditions in accordance with the nature; they neither come nor go, for they are free from all fabrication.

The tenth, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, takes as its primary tenet this very title—the Buddha-vehicle of the Great Vaipulya—and further takes as its tenet the unimpeded dependent origination of the phenomena and principle of the dharmadhātu, wherein causes are perfected and fruits are fulfilled with sovereign mastery.
Therefore, this scripture is titled the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, and it likewise takes the Buddha-vehicle as its primary tenet.

This scripture expounds the resultant virtues of Vairocana’s own essence—his wisdom and compassion—and reveals them universally to all sentient beings, thereby enabling those with the great resolve to believe in the Buddha’s resultant virtues and employ them to form the causal stage.
Having already given rise to faith, one returns to cultivating the wisdom of principle and the myriad practices of great compassion, thereby accomplishing the fruit and virtue of initial realization.

At the very moment of first resolving for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening; by simultaneously cultivating both principle and practice, one ensures that essence and function are sovereign, so that one does not cling to principle alone nor isolate practice, thereby eliminating partial views.
This sutra contains ten kinds of profound, vast, and incomparable teachings that distinguish it from all other sutras.
The first is the fundamental wisdom and great compassion of the essential nature of all Buddhas.
The vehicle of the perfectly fulfilled and limitless Dharma-realm is not a provisional establishment of the three vehicles; therefore, it is profoundly deep, vast, and peerless.
The two Buddha-bodies are themselves adorned by the ocean of immeasurable marks of the Dharma-body and Reward-body.
Each and every pore contains the entire Dharma-realm; all realms are infinitely layered and inexhaustible, profoundly deep, vast, and beyond compare.

Third, this sutra describes the fundamental reward lands of all Buddhas as ten seas of Lotus Treasury World-Oceans. Within each of these Lotus Treasuries, at the very bottom of every world, there are vast lands as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds, adorned with pure splendor. Each of these vast lands is further surrounded by subsidiary lands as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds, with the scale doubling and redoubling upward from there.
Each Flower Treasury World fills all of space, penetrating one another in infinite layers of profundity and vastness beyond compare.

This sutra describes a Bodhi tree that is lofty, eminent, and extraordinary: its trunk is of diamond, its main stem is of lapis lazuli, its branches and twigs are composed of various exquisite jewels, and its fruits are multicolored mani-jewels interspersed with flowers. They stand in alternating rows.

Surpassing the bodhi tree manifested within the body of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, its circumference spanned one hundred thousand trichiliocosms and its height reached one million trichiliocosms; its branches and foliage were proportionate to the trunk, being of incomparable vastness.

Fifth, this sutra states that the Hall of Universal Radiance encompasses the entire Dharma-realm with myriad exquisite and real adornments, where light and shadows multiply in layers; the magnificent array of jewel pavilions, terraces, turrets, and stairways all reflects one another with penetrating clarity, pervading the Dharma-realm in a vastness beyond compare.

Sixth, this sutra states that in every place there is Mañjuśrī, and in every place Samantabhadra; their essence and function mutually penetrate, filling the dharma-realm such that principle and phenomena are unimpeded. Within even a speck of dust, the ocean of conduct is inexhaustible—profound, vast, and beyond compare.

Seventh, this sutra states that although the Tathāgata descends from Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb at the limit of a single kṣaṇa, attains Buddhahood, preaches the Dharma, and enters parinirvāṇa at the conclusion of his transformation, he does not abandon his reward body (vipākakāya), which dwells eternally.

The ocean-like assembly of Bodhisattvas pervades the ten directions; their inexhaustible clouds of bodies are all of true golden color, with deep blue-black eyes and hair, their bodily radiance mutually illuminating one another.

Such oceans of assemblies are all coextensive with the Dharma-realm throughout the ten directions without interval; there is not the slightest void or empty space between them. Their essence is transparent and their forms interpenetrate, with layers upon layers of physical manifestations that are neither obstructed nor hindered. According to what is appropriate and capable, they manifest physical bodies to cause all sentient beings to give rise to the Bodhi-mind without missing the opportune moment.
Thus, these oceans of assemblies are all vast and beyond compare.

Eighth: if there are sentient beings of great resolve who develop deep faith in this Dharma-gate of the sutra, do not read other sutras, and profoundly clarify its essence and function, they shall swiftly attain Bodhi through minor expedient means.
At the moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment, it is the beginning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), its rank equal to the fruit of Buddhahood itself.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata": "Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated and accumulated various factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). If this person has not heard this Dharma-gate of the inconceivable great majesty of the Tathāgata, or having heard it at some time, does not believe it, does not understand it, does not comply with it, and does not enter into it, they are called a 'nominal bodhisattva,' because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata."

If, having heard this Dharma gate of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable, inconceivable, unobstructed, and unhindered wisdom, one believes, understands, accords with, and enters into it, you should know that such a person is born into the family of the Tathāgatas and accords with the realm of all Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage states: "O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish such merits, they attain untaught, spontaneous wisdom with little exertion of effort."
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva said:
"Even those who do not give rise to faith upon seeing the Buddha or hearing the Dharma will likewise accomplish the seeds of the wisdom of liberation.
He then provided analogies such as that of a small amount of gold used for making food, as explained in detail in the sutra.
This sutra contains such a dharma-gate of great majesty and inconceivable power, surpassing all three vehicles and being vast and incomparable.

Ninth, this sutra contains the preeminent symbols of the Dharma: the youth Sudhana, without departing from a single thought-moment, passed through an entire lifetime; without leaving a single location, he reached everywhere throughout the ten directions; he visited fifty-three spiritual benefactors and attained the dharma-gates of one hundred and ten cities.

The individual dharma-gates of each bodhisattva—their various arts, modes of practice, physical forms, complexions, and the methods for gathering and nurturing sentient beings—are all equal to the Dharma-realm, complete and inexhaustible.

These vast gates of practice do not require more than a single lifetime to achieve perfect enlightenment; they are devoid of any distinction between beginning and end, or before and after. Thus, they are as vast as the Dharma-realm and as ultimate as empty space.
Thus it is vast and incomparable.

This sutra contains ten realms of the Buddhas, ten inexhaustible dharma-gates, ten wisdoms, ten stages, ten bodies, ten eyes, ten ears, ten noses, ten eloquences, ten jewels, ten mountain kings, ten dragon kings, ten world-systems as numerous as motes of dust, and ten oceans; each of these possesses ten unspeakable realms, with inexhaustible parables and dharma-gates so vast they are beyond compare.
Furthermore, this sutra possesses ten kinds of virtues.
First, it is like the great ocean to which all streams converge; once the various rivers have entered it, they expand accordingly and all become identical with the ocean's majesty.

This sutra is likewise: if there are sentient beings who can give rise to faith and enter [into it], they will be identical to the Tathāgata’s ocean of nature, the ocean of wisdom, and the merit of fruition.

Just as all wells and springs in the world have the ocean as their essence, if a person drinks from them, they all obtain the taste of the ocean; they are of one substance without difference, yet due to the power of karma, they do not perceive the salty taste.

This sutra is likewise: if there are sentient beings with great resolve who hear, uphold, believe, and enter it, they immediately obtain the flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, Buddha-nature, and great compassionate wisdom.
Although those of icchantika nature lack such capacity, the nature of the Tathāgata’s wisdom constantly acts as the generative cause.

Third, it is like the great ocean which possesses four precious jewels: the first is named Accumulated Treasure, the second is named Inexhaustible Treasury, the third is named Far Removed from Blazing Heat, and the fourth is named Fully Endowed with Adornments.
These four precious jewels cannot be seen by any ordinary beings, nāgas, spirits, or the like. This sutra is likewise:

it cannot be seen by any followers of the two vehicles, nor by provisional-vehicle bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās but have not yet turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]. It can only be seen by those of the supreme Buddha Vehicle with great resolve, who, upon seeing this sutra, give rise to faith and enter it, personally perceiving that their own minds are identical to the Great Wisdom-Jewel of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

In this "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," it is said: "How is it that these sentient beings possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet, being deluded and confused, they neither know nor see it?"

I teach them by means of the Noble Path, causing them to forever leave behind false conceptualizations and attachments, so that within their own bodies they may perceive the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is no different from that of the Buddha.
"Fourth, it is like the great ocean where all dragons, fish, and other creatures alike dwell within its waters and are born therefrom.

This sutra is likewise; it can explain the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings, wherein immeasurable Buddhas arise within the ocean of the minds of sentient beings in a single thought-moment, appearing in the world to attain equal and perfect enlightenment."
As it is said in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" in this sutra: "O Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that within their own minds, in every thought-moment, there is always a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment."
Why is this? Because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas attain perfect enlightenment without departing from this mind.
As it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings.

"5. It is like the great ocean which can receive heavy rains; when immeasurable heavy rains fall all at once, whether it be the water or the ocean, they all share the same taste of the sea without distinction of before or after."

This sutra is likewise; for this reason, it is taught that when one first gives rise to the mind of the ten stages, at that very moment of initial aspiration, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment and partakes equally in the flavor of the Tathāgata’s omniscience.
The Sūtra says, "By means of small skillful means, one quickly attains Bodhi"; those such as Sudhana and the Dragon Girl are examples of this.
Sixth, it is like the great ocean, where beings of massive bodies dwell and reside.
This sutra is likewise: it is the dwelling place for the most supreme beings of great mind, while the dragons of the marshes do not delight in residing there.
7. This sutra is like the great ocean, which does not harbor corpses.

This sutra is likewise: if there are those who see, hear, believe, and rejoice in it, and are thus able to awaken and enter, they will forever leave behind the corpses of ordinary beings, provisional learners, and icchantikas, directly becoming one with the ocean of wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
Eighth, just as the tide of the great ocean never misses its time, so too is this sutra:

if there are sentient beings whose faculties are capable of hearing it, they shall hear it; according to their inclinations, they shall hear it; through the transformative teaching of the Dharma of the five vehicles, it never misses its time.
The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" states:

"O Son of the Buddha! The voice of the Tathāgata is likewise: it has no master and no agent; it is without discrimination, neither entering nor exiting; yet from the power of the Tathāgata’s merit and dharma, four kinds of vast sounds emerge."
What are these four? First:

You should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely suffering—namely, the suffering of hell, the suffering of animals, the suffering of hungry ghosts, the suffering of lacking merit and virtue, the suffering of attachment to self and what belongs to the self, and the suffering of performing various evil deeds.
"Those who wish to be born among humans or devas should cultivate roots of goodness; by being born among humans or devas, they will remain far removed from all states of adversity.
Having heard this, sentient beings abandon their inverted views, practice various virtuous deeds, and, being free from all states of adversity, are born among humans or devas.
This is the vehicle of humans and devas. Second:
"You should know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are ablaze with manifold sufferings, like glowing iron balls."
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to decay; nirvāṇa is tranquil, unconditioned, and blissful, far removed from the blazing fire that consumes all feverish afflictions.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas and attain the "patience of accordant sound" within the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
This is the Śrāvaka-yāna. Third:

"You should know that those of the Śrāvaka-yāna understand according to the words of others, and their wisdom is narrow and inferior. Furthermore, there is a superior vehicle called the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, whose awakening does not depend on a teacher."
"You all should train in this.
Those who delight in the supreme path, having heard this sound, will abandon the path of the śrāvakas and cultivate the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
This is the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas."
The fourth is:
You should know that beyond the stages of the two vehicles there is a further, superior path called the Mahāyāna.

It is the practice of the Bodhisattvas, which accords with the six pāramitās; it does not interrupt the Bodhisattva conduct nor abandon the bodhicitta. Dwelling amidst immeasurable births and deaths without weariness or fatigue—surpassing the two vehicles—it is therefore called the Mahāyāna.
This is the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas.
It is also called the First Vehicle, the Supreme Vehicle, the Most Excellent Vehicle, the Superior Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, and the Vehicle that Benefits All Sentient Beings.

If there are sentient beings who possess vast faith and understanding, whose faculties are sharp and keen, who have planted roots of goodness in the past, who are empowered by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas, and who, possessing superior joy and aspiration, seek the fruit of Buddhahood—they shall, upon hearing this sound, give rise to the bodhicitta.
This is the Buddha-vehicle.
O Son of the Buddha!
The voice of the Tathāgata does not issue from the body, nor does it issue from the mind, yet it is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice.
You should know that the Tathāgata’s voice constantly accords with what the beings of the five vehicles ought to hear, just as the tide of the great ocean never misses its appointed time.

"9. This sutra is like the great ocean; its substance has no active function, yet by means of causes and conditions, four great precious jewels arise within it, and from these four jewels, all manner of rare treasures can be produced."
If these four jewels did not exist, no other jewels whatsoever could arise.
The names of these four jewels have already been explained previously.
This sutra is likewise so: it is the Tathāgata’s single-natured ocean of purity, which all sentient beings share, yet they are unable to expound upon it.

Yet the Tathāgata, in accordance with various conditions, gives rise to the four great wisdoms and the four immeasurable minds, thereby able to produce all dharma-gates and immeasurable treasures of the Path, benefiting and bringing peace to sentient beings without any deficiency.

Within this ocean of nature, if the four wisdoms and the four immeasurable minds are absent, even if the fruits of sainthood are attained, they will all follow the practices of the two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Although within this ocean of nature the four wisdoms and the four immeasurable dharmas of the jewels are accomplished, that ocean of nature has no agent, for it is thus because there is neither attainment nor realization of phenomena.

Tenth, it is like the great ocean which, by virtue of its pure qualities, can reflect the adornments of the seven golden mountains, Mount Sumeru, the four heavenly kings, and all else, such that they all appear clearly within it.

This sutra is likewise; it fully expounds the ocean of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body nature, complete with its virtuous adornments—the ten Buddha-bodies, the ten Lotus Treasury worlds, the five stages, the ten wisdoms, the ten pāramitās, the ten samādhis, and the ten patiences—along with all the factors of the path obtained through the retribution of causes and conditions, each of which is clearly and distinctly manifested.

The general essence of this sutra takes the dharma-realm of the great wisdom of the nature-arising as its substance and function; within the gate of the substance and function of the dharma-realm of the great wisdom of the nature-arising, it establishes the various distinctions of the stages and the methods for the transformational birth of beings.

Therefore, by giving rise to faith within this Dharma and generating the great Bodhicitta, one immediately perceives one's nature and gives rise to the wisdom of the Dharmakaya at the very beginning of the first stage of the Ten Abodes, thereby attaining perfect enlightenment.

However, it is only at the stage of "wisdom arising from nature" that one performs various practices to teach and transform sentient beings; this is the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment and Practice (*juexing yuanyman fo*).

This differs from the provisional teachings, where one first practices the bodhisattva path by studying the provisional because True Suchness (*tathatā*) acts as an obstruction. In those teachings, True Suchness becomes an obstruction due to the observer’s own subjective mind; thus, the practices performed are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the bodhicitta generated has not yet transcended birth and extinction, and the discriminative ignorance (*parikalpita-avidyā*) is merely suppressed through contemplation. Only upon reaching the stage of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) can one see one's nature, and only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* does one finally attain Buddhahood, still requiring another hundred kalpas to separately cultivate the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

If one were to equate this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Buddha’s original vehicle, with those transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya), and thereby lead those of provisional learning—whether of superior, middling, or inferior capacity—who lack complete faith and understanding and remain far removed from the Buddha’s profound mystery, they would fail to comprehend the meaning of the sūtra; thus, throughout vast and long kalpas, they would never have the opportunity to achieve Buddhahood.

If a person of the highest capacity believes and understands this sutra, clearly knowing it to be unerring, they shall immediately mount the Tathāgata-vehicle and proceed directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
At the very moment of mounting it, that is the site of enlightenment; there is nothing further to be reached.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is likewise the Buddha-vehicle, yet it is the transformation Buddha who leads those of the three vehicles to know the true Dharma.

Thus, the three vehicles at the gate of the burning house of the triple world—the goat cart, the deer cart, and the great ox cart—are precisely the three vehicles of the superior, middling, and inferior faculties.
Because those of superior faculties possess a degree of compassion, they surpass the other two vehicles;
yet because they contemplate the conventional and have not yet attained the vision of reality, they are called "untrue bodhisattvas."
These three types of individuals—those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties—all possess the suffering of the three realms.
Those of middling and inferior faculties, as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, loathe this suffering and seek its cessation;
those of superior faculties, as Bodhisattvas, feel weary of it yet do not abandon it, for their compassion surpasses that of the two vehicles and they possess a mind intent on benefiting others.

These three types of persons alike do not know that the essential nature and characteristics of the triple world are the single true realm of the Buddha, as is extensively clarified in the "Chapter on Manifestation.

For this reason, the Buddha taught that all the marks of the retributive fruits of a Buddha’s merits are produced through cultivation, so as to cause those of provisional learning to practice and refine their mental attentions (*manasikāra*).

Having cultivated for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, there was no time when Buddhahood was not attained; therefore, the carriage at the gate is the Buddha’s provisional manifestation, while the white ox in the open field clarifies the Dharma-realm. Nature and characteristics are fundamentally nothing but true wisdom; all conceptual discrimination is but the functioning of wisdom.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "As for the meanings of these various natures and characteristics, only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know this matter;
the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and even the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas are all unable to know it."
This refers to the three vehicles (triyāna) at the gate.

It is because they have not yet clarified that this is the abiding of dharmas, the fixed position of dharmas, and that the characteristics of the world are eternally constant; because they all possess the same mind that seeks to weary of suffering and its origin while delighting in cultivating cessation and the path; and because they have not yet clarified that suffering and its origin fundamentally arise only from ignorance, nor understood that cessation and the path are inherently without cultivation, without construction, and without action—yet manifest like illusions in the world to transform all classes of beings, for when their nature is free from ignorance, they are the Buddha.
To correspond with Buddhahood for a single thought-moment is to be a Buddha; to correspond for a single day is to be a Buddha. Why must one toil in vain to require three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*?

Simply by realizing the karma of the triple world for oneself and being able to empty the locus of that karma, one spontaneously engages in the birth [of beings]; this is precisely what it means to be a Buddha.
Why must one undergo transformation to become a Buddha?
If dragons and devas also undergo transformation, would they not then be Buddhas?
Since those of the Three Vehicles are likewise capable of transformation, why must one wait for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before becoming a Buddha?
Therefore, it is only upon reaching the tenth stage that one is able to see the nature [of reality].

Thus, a verse in the sutra says: "If one wishes to see the Tamer of Men through the great supernatural power of the nature of form, that person has eyes clouded by delusion and sees erroneously; such a person does not recognize the most supreme Dharma."

"Buddha" means awakening. One awakens to the fact that the nature of karma is true and that karma is without arising or ceasing; there is nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized, neither emerging nor submerging. Its nature is without change and is primordially suchness (tathatā); because it is this very state, one is a Buddha.
Following conditions within the six realms of existence, one practices the bodhisattva path, employing transformative supernatural powers to guide and lead the deluded masses.

The Buddha is not a mere transformation; as the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Though he has attained perfect enlightenment and turns the wheel of Dharma, he does not abandon the way of the bodhisattva, for this is the practice of a bodhisattva."

By means of this initial stage of the ten stages of Sudhana’s journey, he received from the bhikṣu Meghashiri on Mount Sumeru the Dharma-door of the Universal Vision of the Wisdom-Light that Recollects the Realms of All Buddhas, and immediately attained perfect enlightenment.
Only then does one approach one's friends to seek the Bodhisattva path and practice the Bodhisattva deeds.

One should know that at the very moment of realizing the essence and function of perfect enlightenment, the mind is in a state of non-action; since this is itself the Buddha, there is no need for further cultivation.
Even if his practice were already perfected, he would not have departed from his present state.

This is like a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) manifesting the signs of accomplishment—such as practicing austerities on hemp and wheat, shaving his hair, wearing robes, renouncing all ornaments, and reclining on grass—solely to transform non-Buddhists who delight in asceticism, and those among the three vehicles whose faculties are prone to negligence.
In the sutras, the Buddha has already reconciled these points; it is not that the Buddha himself must personally engage in such practices.
For one who is free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*), why would such things be necessary?
When one moment of mind rests in the nature of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and the Buddha’s wisdom manifests before one, being without attainment and without realization—that is the Buddha.
It is just as when Sudhana, after realizing awakening, subsequently sought the bodhisattva practices of the path to enlightenment. Why is this so?

Because only after realizing the Way is one capable of entering the entanglements; only by dwelling within those entanglements without being bound can one preach the Dharma for sentient beings to untie their bonds.
If one who is themselves bound were able to untie the bonds of another, such a thing is impossible;
for while the sequence of speech is temporal, the Dharma itself is simultaneous.
One should know that if one wishes to practice the bodhisattva path, one must first achieve perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, at the very beginning of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), atop Mount Meghaśrī, this image [of the Buddha] preached on the summit of Mount Sumeru the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages—the "Dharma-gate of the Universal Vision of the Wisdom-Light that Recollects the Realms of All Buddhas" attained by the Bhikṣu Meghashiri.
The commentary states:

To represent the Dharma through its locus means that one reaches the limit of the Dharma where no marks can be apprehended, just as ascending a high mountain until the point where all characteristics are exhausted.

Because the nature of marklessness can manifest the form-body (*rūpakāya*), and because within the mind of no-mind there is mastery over knowledge and vision, observing capacities and gathering beings for their benefit is termed "wondrous."
Skillfully destroying the afflictions is called a "peak.
Possessing complete knowledge and vision that transcends objective conditions, with wisdom surpassingly lofty and far-reaching, remaining unshakable—this is the mountain.
To explain the Dharma-gate: mindfulness is constant non-mindfulness.

Regarding the realm of all Buddhas: where there is no thought, there is neither internal, external, nor intermediate; because there is no internal, external, or intermediate, it is the realm of the Buddha.

Regarding the radiance of wisdom (*prajñā-āloka*): responding to phenomena and observing faculties is termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*); distinguishing capacities and employing the provisional and the real is termed "insight" (*prajñā*); responding to capacities to shatter delusions is termed "radiance"; the liberation from mental defilements is termed "clarity"; the far-reaching clarity of the Dharma-eye that is equal to the realm of sentient beings is termed "universal"; the perpetual state of non-attainment is termed "vision"; and the initial realization of this principle is termed a "Dharma-gate."

Within this single stage, compassion and wisdom are equally perfected; possessing the wisdom of differentiation, one enters the mundane world to engage with ordinary beings, following the very same model as the conduct of Sudhana.
