From the first *bhūmi*, one’s radiance is equal to that of a Buddha, yet during the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one’s conduct remains exclusively humble, beginning from the level of commoners as a boy or girl.

Those who are unacquainted with the traces of the teaching vainly slander one another; yet for those who have realized the mind and clarified the essence, the mirror of truth remains perfectly intact.
A question is asked:
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are the great ox-carts of the three vehicles at the gate and the white ox-cart on the open ground; since both are oxen, what difference is there between them?

Answer: The three vehicles at the gate correspond to the sufferings of the triple world; they merely cause one to leave the burning of the fire-house and temporarily escape the calamity of fire, but this is not called attaining Buddhahood.

For the sake of Bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching who delight in practicing compassion and possess the will to benefit others, they distance themselves from the perils of fire but do not distance themselves from the triple world.
This is because their partial resolve to deliver sentient beings surpasses that of the two vehicles, which seek only their own liberation.
Furthermore, possessing even a single portion of the mind of transport is termed the "Great Ox," because it is viewed as being vast in comparison to the stage of the Two Vehicles.
This is because one only attains Buddhahood upon seeing the nature at the tenth stage; it is only after passing through many kalpas that one can finally become truly so.
Viewing those of the two vehicles as merely named "Bodhisattva Mahāyāna" rather than "Buddhayāna," the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"There is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third."
Thus, he draws those of the three vehicles back to the single vehicle, just as it is said that those of the Small Vehicle will eventually receive the prediction of Buddhahood.

Although they possess faith and assent to attaining Buddhahood, because it is somewhat difficult for them to turn away from their habitual practices, the distant kalpas are designated as the time frame.

The dragon girl reached the Buddha’s presence in a mere instant; this illustrates that true realization consists in penetrating that suffering is itself the truth, for there is nothing therein to be loathed.
Therefore, the vehicle at the gate is established in contrast to the three vehicles, whereas the white ox on the open ground clarifies arrival at the place of non-reliance.
The "open ground" (lùdì) refers to the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*).
Because the Buddha’s wisdom has no dependence, it is called the open ground.

The "white ox" refers to the compassion and wisdom of the Dharmakāya. The Dharmakāya is termed "white" because it is signless (*animitta*); wisdom is termed the "ox" because it can observe the capacities of sentient beings, while compassion is what rescues them.

Just as one takes a cow for the purpose of its ability to carry loads, [the Buddha] employs the Dharma-body of non-conditioned action (*asaṃskṛta-dharmakāya*) and his compassion and wisdom to rescue and benefit sentient beings; thus, they are analogous to a cow, being called "cows" by virtue of their capacity to provide rescue and benefit.
How does the ox before the gate differ from this ox?

As the ox before the gate, one contemplates emptiness with increasing excellence, breaks through the realms of suffering in the triple world, and possesses a degree of compassion; yet, having departed from a portion of the coarse suffering of the three karmas, one has not yet fulfilled the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* nor seen the Buddha-nature, and has not realized the fundamental wisdom of the wisdom-body.

It does not speak of "white color" nor does it speak of "open ground," because these are provisional designations for True Suchness and the contemplation of emptiness; since the mind still has something upon which to rely, it does not speak of white color, and because there is something upon which to rely, it does not speak of open ground.

Now, although these sons have fled and reached the open space, they all seek the three vehicles—the goat cart, the deer cart, and the great ox cart—thereby clarifying that those of the three vehicles emerge from the suffering of the triple world and are temporarily spared from the calamity of the fire.

Although they have turned their minds to believe in this One Vehicle, they still have not yet reached the first stage (bhūmi), because the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of the three vehicles have not yet been extinguished; thus, they merely follow the Buddha’s words with faith, for their minds have fundamentally established firm conviction, yet they still seek the three vehicles and do not yet dare to rejoice in the Great [Vehicle].
The Buddha then entices and guides them to establish the power of faith, providing them equally with great carts; therefore it is said, "That which you did not expect, I now bestow upon you all.

This clarifies that those of the three vehicles who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] are like the ox-carts at the gate: they are not described as being white, nor are they described as being adorned, because they still possess outflows (*āsrava*).

Furthermore, because one has only attained a portion of the superior bliss of humans and devas, yet has not yet attained the wondrous bliss of the merit of the body of non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*), it is not like the vehicle of the white ox in the open air, which is described in full detail with its ornaments, height, breadth, and other such features.
This is entirely distinct from the vehicle at the gate and that of the open space.
Any further implications will be clarified below in the text.
Therefore, while the *Lotus Sūtra* is for the purpose of reconciling provisional means with entry into the ultimate reality, this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the fundamental vehicle of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, what was symbolized by the dragon girl in that sutra is here presented by Sudhana; the convergence of the modes of conduct of Sudhana and the dragon girl will be explained in detail in the subsequent text.

The intention of the Buddha is that those three provisional means (*upāya*) are transformed so that they all return to this single reality; therefore, this sutra is named the "Root of All-Knowledge, the Buddha Vehicle.
