All the merits of a Buddha are produced through cultivation; for example, one cultivates the karma for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) over a hundred kalpas, attains radiance from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, achieves longevity through non-killing, gains wealth through giving, and attains physical perfection through patience. Each cause and effect corresponds exactly and completely to its counterpart, yet only by applying various methods of counteractive practice (*pratipakṣa-dharma*) can one finally realize one's nature and attain Buddhahood.

It is not so in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where one suddenly realizes the dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm in a single thought-moment. Body and mind, along with their nature and characteristics, are fundamentally nothing but the essence of phenomena; when all activities and applications move and rest in accordance with reality, operating through non-active wisdom, this is itself the Buddha.
For all Buddhas it should be thus: neither long nor short, from beginning to end ultimately so; all phenomena are like this.
Within the single true Dharma-realm, one acts freely according to the Dharma, fully possessing the meritorious functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; this is both cause and fruit.

By means of this universal gate of the dharma-realm, the wisdom of principle and phenomena, all obstacles naturally cease to exist; there is no separate antidote, nor is there any separate cultivation or severance. No transformation is perceived, for there is no difference between the nature and characteristics of that which transforms and that which does not transform.

One universally observes that there is nothing that is not a Dharma-gate and nothing that is not liberation; yet, because one's own mind forcibly gives rise to attachments and becomes preoccupied with manifold affairs, one sinks into the current of suffering. Therefore, the Sage laboriously expounds various distinctions, only for one to again give rise to attachment toward those very teachings.
For this reason, the teachings of the Sages differ—whether gradual or sudden—according to the capacities of various faculties.
Thus, this scripture’s teaching suddenly reveals the Perfect Vehicle (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa), which is what those of the highest and most superior vehicles are capable of receiving.
Even if one is not yet capable of receiving it, one must joyfully cultivate it; in the end, all streams will flow back to and ultimately reside within this ocean.

Therefore, other teachings present the cause first and the result later; this teaching is not like them, as it holds that cause and result are simultaneous, because within the ocean of the wisdom of *dharmatā*, neither cause nor result can be apprehended.
Within the state of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), cause and effect are simultaneous and free from obstruction.
Where cause and effect are apprehended, there is necessarily a sequence of before and after; whatever is apprehended is impermanent, and thus it is not the ultimate teaching.
If the cause precedes the effect, the cause itself cannot be established, and thus the effect is also destroyed.

Because phenomena arising through conditions do not continue in succession, because they would be subject to annihilation, and because self and other would be unestablished—just as when counting one coin without counting the subsequent coins, the "one" is not established in the absence of the "two" that follows—so too, because moments do not continue in succession, the momentary cause is unestablished and the effect is destroyed; because multiple eons do not continue in succession, the causality across multiple eons is destroyed. It is only upon waiting for the time when the subsequent coin is counted that the preceding one finally becomes established.
Cause and effect are likewise: they are only established as cause and effect when they are dependent upon being uninterrupted within a single moment.
If this were so, it would be like counting two coins simultaneously; with neither before nor after, which could be designated as "one" and "two"?
It is like holding up two fingers: which one constitutes the cause and which the effect?
Just as with these two fingers, whichever mental factor arises first serves as the cause, and the subsequent factor serves as the effect.
If there were a "before" and a "after," there would necessarily be an interval between them; and if there is an interval, the relationship of cause and effect cannot be established.
If they were simultaneous, like two fingers held upright with neither before nor after, which would be cause and which effect?
In that case, both would fail to be established.

Thus, regarding the simultaneity of cause and effect in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there is no such conceptual attachment to the delusory thought of priority and posteriority or simultaneity; nor is there attachment to cause and effect through the dualities of existence and non-existence, both or neither, permanence and impermanence, and so forth. Rather, one simply realizes that the essence of phenomena is not something contrived, and that what is called "cause and effect" is not a causal relationship established by the mind—it is not a delusory thought of simultaneity or sequence posited by the intellect.
In this regard, how does this differ from the teachings on gradual instruction found in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*? It is not so.

The previous discussion regarding the difference between the teachers, the difference between the questioner and the respondent, and so forth, clearly demonstrates that Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the Buddha—the three virtues—are the inseparable unity of essence and function, and the non-obstruction of principal and attendant.

In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the transformation Buddha and Mahāmati Bodhisattva engage in a dialogue to refute [inherent] characteristics; however, because they only know how to manifest the principle of non-attachment, they do not discuss the dharma-realm of dependent origination.
Regarding the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as dependent origination: the dharma-realm is neither established nor destroyed, for one simply knows and understands that dharmas are thus.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "First one shows a similar object, and afterwards one shall grant the reality."
It further states: "That which perceives characteristics is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which does not perceive characteristics is wisdom (*jñāna*).
This clarifies the distinction between formation and destruction.

According to the intent of this sutra, there is no provisional dharma within the ultimate truth; all dharmas are collectively the ultimate truth. They are purely true and without falsehood; there exists nothing resembling them wherein one might maintain the distinction between the true and the provisional.
The Sūtra states: "The realm of sentient beings is itself the realm of the Buddha.

Within this scripture, Mañjuśrī unifies practice with principle, while Samantabhadra unifies principle with practice; the two harmonize essence and function to constitute the single true Dharma-realm, wherein the preceding and succeeding aspects mutually encompass one another.

The forty chapters of this sutra encompass one another; they penetrate each other from beginning to end, and their words and meanings mutually contain one another, such that many dharmas are complete within a single dharma-gate.
Therefore, the sutra says: "Within many dharmas, it is made into one dharma; within one dharma, it is made into many."
In the gradual teaching, although there may be a small portion where the meaning is the same, for the most part they do not correspond.

For example, Bodhisattvas such as Jñānacakra and the other nine each expound one dharma to establish the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*); within these ten levels of faith, they collectively form a single level of faith. These ten positions of faith are established through their mutual interpenetration and do not exist as independent constructs; since the ten levels of faith form one level of faith and one level of faith forms the ten levels of faith, those with understanding must not grasp them from the perspective of a single gate alone.

The Bodhisattva Ten Wisdoms, the Bodhisattva Ten Forests, the Bodhisattva Ten Banners, and the Bodhisattva Ten Treasuries further expounded the ten concentrations, the ten supernormal powers, and the ten patiences; in this manner, all such dharma-gates of each successive stage are mutually accomplished, like the net of Indra where they penetrate one another, such that within the one there are the immeasurable, and within the immeasurable there is the one.
The essence and function of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are mutually constitutive, and their causes and effects interpenetrate, being simultaneous and non-dual.
As it is said in a sutra:
when the Bodhisattva Dharmamati entered meditative absorption, Buddhas from the worlds of the ten directions, all bearing the same name Dharmamati, arrived.
When the Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍu entered meditative absorption, the Buddhas named Guṇakāraṇḍu from the worlds of the ten directions immediately arrived.
When the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja entered meditative absorption, the Buddhas named Vajradhvaja from the worlds of the ten directions immediately arrived.
When the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha entered meditative absorption, the Buddhas named Vajragarbha from the worlds of the ten directions came to touch his crown.
Thus, within each stage and throughout each ground, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas mutually accomplish cause and effect, and their essence and function mutually penetrate one another.
The Buddhas who have come are the manifestation of the fruit, while the Bodhisattvas entering meditative concentration are the manifestation of the cause; for cause and fruit are non-dual.

Upon the wisdom-essence of the Buddha’s Dharma-body, the formal characteristics of the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage are established as gateways to guide ordinary beings and transform living beings. Thus, the various stages are the Buddha, and the Buddha is the various stages.

If those of the highest capacity give rise to faith within this teaching, they shall likewise rely upon this Dharma; from the very beginning, at the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they directly realize the wisdom-Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Buddhahood, and only then perform all the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva, because this constitutes the primary realization for knowing the essential nature of the body of Dharma-wisdom.

Even if one were to engage in all activities throughout many kalpas, one’s own fundamental view would not shift for even a moment; at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening simultaneously with the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Because there is no distinction between past and future limits, and because the nature of dharmas is thus, one should understand it in this way.

This differs from the provisional teachings, wherein one attains the fruit of Buddhahood only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Therefore, what is stated here is distinct from the attainment of the fruits by those of the three vehicles.

Furthermore, because one attains the fruit of Buddhahood through the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s omniscience as taught in this sutra-vehicle, there are no followers of the two vehicles who attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; nor is there, as in the provisional teachings, a sequence of causal practices across the various stages (*bhūmi*) of bodhisattvas where the cause precedes and the fruit follows.

Fifth, regarding the distinctions in the modes of practice according to the stages (bhūmi): for all who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind, there are six types of vehicles based on their respective faculties, and three types of five stages with ten distinct levels (*daśabhūmi*) characterized by different modes of practice.

What are their names and numbers? First, the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha’s vow to be reborn in the Pure Land; second, the gate of the Pure Land produced by the practice of *śubha-bhāvanā*; third, the gate of the vehicle of cultivating the contemplation of emptiness and non-self; fourth, the gate of the wisdom that harmonizes and integrates existence and non-existence; fifth, the gate of gradual realization of the Buddha-nature through progressive cultivation; and sixth, the gate of the sudden realization of the Buddha-nature in its perfect fusion.
Those who practice the Mahāyāna do not depart from these six modes of the vehicle's practice.
What are the three types of five stages and ten grounds?
First, there is the establishment of the five stages and ten grounds based on provisional designations such as provisional *tathatā* (suchness).
The first part establishes the five stages and ten grounds based on the cultivation of the two aspects and the realization of one aspect of true suchness (*tathatā*).

The third part establishes the characteristics of the ten grounds and five stages based on the sudden cultivation, sudden realization, and sudden attainment of the Buddha-realm’s perfect suchness; within this Buddha Vehicle, there are no provisional dharmas, for all words, names, and signs are entirely true.

Thus, these three types—the ten stages, the five positions, and their respective modes of practice—encompass all those who are directed toward enlightenment, those who practice the bodhisattva path, and those who fulfill the fruit of Buddhahood; there are none who do not find themselves within them.

Now, by way of a general overview, each shall distinguish the provisional and the ultimate according to the specific tenet they ride upon, so that they may transcend obstacles and advance in their cultivation with merit, refrain from mutual disparagement, clearly understand the distinctions so as to be free from doubt or regret, and cause those who advance in cultivation to have a clear and precise knowledge of the provisional and the ultimate; thus, it ensures that those who attain Buddhahood do not suffer delay or stagnation in their merit.

Those who are born in the Pure Land through the power of reciting the Buddha’s name, cultivating precepts, and generating the power of aspiration, are born in a transformed pure land rather than a true pure land. This is because they have not realized their own nature and do not understand that ignorance is the fundamental wisdom of all Tathāgatas; furthermore, such a land is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Amitābha Sūtra) is an example of this.

Second, regarding the pure land produced through the practice of contemplation for purifying the land: this is a transformation pure land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*). Because it arises from the mind’s thoughts, because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and because one does not yet perceive the fundamental wisdom of Buddha-nature, the *Sūtra on the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life* is precisely such a text.

Regarding the third, the gateway of the practice of the contemplation of emptiness and non-self: for those to whom the *Prajñāpāramitā* was first taught, it serves to shatter the ordinary person’s grasping at substantial existence and the two vehicles’ grasping at a self within the emptiness of persons; therefore, they cultivate the dharma of emptiness extensively.
The gate of the simultaneous emptiness of existence and non-existence is established because the contemplation of emptiness has become predominant.

Although one may practice the six *pāramitās*, cultivate various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), and attain the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and although one’s merit from practicing the bodhisattva path may surpass that of humans and devas, such a person is not born into the Buddha-family and does not see the Buddha-nature. This is because, while analyzing phenomena to clarify emptiness, they fail to realize that ignorance itself is the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* likewise reproves this as previously described. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:

"If one were to uphold the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma and the twelve divisions of scripture, expounding them for others so that listeners might attain the six supernormal powers, this would not be difficult; however, to hear and receive this sūtra is truly difficult."
Because the *Lotus Sūtra* accomplishes the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*) and not the bodhisattva-vehicle (*bodhisattvayāna*),
the Tathāgata has stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"All sentient beings possess buddha-nature, which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure."
There were some bodhisattvas who, repenting of their own transgressions, said:
"Throughout immeasurable kalpas we have wandered in birth and death solely because we were deluded and confused by the notion of self."
Because of such faults, one must turn the mind back [from worldly attachments] before one can perceive the nature; this is the wisdom that realizes "I am.

In various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, those passages where Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva acts as the interlocutor all discuss the principles of the Dharma-body Buddha-nature in a specific aspect, such as the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

When engaging in dialogue with Śrāvakas, it is mostly for the purpose of destroying the two-vehicle practitioners' attachment to a self through the emptiness of persons, and thus teaching the emptiness of phenomena.
When engaging in dialogue with Samantabhadra, it is mostly concerned with the gates of practice.

In general, when teaching the Dharma, one relies on the faculties [of the audience]; however, by observing the dialogue between questioner and respondent, the underlying intent can be discerned, which may be inferred accordingly.

Regarding the gate of contemplating the presence or absence of the four harmonious assemblies and wisdom, this refers to the teachings of the third period in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, which explain the nine consciousnesses as the pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) that serves as the basis for karmic seeds, and further discuss the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) and the three absences of nature (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*), namely: the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Mutually arising and perishing, they are free from all attachments and hindrances; being neither produced nor destroyed, their nature is itself nirvāṇa.

As a verse in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* says: "All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; they are without birth and without cessation, quiescent from the very beginning. The self-nature of all phenomena is eternally nirvāṇic—who possesses wisdom that lacks such profound intent?"

This sutra is intended to refute those who, while practicing the cultivation of emptiness through prajñā, destroy the dharma of dependent origination because their manifest view of emptiness contradicts the true principle.
In this sutra, it is established that all dependently originated phenomena possess a self-nature that is nirvāṇa; they need not be negated or rejected.
The assertions of emptiness and existence mutually refute one another; it is neither appropriate to calculate existence nor appropriate to calculate non-existence.

Furthermore, although this sutra establishes ten stages with names identical to those in the *Avataṃsaka*, its internal meaning and principles differ from that work. Moreover, it lacks the stages prior to the ten stages—namely the three levels of worthies and the ten levels of faith—but instead establishes the manner of severing delusions across the ten stages and designates the Buddha stage as the eleventh stage.
Within those eleven stages, there are further explained eleven kinds of *dausthulya* (coarseness) and twenty-two kinds of ignorance (*moha*).

For this reason, this sutra does not establish the practice gates of the three worthies (*kṣānti*) and ten faiths prior to the stages; this is because the stage prior to the stages in this sutra is not the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Furthermore, because the teachings of the third period merely harmonize existence and non-existence, they have not yet fully encompassed the practices of principle and phenomenon as realized by Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

Therefore, when the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* expounds the Dharma-gates of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten stages, all Buddhas of the ten directions come together to grant their seal of approval; all Buddha-lands collectively proclaim these gates; and the thirteen types of seals manifest the ultimate reality.

In the sūtras of the Three Vehicles, only eleven stages are taught because they do not fully encompass all sentient beings; this is because those [stages] are merely provisional designations for the ten stages, provisional wisdoms, and provisional *tathatā* within the three types of ten stages.

Why is this so? It is because these eleven stages constitute the rank of the Buddha; yet within the rank of the Buddha there still exist obstructions, clarifying that prior to the eleventh stage, the fundamental wisdom of true reality has not yet been attained.
If true reality-wisdom were complete [in each stage], how could there be eleven types of coarse residues (*dausthulya*) across the eleven stages?
Since these coarse residues exist, it follows that within each stage there is no Buddha-wisdom acting as cause and effect.

This sutra merely provides a gradual synthesis of existence and non-existence so as not to allow for stagnation; it does not yet seem to expound the exhaustive great function of principle, phenomena, and wisdom as [taught by] Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī.

For example, as the *Benevolent Kings Sutra* explains, the practice-gates of the five stages and ten grounds are established such that one gradually trains from the level of an ordinary person, accumulating practices over many lifetimes to cultivate provisional and ultimate *tathatā*.
Furthermore, there are teachings stating that one subdues the afflictions prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and realizes the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) upon entering the stages;
or it is taught that one must intentionally retain the afflictions without severing them, requiring three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before one can attain Buddhahood.
Teachings such as these are all provisionally established in accordance with those of expedient faculties; they are not yet the ultimate truth.
All that is spoken by the Transformation Buddha is intended to guide those of middling and inferior faculties and does not exhaustively express the reality.
The rest may be understood by analogy.

Furthermore, when those of the Two Vehicles turn their minds toward the Buddha-fruit as delighted in within the provisional teachings, and the Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings who aspire to that Buddha-fruit, after the completion of an *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, they merely seek the retributive fruit of a Buddha within a trichiliocosm; they do not aspire to the retributive fruit of the realm of the ten Buddhas—the inexhaustible realm of Vairocana throughout the ten directions.

It is not like the joy in the fruit of Buddhahood experienced by Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; rather, it is the state where ordinary beings, through the mind of resolute understanding, fully possess the realm of the ten-fold body of Vairocana and joyfully cultivate it, a profound and vast mind that exhausts the wondrous realm of the infinitely layered mysteries.

The Buddha-realms of the provisional teachings are all established with fixed limits and measures; this is because their faculties are narrow and not yet broad, so they are provisionally established for them.
For example, in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, the limits for severing delusions across the ten stages are set forth:
in the first stage, one counteracts the afflictive, karmic, and birth-related defilements of the evil realms; in the second stage, one counteracts subtle...
The obstacle of the manifestation of subtle transgressions is countered in the third bhūmi; the obstacle of desire and greed is countered in the fourth bhūmi;
the obstacle of attachment to meditative concentration and to dharmas is countered in the fifth bhūmi;
the obstacle of turning exclusively away from saṃsāra and toward nirvāṇa is countered in the sixth bhūmi; and the obstacle of the manifestation of coarse signs is countered in the seventh bhūmi.
In the middle [stage], it counteracts the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle marks;
in the eighth bhūmi, it counteracts the obstacles regarding the effortful application toward the signless and the lack of mastery over signs;
in the ninth bhūmi, it counteracts the obstacle of lacking mastery over all types of skillful speech and eloquence; and in the tenth bhūmi, it counteracts the [obstacle of] not attaining...
The obstacle to the realization of the perfected dharmakāya. Noble son!
This śamatha and vipaśyanā counteract the extremely subtle and most extremely subtle obstacles, as well as the cognitive obstacles (jñeyāvaraṇa), at the stage of the Tathāgata.

As in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the stage of the initial resolve among the three grades of worthies prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), one is able to suddenly realize the dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit, universally sealing all positions—namely, the ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment—just as when a seal is pressed, the pattern is complete without any distinction between beginning and end.
At the very moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment, one suddenly seals the ignorance of the triple world, which immediately becomes the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.

By means of the seal of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, Wisdom-body, and Great Compassion, one simultaneously and instantaneously seals the mundane world as the great function of the Dharma-realm; for there is no sequence of before and after, and such is the nature of phenomena.
This differs from the provisional teachings and external expedients, as it leads those of the three capacities to return to the single reality.

Fifth, regarding the gate of gradual vision of the Buddha-nature through progressive cultivation, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas of the ten abodes see the nature only partially; even those in the ten stages have not yet seen it with complete clarity."
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes perceive the Dharma-body to a small degree, because they manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment through transformation.
According to that treatise’s commentary, this is said to be the result of their power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
Since this is due to the power of vows, it is not a result of true retribution.

It is intended generally for the gradual perception of Buddha-nature; these are all teachings of provisional expedients that gradually lead one through successive stages, and are not the Perfect Teaching.
For such individuals as these, from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the realization of the fruit of Buddhahood, the number of *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is not fixed. Why is this?
As recorded in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the butcher Viśālakṣa will attain Buddhahood within the present Bhadrakalpa.

If even an icchantika who has first awakened the aspiration in their heart possesses the merit to transcend kalpas, how much more so for one who possesses the faculty of faith and is further able to perceive their nature even in small measure—what need would there be for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
There are those of virtue in the world who interpret the butcher Guang'e as a manifestation of Māra; this is merely to conform to human sentiments and fails to grasp the Buddha’s intent.
As he gradually leads [beings] from the provisional toward the ultimate, how could he allow them to remain attached to their delusions and thus cause them to deviate from their fundamental nature?
To gradually lead one to the point where a dragon girl or Sudhana attains Buddhahood within a single thought-moment is the beginning of the true teaching.

Those of the Three Vehicles with their limited views merely contemplate over long periods; since the nature of wisdom is fundamentally non-existent, they sigh in vain and look up in admiration, binding themselves without a rope—how can there ever be a time of rest?
Previously, three types of ten stages were briefly explained.

Furthermore, when measured according to the meaning of the sūtras, there are six types of ten stages: namely, as there are three types of ten stages within the teachings of the Three Vehicles, there are likewise three types of ten stages within the Real Teaching (the Mahāyāna).

As stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, these three sūtras explain the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) primarily by establishing the gate of provisional *tathatā* (suchness) to constitute the characteristics of the ten stages; these are the three types of ten stages within the provisional teachings.

The fourth is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) perceive their nature only partially, while Bodhisattvas of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*) perceive their nature but not with complete clarity.
This clarifies that taking Buddha-nature as the vehicle is the gateway through which the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are cultivated and realized in both partial and complete aspects.

Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that just as a cow eating the fatty grass of the Snowy Mountains obtains only the finest essence, *sarpis* (clarified butter), so too does the initial arousal of the bodhicitta accord with the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha.

The sixth is the ten stages of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), as presented in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which establishes the ten stages by means of the profound and immeasurable, inexhaustible teachings on the gateway of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
These constitute the six kinds of ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

The accounts in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* regarding the butcher and the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood in an instant are all instances of using provisional means to lead toward the ultimate teaching.

However, the realm of the Buddha-fruit aspired to by Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles and ten stages is merely the fruit of a Reward-Buddha (saṃbhogakāya) within a trichiliocosm; this is precisely the third transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) within the True Teaching, and not the actual reward body.
There are three kinds of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*): first, the transformation body that manifests as the bodies of various sentient beings;
second, the transformation body that manifests as the Buddhas who appear throughout the four continents and the twenty-eight heavens;
third, the transformation body that manifests as the Buddha throughout the trichiliocosm.

As for the Body of Real Reward (*sambhogakāya*), it is the realm of profound mystery wherein the ten bodies of Vairocana are mutually fused and their characteristics interpenetrate; its magnitude is equal to the Dharma-realm and penetrates even the finest atom, such that within every atom it is equal to the Dharma-realm, as described in detail in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Since the teachings of the Three Vehicles are provisional, the Dharma-gates they expound and the realm of the Buddha’s fruition have not been fully and truly taught.
Therefore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, these are termed the "Shared Teachings of the Three Vehicles," and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are practiced in common by the three vehicles.

Regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*) taught in the second [scripture], the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, they are intended directly to unravel the profound mysteries. The gateways of the ten stages were expounded through the dialogue and companionship of Bodhisattvas such as Vipula-mati, Pṛthu-mati, and Viśuddha-mati, rather than through the dialogue and companionship of Śrāvakas. This was because the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* was directed toward those who, having been captivated by the *Prajñāpāramitā*, were excessively inclined toward the cultivation of emptiness.

These sutras, such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, merely mention the names of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), but do not include the ten faiths prior to the stages, nor the three levels of worthiness (*śaikṣa*) or the four stages of provisioning (*saṃbhāra*).

Third, as in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, there is the dharma-gate of the complete practice of the five stages. In this manner, the three levels of worthies and ten levels of sages described in the provisional teachings mostly refer to the conventional (provisional) *tathatā*. It is only through a gradual refinement of these stages that one clarifies the Buddha-nature; only then can it be said that one "mounts the Tathāgata vehicle and proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment."
One should know that provisional teachings are not ultimate, and that the stages and sequence described therein are not yet real.

Within the fourth, the Tathāgata Vehicle, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, those in the ten abodes see their nature only partially, while Bodhisattvas in the ten stages have not yet attained complete clarity.

As stated in the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Ten Abidings perceive the nature only partially; yet, through the power of their vows, they are able to attain Buddhahood in eight aspects—this is an instance of that stream.

Although they have not yet reached perfection, because they perceive a small portion of the nature of power, their capacity is such that it is like a crown prince who, for a specific reason, is ordered by his father the king to preside over the administration of state affairs; this is because he is the true son of the king and possesses the strength to do so.

This is for the sake of perceiving the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and for the sake of becoming a true son of the Tathāgata born into the Buddha-family; it differs from other teachings that rely on provisional *tathatā* and provisional wisdom, which only claim one is born into the Buddha-family upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*). Thus, it clarifies that the power of perceiving the nature of reality is truly superior to other schools.
If this is so even for a small portion, how much more so when it is attained in its entirety?

Fifth, regarding the ten stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): because in a single thought-moment the wisdom that embodies the Way is identical to the Buddha, and because the essence of ignorance is realized as being entirely identical to wisdom.
The Sūtra states: "When one is perfected, all are perfected; when one is destroyed, all are destroyed.
This shall be explained in detail later.
These are called the five kinds of ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

These four types of sequential characteristics for the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are largely the same, with minor differences, within the teaching gate of converting those of inferior and middling capacities and receiving them into birth.

However, regarding the teaching gate of the fundamental Dharma, the three provisional teachings establish *tathatā* (suchness) as the contemplative wisdom; this is entirely distinct from the two gates of gradual and sudden established upon the essence of the Buddha-nature of the Dharmakāya.

As in the provisional teachings, although one returns from the first bhūmi to counteract the defilements of birth arising from afflictions and karma in the evil destinies, up until the seventh bhūmi one still counters the manifestation of subtle marks; yet these remain obstacles that hinder the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*), and one has not yet attained full mastery. Even at the eighth bhūmi, where there is signlessness and effortlessness (*anābhoga*), one has not yet attained mastery over the effort involved with signs (*nimitta*).
Thus, because there are obstructions in each stage (*bhūmi*), one lacks mastery within them.
The preceding explanation was based on the sequential dharma-gate for abandoning delusions through the stages as taught in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.

Just as it is definitively established that there are ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) within the three vehicles, with the severing of afflictions occurring through successive levels over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and the cultivation of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) during one hundred eons;
so too has the sequential arrangement of the stages within the framework of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other texts been clarified as previously explained.

As stated in the *Benye yingluo jing*: "A Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes is a Copper-Treasure-Garlanded Copper-Wheel-Turning King; with a hundred-merit son as his retinue, he is born in a single Buddha-field, receives the Buddha’s teachings and practices, and instructs two worlds."

The Bodhisattva of the Ten Practices wears a silver-jeweled necklace and is a silver-wheel-turning king; with five hundred meritorious sons as his retinue, he is born in the lands of the three Buddhas to receive their teachings and travel to transform beings throughout the three continents.

The Bodhisattva of the tenth stage of Dedication is a Wheel-Turning King adorned with a necklace of vajra-jewels; with a thousand sons of merit as his retinue, he enters the lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions, transforms all sentient beings, and dwells throughout the four continents.

On the first bhūmi, there are necklaces of a hundred jewels; on the second, a thousand jewels; on the third, ten thousand jewels; on the fourth bhūmi, the bodhisattva wears necklaces of incalculable jewels; and thus, up to the tenth bhūmi, the jewel necklaces gradually increase in scale.
"Furthermore, the tenth and eleventh stages are those who universally attain the rank of Dharma King of the Buddhas.

Together with the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*trayaḥ-kauśalya-bhūmi*), there are fifteen types of Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) positions in total, as explained extensively in the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*).

Furthermore, it is said that the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness subdue the coarse karma of the afflictions of the three realms and the coarse continuity of the path; they also do not give rise to coarse views regarding the Path of Seeing. Joyful Patience (*pramuditā-kṣānti*) subdues the paths of action of the three [lower] realms;

Stainless Patience (*vimalā-kṣānti*) subdues the karmic paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and humans; Luminous Patience (*arciṣmatī-kṣānti*) subdues the karmic paths of the six heavens; Blazing Patience (*sudurjayā-kṣānti*) subdues all karmic paths; Victorious Patience (*abhimukhī-kṣānti*) subdues the karmic paths of doubt and wrong views; Manifest Patience (*dūraṅgamā-kṣānti*) subdues the karmic paths of causes and conditions; Non-arising Patience (*acalā-kṣānti*) subdues the karmic paths of the cause of form; Radiant Patience (*sādhumatī-kṣānti*) subdues the karmic paths of the cause of mind; Quiescent Patience (*dharmameghā-kṣānti*) subdues the karmic paths of the dual habits of mind and form; and Undefiled Patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) subdues the karmic paths of the fruits of habituation. The habits have already been eliminated prior to this stage, yet their fruits do not perish.

Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, the three stages of the virtuous (śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi) are called "subduing and severing"; from the stage of Joyful Patience (pramuditā-bhūmi) upward, one both subdues and severs all afflictions; when the Patience of Awakening (abhisambodhi-kṣānti) manifests, all ignorance within the dharma-realm is suddenly severed without remainder.

Thus, the eleven kinds of patience described above are employed by the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) to eliminate the coarse afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, as well as to suppress and sever them.
The commentary states:
"The Three Stages of Worthiness refers to the Bodhisattvas."
The ten abidings (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) constitute the three stages prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* states: "O Son of the Buddha!

The wisdom of the non-characteristic Dharma-body in a single thought-moment of the first ground accomplishes millions of asaṃkhyeya merits. It simultaneously illuminates the two truths, and in every thought-moment, it is quiescent. Within this flow of the Dharma, one cannot measure the two kinds of Dharma-bodies with the consciousness of an ordinary person."
The commentary explains:
Regarding the two kinds of bodies, the first is the *dharmatā-kāya* (Dharma-nature body) and the second is the *nirmāṇa-sambhoga-kāya* (manifestation-enjoyment body).

As for the "flow of the Dharma," this refers to a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*), who, within the spontaneous flow of the wisdom of *dharmatā*, proceeds naturally to the state of Buddhahood without any deliberate cultivation or construction; how much more so for those of the second and third stages?

Therefore, another sutra states: "The Bodhisattvas of the Three Sages prior to the stages enter the rank of the sages; within the flowing stream of the Dharma-nature, mind after mind is quiescent and extinguished, naturally flowing into the great ocean of wondrous enlightenment."
"O Son of the Buddha!
Even the names of the Three Sages and the Ten Grounds are called 'formless,' yet they are so designated only for the sake of responsive transformation.

The Dharma-method of the ancient Buddhas includes the names of the Ten Grounds; this sutra is precisely that which, after teaching the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, transforms those of the Three Vehicles, and at another time, once again briefly recounts the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-gate beneath the Bodhi tree where he first attained Buddhahood.

In this *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* (Yingluo jing), it is stated throughout: "I previously expounded the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land in the Hall of Universal Radiance, and even taught the Ten Abodes to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; now I shall explain them once more in brief."
The details are as explained at length in the sutra.

Following the sequence of this sutra, after the ten stages (daśabhūmi) have been taught, the dharma-gate of the eleventh stage is taught within the third dhyāna; however, this sutra has not yet arrived in the Western Regions.
The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!

Previously, within the third dhyāna, I assembled the assembly of the eight dhyānas and spoke of the Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood, who had entered the Buddha-flower Samādhi and recited a hundred trillion verses."
"Now, by briefly explaining the meaning of a single verse, I shall open the minds of sentient beings; you all should receive and uphold it.
Furthermore, he established the gateway of the dharma-characteristics for severing delusions according to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) based on the *Ratnakaranda-śrī-sūtra*.
The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!
Those in the preceding three stages of worthiness subdue the ignorance of the triple world and thereby eliminate coarse karma. Why is this?"
"At the time of taking birth, goodness serves as the causal seed.
The commentary explains:
When the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness first receive the wisdom of the Dharma-nature and are born into the Buddha-family, their compassionate mind increases and becomes preeminent.

Because he regards all sentient beings within the three realms as his own children, he vows never to abandon them; and for the sake of compassion, as well as due to the karma that causes rebirth within the three realms, he takes birth therein.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "Because it moistens karma, one receives future fruits; therefore, it is called 'the cessation of function' (*kṣayopabhoga*).
The commentary explains:
"Because one does not create new karma within the three realms, it is termed 'the cessation of function.'"
Furthermore, a sutra states: "Yet one does not sever the function of craving. The commentary explains:
Although the karma of the three realms has perished, the compassionate karma of taking birth is not extinguished.
The sutra states: "There are eleven types of persons who likewise subdue the karmic fruits of the three realms within the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). The commentary explains:
Regarding the "eleven persons," these consist of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) together with the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*), making eleven.

Furthermore, a sutra states: "From the first stage up to the seventh stage, the karmic fruits of the three realms are all suppressed and exhausted without remainder; it is only at the eighth stage that they are completely ended."
The commentary explains:
From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onward, [afflictions] are fully subdued; at the eighth stage, they are said to be "exhausted according with the Dharma" (*dharmakṣaya*).

From this point upward, one manifests the acts of a Buddha—receiving birth in a royal palace, leaving home, attaining the Way, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa—because one manifests all the realms of the transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇabuddha*). Thus, there is no longer the retribution of the three realms of existence, yet only the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance remain.
The commentary explains:
This refers to the wisdom of non-effort (*anābhoga-jñāna*) that manifests in the eighth stage; although one delivers sentient beings, there is no perception of sentient beings.
Prior to the seventh stage, compassion (*karuṇā*) is predominant; from the eighth stage onward, the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*) is predominant as it manifests.
Although there is no further rebirth, they spontaneously deliver sentient beings;

yet because the habitual tendencies of attachment to phenomena have not been entirely eliminated, these are finally exhausted only at the stage of Buddhahood, whereupon they manifest through transformation by the power of their original vows.
For this reason, I previously spoke in the Heaven of the Thirty-three about the meaning of birth and non-birth: birth through karma and birth through transformation.
O Son of the Buddha!
Within the state of the sages, there are two kinds of karma:
First is the karma of wisdom (*prajñā-karman*): when the mind gives rise to non-illuminating cognition by taking dharmas as its object, this is called the karma of wisdom.

Second is the karma of merit (*guṇa-karman*): because true wisdom emerges from within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as conditioned and untainted (*anāsrava*), and because it accumulates millions of *asaṃkhyeya* merits, it is called the karma of merit.

From the first stage of the noble ones upward, they manifest birth; because it is a transformational body (*pariṇāmika-kāya*), they do not create new karma, yet by the power of their vows, they remain for hundreds or thousands of kalpas, manifesting births through transformation.

The above is all according to the *Bunyō-ryōraku-kyō* (Sūtra on the Ornament of Fundamental Acts). This constitutes both the sudden and gradual gates within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Regarding the "sudden":

this sūtra states, "The bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness (*sanxian*) immediately enter the rank of the sages; they enter the flow of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and reach the ocean of Buddhahood spontaneously, without further effort."
"Furthermore, 'gradual' refers to the progressive stages of severing delusions, advancing step by step in cultivation.

This *Yingluo Sūtra* [teaches] that the Three Worthies and Ten Abidings immediately enter the stream of the Dharma-nature; it differs from the provisional teachings where one perceives the Way at the First Ground, having previously suppressed delusions prior to the Path."

If one consults the "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, it is stated that the first stage is for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) to practice; it does not say that one must be a sage (*ārya*) before studying it, as that sūtra contains explicit textual evidence to this effect.
Furthermore, regarding the clarification of those who regress, the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* states: "O Son of the Buddha!

As for those who regress or advance: prior to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), among all the dharmas of ordinary beings, there are sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who resolve upon bodhicitta and study and practice the Buddha-dharma; yet those who practice within a state of faith and conceptualization possess roots of goodness that belong to the category of regression."
"O sons of good family!

After one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to ten kalpas of cultivation through the Ten Faiths, they enter the Ten Abodes. At that time, from the first abode up to the sixth abode, if they cultivate the sixth *prajñāpāramitā* and correct contemplation manifests before them, and because they are protected and mindful of by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they emerge into the seventh abode, where they abide permanently in non-retrogression and mastery.
Prior to the seventh abode, it is called the stage of retrogression."
O Son of the Buddha!

If one does not regress, they enter the sixth stage, Prajñā; there they cultivate emptiness, non-self, non-personhood, and non-mastership, ultimately giving rise to nothing and ultimately entering the state of definitive certainty.
O Son of the Buddha!
If one does not encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one may fall away from the bodhicitta for one kalpa or two kalpas, just as eighty thousand people in my first assembly fell away.

For example, the Devaputra Viśuddhanetra, the Prince Dharmakāya, Śāriputra, and others, desiring to enter the seventh stage, encountered adverse conditions along the way; consequently, they regressed into the unwholesome states of ordinary worldlings and were no longer termed persons of the nature of the cultivated seeds (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*).

They may retreat and enter the paths of externalists; for one kalpa, ten kalpas, or even up to a thousand kalpas, they commit great false views and the five heinous crimes, committing every kind of evil without exception.
Question: According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, merely hearing the two characters for "eternal abiding" (nitya) prevents one from falling into hell for seven kalpas.

Furthermore, as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Even if one hears the name of the Tathāgata and the Dharma he teaches but does not give rise to faith or understanding, it can still plant the seed; one will certainly attain liberation and reach Buddhahood."
"Why is it that you now state that there is still regression from the sixth stage of mind and even from the ordinary person’s stage of faith?
How should this intention be reconciled?
The explanation says:

Within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), since resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) has not yet been perfected, one may falsely claim to have attained what has not been attained and thereby give rise to arrogance. Failing to draw near to virtuous friends and failing to revere the worthy and good, one becomes negligent due to such pride;
consequently, though dwelling for a long time among humans and devas, evil karma arises, capable of ripening into the karma of the great hells.
If one possesses single-minded faith and is free from arrogance, constantly seeking superior friends, then these faults will not occur.
Within the provisional teachings, there may be regression at the sixth stage of mental abiding;

however, within the ultimate teachings, those who are lingering or stagnant are exhorted to advance in their practice. For instance, Śāriputra was a manifested śrāvaka and not a real śrāvaka; all such skillful means were employed to deliver sentient beings and cause them to exert themselves toward progress.
In the provisional teachings, it may be said that regression occurs at the sixth stage of mental abiding.

Why is this? Because within the provisional teachings, those prior to the ten stages—namely, the three levels of worthiness—have not yet seen the Path; all their cultivated practices are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and all their ignorance is merely suppressed (*vibhāvanā*). If their spiritual power is weak, they will give rise to regression; however, if their power of suppression is strong, they do not fall away.
Just as a snake possesses poison that cannot manifest due to the power of a mantra,

so too, by planting the seed of faith within the Buddha-dharma, being humble and free from pride, revering and following the virtuous, always maintaining compassion and patience toward those with evil minds, inquiring of those superior to oneself regarding what one has not yet heard, practicing and never forgetting the sublime Dharma one has heard, eliminating all falsehoods in accordance with the teachings, and constantly striving without ceasing on the path to the threefold enlightenment— [the poisons of affliction cannot arise].
Now, as for the principle of human life, it is naturally so.
Since one does not grow into evil from birth, why need one worry about falling back?
The above constitutes the five kinds of ten stages (daśabhūmi).

Regarding the three types of ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) within the provisional teachings, such as those in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, there are only the names of the ten stages; the eighth is named the Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), and the ninth is named the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*), with slight differences in their designations.

In the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, although the names of the ten stages are the same as those in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, from the first stage through the eleventh stage, there are eleven types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and twenty-two types of ignorance (*moha*).
Within these two sets of scriptures, there are only the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and altogether lack the four kinds of provisions (*sambhāra*) prior to the stages.

Although the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* speaks of the four kinds of provisions—the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences—prior to the stages, it states that the ten faiths constitute the "inner ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*). This differs from the teachings of the True Vehicle (*saddharma-yāna*), wherein the initial mind of the ten abidings immediately ascends to the nature of the noble ones (*ārya-dharma*), with its essence equal to that of all Buddhas.

Within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), if one does not believe that one's own body and the Buddha-body are non-dual in terms of cause and effect, true faith and understanding (*adhimukti*) will not be achieved.

Therefore, the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" states: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that within a single thought-moment of their own minds, the Buddhas of the ten directions attain equal and perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma."
Why is this? Because the Buddha-mind and one's own mind are non-dual; it is only when faith is such as this that it can truly be called "faith.
How much more so for those in the stage of the Ten Abidings—if they do not realize this mind, how can they be said to "abide"? If they do not realize this mind, why would they be named "Abiders"?

For this reason, abiding in the Buddha-abode is what is called "abiding"; therefore, upon the very first arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one attains perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Furthermore, within the provisional teachings, when describing the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are no Buddhas from other directions who preach the Dharma with the same name; nor is there any Buddha of the same name coming to provide certification, which would signify the identity of cause and fruit.
For this reason, both the stages (*bhūmi*) and the teaching gates are provisional establishments intended to guide sentient beings of inferior faculties;
therefore, those possessed of wisdom should not stagnate therein, but should instead rejoice in ascending further.

Therefore, when the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* expounds the dharma-gate of the five stages and ten bhūmis, specifically at the time when the Bodhisattva Dharmamati enters samādhi within the stage of the Ten Abidings (Daśabhūmika) intending to preach the dharma-gate of the Ten Abidings, there come from beyond a thousand Buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a thousand Buddha-worlds, all sharing the same name, Dharmamati. They touch the crown of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati’s head with their hands, praise him through their vocal karma, and bestow upon him thirteen kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) consisting of the intellectual power of Dharmamati.

When the stage of the ten practices was being taught, Bodhisattva Guṇakara entered meditative absorption; then, from beyond ten thousand Buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions, Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-worlds arrived—all named Guṇakara—along with thirteen kinds of empowered Guṇakara Bodhisattvas and others.

When the ten dedications were being taught, from beyond a million Buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions, there came Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a million Buddha-worlds, all bearing the same name, Vajradhvaja; they likewise empowered the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja in thirteen ways.
The same applies to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The fact that the Buddha and the Bodhisattva share the same name clarifies that their cause and fruit are identical; this shall be explained in detail later.

As for the *Daśabhūmika-vyākhyā*, it was composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and serves as an exposition of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, which is the "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

Regarding the point of interpreting the meaning, as for those who interpret the textual meaning according to the three vehicles and the one vehicle: most understand the meaning of the three vehicles, whereas many do not understand the meaning of the one vehicle, because their intellectual comprehension cannot reach the principles of the one vehicle.

If there are those who seek understanding through intellectual emotion, their web of doubt will not be removed; furthermore, because they merely believe the Buddha’s words, their own doubts remain unsevered.

This [truth] can only be known by those who have long dwelt in non-conceptualization, who do not weary of suffering, who do not stagnate in quiescence, and who have realized the permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Therefore, among the five kinds of ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), three are provisional (*upāya*) and the remaining two kinds of ten stages belong to the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).

Thus, the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* states: "The path and dharma of the ancient Buddhas established these ten stages for the sake of transforming sentient beings. One should know that although the names of the ten stages in the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles are the same, the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) devised to lead sentient beings toward practice and understanding are entirely distinct. This is explained in detail in its own context; there has never been a case where Buddhas of the same name have together established a seal of authentication (*mudrā*) through the mutual verification of cause and effect.

The sixth section clarifies the gate of the sudden realization of Buddha-nature, wherein principle and wisdom, as well as the myriad practices, are perfectly integrated. As described in the first assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata’s Signs," the Tathāgata emits light from between his teeth, and further radiates the light of the fruit-virtue of the Middle Way from between his eyebrows. He then causes Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to enter samādhi and expound the "Chapter on the Formation of Worlds," the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," and the "Chapter on Vairocana," teaching the fruits of all Buddhas so that beings may conceive love and joy for them.

Once they had conceived such love and joy, during the second assembly, he caused Mañjuśrī to preach the "Chapter on the Names and Epithets of the Tathāgata" and the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths."

From beneath the wheels on his two feet, he emitted a radiance; beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, there were ten times the number of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, who all came to assemble. Furthermore, he preached the "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance," the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Clarity," the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," and the "Chapter on Worthy Leader," thereby accomplishing the gateway of the ten levels of faith.

Regarding the light beneath the wheels on the soles of the two feet, it is the lowest; this clarifies that one enters the beginning of faith with faith as the cause. Because faith is the lowest, this is the fruit-light from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows being projected downward.

In the previous "Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs of the Tathāgata," after the Tathāgata emitted light from between his eyebrows, it entered into the wheels of his two feet. This was intended to clarify the raising of the functional power (*de-yong*) of the Buddha-fruit virtues, so that those in the stage of learning who have attained the position of faith (*xin-wei*) might further realize the functional power of the fruit-dharma of faith, thereby achieving the initial entry into the gate of the ten faiths (*shi-xin*). For this reason, from each of the ten directions, there came bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, all from the presence of ten Wisdom Tathāgatas in ten colored worlds. Because the ten faiths constitute the beginning of entering the Way, the bodhisattvas who arrived are all called "leaders" (*shou*).

Regarding the ten worlds of form: these are for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith who have not yet attained actual realization; they are clearly ordinary beings who, although they believe in the Buddha-realm of realized fruition, have not yet departed from the dust of form and thus take form as their land.

The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes possess the perfect clarity of both principle and phenomena; they take flowers as their realm because they have newly caused the principle and phenomena of the mundane stage to blossom.
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices have skillfully mastered the perfect clarity of discerning wisdom; they take wisdom as their realm.
The Ten Dedications and the Ten Grounds take wondrous mastery as their sovereignty and take the wondrous as their land.
This land arises from the dharma-gates of their respective positions; they take the Dharma as their land, not because of the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.
Those who have entered the stage of noble wisdom have already abandoned these hindrances.

Within the stage of the ten faiths, all bodhisattvas are those who have come from the Buddhas of the ten wisdoms, namely: the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom, the Buddha of Unobstructed Wisdom, and the Buddha of Liberating Wisdom.
Regarding these ten wisdoms of the Buddha, wisdom constitutes the merit of the fruit, because within the stage of the ten faiths, one takes the fruit as the object of faith.
This is to clarify that [the path] proceeds from the fruit, taking the fruit as the cause for the sake of clear understanding.
If one does not take the fruit as the object of faith, then because there would be nothing to believe in, faith would have no basis.
Why is Mañjuśrī the leader? It is because Mañjuśrī is the master who initiates enlightenment.

Because the Buddhas of the ten directions all take Mañjuśrī of Wondrous Virtue as the foremost for generating the mind of faith, and because they thereby manifest the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya, they always take Mañjuśrī as the faith that precedes the fruition.
Excellent wisdom and clarity constitute the wisdom of differentiation (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*), as they serve as the practice subsequent to the fruition.

Therefore, when the youth Sudhana first beheld Mañjuśrī, it was the gate of faith; later, when he beheld Maitreya, it was the stage of Buddhahood; and finally, when he saw his own body enter the body of Samantabhadra, this was the practice subsequent to the fruition of Buddhahood.
Mañjuśrī is the younger son and Samantabhadra is the eldest son; when these two sages are unified in essence, they are called the Buddha.

Because Mañjuśrī represents the wondrous wisdom of the Dharmakāya and Samantabhadra represents the majestic virtue of the myriad practices, their essence and function are sovereignly free, and thus they are called the Buddha.

Mañjuśrī the Youngest Son is so called because he is the fundamental wisdom that realizes and attests to the Dharmakāya; he is "first-born" because, by virtue of first realizing the Dharmakāya of fundamental wisdom, he is able to give birth to the Buddha-family.

As for Samantabhadra being the eldest son: it is because, relying on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), he gives rise to the wisdom of the differentiation of practices; and because he possesses mastery over the matters of the various *pāramitās*, which are the family laws of the Buddha, he constantly establishes the family laws of the Buddha through the gate of practice and manages the affairs of the Buddha’s household.

However, within the various sutras, those in which Mañjuśrī acts as the questioner and respondent mostly clarify the gateway of the Dharmakāya and Buddha-nature, while those in which Samantabhadra acts as the questioner and respondent mostly discuss their practice; this serves to illustrate the point.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī riding a lion signifies that he is the steed for severing delusions through the fundamental wisdom of the Buddha-nature of the Dharmakāya, which was first realized.
Samantabhadra riding a fragrant elephant-king symbolizes that his conduct is orderly and majestic in its dignified power.

Furthermore, the reason Mañjuśrī always resides in the Eastern World of Golden Color (Suvarṇavarṇa) at the abode of Akṣobhyajñāna Buddha is to clarify that gold is white in color because it is able to remain free from defilement.
"Golden in color" symbolizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

"Immovable wisdom" refers to the arising of the functional application of wisdom based upon the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*); it is so called because it is indeed without movement.

That Samantabhadra Bodhisattva constantly dwells in the presence of the Buddha Jewel Majestic Virtue Supreme King in the East clarifies that the myriad practices are "jewels," and it is by means of these practices that his majestic virtue is accomplished.
If one is fully accomplished in practice, one possesses mastery through the body of the Dharma-treasure; with majestic virtue and fearlessness, one attains sovereignty as a king.
If one is not fully accomplished in practice, one is subject to all manner of fears; even if one occupies a high position, one cannot become a king because of these underlying fears.

Those who are together with Mañjuśrī in the eastern direction are the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body; for principle and phenomenon, essence and function, have been fundamentally one, and have fundamentally never been two.
Furthermore, the reason Mañjuśrī resides on Mount Qingliang in the northeast is that this mountain corresponds to the hexagram Gen, which governs the northeast.
Gen represents the "younger son" and signifies "childlike innocence."
This is because Mañjuśrī constantly transforms ordinary beings by awakening their initial insight into the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and serves as the foremost of original wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Furthermore, regarding his presence together with Samantabhadra in the East: the East corresponds to the position of the *māo* (卯) hour; *māo* is the hexagram *Zhèn* (震), and *Zhèn* represents the eldest son.

It is also like the sun rising in the east, where the spring sunlight shines forth, such that there is nothing that does not grow and nothing that is not illuminated; this symbolizes the simultaneous penetration of principle and wisdom, wherein essence and function are one and non-dual, because fundamental wisdom and discriminative wisdom do not have separate essences or functions, yet give rise to the myriad practices.

Therefore, Zi corresponds to the stage of Buddhahood; Chou to the ten levels of faith; Yin to the ten abodes; Mao to the ten practices; Chen to the ten transferences; Si to the ten grounds; Wu to Equal Enlightenment; Wei to the period of waning light when one enters the mundane world to follow worldly ways and transform the deluded; and Shen, You, Xu, and Hai correspond to those who are to be transformed.
Thus the laws are established, for it is in accordance with the nature of phenomena that they are so.
In the hexagrams of the *I Ching*, Kan represents the sovereign, Li represents the minister, Zhen represents the high chancellor, and You represents the supreme general.
The east is the Azure Dragon, the west is the White Tiger, the front is the Vermilion Bird, and the rear is the Black Tortoise.

The Azure Dragon represents auspiciousness and celebration; the White Tiger represents calamity and harm; the Vermilion Bird represents brightness; and the Black Tortoise represents darkness. For this reason, the Tathāgata established their order and elucidated their significance.
Samantabhadra serves as the minister, presiding over the myriad practices.
Avalokiteśvara is the foremost of those of great compassion; he governs the perilous and dangerous, acting as the supreme general.
Mañjuśrī is the foremost of those who awaken the ignorant, constantly serving as the teacher who receives the faithful.

Mutually integrating and interpenetrating, they uphold the Dharma of the Buddha’s house, causing all sentient beings to abide in the Middle Way, dwell in a nature of tranquility and harmony, and benefit all things through wisdom and compassion.

Because these bodies are all golden in color, with hair and eyes of deep blue-black and bodies white yet with a yellowish luster, they represent the harmonious breath of the Arhats; they are all forms of formlessness and colors of colorlessness.

If we consider their essential nature and function, each and every bodhisattva fully possesses boundless wisdom and virtue; yet, according to the established principle, Mañjuśrī is always made the foremost leader for initiating faith.
Now, based on the distinction between south and north, we shall provisionally establish one gate for east and west.
If one discusses their mutual fusion and profound mystery, each direction collectively possesses ten aspects.
As the Sūtra says: "In every place there is Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; in every place there is the Golden World; in every place there is Mañjuśrī; in every place there is Acalajñāna Buddha."

The Sūtra says: "The Buddha-body pervades all dharma-realms and appears universally before all sentient beings; filling every vessel capable of being transformed, the Buddha therefore dwells beneath this Bodhi tree."

Within as many pores as there are atoms in all Buddha-fields, Buddhas sit, each surrounded by immeasurable assemblies of Bodhisattvas, who each expound for them the conduct of Samantabhadra in its entirety.
"In this way, one direction is identical to the ten directions, which are inexhaustible; a single atom is identical to the ocean of lands, which is infinite.
Now, for the sake of the ritual of transformation, each is shown according to its partial and total aspects."
Regarding what is now called the "Ten Faiths," one may ask: in reference to which stage does one believe so as to definitively accomplish the gateway of the Ten Faiths?

As stated in the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance" within the section on the Ten Faiths of the Sūtra: "Mañjuśrī, in all places throughout the ten directions, speaks in all places throughout the ten directions the Dharma-gates of all places throughout the ten directions, extolling the ten kinds of fruits and virtues of the Buddha to establish the stage of faith."

As stated in the "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance" (*Prabhāsa-bodhi-parivarta*), it further causes those who have given rise to the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) to become even more luminous and pure.

Mañjuśrī then posed ten questions to the Bodhisattvas such as Daśaśīrṣa, concerning how karma does not know the mind and the mind does not know karma; these ten questions cause those who have given rise to faith to engage in self-observation, making their realization ever more profound and firm.
The Sūtra states: "All phenomena are devoid of activity and possess no intrinsic nature;
therefore, they are all mutually unaware of one another.
It further provides the analogies of flowing water, a blazing flame, the rising wind, and the earth-born, illustrating how these do not know one another.
Furthermore, the following verse states: "Discerningly observe the internal body: who herein is the self?
If one can understand in this way, they will realize the existence and non-existence of the self.

This is the gate of the contemplative practice of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) as established by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-daśa-śīrṣa; it is fully explained in the "Chapter on Inquiring for Clarification" (*Paripṛcchā-vibhāga*).

Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*), it is taught that from the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), one takes faith as the foremost and resolutely seeks the fruit of the Great Bodhi of the Buddha. Thus, from the ground of an ordinary being, one believes that the immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) of the Buddhas of the ten directions is no different from one's own mind; this is solely because one is deluded by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because ignorance and the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions have been fundamentally non-dual from the beginning, one should, from the stage of an ordinary person, believe that the fundamental wisdom of the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions is no different from one's own.
Why is this? Because they are all of one Dharma-nature body and one fundamental wisdom, just as many branches, leaves, and so forth grow from a single root of a tree.
Due to causes and conditions, the formation and destruction on a single branch of that tree differ from one another.

From the stage of an ordinary person, I believe in the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the ten stages of the Tathāgata; I am fully capable of practicing them all. Why is this?

Reflecting upon myself since beginningless time, I have drifted in the ocean of suffering, performing even those things that are of no benefit; how much more so now, when there are matters of benefit—such as the myriad practices of a bodhisattva and the work of saving sentient beings—how could I not be able to perform them?
From the stage of an ordinary person, one believes that the Buddhas of the ten directions are all born from samādhi, and that one shall likewise attain it. Why is this?

Because the samādhis of all Buddhas are born from the skillful means of the Tathāgata’s own nature, and one also possesses the pure nature of the Tathāgata’s own essence, which is equal to that of the Buddha.
From the stage of an ordinary person, one believes that one shall likewise attain all the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Why is this?

The supernormal powers of the Buddhas are attained by relying on true wisdom; I, too, rely solely on the wisdom of true nature (*dharmatā*), wherein afflictions and ignorance are absent and perfected as wisdom. All karma having perished, there remains only wisdom and compassion, through which one transforms beings with sovereign mastery.
From the stage of an ordinary person, one believes that the Buddha’s wisdom is something they too shall attain. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas have come from the state of being ordinary persons.
From the stage of an ordinary person, one believes that the Great Compassion of the Buddhas universally covers all;
I, too, shall attain this.
Why is this? The Great Compassion of all Buddhas arises from great vows, and I, too, have made such great vows like those of the Buddhas.
From the stage of an ordinary person, one believes that the sovereign power of the Buddhas shall also be attained by oneself. Why is this?

Because the sovereign power of all Buddhas resides in the Dharma-gate of the Arising from Nature (*dharmatā-utpatti*); their Wisdom-body and Dharma-body enter the realm of sentient beings, remaining untainted by the dust of sensory objects while possessing mastery over the sense faculties. Since I am likewise not separate from the Tathāgata’s wisdom arising from nature, [I shall attain it].

From the stage of an ordinary person, one’s own initial resolve arises through faith; after passing through inexhaustible kalpas and completing the cultivation of meritorious practices, one’s rank becomes equal to that of all Buddhas without shifting for even a single thought-moment.
Why is this? Because the three periods of time have no temporal duration.
Thus, from the faith and understanding of ordinary beings, one proceeds through beginning and end until reaching the stage of Buddhahood.
As for the ten kinds of faith mentioned above, one will certainly be able to achieve the gateway of the Ten Faiths, abide in the seeds of steadfastness, and never again fall back.
Furthermore, the ten Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths—Mañjuśrī, Jñānacūḍa, and the others—all come from the ten colored worlds.
That which is called the Golden World signifies that they come from within the fundamentally pure Dharma; this is to clarify that the mind of faith relies upon fundamental faith.
The World of Wondrous Colors (*Sudarśana*) is so named because sentient beings give rise to faith through reliance on the principle that the wondrous functions of phenomena are sovereign;
it is for this reason that faith is established. The Lotus-Colored World (*Padmavarṇa*) signifies the practice of faith, as the lotus represents the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*).
The world of Campaka-flower color symbolizes that faith arises from the color of auspicious merit, through the nature of great compassion and the harmony of principle and wisdom.
Among the five colors, yellow is supreme; it is the color of the Arhats and the color of the central palace, for it represents the color of the Middle Way.
