This clarifies that within this stage, at the moment the mind is first generated, cause and effect are mutually established as a non-differentiated essence; therefore, the Bodhisattva and the Buddha share the same name, Dharmamati, because they are sealed as a single entity.
The Buddha’s name being identical to one’s own signifies that this is true for all who have realized the Way.

Among the ten preceding faiths, Akṣobhya (Immovable Wisdom) Buddha represents fundamental wisdom; whereas the lunar names of the Buddhas within these ten abodes represent the fruits obtained through the progressive cultivation of each stage.
As for cause and effect, it is the cause and effect that is not [ordinary] cause and effect; it is designated as "cause and effect" only by virtue of having no basis of dependence.

It is not like the externalists who, through their deluded sentiments, deny cause and effect; nor is it like the ordinary beings of the human and celestial realms who are bound by and constitute cause and effect. Being distinct from these two, it is called the Buddha’s cause and effect.

In this stage, at the very beginning of the first of the ten abodes, one realizes this cause-and-effect that is not [ordinary] cause-and-effect; therefore, at the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one is already a Buddha.

Regarding this stage, the Bodhisattva Anuttara-prajñā states in verse: "Ordinary beings lack awakening and understanding; the Buddha causes them to abide in the True Dharma. All phenomena have no place of abiding; by realizing this, one perceives one's own nature."
"Without a body, yet speaking of a body; without arising, yet manifesting arising; without body and without vision—this is the Buddha’s unsurpassed body. Question:

Why is it that in the preceding stage of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma without entering samādhi, and furthermore, why is there no Buddha named Awakening Head (*Bodhiśiras*) to offer praise?

For what reason, within this stage of the tenth abode, does the Bodhisattva Dharmamati enter samādhi and begin to preach the Dharma, and why do as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a thousand Buddha-worlds, all sharing the same name Dharmamati, come to console and praise him?
Why is it that the first ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) lack these characteristics? What is the reason?
The answer is:

they are presented as the resultant dharmas for the stage of faith; because cause and effect are raised together merely to engender faith, and there has not yet been actual realization, one does not enter samādhi.

Because one enters the realization of reality through the stages of the ten abodes, for this reason, one must enter samādhi before being able to realize it truly; this is so that one may establish the principles of realization for all sentient beings.
This is because, in order to correctly realize the merit of the fruit, Buddhas bearing the same name come to seal and certify the single flavor of cause and effect.

In the preceding stage of faith (*śraddhā*), one merely establishes faith but has not yet realized it directly; therefore, one does not enter samādhi, and there are no Buddhas bearing the same name coming to seal and certify the identity of cause and effect.
One should know it thus and believe and understand it thus.
As for these thousand Buddhas followed by ten thousand Buddhas, this clarifies the characteristics of advancing in cultivation.
It is like the Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma in the "Chapter on the Ten Practices," who entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation.

Having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared before him ten thousand buddhas—each as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields—all bearing the same name, Guṇakūṭa (Forest of Merit), who praised and comforted Guṇakūṭa.
It is just as in the preceding stage, because cause and effect are identical.

The name of the Buddha is the same as the name of the Bodhisattva; taking the Bodhisattva as the cause and the Buddha as the fruit-virtue, their two essences are the same, and for this reason they share the same name.
The lands from which the ten Forest Bodhisattvas originally came were all named Wisdom.

Each of the ten Forest Bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakānanavatī (Virtue Forest), was accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field, coming together from worlds beyond as many lands as there are atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields. Those lands were named World of Intimate Wisdom, World of Banner Wisdom, and World of Jewel Wisdom.

In this manner, in the world-system of Ten Wisdoms, there were Buddhas whom he formerly served, namely: the Buddha Constant Abiding Eye, the Buddha Victorious Eye, the Buddha Non-abiding Eye, and so forth—these ten Buddhas of the Eye.

Question: For what reason, among the ten stages of abiding (*vihāra*), are the Buddhas all named Dharmamati, and is the number [of worlds] cited as being merely the dust-motes of a thousand Buddha-fields; furthermore, the bodhisattvas who come are from beyond a thousand worlds, the worlds they come from all share the same name, "Flower," and the Buddhas they originally served all share the same name, "Moon"? Why, then, in these ten stages of practice (*caryā*), do the lands they originally came from all share the same name, "Wisdom," and the Buddhas they originally served all share the same name, "Eye"?
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is:

because within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one newly realizes [the truth] starting from the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and the qualities of the fruit (*phalaguṇa*) first emerge from that state of being an ordinary person.
The lands all share the same name, "Flower" (Puṣpa), because they are where the newly established Buddhas abide, and because their own Buddha-wisdom has blossomed.

They have realized the Buddha-wisdom and are born for the first time into the family of the Buddhas; thus, the names of the Buddhas are all the same, "Moon" (Candra), signifying that they have attained the coolness of the Dharma like the moon.

Within these ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), from beginning to end, both the Buddha and his surroundings are entirely true; the lands are named after the Dharma, and the Buddhas are titled according to the Dharma.
This initial realization in the preceding stage is used to symbolize the cool clarity of the moon.
This stage is already truly pure; that which is called "the eye" refers to the *dharmacakṣus* (Dharma-eye).
Within this practice, the Dharma-eye is perfected, for its clarity responds to the capacities of beings and illuminates the conventional world to accomplish virtue.

Regarding the gradual expansion from thousands to tens of thousands, this clarifies that the Dharmadhātu is perfectly luminous, neither increasing nor decreasing; it is merely through the skillful means generated by Bodhisattvas at the stage of Buddhahood that ordinary beings are guided and led toward excellence, all of which constitutes the Tathāgata’s intentional skillful means.

In the *Buddhanāmasūtra*, regarding Tathāgatas such as Anantaghoṣa and Sūryacandraprabha, the World-Honored One specifically increases his expressions of reverence and performs three prostrations with added gravity; when he says that these [Tathāgatas] eliminate more transgressions, it is because the Tathāgata uses skillful means to lead the minds of ordinary beings, inspiring them to exert their resolve.
How could it be said that while the essence of all Buddhas is of one flavor, their merits possess differentiation?

At this time, within the fruit of Buddhahood, the stages, positions, and spheres of all Bodhisattvas are established and expanded; thus, through such gradual progression, one speaks of a thousand Buddha-worlds, ten thousand Buddha-worlds, and even until the end of all numbers. Within each and every number, the substance and the conditions of dependent origination mutually penetrate; within each and every number, the beginning and the end interpenetrate without any limit of before or after. This is because these are the secret intentions and skillful means of all Buddhas.
It is like ten coins: if one coin is removed, the ten as a whole cease to exist; yet with that one coin, the ten are fully established as a numerical total.

Just as an echo responds to a sound through simultaneous dependent origination, so too does the beginning and the end coincide. Because their nature is identical, their timing is identical, and their dependent origination is simultaneous, the dharma-gate of establishing the objective realm is herein established.
Treatise on the New Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Five;
Treatise on the New Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan.
A Bodhisattva of the first stage possesses many hundreds of kings of the gates of illumination of dharmas and transforms many hundreds of Buddha-worlds;

a Bodhisattva of the second stage possesses many thousands of kings of the gates of illumination of dharmas and transforms many thousands of Buddha-worlds. This is not like the provisional teachings which maintain that there are actual limitations; rather, as with the numerical methods mentioned previously, they mutually penetrate one another.

Furthermore, it is like a person who uses a finger to draw hundreds of thousands of particles of dust in the air, and then uses their hand to wipe them away until they are gone; yet, in that space, there is neither increase nor decrease.
Because of the measure of one's own perception, one sees that space undergoes increase and decrease in number.
This is likewise the case here: the increase and decrease in the dharma-gates for establishing the various stages of all bodhisattvas is also just like this.
It is for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment that they are urged to advance in their practice; if everything were uniformly equal, there would be no intention to progress.
Ordinary beings lack the mind for advancement; only when they have resolved to cultivate until reaching the state of non-cultivation do they realize that the myriad dharmas are beyond cultivation.

In reality, according to the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), when a bodhisattva attains one thing, they attain all things; this is because within the essence of the Dharma there is no sequence of before or after. It is like the light and shadows in Indra’s Net, which mutually penetrate and interpenetrate one another, without any boundary of before or after.
It is also like a hundred thousand precious mirrors facing a wondrous image; within each mirror, the reflected images interpenetrate one another, their forms and colors perfectly level.
This is as when Bodhisattvas at the stage of Buddhahood arise from the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya through their nature, or when they first realize the mind during the ten stages (bhūmis).
All realms of the various Dharma-gates are entirely based upon the fundamental source, for their essence and function encompass all things through thorough penetration.
They are further equalized by means of their nature, because they are equal in the very moment.
Furthermore, there are other inconsistent doctrines that are untenable.

This is because those who follow provisional teachings have not yet eliminated their emotional obstructions; from the first through the ninth stages, they have not yet seen the Buddha-nature. The stages they establish all possess specific limits and are merely attainable in a conventional sense, for since they have not yet seen the Buddha-nature, what they perceive is but a shadow of provisional True Suchness.
Therefore, a sutra states: "The distinctions between the ten stages are like the tracks of birds in the sky.
Just as the dharma-gates of the stages are provisionally established with increases and decreases to accord with the dispositions of sentient beings.
For one who embodies the Way, the conventional and the ultimate are immediately the ultimate, because when it is one ultimate, all is ultimate; thus, there are no provisional dharmas at all.
One must not harbor views of increase or decrease regarding this Perfect Teaching, for to do so would be to equate it with the gradual teaching.

All the assemblies of the ocean-like multitudes of Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and various spirits mentioned in this sutra are all Bodhisattvas of the ocean-like state of Buddhahood; they are not ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). This is because [the Buddha] desires those who would enter [this teaching] to become identical with the sages, and it clarifies that the realm of Vairocana’s transformative guidance encompasses all sentient beings universally.
All these are assemblies at the stage of Buddhahood, acting as the principal figures and their retinues through their transformative manifestations.
Thus, the assembly of those at the stage of fruition and virtue gathers together to form the Dharma, demonstrating and awakening sentient beings.

After the completion of the "Dharmatā" chapter, Mañjuśrī, through this Dharma-gate of the merit of fruition, departed from the assembly at the Jeta Grove and traveled eastward toward the city of Gandhavatī to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Śāriputra and six thousand bhikṣus conceived the resolve for enlightenment on the road, attaining the ten ears and ten eyes.

At the eastern assembly in the city of Vairambhya, they met Sudhana, who sought out his spiritual friends everywhere until, in a single lifetime, he attained the perfect clarity of the fruit of Buddhahood.

Five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, five hundred boys, and five hundred girls were all like Sudhana; it would be impossible to describe each of them individually in the text, for the entire assembly was likewise so.

If there were no such conditions, one would not hear anything at all; for example, when the Arhat bhikṣus in Jeta Grove were assembled together, they neither heard nor saw the Tathāgata preaching this *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra.
These five assemblies gathered together at the place of Mañjuśrī, heard this Dharma together, and all belong to the stream of those who have realized it.
Therefore, the sutra says: "This sutra shall not fall into the hands of other sentient beings."
Those who are able to have deep faith surpass even those of the three vehicles who study through provisional means, let alone those who are able to realize it.

Therefore, the "Chapter on Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) in this sutra states: "Among all the various classes of sentient beings in the world, few desire to seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas; those who seek the pratyekabuddha vehicle are even fewer still; and those who seek the Mahāyāna are exceedingly rare."
"To seek the Mahāyāna is still relatively easy; to be able to believe in this Dharma is exceedingly difficult.

Therefore, one should know that this assembly gathered at the Ocean-like Conclave consists not of ordinary persons among men, but is exclusively a gathering of Bodhisattvas at the stage of Buddhahood, who have perfected the teachings.
Mañjuśrī was converted at the city of Bodhimaṇḍa; this first clarifies that these teachings will be employed to benefit the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa like medicine.
The five assemblies, including Sudhana and others, collectively represent those who have truly attained this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as previously explained.

Thus, the assembly that has gathered consists exclusively of Bodhisattvas at the stage of fruition; this clarifies that their realized virtues and functions are fully prepared for those of superior faculties. There are no followers of provisional teachings—neither Bodhisattvas, nor those of the Small Vehicle, nor ordinary beings of the human or celestial realms, nor any assemblies concerned with cause and effect—who have come to gather in this assembly.
Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings do not join this assembly from the first stage up through the ninth stage, let alone ordinary beings. Why is this?
Because they are practicing the six pāramitās.

Although there are those who practice the ten pāramitās and, by virtue of three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, achieve the merit of the fruit of the Way, they are not the same as this teaching, which is immediate at all times; for it is not something that can be grasped by the non-sentient mind.

In the *Ji-yuan hui* (The Assembly at Jetavana), when Mañjuśrī traveled eastward, six thousand bhikṣus conceived the aspiration for enlightenment along the way; this clarifies that even śrāvakas are granted the capacity for the most supreme vessel, being capable of entering this Most Excellent Vehicle (*agrayāna*).

Furthermore, those six thousand bhikṣus had all newly gone forth under Śāriputra; they did not yet aspire to the lesser fruits, but because their faculties were sharp, they were able to resolve their minds and reach this stage of the stream.
Having already attained the minor fruits [of the path], it is extremely difficult to turn back completely.
Śāriputra, for instance, was a śrāvaka who was merely a reflection or shadow; he was not a true śrāvaka.
He had already ascended to the rank of a Buddha, entering the stream to lead ordinary beings.
For this reason, the assembly gathered for this sutra differs from that of the provisional teachings.

Even if a transformation Buddha were to appear in a place where only bodhisattvas are assembled and no followers of the Small Vehicle are present, such an assembly would still not be the same as this teaching.
Why is this? Because there are teachings that state:
one who attains Buddhahood through the very cause does not practice the five stages.
Alternatively, because the aspects, substances, and functions of the five stages differ, as previously described,
there is no correspondence when applying this principle by analogy.
Since the dharmas are not identical, the assemblies are also entirely distinct.
Furthermore, regarding all those who have come to this assembly, there are ten kinds of shared dharmas that distinguish them from the assemblies of other sutras.

First, the sameness of the physical body; second, the sameness of the fundamental wisdom of the dharma-body; third, the sameness of the wisdom of compassion; fourth, the sameness of the wheel of the spoken Dharma; fifth, the sameness of the place of origin; sixth, the sameness of the principles of the realized dharma; seventh, the sameness of the cause and effect of the Buddha; eighth, the sameness of serving the Buddha as teacher and disciple; ninth, the sameness of the perfection of the reward-body and its land; and tenth, the sameness of obtaining benefit despite harboring doubts.

First, regarding the identity of the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*): for example, among the five stages, bodhisattvas from each of the ten directions arrive; from every single direction, there come assemblies of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields. All possess golden bodies with deep blue-black hair and eyes, such that the physical bodies of the bodhisattvas within each respective stage are similar to one another. Likewise, the various classes of devas and the eight groups of non-human beings are similar to their respective counterparts. This clarifies that because they have attained the same Dharma, their retributions (*vipāka*) are also identical.

As in the first assembly, there were fifty-five types of categories; although they were distinguished because their gates of practice and methods of gathering and transforming beings differed, their modes of activity, physical forms, and Dharma-gates were such that these fifty-five categories interpenetrated one another. Thus, a single practice became many practices and many practices became a single practice; a single body became many bodies and many bodies became a single body, because they were mutually similar.
The same applies to the ten locations and ten assemblies throughout the preceding and following sections.

Second, regarding the identity of the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya*: as with all the oceans of assemblies within the ten locations and ten assemblies, they are all identical to the Tathāgata’s *dharmatākāya*, because they are fundamentally wisdom.

Should there be any new learners or ordinary beings who enter the assembly, they shall, upon seeing or hearing the Buddha-dharma, realize it in an instant; for all are equal to the Tathāgata’s Dharma-nature body and fundamental wisdom. Thus, among those who enter the assembly and see or hear the Dharma, there are none whose body or wisdom is not identical to that of the Buddha.
The five hundred arhats within the assembly neither saw, nor heard, nor knew, nor were aware of this great assembly or the dharma-gate being preached.

This was entirely different from the bodhisattvas, followers of the two vehicles, humans, devas, and the eight classes of beings of the provisional teachings, who all saw the Buddha together in the assembly, heard the Dharma, and obtained benefits that were completely distinct [from those of the arhats].

Regarding the identity of the three—compassion, wisdom, and sameness: the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the differentiated wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) of the Dharmakāya share the same essence as compassion, because understanding and practice are unified. This is because Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the Buddha-fruit constitute a single dharma from beginning to end.

Regarding the Three Jewels as presented in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: the Buddha is the Buddha Jewel, Mañjuśrī is the Dharma Jewel, and Samantabhadra is the Saṅgha Jewel; this is because it is the ancient teaching of the Buddhas of the past and present.
If they were combined, then all would be identical, because the fundamental nature is thus, being neither created nor subject to formation or destruction.

Regarding the fourth point, the identity of the wheel of Dharma in terms of verbal expression: as described in the sutra, bodhisattvas from five stages come from each of the ten directions; from every single direction, there arrive bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms within ten buddha-fields at this assembly. It is the same throughout all worlds in the ten directions, gathering together like clouds all at once.

With one voice and in unison, the assemblies of beings from the ten directions simultaneously spoke these verses; their phrasing and terminology were identical and perfectly matched, without the slightest difference.
This was because their wisdom was the same and their practice of the Dharma was the same; thus, the Dharma-gates they proclaimed were of one kind throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
This is unlike other sutras where the assembly’s levels of understanding and practice differ, such that some attain [realization] while others do not.

Regarding the "five places of origin being the same," this means that those who have come to assemble as these bodhisattvas of the five stages arrive from every location throughout the ten directions.

Furthermore, within the worlds of the ten directions and amidst every atom, each and every Bodhisattva dwells together; this is because they abide in the essence of the Dharma-realm, wherein all sentiments of self and other, or near and far, have been exhausted. Thus, they do not at all emerge from a single atom, nor have they ever originally entered it.

This is unlike the provisional teachings, wherein the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* have not yet been completed and various views have not yet been extinguished; having arrived here, they each return to their own lands.
Furthermore, it has not yet been discussed that within the realm of a single mote of dust, the Dharma-realm is perfectly complete.
However, because both transformation and penetration are limited, it is said that supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are not the fundamental dharma.

As for the six dharmas that are accomplished being identical: this refers to the practice gates of the Bodhisattvas across the ten stages of faith and the ten abodes; these are established identically throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and all Buddhas of the past and present in the worlds of the ten directions share this same dharma. Thus, cause and effect are shown instantaneously within a single *kṣaṇa*.
This Dharma has no coming, because it is devoid of priority and sequence.

It differs from the provisional teachings, which posit cause before and fruit after, such that one only begins to see one's nature at the conclusion of the ten stages; for those Bodhisattvas prior to the stages are still ordinary beings.
If there were those who attain Buddhahood prior to the stages (bhūmi), this would be attributed to the power of their vows rather than to the fundamental Dharma;

or it would be attributed to Bodhisattvas on the stages leading ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to initiate superior practices, rather than to the fact that the fundamental Dharma is inherently Buddha-nature.

The Dharma principles bestowed by this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* discuss directly the gate of the Buddha’s own vehicle based on fundamental wisdom; they do not discuss the provisional teachings that open the gates of the three vehicles or establish the span of many kalpas.

It is directly clarified that the original essence of sentient beings is inherently without an agent; because their nature is fundamentally the true Buddha-wisdom of the Dharma-realm, it serves as the vehicle upon which they ride.

Regarding the seventh point, those who share the same cause and fruit as the Buddha are already Mañjuśrī’s dharma-body and wisdom-body, the fruition virtues of all Buddhas, and the practice-gate of Samantabhadra; they are fundamentally one and the same Dharma.
Because all these oceans of assemblies are entirely identical, one attains perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta.
Regarding the fact that all obtain this Dharma within a single kṣaṇa, it is not permitted that there be those who attain it at a time other than that kṣaṇa; for such would not be the original Dharma.

If there is someone who, within the Buddha-dharma, perceives the Buddha attaining enlightenment and gives rise to views regarding the duration of kalpas, their place, or their extent, then their faith is not yet perfected; let alone discussing the path of cultivation or the path of vision.

Therefore, those who cultivate the Way must not allow themselves to be deluded by such emotional attachments, falsely claiming to cultivate the Way while revolving through birth and death without rest.
This is merely the realm of worldly sentiment; it is not the Buddha-Dharma.
Therefore, all those gathered for this sutra are equal to the dharmas of the stage of Buddhahood and shall likewise attain the dharmas of the stage of Buddhahood.
Should any see, hear, awaken to, or enter into it, they will all become identical with the stage of Buddhahood, because they rely upon the dharma of fundamental wisdom.

Regarding the eight matters in which the master and disciple are identical: just as reflections in Indra’s net penetrate one another, so too these Bodhisattvas within this ocean of the Dharma-realm of the ten assemblies have bodies present at the abodes of all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma-realm, serving all Buddhas. Thus they are able to accord with the fruit of Buddhahood through the gate of reverential respect between master and disciple, for they do not lose the reverence due to a teacher and a student.
This differs from the provisional teachings, which posit both self-Buddhas and other-Buddhas, and involve coming from those Buddhas to return to one's own land.

It differs from this [provisional] teaching in that it does not shift from its original location nor employ supernatural powers; rather, by virtue of the fundamental dharma being eternally pervasive, one serves all Buddhas and is able to manifest both identity with and distinction from them.
Regarding the ninth point, the perfection of the land of the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) being identical [to that of the Dharma Body]:

it is because one gives rise to faith and practice based on the reality of the Dharma. Since the Dharma is eternally pervasive, the body is likewise pervasive; thus, by relying on the wisdom of the Dharma, both the body and the land are perfected. This is because a single perfection is itself the fulfillment of all, and because the wisdom of non-action ultimately possesses no measure of large or small. This is because it relies upon the Fundamental Dharma Body and the Wisdom Body, and because it is equal whether relying upon the primary retribution (the Reward Body) or others.

Regarding the tenth point, "those who share the same doubts and obtain the same benefits": as in the first assembly, fifty-five groups simultaneously harbored the same doubts and collectively made the same request. The Tathāgata emitted light to manifest his realized virtues, and they all obtained benefits at once; each member of the assembly attained one dharma, while each individual also attained the dharmas of all others. This pattern is consistent throughout the subsequent nine assemblies.
The ten kinds of shared dharmas of the assembly gathered above have no resemblance whatsoever to other teachings.

This fundamental wisdom, this fundamental dharma, this fundamental time, this fundamental place, and the fundamental dharma of the ancient Buddhas—these six stages of the practice-gate, the ocean of the fundamental assembly, fill the entirety of space and within every atom, gathering together in such a manner, layer upon layer, all at once.

In this sutra, the ocean-like assembly from beginning to end consists entirely of those who have realized and manifested the gates of the causes and effects of Buddhahood across the five stages and six positions that the Tathāgata rides; not a single person among them attains the fruits of the three vehicles. Rather, all of them, from the very first thought-moment of the ten abodes, possess both the essence and function equal to a Buddha. Because they rely upon the ocean of fundamental wisdom, they neither increase nor decrease within the nature of the dharma-body, spontaneously benefiting sentient beings.
The characteristics of the assemblies gathered at the ten locations and ten sessions should be analyzed by interpreting the meaning according to the text.

Eighth, regarding the distinction between principle and phenomena within the Dharma-gates of what is bestowed: as stated in the provisional teachings of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, sentient beings possess Buddha-nature while insentient things lack it; thus, all grasses and trees cannot attain the Way or turn the wheel of Dharma.

As in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, this is a teaching that transcends ordinary conceptualization and reveals ultimate reality; it is not like the provisional teachings of the transformation Buddhas, which are taught for the sake of ordinary beings.

For example, regarding the lands from which the ten "Forest" Bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakusuma-vana (Virtue Forest), come: those lands are also named "Wisdom," and all their environments are collectively termed the "Essence of Wisdom."
Why is this so? Because there is neither sentient being nor non-sentient being. Why is this so?
Because there is no dualistic view, it is the realm of the single true wisdom; for therein is neither one who attains Buddhahood nor one who does not.
As for "sentient" and "insentient," these are spoken of in dependence upon karma.
Now, as for the discussion of attaining Buddhahood, it does not pertain to karma.
If it does not pertain to karma, then it is neither sentient nor insentient.
How can one calculate and speak of attaining or not attaining Buddhahood with respect to phenomena that transcend sentience?
That "those beings are sentient and these are insentient" is a matter gathered by karma, not something resolved by the Buddha’s liberation.
How could one use the fetters of one's own sentimental karma to engage in such divinations as to whether things are sentient or insentient, or accomplished or unaccomplished?

As stated in the sutra: "These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness; they are neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure. "These dharmas abide in their dharma-position; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant."
Is such a path for sentient beings or non-sentient things?

According to the great meaning of this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are fundamentally no distinctions between ordinary beings and sages, nor between the sentient and the non-sentient; the entire true reality (*dharmatā*) constitutes the single realm of Buddha-wisdom, with nothing else existing beyond it.
Do not, with the limited capacity of an ordinary person's emotions, recklessly attempt to measure or judge.
If one harbors emotional attachments, one will perceive that sentient beings attain Buddhahood while insentient things do not; this is the karmic clinging of one's own self.
One who understands in such a manner will ultimately never attain Buddhahood.

As for the claim that the principle of nature (li-xing) pervades all insentient things yet sentient beings alone achieve Buddhahood—this arises from not having seen the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā), not relying on true wisdom, and failing to realize that all worldly characteristics are fundamentally and eternally abiding. Instead, one merely perceives the marks of arising and ceasing that follow the transformations of emotional consciousness, and thus falsely speculates, asserting that insentient things possess only their underlying principle because it is pervasive.
As for attaining Buddhahood, how could there be a Buddha existing apart from principle?

If principle itself is the Buddha, then within this principle, sentient and insentient beings originally possess no distinct characteristics; how then could the categories of "sentient" and "insentient" be established based on deluded views?
If, as you claim, the Buddha were a non-sentient being, he could not have attained Buddhahood.
Since there are those who achieve Great Bodhi, they do not rely on these two views; therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* reconciles the provisional with the ultimate.
The Sūtra states: "Regarding the meanings of these various natures and characteristics, only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know this matter.
Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas—all those who study the provisional teachings of the three vehicles—collectively cannot comprehend it."
This is explained in detail in that sutra.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are neither sentient beings nor insentient things; rather, all are merely the realm of wisdom. Thus, all mountains, rivers, trees, and forests can manifest the bodies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and preach the Dharma, being both identical to and distinct from the essence of the Buddha, with sovereign and unimpeded freedom.
The Buddha dwells within the world, sustaining and establishing it with sovereign adornment; the distinctions of his realms are diverse, and their adornments each differ.

Within the adornments of those wondrous lands and territories, the Buddha’s body appears within every single object, even inside a mote of dust. The oceans of lands are layered upon one another with inexhaustible Buddha-bodies, and it is likewise so within the pores of the Buddha’s body.

The realms are layered upon one another, and the Buddha-bodies are inexhaustible as they mutually penetrate each other; they can be identical and distinct, entirely the same and entirely different, with pure and impure lands being without obstruction or hindrance, regardless of whether they are sentient or insentient.
Therefore, it is now said that the gates of teaching herein are distinct.
Furthermore, within the provisional teachings, various practices come first, and the fruit of Buddhahood occurs after the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

In this teaching, the fundamental wisdom of the Buddha-fruit is realized first, with the wisdom of differentiation serving as mutual support; the characteristics of cause and effect are suddenly and simultaneously penetrated, such that throughout the past, present, and future, the perfection of one entails the perfection of all, and the destruction of one entails the destruction of all.
This differs from other teachings in that all stages are cultivated as a single stage, because their nature is equal, their time is equal, their practice is equal, and their wisdom is equal.
When cultivating concentration and wisdom, observe them with discerning intelligence; do not rely on emotional or intellectual interpretations.

The ninth point clarifies the distinctions in the fruits attained by those of the three vehicles. As stated in the sutras: for the sake of śrāvakas, the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is taught to transform birth, old age, sickness, and death;
for the sake of pratyekabuddhas, the practice of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination is taught;
and for the sake of bodhisattvas, the six pāramitās are taught.
Now, this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* also expounds the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, yet it differs from the Four Noble Truths of the Śrāvakas.

As explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths," these Four Noble Truths clarify that the very essence of suffering and its origin is fundamentally primordial wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); thus, they differ from the Three Vehicles, which involve both aspiration and aversion.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva of the fifth stage practices the contemplation of the ten truths, all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions proclaim the Dharma-wheel of the Four Truths; it is only that their voices differ according to the types of beings they address, just as Confucius and Laozi employ various methods for governing sentient beings in this world.

It is always the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; however, according to the varying capacities of those who receive it—whether one expounds the twelve divisions of the teachings or employs incantations—all such methods are subsumed within the wheel of the Four Noble Truths.
Śrāvakas receive only the teaching for severing a portion of suffering according to their individual faculties.
As for the method of severing suffering in the Hīnayāna, it is explained in detail in the various sections of the Hīnayāna scriptures.

Furthermore, if we discuss the general characteristics of the ultimate destination and the resulting fruit according to the four vehicles: the Śrāvaka contemplates the two truths of suffering and its origin, giving rise to a profound sense of weary detachment; they practice meditations on impermanence, impurity, the white bones, and subtle dust, thereby realizing that the body is empty and quiescent.
Following the dharma of emptiness and stillness, wisdom ceases and the body perishes; because neither compassion nor wisdom arises, it is called "extinction.
This state of extinction is termed *nirvāṇa*.

Even after emerging from meditative concentration, one will likewise be free from the faults of the three worldly poisons and so forth; for while still prior to the Path, one cultivates various contemplations and the like, subduing [afflictions] through such contemplation, just as one subdues a venomous snake with a mantra.
Furthermore, one cultivates the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), knowing that the nature of the mind is extinguished and fundamentally lacks a self.

By means of this dharma of the non-existence of a person, one empties the karma of the three poisons; yet, one does not give rise to [mere] compassion or wisdom, remaining inseparable from this cultivation whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration.
That which does not depart from this is ultimately identical to emptiness; the sudden cessation of the compassionate mind is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The subduing and extinguishing of all sufferings is called the Truth of Cessation.
Because of this Truth of Cessation, it is also termed the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: "It is like a person who is intoxicated; only after the alcohol has worn off does he awaken.
The awakening to the Dharma is likewise, whereby one attains the unsurpassed body of a Buddha."
"In such cases as these, those who do not rely on the Buddha’s wisdom but cultivate the samādhi of emptiness exclusively may recognize their error from this point onward,
turn their minds toward the correct path, and be able to attain the Buddha-body."

As stated in the Sūtra: "Regarding 'there is eternal cessation,' because one might become attached to quiescence, [the Buddha] exhorted them to practice early, for one should not seek eternal cessation.
This is for the sake of cultivation and arising, since Nirvāṇa is not eternal cessation."
This is indeed reconciled within the Mahāyāna sūtras themselves.
For instance, this passage does not exist at all in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

As for those of the pratyekabuddha lineage, they understand that the dharma of dependent origination is fundamentally without reality and that its intrinsic nature is entirely empty; they know that both body and mind are inherently without a master. Since body and mind lack a master, their nature is eternally selfless (*anātman*); because there is no self, ignorance (*avidyā*) is extinguished.
Because ignorance ceases, the twelve links of dependent origination cease; thus, one dwells alone as a Pratyekabuddha, wandering at ease according to one's nature.
Because this differs from the Śrāvakas, one does not seek [their] quiescence; because it differs from the Bodhisattvas, there is neither compassion nor wisdom.
Because they do not seek ultimate quiescence, they are superior to the śrāvakas;
because they are able to uphold the Dharma, they are not inferior to the śrāvakas.

Thus, while śrāvakas can also proclaim the Mahāyāna sūtras spoken by the Buddha upon hearing them, they have not personally realized them, as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* rebukes: "Do not use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to speak of the dharma of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)."

The bodhisattvas of provisional teaching who have just begun to turn away from the two vehicles and lesser bodhisattvas, yet are not yet fully endowed with great compassion and wisdom, are exemplified by those in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and other such texts.
It speaks only of the six pāramitās to inspire those of lesser faculties and lead them to the realization of wisdom.
Because they are biased toward the cultivation of meditative concentration and remain stagnant in ignorance, it speaks only of the six pāramitās.

Because their faculties are inferior, they still fear birth and death; therefore, the seven, eight, nine, and ten pāramitās have not yet been taught. This is because the pāramitā of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) is established for the sake of perfecting great compassion (mahākaruṇā), enabling them to transport and deliver others while remaining within the cycle of birth and death.

As stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, those on the outer and inner stages of the ordinary person cultivate the six *pāramitās* and become six kinds of human kings; from the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) upward, the four *pāramitās* are all the four kinds of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*); and those on the ten stages and ten sages cultivate the ten *pāramitās* and are able to become ten kinds of celestial kings.

Furthermore, in other sutras, those of the two vehicles who train gradually or instantaneously transform their faculties into compassion and wisdom. Although they cultivate the ten pāramitās, they still practice the contemplation of provisional and true suchness, performing the contemplation that all phenomena have been, from the very beginning, inherently quiescent, non-transmigrating, and immutable. They break through the dualistic attachments to existence and emptiness cultivated by others, establishing the dharma-gate of non-arising and non-ceasing; yet, they still contemplate according to their own subjective perceptions.

From the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*) onward, one has not yet clearly realized Buddha-nature; as previously explained, this is because the cultivation of that provisional wisdom constitutes an obstruction.

Thus, this sutra provides an immediate revelation of fundamental wisdom for those of superior faculties, such that from the very first moment it arises, at the level of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one’s wisdom is identical to that of a Buddha.
This refers to the meaning of Sudhana attaining the "Light of Wisdom that Recollects All Buddhas" atop Mount Sumeru.

Because one relies on the dharma of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), there is nothing further to be cultivated; because it is fundamentally free from obstruction, compassion and wisdom are spontaneously accomplished without effort. Thus, as one follows conditions within the six realms of existence, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Having realized that the self-nature of dependently arisen phenomena is eternally true and beyond further cultivation or action, all thoughts and reflections arise from wisdom.

One simply knows how to respond spontaneously to manifested physical bodies, preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings like echoes responding to sounds; while constantly abiding within the flow of birth and death, the Dharma-body remains eternally quiescent, its essence remaining unchanged throughout many kalpas.
Entering death and taking birth is not a matter of perishing and being born; it is because one entrusts oneself to the wisdom of great compassion, following dharmas according to conditions.
Such is the nature of dharmas: their essence is free from sorrow and affliction, and they do not abide in realization or cultivation.
Because the Dharma is thus, the Dragon Girl and Sudhana together clarify this point.

This Dharma is difficult to believe; those of the Three Vehicles fold their hands and distance themselves, claiming it is a mere transformation and not something cultivated by a human being. How could they believe in this gate of timeless wisdom, which speaks directly of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and establishes eons according to sentient beings' attachments?
Therefore, when the Sūtra says, "To be able to believe in this Dharma is extremely difficult," it refers precisely to this matter.

Even if one were to practice with diligent effort through many kalpas—seeking gain, seeking attainment, making things long or short, making them right or wrong, making them complete or ruined—even if one were to sacrifice the body and destroy life, how could there ever be a time for attaining Buddhahood?
How wonderful! From the very beginning, one must enter and train within the realm of Buddha-wisdom in this manner; would this not save effort and avoid wasting one's labor?

For this reason, those who follow the vehicles of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the provisional teachings of the Bodhisattvas—lacking true understanding of the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the true wisdom-realm of the *dharmakāya* of True Suchness—are all led by Vairocana through skillful means toward this ocean of the *Avataṃsaka*'s reality, so that they may return to their fundamental nature and act according to their wisdom.

Regarding the various stages practiced, one does not give rise to a sense of agency according to what wisdom performs; yet, all aspects of omniscience are accomplished, unlike the various teachings where distinct remedies are applied on the stages.

However, at the final stage of the Ten Faiths and the initial position of the Ten Abidings, one spontaneously realizes that the Dharma-realm is fundamentally the realm of wisdom; ordinary beings and sages are not different, being entirely and completely true in their essential nature. One no longer perceives distinctions between sentient and insentient beings, nor between those with nature and those without nature; thus, all fetters and hindrances are left as they are, non-arising in accordance with the Dharma.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "When a Tathāgata attains equal and perfect enlightenment and appears in the world, by means of his own wisdom, he universally perceives that all sentient beings have attained equal and perfect enlightenment; their emotions of good and evil are severed, and their nature and characteristics are without distinction."
"Although they deliver sentient beings, there are no beings delivered; this is called planting the various roots of goodness that constitute the marks of a Tathāgata.
Such a teaching is entrusted for circulation, being entirely different in its profound and subtle nature from the shallow depths of the Three Vehicles.
Those who follow the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna, the two vehicles, or the realms of humans and devas do not hear such a scripture as this *Avataṃsaka*.

Only those of the highest faculties—namely, the bodhisattvas who aspire solely to the causal and resultant stages of Buddhahood—are able to hear it; this is clearly evidenced within the aforementioned four vehicles.
Since the vehicles thus mounted are distinct and their realization of the truths is entirely different, they are completely separated in depth regarding a single term.

Furthermore, as stated in the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Bodhisattvas on the fifth stage cultivate ten kinds of contemplation on the Four Noble Truths, while Bodhisattvas on the sixth stage cultivate ten kinds of contemplation on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.

Because this differs from the three vehicles, the four truths, and the twelve links of dependent origination, the tenth [section] clarifies the specific characteristics of the transmission and circulation of the entrusted Dharma-treasury, as stated in this "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata": "O Son of the Buddha!..."

This Dharma gate has not been taught by the Tathāgata for other sentient beings; it is taught only for bodhisattvas who are intent upon the Mahāyāna, and only for bodhisattvas who ride the inconceivable vehicle.
This Dharma-gate of the sutra does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, with the sole exception of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
Son of the Buddha!

It is like the seven treasures possessed by a Wheel-Turning Sage King; it is because of these treasures that he is manifested as a Wheel-Turning King. These treasures do not fall into the hands of other sentient beings, with the sole exception of the eldest son born of the first queen, who is fully endowed with the marks of a sage king.
If a wheel-turning monarch lacks such an eldest son endowed with manifold virtues, then after the king’s life has ended, these various jewels will all vanish within seven days.
O Son of the Buddha!

This jewel of a sutra is likewise; it does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for the true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King—those born into the family of the Tathāgata and who have planted the various roots of goodness that constitute the marks of a Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
If there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate would soon perish and vanish. Why is that?

All followers of the two vehicles do not even hear this sutra, let alone receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, analyze, or explain it; only bodhisattvas are capable of such things. Therefore, when a bodhisattva hears this Dharma-gate, they should feel great joy and, with a heart of reverence, respectfully receive it upon the crown of their head.
"Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who believe in and delight in this sutra will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The commentary explains:

One who is born into the family of the Tathāgata awakens to their own body as the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya*, realizing that it is equal in essence and characteristics to the true nature of the Buddha, devoid of any distinct flavor or identity. Being indistinguishably one with the *dharmadhātu*, the dualistic notions of self and other are exhausted; only the Buddha’s wisdom shines clearly throughout the ten directions. Being without inherent nature and without dependence, and free from the nature of birth and death, this is called being born into the family of the Buddha.

By means of the power of wisdom and compassion that is equal and free from self-made effort, they uphold and promote the True Dharma to govern sentient beings; they subdue them through the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each, causing all sentient beings to eliminate the karma of birth and death, and to delight in all dharmas of peace and happiness—this is called upholding the family dharma of the Buddha.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "planting various roots of goodness that constitute the marks of a Tathāgata," the commentary explains:

to realize the Buddha’s Dharma-body is for one's nature to be identical with the Dharma-realm and identical to the compassion and wisdom of the Buddha; practicing with such faith, principle and phenomena are not distinct, and essence and appearance are equal.

Those who train in this manner plant the marks of a Tathāgata and share in the same roots of goodness as the Buddha; they do not belong to the provisional teachings entrusted to the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles for their common circulation.

Furthermore, while the teachings of the Three Vehicles are mostly entrusted to the various sages and to ordinary beings who have not yet been born into the family of the Buddha, this sutra is entrusted to the most supreme ordinary beings of great resolve who seek only the Tathāgata’s inconceivable vehicle and are thus born into the family of the Buddha. If there were no ordinary beings of great resolve seeking this Dharma-gate to be born into the family of the Tathāgata, this sutra would surely perish.
Why is this? Because this sutra is difficult to believe.
Even if there were noble ones, if ordinary persons do not believe and do not realize it, this sutra shall perish.

If it were not for entrusting ordinary beings in this manner so that they may be born into the Buddha-family, there are bodhisattvas at the stage of sainthood as numerous as the atoms in all buddha-worlds; why would the Tathāgata worry about the dispersal or extinction of this sutra?
It should be understood in this way:

the intention of the Tathāgata is to cause ordinary beings who have been born into the Buddha-family to give rise to faith and practice, rather than thinking that they are already equal in rank to the assembly of bodhisattvas at the stage of Buddhahood.
All practitioners should understand this:

for what reason are the teachings of the Three Vehicles mostly entrusted to the various noble ones (āryas) to ensure their circulation, and also entrusted to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who have not yet been born into the Buddha-family?

Because the teachings of the Three Vehicles have not yet transcended the dust of the emotions and their clarity regarding the Dharma is not yet true, they are easy to believe and understand; thus, for the time being, they are praised by both ordinary beings and sages so that the teaching may circulate and the roots of goodness remain unbroken.
Because they have not yet transcended the realm of ordinary cognition, they do not resemble those at the final moment of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), who immediately become Buddhas.

For this reason, the teachings of the Three Vehicles provisionally lead beings forward while they remain within the dust of sensory objects; it is only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* that they attain Buddhahood. Since these teachings accord with ordinary inclinations and their roots are easy to believe, both ordinary people and sages praise them, and they circulate widely.

Unlike the *Avataṃsaka*, which concerns the fundamental wisdom, the wisdom of differentiation, and the great compassion of the Buddhas of the ten directions—teachings that transcend the dust of emotional afflictions and are so profound they are difficult to believe—it must wait for one to enter and realize the stage of the Ten Abodes, being born into the Buddha-family as a true son of the Buddha, before it can be widely circulated.
If there is only the teaching of the Sages but no one to realize it, it cannot be called "circulation.
If there is only the teaching spoken by ordinary beings but no realization, that too cannot be called "circulation."

Because one's own understanding of the Dharma is not yet clear and doubts still remain, and because one has not dispelled the darkness of others' ignorance, one is unable to definitively know the Buddha’s intent.

For this reason, it is necessary to wait until one enters realization and brings one’s mind into accord with the wisdom-mind of all Buddhas; only then can one decisively understand the gateway of the Buddha’s teaching.
For this reason, it is only when entrusted to great-minded ordinary beings who have entered realization that it is truly called "circulation.
Merely hearing it without attunement does not constitute circulation.
The fourth section clarifies the identity and distinction of attaining Buddhahood: Now, the body of wisdom is vast and boundless, encompassing all phenomena to form its physical frame;
these myriad phenomena are formless, sharing the same substance as the body of wisdom.
Separated by the divergence from reality, yet identical upon attaining the source.

It is solely because of this departure from the fundamental that their manifestations differ, causing their modes of transformation to vary: sometimes one sees a form emaciated at the Bodhi tree, a humble body reclining upon a mat of grass;

sometimes one sees a wondrous form in the Heaven of Ultimate Form, seated upon a lotus flower; or sometimes one sees [the Buddha] dwelling in a pure land beneath a precious Bodhi tree, thereby realizing perfection.
In some instances, one sees them practicing over distant eons; in others, one sees them attaining realization in a single kṣaṇa.

In some, one sees their retribution body (saṃbhogakāya) with its perfect ocean of infinite marks; in others, one sees their transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) manifesting in divided forms, complete with the thirty-two marks.

Such diverse forms and varied appearances pervade all sentient beings; since their emotional faculties differ in ten thousand ways and a thousand distinctions, how could words ever fully encompass them?

For now, focusing on those in the human and celestial realms who share in the provisional and ultimate streams of the four vehicles, I shall briefly compose ten sections on the differences in the attainment of the Way. This is intended to enable the ignorant to give rise to faith and develop understanding, to eliminate doubt and recognize the fundamental source, and to leave behind provisional attachments while aspiring toward supreme virtues.

Regarding the ten gates: first, the distinction of the Buddha-body attained; second, the distinction of the time of attaining Buddhahood; third, the distinction of the Bodhi tree; fourth, the distinction of the seat upon which one sits; fifth, the distinction of the great assembly; sixth, the distinction of the manifested signs; seventh, the distinction of turning the wheel of Dharma; eighth, the distinction of the place where the wheel of Dharma is turned; ninth, the distinction of the adornments of the great assembly; and tenth, the distinction of the Dharma-gates received.

Regarding the first distinction of the Buddha-body of enlightenment: this body of Vairocana Buddha, as described in the sutras, possesses ninety-seven kinds of marks and an inexhaustible body of marks; it is not a body characterized by the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs.

Regarding the second point, the distinction in the timing of attaining Buddhahood: according to the provisional teachings, the time is defined as the moment immediately following the Buddha’s birth, when he left the city to renounce the world and attained equal and perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.
As for Vairocana Buddha, in reality it is not so.

The Tathāgata establishes these manifested forms in order to deliver sentient beings of the three vehicles; thus, they should see him as one who leaves the household life and attains Buddhahood in this manner.
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the ocean of the true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is not like this.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "Since my attainment of Buddhahood, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed."
This refers to turning those of the three vehicles toward reality.

This Vairocana Buddha attains great enlightenment based upon the fundamental dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and likewise abides within that same fundamental dharma-realm, which is without beginning or end, neither arising nor perishing, neither formed nor destroyed, and devoid of temporal divisions.
This sutra states: "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any parinirvāṇa.
This is the true teaching.
Furthermore, wearing a flower crown is fundamentally not the way of one who has left the household life; it entirely lacks the events of the eight signs [of a Buddha's life].

If there is anyone who can know that the Tathāgata neither emerges nor disappears, neither attains realization nor undergoes destruction, they will know that the Tathāgata eternally abides in the world and eternally turns the wheel of Dharma; this is precisely Vairocana appearing in the world.

Furthermore, from descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the mother’s womb by means of his divine spirit, turning the Wheel of Dharma, and entering Nirvāṇa—all these occur within the span of a single kṣaṇa.
Even before he has descended from that heaven, even before he has emerged from this world, he has already entered Nirvāṇa; all matters are thus entirely concluded.

Regarding the third distinction concerning the Bodhi tree: within the context of the Three Vehicles, the tree of the Buddha-way is seen as being made of wood, with its height and proportions corresponding to those of the human world.
However, within the One Vehicle, the tree under which the Tathāgata attained enlightenment is a jewel-tree, its height surpassing that of the six heavens.

The tree manifested within the body of Vajragarbha is one million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems in height, and its circumference is one hundred thousand triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, because its great significance pervades all places.

Regarding the fourth distinction concerning the seat upon which he sits: within the Three Vehicles, the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) attains enlightenment by discarding honors and using a mat of grass.
Within this One Vehicle, the Original Body (dharmakāya) attains enlightenment while seated upon a precious lotus lion throne, exquisitely adorned with all manner of magnificent ornaments.
Regarding the fifth distinction concerning the great assembly: it consists of the entire retinue surrounding Vairocana, which includes the hosts of Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and others;
as well as those who have newly resolved their minds, all of whom are members of the Dharma-realm assembly seeking the fruit of Buddhahood within their own minds.

This is not for those of the three vehicles who study expediently—those seeking the state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha who loathe suffering, nor the assembly of bodhisattvas who delight in being born in a pure land.

Even if there were an assembly of śrāvakas, if they have not yet turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they would be like the deaf who do not hear; they would neither know nor see this profound *Avataṃsaka* sūtra as it is preached.

Nor does it refer to those multitudes who attained the fruit by means of the preceding three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, for these are multitudes whose wisdom is perfected across many kalpas as a single continuum, devoid of any temporal sequence of before and after.

Sixth, regarding the distinction of manifested signs: as in the provisional teachings (*upāya-śāsana*), this refers to such things as taking birth in Tuṣita Heaven, descending from there, entering the womb, and the eight phases of attaining enlightenment.
Within the teaching of the One Vehicle, the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta is taken as perfect enlightenment.

Sentimentality regarding beginning and end is severed; one perceives neither the passage of time nor its lack thereof. Not contradicting the fact that the aggregates are empty in this very thought-moment, one is immediately Buddha, entirely devoid of any characteristic of temporal transition or change.

The true nature of the Arhat constantly turns the Wheel of Dharma; it is not like the provisional teachings involving matters such as the eight signs, nor does it involve sitting upon the precious throne of the Flower King in the realm of Maheśvara, or taking the trichiliocosm as a field of retribution.

When the Tathāgata establishes measures and limits, these are all pedagogical methods for guiding sentient beings, intended to gradually broaden their minds; they do not constitute the ultimate reality of the true mark.

Regarding such a wondrous gateway to the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm, it is described as consisting of ten times the number of atoms in a Buddha-field of Lotus-Treasury World-Oceans, reflecting one another in infinite layers; this is to clarify that inexhaustible Buddha-lands mutually penetrate one another, such that each and every Buddha-field fills the ten directions.

In lands as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields, all are infinitely unobstructed; body and land correspond to one another, such that there is no appearance of coming or going between this and that.
This is unlike the provisional establishment of the characteristics of limited bodies and lands for those of inferior faculties in the Three Vehicles.
Such is the ocean of marks of Vairocana: not even a speck of dust can obstruct his ten directions, nor can a single pore fail to encompass the oceans of lands.

Those who manifest the signs of the Three Vehicles are like fireflies whose light cannot be compared to the illuminating power of the sun and moon; lapis lazuli is difficult to liken to the pure virtue of the maṇi jewel.
This is not due to the Buddha himself, but rather because their capacities as vessels are inferior.
As for the distinction in the seventh turning of the wheel of Dharma: the transformation Buddhas turn the wheel of the Three Vehicles, while Vairocana turns the Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle.

The One Vehicle is what is called the Buddha Vehicle; as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "There is only the One Buddha Vehicle, neither two nor three; it is merely by means of provisional names that sentient beings are guided."

...and so on, until they mount the Tathāgata-vehicle and proceed directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). For the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it brings together the three vehicles and leads them to the ultimate reality, as was already explained previously in the section on the classification of schools based on the analysis of the teachings.

It is solely for the sake of those with the dispositions of the three vehicles that one relies on their respective original dispositions to provide teachings according to the three vehicles; to claim that the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood in an instant is merely an expedient transformation would, on the contrary, constitute a slander of the teaching and would not accord with the Buddha’s intention.

The original intent of the Buddha was to enable the dragon girl to attain Buddhahood in a single kṣaṇa; for in the fundamental Dharma, there is no such thing as time, and the realization that exhausts all time and place constitutes the true Dharma.
To reply that these are merely transformations is truly a tragedy;

what then shall we do? Unexpecting nectar, it has instead become poison; turning precious gems into mere dust; taking the real for the unreal and the unreal for the real. I pray that future sages will not follow in the footsteps of those former worthies.

The Dharma-gates of the former sages have universally bestowed their instructions; according to the capacities [of beings], the provisional and the real follow diverse paths. This is profoundly worthy of long reflection.

One who is fully conversant with the Buddha’s intent, clearly understands the provisional and the real, and transmits the teachings in accordance with them, will not be hindered by various faculties, as both the provisional and the real provide salvation.
One may only lead the small back to the great; yet if one takes the original mind of the myriad sages as being real and thereby treats it as empty, the Buddha would not approve.
Relying on the fundamental school to transmit the teachings brings benefit and merit to humans and devas, causing them to shine brilliantly like gold and jade, so that none shall sink into oblivion.
Therefore, Vairocana Buddha expounds the Buddha Vehicle (Buddhayāna), while the transformation Buddhas expound the Three Vehicles.

Within the teachings of the transformation Buddhas, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sutras gradually lead those who rely on provisional means toward the gate of returning to the ultimate reality;
this is exemplified by such analogies as the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood in an instant, or the cow obtaining pure ghee after consuming the fatty grasses of the Snowy Mountains.
All [other teachings] possess these elements in part but do not fully demonstrate them; each contains the gateway of the complete characteristics of cause, condition, retribution, and appearance.
Only the *Avataṃsaka* of the North is complete in this regard; therefore, it is said that the turning of the wheel of Dharma here is distinct.

Eighth, regarding the distinction of the locations where the Wheel of Dharma was turned: in the provisional teachings, transformation Buddhas turn the Wheel of Dharma; some say it was at the Deer Park, while others say it was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden, and so forth, all of which have specific locations where they move up and down and come and go.

This sutra consists of ten locations and ten assemblies, as well as Buddha-lands and Buddha-bodies within every atom; these are layered upon layered, infinitely upon infinite, constantly turning the Wheel of Dharma—neither departing nor arriving, neither emerging nor disappearing.
The names and locations of the ten assemblies shall be explained further below.
It is stated that they all ascend to every place without departing from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), as is fully expressed in the sutra itself.

Regarding the specific adornments of the ninth great assembly: at the time this sutra was preached, the holy multitudes of the ten directions and sentient beings of great resolve gathered simultaneously and universally across the ten assemblies and ten locations among devas and humans; there were no fixed natures for the three vehicles.
Those who have not yet turned their minds toward enlightenment, even if present at this assembly, do not belong to its current.

Furthermore, the congregations of the ten assemblies have each come from the ten directions; according to the direction from which they came, it is said that a multitude as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields has gathered. On each successive stage (*bhūmi*), the numbers increase by factors of ten, hundred, and thousand, in order to clarify their inexhaustibility.
Furthermore, each and every assembly in these gatherings pervades the entire Dharma-realm, with layers upon layers of interpenetrating light and reflections.

Within even a single speck of dust, there are likewise successive assemblies; within each and every atom, these assemblies are equal in extent to the space of the Dharma-realm. Even within the body of a single small sentient being, they attain perfect enlightenment, and amidst these ocean-like multitudes, they turn the wheel of the True Dharma in successive layers, yet that small sentient being remains unaware and unconscious of it.
Such an assembly as this consists entirely of the bodies, lands, and assemblies of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which are omnipresent in all places; for they pervade every location.

This is unlike the assemblies of transformation Buddhas within the Three Vehicles, which all have specific locations, limitations, and boundaries for their coming and going. This is because the faculties of those beings are inferior, and it is not the case that the Buddhas act in such a manner.

Regarding the specific distinctions of the tenth received Dharma-gate: as in the provisional teachings, one may gradually cultivate the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness within the Lesser Vehicle, becoming weary of old age, sickness, death, and birth, and practicing the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.

Within this, the two truths of suffering and its origin are regarded as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the two truths of cessation and the path are regarded as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

One contemplates that suffering and its origin are truly suffering, thereby generating a profound sense of weary detachment and seeking the state of cessation. This is because one contemplates them through the meditations on impermanence, impurity, the white bones, and so forth, until even those subtle particles are seen to be empty.
Suffering and its accumulation are fundamentally non-existent; when consciousness ceases, wisdom perishes. Taking emptiness as the realization, one first brings suffering to an end.

Only thereafter does one preach the Mahāyāna Dharma for them, causing them to turn their minds toward practicing the contemplation of the dharma-emptiness, to cultivate the six pāramitās, and to gradually give rise to compassion and wisdom.

Alternatively, there may be those of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva lineage whose contemplative practice and antidotes resemble those of the Hīnayāna; yet, possessing compassion by nature and delighting in practicing the various perfections, they do not realize emptiness prematurely but retain their afflictions to benefit sentient beings, thereby accomplishing the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena and so forth.

Alternatively, there are Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas of the lineage who, in a single sudden step, cultivate the contemplations of the provisional and the true suchness; through the preparatory application of the gate of provisional suchness, they undergo subduing for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and only upon seeing their nature in the ten stages do they finally attain Buddhahood.

Some teachings state that by the power of contemplation, Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness prior to the grounds (bhūmi) suppress ignorance through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) on the grounds.
Other teachings state that Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness partially perceive the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Such explanations as these are all taught within the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles.

This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, however, is not like that; it is intended solely for those of the highest faculties, directly bestowing upon them at once the fundamental Dharmakāya, which is the very essence of the Dharma-realm.

The ocean of wisdom of the ancient Buddhas was obscured by ignorance; [the Tathāgata] suddenly causes it to manifest through the samādhi of skillful means, bestowing the entirety of the Buddha-fruit upon the initial mind of the ten abodes all at once—bestowing it in a single thought-moment, a single time, a single limit, and within the single gate of the Dharma-realm.

The myriad practices and the principle-and-phenomena of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra neither expand nor contract according to the measures of sentient beings; they do not cease to accord with worldly time and kalpas, yet remain perfectly present and clear.
The distinctions between the days, months, years, and eons of the three periods of time are clearly and manifestly evident.
Yet, these ages and kalpas do not themselves shift; they are both eternal and impermanent, neither formed nor destroyed, for such is the fundamental nature of phenomena.

To thoroughly understand that the Truth of Suffering is originally the Noble Truth, wherein from the beginning there is neither suffering nor nirvana—if one has such faith and understanding, and enters into such realization, as the Sutra says, "By means of slight expedient means, one swiftly attains Bodhi. Thus, by means of the gate of the illusion of wisdom, one manifests an illusory body, equalizing it with the realm of sentient beings and participating in their affairs;
and by means of the gate of unimpeded mindfulness, one thoroughly understands the faculties of sentient beings.
They establish rules and regulations through the gateway of being a teacher and model;
they instruct and transform sentient beings through the gateway of all arts and skills;
and they remain unattached to any phenomena through the gateway of the field of enlightenment which has no basis.
By means of the gate of non-thought, one contemplates without attachment;
by means of the gate of the radiance of pure wisdom, one constantly illumines all phenomena without obstruction to establish them and deliver sentient beings;
and by means of the gate of inexhaustible marks, one does not destroy the form-body.
By means of the gate of sincere vows, one utters words that are truthful and authentic;
by means of the gate of illusory abiding, one dwells eternally in the world to bring sentient beings to maturity and liberate their faculties.
These ten dharmas are precisely the gates through which the spiritual friends within the stage of Equal Enlightenment enable Sudhana and others to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings.

It enables all practitioners to suddenly cultivate and awaken to entry, practicing these ten dharmas to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings, and to dwell skillfully in the world through the dharma-gate of liberation.

This is by no means like the multitudes of the Three Vehicles who weary of suffering and its origin, and seek joy in cessation and the path; nor is it like those who linger in delusions, delight in emptiness, and seek a pure land by emerging from the entanglements.

Fifth, clarifying the distinctions in the perception of the Buddha: The nature and characteristics of the Buddha’s body are essentially one and without difference. Yet, as there are myriad types of vessels and the faculties upon which they rely differ, sentient beings harbor separations in their minds, and thus their perceptions are severed while the essence remains uniform. When the body stands, reflections arise; when the mind lingers on it, the Buddhas appear diverse. Because the Buddha responds according to the state of the mind, this leads to a deviation from the truth. When the mind is exhausted and the emotions vanish, the Wisdom Body manifests itself.
