Previously, while in the third dhyāna, I assembled the assembly of the eight dhyānas and, for the sake of the Bodhisattvas in their last birth before Buddhahood, spoke one million billion verses while they were in the Buddha-flower Samādhi."
"Now, by briefly explaining the meaning of a single verse, I shall open the minds of sentient beings; you should all receive and uphold it.
This chapter follows immediately after the "Ten Grounds Chapter" (Daśabhūmika-parivarta) and represents the eleventh ground, the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi).
Considering the title of this chapter, it is likewise named "The Buddha-Flower Chapter," as it is titled according to its subject matter.
Furthermore, the text below states: "O Son of the Buddha!
Previously, when I was here beneath this tree preaching the ocean of the dharma-realm, eighty thousand stainless bodhisattvas manifested their bodies and attained Buddhahood."
Therefore, for the sake of this great assembly, I shall briefly reveal the sphere of practice for the fruit of Buddhahood; you should receive this with the highest reverence.

This is as described in the *Sutra on the Original Vows of the Jeweled Necklace*, which states that after the preaching of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was concluded, he transformed the sentient beings of the three vehicles and proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Second, to restate the five-stage Dharma-gate of the *Avataṃsaka* taught at the time of his initial attainment of Perfect Enlightenment, as fully explained in that sutra:

because the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* lacks one chapter on the "Eleventh Stage," I shall now correlate and compare them so that the sequence may be understood. Those who hear this hereafter need not harbor doubts; simply take that sutra for verification, and the truth will become clear.

Now, regarding the "Chapter on the Buddha-Flower" (*Buddhāvatamsaka*) which speaks of the eleven stages within the Third Dhyāna: it comprises ten locations, ten assemblies, and forty chapters in total. All of these were taught simultaneously and instantaneously at the very moment of initial perfect enlightenment, through the Ocean-Seal Dharma-gate (*sāgaramudrā-dharmaparyāya*) in a single kṣaṇa. This is because the fundamental Dharma has no before or after, because the Dharma-nature is thus, because the original body and original wisdom manifest the fundamental Dharma, and because there is no occurrence of repeated assemblies such as those in the Hall of Universal Radiance or the three assemblies.

If there is a layer upon layer, an infinitely repeated layering, regardless of the three assemblies, the ocean-gate of the Dharma-realm encompasses all three periods of time; the before and after of a single thought-moment are simultaneously one, and there is no going from that layer to come back into this.
Because the Tathāgata, by means of the Sea-Seal Gate of the Manifestation of the Form Body through Fundamental Wisdom alone, reveals [all things] universally at once;
what is now called the "threefold assembly in successive layers within the Hall of Universal Radiance" is not like that—it is, in its entirety, the teaching of instantaneous, simultaneous sealing.
As a sutra states: "Within a single utterance, the Tathāgata expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras.

This is merely according to the categories of dharma-gates; the names of the bodhisattvas are distinct only to manifest the teachings. They are not a multitude that arrived earlier or later. Within the ocean of the dharma-realm, one must not conceive of before and after through ordinary sentiment, for such would contradict the fundamental nature of the Dharma.
The manifestation of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment is for the sake of sentient beings; it is not that the fundamental dharma itself possesses the three periods of time.

This is to clarify the fundamental dharma, which cannot be approached through its derivative aspects. A previous generation has already overturned their cart; one must subsequently change one's course. One should not simply take the virtues of former masters as a model for imitation.
Examining the intent of the sutra, there is nowhere the name of a "repeated assembly";
yet, when expressed through the medium of words, it gives the impression that the dharma-gate possesses a sense of repetition.

If one does not observe the intent of the sutra within this chapter, one will see that it consistently describes the dharma-gate of the application of wisdom, which universally encompasses a single time, a single limit, and a single dharma-realm throughout both preceding and succeeding sections.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" and the "Chapter on Leaving the World," it says: "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha, having just attained perfect enlightenment; he entered the Samādhi of the Limit of the Instant within the Hall of Universal Radiance. This is merely according to the positions of the Dharma, where the names of the bodhisattvas differ; it does not mean that the Tathāgata departed and returned again, for the Hall of Universal Radiance is the essence of the resultant wisdom of the dharma-realm.
At one time, he unifies principle and phenomena within the gate of non-active concentration (*anabhisaṃskāra-samādhi*), because these ten gates of concentration are the essence of the *dharmadhātu*.
Since the practices of Samantabhadra are the function of the *dharmadhātu*, this refers precisely to the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*).
These two chapters, when considered together, do not depart from the fundamental capital of wisdom—the great mansion of the fruit-virtue within the Universal Radiance Hall.

These three successive expositions are, in total, a single teaching given at one place and one time, within a single dharma-realm and a single assembly; they are not as perceived by ordinary minds, involving movement back and forth across different times.

Pervading the other nine assemblies, all are unified within a single assembly at a single time, within a single dharma-realm and a single ocean of wisdom; the dharma-gates, layer upon layer, manifest and conceal simultaneously, without obstruction or hindrance.
Now, within this single Dharma-realm, according to the modes of practice for progressive cultivation, ten locations are distinguished by means of metaphorical designations to represent the Dharma.
As for the ten assemblies:
the first is the Assembly at the Site of Enlightenment;...
The second assembly, the Universal Radiance Hall;
the third assembly, ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru;
and the fourth assembly, ascending to the Yāma Heaven.
The fifth is the assembly on ascending to Tuṣita Heaven;
the sixth is the assembly on ascending to Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
the seventh is the assembly on ascending to the Third Dhyāna Heaven.
The eighth is the assembly at the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden;
the ninth is the assembly at the Great Stūpa to the east of the City of Enlightenment;
and the tenth is the assembly throughout all lands and within every atom, pervading all space and the entire dharma-realm.
It is known as the ten locations and ten assemblies.

Within the assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala-kuṭāgāra*), the dharma-gates of the five stages and six positions, the wondrous principles of the ten concentrations, and the essence and function from beginning to end of Samantabhadra’s myriad practices are all contained therein. The ten locations and ten assemblies are collectively situated within the Hall of Universal Radiance—the dwelling place where the one true dharma-realm (*eka-tathatā-dharmadhātu*) abides, its causes perfected and its fruits fulfilled.

The worlds of the ten directions are all encompassed within a single Dharma, a single place, a single time, and a single functional essence; they are subsumed by returning the branches to the root. One must not separately divide them into the doctrines of three assemblies occurring sequentially or reciprocally, nor should one allow the dust of personal sentiment to obscure the true teaching.
Furthermore, within this sutra, all dharmas are rounded off by the number ten; thus, one cannot simply speak of the teachings of the seven locations and nine assemblies.
Again, it is asked:

Why does it reach only the seventh assembly, and why does it proceed only as far as the third dhyāna to gather the assembly of the eight heavens to expound the dharma-gate of the eleven stages, rather than reaching the fourth dhyāna heaven?
Answer: This is for the sake of the heavens of the four *dhyānas*, because they follow a sequential order that constitutes the locus of the Buddha-fruit.

It is precisely at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) that the Buddha correctly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood; thus, the four *dhyānas* and the worlds of the ten directions are collectively encompassed as the single universal hall of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the capital of the abode of retribution. Beyond this, there is no longer any sign of a place where one might go, come, advance, or practice, characterized by higher or lower levels.
It clarifies that the mind and thoughts of the Buddha’s four dhyānas have no basis and no place for further cultivation; therefore, there is no coming or going.
Sentiment is severed and one accords with the truth (satyasaṃdhi), for they are identical with the Dharma-realm.

This is the fourth dhyāna of the Buddha. Because he dwelt beneath the Bodhi tree as if in an āraṇya, the Hall of Universal Radiance is his retribution-residence, his original abode. By these three explanations, the beginning and end of cause and effect are established.
This reiterates the initial moment of attaining Buddhahood in order to clarify that from beginning to end, one is never separate from the fundamental ocean of wisdom, the essence of Bodhi.
Thus, this perfectly integrated dharma-gate unifies the beginning and the end, as well as cause and effect, into a single realm.
Within this sutra, there are six instances of convergence between the preceding and following sections:
two instances within the "Gate of Demonstrating the Fruit and Encouraging Practice," and four instances within the "Gate of Practice Based on Established Faith."

Just as in the first assembly, when Samantabhadra Bodhisattva entered the Tathāgata-garbha-kāya-samādhi and, by means of the Dharma-door of the World-Ocean Revolutions, revealed the gate of the causal and resultant attainment from beginning to end within the ten Lotus-Womb World-Oceans, which are the fundamental source of the Buddha’s Dharma-realm.

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva represents its practice (*caryā*), while the Tathāgatagarbha-body represents its essence (*tattva*); this clarifies that through function one enters into essence, for principle and phenomenon are thoroughly interpenetrated.
Second, the seat upon which Vairocana sits, with all its adornments, likewise clarifies the beginning and end of cause and effect, as essence and function are mutually interpenetrating.

Taking the Buddha Vairocana as the fruit of retribution, taking the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of all phenomena as the substance of the seat, and taking the myriad practices of Samantabhadra as the adornment of its function.

By means of all these ornaments, there emerge from the wheels, terraces, doors, windows, and various other ornaments a multitude of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds, who rain down jewels as offerings to the Buddha. This clarifies that the fruit-virtue of the Tathāgata eternally dwells upon the seat of the emptiness of all phenomena; and that the wondrous functions of Samantabhadra’s manifold practices eternally evoke the adornment of the environment, for principle and phenomenon, cause and effect, essence and function, are always mutually beneficial.

Furthermore, regarding the four gates of harmonizing cause and effect as non-dual within the gate of practice for those who have already attained faith: first, the threefold proclamation of the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment in the Hall of Universal Radiance, wherein all derivative phenomena are subsumed into the fundamental reality of the single-limit Dharma-realm, constitutes one such gate of harmonization.

The twenty-third chapter, consisting of thirty-seven sections, is titled "The Appearance of the Tathāgata. In this chapter, the Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows to moisten the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, and emits light from his mouth to moisten Samantabhadra’s mouth, causing these two to engage in dialogue together to expound upon the gateway to the fruits and virtues of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.

That is to say, Mañjuśrī is the dharma-body of fundamental wisdom and Samantabhadra is practice; this clarifies that body and function are thoroughly integrated. Because they are thoroughly integrated in this way, this very state of thoroughness is named "Buddha."
The "Buddha" in the first assembly clarifies that the Buddha attained Buddhahood through his own inherent nature.
The "Buddha" within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment clarifies the extent reached by the bodhisattva’s own power.
Because of the first Buddha, one gives rise to faith and advances in practice; because of advancing in practice through faith, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood by means of one's own power.

Since this fruit of Buddhahood is no different from that which was previously believed in, throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the Tathāgata, by means of the *Siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*, expounds the causes and fruits of the five stages to guide and benefit humans and devas.

Within the Maitreya Pavilion, the youth Sudhana brings together the beginning and end of the causes and effects of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, as well as the beginning and end of the causes and effects of Maitreya Bodhisattva, into a single reality, for their essence and function are thoroughly penetrating.

Combining this with the preceding "Gate of Revealing the Fruit and Encouraging Practice," we have two locations—the assembly of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and Vairocana Buddha—and adding the subsequent four locations—the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala*), the "Tathāgata-utpatti" chapter, the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden, and Maitreya’s Gabled Pavilion—there are six locations in total. These collectively constitute the Dharma-gate of the non-dual, single-limit reality that harmonizes essence and function, cause and fruit.

Therefore, the name of Maitreya’s pavilion is the "Vairocana-Adornment-Treasury," which corresponds to the name of the samādhi entered by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva in the first assembly, namely the "Tathāgata-Treasury-Body"; thus, the names in the beginning and end are identical.

If one simply takes up the categories and contextual meanings of the scriptural texts and investigates them, their correspondence can be seen through cross-verification: the Tathāgata’s comprehensive synthesis treats all as a single time and a single limit; thus, from the abode of fundamental wisdom at the limit of a single kṣaṇa, there arise both nirvāṇa and the manifestation in the world to turn the wheel of the true Dharma, all of which occurs without deficiency during the very moment of attaining perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time without coming or going.

This Sūtra consists of ten locations and ten assemblies, comprising forty chapters in total. Within nine of these assemblies, the gathered multitudes from all quarters number three hundred and forty-two types; this count also includes the eight types of multitudes from the single assembly in the third dhyāna.

Such assemblies, each numbering as many as the atoms within a Buddha-world, or as many as the atoms within ten Buddha-worlds, gathered simultaneously at the single moment of the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment; they pervaded the ten directions like a great ocean, mutually reflecting one another without obstruction or hindrance.

If one considers those present in all assemblies within the lands, atoms, space, and the dharma-realm as described in the tenth assembly—namely, those within the space of the dharma-realm and even a single atom throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as well as those within the bodies, pores, and oceans of assemblies of all sentient beings—these extend throughout the ten directions like the sea, layer upon layer, infinitely and inexhaustibly.

The ocean-like assemblies of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are eternally thus: the three periods of time are a single thought-moment; past and present are both identical with the present moment; and the inexhaustible kalpas of the past and future are simultaneously complete without deficiency at the very instant one attains perfect enlightenment in a single thought-moment.
Such is the nature of time; whether one attains Buddhahood or not, whether it is the time of awakening or non-awakening, the Dharma is thus.

Second, the explicit instruction on the fruit and exhortation to practice consists of these five chapters of the sutra: the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Manifestation of Signs," the "Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra," the "Chapter on the Formation of the World," the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," and the "Chapter on Vairocana."

In the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs," the Tathāgata emitted light from between his many teeth; through voices within that light, he announced to the multitudes in the ten directions, causing them all to assemble.

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is the eldest son of the Buddha; he upholds the family dharma of the Buddha, enters the samādhi of the Buddha, and manifests the meritorious virtues of the Buddha’s fruition so that all beings may respect and love him, giving rise to faith, joy, and cultivation.

The Tathāgata, regarding his own body and seat, employs the gate of cause and effect throughout his entire being to enable all beings to fully understand: he takes his own person as the Dharma-realm body of great wisdom; he takes all the ornaments as the retributive fruit of Samantabhadra’s practice; and he takes the emptiness of all phenomena as his seat. By means of these three dharmas held in perfect equilibrium, he gives rise to the gates of compassion and wisdom, manifesting and awakening sentient beings without beginning or end; this is what is called a Buddha.

The Tathāgata again emitted a ray of light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, named "The Universal Illumination of the Wisdom-Light of All Bodhisattvas, the Treasury Shining Throughout the Ten Directions. Its appearance was like a cloud of jewel-colored lamps; having universally illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, it circled the Buddha to the right and entered beneath his feet.

Furthermore, from within the ūrṇā-kośa between his eyebrows, there emerged a multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds; they sat together upon a single lotus throne before the Buddha and further extolled the profound nature of the Buddha’s realm.
This clarifies that cause and effect are non-dual.
The light entering beneath the feet signifies that the fruit serves as the cause.
As for the light from between the eyebrows, it is the light of the fruit of the wisdom of the ten stages; its entry now into the Buddha’s feet signifies that the fruit serves as the cause.

At the stage of the Ten Faiths, this light again emerges from the wheels on the soles of the feet; at the stage of the Ten Abidings, it successively reaches the tips of the toes; within the Ten Practices, it emerges from above the ankles; within the Ten Dedications, it emerges from above the knees; and within the Ten Grounds, it returns to emerge from between the eyebrows, thus completing one cycle and beginning anew.

The radiance of the *ūrṇā-kośa* mark is the light that is the fruit of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); that from which Bodhisattvas emerge therein is their causal practice, clarifying that the cause issues forth from the fruit.
Having clarified these five preceding sections of the sutra, this demonstrates the virtues of the Buddha’s fruition so as to inspire faith and joy in the assembly.

Third, regarding the clarification of the fulfillment of faith: this refers to the six chapters of the sutra from the second assembly, namely the "Chapter on the Names and Titles of the Tathāgata," the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths," the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance," the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Clarity," the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," and the "Chapter on Worthy Leader."
These six chapters together constitute one stage of the Ten Faiths.

First is the "Chapter on the Names and Titles of the Tathāgata," which concerns faith in the names and titles of the Buddha, which differ according to where they arise throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Second, the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths" (*Catuḥsatyaparivarta*): It is through faith that one knows the names and designations of the Dharma-gates throughout the worlds of the ten directions all have the Four Noble Truths as their foundation.

Third, the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance" (*Prabhābodhiparivarta*): One knows that the radiance originally issued from the fruit and entered beneath the Buddha’s feet; now it returns from the feet to emit that light of the fruit, thereby establishing the stage of faith (*śraddhābhūmi*).
4. "The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Illumination" (Bodhisattvaparipṛcchā-prakāśa-parivarta) explains the Dharma-gate inquired about by the bodhisattva through faith.
5. "The Chapter on Pure Conduct" (Śuddhacaryā-parivarta) clarifies that the pure conduct of the bodhisattva arises from the power of great vows.
Six: The "Chapter on Worthy Leaders" (Bhadrapāla). It teaches that one knows the attainment of Buddhahood by taking faith as the foremost.
By believing in these six chapters of the Dharma-gate, one collectively completes the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

These six chapters of the sutra were preached within the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāvabhāsa-kuṭāgāra*), for this hall is the fundamental abode where the fruition of the Buddha’s wisdom-function is fully perfected.
Returning once more from within this, he explains the Dharma-gate of Faith (*śraddhā*) in order to clarify that the realization of the fruit constitutes faith.

Having already believed in the qualities of the fruit, from this point onward until the "Flower of the Buddha" chapter of the eleventh stage, he finally elucidates the entry into the Path and the progressive cultivation through the five stages (*pañca-vastu*), detailing the sequence of fulfillment, the commonalities and distinctions, and how what is realized in one stage is universally realized throughout all.

Because there is no temporal interval between cause and fruit, all ten Buddhas—beginning with the fundamental non-moving wisdom—are taken as the gateways of faith; furthermore, one takes the Buddha of the fundamental non-moving wisdom of one's own mind as the very substance and function of the assembly.

The fourth section clarifies the entry into the realization of reality. From the third assembly, [the Buddha] ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru and emitted light from the tips of the two toes of his feet;

therein he preached six chapters of sutra, namely: first, "Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru"; second, "Verses of Praise on the Summit of Sumeru"; third, "The Ten Abodes"; fourth, "Pure Conduct"; fifth, "The Merit of the Initial Resolve for Enlightenment"; and sixth, "The Clarification of the Dharma."

Among these six chapters of the sutra, two—namely the "Chapter on the Summit of Mount Sumeru" and the "Chapter on Verses of Praise"—depict how Śakra and the various devas welcome and praise the Tathāgata, extolling the Buddha’s merits and the excellence of his dwelling place.

The four chapters of the sutra—the "Ten Abodes Chapter," the "Brahma Conduct Chapter," the "Chapter on the Merits of First Resolving for Enlightenment," and the "Chapter on the Clarification of the Dharma"—clarify that one newly realizes the dharma-gate, abides where the Buddhas abide, is born into and dwells within the Buddha-family, and shares the same Buddha-nature, merits, understanding, and practice; such that with both principle and wisdom identical to the Buddha, one attains perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first resolving for enlightenment.
The emission of light from the tips of the two feet in this assembly signifies the beginning of setting forth upon the path of initial realization of the Dharma-gate.

Ascending the summit of Mount Sumeru signifies that from the former stage of faith, one now ascends to the summit of the mountain of the Ten Abodes, the King of Dharma; it represents reaching the limit of phenomena through unimpeded wisdom-illumination, just as one reaches the ultimate point of characteristics when ascending a high mountain.
Furthermore, "mountain" symbolizes that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*).

From this point onward, one acts in accordance with the Dharma without effort, being a Buddha from beginning to end; it is not by following the eight stages that one becomes fully endowed with effortlessness.
The *Sūtra of the Adornment* states: "The Bodhisattvas of the Three Sages reach Buddhahood spontaneously within the stream of the Dharma.
That the initial water and the subsequent water are of one nature as water is because the Buddha of the cause and the Buddha of the fruit are of one nature as Buddha."
Within this, there is no beginning, middle, or end, because there is no interval between moments and because it relies upon the fundamental dharma.
There is no momentary thought that can create an interval; otherwise, cause and effect would terminate, for every moment of correspondence is itself a Buddha-mindfulness.
"Whether it be the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) or supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), these marks and powers are obtained from this perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

If one realizes perfect enlightenment, one does not cling to any marks; yet because one is constantly in accord with the path of awakening, the transformation of marks and powers arrives of its own accord without being sought."
Furthermore, when it comes to the ultimate point of merit and wisdom, the three periods of time are simultaneous and not separated by even a single thought-moment.

Fifth, to clarify the practitioner who initiates and practices: from the fourth assembly, [the Buddha] ascends to the Yāma Heaven palace and emits light from between his two feet to preach four chapters of the sutra:

first, the "Chapter on Ascending to the Yāma Heaven Palace"; second, the "Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Yāma Heaven Palace"; third, the "Chapter on the Ten Practices"; and fourth, the "Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries."

Within this assembly, the two chapters titled "Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven" and "Verses of Praise in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven" describe how the various devas welcomed the Buddha, praising his meritorious virtues as well as the excellence of that place.

The two chapters of the sutra, "The Ten Practices" and "The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries," reveal that the body of clear wisdom is fully endowed with the practices of Samantabhadra; through the perfection of compassion and wisdom, one enters the gateway of the practice of principle and wisdom, thereby accomplishing the inexhaustible merit and wisdom of both the primary and secondary rewards.

Regarding this stage, the emission of light from the two feet of the Tathāgata and the ascent to the Yāma Heaven to teach are intended to clarify that, from the summit of Mount Sumeru to the limit where characteristics cease, one realizes the Buddha’s Wisdom Body; and that reaching the Yāma Heaven signifies the arising of the gateway of Samantabhadra’s ten thousand practices from the fundamental wisdom of the dharma-nature of emptiness. This is done so that the teaching may be easily understood by using locations as symbols, just as those various heavens are situated above the earth’s surface.
The heavens dwell in dependence upon space; this is to clarify that the ten practices proceed in dependence upon the dharma-emptiness of fundamental wisdom.

The sixth section clarifies the mutual interpenetration of principle and phenomena: from the fifth assembly, [the Buddha] ascends to the Tuṣita Heaven palace and emits light from his knee to expound the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

There are three chapters in the sutra: first, the "Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace"; second, the "Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace"; and third, the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications."

The first two chapters of this sutra consist of the various devas welcoming, praising, and reverently extolling the Tathāgata’s buddha-virtues, as well as extolling the excellence of his dwelling place.
The final chapter is the formal exposition of the dharma-gate of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) means causing all phenomenal dharmas to enter into the principle.
Because the ten phenomenal dharmas enter into the preceding ten abodes (*vihāra*) such that phenomena and principle are without obstruction, it is called dedication.

The first ten stages (*bhūmi*) are the fundamental wisdom of Mañjuśrī’s Dharma-body, while the subsequent ten practices (*caryā*) are the myriad deeds of Samantabhadra; clarifying that the essence and function of these two figures mutually penetrate one another is termed "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*).

Regarding the emission of light from the knees: this clarifies that the principles and phenomena (li-shi) are exercised with sovereign mastery in their contraction and expansion, just as a person’s bending, extending, and turning all depend upon the knees.
For what reason is this stage explained in the Tuṣita Heaven?

This is to clarify that this heaven occupies a central position within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), and furthermore, it stands at the center among the five stages, five locations, and five assemblies of the celestial realms.

Below it lie the two assemblies of Śakra and Yāma; above it lie the two assemblies of Paranirmita-vaśavartin and the Third Dhyāna. Because this heaven is situated centrally within the Desire Realm, the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are taught to bring together principle and phenomena without obstruction, so that fundamental wisdom and its differentiated wisdoms, as well as wisdom and compassion, may be harmoniously integrated while abiding in the Middle Way.
Because the Dharma is manifested through its locus, it is necessary to explain the ten gates of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) at this location.

Seventh, regarding the virtues accomplished through the cultivation of the aggregates: from the sixth assembly, [the Buddha] ascends into the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, he emits a radiance named "Flame-Light of Bodhisattva Power."

This light begins again where it ended from the light emitted from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows during the first assembly; because it returns to its original place, it is this single chapter of the sutra, the "Ten Stages" (Daśabhūmika-parivarta), that is being taught.

The absence of a "Chapter on Ascending to the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven" and a "Chapter on Verses of Praise" is intended to clarify that the fruit of the ten stages culminates in abiding within the palace of the fundamental dharma; it is eternally pervasive throughout all things, and as its merit is consummated and its practice perfected, there is no further ascent or progress.

This applies up to the third dhyāna, and it is likewise for all worlds in the ten directions. This is to signify that the fruit is ultimate, that the wisdom of the ten stages is perfected with no further cultivation required, that the Buddhas are always present before one, and that there is no need for new arrivals to offer praise.

These ten stages (daśabhūmi) are merely the accumulation and perfection of merit within the ten abodes (daśavihāra), the ten practices (daśacaryā), and the ten transferences (daśapariṇāmanā), whereby they become smooth and mature; there is nothing further to dwell upon, as they are accomplished spontaneously, naturally bringing all dharmas to fulfillment.
For what reason is the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages taught in this celestial realm?
Because these devas rely on the transformations produced by others to accomplish their own pleasures, this realm is named the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).

In this stage, the Bodhisattva practices compassion and wisdom by relying upon sentient beings; they give rise to clouds of various practices and rain down the rain of the Dharma to bring about happiness, without producing any mental characteristics of their own while performing the characteristics of these practices.
Because the Dharma is manifested through its locus, it was necessary to speak this Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) by means of this locus.

According to Master Zang, when this chapter was spoken, there were three empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and five requests (*adhyeṣaṇā*). Examining the intent of the sūtra, however, the Buddha provided thirteen kinds of empowerment, while the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra and the other bodhisattvas made four requests.

The Buddhas bestow thirteen kinds of empowerments upon the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha; first, the Buddhas of other directions bestow twelve kinds of empowerments upon the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, commanding him to expound this teaching.
Second, Vairocana Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows that illuminates the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha; within this light, he speaks verses exhorting him to preach.
This constitutes the empowerment through light, making thirteen in total.

Regarding the twelve kinds of empowerments bestowed by the Buddhas of the ten directions: first, the Buddhas appear before one, praising and comforting them with words so as to cause them to preach the Dharma.
Second, they bestow the ten kinds of wisdom along with their own roots of goodness; such is the empowerment of the Dharma.
The Buddhas of the thirty directions placed their hands upon his crown and authorized him to speak;
they comforted him with words, which is the empowerment of verbal action (*vākkarman*);
and they bestowed upon him ten kinds of knowledge, which is the empowerment of cognitive action (*jñānakarman*).
Rubbing the crown of the head with his hand is the empowerment of physical action (*kāyakarman*);
the light radiating from the space between the eyebrows of Vairocana and the teaching of the Dharma within that light is the empowerment of the Dharma (*dharmakarman*).
Generally speaking, including these praises along with the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), the rubbing of the crown of the head, and the illumination by light, there are thirteen types of empowerments.

Regarding the fourfold request made by the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha: first, Vimukticandra raised the doubts of the assembly; second, he requested that the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha preach the Dharma for the assembly; third, he made a second request; and fourth, all the great bodhisattvas simultaneously made a collective request—thus, there are four requests in total.
Regarding the "three additions and five requests" that have not yet been explained, from where do they originate?

If these three additions refer merely to the actions of body, speech, and mind, then this would contradict the account of the ten wisdoms, the light from between the eyebrows illuminating the Vajragarbha-body, and the preaching of the Dharma through light; in that case, the "additions" would be incomplete.

If one were to take the words of praise spoken by all Buddhas of the ten directions and treat them as the five requests, this would be improper; for the rank of a Buddha is most honored, and within the rules of propriety, it is not fitting to issue a request to them.
Based on this principle, there are in total thirteen types of augmentations and fourfold requests.

Although these are not distinct from the essence of wisdom when compared with the ten types of wisdom-activities, they function differently at their respective times so that one may not be confused regarding the characteristics of phenomena and may achieve differentiated wisdom; therefore, they cannot be taken as identical in their application.

Because within this single assembly there are thirteen distinct additions and four instances of repeated requests that are all unique, the meaning of transcending and ascending has already been explained previously.
Regarding the eighth [point], "unimpeded according to conditions," it was taught starting from the seventh assembly, gathered among the assembly of the eight dhyānas within the third dhyāna.

A Bodhisattva in the stage of "One Life to Buddhahood" (Ekajātipratibaddha) enters the Buddha-flower Samādhi and expounds the Dharma-gate of Samantabhadra within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) across the eleven stages.

Having completed the ten stages, which clarifies the conclusion of the path of one's own level, one practices the conduct of Samantabhadra within the stage of Equal Enlightenment. This involves universally manifesting entry into the mundane world and pervading the entire Dharma-realm; the successive layers of these practice-gates extend broadly to the oceans of lands within all empty space and even within a single atom, being multilayered yet unimpeded, as vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate like empty space—this is termed the conduct of Samantabhadra within the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
Regarding the term "Buddha-flower Samādhi": "flower" refers to conduct that is capable of being contemplated; it signifies the meaning of blossoming to evoke the fruit [of enlightenment].
This constitutes the Dharma-gate of the Buddha's practice.
"Buddha" means awakening; it clarifies the practice and function of the Perfectly Awakened One across the eleven stages (*ekādaśabhūmi*).

It clarifies that from the tenth stage one attains Buddhahood as the culmination, followed by the fulfillment of the practice of awakening in the eleventh stage; therefore, it is called the "Buddha-Flower Dharma-Gate."

Samādhi is the dharma-gate of the great quiescence of the fundamental substance of the dharma-realm; when the states of concentration and distraction are exhausted, it is termed "fundamental quiescence.
Because of this concentration, one practices all samādhis of the gate of Samantabhadra’s conduct, for these constitute the fundamental substance.

In that celestial realm, for the sake of the assemblies of the eight dhyānas of the form and formless realms, he preached one million billion verses on the gate of the Buddha-flower samādhi entered by bodhisattvas in their final birth before buddhahood.

Because Bodhisattvas at this stage enter the Buddha-flower Dharma-gate and are skillfully clear regarding entering the secular world to extensively benefit sentient beings with mastery, it is called "unimpeded according to conditions.
Since this stage clarifies that the practice of the Dharma-realm is all-pervasive, for what reason is the Dharma-gate of the eleventh stage taught in that celestial realm?

In that celestial realm, the feelings of sorrow and suffering have vanished, leaving only the bliss of samādhi; this is to clarify that for a Bodhisattva at this stage, the feeling of sorrow has vanished because they abide in meditative concentration, while only the joy of wisdom, compassion, and benefiting sentient beings remains.
Because this section symbolizes the Dharma, it expounds herein the Dharma-gate of the eleven stages (*bhūmi*).

The details regarding the stages, positions, and practices are as extensively explained in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng); here, they correspond to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, though the current text is not yet complete.

The ninth section, "Clarifying the Conclusion of the Stage of Cause and Effect," consists of the twelve chapters of the sutra from the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers," "Chapter on the Ten Endurances," "Chapter on the Incalculable," "Chapter on the Lifespan," "Chapter on the Abodes of All Bodhisattvas," "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddha," "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks and Signs of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies," "Chapter on the Merit of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance," "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra," "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata," and "Chapter on Transcending the World. These are the aforementioned twelve chapters.

Why is this so? Because from the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" to the "Chapter on Transcending the World," it comprehensively encompasses the five stages and ten bhūmis, as well as the stage of Buddhahood and the myriad practices of Samantabhadra; thus, the beginning and end, cause and effect, and the preceding and succeeding elements are thoroughly integrated.

Regarding the fact that at the beginning of these two chapters—the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" and the "Chapter on Transcending the World"—it is recounted once again from the first and second assemblies that "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Aranya-dharma Bodhimanda in the kingdom of Magadha, having just attained perfect enlightenment; he entered the 'Momentary Boundary' Samādhi of all Buddhas within the Hall of Universal Radiance," this is not because there was a subsequent gathering. Rather, it is because the "Ten Samādhis" and "Transcending the World" chapters constitute the gates of essence and function, which encompass the beginning and the end.

In the Hall of Universal Radiance, these matters were recounted once more; according to that dharma-gate, the various names and designations of the bodhisattva assembly do not imply that they had departed and then returned again.

Regarding the dharmas of the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten stages, and the eleventh stage, he taught all these positions simultaneously and instantaneously throughout all the celestial realms.
These two chapters clarify that the essence and function [of the Buddha-nature] penetrate from beginning to end, as they constitute the gateway of the Buddha’s cause and fruit.

Mañjuśrī is the essence of the ten stages of concentration (*daśa-dhyāna*), while Samantabhadra is the Dharma that transcends the world (*lokottara-dharma*). Therefore, in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," light is emitted and these two individuals are brought together, because this constitutes the gateway in which cause and fruit mutually penetrate one another.

Light is emitted from between the eyebrows and enters the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head; light is emitted from the mouth and enters the mouth of Samantabhadra, causing them to engage in a mutual dialogue regarding principle and phenomena to expound the gateway to the fruit of Buddhahood.

The gateway to the fruit of Buddhahood lies entirely within the juncture between the fundamental wisdom and the discriminative wisdom of these two types of persons; it can be seen by illuminating them with the power of meditative concentration and insight (*samādhi* and *prajñā*).

These twelve chapters of the sutra converge at once, as they all enter the gate of the Dharma-realm—the great mansion of the merit of fruition and the hall of fundamental wisdom in Universal Radiance—throughout the six stages and eleven grounds. Therefore, both the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" and the "Chapter on Transcending the World" both recount the time when this sutra was preached during the first and second assemblies.

Suppose, for example, that one hundred thousand precious mirrors are set in space, and a single image of a Buddha is placed upon the ground, surrounded and adorned by a multitude of bodhisattvas; these appear all at once within those hundred thousand precious mirrors, and while the reflections in each mirror interpenetrate one another, there is no coming or going whatsoever.

The Tathāgata is likewise: at the moment he first attained perfect enlightenment, the heavens, the human realm, and the lands of the ten directions appeared all at once; they interpenetrate one another without any coming or going. Therefore, the sounds, phrases, and meanings of his teachings are entirely interwoven, without any coming or going, and there is no question of them being encountered again.
One must not form worldly emotional attachments or harbor a mind of repeated coming and going.
As previously stated, matters must be harmonized and explained as they arise.
At the conclusion of this sutra, one must understand the reconciliation of its beginning and end.

The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" clarifies the gateway to the culmination of the fruits of the five stages and eleven grounds—the juncture between the beginning and end of the entire scripture.
For this reason, the dissemination and entrustment are both contained therein.
Prior to the "Chapter on Manifestation" (Samantabhadracaryā-nirdeśa), the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Conduct" clarifies the practices for cultivating one's own Buddha-fruit.

Following the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*), the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) elucidates the conduct for benefiting sentient beings following the realization of one's own Buddhahood.

It clarifies that after attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, all habitual tendencies of the great compassionate wisdom-conduct are completely exhausted; thus, although one performs the myriad practices of Samantabhadra, one remains unstained by the world—hence it is named the "Chapter on Transcending the World."
The "Universal Worthy Practices prior to attaining the Buddha-fruit" clarify that which one personally rides; they encourage others to study for the sake of the Buddha-fruit.

The "Universal Worthy Practices subsequent [to attaining the fruit]" occur once one's own Buddha-fruit is finalized; these consist purely of benefiting others, and by means of this, they enable the Three Jewels to remain uninterrupted.
The ten penetrations (*abhijñā*) and the ten patiences (*kṣānti*) are also like the ten concentrations (*samādhi*); they pervade all five stages, their essence penetrating from beginning to end.
"Penetration" (*tong*) signifies the meaning of universal and comprehensive illumination.
"Patience" is the gateway to the patience of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).
"Asaṃkhyeya" is the gateway that clarifies numerical quantity.
"Life span" is the gateway that clarifies how the Buddha’s life span accords with sentient beings.

The "abodes of the bodhisattvas" clarifies the places where bodhisattvas dwell; it shows that the spheres of their activity for gathering and transforming sentient beings, as well as their sustaining of the teachings, are ever-present and never extinguished.

The "inconceivable dharmas of the Buddha" clarifies that the Tathāgata’s mastery over the rules and methods of his transformative manifestations is not something known by those of the two vehicles or those who study the provisional teachings of the three vehicles.

The "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks and Signs of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata" is intended to clarify that each of the ten Vairocanas within the ten world-oceans possesses ninety-seven kinds of marks, as well as marks numbering as many as the atoms in a lotus-treasury world-system.

The "Chapter on the Merits of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance" is intended to clarify the merit of the Tathāgata’s minor marks and radiance illuminating all, and the benefits obtained by those who receive this light.
The "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" elucidates the practice of advancing toward the fruition.

The "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata" elucidates that the Bodhisattvas of the five stages have reached the culmination of their own-power fruition, manifesting the ultimate stage of cause and effect.
The "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) clarifies that following the attainment of the Buddha-fruit, there is exclusively the benefit of others.
These aforementioned thirty-nine chapters of the sutra conclude the causal stages of the six and five positions, extending their benefits to the various devas and hosts of divine kings.
In the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter of the sutra, the Tathāgata enters the Lion’s Yawn Samādhi, thereby again illustrating how the five stages of the Buddha-fruit benefit the human realm.
Previously, I summarized the dharma-gates concerning the causes and effects of the Buddha’s stages within the first two assemblies and up to the seventh assembly of the eleventh stage.
The eighth assembly took place in Jeta Grove; this shall be further recounted later.

The tenth section clarifies that those who have attained actual realization are instructed: from the eighth assembly, within the Jeta Grove, the Tathāgata entered the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the lion’s yawn samādhi), once again manifesting the fruit and virtue of the *dharmadhātu* throughout all worlds, causing beings to give rise to faith and joy as they hear of the Buddha’s true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Five hundred śrāvakas—Maudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and the others—manifested as if they had not heard [the teaching], thereby paralleling the presence of both faith and lack of faith among those of the Two Vehicles.

Just as in the first assembly there were fifty groups, so too did ten leaders of bodhisattvas such as Jñānottara, ten forest-dwelling bodhisattvas such as Guṇakara, ten banner-bearing bodhisattvas such as Vajradhvaja, and thirty-seven treasury-holding bodhisattvas such as Vajragarbha each assemble with a number of bodhisattvas equal to the atoms within ten buddha-fields. These numbers doubled according to their respective positions to establish the various ranks, enabling all devas, humans, and ordinary beings to attain this Dharma-gate.
In this assembly, six thousand bhikṣus were clearly ordinary persons, yet before Mañjuśrī they suddenly attained clarity regarding the ten ears and ten eyes.
Although these members of the multitude had conceived the aspiration while on the road, their sphere of experience did not depart from the Buddha’s assembly.
Setting forth the aspiration on the road serves as a demonstration of progress in cultivation; it does not mean that one has immediately departed from the Buddha’s assembly.

This continues through to the ninth assembly at the eastern side of the City of Enlightenment, where ten thousand nāgas, five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, five hundred boys, and five hundred girls were present. Because Puming was an ordinary person who attained the rank of Buddhahood together with them, it is said here that he causes ordinary beings to realize the truth.

In the ninth assembly, at the site of the great stupa of a past buddha to the east of the city of Vārāṇasī, Mañjuśrī expounded the Sūtra-gate of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm; immeasurable dragons attained birth in the human realm, and ten thousand dragons resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta.
Although all five groups from the city of Awakening ascended together to the fruit of Buddhahood, only Sudhana is cited as the leader; this same principle applies to the number five hundred.
The number five hundred symbolizes the five stages.
The "six thousand" represents the six stages, with faith also included therein.
The "ten thousand dragons" represent the gateway of the ten thousand practices; since not a single matter is established in vain, they all represent Dharma-gates.

Regarding the great stūpas of the Buddhas of the past as the sites for their assemblies serves to clarify that the traces of the path of ancient Buddhas and present Buddhas are not different, being identical in every respect to those within the assembly of the Tathāgata.

Sudhana’s southern journey to visit his spiritual friends further clarifies the progressive cultivation [of the path] and elucidates the modes of activity through which Bodhisattvas gather and transform sentient beings.

As for the tenth assembly, it comprises all lands, atoms, spaces, and the entire dharma-realm; these ten assemblies pervade every atom within all lands, within space, and within the dharma-realm, as well as the pores of the bodies of sentient beings. Thus, they form a sea-like assembly of infinite layers upon layers, without end.

Regarding this Dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit within the Dharma-realm, those who possess faith and understanding, as well as those who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment and enter it, are like the cub of a lion king at the time of its birth. Although it is not yet able to match the power, majesty, and sovereign mastery of the lion king, the lion’s characteristics are entirely present without difference, and all beasts must stand in awe.

It is likewise for those who have faith and understanding in the dharma-gates of the Buddha-fruit in this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and who have first begun to realize and enter them; they are able to believe that the nature and characteristics of their own body and mind are, in their entirety, identical to the self-substance of all Buddhas' fruition, which is eternally true and fundamentally great wisdom.

Furthermore, those who realize and enter this state share the gateway to the Buddha-fruit of all Tathāgatas; it is fundamentally without cultivation or construction, for its very essence is the complete Buddha.
By means of this true gateway, one fully advances through the myriad differentiated practices of cultivation, which are eternally without beginning or end—the singular, true fruit-virtue.
Although one has not yet been able to exercise power and function like a Buddha, this is called "planting the seed of Buddhahood.
The seed resides within the field of the body, taking faith as its beginning.

For those who enter through the power of concentration and wisdom, at the moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment—the head of the ten stages (*bhūmi*)—they enter the wisdom of the Buddha. This is called being born into the family of the Buddha and becoming a true son of the Buddha; because they share the same Buddha-wisdom and are fully endowed with all the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness, they immediately transcend the three vehicles and attain the vision of the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the *abhijñā* Bodhisattvas.

It is beyond the reach of the wisdom of all those of the three vehicles, devas, humans, and non-Buddhist practitioners; therefore, those whose faculties are capable should single-mindedly practice it.
