Compiled by the Elder Li Tongxuan:
I bow my head to the pure ocean of the ten directions, to the true retribution-body Vairocana of the Dharma-realm,
to the Bodhisattvas of the causes and effects of the six stages, and to the great ocean-like assembly of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
The Dharma-gate of the pure ocean, the vajra-verse of perfect fruition and virtue—
now I shall explain this subtle and wondrous scripture, desiring to bring vast benefit to all sentient beings,
so that they may be unimpeded regarding this Dharma-gate and all who see or hear it shall obtain great benefit.
I only pray that all the Sages will bestow their protection, so that we may all become equal to the pure ocean of Vairocana.
Now, in expounding the teachings and propagating the sutras, one must distinguish four meanings:

first, the long-term structural analysis of the sutra’s intent; second, clarifying the core tenets and purpose of the sutra; third, clarifying the essence of the teaching; and fourth, clarifying the total number of assemblies presented.
To outline the intent of this extensive scripture, it is briefly divided into ten sections and one thousand subsections:

first, clarifying the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment; second, clarifying the exaltation of the fruit to encourage practice; third, clarifying how the fruit establishes faith; fourth, clarifying entry into the realization of reality; fifth, clarifying the initiation of practice and cultivation; sixth, clarifying the mutual integration of wisdom and compassion; seventh, clarifying the accumulation of cultivation to perfect virtue; eighth, clarifying unimpeded benefit for sentient beings; ninth, clarifying the provisional stations of the various sages; and tenth, clarifying the actualization of realization by ordinary beings.
First, the clarification of the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment refers to the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of World Rulers.

Second, the citation of the fruit to encourage practice refers to the five chapters of scripture from the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" down to the "Chapter on Vairocana," as well as the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of World Rulers," which cites the fruit accomplished by the Buddha to cause others to practice.

Regarding the three insights that establish faith through their fruition: these consist of the six chapters of the sutra from the "Chapter on the Names of the Buddhas" down to the "Chapter on Worthy Leaders.
They also comprehensively include everything from the preceding "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World Rulers" onwards.

One then takes the ten Wisdom Buddhas as the fruit of one’s own mind, with Akṣobhya-jñāna Buddha at their head, to clarify that the wisdom of one's own mind is unmoved by its various modes of conceptual differentiation.

Regarding the fourth clarification, the entry into the realization of reality, this refers to the six chapters of the sūtra beginning from the "Chapter on Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru. It takes the Ten Abodes as its essence, because one dwells in the house of the Buddha’s wisdom and is born therein.

Regarding the practitioner who practices through the five vidyās, this refers to the four chapters of the sutra beginning from the "Chapter on Ascending to the Yāma Heaven Palace"; these take the ten practices as their essence, for they practice the conduct of the Buddha.

Regarding the sixth, the mutual entry of wisdom and compassion: this refers to the three chapters of the sutra beginning from the "Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. It takes the ten dedications as its essence; because it perfects both the ultimate and conventional truths, it accomplishes great compassion.

Seventh, regarding the virtues accomplished through the cultivation of the aggregates: this refers to the "Ten Grounds Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) within the *Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations* (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), because it brings to fruition the habitual practice of the first three dharmas of aggregate cultivation.

Eighth, regarding the unimpeded illumination for benefiting sentient beings: this encompasses the eleven chapters from the "Ten Grounds" (*Daśabhūmi*) onwards up to the "Universal Good Conduct" (*Samantabhadra-caryā*). Because one accumulates virtues and accomplishes the stages within the ten grounds, and fulfills the practices for benefiting sentient beings in the eleventh ground, one is then designated as a Buddha whose Dharma-practice is perfected.

From beginning to end, its unconditioned essence does not shift by even a hair’s breadth or a single thought-moment. This is because the nature of the great wisdom of the perfectly luminous *dharmadhātu* serves as the initial stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) for the ten abodes; for it is free from temporal thoughts, lacks inherent existence across the three periods of time, and is the totality of all time. This is not something known through emotional consciousness (*vijñāna*), but is encountered solely through wisdom (*jñāna*).

Ninth, regarding the clarification of the various stages of the worthy ones: these refer to the aforementioned thirty-seven classes of bodhisattvas as well as the Buddhas, and also the "Chapter on Appearing in the World. All of them manifest their bodies through skillful means from within the realm of the great wisdom of the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*). They establish the dharma-gates of the eleven stages—consisting of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment—so that ordinary beings may believe in, enter, and emulate them. By following these traces, they will not be deluded regarding the actual reality.

The tenth [chapter] clarifies that for those who have realized the reality of ordinary beings, the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the other six positions are established within the nature of the *dharmadhātu* as skillful means for progressive cultivation.

Throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one does not depart from the essence and its function, nor does one impair the skillful means; thus, while their wisdom becomes ever more sublime, their conduct becomes ever more humble. Because they fulfill their practice according to the capacities of sentient beings, it is called "progressive cultivation."

According to one's capacity and capability, one establishes the various stages; according to the stages, one practices with knowledge so as not to be deluded regarding cause and effect. This enables the student to clearly understand both the general and the specific, to achieve success based on the traces [of practice], and thus neither stagnate at the beginning nor depart from the origin.

As stated in the following text, the assembly of Sudhana and others—consisting of laymen (*upāsaka*), laywomen (*upāsikā*), youths, and maidens—is each listed as five hundred; these fully elucidate the five stages of the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), ten practices (*caryā*), ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground, with ten members in each stage totaling five hundred.
Regarding the six thousand bhikṣus, they were collectively called "six thousand" because their faith was likewise non-retrogressive.
As for the ten thousand nāgas, they were used to illustrate the ten thousand practices (*sāhasrikā-caryā*).

Such a multitude were all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), yet because they all believed in this Dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit wisdom-realm (*dharmadhātu-buddhaphala-jñāna-viṣaya*), they ascended to the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*) and the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*); therefore, it is said that "ordinary beings are made to realize the reality."
The above ten sections conclude the general outline of the meaning of the sutra; the detailed meaning therein will be clarified as we reach the specific passages.

For instance, the single chapter on the "Dharma-realm" (Dharmadhātu) comprehensively encompasses the preceding and following forty chapters of the sutra, because it is the totality of the Dharma-realm, and because it clarifies that the dharmas of the three periods of time are all the totality of the Dharma-realm.
This single chapter, "The Dharma Realm," is the fruition of all Buddhas and all sentient beings.
Within this one sutra, there are five types of meanings regarding the pervasive nature of cause and effect.

First, the universal pervasiveness of the causes and effects for attaining perfect enlightenment, which comprises the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Lord" (*Lokēśvararāja-vyūha*) and the five subsequent chapters.

Second, the universal pervasiveness of the causes and effects for the stage of faith and progressive cultivation, comprising the six chapters from the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Name" (*Buddhanāma*) onwards; these ten chapters in total encompass the stages of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmana*), and the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*).
Third is the pervasiveness of the essence of the concentrations, which refers to the chapters on the "Ten Concentrations," the "Ten Supernatural Powers," and the "Ten Endurances.
Fourth is the pervasiveness of the ocean of practices, which refers to the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" and the "Chapter on Leaving the World."
The inconceivable great ocean of wisdom of the five dharma-realms pervades everywhere; this is precisely the "Dharmadhātu Chapter.
Because it contains these five meanings of pervasive presence, this single scripture consists of five chapters.

Within these five chapters, the opening of each chapter states, "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha," serving as the heading for the chapter. This clarifies that these five dharmas are of one time, one dharma-realm, one kṣaṇa-limit, and one essence-and-function; they are the common dharma shared by all Buddhas, a single cause and effect, which is equally pervasive and perfect, devoid of any sense of sequence or priority.
All Buddhas are likewise in this way.

Such a Dharma does not depart from even a single kṣaṇa within the ten concentrations; from the descent of the spirit and entry into the womb, to the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood and entering Nirvāṇa, it does not depart from that single kṣaṇa, nor is there any further shifting.

In this single volume of scripture, there are five instances of the phrase "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha. With the exception of the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," these collectively clarify the fundamental essence and purport of this entire sutra: the great, perfect, and bright wisdom of the single Dharmadhātu, which possesses these five kinds of all-pervasive causes and effects.

From the initial stage of faith through the cultivation of all practices, the causal and resultant actions are perfected from beginning to end; yet ultimately, they do not transcend the essence of the ten concentrations and the nature of non-temporality. Ordinary beings and sages are entirely equal, for it has been thus from the very beginning.
The duration of time arises in accordance with the deluded attachments of sentient beings; because of these deluded attachments, birth and old age come to exist.
If one gives rise to views of extension or contraction regarding the fundamental Dharma-realm, these are all merely one's own deluded perceptions, for they do not truly exist.

Thus, those who are deluded regarding the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature, who contravene the dharma-gate of the wisdom-realm that is primordially timeless, and who pursue their own emotions and follow deluded perceptions of time and eons as being extended or abbreviated, do not establish the seed of faith within the Buddha’s true Dharma.

It should be understood that even if such persons practice and attain the fruits of transcending the triple world, they lack the seed for attaining Buddhahood; these are precisely the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the provisional teachings who possess the six supernormal powers.
Even the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* cannot know this.
This clarifies that it is non-retrogression regarding the transcendence of birth and death, not non-retrogression while still remaining within the realm of birth and death.

Furthermore, one merely uses the contemplation of emptiness to subdue manifest afflictions and enter the stage of the Path of Seeing at the first bhūmi; it is not by means of penetrating fundamental ignorance that one attains non-retrogression within fundamental wisdom.

Thus, the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the three vehicles are all bodhisattvas of the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*); none of them possess the non-retrogressive capacity, such as attaining Buddhahood in the ten directions within the initial stage of the dwelling of great perfect wisdom in the fundamental realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*): those of the first, second, and third stages are called the mind-made body of the bliss of meditative absorption (*samāpatti-sukha-manomaya-kāya*); those of the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are called the mind-made body that awakens to the self-nature of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva-abhisambodhi-manomaya-kāya*); and those of the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are called the mind-made body that is spontaneously born in accordance with its class and is free from effort (*nikāya-sahaja-anābhoga-manomaya-kāya*).

These three kinds of mind-made bodies of Bodhisattvas are all the great, perfectly round, and luminous ocean of wisdom of the Dharma-realm; they are established as provisional skillful means—the three vehicles outside the gate of the burning house—to enable the children to temporarily escape the calamity of the fire.
As stated in the subsequent passage of this sutra: "The śrāvakas in the assembly were as if deaf.
Even if bodhisattvas endowed with the six supernormal powers were to hear this sutra, they would be unable to give rise to faith," as explained in detail in the scripture.

Since beginningless time, even if one were to develop faith in the Buddha-dharma, it would be merely a faith born of emotional attachment; because one is deluded regarding the realm of one’s own wisdom, there is no realization of actual wisdom from which true faith and practice could arise.
If one does not turn the mind [toward enlightenment], one will ultimately fail to attain Buddhahood.

Even if one were to teach and transform sentient beings, one could only achieve the seeds of the Three Vehicles and the realms of humans and devas; one would merely abide in a single pure land, lacking the great function of boundless wisdom that is as vast as the ocean and equal in measure to empty space.

Physical bodies manifest in response throughout the lands as numerous as atoms in the ten directions, guiding and receiving all sentient beings according to their faculties; yet, while there is no distinction among the three vehicles, it is simply said that they perceive the realm of the trichiliocosm.
As stated in this sutra: "There are oceans of worlds, natures of worlds, and lineages of worlds; all are profoundly deep and vast, equal to the dharma-realm and space."
This is as described in the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World.

Just as within the Three Vehicles, even if one were to see the Tathāgata’s body with its thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics—or even if it were further expanded to eighty-four thousand—such a person would not see the Tathāgata’s body and its accompanying marks and characteristics, which are equal in number to the atoms of ten Buddha-fields.

Those of the three vehicles perceive only the Tathāgata’s transformations filling the trichiliocosm through equal practices; they do not perceive the Tathāgata’s transformations filling as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in the infinite realms through such practices.

The seeds of the three vehicles and all that they accomplish have limits and measures; yet, within every single atom of the dharma-realm, one does not see the infinite dharmas of Samantabhadra’s practices, which interpenetrate one another without obstruction.
Second, regarding the clarification of the scripture’s central theme and purpose, there are six points:

first, clarifying the scripture’s central theme and purpose; second, identifying which collection (piṭaka) this scripture is subsumed under; third, distinguishing its introductory section (nidāna); fourth, determining its main body (samyak-siddhānta); fifth, clarifying to whom this scripture was entrusted; and sixth, clarifying where this scripture circulates.

First, to clarify the essential purport of the sutra: this scripture is titled *Vairocana*, whose great wisdom is the fundamental reality of the dharma-realm; its self-substance is the perfection of both quiescence and function, and its fruit-virtues—the dharma-body and reward-body—are non-obstructive in essence and appearance. The Buddha’s own vehicle is its central theme.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Riding this precious vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment.

Furthermore, this sutra says: "For those who delight in seeking the fruit of Buddhahood, [the Buddha] speaks of the most excellent vehicle, the superior vehicle, the unsurpassed vehicle, the inconceivable vehicle," and so forth. This is because it causes those who have first resolved their minds toward awakening to aspire to the vast [path], so that they may attain the fruit of such great wisdom of the Tathāgata, becoming one with their own wisdom, non-dual and inseparable.

The essential purport of this sutra is profoundly deep and difficult to believe. If there are those who have faith, their merit would surpass that obtained by serving Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields for the duration of an entire kalpa; yet it would not equal the merit of having faith in the gate of the Buddha-fruit and the dharma-realm—the sphere of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom—contained within this sutra. The merit of such faith is superior to the former.

As stated in a verse later in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (Bhadrapāla-parivarta): "There may be one who holds ten buddha-fields in his hand and remains suspended in mid-air for an entire kalpa;
what he does is not considered difficult, but to be able to believe in this Dharma is exceedingly difficult."
If one were to bestow all articles of pleasure upon as many sentient beings as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields for the duration of an eon, the merit thereof would not be supreme;
one who has faith in this Dharma is the most supreme.
If one were to serve Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields for the duration of an entire kalpa,
yet if one can recite and uphold this chapter, that merit would be far more supreme than the former.

Furthermore, the preceding verse states: "Among all the multitudes of living beings in all worlds, few desire to seek the Śrāvaka vehicle; those who seek the Pratyekabuddha vehicle are even fewer still; and those who set out upon the Mahāyāna are exceedingly rare."
"To aspire to the Mahāyāna is still relatively easy, but to be able to believe in this Dharma is many times more difficult.
This was said to clarify that the essential purpose of this sutra is profoundly deep and difficult to believe.
Those who practice the contemplation of emptiness may cease their delusions and cultivate dhyāna, yet they still harbor attachments to defilement and purity.
Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who have not yet turned their minds [toward the Great Vehicle] do not possess such a portion.

As stated in a later passage of the sutra: "Even if there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās and attained the six superknowledges (abhijñā), they would still be called a 'nominal bodhisattva' and not a 'true bodhisattva.'"

Even if one hears this sutra and does not believe or enter it—just as with the *Lotus Sutra*—it is likewise for the purpose of turning those of the three vehicles back toward the One Vehicle. It is to turn those who were drawn out by the provisional three carts outside the gate, leading them back to the true gate of the Tathāgata’s Great Vehicle, the realm of wisdom and reality (*dharmadhātu*).
Because it shatters the reliance upon limited platforms and conditions, it enables one to attain the Tathāgata’s wisdom of dwelling without dependence and its fundamental mastery.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was taught immediately upon the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment for those of superior faculties; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was taught during the forty years following the Buddha’s appearance in the world for the purpose of turning those of the three vehicles back [toward the One Vehicle].

Furthermore, the Buddha-vehicle and the three vehicles are taught simultaneously as a whole; yet, according to individual faculties, each responds accordingly, and within the single-sound dharma-gate there are distinct differences, giving rise to both general and specific meanings.
Because the true essence is timeless, there is nothing that can be designated as prior or posterior.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third."
"Except for the Buddha’s skillful means, which uses merely provisional names to guide sentient beings.
It further says: "Only this one reality is true; the other two are not real."
Regarding "the other two": it is only the gateway mounted by all Buddhas of the ten directions that is considered real, while the three vehicles are the "other two.

Because those which are merely expedient and not yet true are the "other two," the One Reality is contrasted with all expedients; thus, all are the "other two. This is because the *Lotus Sūtra* rebukes the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive bodhisattvas of the three vehicles for their inability to believe in the Dharma of the One Vehicle.

For bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching, although they possess a partial aspiration for bodhi, they still harbor fear of birth and death; thus, while they may attain non-retrogression by becoming free from defilement, they have not yet attained the non-retrogression of the true equality of defilement and purity.

For instance, Bodhisattvas who cultivate the contemplation of emptiness find their delight in emptiness increasingly superior; likewise, those who exclusively practice the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness) and are free from entanglements both possess longing and aversion.

Furthermore, various assemblies of Bodhisattvas who aspire to be born in pure lands and the like are all able to leave birth-and-death, transcend entanglements, and attain non-retrogression; yet because they have not entered the ocean of the nature of the Dharma-realm—the single truth that is free from the gates of longing and aversion—compared to this Buddha Vehicle, both those who delight in birth-and-death and those who loathe birth-and-death are considered to be retrogressing.

If one practices the gate of contemplating emptiness with increasing excellence and cultivates the gate of conventional truth and suchness, practicing the six pāramitās and attaining the six supernormal powers, this constitutes non-retrogression from birth and death; it is not because of non-retrogression within the single nature of birth and death and nirvāṇa.
For this reason, the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* state that Bodhisattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers do not hear or believe in this sūtra.

As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "If one were to uphold the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, expounding them for others and causing all listeners to attain the six supernormal powers, this would not yet be difficult; however, to hear and receive this sūtra is truly difficult."
Only this realm of wisdom contradicts what the intellect habitually understands; therefore, it is extremely difficult to believe.
The faith and understanding of the Three Vehicles accord with what the intellect delights in. Why is this so?
It is taught that the fruit of Buddhahood occurs only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, and that the Buddha’s pure land is located in another direction, while this Sahā world is a defiled land.
Those who cultivate bodhi feel revulsion for impurity and delight in the true, aspiring to be born in a pure land.

Even those bodhisattvas who remain in the world are said to retain afflictions to sustain their rebirths for the sake of saving sentient beings; this is not because they are compelled by the natural power of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to act in such a manner.
Such teachings regarding bodhisattvas all accord with worldly sentiments, for such doctrines are easy to believe.

This sutra is not like them; it teaches that entry into the fruit of Buddhahood does not exceed a single kṣaṇa, being separated from delusion and awakening by nothing more than that, and it teaches that immeasurable kalpas do not, in total, depart from a single moment.

It is taught that when one first attains the Path from the stage of an ordinary person, cause and effect are simultaneous, lacking any temporal sequence. One does not perceive a time before becoming a Buddha, nor does one perceive a time of attaining perfect enlightenment; one does not perceive the severance of afflictions, nor does one perceive the realization of Bodhi. Ultimately, there is not even the slightest movement of thought. Upon completing the cultivation of the fifty stages, the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is fully accomplished.

Because the simultaneous mastery over the totality and its particulars, their identity and difference, and their formation and disintegration is not something perceived by worldly intellect, it is difficult to believe.

That which is to be believed is as described in the subsequent section of the sutra regarding the stage of the Ten Faiths: in the Golden World, there is the Buddha Immovable Wisdom, whose principal Bodhisattva is named Mañjuśrī, which in this language means "Wondrous Virtue."
That which is called "golden-colored" is bright, pure, and stainless; it is the principle of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*Acalajñāna*) is the wisdom within that principle, for it is equally shared by the bodies of all ordinary beings and sages.
In every place there is Mañjuśrī; in every place there is the Golden World; in every place there is Acala-jñāna Buddha.
Those who now have faith should believe that the nature of their own mind, which is non-abiding, is the wondrous wisdom of liberation—this is Mañjuśrī himself.

Within the state where the mind has no basis for abiding, there is sovereign discernment regarding the wondrous principle of non-substantiality; because this non-substantiality cannot be moved, it is named the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*Acalamati-jñāna*).
Since the wisdom of principle and its wondrous function are non-dual and possess sovereign mastery, he is therefore titled the Bodhisattva of Wondrous Virtue (*Mañjuśrī*).
Therefore, all Buddhas are born from this faith; thus, Mañjuśrī is called the mother of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
He is also called the Youthful Bodhisattva because all [Buddhas] take faith as their primary birth.

When the accomplishment of faith is achieved, it is immediately sealed by the power of wisdom through the contemplation of samādhi and prajñā; when these accord in a single thought-moment, this is called attaining perfect enlightenment at the initial stage of the Ten Abodes.
Taking up the sphere of practice, he is named Samantabhadra.
Taking up the sphere of wondrous wisdom that is without dependence, he is named Mañjuśrī.
Taking up the wisdom that skillfully discerns and knows the faculties [of beings], he is named Akṣobhyajñāna Buddha.
To be in accord with this intrinsic realization is called "right awakening.
To be able to abide in faith is termed "faithful mind.

To be in accord with this intrinsic realization is termed "abiding mind," for one abides in the wondrous wisdom where the Buddhas abide; therein, the marks of liberation are exhausted, as all phenomena are non-arising.
If one perceives a Buddha as existing outside of the mind, this is not called "faith" but is termed being a person of false views.

All Buddhas are identical to one's own mind; all sentient beings are identical to one's own nature. Because this nature has no dependence, its essence is without differentiation, and its wisdom is of a single nature.
One should know it thus.

By means of this wondrous wisdom of identical essence, one knows the minds of all Buddhas and the minds of sentient beings; one should believe and understand it in this way, without deceiving oneself.

Therefore, the essential purport of this sutra is to establish such a Dharma for sentient beings of great resolve. It is the wondrous scripture of the One Vehicle—the gateway through which the Buddhas themselves have traveled—and the principle of the *dharmadhātu*. It causes sentient beings of great resolve to enter the fundamental wisdom of the Buddha and the state of Buddhahood; for by realizing the truth-wisdom in a single thought-moment, they immediately manifest as Buddhas.

This is according to the principle of the *dharmadhātu*, for when seen [in its true nature], there is no beginning, middle, or end. For those of inferior understanding belonging to the three vehicles, who differ from this, it is appropriate that they hear that one ascends to the fruit of Buddhahood through three incalculable eons; it is appropriate that it be taught that Śākyamuni’s pure land lies elsewhere and that this Sahā world is a defiled land.

Therefore, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, for the sake of those whose understanding of the three vehicles is inferior, it causes the dragon girl—who was not a [conventional] vessel—to attain Buddhahood in an instant; this clarifies that the vastness of faith is not a provisional device but is the teaching of reality, because the real teaching one cultivates is neither circuitous nor stagnant.
The statement that the dragon girl was eight years old signifies that she has begun her studies in this present life and is not one who has studied since antiquity.

Her being a female animal indicates that she did not achieve this through cultivation accumulated in past lives; this clarifies that in this very life, her faith in the principles of the Dharma-gate is direct and unimpeded.

The essential nature of the Dharma-realm is not encompassed by the three periods of time; when a single thought-moment accords with reality, the sentiments of the three periods are exhausted, for wisdom that neither arises nor perishes is itself the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, a sutra says: "To deliver sentient beings of inferior understanding, he manifests such matters as the eight marks."
Regarding the passage: "The entire assembly of the Sahā world saw from afar the dragon girl immediately proceeding to the southern world of Vimalā to attain Buddhahood," the commentary explains:
"The south signifies illumination and correctness, as it presides over the element of Fire (Li)."
Li represents illumination, the sun, and emptiness—that is, freedom from defilement.

As for "the multitude seeing from afar," this clarifies that those who study the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles have faith but have not yet realized it for themselves; hence, they are said to see from afar.
Now, the Dharma-realm is the single truth in which self and other are mutually penetrating; if one has already attained it oneself, how could it be called "seeing from afar"?
This sutra enables Sudhana to attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime.

Regarding "the birth of non-arising": after one has given rise to faith from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the initial mind of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) accords with non-arising.
This means that one is born by the power of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, not born through karma; this will be explained extensively in the text.
Now, to briefly set forth the ultimate aim of this sutra’s core doctrine regarding the Dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit, the broad-minded and sagacious gentleman may reflect upon it at length.

Second, as for clarifying which treasury (piṭaka) this sutra is subsumed under: this sutra is named the Vairocana Dharmadhātu Treasury, for it completely contains and stores all Dharma-gates within the ocean of the pervasive Dharmadhātu. This sutra is not permitted to be categorized among the provisional teachings of the transformation Buddhas of the Three Vehicles, nor is it something that can be known or understood by ordinary sentient beings.

In the Transformation Buddha’s teaching, the assembly of bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles cannot understand the Dharma-gate of the Reward Buddha’s One True Dharma-realm, because they know only the distinct dharmas of the three vehicles.

If these bodhisattvas only know that the trichiliocosm is the realm of a single recompense Buddha, and that the thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are transformation bodies, they do not understand this Dharma-gate taught by the recompense Buddha of the real recompense dharma-realm of this One Vehicle.

Therefore, this sutra is further named the Vairocana Dharmadhātu; it is subsumed within the ocean of wisdom of the Buddha-fruit, and is not the same as that which is included in the provisional Bodhisattva-piṭaka taught within the transformation teachings of the Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles.

Therefore, in the subsequent "Dharmadhātu Chapter," the name of the pavilion where Maitreya resides is the Vairocana-alaṃkāra-garbha. Once Sudhana has entered it, he sees only the inexhaustible marks of merit and the adornments of the fruits of practice—the Dharma-treasuries of immeasurable Buddhas—all numbering incalculable *asaṃkhyeya*. Each of these is described in detail as set forth in the sutra.

This refers to the practice of the Dharma-teachings as taught by Vairocana Buddha; because the cause of such Dharma-practice results in the attainment of the palaces and towers where one dwells—being formed through the causes and effects of practicing according to the Dharma-realm treasury (dharmadhātu-garbha)—and because even the causes and effects of the adornments obtained as the fruition of all Buddhas are likewise so.
"Treasury" (garbha) carries the meaning of "containing. It contains all dharmas within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), for the causes and effects of all dharma-gates are inexhaustible.

While the sutras of the Three Vehicles often use the sands of the Ganges as a standard of comparison for the number of dharma-gates to establish the sense of vastness, the sutras of this One Vehicle often use the atoms of a single Buddha-field, ten Buddha-fields, or even the atoms of immeasurable Buddha-fields as the standard of comparison for the number of dharmas.
Furthermore, while the characteristics of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles consist of numbers such as one, two, three, seven, eight, nine, or ten,
each dharma-gate within this sutra is fully endowed with the number ten, thereby clarifying that the dharma-gates of the Buddha-fruit are complete and perfect.
Since the names that designate them differ in their breadth and narrowness, the Dharma-treasuries (dharmakośa) and Dharmas must necessarily be distinct.
Therefore, this sutra is subsumed within the treasury of Vairocana, as it is not included within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka of the Three Vehicles.
This sutra constantly takes the fruit of Buddhahood as the track for progressive cultivation; it is the ancient site of the Buddha’s fundamental great wisdom.
Because one cultivates the wisdom of distinctions, if there were a progressive cultivation that diverged from this ancient site of the Buddha, there would be no principle of attaining Buddhahood.

As with the three vehicles, one merely avoids a portion of the coarse suffering of birth and death; this is not yet relying on the ancient traces of the essence of the Buddha’s wisdom to practice the Buddha-vehicle.
Therefore, this sutra is subsumed within the Vairocana-treasury and is not included within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka of the three vehicles.
Regarding the division of the *Tri-vidyā* (Threefold Knowledge) into its introductory section (*nidāna*), it is divided into two gates:
first, that which encompasses the entire treatise; second, that which belongs specifically to the present chapter.
That which encompasses the entire treatise is the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruling Lord" (*Lokendra-vyuha*).

Second, each chapter has its own introductory section (*nidāna*). As is the case within each chapter of the sutra, every assembly contains the phrase "At that time, thus," which serves as the introduction to the meaning contained within that chapter.
Furthermore, throughout this single section of the sutra, the location of the Bodhimaṇḍa where the World-Honored One resides is introduced five times from beginning to end.
Question: Why is it thus?
Answer:

From the first volume, beginning with "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Magadha," it clarifies that the place where he first attained Buddhahood was within an araṇya (a forest hermitage).

Next, in the second assembly, it is further stated: "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment in the forest retreat (araṇya-dharma-bodhimaṇḍa), having just attained perfect awakening. This clarifies that he did not move from his original location to reside in a retributive dwelling; rather, the Universal Radiance Hall represents the dwelling attained as the fruition of the practice of wisdom and principle. It indicates that by relying on the realization of the forest retreat—which accords with worldly conventions—he has finally arrived at this dwelling.

From this point onward, regarding their ascent to the celestial palaces, it is universally stated that "without leaving their original location, their bodies sit pervasively in all places of practice," or it is said that "they ascend to such-and-such a heaven."
"Those who ascend to heaven" clarifies the advancement through successive stages of cultivation.

"Not shifting from their original place" clarifies the principle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); for the wondrous principle of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) has no coming or going, nor internal or external, and because the essence of great wisdom is inherently all-pervasive.

Furthermore, within the forty fascicles [of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*], the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" (*Daśadharmasamādhiparivarta*) states: "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) for the dharma of the araṇya, having just attained perfect awakening; he entered the samādhi of the 'limit of the kṣaṇa' within the Hall of Universal Radiance. This clarifies that the dharma-realm and the dharma-body constitute the substance of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because they lack the nature of the three periods of time.

From descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the womb, and attaining parinirvāṇa, his forty-year residence in the world and turning of all wheels of Dharma do not, in total, transcend the limit of a single kṣaṇa; for through this samādhi, the beginning and end are perfectly interfused, being neither of the three periods of time nor of past and present.

To summarize this introductory sequence: all Buddhas of the past, present, and future attain Buddhahood simultaneously, and the birth and death of sentient beings likewise does not shift by even a single kṣaṇa; it is only due to the deluded attachments of sentient beings that there appear to be long and short durations of years.
As the Buddha has taught, birth and death occur without even a moment’s interval passing.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: “In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus, one thoroughly knows the affairs of the three periods of time and, transcending all expedient means, accomplishes the ten powers.”
This single chapter of the sutra summarizes the beginning, middle, and end: there is no coming or going, and the nature of past and present is exhausted.

It clarifies that from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), by a single thought of generating the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one suddenly perceives the Way. One then advances through the practices of the five stages—the ten abodes (*vihāra*), ten practices (*caryā*), ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground—attaining Buddhahood, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering *nirvāṇa*, all without shifting by even a single *kṣaṇa*. This is because the gate of the *dharmadhātu* is used as the means for opening, showing, awakening, and entering; it clarifies that such is the nature of the gate of the *dharmadhātu* of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the True Teaching (*saddharma*). Therefore, it is elucidated through the names of various *samādhis*.

This chapter comprehensively presents this gateway of the quiescent function of the fundamental dharma-realm of the One Vehicle; since it is a single limit from beginning to end without distinctions of origin or conclusion, or temporal sequence, it serves as the head of attaining Buddhahood.

The same applies to the subsequent "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*). The introductory section, which extends from "Just Attaining Perfect Enlightenment" up to "the Hall of Universal Radiance," serves as the occasion for Samantabhadra Bodhisattva entering the Buddha-flower Samādhi (*buddhapuṣpa-samādhi*).
"Buddha-flower" refers to the Buddha-activities that have been cultivated.
"Samādhi" clarifies that the functions of quiescence and illumination are unimpeded.

That it corresponds to what was previously stated in the introduction is to clarify that the essence and function of cultivating Buddha-activities have no beginning or end; they are eternally perfect and transcendent of the three periods of time.

This chapter clarifies that cultivation is performed through the practices of Samantabhadra; furthermore, it demonstrates that the great wisdom of the essence of the Dharma-realm constantly accompanies all practices, encompassing the three periods of time while remaining unmoved from the limit of a single kṣaṇa. Thus, it clarifies that these various practices are themselves the essence and function of the Dharma-realm.
This introduction clarifies that time neither shifts nor remains stationary, because the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) has no center or periphery.
All practiced deeds are eternally equal and such-like, for in a single moment, the three periods of time neither increase nor decrease, and there is neither coming nor going.

Next, regarding the statement in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter, "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park," this introduces the main body of the teaching.

The vehicle upon which the Tathāgata rides penetrates from beginning to end; throughout the heavens, the human realm, and the worlds of the ten directions, it takes the Dharma-realm as its essence, for it is not of a false or illusory nature.

Because sentient beings follow delusion and fail to attain realization, this chapter universally presents the inconceivable Dharma-realm—encompassing the heavens, the human world, and the ten directions—in which the essence is quiescent and its function is sovereign, thereby enabling sentient beings to awaken to and enter it.

Therefore, this chapter was spoken by the Tathāgata solely through inconceivable supernormal power, without relying on verbal expression, in order to clarify that the totality of the mundane world is fundamentally true and fundamentally divine, having no arising or ceasing; and to clarify that the Dharma-realm universally encompasses all, for its beginning and end are originally a single limit.

It is unnecessary to have a separate introduction for the Bodhimanda, because enlightenment is itself the Dharma-realm; since the previous assembly was already entirely contained within this assembly of the Dharma-realm, the introduction is thus concluded.
The essence and function of the ten assemblies are all comprehensively encompassed by this chapter, for it is the fundamental matrix of the single body, single time, single nature, and single wisdom.
These five perfections, which sequence the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, collectively clarify that this Dharma-realm is taught as a single moment without before or after.

Within this single scripture, the *World-Ruler’s Sublime Array Chapter*, the *Buddha’s Name-Title Chapter*, the *Ten Samādhis Chapter*, and the *Transcending the World Chapter* all four times reiterate the sequence beginning with the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment in the Universal Radiance Hall; only the *Entering the Dharma Realm Chapter* mentions the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden.
These five chapters of the sutra have, in their general purport, five kinds of Buddha-fruits that are all-pervasive, encompassing the other chapters as a whole.

The intent of these five chapters is to provide a reiteration: it concerns these five kinds of cause and fruit that pervade the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), wherein five matters are manifested instantaneously at a single momentary limit (*kṣaṇa*). They include all stages within themselves, thereby accomplishing the fruit of the great wisdom of the Dharma-realm.
Because there are five titles of sutras that are similar, yet only the *Gandavyūha* (Entering the Dharma Realm) specifically mentions the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden.
What are these five kinds of universal pervasiveness regarding cause and effect?

First, the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World-Ruler" clarifies that the fruit of Buddhahood is all-pervasive; the sūtra states: "Without moving from his original place, his body sits everywhere in all places of enlightenment."

The second, the "Chapter on the Names of the Buddhas," is spoken within the Hall of Universal Radiance; it clarifies that the Dharma-gate of the names of the Reward Body and its lands bestows transformation and benefits beings throughout all quarters.
In this assembly, six chapters of the sutra are expounded to accomplish the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) and the fruit of Buddhahood; this clarifies that the mind of faith is all-pervasive.

In the third chapter, "The Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," the Tathāgata enters the *kṣaṇa-koṭi-samādhi*. By means of this samādhi, he universally encompasses this entire sutra, such that immeasurable kalpas of the three periods of time are, in total, but a single moment—originally thus.

To harmonize with the Buddha-way, he manifests his fundamental dharma to attain Buddhahood and preach the sutras; yet at the time of his parinirvāṇa, there is no shifting or change. This clarifies that the Buddha’s great wisdom is the self-nature of the original essence, wherein the tranquil body and its functioning are eternally fixed and all-pervasive.

Even until his entry into nirvana—remaining in the world for forty years preaching the Dharma—he had not yet emerged from his mother’s womb, nor had he yet descended from Tuṣita Heaven; this is because the essence of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is such that it lacks the nature of coming and going, or of past and present.

Chapter Four, "Leaving the World," clarifies that the essence of Samantabhadra’s practice consists of the great wisdom of the inherently quiescent and concentrated nature of the dharma-realm; it thus elucidates how enlightened practice is all-pervasive.
"Buddha-flower" refers to the practice of awakening.
"Samādhi" refers to the essence of original awakening.
The fifth chapter, "Entering the Dharma Realm," clarifies that the great wisdom of the Buddha-fruit—the fundamental essence of the Dharma Realm—is all-pervasive.
These five kinds of pervasiveness collectively take the dharma-realm as their essence; they constitute, in total, a single dharma-gate of pervasiveness.
These five pervasivenesses encompass all stages and all distinctions.

Fearing that people might fail to understand and lose the intended meaning, the introductory prefaces at five locations within this single scripture are linked by their titles so as to encompass both the preceding and the following; this is to clarify that the essence of this sutra is fundamentally devoid of sequence, beginning or end, extremes or middle, and distinctions of temporal duration.
Just as a king’s precious seal stamps everything at once, forming a complete inscription without before or after, so too does the Dharma-jewel seal universally stamp all stages.

It is only because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of progress—such as the five positions, the ten abodes, and the ten practices—are different that they appear distinct; yet their nature is without differentiation. Through the principles of the ten mysteries and six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*) concerning the universal and the particular, the same and the different, and formation and disintegration, the logic of their mutual interpenetration becomes self-evident.
The meaning of these six characters constitutes three pairs of dependent origination; together, these six characters encompass all phenomena.
First, the pair of the general and the particular; second, the pair of the identical and the different; third, the pair of formation and destruction.
They are never separate; one cannot discard one while retaining the other, nor can they be established as a dual pair, nor can they both be abandoned.

All such views—of annihilationism and eternalism, arising and ceasing, or middle and extremes—are merely the domain of deluded consciousness (*citta-mātra*), failing to realize that all phenomena are spontaneously self-existent through dependent origination.
This is understood only through the power of non-conceptual, correct wisdom;
that which is known through conceptual thought is merely the realm of faith.

This refers to the Bodhisattva of the first stage observing all phenomena of dependent origination in the world: although they arise simultaneously as a whole, they are not bound by simultaneous existence.
Although they possess both the general and the particular, all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is impossible for non-bound phenomena (*aniyata-dharma*) to coexist [with them].
The same applies to the other two pairs.
All these are bound by the conceptualizations of existence and non-existence, both and neither, permanence and impermanence.
Just as all dependently originated phenomena are like echoes in space—fundamentally unconditioned, yet producing sound in response to objects.

It is like a skilled diviner of milfoil stalks and tortoise shells who, through no thought or deliberate action, and being neither a ghost nor a spirit, can respond to conditions to know all things and inform people of the good and ill fortune of past and present as clearly as looking at the back of their hand.
One should understand it thus:
things arise dependently according to the nature of phenomena (dharmas), not according to subjective sentiment.

Whether in terms of unity or multiplicity, totality or particularity, or through various categories of similarity and difference—all instances of formation and disintegration are devoid of any connection such as sequence or simultaneity.
The principle of the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm is likewise thus: none of these possess sequence, nor do existence and non-existence occur simultaneously;
whether they are together or not, whether they perish or remain, is due solely to the attachments of the deluded mind.

All these are the arising of great compassion from the very nature and the effortless great vows; they accord with the dependent origination of phenomena and correspond to non-effortful wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*), being neither old nor new.

The establishment of the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma and the manifestation of birth and extinction are all because they cannot be understood as being produced or newly coming and going; they are entirely due to the sovereign power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of non-arising and non-extinction.

Although they differ from the two vehicles in that those vehicles seek personal quiescence and realization, extinguishing emotion while losing wisdom, [the Bodhisattvas] instead give rise to great vows to benefit all sentient beings without any thought of longing; although they benefit sentient beings through great kindness and great compassion, they have no thought of attachment; although they enter the cycle of birth and death, they do not sink into the mire;
and although they abide in nirvana, their work of benefiting people throughout the worlds of the ten directions never ceases.

All of these are due to the Tathāgata’s power of wisdom which is without intrinsic nature, without dependence, and without fabrication; none of them can be interpreted in terms of past, future, or present, nor of antiquity or modernity.
Regarding the determination of the primary teaching (*zhengzong*), there are three kinds of primary teachings:

first, the primary teaching according to stages (*suowei zhengzong*); second, the primary teaching according to chapters (*suopin zhengzong*); and third, the primary teaching of the great essence (*danti zhengzong*).

First, regarding the primary teaching according to the stages: within the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and the eleventh ground, each has its own primary teaching.
The Ten Faiths take the Buddha’s fundamental immovable wisdom as their primary teaching;
the Ten Abidings take the wondrous wisdom of the rational essence and the fruit-virtue of the Tathāgata—the wisdom that realizes and enters the Dharma-realm—as their primary teaching.
In the Ten Practices, the primary teaching is the cultivation of Samantabhadra’s conduct by means of the Buddha’s fundamental wisdom.

In the Ten Transferences, the primary teaching is the fulfillment of great vows through the perfect integration of principle and wisdom and the ultimate and conventional truths, ensuring that fundamental wisdom, great compassion, and equanimity are balanced and impartial, neither biased toward stillness nor toward activity.

In the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), one cultivates compassion and wisdom through the aggregates, making them habitual until their efficacy brings about salvation; this is established as the primary teaching.

In the eleventh stage, one fulfills the ocean of the Dharma-realm through the practices of Samantabhadra that flow with the sentiments of all sentient beings, employing these to benefit living beings; this is established as the primary teaching.
This constitutes the main body of the teaching according to its respective stages.
Second, if one considers a single section of the teachings, each chapter within the forty chapters has its own main body; the title of each chapter suffices to identify its entirety.

Third, regarding the general essence and the orthodox teaching of one division: it takes the fruit of the One Vehicle Buddha-enlightenment—the nature of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom and the dharma-realm, which transcends past and present and is perfected in both essence and function—as the orthodox teaching.
One should always take this orthodox teaching of the Buddha-fruit as the basis for revealing, awakening, entering, and advancing in practice, thereby bringing it to habitual mastery and fulfillment.
Furthermore, within the forty chapters of this sutra, the "Dharmadhātu Chapter" is taken as the orthodox core, while the remaining chapters serve as its accompaniments.

It is because the Buddhas of the ten directions take the afflictions discriminated by their own minds and transform them into the essence and function of the dharma-realm of all-knowledge and all-aspect knowledge, thereby mounting it to achieve perfect enlightenment.
These root afflictions are not known by those of the three vehicles;

thus, while the followers of the two vehicles merely suppress them so that they do not arise, Bodhisattvas suppress them through the contemplation of emptiness such that they no longer manifest. This is explained in detail in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.

All sentient beings take the gate of the Dharma-realm as the means for opening, showing, awakening to, and entering it; for the fundamental wisdom of the Tathāgata is the very discriminative mind of sentient beings, and because they accord with it non-dually, they attain mastery over the Dharma-realm.
For this reason, one attains perfect enlightenment at the very first thought-moment of the Ten Abodes.

This is because the dharma-gates of the Ten Practices, Ten Transferences, Ten Grounds, and the Eleventh Ground are employed to cultivate and habituate wisdom and compassion until they are perfected; furthermore, these never depart from the essence and function of the dharma-realm wisdom of the initial thought-moment.

However, by means of this gate of the essence and function of the wisdom of the dharma-realm being without dependence or abiding, one treats all habitual afflictions; as the afflictions thin and wisdom becomes luminous, they become increasingly distinguished and superior, requiring only the illuminating function of concentration and wisdom.

All phenomena of body and mind are without support, without root, and without foundation; all greed, hatred, and delusion gradually diminish and fade away, while the wisdom of all Buddhas gradually increases and becomes more luminous.
One finds delight in the Dharma for one's own amusement, not out of craving for worldly pleasures.
This is a gradual process within the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), not something that has a beginning or an end.
Regarding to whom this sutra is entrusted among the five sciences: this Dharma-gate of the sutra is entrusted to ordinary beings of great resolve.
The Sūtra states: "This Dharma-gate of the sūtra shall not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings.
The commentary explains:

"Other sentient beings" refers to those of the three vehicles and the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), as well as those who delight in and are attached to the human and celestial realms, or those who seek the happiness of transcendence from the world.

Why is this? This sutra does not permit bodhisattvas of the three vehicles to possess the six supernormal powers; if they themselves cannot yet give rise to faith upon hearing the sutra, how much less so for those of the two vehicles, devas, humans, or non-Buddhist practitioners?
The Sūtra states: "Except for those born into the family of the Tathāgata as true sons of the Dharma King.
This means that even ordinary beings with great resolve can give rise to faith, realize it, and enter [the path]; therefore, they are born into the Buddha-family.

It is not said that those born into the Buddha-family—the great bodhisattvas—constantly preach the Dharma for sentient beings; because ordinary people lacking the great resolve do not believe or realize it, this is not called "entrustment" nor is it called "circulation," as there is no one to believe and no one to enter into realization.
Regarding the statement in the sutra, "If there are no such sons, this sutra shall perish," the commentary explains:
"If there are no ordinary persons who believe and realize it, this sutra shall perish."

If it were not so, since there are already as many great bodhisattvas born into the Buddha-family as there are atoms in immeasurable oceans of Buddha-worlds, why would the Tathāgata need to concern himself with the thought that this sutra will perish?

Since one does not yet keep in mind the assembly of great bodhisattvas who have already been born into the Buddha-family, one should clearly know that one must keep in mind the ordinary beings of great resolve.
This is not for the sake of those who have already entered the ranks of the noble ones; rather, it should be understood that this sutra is entrusted to ordinary beings of great resolve.

Regarding the sixth point, which clarifies the locations where this sutra circulates: the distribution sections (*pariṇāmanā*) of this sutra appear at the end of each chapter; these include instances where the earth shakes and flowers rain down as bodhisattvas make offerings, all of which constitute the general sections for entrustment and circulation.

As for the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," it marks the conclusion of the beginning and end of the causes and effects of the five stages.

The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" manifests the Dharma to signify the fulfillment of the causes and effects across the five stages from beginning to end; thus, the light from between the eyebrows is poured onto the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, and the light from the mouth is poured into Samantabhadra’s mouth, causing these two figures to engage in mutual dialogue regarding essence and function, cause and effect.
Taking Mañjuśrī as the essence of the dharmadhātu and Samantabhadra as its function, these two serve as essence and function for one another.
Alternatively, Mañjuśrī is the cause and Samantabhadra is the fruit.
Alternatively, these two persons serve as cause and effect for one another.
Throughout this entire scripture, these two figures are constantly used to represent essence and function, as well as cause and effect.
This has been the case for all Buddhas of the past and present; they have all relied upon these traces to clarify the benefits of cultivating the path through cause and effect.
The Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows and from his mouth; together with these two great beings, this clarifies the completion of the beginning and end of the five-stage teaching system.
The light from the mouth signifies the meaning of entrustment and the meaning of circulation, so that the practice of the teaching may be widely disseminated.

The light between the eyebrows signifies the meaning of the fruit; having emitted this light of the fruit, it is entrusted to Mañjuśrī, who is then directed to inquire about the dharma of the fruit. When Samantabhadra explains the appearance of the Buddha, this constitutes the circulation [of the teaching].

Within this chapter, the entrustment and circulation [of the teaching] are fully explained; furthermore, the text is interpreted through metaphors such as being a crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who possesses the complete marks of royalty and is capable of governing the royal throne, which will be clarified upon reaching this specific chapter.

The practice of Samantabhadra prior to the fruit of the tenth stage consists of both self-benefit and benefiting others;

Sixth, it takes the supernatural powers and spiritual penetrations of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as its teaching essence; it manifests various masteries such that those who see them resolve their minds [for enlightenment], without depending on words and phrases.

To state the essential point: the ocean of afflictions of all sentient beings; the fruits of human and celestial bliss resulting from the various degrees of roots of goodness possessed by all sentient beings; the liberation and nirvana of the vehicles of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas; the collections of names, phrases, and syllables, as well as vocal karma and so forth; and all the karmic retributions of good and evil throughout the realm of empty space and the Dharma-realm—whether expressed through speech or beyond words—all phenomena are none other than the substance of the teaching.

Whether through direct observation with the eyes, hearing the Dharma, or through one's own reflection, when wisdom manifests through internal permeation, one is able to abandon all evils and attain nirvana; thus, both what is spoken and what is unspoken constitute the essence of the teaching.
If there were no afflictions, there would be no essence of the teaching.
Regarding the fourth point, the general presentation of the number of assemblies, the main intent therein comprises three aspects:
first, the general enumeration of the number of assemblies; second, the explanation of the purpose of these assemblies; and third, the account of the reasons for the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
First, regarding the general enumeration of the number of assemblies, there are ten such assemblies.
Second, regarding the exposition of the intent of these assemblies:
the first assembly was held within the Bodhimaṇḍa to clearly manifest the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

Regarding the second assembly held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-prāsāda*): this clarifies the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the practices performed; it refers to the dwelling place of the two types of rewards—the primary and secondary—attained as retribution.

For this reason, in this chapter, the phrase "initially attaining perfect enlightenment" is repeated again to reveal that the first assembly does not constitute the initial essence of the *araṇya* Bodhi-field. One does not attain the Way apart from this essence, for one dwells here in the dwelling-place of the reward-body.
It is like a person of the world who attains the Way in a pure place and only then returns; this demonstrates that this Dharma fundamentally has no coming, going, or shifting of time.

As for the third assembly ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru to the palace of Śakra, it clarifies that from within the Hall of Universal Radiance, he expounded the stage of the ten faiths, wherein one first gives rise to the mind of faith upon that ground.
Now, within the celestial palace of Śakra, this is to manifest the stage of his progressive cultivation, wherein his practice of the Dharma has increased and excelled.

It is here in this heaven that the gateway of the Ten Abodes is taught, clarifying that the stage of the Ten Abodes initiates the realization of Arhatship; for his mind merges with emptiness, and he attains a portion of the spontaneous function of wisdom, becoming as sovereign as a celestial being.
Like ascending a high mountain, one’s body merges with space; because the location manifests the excellence of the stage of the Dharma, it does not necessarily require rebirth in heaven.
This clarifies the function of the wisdom of signlessness, which is like the sovereignty of the gods.

Furthermore, it clarifies the nature of the mountain: rising high above the mundane world, it symbolizes the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Like a mountain, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is immovable; its wondrous wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*) transcends the mundane, for it is able to shatter obstacles as they manifest before one.

Regarding the fourth assembly being held in the palace of the Yāma Heaven: this clarifies that the palace of the Yāma Heaven exists at the edge of space and is not connected to the earth; it clarifies that the ten practices are practiced in reliance upon space, as they are not linked to the attachments of craving and desire for the various realms of existence (*bhava*).
In this context, the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*) are explained; the manifestation of the Dharma is thus.
It is not necessary for the body to be born in those heavens, for it clarifies that while abiding in practice, one is constantly empty, having nothing upon which to rely.
The fifth assembly is held in the Tuṣita Heaven palace to clarify that this celestial realm is one of joyful contentment.

The ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are taught to signify that the stage of dedication harmonizes principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma*), ensuring that great vows, great compassion, and great wisdom do not become biased. One does not crave worldly pleasures, nor does one crave *nirvāṇa*; one does not cling to great compassion, nor to great vows, yet remains within them. Thus, one dwells in the world like a lotus flower, remaining untainted by the dust of the mundane.

Furthermore, this indicates that among the abodes of the desire realm, there are the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens below, and the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens above, thereby clarifying the hierarchy from top to bottom. This heaven is situated in the midst of the desire realm;

it explains the ten gates of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) to signify that the great wisdom of the Dharma-body, the myriad practices, the great vows, and the great compassion must be harmonized and maintained in the middle. It prevents one from falling into the error of worldly compassion which is tainted by attachment, or the faults of the three vehicles—such as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas delighting in cultivating a mind for transcendence and seeking quiescence, or Bodhisattvas remaining in birth or abandoning the pure lands—as these are all inconsistent with the natural law (*dharmatā*) of this stage.

The manifestation of the Dharma is thus: it does not necessarily mean one must be reborn in that heaven. It clarifies the turning back from the ultimate toward the conventional so that compassion and wisdom may be balanced.

As for the sixth assembly being held in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, it was for the sake of preaching the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) to the beings of this heaven; because these beings achieve their own pleasure through the power of transforming the transformations of others, it serves to clarify that the great compassion and great wisdom of the Ten Stages are all fully perfected, such that they transform sentient beings alone as their own bliss of *nirvāṇa*, having no personal pleasure of their own.

Why is it that, having transcended the Heaven of Joy (*Nirmāṇarati*), one speaks of the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in the context of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*Paranirmitavaśavartin*)?
The answer is:

It is to clarify that from the tenth stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), wisdom and means are harmoniously integrated; through the fulfillment and increasing excellence of great compassion and great vows, one transcends the Heaven of Joy without following the sequential order, unlike those at lower levels who practice according to a gradual progression.
It is like worldly trade: if one initially gains a double profit on ten coins, and later gains a double profit on twenty coins to reach forty, one thereby surpasses both the first and second profits.

Furthermore, it clarifies that the fruit of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) ultimately abides at the limit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), yet attains mastery therein—remaining identical with it without being defiled, and transcending it without departing from it.

Moreover, it clarifies that because the merit of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages surpasses the bonds of desire, this heaven is identical to them; for they teach Pāpīyān as Māra and Brahmā, and by occupying the rank of the Māra King, they gather the retinue of Māra to teach with mastery, and thus they dwell in this heaven.

Furthermore, this clarifies the characteristics of the Bodhisattva’s progressive cultivation: the stages of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), the power of the Way, and the successive gradations of meritorious practice are naturally so.
This is because the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) has not yet matured and has not yet become clear and pure.

The fruit of the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) only reaches its ultimate end at the very conclusion; even upon reaching the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*), two types of delusion still remain.

Therefore, regarding the teachings of these two chapters of this sutra—the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on the Merits of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks"—the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s practices throughout the eleven stages prior to the fruition of Buddhahood has not yet reached its final consummation. For this reason, the Tathāgata himself declared that while the limits of calculation are known at the beginning and end of the fruition, the merits of the Tathāgata’s minor marks only reach their conclusion at the fruition of Buddhahood itself.

The various dharma-gates of the preceding stages were spoken by the Bodhisattvas of those respective stages themselves; only the final chapter, "Entering the Dharma-realm," was spoken through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata. This signifies that within the Dharma-realm, all phenomena are collectively divine, collectively true, and collectively inconceivable. Because it clarifies that the essence of the Dharma-realm is the single nature of both ordinary beings and sages, it is spoken among humans.
The meaning becomes clear only upon reaching the text.

It is through these two forms of ignorance that the Buddha-fruit is fully realized; therefore, at the stage of the tenth bhūmi, one acts according to what one’s capacity allows, for it is possible to reach this celestial realm.

Although there are distinctions between the successive stages of progressive cultivation, the essence of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is realized all at once in a single moment; thus, by attaining it once, one attains it all, in order to clarify that the dharma-realm is a reality without beginning or end.

One must not immediately conceive of it in terms of beginning and end, or long and short, for such views arise from emotional attachments and conceptual thoughts that contradict the truth; it can only be seen by illuminating it with meditative concentration and wisdom.
The seventh assembly was preached in the third dhyāna; this particular assembly consists of one hundred trillion verses, yet the extant text of this assembly is incomplete.

As stated in full in the *Yíngluò Běnyè Jīng* (The Sūtra on the Original Acts of the Garland): "After that sūtra had completed the transformation of those of the three vehicles, the Tathāgata led them to the foot of the Bodhi tree and subsequently recounted the sequence of the assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as they were preached at the time he first attained Buddhahood."

That sutra states in full: "Calculating this single assembly, it comprises ten locations and ten assemblies consisting of forty chapters; this is because the ten-fold dharmas established within this sutra are all perfectly complete."

This clarifies that within the three dhyānas, the first dhyāna eliminates sorrow and the second dhyāna extinguishes suffering; since sorrow and suffering are absent, the third dhyāna consists solely of the joy and bliss of the Dharma.
Because one still delights in the Dharma, joy and movement persist.
Because of this joy and movement, the form and mind remain present.
This form and mind are the bliss of dhyāna-joy, a state of form without discursive thought; it is not like the form of the desire realm.

The mind is free from volitional thought and possesses the radiance of meditative absorption; while the inhalation and exhalation of breath still persist, one receives a pure body as a karmic reward. This body is like brilliant white snow, and the robes are like gold, measuring one body-length in width. When walking, one traverses through space without the feet ever touching the ground.

The body in the first dhyāna is two and a half *li*; in the second dhyāna, five *li*; in the third dhyāna, ten *li*. The clothing is twice the size of the body, as explained in detail in the *Wén* (Text).

In this heaven, the Dharma-gate of the eleven stages (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*) is taught, signifying that within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one accords with the Dharma-body and practices the myriad deeds, transforming sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm, because of the constant presence of the joy of the Dharma.

Upon reaching the fourth dhyāna, because one abides in the same station as the Buddha, it is said that the true *dharmatā* is without inhalation or exhalation. As it universally pervades according to principle, the delusions of sentient beings regarding the habitual tendencies of the Dharma are simultaneously and entirely exhausted. Since there is no phenomenon, mundane or supramundane, that is not fully understood, this is termed the meaning of "various lights shining everywhere."
Because wisdom is perfected, the manifestation of the Dharma is thus: it does not come and go through ascending or descending in such a manner.

Rather, the physical body is manifested in response to the sun of all-knowledge—the great wisdom of the Dharmakāya—which universally displays various forms within the Dharma-realm according to the waters of sentient beings' capacities.

This single assembly transcends the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and surpasses the two heavens of the first and second *dhyānas*, because it clarifies that the wisdom of these eleven stages increases manifold.

By using the ascending heavens as provisional locations, it symbolizes the gradual mastery of the progressive advancement of the Dharma; it does not mean that the Dharma belongs to those heavens, for it pervades all places.
The eighth assembly was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance, where the Dharma-gate of the Ten Samādhis was taught; the name of that samādhi is "Entering the Limit of a Kṣaṇa.

According to the teachings of the Three Vehicles, eighty cycles of arising and ceasing constitute one kṣaṇa, and eighty kṣaṇas are called one thought-moment (nāṇa); this clarifies the teaching of the Three Vehicles.
Within this One Vehicle, because a single kṣaṇa is so extremely brief that it transcends the reach of thought, one ultimately does not discuss the existence of separate arising and ceasing.

It is clear that from the beginning to the end of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, he never departs from the limit of a single kṣaṇa, as explained in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (Lokottaraparivarta).

When the Tathāgata was correctly dwelling in the womb, residing in Tuṣita Heaven, and [subsequently] being born, renouncing the world to study the Path, attaining bodhi, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering nirvāṇa—all these were, in total, a single moment.
The body remains within the womb and has not yet emerged; as its definitive essence, it is called the nature of the Dharma-realm.
Taking this as its definitive essence, there is no further length or shortness, nor beginning or end; the three periods of time are altogether a single limit.
Furthermore, one must not permit worldly deluded conceptualizations that measure the Buddha’s appearance in the world in terms of duration; for such views contradict ultimate truth.
This clarifies that time reaches its limit here, and it is no longer discussed as having arising and ceasing apart from the moment (*kṣaṇa*).
This is the intended meaning of the sutra within this specific section.
