It differs from the interpretation of former scholars who claimed that this assembly was a "reassembly" in the Hall of Universal Radiance; such is not their intention, for they do not conclude that it is a "reassembly"—or even a "third assembly"—merely because the name and description of the Hall of Universal Radiance are recounted two or three times within the verbal teachings.
To lose its true meaning—how could one allow others to harbor views of coming and going?

According to the intent of the sutra: take the Buddha’s own essence of non-active great compassion as the mother; take all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) as the Buddha; take the naturelessness of phenomena and their lack of dependence as the time, days, months, and years; and take the faculties of all sentient beings as the clear mirror.

Within the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings, the Buddha allows each being to see according to their own capacity and to attain their respective Dharma, causing them all to turn toward goodness and attain Bodhi; it is not because the Tathāgata possesses the characteristic of coming and going repeatedly.

This merely clarifies that this Hall of Universal Radiance is the sovereign essence of the Tathāgata’s self-nature, the omniscient wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-jñāna*), serving as the dwelling place for his dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).

This samādhi of the momentary limit (*kṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of the Buddha’s omniscient wisdom of all-knowledge; its intent lies in encompassing the collective essence of all dharma-realms and the ocean-like assemblies, so as not to allow students to perceive distinctions between coming and going, or self and other.
To now instead form the view of coming and going through successive meetings is, in this regard, unacceptable.

This is explained in its entirety as being like a king’s precious seal, which stamps everything all at once and simultaneously; one must not entertain the view of successive meetings or coming and going, for the sutra does not intend such a meaning.

The ninth assembly, held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-kuṭāgāra*), clarifies that from this point one gives rise to faith and undertakes the practice of the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten concentrations (*samādhi*), the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the ten patiences (*kṣānti*), continuing until the final stage of the fruit of Buddhahood in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" (*Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta*). Throughout all these stages, one never departs from the ancient practices of Samantabhadra.

Therefore, regarding the fruit of Buddhahood prior to the ten stages (bhūmi), when one’s own vehicle’s practice of Samantabhadra is fulfilled, this refers to the thirty-six preceding chapters of the scripture, namely the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata" (Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta).

The "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" (*Samantabhadracaryāparivarta*) follows the stage of Buddhahood; since one's own practice is already perfected, it consists purely of the altruistic conduct of Samantabhadra. Thus, the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*) follows the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāvaparivarta*).

Having aroused the mind of faith from within the Hall of Universal Radiance during the second assembly, one passes through the beginning and end of the five stages of cause and effect; yet without departing from the fundamental and the manifested, one reaches the ancient gate of Samantabhadra where the fruits of all Buddhas are perfected.

In the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" as well, at this very point, it is clarified that the essential substance of the dharmakāya-samādhi is perfectly pervasive, being a single limit and a single locus from beginning to end; the three dharmas are one and the same, such that without departing from the abode of the retributive dwelling in the Universal Radiance Hall, they are simultaneously sealed, with no need for a repeated assembly where the three assemblies depart and then return.

The ancients explained this assembly as the "Third Assembly" held in the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantāvabhāsa-maṇḍala*), because the gateway of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) cannot be understood through worldly sentiments or conceptual thought.

For instance, when Sudhana, proceeding from the site of the Great Stupa to the east of Awakening City where he visited Mañjuśrī, passed through fifty stages of stations (*sthāna*) until he reached the youth Śrīkūṭa and the maiden Guṇavatī, it was because he had not yet completed the practices of Samantabhadra for his own benefit and the benefit of others prior to the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Among the twelve stages, the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) involves beholding the Tathāgata Maitreya; this is the final position of the Buddha-fruit.

It causes Sudhana to look back upon Mañjuśrī, clarifying that reaching the ultimate fruit does not depart from the original gate of initial faith—the Bodhi-wisdom of principle and phenomena. Thus, he hears the name of Samantabhadra, beholds his body, and becomes equal to the body of Samantabhadra; this clarifies the practice of Samantabhadra subsequent to the fruit.
The Sūtra states, "further entering immeasurable samādhis," in order to clarify the realization of the two types of ignorance within the stage of the Buddha-fruit that has been transcended.
These two ignorances are:
first, ignorance regarding the vast number of asaṃkhyeya; and second, ignorance regarding the vastness of the marks and secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana) within the stage of Buddhahood.
These two dharmas are realized only by the Buddha, for even Bodhisattvas of the five stages who have advanced toward self-benefit have not yet transcended them.
For this reason, the Tathāgata himself spoke these two chapters of the sutra.

Furthermore, the teaching on the inconceivable supernatural powers of the Tathāgata in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" is intended to clarify that the dharmadhātu is the ultimate fruit realized in common by all Buddhas; thus, this chapter is presented to instruct and awaken sentient beings.
The remaining thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are taught from the perspective of bodhisattvas at their respective stages.
The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "The ground of abiding ignorance is eliminated only upon the stage of Buddhahood.

Thus, the fruits attained through the three vehicles over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, as well as the distinct attachments regarding pure and impure lands and the returning of bodhisattvas to their original lands, differ greatly from the two views that accord with ordinary sentiment.

Just as with the cause and effect of the Dharma-realm, one should contemplate that they do not shift and that their stages are never deficient; the general and the particular, the one and the many, are mutually integrated, while skillful means remain entirely distinct.

This teaching of the "Chapter on Leaving the World" in the Hall of Universal Radiance clarifies that both the mind of faith and the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood—the practices of Samantabhadra—are never separate from their original traces.

It is also like the tower of Maitreya, which universally manifests the three periods of time within; in a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings of the three periods of time as if they were this very evening, with no distinction between past and present—this is precisely its meaning.
New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Eight;
New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Nine.
Composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan.
Regarding the tenth assembly in the "Dharmadhātu Chapter":

it clarifies that this single assembly universally encompasses all assemblies, as well as the oceans of lands in the ten directions, the dharma-realm, and the realm of empty space, forming a single assembly of infinite, layered profundity; furthermore, the ocean of all Buddhas and the ocean of all sentient beings are collectively unified as one essence within this single chapter, the "Dharmadhātu."

All realms of experience follow the minds of sentient beings; this constitutes their distinction. They are encompassed by the six characteristics and the ten mysteries, and may be seen by illuminating and contemplating them with a mind free from conceptual thought.

Alternatively, one may take the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Ruler" as one assembly and the three assemblies in the Hall of Universal Radiance as another assembly; together with the preceding "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Ruler," these constitute two assemblies.
Ascending to the heavens of Sumeru, Yāma, Tuṣita, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, and the third dhyāna constitutes five assemblies; together with the preceding two assemblies, they form seven assemblies.

The *Dharmadhātu-parivarta* (Chapter on the Dharma Realm) takes the Jeta Grove in the human realm as the eighth assembly; the site of the Great Stūpa of Sudhana as the ninth assembly; and the assemblies in all locations throughout the space of the dharma realm as the tenth assembly.
This should encompass all ten directions from beginning to end; it is also the interpretation of a single school and does not contradict reason.
An ancient said:
"The nine assemblies" refers to the fact that the eleventh stage was previously unknown and was taught in the third dhyāna.
This sutra takes ten dharmas as its standard and cannot be said to consist of nine.

For instance, in the assembly to the east of the city of Awakening where Sudhana resides, it clarifies that the preceding assemblies merely provisionally establish the dharmas of the five stages, yet do not yet provisionally manifest the person who practices them.
The assembly at Vārāṇasī clarifies the person who is capable of practice as well as the skillful means for Bodhisattvas to gather in sentient beings.

Regarding the third point, which explains the reasons for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world: the Tathāgata appears in the world to entrust his stages and manifest the Truth. If one perceives the Tathāgata only as having just attained perfect enlightenment, or views him through the teachings of the three periods—Right, Semblance, and Final—it is not the vision of Perfect Enlightenment, nor is it seeing the Buddha’s emergence in the world. This is merely how sentient beings of inferior understanding perceive him; those who seek Perfect Enlightenment should not view him in such a way.
Question: How does one perceive the appearance of a Buddha in the world? Answer:

When one perceives oneself as being without body and without mind, without arising and without ceasing, without interior and without exterior, neither moving nor quiescent, without thought and without seeking; when one sees that both the mundane and the supramundane have no place of abiding, that there are no mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) and no phenomena (*dharma*), and that mind and phenomena are mutually non-existent; when one realizes that the mind and its factors have no support and that their nature has no beginning or end—then, by means of the wisdom that does not rely on or abide in anything, one preaches such a Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them all to awaken and enter [the truth]. This is called seeing the appearance of a Buddha in the world.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance," Mañjuśrī spoke in verse: "Having transcended all views, both mundane and supramundane, and being able to skillfully know all phenomena, one shall become a great radiance."
If one generates a mind of dedication toward all-knowledge and perceives that the mind is without arising, one shall obtain great renown.
Sentient beings are without arising and likewise without destruction; if one attains such wisdom, one shall accomplish the Unsurpassed Way.
"Understanding the infinite within the one, and understanding the one within the infinite; by comprehending their mutual arising, one shall attain fearlessness.
The first two lines of this verse clarify the appearance of the Buddha, while the latter two lines clarify the wisdom within perfect enlightenment.

One should know that the appearance of a Buddha is likewise: it does not cause sentient beings to grasp at the signs of a Buddha’s appearance or disappearance, nor to perceive a beginning or an end; rather, they see only their own bodies and the body-minds of all sentient beings as having a nature free from arising and ceasing—this is the supramundane.

Now, in the exposition of a single section of this sutra, from beginning to end, there are a total of two hundred and twenty-eight assemblies of followers; their physical forms and categories, as well as their retinues and the adornments of their places of practice, each differ from one another.

The underlying intent of these ritual proceedings all has its symbolic expression, which becomes clear only upon reaching their respective positions; they cannot be understood through mere conjecture.
Furthermore, the first chapter contains forty-five assemblies, whose symbolic meanings are as follows and will be explained in the text itself.
The scriptural texts are vast and extensive, presenting difficult points in advance that are only fully elucidated when confronting specific matters;

thus, one must look toward the path as it exists before one's eyes. As previously detailed in the six-part topical outline of the sutra’s meaning, within the first assembly—beginning with the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment—there are a total of six chapters, comprising eleven fascicles.

As for the titles of the chapters therein: first, "The Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Lord"; second, "The Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata"; third, "The Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra"; fourth, "The Chapter on the Formation of the World"; fifth, "The Chapter on the Flower Treasury World"; sixth, "The Chapter on Vairocana."
Regarding these six fascicles of sutra, there are six types of intentions within the first assembly.

Within this first assembly, from "Thus have I heard" onwards, there are the introductory section (nidāna), the main exposition section (dharmadeśanā), and the dissemination section (parīndanā); the same applies to all subsequent assemblies.
From the six characters "Thus have I heard at one time" up to "attained perfect enlightenment" constitutes the introduction (*nidāna*).
From the passage beginning with "That ground was composed of solid adamant" onwards constitutes the main exposition (*uddeśa*).

The section beginning with "the earth shook and flowers rained down" constitutes the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding) division. From within the *deśanā* (main teaching) division, the causes and conditions for the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood are explained; the fiftyfold assembly of bodhisattvas, devas, and humans represents the multitude through whom the Buddha himself practiced and benefited sentient beings. This enables the bodhisattvas who have come to perceive the causes and conditions, and demonstrates the attainment of the Way and entry into the Dharma, such that they may realize the same Dharma known and seen by the Buddha, serving as a model for future learners.
Because ordinary beings enter the Dharma from that very state, they are identical to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
thus, the principle arises that "at the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one immediately attains perfect awakening.
Hereafter, all subsequent assemblies possess their own sequential sections, which will become clear as we reach the actual text.

Generally speaking, the section concerning the entrustment and circulation is the "Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta," which has already been explained previously; it is like the analogy of the wheel-turning monarch’s eldest son.

First, the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Rulers" clarifies that the Buddha has newly attained perfect enlightenment; the various lords of the world assemble to celebrate the Buddha's attainment of the Way and further seek their own benefit.
Furthermore, regarding the Dharma-gates of the five stages of the Tathāgata’s own practice as they are symbolized:

the second chapter, "The Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata," clarifies that when the Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment, he informed the assembly with light from his mouth and revealed the Dharma with light from the hair-treasure between his brows.

Chapter Three, "The Samādhi of Samantabhadra," clarifies how the Buddha commands Samantabhadra, the eldest son, to enter the Tathāgata-garbha-kāya-samādhi and contemplate the dharmas with precise discernment.

Emerging from this samādhi, he explains the retributive fruits of the Buddha and the karmic power of sentient beings, thereby accomplishing the adornments of the lands—the two types of retribution consisting of the environment and its inhabitants.
Fourth, the "Chapter on the Formation of the World" is taught to clarify that [the world] arises through the karmic power of sentient beings.
Fifth, the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World" clarifies that the Flower Treasury World-Ocean is a majestic adornment obtained as the retributive fruit of the Buddha’s own wisdom.

Chapter Six, "Vairocana," clarifies the citation of antiquity to authenticate the present, causing the assembly to believe and comply; it shows that the Dharma does not arrive in vain, as past and present illuminate one another, so that faith may be free from doubt.
Now, these six chapters of the first assembly all possess profound significance.
Within these six chapters, following the sequence of the assembly, they are further divided into two sections:

First, the single chapter, the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruling Lords," clarifies that the Buddha has newly attained perfect enlightenment, briefly demonstrating the adornments of both the primary and secondary retributions.
The five chapters of the sutra beginning with the second, "The Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Manifestation of Signs," clearly elucidate the fruit and exhort to practice.
Within these two gates, for the first gate—the single chapter "The Sublime Adornment of the World Rulers"—the meaning is divided into ten sections.
The first clarifies Vairocana’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment and the adornments of his two types of retribution: the primary body and the environment.
The second clarifies the assembly of the ten Universal Worthy Bodhisattvas and the assembly that constantly follows the Buddha.
The third clarifies the gathering of the eight classes of spirits and various devas;
the fourth clarifies the conclusion of their assembly;

and the fifth clarifies how the ten great celestial kings, by means of the Dharma-gates through which they themselves have attained benefit, extol the Buddha’s practices and fruits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

The sixth chapter clarifies how the Sun and Moon Devas, the Eight Classes of Kings, and others, through the Dharma-gates they have personally realized, praise the fruits of the Buddha’s ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).

The seventh chapter clarifies how the various deities of the ten assemblies, headed by the deity who presides over crops, each, through their own realized Dharma-gates, praise the fruits of the Buddha’s ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).

The eighth section clarifies the ten great bodhisattvas, beginning with Sāgaramudrāprabhāsa-mahāprabha, together with the nine classes of deities, who, by means of the dharma-gates they have each attained, praise the Buddha’s ten stages of practice and the fruits of their realization.

The ninth chapter clarifies that the throne emerges from the assembly, illustrating the Buddha’s own practice of the conduct of Samantabhadra and praising the fruit of the Buddha’s own practice of the conduct of Samantabhadra.

The tenth chapter clarifies the shaking of the earth and the offering of worship within the Flower Treasury World (*Gandavyūha*), illustrating the appearance of the Buddha and the joyful response of the great assembly through the resonance of merit and majestic power.
In the ten sections of the first assembly above, the Bodhisattvas and Celestial Beings collectively attained the Dharma-gates of the five stages of the Tathāgata.

Those who were transformed and led into these stages all attained a portion of the responsive truth-wisdom (*yǐngshēn zhēnlí zhì*); they are collectively termed "spirits" (*shén*) because they are capable of guiding sentient beings. This is not the spirit of ghosts and deities (*guǐshén*), for they have entered the wisdom of the Tathāgata and possess mastery over the power of the Dharma.
The Ten Stages (Daśabhūmi) are like the heavens and likewise manifest sovereign mastery; these will be explained extensively in the text itself. Section One:

The Exquisite Adornment of the World Rulers (*Lokendra-vyuha*). Now, I shall explain this first chapter, "The Exquisite Adornment of the World Rulers," within the first assembly. As in the first of the ten preceding topical outlines, this clarifies the Buddha’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment.
This section is further divided into two parts:
first, an explanation of the title of the scripture; second, an exegesis of the meaning according to the text.
Regarding the first, the explanation of the title: for what reason is it called the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya*, "Chapter One: The Sublime Array of the World Rulers"?
The commentary states:
"Great" (da) signifies the meaning of being without direction (fang).
"Direction" (fang) signifies the meaning of law or principle (fa-ze).
"Extensive" (*viśada*) means the sense of wisdom and principle pervading everywhere.
"Buddha" means the sense of the essence of wisdom being without dependence or abiding, and the sense of mastery over wisdom.

"Flower" (*puṣpa*) means the sense of inexhaustible practice pervading the entire dharma-realm; because such practice can cause the fruits for oneself and others to blossom, a flower signifies both the attainment of fruit and the act of blossoming.

"Adornment" (*vyūha*) means the sense of embellishment. This clarifies the stage of the first *cittotpāda* dwelling (*vihāra*). Because within the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) there are the flowers of conditioned practice, which cause the fruit of the wisdom of sublime principle to blossom within the ten dwellings; furthermore, the ten kinds of flowers of unconditioned practice arise, constantly using the practices of the Dharma to adorn one another, thereby purifying the path of self-benefit and benefiting others.
This concerns the meaning of the "Adornment of Conduct.

Regarding the title *Lokendrayaśas-vyūha* (The Adornment of the Glory of the World-Lords): because this first chapter contains the various assemblies of gods and the eight classes of beings, all of whom are lords of the world, each leading a retinue of followers from as many worlds as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields—or simply described as "immeasurable"—who come to adorn the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
This is titled "The Sublime Adornment of the World Lords" because it is established based on the assembly [of beings].
Furthermore, both the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas are all lords of the world, for they are able to lead and guide sentient beings, collectively serving as the lords of the world.

Furthermore, this first chapter provides a general outline for the entire work, enumerating a total of two hundred and twenty-eight assemblies. Their forms and appearances differ, each constituting its own distinct category; some are said to be as numerous as the atoms in one Buddha-world, some as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds, and others as immeasurable. Because they adorn the ocean-like assembly, it is called "The Sublime Adornment of the World Rulers."

Alternatively, because the Buddha’s realm of karmic fruition is wondrously adorned in both its primary and secondary aspects (the environment and the inhabitants), it may also be called "The Wondrous Adornment of the World Lord.
Since the Tathāgata is also the Lord of the world, leading and guiding all sentient beings, this name is derived by taking the possessor as the primary referent (an upapada compound).

"Chapter" (*pin*) signifies the meaning of "uniformity and distinction. It clarifies the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*) and the similarities and differences in the degrees of faith, categorically explaining the various types of mental dispositions. It establishes a systematic order for the maturation of practice through progressive cultivation, making the sequence clear so that later students may recognize their own fundamental practices and progress without confusion; thus, it serves as a chapter on the meaning of uniformity and distinction.

The "first" does not refer to a first in a sequential order of before and after; rather, within the gateway of the Dharma-realm, there is no sequence of what precedes and what follows, for all are simultaneous and devoid of dualistic thought-moments.
Simultaneous manifestation is the foremost among all categories;

the dependent origination of the one and the many is the foremost among simultaneous occurrences. This is termed the "Gate of Simultaneous Endowment and Correspondence" and the "Gate of the One and Many Being Mutually Containing Yet Distinct. By means of the harmonious integration of the Ten Mysterious Gates and the Six Characteristics, these cannot be bound by ordinary conceptual attachments; therefore, they are called "foremost."

Second, regarding the word-by-word explanation of the meaning: from "Thus have I heard at one time" up to "such immeasurable merit," there are seventy-one lines of scripture, which are divided into four sections:

first, from the initial "Thus have I heard at one time" down to "first attaining perfect enlightenment," there are eight scriptural sentences that collectively clarify the section on severing doubts and establishing faith.
The first six characters clarify the principal figures who heard the sutra during its compilation; the subsequent five phrases introduce the place where the Tathāgata attained the Way.

Second, from "That ground was firm and solid" down to "its wondrous sounds resounded afar, reaching everywhere," there are twenty-six and a half lines of scripture. These collectively praise the Buddha’s reliance (the physical environment) and the supported (the Buddha himself), constituting the section on the adornment of the site of enlightenment through the spiritual powers of this land, other lands, and bodhisattvas—this is like the "other lands" within Indra’s net.

3. From "At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon this seat" down to "causing all adornments to appear," there are thirteen lines of scripture therein. These verses praise the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment and the fulfillment of his practice, detailing the infinite mastery in gathering and transforming sentient beings through the virtues of the primary and secondary rewards, as well as compassion and wisdom.

Fourth, from "There were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds" down to "immeasurable merit," there are thirty lines of scripture within which the section on the assembly of bodhisattvas surrounding [the Buddha] is clarified.
Furthermore, within the section on severing doubt and establishing faith from the beginning, the meaning is divided into three parts:
first, identifying the person who transmitted the teaching; second, determining the time period when the sutra was spoken; and third, explaining the meaning of the textual passages.

Regarding those who transmit the teachings: as explained in the second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* within the context of the Three Vehicles, "When the Tathāgata was about to enter nirvana, he told Ānanda:
'You should circulate the twelve divisions of the scriptures.'"
He addressed Upāli: "You shall receive and uphold all the precepts.
He addressed Aniruddha:
"You have attained the divine eye; you should protect the relics and exhort others to make offerings.
He addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Whether I remain for a full kalpa or less than a kalpa, this assembly will eventually perish as well."
Having spoken thus, he lay down with his head toward the north between the twin śāla trees and entered parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda’s kinsmen had not yet eliminated their attachments and habitual tendencies;
their minds were submerged in an ocean of grief. Aniruddha said to Ānanda:
"You are one who guards the treasury of the Buddha's Dharma; you ought not to sink into an ocean of sorrow like an ordinary person.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; why do you grieve?"
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entrusted the Dharma to you; yet now you are distressed and have lost the purpose for which you were appointed.
Although the World-Honored One remains today, he will no longer be here tomorrow; you ought to ask the Buddha about matters of vital importance for the future.
Loudou’s instructions on the essential matters contained four points:

first, since all people believed and accepted the Dharma when the Tathāgata was personally present in the world preaching it, what words should be placed at the beginning of all sutras after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa?

The second question is: "While the Tathāgata is in the world, the bhikṣus take the Buddha as their teacher; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, whom shall they take as their teacher? The third question is:
"While the Tathāgata is in the world, the bhikṣus dwell relying upon the Buddha; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, upon whom shall they rely for their dwelling?"
The fourth question concerns how one should dwell together after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, given that while the Buddha was in the world, he personally disciplined the ill-natured Chandaka.
Ānanda asked the World-Honored One according to these instructions, and the World-Honored One replied:
"At the beginning of the sūtras, one should place the six characters 'Thus have I heard at one time' (*evam mayā śrutam ekasmin samaye*) as the opening formula."
Second, it says that all bhikṣus take the Prātimokṣa as their teacher.
Third, it says that all bhikṣus abide in the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni).

Fourth, it says that those bhikṣus of evil character are to be disciplined by *brahmadanda*—here translated as "silent exclusion"—and when their minds have become softened and submissive, the *Kātyāyanāvavāda-sūtra* is preached to them; this is translated here as "departing from existence and non-existence to shatter the mind of *asmimāna*."
Furthermore, as in the five-fascicle *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Ānanda requested of the Buddha:
"How should the Dharma-eye be compiled?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, a bhikṣu of great virtue should ask:
'In what place did the World-Honored One teach the Mahā-ādāna and other such sūtras?
You should answer him thus:"

Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying under the Bodhi tree in the kingdom of Magadha, having just attained perfect enlightenment, preaching the Dharma, and so on, until he preached between the twin śāla trees.
In these and other passages from more than twenty locations where such sūtras are spoken, the Buddha himself personally entrusted Ānanda to compile them in this manner.

Therefore, because the meaning of these six-word phrases was established by the Buddha’s own teaching, it eliminates doubts for those who hear the sūtra later on; they know that it was not spoken by any other person, nor was it spoken by Ānanda himself, but was established according to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* as at the beginning of the sūtra.

According to the structured outline, there are eight phrases from "Thus have I heard at one time" up to "attaining perfect enlightenment," which, as explained in the five-fascicle version of the sutra, serve to eliminate the doubts of the assembly.
The first is "thus" (evam), which constitutes one phrase;
"I have heard" (śrutam) constitutes the second phrase;
"at one time" (ekasmin samaye) constitutes the third phrase.
The Buddha is present within these four lines;
in the Bodhimaṇḍa of the Āraṇyaka-dharma in the kingdom of Magadha, the meaning of these three lines is but one—though expressed in one location, the three dharmas are a single unity.
Together with "attaining perfect enlightenment for the first time," there are six phrases.
Therefore, "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was in the Bodhimaṇḍa, having attained perfect enlightenment for the first time" constitutes these six phrases in total.
Now, regarding the phrase "thus" (*evam*): "thus" means as spoken by the Buddha himself.
"This" (*idam*) refers to what was taught by the Buddha, distinguishing it from other teachings.

Because these two names correspond and accord with one another, their faith is not divergent; this clarifies that this is truly the Buddha’s teaching, not Ānanda’s own words, nor the words of Māra or Brahmā.

Furthermore, I have heard a single phrase which Ānanda heard directly from the Buddha; it was not transmitted through successive hearsay, nor was it composed by non-humans, nor is it like the scriptures of the heterodox paths that were brought by a blue bird or found upon the collapse of a stone cliff. This constitutes the section for severing doubt and establishing faith.
As Tripitaka Master Paramārtha stated:
"According to the *Sūkṣma-vinaya*, at the time Ānanda ascended the Dharma seat, his body was endowed with the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence, just like that of the Buddha."
When the assembly saw this auspicious omen, three doubts arose:
first, they doubted that the Great Teacher Buddha had arisen from nirvana to preach the Dharma once more for the sake of sentient beings;
second, they doubted that a Buddha from another quarter had come.
There are three doubts regarding Ānanda’s transformation into a Buddha.

Now, in order to eliminate these three doubts, the six characters are established: "Thus have I heard this Dharma from the Buddha. This makes it known that these are not teachings spoken by the Buddha arising again, nor did a Buddha from another direction come, nor did Ānanda himself become a Buddha; rather, it is solely through the power of the Dharma that he causes me to resemble the Buddha.
"Therefore, having descended from his high seat, he returned to his original form.
For this reason, these six characters are used to sever all doubts.

As it is said regarding Ānanda within the Three Vehicles: since he was born on the very night the Buddha attained the Way, he became a disciple of the Buddha at the age of twenty; what he heard after those twenty years was heard directly from him, while what preceded that was heard by tradition.
Thus, the *Dharmacakrapravartana-sūtra* states: "When Ānanda was compiling the teachings, he himself spoke this verse:
'When the Buddha first preached the Dharma, at that time I was not present; thus it was heard through successive transmission.'"
"The Buddha traveled to Vārāṇasī and, for the sake of the assembly of five bhikṣus, turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
Thus we know that previously he had not heard it directly from [the Buddha].
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "When Ānanda served as the Buddha’s attendant, he made this aspiration:..."
"I pray that the Buddha will explain to me in full all the sūtras he has taught during the twenty years since his enlightenment.
Do not give me old clothes or leftover food.
One should know that this, too, is contemplation through hearing.
Furthermore, as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Whether the learned Ānanda is present or absent, he naturally and constantly understands the meaning of the permanent and the impermanent."
Furthermore, Ānanda attained the *bodhyaṅga-samādhi*, whereby he constantly heard the sūtras spoken by the Buddha from both near and far.
This account of Ānanda transmitting the Dharma is likewise found within the sūtras of the Three Vehicles.
The transmission of this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* by Ānanda was not as previously described.
For how could the Dharma King among gods, the Tamer of the Ten Directions, and the Lord of transformative rites together with his retinue be the subject of such a minor cause?

Were it not for those whose capacities are of equal stature, who manifest the interplay of yin and yang like shadows and echoes, who exhaustively comprehend the three and nine aeons within a single thought-moment, and for whom the infinite past and present are as constant as this very evening—those who, through the conceptual views of the Three Vehicles, perceive the extension and contraction of beginnings and ends, would be unable to fully understand the masters who transmit the teachings.

Now, regarding those who clarify and transmit the principal teacher and his companions in this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, they are all those who have profoundly penetrated the mysterious source and whose realization is equal to the ocean of wisdom—such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, who serve as mutual teachers and models for one another.
How could one discuss the sequence of before and after based on the age at which one was born?

Thus, when the Buddha appeared in the world and turned the wheel of Dharma, the Tathāgata used the seal of the great wisdom of the ocean of nature to stamp the desires of sentient beings as written characters; within a single sound, there is no distinction between before and after, as all are stamped simultaneously and universally.
According to their differing inclinations, each hears the Dharma that accords with what their own mind desires.

Even if Ānanda is presented as the principal teacher and his associates who transmit the teachings, this is merely the ocean of Samantabhadra’s conduct appearing and disappearing according to the capacities of beings and manifesting traces in accordance with their faculties; none of these can be definitively categorized within the framework of the Three Vehicles.

As stated above, these are all instances where holy sages and worthies secretly conformed to the same activities [as ordinary beings]; they were expedient transformations according to the three vehicles and do not yet constitute the ultimate teaching.
For example, the *Aśokarāja-saṃvarta-sūtra* speaks of three types of Ānanda:
first, Ānanda, which means "Joyous Celebration" (Qingxi), who upholds the Dharma-piṭaka of the Śrāvakas and acts according to his capacity and lot within the two higher vehicles.

Second was Ānandavardhana, here translated as Qìngxǐxián (Joyful and Virtuous). He upheld the Dharma-treasury of the Middle Vehicle; regarding the superior Mahāyāna, he practiced according to his strength and capacity, while for the inferior Hīnayāna, he maintained it with ease and inclusiveness.

Third is Ānanda Sāgara, which in this language is translated as "Ocean of Joy. This Bodhisattva upholds the treasury of the Mahāyāna Dharma, while also concurrently maintaining the lesser vehicles below; he is likewise the Ānanda who transmits the teachings within the Three Vehicles, yet he does not represent the ultimate teaching.

Regarding the transmission of this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* by Ānanda: when Ānanda truly ascended the high seat, his body became identical to that of all Buddhas, and he simultaneously and instantaneously expounded the teachings of the four vehicles and so forth, which were then compiled according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Since Ānanda’s essence and function are not different from those of the Buddha, this interpretation does not contradict the principles of reason.
Furthermore, as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Regarding the sūtras that Ānanda has not yet heard, the Bodhisattva Hongguang shall propagate and circulate them."
If one considers that this sutra is not something known by those of the three vehicles, then it is not erroneous that it was propagated and taught by the Bodhisattva Hongguang (Pṛthuvidhi).
That which is now titled "Thus Have I Heard" refers to the Bodhisattva Hongguang.

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Mañjuśrī proclaimed "Thus have I heard," because that treatise says: "Mañjuśrī, four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, at that time Mañjuśrī was still present in the world."
Furthermore, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "Mañjuśrī and Ānanda compiled the Mahāyāna Piṭaka in another pure location."
As explained above, all of these are the skillful expressions of the Noble Ones.
If discussed in terms of their essential substance, they are all the deeds performed by the Tathāgata, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva in accordance with specific circumstances.

Even if one were to speak of the three bodies, Ānanda, it would be just the same; for all of these are simply the Buddha’s own skillful means within the conduct of Samantabhadra, according to the faculties [of beings] and the varying capacities of their vessels.
The above concludes the determination regarding those who transmit the teachings.
Second, regarding the determination of the timing for preaching the sūtras, ten general types of differing sequences for the preaching of the teachings are established.
First, as stated in the *Malla-sūtra*, after the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he reflected for one week and then preached the Dharma at the Deer Park.

Second, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park; immeasurable multitudes gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka, up to the mind of a pratyekabuddha and the mind of great bodhi, though the specific number of days is not mentioned.
Third, as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he went to the Deer Park after twenty-one days to preach the Dharma.
Fourth, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, it was only after six or seven days that he preached the Dharma.
Fifth, as in the *Sūtra on the Arising of Deeds* (*Qǐxìng xíng jīng*) and the *Sūtra of Luminous Wisdom* (*Chūyào jīng*), he preached the Dharma only after seven weeks.
Sixth, as in the *Five-Part Vinaya* (*Wǔfēn lǜ*), he preached the Dharma only after eight weeks.
Seventh, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he preached the Dharma only after fifty-seven days.
Eighth, as stated in the *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings*, he did not preach the Dharma for one year.

Ninth, according to the Dharma Master Zang of the present Tang Dynasty, it is definitively maintained that the Tathāgata preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* during the second seven-day period following his attainment of enlightenment.

The aforementioned variations regarding the timing of the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma all reflect the differing perceptions of individuals regarding the sequence of the Buddha’s teachings; they do not rely upon the teaching of the ultimate reality established by the fundamental Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Tenth, regarding the current universal penetration of the profound according to this Flower Adornment Dharma-realm gate, the determination of the time for preaching the Dharma still relies on the original teachings to establish its duration; in total, it does not compare with the aforementioned [methods].
The Tathāgata relies on the Truth; appearing in the world to benefit beings, he leads them back to that very Truth.
If each were instead to follow their own deluded sentiments, they would wander through the cycle of suffering for eternal kalpas, deviating from the Truth and pursuing the false.
The Buddha’s intention is not so; the sutras themselves contain clear and explicit teachings—why must one contravene them?
To pursue the provisional while turning one's back on the ultimate, how can the obstruction of karma ever cease?
As stated in the "Ten Samādhis" chapter: "The Tathāgata appears in the world and enters nirvāṇa within a single kṣaṇa"—in truth, there is no time at all.
To speak of the "limit of a single kṣaṇa" is merely a provisional expression.

Because there is no fixed time yet he appears at all times, preaches the Dharma at all times, and enters nirvāṇa at all times—since his quiescence and activity are unimpeded and he manifests according to the minds of sentient beings.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "Since my attainment of Buddhahood, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed.
Because no duration can be measured, it is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
This refers to when the Buddha preaches the Dharma; it is established as such because he does not pursue worldly sentiments or engage in distant reflections on immeasurable concepts.
Since there is no fixed time, this is the time when the Buddha preaches the Dharma; it is the fundamental time as taught in the original teaching.
Regarding "the time of the fundamental": the Dharma-realm is timeless.

As stated in the "Ten Samādhis" chapter, "appearing in the world and entering nirvana at the limit of a single kṣaṇa," the meaning is that time cannot be shifted; like the limit of a kṣaṇa, this generally clarifies that there is no shifting or transition within the Dharma-realm.

Now, to definitively explain the timing of the teaching: it is simply when the sentiments of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—are exhausted; this is taken as the fundamental time for preaching the Dharma, and one must not rely on the provisional teachings of the past that lead and accommodate beings according to their emotional dispositions.

Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning of the scriptural text: first, within the section on "Resolving Doubts and Establishing Faith" consisting of the initial six characters and eight phrases, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it says: "'Tathā' (Thus) means 'in accordance with,' and 'Ayaṃ' (This) means 'a seal.'"
Thus, [the Buddha] was immediately accepted with faith by Indra, and therefore it is said, "Thus" (*evam*).
This term "Thus" summarizes the textual meaning of the entire work; because it refers to the Dharma already heard, it is called "Thus."

Furthermore, according to the explanation by the Tripitaka Master Dīrghanakha based on the Three Jewels: first, regarding the Buddha, it means that what was spoken by the Buddha is "what I have heard," which is the teaching of the Buddha.
Furthermore, according to the explanation by Master Zang regarding the Dharma, it says:
"That which I have heard is what was spoken by the Buddha.
And again: "That which accords with the teaching of reason is what I have heard."
Furthermore, the current *Tongxuan yuefa shi* explains:
"As" (ru) means that all phenomena are as they are (*tathatā*).
"Is" (shi) means that it is precisely the Buddha.
Therefore, it is said "Thus.

Because the true self of the great wisdom of the dharma-realm hears the Buddha’s true scripture of the great wisdom of the dharma-realm expounding the Dharma, it is said "Thus have I heard," which clarifies that the essence of teacher and disciple is one.

This is explained according to the *Avataṃsaka*’s teaching on the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), in order to clarify that from the very first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), the cause and effect, as well as the wisdom and its object, are not different from those of a Buddha.
Furthermore, all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*); because the essence of phenomena is suchness, both the one who expounds the Dharma and the Dharma itself are also suchness.
This wisdom of the dharma-realm is the wisdom that is heard; because this wisdom is also suchness (tathatā), it is called "thus" (evam).

Only when mind and object are non-dual can one hear the sūtras spoken by the Buddha; if there were a discrepancy between mind and object, one could not hear what the Buddha has spoken, nor could one believe in, accord with, or receive it.
That which I hear is the true self of the wisdom of the dharma-realm; I see again the true Buddha of the wisdom of the dharma-realm, and I hear again the true sutra of the wisdom of the dharma-realm.

The true persons of the wisdom of the universal dharma-realm act as mutual leaders and companions, transforming in turn the true sentient beings of the wisdom of the dharma-realm so that they may awaken to and enter the true nature of the wisdom of the dharma-realm; therefore, it is said, "Thus have I heard."

Now, the Buddha is like the rising sun, the paradigm for transforming all living beings; as for those who served as the leaders and their companions in compiling and transmitting the scriptures, they were none other than those whose spiritual natures shone with equal radiance and whose understanding of the Way was mutual, so that they might benefit all things.

It is because the Bodhisattva Hongguang, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata’s own practice of Samantabhadra, and others have upheld the holy teachings that they are authentic; for could those of the three vehicles outside of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) possibly transmit the teachings?

Even if it were Ānanda, he would likewise be of the same class; all would, by means of the true self of great wisdom—characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity—hear the true sutras spoken by the Tathāgata’s great wisdom.

Because it is not a provisional self, and because all things are as known and seen by the Buddha, it is said, "Thus have I heard"; this is not the same as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which describes what is heard through the conjunction of four conditions.
What are the four conditions?
First, the faculty of hearing is unimpaired; second, the sound is within the range of audibility; third, there is no obstruction between them; and fourth, there is the desire to hear.
Such hearing is the hearing of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, there are ten conditions through which ordinary beings and those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) obtain hearing:

first, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as the support; second, the seeds of the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) as the cause; third, the manas as the defiled support; fourth, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the mutual support; fifth, the auditory consciousness of its own kind as the immediate support; sixth, the unimpaired faculty of hearing as the objective faculty; seventh, the attention (*manaskāra*) with the desire to hear; eighth, the object as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*); ninth, the absence of obstruction in the interval; and tenth, the proximity of the object such that it is capable of being heard.

Such hearing as that belongs to ordinary beings and those of the three vehicles, which is limited and finite; it is not like the hearing of the Bodhisattvas of this teaching, who take the great wisdom that pervades the entire Dharma-realm as their hearing. For them, there is no longer subject or object; with a single, perfect, and luminous state of awareness, they hear universally in a single thought-moment all the infinite sounds of the kalpas of the three periods of time, none of which can compare to what has been described above.

Ordinary beings and those of the three vehicles who have been bound for immeasurable eons hear [this] in a single thought-moment within the gateway of the Dharma-realm; this is because wisdom has no interior or exterior, and thus they hear it all at once.
Regarding "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*): according to the Liang dynasty *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are three meanings.
First, the "time of equality," because there is no sinking, floating, or inversion.
Second, the "time of harmony," meaning it causes the listener to hear, the capacity to hear, and the correct hearing [to coincide].
At the time of the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma, it is precisely the time of correct teaching and correct reception.
As stated by various ancient masters, this refers specifically to the time of teaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, not the time of teaching other sūtras;
and specifically to the time of teaching the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, not the time of teaching other sūtras; thus it is called "at one time."
When taking the correct meaning, the term "one time" refers to when one recites the sūtras of a specific school.

However, this is not the case here when reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Rather, it is by means of the essence of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) that, through provisional speech, the world-transcending and the nirvāṇa are manifested within a single kṣaṇa. When a single utterance of sound universally pervades the lands of the ten directions at once to turn the wheel of Dharma, this is called "one time."
This is not the same meaning as "simultaneity" as explained above.
"Buddha" means awakening (*bodhi*).
Awakening has two meanings:
First is initial enlightenment (*shijiao*), and second is original enlightenment (*benjiao*).
This Buddha is one whose enlightenment has neither beginning nor end; because all obstructions throughout the three periods of time have been exhausted, he is called a Buddha.
This is unlike the provisional teachings, which speak of an appearance in the world and a *nirvāṇa*, for those [teachings] possess a beginning and an end.
Furthermore, regarding the term "Buddha," there are four meanings set forth in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
first, he is named "Possessor of Virtue" (*saguṇa*), because *bhaga* signifies virtue and *vat* signifies possession.
The second is named "Skillful Discrimination" (*kauśalya-vibhāga*); *vibhāga* means "discrimination," and *kauśalya* means "skillful.
The third is named "Possessing Sound" (*svara-sahita*); *svara* means "sound," and *sahita* means "possessing."
The four names can destroy lust, anger, and ignorance; "Bhaga" means to destroy, and "Va" refers to lust, anger, and ignorance.

Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains that there are six meanings, as stated in the verse: "Sovereignty, brilliance, and physical excellence, renown, auspiciousness, and nobility—possessing these six distinct meanings, he is therefore collectively titled Bhagavān."
As for the phrase "is located," it refers to a specific place.
There are two meanings: first, pointing to a concrete object; second, citing a dharma.
Regarding the pointing to a concrete object: it is located in the kingdom of Magadha; this specifically points to that country.
As for the locus where phenomena are manifested, it is within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This is because phenomena and the dharma-realm are non-dual; and because the dharma-realm has no center or periphery, nor size, nor this or that.

Furthermore, as for the kingdom of Magadha, this is translated as "The Land of Non-Harming" (*Ahiṃsā-rāṣṭra*). *Mag* means "non-" and *adha* means "harm"; thus, taken together, it is called "The Land of Non-Harming.
It is also said:
*Mag* means "not," and *adha* means "to arrive"; this refers to how the neighboring kingdoms and their enemies, despite plotting with military valor, were unable to invade or reach this country.
Furthermore, "ma" means "pervasive," and "keti" means "wise"; because this country has many wise people who pervade its territory, it is so named.
Alternatively, it is said:
"ma" means "great" and "keti" means "body"; since among the five regions of India this country is the greatest, governing all other nations, it is called the "Great Body."
This king does not carry out executions; those who have committed crimes are sent to the *śmaśāna* (cemetery).
This is to manifest the Buddha’s great compassion, using that location as an expression of his virtue.
The dharma of araṇya is here translated as "a place of tranquility.
There are two meanings to this tranquility:
first, the phenomenal (事), and second, the principle (理).

As for the first matter: it was at the village of Uruvilvā on the banks of the Nairañjanā River in the kingdom of Magadha, five li from the human settlements, a distance of one "cow-bellow" (*gośabdapatha*).
One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* here.
Ten thousand *bodhimaṇḍa*-deities constantly reside in this place.

All Buddhas who manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment do so collectively within it, signifying that the Tathāgata’s ten thousand practices are perfected and that the Middle Way is boundless; for this place is the very center of Jambudvīpa.
Regarding the two aspects of principle: it is because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent, and because they are eternally quiescent even while in motion.
There are two meanings to the term "Bodhimanda": first, the phenomenal aspect; second, the principial aspect.
Regarding the "one matter," it is as previously described by the banks of the Nairañjanā River.
Regarding the "two principles," they are the pervasive Dharmadhātu.
Because the Dharmadhātu is boundless and the Middle Way is boundless, [the Buddha] manifests the attainment of Buddhahood in all lands.

Just as a worldly arena is for the purpose of separating out filth, so the Dharma-arena (*dharmamaṇḍala*) is for the purpose of subduing delusions; it is manifested as the attainment of Buddhahood for the purpose of subduing the delusions of sentient beings.

This "arena" is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, because the Buddha manifests the realization of the Way within it; thus, it is named the "Awakening Arena" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) based on this dependency.

Regarding "initially attaining perfect enlightenment": the exhaustion of all worldly sentiments throughout past and present is termed "initial"; the mind having no dependence is termed "perfect"; the correspondence between principle and wisdom is termed "enlightenment"; and the attainment of such a Dharma is termed "attaining."
Furthermore, awakening oneself and awakening others is termed "awakening.
The above concludes the explanation of the eight phrases concerning the section on severing doubt and establishing faith.

Second is the section on adorning the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). From the passage beginning with "That ground is firm and solid" down to "Its wondrous sounds resonate afar, reaching everywhere," there are twenty-six and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies how the Tathāgata’s two types of retribution—the primary body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the secondary environment—adorn the site of enlightenment.
In this passage, it is clarified that within the Tathāgata’s original practice, four kinds of causes give rise to four kinds of retributive fruits.
Within the single nature of the mind, there are four kinds of causes for practicing the ten pāramitās, and furthermore, within each of these, one attains ten kinds of adornments.
What are the four kinds of causes?
The first is the cause of the Dharma-body, by which one attains the Vajra-ground as a fruition.
This is what the Sūtra refers to when it says, "That ground is firm and solid."

Upon that ground there are ten kinds of adornments; these are formed as the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) by means of the ten *pāramitās*, while the diamond ground (*vajra-bhūmi*) constitutes the primary retribution (*mūla-vipāka*).
What are these ten kinds of adornments?
First, regarding the taking of great wisdom within the *dharmatā* as the essence of *dāna*: this is because within a single practice (*ekakriyā*), the ten practices are fully and universally present.

Since the central theme of this sutra is that one practice is all practices, and the principal and its attendants are eternally perfect, the complete jewel-wheel is used to adorn the golden ground to clarify that "one is all."

Second, regarding "adorned with jewel-flowers upon the golden ground," this clarifies that his natural precepts (śīla) are pure and stainless, like exquisite blossoms and blooming lotuses that people delight to behold, because they give rise to the wholesome causes and effects for both oneself and others.

Regarding "adorned with *maṇi* jewels upon a golden ground": *maṇi* here is translated as "stainless jewel" (*li-gou bao*). This is because the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*) summoned by the practice of patience—which purifies the mind so that it is free from all stains—is such a thing.

Regarding "the ocean of all forms and marks adorns the golden ground": because the perfection of diligence encompasses all practices in their entirety and is able to summon the fruits for both oneself and others;
and because it summons these retributions, the ocean of all forms and marks adorns the golden ground.

Regarding the adornment of the five mani-jewels as banners: this clarifies that because the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is eternally pure and free from fluctuation, it produces such a fruit; for the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) is capable of universal quiescence.

Regarding "the sixfold emission of light and the production of wondrous sounds adorn the Dharma-realm": this clarifies that meditative concentration can give rise to wisdom, and wisdom can expound the teachings; thus, taking these as the fruit of reliance, they adorn empty space.
Furthermore, it clarifies that because the sixth pāramitā, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), is fulfilled;

as for its adornment with nets of the seven treasures, this clarifies that the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) achieves great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), thereby protecting sentient beings by bestowing the practice of the teachings.

The "fruits of reliance" (niśraya-phala) thus summoned are intended to clarify how the seven abodes and seven stages constitute the dharma-gate of great compassion; they provide the net of teaching and practice to filter out sentient beings and establish them upon the shore of Great Parinirvāṇa.
As the causal practice is thus, so too is the resultant fruit.

Regarding the "eight kinds of exquisite fragrant flowers and garlands hanging down to adorn the void," this refers to the ornaments suspended downward from the net; it clarifies that the eighth vow—the perfection of wisdom—enters into the mundane world through spontaneous great wisdom to benefit living beings, which is the resultant fruit summoned by such teaching and practice.

Just as a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages undergoes the seven refinements prior to the seventh stage—likened to refining true gold to make it increasingly bright and pure—the eighth stage is likened to fashioning various ornaments and flower garlands from that refined metal.

"Nine mani-kings manifesting sovereign adornment of space" clarifies the ninth power, the perfection (pāramitā): because the nine stages of abiding (navasthāna) and the nine grounds (navabhūmi), acting as great Dharma-preachers, are the resultant support (niṣyanda-phala) produced by mastery in preaching the Dharma.

This clarifies the ninth stage among the ten abodes, the ninth among the ten practices, the ninth among the ten dedications, and the ninth among the ten grounds, as it collectively elucidates the retributive rewards summoned by the mastery in preaching the Dharma characteristic of the rank of a Dharma Master.

"Ten rains of jewels and flowers adorn the golden ground" clarifies that the great wisdom clouds of the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten stages (*bhūmi*) rain down various Dharma-jewels and perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, pervading everywhere; this is the resultant support (*niṣyanda-phala*) thus summoned.

"From the ninth stage, the sovereign manifestation of the mani-jewel, there rains down the jewels of the Dharma-clouds of the tenth stage" clarifies that the five positions of each stage are mutually identical within the stages of abiding.

Regarding the second cause, the ten thousand practices (*daśasahasrapratipatti*): it has the Tathāgata’s own practice of the conduct of Samantabhadra as its cause, because it brings about the dependent fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of rows of jewel trees adorning the golden ground, pervading the ten directions.
The Sūtra states, "Causing all the ornaments of this *bodhimaṇḍa* to manifest their images within the trees," which clarifies that the essence of awakened practice is all-pervasive.
This is a general description of the adornments upon the trees; subsequently, it specifically mentions a single *bodhi* tree to demonstrate that all the other trees are likewise so adorned.
Regarding the ten kinds of supporting fruits of that Bodhi tree: it constantly takes the vajra-ground as its primary retribution (vipāka), while the adornments upon it serve as its support.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s body is the primary retribution, while the vajra-ground and all the adornments upon the ground serve as its support.

As for the tree now described: taking the practices of the Tathāgata as its cause, it is through the retribution attracted by those practices that the tree serves as the "dependent retribution" (*niśraya-vipāka*).

Furthermore, regarding the tree itself: its adamantine nature constitutes the body, which is the "principal retribution" (*mūla-vipāka*); gold is the principal retribution, while the trunk, branches, twigs, leaves, flowers, and fruits serve as the support. This clarifies that the tree represents the Dharma of practice, the *Lotus Sūtra* represents the fruit of wisdom, and compassion represents the leaves; the ten *pāramitās* constitute the branches and trunk, and the Dharma-body constitutes the stem. Thus, according to the superior retribution obtained through the ten practices, one attains the adornment of the ten kinds of dependent fruits.
What are the ten? First, the adamantine tree-body: because the dharma-nature constitutes the essence of the practice of giving (dāna), it brings about the resultant fruit of the adamantine tree-body.
To clarify that all conditioned phenomena arise from the *dharmatā*, his body is therefore made of vajra.

As for the tree being "tall and prominent," it refers to the tree produced as a result (*phala*) within the practices of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages, as described below in the "Ten Stages" chapter: its circumference is one hundred thousand triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, and its height is one million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems.
If even the fruits resulting from the practice of a Bodhisattva on the tenth stage are already like this, how much more so for a Tathāgata?

Regarding the two *vaiḍūrya* trunks: that which rises above the branches constitutes the trunk, while the portion below where there are no further branches constitutes the main body of the tree. This clarifies that one's own pure precepts serve as the cause, thereby externally summoning *vaiḍūrya* to form the tree trunk.

That which grows directly upward constitutes the trunk; that which grows outwards constitutes the branches; and that which grows upon the branches constitutes the twigs. This illustrates how the myriad practices follow the stream, taking pure precepts as their essence. Because they are untainted, they are all the Dharma-nature body; though following the stream, they remain unstained, being the manifested signs of retribution summoned by the fruits of pure conduct.

The fact that its trunk is adorned with branches made of various exquisite jewels illustrates that the myriad practices, whether pure or mixed, constitute patience when confronted with conditions, for they are able to benefit both oneself and others, thereby bringing about the fruit of reliance.

The four kinds of precious leaves spread luxuriantly, their shade hanging down like clouds to adorn their branches; this luxuriance provides appropriate shelter, illustrating the Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) for self-benefit and benefiting others. Because it provides protective cover appropriately—neither excessive nor deficient, but precisely fitting—it externally manifests as a ripened fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*): the tree’s leaves provide a majestic canopy so that sentient beings may find their proper place beneath it.

Regarding the five kinds of precious flowers of various colors with branching shadows that adorn the precious trees: this clarifies that the Tathāgata, through the skillful means of immeasurable samādhis, manifests according to the capacities and conditions of beings; his reflections respond to the conduct of all sentient beings, appearing in forms according to their respective types, while externally summoning these flowers to adorn the precious trees.
Furthermore, it clarifies that samādhi can cause the fruit of wisdom to blossom; therefore, the *pratibhū* (retributive) and *niṣyanda* (flowing-out) fruits are adorned with flowers.

As for the six *maṇi* jewels serving as fruits interspersed among the flowers, this clarifies that through the flowers of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the fruits of wisdom (*prajñā*) can be made to bloom, because of the sovereign mastery of quiescence and function.

"Containing radiance and emitting flames" means that wisdom is able to illuminate both oneself and others; thus, the resulting environmental fruit (*niśraya-phala*) is adorned with alternating flowers and fruits.

"The seven trees emit light and adorn" means that through the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), one dwells amidst entanglements with a mind of great compassion, employing the skillful means of acting in concert with others (*sabhāga-karman*) to destroy darkness; this is because it is the resulting environmental fruit.

"The tree emits light, and from the eight lights emerge mani-jewels" clarifies that the eighth vow, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), brings forth the fruit summoned by the sovereignty of awakened intelligence.

"Within the mani-jewels, various bodhisattvas appear simultaneously" clarifies that the ninth, the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), manifests through the body of effortless wisdom to respond to conditions according to circumstances and benefit sentient beings.

The Bodhisattva of the Ninth Ground is a great Dharma Master; that which is summoned—the primary and secondary [recompenses]—is analogous to their causes. This is because practice and fruit can summon the tree as retribution, and from the tree emerge the assembly of Bodhisattvas, which in turn clarifies the original practice. This clarifies how the primary and secondary [recompenses] interpenetrate, being complete in both their general and specific aspects.

This clarifies that the adornment of trees is obtained as the retribution for the myriad practices of his original conduct; that the Bodhisattvas emerge from these trees demonstrates the thoroughness of cause and effect.

As for the manifestation of clouds of Bodhisattva bodies within the mani-jewels, this symbolizes the effortless pure wisdom of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), while the emergence of practices and the establishment of teachings to benefit sentient beings represent the ninth stage.
Because the Bodhisattva practices these deeds, he obtains their retribution within the trees; thus, from within the trees, the Bodhisattva’s practices emerge.

As for the ten Bodhi-trees constantly producing sublime sounds to adorn the preaching of the Dharma, this clarifies the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the *pāramitās*, because they bring down the great clouds of Dharma and rain down the rain of Dharma—this is the resultant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) thereby summoned.

Third, regarding the elucidation of the causes and effects of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*): taking the Tathāgata’s great compassion as the cause, the palace wherein the Tathāgata dwells constitutes the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*).
This is accomplished through five kinds of virtues:
first, the virtue of the Tathāgata’s great compassion in its capacity to embrace and nourish, by which his palace is formed.
Second, the virtue of benefiting sentient beings through right wisdom forms its hall;
third, the virtue of benefiting oneself and others through the illuminating observation of wisdom forms its pavilion;
fourth, the virtue of knowing faculties and establishing teachings to benefit living beings through great wisdom forms its upper story.
The virtue of the five great compassionate vows, which universally benefits sentient beings, results in palaces and towers obtained as retribution that pervade the ten directions.
Furthermore, because the practices of the ten *pāramitās* arise in accordance with great compassion, they further accomplish ten kinds of concordant fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*).
What are these ten?
They are the concordant fruits resulting from the Dharma-body, the myriad practices, great compassion, and great wisdom, which are each distinct and do not obstruct one another.
It is like the great earth that gives birth to all grasses and trees; the earth is but one, yet the myriad forms are different.
This can be understood by reflecting upon the analogy of water sustaining life.

However, while the principle of the ten pāramitās is one in essence, they differ according to the myriad practices, great compassion, and great wisdom of the Dharmakāya, as well as their respective retributions.
Just as with the ten pāramitās—great vows, great compassion, and great wisdom of the Dharmakāya—it is impossible to dispense with even one.
Up until the eighth stage, one’s merit remains immature; if even one [practice] is abandoned, then all will fail to be accomplished.

Those who wish to study the Bodhi of the Buddha must be thus comprehensive and not cultivate a single practice alone. If one cultivates stillness exclusively, one becomes stagnant in quiescence; if one cultivates wisdom exclusively, one lacks compassion; if one cultivates compassion exclusively, defiled habits increase; and if one cultivates great vows alone, conditioned sentiments arise.

Regarding these various practices, the Bodhisattva neither departs from nor clings to them; by attaining the state where the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is equanimous and harmonious, they observe them through the power of concentration and wisdom. This must not be subject to the deliberations of abstract sentiments, which would only increase ignorance and craving.

Regarding the ten kinds of practices that serve as the ten kinds of supporting fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) for adornment: first, through the great loving-kindness and great compassion of non-attachment toward the equal dharma-nature of all Buddhas in the ten directions, one practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), which brings about a supporting fruit composed of *maṇi* jewels of manifold colors.

Because the myriad practices within the stage of great compassion are either defiled or pure and thus not of a single color, the resultant supporting fruits they attract are likewise not of a single color; it is with these that the palace is adorned.

Second, because the essence of the dharma-nature is inherently pure, the substance of the unmanifest precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*) follows great compassion to protect sentient beings; this is called the "flower of practice" (*caryā-puṣpa*). Because it can bring about the fruits for both oneself and others, it summons the retribution of precious flowers to adorn the palaces.

Third, by means of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), he dwells in the world to save ordinary beings; because he remains unshaken by either defamation or praise, as an external dependent fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), various jewels emit radiant light, which transforms into banners.
The banner signifies the meaning of being unshakable and the meaning of overcoming enemies, for it triumphs over the enemies of slander and praise.

Fourth, by following the practice of great compassion through the perfection of diligence, one externally attracts the fruit of reliance: the assemblies of boundless bodhisattvas at the site of enlightenment adorn the palace, all gathering at that place.
Fifth, through the dhyāna-pāramitā following the practice of great compassion, external dependent fruits are summoned.
This is because the bodhisattva manifests radiance, for through meditative concentration he is able to give rise to the radiant light of the wisdom of great compassion.

Sixth, by following the practice of great compassion with the perfection of wisdom, one externally attracts the fruit of reliance: obtaining the inconceivable king of mani-jewels to form a net. Because wisdom is able to discern and establish the net of all phenomena, one further obtains the inconceivable jewel-net of sound to adorn the palace.

Seventh, by means of the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), one can accord with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and engage in practices that flow along with both defilement and purity; externally, this invites the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*), whereby one attains the power of sovereign supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), and all spheres of experience emerge from within this.

The Tathāgata, through the gateway of wisdom that is non-reliant and non-abiding in phenomena, takes the practice of great compassionate skillful means as his cause, thereby summoning spiritual powers to adorn his palace.

As for the practice of skillful means carried out during the seven stages that accomplishes the gateway of great compassion, a sutra uses this analogy: "It is like one country being entirely defiled and another country being entirely pure; the affairs of these two countries are difficult to discern."

This clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage, having accomplished the myriad practices through the skillful means of great compassion, find it difficult to sever and difficult to perfect the two views of defilement and purity; therefore, they work tirelessly to transform and benefit sentient beings through this gate of compassion.

Eighth, through the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), it externally summons the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*): the dwellings where sentient beings reside appear within celestial palaces (*vimāna*). This clarifies that the Great Vow of the Tathāgata, which responds to sentient beings, acts as the cause; thus, the summoned fruit of reliance manifests in this manner.

Furthermore, because wisdom and compassion therein are perfectly pure, ninth, by means of the Tathāgata’s power-pāramitā following the practice of great compassion, one acts as a great Dharma-preacher; thus, empowered by the spiritual might of all Buddhas, one adorns the palace as the fruit of reliance.

Tenth, by taking the Tathāgata’s practice of the perfection of wisdom as the cause, external spiritual power is summoned such that, in a single thought-moment, the palace entirely encompasses the dharma-realm of the ten directions; this is because clear wisdom follows the function of compassion to universally contain and cover all.
These ten kinds of practices serve to adorn the palace.
