These supreme adornments are all the concordant results (*niṣyanda-phala*) summoned by the Tathāgata’s practice of great compassion; thus, the textual flow is continuous, mutually integrated, and interdependent, clarifying that each single practice encompasses all practices through their mutual participation.

No retributive fruit can be obtained without a cause; however, if one contemplates this subtly with wisdom, one will see that from the very beginning, causes and effects are similar both internally and externally.

Regarding the fourth point, the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata that accords with the causes and effects of the myriad practices: this refers to penetrating all practices and appearing in the world, wherein attaining perfect enlightenment serves as the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*), and the lion throne serves as the supporting fruit (*adhiṣṭhāna-phala*).
Within this section concerning the lion throne (*siṃhāsana*), the meaning is divided into three parts:
first, the explanation of the throne’s name; second, the description of its height and breadth; and third, the revelation of the causes and conditions for the adornments upon the throne.
Regarding the first [interpretation], the name "lion-seat" (*siṃhāsana*) is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
This is because the Tathāgata has attained fearlessness amidst the great assembly; it does not mean that there is an actual lion upon the seat.
Regarding the description of the arrayed seats, it serves only to clarify the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment).
Second, concerning the height and breadth of the seats, the sutra merely mentions "high and broad" without specifying their exact measurements.
Now, let us compare this by way of analogy:
as in the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), the Buddha’s seat in the palace of Śakra-devendra is ten thousand tiers high;
in the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), the Buddha’s seat in the palace of Suyāma is one million tiers high.
Within the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the Buddha’s seat in the Tuṣita Heaven palace is one hundred thousand million *koṭis* of stories high.
Its height and breadth correspond to the respective stages, each being appropriately proportioned; they may be categorized according to this sequence.

The seat at the stage of the tenth bhūmi in the Tuṣita Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) is many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of layers high; this is because that celestial palace has already transcended the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati).
Within the third dhyāna, eleven stages are taught, which again transcend two heavens and are successively higher by doubling.
The "Chapter on the Ten Grounds" does not explicitly state the height and breadth of the Buddha’s seat, but merely classifies it by analogy.

These four levels of the Buddha’s seat differ in their relative heights and tiers in order to clarify that they correspond to the progressive stages of advancement through the ten abodes, ten practices, ten dedications, and ten grounds; thus, the perceived height and depth vary according to one's respective stage.

Speaking in terms of ultimate reality, the height and breadth of the Buddha’s seat have no fixed dimensions of size, height, or depth; for they are bound by the totality of the Tathāgata’s mental capacity and are thus immeasurable, and the resultant support (*niśraya-phala*) that they attract likewise cannot be measured.

Just as the Bodhisattva Anantagātra could not find the limit of the Buddha’s body because he had already transcended the limits of sentient beings and the measures of the mind, for this reason, his body does not become small while dwelling within a pore, nor does it become large while abiding within the Dharma-realm; this is because the measure of sentient beings has been exhausted.
If the body conforms to its kind, the seat likewise conforms to its kind.
If one speaks in terms of the Tathāgata’s own retributive essence, the Dharma-realm constitutes the substance of the seat.
Since the cause is thus, the fruit that it relies upon is likewise so; therefore, it is also immeasurable.
As stated in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," the size of the seat is fixed as being equal to the extent of the dharmadhātu.

Regarding the causes and fruits of the adornments upon the seat, there are briefly ten kinds. All of these take the Tathāgata’s wisdom that accords with the myriad practices and the attainment of perfect enlightenment in all places as their cause, because they take the ten kinds of adornments in all places as their supporting fruit.
What are these ten?

First, regarding the pedestal made of mani-jewels: this clarifies that the Tathāgata’s wisdom, by bestowing gifts in accordance with the Dharma, accomplishes the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā). It clarifies that the pure essence of wisdom brings about its corresponding environmental fruit (niṣyanda-phala), whereby one obtains stainless jewels as adornments.
"Maṇi" means "stainless jewel" (li-gou-bao) in this language.
Wisdom is able to transcend the mundane; taking this as its pedestal signifies that the essence of clear wisdom transcends the dust of the world and stands far beyond it.

Regarding the second, "the net of lotus flowers": through wisdom that accords with the myriad practices, one accomplishes the gate of the *śīla-pāramitā*. This clarifies that while one possesses the nature of precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*), one attains true non-realization; thus, even while remaining amidst entanglements, one is not defiled, just as a lotus flower remains unstained by water.
Regarding "having a net": this clarifies that the Tathāgata follows the essence of the precepts with wisdom, teaching and practicing the act of filtering sentient beings;

thus, the resulting dependent fruit is similar [to its cause]. Regarding "having wheels made of the three pure, wondrous jewels": this clarifies that the Tathāgata, through wisdom following his conduct, perfected the gate of patience (*kṣānti*). Whether born in a royal palace or manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment, even when provoked by Devadatta, Brahmā, or Māra Pāpīyān, he did not give way to anger. That the resulting dependent fruit consists of wheels made of wondrous jewels clarifies that because the Buddha’s practice of patience was perfected, his karmic fruition is likewise perfected.

Regarding the fourfold assembly adorning themselves with necklaces of various colored flowers: this clarifies that because the Tathāgata, through wisdom, accords with the conduct of the multitudes and accomplishes the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), he brings forth as a resultant support (*niṣyanda-phala*) these flowers of manifold colors, which serve as necklaces to adorn the precious throne.
To clarify that the practice of diligence serves as an adornment for the great Dharma-body of wisdom and acts as a flower garland, it is shown that wisdom and practice mutually adorn one another.

Regarding the five types of halls, pavilions, towers, galleries, steps, thresholds, windows, and all other objects and forms that constitute the complete physical adornment: this clarifies that the Tathāgata, through wisdom following practice, accomplishes the gate of the *dhyāna-pāramitā*. It clarifies that the Tathāgata’s wisdom follows the practice of *dhyāna* such that there is no movement that is not tranquil. It clarifies that this gate of *dhyāna* universally encompasses the Dharma-body, great compassion, and great wisdom, and that the successive stages of the gates for cultivating diligence are fully complete; because the resultant supports (*niṣyanda-phala*) they attract are likewise complete, all objects and forms are cited collectively as constituting the complete physical adornment.
A secular text states: "A large building is called a *she*; its form is flat on top, suitable for serving as a terrace or pavilion.
Eaves are placed around its perimeter, and it is adorned above and below with railings and steps; the center is hollowed out to form its chamber."
It is also said that there is a wooden pavilion upon the terrace;
this is a brief description.

As for the branches and fruits of the six precious trees being arranged in rows all around, this clarifies that the *niṣyanda-phala* (concordant fruit) summoned by the Tathāgata’s wisdom following the application of insight (*prajñā*) and acting in accordance with the faculties is thus manifested. That the precious trees adorn the jeweled seat and their branches and fruits are arranged in rows all around clarifies that fundamental wisdom (*jñāna*), skillful means (*upāya*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and vows (*praṇidhāna*) interpenetrate and function simultaneously, such that the general and the particular attain their proper place because they are not cultivated in isolation.
Examining this through ten gates:

as for the seventh point, "the clouds of mani-jewel light mutually illuminating one another," this clarifies that the Tathāgata’s wisdom, in accordance with skillful means and the capacities of beings, bestows benefit; thus, such adornments of the *niṣyanda-phala* (concordant fruit) are summoned.
"Radiant" refers to the roots of knowledge sharing a common function.

That the pearl-kings manifested by the Buddhas of the eighty directions, the wondrous jewels within the topknots of all Bodhisattvas, all emit light and come to illuminate [it] means that the Tathāgata has brought to completion the great wisdom and great vows of the eighth stage during his causal career; his great compassion is fulfilled and his great wisdom is perfectly luminous. Having been touched on the crown by all Buddhas, he is able to manifest the body of a Buddha throughout the ten directions. Because the vows and practices of all Bodhisattvas are equal, they summon this fruit of reliance.
The Buddha’s transformation of the pearl king illustrates that his sovereign mastery is identical to that of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
That the wondrous jewels of the bodhisattvas come together to illuminate it illustrates the perfection of the bodhisattvas’ practice.

"Ying" (polished) signifies clarity and purity; "zhu" (illuminating) signifies radiance. This refers to the great wisdom of the eighth stage within the causal phase of the Tathāgata, which, by the power of its original great vows, illuminates the faculties of sentient beings. Because it accords with those faculties to provide benefit, it is termed the "fruit of reliance."

All are encompassed by the Ten Mysteries and Six Characteristics; because the general and the particular are fully present within a single moment of time (*kṣaṇa*), they cannot be known through ordinary sentiment.

They are known through the wisdom that is eternally non-different from principle; they become manifest only by relying on the essence of non-constructive meditative concentration (*anabhisaṃskāra-samādhi*).
To know through reflection refers to the stage of faith (*śraddhā*).

The phrase "furthermore, sustained by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas" clarifies that the Tathāgata’s great wisdom follows practice to accomplish the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*); as a great Dharma teacher who expounds the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma, because he shares the power of all Buddhas, this is the fruit of reliance (*niṣyandaphala*) thereby summoned.

The Buddha’s power sustains the seats so that they preach the Dharma; from these ten seats, sounds emerge to expound the realm of the Buddha. That "wondrous sound extends afar, reaching everywhere" means that "afar" (*xia*) refers to distance and "extending" (*chang*) refers to delight. This clarifies that the seats emit sounds to proclaim the Buddha-realm, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*, thereby bringing joy to sentient beings at a great distance.
This is because it is the resultant support (*āśraya-phala*) brought about by the moisture of the Dharma-cloud stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*) during the Tathāgata’s causal stages.

Third, regarding the section clarifying the Tathāgata’s mastery in attaining enlightenment and gathering sentient beings: within this section, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "causing all adornments to appear," there are thirteen lines of scripture that collectively clarify the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood while seated, his mastery over the three karmas of body, speech, and wisdom, the adornment of his retinue, and his mastery in benefiting sentient beings.
The seat upon which the Tathāgata sits takes the dharma-realm as its substance; it is adorned with the fruits of reliance, being the retributive attainment of all the Tathāgata’s myriad practices.

The Tathāgata is the embodiment of great wisdom; all the adornments present upon the seat are the spontaneous retributive attainments that follow from his great wisdom. This is like clouds arising when a dragon moves through them or wind springing up when a tiger roars; such is the natural response of karmic retribution, not something produced by external objects.
The phrase "attaining supreme perfect enlightenment" (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) serves to distinguish this from non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

Within the provisional teachings, those who weary of the mundane world and transcend its entanglements by means of wooden trees and grass seats cause sentient beings of inferior understanding to plant the seeds of the three vehicles and temporarily extricate them from the eight sufferings; however, this is not the perfect enlightenment of ultimate awakening.
Because it is not a discernment such as this, it is said that one achieves supreme perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This perfect enlightenment is neither joyful nor weary, neither emerging nor submerging; the afflictions of both defilement and purity are exhausted.

By means of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which accords with the nature of the Dharma-realm, one freely teaches and transforms all sentient beings; the oceans of worlds and lands are not limited or restricted. All realms of retribution, bodies, and lands are thoroughly interpenetrating and perfectly complete throughout the ten directions. Buddhas and sentient beings, self and other, occupy the same space, mutually entering one another so that reflections appear in infinite layers. One does not say that the realm of retribution fills only three thousand great thousandfold worlds, nor is it called a Pure Land located in some other direction.

Briefly stated, there are ninety-seven kinds of major marks of a Great Man; his secondary characteristics are inexhaustible. He wears a flower crown upon his head, a necklace around his neck, and rings and bracelets upon his hands. This is not like those of the Three Vehicles who renounce worldly life out of weariness with the mundane; rather, it is to exhort all Bodhisattvas to be born in the pure lands of Buddha-realms in other directions.

Since it is not as [the opponents] claim, it is said that he attained supreme perfect enlightenment and was named Vairocana, which means "Universal Radiance. Because his great wisdom teaches and transforms beings according to their faculties and destroys their obstructions, each point is explained in its own respective passage within the sutra.
Regarding "Wisdom enters the three periods of time as entirely equal": this clarifies that wisdom can follow conventional discourse to enter the three periods of time.
Since the very substance of the conventional is fundamentally true, it is said to be "equal."

By means of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*)—the gates of the universal and the particular, the identical and the different, and the formed and the disintegrated—the entire scope is encompassed: that which is the universal is entirely the particular, and that which is the particular is entirely the universal; that which is identical is eternally different, and that which is different is eternally identical; that which is formed is eternally disintegrating, and that which is disintegrating is eternally forming. None of these are the conceptual fetters of identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, or permanence and impermanence, for they are the very nature of arising and ceasing.

All such things are thus because the Tathāgata’s essence and function of wisdom and principle, as well as his environment and inhabitants, are entirely sovereign; they can be seen by illuminating them with the great wisdom of the power of non-thought inherent in his own body.

This section of thirteen lines of scripture generally elucidates how the Tathāgata’s three karmas of body, speech, and mind—along with their environments and manifestations—are sovereign in accordance with their functions; as the text itself is complete, there is no need for further explanation.

The fourth section, from "There were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds" down to "immeasurable merit," consists of thirty lines of scripture that clarify the portion concerning the assembly of bodhisattvas surrounding [the Buddha].
Within this section, it is fully revealed that there are, in total, forty-seven assemblies in the first chapter; all are in attendance and all possess their respective intentions.

Among these forty-seven assemblies, from the assembly of the flowing light within the initial Bodhi tree downward, through the ten eminent names such as Samantabhadra, they are all collectively designated by the name "Universal" (Pu).
The assembly shall be divided into three groups.
*New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Scroll Nine;
*New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Scroll Ten.
Compiled by the Elder Li Tongxuan:

*The Multitude of Radiant Flows Within the Bodhi Tree*. This work elucidates the Buddha’s original cause through the five stages of progressive cultivation, establishing practice to benefit sentient beings and manifesting the causes that bring about retribution.

As explained previously, the assembly within the palaces where the two Tathāgatas reside clarifies that the Buddha’s original cause was the perfection of great compassion; this assembly of those who have attained fruition through the manifestation of causal practices for nurturing and benefiting all living beings is the "assembly of the fruition resulting from causes."

Among the assembly of bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms within thirty buddha-worlds, there are ten groups of bodhisattvas whose names all begin with "Universal" (Puxian)—such as Universal Worthy and others—demonstrating that these are the assemblies of those who have practiced the Universal Worthy conduct together with all Buddhas of the past and present.

The three assemblies mentioned above are all those who have practiced the myriad deeds of great compassion and great wisdom common to all Buddhas of the past and present; they follow the constant path of Samantabhadra by cultivating, throughout the five stages, the self-benefiting and benefiting-others practices of the ten pāramitās, the four means of integration, the four immeasurables, and so forth.

All bodhisattvas take this as their essence, and all ordinary beings ride upon it; like the royal highway, the Dharma is eternally thus—whether one practices it or not, there is no difference in the Way itself.

From this point, starting with the assembly of the Ten Samantabhadras down to the fourth, and from the assembly of the Thirty-three Heavenly Kings up to the assembly of Maheśvara, the deities are further divided into five groups according to their respective ranks.

First, from the time the World-Honored One sat upon this seat and attained supreme perfect enlightenment, together with the assembly of the ten Samantabhadras; this is the section on generating faith through the manifestation of results as causes.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata is the fruit of perfect enlightenment, while Samantabhadra and the other assemblies are the fruits of the Buddha’s practice.
The Flower Treasury Pure Land where the Tathāgata dwells is the fruit of reliance obtained as retribution for his merit.

Because all sentient beings, by means of their own faculties and natures, contemplate the three kinds of cause and effect of the Tathāgata, and give rise to faith by practicing the gate of Samantabhadra’s own conduct.
If it were not so, upon what could faith be based?
Therefore, the Tathāgata causes sentient beings to believe with joy and practice by means of these three kinds of cause and effect.

For this reason, from this first assembly through the twelve chapters of the sutra up to the "Chapter on Worthy Leader" within the second assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance, these constitute the section that presents the fruition to encourage practice and engender faith.

The second section, from the Bodhisattva Samudraprabhāmahāprabha and those below him, together with the nine classes of deities beginning with the second Vajradhara, elucidates the causes and effects of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Why is this so? The Bodhisattva Sāgaracandraprabha-mahādyuti is also among the assembly of Samantabhadra and others; the intention behind assigning him a distinct name is to clarify that he returns from within the state of Buddhahood to engage in the practice-gate of Samantabhadra, entering the mundane world to benefit sentient beings, with his name varying according to his specific activities.

Having already entered the practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct shared by all Buddhas within the stage of Buddhahood to benefit sentient beings in the mundane world, those who are capable of being benefited shall regain their former dharmas without deviating from their former practices.
For this reason, the various names of Bodhisattvas within the stage of Samantabhadra—such as Sāgaracandra and others—are treated as the initial mind of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*).

This clarifies that from the stage of ordinary beings, one cultivates the ten minds of faith (*daśa-śraddhācitta*), believing that the fruit of the Buddhas' perfect enlightenment is no different from the inherently pure nature of one's own mind, which is identical to the nature of all Buddhas.
All conceptual discriminations are pure by nature; this is called the wisdom of non-abiding.

Just like the fundamental wisdom of all Buddhas, when it is sealed with the seal of non-action of the dhyāna-pāramitā, it naturally accords with the nature of the dharmadhātu. Because all practices performed are the conduct of Samantabhadra and because movement and stillness are non-dual, the wheel of Dharma that is turned is in perfect accord with the wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions, being identical and without difference.
Thus, through such cultivation, habituation, and refinement, one’s perfect awakening remains unshakable because its root is one.
One accords with the ancient awakening of all Buddhas because fundamental wisdom is of a single nature;
one’s practice remains unshakable because it is the ancient conduct of Samantabhadra.

For this reason, the ten bodhisattvas within the assembly of Samantabhadra—such as Sāgaracandraprabha and others who bear various names—are brought forward to establish the initial mind of the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi), thereby clarifying that the initial mind of the Ten Abodes does not depart from the original dharma-knowledge.
As the subsequent text states: "At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one immediately attains perfect awakening.

Furthermore, regarding the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sāgaraprabhāsa-arcis, in the section on the benefits obtained and the praise of his virtues, the sutra says: "Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sāgaraprabhāsa-arcis has attained the skillful means and gates of liberation for giving birth to the various stages and perfections of a bodhisattva, for teaching and transforming sentient beings, and for adorning and purifying all buddha-fields."

This clarifies that by accomplishing sentient beings through the practices of Samantabhadra, one enters the Buddha’s great wisdom-dharmadhātu; because one practices the dharma-gates of the sequential cultivation of the five stages of Samantabhadra’s conduct, this fruit-stage practice of entering the mundane world is named "Sea Moonlight."
Including those below, these collectively constitute ten assemblies, establishing the gateway to the stages of the Bodhisattva’s Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
From the deities below up to the Medicine King (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*) and others, it clarifies that these are the practices of the fruit resulting from entering the Ten Abodes.
To enter the ten stages (daśabhūmi) as an arhat is what is termed "divine" (shen).

It clarifies that a bodhisattva who has entered these stages is called "divine" because they unite with the dharma of their own arhatship; because they nurture and sustain all sentient beings, and because they save and liberate living beings through the spiritual penetration of wisdom and sovereign mastery, they are called "divine"—they are not the ghosts or spirits of the mundane world.
Subsequently, the various devas and celestial beings clarify the progressive advancement through the five stages; thus, they gradually attain mastery.

Because these Bodhisattvas and devas collectively clarify the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), those Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages above all sustain sentient beings according to their respective positions, as they practice with mastery over cause and effect; therefore, they are not the "spirits" of ghosts and deities.

If one’s own mind realizes the principle and does not conjoin with delusion, its wisdom becomes spontaneously divine; because it is not through non-thinking that this wisdom skillfully penetrates all phenomena.

These various hosts of deities are all those whom the Tathāgata has gathered to benefit sentient beings through the practices of the five stages. He has further provided the sequential patterns and ritual forms of these practice-phenomena so that later students may each emulate them, thereby gaining a thorough understanding of cause and effect.

The third section, from the "Deity of the Chief Crops" down to the "Deity of the Day," comprises these ten classes of deities; they clarify the causes and effects of the ten practices for benefiting sentient beings.

The fourth section, from "Asura King" down to "Sūryadevaputra," comprises ten assemblies that clarify the causes and effects of the ten *pariṇāmanā* (dedications) as methods for benefiting sentient beings.

Fifth, from the "King of the Heaven of the Thirty-three" down to the "King of the Heaven of Maheśvara," there are ten heavenly kings therein, clarifying the causes and effects of the ten stages of the arising of beings.
The five assemblies mentioned above represent provisional stages (*jìwèi*), as they manifest the causal and resultant practices of the five stages of the Buddha-fruit.

For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, these provisional stages are established to reveal the Dharma and to provide entry into the Dharma; they serve as a model for sentient beings, enabling them to realize and cultivate it.
From the assembly within the Tathāgata’s seat to the assembly emerging from the ūrṇā-kośa between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, there are four kinds of assemblies therein.
What is their significance?
The first is the assembly within the Tathāgata’s seat, clarifying those who manifested the fruit by virtue of the Tathāgata’s own past practice of causes identical to those of antiquity.
The second is the assembly of bodhisattvas from the ten directions who have gathered to present offerings.

Third is the assembly of the light from the pores of all the bodhisattvas who have come, which is the unimpeded arising of the nature of the dharma-realm; it is an inconceivable assembly of inexhaustible great compassion, wherein the one and the many, as well as their identity and difference, are sovereignly free.

It is clarified that this gateway of the dharma-realm is such by the nature of things; its essence is fundamentally thus. The dharmas of practice—both the environment and its inhabitants—are multilayered and unimpeded, because the realms of wisdom, bodies, lands, unity, and multiplicity are mutually inclusive through the harmony of the dharma-realm.
The fourth assembly, that within the tuft of hair between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, is the assembly that demonstrates the causes for attaining fruition, engenders faith, and benefits sentient beings.

This refers to the assembly of dharma-gates of the ten levels of faith, as well as the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage, which pervade the Dharma-realm after the attainment of Buddhahood; by citing these causes and fruits of his own cultivation, he causes students to emulate them.

The above-mentioned assemblies, including their assigned positions and the reasons for their appearance—namely, the assembly of those with flowing light within the trees and the assembly of those in palaces and pavilions—comprise eleven assemblies in total.
When assigned individually according to their respective positions, there are forty-seven assemblies.
Within these five positions, the ten Samantabhadras are collectively treated as a single assembly, because within each position they are not divided into ten distinct sub-categories.

The assembly of Bodhisattvas such as Sāgaraprabhāmahāprabha and the deities and spirits below them—consisting of ten distinct divisions each for those in the Ten Abidings, the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, and the Ten Grounds—total forty in all.
Including the ten Samantabhadras as one assembly, and taking the aforementioned forty [assemblies] together, they total forty-one.

Together with the assembly of light-radiating beings within the Bodhi tree, the assembly of beings in the palaces where the Tathāgatas reside, the assembly within the seats of the Tathāgatas, the assembly of bodhisattvas who have come from the ten directions, the assembly of beings from the light of the pores of the bodhisattvas, and the assembly within the ūrṇā-hair between the eyebrows of the Tathāgata, there are altogether forty-seven assemblies.
Furthermore, the general outline of the assembly’s intention is as follows; the underlying meaning therein will become clear when we reach the actual text.
As for the assembly within the Bodhi tree and the assembly within the Tathāgata’s palace, these have already been explained previously.
The above concludes the initial section on the assembly of the first chapter; the remainder shall await the relevant passages.
Thus far, it has been generally explained that the universal pervasiveness of the practice of manifesting the fruit establishes the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

From this point forward, regarding the forty-seven assemblies—if one were to list them separately, including the ten assemblies of Samantabhadra—there would be fifty-six assemblies of the great ocean-like masses. All of these constitute the "Section on Being Surrounded by the Great Assembly."
Within this first section, there are thirty lines of scripture, which are divided into three parts:
first, there are seven and a half lines of scripture that collectively enumerate the number of bodhisattvas and present the names of the various Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas who share the same title.

Second, from "the Bodhisattva Sāgaraprabhāsa-mahāprabha" down to "as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds," this section of the text consists of seven and a half lines of scripture; it enumerates the assembly of bodhisattvas by their various names and provides a collective total for all the aforementioned bodhisattvas.

Third, from "These bodhisattvas... down to "...accomplish immeasurable merit," there are fifteen and a half lines of scripture within which the causes for the original practice of the great assembly are set forth, as well as praise for the virtues of the great assembly.
Within the first section of the sutra, spanning seven and a half lines, the names of those sharing the same title, Samantabhadra, are listed; this is divided into three parts in meaning:

first, the explanation of the meaning of the name "Bodhisattva"; second, the explanation of the meaning of their shared title; and third, the presentation of the causes and conditions for the assembly’s actions.
First, regarding the explanation of the meaning of the name "Bodhisattva": to briefly explain the single title of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, the others may be understood by analogy.
Because his practice is equal to principle and his benefit for sentient beings is universal, he is titled "Samanta" (Universal).
One who knows the faculties and is sharp in worldly affairs is called a "worthy one" (xian).
"Buo" means awakening, and "sa" means sentient beings; one who awakens sentient beings well is titled a "bodhisattva," which in full is called *mahābodhisattva*.

In the Sanskrit language it is called *mahābodhisattva*, which here is translated as "Greatly Awakened Being of Sentient Beings," because they constantly awaken inexhaustible sentient beings within the ocean of birth and death.

The nine names below that share the title "Pǔ" (Universal) refer to the universal name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; this clarifies that each and every bodhisattva possesses these ten kinds of virtuous conduct, and thus they are named according to their virtues.
This is to manifest that their perfected virtues are complete from beginning to end, numbering ten, and because the names following each Bodhisattva are inexhaustible.
Because they practice inexhaustible deeds, the meaning of each name itself reveals their own cultivation.
The rest may be understood by analogy.
In general, these are taken as having the ten pāramitās as their essence.

Regarding the second explanation of the meaning of the shared title "Bodhisattva": it clarifies that the meaning of these ten "universals" (pāramitās) is the universal of a single person—that is, each and every bodhisattva possesses the ten universals—and this is true for all bodhisattvas collectively.

Regarding the distinction of names at the lower level: it clarifies that each and every one is universally able to pervade the particulars; only then can the meaning of "universal" (pu) be understood as being established.
In total, this is the common practice and shared practice of all Buddhas of the ten directions, wherein there is neither new nor old.
It is like the Great King’s Road: for those who set out upon its path, there is simply no way not to travel it.

When one follows goodness for even a single thought-moment, one perceives the nature to a small degree and wisdom manifests before them; all of this is because they do not depart from the fundamental wisdom of the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, nor do they depart from the practices of Samantabhadra.
Just as in the conduct of Samantabhadra, even a slight moment of wholesome mind within a single thought is entirely directed toward the flow of the Dharma.

As the sutra below states: "If, upon hearing the names of the Tathāgatas and the Dharma-gates they teach, one does not believe them, yet still ultimately reaches the stage of Vajra-wisdom, how much more so for those who give rise to faith and practice accordingly!"

Regarding the third point, the causes and conditions for the assembly’s action: this clarifies that the Buddha’s appearance in the world manifests both the primary and secondary rewards (the dharmakāya and rūpakāya), and that the ocean-like assembly of Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas gathers for the purpose of causing sentient beings to see these fruits, thereby engendering faith and engaging in practice.
This is the section on exhorting cultivation by citing the fruits to inspire faith.

The Tathāgata is the fruit of the fundamental wisdom of the perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas of the ten directions; the ten [bodhisattvas] such as Samantabhadra are the fruits of the differentiated practices of all Buddhas of the ten directions. By citing these two—the causes and effects obtained through retribution within these two categories of phenomena—it is intended to cause sentient beings to believe with joy, practice, and enter [the path].
As in the Three Turnings of the Wheel of Dharma: first, the demonstration, which refers to the accomplishment of the path through the eight phases;
second, the exhortation to practice, wherein one knows the cause by observing the fruit, thus encouraging devas, humans, and others to train;
third, the realization of sameness, wherein the three vehicles and the one vehicle are realized as such.

Now, within this One Vehicle, these—the fruit of the fundamental wisdom of the Buddha-vehicle and the fruit of Samantabhadra’s practice that pervades the Dharma-realm—are used to exhort those of great resolve to give rise to faith and engage in cultivation. This is precisely the gate of the stage of Samantabhadra’s Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) within the eleventh stage of the five stages; it is that which the Buddhas of the ten directions continue to practice without ceasing even after they have attained Buddhahood, just as one who has first resolved upon Bodhicitta practices without ceasing.
Now, this stage is taken as the gateway of faith; were it not so, by what means could one enter through faith?

Therefore, the conduct of Samantabhadra subsequent to the fruition of Buddhahood is purely for the benefit of others, whereas from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment onward, the conduct of Samantabhadra consists of practices that benefit both oneself and others.

Now, this first assembly and that which the Buddha has performed for them are thus: by presenting the fruit, they are exhorted to practice, so as to give rise to faith and joy, and thereby enter into cultivation.
Such is the general purport of this sutra: it uses past fruits to exhort those at the beginning of their resolve.

Below, for the Bodhisattva Sāgaramudrāprabhāsa and the assembly of devas and spirits, having attained clear faith, they enter the ten abodes and ten stages to practice and progress, gradually cultivating and increasing their cause and effect.

This clarifies the establishment of the causes and effects specific to each stage, so that later students may perceive their essential forms and gain confident faith without doubt, as they enter into the distinct characteristics of each respective stage.
If it were not thus, one would remain stagnant in a single dharma, for wisdom would lack further increase or excellence.

The preceding section briefly describes the initial vision of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment—the fruit of Buddhahood—and the manifestation of the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the five stages entering the Dharma. "Entering" means that they are identical to what the Buddha knows and equal to the Buddha's vision.

If one believes in other Buddhas, yet a bodhisattva at the initial stage has not yet attained such [realization]; for they have not yet gained self-confidence that their own mind and own body are the Buddha, nor realized that the realm of great wisdom is the Dharma-body of the Buddha, and thus are not yet capable of practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra.

From the "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance" in the second assembly onwards, all locations—such as the World of Golden Color and the World of Jewel Color—clarify that the dharma-nature of one's own mind is golden, pure white, and unstained; this is termed the world in which one dwells.
The Buddha Akṣobhyajñāna is one's own mind; within the principle of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*), the wisdom that discriminates is fundamentally unmoving.

The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the foremost, clearly represents the sublime wisdom of skillful discernment within the non-substantiality of one's own mind. The Bodhisattva Bodhyaṅga is the head of such true faith within one's own mind. The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha is one's own mind, clearly perceiving that the mind and its objects are both Buddha.
According to the laws of the country of Samudramukha, because one universally perceives that both self and others are equally Buddhas, this will be explained extensively in the text below.
Only then can it be clarified that this very body is the Buddha and this very mind creates the Buddha; to perceive a Buddha outside of the mind is not called having faith.
The above concludes the explanation of the assembly with identical names within the section on the surrounding multitudes.
Second is the explanation of the assembly with different names, such as Sāgaraprabhā and others.
What is the intent of this?
This passage of seven lines and a half is divided into four sections in terms of its meaning:
first, the statement of the Bodhisattvas' intention; second, the explanation of the Bodhisattvas' names; third, the summary of the number of the assembly; and fourth, the praise of their virtues.

First, to explain the intention behind the assembly of Bodhisattvas: as for why these ten assemblies have distinct names, the meaning of their shared titles has already been explained in the preceding section. Furthermore, the significance of the specific names has likewise been elucidated as previously discussed.

The intention behind these various alternative names is to clarify that by means of those practices of Samantabhadra, one enters the mundane world to benefit sentient beings; as the practices differ, the names likewise differ accordingly.
It is to clarify that because they pervade every distinct direction, they are called "universal" (samanta).

The intention of this assembly is to clarify the entry into the mundane world to benefit and transform sentient beings, thereby enabling those beings to attain the Dharma of their own selves; for this reason, they are assigned a position at the initial stage of the ten abodes.

By clarifying its application, it manifests the sudden vehicle of the ancient dharma for those at the initial stage of the ten abodes; because it does not deviate from the ancient traces, it is no different from the old path, just as the great royal highway is traversed by both the new and the old alike.
By means of this ancient method, one enters into worldly affairs to benefit sentient beings, awakening the deluded masses and causing them to return to the study of antiquity.

For this reason, the various names of Samantabhadra from within the stage of Buddhahood are provisionally assigned to the initial mind of the Ten Abodes, in order to demonstrate that subsequent enlightenment does not deviate from the ancient traces.

Furthermore, it clarifies that the fruit of Buddhahood attained by the Tathāgatas of the past who realized perfect enlightenment, as well as the fruit of Samantabhadra’s conduct, constitute the eternal path traversed by all Buddhas of the past and present; this clarifies the gateway of faith.

This multitude of various names for entering the mundane world to benefit sentient beings clarifies that the initial aspiration of the sentient beings to be converted to enter the Path remains identical to their own original Dharma and does not deviate from its ancient traces.

Later, there may be those who resolve their minds to practice; each should examine this within their own mind through the power of concentration and wisdom, for it cannot be grasped through mere emotional faith. Only those who have long planted roots of goodness are capable of hearing this and remaining undeluded.
Even Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles who possess the seeds of the faculties and the six supernormal powers still harbor doubts;
yet among the ranks of ordinary beings, those with the nature of the One Vehicle enter through faith while remaining within that common stream.

As the sutras themselves clearly state, for those of the three vehicles who possess inferior understanding, the Buddha, in accordance with their faculties, provisionally taught that this Sahā world is an impure land because it is characterized by the five turbidities, while the pure lands exist in other directions.
Some say that this world-realm is defiled, and that above the fourth dhyāna there exists a separate pure land for bodhisattvas;
others claim that the fruit of Buddhahood is only accomplished after an incalculable aeon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
It has not yet been taught that the pure and the defiled coexist, that the mundane contains the Dharma-realm, and that ordinary beings and sages dwell together without mutual obstruction.
Those who adhere to the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles as being ultimately real find it difficult to believe in this gateway of the One Vehicle of the Dharma-realm.

In order to study through provisional expressions, provisional teachings, and provisional contemplations, and thereby break through the attachments of coarse, manifest ignorance, one practices a portion of the coarse *pāramitās*, attains the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*), and perceives that among the various Buddha-lands there are those that are self-originated and others-originated, as well as those that are pure and those that are defiled; thus, one rejoices in the former, feels aversion toward the latter, and concurrently cultivates pure practices.

By practicing various provisional contemplations on *tathatā* (suchness) as well as the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth, one attains a portion of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). One’s retribution becomes superior to that of the various devas, and one’s supernormal powers are likewise superior; with a mind of superior joy and revulsion, one will never again be born in evil lands or defiled realms.
By the power of their original vows, they come briefly to the places where Buddhas attain enlightenment and then depart.
As it is said in the teachings of the Three Vehicles, there are many such instances; those who have not yet turned their minds toward awakening shall always be like this.

Regarding those who study the provisional teachings: because their faculties are inferior, they do not hear these teachings, and even if they were to hear them, they would not believe them, as is fully explained in the subsequent sections of the sutra.

Thus, in order to refute such views, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* only provide a partial and brief exposition; they have not yet discussed the matter in its entirety.
Therefore, those who study the teachings should be careful not to practice only one school.
One should reflect deeply upon the underlying intent of the scriptures of all the various traditions.
There have been many who spent their entire lives studying the Path, yet because their wisdom derived from hearing was neither refined nor extensive, they instead slandered the Mantras.
The details have been explained at length; for now, they shall be presented in brief.
The above concludes the explanation of the intended meaning of the various names of the assembly of bodhisattvas.

Second, regarding the interpretation of the term "bodhisattva": these ten names of bodhisattvas are each a general designation for one of the *pāramitās* within the stages of the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*).
Within each [of these stages], ten [perfections] are fully present, because they are established as the names of the practices.
These ten pāramitās practiced by the ten bodhisattvas are each the common practice of bodhisattvas throughout the five stages.

Furthermore, according to the practices within the five stages: the ten abodes possess ten, the ten practices possess ten, the ten transferences possess ten, the ten grounds possess ten, and the eleventh ground possesses ten; collectively, these constitute the number one hundred.
This clarifies that within each single pāramitā there are ten, and within those ten there are a hundred.
Furthermore, within each of the ten stages (bhūmis), all ten are fully present; thus, within the ten stages, there are a hundred.
Taken together, these five stages collectively constitute five hundred gates of *pāramitā*.
According to the names assigned to their respective practices and stages, the fruits they evoke differ; yet, in terms of their general stages, these are simply the ten titles of the Bodhisattvas.
For what reason is he titled the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ocean-Light Moon Great Radiance?

Because his practice of the Dharma is boundless, his great compassion is vast, and his benefit to others is as extensive as the ocean; all who receive his benefit are led to see their nature and attain the coolness of liberation, and for this reason he is named Moonlight.
Once one has attained this state of coolness, there is no wisdom that does not illuminate; it is called "Great Illumination" because it brings all sentient beings in every world to great awakening.
*Mahābodhisattva*: *mahābodhi* means "Great Awakening."
*Satva* means "sentient being" (*sattva*).
Because one does not abandon sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is called *mahābodhisattva*; this is abbreviated as *bodhisattva*.
In Sanskrit, this is called *mahābodhisattva*; here it is translated as "beings with the mind for the path of great enlightenment.
This is because, in order to realize the path for themselves, they do not abandon the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and thereby bring about the great awakening of sentient beings.

Furthermore, because the birth and death of sentient beings is itself the bodhi of a bodhisattva, and because it clarifies that the dharma-realm is a single truth without differentiated characteristics, this is characterized primarily by the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).

The names of the other nine bodhisattvas serve as their companions, clarifying that through the practice of the great gate of giving within the *dharmadhātu*, they extensively save others like the ocean; they are called Moonlight because they benefit others by removing the heat of afflictions and attaining refreshing coolness.

These names are themselves the practices to be performed; that is, these ten names of bodhisattvas represent the myriad practices of the primary and attendant *pāramitās* of the initial resolve within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
In the passage below this image, within the "Ten Abodes" chapter, the names of the Buddhas whom the Bodhisattvas originally served are all titled "Moon.
This follows the same pattern as the ten Buddhas within the Ten Abodes, whose names are all likewise titled "Moon. This is according to that method.

Next, regarding the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Cloud-Sound-Ocean-Light-Undefiled-Treasury within the Perfection of Precepts (*śīla-pāramitā*): he is called "Cloud-Sound" because his nature-precept and great compassion universally rain down the sound of the Dharma.
The nature-precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) are undefiled, for they are like the great ocean which does not harbor corpses.

One clarifies that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) as the essence of the precepts; there is no phenomenon that is not pure, for it is as vast as the ocean.

"Light" refers to the essence of the precepts of purity; when both mind and environment are true, it is called light. Furthermore, because pure wisdom constantly illuminates the conventional world, it is called light.
"Stainless" means that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is free from defilement.
"Treasury" means that the nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) constantly contains all phenomena; there is nothing that is not pure, because it clarifies the single reality.
Because both the general and the specific are truly without defilement or impurity, he is named Cloud-Sound Ocean-Light Stainless-Treasury.
The Bodhisattva is as described before.

Next, regarding the Bodhisattva named Merit-Jewel-Crest Wisdom-Arisen within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), because his body is adorned by the patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*), he is named Merit-Jewel-Crest.

"Jewel Topknot" (Ratnaśikhin) refers to the ornament upon the head; it clarifies that for a bodhisattva, the arousal of the mind and patience are the foremost, and thus the head is adorned with jewels.
"Born of Wisdom" (Jñānajāta) means that because one is able to practice patience, wisdom is thereby born.
As previously stated, this clarifies that patience constitutes the meaning of the "Flower Topknot.

Next, regarding the Bodhisattva named King Sovereign of Merit Great Radiance (*Guṇendrarāja-mahāprabha*) within the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), this clarifies that through the diligent practice of benefiting sentient beings, one summons manifold merit; for among the myriad practices performed, there is none that does not benefit others.

The "Great Light of the Sovereign-like King" refers to universal illumination; because he constantly employs the light of wisdom within the ocean of birth and death to benefit sentient beings without weariness, causing them all to attain understanding, he is called the Great Light.

As with the preceding Bodhisattvas, next, regarding the one titled the Bodhisattva Good Valiant Lotus Topknot within the *dhyānapāramitā*, it clarifies that the *dharmadhātu* constitutes the essence of dhyāna; having given rise to faith from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), this marks the initial entry into realization.
To clarify that in a single thought there is no deliberation, one suddenly transcends all conceptualizations; because true wisdom is darkly united with reality, it is called "valiant.
Because this wisdom can penetrate the conventional world while remaining unstained by worldly existence, it is named the "Lotus."

The topknot signifies that within the dharma manifested by the Bodhisattva of this stage, he wears a lotus-flower crown upon his head; this clarifies that the essence of meditative concentration abides in the world as the ultimate truth, remaining unstained by either stillness or agitation.
Next, regarding the one titled Bodhisattva Universal Wisdom Cloud Sun Banner within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this clarifies that the sixth wisdom is like a cloud, for it rains down the rain of Dharma.
The light of wisdom destroys darkness, and thus it is named the Sun;
it subdues the heterodox and reveals the orthodox, and is therefore called the Banner.

Next, regarding the Bodhisattva Great Diligence Vajra-Navel within the *Upāya-pāramitā*, this clarifies that the seventh dwelling, the seventh practice, the seventh dedication, the seventh stage, and all seventh positions among the five stages collectively cultivate the stage of compassion.
Because its ultimate truth is perfectly interfused with both the defiled and the pure, it is called "skillful means" (*upāya*).

As illustrated by a metaphor given by a Bodhisattva in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) among the ten stages: "Suppose there were one country that was entirely pure and another country that was entirely defiled; it would be difficult to discern the distinction between this purity and this defilement."

For instance, when the youth Sudhana, in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), beheld the laywoman Śrīprabhā—here translated as "Fulfilling Wishes"—it was to clarify that this seventh stage accomplishes profound and deep great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) in order to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings.
He further addressed Sudhana, saying:
"I have eighty-four thousand nayutas of fellow-practitioners and attendants who constantly dwell in this garden.
This intention clarifies that within each stage, the seventh perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) constitutes the stage of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā).

Regarding the statement "eighty-four thousand companions of like practice," it means that I have practiced in accordance with all eighty-four thousand gates of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), for I constantly take birth and death as my garden and grove.

Thus, this Bodhisattva clarifies that within the stage of the first resolve among the ten stages of dwelling, it refers to the seventh *pāramitā* within the ten *pāramitās* of that single dwelling; it does not refer to the seventh *pāramitā* within the seventh dwelling.

Within the ten stages (bhūmis), there are ten instances of the seventh stage; the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) is present within each individual stage, for in each case, skillful means brings to completion the myriad practices of compassion and wisdom.
The same applies to the other pāramitās.

Within the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), each one possesses the ten; likewise for the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*adhimukti*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh stage—each has its own ten, following this pattern of the names of these ten bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, because it is the seventh door of skillful means (*upāya*) among the ten *pāramitās* within the first stage of the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), and because it encompasses the ten *pāramitās* as the primary and auxiliary aspects of compassion and wisdom within a single stage, it clarifies that great compassion is firm and steadfast; dwelling amidst birth and death without weariness is called "great diligence" (*mahāvīrya*).
It destroys the stubborn defilements of others and is therefore called "Vajra" (Diamond).
While dwelling in the mundane world amidst the same fetters as others, it does not impair the Middle Way and is thus called "Nābhi" (Navel).
"Navel" signifies the point where wisdom and compassion meet in the center.

As for the Buddha emitting the light of taking birth at the navel wheel, this symbolizes the intermediate state of wisdom and compassion; its extensive meaning will be clarified in the subsequent text.
The Bodhisattva is as described above.

This refers to the seventh skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) within the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (prathamacittotpādabhūmi), among the ten stages; it serves to clarify how the ten pāramitās function as the primary and auxiliary factors within a single stage.

In the Dwelling of the Ground of Cultivation and the Dwelling of Practice—these ten dwellings—each is fully endowed with the ten pāramitās in a state of mutual integration and perfect harmony. One dwelling possesses ten, and ten dwellings possess one hundred; this pattern applies to the five stages as well, totaling five hundred, extending even to infinity.

Next, regarding the name "Fragrant Flame Light Banner" (*Gandhārci-prabhā-dhvaja*) among the bodhisattvas within the eighth vow, *pāramitā*: their great vows are vast and fragrant, hence they are called "fragrance" (*gandha*); because their wisdom follows their vows and, according to the faculties of beings, destroys delusions, it is called "light" (*prabhā*); and because they enter into [the realms of] the heterodox and destroy obstacles, they are named "banner" (*dhvaja*).
As in the eighth stage, one frequently acts as a heterodox teacher of external paths, associates with those of such wrong views, and then destroys the path of those heterodox teachers.

Examples include the seer Vemacitra and others during the eighth dwelling; these are the spiritual friends within the eighth dwelling of Sudhana, for it is only through clear wisdom and purity that one can destroy what is heterodox.

Regarding the ninth power among the *pāramitās*, the Bodhisattva named Greatly Luminous Virtue and Profound Beautiful Voice (*Mahāprabhāsa-gambhīra-svarābhigīti*): this clarifies that the power of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*) constitutes the stage of a great Dharma teacher (*mahādharma-bhāṇaka*), for he is skilled in preaching the Dharma; therefore, he is named Greatly Luminous Virtue and Profound Beautiful Voice.
"Bodhisattva" is explained as before.

Regarding the name "Born from the Light of Great Merit and Wisdom" for the Bodhisattva within the tenth perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*), it clarifies that this refers specifically to the perfection of wisdom.

These ten names of Bodhisattvas clarify that within the stage of the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), one employs the ten *pāramitās* to remedy the obstacles inherent in the Initial Resolve, thereby perfecting the gateway of compassion and wisdom of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Regarding this cultivation and purification, the dharmas are unified into a single dharma.

Now, in explaining the various pāramitās, each is practiced differently; this clarifies that upon a single dharma, one cultivates and purifies it through ten dharmas. Through habitual practice, these become increasingly luminous, and because they are perfected as one, that dharma does not depart from its original practice, nor does its timing deviate from its original time.

Because there is no intrinsic nature at that time, and because the three periods of time have no coming or going, one simply possesses within a single dharma the essence and function of the ten pāramitā practice-gates; one simply distinguishes the stages of the first and second dwellings (*vihāra*) through the maturation of cultivation within a single dharma; and one simply distinguishes the differences in the levels of the stages according to the varying degrees of depth and maturity in the realization of wisdom, compassion, vows, and practice within a single dharma—this is because the dharmas themselves are not different.
The meaning of the six characteristics—totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration—can be understood through their perfect interpenetration.

Third, regarding the summary of the number of the assembly, the Sūtra says: "With these as their leaders, there were as many [bodhisattvas] as there are atoms in ten Buddha-worlds. This refers to that very passage.
Fourth, regarding the praise of virtues, this is contained in the following fifteen and a half lines of the sūtra.
As the text itself provides the full account, there is no need for further explanation.

Thus, this ocean-like assembly as a whole represents the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s practices, eternally abiding in the world to establish the laws of Dharma, and accomplishing the successive stages of the Bodhisattva’s ten abodes, ten practices, and ten grounds, thereby causing all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter [the truth], constantly serving as a refuge and protection for all in the world.
As was fully elucidated in the preceding section on praising virtues, it is likewise fully elucidated in the following section on obtaining benefits.

As in the section on obtaining benefits, this constitutes the sequential order of entering the Dharma through skillful means for benefiting sentient beings; "entering" here means becoming identical with what the Buddha knows, serving as a model for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) for future learners.

Delusion is simply the state of an ordinary being, while awakening is identical to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; both are fundamentally and primordially attained, and all are members of the assembly of "shadows and echoes.

The same principle applies to the deities and spirits mentioned below: they all assist the Buddha in propagating his transformation and manifesting his virtues, so that the Buddha-dharma may circulate throughout the world and sentient beings may obtain benefit.
Second, there were vajra-holding spirits as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-world.
This section consists of thirteen and a half lines of scripture;
its meaning is divided into four parts:

First, indicating the Dharma by way of assigned stages; second, explaining the names and correlating them with practices; third, enumerating the numbers; fourth, extolling their spiritual virtues. Regarding the first, indicating the Dharma by way of assigned stages:

it clarifies that these spiritual beings (*devas*) have already attained the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*); their nature is equal to that of all Buddhas and their wisdom is identical to ultimate truth. They follow the conduct of Samantabhadra to dwell in the world and provide protection, and are thus called "spirits" (*devas*), because they protect and uphold the True Dharma.

Regarding the manifestation of the dharma through practice: this serves to manifest the second stage, the Dwelling of Refining the Ground (*viśuddhabhūmi*), within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); it takes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) as its primary focus, clarifying that ethical discipline has the meaning of protection and defense.
Taking the Dharma-body as the essence of the precepts, it accords with reality and is indestructible; thus it is called "Vajra.

As for the Bodhisattva Candraprabha-mahāprabha mentioned previously, he refers to the first stage among the ten abodes, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*); the meaning within this has already been explained in the preceding section.

This assembly consists of ten deities; they clarify the second stage, the Dwelling of Purifying the Ground (*viśuddhabhūmi*), as the masters of the Dharma-gate of Precepts (*śīla*). Because their purpose is protection, they are titled the Vajra-holding Deities (*Vajrapāṇi-devas*).
"Adherence" (zhí) means maintaining the precepts without transgression; this is termed "adherence.
When that wisdom accords with reality, it is designated as "divine" (shén).

Regarding the correlation between these two definitions and their practice: this assembly of deities takes the *śīla-pāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline) as its essence. The ten names of the deities are precisely the names of the ten *pāramitās* corresponding to the essence of the precepts; each deity represents one practice.

The first is the Vajrapāṇi deity of exquisite form, Nārāyaṇa; he presides over the gate of the *dānapāramitā* within the *śīlapāramitā*, whereby the perfection of giving is accomplished through natural morality (*dharmatā-śīla*), thereby invoking and manifesting exquisite form.
The emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) destroys delusions; therefore, it is called Nārāyaṇa, which signifies "indestructible.
This stage clarifies that by upholding the nature-precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*), one attains an indestructible body.
"Grasping" (*dharana*) carries the meaning of "guiding and maintaining."
"Vajra" means indestructible.
The Vajrapāṇi deity, Swift Banner of the Solar Disc, presides over the perfection of morality within the essential morality.
Because his light of morality is without flaw, he is named "Solar Disc."
One who sees thus is an Arhat, called "The Swift.
With the delusions of self and others exhausted, he is called "The Banner.
With no divergent thoughts in his mind, he is called "The Grasper."
Its nature is indestructible and is thus called "Vajra" (Diamond).
It is termed "True Sovereignty" and named "Divine" (*deva*), because it takes wisdom as its divinity.
The third is the Vajra-holding Divine Being of Flower-Light on Mount Sumeru, who presides over the perfection of patience within the perfection of ethical discipline.
Because his patience regarding the Dharma was lofty and supreme, he was named Sumeru.
Because he adorned his conduct with patience, all who saw him were delighted, and he was named Flower.
Because he personally subdued arrogance, he was named Light.
To maintain patience without fail is called "grasping.
Taking the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as patience is like a diamond.
Wisdom that knows all things without conceptual thought is designated as "spiritual" (*shen*).
The Vajra-holding Spirit Pure Cloud Sound presides over the perfection of diligence within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
To tread upon the mundane while remaining eternally true is called "purity."
He expounds the Dharma without ceasing, moistening and nourishing all sentient beings; thus he is called Cloud-Sound.
Hearing his Dharma, they shatter their delusions; thus he is called Vajra.
His wisdom knows all phenomena without striving to know them; thus he is titled Divine.
Fifth, the Vajrapāṇi deity of exquisite sense faculties presides over the dhyāna-pāramitā within the śīla-pāramitā.
Because there is no discursive thought in dhyāna, yet the six sense faculties function in accordance with wisdom, they are called "exquisite sense faculties."
To employ [the mind] while remaining eternally quiescent is termed "grasping.
That which cannot be destroyed by thought is designated as "Vajra.
Furthermore, because the wisdom of non-thought can destroy the delusions of both self and others, it is designated as "Vajra."
In tranquil wisdom there is no movement; when correct insight functions accordingly, it is designated as "spiritual power" (*śakti*).
The Vajrapāṇi Spirit of the Six Delightful Radiances presides over wisdom, for it is capable of destroying darkness.
The seventh, the Great Tree Resounding with Thunder, presides over the seventh gate of great compassion.
"Tree" signifies the meaning of providing shelter and shade; it clarifies that the gate of the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means) provides shelter and shade for sentient beings.
The radiance of the eight lion kings represents the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
It gives rise to non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), being as sovereign as a lion king, for it is able to shatter the various heterodox arguments of external paths.
As for the "Nine Secret Flames of Supreme Vision," their primary power is the *pāramitā* [of skillful means].

Possessing sovereign mastery over the Dharma, they flow secretly through "sameness of purpose" (*sāmānārthya*), sometimes acting as teachers of heterodox paths to break the bonds of those who are attached.

This stage is the stage of the Great Dharma Master; for every ninth pāramitā that pervades the five hundred gates of pāramitā within the five stages, the ninth is invariably the stage of the Dharma Master.
The ninth of the ten stages is the Stage of the Dharma Prince.

Just as the spiritual friend of the youth Sudhana, within the ninth stage of the ten stages, acts as the Brahmin Jvalanaprabha in the position of a Dharma Master; he manifests the entry into the five fires of the heterodox paths, such as climbing the mountain of blades and entering the mass of fire.
This is called "Secret Flame and Supreme Eye.
Because they secretly engage in common activities and establish teachings to shatter ignorance, it is named "Secret Flame.
Because their eye of wisdom knows the faculties [of beings], it is named "Supreme Eye."
The Vajradhara deity named Daśapadmaprabhamaṇicūḍa presides over the perfection of wisdom within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
He is like the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) encountered by the youth Sudhana during the tenth stage, the "Stage of Consecration" (*abhiṣekabhūmi*), who appeared as a young girl named Maitrīcaryā.
Attaining the truth without realization, dwelling in the mundane world without defilement—this is called "Lotus.
Great wisdom that knows the faculties of beings is named "Light.
Ascending to the rank of consecration is named "Maṇi Topknot."
"Maṇi" means "stainless jewel" (vimala-ratna) in this language.
This constitutes the ten positions and ten pāramitās within the second stage, the Dwelling of Purifying the Ground (śuddhādharā-vihāra).
These ten positions and their attendant practices are called the "ten Vajradharas. The names of these deities are all established based on their respective practices and stages.

In the explanation of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), each single abode contains ten; thus the ten stages contain one hundred. This applies to all five groups [of ten]. One by one, in their proper sequence, the names and meanings are to be correlated accordingly; such is the conformity of the Dharma.
The third section below consists of two parts: the enumeration [of the stages] and the praise of their virtues, which may be understood according to the text.
The third is the Stage of Practice (*caryā-pratipatti*) among the ten stages (*daśa-vihāra*).
Within this, the six lines and a half of sūtra are divided into four sections in meaning:

First, the enumeration of the numbers; second, the assignment of positions to represent the dharmas; third, the explanation of names and their correlation with practices; fourth, the reiteration of the numbers and the praise of spiritual virtues.
Regarding the first, the enumeration of the numbers, it is as in the first line above.

Second, regarding the assignment of these [deities] to specific stages to symbolize the Dharma: these ten groups of body-deities (kāyika-devatās) are assigned to represent the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) within the ten abodes (daśa-vihāra).
Because they have accomplished the patience of the Dharma (dharma-kṣānti), they act with mastery to benefit sentient beings amidst birth and death; thus, they are called "deities" (devatās).

In the following section on praising his virtues, it is stated that he has accomplished great vows and made offerings to and served all Buddhas. This clarifies that in the past, while abiding [in practice], he served all sentient beings with a mind of discipline and patience, causing them to attain Buddhahood, because the essence of the Buddhas and sentient beings is non-dual.
Since they have already become Buddhas, why would they need to rely upon offerings?

By serving with immeasurable bodies and immeasurable varieties of ritual requisites, they make offerings to all sentient beings at all times, causing them to attain Buddhahood; this is the meaning of "discipline and patience" (kṣānti) and the meaning of "body and assembly" (kāya-gaṇa).

Third, regarding the explanation of the names and their correspondence to the practices: these ten deities represent the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of patience; thus, it clarifies that each individual practice pervades all practices.
The first, known as the Deity of the Flower-Tuft Adorned Body, presides over the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
This is because patience is clarified as the fruit of the flower-garland, by which one obtains adornments to grace the crown of the head.

Regarding "the multitude of bodies": this refers to practicing generosity during the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), clarifying that one serves and makes offerings throughout the entire Dharma-realm by means of numerous clouds of bodies and numerous ornaments, for the sake of extensively benefiting sentient beings.
"Divine" (*deva*) means that wisdom follows the practice of patience with sovereign mastery; thus it is called "divine.
These ten *pāramitās* take patience as their essence.
Regarding the second light, the "Body Deities Illumining the Ten Directions," they preside over the *śīla-pāramitā* within the *kṣānti-pāramitā*.

In this stage, the essence of the precepts is taken as the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*); it clarifies that the perfection and luminosity of the precept of patience cause those who see it to rejoice.
The radiance of the precept of patience is called "light," which illuminates bodies throughout the ten directions.
The various deities are as explained previously.

Regarding the deity "Subduer of the Multitude through the Melody of the Three Oceans," this is because he presides over the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) within the perfection of patience.

As for "Melody of the Ocean": it clarifies that although one hears a vast multitude of sounds—whether good or evil, disparaging or praising—they are like the sound of ocean tides; one gives rise to neither sorrow nor joy. This is the meaning of subduing, and it constitutes the capacity for patience.
Furthermore, because their own voices are like the sound of the ocean tide, they know the proper time to teach and transform sentient beings so that no opportunity is lost.
The fourth is the Host of Devas Adorned with Pure Flower Topknots, who presides over the perfection of diligence within the perfection of patience.
Advancing by means of the patience of dharmas is called "purity.
Advancing in a manner that is observable is called "flower.
Because practice brings forth its fruit, which is used to adorn the topknot—since diligence is the foremost of the long path—the flower is used to adorn the head.
The five kinds of immeasurable body-attendants of majestic deportment preside over the dhyāna-pāramitā within the kṣānti-pāramitā.
Because they manifest dharmas in accordance with the faculties [of sentient beings], they are called "immeasurable."
Constant tranquility in movement and stillness is called "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*).
To clarify that walking, standing, sitting, and reclining never depart from the essence of meditative concentration is termed "dignified deportment.
As for the six supreme light-adorned deities who attend the body, they preside over the illumination of both self and others through wisdom.
"Clarity" refers to using the radiant light of meditative concentration and wisdom to illuminate the mind and its objects, thereby adorning the Dharma-body.

As for the "multitude of deities whose bodies are clouds of pure radiant fragrance," this clarifies the seventh [perfection], the skillful means of great compassion; because it is neither constrained by defilement nor purity, it is called "pure radiance."
Encompassing all with compassion, his speech forms the Dharma and delights the hearts of the multitude; thus he is named Fragrant Cloud (Gandhamegha).

Because he clearly moistens sentient beings with the rain of Dharma, this clarifies the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body: precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Regarding the eighth, the "Body-Protecting Gathering Deities": it refers to the clear wisdom that, in accordance with great vows, gathers and sustains all sentient beings.

Abiding in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), within the fifth of the eight stages, when the accomplishment of effortlessness is realized through clear wisdom, one immediately receives the empowerment upon the crown of the head by the hands of the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is the meaning of being sustained by those Buddhas.
The ninth, the Universal Manifestation and Gathering Body Deity, clarifies the stage of the Dharma King who possesses sovereign mastery over the power of the ninth *pāramitā*.

Because he universally manifests all teachings and causes the ninety-five kinds of heterodox views to flow forth and act in concert with all sentient beings, it is called "Universal Manifestation and Gathering. This refers, for example, to the Brahmin Jvalanāmukha and others.
The ten classes of deities of immovable radiant bodies clarify the tenth perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
They are named "Immovable Radiance.
Furthermore, they constitute the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka), which is also called "Immovable Light."
Furthermore, this clarifies that within this stage of patience (*kṣānti*), it is one of the ten *pāramitās*.
At the conclusion, the enumeration of the four fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the praise of its virtues may be understood according to the text.

These aforementioned ten *pāramitās* take patience as their essence; this clarifies that through good or evil, and through defamation or praise, one attains the wisdom of immovability (*akampya-jñāna*).
The fourth section contains six and a half lines of scripture, which are divided into four parts:
