first, enumerating the number of the assembly; second, using stages to symbolize the Dharma; third, explaining the names and correlating them with practices; and fourth, concluding with the enumeration and praise of virtues.
First, regarding the enumeration of the entire assembly: this refers to the total number listed at the beginning of the first line.

Second, regarding the symbolic representation of the stages (*bhūmi*): these ten "feet-walking spirits" symbolize the stage of "Noble Birth" (*janma-bhūmi*) within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), presiding over the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
As stated in the section on praising virtues, "approaching and following the Tathāgata without abandoning him throughout immeasurable kalpas" is the meaning of diligence (*vīrya*).
This is to clarify that the true nature of reality (*dharmatā-tathatā*) serves as the essence of practice, and that this dharma-practice is used to adorn the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
"Foot-traveler" (*padaja*) signifies the meaning of diligence; because all practices are fulfilled, he is named the Deity of Foot-traveling.
"Deity" (*deva*) refers to the wisdom that follows along with these practices.

Third, regarding the explanation of names and their correlation with the practices: first, as for the Foot-and-Hand Attendant Spirit named Jewel Seal, she presides over the *dāna-pāramitā* within the *vīrya-pāramitā*. This clarifies that by means of the wisdom-seal of the Dharma-jewel, she performs diligent practice to guide and receive sentient beings.
The hand signifies the meaning of grasping and taking.

As for the foot-traveling spirit Lotus-Radiance, this clarifies that within the perfection of vigor and the perfection of ethical discipline during the stage of Abiding in Noble Birth, one constantly dwells within the ocean of birth and death, yet remains unstained, just like a lotus flower.
That which causes those who see it to resolve their minds is called "light.
Walking with the feet signifies the meaning of practicing diligence without weariness.
Because of mastery over wisdom, it is termed "divine" (*deva*).
The foot-attendant deity Pure Flower Topknot primarily presides over the dharma of the perfection of patience within the perfection of diligence.
Patience is called "stainless," which constitutes purity.
Patience brings about the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*); it is the crown ornament of the *Avataṃsaka*, in the sense that patience constitutes its flower garland.

Regarding the deity "Whose Feet Are Seen as the Four Means of Attraction" (*Catur-saṃgraha-vastu-dṛṣṭa-pāda-caraṇa-devatā*), she presides over the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) within the perfection of vigor.
"Comprehending all right views" is the meaning of diligence (*vīrya*).
Because one constantly restrains the sense faculties so that views do not arise, there is no unwholesome view.

As for the footstep-moving spirit *Pañcābhijña-ratna-tārakā-dhvaja*, he presides over the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*); because he takes sublime principle as his meditation, he is called "Sublime."
"Jewel" (Ratna) refers to the Way (Dharma).
Because one follows the practice to shatter delusions, it is called "Star Banner" (Tārakadhvaja).

The myriad practices are the stars; as they do not depart from the essence of dhyāna and all possess illuminating light, they shatter delusions according to the faculties. To know the faculties with perfect clarity is what is meant by "star."
In this stage, vigor is taken as the essence of dhyāna; dhyāna is able to manifest, and wisdom is able to know phenomena. Because one returns to skillfully knowing phenomena, it is called a "star."
The banner represents meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
As for the foot-traveling deity "Delighting in Emitting Sublime Sounds," he presides over the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
He is called "Delighting in Emitting Sublime Sounds" because he takes diligence as the essence of wisdom and constantly delights in preaching the Dharma for others.
The Light-Footed Spirit of the Seven Sandalwood Trees presides over the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
Because he accomplishes the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he is named after fragrant trees; this signifies the meaning of compassion providing shelter and shade.
"Light" signifies the meaning of illuminating and guiding sentient beings.
The Lotus Radiant Footstep Deity presides over the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
This is because wisdom follows great aspirations, benefiting sentient beings according to their needs without being stained by anything.

As for the ninth, the Foot-Attendant Spirit Subtle and Wondrous Radiance, his primary station is that of the Dharma King of the Perfection of Power, because he transforms sentient beings through the light of the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
The footstep-following spirit named Accumulating Wondrous Flowers presides over the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
By means of wisdom, she accumulates all teachings, just as one strings flowers together to form a garland so that they are not lost; thus she teaches and transforms sentient beings.
The ten pāramitās mentioned above all take the vīrya-pāramitā as their essence.
Within each stage, there are both common and specific meanings; these can be seen by reflecting upon them, and one must not apply a single, uniform standard to them all.
The fourth section consists of a numerical summary praising their virtues, which may be understood from the text itself.
The fifth section comprises six and a half lines of scripture, the meaning of which is divided into four parts:

first, citing the number of the assembly; second, using specific positions to symbolize the Dharma; third, explaining the names and correlating them with the Dharma; and fourth, providing a numerical summary praising their virtues.
First, regarding the enumeration of the assembly: this refers to the initial practice mentioned above.
Second, regarding the designation of stages to symbolize the dharmas: this single stage symbolizes the ten pāramitās within the dwelling of the complete skillful means.

It takes the dhyāna-pāramitā as its essence; it takes the bodhimaṇḍa as the meaning of removing the defilements of the aggregates (skandha), because it clarifies that dhyāna can remedy the aggregates, just like a worldly threshing floor.

This is to clarify that meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) purifies the defiled grasping of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, and to demonstrate that wisdom (*prajñā*) can open up sublime insight by discerning the fundamental reality of the essence of principle and cognition.

Taking the dhyāna-pāramitā as the substance of the field, the prajñā-pāramitā as human effort, and the myriad practices of Samantabhadra as the means of transport to the Dharma-realm; taking the Palace of Universal Radiance Wisdom as the primary residence, and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) as the great treasury.
Among these, there are ten deities, each deity representing one *pāramitā*, serving as a model for practice that benefits both oneself and others.

Regarding the third section, the explanation of names and their correspondence to the dharmas: first is the Deity of the Pure Ornament Banner Altar, who presides over the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) while abiding within the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), endowed with skillful means.

Taking the essential nature of the concentration of the dharma-nature as the pure ground of *dāna*, and taking the essential nature of that undiminished concentration as the banner of adornment for the myriad practices.
The "banner" clarifies the meaning of the immovability of the essential nature of concentration.
Taking the nature of phenomena as being without intrinsic nature as that which is mounted upon is called the "Path.
Taking the meditative concentration of non-nature as that which can treat the aggregates which serve as its basis is called the "Field."
The "Divine" (shen) is the great wisdom within that which is without dependence and without intrinsic nature.
Because it is inconceivable and non-active, formless and without substance, yet pervades the entire dharma-realm and knows all phenomena, it is called the Divine.

Second is the Site-Protecting Spirit Jewel-Light of Mount Sumeru. "Mount Sumeru" signifies the meaning of loftiness and prominence; "Jewel-Light" signifies the meaning of being stainless. This is because the light of the precepts illuminates the mundane world, causing those who see it to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
Taking meditative concentration as one's precept and transcending emotional consciousness is the meaning of Sumeru.
That concentration can eliminate delusion is the meaning of "stainless.
That concentration can give rise to wisdom is the meaning of "precious light."
The third is the Site-Spirit named Thunder-Sound Banner-Mark, who presides over the perfection of patience within the perfection of meditation.
She is called "Banner-Mark" because she remains unmoved by the thunder-like sounds of praise and blame, maintaining the patience regarding phenomena (dharmakṣānti).
The meaning of "maṇḍala deity" is as explained previously.
Regarding the ten pāramitās, each possesses the significance of a maṇḍala within its respective stage among the five stages.
The Maṇḍala Deity of Sublime Eyes Showering Fourfold Flowers presides over the pāramitā of diligence within the pāramitā of dhyāna.

The Dharma-body is clarified as the essential substance of meditative concentration; based on this concentration, one gives rise to the vigor of the myriad practices, which is termed "Raining Flowers"—this is the meaning of vigor.
Because concentration can give rise to wisdom, it is called the "Sublime Eye."
Because they practice with the Flower of the Dharma-Eye and benefit sentient beings without weariness, this is due to diligence.
The fifth is the Way-Place Spirit Adorned with a Flower-Garland and Radiant Topknot, who presides over the perfection of meditation within the perfection of meditation.
Based on the fact that the self-nature of the Dharma-realm is devoid of movement or stillness, one initiates the practice of dhyāna to transform all distracted thoughts;
this is called "necklace" (yīng). Because concentration can give rise to wisdom, it is called "light" (guāng).
Because they attract their fruits through practice and adorn the crown [of the head], they are named as such.
Furthermore, these ten pāramitās are all "crown dharmas" (mūrdha-dharma). Why is this so?

This is because each of the gates of deliverance within the initial mind of the ten stages leads to the fruit of Buddhahood; because there is no distinction of beginning, middle, or end; and because one proceeds from the fruit of Buddhahood toward further superior advancement.
Sixth is the Ritual Ground Spirit named Rain of Jewel Adornments, who presides over the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), for wisdom can rain down the jewels of the Dharma.
Seventh is the Ritual Ground Spirit named Courageous Fragrant Eye, who presides over the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).

Because this stage is the stage of compassion (*karuṇā*), one who constantly dwells within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is called "valiant. One who gazes upon sentient beings with eyes of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is called "Fragrant Eyes" (*Gandhacakṣus*).

By means of the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body—the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—one gazes upon sentient beings, uprooting their suffering and bestowing happiness; thus, one is called "Fragrant Eyes."
The eighth is the Vajra-Colored Cloud Ritual Ground Deity, who clarifies the eighth vow-paramita (praṇidhāna-pāramitā), because he acts as a cloud of vows to cover all sentient beings.

Since this stage is the wisdom of effortlessness (anābhoga-jñāna) that can destroy heterodox currents, he is titled "Vajra-Colored Cloud," clarifying his ability to harmonize with and enter diverse paths.
The ninth is the Site-Protecting Spirit Lotus Radiance, whose primary power is the perfection of skillful means; this is the rank of the Dharma King.
He dwells in the world like a lotus flower, for his preaching of the Dharma constitutes his radiance.
The tenth is the Spirit of the Radiance of the Ten Sublime Lights who Illuminates the Bodhimanda; she presides over the Perfection of Wisdom.
Because she knows the faculties [of beings] through great wisdom, she is named "Sublime Light.
Because she knows the faculties and thereby destroys delusions, she is called "Illuminating."
The ten *pāramitās* mentioned above all have the *dhyāna-pāramitā* as their essence.
The four concluding verses praising these virtues may be understood according to the text.
The sixth stage, the Stage of Rectifying the Mind (*samyaktva-cittavihāra*), has the *prajñā-pāramitā* as its primary essence.
Regarding the ten city-protecting goddesses (*purī-devatā*), this is because within this *prajñāpāramitā* there are ten *pāramitās*.
Within this section, there are six and a half lines of scripture, the meaning of which is divided into four parts:

first, enumerating the number; second, assigning positions to symbolize the dharmas; third, explaining the names and correlating them with the practices; and fourth, concluding the enumeration and praising their virtues.
First, regarding the enumeration of the assembly: it is as in the initial practice.

Second, regarding the use of positions to symbolize dharmas: by means of this assembly of deities, the accomplishment of the contemplation of emptiness within the Abiding in the Right Mind is symbolized; it clarifies the skillful guarding of the city of the mind, which is named the Abiding in the Right Mind. This is like the sixth spiritual friend among the Ten Abidings of the youth Sudhana, namely the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha.

While standing by the side of his walking path, he entered into samādhi; his breath ceased, and from his feet emerged elders, householders, and brahmins, and even from the crown of his head emerged all the Buddhas and others, who, through vast clouds of bodies pervading the entire Dharma-realm, taught and transformed sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding the stage of Right Mind (samyak-citta) within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the Sūtra states:
"When this Bodhisattva hears the ten kinds of dharmas, his mind is settled and immovable.
This clarifies the stage of Right Mind, for it skillfully guards the city of the mind.
The City-Ruling Goddess is employed here to represent the station of rectifying the mind.

Regarding the threefold explanation of names and their correlation with the practices: the first is the City-Ruling Goddess Radiant Light of the Jewel Peak, who presides over the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Because he illuminates all sentient beings with the wondrous wisdom of non-substantiality, he is named Jewel Peak Radiance.

Just as a mountain peak reaches the limit where its characteristics merge with space, so too does his illumination through the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena reach the limit where all characteristics are exhausted.
To extensively bestow the wondrous wisdom of signlessness upon sentient beings is called "Illumination.
As for the "Lord," it refers to mastery over the wisdom of emptiness; thus, he is named the Lord.
As for the "City," it refers to mastery over both emptiness and existence; because it neither conjoins with nor disperses from nirvana and saṃsāra, it is named a City.
Furthermore, because they bestow the wisdom of the Dharma upon others and do not conjoin with the outflows of sensual desire, they are called "cities.
Second is the City-Ruling Goddess Subhavyūharājadhānī, who clarifies the benefit of sentient beings through wisdom and takes this as the essence of her precepts.
Sublime wisdom serves as the palace, governing others as the hall, and the myriad practices as the adornments.

Furthermore, the correct wisdom of the bodhisattva constitutes the exquisite ornamentation, great kindness and great compassion serve as the palace, and a mind free from discursive thought is the principal city.
The wondrous wisdom of signlessness is known through both principle and cognition; this is termed "spiritual power" (*śakti*).
Here, sharp wisdom is primary, while ethical discipline serves the sense of protection, acting as a fortress that protects all sentient beings.
The City-Ruling Spirit Pure Joy Treasure primarily presides over the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
She is named "Pure Joy" because she achieves patience through the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and because patience itself is joy.
Because the joy of the Dharma (dharmaprīti) is itself called a treasure, it is clarified that the ability to endure is a treasure.

From this point downward, the seven classes of spirits are assigned positions according to the sequence above; as the scriptural text is vast, it cannot be explained word by word, but one should know briefly that the principles are thus.
Such as the presiding deity of the *maṇḍala*, the presiding deity of the city, the presiding deity of the earth, and others—all of whom are goddesses, for the purpose of clarifying compassion.
Yet, in their true essence, they are neither male nor female; they merely manifest according to circumstances.

The seventh earth-ruling goddess presides over the ten pāramitās within the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), which is characterized by the skillful means of the pāramitās; thus, ten divine names are assigned to each of these ten pāramitās respectively.
This takes the Dharma-body as the substance of the earth, capable of giving rise to the myriad practices.
It takes wisdom, principle, compassion, and kindness as its divine nature because it is without retreat or movement; and because great compassion nourishes all things like the earth.
The eighth presiding mountain deity is the stage of Youthful Innocence (*kumārabhūta*), which corresponds to the ten *pāramitās* within the practice of the *pāramitā* of Vow (*praṇidhāna*).
"Mountain" signifies immovability and supreme loftiness.
The "Spirit" (deva) refers to the essence of wisdom that accords with the truth and is sovereign.

It clarifies the eighth abiding, the eighth practice, the eighth dedication, and the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), wherein the meritless wisdom is as immovable as a mountain; therefore, it is represented by a mountain spirit.
Among them, the ten deities represent the practice of the ten pāramitās within this stage.
They are also called "Intelligence Transcending the World," as they are as lofty and supreme as mountains.
The ninth deity, the Lord of the Forest, represents the stage of the Dharma Prince and primarily embodies the pāramitā of power.
The clarity of the Dharma being taught is like a forest because it provides vast and abundant shade; this is the rank of the Dharma Master.
The tenth is the Lord of Medicine Deity, who clarifies the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*) and presides over the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

Among these, one [aspect] concerns the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*): within this perfection of wisdom, there are ten perfections; clear wisdom knows the faculties [of beings] and bestows the medicine of the Dharma.
The fourth section praises its virtues, as can be understood from the text itself.
From the Bodhisattva Sāgaraprabhāmahārcis above until this Medicine King Goddess, the hundred pāramitās of the ten abodes among the assemblies of the Tathāgata’s five ranks are completed.
The assembly of those on the ten stages of practice should be understood as follows.
In this single scripture, every provision is entirely a dharma-gate; none are established in vain.

Every single matter and every single word are, in their entirety, the rules for the practice, awakening, and entry into the Dharma within the five stages; thus, they are the gateways of skillful means for entering the Dharma.

This clarifies the manner in which one enters the Dharma and nurtures and protects others through the five stages of the Buddha-fruit; therefore, those who enter it initially achieve union with wisdom, which is termed "divinity" (shen).
Furthermore, because they cover and nurture sentient beings, they are blessed by divine protection.
Because they dwell in the state of sovereign cultivation like the heavens,
and because they transform and benefit the various devas, they manifest the reception of celestial retribution throughout the ten directions and the three realms.

Furthermore, by means of the gate of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), they assume the bodies of asuras to enter the realms of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*), thereby manifesting sovereignty like that of a king.
*New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Scroll Ten;

Compiled by the Elder Li Tongxuan:
Section Three, from the Deity Who Oversees Cultivation down to the Deity Who Oversees Daytime.

These ten assemblies of deities constitute the dharma-gate of cause and effect for benefiting sentient beings through the ten practices; the Deity Who Oversees Cultivation is taken as the primary representation because its practice serves as the necessary provision.

Just as in the world one uses grain crops as provisions to nourish the conditioned body, so too in the Buddha-dharma one takes the practice of the ten pāramitās as provisions to nourish the Dharma-body.
This causes worldly habitual tendencies to gradually diminish, while supramundane habitual tendencies—great loving-kindness, great compassion, and great wisdom—are brought to fulfillment.

As in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), according to the exposition of the three vehicles: the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abidings (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) constitute the four kinds of equipment prior to the path;

from the first ground (*bhūmi*) upward constitutes the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). These are the conditioned and outflowing (*sāsrava*) practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles during one great *kalpa* (*mahā-kalpa*) prior to their respective grounds.

The path of seeing at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is as follows: throughout the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one fully believes that one’s own mind and the nature, characteristics, and great wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions are of an undifferentiated essence.
The initial mind of the ten abodes (daśabhūmi) perceives the Path through the power of the samādhi of skillful means (upāya).
From the first abode of the Initial Resolve (prathamacittotpāda) and all subsequent abodes, these collectively constitute the stage of the Path of Vision (darśanamārga).

The ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) are collectively termed the "preparatory application" (*prayoga*) and collectively the "provisioning preparatory application.

They are called "preparatory application" because one advances in tandem with the causes and effects of a Buddha; they are "provisioning" because they employ the conduct of Samantabhadra to equal the Buddha-fruit and bring compassionate vows to fulfillment. The provisions for the nature-fruit of the principle and wisdom of the Dharmakāya, as perceived by the initial mind of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), consist of the conduct of Samantabhadra and do not belong to the conditioned, impermanent states of humans or devas.

From the initial stage of generating the bodhicitta, one progresses through the five stages to cultivate the fruit of the Tathāgata’s dharma-body—the nature of wisdom and principle—and the fruit of Samantabhadra’s conduct; within the single true dharma-realm, these serve as mutual provisions for one another.
If one is discarded, both are not established; thus, a mind that is simultaneously defiled and pure arises.
Therefore, by adorning practice with the fruit of the Buddha’s wisdom and insight, and adorning the fruit with practice, it is called the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*.

Therefore, throughout the stages of the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications, all bodhisattvas entering these stages receive from the Buddhas of the ten directions names identical to their own, as well as the bestowing of wisdom and the touching of the crown of the head, thereby realizing the wisdom of the same essence.
For instance, Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles are mostly reborn in the pure lands of other directions, as well as in the distinct Bodhisattva pure lands above the fourth dhyāna.
Even if they remain in the desire realm, it is said that they do so by retaining their afflictions through the power of their compassionate vows to sustain rebirth.

This Dharma-gate of the sutra is not like that; it is the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s dharma-realm. From the first arousal of the mind, one dwells by means of the fruit of the nature of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom-dharmakāya and the fruit of Samantabhadra’s practice, which universally pervades birth and death. With movement and stillness equally balanced, and principle and phenomena advancing together, one uses the essence and function of the dharma-realm to treat residual habits; thus, dharmas have no precedence or succession, and new and old are equalized in their retribution.
This is not like the distinct teachings of the Three Vehicles, which speak of other directions having separate pure lands,

of lingering in afflictions within this Sahā world, and of the stage of application being at the first bhūmi, while the initial stage of provisioning occurs during the ten faiths, the ten abidings, and the ten transferences.
Since there is no fruit of Buddhahood within these five stages, it is clear that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is not yet ultimate.

Thus, according to this sutra, within the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhācitta*), one personally realizes that within one’s own mind there are ten kinds of worlds—namely, the Golden World, the World of Wondrous Colors, the Lotus-Colored World, and so forth, totaling ten such colored worlds. Because these ten levels of faith are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the Buddha-realm that they take as their object is likewise of the nature of form (*rūpa*).

The Buddhas whom I have served are the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom, the Buddha of Unobstructed Wisdom, and the Buddha of Liberated Wisdom; these ten Buddhas of Wisdom are none other than one's own mind.
Because the ten kinds of fruits of the wisdom of one’s own mind, which is the object of faith, are designated as the ten titles of the Buddha-fruit;
one ultimately realizes and cultivates the perfected state of all Buddhas, achieving this wisdom such that it is not different from that wisdom.

Excluding these, within the stage of the Ten Faiths, one uses the mind of arising and ceasing to believe in the ten material worlds and the ten Wisdom Tathāgatas; continuing through the Ten Abidings, Ten Practices, Ten Transferences, Ten Grounds, and the eleventh ground of Equal Enlightenment, there are fifty instances of cause and effect in total. In all of these, the conduct of Samantabhadra serves as the cause, while the nature of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body—its wisdom and principle—constitutes the fruit; alternatively, these may be intermingled to mutually support and stimulate one another.

Within these two types of cause and effect across the five stages, there are a total of one hundred layers of Buddha-causes and -effects; by taking all five layers of causes and five layers of effects from each of the five stages, they collectively constitute one hundred and ten layers of cause and effect.

Regarding the causes and effects of the Buddha within the stage of the Ten Abodes, these consist of the Indrakusuma World, the Padmakusuma World, and the Ratnakusuma World; the names of the Buddhas therein are Viśeṣacandra Buddha, Akṣayacandra Buddha, and Acalacandra Buddha.
In this way, the ten worlds of flowers and the ten Buddhas, all sharing the same name "Moon," constitute the fruit of Buddhahood;
the ten Bodhisattvas of Wisdom, headed by Dharmamati Bodhisattva, constitute the cause for practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra.

For these ten stages, by the power of entering the Samādhi of Skillful Means, one truly realizes the wondrous wisdom of the Dharmakāya; thus, in this world, it is called "Flower," because the fruit is manifested through the blossoming of the flower.

The reason all the manifested Buddha-lands are named "Moon" is to clarify that within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one first beholds the Dharma-body and sublime wisdom manifests before them; being free from the heat of afflictions and having attained the Buddha's Dharma-body, which is as cool and refreshing as the moon, the world is thus established based on the state where the path of vision eliminates delusions.
The *Indra-flower* (因陀羅花) is here translated as the "Flower of the Sovereign" (*nengzhu hua*).

It clarifies the stage of the "Abiding in the Initial Aspiration for Enlightenment" (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), wherein one is born into the family of the Buddhas and is able to act as a master of the Dharma for all sentient beings.
The *pāṭala* flower is the red lotus. It signifies the purification of the stages of abiding and the progressive advancement toward excellence;
its brilliant blooming represents the meaning of being worthy of contemplation.

In general, by means of the causes and effects of entering the Way according to each stage, it is shown that the names of the Buddhas, their lands, and the worlds, as well as the Bodhisattvas, do not exist externally; this collectively clarifies the practices undertaken in one's own cultivation.
As in the stage of the Ten Practices, the ten worlds of wisdom and the ten names of the Buddhas are all termed "Eye," constituting the fruit of Buddhahood;
the ten forest-dwelling Bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakāraṇḍa-vyūha, constitute the causes for these practices.
The sequence of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) may be understood from the sutras;

their specific details will be clarified when we reach those respective positions. To state the essentials: the ten Buddhas of each stage constitute the fruit of that stage, while the ten Bodhisattvas of each stage constitute the cause for the practice of that stage.

Thus, in this first assembly, the Tathāgata is taken as the fruit of the five stages, while Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and the various deities are taken as the causes for the practice of the five stages.

Furthermore, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and the various deities and spirits take the fundamental wisdom of Vairocana as the primary cause for initiating their practice, and they regard their own bodies of practice as the fruit of the Buddha’s differentiated wisdom.

This is because the fruit of the Buddha-nature wisdom serves as the cause, and the present body of cultivation is itself the nature-fruit of principle and wisdom; thus, they mutually function as cause and effect, essence and function.
For this reason, within the praise of divine virtues, one first praises the Buddha’s virtues, and subsequently praises oneself for possessing the same wisdom and virtues as the Buddha.

This is the manner of entering the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which causes all practitioners to realize that delusion is itself ordinary and awakening is itself Buddhahood; therefore, wisdom and compassion must advance together.

This is like the land where the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of the first stage of the Ten Practices—the Practice of Joy—resides for the youth Sudhana, which is named "Three Eyes" (Sāyana); it corresponds to the worlds inhabited by Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices, such as the world named "Intimate Wisdom," the world named "Precious Wisdom," and so forth, comprising the Ten Wisdom Worlds.
Regarding the "three eyes": first is Mahāprajñā, second is liberation, and third is the Dharmakāya.
This is because the three eyes are also identified as the eye of wisdom (*jñāna-cakṣus*), the eye of insight (*prajñā-cakṣus*), and the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*).

It is like the character for "world" (loka), because it is like the three eyes on the face of the Heavenly King Maheśvara; for all Buddha-dharmas do not depart from this Dharma-body of great wisdom and great insight.
The meaning of these ten wisdoms of the world penetrates these three eyes.

For this reason, among the ten practices of Sudhana, the first spiritual friend’s land is named "Three Eyes," and the bhikṣu is named "Good Vision" (Sudarśana); this corresponds precisely to the stage of the ten practices.
The Buddhas are named Constantly Abiding Eye Buddha and Unconquerable Eye Buddha.

They are called "Those of Good Vision" because they possess the three eyes; among the ten practices, they employ the wisdom-eye to know the faculties of sentient beings and act in accordance with them.
The Buddha is named Eye (Akṣi), and the spiritual friend is named Good Vision (Sudarśana).

With hair as deep blue-black as a sapphire, skin the color of gold, and a halo extending one fathom, his marks and signs are like those of a Buddha; this clarifies that the cause is the practice of the three eyes within the ten stages of practice, and the fruit is the Buddha himself.
Regarding "practicing the path within the forest": this clarifies that the dense forest of myriad practices provides shelter and shade for sentient beings.

It is analogous to the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), where the bodhisattvas are named the Ten Forest Bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakusuma-vana (Forest of Merit), Prajñā-vana (Forest of Wisdom), and Jayavṛkṣa-vana (Forest of Victory).
The spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) within Sudhana’s ten stages of practice (daśa-caryā) take the bhikṣu in the Forest of Merit (Guṇakānanā) as the locus of practice for the tenth stage.
As indicated in the subsequent text, the ten bodhisattvas of the forests, such as Guṇakānanā and others, serve as the objects of his practice.

Now, within this first assembly, the deity presiding over agriculture serves as the provision for the ten practices leading to the fruit of Buddhahood; for when sentient beings enter the stage of Buddhahood, the Bodhisattvas on the path of provisions and the path of vision expand their great compassion.

Thus, the five stages of the Buddha-fruit in this assembly correspond to the five stages practiced by the bodhisattvas from the second and third assemblies onward, as well as the five stages demonstrated and practiced by the youth Sudhana; these are mutually correlated in their sequence and structure. Collectively, they clarify that the essence and function of the Buddha-fruit and the fruit of Samantabhadra’s practice support one another, remaining identical from beginning to end.

For this reason, within the five stages, the fifty kinds of provisions and the fifty kinds of Buddha-fruits are mutually primary and secondary, mutually cause and effect, and mutually essence and function.

Because the nature of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and principle constantly sustains the practice of Samantabhadra so that it remains untainted, and the practice of Samantabhadra constantly sustains the nature of the Tathāgata’s fruition so that compassion and wisdom are brought to perfection; if either side were abandoned, nothing would be accomplished.

All gateways of practice are the causes and effects of humans and devas; even if one attains transcendence, it is merely the stage of the śrāvakas and the two vehicles, as well as that of the bodhisattvas of the supramundane pure lands who retain delusions to moisten their rebirths.

Therefore, it is because the principle of the intrinsic nature of reality (dharmatā) and the wisdom of realization are dynamically integrated with the mundane and supramundane great compassion, such that movement and stillness, defilement and purity, are sovereignly and perfectly interfused.

These ten practices and the provisions for the fruit of Buddhahood are like a cucumber, wherein the flower and the fruit emerge together and the flower and fruit mutually support one another; they take non-conceptual merit as their sovereignty, for the practice of the principle of the intrinsic nature of reality and the wisdom of realization is all-pervasive.
In this passage concerning the deity who presides over the harvest, the meaning is divided into four parts:

first, enumerating the number of the assembly; second, assigning positions to symbolize the dharmas; third, explaining the names and correlating them with their functions; and fourth, concluding the enumeration and praising their virtues.
First, as for enumerating the number of the assembly, it is like the single line concerning the initial practice.

Second, as for indicating the dharmas by means of their assigned stages, this refers to the ten stages of practice within the stage of provisions (*sambhāra*) of the deity who presides over the cultivation of crops.

Third, regarding the explanation of the names and their correlation with the practices: the deity known as Mṛdusvarāgra-sasyādhipati presides over the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) within the practice of joy.
Within this giving, there are two aspects: first, the gift of Dharma (dharma-dāna); second, the gift of material things (āmiṣa-dāna).
Regarding the first, the dharma-dāna: when one sees those who come seeking the Dharma, one rejoices without weariness; therefore, it is called the "supremely delicious flavor of gentleness.
By providing the flavor of the Dharma to others, it causes their minds to be tamed.

The second type of Dāna deity is the presiding deity of agriculture, who belongs to the lineage of Hou Ji; because this deity blesses the five grains to produce superior flavors that sustain all living beings, it is known by various names throughout the worlds of the ten directions according to its location.
The second is the Flower-Purity-Light Chief of Crops Deity; this is the perfection of ethical discipline within the joyful practice of the perfection of generosity.
Because he knows the faculties [of beings] and acts in accordance with them, he is named "Timely Flower."
It causes the blossoming of the natural precepts (prakṛti-śīla), which is named "Pure Radiance" (Vimalaprabhā).
It is also like the flowers of the five grains of the world, which, being nurtured by the seasons, cause them to bloom with pure radiance.
The Three-Colored Power, the Lord of Vigor, and the Deity of Harvest clarify the perfection of patience within the perfection of giving.
Because the merit of the patience toward dharmas has been perfected, it is named "Vigor."
Because the fruit is attained through the power of patience (*kṣānti*), one obtains a body adorned with physical strength.
Among all powers, the power of wind is supreme; among all practices, the power of patience is supreme, for it cannot be moved by the eight winds.
Because one can practice accordingly and achieve patience, they are called "valiant.
For example, among the ten practices of Sudhana, the third practice is that of the Upāsikā Guṇavatī; because she clarifies that patience is the fruit among all practices, it is called "complete."
The fourth is the Spirit Who Increases Vital Energy and Governs Crops, who presides over the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) within the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

By means of the power of diligence as a provision of the Dharma, and the power of great loving-kindness and great compassion, he dwells in the ocean of birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings without weariness. Because he himself has no personal seeking, he is named the Spirit Who Increases Vital Energy and Governs Crops; this signifies that without the power of diligence, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) cannot be established.
The fifth is the presiding deity of the universal roots of birth and fruit, who presides over the *dhyāna-pāramitā* within the *dāna-pāramitā*.
Taking the *dharmatā* as *dhyāna*, it gives rise to the wondrous wisdom of principle and knowledge that produces the myriad practices; this is named "Universal Roots of Birth and Fruit."

Taking the principle of *dharmatā* as meditation, because it gives rise to wisdom and the myriad practices, it is both root and fruit. Since the root arises from the fruit and there is no difference between the fundamental and the derivative, it is like the fruit of Buddhahood and the fruit of Samantabhadra’s practices mutually supporting one another; thus, it clarifies how the root arises from the fruit and how the root supports the fruit.
The sixth is the Crop-Master Spirit, Adorned with a Wondrous Ringed Topknot, who presides over the perfection of wisdom within the perfection of giving.

She clarifies that one adorns conduct with wondrous wisdom, and conduct in turn adorns wisdom; as conduct and wisdom mutually adorn one another, she employs them to benefit sentient beings, thereby summoning the fruit of reliance.
By encircling her topknot to adorn her head, she represents a topknot hanging like a ring, signifying the perfection of understanding and practice.
Seventh is the deity of the Moistening Pure Flower who presides over the harvest, who presides over the perfection of skillful means within the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

This stage clarifies the accomplishment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); it serves to moisten and purify the flowers of altruistic practice, and causes the flowers of the Dharma of practice to bloom so that others may understand them.
This is the gateway of skillful means (*upāya*) within the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), for it brings about the fulfillment of great loving-kindness and compassion.
The eighth is the Sovereign Spirit of Excellent Fragrance Who Oversees Crops, who presides over the perfection of aspiration within the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

In the eighth stage of the ten stages of practice, it is identical to the eighth ground (*bhūmi*) in that wisdom is effortless (*anābhoga*), for the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*) is fully accomplished therein.

Furthermore, by means of pure wisdom, one knows the faculties (indriya) and establishes teachings based upon those faculties, so as to produce the wondrous fragrance of the perfections of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
As for the ninth vision, it is the deity who loves and delights in cultivation, presiding over the perfection of power (bala-pāramitā) within the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā).
The Dharma Master achieves accomplishment; through the power of the Dharma, he benefits sentient beings, for all who see or hear the Dharma find joy in it.
Tenth is the Crop-Protecting Spirit Pure Light Free from Defilement, who presides over the perfection of wisdom within the perfection of generosity.

Because one is able to leave behind the defilements of both self and others through wisdom, there is the consecration of all dharmas; this is equivalent to the stage of consecration within the ten abodes and ten grounds.
The fourth section concludes by enumerating and praising these virtues, as can be understood from the text itself.

The ten presiding deities of the harvest mentioned above are all the provisions for the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) practiced with joy; they receive their titles based on these practices.
The subsequent examples are likewise; the principles are as stated above.
The twentieth lord of river deities is Beneficial Conduct, who practices the ten pāramitās within the practice of the śīla-pāramitā.

The first is the River Goddess Universal Emission of Swift Currents, who clarifies the dāna-pāramitā within the śīla-pāramitā among the ten practices; she received her name from the accomplishment of those practices.
The following cases are similar, and the principle is as stated above.
If we consider the specific instances, the example of Māṭṛkā (Mencius’s mother) is such.

Likewise, among the spiritual friends encountered by Sudhana in the "Practice of Benefiting Others," there were ten thousand youths led by Śakra-devendra who played at the riverbank, using sand for their games and taking the river as their path; this was because they clearly benefited others through the essence of the precepts.

In this first assembly, the River Deity represents the precept-body being similar before and after, universally emitting swift currents to clarify its correspondence to the seed of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The second, the Universal Purifier of Springs and Streams River Deity, clarifies its correspondence to the wholesome dharmas of the Three Vehicles, humans, and devas, presiding over the *śīla-pāramitā* within the ten practices.
The various assemblies of deities listed below establish their names based on their practices; their meanings may be understood by correlating them with the preceding explanations.

For instance, regarding the "precept-essence" within the Ten Practices, it is like the youth of the Deva Śakra, who, through the arts of calculation, physiognomy and moles, the Five Elements and Yin-Yang, and skillful techniques for benefiting others, established the precept-essence within the Ten Practices; thus, it is named according to the meaning of "Universal Purity of Springs and Streams."
If it were not thus, the practice would remain incomplete.
To clearly transform humans, devas, and those of the three vehicles, benefiting sentient beings through skillful means—this is the meaning of universal purification.
The third lord is the Sea God, who clarifies the practice of non-opposition.
He clarifies that the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) is like the ocean’s ability to receive all streams; this is non-opposition.
The Lord of the Perfection of Forbearance has ten ocean deities; these represent the ten perfections within the perfection of forbearance.
Each should be assigned according to the meaning of its respective name, as previously detailed.

In brief, within these ten practices of patience, the essence of patience consists of the great compassion of the dharma-nature; therefore, like the ocean which contains moisture, it can accommodate all things while remaining at their lowest level.
The streams of ignorance, pride, and birth-and-death are all transformed into the stream of Dharma, without any obstruction; therefore, it is called the "Practice of Non-Contradiction.

Just as with the spiritual friends encountered by Sudhana during his practice of non-contradiction, there is a city in the south named Sāgarāvāsā, where there is a laywoman (upāsikā) named Paripūrṇā. She wears plain garments and lets her hair hang loose; she possesses a countenance of loving-kindness and patience, having fully perfected the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Because there is no conduct that is not all-pervasive, it is called "complete.

As for the Sea Deity, she is a goddess who clearly possesses compassion and gentleness; she abides in conduct with the capacity for patience, her mind is like the ocean, and she is fully endowed with merit and wisdom to benefit sentient beings.
Therefore, patience is the fruit among the myriad practices, for it can accommodate all streams.
The fourth water-governing spirit clarifies the practice of being unbending and unyielding, presiding over the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

To clarify that the essence of water can purify all impurities, this stage of the Bodhisattva is illustrated by using the water of *dharmatā* to constantly and diligently apply effort in teaching and transforming sentient beings; knowing each one’s faculties, they benefit them without ever succumbing to discouragement or weariness.
Their minds are like water that moistens all things, benefiting them according to their nature; each receives what it requires without being bent or obstructed.
Within this, the ten water deities represent the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of diligence.
It is explained that the myriad practices are like water, moistening birth through shared activity; each is accordingly paired with its name according to its meaning.

It constantly takes the vigor within the ten practices as its essence, just as the gate of vigor within the ten abidings takes the joyful and diligent contemplation of the dharma-nature as its essence.
Among these ten practices, the gate of vigor has as its essence benefiting others while dwelling in the world by nourishing all things through one's conduct.

Within each stage, it takes the primary practice of that specific stage as its essence; the remaining nine practices function as distinctions upon this primary essence, for they cannot be understood in isolation. Therefore, to interpret them otherwise would be incorrect regarding their essential meaning.
As in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*’s section on the Perfection of Diligence within the Ten Dedications, the integration of wisdom and principle with great compassion brings about equilibrium and mastery.
Thus, when one attains [the realization of] any single stage among these five, all five stages are simultaneously present in equal measure.

Because the maturation of habitual tendencies must proceed through a sequence, although a sequence is established, the essence of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* has no priority or posteriority; thus, it is a sequence without before, after, or middle. It is a sameness and difference within a single nature devoid of differentiation, and one must not interpret this as a sequence of priority and posteriority based on emotional or conceptual constructs.

Speaking according to reality, when one first enters the stage of the Initial Resolve (prathamacittotpāda-vihāra), it is like a single drop of water entering the waters of the great ocean; it becomes identical with the essence of the ocean, and all the dragons, fish, and jewels are contained therein.
For the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, the methods of the teaching-net and the fish-trap must be fully prepared.

By recording [the teachings] upon bamboo and silk, the principles of sequence and succession appear; yet for one who embodies the Way, this is like holding a precious mirror that universally reflects all myriad forms.

The ten stages (daśabhūmi) clarify that through habitual practice, one’s merit reaches completion; the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyag-avabodha) clarifies that one’s sovereign conduct pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
If only the single stage of the Ten Abidings (daśavihāra) were established, it would merely clarify the initial merit of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).
Furthermore, one establishes the ten practices of cultivation;

though these possess the excellence of the supramundane mind, one adds the ten dedications to raise clouds of great vows, thereby causing the myriad practices of compassion and wisdom to reach fulfillment.
In the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), one merely accumulates merit and perfects virtue, ensuring that habitual practice is fully established.
In the eleventh stage, one enters the world with sovereign conduct, benefiting others according to the Dharma and clearly spreading the net of the teachings so that students have a place of refuge.
If it were not thus, how could those who have resolved their minds proceed?
The fifth lord is the Fire God, who clarifies conduct free from delusion and confusion, presiding over the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.
Within this, there are ten deities who clarify the ten *pāramitās* within the *dhyāna-pāramitā*; all take the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of the ten stages of practice as their essence.

It is because universal wisdom illuminates while remaining eternally quiescent; thus, the Fire Deity is taken as the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It is because within quiescence there is constant illumination, and within phenomena there is eternal principle; since compassion and wisdom, as well as their illuminating functions, are unimpeded, the Fire Deity is taken as the essence of meditative concentration.
If it pertains to worldly phenomena, it is the deity Fire (Rudra) of the south.
If it pertains to the person, it is their mind, because the mind is characterized by the quality of detachment (virāga).
If it pertains to the Dharma, it is the wisdom of emptiness.
If it pertains to external affairs, it is the sun.
If it pertains to one's own person, it is the eyes.

If she is the method, she is the Middle Way and the True Illumination; she is the illumination that is empty and non-existent, the wisdom that illumines all phenomena, and the Hall of Universal Radiance, for she is the Goddess.
Such was the intention of Sudhana Kumāra as he traveled southward:
to clarify the practice free from delusion and confusion, for the Fire Deity is able to destroy darkness, because she is not bewildered and possesses no obscuration of darkness.
This section establishes the meditative concentration based on function.
The sixth is the Lord Wind Deity, who clarifies the skillful manifestation of conduct, taking the Prajñāpāramitā as its essence.
The ten wind deities represent the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of wisdom.
In worldly terms, they correspond to the deity of the *xun* trigram during the hours between the *chen* and *si* periods; this is because she is a female deity.
It serves as a model for the Dharma, as a discourse, and as an injunction; it is like the fifth-generation hexagram of the *Zhouyi*, where Qian is above and Kun is below, called Guan (Contemplation).
The *Yi* says: "Wind blowing over the ground: one may observe the images therein.
The nobleman establishes his teachings, and the multitude follows them as a model; thus one may observe."
For this reason, the hexagram Xun represents wind-like instruction.
It clarifies that the merit of the sixth pāramitā, wisdom, has been perfected; Subhūti’s verbal teachings are used to transform sentient beings, and this is called the practice of Subhūti.

Furthermore, during the hours of the Dragon (辰) and Snake (巳), the Tathāgata took them as the rules for fasting and precept-observance; this clarifies that the juncture between good and ill fortune may culminate therein, until at the hour of the Horse (午), all phenomena are correctly aligned.

Above, it coincides with the Jue (Horn) lunar mansion; Jue is the Gate of Heaven, presiding over monks, nuns, and Daoists who dwell therein. This clearly establishes the teaching, serving as the gateway for the accomplishment of all manner of goodness.

All transformations and influences arise from this; the elephant takes its mouth as the "Gate of Heaven," for by exhaling and inhaling the vital breath it establishes the True Teaching, and thus takes wisdom as its spirit.

Furthermore, it spreads flowers and produces fruits, giving rise to all things; it can sustain the world, and can both form and destroy it. Therefore, it is called the "Excellently Manifested Conduct" (*sudarśana-caryā*).
As stated in the later sections of this sutra, there are four kinds of winds in the ocean:
the first is named "The Able to Gather," which can gather all manner of jewels, clarifying the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
The second is "Capable of Accomplishing," which can accomplish all manner of jewels; it clarifies the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
The third is named "Discrimination," which can discriminate among all manner of jewels; it clarifies the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
The fourth is named "Capable of Dispensing," which can dispense all manner of jewels; it clarifies the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*).
Therefore, the four wisdoms are taken as the Wind Spirit (*vāyu-devatā*), because they are able to manifest mastery over all phenomena.

The Wind Spirit is taken as the manifestation of wholesome conduct, for this reason it constitutes the sixth wisdom-dharma; by means of the Wind Spirit of Wisdom, one skillfully manifests the practice of all dharmas with complete mastery.
As in the stage of the Ten Faiths, the fruit of Buddhahood is assigned to the sixth faith-position in the southeast; the Buddha’s name is Ultimate Wisdom (Kung-chiu Chih).
Since the southeast corresponds to the trigram *Xun*, and *Xun* represents the Wind Deity.
Furthermore, the *Yi Jing* states: "Xun represents speech.
By using this object to symbolize the Dharma, it signifies that wind-like spiritual intelligence can skillfully manifest all phenomena.
"Method" (fang) means "Dharma"; by taking this Dharma, one grasps the Great Image which is itself without fixed direction.

The seventh is the Lord of the Devas of Space, who clarifies the practice of non-attachment and presides over the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) to accomplish the gate of great compassion.

Because one initiates practice through the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) to teach, transform, and gather all sentient beings, it is called "skillful means" (*upāya*) and the "practice of non-attachment.
Within this, the various deities clarify the ten *pāramitās* within the *pāramitā* of skillful means.
Taking the emptiness of all phenomena as its essence and taking wisdom as its spirit, it is therefore free from attachment.
Because the emptiness of all phenomena can give rise to compassion and wisdom, the myriad practices are likewise free from attachment.

The eighth is the presiding deity of the directions, who clarifies the practice that is difficult to attain. Because wisdom functions without effort yet its accomplishment is difficult to achieve, he presides over the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

Since the essence of wisdom is pure, one uses aspiration to guard it; by recollecting one’s original vow, one draws forth wisdom to give rise to practice, causing that practice to become all-pervasive, so that one neither dwells in saṃsāra nor dwells in nirvāṇa.
Within this, the ten deities represent the ten *pāramitās* within the *pranidhāna-pāramitā*.
"Direction" (*fang*) means "Dharma.
By accomplishing the great wisdom of the eighth stage, one establishes the Dharma through that wisdom to benefit sentient beings.

This refers to the Great Wisdom as the Spirit; it encompasses all the spirits of the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate points, above and below, and the four corners, because it universally raises up and perfectly gathers the wisdom of non-action.
The ninth night goddess is named *Saddharmacāriṇī* (Practitioner of the True Dharma). Her primary power is the perfection (*pāramitā*) of wisdom.

Having perfected the power of the Dharma and accomplished the deeds of a Dharma King, she dwells constantly within the long night of birth and death, illuminating the world with the light of the Dharma; therefore, she is named *Saddharmacāriṇī*.
Among them, the ten deities primarily represent the ten pāramitās within the pāramitās.

These are goddesses, and because they serve as the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) for the youth Sudhana throughout the ten stages (bhūmi), they clarify that the essential nature of the practices in these positions penetrates the dharmas of the ten stages.
The tenth daytime deity is Illuminator of True Practice (Vidyā-satya-caryā), who presides over the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Among these ten deities, they represent the ten perfections within the perfection of wisdom.
Because the sun of wisdom is ever-luminous, they are called "Masters of Day.
Because wisdom is unconditioned yet responds to all phenomena, it is termed "Divine.

Within the praise of their virtues, it says that those who constantly and diligently adorn the palace together do so because their wisdom is universally pervasive; they teach and transform sentient beings, thereby perfecting the palaces of the Dharma.
Compassion is the palace and wisdom is the hall.
This is because, in bringing sentient beings to maturity, the palaces of compassion and wisdom mutually benefit one another.
The above concludes the explanation of the stage of the Ten Practices (daśa-caryā).
The ten gates of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) are as follows.
The fourth section, from the Asura King to the Sun Deity (*Sūryadeva*), contains ten assemblies, which serve to symbolize the ten dedications.

Why is this so? It is because the asuras dwell within the great ocean without their bodies sinking; this symbolizes that the ten dedications are the perfect fusion of the ultimate and the conventional, such that one constantly dwells within the great ocean of birth and death without one's body sinking.
The preceding ten abodes and ten practices involve merely cultivating supramundane compassion and wisdom so that these mental states increase;
by adding the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one turns toward the ultimate truth and enters the mundane world, thereby perfecting the compassion and wisdom required for dwelling in the world.
By means of the ten assemblies, beginning with the asuras, this represents the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) which, like entering the great ocean, do not result in drowning.

This symbolizes that the Bodhisattva at this stage, through the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), attains true realization without falling into [the extreme of] non-attainment; they know the ultimate truth to be identical to the conventional, and while dwelling in the conventional world, they remain untainted, acting with mastery to benefit sentient beings.
Regarding the first [section], concerning the initial assembly of the *asura* kings, it is divided into four parts: first, citing the number of the assembly;

To clarify this initial dedication: although an asura dwells within the great ocean, he is not submerged by its waters;
yet, though he belongs to the same realm of existence as the devas, he lacks their sublime bliss.
Thus, a Bodhisattva in this stage dwells within birth and death, yet lacks the pleasure of the five desires found therein;

though dwelling in nirvana, they lack the pleasure of quiescent extinction found therein. Therefore, it is called the Dedication of Saving and Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Appearance of Sentient Beings.

The old translations—calling him "High Resonance" (Xiǎnggāo) or "Cave-Dweller" (Xuējū)—are incorrect.
This is based on the translation by Dharma Master Li and others of the Tang Dynasty; it is included within the fourth evil destiny (*durgati*).

As stated in the sutras regarding the ten types of *asura* kings who manifest their status and advance in practice, this clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s great compassion penetrates to the lowest realms, reaching their very bottom like the great ocean.
The body emerges from the great ocean, signifying that the Bodhisattva does not sink into the evil realms because they are able to abandon self-conceit.

By subsuming the conventional within the ultimate, the ultimate and the conventional are perfectly interfused; though dwelling in the sea of suffering, one constantly emerges from it. This stage is established to represent the Dharma-gate of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Third, regarding the explanation of the names and their correspondence to the practices: first, as for Rāhula, the King of Asuras, this clarifies the gate of the *dāna-pāramitā* within the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Within these dedications, the ten *pāramitās* are used to symbolize the dharmas; herein, the *asura* is taken to represent them, clarifying that these ten dedications take the ten great compassionate vows as the essence of the ten perfections.

There is no intention of seeking personal benefit; rather, because the abode of those asuras extends downward and their bodies reside in the sea with half their forms emerging above, this is intended generally to clarify that phenomena are manifested through metaphorical events so that the Dharma may be easily understood.
To manifest this stage, it takes as its essence the thorough penetration of both the ultimate and conventional truths through pure great wisdom, great compassion, and great vows.

As for Rāhula, which means "the Obstructor," this indicates that the Bodhisattva of this stage enters the realms of birth and death with a heart of great compassion to reveal the emptiness of the Great Dharma and obstruct all evil destinies.
Second, regarding Vemacitra, the King of the Asuras: this clarifies the precept-pāramitā within the context of the dāna-pāramitā.

"Vemacitra" is translated here as "High Resonance" (Xiǎnggāo). This signifies that by means of the sound of great compassion and great vows, he pledges to deliver beings from the three realms and six paths; thus, he takes compassion and vows as the essence of his precepts.
A "King" (rāja) signifies mastery; because he possesses mastery over floating and sinking within the ocean of suffering.
The third, the King of the Asuras with skillful illusory arts, elucidates the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Although a Bodhisattva in this stage dwells within the great ocean of birth and death, they constantly attain the patience that perceives all things as like an illusion.
The four great kinsmen, the Asura Kings, preside over the perfection of diligence; it is clear that they do so because they universally gather in sentient beings through the myriad practices.

The fifth is the Great Powerful Asura King, who, by means of the great power of meditative concentration within the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), remains in the ocean of suffering yet experiences no suffering.
The sixth is the Universal Illumination Asura King, who, through the light of wisdom, universally gathers and transforms sentient beings.
The Asura King Subhavyūha-dṛḍhacaryā is so named because he takes great compassion and skillful means as his adornment.
The Asura King Vipula-hetumati is so named because he increases the brilliance of wisdom and takes the benefit of sentient beings through his original vows as his cause.

In order to attain the further increase of wisdom while abiding in the eighth stage, one must in all cases take the great vows made at the time of first generating the bodhicitta as the cause, so as to bring sentient beings across.
The Asura King Manifesting Supreme Virtue represents the stage of the Dharma Master, accomplishing the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
The Asura King Wondrous and Beautiful Voice represents the stage of Wisdom, accomplishing the wondrous voice because he skillfully expounds the Dharma.
The fourth section consists of verses praising these virtues, which may be understood according to the text.
The ten *pāramitās* mentioned above all involve knowing the ultimate while dwelling in the conventional, fusing them within the nature of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as the ten *pāramitās*.

These ten perfections, having great compassion as their essence, manifest through phenomena by relying on events within the realm of the asuras; this serves as a metaphor for how a bodhisattva dwells within the ocean of birth and death while reaching its very bottom, yet never sinks into that ocean of birth and death.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "He achieves the Tathāgata’s eminence that transcends the world, like a king of asuras.
Furthermore, the Ten Abodes and the Ten Practices clarify only the realization of wisdom and its correspondence with truth; these are designated as "divine" (shen).

The ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) and the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) are all represented by the ten kings, clarifying that they are attained through the mastery gained from the growth of habitual practice.
The broader implications thereof will be explained in detail only upon reaching the "Chapter on the Ten Stages of Dedication" (*Daśa-pratipatti-parivarta*).

The second is the indestructible dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*), which clarifies that by means of the wisdom of ultimate truth, one simultaneously wraps oneself in the benefit of sentient beings to accomplish the precept of great compassion; this is for the purpose of realizing that the conventional nature is the ultimate and that the conventional and the ultimate are non-dual.
That the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is named "The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma" is its meaning.

That this scripture is named *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka* is likewise its meaning; because it gives rise to the myriad practices through the wisdom of principle and great compassion, which is the inherently pure awakening of the dharma-realm, it is titled the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*. It clarifies that Bodhisattvas, by means of the great wisdom and great compassion of the dharma-nature, do not abandon the worldly flow but engage in communal activities with sentient beings, which is termed "water."
Possessing the practices of Samantabhadra, it is named "Lotus.
Because awakening and practice mutually support one another, it is called the "Sublime Dharma"; thus, it is named the "Unbreakable Dedication.
Since true nature is without deficiency and flows equally into the conventional world, it is called "unbreakable."
This clarifies the bodhi of non-nature, because of the mastery of wisdom that abides nowhere.
Now, this is manifested through the entrusting of the matter of the Garuḍa King; he is the Golden-Winged Bird.
Within this single passage, the meaning is divided into four parts:

first, enumerating the number of the assembly; second, assigning stages to represent the dharmas; third, explaining the names and correlating them with practices; and fourth, concluding with the enumeration and praise of virtues.
First, regarding the enumeration of the assembly, it may be understood as in the initial practice.

Second, regarding the symbolic representation of the dharmas through assigned positions: by relying on the actual event and assigning it to the position of the King of Garuḍas, it is clarified that upon the great ocean, he observes with his pure eyes a dragon whose life is ending, and seizes it with his two wings—this clarifies the meaning of deliverance.
As stated in the "Dharmadhātu Chapter": "One constantly vows to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the ocean of existence.

The Garuḍa King—here translated as the "Golden-Winged Bird King"—manifests the Bodhisattva of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*). Constantly above the great ocean of birth and death, he uses the eye of the pure wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) to observe those sentient beings whose faculties are matured; then, with the two wings of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), he seizes them and establishes them upon the shore of self-nature pure nirvāṇa.

In this śamatha and vipaśyanā, the essence of śamatha is the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the essence of vipaśyanā is the wisdom that realizes self-nature as being without intrinsic nature; these are not two distinct entities consisting of a subject and an object of observation, because the primary factor is the purity of the precept-pāramitā.

Just as the great ocean does not harbor corpses, this elucidation of the precepts of great compassion and great wisdom does not harbor the corpses of the two views—defiled and pure—held by humans, devas, and those of the three vehicles.
As for this garuḍa, the distance between its two wings is three million six hundred thousand li.

Regarding the third explanation of the names in relation to the practitioner: the Great Swift Power Garuḍa King clarifies the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) within the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).

This clarifies that the Bodhisattva of this stage, by giving rise to great compassion through their inherent nature, enters the ocean of birth and death to deliver those sentient beings whose faculties are matured.
By the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they reach the shore of the Buddha-fruit and *nirvāṇa* in the duration of a single thought-moment.
This is to clarify that within the nature of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), a single thought-moment is not bound by the three periods of time—past, present, or future.

It is illustrated by the metaphor of the garuḍa seizing a nāga: by its power of extreme swiftness, when the garuḍa seizes a nāga, it plunges its body into the ocean waters in a single thought-moment; before the waves have even closed together, it seizes the nāga and emerges. This is called the power of swiftness.
Therefore, in the subsequent passage praising his virtues, it says: "He is well able to rescue and gather in all sentient beings, delivering them from the sea of birth and death.

A Bodhisattva who has attained the Way is likewise so: by the power of observation through concentration and wisdom, from the very edge of the great ocean of ignorance, he binds the long and short minds and, in a single thought-moment, responds to reality; thus, the three periods of time—past, present, and future—are seen exhaustively all at once.

Such is the path of seeing; such is the path of cultivation. This is what is meant by "the initial resolve and the ultimate [resolve] are not two different things," and between these two resolves, the former resolve is more difficult.

This merely clarifies that the initial mind of the ten abodes (daśabhūmi) is difficult to attain because it requires a single thought-moment of responding to truth from the stage of an ordinary person; it does not refer to the difficulty of the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood.

Since the ultimate state is no different from the initial mind, it clarifies that the Dharma is not different, wisdom is not different, and time does not shift. This is because it clarifies the essence and function of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). It can be seen by illuminating it with concentration and wisdom, but if one attempts to conceive of it through emotional thought, one will immediately become deluded.
Below, one may understand the application of the various *pāramitās* according to their names and meanings.
The fourth section concludes by enumerating and praising these virtues, as can be seen in the text.
Third is the King of the *Kiṃnaras*, which clarifies the dedication equal to that of all Buddhas.
Because all Buddhas abide within birth and death, taking the gate of dharma-patience as the sovereign of all practices, so that all sentient beings may attain the unsurpassed dharma-bliss of bodhi.

This was sent as a representation to the King of the Kinnaras—here translated as "Doubtful Deity"—who also served as the leader of the procession; he resembled a human being but had horns upon his head and a mouth like that of an ox, such that all who saw him were filled with doubt: "Is this a human? or "Is this not?"
"Is he not a non-human being?
Therefore, it is called "doubting the divine.

It clarifies that the Bodhisattva at this stage, having perfected the mind of great compassion through the ten dedications, is born within the six realms by the power of the patience of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*). Practicing together with others to benefit them, all who see him are filled with doubt as to whether he is an ordinary person or a sage.
If he were an ordinary person, his wisdom would be like that of a Buddha;
if he were a worthy sage, his conduct would be identical to that of an ordinary person. Therefore, the spirit was made to appear in doubt in order to manifest his practice.
This deity can act as the master of practice and play with the heavens.
He presides over the gate of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), taking patience as the master of the myriad practices.
Without patience, the myriad practices cannot be accomplished; therefore, patience is the master of practice.
Regarding the four meanings therein, they should be understood by analogy with what was stated above.
As for the ten deities of doubt, they may be seen by correlating the ten pāramitās within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) with their respective names and meanings.

Regarding "crawling on the chest and belly": it clarifies that those who seek the benefit of the Dharma do so by crawling—that is, by abandoning pride and practicing humility and reverence; this is the meaning of diligence.
This is the dedication that reaches all places; there is no place among the births of the six realms where it does not enter.

As stated in this "Dharmadhātu Chapter": "The Mahoraga King, seeing the Buddha, rejoiced, bowed his body, and paid homage.

The fifth Yakṣa King is the one who illumines the inexhaustible treasury of merit through dedication; he presides over the perfection of dhyāna.

There are five kinds of nāgas: first, those in the form of elephants; second, those in the form of snakes; third, those in the form of horses; fourth, those in the form of fish; and fifth, those in the form of frogs.
First is the Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita, who presides over all dragon kings with the forms of elephants.
Second is the Dragon King Nanda—translated here as "Joy"—who presides over all dragon kings with the forms of snakes.
The third is the Nāga King Anavatapta, which in this language is translated as "Free from Heat and Torment" and is also named "Cool. He is the sovereign of all horse-shaped nāgas.
This single nāga king is far removed from the three kinds of afflictions of the nāgas:
first, hot sand does not fall upon his head; second, he does not engage in sexual desire in the form of a snake; and third, he has no fear of the garuḍa bird.

Furthermore, there is yet another suffering: when the wind blows against their jeweled robes, their bodies are exposed, giving rise to pain. Only this Dragon King is exempt from such affliction; therefore, he is called "Cool."
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this dragon king is a bodhisattva of the seventh stage.
For example, there is the Dragon King Varuṇa—here translated as "Water Deity"—who is the lord of all fish-shaped dragons.
The Dragon King Mānasvati is also named Mānasa; this is translated as "Compassionate Heart. When he manifests, the wind does not rustle the branches and the rain does not break the clods of earth.
He is also named "Attaining the Intention."
It is also said that "Mona" means "high-minded.
Because this dragon possesses majestic power and virtue, he is named "High-Minded," and he serves as the Dragon King for all those in the form of frogs.
As stated in the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:

"When nāgas are first born, when they sleep, when they are angry, and when they engage in sexual desire, during these times they cannot transform their bodies; at other times, they are all able to transform them."

This refers to the dragon kings within the context of the Three Vehicles; their affairs are as described above.
