This is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) among the ten dedications.

Sāgara Dragon King—here translated as "Salt Sea"—attains in a single thought-moment the liberation door of manifesting immeasurable bodies of sentient beings while transforming his own dragon form. This clarifies that this is entering into birth and death to fulfill the precept of great compassion, due to the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) obtained through the fulfillment of vows.
The general substance of these ten dedications accomplishes the practice of compassionate vows and attains the supernormal powers of the power of vows.
The Dragon King Cloud-Sound Sublime Banner attained the liberation door of proclaiming the ocean of the Buddha’s boundless names with a pure voice throughout all realms of existence.
This clarifies that patience brings forth renown, as explained in detail within the section on "obtaining a share of benefit.
Regarding the Nāga King Takṣaka: this is translated as "the one capable of harming what is to be harmed.
Here, *takṣa* is the sound for "that which is to be harmed," and *ka* is the sound for "the one capable of harming."
It is said that when this dragon becomes enraged, its mere gaze upon humans or livestock brings them to their end.
As for the old translation "Many-Tongued Dragon" (Duoshé Lóng), it refers to having many tongues due to excessive speech, not because there are actually multiple tongues within its mouth.

In the progression of the manifest advancement, this is the sixth gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*; because it skillfully expounds many dharmas, it is called "many-tongued. It is so named because the dragon serves as a locus for entrusting the manifestation of the Dharma.
The following should be understood by analogy with the above, as can be known by correlating names with their meanings.
These ten dragon kings take the *prajñāpāramitā* of the Ten Dedications as their essence, symbolizing the sovereignty of wisdom that traverses emptiness and rains down the Dharma.

The seventh is the dedication that accords with all sentient beings, presided over by the Kumbhāṇḍa King; it clarifies that the Bodhisattva of this stage achieves great compassion, entering all realms and benefiting beings through universal loving-kindness.
These are spirits of loathsome seduction who devour vital essence; they are also called "winter melon ghosts," their names being recounted according to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*.

The "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" states: "Always diligently strive to eliminate the realms of the hungry ghosts.
The Kumbhāṇḍa kings illustrate that their passionate attachment and greedy seeking are like those of hungry ghosts.
The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion gives everything away along with his retinue, because he has severed all craving and seeking.
The eighth dedication, the Dedication of the Mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*), uses the Gandharva King as a metaphor to represent the Dharma.
This is called "Seeking Fragrance" (gandharva), for they seek their sustenance by finding entertainment wherever there is fragrance.

Using this phenomenon to symbolize the ultimate truth, it is like the Bodhisattvas in the stage of characteristics, who constantly use the fragrance of the undefiled fivefold Dharma-body—the True Suchness Dharmadhātu, precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—to entertain sentient beings, causing them to cherish and delight in it.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "All have generated profound faith and understanding in the Great Dharma; with joy and reverence, they practice diligently without weariness.

The *Gandavyūha* (Entering the Dharma Realm) chapter says: "He constantly causes sentient beings to increase in joy," because the Gandharva King gladdens sentient beings through the meaning of the Dharma.
Among these, the ten kings clarify the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of aspiration.
In this stage, wisdom predominates; by establishing teachings according to the faculties [of beings] and gladdening sentient beings, one causes them to rejoice.
The ninth dedication is the "Unfettered and Unattached Liberation. It relies on the moon deity as its symbolic basis to represent the *pāramitā* of power (*bala*).

This is because, through the wisdom of the space-like *dharmatā* that is unfettered and unattached, one illuminates sentient beings, purifies the heat of their afflictions, and attains the coolness of the Dharma.
Among these, the tenth month corresponds to the ten *pāramitās* within the *prajñā-pāramitā*; their respective names and meanings may be understood by correlating them accordingly.
The tenth stage, the immeasurable dedication of entering the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), is symbolized through the event of the Sun Deity (*Sūrya-devaputra*).

In the tenth of the *daśapariṇāmanā* (ten dedications), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is like the sun situated in the sky: it looks down and illuminates all things; its position is high, yet its merit benefits those below. A Bodhisattva in this stage is like this: his wisdom is exceedingly lofty, yet his conduct extends most widely downward. It reaches through humans, devas, asuras, and ghosts, as well as the heterodox practices of outsiders, the animal realm, and even the hells, making them all identical with his own conduct. This is just like the sun and moon: their form is above, yet their merit is below, for they illuminate both the good and the evil alike.
Among these, the ten days correspond to the ten pāramitās within the Prajñāpāramitā; each is assigned according to its name and meaning.
They always take the Prajñāpāramitā as their essence.
The above ten kings correspond to the ten pāramitās within the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).

Just as with the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten dedications, and even the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), the pāramitās in each respective stage may be understood by taking their essential meaning according to that specific level.
To take one example, its true nature remains unknown;

for instance, regarding the forms and altitudes of the two celestial bodies, the sun and moon, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The moon is forty thousand yojanas from the earth and forty yojanas in width. It is composed of both crystal and white silver on its two faces; because they revolve and reflect one another, there is waning and waxing."
Since this treatise speaks in such a manner, it cannot be taken as a definitive authority; rather, one should rely on the scriptural teachings as the guide.
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*: "Upon the Moon there is a city; that city is square, measuring one thousand nine hundred and sixty li on each side, and its height and depth are likewise."
Two parts are made of celestial gold and one part is made of lapis lazuli; viewed from afar, it appears circular.
The lifespan of its inhabitants is five hundred celestial years, and their lineage succeeds one another for the duration of one kalpa.
When the sun and moon are near each other, their light and shadows reflect one another, resulting in their waning and waxing.
The sun is fifty yojanas in breadth; its city is square, measuring two thousand forty li on each side, and its height and depth are likewise the same.
That city was made of pure gold and adorned with the seven treasures.
The king’s domain extended for two thousand *li*; his lifespan and that of his descendants were equal to those of the Son of Heaven (*Tianzi*).
Sustained by the wind, he circles Mount Sumeru.
"The Sun and Moon Devas are always encompassed by the Four Heavenly Kings.
This and more is based on the teachings of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

Thus, these Sun and Moon Devas represent the gateway of the ten dedications that perfect the practice of great compassionate vows. They clarify that compassion and wisdom are without dependence, constantly taking the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) as their essence; they shine universally according to capacities without any deliberate action, allowing the sun of non-effortful wisdom to bring benefit to all things in accordance with their myriad forms.

Fifth, from the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven down to the Great Lord Maheśvara, there are ten great celestial kings therein who clarify the causes and effects of the ten stages for the benefit of sentient beings.
From the first among the ten great heavenly kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the entrusting of events symbolizes the initial Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
This is divided into four parts:

first, listing the names of the heavenly kings; second, correlating their positions with the Dharma they represent; third, explaining their names and assigning them to specific practices; and fourth, concluding with the enumeration and praise of their virtues.
First, regarding the recitation of the names of the celestial kings: as stated in the sutra, this refers to the names of the ten great celestial kings, such as Śakrendra and others.
Second, regarding the symbolic representation of the stages (*bhūmi*): by relying upon these heavens, it symbolizes the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

When a bodhisattva attains the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), they obtain the rapture of the Dharma; because their mind is free from all attachments such as the five worldly desires, their delight consists solely in the joy of the Dharma.
For this reason, there is great joy and great rapture, just as when worldly people are first born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and experience celestial wondrous bliss.

It is also like ascending a mountain peak to the limit of the signless, where the body merges with space; this clarifies that the Bodhisattva at this stage rises from the conditioned habitual tendencies of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications to the limit of dharma-emptiness in this ground, because a portion of the habitual tendencies has been exhausted.
The summit of Mount Sumeru and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are used as metaphors for its position in order to facilitate understanding.

The ten abodes (bhūmi) and ten practices (caryā) are metaphorically represented as being like spirits; the stage of the ten dedications (pariṇāmanā) is metaphorically represented as being like a king; and within these ten stages (bhūmi), it is metaphorically represented as being like devas. This clarifies that through progressive cultivation and gradual habituation, one attains ever more sublime excellence. This is encompassed by the six characters of the three pairs—the gates of the general and the particular, the same and the different, and formation and destruction—and is likewise encompassed by the ten mysterious gates (daśa-guhya-mukha).

Such distinctions in progressive cultivation are, in total, the similarities and differences within a single moment; none can be grasped according to how they appear to the ordinary mind, but may be seen through reflection in accordance with reality.

Furthermore, as the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "The Pratipannaka-type (習種) possesses a copper wheel over two continents; the Silver Wheel [type] over three continents; and the Svabhāva-type, Mārga-type, and Dṛḍhaguṇa-type possess the seven treasures and a golden wheel as Universal Monarchs (Cakravartin) over four continents."

The Bodhisattva of the first stage is the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the Bodhisattva of the second stage is the King of the Yāma Heaven. By assigning these stages in succession, it is made clear that their excellence in merit and wisdom cannot be compared to worldly pleasures.

To speak in terms of reality, these beings—born throughout the six realms of existence as embraced by the Bodhisattva’s compassion and wisdom—do not abandon even the most minute or lowly classes of sentient beings. It is solely for the sake of benefiting them and because of the sovereignty of the *dharmatā* that they are metaphorically represented as being like gods or kings; this expresses the meaning of such sovereignty, rather than expressing a delight in worldly pleasures.

Thus, regarding the later passage in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* which states that "Bodhisattvas of the first stage mostly become kings of Jambudvīpa," the present ten Great Heavenly Kings merely serve to symbolize the progressive cultivation of the Dharma, wherein one gradually becomes increasingly sublime within a single kṣaṇa.

Furthermore, this heaven is named the Heaven of Mount Sumeru. This mountain stands in the great ocean; it rises eighty million *yojanas* above the water and extends eighty million *yojanas* deep into the water. It is composed of four precious substances: its northern face is of gold, its southern face of lapis lazuli, its western face of crystal, and its eastern face of white silver. Its shape is like that of a waist drum (*kaṭhaka*), and it has four tiers upon which the Four Heavenly Kings each dwell on their respective sides according to their directions.
Upon its summit are four terraces; on each terrace dwell one of the Eight Heavenly Kings, each with their own retinue.

At the central peak dwells Śakra, adorned with various jewels. For this reason, it is named Sumeru (Wondrous High), also named Śṛṅgagiri (Peak Mountain), and also named Trāyastriṃśa (The Thirty-three). This is translated as "The Sovereign Lord Heaven" (*Nengzhutian*), because Śakra is able to serve as the Lord of the Devas; the name is derived based on his lordship.
Below are seven layers of seas, each encircled by a distinct mountain of gold. A garuḍa can fly across them at great speed, taking seven days to reach the end.
Upon these golden mountains dwell devas, all of whom are under the jurisdiction of the Four Great Kings.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven above have bodies one yojana in height; their garments are two yojanas long and one yojana wide, weighing six zhu.
Their lifespan is one thousand years; one day and night there is equivalent to one hundred years in this human world, thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year.
The above is according to the explanations in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Tridharma-sūtra*, and other scriptures.
This Heavenly King has five names:
first, Śakra; second, Śakradevendra; third, Kauśika; fourth, Śakro devānām indraḥ; and fifth, Indradeva. These names refer to the Lord of Devas.
In full, his name is Śakrendra; "Śakra" here means "hundred," for because he previously offered a hundred times the *paṃcavārṣika* (unrestricted) feast, he attained the status of Lord of Devas.
This corresponds to the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) within the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
The ten celestial kings below represent the ten perfections within the perfection of giving; they may be understood by correlating each with its respective name and meaning.
The arrangement of these four sections can be understood as before.

At this stage, the bodhisattva practices the contemplation of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence as antidotes; he realizes that worldly phenomena are not real, all arise from the twelve links of dependent origination, and fundamentally lack any intrinsic essence or characteristics.
Having accomplished the practice of relinquishing body, life, wealth, and so forth, one thus follows and practices with faith in all the Buddha-dharmas;

for the time being, this remedies the coarse karma of stinginess within the desire realm as one practices the *dāna-pāramitā*, yet one has not yet fully mastered the understanding of the twelve links of dependent origination.

It is only at the sixth stage that a Bodhisattva clearly understands the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination; this is illustrated by the analogy of refining pure gold through repeated entry into fire, clarifying the antidote to the obstacle of stinginess.

Second, there are immeasurable kings of the Yāma Heaven who, by means of a symbolic event, represent the Stainless Stage (Vimalā-bhūmi). Because these devas have transcended the terrestrial realm, they dwell in the void and enjoy manifold sublime pleasures.

In this stage, the Bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) increases and excels, possessing sublime bliss; for the Dharma-body constitutes the essence of their ethical discipline, and they gradually advance, becoming detached from the worldly fetters of the preceding stage.

On the first stage (*bhūmi*), the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is preeminent; on this [second] stage, the pure precepts of the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*) in their highest degree are preeminent, and it is therefore named the "Stainless Stage" (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

Just as the summit of Mount Sumeru connects with the human realm and is thus associated with the mundane world, this stage dwells in emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and is thus associated with the supramundane; hence it is called "Stainless."
The first stage is likened to refining pure gold; it has not yet mentioned the addition of medicinal agents, but rather that by repeatedly entering the fire, it becomes increasingly bright and pure.
On this stage, the refining of gold is like adding alum, which makes it even more brilliant and clear, taking the precepts as the alum.

However, the essence of gold is non-dual; it is clarified by using the precepts as an antidote to the coarse obstructions of craving and desire within the realm of desire. Yet, it is by means of the medicinal dharma of the Dharmakāya’s great kindness, great compassion, and great vows, the four means of integration, the four immeasurables, the ten pāramitās, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, that they are mutually polished and refined, so as to bring about mastery over wisdom and compassion.
The Yāma Heaven is here translated as the "Time-Portion" Heaven (*kāmadeva*).

This is because this heaven lacks the sun and moon; its deities illuminate one another by their own radiance, such that day and night cannot be distinguished. One knows the divisions of time for day and night only through the opening and closing of the lotus flowers.

The bodies of these devas are two yojanas in height and two yojanas in breadth; their garments weigh three zhu; their lifespan is two thousand years, with the number of days, months, and years being double that of the preceding heaven.

This Heavenly King has ten retinues of devas; this clearly illustrates the ten pāramitās within this śīla-pāramitā, which may be understood by correlating their names and meanings according to their respective positions.
In this stage, one cultivates the superior and most excellent ten wholesome precepts to remedy the habitual tendencies of coarse afflictions currently active in the desire realm.

In the third stage, one cultivates the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), whereby one is finally free from the afflictions of the three realms, is born into the family of the Tathāgata, and shares the same nature as the Tathāgata.

Third, there is the inconceivable King of the Tuṣita Heaven; this symbolizes the Ground of Radiant Light through its reference to a concrete object.
This is named the Heaven of Contentment (*Tuṣita*), and the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva in his final existence teaches and transforms beings here."

As stated in the *Yingluo benye jing*: "The eleventh stage, the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi-bhūmi*), is first called 'one birth remaining' (*eka-jāti-pratibaddha*) and is designated as the 'final body' (*carama-deha*); it is assigned to the third dhyāna."

"This Deva of Contentment is in his final existence; as for those Bodhisattvas among them, they are all Tathāgatas employing skillful means according to the occasion to establish the Dharma and benefit sentient beings—they cannot be fixed."

The preceding stage clarifies the purification of the ten wholesome courses of action through the highest-of-the-high [levels], because it abandons the stains of coarse afflictions manifesting in the desire realm.

In this stage, the Bodhisattva, by means of the nine successive meditative absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), purifies the mental tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the form realm, the formless realm, and the desire realm, thereby attaining a mind that transcends the three realms. This is likened to refining gold: skillfully refined so as not to lose even a *zhū* or two [of its weight], it becomes increasingly bright and pure.

One refines it with the nine successive concentrations, observes it with the Dharma-eye, and harmonizes it through practice; thus, while the fundamental dharma remains unimpaired, it becomes increasingly bright and pure.

One cultivates concentration in the desire realm to remedy the obstacle of desire, and cultivates wisdom in the higher realms to remedy the obstacle to concentration. Through such counteractive measures—just as a Bodhisattva at the stage of the sixth ground cultivates the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination within the first dhyāna of the form realm to remedy the obstacle to concentration—one accords with the practice of the Dharma and benefits sentient beings through skillful means without any attachment; this is called the Ground of Radiant Light (Prabhākārī-bhūmi).
It has the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence.
Within this realm, there are ten great celestial kings; these represent the ten perfections within the perfection of patience.

These deities are four *yojana* in height; their robes are eight *yojana* long and four *yojana* wide. Their lifespan is four thousand years, and both the duration of their days and months and the number of years are each double those of the preceding heaven.
These gods of the Heaven of Contentment (Tuṣita) shall attain birth therein by practicing three dharmas: namely, ethical discipline (śīla), meditative concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā).
If one practices only ethical discipline and generosity (dāna), one will be born in other heavens, all of which are characterized by negligence (pramāda).
If, within the Dharma of the One Vehicle, the matter were not thus, it would be because wisdom is all-pervasive and constitutes the very essence of the celestial realm.
The fourth, the King of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), relies upon this phenomenon to represent the Bodhisattva of the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī).

While observing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment with equanimity as their essence, he does not abandon the teaching and transformation of all sentient beings due to his original vow and because such is the nature of the Dharma.

One adorns the work of wisdom with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, intending to benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings as one's own joy; just like this celestial realm, one constantly delights in self-joy through transformations.
It is also called the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), because there are no objects external to the mind, as they arise through mental transformation.

This indicates that from the first stage of the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) manifests before them and there are no objects external to the mind. For the sake of further cultivation, the Bodhisattva employs the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmas*) as auxiliary means to counteract the obstacles of this heaven and the false views of the triple world. By refining and polishing the ground of the mind to adorn the work of wisdom and making it luminously pure, the Bodhisattva intends to use this purity to teach and transform all sentient beings as their own joy; therefore, it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

As stated in the *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-sūtra*: "The Bodhisattva of the Stage of Joy is called 'Flowing Against the Stream'; the Stage of Freedom from Defilement is called 'Stream of the Path'; the Third Stage is called 'Entering the Stream'; the Fourth Stage is Srotāpanna; the Fifth Stage is Sakṛdāgāmin; the Sixth Stage is Anāgāmin; the Seventh Stage is Arhat; the Eighth Stage is the Transformation of Birth and Death; the Ninth Stage is the Stage of Sublime Wisdom; and the Tenth Stage is the Stage of the Dharma Cloud."
Furthermore, the *Āḍakavatī-sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas of the ten abodes enter the flow of the Dharma and spontaneously reach Buddhahood.

Thus, within the five stages—the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and the eleventh ground—of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, each stage individually possesses tenfold aspects of the Buddha-fruit, with the conduct of Samantabhadra serving as the cause.

In the stage of the ten faiths, one comes to believe that the nature of the mind’s own discrimination constitutes the ten fruits of Buddhahood—such as the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom and the Buddha of Unobstructed Wisdom—and that these are collectively the wisdom of one's own mind; only then is it called the "faith-mind."
Thus, by reconciling many similarities and differences, one accords with the varying degrees of intimacy and disparity among different faiths and understandings.

One simply relies on the specific practice-gates of their respective schools; yet all are encompassed and harmonized through the gates of the general and the particular, of identity and difference, and of formation and disintegration. All of these do not depart from the limit of a single kṣaṇa; this is what is meant by the universal penetration of meaning.
If one seeks understanding by stretching or compressing the temporal sequence, it would contradict the principles of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).

Among this assembly of celestial kings, there are ten celestial kings; these are all the ten pāramitās within the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), each of which may be understood by correlating them with their respective names and meanings.
It always takes the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) as its essence.
This stage employs the analogy of refining true gold to create ornaments;

for through the clarity of diligence, one cultivates the contemplations of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*) to counteract the habitual tendencies of erroneous karma within the three realms.

The bodies of these devas are eight yojanas in height; their garments are sixteen yojanas long and eight yojanas wide; their lifespan is eight thousand years, with the number of days, months, and years being double that of the preceding heaven.
Their robes weigh but one *zhū*, and they partake of the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
The remaining sections praising their virtues may be understood as previously explained.
Fifth, there are further countless kings of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven who, by means of these events, symbolize the Ground of Difficult Victory (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

For this reason, this heaven is at the summit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); it clarifies that the bodhisattva’s realm of desire is difficult to transcend, and thus it is called the "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*) stage.

It clarifies that from the fifth stage onward, bodhisattvas have not yet attained complete mastery over the five sensory objects; they merely contemplate the various *pāramitās* and, by the power of their cultivation, do not sink into them. Yet they are not yet equal to those in the eighth stage, who possess the spontaneous flow of effortless practice (*anābhoga*).

In this stage, the Bodhisattva cultivates the contemplation of the ten truths (*daśatattvadarśana*) in order to remedy the remaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations regarding the defiled and purified states of the three realms; thus, he attains the gateway to the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*), whereby the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) manifest.
In this celestial realm, if one does not cultivate the contemplation of the ten truths to remedy these conditions, it becomes a realm of Māra.
Because one cannot attain mastery over the karmic habits of defilement and purity within the three realms, it is called the "Difficult-to-Conquer" stage (*sudurjayā bhūmi*).
In this stage, the Bodhisattva constantly takes the dhyāna-pāramitā as the essence of his contemplation.

Māra Pāpīyān, while dwelling in this heaven, practices the contemplation of the ten truths and thus attains the rank of a Bodhisattva; those who do not practice this contemplation remain among the retinue of Māra.

Furthermore, this heaven is named Paranirmita-vaśavartin because its inhabitants take the transformations produced by others as their own pleasure; likewise, a Bodhisattva at this stage constantly teaches and transforms sentient beings, taking it as his own pleasure that they attain happiness.
This is the analogy of using *musāragalva* to grind gold, clarifying that the ten truths (*daśatattva*) serve as the *musāragalva*.
Within this, the ten great heavenly kings clarify the ten *pāramitās* within the *dhyānapāramitā*; these can be understood by correlating the names with their underlying meanings.
The bodies of these devas are sixteen yojanas in height, and their garments are thirty-two yojanas in length; their lifespan, in years and months, is all double that of the former.
In the sixth [heaven], there are again an inconceivable number of Great Brahma Kings, who clearly manifest the Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī-bhūmi).

By means of the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, one attains the supernormal power of cessation and the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; wisdom becomes increasingly luminous, thereby removing the obstacle of being deluded regarding true reality while attached to the blissful tranquility of the first dhyāna.
When clarity arises while practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as is the case with Bodhisattvas on the third stage,
one should employ the Dharma to govern it when practicing the excellence of wisdom (*prajñā*) within the dhyāna realms, so as not to allow it to obstruct the truth.
Because its nature is without dependence, it constantly dwells within the three realms yet does not abide therein.
He is named Śikhin Devendra; this is according to the new translation. The old translation was Brahmā, which means "pure and tranquil."
Because the first dhyāna belongs to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), no women are born there, as it is free from the defilements of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is said: "Because it is free from desire and is tranquil, it is called the Brahma-body (*brahmakāya*)."
Furthermore, according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it is said: "Because they speak with the Brahma-voice among the Brahma-multitude, they are called 'Brahma'.
As for Śikhin, he is sometimes called "Holding the Topknot," sometimes "Conch-like Topknot," or "Fire-Crest," because the calamity of fire reaches this heaven.
Those who have cultivated and attained the first dhyāna are born in this heaven.
Within this assembly of Brahmakāyika devas, the King of Devas utters the great Brahma-sound, yet each of the devas thinks to themselves, "He is speaking only with me."

They attain supreme mastery within the great trichiliocosm; their countenances are like those of youths, their bodies are the color of white silver, they are half a yojana in height, and their garments are golden in hue. They possess neither male nor female forms, take the joy of dhyāna as their sustenance, and have a lifespan of one kalpa.
This is based on the explanation in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

This stage employs the analogy of true gold being polished with lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*) until it becomes increasingly bright and pure; it clarifies that by means of the ten types of direct and reverse dependent origination, one attains the ten gates of the emptiness concentrations, which constitute the lapis lazuli. Here, "vai" is translated as "light."

In this stage, the Bodhisattva employs the ten types of contemplation on the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and the ten emptiness samādhis (*daśa-śūnyatā-samādhi*). Represented by the contemplation of the twelve links as clear and pure lapis lazuli, they use it to polish wisdom until it becomes increasingly clear and pure; through contemplating ignorance (*avidyā*), they realize fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), making it even more luminous and pure.
Within this, there are ten Great Brahma Kings, which clarify the ten *pāramitās* within the *prajñāpāramitā*; each may be understood by correlating its name with its meaning as previously assigned.

This sixth stage, comprising the six abodes and so forth, generally clarifies the manifestation of karma that transcends the three realms, as well as the mastery over the three voids through the quiescent divine intelligence.
This is illustrated by the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja within the Ten Abodes;

and in the sixth stage of the Ten Grounds, it is represented by the night goddess named Sarvanagararakṣāsaṃbhavatejaḥprabha. In all such cases, these are collectively represented by the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) encountered by Sudhana.
The seventh stage clarifies the entry into shared activity amidst entanglements, as follows.
Furthermore, there is the King of Gods of Immeasurable Light and Sound in the seventh stage, which clarifies the Ground of Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi).
Just as with these two dhyāna heavens—wherein sorrow is extinguished in the first dhyāna and suffering is extinguished in the second.

This clarifies that the Bodhisattva in this stage resides in the seventh bhūmi; all conditioned practices have already come to an end, great compassion is perfected, and the four means of integration, the four immeasurables, the ten pāramitās, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are constantly manifest in their conduct.

Having personally exhausted all suffering, one constantly delivers others from their suffering; having transcended both the afflictive and cognitive obscurations at this stage, it is like pure gold adorned with various exquisite and diverse jewels, becoming even more magnificent. Here, the *dharmakāya* is taken as the essence of the gold, while the perfection of the myriad practices of compassion and wisdom constitutes the exquisite jewels that mutually adorn one another. Because one constantly employs the net of practice and the light of teaching to universally transform all sentient beings, this stage resembles that celestial realm where sorrow and suffering have already been extinguished.
Because the mind is pure, light arises from the mouth as speech issues forth; this serves to clarify that for a Bodhisattva at this stage, the light of teaching dispels darkness.

Within this stage, there are ten *Mahāprabhāsvara* (Great Radiant) Heavens, which clarify the ten *pāramitās* within the *upāya-pāramitā*; each may be understood by correlating them with their respective names and meanings.
The bodies of these devas are two yojanas in height and their lifespan is two kalpas; for these devas, the calamity of water arrives.
In the eighth [heaven], there are furthermore immeasurable Śubhakṛtsna devas, who clarify the stage of the Bodhisattva Immovable (Acalā-bhūmi).

Having clarified that the sorrow and suffering of this heaven have ceased and only the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prīti*) remains, it is like the Bodhisattva at this stage whose functional effort (*prayoga*) has ended and only the joy of the Dharma (*dharma-prīti*) remains.
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of this joy of the Dharma are first eliminated at the tenth stage.

When this great wind disaster arrives, there are those whose natures are moved by the joy of dhyāna-pleasure; for a Bodhisattva at this stage, non-conceptual wisdom manifests, yet there still remain the pure habitual tendencies of the wisdom of the bliss of the non-arising of dharmas.

Through the Buddhas’ three empowerments and sevenfold exhortations, they are caused to recall their original vows; only then do they proceed according to wisdom to extensively benefit sentient beings, delivering them throughout the worlds of the ten directions without limit.
This is the Tathāgata’s establishment of the teaching to prevent [such obstacles], guarding the perfect integration of compassion and wisdom at the very moment the initial resolve is first awakened.
It is not only at this stage that there is the function of preventing attachment to purity; it is a prevention within the principle that "one is all."

If all matters are fully present within the seventh stage, how can it be that the Buddha’s fruit of knowledge and vision has not yet reached its conclusion within the eighth stage, such that one must still rely on the mutual interpenetration of the Ten Mysteries and Six Identities?

One must not interpret the essence of the *dharmadhātu* as having a temporal sequence of before and after; though ordinary beings falsely conceive of it as lasting for immeasurable eons, within the *dharmadhātu* there is neither beginning nor end.

This stage is like the analogy of true gold used for the crown of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), which cannot be surpassed by the crowns of his ministers; this clarifies that the wisdom of non-effort regarding the *dharmatā* of the eighth stage is supreme.
The ten powers and four fearlessnesses are completed in the tenth stage; the ocean-like conduct of Samantabhadra is fulfilled in the eleventh stage.
Furthermore, in the ninth [stage], there are immeasurable devas of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala), clarifying the stage of Excellent Intelligence (Sādhumatī).
For this reason, the fourth dhyāna is free from inhalation and exhalation, and is not affected by the three calamities.

Furthermore, as described in the "Praise of Virtues," none of these ten heavens fail to take the dharma-gate of tranquility as their palaces, manifesting the adornment of the excellent wisdom of the ninth bhūmi; they teach and transform sentient beings through palaces of the dharma-treasure consisting of hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya dhāraṇī-gates.
One is able to use a single utterance to preach various teachings for all sentient beings.

Being without mind, intellect, or consciousness, one acts as a great Dharma Master; endowed with the illumination of wisdom and the Dharma, all things are fully perfected. Thus, like this deva, one is able to produce speech without thought or consciousness.

This deva lacks consciousness belonging to the lower realms; he possesses the mental consciousness of the form realm, and even up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, there is subtle consciousness. If perception and consciousness were entirely exhausted, one would no longer be subsumed under the karma of the three realms.
In this stage, it is like the analogy of refined gold used for the precious crown of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), which cannot be surpassed by the crowns of any minor kings;
likewise, the precious crown of wisdom of a Bodhisattva in this stage cannot be surpassed by Bodhisattvas of the lower stages.

Within this realm there are ten celestial kings, corresponding to the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of the power of clarity (*prabhāva*). Each may be understood by correlating it with its respective name and meaning.

The bodies, garments, and lifespans of these deities are all double those of the preceding heavens; this indicates that the bodhisattvas at this stage constantly take the Dharma-palace as their dwelling place. Because their merit and fame are vast, they are called the Vast Fruit Heaven (*Bṛhatphala*).
The tenth Great Lord of Heaven, Maheśvara, represents the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).

As stated in the subsequent section on the praise of virtues, he diligently observes the signless (*animitta*) dharmas and acts with equanimity; this clarifies that the wisdom of signlessness is perfected at this stage.

As the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness can subdue the coarse karma and the coarse continuity of results within the triple world; from the First Stage upward, they both subdue and sever them. From the Eighth Stage onward, the karma that serves as the cause for form is superior, because of the habitual tendencies of grasping at objects and conditions."

This is because even at the stage of "Luminosity" (prabhāsvara), the vision regarding objects is not yet fully matured, as the habitual tendencies of clinging to phenomena (dharmagrāha-vāsanā) still persist.
From the ninth stage onward, the mind’s causal karma is superior; it internally self-reflects due to the habitual tendencies of clinging to phenomena.
In the ninth stage, there remains an internal mental object due to the habitual tendencies of the clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

Within the tenth stage, the two habitual tendencies of mind and form are simultaneously and completely exhausted; it is only in the tenth stage that one attains unimpeded mastery regarding both the objective realm and the subjective mind.

From the eighth stage through the tenth stage, within the state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), the internal and external habitual tendencies of clinging to true dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) are extinguished; yet, regarding the gateway of Samantabhadra in the eleventh stage, one has not yet attained mastery.
This refers to the passage in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" where one seeks for Samantabhadra but does not see him.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Beyond the ninth heaven, there are further distinct bodhisattva devas of the ten stages, named Maheśvara."
"This deity has eight arms and three eyes, rides a white ox, and in a single thought knows the number of raindrops in a trichiliocosm.

This is an expedient teaching introduced by the Bodhisattva to manifest the Dharma through phenomena and events, as well as because the scope of his transformative influence gradually increases in excellence.

I aspire to participate in the Dharma-realm of the One Vehicle, where principle and phenomena are co-extensive; wherein within a single atom, the Buddha-lands and the realms of humans and devas exist together, and the pores of one's body and the atoms of the world enter one another like reflections.

Those who cultivate the Way must know things as they truly are; they must not follow along with conditioned correspondences. They must encompass [all phenomena] by means of these ten gates of profound mystery: the gate of simultaneous and complete correspondence; the gate of the mutual inclusion of the one and the many without confusion; the gate of the free interpenetration of all dharmas; the gate of the realm of Indra’s net; the gate of the subtle inclusion and establishment of all things; the gate of the secret formation of both the hidden and the manifest; the gate of the distinct formation of the ten ages; the gate of the unimpeded intermingling of principal and attendant elements; the gate of generating understanding through phenomena based on events; and the gate of the skillful accomplishment of the revolving of the mind-only. By means of these ten gates of mystery, one encompasses [reality], for it is thus that principle accords with reality.
The aforementioned positions of the celestial deities are merely for the purpose of facilitating understanding within the gate of benefiting sentient beings by using phenomena as metaphors.
For example, although the Tathāgata is in reality not a king of oxen, a king of dragons, or a king of elephants, these are used as metaphors to induce understanding.
That which one aspires to attain upon the path—wherein wisdom is formless and non-active yet capable of knowing all that exists—is precisely what constitutes the spirit (*shen*).
When this spiritual nature accompanies one’s conduct to bless and sustain life, then one’s actions are not in vain.

By means of wisdom, they constantly dwell within the triple world without being defiled by it, nor do they follow after its purity; through this sovereignty, they occupy a station like that of a king.
Through their unhindered transformations and boundless merit that surpasses all classes of beings, they occupy a station identical to that of the heavens.
Thus, as they follow in practice, they are born everywhere; their practice is not in vain.
Whether in commonality or distinction, they are all attained; this does not hinder the manifestation of reality.

From among the assembly that constantly surrounds the Buddha, starting from Samantabhadra Bodhisattva down to Maheśvara, these forty-one assemblies are divided into two categories according to their meaning:
First, the section on manifesting the causes that produce results to clarify the stages, such as the assembly previously listed above.

Second, the section on advancing in practice by taking up the dharmas from these stages, based on the shared attainment of benefits, such as the sections extending downward to Samantabhadra, Sāgaracandra, and so forth.

From the beginning of the second fascicle, starting from "At that time, the ocean-like assemblies at the site of enlightenment had all gathered like clouds," down to the "Assembly of the Bodhisattvas of Ocean-Light Moon-Brightness" within the fifth fascicle—these forty-one assemblies represent the section on "Advancing in Practice by Taking Ranks as the Basis for the Dharma, Entrusted with Attaining Shared Benefits."

In this context, there are fifty assemblies in total. The ten bodhisattvas, such as Samantabhadra and others, represent the dharma-gate of the eleven stages of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
As these ten mutually interpenetrate, each one inherently possesses all ten assemblies; thus, with each individual embodying the ten, they collectively constitute the fifty assemblies.

As stated in the section on "Attaining Benefits," entering [the path] is identical to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; this is established as a model for later students so that they may emulate it. Not realizing this, one is an ordinary person;

once realized, one is identical to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, it is said that "at the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening."

Within the following sections on how the devas and deities obtain benefits, there are twenty verses each; in all cases, the first two lines praise the virtues of the Buddha, while the subsequent eighteen lines consist of three phrases praising the Buddha and one phrase expressing their own realization that they share the same knowledge as the Buddha.
The examples are as follows: the classification of the text according to the occasion and the eulogies given according to the occasion need not be further explained.
As for the fact that only the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra alone enters the ten dharmas, this is because Samantabhadra’s single stage of universal illumination universally encompasses all practices.

The assembly of Samudrareṇuprabha merely extols the Buddha’s virtues as being similar to the Dharma they themselves have entered; for this reason, their own individual virtues are not separately extolled within these verses.
This is like the addition of the Bodhisattva Śuddhaguṇavimalaprabha among the assembly of Samantabhadra, who is an alternative name for Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī is here translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode).
Furthermore, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he was formerly named "Wondrous Light" (Miaoguang); thus, the meanings of "Wondrous Virtue" and "Wondrous Light" are similar.
He takes virtue as his light, for he is able to shatter darkness and manifest illumination.
He now stands within the assembly of Samantabhadra to manifest the Dharma, clarifying that cause and effect, wisdom and prajñā, and the myriad practices are perfectly integrated.

That Samantabhadra alone attains these ten kinds of benefits clarifies that the one is identical to all; it clarifies the sovereign mastery over the one and the many, and the freedom to extend or contract time—this is the meaning of universal integration.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, the ocean-like assembly at the Tathāgata’s place of enlightenment" onwards, there are twenty-six lines of scripture, which are divided into two parts.
First, from "At that time" onwards, there are eleven lines of scripture clarifying that the assembly has already gathered like clouds.
In this section, there are five points: first, the description of the assembly’s gathering;

second, the description of the distinct categories [of the assembly]; third, the general praise of the assembly’s virtues; fourth, the clarification that their original cause was the Buddha’s transformation; and fifth, the clarification that they now enter what the Buddha knows through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
The second section, beginning from "That is to say, the Great Lord Indra of the Ocean of Sublime Flames," consists of fifteen lines of scripture. Within this passage, there are two points of meaning:
first, it clarifies the benefits obtained by the Heavenly King; second, it clarifies how the Heavenly King, riding upon [the Buddha's] majestic power, recited verses.
Within these twenty verses, there are two meanings:
first, the initial two verses exclusively praise the Buddha’s virtues;

second, from the third verse through the eighteenth, each praises the Buddha with three lines, while one line praises oneself for possessing knowledge equal to that of the Buddha—the subsequent verses follow this pattern.
Only Samantabhadra differs slightly, as the intent has already been explained above.
All the aforementioned assemblies are exactly as described; the text is categorized according to its meaning, and they are praised in accordance with that meaning.
The gateway of the teaching is vast and expansive; it does not require prolixity of words, for one attains it simply by grasping the meaning.
Within these first four assemblies, among the forty-seven groups of followers, the first seven groups have already been explained.

Regarding the assembly within the Tathāgata’s seat, the sutra states: "From the Tathāgata’s lion throne—its wheel-shaped base, its terraces and steps, and all its windows and doors, as well as from every such article of adornment—there emerge from each one bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field."
In this section, the meaning is divided into two parts:
first, an account of the purpose for which the assembly has come; second, a detailed analysis of the sūtra text.
Regarding the first, the account of the purpose for which the assembly has come, there are three points therein:

First, it clarifies that all bodhisattvas have practiced the ancient path of former Buddhas; second, it clarifies that the present Buddha accords with them; third, it clarifies the non-duality of past and present, demonstrating that the seat upon which he sits accords with the practices of antiquity, for the bodhisattva practice follows that ancient precedent.

As stated in the verse, "What all Buddhas have realized, I have known," the Dharma-body is taken as the seat itself, adorned with the myriad practices of Samantabhadra, and the wisdom of unconditioned great compassion is taken as the Buddha upon the seat.

The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future are all identical in this regard; they clarify that the Buddha’s realization accords with ancient traces and resolve the doubts of sentient beings. For this reason, he must come; this is called the Tathāgata’s own practice being identical in cause to that of antiquity.
The assembly constitutes the substance of the seat; this is the dharma-realm and that which is traversed, for the act of traversing is likewise the dharma-realm, due to its unimpeded sovereignty.
The body of the seat is the primary retribution (vipāka), while the adornments upon the seat are the secondary retribution (niśraya-vipāka) summoned by that practice.

Now, from within the fruits obtained as retribution for their original practices, there again emerge the assemblies of Bodhisattvas who were originally the causes of their own practice; this also clarifies that cause and effect are non-dual in essence.
As stated in the "Dharmadhātu Chapter," the lion throne of the Tathāgata has the entire dharmadhātu as its substance.
Second, regarding the long division of the scriptural text: from the passage "At that time, the Tathāgata’s lion throne" onwards, there are twenty-nine lines of scripture.
Within this, there are seven points of meaning: first, the manifestation of the assembly’s adornment upon their seats;

second, the enumeration of the names of the manifested assembly; third, the arrival of the assembly and the presentation of offerings; fourth, the assembly circumambulating the Buddha to pay homage; fifth, having paid homage, ascending the seats and taking their places; sixth, praising the virtues of the assembled multitude; and seventh, delivering verses by means of that majestic power.

From this point onward, there are ten bodhisattvas, each of whom speaks twenty verses in praise of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom—both the primary and secondary supports resulting from his attainment of enlightenment—as well as the causes he cultivated in the past.
Let later scholars praise this according to the words and their meanings; there is no need for further explanation.

This section clarifies that the present Buddha accords with the ancient practice, and the ancient practice accords with the present Buddha. It clarifies that the assembly of Samantabhadra outside the seat represents the Buddha’s altruistic activity, while the assembly within the seat represents the assembly of Samantabhadra realized through the Buddha’s own practice.
This great assembly shares the same path as all Buddhas of the past and present; there is no other way.

When sentient beings mount it, it is called the inconceivable Tathāgata-vehicle, the most supreme vehicle, and the unsurpassed vehicle that leads to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for all these dharmas constitute the site of enlightenment.

Taking the dharma-realm as the site of practice and the various pāramitās as human effort, one purifies all defilements because they are inherently pure from the beginning; one purifies ignorance to realize fundamental wisdom.
The teachings of this school are vast and expansive; I have briefly set forth their essential meaning here.
As for the eulogies accompanying each passage, these shall be left to future sages.

Among these ten stanzas, there are twenty lines of verse below that praise the Buddha’s ten *pāramitās* and the ten stages (*bhūmis*); it should be understood that all the remaining sections likewise consist of twenty lines each.

From the passage beginning with "At that time, in the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean" onwards, there are twenty-one lines of scripture clarifying the shaking of the earth and the offering of worship.
Within this section of the text, there are seven points of meaning: first, the naming of the world;

second, the sixfold trembling of the earth through the Buddha’s spiritual power; third, the joyful offering of the world-protectors; fourth, illustrating that this pattern applies equally to many lands; fifth, showing that the Buddha is universally present throughout all worlds; sixth, showing that the world-protectors each act according to their own understanding; and seventh, showing that the offerings made at the Dharma assembly pervade the ten directions.
Question: What causes the earth to quake? Answer:
Regarding the earthquake, there are five general meanings:

first, the great assembly at this gathering attains the Way; second, a person of wisdom appears; third, a person of wisdom passes away; fourth, a calamity occurs in the world; and fifth, the joy of attaining the Way. This [passage] clarifies that the great assembly has obtained benefit and rejoices.
Regarding the attribution of the earthquake to the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), this clarifies the reverence between teacher and disciple, ascribing merit to the superior.
It is asked:
for what reason does the earthquake arise as an offering within this section?

Answer: To explain this section, it clarifies that within the first assembly, there are the followers who constantly attend the Buddha, the divine and celestial hosts within their respective realms, the hosts of Buddhas of past and present sharing the same causal roots seated within the Tathāgata’s throne, the hosts of flowing light within the Bodhi tree, and the hosts of Great Compassion within the Tathāgata’s palace. Because these various assemblies of the Buddha himself have gathered and attained further benefit, and because they rejoice at the Buddha’s appearance in the world, the minds of sentient beings are moved with joy; and as their minds are moved with joy, the earth likewise trembles in accordance with those minds.

This clarifies that within the primary assembly’s own realm, one cycle of the Great Assembly concludes; thereafter, light is emitted from the face-gate so that those from other lands also gather at this assembly. This "other" exists within a state where there is neither self nor other, thereby elucidating the ritual of transformation through the roles of principal and retinue.
This is the natural response of the dragon’s movement and the clouds’ appearance; such is the proper manner for dharma-activities, serving as the model for transforming sentient beings.

Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) pervades all lands and atoms, the three periods of time share a common boundary within a single kṣaṇa. Thus, by means of the "gate of the unity and multiplicity being mutually inclusive yet distinct," the emission of light and the gathering of the assembly are encompassed in this way, intending to make known that the characteristics of the Buddha’s realm interpenetrate without duality.
The above constitutes the first section, which reveals the five stages of practice and the single cycle of cause and effect for the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment.
This entire scripture contains six layers of cause and effect:

first, from the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruling Lord" through the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," these five chapters clarify the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, revealing the retributive attainments of the five stages of practice and demonstrating the first layer of cause and effect regarding the entry into the Dharma.

Second, the "Vairocana Chapter" concerns the causes and effects of ancient Buddhas; by citing the past to verify the present, it clarifies that the Buddha’s practices were inherited and that the Way did not arrive without cause.
Third, the second assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance reveals the causes and effects of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
From the fourth chapter, "The Summit of Mount Sumeru," up to the "Chapter on Leaving the World," the causes and effects of the bodhisattva’s realization and cultivation are revealed.

The fifth, the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm," elucidates the inconceivable causes and effects of the fundamental reality of both past and present; this is the doctrine upon which all Buddhas ride together and constitutes the very essence of all Buddhas.
Sentient beings all possess this [nature], yet they are merely deluded by it.

At the assembly to the east of the City of Six Awakenings, the Bodhisattva Mingxian revealed the gate of practice for benefiting sentient beings and the methods for a spiritual friend to gather in and transform beings; these are the causes and effects of progressive cultivation.
If one were to speak only of the Dharma, one would still be bewildered even while practicing.

This sutra establishes the teachings and the sequential practice and realization of the six perfections; it summarizes the causes and effects of understanding, practice, realization, and cultivation, so as to make them easy for beginners to comprehend and ensure that their efforts do not falter.

Chapter Two: The Tathāgata Manifesting Signs. From this point onward, up to the "Vairocana Chapter," constitutes the second section within this extensive treatise: the Gate of Exhortation to Practice by Way of Presenting the Fruit.
The commentary on this chapter is divided into three sections:
first, the explanation of the chapter title; second, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; and third, the word-by-word exegesis of the text.
Regarding the first, the explanation of the chapter title: why is this chapter titled "The Manifestation of Signs" (Xianxiang-pin)?
When the great assembly of bodhisattvas, spirits, and devas had all gathered, they remained silent in contemplation, mentally requesting the Dharma; there were thirty-seven such questions.

The Tathāgata, knowing their thoughts, immediately emitted light from his face to manifest a sign and, having assembled the multitudes from the ten directions, answered the questions previously asked.

Within this chapter, the Tathāgata twice emits light: first, the light from his teeth summons the assembly; second, the light from the hair-treasure between his brows reveals the Dharma, inspiring faith in the Buddha’s realm and the gates of practice regarding cause and effect.
The Bodhisattvas who have come forth emit light from their pores; this is because they collectively emit light for the third time.

Furthermore, it assembles the ocean-like multitudes of the ten directions and the characteristics of the Buddha-realm and the Bodhisattva-realm to answer the questions posed by the assembly; therefore, it is named the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs."
This sutra manifests the Dharma and assembles the multitudes through the Tathāgata’s emission of light; since he emits light ten times in total, both before and after, there are two aspects:
first, the light from his face, teeth, and mouth assembles the multitudes from other directions;
second, the light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows demonstrates how the cause is formed to achieve the fruit.
From within the wheels beneath his three feet he emits light, accomplishing the ten levels of faith; fourth,
from the tips of his toes within the palace of Śakra, he emits light to assemble the multitudes and lead them into the Way, accomplishing the stage of the ten abidings.
5. From the tops of the feet in the palace of the Yāma Heaven, light is emitted, forming the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*);
6. From above the knees in the palace of the Tuṣita Heaven, light is emitted, forming the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*);
7. From the ūrṇā-kośa between the eyebrows in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, light is emitted, forming the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).
Eighth, in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," light is emitted from between the eyebrows and enters the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head;

ninth, light is emitted from the mouth and enters the mouth of Samantabhadra, causing these two persons to engage in a dialogue regarding the principles of the causes and effects of the Tathāgata’s appearance from beginning to end;
tenth, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Realm," light is emitted from between the eyebrows, named the "Gate of Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm of the Three Times."
These are the ten.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Minor Marks and Radiance," it constantly emits light that universally illuminates according to [the capacities of] the faculties; this light does not merely symbolize the practice and advancement through the five stages, but is the light that constantly relies upon the faculties to gather and transform beings.

Second, regarding the purpose of this chapter: This chapter must appear because, following the previous section where the World Lord and others silently contemplated thirty-seven questions, this chapter emits light to assemble the multitude and reveals the characteristics of those dharmas, thereby answering the thirty-seven questions posed by the assembly. Thus, this chapter is required.
Third, the explanation of the meaning according to the text is further divided into two parts:
first, a general outline of the intent of the sūtra; second, a detailed analysis of the specific chapters.

Regarding the first, the general outline of the intent of the sūtra: from this "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" through the "Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra," the "Chapter on the Formation of Worlds," the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," and the "Chapter on Vairocana"—these five chapters of the sūtra collectively answer the preceding thirty-seven questions, clarifying the presentation of the fruition and the exhortation to practice.
Regarding the two sections that correspond to this chapter, within this chapter there are four parts of meaning:

first, from the prose passage beginning with "At that time, the bodhisattvas and all the lords of the world" through the following verses, is the section on the lords of the world requesting the Dharma.

Second, from the passage beginning "At that time, the World-Honored One knew what was in the minds of the bodhisattvas" onwards, there is a section consisting of prose and a verse; this is the portion concerning the Tathāgata emitting light from his face and teeth to summon the assembly.

Third, from the prose section beginning with "At that time, the oceans of worlds in the ten directions" down to the single verse, this constitutes the "Manifestation of the Dharma" portion, wherein the oceans of worlds in the ten directions, having been illumined by the light, all come together in a cloud-like assembly.

4. From "At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause all bodhisattvas... onwards, this section consisting of the prose passage and ten verses in total answers the previous thirty-seven questions.
First, from the section on the World-Honored One’s mental inquiry regarding the Dharma, the meaning is divided into three parts.

First, from "At that time" down to "I only pray that the World-Honored One will have compassion for us," there are eight lines of prose within which he purely requests eighteen kinds of Buddha-dharmas.

Second: From "Furthermore, the ocean of worlds in the ten directions" onwards, there are six lines and a half of scripture. There are nineteen questions concerning the oceans of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, totaling thirty-seven questions in all.

3. The two lines of scripture beginning with "I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One" clarify the supernormal power of the Bodhisattvas; thus, all the ritual implements emit light, and within that light, verses are spoken to request the Buddha to sever doubts. This constitutes the section on requesting the Buddha to resolve doubts.
First, from the beginning—"At that time, all the bodhisattvas and the lords of all worlds had this thought"—it clarifies the silent petition made through mental reflection.
What is the ground of the Buddhas?
The inconceivable stage of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the stage of the Buddha;
as the subsequent text states: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like space, and all Buddhas abide therein.
This is the stage of the Tathāgata.
What is the realm of all Buddhas?
As the sutra below states: "When the Tathāgata sits upon this seat of enlightenment, he manifests many oceans of lands from a single hair; it is likewise for every single hair."
"This is the domain of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the dharma-realm is the domain of the Tathāgata.
What is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas?"
In the following passage, the Tathāgata empowers Samantabhadra to enter samādhi; this is due to the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas.
What is it that these Buddhas practice?
The Sūtra states: "Unimpeded conduct is the conduct of the Tathāgatas."
Furthermore, the conduct of Samantabhadra is that which is practiced collectively by all Buddhas.
What are the powers of the Buddhas? As the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata possesses ten kinds of powers, such as the power of what is possible and what is impossible," and so forth. This is it.
What is the fearlessness of all Buddhas?
It is that the Tathāgata is free from the five fears and possesses the four fearlessnesses.
What is the inability of others to grasp [the Buddhas]?
The Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom of non-substantiality cannot be grasped by anything.
Why is this the eye of all Buddhas?

Because the wisdom that knows all phenomena and the wisdom that knows the faculties of all sentient beings is called the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*); it is for this reason that it is the Buddha-eye.
Furthermore, this is as stated in the latter part of this sutra regarding the ten eyes and so forth.
Also, as it says in the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies": "The Tathāgata’s eye possesses a mark of a great man called 'Cloud of Sovereign Universal Vision'."
"What is the ear of all Buddhas?
As stated in the 'Dharmadhātu-parivarta': 'All Buddhas possess unobstructed ears, capable of fully understanding and comprehending all sounds.'"
"What is the nose of these Buddhas?

As the following sutra states: 'The Tathāgata’s nose possesses the mark of a great man called "All-Pervading Supernatural Powers and Wisdom. From within it appear immeasurable transformation Buddhas, who sit upon precious lotus flowers and travel to all worlds.'"
"What is the tongue of the Buddhas?
As stated in the sutra below: 'The Tathāgata’s tongue possesses the mark of a great man, called the Cloud that Manifests the Images of Sound.'"
What is the body of these Buddhas?
As the sutra below states: "All Buddhas share the same Dharma-body; it is without dependence and without distinction.
Furthermore: "The Buddha-body fills the entire Dharma-realm, universally appearing before all sentient beings."
"What is the intention of these Buddhas?
The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" states: "How does one know the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
O Son of the Buddha!
The mind, intellect, and consciousness of the Tathāgata are immeasurable and, in their totality, cannot be apprehended.
One should know the mind of the Tathāgata only through the immeasurability of wisdom.
"What is the bodily radiance of the Buddhas?
It is the constant light of the Tathāgata’s secondary marks (anuvyañjana), which illuminates objects according to their faculties and pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
What is the luminosity of the Buddhas?"
There are two kinds of light:
first, the light of the teaching;

second, such as that found in the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance" (Guangming jue pin) of this sutra, as well as the radiant illumination of the dharmas symbolized by the ten perfections (daśapāramitā) throughout its preceding and following sections.
What is the wisdom of all Buddhas?
It is omniscience (*sarvajñā*) and the wisdom that discriminates all various phenomena.

Furthermore, as stated in the passage below: "The Tathāgata’s wisdom is profoundly deep; it universally enters the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), can revolve according to the three periods of time, and serves as a guiding light for the world."
The above constitutes the inquiry regarding eighteen kinds of dharmas.

The Sūtra states, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us," which consists of three phrases of scriptural text; this concludes the formal request for the Buddha to speak on nineteen kinds of oceans. The Sūtra further states, "All Buddhas expound the world-oceans for the sake of all Bodhisattvas," which summarizes the entirety of the inquiry.
Regarding "the ocean of sentient beings," the commentary states:
it is because the worldly multitude of sentient beings is as vast and numerous as the ocean.

Regarding "the ocean of Buddhas," the Sūtra says: "When the Tathāgata is seated upon the Bodhi throne, he manifests many oceans of lands from a single pore; every single pore manifests in the same way, thus pervading the entire Dharma-realm."
"The ocean of the Buddha's *pāramitās*, because the ten *pāramitās* pervade all bodhisattva practices.

The ocean of the Buddha's liberation: the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the Buddha's liberation; furthermore, it includes wisdom-liberation, as well as the fivefold Dharma-body consisting of precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation."
The ocean of the Buddha’s transformations is as described in the following passage: "Without substance and without a place of abiding, and with no birth to be found;
without marks and without form, all that is manifested is like a shadow."
It is further said: "In numbers equal to the atoms of all lands, clouds of manifested bodies constantly appear, filling them all.
And it is also said: "Upon the body of a single Buddha, he transforms and creates infinite bodies."

The Buddha expounds the ocean [of teachings]; as stated in the subsequent passage: "From each and every pore, nets of light pervade the ten directions, proclaiming the wondrous voice of the Buddha to discipline those who are difficult to discipline."
Furthermore, because a single sound pervades all sense faculties, the voice of the Tathāgata does not issue from the mind nor does it issue from the body.
The ocean of the Buddha’s names is as described in the "Chapter on Names" below; the name of the Tathāgata is equal to the minds of all sentient beings.
The ocean of the Buddha’s lifespan is as described below: "The Buddha’s body appears like a reflection; its arising and ceasing cannot be apprehended.
This is the ocean of the Buddha’s lifespan.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage states: "His lifespan is thus."

Furthermore, there is the ocean of vows of all bodhisattvas, such as those in the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Śīla-parivarta*) and others, as well as the great vows within the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications" (*Daśa-praṇidhāna-parivarta*).

Regarding the ocean of all bodhisattvas' resolve for enlightenment, as it says below: "All these sons of the Buddha in this assembly have skillfully cultivated manifold wisdoms; such persons are able to enter this kind of gateway of skillful means."

Furthermore, the subsequent passage—“From stage to stage one attains; abiding within the stage of power (*balabhūmi*), one diligently practices for billions of eons, and the Dharma thus obtained is such”—clarifies that “attaining from stage to stage” means proceeding without departing from the inherently pure nature-ground (*prakṛtiviśuddhabhūmi*) of the true *dharmadhātu*, while advancing to cultivate the dharmas of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) and the ten practices (*daśacaryā*). Therefore, it is said: “from stage to stage one attains.”

Furthermore, the "Ten Practices" chapter represents the accomplishment of the preparatory applications for the ten stages of departure, because it brings the wisdom, mind, and compassion of bodhi to full maturity.
The ocean of factors conducive to the path consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which take the contemplation of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena as their primary focus.
The ocean of all vehicles consists of the Tathāgata vehicle, the inconceivable vehicle, and the Dharma-realm vehicle, extending even to the eighty-four thousand vehicles and so forth.

The ocean of all bodhisattva practices is the practice of Samantabhadra; as the sutra below states: "Such a realm of wisdom for the manifested bodies is established within the practice of Samantabhadra."

The ocean of renunciation for all bodhisattvas is like the skillful means of application within the five stages, as the subsequent sutra states: "The bodhisattvas in this assembly have entered the inconceivable stages of the Buddha; each and every one is able to perceive the spiritual powers of all Buddhas."

Furthermore, the subsequent passage states: "The various practices and vows of Samantabhadra have been cultivated until they are pure and bright; thus, one can universally behold the spiritual transformations of the Buddhas in all lands.
Abiding in all places, with all things being equal, one whose wisdom can act in this way enters the realm of the Buddha."

"The ocean of all Bodhisattvas' supernormal powers refers to the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have gathered from the Buddha-fields of the ten directions as described below, as well as those emerging from the pores [of the Buddha], and their various activities such as benefiting sentient beings according to their conduct."
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers" is also [relevant].

Moreover, the subsequent passage states: "In each and every Buddha-field, they go without exception; beholding the Buddha’s power of supernatural penetration, they enter the sphere of the Buddhas’ practice."

Regarding the ocean of all bodhisattvas' *pāramitās*, as described in the following passage of the sutra: "The great assembly gathered from the ten directions emitted from each of their pores rays of light as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds; from each ray issued forth bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds, all of whom were able to enter everywhere into the oceans of all established realms within the entire dharma-realm to teach and transform sentient beings."
This is explained in full detail as set forth in the sutra.
This is the ocean of *pāramitās*, which serves as the model of Samantabhadra for those who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment].
Regarding the ocean of all bodhisattva stages, it is as stated in the subsequent sutra: "From stage to stage one attains."
Furthermore, it is the "Ten Grounds Chapter.
Moreover, the Tathāgata-ground is the Bodhisattva-ground, as the sutra below states: "The bodhisattvas in this assembly have entered the inconceivable ground of the Buddha."

"The ocean of wisdom of all bodhisattvas has the wisdom of the Tathāgata as its root. From this root-wisdom, they give rise to differentiated wisdom to teach and transform sentient beings; this is the ocean of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, which extends even to the ten inexhaustible wisdoms."
The three phrases beginning with "I only pray that the World-Honored One" serve as a summary exhortation.
Following this precedent, since the Buddhas of the ten directions have already spoken, it is fitting that the present Buddha, the World-Honored One, should likewise speak.
Furthermore, the four lines beginning with "At that time" clarify the offering implements and the recitation of verses.
Regarding the thirty-seven questions above, from here down to the "Vairocana Chapter," there are three ways in which the preceding questions are answered:

first, as in the passage where light is emitted from between the lower teeth to gather the assembly, answering by manifesting signs and supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*); [the other two follow].
Second, as in the manifestation of signs from the light-ray of the hair-tuft between the eyebrows and the response in the verses of the ten Bodhisattvas;
