The preceding scriptural text is sufficient for understanding this on its own; the brief topical outline (*śīrṣaka*) is as follows.
Within the second section, the Main Exposition (*samyag-deśanā-bhāga*), there are ten scriptural passages.
In the first section, the prose portion consists of eighteen and a half lines of scripture. Within this, there are six main points:
first, it clarifies that Samantabhadra addresses the assembly, intending to expound the Dharma;
second, it correctly explains that the ocean of worlds possesses ten dharmas which all Buddhas of the three periods of time equally proclaim.
Third, the correct exposition of the world’s shape and essential nature, which consists of ten vast and inexhaustible aspects;
fourth, the correct exposition of worlds already formed, currently forming, and yet to be formed, possessing ten kinds of causal conditions;
fifth, the correct exposition that these arise through the Tathāgata’s spiritual power and the suchness of phenomena, as exemplified by the ten matters of causal conditions below.
The six vehicles, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, spoke these verses.

Within these eighteen lines of verse, the preceding prose method is reiterated to clarify that the realm of sentient beings is vast and numerous, and that it is encompassed by the compassionate vows of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Because their practice is vast, the adornments of their buddha-fields are vast.
Because the karma of sentient beings is immeasurable, the practices of bodhisattvas are immeasurable.
Because the bodhisattvas’ faith is vast and free from defilement, the buddha-fields where they dwell are composed of radiant jewels, pure and stainless.
This clarifies that the pure and the defiled coexist, yet their karmic manifestations differ; this may be understood from the text as it stands.
Therefore, the sutra says: "The Bodhisattva practices an ocean of vows, universally according with the desires of the minds of sentient beings."
"The mental activities of sentient beings are vast and boundless; the lands of the Bodhisattvas pervade the ten directions.

In the second section, the nine and a half lines of sutra text beginning with "At that time," along with the forty-four lines of verse, clarify the basis upon which the worlds rest, as clearly explained in the full text.

In the third section, from "At that time" onwards, there are six lines of prose and twenty lines of verse which clarify how the distinct forms of the world arise from karma, as explained in detail in the full text.
The fourth section, from "At that time" onwards, consists of thirteen lines of prose and ten lines of verse, which clarify the distinctions in the essence of the world-system.
The fifth section, from "At that time" onwards, consists of eleven lines of prose and twenty lines of verse, which clarify the distinctions in the adornments of the world-system.

The sixth section, from "At that time" onwards, consists of ten lines of prose and twenty lines of verse. Due to the power of the vows and the skillful means practiced, the adornments of the oceans of worlds are produced; because karma is pure, the adornments are pure, and because karma is defiled, the adornments are defiled.

Seventh, the passage from "At that time" onwards consists of eight lines of prose and twenty lines of verse, clarifying the distinctions in the appearance of Buddhas across various worlds; it explains how the manifestations of Buddhas differ according to the karmic actions and the length of lifespans of sentient beings.
The eighth section, from "At that time" onwards, consists of seven lines of prose and twenty lines of verse, clarifying how the duration of the world's kalpa differs due to karma.
The ninth section, from "At that time" onwards, consists of fourteen lines of prose and ten lines of verse, clarifying how the kalpa transforms into purity or defilement according to karma.
Tenth: From "At that time" onwards, there are fifteen lines of prose and twenty lines of verse, clarifying that the appearance of Tathāgatas throughout all world-oceans is without distinction.
Each point is clearly elucidated according to the text.
This chapter answers the previous thirty-seven questions, intending to enable those who have generated the bodhicitta in the present or future to recognize the conduct of the Buddha.

The ocean of sentient beings' karma is boundless; the Tathāgata universally saves them through the practices of Samantabhadra. With the unimpeded wisdom of the principle of dharmatā, from the first arousal of the bodhicitta he has raised clouds of great vows, covering all with compassion and wisdom. Through the oceans of *pāramitās* and lands, there is nowhere his body does not appear, and no practice that is not identical to his deeds. Within a single speck of dust or a hair’s breadth, lands manifest in infinite layers; his body of equalizing wisdom enters them all, yet by the very essence of the *dharmadhātu*, it is without coming or going.
The Dharma is always thus; it causes those who study it to emulate it so that their pursuit is unerring.
This is like the royal road—the nature of the Dharma is eternally such.
To seek otherwise is deviant and improper.

Chapter Five: The Flower Treasury World System. In order to explain this chapter, it shall be briefly analyzed through ten topical divisions: first, explaining the purpose for the chapter’s appearance; second, explaining the title of the chapter; third, explaining by what karmic retribution the Flower Treasury World-Ocean is obtained;

fourth, explaining the configuration and establishment of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean; fifth, correlating the establishment of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean with its causes; sixth, explaining the non-obstruction between the pure and the mixed aspects of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean; seventh, explaining how the Flower Treasury World-Ocean perfectly encompasses the realms of activity across the three periods of time; eighth, explaining why the Buddha-lands are fundamentally empty yet serve as the objective conditions for the manifestation of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean; ninth, clarifying by what means the Flower Treasury World-Ocean attains mastery over concealment and manifestation; and tenth, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.

First, regarding the intent of this chapter: it answers, among the previous thirty-seven questions, those concerning the ocean of Buddha-worlds, the ocean of sentient beings, the ocean of *pāramitās*, and so forth.
This chapter must appear because it presents the karmic causes, actions, and resultant rewards within the five stages of the Tathāgata, thereby answering the previous thirty-seven questions.

Second, regarding the explanation of the title: it is called "Flower Treasury" (*Huazang*) because this land, which is the resultant reward of the Buddha’s realm, is supported by lotus flowers; it contains and holds all pure and impure environments within it.

Regarding the third explanation of how the Flower Treasury World-Ocean is obtained as a retribution: from the initial stage of faith up until the eighth bhūmi, one has constantly maintained it through the power of great vows, ensuring that one does not regress from bodhi. Through the ocean of the various pāramitās, one teaches and benefits all sentient beings; upon reaching the eighth bhūmi, one spontaneously benefits others without effort.
One should know that the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) is the retribution produced by the perfection of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
The world of sentient beings is sustained by the winds of karma born of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*);

the world of the Tathāgata, however, sustains all objects through the wind of wisdom (*jñāna-vāyu*) empowered by the force of great vows. This is because wisdom can accord with vows, and vows can bring wisdom to fruition; thus, it is obtained as the retribution of the great wisdom of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of great vows.
If the substance of the wind-circle were not the Dharma-body, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would be entirely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If there were no aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), the Dharma-body, lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), could not be established for itself, much less for others.
Only by taking these three matters as conditions can one truly be capable of benefiting sentient beings, without becoming mired in emptiness or existence.
When the cultivation of progress reaches maturity, one benefits others spontaneously and without effort.
Furthermore, taking the primary cause—the great vow—as the foremost, one causes the myriad objects of experience to be sustained.

In general, the wind of the wisdom of great vows serves as the support for these objects; therefore, this chapter later states: "The exquisite mani-jewel flowers are scattered everywhere, abiding in the air through the power of past vows."
Thus, all the adornments of the Flower Treasury World (Puṣpasaṃcayadhātu) are sustained by the wind-circle (vāyumaṇḍala).
Since all meritorious actions (puṇyakarman) originally arise from vows, they in turn sustain their various fruits by means of those original causes.
By means of this perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), one is able to accomplish all perfections; because the fundamental cause is thus, the cause and effect mutually sustain one another.

Now, by means of the ten perfections within the perfection of vows at the time of the eighth stage and the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment, one forms ten kinds of wind-circles (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) to support the ten kinds of all-encompassing adornments above them. Because the essence of the perfection of vows interpenetrates one another, they are able to support all the adornments obtained as the retribution for those superior practices.

Just as the very lowest wind-circle is named "Abiding in Equanimity" (Samatala), because it is obtained as the retributive fruit of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) within the perfection of aspiration, it is able to support all the blazing jewel-flames and adornments above it.
Or rather, it is born as a result of the gift of Dharma-wealth through the practice of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) among the perfections; thus, they mutually sustain one another.
Cause and effect penetrate each other; the Dharma is not obtained in vain, and the cause is never wasted.

Applying this principle to the ten dharma-gates of the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā*, they correspond to the ten kinds of wind-circles (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). This is because the retribution obtained through cause and effect mutually sustains one another.

It is just as in the world of sentient beings: the wind of karma dwells at the very bottom of their delusions; it supports the water-limit, the diamond ground, and the mountains above, causing them to abide securely. Like the image of the planet *Bhauma* (Mars) and its profound light, this establishes the movement of celestial bodies so that they do not fall.

The essence of the Lotus Treasury is the retribution-obtained fruit of the Dharma-body’s wisdom that follows all practices without dependence or abiding; the palaces are the retribution-obtained fruit of Great Compassion that nurtures and sustains all beings; the towers and pavilions are the retribution-obtained fruit of wisdom-illumination that observes faculties and accords with compassion to save sentient beings; and the ground of adamant is the retribution-obtained fruit of the Dharma-body’s own nature of equality.
However, among all these adornments, those that consist of vajras as adornments are all rewards obtained through the practice accompanying the Dharmakāya.
Those that consist of mani-jewels as adornments are all rewards obtained through the practice accompanying the formation of the precept-body within the Dharmakāya.

The Vajra-Circle Encircling Mountains are the retribution obtained from the protection of karma through the precepts of great compassion; they are adorned with myriad flowers because they are the retribution obtained from the blossoming of manifold virtues through the ten thousand practices that benefit sentient beings.
Regarding the adornment of jewel trees: this is the retributive attainment of establishing practices to benefit sentient beings and providing shelter for all conscious beings.

For instance, within the stage of the Ten Practices, the names of the ten bodhisattvas such as Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha (Forest of Merit) are all called "forests" because their practices provide shelter and protection.
As for the adornment of the lion throne, it is because the Dharma-body, in accordance with wisdom, establishes the wheel of the Dharma as a result of retribution.
To speak briefly, it is thus; however, a full and exhaustive explanation of the causes of the karma of retribution cannot be completely set forth.
Now, retribution is never obtained without cause; all things have their origins.
If one does not know the cause, how can one cultivate the fruit?

This is the beginning of this chapter: this Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean was purified by Vairocana Tathāgata in the past through the cultivation of world-ocean-microdust-numbered great vows at the abodes of each of the world-ocean-microdust-numbered Buddhas.
The mere mention of "vows" is because practice is accomplished through vows.
Furthermore, it says below: "The practices of Samantabhadra’s ground of wisdom are all perfected; all adornments emerge from this."
The fragrant water ocean is the retribution obtained through the karma of great compassion;
the fragrant water river is the retribution obtained through the practice of progressive cultivation.
As in the assembly constantly following Mañjuśrī below, names are used collectively to represent dharmas; thus, by seeing the name, one knows the practice.
Regarding this Flower Treasury World-Ocean, one knows the cause by seeing the fruit; it is not possible to cite other sutras separately to corroborate this.
Only when one sees the names in this sutra and thereby knows the phenomena, and sees the fruit and thereby knows the cause, can one truly understand the intended meaning of this sutra.
The categories of dharmas in other sūtras mostly do not correspond with this sūtra.
While other sūtras speak of the "Truth of Suffering" (*duḥkha-satya*), this sūtra speaks of the "Noble Truth" (*ārya-satya*); thus, the meaning is incomplete [in those others].

Other sūtras speak of the Four Truths, while this sūtra speaks of the ten noble truths and the ten [aspects of] the twelve links of dependent origination; if explained in detail, their immeasurable distinctions could not be fully set forth at once.
For this reason, these are correlated with cause and effect; one must not cite other teachings to correlate them with the text of this sutra.
This sutra reveals names through practice and knows the cause through its resultant consciousness.

They are like the assembly that constantly follows Mañjuśrī: for example, the directional deity who presides over the rituals of the ten directions with clarity and skill, the nocturnal deity who dispels the darkness of ignorance, and the diurnal deity who tirelessly illuminates the sun of the Buddha with single-minded devotion. These are the cases in point.

Regarding the essential substance of this Flower Treasury World obtained as a result of retribution, to state it in brief: it consists of the Dharma-body of great vows, great wisdom, myriad practices, and great kindness and compassion.

Through the fulfillment of these five matters, throughout the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space—even within the minute particles and hairs of the infinitely layered oceans of lands—all sentient beings are equally benefited by their actions.
Upon reaching the eighth stage, its functioning is effortless and it naturally pervades all; this is taken as its essence.

It is not the realm of those who dwell in stagnant quiescence for their own peace, nor of those in the human or celestial realms who seek their own pleasant fruits; nor is it the realm of Bodhisattvas who delight in being born in pure lands.

Even if the bodhisattvas of this Pure Land cultivate the six pāramitās and attain the six supernormal powers, they are still unable to give rise to faith; for originally, they did not resolve their minds upon or practice with faith by means of the fundamental wisdom of the dharma-realm and its discerning wisdom.

Fourth, regarding the explanation of the shape and arrangement of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean: by means of the wind-circle of inexhaustible great vows, it sustains the water of great compassion, which gives rise to the flowers of boundless practices.
Because the nature of phenomena is like space, it can accommodate myriad objects without obstruction, even when they are layered one upon another.
Upon that water, a great lotus flower arises, its petals extending throughout the dharma-realm of space, named "Various Stamen-Scents Banner."
The arising of the wisdom of differentiation from the fundamental wisdom and the performance of differentiated practices is called the "Stamen-Perfume Banner.

Within the lotus, atop a sun-jewel king gem, there is a Great Cakravāḍa Mountain. When the Sūtra says, "upon the sun-jewel king lotus," it simply means that within the flower there is a gem named the sun-jewel king; it does not mean that there is a separate lotus.
The forest trees are composed of various jewels, and fragrant waters abound with exquisite blossoms in full bloom; these matters are fully described in the text of the Sūtra itself.
The ground beneath those flowers is composed of vajra, and the earth is adorned with an intermingling of various jewels.
The sūtra itself states in full detail:
upon that ground are innumerable seas of fragrant water with various jewels as their floor, as described extensively in the sūtra.

Each of these seas of fragrant water is encircled by rivers of fragrant water, numbering as many as the atoms in four continents, spiraling to the right; they flow from south to east in succession, circling around like the six auspicious marks (ṣaḍ-aṅga) turned to the right, and these rivers are magnificently adorned.
The Sūtra itself states:
Within each and every one of the unspeakably many seas of fragrant water, there dwells a single great world-system.
Regarding these world-systems, that which is inhabited by those of a common stream is called a "seed" (*gotra*).
A "seed" refers to a category or lineage.
As the former masters have explained:

A number of three thousand great thousandfold world systems equal to the sands of the Ganges constitutes one world-ocean; a number of such ocean-worlds equal to the sands of the Ganges constitutes one world-nature; and a number of such world-natures equal to the sands of the Ganges constitutes one world-lineage. Within this world-lineage, there are as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Within each and every fragrant water ocean, there is one world-system; as the sutra briefly enumerates these world-systems:

at the very center is the fragrant water ocean named Boundless Light of Wondrous Flowers. This name is given because it represents the sublime function of the Middle Way’s wisdom and compassion. It is the central fragrant water ocean situated within the great lotus of various stamens and fragrance-banners atop the wind-circle.

Within this ocean there emerges a great lotus flower named Adorned with the King of All Fragrant Maṇis; within it dwells a world-system named Blazing Jewel Radiance Universally Illuminating the Ten Directions.

In this world-system, there are twenty tiers of worlds stacked vertically, each separated from the next by a distance equal to the number of atoms in a buddha-field; this Sahā world is situated within the thirteenth tier.

In the lowest tier, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in one buddha-field surrounding it; in the next tier above, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in two buddha-fields surrounding it; in the next tier above, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in three buddha-fields surrounding it. Increasing by one for each successive tier, up to the twenty uppermost tiers, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in twenty buddha-fields surrounding it, thus revolving in this manner.
At the center of the thoroughfare, there are eleven world-systems, each consisting of twenty layers, with their vertical distances from top to bottom being similar.

Surrounding these eleven world-systems as far as the Cakravāḍa Mountains, there are another one hundred world-systems—ten in each direction—arranged in straight lines and situated in rows according to their respective directions.

Near the Cakravāḍa Mountains, there are ten world-systems surrounding it; each has four layers above and below. Although the number of layers is small, the distance between the uppermost and lowermost layers is extremely vast.
Each of the thirteenth layers is equal in height to this Sahā world.

Regarding the distance between the uppermost layer and the one below it, some say it is seven Buddha-fields of dust; as for the second layer from the bottom, the distance to the layer below is often said to be ten Buddha-fields of micro-dust. Calculated in this way, the four layers of worlds are equal in height to the eleven sets of twenty-layered world-systems at the center.
This system of ten world-systems near the Cakravāḍa mountains consists of four tiers; for the remaining ninety world-systems, the number of tiers is not mentioned.

To provide a brief illustration, there are eleven world-systems at the center, surrounded by one hundred world-systems, totaling one hundred and eleven world-systems, which abide distributed like the net of Indra.
In total, there are world-systems as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.

From each of the various fragrant lotus-stalk banners atop the great lotus flowers within the various seas of fragrant water, individual world-systems emerge and abide; that is, they dwell upon distinct lotuses atop those great flowers, which constitutes their arrangement and abiding upon the second tier of distinct lotuses.

At the very bottom are wind-circles as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru, which support the various adornments above them and the successive worlds upon them, just as the sun, moon, and many stars abide in space, sustained by the wind.
For further details, the sūtra itself contains the text.
Were I to cite the full passage, it would be cumbersome and I fear you might not see it; therefore, I shall briefly set forth the general framework and speak of it in outline.

Regarding the fifth point, the correspondence with the ocean of the Flower Treasury World-System (*kusumatalagarbhavyūha-lokadhātusamudra*) as established by way of causes: Now, effects do not arise of themselves; they are obtained through causes. As the Sūtra says:

"The vast clouds of vows pervade the Dharma-realm; throughout all kalpas, they transform sentient beings. The practices of the ground of Samantabhadra’s wisdom are fully accomplished, and all adornments emerge from this."

As for the sutra’s general mention of world-systems as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, this clarifies that the sphere of Samantabhadra’s practice of gathering and transforming beings pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

This refers to what is attained as the retribution for the practices and realizations cultivated by the assemblies within the seat and the assemblies between the eyebrows; it encompasses the entire sphere of perfected and universal conduct and fruition.

Regarding those [assemblies], they are merely described as being "as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-world," whereas here they are described as being "as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields. Thus, the former is a brief enumeration, while this is a detailed enumeration.

Regarding the so-called "conduct of Samantabhadra," although it is briefly described as the "ten thousand practices," this is merely a concise statement; the underlying intent refers to practices that are inexhaustible and equal to the Dharma-realm.

Within these two layers of presenting the fruition, the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s conduct corresponds to the assembly within the seat and the assembly from between the eyebrows. These are the world-systems within the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean, numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, distributed like the net of Indra amidst various stamens, fragrant banners, and great lotus flowers.

Regarding the realms obtained as the full fruition of birth resulting from the conduct of those fruits—which are not enumerated in their entirety within this sutra, but rather represent eleven world-systems at the center, with twenty tiers above and below, each tier separated by a distance equal to the number of atoms in a buddha-field—within these, the worlds of the lowest tier are each surrounded on all sides by a number of worlds equal to the atoms in a buddha-field, and he dwells therein.

Next, above the third layer, it is said that it is surrounded on all sides by worlds as numerous as the atoms in three buddha-fields; proceeding upward layer by layer, adding one more at each level, until reaching the uppermost layer, where it is surrounded on all sides by worlds as numerous as the atoms in twenty buddha-fields.

Among these, the eleven world-systems at the center are all likewise so; this clarifies that the realms attained as retribution through the progressive cultivation and gathering of beings via the practice-gates of the eleven stages (bhūmis) constitute the eleven world-systems at the center, which are the retributive attainments of the eleven stages.

Regarding the statement that "the twenty layers from top to bottom gradually increase in breadth," this clarifies that within the practice-gates of the eleven stages (*bhūmi*), each stage contains two layers of cause and effect; for throughout the progressive cultivation of the stages, there is always one primary fruit (*phala*) and one concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
The names of all the Buddhas in those twenty tiers are all Buddhas of the causes and effects within the stage of supreme progress (*viśeṣa-gāmin*).

All the worlds therein are the spheres of transformation according to each respective stage; this clarifies that through the progressive cultivation and gathering of beings in the eleven stages, one attains the increasingly exalted fruits of Buddhahood.
Each may be seen by assigning them according to their respective positions.

Beyond these eleven worlds, the separate enumeration of one hundred world-systems surrounding them clarifies that these eleven stages encompass and transform the ten *pāramitā* practices throughout the entire Dharma-realm within the Cakravāḍa mountains.

Furthermore, as each direction sequentially contains ten, they are collectively said to be one hundred; this clarifies that the realm is filled with as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in an ineffable number of lands.

Near the Vajra-circumference Mountains (Vajrāvalī-parikhā), there are ten world-systems (lokadhātu-jāti) surrounding it; the fact that they have four layers above and below clarifies that the four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu) pervade the eleven stages (bhūmi).

The reason the remaining ninety world-systems are not described as being multiplied in number is to clarify that these ten *pāramitās* encompass one hundred realms of beings to be transformed and guided within each of the ten.
This concludes one correspondence regarding cause and effect.
As for the remaining ten sets of fourfold worlds, they are correlated with the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); this shall be presented as another correspondence.

Taking the eleven world-systems centered in the middle, together with the hundred world-systems extending to the surrounding Diamond Rim Mountains (*vajrakaṇikāra-parvata*), there are a total of one hundred and ten world-systems, which are correlated with the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground.
Each of the five stages of dharma possesses its own Buddha-causes and -effects, totaling one hundred.

Within the original five stages, there are inherently ten layers of cause and effect as the foundation; within each of these five stages, there are two layers of cause and effect, which constitute these ten. These serve as the foundation because the Buddha-causes and -effects of the five stages function as progressive cultivation within those five stages.
Thus, these five stages of the Buddha’s cause and fruit in this first assembly total one hundred and ten.
There is yet another world-system included to clarify the stage of Buddhahood, as it constitutes the "one" within that which pervades all.
If this one position did not exist, the various positions would not be established.
Furthermore, it clarifies that all phenomena produced through dependent origination must necessarily possess a "one.

Only when the phenomenon of dependent origination is first established does it function as a condition for one, three, five, seven, and nine; however, by merely setting aside two, four, six, and eight, the number ten becomes complete.
This perfect number cannot be increased or decreased, for the dharmas of the Buddha and the dharmas of the world are all similar.

Just as with one day, three days, five days, or seven days—wherein one, three, five, seven, and nine serve as the fundamental principle—they constitute the inexhaustible nature of dependent origination, because the one and the many mutually penetrate one another.
To clarify that it is "one": it is not one in the sense of being simultaneous, for there is neither before, after, nor middle.
It is "one" because it does not itself constitute oneness, but acts as the oneness for the myriad dharmas;
it is "many" because the myriad dharmas do not themselves constitute multiplicity, but act as the multiplicity for the one.

To establish the principle of dependent origination, these are combined as such: the mastery over unity and multiplicity is non-acting, because they are established according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
It is like worldly phenomena where one represents the yang and two represent the yin; the yang moves and the yin follows, and neither can act on its own.
If the yin were to act on its own, then heaven and earth would be at odds with one another; clouds would not arise and rain would not fall.

It is only when the primary and secondary, the yin and yang, and movement and stillness accord with one another, mutually serving as primary and secondary, that they together constitute dependent origination.
Two yang lines constitute *que*, and two yin lines constitute *li*; these do not form a union because they cannot provide mutual support.

Thus, when the Tathāgata appears in the world, his intention lies in benefiting sentient beings; as he truly does not conform to worldly conventions, there is no contrived practice and no contrived virtue—therefore, the Buddha remains the Buddha, and sentient beings remain sentient beings.

If one establishes the principles of the Dharma for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, then the Buddha is the Yang virtue and the teachings he has established are the Yin; therefore, this sutra is called the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
The Buddha resides in the single line of the *kan* hexagram, yet establishes ten teachings because he takes *kan* as his teacher and domain.

To clarify the causal origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of the teachings for the benefit of living beings, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva demonstrates that the Dharma must be sovereign and unimpeded by dependent arising; thus, he cites one hundred and eleven world-systems to correspond to the causes and fruits of the five stages, establishing one hundred and ten gates for the maturation and attainment of sentient beings.
There is one world-system, which clarifies that the Buddha’s state and the five stages, as well as all conditioned activities, are one.

This is like the assembly at the brow-centre: the Bodhisattva Supreme Sound sits alone upon the lotus pedestal, while the host of Bodhisattvas sit upon its filaments, clarifying that the principal and the attendants, and the myriad practices, are the mutual identity of the one and the many.
This can be seen through the contemplation of meditative concentration and wisdom.
Taking ten units below and making them one constitutes the character "shi" (士), which clarifies the dharma of the benevolent scholar (*renshi*).
This dharma corresponds to eleven; thus, it causes eleven worlds to be established as the dharma-gate of the eleven stages (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*).
The fourfold world-system clarifies the skillful means of the ten *pāramitās* and the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
In its general purport, it cites the assembly within the seat and the assembly between the eyebrows to clarify the practices they perform.
This Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*) clarifies the environmental fruit obtained as retribution within those practices.

Among these, the various types of worlds clarify that the sentient beings encompassed therein dwell together in one place while their respective environments differ; this is because, in terms of the Dharma-realm, the principle and wisdom, and the ultimate and conventional truths, they are not distinct.

Regarding the sixth explanation—that the Flower Treasury World-Ocean is characterized by the non-obstruction of the pure and the mixed—it is because the Buddha’s practice pervades both the Dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings.

Since this is obtained through such pervasive practice, its resultant environment is likewise pervasive; however, those whose karma does not correspond to it may dwell together yet fail to perceive it.
It is just as when spirits and various beings of the ghost realms dwell together with humans, yet humans cannot see them.
As a sutra says: "For example, two devas constantly follow a human being."
"The devas constantly see humans, yet humans do not see the devas.
This sutra demonstrates that the Buddha's practice is all-pervasive, such that both the primary [the Buddha] and the secondary [the environment] are likewise pervasive.
It differs from the three vehicles, which project the Pure Land to other directions, thereby giving rise to the notions of coming and going, or self and other.
This is because such provisional nets of teaching were established for those of narrow-mindedness and inferior faculties.
Ultimately, however, those who seek the mind of great bodhi must still return to this gate of non-duality and give rise to practices and vows that pervade the entire dharma realm.

Seventh, regarding the clarification of how the Flower Treasury World-Ocean perfectly encompasses the realms of karma throughout the three periods of time: this Flower Treasury World-Ocean clarifies that within a single thought-moment of this teaching, the three periods of time are fully contained.
A single thought is non-thought.

Non-thought is the absence of dharmas such as the three periods of time, antiquity, or modernity; it clarifies that the Dharmakāya is non-thought, and that the deluded thoughts of all sentient beings regarding the dharmas of many kalpas across the three periods of time do not depart from within this state of non-thought.

For this reason, all the adorned realms within this Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) are able to mutually manifest the karmic activities of all Buddhas. The causes and effects of the actions performed by sentient beings throughout the three periods of time are entirely manifested therein: sometimes past karma appears within the future; sometimes future karma appears within the past; sometimes past and future karma appear within the present; and sometimes present karma appears within the past and future. This is like hundreds of thousands of bright mirrors suspended together, where the reflections on the four sides, front, and back mutually penetrate one another.
Because the essence of the dharma-realm is timeless, the karma bound to the three periods of time suddenly manifests within this timeless dharma.
Therefore, the sutra says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time without coming or going."
The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, you should observe the majestic spiritual power of the world-systems: all future lands are made visible as if in a dream.
All the oceans of past lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions appear within a single land, like magical emanations."
"All Buddhas of the three periods of time, along with their respective lands, are entirely perceived within a single dharma-realm system.
The Master of the Treatise says in verse:
"There is no such thing as 'time' throughout the three periods; it is through delusion that dharmas are bound to the three periods."
Because in reality there is no delusive thought, a single moment manifests the three periods of time.
Since the three periods have no temporal duration, there is likewise not even a single moment;
yet, being unattached to the dharmas of the three periods, they all manifest within that which has no time.
Having thoroughly realized that dharmas have no temporal existence, one attains perfect enlightenment in a single thought-moment.

Regarding the eighth explanation of why the Buddha-lands are fundamentally empty yet give rise to the Flower Treasury World-Ocean as their objective support: what is the object of this support? There are four types of objects; the first is to clarify that although those of the Two Vehicles have attained liberation from the coarse karma of the triple world, they lack merit and wisdom, do not benefit sentient beings, and remain stuck in *nirvāṇa*.

Second, because Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles maintain a persistent thought of desiring birth in a pure land, this obstructs the principle of the *dharmatā*. Since their perception of defilement and purity is biased and not universal, they harbor attachment to the pure land and fail to attain mastery.

This Dharma is not like that; it manifests and conceals with sovereign mastery, and because it benefits sentient beings by manifesting supreme merit, it is endowed with ten thousand variations of marks and radiates brilliant light.

If it causes sentient beings’ minds to be free from grasping and attachment—like clouds dispersing from an illusion so that not a single thing remains to be grasped—then there is nothing left to bind them.

Third, for the sake of all sentient beings who fear emptiness, and for the sake of the principle of the emptiness and signlessness of phenomena, it is said that those who hold nihilistic views—claiming that emptiness lacks merit and wisdom, who do not delight in contemplating emptiness but instead delight in grasping at signs and fetters, and who follow after objects and persist in their karma such that they cannot attain liberation—are shown the fruits of the primary and secondary bodies resulting from merit. This causes them to contemplate the dharma of emptiness, whereby ignorance is vacated and the karma of merit is accomplished.

Fourth, for the sake of all those of the three vehicles and all ordinary beings, he manifests the scale and patterns of the vast realms of vows, practices, merit, and wisdom, so that they may emulate and study them without falling into partiality or attachment.

The Sūtra says: "The lands of all Buddhas are like space—unequaled, unborn, and without marks; yet, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they universally adorn and purify them, abiding therein by the power of their original vows."

Regarding the ninth point, explaining how the Flower Treasury Ocean of Worlds attains mastery over concealment and manifestation: it is because they manifest in accordance with wisdom from the principle of the emptiness of all phenomena that they attain mastery over concealment and manifestation.
If the dragons and ghosts of the world, who possess the three poisons, are still able to manifest and conceal themselves at will,

how much more so should those of the emptiness of dharmas— who have eliminated the three poisons and consist of pure, pristine wisdom— not be able to manifest and conceal themselves with sovereign mastery?
It is like when Sudhana entered Maitreya’s pavilion and, through the power of samādhi, beheld all manner of exquisite adornments;
yet upon arising from that samādhi, they suddenly vanished, leaving not a single mark behind.
Sudhana said, "Where has this array gone? Maitreya replied:
"Go from where you came.
He asked, "From where did you come?"
He replied: "I come from the realm of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom and abide by the power of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom.
Having no place of departure, there is no place of abiding; it is neither accumulated nor permanent, being far removed from all things."
Furthermore, it is like a magician performing various illusory feats; they come from nowhere and go nowhere.
Although there is no coming or going, they are clearly visible due to the power of illusion.
The matter of that adornment is likewise so: it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.

Although there is no coming or going, it nevertheless manifests in this way due to the power of the inconceivable wisdom of illusory mastery through habitual practice, and due to the power of former great vows.

The Flower Treasury World is likewise thus: by the power of the Tathāgata’s great vows and wisdom, and by the power of the self-nature of dharmatā being empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, it manifests and conceals itself with sovereign mastery.
If one follows the dharma-nature, all myriad phenomena are entirely non-existent; yet, following the power of wisdom and vows, the various marks appear accordingly.

Their concealment and manifestation follow conditions and have no creator; it is simply because the principle of wisdom and reality is thus, naturally possessing inconceivable efficacy and inconceivable transformations. There is no agent who can create them, yet they manifest and conceal themselves with sovereign ease.
Ordinary beings cling to its functioning as the obscuration of ignorance. When the functioning of wisdom is absent, there is no mastery;

thus, in accordance with the Dharmakāya, all phenomena are simultaneously quiescent. Following the functioning of wisdom, all phenomena are simultaneously manifested. Following great compassion, one constantly dwells within birth and death; yet, following the principle of wisdom, birth and death are eternally true.
Through these three matters, myriad manifestations of concealment and revelation do not depart from the wisdom of the single truth, while the ritual of transformation undergoes a hundred variations.
Regarding the ten points for explaining the meaning according to the text: this chapter of the sutra is divided into twelve sections.

First, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" onwards, there are twenty-four lines of prose and twenty lines of verse which clarify the praise of the Buddha’s past causes—his practice of the bodhisattva path and cultivation of the power of great vows—and how he obtained, as a karmic reward, a wind-wheel to support the Flower Treasury World (Puṣpakaraṇḍa-vyūha) and its various adornments.

2. From "At that time" onwards, there are eight and a half lines of prose and twenty lines of verse, which clarify the praise of the Jewel-Rimmed Mountains atop the lotuses, complete with manifold adornments produced by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.

3. From "At that time" onwards, the ten and a half lines of prose and twenty lines of verse praise the level ground within the Cakravāḍa mountains, which is composed of vajra and adorned with various jewels interspersed throughout the earth, decorated with nets of flowers.

4. From "At that time" onwards, the following sixteen lines of prose and twenty lines of verse clarify that within the diamond-jewel ground there are numerous fragrant oceans, with various jewels as their floor and exquisite incense adorning their shores, complete with all manner of magnificent adornments.

5. From "At that time" onwards, the following twelve lines of prose and twenty lines of verse clarify that each fragrant sea possesses various fragrant rivers; the beds and banks of these rivers are adorned with all manner of ornaments and wind to the right, circling the seas.

Sixth: From "At that time" onwards, fifteen and a half lines of prose and twenty lines of verse clarify the level ground between the two fragrant-water rivers; this ground is adorned with myriad wonders, and its trees are likewise adorned with myriad wonders of flowers and fruits.
*Puṇḍarīka* flowers—this is translated as "hundred-petaled white lotus flowers.
7. From "At that time" onwards, five lines of prose and twenty lines of verse collectively conclude and praise this ocean of worlds, adorned by the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata.
8. From "At that time" onwards, thirty-eight lines of prose and twenty lines of verse clarify the essential nature, form, and basis of the world-systems.
9. From "At that time" until the end of the volume and its beginning, it summarizes how all these world-systems are distributed and abide upon this great lotus flower.

Furthermore, within this central Flower Treasury Ocean of Worlds, there is a world-system named Blazing Jewel Radiance Universally Illumining the Ten Directions, consisting of twenty tiers of worlds stacked vertically.
The general meaning therein has already been explained as before.

In this ninth fascicle, there are ten sets of twentyfold world-systems (*lokadhātu-vīja*) in total; surrounding this central world-system, there are altogether eleven sets of twentyfold world-systems.
The circumstances therein have already been explained previously.

In this eleventh [section], the tenth fascicle, one hundred world-systems (*lokadhātu-jāta*) are collectively enumerated, surrounding the central eleven twenty-tiered world-systems which are arrayed and abide there.

The ten world-systems near the Cakravāḍa Mountains are arranged in four tiers above and below; their height and depth are similar to those of the eleven world-systems at this center, yet they are separated from one another by immense distances.
The remaining ninety world-systems are not mentioned as being counted in multiples; in total, there are one hundred and ten world-systems.
The intended meaning therein has already been explained as before.

The final verse at the end of the twelfth [fascicle], tenth [chapter] states that all the aforementioned oceans of worlds abide within space—whether pure or impure, and whether consisting of homogeneous or mixed inhabitants—yet they do not obstruct one another; all of these arise through the power of karma.
The scriptural text is vast and extensive, such that it cannot be minutely categorized; its disordered and cumbersome phrasing would obstruct its underlying meaning.
The essential flavor and general purport of this work have already been briefly described above.
The broader meanings of the remainder are already fully contained within the sūtra text itself.
This differs from minor sūtras, for which one must frequently cite external texts to embellish their meaning.

This great compendium of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is such that its meanings do not largely correspond with those of other sūtras; its purport is entirely distinct from that of the Three Vehicles (Triyāna), and thus it cannot be treated as an example of those [minor] scriptures.
The ten fascicles of sutras above clarify three instances where the fruit is raised:
first, at the time when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment and while within his assembly, he raised the fruit of the Buddha’s practice to clarify his own self-realization.
Second, the assembly at the space between the eyebrows illustrates the fruit of the Buddha’s practice of the Middle Way, serving as the cause for those who have not yet attained faith to develop it.

Third, the Flower Treasury World-Ocean clarifies the practices performed by the assemblies previously mentioned—the one within the seat and the one at the space between the eyebrows—as well as the fruits obtained as their retribution.

The underlying intention is to answer the previous thirty-seven questions by means of the fruits of the Buddha’s retributive karma; by seeing the fruit, one knows the cause, so that future learners may emulate this, practicing such vows and deeds to attain such retributive results.
Chapter Six: Vairocana. In order to explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to three sections: first, the purpose for which the chapter appears;
second, the explanation of its title; and third, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.

First, regarding the intent of this "Chapter on Explanation": the preceding five chapters presented the fruit of Vairocana Buddha in the present world; however, there is concern that this may not inspire conviction. Why is this so?
Since there were no ancient traces in the past, from where would they have come now?
By using this to cite the past as evidence for the present, it clarifies that the Way is not erroneous.
Furthermore, it clarifies that the dharmas of the Buddhas of the three periods throughout all time are similar, so that those who achieve faith will have no doubts.
Second, regarding the explanation of the chapter titles: as for the "Vairocana Chapter," this chapter is named by means of the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
It cites the realization of ancient Buddhas to inspire present faith, and thus uses the name of the Buddha himself as the title of the chapter.

"Vairocana" means "various," and "Cana" means "light. This signifies that by means of the compassion and wisdom of the Dharmakāya, various lights of teaching and practice are established to shatter the darkness of the karma of sentient beings.
Question: Are the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the present one and the same, or are they different? Answer:
Are they one or are they different? Why is this so?
Because the Dharma-body, the Wisdom-body, the ninety-seven marks of a great man, and great kindness, great compassion, wisdom, and liberation are one; yet [they appear as many].
That each and every sentient being resolves their mind to attain Buddhahood is a point of distinction.
Furthermore, that all Buddhas of the immeasurable three periods of time attain Buddhahood within a single thought-moment, without any boundary of before or after, is a point of unity;
yet, that within this single thought-moment one does not destroy the perception of the immeasurable kalpas and lifespans of sentient beings across the three periods of time is a point of distinction.
This can be understood by encompassing it within the ten mysteries (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*) and the meaning of the six characteristics (*ṣat-lakṣaṇa*).
As the Sūtra says: "The bodies of all Buddhas are but a single Dharma-body; they are one mind and one wisdom, and their powers and fearlessnesses are likewise so."
Third, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning: within this chapter of the sutra, there are fifteen sections of text in total.

Among these fifteen sections, four Buddhas appear in the world; this collectively clarifies that while Vairocana has a single name, his titles vary according to the conditions of each respective world, yet it is not that the Buddha’s name itself differs.

In the subsequent section of this sutra, the "Chapter on the Names of the Buddhas," each and every Buddha possesses a name that accords with conditions and is equal to the realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm.
All names in the world are the names of the Buddhas, because the virtues of the Tathāgata pervade all phenomena.
It is like space, which universally contains all phenomena because there is nothing impure within it.
All sentient beings are said to enter the name of the Buddha because there is nothing impure within them.
Furthermore, it is like a fragrance named "Dragon Strife," which is produced from the strife of dragons; if one pellet of it is burned, its scent will linger for seven days.
When the rain of golden light falls and moistens the bodies of people, they all become golden in color.
In the same way, all names and designations that enter the name of the Buddha are likewise completely purified.
Because the name of this Buddha pervades all worlds as their designation, he is first named Vairocana.
He universally illumines all things with the light of various teachings and practices, illuminating them with the eye of all dharmas.
Regarding the division into fifteen sections:
first, the initial section of eight lines beginning with "At that time" clarifies how Samantabhadra addresses the assembly, intending to expound the Dharma.

This section is further divided into ten parts: first, citing the number of eons passed by the ancient Buddhas; second, citing that there are world-oceans and worlds with names twice as many as that number; third, citing the specific names of worlds within those world-oceans; fourth, citing the substratum upon which the worlds rest; fifth, citing the number of surrounding retinues of worlds; sixth, citing the shapes of the worlds; seventh, citing the adornments upon the ground of the worlds; eighth, citing the precious trees and the multiple layers of mountain ranges surrounding the worlds; ninth, citing the cities and palaces of the worlds; and tenth, citing how the food, drink, and clothing of the people in the worlds arrive according to their thoughts, as well as the name of the eon.

The above sections are fully explained by the text itself and need not be further elaborated upon. Second, regarding the eight lines of scripture beginning with "O Children of the Buddha," the general meaning is divided into eight points:

first, it clarifies the fragrant water ocean within the world-system of Supreme Sound and mentions its name; second, it clarifies that a flower-mountain appears within the ocean, shaped like Mount Sumeru; third, it clarifies that there are ten kinds of adornments for the mountain; fourth, it clarifies that there is a great forest on the mountain and mentions the name of the forest; fifth, it mentions the five kinds of immeasurable matters that adorn the mountain; sixth, it clarifies that the entirety of these adornments is difficult to record; seventh, it clarifies the number of cities upon the mountain; and eighth, it clarifies that various classes of beings dwell together there.
Regarding the term *puṇḍarīka*, this refers to the white lotus flower (*śvetapadma*).
This preceding section of the text is self-evident and need not be further explained.
Third, the nineteen and a half lines of scripture beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha" clarify the city to the east of the grove.
The meaning of this section is divided into ten parts:
first, naming the city;
second, the place where the human king resides.
Third, it describes how various cities surround [it].
Fourth, it clarifies that the substance of the city is composed of various jewels.
Fifth, it clarifies the dimensions of the city’s breadth and width.
Sixth, it clarifies that the adornments of the city walls are all lofty and magnificent.
Seventh, it clarifies the adornments of the various matters throughout the upper and lower parts of the city.

Regarding the term *lǔ* (rampart), according to the *Yinjie* (Explanations of Pronunciation): "The defensive structure atop the city wall is called a *yán* (eaves/parapet); the projecting front portion is called an *dí* (enemy-stopping tower); being highly decorated and superior is called *chóng* (lofty); being beautiful and worth beholding is called *lì* (magnificent)."
"A moat" refers to a long, winding ditch surrounding a city that is deep and wide; one that is narrow is called a "trench.

As for the *utpala* flower, it is translated here as the "blue flower"; it resembles a lotus root, with leaves that are narrow and long, small and rounded at the base and gradually tapering to a point at the top, resembling the eyes of a Buddha.
The stem of its flower is thornless.
According to the *Buddhastotra*, the description "eyes pure and long as a blue lotus" refers to the petals of the blue lotus (*utpala*).
As for the *padma* flower, this is translated here as the red lotus; the stem of its flower is thorny.
As for the *kumuda* flower, its stem has thorns.
Some say it is a red or white flower; when the tips of its petals have not yet opened, its shape is like that of a tightly knotted bud.
The *puṇḍarīka* flower is the white lotus.
As for the *ratnatāla* tree, it is sometimes called the *aśoka* tree; this remains uncertain, as I have not been able to find a definitive textual source.
In the ritual procedures for the sevenfold encirclement, the numbers one, three, five, seven, and nine correspond to the yang numbers.
*Śīla* means "purity," which here is translated as "purity."
The aforementioned adornments of the Jewel Banner are all made of jewels.
Regarding the inhabitants of the eight cities of clarity:
the people of the ninth city of clarity attain supernatural powers as the retribution for their karma, such that whatever they think of arrives before them.

The city of Daśāntī is surrounded on all four sides by seven classes of beings—devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and so forth—who dwell within its various districts; furthermore, it is entirely bound together with immeasurable adornments.

Question: Among these, one class consists of humans who are not devas, nāgas, or spirits. How is it that they obtain supernatural powers as karmic retribution, such that their clothing, food, and drink arrive according to their thoughts?
Furthermore, as for the fact that the dwelling place is exalted and adorned with the precious adornments of the environment, by what karma is such a retribution obtained?
The answer is:
because the cause is vast, the karmic retribution is vast.
Because the cause is lofty and supreme, the abode resulting from karmic retribution is lofty and supreme.
Question: What constitutes a cause that is vast, expansive, lofty, and supreme?
The answer is:

For the sake of past causes, one gives rise to faith in this gate of the non-abiding nature of the essence and function of Vairocana’s Dharma-realm wisdom, which is pure by nature; one cultivates the power of faith and understanding, constantly believing that self and others, ordinary beings and sages, are of one substance, identical to the Tathāgata’s wisdom in its non-abiding, devoid of self and what belongs to self, with mind and object equal and without dualistic marks—because there is no duality and no "mine. Since all ordinary beings and sages are fundamentally only the Dharma-realm, characterized by a nature free from fabrication and a nature free from arising and ceasing, they abide in accordance with the Truth, abiding in non-abiding, sharing the same mind and wisdom as all Buddhas and sentient beings, dwelling in the true Dharma-realm of nature.
All conceptual discriminations are the fundamental non-moving wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*) of all Buddhas; ordinary beings and sages alike share this one true wisdom.

Because one has full faith that one’s own mind is the Buddha’s seed-wisdom and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is no separate mind that believes in a Buddha apart from the mind itself, nor does one perceive any marks of a Buddha within one's own mind.
Believing in this Dharma, though their own power is not yet sufficient, such persons obtain every supreme retribution among all people;
by the power of this faith, they further attain co-residence with Vairocana Buddha in his realm, constantly manifesting the supernormal powers of spiritual transformation.

They dwell together with the devas, for all the spirits, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings residing in all cities have likewise given rise to faith and understanding within this Dharma through shared conditions.
Because the causes of faith were lofty, supreme, and vast, one obtains such excellent and wondrous retributions of both the primary and secondary fruits.

Fourth, from "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, there are nine lines of scripture that clarify the site of enlightenment within the grove of jewel-flower-branch wheels, as well as describing its vast and magnificent adornments.
This grove is adorned with various flowers and is constantly filled with the sounds of music and song.

(5) From the words "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, there are twelve and a half lines of scripture which clarify the number of Buddhas appearing during the first eon, list the name of the first Buddha, and cite the auspicious omen that first appeared in the Great Forest of Flower Branches.

6. From "At that time" onwards, there are nine lines and a half of scripture which clarify how the first Buddha suddenly appeared from within a lotus flower, as well as the matters such as the Buddha’s body pervasively sitting at the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) throughout the entire Dharma-realm, and all sentient beings seeing [him] and so forth.
Question: For what reason does this Buddha manifest through the transformation of a lotus flower, rather than appearing from the womb of Śākyamuni’s mother? Answer:
It appears according to the faculties [of beings].
Its manifestation from a mother’s womb is seen by sentient beings of inferior understanding through their own faculties alone.
As stated in the "Chapter on Transcending the World": "For sentient beings of inferior understanding, it appears as emerging from a mother’s womb."
"For those sentient beings with great faculties, lotus flowers shall all appear. 7.

From "At that time" onwards, there are eight lines of scripture which clarify the appearance of the first Buddha, his emission of light to assemble the multitude, and the presentation of how the assembly of the Light-Virtue [Buddha] gathered.

8. From the passage beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha" below, there are fourteen and a half lines of scripture that clarify how, in the Great City of Blazing Radiance, there was a human king named King Joyful Vision and Good Wisdom (Priyadarśana-sudhīra-rāja) who, together with his retinue, assembled; and how, along with the Crown Prince Majestic Light (Tejaprabha), through their own roots of goodness, they beheld the light of the Buddha and attained ten kinds of Dharma-gates.
This is exactly as explained in the sutra.
The final three lines clarify the proclamation of verses in praise of the Buddha by Ābhāsvara.
Within these ten lines of verse, the virtues of the Buddha and the benefits he brings to sentient beings are praised; these may be understood according to the text.

9. From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, there are two and a half lines of sūtra text clarifying that the King spoke these verses through his majestic radiance; by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the sound was heard everywhere, and upon hearing it, the Father-King joyfully spoke these verses.
Within these eleven verses, it is clarified that King Supriya commanded the assembly to gather and ordered the preparation of offerings.

From "At that time" onwards, there are thirty-four and a half lines of scripture which clarify how the ten kings raised offerings to see the Buddha, presented the *sūtra* they had heard, and how Prajñāprabha attained benefit.
The term *sūtra* refers here to the prose portion of the scripture.
The final two lines clarify that it was Prabhāsa who spoke these verses.

Within these ten lines of verse, it is shown that Prabhāsa, upon hearing the Dharma, attained the power of knowledge regarding past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*), thereby perceiving the events of the Buddha’s past causes and conditions, and subsequently made a vow for himself to act as the Buddha had done.

11. From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, there are eleven lines of scripture which clarify that because the Bodhisattva Vidyutprabha had seen and served the first Buddha, he attained ten kinds of manifestations of the dharmas practiced by the Tathāgatas, thereby causing sentient beings as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
The Tathāgata Meruśrīmeghottama spoke these verses to Prabhāsa, praising his virtues.

Within these eleven lines of verse, it is clarified that the Tathāgata Meruśrī praises the vastness of Prabhāsa’s attainment of the conduct of a Buddha; this may be understood from the text as it stands.
Twelfth: The following fifteen lines of scripture, beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha," clarify the length of the lifespans of the Buddhas and humans during the *Kṛta-yuga* (Adorned Eon).

It describes how, after the first Buddha passed away, the second Buddha appeared; it further explains the ten kinds of benefits obtained by Vigraprabha upon seeing the second Buddha, as well as the verses he spoke for his retinue.

Within these twenty verses, it is clarified that the majestic light praises the Buddha’s compassion and the difficulty of encountering his appearance in the world, exhorting his retinue to go together to the Buddha’s presence.
From "O Sons of the Buddhas" onwards, there are sixteen lines of scripture clarifying that the majestic light spoke these verses, and their sound was heard everywhere.
Together with his retinue, Prajñāprabha went to the Buddha’s dwelling and attained ten kinds of benefits.

The second [section] consists of verses spoken by the Buddha for Prajñāprabha; within these twenty lines of verse, the second Tathāgata praises Prajñāprabha for entering the Path and attaining benefits—the benefits attained being the Dharma-gate of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
As the sutra says: "Attaining the ocean of wisdom through consecration, it is named 'Effortless,' and one cultivates the most sublime vision.

(14) From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, there are twelve lines of scripture which clarify that after the second Buddha has passed away and King Good Wisdom (*Sukhadatta*) has also passed away, Great Radiance (*Mahātejaḥprabha*) assumes the position of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
The third Tathāgata appeared at the ancient site of enlightenment; having seen the Buddha’s majestic radiance and heard the Dharma, Vairocana gained great benefit.
This third Tathāgata then spoke verses in praise of Vairocana’s virtues.
These twenty-two lines of verse clarify the third Tathāgata’s verses praising the dharmas attained through his majestic radiance.
The subsequent eight and a half lines of sūtra, beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha," clarify the fourth Tathāgata’s manifestation within the ancient site of enlightenment.
After Mahātejas passed away, he was reborn on the summit of Mount Sumeru as the Great Heavenly King; he returned once more to see the Buddha, obtained benefit, and departed.
This single chapter of the sutra is incomplete in its extant text and lacks a concluding section.
This chapter merely clarifies that by citing the past to seal the present, the Dharma of Vairocana’s appearance in the world remains unchanged across the succession of ages.

Furthermore, it clarifies that the path one believes in and delights in is sublime and the Dharma is supreme; that the lifespan of human beings is long; that the fruits of the primary and secondary environments inhabited through merit are superior; and that the benefits obtained from seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma are supreme.

The second assembly consists of six chapters of sutra, clarifying the Gate of Bodhisattva Faith.
Within this single assembly, there are naturally the introductory section (nidāna), the main exposition section (dharmadeśanā), and the dissemination section (parīndanā).

From the beginning of the twelfth fascicle, starting from "At that time" and below, there are four and a half lines of sūtra that constitute the introduction (nidāna). From here down to the "Chapter on Worthy Leader" (Bhadrapāla-parivarta) is the main exposition (deśanā). At the end of the "Chapter on Worthy Leader," there are three and a half lines of sūtra that constitute the dissemination (pariṇāmanā).

Chapter Seven: The Names of the Tathāgatas. From this chapter through the "Chapter on Worthy Heads," this constitutes the third major section of the structural outline, which establishes faith through the fruition [of Buddhahood], specifically the portion concerning the conviction that one's own mind is itself the Buddha.
Within this section, there are approximately six dharmas that establish the Buddha-fruit of one's own mind, so as to enable those with faith to enter the Buddha-fruit.

First is the "Chapter on the Names of the Buddhas," which causes those with faithful minds to believe that the names of the Buddhas pervade all worlds, and to know that the nature of names is detached [from inherent existence].
Second, the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths," which causes those with faith to personally realize that all worldly suffering is itself the Noble Truth, so that they do not seek it elsewhere.

Third, the "Chapter on the Radiance of Awakening," which causes those with faith to personally use the radiance of their own minds to illuminate the entirety of the infinite and inexhaustible great trichiliocosm as the universal realm of the Buddhas, realizing that they themselves are likewise equal [to the Buddhas].
Following the light with the mind, illuminate each [world] one by one; when the mind and its objects merge as one, the distinction between internal and external vanishes.
Having first illuminated the three thousandfold world-system, next return to taking the eastern direction as the starting point.

The light reaches the thirteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction and illuminates a hundred such triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems; thus it revolves ten times through each of the ten directions, doubling at each stage, universally illuminating the ten directions so that body and mind are of one nature, unimpeded and all-pervading, identical to the realm of the Buddha.

Contemplating each one in this manner through focused attention, he then seals them with the meditative seal of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-upāya*), enters the initial mind of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and becomes a true son of the Dharma King of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Just as light illuminates, so it is clearly explained in the sutras.

One must not think that the Buddha’s light lacks its own portion [of efficacy]; rather, one must personally employ the light of the mind to be like the Buddha’s light, awakening the mind so that it perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm.
4. The "Chapter on Questions and Clarifications" (Prajñāparipṛcchā-parivarta) causes those with faith to believe in the dharmas that are to be believed.

5. The "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (Caryā-viśuddhi-parivarta) causes those with faith to believe that when Bodhisattvas first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], they invariably take the making of great vows as the foremost.
Furthermore, it causes those with faith to turn back their beginningless deluded thoughts, thereby forming an ocean of wisdom characterized by the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.

Chapter Six, "The Chapter on Worthy Leader," causes those with faith to believe in the Buddha’s spiritual power that universally transforms the boundless, so that they may attain great sovereignty as well as the merit of faith.
To have faith in these six dharmas is called being a "Virtuous Head" (Bhadramukha); to practice contemplation in accordance with these six dharmas is called "faithful mind.

All ten Tathāgatas of the Wisdoms, such as the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom, are the fruits of one's own mind; the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom constitutes the essence, while the remaining wisdoms constitute its function—this will be clarified below.
Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva Chief of Awakening, Chief of Eyes, and the other nine "Chief" Bodhisattvas are the embodiments of those who practice with faith.

From this chapter down to the "Chapter on Chief of Worthies," these six chapters of the sutra constitute the third major section within this single scripture: the Gate of Establishing Faith through the Fruit.
The first assembly was held to clarify the fruit of Buddhahood and encourage its cultivation, so that one may have faith in what all Buddhas have attained.

This second assembly establishes faith through the fruit, leading one to believe that one's own mind is the Buddha because it is no different from the Buddha of the fruit; this will be clarified in the text itself.
The preceding section used the fruit of Buddhahood to encourage practice; this section encourages practice by citing the names of the Buddhas as the fruit.

Within the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single name that is not the name of a Buddha, for the essential nature of names is itself liberation; it is only because they accord with the diverse perceptions of sentient beings that they appear different.
This clarifies that the Buddha’s name is all-pervasive, which means he is unattached to all names.
To explain this chapter, I shall briefly present three sections:
first, the purpose for the appearance of this chapter; second, the explanation of its title; and third, the word-by-word commentary on its meaning.

First, regarding the intent of this "Chapter on Explanation": it clarifies that while the first assembly previously explained only the Tathāgata’s body of attaining equal and perfect enlightenment and his wisdom that encompasses sentient beings, it did not yet clarify the breadth or narrowness of the Tathāgata’s name and title in encompassing sentient beings.
Now, in this second assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance, it is precisely to clarify that the names of the Buddha-fruit encompass all living beings that this chapter must appear.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of citing the names of the Buddha-fruit to inspire faith and understanding that this chapter must appear.
In the previous assembly, it was clarified that the body and wisdom are all-pervasive; in this assembly, it is clarified that both the name-body (*nāma-kāya*) and wisdom are equally all-pervasive.
Although the World Lord posed questions in the first assembly, no answer had yet been given;

this chapter answers those prior inquiries, thereby causing the minds of future believers to have faith that the Buddha’s name-body and wisdom universally pervade the Dharma-realm, covering sentient capacities to benefit beings, illuminating the mundane world to shatter delusion.

It is named the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala*). Because the hall is established based on its virtues, and because those virtues are manifested through the hall, this chapter must appear here.
Second, regarding the explanation of the chapter title: within this Buddha-name, there are five conditions by which the Buddha-name is established:

first, the Buddha-name is established through the condition of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) that is the self-substance of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); second, the Buddha-name is established through the condition of the Tathāgata’s own virtue in manifesting perfect enlightenment; third, the Buddha-name is established through the condition of the Tathāgata’s skillful means for benefiting sentient beings, specifically the progressive cultivation of the stages; fourth, the Buddha-name is established through the condition of all sentient beings according to their faculties and inclinations; fifth, the Buddha-name is established through the condition of the equality of the essence and function of the dharma-realm, wherein all phenomena are collectively termed the Buddha-name.

First, regarding those who attain the title of Buddha by taking the fundamental wisdom of the self-nature of the Dharma-realm as their object of focus: these are the names of the ten Wisdom Buddhas, such as the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom, the Buddha of Unobstructed Wisdom, and the Buddha of Wisdom that Extinguishes Darkness.

Based upon this fundamental wisdom of the dharma-realm, ten names are bestowed to establish ten kinds of the power of faith; the extensive meaning will be clarified once the respective stages are reached.

The general purport is to cause sentient beings to realize that their own fundamental ignorance is, in its original state, nothing other than the Tathāgata’s fundamental great wisdom; this is so that all sentient beings may suddenly recognize their original nature and suddenly become Buddhas.

Second, regarding the Tathāgata’s manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment as the causal condition for his own virtues, thereby establishing his title as a Buddha: this refers to the manifestation of perfect enlightenment by all Buddhas of the ten directions, who share the ten common titles, namely: Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, Vairocana is a collective name; it is the light of great wisdom that illuminates all various phenomena and various sentient beings.
Thus, "Vai" means "various," and "rocana" means "pervasive illumination."

Regarding the Tathāgata of the Three Clarities’ skillful means for benefiting sentient beings, which involves advancing through stages to achieve the title of Buddha, this is precisely as follows: ten fundamental Immovable Wisdom Buddhas are cited below to establish the Ten Faiths.

Listing ten months, the names assigned to each Buddha are all identical and called "Moon," thereby completing the Ten Abodes; this clarifies that one has newly realized the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya, and the mind attains cool serenity.

To clarify that at this stage the Bodhisattva accords with reality and delusion has vanished, thereby attaining the cool clarity of the wisdom of *dharmatā*, the Buddha-name is established based on the qualities of the benefits attained by himself.

Within the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten "Eye-Buddhas" are all uniformly named "Eye" to clarify that the ten practices benefit and assist sentient beings through the eye of wisdom-knowledge (*jñāna-jñāna*). Because these Buddhas possess excellent knowledge of the faculties and natures (*indriya-gotra*) of beings, they are all designated as "Buddhas" based on the benefits conferred upon others.

Within the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the ten sublime names of the Buddhas are all uniformly designated as "Sublime" (*Miao*). This is to clarify that because the Bodhisattvas in the stage of the ten dedications advance in their practice until their refined wisdom gradually matures and manifests before them, the Buddhas' names are termed "Sublime."

From "The Ten Grounds are Identical to the Wondrous" onwards, it clarifies that from within the ten faiths, one’s own mind’s discriminative wisdom and the fundamental immovable wisdom of all Buddhas have been primordially one; thus, faith is established.
To perceive phenomena as existing apart from the mind does not constitute true faith.

From this point of faith onward, one accords with principle and unites with the source through the power of samādhi; this is called the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*).
