The Buddhas are given names such as "Moon," all of which are titles of Buddhahood conferred according to the dharmas attained by practitioners during their cultivation.

The fifty names of the Buddhas are established across five stages, consisting of fifty causes and fifty fruits; because each stage is complete with both cause and fruit, they constitute one hundred layers of cause and fruit.

Within the five fundamental stages, there are originally five causes and five fruits, which constitute a dharma-gate of one hundred and ten layers of cause and effect; this is not different from the essence of the Dharma-realm, nor is it different from the dharmas believed during the stage of the ten faiths.

The Fundamental Immovable Wisdom Buddha serves as the basis for the progressive cultivation of all stages; this is explained provisionally here, while its full significance will be elucidated extensively below in the section on the fundamental positions.
This is termed "attaining the Buddha-name through progressive cultivation according to the stages."

The Tathāgata of the Fourth Clarification explains that because all sentient beings attain the name of Buddha according to their faculties, inclinations, and conditions, he manifests within the realm of sentient beings as a Buddha, a deva, a spirit, a lord, a benevolent one, or an immortal.

That the Buddha’s name pervades the realm of all sentient beings, causing them not to commit evil, is entirely beyond the scope of measurement by one's own ordinary, mundane mind; it is simply that the Buddha’s names are omnipresent.

Regarding the statement that the five sciences, the essence and function of the dharma-dhātu, and all phenomena in their equality are collectively named "Buddha," this is because all phenomena and their names and expressions are by nature devoid of intrinsic selfhood.

The self-nature of all phenomena is the detachment from inherent existence, which is the nature of the Dharma-realm; because the nature of the Dharma-realm is the name of the Buddha, and because all phenomena and their designations are the name of the Buddha, the Tathāgata attains Buddhahood by proclaiming this dharma of the detachment from the self-nature of all phenomena.

If one were to extensively cite scriptural passages to substantiate these meanings, the text would become overly expansive and verbose, obscuring the sense; furthermore, those who have performed the original karma would find it difficult to understand. Therefore, by relying solely on the internal consistency of this sutra from beginning to end, those who have performed the karma will find it easy to comprehend.

Just as within the Three Vehicles it is also taught that there is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) followed by subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), here, in order to cause those of the Three Vehicles to turn their minds [toward the Great Vehicle], this Golden World and its Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*Acalamati-buddha*) are pointed out so that they may directly recognize them as the discerning wisdom of one’s own mind, which is fundamentally unmoving. Mañjuśrī is precisely the sublime, signless wisdom (*anākāra-prajñā*) of one’s own mind that skillfully discriminates; and Bodhisattvas such as Buddhamati and Vidyumati are the principle-wisdom (*jñāna-dharmatā*) perceived within one’s own mind according to faith and understanding.
Those of the three vehicles who have not yet turned their minds will certainly not believe this.
Why is this? Because it is established that they shall attain Buddhahood only after three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

This is simply to acknowledge that one's own body and mind are entirely those of an ordinary person, and to believe only in the Buddha’s immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) and so forth, rather than having confidence that one's own mind is the fundamental immovable wisdom Buddha (*mūla-acala-jñāna-buddha*), no different from the Buddha himself.

For this reason, it is not established that within this vehicle of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-yāna), fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) is taken as faith. The faith of this sutra should be understood in this way:

one directly believes that the very nature of the conceptualization of one’s own mind is the Fundamental Immovable Wisdom Buddha within the nature of the Dharma-realm; that the Golden World is the principle of the non-defilement of one’s own mind; and that Mañjuśrī is the sublime wisdom of skillful discernment within one’s own mind. Bodhisattvas such as Bodhirāja and Śrīcakra are the manifestation of principle and wisdom within the context of that faith. Only when one accords with the fruit-dharmas of all Buddhas through the cause of faith, without the slightest error, does one truly establish faith.

Having attained this faith, one advances through meditative concentration and wisdom, traversing the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground. Throughout these stages, the divisions of time—days, months, years, kalpas, and seasons—do not shift; the dharma-realm remains as it was, and the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom remains as he was, until one accomplishes the ocean of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
To transform sentient beings, one must realize that cause and effect do not shift and kalpas do not change; only then is true faith established.

If one posits a fixed reality within the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, considering oneself an ordinary person while viewing the paths of the ordinary and the sage as separated by shifting kalpas, or believing that there is a Buddha external to the mind, true faith is not achieved.
As stated above, there are these five kinds of Buddhas, whose names and titles differ.
Question: What is the difference between a "name" (ming) and a "title" (hao)?
The answer is:
There are two types of similarities and differences. What are these two?
Based on the fact that one is a young child born of parents and lacks virtue, one is given a name as a mere appellation; when one possesses virtue, a name is established based upon that virtue.
When such a name becomes worthy of honor, it is designated as a title.
A "name" (*nāman*) is that which even a person of low status may not invoke; a "designation" (*adhivacana*) is that which even a person of low status may invoke.
Therefore, although there is a distinction between those with virtue and those without, both are subsumed under the category of "name," as they are encompassed by verbal expression.
Regarding the names of the Buddhas according to this sutra, they are all established based on the Dharma and their virtues, differing from worldly conventions.
Third, as for the word-by-word commentary, the meaning within this section is divided into two parts:
first, a general outline of the intent of the thirty-two chapters of the sutra.
In the third dhyāna, eleven stages and one category of the future are explained.

Regarding the intent of the scripture within these two sections—from the second assembly, the "Chapter on the Names and Epithets of the Tathāgata," following the twenty-eight questions raised by the World Ruler (Lokendra), up until the subsequent "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata"—this constitutes the complete cycle of cause and effect concerning that which was questioned by the World Ruler.
The responses comprise thirty-two chapters of sutra, which answer twenty-eight questions.

Therefore, beginning from the palace of the fruition of Buddhahood within the Dharma-realm of Universal Radiant Wisdom, the names of the Buddhas' fruits are cited; likewise, the Four Noble Truths—the Dharma-gate for teaching and transforming sentient beings practiced by the Buddhas' fruits—are cited; and the name of the Buddha of the fundamental wisdom-essence of the Dharma-realm, Immovable Wisdom Buddha, is cited to establish faith and cultivation, continuing all the way through the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata."
The thirty-two chapters of this sutra constitute the completion of the practice of faith and vigor and represent the ultimate of cause and effect.

From the elucidation of this Palace of Universal Radiance Wisdom up to the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," there is no duality between the cause and effect of this practice of faith and vigor.

Furthermore, it clarifies that one generates faith and practices upon the fruit-virtue of this initial attainment of perfect enlightenment; subsequently, in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," it is clarified that because the Dharma-realm has no temporal separation, within the essence of the Dharma-realm, the deluded perceptions of ordinary beings [manifest as] immeasurable kalpas.

As for those who give rise to faith and advance in practice, they rely on the Truth to initiate their practice as their progressive cultivation; because they pass through the practice-gates of the five stages without ever deviating at any time.
When one has not yet given rise to faith and is practicing, one always thinks that the Buddhas of the past attained Buddhahood long ago, having passed through immeasurable kalpas;

yet, when one relies on the power of right faith, one sees those who have already attained Buddhahood throughout the ten directions over immeasurable kalpas, and realizes that oneself and those who previously attained Buddhahood attain Buddhahood simultaneously, with no distinction of before or after.

For this reason, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he was like an ordinary person today who has first resolved upon bodhicitta; having initiated practice and cultivated it until his own path was fulfilled, he ultimately never departs from the moment the Tathāgata first appeared at the time of his initial attainment of perfect enlightenment.
This is established as the measure of the insentient because the fundamental dharma-dhātu has no beginning in time.

Therefore, when the Sūtra says, "The initial resolve and the ultimate [attainment] are not two different things," it is because the nature of the dharma-dhātu is devoid of distinctions across the three periods of time.
Because there is no distinction between the three periods of time, and because there is no distinction of time, there is no distinction because wisdom is without distinction.
Since it is not different from the essence of the Buddha Akṣobhya-jñāna, the function of wondrous wisdom is without distinction.
Because there is no difference from Mañjuśrī’s skillfully discerning sublime wisdom, their practice is not distinct.

Because they have practiced from the first generation of the mind of awakening by practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra without differing from the ten pāramitās, their great compassion is not distinct.
Because they constantly engage in teaching and transforming others, their great vows are without distinction.

Because they do not abandon sentient beings, the four means of integration are without distinction, the four immeasurable minds are without distinction, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are without distinction.
Because these ten kinds [of faith] are non-distinct, it is said: "The initial resolve and the ultimate [resolve] are not two; thus, between these two resolves, the former is more difficult.
This is to clarify that it is difficult for one to enter into these ten kinds of faith and understanding.

If one believes in one's heart that there are other Buddhas who have attained the Way while considering oneself an ordinary person, this is merely the measure of worldly sentiment; it does not involve faith, progress, or cultivation, but is simply the long-flowing stream of birth and death constantly following the net of views—how great a suffering this is!
Thus, as in the second assembly and the first assembly, it clarifies the appearance of the Tathāgata who has just attained perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, in the subsequent thirty-two chapters, it again emphasizes the appearance of the Tathāgata to clarify that those who practice with faith and diligence from beginning to end appear simultaneously with the Buddhas of the three periods, because the entire Dharma-realm appears all at once.

Just as holding a precious mirror facing all images causes them to be suddenly illuminated and manifested without before or after, so too, within the fundamental Buddha-wisdom realm of the *dharmadhātu*, all phenomena are suddenly manifested; one must not employ the measures of the deluded mind to interpret this as having a sequence of before and after.
First, regarding the realm within Maitreya’s pavilion:
the Buddha who has just attained perfect enlightenment in the first assembly illustrates the exhortation to practice by pointing to the fruition.

The Buddha in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Buddha" clarifies the Buddha at the culmination of the causal practices of the five stages for all bodhisattvas; this is because he corresponds to the Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*acalajñāna-buddha*) within the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

Question: For what reason are the various chapters spoken by the various bodhisattvas, while only the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on the Minor Marks" (*Anuvyañjana-parivarta*) are spoken by the Buddha himself?

Answer: It is as in the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of a bodhisattva, and as in the afflictions and ignorance of the five stages. Within the stage of the Tathāgata, the inconceivable assembly of bodhisattvas is provisionally established to constitute these five stages; thus, the successive dharma-gates are manifested within the respective positions of the bodhisattvas, namely the bodhisattvas of the Ten Wisdoms, the Ten Forests, the Ten Banners, the Ten Treasuries, and so forth.

Regarding the ignorance regarding phenomena within the stage of Buddhahood, the Tathāgata himself has stated that such as these—the "Asaṃkhyeya Chapter" and the "Anuvyañjana Chapter"—are the ignorances within the stage of Buddhahood; it is only upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood that these two delusions are finally resolved.
Therefore, the stage of the abiding ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is only finally brought to an end at the level of Buddhahood, as stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.

This is because a portion of the scriptural net—namely, the teachings common to the two vehicles (*yāna*)—does not permit the two vehicles or the bodhisattvas of the Pure Land to sever and realize fundamental ignorance, for they do not understand that ignorance is [identical to] fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
This One Vehicle teaching takes the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom as the mind of faith; for all other dharmas practiced and realized through illumination differ from this sutra.

This teaching clarifies that one should contemplate the initial mind and the ultimate mind as being entirely exhaustive, because within the *dharmadhātu* there are no three periods of time (*tryadhvan*).

The fulfillment of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) requires a fixed number of *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; furthermore, the paths of progress for the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of sagehood (*daśārya-bhūmi*) are distinct. The preparatory practices (*prayoga*) on the stages (*bhūmi*) and the four provisions (*catuḥ-sambhāra*) prior to the stages, as well as the fruit of Buddhahood, all require a fixed number of *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, as was explained previously.

The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of this sutra constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the stage of application (*prayogamārga*), and the stage of equipment (*sambhāramārga*) simultaneously. Why is this so?

Because the great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* serves as equipment for one's practice, ensuring that the practice remains untainted; and because the body of the *dharmadhātu*-wisdom, through the equipment of practice, is made habitual and matured. This is to clarify that from the state of an ordinary being, one first perceives the nature of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and principle (*jñāna-dharma*).

Furthermore, within these five stages of practice, each stage possesses its own fruition of Buddhahood; the distinctions in nomenclature are established according to the specific habituation and station of each stage.
This is because, within the teachings of the Three Vehicles, as one progresses from a preceding stage to a subsequent stage, there is only the fruit of a Bodhisattva, not the fruit of a Buddha.
This will be explained in detail later in the section on the stages.

Regarding this Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm, speaking of it for immeasurable eons does not prolong it; speaking of it in a single kṣaṇa does not shorten it. Only those who are deluded falsely conceive of it as having length or brevity, extension or contraction; such a view does not accord with the mind of the truly realized ones.

From this "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgatas" onwards, up until the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," there are thirty-two chapters in total; these constitute the causes and effects of the progressive cultivation of the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten stages, and the eleventh stage.

Because the beginning is identical to the end and the end is identical to the beginning, they constitute a state of non-duality; like the Great King’s Highway, this Dharma is eternally thus, being neither something old nor something new in essence.

As stated in a verse by Mañjuśrī: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus understanding the affairs of the three periods of time, one transcends all skillful means and achieves the ten powers."
Regarding the two sections of this chapter: within this chapter, it is further divided into four parts.
First, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, there are eight lines and a half of scripture, which clarifies the section on praising virtues and assembling the assembly.
2. From "At that time, the bodhisattvas had this thought" onwards, the fourteen lines of scripture constitute the section on the Great Assembly’s Request for the Dharma.

3. From "At that time, the World-Honored One knew what the bodhisattvas were thinking in their hearts" onwards, the forty-one lines of scripture clarify the section on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Manifestation of the Dharma.
4. From "At that time, Mañjuśrī... down to the end of the chapter is the section on the exposition of the Dharma.
Within this, from the beginning, there are two parts:
first, praising the virtues of the Tathāgata; second, praising the virtues of the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
From the initial section on the virtues of the Tathāgata, the two lines of scripture beginning with "At that time" constitute the introduction (*nidāna*).

This passage recounts the original site where he first attained Bodhi as well as the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala*), intending to clarify that these two locations are not distinct. This is because his body pervades all places without moving from the original site of the Bodhimanda; because the essence of the Bodhimanda is the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); because the Universal Radiance Hall is the central abode of the retributive dwelling within the Dharma-realm; and because the two natures of Dharma-body and retribution are identical in their essential nature and characteristics, being one true reality where the fundamental and the derivative, and cause and effect, are without difference.
For this reason, it is restated.
An ancient commentator explained:
"Because they are closely related, it is necessary to restate them."
The meaning of the sutra is not so.
Furthermore, it says:
seeing that the Buddha was dwelling in the open air, the dragon constructed the Hall of Universal Radiance (Puguangdian).
This interpretation is also incorrect.
Even if such a thing were to exist, it would be a teaching intended for those of the three vehicles.
Furthermore, it is said:

The site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River, three *li* distant from the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-prāsāda*). Located to the southeast of the site of enlightenment, it is understood that the site of enlightenment is the place of solitary retreat (*āraṇya*) where the Way was attained, while the Hall of Universal Radiance is the dwelling of retribution.

In this section of the sutra, the text extends from the beginning through the "Dharmadhātu Chapter," and the phrase "At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling... appears five times in succession. This is intended to clarify that the dwelling place consists of the Dharmadhātu, the Tathāgata’s body, and the adornments of the palace; all of these are fundamentally non-dual with the nature and characteristics of the Dharmadhātu, which is the root wisdom.
The five preceding sections have already been explained in the previous assembly.

From the passage "The wondrous realization is already fulfilled" down to "universally seeing the three periods of time," there are two and a half lines of scripture; these constitute the formal praise of the Buddha’s virtues. They demonstrate that his wondrous realization is already fulfilled, clarifying that his ten knowledges are all-pervasive and sovereign.

"Both modes of activity are forever severed" means that because both conditioned and unconditioned modes of activity have been exhausted, one realizes the dharma of signlessness, wherein grasping and abandoning are both ended.
"Abiding in the Buddha-abode" means that one dwells together with all Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—in the great wisdom and great compassion of the dharmadhātu.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata and all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time abide in five kinds of universal pervasiveness:
first, the universal pervasiveness of manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment, as exemplified by the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in the first assembly.

Second is the pervasive nature of the adornments of the primary and secondary retributions as well as the names and titles, which refers to the second assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*).
Third is the pervasive nature of the essence of meditative concentration, which refers to the "Chapter on the Ten Concentrations" (*Daśa-samādhi-parivarta*).
Fourth is the universal pervasiveness of the teachings on the practices of Samantabhadra, which refers to the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*).
Fifth is the universal pervasiveness of the inconceivable, unimpeded, and perfect wisdom-functioning of the Dharma-realm, which refers to the "Dharma-realm Chapter" (*Dharmadhātu-parivarta*).
Because these five kinds [of dharmas] pervade everywhere throughout all Buddhas, it is called "abiding where the Buddhas abide.

For this reason, within this single division of the sutra, the five perfections are established [beginning with]: "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha. With the exception of the slight variation in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," this clarifies the layered and pervasive nature of reality—how it does not depart from a single location, a single essence of bodhi, a single dharmadhātu, a single fundamental wisdom, or a single moment devoid of before and after.
Fearing that the meaning of the sutra might be lost, these five sections are recounted repeatedly so that later students will not be confused by its events.

To clarify these five cycles, it is shown in their entirety that there is only a single limit without before or after; within a single kṣaṇa-limit there are no two moments. Thus, the turning of the Wheel of Dharma throughout forty years—from the time he had not yet descended from Tuṣita Heaven nor emerged from his mother’s womb until he had already entered nirvāṇa—is all contained therein.
"Attaining the equality of a Buddha" means that because principle and phenomena are non-dual, one reaches the state of being free from obstructions.
"The dharma that cannot be turned back" clarifies that the Buddha constantly dwells within birth and death, yet is not transmuted by karma.
Furthermore, it can transform the dharma of non-transmigration.

That "his conduct is unimpeded" clarifies that the Buddha is able to engage in communal activities (*samānārthatā*) within the cycle of birth and death, because the ultimate and conventional truths do not obstruct one another.

Regarding "establishing the inconceivable": this refers to the completion of the Buddha’s path and practices; it signifies that, being entirely effortless and spontaneous in benefiting sentient beings, his wisdom is sovereign and cannot be measured by thought, intention, or deliberation.

Regarding "one who universally perceives the three periods of time," because their vision is perfectly clear and bright, it does not mean that they perceive the affairs of sentient beings within the three periods from within the three periods themselves.

From the passage beginning with "Together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields" down to "past, present, and future," there are approximately four lines of scripture therein that praise the virtues of the bodhisattvas.
"Accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields" clarifies that they come from the ocean of the Dharma-realm, which is perfectly complete and pervasive.
"Accompanied" means arriving simultaneously, for there is no coming or going.
"There are none who are not all Bodhisattvas in their final birth" means they are all Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage; thus, they are designated as being on the tenth stage.

According to the *Sūtra on the Original Acts of the Garland* (*Yíngluò Běnyè Jīng*), within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*Samatābhisambodhi*), the stage of Samantabhadra matures the path, fulfilling its merit and completing its function, only then ascending to the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, it is called "the final birth. This is as explained in the *Yíngluò Běnyè Jīng*.

Furthermore, from the initial dwelling of the first aspiration, one is also called a "Bodhisattva of One Life. Because, through the fundamental wisdom that first perceives the nature, one does not perceive the prior or posterior limits of birth, they are termed "One Life."
The *Sutra of the Necklaces* (*Yingluo jing*) states: “The Bodhisattvas of the Three Sages reach Buddhahood spontaneously within the flow of the Dharma.

As for the phrase “all come together from other directions,” the mention of coming together from other directions distinguishes them from the original assembly; they are all those who arrive without coming and pervade everywhere without going.

Furthermore, it was clarified in the previous assembly that by citing the fruition to encourage practice, one relies on the fruit of another Buddha’s realization; now, in this second assembly, it is clarified that through the conduct and understanding of another Buddha’s fruition, one perfects the path of faith and realization within one's own mind—this is what is meant by "coming together from other directions."

Those who have come from the fruit of faith in the Buddha in the past and are all in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) clarify that, having given rise to faith and understanding in the first assembly, they reach this assembly where their faith is fulfilled and they enter the stage of realization, thereby attaining Buddhahood; such is the case with the Dragon Girl, Sudhana, and others.
For this reason, those who have come from other regions are all members of the single-life assembly.
This is precisely what is meant by the expression "entering the Dharma," signifying that they have come from other regions.
Delusion is called "other," and awakening is called "coming.

The three lines of scripture beginning with "Universally and skillfully observing the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, and the world-realm" praise the assembly that has come, because they skillfully observe the non-dual nature of these three kinds of realms; furthermore, it shows that they know sentient beings follow afflictions and karma, and they also know the matters of the afflictions, karma, and activities of bodhisattvas according to their respective stages.
The remainder is as explained in the sūtra.

Regarding the second section, "The Request for the Dharma by the Great Assembly," the passage beginning from "At that time, the bodhisattvas, having reflected thus" and extending for fourteen and a half lines of scripture, contains thirty-two questions. These are divided into two parts in meaning:
first, there are four initial questions concerning the four kinds of buddha-fields.

2. Following the section "Accomplishing the Great Bodhicitta and Being Exhorted by the Buddhas of the Ten Directions," there are twenty-eight [sections] below concerning the questions regarding the bodhisattvas' stages, their buddha-eyes, buddha-ears, and so forth.
These thirty-two questions are answered as far as the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," as detailed in the sutra.
It is asked:

The questions posed by the World Rulers in the first assembly are largely similar in meaning to these; they differ only in their degree of detail. Why, then, are the same questions as above asked once again in this second assembly?
The answer is:
At the previous assembly, it was the World-Honored One who questioned; he cited the fruit of Buddhahood to encourage practice and the attainment gained through faith in the Buddha.

At this assembly, however, [the Bodhisattvas] must question again because they now personally believe that their own bodies and minds are the Buddha, and they are entering the stages of cultivation. Therefore, further inquiry is required.
The preceding section describes Samantabhadra entering meditative absorption to manifest the fruit; this assembly, however, clarifies Mañjuśrī’s emergence as the beginning of entry into faith.
This indicates that for ordinary beings at the initial stage of faith, because their confidence is coarse, he does not enter absorption when teaching;
it is only from the Ten Abodes onward that the Bodhisattvas of those respective stages enter absorption before beginning their discourse.
For this reason, although the preceding inquiry shares some similarity in its underlying principles, it must differ from the previous assembly because of the distinction in its objective conditions;
thus, while the former assembly involved faith in the attainment of other Buddhas, this assembly involves one's own entry into faith and practice.
The ancients said:
"The former assembly was for invitation; this assembly is for inquiry.
This interpretation is not correct.
From beginning to end, this is always a request, for it is precisely because of this request that the inquiry is made.
However, there is a slight difference in the ritual procedure regarding the exhortation to practice and one’s own entry [into the path].

This is as in the previous assembly: the Tathāgata’s fulfillment of the Way through his own cultivation, as well as the fruit of the fulfillment of practice by the past Buddhas who have already attained the Way.

This second assembly presents the fundamental wisdom of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions—the fruition shared by both ordinary beings and sages—which is precisely the Golden World in every place, and the Buddhas of Immovable Wisdom and the Ten Wisdoms in every place.
It clarifies that all Buddhas and sentient beings alike possess this Immovable Wisdom.
Its golden color represents the Dharma-nature body of principle; it is called "color" because it arises from the mind of faith.
This is represented by the ten material worlds, which is precisely what is being inquired about in this assembly.
Regarding the Buddhas who dwell in the four kinds of Buddha-fields, it clarifies that these are the common abodes of all Buddhas and all sentient beings.

It is the wisdom that serves as the root for all ordinary beings and sages; it is the wisdom by which one is led to believe that the Buddha resides within one's own mind. All Buddhas arise from this faith, and all ordinary beings likewise originate from it.

Regarding "adorned with the nature of the Buddha-dharma and Buddha-lands," this refers to the ten names of the Buddhas associated with each stage among the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), ten practices (*caryā*), ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground.

Therefore, one should give rise to faith in the fundamental wisdom of one’s own mind and proceed with its cultivation; by adorning each stage and practice with the various *pāramitās*, one thereby ornaments the *dharmakāya* and *jñānakāya* so that they may reach full maturity.

By employing the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body to adorn the myriad practices, one causes those practices to be free from attachment; therefore, it is called the "Buddha-field of the Buddha-nature adorned by the Buddha-dharma.
As for the "Buddha-field where the pure Buddhas preach the Dharma," this refers to the Tathāgata manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment and turning the wheel of Dharma.

Regarding the "Buddha of Essential Nature" and the "Buddha of Majestic Power," these refer to those who manifest through supernatural powers (ṛddhi) and appear in the world according to the faculties [of beings].
This clarifies that the latter two Buddha-fields are attained by generating faith, practicing, and reaching maturity based on the former two Buddha-fields.
For this reason, one should know that the Buddhas of the ten directions are all born through this single path.
One should know thus and believe and understand thus; by doing so, one attains the fulfillment of faith and understanding, for it is identical to what the Buddhas themselves believe.

Those who attain this faith are superior as described in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (Bhadrapāla-parivarta), for they can lift the trichiliocosm with their hands and remain suspended in mid-air for an eon; this is to clarify that such faith is difficult to believe.
Furthermore, the merit of making superior offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the dust motes in the worlds of the ten directions over the course of an eon is not equal to such faith.
The following twenty-eight questions are answered in full by the Sutra itself.
Those meanings that are obscure and difficult to clarify are explained; those meanings that are manifest can be understood from the text as it stands.

Among these thirty-two questions, there are inquiries concerning the Ten Penetrations (*daśābhisamaya*) and the Ten Summits (*daśa-mūrdhan*); yet in the sūtra, there are only the Ten Penetrations and the Ten Patiences (*daśakṣānti*), with the name "Summit" not being seen. Thus, the Ten Patiences are redundant and the Ten Summits are missing.
"May the Buddha, the World-Honored One, [also] speak for the sake of all bodhisattvas and for me as well"—these two lines conclude the request.
From this point onward, the Tathāgata provides a manifest response by employing his supernormal powers to raise up the Dharma.
Regarding the third section, "The Manifestation of Dharmas through the Tathāgata’s Supernormal Powers," this section is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the manifestation of dharmas according to the various types of beings; second, clarifying [the manifestation] in relation to initial faith.
First, regarding the manifestation of dharmas according to their respective categories: within each of the five stages, the Bodhisattva manifests ten kinds of Buddha-abodes.

Within the Ten Abodes, the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, the Ten Grounds, and the Eleventh Ground, there are respectively the names and titles of the Buddha-fruit corresponding to each stage. This is what is meant.
In accordance with all buddha-fields and all classes of sentient beings, he manifests various different names and titles, such as those of the Buddhas spoken of by Mañjuśrī in the following passage.
Second, regarding the clarification for those at the initial stage of faith: this refers to the present chapter as well as the entire treatise taken together as "faith.
Only when one possesses a comprehensive faith in the cause and effect within the five stages, free from doubt or stagnation, can one truly practice.
As it is taught in a scripture:
For example, suppose there is a person who must traverse a perilous road five hundred *yojanas* long; he first discerns where it is passable and where it is obstructed before proceeding.

This is analogous to a Bodhisattva of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), who, within the state of faith, first discerns the points of progress and obstruction throughout the five stages of cultivation. He preemptively employs vows and practices to guard against them, for he realizes through the faculty of faith that the nature of his own mind’s discrimination is fundamentally the immovable wisdom-body (*acala-jñāna-kāya*) of all Buddhas. He uses this realization to guard against false views, which arise from grasping at external objects as other than oneself.
Because one falsely claims that mental agitation occurs in accordance with each stage, thereby obstructing true wisdom, one employs the *dhyāna-pāramitā* to prevent it.

Because in the eighth dwelling, the eighth practice, the eighth dedication, and the wisdom of the eighth stage, one becomes attached to and stagnates in quiescence, thereby obstructing true non-conceptual great compassion, one employs the one hundred and forty great vows to prevent it.

Because attachment to birth and death obstructs true wisdom, one must prevent it by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness, as well as the contemplation of the ten truths and the twelve links of dependent origination.

Because the benefit to sentient beings through the ten *pāramitās* might not be sufficiently vast and extensive, one employs the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) to guard against this.

Because teaching and transforming sentient beings by seeking a pleasant fruit for oneself would be incomplete and narrow, one gives rise to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), augmented by great vows, great kindness, and great compassion. This is so as not to abandon any of the evil realms, the hells, humans, or devas, but to be born everywhere among them to prevent self-indulgence and the violation of the bodhicitta that arises from grasping at attainments.
For this reason, the mind of the ten faiths universally permeates all five stages; even in delusion, one is entirely within the state of faith.
If one’s self-confidence is thorough, then in pursuing the goal, there is no dharma that cannot be attained.
If doubt is not eliminated from the mind, how can faith be established?

Thus, this chapter introduces the gateway of the Buddha-fruit, while the "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (Xianshou-pin) introduces the Buddha’s supernormal powers and his various practices; because these cause those with initial faith to attain thorough conviction, it is first termed "faith."

Now, this single section of the sutra suddenly presents the gates of fruition of all Buddhas—the causes and effects of the five stages—thereby collectively establishing the practice for those who have already entered the stage through faith; only then does one begin to no longer lose oneself in the confusion between principle and wisdom.
It is like when someone prepares food: the five flavors are all cooked at once, and only then does one begin to eat it.
From the first moment of eating until the meal is finished, the flavors remain inseparable from these five.

To clarify the cause and effect of the five stages, the ten faiths are explained collectively; this is because time does not shift between the beginning and the end, as one must believe that the three periods of time are a single limit.
Ultimately, the fruit of Buddhahood is not separate from the dharmas of the initial stage of faith, as can be understood through analogies such as painting a portrait based on a model.
Within this section on the Dharma-gate of manifesting supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), there are forty-one lines of scripture, divided into eleven segments.

The first, consisting of one and a half lines of scripture beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of the bodhisattvas," clarifies how the Tathāgata, aware of what the assembly was contemplating, manifested the Dharma through his supernatural powers.

First, the thirty-nine and a half lines of scripture beginning with "To the east, beyond the dust-motes of ten Buddha-fields" collectively clarify the gathering of Bodhisattvas from the ten directions; as each direction has its own distinct portion, there is no need for further sub-sectioning.
Within this assembly of bodhisattvas gathered from the ten directions, the meaning may be divided into ten parts:

first, the direction of the buddha-field; second, the distance of the buddha-field; third, the name and form of the world-system; fourth, the name of the Buddha; fifth, the names of the leading bodhisattvas; sixth, the number of the great assembly; seventh, the paying of respect by the assembly upon their arrival; eighth, the transformation of seats according to their respective directions; ninth, the names of the seats; and tenth, the ascending of the assembly onto the seats and taking their places.
Regarding "first raising the direction of the Buddha-field," this refers to the East.
The East corresponds to the hexagram Zhen, to the spring season of birth and growth, and to the beginning; it clarifies the eldest son.

It represents the head, the Azure Dragon, auspiciousness, and vibration; it clarifies the initial stage of the movement and application of ritual activities. Because both monastics and laypeople employ it universally, and because the East is raised first as the primary direction, it is mentioned at the outset.
"Direction" (fang) means "method" (fa); it simply takes the sense of a method of approach.
The beginning of its dynamic application is not like the directions of east, west, south, and north as perceived by the world, which can be grasped as fixed points.
In every direction, from the east to the south, it is solely for the sake of grasping that Dharma; the other directions are to be understood accordingly.
Second, regarding the distance of the Buddha-fields: beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields to the east.
There are four meanings to this:
first, to clarify that ten is a perfect number, in order to demonstrate the inexhaustibility of both the distant and the near;
second, to clarify that it causes those with faith to know the vastness of the Buddha’s realm, thereby expanding their own minds.
The third clarity reveals that the Buddha-realm is all-pervasive, such that images within a mirror reflect one another without obstruction.
The fourth clarity shows those who have not yet given rise to faith, using the dust motes of ten buddha-fields as a metaphor for their state of delusion.
The ten types of ignorance have not been reached; they obstruct the Buddha-realm from manifesting before one, and thus dust is cited to represent delusion.

As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni’s pure land lies beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers to the west. This is entirely a numerical expression for representing the Dharma, as has already been explained in the commentary.

The statement that these beings come from "beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields" clarifies that they are separated by ten levels of ignorance (*avidyā*). Within each of these ignorances, there are immeasurable afflictions—consisting of active defilements (*kleśa*), karmic tendencies (*vāsanā*), and their associated factors—which mutually permeate one another. These afflictions exceed the number of atoms in worlds, their limits being unknowable; because they are able to obstruct the realm of wisdom (*jñāna-viṣaya*), it is said they come from "beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields."
"Coming" clarifies that one enters faith from delusion; therefore, it is termed "coming.

As for the statement that there is a Buddha in that world named Acalamati (Immovable Wisdom), it clarifies that the Buddha Acalamati is the fundamental wisdom common to all ordinary beings and sages throughout the ten directions.
Because one can give rise to faith through wisdom that is clear regarding this, it is termed "coming.
This Buddha of Immovable Wisdom is eternally possessed by all sentient beings.
If one grasps at signs and follows delusion, then the obstructions of sensory objects will be inexhaustible;
if one awakens to delusion in a single thought-moment and penetrates these signs, they will be pure like empty space.
It is only because one follows delusion that we speak of "external" in reference to the place of awakening.

In reality, the Buddha-fields are fundamentally free from such obstacles as distance, nearness, interior, or exterior; they neither come nor go, and infinite Buddha-fields do not transcend the surface of a single pore or a minute speck of dust.
Now, to convey the intention regarding the far and the near, so that those with initial faith may expand their minds, it is said that he comes from that world.
Furthermore, to clarify the transition from delusion to awakening, it is said that he comes for this purpose.
There is a Buddha named Immovable Wisdom; this clarifies that faith is one's own fundamental wisdom.
Because of the existence of this wisdom, all sentient beings are able to give rise to the bodhicitta.

Because the essence of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is able to comprehend that the nature of delusion gives rise to faith and understanding, it manifests those deluded objects; this is termed "coming.
As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The aspect of inconceivable karma refers to the ability, based on the aspect of pure wisdom, to produce all kinds of supreme and wondrous realms."
That which is called the mark of immeasurable merit is eternally uninterrupted; it naturally accords with the faculties of sentient beings, manifesting in various ways for the sake of their benefit.
It is also said: "Because of fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi), there is non-awakening (a-bodhi).
And it is further said: "Depending upon wisdom (jñāna), suffering and pleasure arise.
These points are explained in detail in the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith).
This clarifies that all sentient beings are deluded regarding fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and thus there exist worldly phenomena of suffering and pleasure.
Because wisdom has no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it follows conditions; through non-awakening, the karma of suffering and pleasure arises.
Because wisdom is devoid of intrinsic nature, one is entangled by suffering; only then can one realize for oneself that the root is devoid of intrinsic nature.
Since all conditions lack intrinsic nature, the myriad dharmas are inherently quiescent.
When suffering is not perceived, because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one does not know at all whether there is intrinsic nature or the absence of intrinsic nature.
Just as a person falls because of the ground and rises because of the ground;
so too do all sentient beings fall because of the fundamental wisdom of their own minds and rise because of the fundamental wisdom of their own minds.

For this reason, within this sutra of the One Vehicle, the Tathāgata suddenly reveals the fundamental dharma as the Golden World, clarifying that the Dharmakāya is pure and unstained; he suddenly reveals the fundamental wisdom as the Buddha Immovable Wisdom; and he suddenly reveals Mañjuśrī as the wondrous discerning wisdom of one's own mind.

The remaining nine worlds, the nine Wisdom Buddhas, and the nine Bodhisattvas represent the progressive advancement and increasing excellence on the stages of practice according to one's own faith and understanding; they are thus alternative names for the Dharma-body as it accords with these various modes of practice.

From this Buddha of the Primordial Immovable Wisdom of one’s own mind, through the supremacy of self-awakening, one perceives the Way and enters the stages, giving rise to the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the preparatory practices for each of the ten stages; thereupon, one progressively cultivates the great vows, great kindness, and great compassion of the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body, as well as the four means of integration, the four immeasurables, the ten perfections, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

From the very beginning of the aspiration for enlightenment, based upon the fundamental Dharma-body and the essence of primordial unmoving wisdom, one employs these to support the myriad practices; compassion and vows interpenetrate and harmonize to mutually mature one another, such that the Dharma-body supports practice to ensure it remains undefiled, and practice supports the Dharma-body to bring it to full maturity.

Within each of the five stages, ten Buddha-fruitions and ten Bodhisattvas are established respectively; this clarifies that within the progressive cultivation of each stage, these names are established based on the fruits of the Buddha and the practices of the Bodhisattva attained through one's own practice, rather than being names of other Buddhas or other Bodhisattvas.

Following the fruit of Buddhahood through wisdom and the fruit of its practice, there are fifty causes and effects for each of the five stages, totaling one hundred; when combined with the five fundamental stages, which themselves comprise five sets of cause and effect, these constitute the one hundred and ten dharma-gates of the "cities."

This answers the previous Bodhisattva’s question regarding the four kinds of Buddha-fields: the Buddha-field where the Buddha dwells, and the Buddha-field of the pure nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as adornment.

Beyond these two Buddha-fields, there are the Buddha-field that manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment and the Buddha-field of the majestic power of the Buddha’s sovereign spiritual powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*).
Therefore, the questions posed by the World Ruler (*Lokendra*) in the previous assembly concern the fruit of the mastery attained by that Vairocana Buddha;
whereas the questions posed by the Bodhisattvas in this second assembly concern the causes and effects of the bodhisattva practices within a buddha-field for those who practice for themselves.

From this point onward, up until the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," constitutes the final stage of the five levels of the bodhisattva’s progressive practice through the power of self-exertion.

This chapter clarifies that it is the fruit of advancing through faith; whereas the "Appearance Chapter" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) represents the characteristics of cause and effect at the ultimate stage of cultivation, because one generates faith, advances, and practices upon the fundamental Buddha-wisdom within one's own mind.
This Immovable Wisdom is the ground of all Buddhas and all sentient beings; it is by virtue of this wisdom that they manifest as sentient beings.

When they follow delusion and act as sentient beings, throughout the six realms—whether among devas, humans, or within the evil destinies—they all experience the karmic retributions corresponding to the sentient beings' environments and their own bodies.

As the coarseness or subtlety of karma varies, by means of this wisdom, at the time of awakening, one achieves the fulfillment of the fruits of the Dharma and the three vehicles, as well as the wondrous retributions of the primary and secondary marks of the fruit of Buddhahood in the One Vehicle.
If this wisdom did not exist, there would be no such thing as space, nor would there be sentient beings, nor Buddhas.
Question: All sentient beings inherently possess the immovable wisdom; for what reason do they not themselves correspondingly realize the eternally true and pure state?
Why does it follow along with defilement?
The answer is:

because all sentient beings give rise to the three realms by means of this wisdom, yet since this wisdom lacks intrinsic nature, they are unable to know for themselves whether it is wisdom or not wisdom.

Phenomena such as good and evil, suffering and pleasure, have no intrinsic nature within the essence of wisdom; they merely manifest in accordance with conditions. They are like echoes in the sky, which produce sounds in response to objects.

Wisdom, being devoid of intrinsic nature, merely discriminates in response to conditions. Because of this discrimination, delusion and craving arise; because of delusion and craving, the sickness of "mine-ness" (mama-kāra) arises. Because of mine-ness, the karma of grasping at self and other arises. Because of this grasping, it is called *manas*. Because *manas* grasps, it is termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). Due to the seeds of consciousness, birth and death continue in succession; because of birth and death, there is immeasurable suffering.
Because suffering is immeasurable, one seeks the Way that is free from suffering.
Those who are deluded and do not recognize suffering cannot give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment;
those who recognize suffering and seek the Truth, however, possess what is fundamentally innate wisdom.
Only by encountering the conditions for suffering can one come to know suffering; because one does not encounter the conditions for suffering, one cannot know suffering.
Because one knows the conditions for suffering, one is then able to resolve to seek the unsurpassed path.

Bodhisattvas of the lineage who, due to their past lives, have already understood suffering and thereby resolved their minds, and whose strength of faith and understanding is powerful, are able to resolve their minds and seek the unsurpassed path even while experiencing the pleasant fruits of human and celestial realms.
Therefore, wisdom follows delusion, and wisdom follows awakening; it is like a person who falls because of the ground and rises because of the ground.

When one is precisely following delusion, it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); when one is precisely following awakening, it is called wisdom (*jñāna*). In the state of being entangled in afflictions, it is called consciousness; in the state of enlightenment, it is called wisdom. Consciousness and wisdom originally have no names of their own; they are established only in accordance with delusion and awakening. Thus, they cannot be bound by the labels of permanence or annihilation.
This wisdom and this consciousness are merely names established according to delusion and enlightenment.
If one seeks their beginning or end, it is like seeking tracks in the sky, like seeking a person within a shadow, or like seeking a self within the body.
Because they depend on their respective locations, the characteristics of newly arising long or short places can ultimately never be apprehended.
In this same way, ignorance and wisdom have neither beginning nor end.
When one attains bodhi, ignorance is not extinguished. Why?
Because it is fundamentally non-existent; thus, there is nothing further to be extinguished.

If one follows along with ignorance (*avidyā*), the immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) is likewise not extinguished; because it is fundamentally non-existent, there is furthermore nothing to be extinguished.
It is only when following after the conditions of grasping at forms, sounds, and fragrances that it is called ignorance;
it is only when knowing suffering and giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment that it is called wisdom.
It exists only as a name following conditions; therefore, its essence has no fundamental basis.
This can be understood by reflecting on it like an echo in the sky.

Third, regarding the mention of the world’s name and form: the world is named "Golden" to clarify that the essence of gold is white, pure, and unstained; this is cited as a metaphor for the fact that the Dharma-body has no inherent nature, as its essence is free from defilement.
Just as in the world of the West, gold is white in color;
its substance is white and yellow, signifying that the Bodhisattva Saṃyaksatya internally accords with the white dharma while externally manifesting a yellow appearance.
Yellow is the qi of the Arhat (Arhant). Xu Fu said:
"Among the five colors, yellow is the most excellent."
"A person's face may resemble a gourd, yet within lies noble conduct.
The Sūtra states, "The Arhats and Bodhisattvas are all of a true golden color.
Furthermore, the clarification of the Golden World elucidates the stage of faith.
Although one may believe that one's own body and mind are the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body, pure and originally unstained,
because one believes this to be a mind subject to arising and ceasing and characterized by outflows, it is therefore merely the physical and mental aggregates.

The reason for citing the eastern direction as the primary one is to clarify that the east is the beginning; it is the source from which all things emerge and are set in motion. Therefore, it is taken to represent the Dharma, serving as a metaphor for the very commencement of the ten stages of faith.

Although space is without spatial dimensions, it is merely cited as a dharma to illustrate its principle and to manifest its essence and function, just as the "bull-king" or "dragon-king" are used to illustrate the virtues of the Buddha.

Question: Since the East is used as a metaphor to represent the initial stage of the ten faiths, and since gold is located in the West, why is the Eastern direction designated as the Golden World? Is it to symbolize the Dharma-body as golden in color, thereby manifesting fundamental wisdom as the Immovable Wisdom?
Answer: This question clearly elucidates the underlying principle.
As stated in the sutras, taking faith as the womb and reaching the stage of the ten abodes is called being "born for the first time into the Buddha-family."

Now, the reason the eastern direction is designated as the Golden World is to clarify that gold corresponds to the first month [of pregnancy] as the *bao* (embryo), the second month as the *tai* (fetus), the third month as the formation of shape, the fourth month as birth in the *ji* position, the fifth month as nourishment in the *wu* position, the sixth month as the wearing of the cap and sash in the *wei* position, the seventh month as the development of features, and the eighth month as the attainment of royal status.
Because the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are like a fetus, they are symbolized by the golden womb (*suvarṇagarbha*) of the eastern direction.

Subsequently, the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir are used to symbolize the progressive advancement and increasing excellence of the ten stages of faith; thus, these phenomena are employed as metaphors to facilitate understanding.
As stated in this chapter by Mañjuśrī:

"When the World-Honored One was formerly a bodhisattva, he attained accomplishment through various discourses, skillful means, and the stages [of the path]; he likewise causes sentient beings to perceive and know in such a manner as he preaches the Dharma."
Later scholars, because they are able to observe that all [teachings] are explained through these directional indicators to represent the Dharma,
should know that one uses a net to seek fish, yet the fish is not the net.
If there were no net, one likewise could not catch fish.
Reflecting on this through its underlying principle, the ultimate truth alone becomes credible.

Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "In every place is the Golden World; in every place is the Buddha Acalamati; in every place is Mañjuśrī. This clarifies that the Dharmakāya pervades the bodies and minds of all sentient beings, because it is the totality of the Buddha Acalamati and the totality of Mañjuśrī.
One should know it thus and believe and understand it thus.
It should be understood that the world named Golden Color is so called because the principle one believes in serves as the name of the world; it is also for this reason of faith.

In return, one shall obtain birth that is free from defilement and a dwelling that is free from attachment; this is precisely the meaning of the Western World of Lotus-Colored Radiance (*Padmavarṇa*).
As for the World of Golden Color (*Suvarṇavarṇa*), this is cited as the initial cause of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Just as there are the World of Wondrous Colors in the south, the World of Lotus Colors in the west, and so forth, these represent the superior functions of advancing through the ten stages of faith; for within them, there are ten causes and ten fruits.
The ten fruits refer to the ten wisdom Buddhas.
The ten causes refer to the ten bodhisattvas, such as Mañjuśrī and Bodhyaṅga.
As for the causes of practice, the benefits obtained within those causes constitute the fruits within the causes; these are the ten wisdom Buddhas, such as Akṣobhyajñāna and the others.
The ten worlds are the dharma-gates that are cultivated.
Regarding the fourth point, the mention of the Buddha’s name, Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*Acalamati*), clarifies the fundamental essence of wisdom of all Buddhas and all sentient beings.
I shall now first cite this to establish the initial faith.
This clarifies the response concerning the Buddha dwelling in the Buddha-field.
The remaining nine types of wisdom-Buddhas are all names for progressive cultivation based upon this fundamental Immovable Wisdom; they do not exist elsewhere as separate entities.

The Buddhas of the ten directions all share these same traces of name and title; by giving rise to faith, advancing in practice, and passing through the five stages, one attains the manifestation of perfect enlightenment, the Buddha-fields, and the majestic virtue of the Buddhas.
The Buddha-field is the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata.
The remaining points are as previously explained.

Regarding the fifth point, the mention of the name of the foremost Bodhisattva: his name is Mañjuśrī. He is the sublime wisdom that discriminates phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) within the non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all Buddhas of the ten directions; for it is from this wisdom that all Buddhas distinguish between the correct and the erroneous to achieve perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Mañjuśrī is titled the teacher of all Buddhas of the ten directions and is also called the Mother of Buddhas, because it is clarified that all Buddhas are born from this wondrous wisdom.

If one lacks this wisdom, even if they cultivate liberation, they will only attain the vehicles of the two vehicles or become a Bodhisattva of the Pure Land; they will not ride the Tathāgata Vehicle to achieve perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, by mounting this essence of immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*), the wondrous prajñā of Mañjuśrī, and the great wisdom of the wondrous principle of the Dharmakāya, one traverses the five stages from the level of faith; because one attains perfect enlightenment without departing from the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom and the wondrous prajñā of Mañjuśrī, it is called "mounting the Tathāgata Vehicle," the "Inconceivable Vehicle," the "Most Victorious Vehicle," and the "Unsurpassed Vehicle" to attain perfect enlightenment.

Mañjuśrī is also called the Youngest Son or the Youthful One, because it is through this wondrous wisdom that all Buddhas thoroughly understand the True Dharma and are thus born into the Buddha-family for the first time; therefore, he is titled the Youthful Bodhisattva.

After the Tathāgata has passed away, Mañjuśrī will still remain in this world; later, when his transformative conditions have been exhausted, he will manifest entry into nirvāṇa upon the summit of Mount Gandhamādana.
This is the teaching of the Three Vehicles.
This sutra states, "Mañjuśrī is present in all places," which clarifies that he is equally shared by all sentient beings everywhere.

Now, at the beginning of this sutra, the name is raised to clarify what it means to have faith; here, the wisdom of discerning the wondrous nature of one's own mind is identical to this [faith]. It does not deviate from the ancient traces; it is the fundamental wondrous wisdom common to all Buddhas and sentient beings, shared equally by both ordinary persons and sages, possessing no different nature. It is like the great royal road: the Dharma-principle is eternally thus.
However, in all sutras where Mañjuśrī serves as the primary interlocutor, they clarify the gateway to the wondrous wisdom of the Dharmakāya;
whereas those where Samantabhadra serves as the primary interlocutor, they clarify the essence and function of the myriad practices of wondrous wisdom.

These two sages are the gateway to the wondrous functioning of the wisdom and principle of all Buddhas and to the myriad practices; they establish their titles based on these dharma-gates, manifesting their bodies to bring about transformation and benefit sentient beings.

All sentient beings who have resolved their minds to attain enlightenment shall together cultivate these practices, each possessing conduct that benefits both themselves and others, establishing this as their constant model.
Regarding the statement in the teachings that Mañjuśrī and ten thousand bodhisattvas dwell upon Mount Qingliang in the northeast, there are three meanings:

first, to cause all sentient beings in this realm to give rise to a joyful mind and ensure that their roots of goodness do not cease; second, to demonstrate that bodhisattvas abide eternally within the world; and third, to clarify that the Dharma is revealed according to specific regions so that the teaching may be easily understood.
The first two sections may be understood as before.

Regarding the third section, which clarifies the Dharma according to its location: as for the clarification of the northeast, this refers to the northeastern region of this single realm of Jambudvīpa, which is this Mount Qingliang.
According to investigation, it is located in the land of Zhendan, also called Jitianā, which translates as "Contemplation" (Sītuí).
It is so named because the people of that country engage in much reflection and much deliberation; thus, it is none other than the land of Han.
The symbol of the Dharma-light represents the *gen* hexagram in the northeast; *gen* signifies the "younger son" and the "ignorant child.

Because the period between *chou* and *yin* marks the initial dawn of illumination, it is likened to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, who constantly inspires ordinary beings to enter right faith and the ignorant children who first perceive the Path, causing the light of sublime wisdom to arise.

Furthermore, it is like reaching the summit of a mountain where all characteristics are exhausted; its clarity is like that of a beginner who has newly entered right faith and first believes in the emptiness of all phenomena, for through this ability to believe in the emptiness of phenomena, wondrous wisdom arises.
The month of Chou (December–January) corresponds to the initial faith; the month of Yin (January–February) corresponds to the initial realization of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The months of Mao, Chen, and Si constitute progressive cultivation; Wu represents the Middle Way; Wei, Shen, You, Xu, and Hai represent working for the benefit of sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*); and Zi represents the stage of the Master (*ācārya*).

The Kan hexagram represents the sovereign and the teacher; it establishes a model for those in the midst of ignorance and provides a standard for regulation. Because its principles benefit all living beings, it is therefore the dwelling place of the North, of the sovereign, and of the honored teacher, who governs through the manifestation of brilliant virtue.
Sixth, regarding the number of the great assembly: there were as many as the atoms within ten buddha-fields, in order to manifest that his physical activity is all-pervasive.
If even the atoms of a single buddha-field already pervade everywhere, how much more so those of ten buddha-fields?

7. "Clarifying that the Great Assembly has arrived and pays homage" clarifies the rules for teacher and disciple, as well as the etiquette of respectful compliance. This is because it clarifies the infinite, layered pervasiveness of the body.
Eighth, to clarify the seat that transforms according to the directions: it remains in the eastern quarter.
Ninth, to clarify the name of the seat: it is called the Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne.
Within this section, the meaning is divided into three parts:
First, the lotus signifies freedom from defilement; this is obtained as the retribution for one's practice.
Because the nature of the practice of the Dharma-body is undefiled by the world, it is able to cause the fruit of wisdom and principle to blossom forth with increasing clarity and purity.
It clarifies that cause and effect mutually support one another so as to bring them to full maturity.
It clarifies that the blooming lotuses serve as adornments for phenomena, possessing a quality worthy of contemplation.
By means of the flower of practicing this Dharma, one invokes this retribution, resulting in a lotus flower serving as a seat.

The two "treasuries" (pitakas) carry the meaning of "containing. They are called treasuries because they clarify how the Dharma-body, through its wisdom and principle, abides in the world and acts in accordance with circumstances to benefit sentient beings; as it universally contains the entire Dharma-realm and provides benefit to all through manifold merits, it is termed a "treasury."
The three "Lions" derive their names through the *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent designation).
This is because, by means of the body of great wisdom of the *dharmatā* which is without arising or ceasing, they dwell in the world for the benefit of beings, being fearless amidst birth and death.
Furthermore, by means of the light of correct wisdom, eloquence, and fearlessness, he is like a lion who possesses no fivefold fears.

When the assembly of the ten lights ascends and sits upon their seats, they take the *dharmadhātu* as the substance of the seat; this is because one must first accord with the substance of the *dharmadhātu* as an ordinary being, and only through the practice of faith and diligence does one finally achieve that faith.
This is the fruit-seat of all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
It clarifies that at the initial stage of faith, one must have sudden faith in the Buddha-fruit as the dharma to be practiced in one's own conduct; only then is faith truly established.
This section is further divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the breadth and narrowness of the seat; second, clarifying how the bodhisattvas sit upon it.

Regarding the first, the breadth and narrowness of the seat, as stated in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta": "That lion throne encompasses the entire dharmadhātu," and so forth, as clearly explained in the full text.
The general meaning is that because the essence of the mind-nature is neither dependent on concentration nor on distraction, it is taken as the substance of the seat.
Second, to clarify how the Bodhisattva sits: it is said that he sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
To unify the various conditions of the world into a single Dharma-realm is called *kṣepa* (binding).
To designate many conditions by means of a single dharma is called *ka*.
Furthermore, as for "sitting cross-legged" (*paryaṅka*), it refers to the characteristic of a dignified deportment that is tranquil and unmoving.

In this stage, ten *pāramitās* are subsumed within the primary *dāna-pāramitā*. Regarding the four lines of scripture beginning with "To the south," the meaning of this section is divided into ten parts: first, indicating the direction of the Buddha-field; second, indicating the distance of the Buddha-field;

third, indicating the name and form of the world-system; fourth, indicating the name of the Buddha; fifth, indicating the names of the principal bodhisattvas; sixth, clarifying the number of the great assembly; seventh, clarifying that the assembly has arrived and paid homage; eighth, clarifying the transformation seats according to their respective directions; ninth, clarifying the names of the seats; and tenth, clarifying that the great assembly ascends the seats and sits.

Regarding the first movement toward the direction of a buddha-field: as stated in the Sūtra within the section on the symbolism of the south, "south" signifies correctness, the sun, illumination, emptiness, and the voidness at the center of the hexagram Li. This clarifies that through the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one advances in practice, realizes the emptiness of all phenomena, and gradually increases in illumination.

Therefore, Mañjuśrī, the Mother of Awakening, initiated the instruction that leads to faith; immediately following this, at the eastern gate of the city of Bodh Gaya, Sudhana entered the Path for further cultivation and traveled south to visit various spiritual friends, symbolizing that the South represents the Correct, the Sun, Illumination, and the Principle of Emptiness.
Therefore, when paying homage to the Buddha, one always says "Namo," which clarifies that the south is empty and void.
However, the principle of emptiness and voidness is the meaning of the south; it is the south in all places.
Yet, the initial arising of faith is the meaning of the east in all places.
Therefore, regarding the Four Noble Truths, East and West are assigned to Suffering and its Accumulation, while South and North are assigned to Cessation and the Path.

Yet, dharmas have no fixed location; they are established to transform ignorant beings and cause them to give rise to understanding and faith, for otherwise the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) would be difficult to clarify.

As stated in the subsequent passage of this chapter: "When the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva, he attained accomplishment through various discourses, various modes of speech, and even various inclinations and understandings."
"Furthermore, he causes sentient beings to know and see in this way, and for their sake he preaches the Dharma," as fully explained in the sutra.
Moreover, "namas" signifies correct compliance; because one correctly complies with the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is called *namas*.
"Such-and-such Buddha" refers to one who has realized the wisdom of emptiness and non-existence; therefore, one pays homage by saying "Namo Such-and-such Buddha.
Second, regarding the enumeration of the distance of the buddha-fields, it is said to be "the number of atoms in ten buddha-fields," the meaning of which is as explained previously.
Beyond the clouds of delusion, one enters the Cloud of Dharma.

Regarding the third mention of the world’s name and form: its name is "Sublime Form" (*Miaose*). This constitutes the second stage of faith, because the sublime qualities gradually increase and it surpasses the preceding stage of faith.
This is because one realizes that phenomena are void and non-existent, and thus phenomena themselves are inherently wondrous.

Fourth, regarding the invocation of the Buddha’s name as "Unobstructed Wisdom," this clarifies that by advancing in practice through the essence of Immovable Wisdom, one's faith becomes increasingly clear and luminous, such that wisdom itself is unobstructed.
This collectively clarifies that the Buddha of the stage of faith is one's own mind; it is not another Buddha.
Because the Buddha-mind, the sentient-being mind, and one's own mind are, in total, a single mind, a single nature, a single dharma-realm, and a single wisdom, faith is first established.

Regarding the mention of the names of the foremost bodhisattvas as five: Mañjuśrī is the "Head of Awakening" because he possesses wondrous wisdom and is able to correctly discern the right from the wrong through his own awakening, and because he awakens others to the dharmas he himself has awakened to.
What phenomena does the bodhisattva of this stage awaken to?
Within this stage, his awakening is threefold:
first, he awakens to the fact that the fundamental nature of his own body and mind is the dharmadhātu, pure and undefiled, just as was the case with the Golden World mentioned previously.
Second, awakening to the nature of one’s own mind and mental discriminations as fundamentally lacking subject and object, which is primordially the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom;
third, awakening to the sublime wisdom of one’s own mind that skillfully discriminates between the correct and the erroneous, which is Mañjuśrī.
At the inception of the mind of faith, one awakens to these three dharmas; this is called "Awakening Chief" (Bodhi-mukha).
This clarifies that within the mind of faith, the practice of skillful awakening is named the Bodhisattva Awakening Chief.
In all cases, one must personally realize that this is the dharma-gate one practices for oneself; only then does faith become established.
If faith exists through another while one lacks it within oneself, it cannot be called true faith.
Sixth, regarding the number of the great assembly: it consists of as many beings as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields; the meaning is as explained in the initial commentary.
Seventh, regarding the great assembly’s arrival and their paying of respects: this may be understood as before.
Eighth, regarding the clarification of the seats according to the directions, this may be understood as previously explained.

Ninth, regarding the clarification of the names of the seats: this is for the purpose of clarifying the accomplishment of entering faith, so that one may attain fearlessness amidst birth and death, and because they are obtained through mastery over the primary [elements].
The remaining meanings are as explained previously.
Regarding the tenth point, that the great assembly ascends the seat and sits, the meaning is interpreted as before.
In this stage, the Perfection of Morality (*śīla-pāramitā*) is the primary leader, while the other nine serve as its companions.
New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
Volume Fourteen (Volume Fifteen) Compiled by the Elder Li Tongxuan (Li Tongxuan)
The third section, from "To the west, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are atoms" onwards, consists of approximately four lines of scripture;
herein, ten points are as previously described.
First, regarding the direction of the buddha-field mentioned: it is the western direction.
Second, regarding the distance of the Buddha-fields, the meaning is as explained in the initial commentary.

Third, regarding the naming and appearance of the world: it is named "Lotus Color" (*padmavarṇa*). This is to clarify that within the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), progressive cultivation becomes increasingly superior; the mind is like the color of a lotus because, within the stage of the ten levels of faith, through progressive cultivation, the mind is free from defilement, just like a lotus flower.
