The ten thousand kinds of canopies signify the meaning of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), for they are obtained as the fruit of nurturing all sentient beings with a mind of great compassion.

The ten thousand silken brocades signify the fruit that is clear and manifest to behold: the inexhaustible differentiation of practices within a single practice, and the possession of differentiated teachings within a single utterance.

The "ten thousand pearl necklaces" signify that the fruit attained through the ceaseless transformation and benefit of sentient beings is the adornment of the realm of wisdom by means of the ten thousand practices (daśasāhasra-caryā) pervading everywhere;
it refers to the fact that within every single atom there exists the inexhaustible body of Samantabhadra.
The ten thousand garments signify the fruit of nurturing and protecting all sentient beings through gentleness and virtuous patience amidst the ocean of all birth and death.
The ten thousand devaputras clarify those who are able to practice the ten thousand deeds.
The ten thousand Brahma kings signify mastery in wisdom regarding the practice of conduct.
The ten thousand radiating lights signify the illumination of wisdom, which is able to shatter the long night of delusion for oneself and others, bringing forth great clarity.

All of the above serves to illustrate the fruit, virtue, and function of this stage as a means of adornment, so that bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds and entered this stage may recognize the fruit and practice the cause without any doubt or confusion.

From the passage beginning with "Bowing his body" onwards, it clarifies that Śakra, King of Devas, paid homage to the Tathāgata and invited the Buddha into his palace, thereby demonstrating his practice of humility.
That the Tathāgata accepted the invitation clarifies his entry into the dwelling of faith; this may be understood according to the text.

The passage clarifies that Śakra Devendra attained the power of recollecting past lives and planted roots of goodness under past Buddhas when he spoke these verses in praise of the Buddha; it further clarifies that by the power of samādhi, he personally perceived that the essential nature of his own body and mind was identical to the wisdom and roots of goodness of the Buddhas of the past and present.
The ten Buddhas listed below represent the functional application of their respective positions throughout both past and present.
Within these verses, there are twenty lines of verse, with two lines constituting a single stanza.
The first two verses praise Kāśyapa Buddha.
His full name is Kāśyapa, which here is translated as "Drinking Light" (Yìnguāng); this is his clan name.
It is also because his bodily radiance was so extraordinary that it could "drink up" the light of the sons of gods, the sun, the moon, and so forth, causing them all to disappear.
The next two lines praise Kanakamuni Buddha—properly called Kaṇakamuni. "Kana" means gold; "muni" means Buddha.
He was named after his golden complexion.
Next, two lines praise Kālakodra; in full, he is called Kālakodravu Buddha, which means "one who has severed what ought to be severed."
The next two lines praise Viśvabhū Buddha, which is translated here as "Pervasive Sovereignty over All.
The following two lines praise Śikhin Buddha; his name is correctly rendered as Śikhiṇa, which means "Wearing a Topknot" or "Having Hair."
The next two lines praise Vipaśyin Buddha, which is translated here as "Pure Vision," or alternatively "Supreme Vision," or "Diverse Vision.
The following two lines praise Puṣya Buddha, who is correctly called *Puṣya* (勁沙), and is translated here as "Flourishing" (增盛).
The next two lines praise the Buddha Tiṣya—properly called *Tiṣya*, which here means "one who teaches the Dharma to deliver beings.
The following two lines praise the Buddha Padmottara—properly called *Padmottara*, which here means "red lotus flower."
The next two lines praise the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.
The first three Buddhas are those of this present Bhadrakalpa, while the latter seven Buddhas are those of a previous kalpa.

This clarifies that one has newly entered the gate of the ten abodes; here, the laws of past and present converge because the Dharma of ancient Buddhas and the Dharma of present Buddhas are not different, and those who enter this stage meet in unity without distinction.
"Speaking of 'Auspicious' refers to praising this mountain peak as a place of merit and goodness.

'Clarifying Advancement' means that through the power of samādhi, one's body and mind are as immovable as the King of Mountains, thereby uniting with the wisdom of all Buddhas of the past and present."
The ninth section, beginning with "In this world, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven," consists of four lines of sūtra, the meaning of which is divided into four parts:

first, praising the Buddha’s virtues by citing this world; second, stating generally that it is the same throughout the ten directions; third, from "At that time" onwards, clarifying how the Tathāgata entered the hall and ascended the seat to sit.
The fourth clarifies that the palace suddenly became vast and expansive, universally accommodating the dwellings of all the devas.

This clarifies that, in accordance with the Tathāgata’s virtue of being without self or other, it naturally occurs so as to allow the great assembly to see it; thereby, it clarifies that the great assembly is enabled to enter the same stage.
This concludes the explanation of the "Chapter on Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru.

It is explained in general terms that when one correctly enters meditative concentration through the power of samādhi, body and mind become utterly serene and accord with the nature of the Dharma-realm; being without interior or exterior, its radiance is bright and penetrating. This is the meaning of "suddenly becoming vast and expansive," and it is also the meaning of the "Lion Throne of the Universal Radiant Treasury."
The manifestation of wisdom is the meaning of the Buddha’s coming.
One should practice by realizing the principle in each instance in this manner; one must not merely follow names.
Chapter 14: Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru In order to explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to four sections:

First, an explanation of the chapter title; second, an explanation of the purpose for the chapter’s inclusion; third, a general summary of the meaning of these ten chapters on the Ten Abidings; and fourth, an exegesis of the meaning according to the text. Regarding the first, the explanation of the chapter title:

the ten bodhisattvas, beginning with Dharmamati, each describe the methods of practice appropriate to their own respective stages and advance accordingly; they then praise themselves in verse so that bodhisattvas at the final stage of faith may emulate them and thereby attain awakening and entry.

This chapter is titled "The Chapter on Verses of Praise. It clarifies that all Buddhas of the past and present assemble together in this Hall of Wisdom and Palace of Compassion; for one assembles with the Buddhas of the past and present because one's own person is a Buddha of the future, and thus accords with the path of the ancient Buddhas.
Second, regarding the purpose for the arrival of this chapter: it clarifies that previously [the Buddha] first ascended Mount Sumeru, where Śakra praised the Buddha with verses.

This chapter elucidates the Bodhisattvas of each stage within the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi), using verses to praise the Dharma-gates of their respective stages, so that those with faith may enter these stages; therefore, this chapter must appear.
First, there is praise for the Buddhas of the past; next, there is praise for the Buddhas of the present.
As for the Buddhas of the future, they are those who shall enter this very stage; therefore, the sutra does not mention them.
The ten Buddhas are the Buddhas of the past; Vairocana is the Buddha of the present; and those who have begun their practice and entered the stages are the Buddhas of the future.

To unify the intent of these ten chapters and six sections of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the first is the "Chapter on Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru," which clearly explains the ultimate ascent and progress.

2. The "Chapter on Verses of Praise at the Summit of Mount Sumeru" clarifies the dharmas of praise through verse appropriate to this stage and exhorts the principle of cultivation for ascending progress.
3. The "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" clarifies the practices to be performed while in these stages.
4. The "Chapter on Holy Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-varga*) elucidates the nature of signless ethical discipline (*śīla*) maintained throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
5. The "Chapter on the Merit of Arousing the Resolve" (*Cittotpāda-puṇya-varga*) elucidates the magnitude of the merit obtained by arousing the resolve within the ten stages.

The sixth is the "Chapter on Clarifying the Dharmas" (Mingfa pin), which clarifies the dharmas pertaining to the current stage and the causes for ascending toward the ten practices (*daśapratipatti*).
These six chapters clarify the causes and fruits of cultivation pertaining to the current stage, as well as the causes for advancing toward the ten practices.
Within the section explaining the meaning according to the text, there are further two divisions:
first, a general outline of the intent of this chapter; second, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning.
Regarding the general outline of the intent of this chapter, the meaning is divided into eleven sections.

From "At that time, by the Buddha's supernatural power" onwards, for nineteen and a half lines of scripture, it clarifies the section on how the Buddha, through his supernatural power, caused the assembly to gather.

Second, from "The Bodhisattva Dharmamati, receiving the majestic power, spoke these verses" onwards, there are ten lines of verse; these clarify the section in which the Bodhisattva Dharmamati praises the Buddha’s emission of light and the gathering of the assembly.
3. From "At that time" onwards, it clarifies how Sarvajñā (All-Wisdom) receives the majestic power [of the Buddha] to recite ten verses of practice, praising the signless dharma as the reality.

4. From "At that time" onwards, it clarifies how Vijñāna (Supreme Wisdom) Bodhisattva recites ten verses of practice, praising how ordinary beings are deluded regarding the true nature of the five aggregates, and that this is only understood through the teaching of others.
5. At that time, Guṇamati spoke ten verses to clarify how one falsely grasps at the true nature of all phenomena.
6. At that time, Vīramati spoke ten verses to praise the fact that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is invisible, and that false views lead to delusion regarding the truth.

7. At that time, the Bodhisattva Good Wisdom (Suvijñāna) spoke ten verses of practice, praising how there are no sentient beings to be exhausted, and that phenomena transcend the dualistic views of existence and non-existence.
8. At that time, the Bodhisattva Wisdom (Jñāna) spoke ten verses of practice, praising how verbal expressions cannot reach the ultimate truth.
9. At that time, the Bodhisattva Real Wisdom (Tattvabuddhi) spoke ten verses of practice, extolling how all phenomena possess a nature that is neither joined nor dispersed.

10. At that time, the Bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom (Anuttarabuddhi) spoke ten verses of practice, extolling how the essence of the Dharma attained by the Buddha is non-discriminative and does not belong to names or numerical categories.
11. At that time, Resolute Wisdom (Dṛḍhamati) spoke ten verses of practice, praising the Buddha’s great compassion in appearing in the world for the benefit of beings.

Thus, the ten bodhisattvas above each spoke ten verses of practice, harmonizing and entering the methods of the stages, causing all mental and physical calculations to have no basis, departing from biased attachments, and abiding where the Buddhas abide.
Furthermore, from the beginning of the Bodhisattvas’ Arrival section up to the nineteenth line and a half, the text is further divided into seven sections:
first, from the five lines and a half of scripture beginning with "At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power," the arrival of the bodhisattvas is elucidated.
2. The three and a half lines of sūtra beginning with "the lands from which they have come" clarify the names of the worlds of these bodhisattvas.
3. The three lines of sūtra beginning with "each having practiced the pure brahma-faring in the presence of a Buddha" clarify the Buddhas whom they originally served.

The fourth is the two lines of sutra beginning with "All the bodhisattvas having arrived at the Buddha’s place," which clarifies that after the bodhisattvas have arrived, they transform their seats and sit down.
The fifth is the two lines of sutra beginning with "In this world-system," which clarifies that the same applies to the bodhisattvas in all the world-systems of the ten directions.
Six: From "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, for two lines and a half of the sūtra, light is emitted from the tips of the Buddha's toes, universally illuminating all the palaces of Śakra.
In the stage of the Ten Faiths, light is emitted from below the soles of the feet; in these Ten Abidings, light is emitted from the tips of the toes, signifying the advancement of the stage.

In the Ten Practices, it is from the insteps; in the Ten Dedications, from above the knees; and in the Ten Grounds, light is emitted from the tuft of hair between the eyebrows, signifying the ascent through the stages of the Dharma.

Alternatively, the light emitted from between the eyebrows during the first assembly in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" (Prakṛtyabhisaṃbodhanaparivarta) is the light that brings about faith through the fruition and leads one into the stages (*bhūmi*).

As for the light from the toes, it clarifies the entry into the palace of body, mind, and wisdom within this stage (*vihāra*); because it signifies the initial entry into the state of a noble one (*ārya*), it refers to the emission of light from the tips of the toes.
7. From the line beginning with "At that time" onwards, one section of the sutra clarifies how the Bodhisattva Dharmamati speaks in verse to praise the Buddha.
The remaining meanings may be understood according to the text; by following the structure of the text, their significance will be fully grasped.

Just as when the Bodhisattvas first gathered together, sharing a common world-name and their respective original Buddhas, it was only by assembling and correlating their practices and the causes and conditions of their Dharma-gates that one could begin to perceive the full significance of their situation.
From the Bodhisattva Dharmamati: this refers to one who practices within this stage, so named in accordance with the Tathāgata’s wisdom they have attained.
The world is named Indrarāja-puṣpa; this refers to the Dharma that is practiced.
The Buddha Viśeṣacandra is the fruit cultivated through the Dharma within the stage of the first arousal of the bodhicitta.
As for "Indra," this is translated as "Capable Lord."
"Flower" (puṣpa) signifies the meaning of blossoming and the realization of fruition.
This is because a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind within these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is able to manifest the attainment of Buddhahood throughout all worlds in the ten directions.

The world-system is named "Capable Leader" (*Īśvara*), because it is able to manifest as a leader for all sentient beings, and because its flowers of conduct can cause the fruits of wisdom in oneself and others to blossom.

The Sūtra states: "Each is accompanied by as many Bodhisattvas named Dharmamati as there are atoms in a Buddha-field. This clarifies that through wisdom, understanding, and practice, one realizes and fully knows this realm, because one has attained the realization that all things within one's own mind are likewise so.
When one is deluded, all are deluded; when one awakens, all awaken.
This clarifies that it is solely those who are to be delivered who, through their own resolution of delusion, possess pervasive wisdom.
As for the phrase "coming from worlds outside the lands as numerous as the atoms of a hundred buddha-fields," "outside the lands" refers to delusion, while "coming" refers to awakening.
However, because the obscurations of deluded ignorance are vast and numerous, they are compared to the number of dust motes in a world;
because the practices of awakening and understanding are likewise vast and numerous, they are also compared to the dust motes of a world.
Wisdom and ignorance are similar, differing only in their states of delusion and awakening.
Therefore, this sutra states later on: "There is a scripture equal in size to a trichiliocosm contained within the body of a minute sentient being."
This is its meaning. Regarding the Buddha’s title "Extraordinary Moon" (*Viśeṣacandra*): "extraordinary" (*viśeṣa*) means superior;

"special" (*viśiṣṭa*) means marvelous; and "moon" (*candra*) means coolness. This signifies that when a Bodhisattva enters this stage and dwells in the house of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the scorching heat of beginningless ignorance and afflictions, as well as the blazing fires of the evil realms, are all extinguished at once. Only the Tathāgata’s wisdom remains, radiant and cool like the moon.

It clarifies that at this stage, the Bodhisattva first enters the True [Dharma], establishing for themselves the name of their own Buddhahood by virtue of being able to destroy the feverish afflictions of delusion.

Subsequently, through the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), they advance and ascend according to their respective stages; thus, the names of the Bodhisattvas, the Buddhas, and the worlds each differ according to their respective positions.

Among the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), the names of the Buddha-fruit (*buddhatva*) are all uniformly designated as "Eye" (*cakṣus*); this name is established because it represents the faculty of knowing the capacities of sentient beings and benefiting them.

Among the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the names of the Buddha-fruit are all uniformly designated as "Sublime" (*praṇīta*); this is because its sublime function of benefiting sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is sovereign and autonomous.
It is only upon reaching this stage that the meaning becomes clear.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "The ten bodhisattvas, such as Dharmamati and others who have come from the ten directions, each purify their brahmacarya in the presence of the Buddha," this clarifies that each is able to purify afflictions through the wisdom of the dharma-body within their own mind; being as cool as the moon in this state is what is meant by "each purifying their brahmacarya in the presence of the Buddha."
"Brahma" means purity; it indicates that for Bodhisattvas at this stage, sublime wisdom manifests before them because the essence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inherently pure.
It refers to the functioning of the wisdom of *dharmatā*, which operates according to the Dharma, because its essence is without arising or ceasing.
This is because one clarifies that, in its essence, there is no place for arising or ceasing, thereby designating the Buddha-fruit within one's own mind.

Therefore, any person who has resolved to attain enlightenment should, through this samādhi of non-action, non-conceptualization, and natural spontaneity as a skillful means, manifest for themselves the gate of the Buddha’s wisdom of non-substantiality within their own mind. Thus, they will remain undefiled by afflictions and shall be named the Extraordinary Moon Buddha.

Regarding the statement that "in each direction from which [the bodhisattvas] came, he manifested a lion throne of the Vairocana-treasury": this Bodhisattva Dharma-wisdom occupies the position of the East. He represents the beginning of entering the stages and the first breaking of darkness; just as the sun first rises in the east and is able to dispel the gloom, so too does he.

Because the light of wisdom can shatter the delusive darkness of oneself and others throughout the long night since beginningless time, the fruit of Buddhahood is named the Extraordinary Moon Buddha (*Viśiṣṭacandra*).
Because he has already served as a teacher of gods and humans from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, this world is named Sovereign Flower (*Puṣpādhipati*).
The seat produced through transformation, named the Vairocana-garbha Lion Throne, is the seat of the Buddha-fruit. To clarify: *Vairo* means light, and *cana* means pervasive.

It signifies sitting pervasively upon all beginningless ignorance and afflictions, thereby manifesting as the treasury of the great wisdom-light of all things, universally illuminating all states of mind and objects, and transforming them into the gate of sovereign liberation within the Dharma-realm.
"Siṃha" (Lion) refers to the attainment of fearlessness.
The above is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
As for "sitting in the full lotus posture" (*paryaṅka-bandha*), it is called sitting in the full lotus posture because one brings together delusive thoughts to constitute true wisdom.

Within these ten stages of the *daśabhūmi*, the ten bodhisattvas correspond to Sudhana’s own progression from his initial entry into faith atop Mount Supratiṣṭhita to his reception of the Dharma-gates from the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī down to the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, who resembles [the Buddha],
clarified the initial arousal of the mind of faith by means of this scripture,
perfectly harmonizing its teachings and practices so that later students may easily understand them.
However, he speaks only of the teaching and does not dwell upon the person who can practice it, because such a person is difficult to understand.

For this reason, in the first assembly, he brings forth the Buddha-fruit and the divine beings to demonstrate the entry into the Dharma and to encourage its cultivation, thereby clarifying that each and every thing is identical to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
In the second assembly, he exhorted them to give rise to faith and understanding, establishing the gateway of faith through the Buddha Immovable Wisdom (*Acalamati*).

Next, he taught the instructions for entering the stages and advancing in practice, namely the Dharma-gates of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the ten transferences (*daśapariṇāmana*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*).

At the conclusion of the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," the youth Sudhana is cited as one who can practice the five stages of the path; this is done so that the teachings and practices may be fully manifested, making them easy to understand.
If it were not thus, although one might encounter the teachings, one would remain deluded regarding their practice.

Therefore, within this single section of the sutra, the causes and effects, as well as the principles and wisdom, and the teachings and practices for practitioners, are each fully elucidated, so that those who cultivate the Way may emulate them without error.

This initial mind of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), which enters the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), serves as the cause for the subsequent ten practices (*daśacaryā*), ten transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*), ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), and the eleventh ground (*ekādaśabhūmi*), which constitute the fruit of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Just as a person who is one hundred years old is considered the eldest because they were born first,
so too when a man fathers ten sons, the one born first is considered the eldest.

New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary, Volume Seventeen, composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan. Second:
The Bodhisattva’s name is Sarvajñāna; the world’s name is Padmapuspa; the Buddha’s title is [as follows].
Regarding the "Inexhaustible Moon," within this context, the meaning is divided into five parts:

first, an explanation of the name of the Bodhisattva; second, an explanation of the name of the world; third, an explanation of the title for advancing toward the fruit of Buddhahood according to the stages; fourth, an explanation of the substance of his seat; and fifth, the determination of the direction from which he has come.

First, regarding the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva": he is called "One of Universal Wisdom" because, throughout his progressive cultivation according to the stages, he realizes that all phenomena are without substance or intrinsic nature, and thus is free from deluded attachment.

This corresponds to the second stage, the Dwelling of the Ground of Refinement (*viśuddhabhūmi*). Within the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), there are ten perfections; for the essence of ethical discipline consists in the fact that all phenomena are without substance or intrinsic nature, and are neither defiled nor pure.
Regarding these ten stages of abiding (*bhūmi*), the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" constitutes their essential body of precepts (*śīla-ātman*).
Second, as for the explanation of the name of the world: the reason this world is named *padma* is that it means "red lotus flower" in this language [Chinese].

To manifest that the characteristics of the precepts are untainted, shining brilliantly while abiding in the world, fully blossoming and adorned, and yielding fruit through the myriad practices—this is the meaning of what may be observed.

Regarding the third explanation, which concerns the titles for advancing toward the Buddha-fruit according to each stage: the Buddha’s title is "Inexhaustible Moon," and the Bodhisattva’s name is "All-Wisdom"; the Buddha-fruit is again titled "Inexhaustible Moon" to clarify that cause and effect are similar.

This clarifies that "all-encompassing wisdom" refers to the person who attains the wisdom of all Buddhas through practice; "the world" refers to the fruit of Buddhahood which is the dharma being cultivated; and this is the fruit obtained within the stage of "Purifying the Ground," as it clarifies the ability to cool all afflictions.
The substance of the four seats has already been explained as before.
Fifth, regarding the determination of the direction from which they come: these are the assembly from the south.

This serves to signify that the south is the position of *Li* (the Trigram Li), which signifies emptiness and non-existence, the meaning of literary composition, and the meaning of brilliant crimson radiance. It is like the sun shining directly south, its face illuminating all phenomena with perfect clarity; for this reason, the Bodhisattvas are named "All-Wisdom" (*Sarvajñā*).
The world is named Red Lotus, and the Buddha’s name is Infinite Moon.

This refers to when the youth Sudhana saw the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha and heard the Buddha preach the *Puyan-jing* (Universal Eye Sūtra); by reflecting upon its meaning, he will naturally understand it clearly for himself.
The third section, on the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa, is divided into four parts:

first, clarifying the name of the bodhisattva; second, clarifying the land in which he resides; third, clarifying the title of the Buddha-fruit according to his stage; and fourth, clarifying the direction from which he has come.

First, regarding the explanation of the Bodhisattva’s name: he is named "Supreme Wisdom" (*Jñānavatī*) because his cultivation and progress according to the stages become increasingly clear and pure; yet he does not shift a single dharma, for he excels the preceding stages.

Second, regarding the explanation of the world's name: it is called the "World of Precious Flowers" because, through the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), one attains the wisdom of all Buddhas and is able to practice the conduct of patience by means of the essence of the Path.
"Flower" refers to practice; it clarifies that one adorns the Dharma-body of wisdom through the practice of patience (*kṣānti*).

The three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) are the designation for the fruit of Buddhahood. As for why the Buddha’s name is "Immovable Moon," it is because he has realized the principle and perfected his practice; having attained mastery over the mind and its objects, he is incapable of being moved, thereby clarifying his capacity for endurance.
The moon signifies the meaning of coolness.

Regarding the four directions from which [the Buddhas] come: these are the assembly of the West; for the West is associated with autumn, with killing, and with the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), while the position of compassion is held in the center.

As in the *Daśabhūmika-vyākhyāna* (Ten Stages of Dedication), when Sudhana beheld Avalokiteśvara to the west of Mount Vajra, it was to clarify that the position of the "Killing" (Kṣaya) station represents a place of manifold sufferings, wherein one cultivates loving-kindness and patience.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva is named Supreme Wisdom (Jñānavara), the world is named Jewel Flower (Ratnapuṣpa), and the Buddha is titled Immovable Moon (Acalacandra); these collectively clarify the superior power and function of attaining the Dharma and achieving patience (kṣānti).

This is the meaning of the Jewel Flower; this is the practice of dwelling in the remedial dharmas; this is how Sudhana, upon seeing the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita, attained the dharma-gate of non-obstruction through his ability to endure.
The fourth bodhisattva is named Guṇamati. Within this section, it is divided into four parts:
first, clarifying the name of the bodhisattva; second, clarifying the name of the world; third, clarifying the title of the Buddha-fruit; and fourth, clarifying the direction from which he has come.
First, to clarify the name of the Bodhisattva: why is he named Guṇamati (Virtuous Wisdom)?

Because in this stage he cultivates the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), zealously practicing for the benefit of others and extensively aiding sentient beings, he acquires manifold merits; it is on account of these that his name is established.
Second, to clarify the name of the world: it is named *Utpala*, which in this language means "blue lotus"; among all colored lotuses, this flower is the most excellent.
Because diligence is the most supreme among all practices, and because this flower serves as the dharma-body of their abode, all myriad practices take this as their merit.

Regarding the title of the Buddha-fruit as "Wind and Moon": it is so named because the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) is free from pride and indolence; thus, one attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment with a swiftness like the wind.

Furthermore, it clarifies that diligent contemplation and observation of concentration and wisdom are like the wind; they can eliminate the defilements and impurities of ignorance, blowing away both fragrance and stench, for just as the wind is able to purify.
Regarding the direction from which the Four Illuminations originate, it is the assembly of the North.
The North corresponds to the position of *kan* (the trigram for water), which signifies blackness, ignorance, and the meaning of worldly peril and banditry.
Furthermore, occupying the positions of teacher and sovereign,
for this very reason, one should diligently cultivate beneficial practices through the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), shatter delusion, depart from darkness, and swiftly attain Buddhahood.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva is named Guṇamati; the world is named Blue Lotus; and the Buddha’s title is Vāyu-candra, because wind can purify all defilements.
This concludes the section on the "Abiding in Noble Birth" (*jātapravara-vihāra*), presented here as an antidote through the Dharma-gate.

This corresponds to the teaching of the Dharma-gate of the "Wheel of Syllables" (*akṣara-cakra*) by the fourth spiritual friend, the Elder Megha, to Sudhana; it is intended to bring those who are ignorant and darkened to an understanding of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and cause them to attain supramundane bliss.
The fifth bodhisattva is named Vīramati (Exerted Wisdom). Regarding this meaning, four points are as previously stated.

First, as for why he is named Vīramati: it clarifies that this stage is the dwelling of perfected skillful means (*upāya*). Because he manifests profound wisdom by diligently practicing the gateways of skillful means and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he is established with this name.

Because a single practice contains immeasurable practices, the name "diligence" arises within the state of meditative concentration, and the name "merit" arises above diligence; this clarifies that while various practices are employed, a single practice encompasses immeasurable practices.

Regarding the two worlds named Vajrapuṣpa: they take the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as the essence of dhyāna, giving rise to sublime wisdom that discriminates between the correct and the erroneous.
Because there is nothing it cannot shatter, this is the meaning of "vajra."
"Flower" refers to practice (*caryā*), because it possesses the wondrous function of discernment through the illumination of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*).
The three fruits of Buddhahood are named "water-moon" because the essence of concentration can purify, can cool, and can manifest myriad images, just like water.
Regarding the direction from which the Four Clarities originate, it is the assembly of the Northeast.

The Northeast is the position of Gen; it represents mountains, stones, gate-towers, the ignorant, the initial illumination, the lofty and manifest, tranquility, and cessation. This is because the essence of clarity and concentration pervades all positions and practices of cultivation and progress, serving as the fundamental basis for the beginning and end of advancing in practice—enlightening the uninitiated, illuminating the mind, cooling the fever of delusion, and progressing through the entirety of the path.
Because it represents Mount Gen (艮), the beginning of the year and the end of the year—the source and the culmination—it signifies the initial illumination and cessation.

The Bodhisattva is named *Vīryamati* (Wisdom of Diligence), the world is named *Vajrapuṣpa* (Diamond Flower), and the Buddha’s title is *Jalam-candra* (Water Moon). This is the fifth spiritual friend of Sudhana, the householder Vimokṣa, who presides over the gate of dhyāna. Within his body, he manifests ten buddha-fields; the dust-mote number of buddha-lands in their entirety is contained within his body, and the dust-mote number of buddha-lands from each of the ten directions is likewise entirely contained within his body, illustrating that the essence and function of dhyāna are all-pervasive.
Regarding the sixth stage, the Bodhisattva of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī*), the four meanings are as previously explained.

First, to clarify the name of the Bodhisattva: because this "Abiding in the Right Mind" (*samyaktva-nyāma*) cultivates the gateway of wisdom through the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Bodhisattva is named "Excellent Wisdom."

Regarding the second, the World of Sublime Fragrance and Flowers: this clarifies that the fragrance and flowers of the wisdom of sublime function cause the fruits of Buddhahood for oneself and others to blossom; it is because the teaching spoken through wisdom is the meaning of "fragrance and flowers."
The third Buddha is named Moon of Liberation (*Vimukticandra*), which clarifies that through the discernment of wondrous wisdom, both mind and objects are liberated.
The fourth clarifies the direction from which [the assembly] has come; these are the multitude from the southeast.

The southeast is the position of Xun; Xun represents wind and instruction, as well as speech. This position symbolizes the use of wisdom to skillfully expound the sublime Dharma in order to teach and transform sentient beings so that they may attain liberation. For this reason, the Bodhisattva is named Good Wisdom (Sudhī), the world is named Sublime Fragrant Flower (Gandhapuṣpa), and the Buddha is titled Moon of Liberation (Vimukticandra).

This corresponds to Sudhana’s sixth stage, that of the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, whose body and mind are tranquil and free from inhalation and exhalation, because his body emanates transformation-bodies that pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
This clarifies that his quiescent function is sovereign, and he has attained the supernormal power of cessation (*śamatha*).
The seventh bodhisattva is named Wisdom (*jñāna*). The four meanings are as previously explained.

First, to clarify why the bodhisattva is named Wisdom: this seventh stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-vihāra*) constitutes the gateway to the fulfillment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Only by perfecting wisdom can one skillfully enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) in accordance with worldly conventions; it is for this reason that he is so named.

As for the two worlds named *Rucirapuṣpa* (Pleasant Flower), because they possess wisdom, they remain within birth and death to benefit sentient beings by acting in concert with them across the six realms; knowing their faculties and gladdening the mundane, they cause all to enter the joy of the Dharma and attain freedom from sorrow; therefore, they are named *Rucirapuṣpa*.

Regarding the third Buddha, named Anuttara-candra (Moon of the Unsurpassed), it clarifies that among all practices, compassion is paramount; because it is the most supreme for the sake of saving and benefiting sentient beings, he is thus named Moon of the Unsurpassed.
As for the direction from which he came, it was the southwest; this is the position of *Kun*, representing faith and compliance, the mother, the earth, and the multitude.

It clarifies that the *pāramitā* of skillful means takes great compassion as its mother, entering the realm of birth and death of all sentient beings, sharing in their welfare to teach and transform them, so that they may enter the True Dharma through faith and compliance. For this reason, the Bodhisattva is named Wisdom, the world is named Joyful Flower, and the Buddha is titled Moon Without Superiority.

This is the seventh spiritual friend encountered by Sudhana, the laywoman (upāsikā) Śrīmati, which here means "Fulfiller of Vows," because she fulfills the vows of sentient beings through the practice of great compassion.
Just as in this region, the southwest represents the meaning of the mother, because it symbolizes the stage of compassion.
Regarding the eighth, the Bodhisattva *Tathatājñāna* (True Wisdom), the four meanings are as previously explained.

First, to clarify the name of the Bodhisattva: because in this eighth stage, *Kumārabhūmi* (Youthful Abode), one practices the *pāramitā* of vows and conduct (*praṇidhāna-caryā-pāramitā*), employing true wisdom to ensure that sentient beings do not fall into error.
Second, to clarify the name of the world: the world is named Aruṇapuṣpa, which in this language means "Red Lotus.
This flower is clearly distinguished as being both red and white; its red color constitutes this stage.

This is the eighth stage, the level of the increase of wisdom, which clarifies that one practices compassion according to vows through great wisdom, thereby bringing both wisdom and compassion to fulfillment; it is like a red lotus where the red and white are clearly distinguished, for white represents wisdom and red represents compassion.

The world is named "Red Lotus," signifying that while abiding in birth and death through conforming to true wisdom, one remains untainted—just as a lotus dwelling in water, with its red and white petals fully blossomed, is worthy of contemplation.

Regarding the Buddha of the third enlightenment named Star-Moon (Jyotir-maṇḍala-candra): it is because at this stage, true wisdom is luminously clear, knowing the capacities of sentient beings and discerning their distinctions.
The name of the Buddha is Star-Moon to signify that he clearly understands and distinguishes the diverse root-natures of sentient beings.

Regarding the direction from which the Four Clarities originate: it is the northwest, corresponding to Qian, to the Father, to firmness and hardness, to Heaven, and to the circle; it is pure white and capable of manifesting all colors, with all colors residing within it.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva is named True Wisdom, the world is named Red Lotus, and the Buddha is titled Star-Moon.

This collectively clarifies that his great wisdom is perfectly luminous and capable of manifesting the differences in the faculties and capacities of sentient beings, just as celestial images appear with distinct clarity.
This is the eighth spiritual friend encountered by Sudhana, the rishi Vimalacitra, which means "One Whose Utterance Is Terrifying.
He is so named because his true wisdom is perfectly luminous, and the words he utters are terrifying to all that is heterodox.

The "Sage" (ṛṣi) is used to signify that at this stage, wisdom increases and is free from defilement; furthermore, it signifies that the wisdom attained here is similar to [the wisdom of] false views.
Regarding the ninth stage, the Bodhisattva of Unsurpassed Wisdom, the four meanings are as previously explained.

First, regarding the name of the Bodhisattva: because this stage is the dwelling place of the Dharma Prince of the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) and because he skillfully expounds the Dharma, he is named "Supreme Wisdom" (*anuttara-prajñā*).

Second, to clarify the name of the world: the reason this world is named Nārada-puṣpa is as follows. "Nāra" here means "person," and "da" means "to hold. Because the fragrance of these flowers is pure and exquisite, people wear them as ornaments; this signifies that the Bodhisattvas of this stage, through their skillful preaching of the sublime Dharma, enable those who hear it to obtain the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body—namely, precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Since all people wear and carry these verses [of the Dharma] like ornaments, the world is named Nārada-puṣpa.

Regarding the Buddha of this third stage named Pure Moon: because this stage’s Bodhisattva skillfully expounds the Dharma, acts as a great Dharma teacher, and is able to purify the afflictions of both self and others, the Buddha is named Pure Moon.

Regarding the four directions from which [the assemblies] come: these are the multitudes from the lower direction; this clarifies that the lower direction consists of the vajra, water, and wind wheels, which are able to support the world.
In this stage, the Bodhisattva skillfully expounds the sublime Dharma and is able to uphold the worldly norms and rules, causing others to emulate and learn from them.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva is named Supreme Wisdom (Anuttara-prajñā), the world is named Naradapuṣpa, and the Buddha is titled Pure Moon (Vimalacandra).

In this stage, he is like Sudhana seeing the Brahmin Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa ascending the mountain of blades and entering the mass of fire; all those gods and humans who come to witness these acts attain the Way before departing.
This clarifies that the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom appears identical to the heterodox, thereby gathering those of various paths and causing them to enter right view.
Regarding the tenth, the Bodhisattva Firm Wisdom (*Dṛḍhamati*), the four meanings are as before.

First, to clarify why the Bodhisattva is named "Firm Wisdom" (Dṛḍhamati): because this stage is the Abiding of Consecration (Abhiṣeka-vihāra), wherein one practices the perfection of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā) and is able to firmly benefit all sentient beings; thus, it is by virtue of this that he receives his name.

As for the two worlds named "Flowers in Empty Space," they are so named because the sun of wisdom illuminates both the mundane and supramundane realms such that neither has any basis or abode; it is for this reason they are given this name.

As for why the Buddha is titled "The Moon of Clear Illumination" (Mingliao Yue) because he possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*): it is because at this stage his great wisdom is perfectly luminous, universally illuminating the world such that nothing remains unclear; it is for this reason that he is so named.
Regarding the four directions from which they come, these are the multitudes from the direction above.

"The direction above" refers to empty space, the sun, the moon, and the stars; it symbolizes that great wisdom has no dependence, for it does not rely on either emptiness or existence, clearly reflecting all phenomena just as the sun, moon, and stars do.
In this stage, the youth Sudhana beheld the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja, named the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
This daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja was one whose wisdom and compassion were perfected.

With the completion of these ten stages (*bhūmi*), one has already been born into the family of the Buddha; having integrated the ten dharmas of compassion and wisdom, this constitutes the perfection of the final stage.
Since one is first born into the family of the Buddha at the initial stage, cultivating wisdom and practicing compassion is precisely the compassionate conduct of the royal daughter.

Having perfected the cultivation of compassion through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), at the beginning of the eleventh stage, one employs the wisdom of compassionate action. This is the Buddha-mother Māyā; she who manifests all Buddhas through illusion is Great Wisdom, and she as the mother is Great Compassion. The full clarity of this expansive meaning will be understood from the text itself.
The following ten sections of verse can be understood according to the text itself.
First, the faults are explained based on the headings as previously categorized.

All the aforementioned names of Bodhisattvas, names of worlds, and ten fruits of Buddhahood are collectively titles for the causes and effects of progressive cultivation according to their respective stages within these Ten Abodes. These are established by symbolizing the Dharma according to various directions and by forming names through entry into the Dharma; they may be understood by correlating them with the above.
Chapter Fifteen: The Ten Abodes (Daśabhūmi). In preparing to explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to five sections:

first, an explanation of the title; second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; third, clarification of the chapter’s central theme; fourth, a comprehensive overview of the sequence for severing delusions; and fifth, an exegesis of the meaning following the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the chapter title: this chapter expounds ten types of dwelling-gates, and is therefore titled "The Chapter on the Ten Dwellings" (*Daśabhūmika*).

Second, regarding the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion: since the preceding chapter was a gateway of verse-praise and exhortation to practice, this chapter clarifies the actual presentation of the practice of the ten dwellings; for this reason, this chapter must follow.
Regarding the "Ten Abodes" (daśavihāra): one dwells within the great wisdom born of all Buddhas; because one enters these abodes and never again regresses, they are called "abodes.

As for the essential purport of the "Chapter on the Three Clarities" (trividyā), it clarifies that this chapter takes as its primary subject matter the ten types of abodes and the twenty types of progressive cultivation of cause and effect.
Furthermore, dwelling in that which the Buddhas dwell is taken as the primary teaching.
This clarifies that within each of these ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are two kinds of cause and effect, each corresponding to the specific stage in which they reside.
The first set of ten dharmas presented serves as the superior conditions for joyful progress;
the latter set of ten dharmas represents the fruits of internal cultivation and training to be maintained.
This is clearly elucidated in the full text.

Regarding the sequence for severing delusions through the four assemblies: in the first three stages—the Stage of Initial Resolve, the Stage of Cultivating the Ground, and the Stage of Practice—it is clarified that one universally cultivates the supramundane mind within these three stages to shatter the entanglements of all mundane afflictions.
Regarding the afflictions of the world, as in the verses of Sudhana, there are ten root afflictions and six secondary afflictions in total.

As for the ten root afflictions: first, desire; second, form; third, formlessness—these are the points of bondage that constitute the roots of the three realms; fourth, pride; fifth, the various destinies; sixth, craving; seventh, delusion; eighth, greed; ninth, anger; and tenth, the King of the Mind-māra—these are the ten.
Furthermore, there are six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) in total: first, guile (*śāṭhya*); second, deception (*māyā*); third, doubt (*vicikitsā*); fourth, stinginess (*mātsarya*);

fifth, envy (*īrṣyā*); and sixth, arrogance (*mada*). As the Verse of Sudhana says: "The three realms of existence are its city walls; pride is its ramparts; the various destinies are its gates; the waters of craving are its moats; it is shrouded in the darkness of ignorance; the fires of greed and hatred blaze within; Māra acts as its sovereign, and the deluded dwell therein."
Craving serves as their fetters, and flattery and deception as their bridles; with doubt obscuring their eyes, they enter upon various wrong paths.
Due to stinginess, envy, and arrogance, they fall into the three evil realms.
"This refers to the direction of the inner mind, not to the view of a self, the view of extremes, the grasping at views, the grasping at precepts and rituals, or false views.
When the inner mind achieves wisdom, all such views are naturally liberated."

Since the essence of the One Vehicle teaching consists solely in realizing that ignorance constitutes great wisdom and employing various views as sovereign mastery, the five [wrong] views are not discussed herein.
As in the stage of the ten faiths, in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-dharmottara-bodhisattva-sūtra*, there are eleven kinds of afflictions.

What are these eleven? First, greed; second, anger; third, delusion; fourth, pride; fifth, concealment; sixth, indignation; seventh, resentment; eighth, envy; ninth, stinginess; tenth, deception; and eleventh, guile.
As in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* regarding the five aggregates, the twelve links of dependent origination, and so forth;

the aforementioned afflictions are simultaneously and instantaneously resolved into fundamental wisdom through these three stages among the ten abodes: the Abode of Initial Resolve, the Abode of Cultivating the Ground, and the Abode of Practice.

This is just as when Sudhana, on the summit of Mount Meghaśrī, beheld the bhikṣu Meghadatta and attained the gate of the light of wisdom of all Buddhas; by means of this, he immediately eliminated all the aforementioned afflictive obstructions of the mundane world, because he had realized the light of the Buddha’s wisdom.

Just as when Sudhana was on Mount Supārśva, his eye of faith was clear and pure, the light of wisdom shone brightly, and he universally observed all realms free from every obstruction—this is the stage of the first production of the thought of enlightenment (prathamacittotpādavihāra).

In the second country, Sāgaradvāra, one beholds the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha; by removing the obstacle of the mind’s delusion regarding reality that gives rise to the twelve links of dependent origination, and thereby becoming free from such obstacles, one immediately sees a Buddha appear within the ocean, preaching the *Samantacakṣus Sūtra*.
Clearly seeing the twelvefold dependent origination of oneself and others, one realizes the great ocean of wisdom; this is the meaning of "Buddha," for both mind and objects are entirely the Sūtra.

Having clearly attained the Buddha-wisdom previously, one contemplates the formation of the twelvefold dependent origination to realize the great ocean of wisdom, because mind and objects are universally pervasive and sovereignly all-encompassing.

This is the Dwelling of the Ground of Purification (*bhūmi-parikarma-sthiti*), because by means of the twelvefold dependent origination, one purifies [the mind] so as to perfect the ground of Tathāgata-knowledge.

In the third country, Kūṭaśālmali, he saw the bhikṣu Susthita, who removed the obstacle of the lack of clarity and purity regarding the mind and its objects, and attained the bodhisattva liberation door of unimpeded understanding (*pratisaṃvid-vimokṣamukha*). He was able to see the faculties, karmic actions, and conduct of all sentient beings, as well as their deaths here and births there, perceiving them all with complete clarity.
This is the dwelling of practice.
Within these three types of dwellings, one clearly attains liberation from entanglements and mastery over the mind.
By means of the ten faiths, one gains self-confidence that all the conceptualizations of the triple world and ignorance are fundamentally the Immovable Wisdom Buddha.

Within the stage of the initial resolve, by the power of sovereign and decisive understanding, with the eye of faith purified and the light of wisdom shining brightly, one universally contemplates all objects, becomes free from all hindrances, and attains realization and entry into the initial mind of the ten stages.
By means of the skillful methods for establishing fifty sequential dharma-gates within the progressive cultivation according to the stages, all take Immovable Wisdom as their fundamental basis.

The above—namely, the Dwelling of Initial Resolve, the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground, and the Dwelling of Practice—clarify the excellence of the mind that has emerged from entanglement within the Ten Dwellings.
Therefore, Sudhana’s three spiritual friends were all bhikṣus; they clearly demonstrated liberation from the fetters to represent the modes of practice within these three stages of dwelling.

The fourth stage, the Abiding in Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*), clarifies the remedial methods for worldly conventions and the obstacle of lack of mastery amidst the bustle of birth and death, thereby bringing about mastery.

This is illustrated by Sudhana’s encounter with the elder Megha at a marketplace, where Megha preaches the *Akṣara-cakra-sūtra*; this signifies that although the marketplace of birth and death is tumultuous, it is eternally quiescent.
Each individual character is like a wheel, wherein the one and the many are perfected and mutually constitute one another's essence.
Furthermore, they are like the jewel-net of Śakra, wherein each element arises through mutual conditionality, reflecting and penetrating one another in infinite layers.

Within a single syllable there are inexhaustible words and phrases, which constitute the world’s bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes; they lead those who have not yet studied toward the establishment of the rules of teaching, and through the example of the layman Megha, they bring about the perfection of practice, so as to cause them to give rise to the supramundane mind.

Subsequently, one must clarify the nature of the mundane arising and ceasing of life and death through the conditions of tranquility and turmoil; that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; and the mutual accomplishment of the names, meanings, and principles of the world, as well as the languages of all sentient beings—such as the ancient Fuyi (Fuxi) and others.

The fifth is the stage of being fully endowed with skillful means (*upāya-saṃpanna-vihāra*). It serves as the antidote to the two views of self-identity regarding the ultimate and the conventional, thereby removing the obstacle that prevents the sphere of great wisdom from being sovereign.

For example, when Sudhana saw the elder Vimokṣa enter the samādhi called "The Universal Gathering of All Buddha-fields and Boundless Dhāraṇīs," he beheld oceans of Buddha-lands, as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, each appearing in the ten directions, all pure and adorned, entirely within the elder’s body.
This clarifies that the bodies of all sentient beings collectively contain boundless Buddha-fields, their essence and form being without obstruction.

This is to clarify that the phenomenal characteristics of both the ultimate and conventional truths are like light and shadows, mutually accommodating one another because they have neither center nor periphery;
it is intended to bring about the liberation of the nature of the sixty-two views and all limitless perspectives.
The sixth stage, the Abiding of Rectified Mind (*samyakcittavihāra*), counteracts the obstacle of wisdom being tranquil yet lacking mastery in its application.

This is illustrated by Sudhana’s encounter with the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, who was sitting cross-legged beside his walking path, free from inhalation and exhalation and devoid of distinct thoughts or perceptions.
From each part of their bodies, transformation bodies emerge like clouds, extensively covering all directions and appearing to all according to their needs.
This clarifies that stillness and function are unimpeded.
The above summarizes the convergence of the mundane and the supramundane, as both lead to liberation.
Following this, the subsequent four pāramitās involve entering the secular world to practice compassion, thereby bringing about mastery.

The seventh stage, the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avivartya-vihāra*), serves to remedy the obstacle of lacking mastery over the complete fulfillment of gathering sentient beings through the practice of great loving-kindness and great compassion; it does so by bringing that mastery to perfection.
This is illustrated by Sudhana’s encounter with the laywoman Śrīprabhā in the Garden of Universal Adornment, who said to him:
"I have eighty-four thousand nayutas of companions and followers who constantly dwell in this garden."

This clarifies that within the stage of great compassion, one practices the perfection of skillful means; being identical to the eighty-four thousand unspeakable afflictions of all sentient beings, one collectively performs deeds to teach, transform, benefit, and bring them joy.
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, all other sentient beings who dwell in this garden shall also universally attain the stage of non-retrogression.
This clarifies that those who are able to practice compassion and wisdom are all identical to this.

The eighth stage, the Abode of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*), serves as the antidote to the obstacle of impure wisdom regarding residual habits shared with the world while dwelling amidst entanglements; it causes such wisdom to become pure.
This is illustrated by Sudhana’s vision of the seer Vimalakīrti, which symbolizes the purity of great wisdom that remains unstained.

The fact that the laywoman Śūradattā and the dwelling place of the rishi share the same name and both are located at the seashore clarifies that this unity of compassion and wisdom is stained yet remains undefiled.

If one cultivates wisdom in accordance with compassion, yet there still remains a mind that is stained by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) toward objects, this is precisely the point where the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are unified as one.
If one practices compassion in accordance with wisdom without any defiled habituation, it is none other than the girl Maitrāyaṇī, daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja.
One should reflect upon this to perceive its meaning.
The ninth stage, the Dwelling of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputra-vihāra*), serves as the antidote to the obstacle of lacking mastery in teaching the Dharma, thereby bringing about such mastery.

This is illustrated by the case of Sudhana seeing the Brahmin Jvalanānta performing ascetic practices—climbing a mountain of swords and entering a mass of fire—wherein every god, nāga, spirit, human, and non-human who came to him did not fail to receive benefit.

The tenth stage, the Stage of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*), serves as the antidote to the obstacle of impurity regarding the lack of mastery over compassion and wisdom, thereby bringing about their purification.
This is illustrated, for example, by Sudhana’s encounters with the princess Siṃhadhvajā and the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.

Because the King possesses mastery over wisdom, the woman symbolizes following others through compassion and shared activity (*samānārthatā*) without the habituation of defilement; because his clear wisdom is perfected, he dwells in the world from the standpoint of compassion, which is precisely shared activity free from habitual tendencies.

The ten types of remedies mentioned above all arise within a single thought-moment on the mind at the initial moment of generating the bodhicitta; they occur within a single practice and a single instant, devoid of any temporal sequence or boundaries.
The ten methods for counteracting obstacles constitute a single mind and a single wisdom.

Within a single practice, there are ten inexhaustible dharma-gates, all of which take the Immovable Wisdom Buddha of one’s own mind as their essence; this is because within the performance of dharmic activities, these ten kinds of inexhaustible dharma-gates are fully present, such that identity and difference, unity and multiplicity, are sovereignly interpenetrating.
By means of these ten kinds of remedies, one simultaneously brings mastery over habitual tendencies.

This differs from the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, which—addressing sentient beings of inferior understanding—maintain that the nature of the three periods of time exists within the mundane world and teach that the fruit of Buddhahood lies beyond three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
By means of the seeds of discrimination within the fundamental ignorance of one's own mind, one becomes the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom.
Taking the essence and function of the Dharma-realm as the gateway for entering through faith and diligence.

From the stage of faith and the entry into the positions (*bhūmi*), through the progression up to the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh stage, one never departs from the Buddha of Fundamental Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*). Within a single moment, a single thought, a single dharma, and a single practice, there exist boundless, immeasurable, unspeakable, and ineffable Dharma-gates as numerous as the atoms within the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Why is this? It is because one enters through faith and progress from the Dharma-realm and the fundamental immovable wisdom; for the nature of phenomena is such.

It is like the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood in an instant, or Sudhana attaining the fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime. In the Dharma-realm, there is no intrinsic nature of birth, so "one lifetime" refers to a non-prolonged and non-abridged birth. This is because the essence of the Dharma-realm is devoid of the mental constructs of prolongation or abbreviation, length or shortness, and past, future, or present.
Those with faith should understand it thus:
attaining Buddhahood now is simultaneous with all Buddhas of the past and future attaining Buddhahood, because the essence of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* is without distinction of time.
Just as a single drop of water entering the great ocean becomes identical to the ocean, for there is no distinction between new and old water;
so too, one must transcend emotional attachments to see [the truth], for it is not known by the conscious mind.

As it is within the Three Vehicles, even Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage still undergo the segmented birth and death (*bhavāgra-cheda*) of the triple world; they cultivate the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) as an antidote to the obstacle of the icchantika’s lack of faith.

The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices (daśabhūmi-pratipatti) differentiate their cultivation of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasunyatā-darśana), practicing deeds that benefit both self and others to counteract the obstacle of the Śrāvaka’s self-interest.

The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Dedications (daśapariṇāmana) cultivate the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena, accomplishing the arousal of the power of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-praṇidhāna); they manifest forms within the six realms of existence to teach and transform sentient beings, thereby counteracting the obstacle of the Pratyekabuddha’s solitary liberation.

This clarifies that among the three vehicles, Bodhisattvas of the thirty minds counteract the three types of obstacles prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), eliminating only the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) but not yet the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*); it is the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages who sever these remaining habit-energies.
As with a Bodhisattva on the first stage (*bhūmi*), because they perceive the *tathatā* (suchness) of their own Buddha-nature, this is called the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
From the second stage through the seventh stage is the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), wherein one still practices with effortful application (*sābhisamskāra*).
From the eighth stage to the tenth stage is called the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), because one reaches the fruit of Buddhahood spontaneously without depending on further effort.
Furthermore, within the twelve stages of the three vehicles, there is the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*),
which refers to the ten stages of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*).
The second is the stage of conduct through understanding, which consists of the ten stages of dedication;
the third is the stage of joy, which is the first bhūmi;
and the fourth is the stage of superior ethical discipline, which is the second bhūmi.
The fifth is the dwelling of superior intention, which is the third stage;
the sixth is the dwelling of superior wisdom associated with the categories of phenomena, which is the fourth stage;
the seventh is the dwelling of superior wisdom associated with the truths, which is the fifth stage.
The eighth is the dwelling of superior wisdom associated with dependent origination; this is the sixth stage.
The ninth is the dwelling of signlessness with effort and development; this is the seventh stage.
The tenth is the dwelling of signlessness without effort or development; this is the eighth stage.
The eleventh is the Dwelling of Unimpeded Wisdom, which corresponds to the ninth stage;
the twelfth is the Supreme Bodhisattva Dwelling, which corresponds to the tenth stage.

Furthermore, within the context of the Three Vehicles, bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness prior to the bhūmis attain the Patience of Subjugation (*vinaya-kṣānti*), while those in the ten stages and the Buddha-stage attain the Patience of Quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*).

Furthermore, in light of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the Pure Land are all at the stage of "subduing patience" (*vinīyaka-kṣānti*); because they manifest the practice of the contemplation of emptiness, the ten proclivities (*daśa-anuśaya*) do not arise. However, because they do not recognize the afflictions of the "ground of ignorance" (*avidyā-āśraya*), they are said to be "unaware."
What is meant by "severing afflictions"?

It refers to merely suppressing their active manifestation so that they do not arise, thereby attaining the three kinds of mind-made bodies and undergoing the transformation-death outside the triple world.

In this way, although these bodhisattvas practice the six pāramitās and attain the six superknowledges (abhijñā), such that their merit and supernormal powers surpass those of humans and devas, because they have not yet cultivated the gateway to the Buddha-fruit dharma-realm, they remain outside this gate in the three carts, still within the thatched hut.

The śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the three vehicles differ in their virtues; although they are similar in name in that they have transcended the triple world and exercise the six supernatural powers, they differ in the fruits and retributions of the merit of the six pāramitās.
Thus, bodhisattvas of the three vehicles who possess the six supernormal powers and the like do not hear or believe in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

As this sūtra states: "Suppose there is a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable billions of nayutas of kalpas, cultivates the six pāramitās and attains the six supernormal powers; yet if they have still not heard this *Avataṃsaka* scripture, they are merely called a 'nominal bodhisattva' and are not a true bodhisattva."
Furthermore, even if one hears [the teaching] at that time, it does not enter [the mind], as is also the case in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Regarding the three kinds of "mind-made bodies" (*manomaya-kāya*) within the Three Vehicles: first, those of the first, second, and third stages are called the "mind-made body of delighting in the Dharma through meditative absorption" (*samāpatti-dharma-rati-manomaya-kāya*);
second, those of the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are called the "mind-made body of awakening to the self-nature of phenomena" (*dharma-svabhāva-avabodha-manomaya-kāya*).

Third, regarding the categories of the stages from the third to the tenth, there are those born spontaneously (*upapāduka*), those without effort (*anabhisamskāra*), and those with mental application (*manasikāra*).
If one were to cite them at length, they are already clearly elucidated within the teachings of the Three Vehicles themselves.
The remedy for such [delusions] regarding appointments is as follows.
In this teaching of the One Vehicle, there is altogether no pursuit of the three vehicles mentioned above.
Because fundamental ignorance-abiding-ground afflictions are themselves the immovable wisdom of all Buddhas, all sentient beings inherently possess it.
It is simply because the essence of wisdom has no inherent nature and no support, and thus cannot understand itself; it understands only by meeting with conditions (*pratyaya*).
What is meant by "meeting with conditions"?
There are three kinds of conditions:
First is the condition of suffering: it is only by encountering suffering that one can resolve to cultivate the mind.

Second is the condition of happiness: having long dwelt among humans and devas with clear inner wisdom, one realizes that worldly fruits of happiness are impermanent within the cycle of birth and death, and only then does one begin to seek the Truth.
Third, by beholding the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle, one seeks to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and seeks the Buddha’s seed-wisdom (*jñāna*).

By bringing these three conditions together and drawing near to a true and virtuous spiritual friend, one is able to realize for oneself that the very root of ignorance is fundamentally Buddha-wisdom.

The same applies to the three vehicles; however, because their inclinations (*āśaya*) differ in depth, they generate faith based upon the primordial wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and enter into realization by means of that primordial wisdom. Since they do not depart from primordial wisdom, the five stages are fully perfected even at the initial stage of the first resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*).

Although the dharma-gates of the stages and practices—the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and the eleventh ground—are set forth as the rules for progressive cultivation, they are like a king’s precious seal: a single seal, without discrepancy.
By means of the seal of the great wisdom of the single mind, one seals the beginningless three periods of time as being entirely contained within a single moment.

The wisdom-seal of all boundless phenomena is universally pervasive; for this wisdom is equal to all Buddhas, equal to the minds of all sentient beings, and equal to all phenomena. This is because wisdom has no center or periphery, nor interior or exterior, and is free from the distinctions of the three periods of time—long or short, near or far.
Because wisdom exceeds the measure of empty space, it is like the worldly void which has nothing to be cognized.
Just as non-conceptual wisdom is like space, in a single thought-moment it can discern dharma-gates that exceed the measure of empty space.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "All of space may still be measured, but the realm of the Buddhas is unspeakable.

For this reason, by means of the essence and function of the fundamental ignorance of one's own mind, one perceives that the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) is of the same essential nature, the same realm, and the same ocean of wisdom as all Buddhas and all sentient beings.

Because this initial arousal of the mind places one within the family of the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes, at the very moment the mind is aroused, one manifests the attainment of Buddhahood throughout the ten directions, as is clearly explained in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Initial Arousal of the Mind."

For this reason, among these ten stages of dwelling (*daśabhūmi*), one who enters the stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*) dwells within the sphere of the ocean of great compassion and wisdom of all Buddhas; thus, they cultivate all five stages simultaneously, because the first stage and the tenth stage are not separate from the single sphere of a Buddha’s wisdom.

It is merely to clarify the distinctions between the matured and the habitual, as well as the superior and the inferior, that the names of the "stages" (bhūmi) are established; for within the essence of wisdom, it is not subsumed by the temporal conditions of the three periods.
This is just as the Dragon Girl, in a single kṣaṇa, already possessed the three births, and thus fulfilled the conduct of Samantabhadra and attained the fruit of Buddhahood.

As the verse by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva states: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus understanding the affairs of the three periods of time, one transcends all skillful means and accomplishes the ten powers."

It is clearly known that the teaching concerning the three vehicles, the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, and the attainment of Buddhahood through worldly emergence is a provisional, skillful means (*upāya*).
This teaching, based on the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dharma*), does not speak of such matters as attaining Buddhahood through the power of vows.

If one accomplishes practice through the power of vows, one attains Buddhahood by returning to the ultimate reality; it is not said that Buddhahood is temporarily achieved through the power of vows alone.

Therefore, one should know that from among the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), the Bodhisattva who has first entered the stages practices all five positions simultaneously, because the common characteristics of the ten abodes universally encompass the dharma-gates of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the ten transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*), and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Just as in the ten stages, the seventh and eighth stages involve the cultivation of compassion and wisdom, and in the ninth stage—the position of the Dharma Master—compassion and wisdom are perfected; it is because the characteristics of these five positions are similar in this way.

Just as with the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in the Ten Abodes of Sudhana, each and every realm of wisdom is utterly boundless; yet, because the supreme Dharma of the Dharmakāya’s great wisdom and great compassion is endowed with inexhaustibility, one must establish the practice-gates of the five stages. In essence, these constitute the path of practice wherein a single mind, a single wisdom, and the simultaneous wisdom pervade all things.

Therefore, those who give rise to faith and advance in practice should not form views of the three periods of time as being distant or near, prolonged or abbreviated, regarding the realm of great wisdom; for such views would contradict the realm of wisdom.

One loses the realm of fundamental great wisdom because one pursues emotional consciousness and follows after appearances. This concludes the fourth sequence of severing delusions within this assembly. This sequence of severing delusions across the five stages is like space, which has no time;

it is like a perfect mirror that reflects all at once; it is like a mani jewel that can assume all colors; and it is like a single drop of water entering the great ocean, becoming identical and non-dual. Because the perfect mirror of great wisdom universally seals all activities, there is nothing that does not achieve the great function of non-action; thus, there is no "one time" apart from the three periods of time.
Regarding the fifth section, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, the text is divided into six parts.

The first part, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati" down to "I shall now explain the dwelling of those bodhisattvas," consists of nineteen and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies the stage where the Bodhisattva Dharmamati enters meditative absorption and is empowered by all Buddhas.
The second [section], following the emergence from meditative absorption, clarifies the division on the enumeration of the ten types of abodes.
The third contains ten dharmas, clarifying the division on the formal explanation of the causes for generating the resolve [for awakening].
The fourth [section] contains ten dharmas, clarifying the section on the ten kinds of supreme wisdom of the Tathāgata that serve as the objects of focus for the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
The fifth clarifies the section on the manifestation of the majestic power of the teaching, which causes the great earth to tremble.

The sixth section clarifies the division of praising the Dharma through verses. Within the first part, "The Entry into Samādhi by the Bodhisattva Dharmamati and the Empowerment by All Buddhas," there are ten main points:

first, the explanation of the Bodhisattva’s name; second, the clarification of the purpose for entering samādhi; third, the clarification of the power of the samādhi; fourth, the clarification that the Buddhas of the ten directions come to appear before him and share the same name as Dharmamati; fifth, the clarification that the Buddhas of the ten directions bestow their power in common; sixth, the clarification that this is brought about by the power of Vairocana Tathāgata’s past vows; seventh, the clarification that the Bodhisattva Dharmamati is able to enter samādhi through the power of his own roots of goodness; eighth, the clarification of the causes and conditions for entering meditative concentration; ninth, the clarification that the Buddhas of the ten directions grant wisdom; and tenth, the clarification that Dharmamati emerges from samādhi to expound the ten gates of dwelling.
