It is said that attaining Buddhahood definitely requires the completion of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Regarding the realm of the Buddhas perceived therein, a Bodhisattva on the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) merely speaks of making offerings to a hundred Buddhas, transforming and guiding a hundred Buddha-worlds, and attaining the "Gate of Illumination of a Hundred Dharmas" (*śata-dharma-prakāśa-mukham*).
Regarding this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of the Tathāgata’s omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is called the bodhicitta.

Just as in the first stage of the resolve for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), one is born into the great house of the wisdom of all modes of all Buddhas; at the very moment the resolve is first made, one attains perfect awakening, because one brings together the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) of all Buddhas and makes it one with one's own wisdom.
Attaining Buddhahood does not occur outside of a single kṣaṇa, because the realm of wisdom is neither extended nor compressed.

The realm of gathering and transforming beings pervades as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in a hundred Buddha-fields; furthermore, because the merit, function, and power of the wise and enlightened realm of a hundred Buddhas are inexhaustible, limitless, and infinitely layered.
This is still based on the terminology of "progressive cultivation according to stages," yet when reckoning the essence, one is identical with all, which is infinite.

For example, among the ten stages, a Bodhisattva in the first stage makes offerings to many hundreds or many thousands of Buddhas; although the number does not exceed the category of "hundreds," these "many hundreds" are themselves infinite and cannot be compared to a mere "single hundred."
Therefore, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four means of integration, the four immeasurable minds, and the ten perfections—each and every one of these dharmas is entirely limitless.
Consequently, the meditative practice cultivated by a Bodhisattva of these ten stages does not belong to the mundane or supramundane concentrations characterized by sinking or agitation.
The explanation of abiding in profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without sinking or agitation is now complete.

Regarding the passage stating that one who enters deep *dhyāna* attains the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a Buddha: these are like those of the gods of the form and formless realms, as well as the supernormal powers of the three vehicles. The supernormal powers of the form and formless realms arise from the purification of mental conceptions through the cessation of thought; they are supernormal powers obtained as a result of karmic retribution (*vipākaja*).

The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the two vehicles depend on what was previously contemplated during meditative concentration; the supernormal powers of Bodhisattvas in the Pure Lands attain the supernormal power of pure intention (*āśaya*), such as the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*).

In this sutra, those who enter deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and attain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a Buddha do so because their minds accord with principle. In its source, there is neither entering nor exiting; in its essence, there is neither stillness nor agitation, and in its essence, there is no contrived activity. Its nature spontaneously accords with principle and is inherently true; it neither arises nor is suppressed.

The principle accords with true wisdom, and its nature is inherently all-pervasive; it universally responds throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions simultaneously, manifesting physical bodies in accordance with beings.

It transforms the various classes of sentient beings in response to their wisdom, yet there is no coming or going, nor is there any transformation; this is called the supernatural power of the Buddha.

Wisdom has no basis of reliance; it has no form or substance and no nature of coming or going. Its nature is inherently all-pervasive and is not subsumed within the three periods of time, yet it can universally respond to the phenomena of the three periods of time; this is called supernormal power (abhijñā).
Therefore, a sutra says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time without coming or going.
This is because the three periods of time are falsely established by the deluded sentiments of sentient beings and do not exist as substantial realities.
The essence of wisdom is formless and colorless; it acts without deliberate effort yet responds to all classes of beings—this is called the "spiritual" (shen).
It is perfectly complete throughout the ten directions; there is no phenomenon it does not know and no faculty it does not discern—this is called "penetration" (tong).

As for the scripture’s statement, “One cultivates all pure practices by way of the gate of non-action,” it is because one cultivates the ocean of practices of the dharma-realm and the space-realm through this gate of non-action, such that they are universally and completely purified.
Wisdom that is without purposeful activity is called cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Knowing that the faculties share a common function is called practice (*caryā*).
When practice is such that nothing is not beneficial, being neither created nor born, it is called the gate of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-mukha*).

Because one constantly dwells throughout the ten directions within all three realms of existence, benefiting the mundane without being defiled by them or seeking purification, this is called "pure conduct.
As the Sūtra says, "To be of the same single essence as the Buddhas of the three periods of time" means that their Dharma-body wisdom is identical.

The vast eons of the three periods of time are identical within a single thought-moment; the great wisdom and great compassion practiced by all Buddhas of the three periods are universally shared and perfectly identical with those of Samantabhadra.

As the Sūtra states, "There are ten kinds of dharmas that cause Bodhisattvas to swiftly enter the various stages," this clarifies that at the stage of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), one universally knows the dharma-gates of all the stages, practices, dedications, and grounds, because the one is all and all is one, and because cause is itself the fruit.
This is just as when the youth Sudhana, having seen Maitreya Bodhisattva, was then led by Maitreya to see Mañjuśrī once again; this clarifies that cause and effect are neither different nor separate.

This is also like that: from the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one proceeds simultaneously toward the stage of Buddhahood in a single thought-moment; yet, one does not depart from this single thought-moment in accomplishing perfect enlightenment, for both the causes and fruits of Buddhahood as well as the practices of a bodhisattva are all fully perfected therein.
This is because Sudhana’s attainment of Buddhahood in one lifetime and the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood in less than a single kṣaṇa are essentially similar.

As for the expression "attaining Buddhahood in one lifetime," it clarifies that this present life—this body of segmented birth derived from parents—is itself a "lifetime" produced through the practice of faith and the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga).
To cast off the body of segmented birth and enter into the birth of transformation is called "one life.

Yet this does not transcend the limit of the moment (*kṣaṇa*). It possesses no nature of past or present, no nature of segmentation, and no nature of transformation; for all phenomena are like illusions, like transformations, non-extinguishing, and devoid of the three periods of time.

Because one universally cultivates all dwellings and stages from this first dwelling, one penetrates all dharmas; thus, in a single moment of time, one attains mastery over the many and the few, the long and the short, without obstruction, for not a single instant is transcended—such is the nature of dharmas.
By removing emotional attachments through wisdom, this can be seen through contemplation.

When the Sūtra states, "One knows that all sentient beings and all Tathāgatas share the same single essence," the Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles understand that all sentient beings equally possess the Buddha-nature and the nature of reality; this sūtra, however, understands that all sentient beings equally possess the nature of the Tathāgata’s *sarvākārajñatā* (all-encompassing wisdom).
As stated in a later passage of the sutra: "There is a scripture scroll as large as a trichiliocosm, contained within the bodies of small sentient beings.
When someone attains Buddhahood, they shatter these atoms and bring forth this scripture scroll."
To say that it is as large as a mote of dust means that all sentient beings possess the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
When a bodhisattva attains buddhahood and transforms them, they collectively obtain the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes.
The wisdom that realizes the ultimate principle is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā); the wisdom of differentiation is called "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā).

As the Sūtra says, "Hearing of all Buddha-lands, one vows to be reborn in them," this does not mean departing from the mundane world; rather, it is the manifestation of pervasive wisdom through responsive transformation, making offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions without coming or going.

The Sūtra states: "Regarding the 'successive meditative concentrations' (anupūrva-samāpatti), these refer to the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which the bodhisattva is able to enter in successive order.
As for the four dhyānas of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the bodhisattva is fully able to enter them in regular succession, or may enter and emerge from them by skipping stages."
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the section on cremation:

one enters the third dhyāna from the first dhyāna and emerges; enters the sphere of nothingness from the sphere of infinite space and emerges; enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception from the sphere of infinite space and emerges. Such is the skipping of stages (*vyutkrāntaka*), and such is the sequential order (*anupūrva*).

Regarding this "Sūtra-Method Net Samādhi," such as entering meditative absorption in one direction and arising in the ten directions, or entering absorption in the ten directions and arising in one direction, it is fully explained as described in the section on the stage of the Ten Faiths.

As for the Samāpatti-jñāna-mudrā (the Wisdom Seal of Meditative Absorption), it clarifies that stillness and function arise simultaneously; it seals all myriad phenomena such that none are not clearly manifest, like the waters of the great ocean manifesting ten thousand images.
Pure wisdom universally seals all phenomena, enabling one to comprehend them all; yet there is neither subject nor object, nor is there an agent.

As the Sūtra says, "Skillfully observing all phenomena, one attains the seal of the true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*). Because the great wisdom-seal—characterized by non-action, non-reliance, and non-conceptualization—stamps all phenomena, what arises is only the arising of phenomena themselves. Being free from ignorance and the fetters of the three periods of time, this is called the seal of the true mark.
The Sūtra states that "entering true samādhi" refers to being free from the defilement and purity, as well as the sinking and agitation, of the three realms and the three vehicles.
To be "separated from all deviant views" refers to the two views of existence and non-existence.

The view of the internal, the view of the external, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), the clinging to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), and so forth—all these, up to the sixty-two views, are included herein.
Regarding the sixty-two views, there are four types of views applied to all phenomena:
first, eternalism; second, impermanence; third, both eternal and impermanent; and fourth, neither eternal nor impermanent.
Regarding each of the five aggregates (*skandha*), there are four views; thus, four times five makes twenty.
When these are combined with the five aggregates of the three periods of time, they total sixty.
Together with the two fundamental views, these constitute the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*).
All deviant views do not depart from this.

"Universal-gate wisdom" refers to the wisdom that universally knows the various faculties of sentient beings, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñajñāna*), and the various differentiated types of wisdom.
For the sake of those sentient beings in the realm of form who abide in meditative concentration, he teaches them to give rise to contemplation.

For the sake of those sentient beings in the formless realm who cultivate the contemplation of signlessness, he teaches subtle and wondrous wisdom, so that signs do not engage their minds and their wisdom may be sharp.

The six dharmas of concordant respect consist of: first, the body; second, speech; third, the mind; fourth, precepts; fifth, giving; and sixth, views. These are called the six dharmas of concordant respect.

Regarding the sowing of the seeds of the Buddha within the field of sentient beings: this is to demonstrate the bodhi-wisdom and principle to all sentient beings, and because even a slight root of goodness serves as a superior condition.
The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) have already been explained previously, as described in the "Chapter on the Ten Supernormal Powers" (*Daśābhijñā-parivarta*).
The ten supernormal powers are fully elucidated in the sutra.
Below, in the verses, there is one verse per two lines; the text is self-sufficient, and the praise follows the wording of each line.
The final single line of prose clarifies the section on the Great Assembly’s joyful reception and practice of the Dharma.

Within this assembly, the "Chapter on Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven" constitutes the introductory section (nidāna); from the "Chapter on Verses of Praise" onwards is the main exposition (dharmadeśanā); and the shaking of the earth and the offering of worship constitute the section on dissemination (pariṇāmanā).
Chapter Nineteen: Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven. In order to explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to three sections:
first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; and third, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning.
First, regarding the explanation of the title: why is it called the "Palace of the Yāma Heaven"?
It is intended to clarify that the location represents the Dharma.

This heaven is named the "Time-Portion" (Yāma) Heaven because this heaven lacks the sun and moon, and thus has no distinction between darkness and light; instead, the opening of the lotus flowers constitutes the day, and their closing constitutes the night. For these reasons, it is called the Time-Portion Heaven.

To manifest that the Dharma-gate of the ten practices must respond according to the proper time—since one cannot fail to know the proper time for universal transformation—it uses the *Kāla-deva* (Time-God) to symbolize knowing the faculties (*indriya*) in order to correspond to the practices; one must not act in a one-sided manner.

This is because one must know whether a person belongs to the lineage of devas and humans, or to the lineages of the two vehicles, the three vehicles, or the single vehicle, so as to guide them by means of whatever roots of goodness are appropriate.
Furthermore, the "heaven of time" (*kāladivya*) is used to symbolize the practice to be performed, for it is necessary to know the proper timing.
Mount Sumeru symbolizes the dharma-gate of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), clarifying that one ascends from faith and leaves behind the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, it symbolizes the positions of the ten stages, representing the initial ascent to the summit of the Dharma and reaching the point where all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are exhausted.
Furthermore, it represents Mount Sumeru situated within the great ocean, rising eighty-four thousand yojanas high; for it cannot be ascended by grasping with hands or feet.
This clarifies that the stage of the first ten abodes is not something reachable through the grasping of contemplative practices (vipaśyanā) pursued with a deliberate mind;
rather, it is only by being free from thought—where wisdom responds in a state of total openness and all phenomena have no basis—that one may ascend.
This stage of the Ten Practices resides within the Yāma Heaven; it clarifies that one dwells by relying on emptiness and is not connected with ordinary people.

The Ten Practices are likewise: one acts in accordance with the emptiness of phenomena, and while practicing these deeds, one benefits the mundane world at the appropriate times. Therefore, this stage is represented as being situated in this heaven.

The *Ten Dedications* (*Daśapariṇāmanā*) are taught in Tuṣita Heaven in order to clarify that this realm resides within the heavens of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), and furthermore, to clarify that this heaven is characterized by contentment with its bliss. This serves to symbolize that the Ten Dedications employ right wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) to engage with the mundane world for the benefit of sentient beings; they abide in the gateway of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to enrich all beings, remaining free from craving or seeking after any sensory objects. Thus, this heaven is taken as the symbolic representation.

Regarding the teaching of the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages while ascending to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*): it signifies transcending the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (*nirmāṇarati*) and reaching the limit of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). This represents the sovereign transcendence of the Ten Stages from the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations up to the summit of the Desire Realm, because the *māra* who transforms his mind reaches the very limit of desire's exhaustion.

Ascending to the third dhyāna, he expounds the Dharma-gate of the Buddha-Flower, clarifying the fulfillment of the practices of Samantabhadra; this signifies that through the practice of the Dharma, he brings joy to infinite sentient beings.
Furthermore, it demonstrates that the fourth dhyāna is the stage of Buddhahood.

This is established as such by way of a symbolic representation of the progression and regression of spiritual cultivation; however, each instance of wisdom and reality is all-pervasive and devoid of coming or going. For this reason, it is said that [the Buddhas] "ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, and other realms without ever departing from the Bodhimaṇḍa in the Samantaprabhā Hall."
As for the Third Dhyāna surpassing the First and Second Dhyanas, this clarifies that each successive stage is doubly superior.
This specific assembly has not yet appeared in previous texts.

It is from the *Yingluo Benye Jing* (The Sutra on the Original Acts of the Garland), wherein the Tathāgata, leading the assembly of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas toward the foot of the Bodhi tree, recalled what he had previously taught as the *Dharmadhātu Sūtra* when first attaining perfect enlightenment under the Bodhi tree; because [the stages] were arranged one by one up to the Third Dhyāna, it is therefore used here at the Yāma Heaven to represent the Ten Practices.

Second, regarding the purpose of this chapter: the preceding section clarified the advancement through the ten stages (*bhūmi*) by ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru; this section clarifies the advancement through the ten practices (*caryā*) by reaching the Yāma Heaven. Consequently, this chapter must follow in sequence.
Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text, the major themes therein are divided into two parts:
first, a general outline of the intent of the sūtra; second, a word-by-word commentary.
First, concerning the general outline of the intent of the sūtra: within these forty-nine lines of this chapter, the text is divided into ten sections.

First: from "At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata" down to "constantly facing the Buddha," there are three and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on how those in the ten directions simultaneously see the Tathāgata without leaving their own places.

2. From "At that time" onwards, up to "the Palace of Precious Adornment," there are approximately two lines of scripture which clarify the section on ascending to the Yāma Heaven without departing from the Universal Radiance Hall at all the sites of enlightenment throughout the ten directions.

3. From "At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven" down to "at that time, the king having prepared the seat," there are fourteen lines of scripture which clarify the section on the King of the Time-Interval seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, the transformation and adornment of the seat, and the section on respectful homage.

4. From "He approached the Buddha, the World-Honored One" down to "entered this palace," approximately two and a half lines of scripture, clarify the section concerning the timely invitation by the Heavenly King to the Buddha to enter the hall and ascend the seat.

5. From "At that time, the Buddha accepted the invitation" down to "all were likewise," there is approximately one line of scripture which clarifies that the Tathāgata accepted the invitation and concludes by showing that this was the same throughout the ten directions.

6. From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Heavenly King" and extending for one and a half lines of scripture, there is the section on the Heavenly King recollecting his past causes and praising the Buddha through verses.
7. Within these verses, there are twenty lines of verse comprising the section on praising the ten Tathāgatas who previously came to enter this celestial palace.

8. From "In this world" down to "praising the Buddha’s merits," there are two and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section where the ten directions simultaneously praise the Buddha in the same manner as here.

9. From "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "all the places where he dwells," approximately two lines of scripture, clarify how the Tathāgata accepted the invitation and entered the hall, which was vast, spacious, and capacious.
10. "The worlds of the ten directions are all likewise" is the summary concluding that the ten directions are identical to this section.

Regarding the second part, the word-by-word explanation: from the initial phrase "At that time" down to "constantly facing the Buddha," it clarifies that [the Buddhas] are eternally and universally present in all places throughout the ten directions, without increase or decrease.

As for the statement that he ascends to the Yāma Heaven without departing from the summit of Mount Sumeru at the Bodhi tree, it means that his wisdom pervades all places and thus manifests his body; it is not a matter of coming or going.
The statement that they saw the Buddha coming from afar clarifies that [the practitioner] proceeds from the Ten Abodes toward the stage of the Ten Practices.

The immediate manifestation of a seat through spiritual power clarifies that the practice is established upon the wisdom of emptiness, wherein subject and object are non-existent, and it is firmly established in meditative concentration.
The seat symbolizes practice; it is called "Lotus" because it clarifies that the practice of non-action has been perfected, being free from all defilement and attachment.
"Treasury" (garbha) carries the meaning of containment, clarifying that the practice of non-practice contains and stores all manner of virtues.
The lion signifies fearlessness; because one dwells within birth and death with the wisdom and principle of non-action (*wuwei*), one is without fear.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound used as the name for the seat.

"Ten million tiers" clarifies that within the ten abodes there are ten thousand, and within the ten practices there are one million, because this clarifies the successive stages of advancement according to each rank.

"With ten million golden nets serving as interlacing cords" clarifies that within this stage, one transforms sentient beings through the net of practice; this is because it is the fruit of reliance obtained as a result of retribution.
The ten abodes amount to ten thousand and the ten practices to one million, which clarifies the ascending progression.

The flower garlands, fragrant jewels, and the four kinds of canopies clarify that through the skillful means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one gathers and encompasses sentient beings.

The "four kinds of hindrances" (catvāra āvaraṇāḥ) clarify that one covers and protects sentient beings by means of the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa-citta): loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
"Illuminating with a million rays of light" clarifies that one observes the faculties [of beings] with the eye of wisdom (jñāna-cakṣus) and thereby gathers and transforms them.
The Heavenly King represents mastery over conduct.
Paying respectful homage signifies practicing all deeds without pride.
The Brahma King’s exultation signifies that through pure conduct he benefits sentient beings, feeling joy without weariness upon seeing those who come to beg.
That "a million bodhisattvas extolled him" clarifies that he saves sentient beings through his practice, and that the multitude of sages joyfully praise him.
That "celestial music played its melodies" clarifies the fruit summoned by his skillful preaching of the Dharma.
Regarding the "four kinds of clouds," they cover the mundane world through the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

The preceding mention of "cloud-canopies" and the subsequent mention of "four kinds of clouds" clarify that these are distinguished according to the size of the vessels [of sentient beings] they cover and nourish.
The mani-clouds are likewise; they illuminate and benefit according to the capacity of each root.
The phrase "produced by ten million roots of goodness" clarifies the aforementioned adornments, indicating that they are all produced by the roots of goodness within the context of practice.
By practicing deeds that benefit others and accumulate merit, one immediately attains all forms of protection and is adorned by manifold blessings.
The following may be understood according to the text.
As for the phrase "Welcome, Sugata," it means that [the Buddha] has excellently extinguished all evils, sufferings, and calamities.
"The departed" refers to those who deliver sentient beings and leave behind their bonds.
When it says "the Buddha accepted the invitation and ascended the hall," it clarifies that he has advanced upward and correctly entered the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*).
The above points demonstrate that the Buddha’s own virtues naturally pervade and encompass the ten directions at all times.
The present discussion of "ascending and descending" is made in general terms regarding the progress and advancement of sentient beings.

Within these twenty verses, the praise of the ten Buddhas who previously entered this hall clarifies that the principle and wisdom of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*) entered now are no different from those of antiquity; these ten Tathāgatas are titles established according to the advancement achieved through practice.

The ten names of the Tathāgatas at the summit of Mount Sumeru during the first ten stages (*bhūmi*) are likewise titles that accord with the ancient teachings of those stages; they clarify that the Dharma entered is no different from that of all Buddhas of the past and present.

As described in the stage of the Ten Abodes, when Śakra, Lord of the Devas atop Mount Sumeru, saw the Buddha approaching from afar, he immediately prepared the Lion Throne of Universal Radiance within his palace. This was to clarify that one has newly entered the arising of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; thus, by means of the gate of the Samādhi of Expedient Means, it is named "Establishing the Universal Radiance Treasury," which clarifies that wisdom illuminates the treasury of the Dharma-realm.

Regarding these ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), when the Heavenly King Timingila (Kālakarnin) sees the Buddha approaching from afar and transforms himself into a precious lotus lion-throne, it clarifies that through the flowers of practice he establishes a net of teaching to filter out all sentient beings, causing them to enter the treasury of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-realm; for the lotus symbolizes the meaning of non-attachment in practice.

The "transformed seat" clarifies the essence of practice: by relying on the wisdom of the ten stages, the dharma-body of emptiness has no fixed establishment; its manifestations are like illusions, which is what is signified herein.
The final five lines of the sutra collectively conclude with the simultaneous praise of the Buddha by those from the ten directions.

The passage stating that when the Tathāgata enters the hall, the hall encompasses him as if he were dwelling in the celestial realm, clarifies that upon entering the stages and ascending therein, one’s own wisdom becomes vast and inclusive, and only then does one come to know the realm of the Buddha.
Chapter Twenty: The Chapter on Praise in Verses in the Yāma Heaven. In order to explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to three sections:
first, an explanation of the chapter title; second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; and third, an explanation of the meaning following the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the chapter title: it clarifies that [the Buddha] ascended to the palace of the Yāma Heaven to preach the Dharma of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*).

In this chapter, the assembly of ten bodhisattvas, including Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha, each uses verses to universally praise the Dharma of their respective stages through the practices appropriate to those stages; therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on Verses of Praise" (*Gāthā-stotra-parivarta*).

Second, regarding the purpose for which this chapter is introduced: it clarifies that, in order to explain the dharma of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), one must first present a verse that provides a comprehensive praise of the causal and resultant dharma-gates within those Ten Practices; therefore, this chapter must appear here.
If the causes and effects of the practices were not first set forth, upon what would the ten practices depend for their accomplishment?
Regarding the third section, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, this chapter is divided into two parts:
first, a general outline of the intent of the scripture; second, a detailed explanation following the text.
Regarding the first major structural division of the sutra’s meaning, it is divided into five sections.

The first section, from "At that time, by the Buddha's supernatural power" down to "sat cross-legged," consists of thirteen and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies the section on the assembly of the ten bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakusuma (Flower of Virtue) and others, who have come together having manifested their own practice of the Buddha’s cause and fruit according to their respective stages.

The second section, from "In this world" down to "all are equal and without distinction," comprises approximately two lines of scripture; it collectively cites the bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions who have gathered together for this same division.

The third section, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "there was none who did not manifest," comprises approximately two lines of scripture; it clarifies the division concerning the locations where the light was emitted.

The fourth section, "At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakaraṇḍa," comprises approximately one line of scripture; it clarifies the division concerning the contemplation of the Dharma and the recitation of verses.
Fifth, from the first verse below, there are ten sections of verses that clarify the causal and resultant divisions of the individual practice gateways within each of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Regarding the second part, the exegesis of the meaning according to the text: within the first section of thirteen and a half lines at the beginning of this chapter, the meaning is divided into three parts:

first, the explanation of the Bodhisattva’s name and its correlation with the causes and results of progressive cultivation through the stages; second, the explanation of the significance of the distance between the Buddha-lands (*kṣetra*); and third, the explanation of how the Bodhisattvas are each given the same title and are universally pervasive.

The first [section] explains the names of the bodhisattvas and correlates them with the causes and effects of progressive cultivation through the various stages; there are ten such types of cause and effect.

Regarding the first, Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha: because he has been born into the family of Buddha-wisdom within the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśabhūmi*), the bodhisattva is named Dharmamati and Arthamati, among others.
This stage is called "Forest" because it clarifies that from wisdom one practices both merit and knowledge; since the two resulting rewards are vast and manifold, it is named after a forest.
Furthermore, "forest" carries the meanings of being vast and manifold, providing shelter and shade, being adorned, and the mutual support of the trunk, branches, twigs, flowers, leaves, and fruits.

This clarifies the stage of the Bodhisattva of the Ten Practices (*daśaparikarman*): by means of the wisdom of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*), they adorn the branches of the myriad practices; with great compassion as their leaves, they provide shelter and shade to gather in and transform all sentient beings, so that the flowers and fruits of enlightenment for both self and others may fully blossom and ripen.

Just as birds flock to forests by rivers and marshes, and many people rely upon a benevolent person who practices virtue, for this reason the ten practices of a bodhisattva are designated as "forests.
This refers to the gate of practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) with joy.
Just as in the beginning of Sudhana’s Ten Practices, when the spiritual friend named Sudarśana was walking back and forth in a grove, it was also like this.
As for the land named "Three Eyes," it is because at this stage the fruit of Buddhahood is designated by the term "eye."

The world is named "Beloved Wisdom" (Priyaprajña) because these ten practices are clearly seen to arise from the Buddha’s wisdom as their cause, and because they also constantly serve as a source of intimacy for all sentient beings.

The Buddha-fruit is called the "Ever-abiding Eye" because it arises directly from the Buddha’s wisdom; its faculty of knowing benefits the mundane world by enabling one to directly attain the eye of ever-abiding wisdom.
It clarifies that one has personally attained the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom, so that all acts of benefiting sentient beings also cause others to attain the eye of wisdom.
It clarifies that the wisdom which observes the faculties of sentient beings with the Tathāgata’s wisdom to benefit them is precisely the Buddha-fruit of this stage.
Guna-kānana (Forest of Merit) represents the person who practices the conduct to be performed.
Priyamedha-loka (World of Intimate Wisdom) is the cause of the wisdom practiced within that stage.
The Buddha Constantly Abiding in the Eye is the fruit of knowing the faculties and perspectives within that stage.
Being in correspondence with fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), he is named the Buddha of the Permanently Abiding Eye.
As for the second, the Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom (Prajñāvana): it signifies that his wisdom is like a forest, because its meanings are vast and manifold.
This is the practice of benefiting others, because one benefits all sentient beings through wisdom so that they do not become deluded.
One practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), because in this stage, wisdom constitutes the very essence of ethical discipline.

For example, among the ten practices of the youth Sudhana, the spiritual friend Śakranandana practiced the perfection of ethical discipline; by means of the arts of calculation, physiognomy, and seal-marking, he established the auspicious and inauspicious locations for villages, camps, cities, and towns, which was due to his wisdom.
Within the Ten Abodes, the dharma-body serves as the essence of the precepts; within these Ten Practices, wisdom serves as the essence of the precepts.
Thus, Bodhisattva Hui-lin is one who practices such cultivation.

The world-system of Banner Wisdom (*Dhvaja-prajñā*) is the cause of the practice undertaken, for wisdom serves as the essence of the precepts (*śīla-ātman*), remaining unshakable amidst birth and death.
The Buddha Unsurpassed Eye (*Anuttara-cakṣus*) is the fruit of that practice, for with the eye of wisdom he knows the faculties of others, such that none are superior to him.
The third is the Bodhisattva Jayasena; this is the practice of non-opposition, presiding over the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Among all practices, the practice of patience is supreme; for if one lacks patience within their conduct, no practice is perfected. Therefore, he is named the Bodhisattva Jayasena.

For example, in this stage, for the youth Sudhana, the spiritual friend is the laywoman (upāsikā) named Guṇavatī; she embodies the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) as the comprehensive synthesis of all practices, wherein loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are all fully contained.
The "Enlightened Upāsikā" represents the practice of compassion.
Her plain clothing and disheveled hair signify the marks of precept-keeping and patience.
Her dwelling in a single room with four doors symbolizes the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) used to compassionately nurture sentient beings.
The ten thousand female attendants represent the perfection of the ten thousand practices (*daśasāhasra-caryā*).

The fact that she provides inexhaustible aid with a single small vessel symbolizes her freedom from pride and self-exaltation, as well as the boundlessness of the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*); it clarifies that each and every *pāramitā* mutually contains and accommodates the others.
Jeta-vana Bodhisattva is one who practices such conduct.
The world-system Ratnaprajñā is the dharma that he cultivates; it is illuminated by the fact that patience is the jewel among all practices, for it is worthy of being highly valued.

The Buddha Anihitacakṣus (No Abiding Eye) represents the fruit of Buddhahood within the perfection of patience; it clarifies that although one practices patience, one does not dwell on the act of practicing while doing so.

As for the fourth, the Bodhisattva Abhayavanavāsī (Dweller in the Forest of Fearlessness), he clarifies that one constantly practices diligence, which constitutes fearlessness in benefiting humans and devas amidst birth and death.

The Master’s conduct is free from yielding or flinching because, through wisdom, he knows the proper time, knows the Dharma, and knows the faculties of beings to benefit them; thus, he does not falter in his tasks nor stagnate in his merit.
For example, the wise layman Sudhana, a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), is a spiritual friend within this stage.
This is because he benefits sentient beings through his wisdom and acts with unyielding perseverance.
"Residing in the city of Great Flourishing" signifies the meaning of diligence.

"At the crossroads of the marketplace" clarifies that the benefit is vast and manifold, providing limitless advantage, and that one applies the skillful means of focused attention and mental engagement for even a brief moment.
Looking up at the void, all things required to benefit sentient beings descend from the sky; this is because wisdom is like the void, corresponding to the mindfulness of that wisdom.
The void is the root of wisdom, for wisdom is not distinct from the void.
Therefore, the contemplation of emptiness is the universal manifestation that accords with wisdom.
Thus, emptiness is the foundation of all dharmas.
Contemplating it in this way, one clarifies that all merits arise collectively from the wisdom of emptiness.
The Bodhisattva Abhayavana is one who practices the conduct of this stage.
The world-realm Vijñānamati is the dharma of cultivation for this stage.
The Buddha Acalanetra is the fruit of Buddhahood within this stage.
The stage of luminous diligence is so called because it does not follow the transformations of external objects; thus, the Buddha is named the Unwavering Eye.
To remain unmoved amidst sensory objects is what is termed diligence.
The fifth, the Bodhisattva Forest of Shame and Remorse, practices conduct free from delusion and confusion, presiding over the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
One practices dhyāna out of a sense of shame and remorse; one gives rise to wisdom through meditative concentration, because one thus practices without delusion or distraction.
The elder Ratnacūḍa, a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of Sudhana, is the spiritual friend within this stage.
Being in the midst of the marketplace, he clarifies the essence of dhyāna within active conduct; though amidst clamor, he is ever tranquil.

He takes Sudhana by the hand and leads him to his dwelling; this signifies guidance and reception. It signifies that within the marketplace of birth and death, he guides and receives others, leading them to the abode of the fruit of wisdom; thus, it signifies observing the fruit to understand the cause.

That residence is adorned with jewels, consisting of ten stories and eight gates; the courtyards have eight gates and the pavilions have ten stories. The eight gates clarify the Eightfold Noble Path, while the ten-story pavilion represents the retribution of the ten *pāramitās*. These are arranged from bottom to top according to the practice of the ten perfections, each possessing its own inherent principle, which will be clarified in the text below.
This refers to the total inclusion of the myriad practices within the essence of dhyāna.
The Bodhisattva Forest of Shame and Remorse is the practitioner of this stage.
The world Lamp-Wisdom is the dharma practiced therein; because meditative concentration can give rise to the illumination of wisdom that shines upon all things, the world is named "Lamp."
The Buddha Celestial Eye is the fruit of Buddhahood at this stage; because he is definitively able to purify all the faculties, he is titled the Buddha Celestial Eye.
The sixth, the Bodhisattva Forest of Vigor, represents the practice of excellence and presides over the gateway of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Because he uses the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to bring all practices to fruition for the benefit of sentient beings, he is named "Forest of Diligence" (*Vīryavana*).

Just as the spiritual friend in this stage of Sudhana is named the Elder Universal Eye (*Samantanetra*), who first saves his life, next provides food and drink, and finally bestows the Dharma—each according to the individual's capacity—to clarify the accomplishment of wisdom.
The Forest of Diligence is the person who practices;
the World of Vajra Wisdom is the Dharma of practice, for it is called "Vajra" because clear wisdom can shatter afflictions.
The Buddha Liberation-Eye is the fruit of Buddhahood at this stage.
The Bodhisattva Seventh Forest of Power is of unattached conduct and presides over the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).

To manifest through skillful means within the mundane world to benefit sentient beings, to conform to their conduct and ways, and to dwell in the world without attachment while accomplishing the practice of great compassion—this is the Forest of Power (*balavana*).
To enter the mundane world with reality (*tattva*) and remain undefiled while dwelling amidst the fetters (*saṃyojana*)—therefore it is named the Forest of Power.

Just as in this stage, Sudhana’s spiritual friend was named King Never-Weary; for the sake of practicing great compassion, he manifested himself through transformation to perform various unwholesome acts, and then again manifested himself to pursue, capture, and punish them, or even to sever their life-force to inflict suffering upon them as a means of correction, so that sentient beings would truly fear and abandon evil.
To rescue and protect sentient beings with love, never abandoning them, is called "insatiability.
Bodhisattva Power Forest (Balavana) is the person capable of such practice;
the World of Peaceful Wisdom (Sukhamatī) is the dharma that is practiced.
The Buddha Pure Vision (Śuddhacakṣus) is the fruit of this stage.

Because this stage constitutes the gateway to the Great Compassion, it is named the World of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī); it receives its name by virtue of bringing peace and bliss to sentient beings.
The Buddha is named Discerning Eye (*Sudṛṣṭin*), for he thoroughly knows by what Dharma each sentient being should be transformed before he begins to discipline them.
The eighth is the Bodhisattva Forest of Practice (*Caryāvana*); this is the practice that is difficult to attain, presiding over the perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
That which is difficult to attain yet can be attained is called the Forest of Practice (*caryā-vana*).
Because this stage of wisdom is difficult to ascend, it is termed the "Practice Difficult to Attain" (*dur-labha-caryā*).
For example, at this stage, the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the youth Sudhana was named Mahāprabha, the King.

The eighth wisdom follows great vows to fulfill the intentions of sentient beings; it performs great benefit by universally bestowing upon sentient beings the requisites for worldly happiness and grants them all the jewels of omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Gaṇeśvara is one who is capable of such practice;
the world-system *Sūryaprajñā* is the dharma that he has cultivated.
In this stage, the essence of wisdom increases and becomes luminous; thus, the world is named *Sūryaprajñā*.

The Buddha Luminous Appearance Eyes (*Prabhāsa-lakṣaṇa-cakṣus*) is the fruit of this stage; because the essence of wisdom for this stage increases in luminosity, the name of the Buddha-fruit is "Luminous Appearance Eyes.
The ninth, Bodhisattva Forest of Awakening (*Bodhivana*), is the practice of wholesome dharmas, with the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) as its primary force.
Just as for Sudhana at this stage, the spiritual friend is named the Upāsikā Acalā; she represents the ninth station of the Dharma Master.
Why is she female? It is to clarify that when one occupies the station of a Dharma Master, being chaste, compassionate, and gentle, these qualities are symbolized by a woman.

This woman has already cultivated the resolve for enlightenment for as many eons as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa; since she first resolved her mind upon it, not a single thought of the five desires has arisen in her heart.
She is brilliant, pure, firm, compassionate, and gentle—such are the virtues of this Dharma Master.
For this reason, this bodhisattva is named Forest of Awakening (Juelin), and his primary power is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Bodhisattva Forest of Awakening is one who practices the practice;
the World of Pure Wisdom is the dharma of cultivation.
The Buddha Most Supreme Eye is the fruit of the practice cultivated; because his wisdom is pure, the Buddha is named Most Supreme Eye.
The tenth Bodhisattva, Forest of Wisdom, is so called because he practices true wisdom and presides over the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this stage and position, the similarities may be understood as follows:

for example, at this stage, Sudhana’s spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) was a renunciant non-Buddhist named Viśvāmitra, who had attained mastery over wisdom and was able to manifest in the form of those with false views to gather in all such adherents, saying, "Of the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhists within the realm of the three thousandfold world-system, I have become each and every one of them."
The Bodhisattva Jñānaketu is the practitioner;
the world-system Brahmajñāna is the Dharma practiced;
and the Buddha Indranīlanetra is the fruit of this stage.
The deep azure is the wisdom of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*), representing the fulfillment of a single cycle, as it is the ultimate state of luminous, pure illumination.

Second, regarding the meaning of the distance of the buddha-fields (*kṣetra*): the Sūtra states, "From each of the ten directions, there is a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field, who have come from worlds beyond as many lands as there are atoms in one hundred thousand buddha-fields to assemble here. While the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* speaks of "atoms in a hundred fields," this text says "one hundred thousand" to clarify the expansion and increase of ascending wisdom.
The deluded mind and its various objects constitute the measure of the sensory realms; the dwelling place of deluded attachment is called a "country.
When the mind turns in accordance with these objects, it is called being outside of all such countries.
Holding the seal of lost wisdom is called "coming.
When clear wisdom is all-pervasive, there is no realm it does not reach; they are collectively termed Bodhisattvas, and this applies to each and every Bodhisattva alike.
This generally clarifies that wisdom pervades both penetration and delusion.

Third, regarding the explanation of how each Bodhisattva is universally designated by the same name: it clarifies that when the mind is deluded regarding various objects, ignorance manifests extensively beyond the sensory realms.

When the mind awakens and wisdom penetrates, it extends far and wide throughout the oceans of lands; there is no aspect of omniscience that does not accord with its vision, and thus each of its various names pervades everywhere.
It clarifies that in the state of delusion, there is no object that is not confused about, and once awakened, there is no object that is not known by wisdom.
From "these bodhisattvas" onwards, they prostrated at the Buddha's feet, clearly expressing their reverence.

They ascended the *maṇi-garbha* transformation seat to signify that while abiding in the cycle of birth and death through the ten practices, they transform sentient beings, for their conduct is eternally stainless.
The "mani-treasury" refers to the stainless jewel.
"Treasury" (garbha) carries the meaning of containing or encompassing. "Lion" signifies fearlessness.
This clarifies that the conduct of ordinary beings is defiled, whereas the conduct of the noble ones is stainless.
The term "Lion" is established as a name based on its primary referent (*adhīśvara*).
This collectively elucidates the dharmas practiced by the wisdom-virtue of the practitioner.

At that time, as for the World-Honored One emitting hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light from his two feet: light is emitted from the wheels on the soles of the feet during the Ten Faiths; light is emitted from the tips of the toes during the Ten Abidings; and light is emitted from the tops of the ankles during these Ten Practices. This clarifies the successive advancement through the stages, signifying that the light of the Dharma proceeds from ten thousand, to a hundred thousand, to a hundred thousand billion wondrous colors and lights, collectively illustrating the advancement through each stage.
Generally, from the soles of the feet, the tips of the toes, and the tops of the insteps, everything is not separate from the practice being performed.

From this prose section below, there are ten stanzas; these are the individual verses of the ten forest Bodhisattvas on the methods of practice cultivated in their respective stations, whereby these ten dharmas together constitute a single practice.

In this way, each and every practice contains all ten practices; according to the specific names and meanings within their respective stages of practice, these are the dharmas that are praised, as clearly elucidated in the full text.

From here on, the meanings corresponding to the names are presented; each praises the dharmas practiced in their respective positions. It should be understood that by comprehending the names, one knows the dharmas.
*New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Volume XVIII;
*New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Volume XIX.
Compiled by the Elder Li Tongxuan.
Chapter Twenty-one: The Ten Practices. Regarding the explanation of this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to three sections:
First, explaining the title of the chapter; second, explaining the purpose of the chapter’s inclusion; third, explaining the meaning according to the text.
Regarding the first, explaining the title of the chapter: this chapter correctly expounds ten kinds of practice-gates, and is therefore titled "The Chapter on the Ten Practices" (Shixing-pin).

Second, regarding the purpose of this chapter: the original intent of this Yāma Heaven palace is to explain the "Chapter on the Ten Practices. This is because for this heaven, the opening of the lotus flowers signifies day and their closing signifies night; as the natural light of this heaven illuminates one another and there is neither sun nor moon, day and night are distinguished solely by observing the opening and closing of the lotuses. Thus, it is called the Heaven of Time-Divisions (Kāmadeva).
"Yāma" is a term from the Sanskrit language.

When Bodhisattvas at this stage perceive that the minds of sentient beings are ready to be awakened, they guide them accordingly; for those who are not yet ready to be delivered, they establish the causes and conditions for their deliverance. Because this stage serves as the representation of such activity, ten types of practice-gates are explained here.

The preceding two chapters merely clarified the arrival at this celestial realm and offered praise for it; since this chapter specifically explains the gateway of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), this chapter must follow.
The preceding ten stages (*bhūmi*) are like relying on the summit of Mount Sumeru; these ten practices (*caryā*) rely upon the void, signifying that their practice is unattached.
Third, regarding the word-by-word commentary, it is divided into two parts:
first, a general outline of the sūtra’s meaning; second, an explanation following the text.
Regarding the first major structural division (*dīrgha-khaṇḍa*) of the sūtra’s meaning: this chapter is divided into fourteen sections.

The first section, from "At that time" down to "These are the ten," consists of twenty-five lines of scripture; it clarifies that the Buddhas collectively empower the Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma to correctly expound the section on the Ten Practices for those who share the same name, Guṇakusuma.

The second section, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "the first stage of the Joyful Practice," consists of forty-three lines of scripture, which clarify the dharma-gate for correctly expounding the initial Joyful Practice.
The third section, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "the second Beneficial Conduct," consists of forty-two lines of scripture that clarify beneficial conduct (*anugrahacaryā*).
Thus, this entire chapter, comprising both prose and verse, contains fourteen segments of scripture in total.
The final two sections of the prose narrative consist of:
first, the section on the earth quaking and the offering of worship; second, the section on Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha observing the assembly and speaking in verse.
Following these are two hundred and two lines of scripture, comprising the section on praising the Dharma in verse.

The first fascicle, comprising both the upper and lower sections, consists in total of fourteen divisions; as these have their own internal structural boundaries within the sutra itself, there is no need for further formal sub-sectioning.
For instance, within the initial "Section on the Empowerment of Buddhas of Identical Names," there are four analytical gates:

first, clarifying the name of the samādhi; second, clarifying the number of Buddhas of identical names; third, clarifying the empowerment bestowed by those Buddhas of identical names; and fourth, clarifying the reason why the Buddhas collectively enter into meditative concentration with the Bodhisattva who shares their name.
Regarding the first point, the clarification of the name of the samādhi: why is it called the "Samādhi of Good Contemplation"?
As for *samādhi*, it refers to being free from dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*); it is an alternative name for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there are four kinds of dhyāna:
first, the dhyāna practiced by foolish worldlings; second, the dhyāna that examines meanings; third, the dhyāna of mindfulness of true thusness (*tathatā*); and fourth, the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
What is now called the Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation is the dhyāna of the contemplation of meaning.
In order to ascertain that Dharma, one must skillfully observe and contemplate with right mindfulness, establishing the gateway of the Dharma so as to serve as a model for future learners.

Regarding the second point, the number of Buddhas sharing the same name: it refers to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-fields, all of whom are named Guṇakūṭa (Forest of Merit), sharing the same name as those who have entered meditative concentration.
If one is deluded regarding the nature of the mind and its objects, ignorance is no different from the infinite atoms of all lands;
if one thoroughly realizes the source of the mind, wisdom and merit will be equal to the ten directions and inexhaustible.
Through his own single-minded penetration, he is no different from the merit and wisdom of the Dharma-realm.

Now that this Bodhisattva has entered this gate of samādhi, because his merit and wisdom accord with those of all Buddhas, he consequently receives the empowerment of Buddhas bearing the same name, clearly because his wisdom, understanding, and practice are identical to those of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and his merit and virtues are identical to theirs.
Third, regarding the explanation of the empowerment conferred by Buddhas of identical name, there are six kinds of empowerment:
first, empowerment through speech, because they praise and extol with words;
second, empowerment through the power of Vairocana’s vows, because he relies upon his past aspirations.
Third, the empowerment of the spiritual power of Vairocana, because it accords with the spiritual power of the Buddhas;
fourth, the empowerment of the roots of goodness of the assembly of bodhisattvas,
because their roots of goodness are identical.
Fifth, the Buddhas bestow the empowerment of wisdom, because [the bodhisattva] attains the ten kinds of unimpeded knowledge;
sixth, the Buddhas empower him by stroking his head with their hands, comforting him and granting permission to preach the Dharma.
The following clarifies that Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha arises from meditative concentration and correctly expounds ten types of practice-gates.
Within these ten types of practice as described below, the ten pāramitās constitute their essential substance.
The first is the Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*), which takes the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) as its essence.
It consists of forty-three lines of scripture, divided into five sections.

The first section, from "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Practice of Joy? down to "causing all sentient beings to rejoice and delight," comprises nine and a half lines of scripture; it elucidates the practice of the perfection of giving and constitutes the portion concerning training in all the practices of the Buddhas.

The second section, from "In whatever regions there are places of poverty" down to "not contradicting the minds of any sentient beings," consists of ten and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies that a Bodhisattva in this stage, upon seeing places of poverty, vows to be born into wealthy and noble families, and fully relinquishes their wealth, resources, as well as their own body and life, to benefit others.

The third section, from "Again, he thinks" down to "samyaksambodhi," consists of eight and a half lines of scripture, clarifying how the Bodhisattva, during the kalpa of famine, assumes a vast body and relinquishes it to relieve the destitute.

The fourth section, from "In this way, the bodhisattva" down to "neither seeing a great fruit nor seeing a small fruit," consists of six and a half lines of scripture, which clearly elucidates the stage of true non-conceptualization (*tathatā-nirvikalpa*).
The notion of a "person" (*pudgala*) refers here to one who repeatedly takes up a rebirth.
The notion of a "young man" (*māṇava*) refers to a youth, also called a "scholar-child.
The meaning is that one should give to all without discriminating between good and evil, old and young.

The fifth section, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva contemplates the past, future, and present" down to "the first joy," consists of seven and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies the stage of observing that the bodies of sentient beings are not solid and seeking a solid body so that they may attain eternal peace and stability.
The second is the Beneficial Conduct (*anugrahacaryā*), which has the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) as its essence.
It consists of forty-two lines of verse, divided into five sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s beneficial conduct? down to "attaining the equal and true Dharma praised by the Buddhas," there are six lines of verse, which clarify the stage of non-attachment to the objects of the five sensory realms.

2. From "When a bodhisattva maintains the pure precepts in this way" down to "the mind of omniscience," there are eight lines of scripture clarifying the section on how Māra and his celestial maidens cannot cause confusion or distraction.
3. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "nirvāṇa without remainder," there are eight lines of scripture clarifying the section on how Bodhisattvas do not afflict sentient beings with the five desires.

4. From "For what reason" down to "causing others to attain happiness," there are thirteen lines of scripture which clarify that only by being well-disciplined oneself can one preach the Dharma so that others may obtain their share of happiness.

5. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "the practice of benefiting others," there are six lines of scripture that clarify attaining the practice of transcending the world and entering the stage of profound wisdom.
The third is the practice of non-opposition, which has the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence.
It consists of thirty lines of scripture, divided into three sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "patience, gentleness, and flexibility," there are five and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on patience and gentleness that does not harm oneself or others.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "causing the minds of others to attain purity," there are thirteen and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on the bodhisattva’s endurance of physical and verbal harm.

3. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva... down to "...the practice of non-opposition," there are ten and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of patience through the contemplation of emptiness.
The fourth is the practice of being unyielding, which has the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) as its essence.
It consists of thirty-seven and a half lines of scripture, divided into three sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "because of the phrases and meanings of all Buddha-dharmas, one practices vigor," there are twenty-two and a half lines of scripture; this is the section clarifying that the Bodhisattva does not seek worldly gain, but practices vigor for the sake of seeking the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*) of a Buddha.

Second, the six lines of scripture from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to "He replied, 'I am able'" clarify the section on how Bodhisattvas enter the hells for the sake of sentient beings and undergo suffering without complaint.

3. From "Furthermore, if there should be a person" down to "unyielding conduct," there are eight and a half lines of scripture which clarify the section on how Bodhisattvas, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, do not shrink from the toil of undergoing suffering throughout many eons.
The fifth is the practice of being free from delusion and confusion, which takes the *dhyāna-pāramitā* as its essence.
It consists of forty-nine lines of verse, divided into six sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "cultivating the bodhisattva practice with a mind free from delusion and confusion," there are ten lines of verse, clarifying the stage of using right mindfulness to benefit sentient beings amidst the cycle of birth and death without confusion.

2. From "This bodhisattva" onwards, up to "the mind constantly recollects without interruption," there are nine and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the bodhisattva’s retention of what is heard and undisturbed right mindfulness.

3. From "For what reason" onwards, up to "never for a single moment has his mind been distracted," there are seven and a half lines of sūtra text, clarifying the section on how, through right mindfulness, one remains undistracted by pleasant or unpleasant sounds.

4. From "What is called right mindfulness without distraction" down to "and cannot destroy this bodhisattva's mind," there are eight and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the absence of any obstacles regarding hearing the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings.

5. From "The Bodhisattva enters into samādhi" down to "without distinction," there are five lines of sūtra that clarify the section on the patient endurance of observing that sound has no intrinsic substance.

Sixth: From "The bodhisattva thus accomplishes the tranquil conduct of body, speech, and mind" down to "free from deluded and distracted conduct," there are nine and a half lines of scripture that clarify the purity of body, speech, and mind, demonstrating their fitness for entering all dharmas without departing from the single nature.
The sixth is the practice of excellence (*sādhumatī*), which has the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as its essence.
It consists of forty and a half lines of scripture, divided into four sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "manifesting birth through skillful means," there are ten and a half lines of scripture; this section clarifies that the nature of wisdom is non-nature, and demonstrates the stage of manifesting birth through skillful means.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "acting as a place of reliance for all sentient beings," there are ten lines of scripture that clarify how Bodhisattvas, having realized that all phenomena within the mind and its objects are without intrinsic nature and without reliance, teach and transform sentient beings, providing them with a place of reliance.

3. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva... down to "...does not practice the right path," there are eleven lines of scripture, clarifying the section on mindfulness regarding the deliverance of sentient beings.

4. From "The Bodhisattva contemplates all sentient beings in this way... down to "...skillfully manifests [the path]," there are nine lines of scripture, clarifying the section on not attaining self-realized *nirvāṇa* because the deliverance of sentient beings is not yet complete.
The seventh is the Practice of Non-attachment, which takes the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) as its essence.
It consists of fifty-five lines of verse, divided into six sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "and there is no attachment even to the various Buddha-dharmas," there are twelve and a half lines of verse, clarifying the section on the Bodhisattva’s purification of Buddha-fields and making offerings to all Buddhas with a mind free of attachment.

Section Two: From "This bodhisattva" down to "is able to be thus unattached," there are fifteen lines of scripture that clarify the bodhisattva’s tireless making of offerings to the Buddhas, and the stage of practicing within the dharmas of worldly affairs while remaining constantly unattached in the midst of them.

3. From "In the Buddha-dharma, the mind is without obstruction" down to "giving rise to all roots of goodness while remaining unattached," there are eleven lines of scripture that clarify the section on observing the suffering of sentient beings and increasing great compassion.

4. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva... down to "...for what reason? there are nine and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on how the Bodhisattva constantly dwells within birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings without attachment.

5. From "The Bodhisattva forms this thought" down to "the mind is without weariness," there are nine lines of scripture that clarify the section on teaching and transforming sentient beings by contemplating all phenomena as being like illusions.

Sixth: From "Because of being free from weariness" down to "unattached conduct," there are seven and a half lines of sūtra, clarifying how the bodhisattva, seeing sentient beings who have not yet been tamed, goes to be born among them.
The eighth is the practice that is difficult to attain, which takes the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā* (perfection of aspiration) as its essence.
It consists of seventy lines of scripture, divided into six sections.
First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the roots of goodness of a single nature," there are four lines of scripture, clarifying the ten roots of goodness within this stage.
2. From "This bodhisattva" down to "attains non-retrogression," there are eight and a half lines of sūtra, clarifying the section on being untiring despite dwelling in suffering.

3. From "Although this bodhisattva realizes that sentient beings do not exist" down to "Why is that? there are ten lines of sūtra, clarifying the section on not abandoning yet not clinging to the realm of sentient beings.

4. From "The Bodhisattva deeply enters the realm of sentient beings" down to "not attaining the fruit," there are fourteen lines of scripture which clarify that while the Bodhisattva enters the realm of sentient beings without attachment, they do not neglect their constant manifestation in the world to deliver sentient beings.

5. From "The bodhisattva, having accomplished such [qualities]" down to "not clinging to the world," there are nineteen and a half lines of scripture that clarify the section on the mastery of teaching the Dharma without speaking.

Sixth: From "The bodhisattva is thus" down to "the eighth difficult-to-attain practice," there are fourteen and a half lines of scripture that clarify the section on practicing the bodhisattva path without seeking karmic retribution.
The ninth is the practice of wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-caryā*), which takes the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*) as its essence. This section is divided into five parts.
First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the inexhaustible eloquence of the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*," there are twelve lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the ten inexhaustible eloquences.

2. From "This Bodhisattva" down to "all are likewise," there are nine lines and a half of scripture, clarifying the section on the unimpeded eloquence of manifesting as a Buddha throughout the trichiliocosm.

Third: From "Furthermore" below, up to "and perform the Buddha-work," there are sixteen and a half lines of scripture. This section clarifies that within a single hair-tip site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there is inexhaustibility; it constitutes the part concerning manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood throughout all hair-tips and unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosms.

4. From "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva" down to "because he is well able to observe the characteristics of phenomena," there are six lines and a half of scripture, which clarify the ten types of mastery as constituent parts.

5. From "The bodhisattva, having accomplished these ten kinds of bodies" down to "because it is the source of all Buddha-dharmas," there are nine lines of scripture that clarify the aspect of being the locus of reliance for all sentient beings.
The tenth is the practice of reality (*tattvācaryā*), which has the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as its essence.
This section is divided into three parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "for the sake of making all completely pure," there are ten lines of scripture that clarify how the bodhisattva of this stage studies the truthful body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, thereby attaining the tenfold divisions of the Buddha’s wisdom.

2. From "This bodhisattva further gives rise to such a superior mind" down to "the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space," there are sixteen and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the aspect of not taking [final] enlightenment while teaching and transforming sentient beings through the power of vows.

3. From "This bodhisattva" below, down to "the tenth true practice," there are sixteen lines of scripture that clarify the section on the mastery of containing all lands within one's body, knowing faculties, and benefiting sentient beings.
In the section concerning the shaking of the earth and the offering of worship that follows, there are fifteen lines of scripture, which are divided into three parts.

First, from "At that time" down to "the subtle and wondrous sounds of the devas," there are five and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the shaking of the earth and the offering of worship.
2. From "In this world" down to "all are likewise," there is one and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section that concludes that all ten directions are likewise so.

3. From "Furthermore, by the Buddha’s spiritual power" down to "In all worlds of the ten directions it is likewise," there are eight lines of scripture that clarify the section on the assembly of Bodhisattvas from the Forest of Merits in the ten directions coming to bear witness.

For instance, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there are Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand Buddha-fields, all named Guṇakūṭa (Forest of Merit), in order to clarify that the ten practices are all-pervasive.

The name of the Buddha is "Universal Merit" (Samantaguṇa) in order to clarify that these ten practices are all-pervasive, which is to say that merit is all-pervasive; this is the fruit obtained within this stage, for it is the merit summoned by the pervasiveness of the practices.

The name of the Buddha is Universal Merit (*Samantaguṇa*). The phrase "each surpassing ten buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms [in them] throughout the ten directions" also clarifies the dharmas reached by wisdom.
It further clarifies that the measure of the gate of practice is vast, which is to say that the merit of the fruit of Buddhahood is vast.
The ten practices described above are established as progressive stages in relation to the ten *pāramitās*; they are inherently clear within the Dharma itself and need not be further explained.

These ten practices, taken as a whole, constitute a single gateway of practice within one moment of consciousness (*ekakṣaṇa*), devoid of before and after. One must not harbor views of temporal sequence or duration; rather, all must be understood as gateways for cultivation formed through the essence and function of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.
As it is said in the verses praising the Dharma, there are seven lines of sutra that clarify the non-interruption of the ten kinds of *gotra* (lineages); these are restated here in verse.
Regarding the phrase "extending as far as the *dharmadhātu*": *ji* means "to reach"; thus, it means "reaching as far as the *dharmadhātu*."
As for the section on verses (*gāthā-vibhāga*), there are two hundred and two lines of verse, with two lines constituting one verse, as clearly explained in the full text. 22.
The Twenty-second Chapter: The Storehouse of the Ten Inexhaustibles. Regarding the explanation of this chapter, the three introductory sections are as before.
First, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter: it should be understood that this chapter is titled according to the ten kinds of *dharmakośas* (treasuries) upon which it is based.
Second, regarding the explanation of the purpose for the chapter’s inclusion: in this stage, the ten kinds of practices have already been explained.

By means of these ten inexhaustible treasuries, the preceding ten practices are brought to completion so that they become inexhaustible, and the subsequent ten dedications are brought to fulfillment so that one may progress toward them; thus, the gates of practice are rendered free from obstruction. For this reason, this chapter must appear.
Regarding the intent of the three-part structural analysis (*changke*) of this sutra, it is divided into two sections:
first, the structural analysis of the intent of the sutra; second, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.

As for the structural analysis of the intent of the sutra: within this single chapter of the sutra, there are eleven major sections in total, corresponding to the titles of the ten scriptural collections (*daśapiṭaka*).
The text is as follows.

First, from the initial passage "At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakūṭa" down to "he preaches for the sake of sentient beings, causing them all to attain awakening," there are twenty-eight and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the formal presentation of the names of the ten inexhaustible treasuries (*daśākṣayākarāḥ*), along with the exposition of the ten types of dharma-factors of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-dharmapada*).
Within this section, it is further divided into six parts.
First, from "At that time, Guṇakusuma" down to "these are the ten," there are four lines of scripture which clarify the section on the formal exposition of the names of the ten treasuries (daśakośa).

The second section, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "having given rise to pure faith," consists of five and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the first presentation of the ten kinds of dharmas of faith.
