That this does not transcend the Tathāgata’s great, perfect, and wise illumination is called "coming together as one."
That the assembly is pure means it is devoid of mental consciousness.
That the Dharma-body is non-dual means it shares the same essential nature as the Buddha, being equal in its lack of intrinsic nature.
That there is no basis for reliance means there is neither attainment nor realization.
That one is able to spontaneously manifest the practice of the Buddha-body signifies that non-active wisdom is identical to the functioning of the Buddha.
Having sat upon this seat means one has realized the fundamental source of this Dharma-realm of the ten dedications.
That the Hall produced such extraordinary excellence was due to what is moved by wisdom (*jñāna*).
That it surpassed all the heavens was due to the response of the retribution of wisdom, not the work of sentient beings (*sattva*).
The commentary says:
The marks manifested by a bodhisattva arise from their practice.
The Master of the Treatise says in verse:
"A bodhisattva takes patience as a hanging garland, And always uses shame and remorse as garments and ornaments."
The precepts are the unguents and powdered incense; compassion, universally covering all, serves as the canopy.
The unmoving banner of meditative concentration is the upright mind, and the streamer of wisdom shatters all false views.
Abiding eternally in the sea of birth and death through skillful means, one brings benefit to sentient beings as their music and dance.
The *dhāraṇīs* proclaim the wondrous sound of the Dharma; those who hear it attain liberation as their song and music.
The above may be understood according to the text.

This section contains an unspeakable number of bodhisattvas from other quarters. This particular section consists of the various devas dwelling in the Tuṣita Palace; the total number of this assembly of bodhisattvas is one hundred and fifty million billion.
The bodhisattvas who have come from other directions are unspeakably many.
There are one hundred and eighty kinds of distinctions in the colors and types of the celestial thrones and palaces that serve as adornments, with each category numbering in the hundreds of billions.
The adornment of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas through their own merit is without limit or number.

Yet the great compassion, wisdom, and myriad practices brought forth in this assembly are intended solely to nurture the wisdom and great compassion of those who have first resolved for enlightenment and are newly born into the Buddha-family, so that they may become habituated and attain mastery.

The time does not change, the Dharma does not differ, and wisdom does not shift; it is just like a bamboo stalk that grows according to its natural course, where there is no difference between coarseness or fineness from its initial birth to its final end.
It is also like a child growing up; from the moment of birth, one becomes "large," yet there is no difference between that [initial] largeness.

This simply takes the ten practices (*daśapratipatti*), the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and the eleventh stage as the skillful means for nurturing the Way, while the fruit of Buddhahood resides in the initial aspiration (*prathamacittotpāda*).
Furthermore, within the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), each single abode possesses the functional efficacy of all ten abodes;
and because the ten abodes, the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are collectively and fully contained within the ten abodes.

It is just as when a divine dragon-horse king gives birth to a divine colt; though born in that same land, the colt resembles its father in speed and swiftness, yet its strength and utility do not yet equal those of its mother.

Just as a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment, by mounting the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, is born into the family of the Buddhas and possesses wisdom identical to that of the Buddhas; yet, their supernatural powers and spiritual faculties are not yet equal [to those of the Buddhas], as they await nourishment through the myriad practices of great compassion.
Although the function of cultivation is ultimately complete, the Dharma does not change and time does not shift; in the end, it does not transcend the power and function of the initial aspiration.
This is like the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood in three lifetimes within a single kṣaṇa, and likewise, it is as with Sudhana attaining the fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime.

The meaning of "one life" (*ekajāti*) is the attainment of non-arising (*anutpāda*). For now, we shall establish ten aspects of this non-arising: first, the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates;

second, the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of all views; third, the non-arising of emptiness; fourth, the non-arising of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); fifth, the non-arising of the non-transmigration of time and kalpas; sixth, the non-arising of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra; seventh, the non-arising of the silence of the sounds of the Dharma-teaching; eighth, the non-arising of the discrimination of wisdom; ninth, the non-arising of the spontaneous pervasiveness of the nature of supernormal powers; and tenth, the non-arising of the body prior to the manifestation before all sentient beings throughout all kalpas from antiquity to the present, within the limit of a single *kṣaṇa*.
Because there are these ten meanings of non-arising, it is said that "in one lifetime one shall attain Bodhi"; this is the intended meaning of this sutra.

By means of the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pratiṣṭhāna*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh stage, the skillful means of these dharmas serve to support the fruit of Buddhahood from the initial resolve. Because they sever the expectations of temporal sequence—since the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the fruit of Buddhahood are simultaneous and mutually function as essence and function—they are termed "the mutual adornment of awakening and practice."
This sutra employs the fruit to support practice so that practice may become free from attachment, and employs practice to support the fruit so that great attainments are accomplished.

For example, regarding the three vehicles, it is not yet said that Bodhisattvas possess the mind-made body; those who have not yet mounted the Buddha’s vehicle of omniscience infer that the fruit of Buddhahood lies beyond the eleventh stage, at the conclusion of the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Thus, the three stages of worthiness prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) constitute the path of provisions (*sambhāramārga*), the ten grounds constitute the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), and the fruit of Buddhahood is attained after the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas on the eleventh ground.
Such a teaching differs from the characteristics of the five stages within the Three Vehicles by being a complete inversion of their sequence; this shall be further clarified later.
Chapter Twenty-Four: Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. Regarding the explanation of this chapter, the three gates are as before.

First, regarding the explanation of the chapter title: it clarifies that ten bodhisattvas, beginning with Vajradhvaja, each come from different buddha-fields and dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven palace. Upon arriving at the place of the Tathāgata, they each magically manifest lion thrones of exquisite jewel-treasuries and then praise him with verses concerning the causes and fruits of the ten methods of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Therefore, this is named the "Chapter on Verses of Praise."
Regarding "differing Buddha-fields," this refers to proceeding from the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*) and entering the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*).
Second, concerning the purpose of this chapter: since this chapter aims to establish the dharma-gate of cause and effect within the ten stages of dedication, this chapter must be included.
In the third section, the word-by-word commentary, the meaning is divided into two parts:
first, a general outline of the sūtra’s intent; second, the word-by-word explanation of the meaning.
Regarding the first, the general outline of the sūtra’s intent: within the overall purport of this chapter, the text is broadly divided into eleven sections from beginning to end.

From "At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha" down to "and spoke these verses," there are fifty-two lines of scripture which clarify how the assembly of ten bodhisattvas, including Vajradhvaja and others, gathered from the ten directions, manifesting the non-duality of cause and fruit.
2. From "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world" onwards, there are ten verses that clarify how the Buddha reveals provisional means through reality.

3. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhadhvaja" onwards, there are ten verses that clarify praising the Buddha’s body, nature, and marks as being peerless; they further clarify that one must constantly approach and make offerings without weariness, for only when great vows are fulfilled can one tread the path traveled by the Buddha.

4. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīradhvaja" onwards, there are ten lines of verse which clarify that the Buddha and the Dharma can only be fully realized through a pure mind and pure conduct; they show that seeing the Buddha as having conditioned existence is insufficient.
5. From "The Bodhisattva Prabhāketu" onwards, there are ten verses which clarify how a single Buddha-body gives rise to many Buddha-bodies, as in the section on arising like an illusion.

Six: From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu" onwards, there are ten lines of verse clarifying that the Buddha’s wisdom is without dependence, without activity, and without fabrication; it is neither internal nor external, yet it is able to manifest forms universally and pervasively.

7. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu" onwards, there are ten lines of verse which clarify that all manifestations of the Tathāgata are not the product of insentient things, but are effortless and function through wisdom; they are the portions to be seen by sentient beings according to their own karma.
This section establishes the "knowledge of non-temporality" (akāla-jñāna) because it accords with the wisdom of practice as it manifests within one's own cultivation;
for "temporality" refers to sentient beings, and both long durations and short durations are attributes of sentient beings.

8. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīradhvaja" onwards, there are ten lines of verse clarifying that the Buddha-body is neither internal nor external; that the Buddhas of the ten directions are identical; that there is no body that is internal or external; and that it manifests as distinct portions in accordance with the karma of sentient beings.

9. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja" onwards, there are ten lines of verse which clarify how the Tathāgata, through wisdom that is mindless, thoughtless, and non-reliant, being by nature without interior or exterior, manifests before the ten directions, responding universally to all according to their faculties.

10. From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatradhvaja" below, there are ten lines of verse clarifying that the Tathāgata is devoid of mind, thought, and consciousness, and may thus be called a Buddha; yet sentient beings—whether possessing mind, thought, and consciousness, or abiding in a mind of quiescent extinction—are collectively unable to perceive even a portion of the Buddha.

11. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmadhvaja" onwards, there are ten lines of verse which clarify that one would rather undergo all manner of suffering than forsake a portion of the Tathāgata.
Above, each has explained a single dharma, together constituting the ten minds of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
Sometimes it is taught that there are sentient beings who cling to existence, and sometimes it is taught that there are no sentient beings who cling to non-existence.
As the verse by the Bodhisattva Nakṣatradhvaja in a sutra says: "Sentient beings have conceptual discrimination; these are the Buddhas and these are the worlds."
"One who thoroughly realizes the nature of phenomena sees neither Buddha nor world.

As the verse by Dharmadhvaja in the following text says: "One would rather constantly endure all the sufferings of the world than ever distance oneself from the Tathāgata or fail to behold his sovereign power."
These two verses both establish the existence and non-existence [of phenomena] to prevent falling into extreme views; other cases should be understood by analogy.

As for "observing the ten directions," the intention is to observe whether the minds of sentient beings are identical or distinct, and also to observe that the dharmas of all Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions are identical and non-dual.
Second, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: from the first section up to the fifty-second line of the sūtra, the meaning is divided into ten parts.
First, from "At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power" down to "came to where the Buddha was," is the section on the assembly of the various multitudes.
2. From "Their names were" down to "Dharmadhvaja Bodhisattva," this is the section enumerating the names of the ten bodhisattvas who have come.
3. From "The lands from which they came" down to "the World of Wondrous Fragrance," this is the section concerning the lands from which these bodhisattvas have come.

4. From "Each [attained] pure cultivation of the brahmacarya under a Buddha" down to "the Buddha Observing Banner," this constitutes the section enumerating the names of the Buddhas whom [the Bodhisattvas] served in their past lives.

5. From "All those bodhisattvas" down to "immeasurable merit," there are eight lines of scripture that clarify the section on the benefiting [of beings] through the manifestation of light and the display of virtue as the arriving bodhisattvas sit upon transformed seats.

Sixth: From "That which is called" down to "just like empty space," there are seven lines of scripture that clarify the section on how the bodhisattvas who have come see the wisdom of the pure *dharmakāya*—which has no basis—and travel freely and without obstruction throughout the ten directions to serve the Buddhas.
7. From "In this world" down to "there is no distinction," it clarifies the section on the conclusion that all ten directions are identical and have gathered here together.

8. From "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "the signs of spiritual transformations," it clarifies the section where the Tathāgata emits light that shines universally throughout the ten directions, so that the great assemblies on both sides can see one another.

9. From "In this way, the bodhisattvas... down to "...all have gathered," there are sixteen lines of scripture that clarify the section on the ultimate mastery of the Dharma, wherein the past causes of the assembled bodhisattvas—consisting of roots of goodness identical to those of the Buddha—have reached their consummation.

10. From "In the presence of the Buddha, by means of the light they were seen" down to the verse, there are two lines of scripture that clarify the concluding section on how the assemblies of bodhisattvas from the ten directions are identical to those in this world.

Second, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: within these fifty lines of scripture, ten topical gates are established: first, clarifying the Dharma from which the bodhisattvas of the ten directions have come;

second, explaining the meaning of the names of the bodhisattvas; third, explaining what the ten worlds symbolize; fourth, explaining the causes and effects of the ten Buddhas' names; fifth, explaining the nature of the seats upon which the ten bodhisattvas arrive at the Buddha’s abode to transform others; sixth, explaining the cause of the bodhisattvas’ bodily radiance; seventh, clarifying what Dharma the bodhisattvas have attained that enables them to freely transform and fill the ten directions; eighth, explaining the Dharma symbolized by the locations where the Tathāgata emits light; ninth, clarifying from whom the ocean-like assemblies of bodhisattvas who have come have generated the resolve for enlightenment; and tenth, clarifying the causes and effects of their progressive cultivation according to their respective stages.

First, regarding the Dharma from which the Bodhisattvas come: the Sūtra states that "each [Bodhisattva] is accompanied by a number equal to the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields. This clarifies the method of progressive advancement, for their wisdom and insight surpass those of the preceding stages.
The ten abodes are called "hundred," the ten practices "thousand," and the ten transferences "ten thousand.

Those who come from worlds beyond as many lands as there are atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields do so to clarify that the "worlds outside the clouds of the Dharma" are characterized by delusion, whereas reaching through wisdom is termed "coming to the place where the Buddha is."
Regarding the phrase "the dust motes of ten thousand Buddha-fields," this refers to the numerical count of delusion and awakening.
Second, as for explaining the meaning of the names of the Bodhisattvas: regarding the one named Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva, the term "Bodhisattva" has already been explained previously.
"Vajradhvaja" (Diamond Banner) clarifies the meaning of firmness and immovability.
The Bodhisattvas in the preceding ten stages of practice are called "forests," signifying that their practices provide extensive and abundant shelter and protection.

That a Bodhisattva at this stage is designated by the name "Banner" clarifies the practice of great compassion; dwelling within the great ocean of birth and death, they are able to crush and destroy all the afflictions of sentient beings, for their own wisdom remains unshakable.

The Ten Practices clarify the meaning of humbling oneself through practice to harmonize with enemies; the Ten Dedications clarify the meaning of mastery in destroying enmity through great wisdom that is firm and follows compassion.
This is in terms of the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhadhvaja (Firm Banner) is so named because this great compassion constitutes the essence of his precepts.
The Bodhisattva Vikramadhvaja (Valiant Banner) is so named because, in relation to this great compassion, he practices patience; this is the meaning of "valiance."
As for the Bodhisattva Light-Radiance Banner, this refers to taking great compassion as the essence of diligence; for he dwells long within the night of birth and death, illuminating it with wisdom.

As for the Bodhisattva Wisdom Banner (Jñānadhvaja), his essential nature is defined by great wisdom at this stage, which remains perpetually luminous amidst birth and death, constantly shattering darkness.
As for the Bodhisattva Jewel Banner (Ratnadhvaja), he is called the Jewel Banner because he clearly employs great compassion and great wisdom to skillfully deploy the net of the teachings.
Because enlightenment is noble and precious, it is not a worldly treasure.

As for the Bodhisattva Banner of Diligence (*Vīryaketu*), this stage is the seventh, the practice of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya-caryā*). It is characterized by the ability to skillfully know the faculties of others and engage with them through shared activities; while dwelling in the secular world, one is neither deluded nor defiled by the dust of the mundane—this is the meaning of the "Banner of Diligence."

As for the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, he represents this eighth perfection of the vow; because he is himself free from birth and death and benefits sentient beings by following his vows through wisdom, he is eternally stainless.

The Bodhisattva Nakṣatradhvaja is one who has perfected the wisdom of differentiation regarding the rank of the Dharma King of the perfection of power; he clearly and skillfully knows the faculties of all beings, just as the various sizes of the stars are all clearly visible.

Regarding the Bodhisattva Dharmadhvaja: this stage is the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*); because it skillfully establishes all phenomena such that nothing can destroy them, it carries the meaning of "Dharma-banner" (*dharmadhvaja*).
The above describes those who are capable of practicing the path.

Third, regarding the explanation of the name of the world: the land from which [the Buddha] comes is called the World of Wondrous Jewels (*Ratnavyūha*). This clarifies that the meaning of "wondrous" is that he universally bestows the sublime Dharma upon all sentient beings, which is a quality worthy of esteem.
The world named "Wondrous Joy" (Miaole) clarifies that great compassion constitutes the precepts; dwelling within birth and death to benefit sentient beings, it causes them to attain great bliss.
The world of "Wondrous Silver" clarifies that the essence of patience is perfected through the principle and wisdom of the Dharma-body, which is like white silver—supple, luminous, and pure.

As for the World of Wondrous Gold: it clarifies that through the benefit of diligence in worldly affairs, one remains free from weariness; without failing the True Principle, one brings forth blessings through the central virtue of yellow, such that everything becomes golden in color.
The World of Wondrous Maṇi illustrates that the pure and white functioning of the dharma-nature is inherently stainless and sovereign, as it constitutes the very essence of meditative concentration.
The World of Wondrous Vajra illustrates that wondrous wisdom, being devoid of intrinsic nature, can shatter all that is false and illusory without itself being destroyed.

The world of *Padma-vicitra* (Wondrous Red Lotus) refers to the red lotus; this clarifies that through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one is able to share its color and fragrance while remaining unstained.

The world of *Utpala-vicitra* (Wondrous Blue Lotus) refers to the blue lotus color; this clarifies that the eighth stage involves conduct where wisdom follows compassion, remaining pure and untainted. This is symbolized by the blue lotus, which, though situated in the mud, remains unstained.
The World of Wondrous Sandalwood (*Candana*) signifies that through this stage of the Dharma Master, one perfects the fragrance of preaching the Dharma.

The World of Wondrous Fragrance (*Gandha*) clarifies that at this stage, the merits of great wisdom and great compassion according to the position reach their consummation; by means of the subtle and wondrous wisdom that is non-reliant and non-constructive, one fulfills the wisdom of no coming or going throughout the ten directions, for the sound of the Dharma pervades everywhere without having any form.
It merely mentions "wondrous fragrance" and does not mention "form or type," because this indicates that it surpasses what preceded it.
These names for the worlds above [the first ten] are the dharmas within the practices of these ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

What is called the "World of Sublime Fragrance" (Gandhavatī) refers to the wondrous application of the principle and wisdom used to teach and transform sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
While worldly people take lands, mountains, and rivers to be their world, the wise take the wondrous application of wisdom and virtue to be their world.

Regarding the fourth explanation, the causes and effects of the ten Buddha names: the Sūtra states, "Each, in the presence of a Buddha, purely cultivated the Brahma-faring. This clarifies that one advances through the stages by practicing preparatory applications (*prayoga*) toward the fruit of Buddhahood; these are precisely the ten Buddhas mentioned below.

Regarding the so-called Buddha Akṣayadhvaja (Inexhaustible Banner): this clarifies that the giving performed at the stage of the ten dedications of great compassion is inexhaustible, and thus it is used as the name for the fruit of Buddhahood.
This giving is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Dedication" (*Parivarta*) below.

Regarding the Buddha Wind-Standard (Vāyu-dhvaja): it clarifies that the trigram Xun represents wind, represents pure white, represents speech, represents red, represents the sun, represents illumination, and represents pure white; this is because, just as wind has no form or color yet wafts all fragrances and odors, making them all pure.
Furthermore, Xun represents the rooster; because it knows the time and crows accordingly, it serves as a metaphor for this faculty of cognition (jñendriya) which bestows instruction.
Its upper position coincides with the Gate of Heaven, opening the way for all that is wholesome.
Xùn represents the beginning of the Yang energy that has already become full; it is the time for determining right and wrong.
It is because this is the time for the laws of fasting and purification.
Xùn represents speech, the mouth, and the gateway of the face, through which one discusses all manner of goodness.
He is able to subdue the Xin-Chou year; as for the Earthly Branch *Chou*, it represents the "youngest son," signifying the transformation of the ignorant through manifold teachings.
Speaking from this perspective, Feng-chuang Buddha is the fruit-name resulting from the wind-like transformation of this *śīla-pāramitā*.
The Buddha Victory Banner of Liberation is the fruit within the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*).
Once the power of patience is perfected, there is nothing that is not liberated.
This corresponds to the West, the trigram *Dui*, which carries the meaning of being lowly or downward-tending.

The Buddha Vidyutketu (威儀幢佛) presides over the fruition of Buddhahood in the north; he shares his name with the Buddha Vidyutjñāna (威儀智佛) of the northern direction within the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

He presides over the north as the Teacher’s Exemplar (*ācārya-sthāna*), for he receives the spiritually immature with dignified and orderly deportment (*īryāpatha*); thus, his title of fruition is derived from his conduct.

Regarding the Buddha Mingxiangdang (Luminous Sign Banner): because his name is identical to that of the Buddha Mingxiangzhi (Luminous Sign Wisdom) in the northeast during the stage of the Ten Faiths, it is clear that "Ming" (luminous) refers to Kan as the object to be remedied, Chou as the mind of faith, and Yin as the realization of principle; thus, it begins by using directions to symbolize the Dharma.

The master [of the cycle] is the Ox (Chou), which represents the mountain; the mountain is immovability, and immovability is purity. Purity is able to bring forth illumination, and illumination is the beginning of dhyāna.

At the commencement of entering meditative concentration, right wisdom unfolds, for the stage of the Ten Transferences does not depart from the dharmas believed in during the Ten Faiths; thus, one establishes oneself upon those dharmas.

This clarifies the essential nature of the Ten Transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*), for it is capable of giving rise to the luminous wisdom that manifests great compassion and benefits the mundane world.

It is similar to the Buddha Constant Banner (*Sadāsena*) and also resembles the Buddha Ultimate Wisdom (*Niṣṭhājñāna*) of the sixth stage within the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). In general, these names for the fruits of Buddhahood are established based on the perfection (*pāramitā*) attained through advancement through the respective stages; they do not, in total, depart from the fruit of what is believed during the Ten Faiths.
This is just as when Sudhana reaches the fruit of Maitreya Buddha, he is directed back to see Mañjuśrī;

this clarifies that Mañjuśrī represents the stage of the fruit of faith for those beginning their enlightenment, wherein the practice of setting out and advancing does not depart from the original traces.

Now, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva dwells on Mount Qingliang, located in the northeast of this realm of Jambudvīpa; presiding over the position of Gen (艮), he represents the beginning of enlightenment and the first manifestation of wisdom, and is therefore known as the Youthful Bodhisattva.

To speak according to reality, this is fundamentally the wondrous wisdom of the principle of non-nature of the Buddhas of the ten directions; there is no attaining Buddhahood that does not proceed through it.
This gate is possessed by all sentient beings without exception, yet they fail to see it because they are deluded by their own confusion regarding this principle.
If one awakens to the principle, it is the active manifestation of discrimination; it is only through meditative concentration that this becomes clear.
*Gen* (艮) signifies "stopping.
For all other instances, follow this precedent and understand them by correlating their names with their respective positions.

Fifth, regarding the explanation of the substance of the lion thrones upon which the various bodhisattvas come to transform beings, the sutra states: "They emanated exquisite lion thrones of jewel-treasuries. This is because they employ the net of teaching and practice to benefit sentient beings through the Dharma-jewel.
A jeweled net covers the seat; within the stage of the Ten Faiths, the substance of the seat is established by way of its fruit, taking the treasury of jewel lotuses as its essence.

Within the stage of the Ten Abidings, it is established as its essence by way of attaining the Tathāgata’s wisdom and great compassion, thus taking the Vairocana-treasury as its essence; this lion throne is therefore named the Vairocana-treasury.
In the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*), one sits upon a lion throne purified by conduct and free from defilement, which takes the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*) as its substance.

In the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmana*), one clarifies the abode of great compassion within birth and death, establishing teachings and practices that universally encompass all phenomena without being restricted to any single one; thus, the substance of the throne is simply named "Jewel" (*ratna*) without limitation to specific types of material, for its teaching and practice pervade everywhere to rescue sentient beings, and the throne is covered above by a net of jewels.

Regarding the sixth explanation of the Bodhisattva’s bodily radiance: it clarifies that the Bodhisattva of this stage dwells in the world for the benefit of beings through the practice of great compassion; relying on wisdom to illuminate sentient beings, they possess a pure light that shines perpetually.

Seventh, regarding what dharmas a bodhisattva attains to achieve mastery, the sūtra states: "One perceives the pure dharmakāya which has no basis," because the wisdom-body manifests in immeasurable ways.

This clarifies that one perceives the nature of phenomena as being without dependence; thus, all ignorance becomes the sublime function of wisdom, enabling unhindered transformation in every direction.

Regarding the eighth explanation of the significance of the Tathāgata’s emission of light: it clarifies that light is emitted from the wheels beneath the feet during the stage of the Ten Faiths, taking faith as the beginning.
The toes of the feet represent the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), clarifying the initial entry into the stage of the sages (*āryabhūmi*).
The insteps of the feet represent the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), clarifying that one initiates practice based on the Dharma-body of the sage-nature (*āryadharmakāya*).

As for the emission of light from above the knees during the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), this clearly symbolizes the radiance of the Dharma; for the knees are the locus from which a person’s sitting, rising, turning, and stretching are freely accomplished.

This dharma-gate of the stage of dedication is the great wisdom that returns from the mundane to the true liberation free from defilement; it benefits sentient beings through compassionate vows, abiding in birth-and-death while ever remaining in nirvana, and dwelling in nirvana while being unimpeded and sovereign within birth-and-death—a state symbolized by the radiating of light.
The space between the eyebrows on the tenth stage represents the light of the fruit of the Middle Way.
As for the ninth point, clarifying from whom the various bodhisattvas develop their resolve: it is all from within their own minds' beginningless conceptualization.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the beginning of the arousal of the bodhicitta; because one realizes that this beginningless ignorance is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), one shares the same roots of goodness as the Tathāgata Vairocana of the ten directions.
If one is separated from this wisdom, there will be no time for attaining Buddhahood, nor will there be a vision of the Buddha-sun.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Such Bodhisattvas all share the same roots of goodness as those of Vairocana in the past. This clarifies that by penetrating one's own ignorance, one realizes the essence of Great Wisdom, which is shared by all Buddhas.

Regarding the tenth [section], clarifying the cause and effect of progressive cultivation according to the stages: it clarifies that the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja is the person who practices, the World of Wondrous Jewels (Ratnavyūha) is the practice itself, and the Buddha Anantadhvaja is the fruit of that practice.
The remaining nine examples should be understood by analogy with this.
Below are ten sections of verse, each verse consisting of ten lines, with one verse for each [stage].
The dharmas being versified are the gates of the comprehensive governance within this very stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), as they are fully contained within the text itself.

Furthermore, if the prose commentary were expanded, the text would become cumbersome and the meaning submerged; the manifestation of the Dharma would be difficult to comprehend, and only then could it be explained by way of summary.
The rest is fully contained within the text itself.
Chapter Twenty-five: The Ten Dedications. Regarding the explanation of this chapter, there are three sections as previously stated.
First, regarding the explanation of the title of this chapter: Why is this chapter named "The Ten Dedications" (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*)?
The answer is:

Although one is born into the family of the wisdom of all Buddhas at the beginning of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), and although there is the seventh perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) which accomplishes the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), because this is the initial stage, the mind that cultivates true reality and transcendent wisdom (*lokottara-citta*) predominates, while the practice of compassionate deeds is still inferior.
In the stage of the Initial Resolve, atop Mount Sumeru, he saw a bhikṣu named Meghaśrī, from whom he attained the gate of the light of wisdom of all Buddhas through mindfulness.

Although one knows that subsequently, through the ten virtuous spiritual friends, the ten pāramitās mutually interpenetrate, such that all practices are already fully perfected in their harmonious integration.

However, one must follow the practice gates according to their original positions, as their superior or inferior qualities differ entirely; this clarifies that within the state of sameness, there is a specific progression toward advancement.

For instance, among the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), it is the first stage of practice; thus, the bhikṣu from the country of the Three Eyes is named Sudarśana (Good Vision), and he uses his walking meditation in the forest to symbolize these ten practices.

Observing the faculties of sentient beings with the eye of wisdom, the eye of insight, and the Dharma-eye, one transforms them so that they transcend the world; thus, what is symbolized by the bhikṣu constitutes the ten practices.
Because it provides vast shelter for the multitude, it is symbolized by the forest.

Thus, within these ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), it is clarified that in the preceding two stages, the mind directed toward transcending the mundane was predominant while the practice of great compassion was deficient; therefore, by employing the wisdom of all Buddhas attained at the initial stage of the ten abidings (*vihāra*) to perform supramundane practices during the ten practices (*caryā*) for the benefit of living beings within the mundane world, they are called "dedications."
Turning back from the ultimate truth to enter the mundane world to benefit sentient beings is called "dedication" (pariṇāmanā).
Therefore, the spiritual friend who symbolizes this stage is represented by the name of the incense merchant, Blue Lotus (Utpala).

This dharma-gate of the ten dedications is like the method of compounding incense: by combining various fragrances into a single pellet, they mutually benefit one another to form a pervasive fragrance.

The ten dedications are likewise so: by means of the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body—precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—one blends together great kindness and great compassion, the various *pāramitās*, the four means of integration, the four immeasurables, and all the gates of worldly toil such as nirvana and birth-and-death, to collectively form a single true fragrance of the Dharma-realm. Since all of these take the Great Vow as their primary source, this stage is called "Dedication."
The elder named Utpala symbolizes that the practice of this stage is unstained by defilement, being pure with respect to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, "elder" (śreṣṭhin) clarifies that he dwells among the worldly stream yet his wisdom excels that of ordinary people; thus he is called an elder.

The blue lotus flower signifies that among all flowers, this flower is foremost in both color and fragrance; it symbolizes the practice-gates of the five stages, as this Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications is the foremost.

Why is this so? It is because this Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications, through the power of its great vows, unifies compassion and wisdom, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana, into the true sovereignty of a single Dharma-realm; thus it can support the fruition of Buddhahood in the preceding stages, enabling the fulfillment of the gates of Samantabhadra’s practices.
It also accomplishes the practice-gates of the subsequent stages—the ten bhūmis and the eleventh bhūmi—so that one may attain mastery through habitual cultivation.

This clarifies that the preceding ten abodes, ten practices, ten bhūmis, and the eleventh bhūmi are all, in their entirety, the perfect integration of principle and wisdom, great vows, and great compassion within this stage of the ten dedications.

Therefore, because these ten stages of dedication encompass everything from the preceding to the succeeding stages, they are represented by the blue lotus; among all flowers, its color and fragrance are the most excellent, surpassing all other blossoms.
Furthermore, it symbolizes that among all the three realms, this Tuṣita Heaven is preeminent.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the three periods of time in the world reside in this heaven, there to cultivate the bodhicitta and fulfill their transformation of the world.
Above, in the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, there is pleasure because of the abundance of heedlessness.
Furthermore, above that, in the Form and Formless Realms, there is pleasure because of the predominance of a mind characterized by purity.
The heavens below Yāma and Trāyastriṃśa are places where the gods are attached to pleasure, for they lack contentment.
The gods of the Four Great Kings dwell on four sides, for they do not occupy a central position.
Therefore, this heaven is situated among the heavens of the desire realm, occupying a middle position between those above and below.
Furthermore, this heaven is the common dwelling place for those who have cultivated the three types of merit.
What are these three? First, the cultivation of giving; second, the observance of precepts; and third, the cultivation of meditative concentration.
Because the other various devas do not cultivate these three merits in equal measure, they all possess them in partial excess.
Because they have cultivated the two merits of precepts and giving, other devas are either prone to much negligence or take great pleasure in purity.
Therefore, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* states: "Those who desire to long for the bodhicitta shall be reborn in this heaven."
Therefore, this deva expounds these ten gates of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), because the representation of the Dharma is preeminent here.

Furthermore, as it lies below the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens and above the Paranirmitavaśavartin and Nirmāṇarati heavens, this deva occupies a central position among these five celestial realms. Thus, the ten dedications are taught so that wisdom and compassion may be harmonized and balanced to abide in the center; for this reason, the ten dedications are taught to this deva, and this location is used to represent the Dharma-gate being taught.
Furthermore, the meaning of the Dharma-position symbolized by the incense merchant named Blue Lotus can be understood through this principle.

Therefore, it is called the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), because they symbolize the gate of the integration and differentiation of the ten *pāramitās*—the unity and multiplicity, the identity and distinctness; because they constitute ten kinds of dedication to manifest inexhaustibility; and because the winds of great vows blow upon the clouds of wisdom and compassion, causing them to rain universally.
Second, regarding the purpose of this chapter’s introduction: its general meaning may be understood as previously described.
Third, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, it is divided into two parts:
first, the structural outline of the sutra’s intent; second, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning.

Regarding the general structural outline of the sutra's meaning: from the section beginning with "At that time" down to the end of the thirty-third fascicle, the entire text is divided into fifteen long sections.

First, from the beginning of the chapter, starting from "At that time" down to "the dedication of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present," there are thirty-three lines of scripture; these constitute the section on the Ten Dedications as taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions through the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja.

The second section, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to "the Buddhas of the past, future, and present have already taught, will teach, and are now teaching," consists of nine and a half lines of scripture; this is the portion that formally enumerates the titles of the ten dedications.

From this point onward—beginning from "O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva... and continuing through the thirty-third fascicle up to "...all attain purity and reach the other shore"—there are ten fascicles of scripture that clarify the section on the progressive practice gates of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) in accordance with the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*). This constitutes the main exposition.
The ten dedications above each constitute one *pāramitā* practice, forming ten sections in total.

From the thirteenth section, "By the Buddha’s spiritual power," down to "In all worlds, the Tuṣita palaces are likewise," there are sixteen lines of scripture; this constitutes the section on the shaking of the earth and the presentation of offerings.

Section Fourteen: From "At that time, again by the Buddha’s spiritual power" down to "it was likewise so," there are ten lines of scripture clarifying the section on the gathering and testimony of the Bodhisattvas of Identical Name.
Fifteenth: From "At that time" onwards, there are six and a half lines of scripture clarifying the section on the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja’s recitation of verses.
Within the first segment, "The Buddhas Empower Vajradhvaja," it is further divided into four sub-sections.

1. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja" down to "expounding the ten dedications of all bodhisattvas," there are eighteen and a half lines of scripture. This section clarifies the stage where the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and all Buddhas bestow empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon him by means of identical names.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, you should rely on the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority" down to "because of the light of the unobstructed Dharma," there are four and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on the Buddhas’ exhortation to expound the dharma-gate of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

3. From "At that time" onwards, up to "by the power of their roots of goodness," there are six lines of scripture clarifying the section on the ten kinds of empowerment through the dharmic powers bestowed by all Buddhas upon Vajradhvaja.

4. From "At that time" onwards, up to "all Buddhas of the past, future, and present dedicate," there are four lines of scripture clarifying the section in which all Buddhas stroke the crown of the head with their hands, causing the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja to emerge from samādhi and preach the Dharma.

Second, regarding the exegesis of the text according to its meaning, ten sections are established: first, the explanation of the causes and conditions for entering samādhi; second, the explanation of the name of the samādhi;

third, clarifying the distance of the various Buddha-fields from which the Buddhas have come; fourth, clarifying the number of the Buddhas; fifth, clarifying the common name of the Buddhas and its objective basis; sixth, clarifying the manifestation of the Buddhas before one’s presence and their praise; seventh, clarifying the Buddhas’ collective entry into meditative absorption; eighth, clarifying the causes and conditions for the Buddhas’ touching of the crown of the head; ninth, clarifying the emergence from concentration, the addressing of the assembly, and the eulogy of the Dharma; tenth, clarifying the formal exposition of the Ten Dedications.

First, regarding the causes and conditions for entering samādhi: it is because one wishes to enable future student bodhisattvas to know the proper rules of conduct; because one wishes to make clear and pure the manifest wisdom through the skillful means of samādhi; because one wishes to know that the power of samādhi can cause the wisdom of preaching the Dharma to be discerning, sovereign, and distinct; and because the dharma-rules of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are consistent with this—therefore, it is necessary to enter meditative concentration.
Regarding the second explanation of the name of this samādhi: why is it called the "Wisdom-Light Samādhi"?
It is because the gateway to the accomplishment of great compassion is not manifested without great wisdom.

As revealed in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the Buddha’s wisdom is shown to be identical with and unified within one's own mind; through the samādhi of skillful means—which is effortless and thoughtless—it is like clear, still water in which the sun, moon, and myriad forms naturally appear with perfect clarity.

Within the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), the samādhi is named "Excellent Reflection" (*suvicintita*); this clarifies that one discerns the distinctions between principles and phenomena according to their specific circumstances, which is called "excellent reflection.

Similarly, the samādhi entered during these ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is named "Light of Wisdom" (*jñānāloka*); this clarifies that one practices compassion through wisdom and remains unstained while dwelling in the mundane world. By means of this light of wisdom illuminating the mundane, there is nothing within the mundane that is not true.
Therefore, the elder who sells incense is represented by the blue lotus to clarify his state of being unstained while remaining in the secular world.

The bhikṣus of the ten abodes and ten practices are taken as the primary exemplars to clarify the merit of transcending the secular world; this is entirely modeled upon the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) encountered by Sudhana.
Therefore, because this stage possesses the sovereign mastery of perfect compassion and wisdom, the samādhi is named "Light of Wisdom.
As for the illumination of the distant and near Buddha-fields that come forth, it clarifies the progressive advancement through the stages and the expansion of wisdom.

The stage of the Ten Practices (Daśabhūmika) is described as [the number of] atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra*), while this stage is described as [the number of] atoms in one hundred thousand Buddha-fields; this indicates that its superior progress surpasses the former.

Regarding the number of Buddhas of the four directions, the Sūtra states: "In each of the ten directions, there are [Buddhas as numerous as] the atoms in one hundred thousand Buddha-fields. This clarifies that the wisdom-practice (*jñānakarma*) of further cultivation is vast, for it accords with the functional power of the wisdom-essence (*jñānadhātu*) of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

Regarding the five clarities where all Buddhas share the same name as the object of focus: why is it that the Buddhas of the ten directions bear the same name as the bodhisattva who has entered meditative absorption—namely, Vajradhvaja—and appear before him? There are two reasons:
first, it is as previously explained regarding the convergence of wisdom through progressive cultivation;

second, by appearing before the bodhisattva in the form of the Buddha’s name and the Tathāgata’s body, it clarifies that one is not deluded regarding their respective positions, thereby severing doubts concerning self and others and establishing the Dharma-seal.
Furthermore, since wisdom is already unified and the body is likewise non-dual,

the sixth section clarifies that the Buddhas appear to praise the Vajradhvaja; this clarifies that they bestow empowerment through speech to cause him to enter meditative absorption, so that he may not be confused regarding the Dharma-seal, and also causes his future disciples to sever all remaining doubts.
Furthermore, since their bodies and wisdoms are identical, their preaching of the Dharma is also equal.
Seventh, regarding the common empowerment (*sādhāraṇādhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas when entering meditative absorption: what is called "common empowerment" has two meanings.

First, it is because the Buddha's virtues are united and harmonized through one's own wisdom. Second, it is because all Buddhas, in accordance with that wisdom, bring together the two conditions of power (*bala*) and influence; this is termed "empowerment."
Furthermore, it is for the sake of severing the delusions of others even though one has no doubts oneself;
and because the Buddhas bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) so that the Dharma may be established.
Moreover, it is said that there are six types of Buddha-empowerment:
First is the empowerment of the same name, because they share the same name;
second is the empowerment of manifesting the body, because [the Buddha] appears before them;
third is the empowerment of verbal praise, because he praises them with words.
Fourth is the empowerment through the power of Vairocana’s past vows;
fifth is the empowerment through the ten kinds of dharmas, as clarified by the text itself;
sixth is the empowerment by the hands of the Buddhas of the ten directions rubbing the crown of one's head.
Eighth, regarding the causes and conditions for the Buddhas stroking the crown of his head with their hands: why do they stroke the crown of his head?

It clarifies the functional utility of the right hand; it clarifies that the Buddhas receive and guide him with their right hands, causing him to emerge from meditative absorption and preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, because one's own activity and the activities of all Buddhas reach one another;
and because all Buddhas grant permission to reach the limit of reality (*dharmaparyanta*), for within each respective stage there exists the reality that constitutes the limit of that stage.
9. To clarify the emergence from meditative absorption and the proclamation of the Dharma to the assembly, the scriptural text itself provides the details.
10. To clarify the formal exposition of the ten kinds of dedication, it is as found in the subsequent sections of the sutra.
This concludes the first section consisting of thirty-three lines.

The second section, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva" down to "the Buddhas of the past, future, and present have already taught, will teach, and are now teaching," comprises nine and a half lines of scripture; it formally enumerates the titles of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
This will be explained in detail later according to its respective section.

Third, within the section on the progressive cultivation of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) in accordance with the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*), it begins from the passage: "O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
What is the dedication of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva that rescues and protects all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings?
Within this section, there are two points:
first, to analyze the meaning of the scripture for this specific section; second, to provide a word-by-word explanation.
Within these ten dedications, there are one hundred and eighty sections of scripture. To explain the meaning of the scripture for each respective section:
within this section titled "The Dedication of Saving and Protecting All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings," it is further divided into ten subsections.

1. From "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s dedication of merit for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings? down to "such immeasurable roots of goodness," there are five lines of scripture that clarify the cultivation of the six *pāramitās* and the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) to accomplish the first stage of dedication.

2. From "The time of cultivating roots of goodness" down to "causing all to attain omniscience," there are fourteen and a half lines of sūtra text, clarifying the section on generating great vows and the mindfulness of delivering sentient beings.

3. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," there are thirty-three and a half lines of scripture that clarify the impartial division between the near and the distant, and between the good and the evil.

4. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva" down to "dwelling where the Buddhas dwell," there are twenty lines of scripture that clarify how, by taking the dharmas of all Buddhas as supreme conditions, one deeply plants one's own roots of goodness and vows to share them with sentient beings.

5. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to "causing them to attain liberation," there are thirty-eight lines of scripture which clarify how the bodhisattva enters the evil realms to undergo suffering on behalf of all sentient beings, thereby enabling those beings to obtain their share of happiness.

Sixth: From "The Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, further form this thought" down to "causing them to reach the other shore," there are seven lines of scripture which clarify how the Bodhisattvas, by means of their own roots of goodness, cause all sentient beings to attain ten kinds of ultimate happiness.

7. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to "immeasurable roots of goodness," there are five lines of scripture that clarify the section concerning how bodhisattvas, according to their capacities, rescue and protect sentient beings so that they may transcend birth and death, make offerings to all Buddhas, and draw near to virtuous friends.

8. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "in order to cause all sentient beings to sever their doubts," there are eleven and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the great vows of the Bodhisattva: although sentient beings are numerous, they do not require many sages; rather, I alone am capable of delivering them all to the end.

9. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "The Dedication of Saving and Protecting All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings," there are thirty-one lines of scripture that clarify the stage of dedication wherein the Bodhisattva shines universally like the sun, seeking no reward for his kindness and remaining unattached to the phenomena of sentient beings.

10. From "At that time" onwards, up to the recitation of the verses, there are six and a half lines of sūtra text clarifying the section on the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja observing the assembly and reciting verses.
Regarding the word-by-word commentary: why is this called the "Dedication for the Protection and Rescue of All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings"?
There are two meanings for explaining these names and titles:
first, to clarify the sequential methods of practice according to the stages; second, to clarify the designations of the fundamental stages themselves.

Regarding the first—clarifying the sequential methods of practice according to the stages—it is as follows: within the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), one seeks all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*) during the initial stage of the Abode of Generating the Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*).

This bodhisattva gives rise to the mind by taking as objects of focus the ten kinds of dharmas that are difficult to obtain; that is to say, they give rise to the mind through the ten powers of a Tathāgata’s wisdom, such as the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible, and is thus born into the family of the Buddhas as a true son of the Buddha.

As it is said among the ten practices: practicing the conduct of joy, one acts as a great donor, able to bestow all possessions without regret or stinginess, taking the practice of the bodhisattva path as the object of focus.

Among these ten dedications, the first dedication is named "Rescuing and Protecting All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings. It takes the six *pāramitās* and the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*) as its objects of focus. By means of the great wisdom, dharma-body, and unattached pure conduct attained through the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*), it gives rise to vast vows and practices. Abiding within birth and death, it takes the six *pāramitās* as the primary conduct and compassion, joy, sympathetic joy, and equanimity as the conditions for benefiting sentient beings while remaining in the cycle of existence. Therefore, it is called the dedication of "Rescuing and Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings."

One takes loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity as protection; one takes the six pāramitās, which are supramundane dharmas, for the purpose of abandoning the perception of sentient beings, because these practices of the six perfections constitute supramundane conduct.

Therefore, while this established sequence exists in its entirety within the single moment of the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*) in the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is merely due to the sequential nature of names and words on paper or bamboo slips that divisions are produced; it is not because there is any sense of temporal succession within the Dharma itself.

As illustrated within the Dharma-allegory of Sudhana’s journey during the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), his observation of the great ocean in the kingdom of Samudramukha—including the offerings made by the ten kings such as the asuras—signifies the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Nevertheless, the sequential progression of the teaching’s gates must be maintained; for if it were not so, it would cause later students to sink into worldly existence and fail to advance.

Second, regarding the name of the fundamental stage: taking the Dharma-body of Great Wisdom as the essence of detachment, and the ten *pāramitās* and four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) as the objects of focus for dwelling in birth-and-death to rescue and protect sentient beings, it is therefore called the "Dedication of Rescuing and Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings."

Because the mind takes wisdom as its essence and has no basis for support, those who are to be rescued and protected have no fixed abode; because sentient beings are without marks, there is truly no agent who performs the act of rescuing and protecting. Thus, because sentient beings are themselves true and without arising or ceasing, it is called the "Dedication of Rescuing and Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Mark of Sentient Beings."
The accomplishment of this first Dharma-gate of Dedication possesses five conditions: first, the condition of possessing the understanding that one's own Dharmakāya is inherently pure and liberated;

second, the condition of attaining great wisdom and liberation; third, the condition of possessing the power of great vows to serve all Buddhas and benefit sentient beings; fourth, the condition of fulfilling the superior practices of the ten pāramitās; and fifth, the condition of not abandoning any sentient being through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Only by possessing these five dharmas can one accomplish this first dedication.
How does one practice the purity of the dānapāramitā and the śīlapāramitā?
It is because by being able to relinquish unwholesome dharmas, the essence of morality (śīlaskandha) becomes naturally pure.
How does one cultivate the kṣāntipāramitā?

When the perfections of generosity and ethical discipline have already been accomplished, one must cultivate the power of patience. Because the essence of generosity consists in the ability to relinquish, it serves as the cause for the purity of the essence of ethical discipline; however, the essence of patience requires the application of deliberate cultivation and study. Since patience functions to prevent others from insulting or humiliating one, rather than involving the voluntary relinquishment of one's own possessions, it is necessary to apply deliberate effort in training in patience.
How does one give rise to the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*)?

Since the essence of patience (*kṣānti*) consists in the natural subsiding of anger and resentment, rather than the joyful cultivation of deeds that benefit others, it is necessary to initiate such deeds for the benefit of others; this is the meaning of diligence in this stage.

How does one give rise to the perfection of vigor and enter the perfection of meditative concentration? Because the practice of diligently benefiting sentient beings through vigor may involve much distraction and agitation, it is necessary to enter the perfection of meditative concentration.
How does one dwell in the perfection of wisdom?
Because through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), pure wisdom can be generated.
What are great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity?

Because these six *pāramitās* consist largely of supramundane states of mind, they are further augmented by the dharmas of benefiting sentient beings—compassion (*karuṇā*), joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—thereby harmonizing all practices.

Having thus balanced the aforementioned six perfections and four immeasurable minds, wisdom and compassion attain their proper place; this is the initial gate of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). This dharma-gate of dedication is possessed in its entirety from the stages of the ten faiths (*śraddhā*), the ten abidings (*vihāra*), and the ten practices (*caryā*), yet it is only upon reaching this fundamental stage that they are made perfectly equal.

If one considers this from the perspective of the gate of practice through understanding (*pratipatti-mukha*), there are such gradations; however, from the perspective of the gate of principle and wisdom (*jñāna-mukha*), there is altogether no dharma of before or after, beginning or end.

Hereafter follows the method for cultivating and harmonizing the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) within their respective stages, as fully elucidated in the subsequent text. There is no need for further explanation; simply practice according to the text as it is presented.
Why are the six pāramitās alone considered the practice for benefiting sentient beings?

It is to clarify that within the gateway of great compassion, one first causes sentient beings to transcend the mundane world, and only thereafter causes them to enter into the cycle of birth and death.
In the following verses, there are fifty-six lines that versify this dedication of "Rescuing and Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.
Within this section, it is clarified that the practices performed by the Bodhisattva are harmonized and appropriately balanced.
Two lines form one verse, as is fully contained within the text itself; one should practice by grasping its intended meaning.

In this section, the *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving) serves as the primary theme, with the other nine *pāramitās* acting as its companions. Sudhana, the merchant of incense known as Blue Lotus (*utpala*), represents the person who practices these deeds. This can be understood by reflecting upon the significance of his name.
Regarding the practices performed therein: "the incense-seller" refers to one who sells incense; such a person is able to prepare various incenses, blend them together, and sell them to others.
The practice of this stage has already been explained previously.
Second is the "Non-Perishing Dedication" (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*), which takes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) as its essence, with the other nine perfections as its companions.
Sudhana, taking the boatman named Vāsava—here translated as "Mastery"—to represent one who practices the path, found him dwelling on the seashore outside the gate of the city of Lokeśvarā;
he was abiding in the dharma-gate of the practice of the Banner of Great Compassion.

It clarifies that within this stage of dedication, great compassion serves as the essence of the precepts; by viewing the ocean of all birth and death, one causes it to become the ocean of all great wisdom. Because one dwells within the ocean of birth and death while attaining mastery, it is called "Mastery" (Vasitā).
The detailed explanation is as found in the sutra text.

Furthermore, representing the nature of the precepts as being like the ocean—pure by nature and not harboring corpses—it clarifies that the Dharma-body is fundamentally pure and does not harbor the corpses of afflictive defilements.
The broad meaning follows the text. Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that asks, "O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s ‘Unshakeable Dedication’ (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*)?", the meaning of this section of the scripture is divided into two parts:
First, a general outline of the meaning of this section of the sutra; second, an explanatory commentary following the text.

Regarding the first, the general outline of the meaning of this section of the sutra: from the words "O Son of the Buddha" down to the conclusion of the verses, the entire section is divided into six parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "because of the realm of immeasurable and innumerable practices," there are thirteen and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the stage where Bodhisattvas attain indestructible faith.

2. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, up to "causing all great vows to be fully satisfied," there are eleven lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the Bodhisattva’s sustaining power in teaching and transforming sentient beings.

3. From "The Bodhisattva, in this manner" down to "incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) robes were spread upon the ground," there are thirty-three lines of scripture that clarify the section on the adornment of the resultant environment (*niṣyanda-phala*).

4. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the supreme mind of faith and understanding dedicated [to awakening]," there are twenty-one and a half lines of scripture. These clarify that the Bodhisattva, by means of the aforementioned adornments of the fruits of reliance (*niṣyanda-phala*), makes offerings to all Buddhas, all for the sake of liberating sentient beings.

5. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, up to the "Second Indestructible Dedication," there are twenty-four lines of scripture which clarify that Bodhisattvas are able to follow the cycle of birth and death to deliver sentient beings, participate in all their activities, and never abandon the portion of seeking the pure dharmas of omniscience and so forth.

Sixth: From "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" down to the verses, there are seven lines of scripture that clarify how the bodhisattva attains the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas and severs doubt; having realized it for themselves as they heard it, they are able to enter all lands according to the power of their mental conceptions and universally illuminate sentient beings.
The following verses consist of fifty lines, with two lines forming each stanza; all of them praise the practices performed within their respective stages as dedicated toward enlightenment.
As these are fully contained within the text itself, there is no need for further commentary; one should practice according to the text.
Regarding the second part, the explanation according to the text: What is meant by "unbreakable dedication"?

Although one follows the ocean of birth and death, one does not break the Dharma-body; although one follows conceptual discrimination, one does not break non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*); although one follows various views, one does not break the Dharma-eye; although one follows various practices, one does not break the bodhicitta; although one teaches and brings sentient beings to maturity so that they all reach the fruit of Buddhahood, one does not break the door of non-abiding in body or mind; although one follows all sentient beings by knowing their faculties and acting in concert with them, one does not break the essence of the precepts, which remains eternally pure. Therefore, it is called "unbreakable dedication."
Furthermore, all mundane and supramundane phenomena possess no essence of formation or destruction.

These incalculable jewels (*asaṃkhyeya-ratna*) are the fruit of the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) resulting from benefiting sentient beings through the Dharma during his past practices.
"Immeasurable flowers" refers to the ability to benefit oneself and others through practice, thereby causing the fruits that depend upon manifold virtues to blossom.
"Immeasurable garlands" refer to the retribution for patience.
The incalculable robes arise from a sense of shame and dread of blame.
The incalculable parasols arise from great compassion.
The incalculable banners arise from the mind of dedication.
The "incalculable banners" are produced by the power of non-retrogression in accordance with practice.
The "incalculable ornaments" are produced by the various factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
The incalculable number of attendants arises from humility, respect, and the abandonment of pride.
The incalculable number of those who adorn the ground arises from the category of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) unguents arise from the precepts pervading all phenomena.
The incalculable powdered incenses arise as the retribution for having scattered flowers and incense in the past.

Generally speaking, one may understand this by knowing that the fruits of action correspond to their causes, just as a shadow follows a form, with each being exactly alike; this can be explained by applying the principle of analogy to the nature of things.
Furthermore, it is because one has previously made offerings of such things to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha that one obtains such fruits.

The remainder may be understood by analogy with this. Regarding the essence of this dedication, as the Sūtra says: "Sealing all doors of karma with the seal of the Dharma as it truly is; attaining the non-arising of dharmas and abiding where the Buddhas abide; contemplating the nature of non-arising and sealing all objective realms; being protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas and dedicating the arousal of the resolve; dedicating in accordance with the nature of all dharmas; and dedicating through entering the unconditioned to accomplish the skillful means of what is to be done."
This is the general essence of indestructible dedication.
Wisdom is indestructible, saṃsāra is indestructible, the great vow is indestructible, and great compassion is indestructible, for all are suchness.

In the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), taking great compassion free from defilement as the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*), the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha of the country of Samudramukha serves as its symbolic representation.

Within the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), taking craftsmanship and mathematics as the essence of the precepts, the youth Śakradeva calculating the methods of seals (*mudrā*) on a sandbank by a river serves as its symbolic representation; this is to clarify that the practices are like rivers that flow back to the ocean.

Within the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), taking great compassion for those dwelling in the secular world as the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*) is symbolized by mastery over the sea and the shipmaster.

The third category, "The Dedication of All Buddhas," was compiled by the Elder Li Tongxuan; it takes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence,
with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.
In the representation of the Dharma, he is the Elder Anuttarajaya (Unsurpassed Victory) within the Great Adorned Banner无忧林 (Aśoka Forest) to the east of the delightful city seen by the youth Sudhana.
It is named "Delightful" because it is established according to the conduct practiced by its presiding lord;
it is so called to clarify that one who has attained the Dharma achieves patience (*kṣānti*), and thus people perceive it as delightful.

As for those dwelling to the east of the city, this is to clarify that patience is the foremost of the practices leading to awakening, and to signify the position of the constellations Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and Cancer in the eastern quarter, which presides over the head of all virtues.
The quarters are the Azure Dragon, for they preside over the position of auspiciousness.
Since the East is yang and is the source from which all things are produced,

The "Great Ornament Banner" signifies that patience remains unmoved in the face of adverse conditions; this is the meaning of a banner.
The "Forest Without Sorrow" clarifies that through the perfection of the practice of patience, one provides vast shade, like a forest.
He is called the Unsurpassed Victor because, among all practices, nothing surpasses patience.
For among all practices, if there is no patience, those practices cannot be perfected.
