This clarifies that the great vows and great compassion of the wisdom of principle, which fully pervade the ten directions and are harmoniously integrated without obstruction, do not fail to depend entirely upon the stage of the ten dedications.
Just as the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi) proceed by relying on this [wisdom], accumulating and maturing it, there is no separate dharma.
Thus, in the sixth assembly at the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Ten Grounds were taught to signify reaching the summit of the realm of desire.
Furthermore, because it manifests in accordance with sentient beings through transformation, there is no self-transformation.
Thus, this celestial realm is borrowed to symbolize the wisdom that transforms others.

Moreover, as this celestial realm is the abode of Māra Pāpīyas, it clarifies that the wisdom of the ten stages subdues the mental Māras, thereby accomplishing the practice of great compassion to bring beings to maturity.

The seventh assembly takes place in the third dhyāna, signifying that the practices of Samantabhadra are fulfilled and that one benefits sentient beings through the joy of the Dharma; this indicates that the deities of this heaven are moved solely by the joy of meditative concentration.

The eighth assembly, held in the Hall of Universal Radiance, expounds the "Ten Samādhis" and the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," clarifying that the Buddha’s appearance marks the culmination of the path of progressive cultivation. It demonstrates that without leaving his original station, he does not depart from a single universal radiance-wisdom as the basis for his progressive cultivation.

The clouds ascending to the heavens symbolize the advancement of the Dharma; from the very beginning, this does not depart from the single dwelling of the great samādhi of universal radiance and fundamental wisdom.
Although one cultivates advancement through clarity, when practice is perfected, it never shifts from the universal, great function within the fundamental, immovable wisdom.

The ninth assembly was again held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-maṇḍapa*), where the *Dharmaparyāya on Transcending the World* (*Lokottara-dharma*) was preached. It clarifies that through the wisdom of universal radiance, which pervades the ten directions, one universally benefits sentient beings while remaining unstained by worldly phenomena; thus it is named "Transcending the World."

By means of the wisdom of universal radiance, one is endowed with the practices of Samantabhadra; constantly abiding in the world without emerging or entering, this is called "leaving the world" because it transcends the world.
Because the essence of wisdom is eternally active yet without dependence, it is called "leaving"; it is not a leaving born of aversion.

That these three assemblies are all contained within the Hall of Universal Radiance (Puguangming-dian) clarifies that the causal practices and their fruits, as well as the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s conduct, are collectively one single Universal Radiance; it is because this is the sovereign great wisdom that has no beginning or end and is free from any fixed abode.
If sentient beings give rise to the bodhicitta, they do not truly give rise to it unless they perceive this wisdom; only upon perceiving this wisdom is it called the arising of the mind.

Those who perceive a Buddha outside of the mind, or who grasp at signs while seeking the truth, may indeed perform wholesome deeds for the time being, but they have not yet been said to have given rise to the mind of omniscience (sarvajñā-citta).
The Sūtra says: "Riding upon the vehicle of all-knowledge, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

Because one rides upon the vehicle of universal radiance and great wisdom, one does not depart from the site of enlightenment of universal radiance and great wisdom; this is what is meant by "arriving."
This is called: "The initial resolve and the ultimate realization are not two; of these two states of mind, the former is more difficult.
Therefore, the initial resolve is difficult because this wisdom is difficult to believe; yet once one attains faith, one is able to enter.

Now, it is easy to realize the arousal of the mind [of enlightenment], whereas it is difficult for the arousal of the mind through faith to precede it, because faith reaches its ultimate limit only upon entering the stages.
One must simply manifest it through the samādhi of skillful means, and the realm of wisdom will then appear.

The fact that these three assemblies are all situated within the Hall of Universal Radiance clarifies that the essence and function, the beginning and end, the cause and effect, and the myriad practices of meditative concentration are one and the same wisdom, as previously described.

In the tenth assembly, at the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden, the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" is taught; because it clarifies that the dharmadhātu is not separate from the worldly provision of sustenance, it signifies that the gardens and groves of worldly saṃsāra are themselves the essence and function of the dharmadhātu.

Therefore, the multi-storied lecture hall where the Tathāgata dwells encompasses the lion throne that pervades the entire Dharma-realm throughout the ten directions; only those who are ready for deliverance can perceive it.
Those dwelling in delusion do not realize this; these are the five hundred śrāvakas and other sentient beings.

The eleventh assembly was held to the east of the city of Awakened (Vaiśālī), where Mañjuśrī expounded for the great multitude the *Sūtra-Door of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma-Dhātu*, as well as the account of the Youth Sudhana and his spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). This clearly establishes that Mañjuśrī is the foremost guide for the ignorant, for all Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings collectively rely upon him as their teacher and leader according to this Dharma.

Because it is the foremost of the sublime wisdom of non-substantiality, and because Samantabhadra is the foremost of practices, these two "foremost" aspects arise simultaneously without priority or sequence.
The above concludes the description of the location of the assembly and its symbolic significance.
However, regarding the Tathāgata’s own person as the manifestation of the Dharma, there are ten degrees of emitting light.
Second, concerning the description of the locations where the light is emitted and its underlying intent: this describes the manifestation of the radiance of progressive spiritual cultivation.
There are approximately ten such instances.
Within the first assembly, in the "Chapter on the Tathāgata Manifesting Signs," light is emitted twice from between his teeth:

first, he emits light from between his teeth to inform the multitudes in the ten directions that the Buddha has attained enlightenment, causing them all to assemble so that he may preach the Dharma of the causes and effects of Buddhahood.

From the tuft of hair between his two eyebrows, he emits light that universally illumines the ten directions; it is named "The Radiance of the Power and Wisdom of All Bodhisattvas Illuminating the Treasuries of the Ten Directions. Having illuminated the ten directions, the light returns and enters the wheel-mark beneath the Buddha’s feet, clearly manifesting the fruit as the cause for entering the light of faith.

Furthermore, from within each pore there emerged Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field, with Supreme Sound (*Jyotisvara*) at their head; they clearly elucidated the universal pervasiveness of the Tathāgata’s own practice and clearly elucidated the universal pervasiveness of the fruit of the Tathāgata’s self-awakened practice, in order to establish faith.

This light enters the wheel-mark beneath the Buddha’s feet; this illumination is similar to the light emitted from between the eyebrows when the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) are expounded. This is the fruit of Buddhahood that is the object of faith, whereas that [light] is the radiance of the fruit attained through one's own progressive cultivation.

In the second assembly, the Tathāgata emits light from the wheels on the soles of his two feet; this is the light that establishes the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*). It is the same light that was emitted from the wheels on the soles of his feet during the first assembly, now emitted again to bring the fruit of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) to completion.
The "Light" (ābhā) clearly explains the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

It is represented by the feet below, because the wheel symbolizes perfection; thus, it clearly explains that the qualities and functions of the Buddha-fruit (*buddha-phala*) establish faith, representing how, within the state of faith, one has faith in the perfection of the Buddha-fruit.

In the third assembly, the Tathāgata emits light from the tips of his toes to signify the beginning of entering the inner stage, the first step upon the noble path, the commencement of birth into the Buddha-family, and the initiation of the practice of the holy conduct; therefore, this light represents these meanings.
This clarifies that the light spoken of here marks the beginning of setting out to enter the state of the noble ones during the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
In the fourth assembly, the Tathāgata emits light from the soles of his two feet to signify that he practices in reliance upon the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
This clarifies the exposition of the light of the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), because it demonstrates that practice arises based upon emptiness.

In the fifth assembly, the Tathāgata emits light from his knees to symbolize the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*); here, the great vows interpenetrate both principle and phenomena, and wisdom and compassion provide simultaneous relief, just as a person’s knees are the means by which one extends and retracts.

This describes the light of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), symbolizing the arousal of vows and the arising of compassion, wherein wisdom and compassion are sovereign over both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

In the sixth assembly, light was emitted from between the eyebrows, named "Flame-Brightness of Bodhisattva Power" (*bodhisattvabalajvālāloka*); this light is the same as that emitted from between the eyebrows in the first assembly, which was named "Wisdom-Light of Bodhisattva Power" (*bodhisattvabalajñānāloka*).
This cause and effect are similar; the former is named "Power-Wisdom" (*balajñāna*), signifying fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*).

This is named "Power-Flame-Illumination" (*balajvālāloka*), signifying that through the realization of one's own merit, one reaches the source and is thus able to illuminate the conventional; hence it is called "Power-Flame-Illumination."

As it is designated in the Three Vehicles, that which is called "fundamental wisdom" (mūla-jñāna) and that which, when taking conventional reality as its object, is called "subsequently attained wisdom" (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna):
this clarifies that fundamental wisdom is itself able to illumine the conventional; there is no duality of essence, nor any sequence of before and after.

Although one establishes stages and ranks for advancement, wisdom does not differ, great compassion does not differ, eons and kalpas do not differ, and the practices of Samantabhadra do not differ; because there is fundamentally no phenomenon that undergoes transition, it is said that immeasurable wisdoms are all spoken of according to their specific functions, yet they do not deviate from the fundamental source.
When viewed through wisdom, it can be clearly perceived; when viewed through emotion, one immediately becomes deluded.
Within the gate of great compassion, one guides the mundane world, wherein time, kalpas, and dharmas are each distinguished.

If one speaks of time and kalpas from the perspective of Great Wisdom regarding the ultimate reality, there is fundamentally no dependence on length or brevity; this is explained through the six aspects of totality and particularity.

In the eighth assembly, the Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows to anoint the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head and emits light from his mouth to anoint the mouth of Samantabhadra, signifying that fundamental wisdom (*prajñā*) and phenomenal knowledge (*jñāna*), as well as the myriad practices, are to be mutually integrated, thereby expounding the virtues of the Buddha-fruit.

The intent clarifies that Mañjuśrī represents principle (*li*) and wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*), while Samantabhadra represents wisdom (*jñāna*) and the function of the myriad practices (*caryā*). This signifies the mutual penetration and interpenetration of principle and wisdom, as well as stillness and function; it constitutes the gateway to the fruit of Buddhahood through the format of question and answer.
Mañjuśrī is the formless Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, the fruit of wondrous wisdom that skillfully discerns the correct from the deviant.
Samantabhadra is the all-pervading great wisdom of the Tathāgata, manifesting as a form-body; he is the fruit of practices that benefit the mundane world by knowing the capacities of sentient beings.

Because all Buddhas attain Buddhahood by means of these two dharmas, within this teaching, the "Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta" (Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata) causes these two dharmas to be harmonized, integrated, and thoroughly penetrated; only then does one enter the gate of the unimpeded, perfectly interfused fruit of Buddhahood—the non-obstruction between principle and wisdom, and between the myriad practices and the dharma-realm.
He emits light to illuminate them so that they may engage in dialogue, enabling later students to see the Dharma with ease.

Regarding the cause and effect of these two individuals—from their initial arousal of faith until the ultimate consummation of the fruit—they are mutually integrated and thoroughly penetrating. Contemplate this through principle; let wisdom illumine one’s own mind, and the essence and function will become visible.

In the first assembly, the Buddha-fruit is that which the Buddha himself has spontaneously realized; whereas this Buddha-fruit, following the tenth and eleventh stages, is accomplished through the self-power of the practitioner.
This is because, by integrating the two practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, one clarifies that the myriad practices are fulfilled through the union of principle and wisdom.

The ninth chapter, "The Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks," describes emitting light from the palms of the hands to illuminate the sufferings of the evil realms; it is the radiance that clarifies the path, fulfills great compassion, and reaches out to embrace worldly beings.
From this point onward, since the second assembly, this has been the conclusion of the progressive advancement for those who practice for themselves.
This teaching on the final stage has not yet been entrusted for circulation, and it is likewise contained within this "Chapter on the Manifestation," as previously explained.
In the tenth chapter, "The Dharma-realm," light is again emitted from between the eyebrows, named "Illumination of the Dharma-realm Universally Shining upon the Three Times.
Because the three times are integrated into a single moment, the Dharma-realm as a whole is taken as the essence of the fruit.

From the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and dedication, through the ten bhūmis, the eleventh bhūmi, and up to the fruit of Buddhahood, the entire range takes the Dharma-realm as its essential substance.

Mañjuśrī represents the principle of the Dharma-realm, while Samantabhadra represents the wisdom of the Dharma-realm; the sublime functioning of this principle and wisdom constitutes the single gateway of the Buddha.
Taking this single gateway as a means to transform the ignorant masses, it is divided into two dharmas.
If one follows the faculties of beings and accords with worldly conventions, the dharma-gates are inexhaustible.
However, if one discusses the ultimate principle, there is not even a single dharma apart from the midst of non-nature; the non-obstruction of the one and the many is what is called Samantabhadra.

Beginning with the guidance of the ignorant and reaching the profound principle of non-substantiality, he skillfully discriminates between the correct and the heterodox, entering the wisdom of non-arising; his name is Mañjuśrī, and he is also called the Youthful Bodhisattva.
To be able to arise together with sentient beings at the limit of suffering to practice for their benefit, and to govern the Dharma of the Buddha-family, is called Samantabhadra.
When these two aspects merge into one essence, it is called the Buddha.
That which is inherently sovereign is called the Dharmadhātu.
From the beginning to the end, this entire Dharma-realm constitutes the essence, with no other separate phenomena existing.
This chapter is the great totality of the cause and fruit of all Buddhas, and it is also the great highway traversed by all the sages and worthies; there is nothing that transcends it.

It is also the great palace wherein the sovereign of all-knowledge of one's own mind dwells and contemplates; it is also that upon which all sentient beings rely, and is therefore called the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Third, regarding the description of the substance and the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) of the assembly: there are ten types of intent concerning their similarities and differences.

First, as for the substance of the assembly in the first convocation having a *maṇi* jewel as its pedestal: this refers to the fundamental essence; because the nature of the *dharmakāya* is inherently stainless, it is designated as a *maṇi*, being called the "stainless jewel" (*vimalaratna*).

The intention is that the fruit of Buddhahood, bodhi, takes the stainless dharmakāya as its essence, while the retributive body and the transformation bodies constitute its wisdom-function; this clarifies that the wisdom-function arises based on the essence, and thus the mani-jewel serves as the substance of the seat.

Regarding the second assembly, whose essential body is a lotus-flower treasury: this signifies that the second assembly concerns the transformation and benefit of sentient beings by causing them to establish the seed of faith, and within that state of faith, it represents practice.
Being unstained while in the world signifies that benefiting sentient beings without defilement is one's merit; thus, it is represented by the lotus flower as a treasury.

The third assembly was held in the Palace of Sublime Victory (Vaijayanta) of Śakra-devendra, where a lion throne of universal radiance-treasury (Samantaprabhā-kośa) with hundreds of thousands of tiers was established, signifying the entry into the stages from the level of faith.
By means of the samādhi of skillful means, which is non-conceptual, non-active, and tranquil, it is called "establishment.

Through the power of this samādhi, one manifests the fundamental wisdom of the Tathāgata; having newly entered the Buddha-family and attained fearless wisdom, one clearly perceives the Lion Throne of the Universal Radiance Treasury.
"Treasury" (garbha) signifies that this stage enters the treasury of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
"Lion" clarifies the fearlessness of wisdom.
"Universal Radiance" signifies the realization of the Tathāgata’s fundamental great wisdom of the universally radiant *dharmadhātu*.

The "hundred thousand tiers" symbolize the stages of progress through the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) that transcend the world; they signify the surpassing of the hundred thousand fetters of the passions and ignorance, as well as the destruction of the hundred thousand karmic obstructions.

Regarding the seat of the Buddha-fruit, no tiers or levels are mentioned at all, because there is no progression or regression in cultivation, no depth or shallowness in awakening or delusion, and no superiority or inferiority in wisdom.

In contrast, the first stage within the Ten Abidings has hundreds of thousands of tiers, which serves to clarify the demarcation of entering the position, advancing in cultivation, and transcending karmic obstacles.
The fourth assembly was held in the palace of the Yāma Heaven, where a lion throne made of precious lotus-wombs was manifested to signify the exposition of the stage of the Ten Practices.
Because one is unattached while abiding in the sphere of practice, it is symbolized by the lotus.
"Siṃha" (Lion) is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound as previously stated.
Regarding the "one million tiers," these surpass the preceding ones because they transcend karma and are superior.

As for why it says "transformed into a seat" rather than "placed," this signifies that by entering the Tathāgata’s wisdom, one acts in accordance with that wisdom; since the practices performed are transformed by wisdom, they are like a magical manifestation (*nirmāṇa*). Therefore, it does not say "placed," clarifying that practice proceeds from the transformation of principle.
The fifth assembly was held in the Tuṣita Heaven palace; there, upon the dais, a lion throne of the maṇi-treasury was spread with a hundred trillion tiers, symbolizing the ten stages of dedication.

Within this, by means of the supramundane wisdom and insight, one dwells in the world without defilement based on the fundamental Dharma-body; one advances by relying on the seat of the fundamental Buddha-fruit, returning to the source.
By means of the skillful means of dedication and the power of vows, one brings forth compassion and wisdom; yet this does not alter the stainless nature of the Dharma-body itself.

Because dedication integrates compassion and vows so that essence and function are balanced, it is said that "the seat is spread," rather than saying "it is placed" or "it is manifested through transformation."
The "hundred trillion levels" refers to the advancement beyond what preceded.
Having eliminated both the afflictive and cognitive obscurations, one realizes the unimpeded dharma-realm of great compassionate wisdom (*mahākaruṇājñāna*).

Although the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) and ten practices (*daśacaryā*) are cultivated simultaneously across these five stages, the teachings distinguish them according to their specific functions: it is clarified that in the first two stages, the mind of renunciation (*pravrajyacitta*) is superior while the mind of great compassion is inferior; whereas in this stage of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), wisdom and compassion are brought into harmony through the power of aspiration (*praṇidhānabala*), thereby attaining their proper place.

Regarding the sixth assembly in the palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, it mentions only the "Maṇi-treasury Hall" (*maṇi-garbha-maṇḍapa*) and does not mention the substance of the seat. This is intended to indicate that this seat is no different from the maṇi-seat of Tuṣita Heaven; rather, it highlights how the stainless great wisdom of the *dharmatā* constitutes the gate of great compassion, thereby nurturing and sustaining all sentient beings. For this reason, it refers only to the "hall" and not to the "seat."

This clarifies that by relying on the aforementioned method of dedication, one nurtures the palace of great compassion to shelter and sustain all sentient beings; thus, there is no separate progression.
The seventh assembly takes place in the third dhyāna; its ritual principles are taught for future practice, and they are briefly presented here through the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra."

The "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" is the thirty-sixth among its chapters; this is but a brief summary, for the full original text has not yet appeared, consisting of one hundred million verses.

The eighth and ninth assemblies, as well as the second assembly, all take place in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsabhavana*). These clarify the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the Buddha-fruition reached through progressive cultivation, as well as the constant practices of Samantabhadra in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*), the ten concentrations (*daśa-samādhi*), the ten supernatural powers (*daśābhijñā*), and so forth. Because these are all inseparable from the single essence of wisdom—the Universal Radiance—and because they constitute the progression through the five stages, the ten faiths, and other practices, they are presented here together.

In total, it does not transcend this wisdom; this Wisdom of Universal Radiance is shared equally by all Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings alike. It is because the Buddhas have already realized it, whereas sentient beings are deluded regarding it.
Nevertheless, essence and function are one, though delusion and enlightenment differ.
From the perspective of those who resolve their minds within this teaching, once they awaken, their knowledge and vision are identical to that of a Buddha.

As the *Lotus Sūtra* teaches the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings to cause them to awaken, desiring to lead sentient beings into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and even to have them ride upon the vehicle of omniscience straight to the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, this sutra says: "It is the vehicle of the Tathāgata, the inconceivable vehicle, the most supreme vehicle, the unsurpassed vehicle," and so forth.

This is as described in the first fascicle, in the praise of the virtues of the bodhisattvas, where it is said that after they have thoroughly understood the equal Dharma of all Buddhas, they tread upon the stage of the Tathāgata’s Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-bhūmi*).

This is the Wisdom of Universal Radiance. For sentient beings, delusion regarding this wisdom constitutes their own delusion; for those who awaken, awakening to that delusion constitutes the realization of the Wisdom of Universal Radiance.

Therefore, in the first assembly, the deities manifested their entry into the Dharma to obtain benefit; their "entry" was identical to that entered by the Buddha and identical to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, serving as a model for sentient beings to enter the Dharma and enabling later students to emulate it.

Therefore, the intention behind the fact that these three assemblies are collectively situated in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-maṇḍala*) is to clarify that as one ascends through the five stages, faith does not depart from this wisdom; awakening and entering into practice likewise do not depart from this wisdom. Since time and kalpas have no substantiality that can be transmuted, wisdom, moreover, is not different from this Wisdom of Universal Radiance.
When the ten methods of dedication are harmonized with compassion and vows, sovereign supernormal powers are entirely contained within them.

For example, if one practices the ten wholesome paths of action while still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) for a single lifetime, one may yet be reborn in the heavens and attain supernormal powers as a karmic retribution.

If one achieves rebirth in the Pure Land through even ten recitations, how much more so for one who resolves their mind according to wisdom, further augmenting this with compassionate vows and the practice of the various *pāramitās*? How could such a person not attain the essence of wisdom and sovereign supernatural powers after this single lifetime?
If one seeks to discuss this by reconciling the realm of wisdom with ultimate reality, even throughout incalculable eons, it fundamentally never departs from a single thought-moment.
What is now called "one lifetime" is such that time ultimately does not extend, wisdom ultimately does not differ, and birth ultimately has no birth.

One must by no means follow emotional perceptions to give rise to views of arising and ceasing; rather, one should simply know through true wisdom, whereby the myriad delusions will not cause confusion.

For example, the sixteen contemplation gates of the Western Pure Land are all forms of mental visualization; once these visualizations are perfected, one naturally attains supernormal powers as a karmic reward.

How much more so for one who has realized that the principle of wisdom (*prajñā*) is without dependence, luminously pure, and universally illuminating; who understands that body and mind have no substantiality, and whose internal and external views have vanished. Such a person simply allows the principle of wisdom to remain vast and open, giving rise to an ocean-like sea of great vows where compassion and wisdom are fused. In a single instant, they manifest physical bodies to make offerings to all Buddhas and transform sentient beings, yet there is no agent. Their nature is entirely equal—without mind, without master, without essence, and without form. Ordinary beings and sages are as one, with nothing upon which to rely or dwell. By means of the dharma of non-abiding, following the wisdom of non-abiding, they make offerings to the Buddhas and benefit living beings.
If one practices in this manner, why worry about not attaining great power and supernormal faculties?
By simply relying on the "Ten Dedications" chapter (*Daśapariṇāmanā-parivarta*) for study and practice, they will be attained.

In the tenth chapter, the "Dharma-realm" (*Dharmadhātu-parivarta*), it is merely stated that his seat universally pervades the dharma-realm; no tiers or levels are mentioned, as it clarifies only that the essence of the Buddha’s fruition-seat is composed of *maṇi* jewels.
From the first assembly to the fifth assembly, the substance of the seat is uniformly composed of *maṇi* jewels, because the essence of the Buddha-fruit is identical across these assemblies.
The general meaning is that wisdom gives rise to compassion; they do not differ from this single, universal radiance of wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*).
Abiding in the world without defilement, it is no different from a single wondrous principle: the wisdom-body and the dharma-body are one and the same.

Together they constitute a single state of sovereign freedom, devoid of substance yet manifesting function without effort; it reaches everywhere without moving, responding to things as they arise, and can only be known through the harmonious integration of principle and wisdom.

The foregoing expresses the essential meaning; it is intended merely to enable sentient beings to understand the Dharma through observed phenomena so that it may be easily comprehended, and to inspire them to undertake practice without doubt.
To elaborate further, [the text] discusses this extensively in terms of knowing the destination toward which one is heading.
The Master of the Treatise states in verse:
Universal radiant wisdom is equal to space; Space is merely empty, while wisdom is sovereign.
From the first generation of the mind, one relies upon this; In the end, one returns to this very place to reach fulfillment.
Therefore, in the Hall of Radiance during the three assemblies, cause and effect are harmonized as having no separate essence;
yet according to the stages, there are distinctions in the advancement of practice. Wisdom follows the arising of beings, and the realms of retribution differ;
yet they do not depart from fundamental wisdom, which is without birth or extinction. For this reason, the Buddha sits upon the mani throne.

This passage clarifies that throughout the five stages of advancement toward the fruit of Buddhahood, the essence and function are always the fundamental wisdom of the universally radiant light of the dharma-realm; therefore, from beginning to end, cause and effect do not depart from within the Hall of Universal Radiance.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: within this chapter of the sutra, it is divided into four sections:

first, the introduction; second, the main exposition; third, the section on the shaking of the earth and the offering of worship; and fourth, the section on the recitation of verses in praise of the Dharma.

First, regarding the introduction (*nidāna*): from the initial phrase "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "because of being well-sealed by the seal of the wisdom of the dharma-realm," there are four sections within this portion, which are called the introduction.

Regarding the second part, the Section of the Formal Exposition (*samyag-deśanā-bhāga*): from the passage beginning with "At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hands" down to the thirty-ninth fascicle, where it says "Having received, upheld, and practiced [this], one subsequently reaches the ground of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*)," this entire section constitutes the Section of the Formal Exposition.
Third, the section on the earth shaking and the offering of worship begins from "At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power" and continues until the verse is spoken.
Fourth, the section on the recitation of verses in praise of the Dharma begins from "His mind is tranquil and ever-disciplined" and extends to the end of the thirty-ninth fascicle of the sutra.
Within the first introductory section, there are further four divisions.

First, from "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations" down to "the teaching is inexhaustible," there are eighteen lines of scripture; this is the section praising the resolve and virtue of the bodhisattvas who have come.
2. From "Their names were" down to "serving as the leaders," there are eighteen lines of scripture; this is the section listing the names of the bodhisattvas. 3.

From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha" down to "in order to fulfill the knowledge of all-knowledge," there are twenty-five lines of scripture; this clarifies the section on the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha entering meditative absorption, where Buddhas bearing the same name all appear before him to exhort and remind him to expound the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages.

4. From "At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions" down to "because they are well-sealed by the seal of the wisdom of the dharma-realm," there are nine lines of scripture clarifying the section on how the Buddhas of the ten directions bestow upon the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha ten kinds of powers, enabling him to preach the Dharma with mastery.

Regarding the exegesis following the text: from the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven," it is clarified that the wisdom-body of the Tathāgata manifests in accordance with its station; thus, the location upon which he relies symbolizes the Dharma.
This clarifies that the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of this bodhisattva extend from the beginning up to the peak of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, because he practices these ten stages for the sake of sentient beings and not for any personal seeking of his own, it is called "Paranirmita" (Other-Transformation).
Furthermore, because they have reached the end of the ten stages of the path, subdued the demons of mind and world, and attained mastery, they enter the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement;
being pure and immaculate, as is the natural law of reality, they abide at the summit of the Desire Realm.
Because they constantly abide in samādhi without dwelling in a mind of purity, and do not reside within the realms of dhyāna;

and because it clarifies that the merit of these ten stages culminates in the Dharma-cloud which universally moistens all, and because the manifestation of the form-body is not restricted by the opposition of defilement and purity, these ten stages are taught here in this heaven.

As in the first assembly, the Sovereign Heavenly King attained benefit, as expressed in this verse: “The Buddha’s body pervades everywhere, equal to the Dharma-realm; Universally responding to sentient beings, he appears before them all. Through various gates of teaching, he constantly transforms and guides; Sovereign over the Dharma, he is able to bring awakening.”
Question: For what reason did the Tathāgata descend into this realm of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods?
Why is it not mentioned that the Heavenly King saw the Buddha approaching from afar, prepared a seat, escorted him, or offered verses of praise for his adornment?

Answer: In this stage, one merely practices the dharmas of dedication, vows, conduct, compassion, and wisdom according to the dharma-gate of the previous Tuṣita Heaven palace; there is no other distinct dharma.

Because one does not present other matters here but merely accumulates merit, and because the function reaches its consummation and wisdom its ultimate limit based on the preceding ocean of vows, there is no need for further ritual acts to manifest this advancement and harmonious convergence; one simply follows the previous method.
It was further asked:

"For what reason does it not proceed in sequence to the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), but instead bypasses it to ascend directly to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) to explain its ten stages?
He replied:

It clarifies that prior to the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), one must sequentially harmonize and integrate wisdom (*jñāna*), principle (*li*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and vows (*praṇidhāna*) so as to achieve their balanced fusion. In the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), compassion, vows, wisdom, and principle are equally blended; their breadth and narrowness correspond to the measure of the Dharma-realm and the number of sentient beings. This represents the Dharma abiding in the Middle Way, wherein the meaning of the Middle Way is explained within the state of "abiding in the center. Thus, the Ten Dedications harmonize compassion, vows, wisdom, and principle precisely within the central position of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), because Tuṣita Heaven is situated between the two extremes of the upper and lower heavens.
In the exposition of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), this refers to the upper limit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the lower limit of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This is intended to clarify that [the Buddha] is not constrained by defilement or purity, because he possesses mastery over wisdom, principle, and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Furthermore, it is taught that the Dharma-gate of the Perfect Enlightenment of the Eleven Stages is expounded within the Third Dhyāna; this signifies the fulfillment of practices for benefiting sentient beings, wherein the joy of benefiting others through the bliss of the Dharma resembles the meditative rapture (*dhyāna-prīti*) that constitutes the pleasure of that Third Dhyāna.
The fourth dhyāna represents the Buddha-fruit as all-pervasive and subtle, because its function is perfected.

Furthermore, the tenth stage transcends the Heaven of Joy (Nirmāṇarati), and the eleventh stage transcends the second dhyāna; this clarifies that wisdom increases twofold at each level, thereby surpassing the sequential order.
The Mani-jewel Treasury Palace symbolizes that stainless great compassion is able to contain, cover, and nurture all beings.

It indicates that at this stage, one has no thought of seeking personal peace and happiness for oneself, but instead exclusively benefits sentient beings through the cultivation of great compassion; therefore, dwelling in the Mani-jewel Stainless Treasury Palace serves to represent this.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of bodhisattvas, namely the thirty-seven beginning with Vajragarbha, representing the assembly of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
Mañjuśrī Vimukticandra alone represents that each and every factor of enlightenment, when examined in its own essence, is itself the cool bliss of liberation.

Illumination (*vidyā*) is itself the auxiliary and the direct path; for those on the stages prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the correct vision (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) has already been completed, and throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the auxiliary serves to manifest and bring it to maturity.
This differs from the three vehicles (*triyāna*), wherein the path of seeing occurs during the ten stages and the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) are accumulated prior to the stages.

Because this teaching of the One Vehicle proceeds from the beginning by relying on the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom to give rise to faith and cultivate the wisdom of *sarvajñatā*, one does not rely on the contemplation of emptiness to suppress active afflictions, for it is only upon the tenth stage that one attains the *manomayakāya*.

Although this teaching speaks of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as mind and intellect, it clarifies that one does not destroy conventional reality in order to achieve discriminative wisdom; it is not the same as suppressing afflictions to remain in this life or to be reborn in a pure land.

Some say that because the realm of the three thousandfold world-system is the Buddha-realm, within this teaching, from the very first stage of faith, one practices with progress based solely on the infinite Buddha-realm—in which a single mote of dust contains the ten directions and a single hair-pore accommodates the entire Dharma-realm—rather than stating that the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system is the retributive realm of the Buddha. This is exactly as the "Chapter on Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) is the gateway for what is believed, aspired to, and cultivated, while the "Chapter on the Merit of Arousing the Mind" (*Cittotpāda-guṇa-parivarta*) represents the virtue of awakening and entry into the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The Sūtra states: "All those bodhisattvas have attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Regarding enlightenment (*bodhi*), there are five types:
first, the enlightenment of the Hīnayāna; second, the enlightenment of the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha); [and so forth].
1. The Bodhi of a Bodhisattva through the three contemplations of emptiness and the six pāramitās; 2.

The Bodhi of ten kinds of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) and twenty-two kinds of delusion, which arise when one cultivates the ten types of contemplation on semblance-tathatā and practices the ten pāramitās;

3. The Bodhi of Buddha-wisdom, wherein delusion and liberation are identical, by relying on the ten kinds of Tathāgata-wisdom to practice the ten pāramitās, taking inexhaustible eons as a single kṣaṇa-limit, and realizing that inexhaustible many lifetimes are but a single life and a single thought-moment.
This clarifies that the arousal of the bodhicitta is based upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

As stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, there is the passage: "Because of fundamental awakening (*prakṛti-āśraya-bodhi*), there is non-awakening (*a-bodha*)," and further: "Because one awakens to the source of the mind, it is called ultimate awakening. It is thus clearly understood that non-awakening exists in dependence upon Tathāgata-wisdom, while awakening exists in dependence upon ignorance (*avidyā*).
Regarding these awakenings, there are five distinct types of awakening-dharmas corresponding to the faculties and spiritual lineages.

As for the bodhi mentioned in this sutra, it refers to the non-retrogressive bodhi within the fundamental wisdom of the single vehicle (ekayāna) and the fruit of Buddhahood; as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, whether it is said that one attains Buddhahood by transcending kalpas, or that "I have practiced and attained the path to Buddhahood over immeasurable kalpas," these are all countless skillful means employed for the sake of indolent sentient beings.

As for those who say, "One must pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before attaining Buddhahood," these are all explanations given according to worldly sentiments regarding the Three Vehicles; they do not rely on the fundamental wisdom to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.

This teaching relies on wisdom to give rise to the bodhicitta. If one discusses it from the perspective of wisdom, one does not follow deluded sentiments; rather, one takes incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as being "no time. By means of this provisional designation of "no time," a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) encompasses infinite kalpas of the three periods of time, and these infinite kalpas of the three periods do not, in total, transcend a single moment.
The Sūtra says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time without coming or going.

Thus, throughout these three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, while emotion (*qing*) exists, wisdom (*zhi*) does not; yet by means of wisdom, emotion is subsumed, and emotion resides within wisdom. The existence of emotion across immeasurable kalpas is contained within the momentary limit (*kṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*) of wisdom.
If one takes the emotional as empty and wisdom as real, then from the beginning there has never been a substance of time, for from start to finish there is no time that can shift.
When comparing these two matters, one may only follow the real and not the empty.

As for the scripture’s statement that “they have all come together from other worlds,” it is because they have come from the ten stages of dedication (daśa-pariṇāmanā) to achieve the ten grounds (daśa-bhūmi); therefore, these are designated as "other worlds."
Within the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, there are no separate "other directions," for it is only at the stage prior to arrival that one speaks of "other directions.
This applies analogously to all stages.

Regarding the phrase "abiding in the realm where the wisdom of all bodhisattvas dwells": this is because the wisdom-realm of the bodhisattvas of the five stages is collectively identical to the Buddha-wisdom realm reached within these ten stages.

Regarding "entering the sphere entered by the Tathāgata’s wisdom": this means generating the mind of awakening based on the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom, entering into the distinctions of practice, and thereby perfecting great compassion through wisdom.

Regarding "skillfully entering all bodhisattva meditative concentrations," this is as explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Concentrations" (*Daśadhyāna-parivarta*): through the supernormal powers of *samāpatti*, the clear knowledge of wisdom, and the clarity of insight, these samādhis are able to give rise to the supernormal power of the seal of wisdom (*jñānamudrā*).
The term *samyak* is translated here as "right wisdom" (*zhèng huì*).
In this context, *sam* refers to *samādhi*,
and *bodhi* refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).

To be able to proceed to all places of enlightenment in a single moment without any movement is because the nature of the seal of samādhi-wisdom is inherently pervasive and lacks interior or exterior.
Illumination is always accompanied by wisdom because it is free from distraction and movement.
As for the one named Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, he takes wisdom as his vajra, for it is capable of shattering all delusions.
As for "Treasury" (Kośa), it is called a treasury because the wisdom and virtue of its enlightened intelligence pervade everywhere.
As for the Bodhisattva Ratnakośa, he is named "Jewel Treasury" because the Dharma-jewels pervade everywhere.
The Bodhisattva Padmagarbha is so named because he is clear regarding all practices and is unstained by nirvana or birth-and-death.
The Bodhisattva Guṇagarbha is so named because his manifold virtues are perfected.
The Bodhisattva Padmagarbha signifies the wisdom and virtue adorned by various practices that are free from defilement.
The Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha signifies the illuminating function of great wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha means "the illuminating function of the sun" in this language.
The Bodhisattva Vimalacandragarbha signifies that the mind of great compassion illuminates the mundane world and destroys the flames of affliction.
The Bodhisattva Universal Manifestation of the Treasury of Adornments in All Lands is so named because his two matters of merit and wisdom are all-pervasive.
The Bodhisattva Vairocanagarbha means "wisdom that universally illumines with light."
Thus, these various bodhisattvas can be understood by interpreting their names according to their meanings.

In this section, there are thirty-eight bodhisattvas; for instance, the fact that thirty-seven of these bodhisattvas share the same name, "Treasury" (Kośa), symbolizes the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ).

The single figure of Vimukticandra represents the fruit of the "cooling" stage within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist toward awakening; furthermore, as he acts as the primary requester of the Dharma for all bodhisattvas, he causes the great assembly to hear and practice the teaching so that those who attain pure vision find delight like a flower. Therefore, he is named "Delightful Flower" (Ruciraprabhāsa).
The Bodhisattva Utpalaguṇasaṃbhava takes the blue lotus as a metaphor; its meaning can be understood through this analogy.
The King of Constellations (Nakṣatrarāja) signifies mastery and unimpeded clarity, for his discerning wisdom is distinct and lucid.
Within the third section on entering meditative absorption, there are twenty-five lines of sūtra, which are divided into four parts in meaning.

First, the passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha" consists of one and a half lines of sūtra; it comprises three sentences in total, clarifying the section on the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha’s entry into meditative absorption.

Second, from "having entered this samādhi" down to "appeared before him," there are two lines of scripture that clarify the section on the Buddhas of identical name appearing before [the bodhisattva].

3. From "Having spoken thus" down to "because of being able to reach all places and bring about certain awakening," there are sixteen lines of scripture that clarify the section on entering this samādhi by means of twenty-six causal conditions.

4. From "Good son" onwards, there are five lines of scripture clarifying the section in which the Buddhas of the ten directions exhort Vajragarbha Bodhisattva to preach the Dharma. The scripture states:

"Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom. This means that taking the Tathāgata’s wisdom as the basis for faith and progress in practice, all the Buddha-works performed therein are entirely the Buddha’s spiritual power, for there is no sense of "I" acting of my own accord.

The samādhi named "Great Wisdom Radiance of the Bodhisattva" is precisely the radiance of the Middle Way of the wisdom of the ten stages emitted from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows; it is called the "Blazing Radiance of the Bodhisattva’s Power."
This is also the light emitted from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows during the first assembly, named "The Light of the Power and Wisdom of All Bodhisattvas.
It is, in its entirety, the light of the Buddha-wisdom at the conclusion of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Entering samādhi now refers to this wisdom-samādhi which explains the wisdom of the ten stages of the path; it is called the "Great Wisdom Radiance of the Bodhisattva" because one accomplishes the bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion through fundamental wisdom.

Beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there are Buddhas, numbering as many as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields, all sharing the same name, Vajragarbha; the number ten billion signifies the perfection and inexhaustibility of their count.
Regarding the phrase "beyond the world," within the stages of the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications, the fruit of Buddhahood is considered "external.
Now, having perfected the wisdom and virtue of these ten stages, the name of the fruit of Buddhahood arrives and manifests before one.

The reason for sharing the same name as the Bodhisattvas who have entered meditative concentration is to clarify that those who have entered concentration have attained the realization of wisdom and merged with the fundamental Buddha-wisdom of their original station.

As for the statement that the number is equal to the atoms within ten billion Buddha-lands, it clarifies that the essence of the function of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirnimitta-jñāna*) is all-pervasive.

Regarding the statement that "ten billion buddha-lands of atoms of buddhas collectively empower [the practitioner]," this clarifies that when one reaches the source of the assembly, one's own power merges with the power of the buddhas.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "This is also due to your own superior power of wisdom."

Regarding the phrase, "By the power of the original vows and the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata Vairocana, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha," this clarifies that the ascending into this Dharma-gate of the ten stages is entirely initiated by the original vows of all Buddhas within the ten dedications; for without these ten great vows of dedication, this stage could not be spontaneously realized.

Regarding "powerful spiritual authority": because from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, they all ascend these ten stages by means of the powerful spiritual authority of the Tathāgata’s vehicle of omniscience, and because they do not depart from the Tathāgata’s application of the functions of omniscience.
If one does not rely on the vehicle—the Tathāgata’s vehicle of omniscience—how could one reach this stage of the ten bhūmis?
This wisdom penetrates from cause to fruit, for it is identical to the ground of wisdom (jñāna-bhūmi).
Therefore, within this teaching, because the fruit of Buddhahood exists at each stage of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications,
the fruit of Buddhahood within these ten stages and the eleventh stage takes the fruit of Buddhahood within the ten dedications as its identical wondrous function.

Including the ten stages of faith and the progressive cultivation of the five positions, there are sixty levels of the Buddha-fruit; if one takes only the entry into these positions, there are fifty levels of the Buddha-fruit.
Including the causal stage of practice, there are altogether one hundred levels of cause and fruit.

Based on the ten *pāramitās* within the Buddha’s fundamental state, which inherently possess ten layers of cause and effect, it is clarified that all practitioners initiate their five-stage cultivation and advancement upon this very foundation of the Buddha’s original causes and effects. Because they arise based on this fundamental source, it is called the Dharma-gate of the One Hundred and Ten Cities.

In general, throughout the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*), the Buddha-fruit is uniformly designated as "Sublime" (*miao*); this is because the Buddha-fruits of the tenth and eleventh stages are not established with separate names, as the dharmas of the tenth and eleventh stages are identical to the dharmas of the ten stages of dedication.
Regarding the ten *pāramitās* of the Buddha’s fundamental position: as in the first assembly, within the section on exhorting practice by citing the fruit, the Tathāgata represents the Buddha-fruit.

Next, regarding the ten bodhisattvas whose names are all identical as "Universal" (*Samantabhadra*), this clarifies that within the stage of the Buddha-fruit, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra cultivates the ten *pāramitās*; although their names differ according to their specific practices, these constitute the gate of causal practice for the Buddha’s fundamental nature.

The forty classes of celestial deities arise in imitation of this; according to the distinctions in their progressive cultivation through the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the ten stages, the ten pāramitās likewise ascend and progress accordingly, and are thus also termed distinct.
Including the ten Universal Worthy Bodhisattvas and the forty deities, there are fifty celestial beings.
As one ascends through the five stages by practicing the ten *pāramitās*, there are fifty bodhisattva causal practices and fifty buddha fruits; together, these constitute one hundred.

Constantly not departing from the original fruit of Buddhahood, the ten fundamental practices of Samantabhadra are called the "Ten. These ten, together with the forty classes of divine beings, constitute the fifty *pāramitā* practices. Within each one, ten are subsumed, resulting in five hundred distinct gates of wisdom; only then is the perfection of the myriad practices achieved, which is the Buddha.
Thus, a single momentary limit (*kṣaṇāntika*) is established as the time for the beginning and end of spiritual advancement.
For example, it is like the Dragon Girl, who attained Buddhahood in three lifetimes within a single moment.

Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," it is taken that the descent of the spirit at the limit of a single kṣaṇa, the initial birth, and the entry into nirvāṇa constitute the temporal essence, which is fundamentally thus.
As for the phrase "when seeing, time passes," it means that the emotions follow after deluded thoughts.
The above concludes the explanation of you [the listener] by virtue of the power of the original vows and the majestic spiritual power of Vairocana Tathāgata, the Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

This section concerning the causes and conditions for the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and the attainment of fruition is practiced by relying upon the power of Vairocana’s wisdom, the ten practices of Samantabhadra, and the power of the practices performed by the forty classes of devas and spirits during the first assembly; thus it is called "riding upon the Buddha's spiritual power."
This is due to the power of the Tathāgata’s vows and also because of your own superior power of wisdom.
The following twelve lines of scripture collectively set forth the purpose for entering samādhi; there are twenty-four causal conditions, the meaning of which can be understood from the text.
The fourth section, "Good Son," consists of five lines of scripture; it is the section on exhortation.
There are ten causal conditions, which are self-evident from the text itself.
Regarding the phrase "to fulfill all-knowledge wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*)," first, it fulfills fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), and second, it fulfills differentiated wisdom (*prabhedaprajñā*).
Regarding the fourth section, "The Empowerment and Sustenance Provided by All Buddhas," the meaning is divided into three parts:

first, clarifying the ten kinds of empowerment provided by all Buddhas; second, clarifying how the ten kinds of causal conditions lead one into this samādhi; and third, clarifying the request by all bodhisattvas for the teaching of the Dharma.

First, from "At that time" onwards to "fully adorned," there are five lines and a half of scripture, clarifying the section on how the Buddhas of the ten directions bestow upon the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha the empowerment of the ten powers.
2. From "For what reason" onwards, there are four lines of scripture that clarify how ten kinds of causal conditions are subsumed within this section on entering samādhi.
When about to expound the dharmas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), there are six types of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) bestowed by the Buddhas:

first, the empowerment of all Buddhas of the ten directions appearing before one under the same name; second, the empowerment of the majestic spiritual power of Vairocana’s original vows; third, the empowerment of the ten kinds of dharma-power bestowed by the Buddhas upon Vajragarbha; fourth, the empowerment of the Buddhas praising him with words; fifth, the empowerment of each Buddha extending his right hand to stroke the crown of the head; and sixth, the empowerment of the Tathāgatas emitting light to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
There are four ways in which Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas request [the teaching]:

first, the Tathāgata emits light from his light-pavilion to exhort [the teaching]; second, the three requests of Vimukticandra; third, the collective request of all the Bodhisattvas; and fourth, the universal emission of light by all Buddhas to exhort [the teaching].
In total, there are six kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), fourfold requests, and two exhortations.

Within the second section, the "Section on the Correct Exposition," from the passage beginning with "At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hands" down to "the earth shook and offerings arose," the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are correctly expounded.
Furthermore, from the very beginning within the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the text is divided into ten sections.

The first section, beginning with "At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hands," consists of sixteen and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies the portion in which the Buddhas of the ten directions touch the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, thereby causing him to arise and correctly expound the names of the ten stages.

Second, from "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" onwards, there are five lines of prose and ten lines of verse in total, clarifying that Vajragarbha Bodhisattva remained silent and did not preach the Dharma; then, Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, perceiving the thoughts of the assembly, requested on their behalf that the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) be expounded. This constitutes the section on the request for the teaching.

3. From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha of Great Wisdom and Fearlessness" onwards, there are seven lines of prose interspersed with verses which clarify the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha’s intention for maintaining silence and not speaking.

4. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra" onwards, there are nine lines of verse in total, clarifying the section in which the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra again requests the teaching of the Dharma.

5. From "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" onwards, there are nine lines of prose and verse in the sūtra, clarifying the section in which Vajragarbha Bodhisattva fears that those of inferior understanding who follow their consciousness will be unable to give rise to faith.

Sixth: The section beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra" comprises fourteen lines of verse in total. It clarifies the three requests made by Vimukticandra that this assembly is capable of hearing [the teaching], and that if they are able to hear it through the Buddha’s protective mindfulness, he prays that the "Section on the Absence of Doubt" be expounded.

7. From "At that time, the assembly of great bodhisattvas" onwards, including six and a half lines of verse, constitutes the section clarifying how the great assembly collectively requested [the teaching]. 8.

From "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, including twenty-one lines of verse, constitutes the section clarifying how the Tathāgatas of the worlds of the ten directions each emitted light from between their eyebrows to drench the crown of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha; how these lights mutually illuminated one another to form a radiant platform; and how sounds issued from this radiant platform to exhort and explain the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

9. From "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" onwards, there are thirteen lines of prose and verse in the sūtra, which clarify how Vajragarbha Bodhisattva extols the profound Dharma-gate of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). He explains that it transcends the functioning of thought, intellect, and consciousness (*manovijñāna*), is known only by wisdom (*jñāna*), and is beyond the reach of words; thus, empowered by the majestic spiritual authority (*anubhāva*) of all Buddhas, he briefly expounds upon a small portion of it.
10. From "O Son of the Buddha, if there are sentient beings... onwards until the end of the scroll is the section on the practice gate of the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Within these ten sections, there are ten main themes which are fully contained within the text itself, so there is no need for further explanation. These ten matters are:
first, the Buddhas touching [the crown of] his head to signify their approval and permission for him to teach;
second, the general enumeration of the names of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Third, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva remained silent to stop [the teaching] and waited for a formal request before proclaiming it, clarifying that the Dharma is precious and should not be bestowed lightly;
fourth, Vimukticandra knew the proper time and made three requests;
fifth, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva feared the vessels were inferior and stopped [the teaching] three times.
1. The six great assemblies all join in the request;
2. It clarifies that those capable of hearing are empowered by all Buddhas, while those incapable do not hear it from the outset; 3.
It clarifies that sounds emerge from the light-platform to provide exhortation and instruction.
Ninth, it clarifies the empowerment by the Buddha’s light;
tenth, it clarifies how Bodhisattva Vajragarbha departs from the profound Dharma that is near at hand, providing a brief exposition of only a small portion.

The general meaning clarifies that the essence of these ten stages (*bhūmi*) serves as a mutual basis for the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the eleventh stage.

Therefore, from the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences, there is a sequential gateway of practice for the ten stages (*bhūmi*). This is because, by means of a single Tathāgata’s sovereign, unimpeded great wisdom, one practices the same single set of ten *pāramitās* as a skillful means for progressive cultivation; thus, they all constitute the ten Universal Worthy (*Samantabhadra*) Dharmas of the first assembly.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"By means of analogies such as the alphabet, all written characters and numbers are explained as being inseparable from the alphabet.

All Buddha-dharmas take the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as their foundation; it is clarified that these ten stages serve as the basis, and that the dharma of these ten stages permeates both cause and fruit, never departing from the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*).
By relying on the ten practices of Samantabhadra, one cultivates differentiated wisdom in order to fulfill the ocean of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).

For this reason, from the very beginning, within the exhortation to practice by presenting the fruit, light is emitted from between the eyebrows, named "The Radiance of the Bodhisattva’s Power and Wisdom."
He entered into the wheels beneath the Buddha’s feet to accomplish the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Now, the Tathāgata again emits a light from between his eyebrows called "Blazing Radiance of Bodhisattva Power" (*bodhisattvabalajvālāprabhā*), which drenches the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, so that he may expound upon the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

The radiance from his feet uses the fruit to cause the arising of faith in the cause; this radiance explains that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the culmination of the fruit of what is to be believed. Therefore, he now again emits the light of the fruit of the wisdom of the ten stages—the initial stage of faith—and uses it to empower the crown of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, causing him to expound these practices of the ten stages.

Regarding "entering from the crown": this clarifies that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the pinnacle of the fruit of wisdom—the middle way among all bodhisattvas—because they reach the ultimate limit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Therefore, in both the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" and the "Chapter on the Dharma Realm," light is emitted collectively from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, as these chapters collectively clarify the state in which the light of wisdom—the essence of the fruition—is perfected.

Furthermore, as for the light entering through the crown of the head, this clarifies that one proceeds through the world with compassion from the summit of wisdom, fulfilling the great vows generated during the ten stages of Dedication (daśa-pratipatti) so that their practice may reach completion.
This clarifies the gate of nurturing great compassion throughout these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), so as to fulfill one's vows.
For this reason, the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of Sudhana represent this by means of the ten goddesses.
The eleventh stage clarifies that compassion is perfected through wisdom to universally benefit sentient beings, symbolized by the birth of the Buddha from Māyā, the Mother of Buddhas.
One must skillfully grasp its meaning to be able to know the truth; this constitutes the gateway to faith and understanding and the path of spiritual advancement.
Without exhausting the Great Teaching, there would be no means by which to provide guidance.
From within the tenth section, the "Gate of the Characteristics of Practice on the Stage of Joyful Enlightenment" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), it is further divided into two parts:
first, a general outline of this stage; second, an explanation of the meaning according to the text.
Regarding the first major section of this stage: within this Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), it is divided into twelve sections.

The first, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, if there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness," consists of seventeen lines of scripture, clarifying the initial arising from the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) through thirty kinds of vast aspirations and profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*) to enter the rank of Bodhisattvas and be born into the family of the Tathāgata.

2. From "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva dwells on the Stage of Joy" onwards, there is a passage of twenty-three lines of scripture that clarifies the Bodhisattva’s initial entry into the stages (*bhūmi*), characterized by a great abundance of joy.

3. "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva takes great compassion as the foremost," and so forth—the following sixteen lines of scripture clarify that after entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one further gives rise to thirty-four kinds of vast aspirations and inclinations (*adhimukti*).

4. From "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy" onwards, there are fifty-eight lines of scripture clarifying the section on dwelling in the Stage of Joy and giving rise to ten kinds of inexhaustible, vast vows.

5. "O Son of the Buddha, this great vow" and the following seven and a half lines of scripture clarify how the ten inexhaustible vows are accomplished through the ten inexhaustible phrases (*daśākṣayamukha*).

Sixth: From "O Son of the Buddha, once the Bodhisattva has made such great vows" onwards, there are eight lines of scripture which clarify that after having generated the ten inexhaustible vows, one attains the section on the ten kinds of beneficial minds and the ten kinds of functional power of faith.

7. "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva further reflects... and so forth; the following eighteen lines of scripture clarify the section on the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of reality and compassion for the mundane, wherein great loving-kindness and compassion arise in accordance with the conditions of delusion.

8. From "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" onwards, there are twenty-one and a half lines of sūtra text, clarifying the section on the Bodhisattva entering the first bhūmi and practicing giving in accordance with great loving-kindness and great compassion.

9. "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy" and so forth—comprising eighteen lines and a half of scripture—clarifies the section on how, through the power of great vows, one comes to see many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, as well as the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) for gathering sentient beings.

10. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva" onwards, there are twenty-eight and a half lines of scripture which clarify the section on the Bodhisattva’s skillful inquiry into the successive stages of cultivation and the remedies for obstacles at the time of entering the first stage (*bhūmi*).

11. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" onwards, there are twenty and a half lines of prose that clarify the stage of entering the position and receiving the office of a Bodhisattva.
12. From "If a person accumulates various virtues" onwards, there are forty-six stanzas that versify the preceding teachings.

Second, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: from the first section, the Sūtra states, "O Son of the Buddha, if there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness," which refers to the thirty kinds of vast aspirations (*adhimukti*) produced in this section.

"Those who skillfully cultivate all practices and skillfully gather the aids to the Path" refers precisely to the ten *pāramitās* and the contemplation of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

Beginning with the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one constantly contemplates the body as empty, devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics; one contemplates sensation as being neither internal, nor external, nor in between; one contemplates the mind as having no abiding place; and one contemplates phenomena as being without self.
Diligently practicing this contemplation is called the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*).
When the mind accords with what is contemplated and one attains the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), it is called the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Because one has attained the selflessness of phenomena, one obtains the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Because one attains penetration through contemplation and does not regress, these are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

The five faculties are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; they are so named because, by not regressing from the cycle of birth and death, the faculty of right faith is perfected.
To follow along with objects of perception without being stained by them, and not to act in concert with the afflictions, is called "power.

As for power, it is like the aforementioned five faculties (*pañcendriya*): when they follow objects without retreating and do not unite with the afflictions, but instead act in concert with wisdom (*jñāna*), it is called power.
Even having attained the seven factors of enlightenment:
the seven awakenings are the awakening factor of mindfulness;
the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena;
The factor of enlightenment of energy;
the factor of enlightenment of joy;
the factor of enlightenment of equanimity;
The awakening factor of tranquility: this mind is called "tranquil" because it accords with principle;
the awakening factor of concentration.
By attaining these seven factors of awakening, one obtains the eight factors of the noble path.
The Eightfold Noble Path consists of right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
The commentary states:
Entering into the Buddha’s wisdom is called right view;
observing phenomena with that wisdom is called right thought.
To practice and cultivate according to the dharmas of the five stages is called right effort (*samyag-vīrya*).
To be constantly united with wisdom and not to dwell with deluded emotions is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

For the mind to be without arising or ceasing, yet to be able to give rise to the wisdom of all Buddhas and to manifest immeasurable great supernormal powers, is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).

To be skillfully able to distinguish between humans and non-Buddhists, the three vehicles and the one vehicle, wrong views and right views, wrong determination and right determination, and wrong conduct and right conduct is called right speech.

Skillfully discerning all erroneous actions of oneself and others, and skillfully manifesting that the Buddha’s wisdom and so forth are shared equally by all sentient beings, is called Right Action (*samyak-karmānta*).

Causing all sentient beings—including humans, devas, non-Buddhists, worldly beings in the cycle of birth and death, and those following the liberation methods of the three vehicles—to dedicate [their merit] toward the Tathāgata’s fundamental mind of omniscience, remaining fundamentally free from emotional agitation, is called Right Livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
As for the thirty kinds of vast aspirations and inclinations, they are fully explained in the sutra.

From the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva first gives rise to such a mind" and following, there are five lines of the sutra that collectively conclude that a bodhisattva is able to give rise to these thirty kinds of vast aspirations and inclinations; by first giving rise to such a mind, one immediately transcends the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), enters the rank of a bodhisattva, and is born into the family of the Tathāgata.

This section comprehensively subsumes the initial stage of "First Resolve" (*prathamacittotpāda*) within the preceding ten stages (*bhūmi*), which corresponds to the first stage, "Joyful" (*pramuditā*), within these ten stages. It establishes that one is born into the family of the Tathāgata as a true son of the Buddha, clarifying that they share the same vehicle, taking the wisdom of the Tathāgata as their essential nature.

This clarifies the distinct practices and distinct wisdoms within the five stages; because they advance simultaneously as one without beginning, middle, or end, they are not like the three vehicles which follow dharmas according to emotional attachments.
Although the practices of the Dharma are vast, they constitute the single seal of a Buddha’s wisdom, for all dharmas are neither prior nor posterior.

Thus, these dharmas of the ten stages (bhūmis) actually fulfill the preceding dharmas of the ten abodes (vihāras), the ten practices (caryās), and the ten transferences (pariṇāmanās); it is not that there are separate dharmas that come into being within these ten stages.
It is like a radish, which produces leaves from its root, and those leaves in turn nourish the root;
or like sowing grain, where the fruit gives rise to the sprout, and once the sprout has matured and the fruit is formed, it returns to the original fruit.
It is like Sudhana seeing the Tathāgata Maitreya, yet Maitreya causes him to see Mañjuśrī once again; this clarifies that the fruit does not depart from the fruit within the cause.
