The practitioners of the Three Vehicles, through the contemplation of emptiness and the practice-gates of the five stages, rejoice in the principle and the ultimate truth; only then do they rejoice in the gateway of the Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom. Nevertheless, they must further enter into the vows and practices of Samantabhadra.
That is to say, the fruit of Buddhahood lies beyond the ten stages of faith; it is said that one reaches it only after completing three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
If one does not turn the mind [toward awakening], both remain outside the gate in a grass hut.

The gate of the supreme ten wholesome acts and the One Vehicle takes the Tathāgata Sarvatrāgata-acala-jñāna Buddha as the object of faith; within the stage of the Ten Abidings, one immediately enters the fruit of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

The ten stages of faith and the five ranks all take the great wisdom of the Buddha-fruit as the basis for their practice; they take the Tathāgata’s universal radiance wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*) as the essence of the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, and the eleventh ground. Thus, the Buddha-fruit and the conduct of Samantabhadra mutually support one another. Because this wisdom-essence is perfectly luminous and transcends conceptual perception, it is not encompassed by the three periods of time.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* takes the three vehicles and turns them back toward the ocean of wisdom, which is symbolized by the dragon girl;
this sūtra reveals the gateway to Buddhahood instantaneously, as exemplified by Sudhana.
Although Sudhana traveled extensively among his spiritual friends, he did not move a single step from before the ocean of awakening.
Although Maitreya attained the merit of becoming a Buddha in a single lifetime, he never departed from the ocean of wisdom that is non-dual in terms of past and future, and free from arising.
This is the vehicle of omniscience, wherein all views of the past and present are exhausted.
Those whose minds remain attached to temporal succession do not enter the gate of Buddha-wisdom; they merely dwell in grass huts and stop outside the door.
The Master of the Treatise states in verse:
All sentient beings possess the golden realm, Pure, stainless, and indestructible wisdom;
The jewel of wisdom lies within their inner garments, Yet they remain outside the gate, enduring perpetual poverty.
The vast and precious vehicle stands at the crossroads; Mañjuśrī guides from the front, Samantabhadra supports from behind.
Drawn by a robust white ox of immense strength, It traverses all realms in a single thought, without expanding or contracting.
Thus unable to enter this precious vehicle, they take pleasure only in standing before the gate of arduous toil;
unaware that they themselves dwell within it, they constantly say, "I am not yet fit."
The forty lines of scripture in the fourth section clarify the stage of generating compassion within the Second Ground (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*).
This is further divided into ten subsections.

First, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" (*jinaputra*) onwards, there are forty lines of scripture that collectively comprise ten kinds of compassionate thoughts toward sentient beings and ten ways of contemplating the path of suffering of sentient beings, intended to establish them within ten kinds of happiness. These are fully contained within the scripture itself, consisting of ten successive instances of the phrase "He further forms this thought."
Just as the two views of self-identity and extremes are placed at the head [of the list] because both the view of grasping at views and the view of grasping at precepts arise based on false view;
so too, ignorance within the six destinies and three realms arises based on name-and-form, giving rise to unwholesome wisdom and unwholesome desire.
"Those who depart from the Buddha's intent" clarifies that the faculties follow the transformations of objects because they are deluded regarding their own Buddha-wisdom.

"I pull them out from such perilous difficulties and cause them to dwell in the fearless city of omniscience" clarifies that by recollecting suffering, one gives rise to compassion, thereby enabling them to realize fundamental wisdom.
Furthermore, he reflects:
"The fact that all sentient beings are submerged by the waves of a great torrential flood clarifies that they are submerged by the water of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

The fact that they enter the whirlpools of birth and death within the flow of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flow of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flow of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*), and the flow of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*) clarifies that they are collectively adrift and tossed about by the eddies of the river of craving."

"The turbulent current rushes and surges so that there is no leisure for observation" clarifies that the preceding four floods pursue objects with such steep and rapid velocity that, arising from views, various deluded karmas are produced; thus, there is no leisure to give rise to contemplation and subdue them.

Regarding those who are pursued and not abandoned by thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty: this clarifies that these three streams of evil conduct arise from being seized by the rākṣasa of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), leading one to enter forever into the dense forest of craving and desire.
Based on the body and so forth, the five views arise together.
When the five views arise together, the sixty-two views arise simultaneously.
Regarding these sixty-two views, according to the *Vibhāṣā*, four views arise for each of the five aggregates; thus, four times five makes twenty.
There are twenty views for each of the three periods of time, totaling sixty.
When combined with the two views that the body is identical to the self and that the body is distinct from the self, these constitute the sixty-two views in total.
Furthermore, regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), one considers: "form is the self," "the self is apart from form," "form is within the self," or "the self is within form.
Relying on one's own Buddha-wisdom, one gradually clarifies the vision of the truths through the five stages.
Furthermore, there are five causes and five fruits; these are established based on the original five [causes] above, totaling ten.
Altogether, there are one hundred and ten dharma-gates, all of which involve dharmas such as delusion, obstruction, and ignorance.
Just as the obstacles encountered by the youth Sudhana are fully elucidated upon reaching his respective stages,

so too is this called the delusion regarding the lack of mastery in progressive cultivation according to the stages, which persists until the fruit of Buddhahood— namely, the delusion regarding the vastness of numerical calculation and the delusion regarding the vast magnitude of the proportions of the marks and signs and the radiance of their merits, which can only be fully known by a Buddha who has reached the ultimate fruit.

This is as the Tathāgata himself has explained in the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks" (*Anuvyañjana-prabhāsa-guṇa-parivarta*).

Thus, regarding the delusions and obstacles encountered during progress through the stages (*bhūmi*), they are clearly elucidated in correspondence with each of the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) represented by Sudhana, so that they may be easily understood; for [otherwise] one would follow erroneous paths.

Furthermore, all sentient beings—including humans, devas, māras, and brahmās, as well as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the pure lands—all possess false views; it is merely that their experiences of suffering and pleasure differ, yet none of them practice according to right view.
Those who act with perversion include the four perversions, the eight perversions, and so forth.

The phrase "like a blind person without a guide" clarifies that the Bodhisattva, observing such delusion, gives rise to compassion and seeks the essential path of deliverance to save all beings through wisdom.
The following may be understood accordingly.
Those who have entered the realm of Māra are the five aggregates-māra, the afflictions-māra, the death-māra, and the celestial-māra.
Those who are seized by evil bandits are the six sense faculties that pursue their objects and give rise to various false views.

Following the mind of Māra, they give rise to delusion regarding the truth and falsely grasp at name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Enmeshed by their own nets of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), they revolve within the stream of suffering, bewildered by the dense forest of ignorance. Just as all sentient beings are bewildered by this dense forest of ignorance, there are, in brief, eighty-four thousand such types.

In general terms, the first delusion is the delusion that is equal to space; it is the delusion regarding one's own self as the ocean of the Tathāgata’s universal radiance and fundamental wisdom, which is a total delusion equal to the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Such ignorance is vast and manifold, obscuring and obstructing fundamental wisdom; therefore, it is called a "dense forest.

It is like the ignorance of a bodhisattva who has entered the stages and is lost on the path: there are one hundred [factors] according to the causes and effects cultivated as they progress through the five stages, because within each of these five stages there are ten kinds of pāramitās.

This is considered the embodiment of the practice of ascending progress. It is like the cultivation of the Samādhi of Expedient Means from the stage of Ten Faiths onward within the Ten Abodes; it is the cultivation of the Initial Stage of Resolve within the Ten Abodes, directed toward entering the fruition of the Initial Stage of Resolve. This is what is called attaining the recollection of the light of the wisdom of all Buddhas, which is the entry into the Country of the Sea Gate.
Contemplating and cultivating the stage of Abiding in Observation, one observes the ocean of all sentient beings; this is the ocean of the pure *dharmadhātu*.
Attaining the Dharma-door of the Universal Eye is the correct entry into the fruit of the stage of Abiding in Cultivation.
Thus, these five stages consist of fifty dharma-gates, each possessing two kinds of cause and effect, totaling one hundred dharma-gates for ascending progress.
Furthermore, because they begin from the dense forest of birth and death at the initial arousal of the mind, this stage is designated as the first.

If one understands that these views have no intrinsic substance, then all views are the dharma-realm arising through conditions; their arising is merely the arising of dharmas, and their perception is merely the perception of dharmas. They turn according to wisdom as objects of cognition, and all unwholesome paths within the three realms and six destinies arise collectively from these five types [of views].
If one realizes this, one immediately enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thereafter, all afflictions will never arise again.
Thus, the destruction of the characteristics of these five views is the transcendence of worldly karma.
Thus, from these five views arise strife, contention, and resentment; just as greed gives rise to wrong livelihood, and the three poisons give rise to the karmas of greed, hatred, and delusion.
When evil karma increases and flourishes, it is called "blazing."
Regarding "cooling nirvana": when karma ceases and wisdom manifests, this is bliss.

Furthermore, the mention of those with the heavy darkness of ignorance and the film of false views collectively clarifies that many are obstructed by deluded karma; they are deluded regarding name-and-form (nāmarūpa), thereby obstructing right wisdom.

Furthermore, regarding those cited as falling into the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts: this clarifies that due to the delusions and obstructions of the past, they fall falsely into the hells—specifically, the eighteen hells.

The eighteen are: the cauldrons of boiling water and the furnaces of burning charcoal; the mountains of knives and the trees of swords; the darkness and the freezing ice; the fire chariots and the fire wheels; the iron net and the copper pillar; the boiling excrement and the plucking out of tongues; the nailing of the body and the spitting of fire; drinking molten copper out of folly; the city of fire and the river of ashes, and so forth.
The eighteen types of hells mentioned above are experienced precisely where the evil karma created by the mind is produced.

Regarding those who enter the net of wrong views, it clarifies that within each of the five aggregates of the "self," these four [types of views] are present; such views all arise based upon the body. Therefore, this sutra states: "Without a body, there are no views; thus one attains the unsurpassed state of Buddhahood."
"Those who are about to enter the dense forest of craving and desire" clarifies that all birth and death arise from craving and desire.

Because birth and death are manifold, they are like a dense forest; in a single kṣaṇa, eight hundred moments of arising and ceasing arise simultaneously in a continuous, uninterrupted flow, such that at the very end of that kṣaṇa, arising and ceasing occur together.
Regarding those who give rise to deep defilement and attachment toward what they crave, this clarifies that they perform the karma of birth and death repeatedly and without ceasing.

As for the "highlands of conceit," there are seven types of conceit: conceit (*māna*), excessive conceit (*atimāna*), pride of self (*asmimāna*), pride of arrogance (*abhimāna*), pride of superiority (*adhimāna*), pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*), and false conceit (*mithyāmāna*).
Regarding "original eminence" (*yuanfù*): it clarifies that when pride (*māna*) is further increased by pride and over-pride (*atimāna*), it is termed an "eminence.
It is like a high ground upon level earth; that which is level atop it is called an "original plain" (*yuan*).
That which is higher than the original mound is a heap; that which is higher than the heap is a hillock.
This illustrates how the six types of conceit are added upon the original conceit of self, which constitutes this "hillock.

Regarding the establishment of the six sense bases as a village: atop the mounds and hillocks of pride, one further adds the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind to grasp at the objects of name and form.
The fourteen lines of sutra beginning with "Increasing the causes of suffering" can be understood according to the text.
These ten sections of sutra clarify the stage within this [ground] of observing suffering and giving rise to compassion for the purpose of providing protection and rescue.

The fifth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," consists of thirty-one and a half lines of scripture, clarifying that the bodhisattvas of this stage, through the power of their vows, are able to see many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
This section is further divided into ten parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "ten billion Buddhas," there are three and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the aspect of this stage’s bodhisattva perceiving many Buddhas through the power of their vows.

2. From "At the abodes of all Buddhas" down to "and also making offerings to the entire Sangha," there are two and a half lines of scripture that clarify the division of offerings to the Buddhas and the Sangha by means of two mental states and five types of material things.
Regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha herein: Vairocana is the Buddha Jewel; Mañjuśrī is the Dharma Jewel; and the conduct of Samantabhadra is the Sangha Jewel.

This encompasses all those of the three vehicles, the six realms of humans and devas, and the Three Jewels; they are all contained within these Three Jewels, for they are all accomplished through following the teachings of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
The four lines of sūtra from "The Roots of Goodness" down to "the purity and fulfillment of generosity and precepts" clarify the section on the re-acceptance of the ten wholesome precepts.
This clarifies that the first stage (*bhūmi*) also receives the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) in their highest degree; this further emphasizes the process of refinement and polishing.

The passage from "For example, like pure gold" down to "the purity of precepts is fulfilled" consists of three and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the analogy of refining pure gold by adding alum so that it becomes even more brilliant and pure.

5. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, up to "only according to one's power and according to one's lot," there are two and a half lines of scripture that clarify the portion of practice performed by the Bodhisattvas of this stage.
6. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the knowledge of all-knowledge," there are six and a half lines of sūtra, clarifying the section on the reception of office by the bodhisattva of this stage.

7. From "Furthermore, he thinks thus" down to "the basis of the knowledge of all-knowledge," there are two and a half lines of sūtra, clarifying the section on the bodhisattva of this stage personally knowing the excellence of his own virtues.

8. From "This bodhisattva" below to "as his retinue," there are four and a half lines of scripture which clarify that this bodhisattva is also able to renounce home, wife, and children to leave the household life, attain a thousand samādhis, and obtain a portion of the vision of the Buddha.

9. From "If by the superior power of a bodhisattva’s vow" down to "cannot be known by calculation," it clarifies that seeing the Buddha through the power of superior vows surpasses the previous section on the power of the karma of the environment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
10. From "At that time" onwards clarifies the section on the recitation of verses by Vajragarbha.
Following the sixth recitation of verses, there are forty-two lines of verse, which are further divided into five sections.

First, from "Honest, supple, and capable" down to "For the sake of the sons of the Buddhas, it has been expounded," there are thirty stanzas that clarify the ten preceding sections of the Dharma-gates.
Two lines form one verse, as is fully contained within the text itself.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards until "the characteristics of practice in the second stage," there are four lines of verse, clarifying the section on the great assembly hearing the Dharma and making offerings.

3. From "These bodhisattvas" down to "Please expound the third bhūmi," there are three lines of verse which clarify that the bodhisattvas, having heard about the second bhūmi, further request the exposition of the section on the dharmas of the third bhūmi.

4. From "The various activities of wisdom corresponding to the Dharma" down to "the Buddha’s pure vows of conduct are all proclaimed," there are three verses clarifying the section on the collective request for the teaching by all the bodhisattvas.
5. "At that time, Vimukticandra again requested," and so forth; the two lines of verse below clarify that Vimukticandra once more requested the exposition of the section on the Third Bhūmi.

As stated above regarding "all modes" (*sarvākāra*), by means of the cultivation of seeds through preparatory application (*prayoga*), one attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), which is precisely the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the "wise one," it is clarified that through the application of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one accomplishes differentiated wisdom (*prabheda-jñāna*). Just as fundamental wisdom manifests by virtue of samādhi, differentiated wisdom is accomplished through the power of cultivation based on the observation of fundamental wisdom during its preparatory application (*prayoga*).

If one does not employ the power of application, the power of observation, and the power of great vows for each [moment], then the fundamental wisdom will simply stagnate in quiescence, becoming identical to the vehicle of the śrāvakas; therefore, it would be of no use.
3. The Third Stage, the Radiant (Prabhākari-bhūmi). Regarding the explanation of this stage, five sections are established as in the preceding stages.
First, concerning the explanation of the name of the stage: for what reason is it called the Radiant Stage?
This stage clarifies the cultivation of the eight dhyānas of the form and formless realms, and the thorough mastery of those realms.

It involves the mutual counteraction between the meditative bodies of the world and consciousness, and provides clear insight into the divisions of the obstacles and delusions within the three realms.
It is called the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākarī-bhūmi*) because it causes wisdom to become increasingly bright and pure.

Furthermore, having thoroughly mastered the phenomena of the secondary fetters within the desire realm from the first and second grounds, and having thoroughly mastered the dharma-gates of the four dhyānas and eight meditative attainments of the form and formless realms on the third ground, one emerges from the three realms; thus, because the light of wisdom manifests before one, it is named the Ground of Radiant Light.

If one only cultivates the afflictions of the desire realm and does not cultivate the eight meditative absorptions to reach the form and formless realms, because the obstacles of those two higher realms still remain, it is not called "Emission of Light."

Because one cultivates this stage to exhaust the karmic obstacles of the three realms, it is named the "Radiant Stage" (*Prabhākarī-bhūmi*), for meditative concentration can give rise to the light of wisdom.
Second, as for what practice-gate is cultivated on this stage: it takes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence, with the other eight perfections as its companions.
This clarifies that because the karmic obstructions of the three realms have been exhausted, this patience is called "patience in accordance with non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

If, upon entering the first stage of the Bodhisattva path (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), the wisdom of a Buddha manifests before one, it is called being "born into the family of the wisdom of all Buddhas. Having attained non-arising patience throughout the ten stages, the ten practices, and the ten transferences constitutes the general meaning.

If we speak in terms of the progressive cultivation of the coarse and the subtle: the three stages of worthiness prior to the [ten] grounds are called "subduing through the Buddha’s wisdom" and are termed the "Patience of Subduing" (*vinaya-kṣānti*);
the first, second, and third grounds are termed the "Conformity to the Patience of Non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti-anuloma*);
from the fourth, fifth, and sixth grounds onward, having emerged from the triple world and being free from worldly obstacles, they are finally termed the attainment of the "Patience of Non-arising."
The seventh, eighth, and ninth stages are called the "Effortless Patience of Quiescence" (*anābhoga-śānti-kṣānti*);
at the tenth stage, compassion and wisdom are perfectly integrated, and the rank is equal to that of the Buddhas.

Regarding Sudhana’s manifestation of the Dharma within these stages: in this position, Sudhana beholds the Night Goddess *Priyadarśanā-sattvāvalokanī*, who, not far from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), sits upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury.
Sudhana attained the liberation gate of the Banner of Universal Joy and Great Power, which symbolizes the initial aspiration at the very beginning of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

The second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā*), is the essence of enlightenment from the first assembly, serving as the essence of ethical discipline (*śīla*). The third stage is the cultivation of patience (*kṣānti*) based on the principle of enlightenment; since patience is the foremost of practices, one is not far from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for it is through enlightenment that the practice of patience is perfected.
He sits upon the lion throne of the Lotus Treasury; the lotus signifies being unstained amidst practice, while the lion clarifies the principle of relying on the Dharma.
He is titled "The One with Joyful Eyes Who Observes Sentient Beings," which clarifies the practice of loving-kindness through the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
The Night Deity is explained as before.

As for Sudhana’s attainment of the liberation of the Banner of Universal Joy with Great Power: this clarifies that he has transcended the three realms and exhausted all obstructions; because afflictions such as greed, hatred, anger, resentment, and delusion can no longer arise, the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) is perfected and manifests before him, whereby he possesses great power.

Regarding the liberation of the Universal Joy Banner: it clarifies that one is able to destroy the afflictions of both self and others; that one is not shaken by any sensory objects; and that one achieves the joy of the Dharma amidst all circumstances, whether adverse or favorable.
Regarding the fourth clarification—what kind of liberation from the three realms is attained at this stage—it is the attainment of liberation from all three realms.

While the first two stages serve as the antidote to the desire realm, these [subsequent] three stages successively serve as the antidotes for the two higher realms; thus, the eight dhyānas collectively exhaust all obstacles within the three realms.

On the fourth stage, one cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; on the fifth stage, one cultivates the contemplation of the ten truths; and on the sixth stage, one cultivates the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, because one is training in supramundane and mundane wisdom.
Regarding the fivefold commentary on the meaning according to the text, two points are as previously explained.
First, concerning the long division of the intent of the sūtra: within this section of the *Prabhākarī-bhūmi*, it is divided into seven sections.

First, from "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" down to "attaining the third stage," there are five lines of scripture that clarify the section on the arising of the ten kinds of mind as one cultivates the third stage from the second stage.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the fifty-two and a half lines of scripture stating that "it is not merely by verbal expression that one can attain purity" clarify the correct abiding in the third stage (*bhūmi*). This explains how one contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), gives rise to compassion for all sentient beings, honors the Dharma and respects those who uphold it, and is able to enter a pit of fire to undergo suffering for the sake of hearing the Dharma.

The third section, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "and there is no attachment or delight," consists of ten and a half lines of scripture. It clarifies the stage of dwelling in the Radiant Ground (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), wherein one cultivates the four dhyānas and eight samādhis of the form and formless realms, proceeding in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) without any attachment.

The fourth section, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "is likewise so," consists of two lines of sūtra that clarify the stage of cultivating the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

The fifth section, from "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) down to "by means of the power of vows one is born therein," consists of thirty-three lines of scripture; it clarifies the stage of dwelling in this ground where, through the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which constitutes the division on the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*).

The sixth section, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "and spoke these verses," consists of thirty lines of scripture, clarifying the extent of the Buddhas seen by the Bodhisattva of this stage, as well as his reception of office.
The seventh section, “Then he spoke in verse,” constitutes the portion on the recitation of verses.

Within these seven segments of the sūtra, the first—beginning with “At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha” and comprising five lines of scripture—clarifies the transition from the second bhūmi toward the cultivation of the third bhūmi by giving rise to ten kinds of mind, as detailed in the sūtra itself.
The second section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" and below, consists of fifty-two and a half lines of sūtra, which are further divided into five parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in the third stage" down to "these are the ten," there are nineteen lines of sūtra that clarify the contemplation of conditioned suffering and impermanence through ten modes of compassion for sentient beings.

Second, from "The Bodhisattva, having thus perceived the realm of sentient beings" down to "the bliss of ultimate nirvāṇa," there are seven and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies how the bodhisattva contemplates the deliverance of sentient beings, by what means and in what state they are established, so that they may attain the portion of the bliss of ultimate nirvāṇa.

3. From "Then he formed this thought" down to "having thus observed and fully understood," there are approximately five lines of scripture that clarify what the Bodhisattva contemplates, namely the section concerning the knowledge of how to establish sentient beings in their ultimate destination.

4. From "Twofold [the Dharma]" down to "observing and practicing," there are nineteen lines of scripture which clarify that when Bodhisattvas wish to deliver sentient beings, they redouble their diligent cultivation to seek the Dharmakāya; such that they would be able to abandon their lives by entering a great pit of fire without a trace of suffering.
5. From "This Bodhisattva" onwards, there are two lines of scripture clarifying that this is definitive practice, not merely a matter of verbal expression.
*New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle 24;
*New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle 25.
Regarding the commentary on the meaning of each passage composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan, the remaining text is self-evident.

As for the desire to deliver sentient beings and cause them to abide in the bliss of nirvana, this does not depart from the wisdom of unobstructed liberation; this is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Up to and including the realization, as it truly is, of non-activity and non-arising; the certainty of skill in the meditative concentration of the light of wisdom;

and the skill in analytical knowledge and extensive learning—these five dharmas collectively constitute the secondary functions of the single fundamental gnosis, which are manifested and made visible by the practitioner through the cultivation of skillful means and meditative absorption.

Just as those who diligently seek to practice the True Dharma with redoubled vigor, who day and night aspire only to hear the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, because clear wisdom manifests and there is no sorrow;
who rejoice in the Dharma because they are free from birth and death; and who rely on the Dharma because they rely upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
One who follows the Dharma does so because they accord with right liberation.
One who understands the Dharma does so because they understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
One who conforms to the Dharma does so because they conform to right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Regarding "reaching the Dharma": it means that while one has personally reached nirvana, one is able to enter into birth and death to deliver sentient beings, and also causes others to reach nirvana.

This is because, as it is said that obtaining even a single verse of the Dharma is superior to obtaining the treasures of the great trichiliocosm or the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, it clarifies that worldly dharmas cannot escape birth and death.
The subsequent sections should be understood accordingly.

Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, there are ten and a half lines of scripture; these belong to the section on "Conformity with the Nature of Reality Without Attachment" within the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, and are further divided into nine segments.
1. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the joy and happiness born of seclusion," this one and a half lines of sūtra constitute the section on abiding in the first dhyāna.
2. From "the cessation of applied and sustained thought" down to "the joy and happiness born of concentration," this one line of sūtra constitutes the section on abiding in the second dhyāna.

3. From "dwelling in equanimity, free from joy" down to "experiencing bliss with mindfulness and equanimity," there are two lines of scripture; this constitutes the section on abiding in the third dhyāna. 4.
From "abandoning bliss" down to "abiding in the fourth dhyāna," there is one line of scripture; this constitutes the section on abiding in the fourth dhyāna.

5. From "having transcended all perceptions of form" down to "abiding in the sphere of infinite space," there is one line of scripture; this constitutes the constituent part of the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.

6. "Transcending the sphere of infinite space and attaining and abiding in the sphere of infinite consciousness" constitutes one line of sutra; this is the factor of the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*). 7.

From "transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness" down to "the sphere of nothingness," one line of sutra; this is the factor of the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

8. From "Transcending the Sphere of Nothingness" down to "the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception," this single line of sūtra constitutes the section on the meditative attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; it is the pinnacle of these three realms.

9. "To accord with the Dharma alone and thus have no attachments" refers to the concentration of a mind without dependence; this is the essential nature of the *dharmadhātu-samādhi*. To explain the meaning according to the text:

it clarifies that upon attaining this Radiant Ground (*prabhākarī-bhūmi*), one acquires a mind that transcends the three realms and enters the gate of the great non-conditioned samādhi, which is the very essence of the *dharmadhātu*. Although one cultivates the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, one constantly accords with the *dharmatā* without any point of reliance, doing so solely to refine and polish the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the three realms so that wisdom may become bright and pure.
Because one should cultivate and progress in this manner, it is like the analogy of well-refined gold that does not lose a single *zhū* or *liǎng* in weight.
In this way, through repeated refinement by means of precept, concentration, and wisdom, one does not lose even a fraction of the great, perfectly round, and luminous wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.

By means of these eight kinds of meditative concentration, one refines and polishes them so that wisdom becomes increasingly bright and pure; because the essence of the Dharma-body wisdom is fundamentally without increase or decrease, it is called the Ground of Radiance (Prabhākarī-bhūmi).

According to the provisional teachings, bodhisattvas who attain the eight dhyānas transcend the suffering of the triple world and are reborn in a pure land; those possessing great compassion, however, retain their afflictions to moisten their rebirth and remain in the mundane world.

When Śrāvakas and Arhats emerge from the eight dhyānas and enter the ninth concentration, they rely on the wisdom of emptiness to bring about cessation; thus, both body and wisdom are entirely absent.

In contrast, when Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle practice the eight dhyānas, they skillfully understand that worldly phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Because they accomplish the wondrous function of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), because they realize that the essence of the three realms is inherently without arising or ceasing, and because they give rise to transcendent great wisdom to know worldly phenomena, it is therefore called the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

On the first stage (*bhūmi*), one cultivates generosity (*dāna*) while abiding in the world; on the second stage, one cultivates ethical discipline (*śīla*) and clearly purifies the world; on the third stage, one cultivates the eight meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and clearly attains transcendence from the world; on the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one clearly cultivates the wisdom that is both transcendent and worldly; on the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages, one clearly cultivates entry into the world to achieve the perfect integration of compassion and wisdom; and on the tenth stage, one clearly cultivates the perfection of wisdom and compassion to attain the state of Buddhahood.

In reckoning their essence of principle and wisdom, there is no actual substantiality or hierarchical gradation of stages; rather, the various stages (*bhūmi*) are established to counteract habitual tendencies, to integrate compassion and wisdom, and to bring about the maturation of these qualities, as well as to distinguish between the cultivation of mundane and supramundane differentiated wisdoms according to their depth and shallowness. Thus, a systematic framework has been provided for others to emulate.

The fourth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" and comprising two and a half lines of scripture, clarifies the cultivation of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), with great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) as the primary part.

The fifth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" and continuing until "by the power of their vows they are born therein," consists of thirty-three lines of scripture; it clarifies the section on the mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vaśitā*).
This section is further divided into six parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva attains immeasurable supernormal powers" down to "the Brahma world," there are six lines of scripture that clarify the division on supernormal powers.
2. From "This bodhisattva" down to "is also able to hear everything," there are two lines of sūtra that clarify the portion concerning the supernormal power of the divine ear.

3. From "This bodhisattva" down to "knows the minds of sentient beings through the knowledge of others' minds," there are seven lines of sūtra that clarify the portion concerning the attainment of the knowledge of others' minds.
4. From "This bodhisattva" onwards to "are all able to recollect," there are eight lines of scripture, which clarify the attainment of the power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsajñāna).
5. From "This bodhisattva" onwards to "knows them all as they truly are," there are seven and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the attainment of the divine eye (divyacakṣus).

The above clarifies the mastery of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of Bodhisattvas. Because their wisdom and compassion have not yet fulfilled their original vows, because they possess the practices of Samantabhadra, because they differ from Bodhisattvas in pure lands, and because they differ from those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), they do not realize the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). This is because their wisdom exercises mastery in accordance with their conduct within birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"Though they have realized the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they do not exhaust their outflows (*āsrava*).
The two lines of sūtra from "This bodhisattva" down to "is born therein by the power of his vow" clarify the section on being born without following the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The sixth section, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "and spoke these verses," consists of thirty and a half lines of scripture; this segment is further divided into six sub-sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "practicing according to one's power," there are six and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the stage where this bodhisattva, by the power of their vows, attains the vision of many Buddhas and performs offerings while hearing the Dharma.
2. From "This bodhisattva" down to "becomes even more bright and pure," there are four and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on observing phenomena and liberation from bondage.

3. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "becomes even more bright and pure," there are three lines of scripture, which clarify the analogy of refining gold; the gold is compared to the bodhisattva’s wisdom of preparatory application (*prayoga*) on the stages (*bhūmi*), clarifying its increasing brightness and purity.

4. From "This bodhisattva" onwards, up to "all become transformed and purified," there are three lines of scripture that clarify the section on the thirteen types of mind that become increasingly bright and pure through patience and gentleness.

5. From "This bodhisattva" below, down to "according to his power and according to his lot," there is one and a half lines of scripture that clarify the portion of the Dharma practiced by the bodhisattva at this stage.

Sixth: From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "cannot be calculated," there are ten and a half lines of scripture that clarify the section on the number of Buddhas seen by Bodhisattvas in this stage, based on their reception of office and their meditative concentration.
Seventh, from "At that time" onwards, is the section clarifying the verses spoken by Vajragarbha.
Within these verses there are thirty-six lines, with two lines constituting one verse; they reiterate the preceding teachings as they appear in the text itself.
4. The Fourth Ground: The Ground of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi). In order to explain this ground, five sections will be presented as before.
First, regarding the explanation of the name of the ground: why is it called the Ground of Blazing Wisdom?

Because one cultivates the eight dhyānas of the upper realms in the preceding stage and thereby attains the wisdom that transcends the three realms, it is named the Stage of Radiant Emission (Prabhākārī-bhūmi).

In this stage, one cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; as one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, they become increasingly bright and pure, and thus it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
Because it is brought forth by the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the preceding stage, it is named the Stage of Radiant Light (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).

In this stage, one contemplates the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*) through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); because the wisdom that is inherently without dependence becomes further clarified and purified, it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
Second, regarding what gateways of practice are cultivated on this stage: the perfection of diligence is primary, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.

Third, regarding Sudhana’s representation of the Dharma: within this stage, Sudhana beholds the Night Goddess Sarvasattvatrāṇaśriyā and attains the bodhisattva liberation door of universally manifesting in all worlds to discipline sentient beings.

The fact that this deity dwells within this assembly indicates that he is present together with the previously mentioned deity Joyful Eye; this is to signify that the preceding Stainless Ground (vimalā-bhūmi) takes the unconditioned nature of the Dharma-body as its essence of bodhi, and that the perfection of patience and the perfection of diligence constitute the practice of bodhi.

The Universal Virtue Pure Light resides within the site of enlightenment; the abode of the deity Joyful Eyes is not far from the site of enlightenment. This Night Goddess Who Universally Saves Sentient Beings is present in this assembly within the fourth stage, clearly because the two positions of patience and diligence are not separate from the myriad practices.

Furthermore, it is clarified that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) are auxiliary practices for attaining bodhi; therefore, it is said that they are present within this assembly.

This stage clarifies that by means of the essence of bodhi, one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*), thereby accomplishing mundane wisdom (*laukika-prajñā*).

In the first three stages, one has already sought the supramundane bodhicitta; in these fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one uses that bodhicitta to cultivate mundane wisdom in reverse. This refers to being present within this assembly.

Regarding the vision of the Night Goddess Sarvasattvatrāṇaśri within this stage: it clarifies that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness are the skillful means for the Buddhas of the three periods of time to transform all sentient beings and assist them on the path. Because all Buddhas, from their initial resolve until the attainment of ultimate wisdom, rely upon these very means to increase and clarify their various wisdoms, this goddess is named Sarvasattvatrāṇaśri (Wondrous Virtue Who Universally Saves All Sentient Beings).
"Sublime Virtue" (Prabhākari) refers to the fact that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment clearly manifest the sublime wisdom of both oneself and others.

It clarifies that through the cultivation of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and patience in the preceding three stages, one attains the supramundane mind; in this stage, these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are once again applied to further refine it, and thus it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī).

Regarding the liberation door of "Universally Manifesting in the World to Subdue All Sentient Beings," it is so named because this stage clarifies that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*) are the great path of subduing practiced in common by both the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle; hence, it is called the liberation of universally manifesting to subdue all sentient beings.
One may discern its meaning by comparing each point with the corresponding practices in Sudhana’s journey;
otherwise, it would be impossible to understand the stages and the gates of practice.
This will be explained in detail later in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Lokadhātu-praveśa-parivarta*).

Fourth, regarding what kind of liberation from the three realms is attained at this stage: if considered according to its general characteristics, one attains the liberation of the single characteristic of the three realms;

if considered according to its specific characteristics and progressive advancement, it is clarified that within this stage, by practicing the contemplation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*), one predominantly attains the liberation of wisdom within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The general meaning clarifies that, following the previous treatment in the third bhūmi concerning the remaining habitual tendencies of the three realms, this section elucidates the cultivation of the ten-fold contemplation of truth (*daśatattvavipaśyanā*) within the dhyāna-pāramitā of the fifth bhūmi. It demonstrates how one attains supramundane liberation within both the two upper realms and the desire realm; all of these must be discussed through the analytical categories of totality and particularity, sameness and difference, and formation and disintegration.

Just as the Earth-Dharmadevatā of the Stage of Joy at the beginning [of the path] clearly manifests birth into the Buddha-family—because the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) can nourish the holy path—the deity is named "Mistress of Springtime Birth."

Just as in the second stage, the Stainless Ground (Vimalā-bhūmi), where the precept-pāramitā takes the unconditioned Dharma-body as its essential nature, the spirit is named Universal Virtue Pure Radiance Precept-Light (Pude Jingguang Jiguang).
He immediately dwells within the precincts of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, signifying that the *dharmakāya* is the essence of the *bodhimaṇḍa* and that the body is the essence of *bodhi*.

In the third stage, the Radiant (*Prabhākārī*), the essence is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). His spiritual name is Joyful-Eye-Contemplating-Sentient-Beings; because of his patience, there is nothing he does not find joyful.
"Being not far from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)" clarifies that patience takes the non-activity of the Dharma-body as its essence.

The fourth stage, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi), takes the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) as its essence; the spirit is named "Universally Saving All Sentient Beings," because the perfection of vigor carries the meaning of universal salvation.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of universally purifying the residual habits (*vāsanā*) of the three realms that have persisted since the previous three stages.
Those who dwell in this assembly clearly do not depart from the *dharmakāya*, and they practice within the conduct of natural precepts, patience, and diligence.
Thus, by summarizing the names and abodes, the sequential order of the stages (bhūmi) is made easy to perceive; this can be understood through reflection.

Furthermore, the reason that "spiritual power" (ṛddhi) is frequently used as a metaphor for entering the stages is to clarify that entering the stages arises from the assistance of practice through noble wisdom (āryajñāna), which is therefore termed "spiritual power."
Furthermore, one must contemplate this through the sixfold dharma-gate of totality and particularity, sameness and difference, and formation and disintegration; only then will there be no confusion.
Regarding the second [section], the "Explanation of Meaning According to the Text," there are two aspects:
first, the extended analysis of the sutra’s intent, and second, the word-by-word explanation of the meaning.
Regarding the general outline of the meaning of this scripture: within this stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), it is divided into seven sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) onwards, there are twelve lines of verse which clarify that the great assembly, having heard of the preceding stage, rejoices and further requests the teaching for the subsequent stage.

The second section, beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha," consists of the following six and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the stage of entering the fourth bhūmi by means of ten dharmas.

The third section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Blazing Wisdom," consists of thirty-seven and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the division concerning the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The fourth section, consisting of five and a half lines of scripture beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," clarifies the stage of counteracting the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

The fifth section, a passage of fifteen lines beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva," clarifies the stage of attaining great benefit and gentleness through the skillful means of the aforementioned contemplative wisdom.

The sixth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Blazing Wisdom," consists of thirty lines of scripture that clarify the portion concerning the further expansion of the vision of the Buddhas in this stage.
The seventh section, "The Bodhisattva has already purified the Second Ground," consists of fifty-three verses below, which clarify the reiteration of the preceding section on the Dharma.
Within the first twelve verses, it is further divided into two parts.

First: From "The Sons of the Buddha, having heard this vast practice" down to "the sublime Dharma-sound of the Bodhisattvas' superior conduct," there are eight verses of verse which clarify the section on the great assembly hearing the Dharma of the third stage, rejoicing, making offerings, and offering praise.
Second, from the line "I pray that the wise one will further expound," there are four verses which clarify the section on the further request for the Dharma-gate of the Fourth Ground.
The meaning of the preceding text is fully contained within the words themselves; there is no need for further explanation.

Regarding the phrase "just as the Sovereign Lord of Devas is greatly rejoicing": this is because he is the one for whom this teaching on the Ten Stages is expounded; it is not that other devas do not rejoice, but rather that the sovereign of the place where the Dharma is taught is being singled out.

The second section, beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva," contains six and a half lines of sūtra within the cultivation of the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), which is divided into two parts.

First, from "At that time" down to "should cultivate the ten gates of dharma-illumination" (two and a half lines of sūtra), clarifies the section on exhorting the cultivation of the ten dharmas for the purpose of entering the fourth stage.
The three lines of scripture beginning with "What are the ten? constitute the section on the examination of the names and categories of the ten dharmas.

Why are these ten dharmas presented again for contemplation? It is to clarify that while one has attained supramundane wisdom in the preceding three stages, the present re-examination of these ten dharmas clarifies that one will employ this supramundane wisdom to return to the mundane world, thereby making the mundane identical to the supramundane.
The third section, consisting of thirty-seven and a half lines of scripture beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," is divided into nine parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "born into the family of the Tathāgata," there is one and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the stage of being born into the Buddha-family by means of ten kinds of wisdom.

If the first stage of the Ten Abodes, the Stage of Initial Resolve, is called "being born into the family of the Tathāgata," and reaching the first ground (bhūmi) is also called "being born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom," and these four grounds are likewise called "being born into the family of the Tathāgata," what is the difference between them?
Answer: Considering their general characteristics, those born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom are of one essence and non-dual.
However, when discussing their specific characteristics, there are degrees of depth in their spiritual advancement.

Just as within the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi), at the summit of Mount Sumeru, one first awakens from ordinary sentiment and begins to open the Buddha-wisdom; because wisdom merely dispels delusion and one attains a portion of the coolness of liberation from afflictions, the fruit of Buddhahood is named "Moon. This is like the ten lunar Buddhas within the stage of the Ten Abodes.

As illustrated in the section on Sudhana’s manifestation of the Dharma, his vision of the bhikṣu on Mount Megha-dhara primarily demonstrates the Buddha’s wisdom and liberation (*vimukti*), yet does not yet clarify his wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Just as one born into the family of the Tathāgata at the first stage (*bhūmi*) possesses wisdom, virtue, and supernormal powers, they have merely attained the spiritual intelligence that transcends the three realms; their teaching of sentient beings is likewise limited to what they themselves know, and they have not yet attained mastery and unimpededness in both worldly and world-transcending wisdom.

In this fourth stage, one is born into the family of the Buddhas because of the clear realization of both mundane and supramundane wisdom; thus, although it shares a commonality with the spiritual nature entered in the first stage, there is a distinction in the depth of mundane versus supramundane wisdom.

It clarifies that the previous three stages involve practicing only the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the two upper realms, thereby attaining liberation from the three realms; this is the principle of the "single [vehicle].

In this stage, one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*); thus, the Sūtra states: "Having attained those internal dharmas, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata."
Regarding "inner dharmas," this clarifies that through wisdom one turns back to contemplate and penetrates conventional knowledge; for there is no conventionality that is not true.
Second, from "What are the ten? down to "These are the ten," there are four and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on the wisdom of this stage accomplished by means of ten dharmas.

Regarding the phrase "because of not retreating from what is called the profound mind, and because pure faith in the Three Jewels is ultimately indestructible": these Three Jewels encompass all phenomena throughout the three realms and the three periods of time, being subsumed within the universal Three Jewels; they are not like the Three Jewels according to worldly conventions, and thus they are called the "profound mind."
To contemplate that the dharma-nature of the three realms is inherently devoid of self-nature is called the Buddha Jewel.
To thoroughly understand the similarities and differences, the general and the specific, as well as the formation and destruction of the dharmas of the three realms, is called the Dharma Jewel.

By means of the gate of one's own practice, they harmonize the minds and intentions of sentient beings through skillful means to guide and receive them, enabling them to attain the state of an Arhat as well as the bliss of humans and devas; this is called the Sangha Jewel.
Regarding the phrase "observing the formation and destruction of the world," the subsequent text states: "Birth occurs because of karma, and it likewise ceases because of karma."

Because the fundamental dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is without formation or destruction, it is clarified that within this state of non-formation and non-destruction, sentient beings falsely perceive formation and destruction.
Regarding the observation of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, it is clarified that saṃsāra is fundamentally nirvāṇa, because they both lack any inherent substance.

Regarding "observing the lands and karma of sentient beings," this clarifies that nations arise from karma; because they were originally non-existent and now exist; and because one observes their prior limit and subsequent limit.
Regarding "observing the exhaustion of non-existence," this clarifies that the three periods of time are fundamentally non-existent, as there is no characteristic of exhaustion.

It does not say that there is something inexhaustible across many kalpas; rather, it says that the three periods of time are fundamentally non-existent, and that which is fundamentally non-existent cannot be exhausted.
This constitutes the tenth [point], as it summarizes the ten preceding dharmas.

3. From "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this fourth stage" down to "removing worldly craving and attachment," there are six lines of scripture that clarify the section on the contemplative gate of the four foundations of mindfulness—body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.

Regarding the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness: first, as for the foundation of mindfulness of the body, "following" means to accord with. This refers to clearly and skillfully following the observation of the internal body—the five viscera (liver, gallbladder, heart, lungs, spleen, kidneys) and the six receptacles—to realize that within them there is absolutely no self, person, sovereign, or substantial characteristic.
The "diligent hero" refers to one who clearly practices diligent contemplation without weariness.
"Mindful awareness" refers to the non-forgetfulness of mindfulness.

"Eliminating worldly greed and sorrow" means that through diligent contemplation of the internal body, one rightly knows it has no master, thereby eliminating the afflictions of worldly greed and desire.

One contemplates the external body by means of mindfulness of the body. "Mindfulness of the body" (kayānupassanā) means to survey the body; it is also called "following" (anupassanā) and "skillful" (kuśala).

This refers to the thorough investigation of the external body—its skin, flesh, sinews, bones, hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, feet, waist, and hips—to see that there is therein no sovereign self, person, or human characteristic. All arise from false attachments born of karma; there is no substantial dharma. Where there is karma, there is existence; where there is no karma, there is non-existence.

One should contemplate that the essence of karma fundamentally has no basis; realizing that the body has no substance and the recipient is absent, there is great wisdom, perfect and luminous, wherein there is absolutely no self, person, or recipient.
Movement and stillness are left to wisdom; internally and externally there is no dependence; one applies diligent vigor and mindful awareness.

As previously stated regarding "removing worldly greed and grief," this refers to removing the greed and grief associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Regarding "observing the internal and external body by surveying it all around": the internal and external body are observed separately as before; here, one observes the body as a whole, seeing that both internally and externally there is no self-mastery.
Just as in empty space not a single dharma can be apprehended, this is the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Having already observed internal and external sensations by circling through both internally and externally, one observes the subject that experiences and the object experienced within the internal, external, and intermediate [realms].
From the passage "The nature has no dependence" onwards, one observes the inner mind and outer mind, as well as the knower and the known.
From "There is no place of abiding" onwards, one contemplates that within internal and external phenomena there is no self or person.
The above constitutes the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

From the four instances of "Furthermore" onwards, up to "dedicating [merit] toward equanimity," there are eight and a half lines of scripture; this is the section on practicing the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*).

Furthermore, when this bodhisattva practices the cultivation of the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*) for the abandonment of unwholesome states, he clearly and diligently contemplates the first four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). This undistracted state is the concentration of desire, because it is characterized by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

As for the practitioner who abandons, they diligently contemplate the four preceding foundations of mindfulness to abandon the view of a self-identity, extreme views, false views, and so forth, as well as the formations of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
In this stage, one again subdues and refines the afflictions of the desire realm and the afflictions of the two upper realms, further refining them through the *dhyāna-pāramitā* of the five stages.
While the first two stages used the essence of ethical discipline (*śīla*) to subdue the coarse [afflictions], these four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) subdue the subtle ones.

Regarding the accomplishment of the *ṛddhipāda* (bases of supernatural power): the *ṛddhipāda* of the various devas and others in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is the retribution for the inferior grade of the ten wholesome karmic paths. This [accomplishment], however, is distinguished by its excellence as a portion of the wisdom-penetration of the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena); it cannot be compared to the limited penetrations of the three realms or those of the two vehicles and three vehicles.

Furthermore, looking toward subsequent stages, this present stage is not yet as refined; although all contemplative practices take wisdom and principle as their essence, they are made even more subtle in order to achieve discriminating wisdom, and to give rise to the full realization of original vows through contemplating all phenomena, thereby accomplishing great compassion.
Relying on revulsion counteracts the grasping of unwholesome worldly phenomena.
Relying on detachment is because one’s nature is inherently free from attachment.
Relying on cessation is because it extinguishes all unwholesome phenomena so that they do not arise.
"Dedicating toward relinquishment" means reaching the state of non-reliance.

This clarifies that by universally relinquishing both the right and the wrong, one reaches the wisdom of the open space; thus, through the cultivation of diligence, one universally rescues all sentient beings.

Regarding the practitioner who cultivates diligence, concentration of mind, and contemplative concentration through abandonment: it is because they apply themselves single-mindedly and exclusively without error.
The subsequent sections are as explained previously.

Fifth, from "Furthermore" onwards until "dedicating toward equanimity," there are two and a half lines of scripture that clarify the division of the cultivation of the five faculties: faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Relying on revulsion, cessation, and dedication toward equanimity—since these four factors collectively constitute the essence of the antidote—the meaning may be understood from the text itself.

Sixth, the passage from "Furthermore" down to "dedication toward equanimity" consists of two and a half lines of scripture; this is the section on the cultivation of the five powers (*pañcabala*). It likewise takes reliance on revulsion, cessation, and dedication toward equanimity as its essence; that is to say, being unshakable regarding the object is what is termed "power."

7. From "Furthermore" onwards, up to "dedicating [the merit] toward equanimity," there are three and a half lines of scripture which clarify the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment; they likewise take as their essence reliance upon disenchantment, cessation, and equanimity.
Clearly distinguishing between the correct and the erroneous is called the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
To benefit oneself and exhort others constantly without weariness is called the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The manifestation of the joy of the Dharma, seeing those who come seeking it with delight and without satiety, is called the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
*Praśrabdhi* (serenity) means reliance and joy.

Because the wisdom and insight that abide without reliance are constantly manifest before one, there is a joyful rapture of the Dharma; and because one is not wounded by worldly sorrow or resentment, it is called the awakening factor of serenity (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

When internal and external observation are complete, if the sensations and mind follow wisdom rather than revolving with objects, this is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

When views of self and body have perished and the objects of self and other are extinguished, such that the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena have no basis whatsoever, this is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

When the mind and its objects are seen as non-existent, what arises is solely the arising of wisdom; because there is no confusion, this is called the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The following sections are as previously explained.

Eighth: From "Furthermore" onwards, up to "dedicating toward equanimity," there are three lines of scripture that clarify the factors of the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Taking disenchantment, cessation, and equanimity as their essence, they transform the eight wrong paths into the Eightfold Noble Path.

9. From "The Bodhisattva practices such meritorious virtues" down to "by means of skillful expedients," there are five lines and a half of scripture that clarify the intent behind performing such contemplative practices. These are for the sake of ten dharmas, with "not abandoning any sentient beings" as the foremost, as clearly explained in the full text.
As previously explained, these begin with the ten powers (*daśabala*), starting with the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*).

Regarding the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), there are four: first, fearlessness regarding omniscience; second, fearlessness regarding the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); third, fearlessness regarding the teaching of obstacles to the path; and fourth, fearlessness regarding the teaching of the path leading to the end of suffering. In these four ways, neither humans, devas, nor non-Buddhists are able to challenge them with any fault.
The "unshared Buddha-dharmas" refer to the eighteen unshared dharmas.
First, the Buddha’s body is without fault, because his bodily conduct is virtuous.
Second, his speech is without fault, because his verbal karma is virtuous.
Third, mindfulness is without loss, because there is no distracted thought.
Fourth, intention is without differentiation, because there is equality toward enemies and kin.
Fifth, the mind is never unsettled, because it is the non-conceptual wisdom that is not distinct from the dharma-realm.
Sixth is being all-knowing, because there is nothing that is not clearly understood.
Seventh is the non-diminution of desire, because one fulfills the hearts of sentient beings, acting according to their wishes and bringing them to birth in accordance with what is beneficial.
Eighth, vigor is without loss, because although one’s own path is perfected, one establishes the Dharma to benefit sentient beings without ceasing.
Ninth, mindfulness is without decrease, because one skillfully knows the faculties of all sentient beings as well as the appropriate and inappropriate times [to act].
Tenth, there is no regression from meditative concentration, because it is fundamentally unmoving.
Eleventh, wisdom does not diminish, because it skillfully discerns all phenomena as being without arising or ceasing.
Twelfth, the knowledge and vision of liberation do not diminish, because its luminous wisdom reaches everywhere without exception.
Thirteenth, his physical actions follow the movement of wisdom, because among the four modes of deportment there is nothing that does not benefit all sentient beings.
Fourteenth, his verbal actions follow the movement of wisdom, because he engages in no frivolous discourse.
Fifteenth, his mental karma proceeds in accordance with wisdom, because he is forever free from the characteristics of perverse thoughts.
Sixteenth, his wisdom knows the unimpeded matters of the past.
Seventeenth, wisdom that knows unimpeded matters of the present world.
Eighteenth, wisdom that knows unimpeded matters of the future world.
These eighteen kinds belong exclusively to the Buddha alone and do not extend to lower fruits.
Regarding the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*), there are ninety-seven marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Regarding the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), they are as described in the "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of Secondary Characteristics.

To cite but a single secondary characteristic of the hand: it is called the "King of Perfection" (*Pūrṇacandra-rāja*) which emits a blazing radiance, with seven million *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light as its retinue.
To mention but one, his secondary marks (anuvyañjana) are inexhaustible.

Furthermore, he possesses the major marks (lakṣaṇa) of a great man, as numerous as the atoms in ten oceans of Flower Treasury worlds, each physical mark being adorned with various jewel-like characteristics.
This clarifies the inexhaustible marks and inexhaustible minor characteristics, as they are equal in measure to the dharma-realm and empty space.
Regarding "the voice being fully endowed," speaking generally, there are sixty kinds of Brahma-sounds.
If one follows the distinctions, the Sūtra says: "The vast and subtle voice pervades all lands, because for immeasurable kalpas it has sought the most supreme and excellent path."
This is because the dharma-gate of the fruit of Buddhahood itself encompasses all other dharmas.
Those who accord with the profound liberation of the Buddha as they have heard it do so by mounting the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s omniscience.

Regarding "contemplating great wisdom and skillful means": this refers to being skillfully able to follow the inclinations of the faculties of all sentient beings in order to lead them across from suffering.
The fourth section contains five lines and a half of scripture, which is divided into two parts.

First, from "The Buddha-sons dwell in this Stage of Blazing Wisdom" down to "all are detached," there are three lines of scripture. This clarifies that on this stage, one uses the contemplations of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) to counteract the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as the primary focus; by universally contemplating body, sensation, mind, and phenomena, one is able to become detached from all other notions such as self, person, and sentient beings.

Second, from "This bodhisattva" down to "all practice," there are two lines of sūtra that clarify the section on this bodhisattva’s vision of karma as that which is censured or praised by the Tathāgata.

One should clearly understand that the paths of action created by all sentient beings cause them to perpetually transmigrate through birth and death; this is what the Tathāgata has censured, and it should be remedied through contemplation.

If one uses contemplation to bring oneself under control such that there is no [further] karma, one should then employ the skillful means of wisdom to follow along with the cycle of birth and death, engaging in the same activities as sentient beings to deliver them.
This accords with the bodhisattva path because one is able to cultivate all that is praised by the Tathāgata.
The fifth section consists of fifteen lines of scripture, which are divided into four topical segments.

First: From "O Sons of the Buddha, as for these Bodhisattvas’ application of skillful means" down to "the mind that is well-cultivated," there are four and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies that in this stage, having cultivated and accumulated the Path and the factors conducive to the Path as described above, one attains ten kinds of beneficial mental states.

2. From "This bodhisattva" down to "attaining the intention of the speaker of the Dharma," there are approximately two lines of scripture; furthermore, this constitutes the section on attaining ten kinds of minds to grasp the intention of the speaker of the Dharma.
"Those who do not walk in the dense forest" refers to being clearly free from the obscuration and concealment of delusive obstructions.

Third, from "this bodhisattva" down to "diligence in what is the path and what is not the path," there are five lines and a half of scripture, clarifying that the bodhisattva of this stage attains ten kinds of diligence.
These ten types of diligence serve to make the current stage firm and to bring about the subsequent stages so that they may be attained in accordance with one another.

Fourth, from the passage beginning with "This bodhisattva’s realm of mind is pure" down to "all are fully accomplished," there are three lines of scripture which clarify the section on how the bodhisattva in this stage attains the protection and mindfulness of the Buddhas through the purity of the realm of mind.

The above clarifies that having already practiced the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness, one possesses profound subtlety regarding phenomena, clear and sharp realization, and the full perfection of discernment.
From the sixth section, "O Son of the Buddha," and below, there are thirty lines of scripture.
In this section, the meaning is divided into eight parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Blazing Wisdom" down to "all the Sanghas," there are four and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the portion on seeing many Buddhas through the power of vows and making offerings to them.

2. From "By means of these roots of goodness" onwards, up to "becoming even more bright and pure," there are four lines of scripture that clarify how, through seeing the Buddha and serving him while dwelling for many eons, the aspect of the profound mind of faith and understanding becomes further increased and purified.

3. From "O Son of the Buddha, it is as if a goldsmith... down to "...none can destroy it," there are six lines of scripture. This clarifies the analogy of a goldsmith refining pure gold to create ornaments that become increasingly bright and pure.
4. From "This bodhisattva" below until "the fourth stage, the Blazing Wisdom," there are two and a half lines of sūtra, clarifying the categories of practice performed within this stage.

5. From "The Bodhisattva abides in this stage" down to "being fully endowed with the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all-knowledge," there are approximately four lines of scripture that clarify the duties and responsibilities assumed by the Bodhisattva at this stage.
"Like all aspects" clarifies that the application of practice constitutes the seeds.
"The knowledge of all modes" clarifies that one may seek entry into both fundamental wisdom and its differentiated wisdom.

6. From "He further thinks" down to "the one who is the basis for all-knowledge," there are approximately two lines of scripture that clarify how this stage is capable of serving as the leader and teacher for all sentient beings.

7. From "This bodhisattva" down to "as his retinue," there are three lines of sūtra; this is the section on entering samādhi based on one's own karmic retribution to see the Buddha and witness the expansion and contraction of his majestic power.
