By means of the skillful means of the *pāramitās* practiced on this stage, and through the three emptinesses and three samādhis within the sixth stage, one manifests immeasurable gates of non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*), enabling entry into immeasurable realms of sentient beings, entry into immeasurable karmic activities for teaching and transforming sentient beings, and entry into immeasurable networks of worlds.

Because one enters all worlds with non-conceptual wisdom (*nirnimitta-prajñā*), equalizing the conduct of sentient beings so as to pervade them universally, it is called the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*).
Because one enters the pervasive and vast conduct within the world, it is named the Ground of Far-Going.
Second, to clarify what gate of practice is cultivated on this stage: on this stage, one cultivates the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means).

By means of the gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—one is able to enter the world and engage in the myriad practices of sentient beings; yet, because one does not leave the world and does not follow the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and because one has brought great compassion to full maturity, it is called the *upāya-pāramitā*.

Regarding Sudhana’s manifestation of the Dharma at this stage: the fact that the spiritual friends Sudhana encounters here are situated within the assembly of the Buddha clarifies that one does not depart from the essence of bodhi while practicing all manner of deeds.

The name "Flowering Tree Blossom" symbolizes the blossoming of the tree of signless, wondrous wisdom with the flowers of Samantabhadra’s practices; it also signifies causing the flowers of the tree of ignorant conduct of all sentient beings to blossom into the flowers of Samantabhadra’s practices. This is to represent the fulfillment of the gate of compassion and worldly conduct achieved at the seventh stage.

That his body is within a pavilion of various jewel-trees, seated upon a lion throne composed of exquisite jewels, symbolizes that the various jewel-trees represent the manifold practices, clarifying the environment as the result of retribution.
The formation of a pavilion from jewel trees represents the wisdom that accords with practice.
The exquisite jewel lion throne symbolizes the fearless conduct of sublime function.

As for Sudhana’s attainment of the Bodhisattva liberation of "Vast Joy," it clarifies that the Bodhisattvas on this stage accomplish the practice of great compassion and are universally able to skillfully transform sentient beings, rejoicing without weariness.
Because it does not abide in either defilement or purity, it is called liberation.
The seventh stage is the teaching bestowed; since this refers to the practice performed within the seventh stage, it is designated as "abiding in its own place" to represent it.

Regarding the fourth clarification—what kind of liberation from the three realms is attained on this stage—it clarifies that in this stage, one employs skillful means through all worldly activities to benefit sentient beings; it is the gate of liberation characterized by non-attachment to worldly dharmas.
This is also because of Sudhana’s attainment of the bodhisattva liberation door of vast joy.
As the sutra says: "In this seventh stage, having perfected the practice of effortful application, one enters the practice of mastery over wisdom."

It is further said: "In the first bhūmi, because one seeks to fulfill the aspiration for all Buddha-dharmas; in the second bhūmi, because one is free from the defilements of the mind; in the third bhūmi, because the aspiration increases further and one attains the dharma of the light of the Dharma; in the fourth bhūmi, because one enters the Path; in the fifth bhūmi, because one accords with worldly activities; in the sixth bhūmi, because one enters the profound gateways of the Dharma; and in the seventh bhūmi, because one gives rise to all Buddha-dharmas—all of these also bring the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) to fulfillment."

Furthermore, it clarifies that from the first stage through the seventh stage, one accomplishes wisdom through effortful application (*sābhoga*), whereas from the eighth stage through the tenth stage, one accomplishes practice without effortful application (*anābhoga*). This clarifies that prior to the seventh stage there is always effortful application, while from the eighth stage onward, one attains practice without effortful application.
Regarding the fifth section, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, there are two aspects as previously stated.
First, concerning the long division of the sūtra’s intent: within these seven stages, the text is divided into ten sections.
From "At that time, the great assembly’s hearts were filled with joy" onwards, there are twenty-four verses, divided into two sections.

The first section, from "At that time, the great assembly’s hearts were filled with joy" down to "Gazing up at the Honored One among Men, they wish to hear the Dharma," consists of twenty-two verses, clarifying the portion concerning the great assembly’s joyful response and offering of worship upon hearing the sixth stage.

The second section, consisting of two lines of verse beginning with "Then Vimukticandra," clarifies the division concerning the further request for the Dharma-gate of the subsequent stages; its meaning is as expressed in the text.

The third section, beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" and comprising fifty and a half lines of scripture, clarifies the cultivation of the seventh stage through ten dharmas, as well as the division on the initial entry into the dharma of the seventh stage.

The fourth section, beginning with "At that time," consists of forty-four and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the section on the similarities and differences in the advancement through the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The fifth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," consists of seven and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the section on the ten kinds of well-discriminating samādhis.

The sixth section, "Bodhisattva" and below, consists of twelve and a half lines of scripture, clarifying that from the first bhūmi onward, there are three types of superior activity (trikarma) that distinguish [the Bodhisattva] from the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

The seventh section consists of nine and a half lines of sūtra, clarifying that this stage is far removed from existence and non-existence; it describes the constant practice of the actions of body, speech, and mind, and the constant entry into the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) without yet realizing its final fruit.
The eighth section consists of eleven lines of scripture, clarifying the stage of manifesting entry into all paths of birth and death through skillful means while abiding in the Buddha-dharma.

The ninth section consists of twenty-nine and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the stage where the bodhisattva, by the power of their vows, perceives a vast multitude of Buddhas and receives their empowerment.
The tenth section contains forty-two verses, which are a reiteration of the preceding *dharmabhāṇaka* section.

Second, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning: the first section of the initial prose portion consists of fifty and a half lines of scripture, which may be divided approximately into three segments.

First: From "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" down to "dwelling in the seventh stage, Dūraṃgamā," there are eighteen lines of scripture clarifying the entry into the seventh stage by cultivating ten dharmas.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to "accomplishing perfection through effortlessness," there are fifteen lines of scripture that clarify how a Bodhisattva dwelling in the seventh stage possesses twenty ways of entering the realm of sentient beings, as well as the section on teaching and transforming sentient beings through all dharma-gates.

3. From "O Son of the Buddha, by means of profound wisdom" down to "all are fully perfected," there are seventeen and a half lines of scripture which clarify the portion of this stage where the Bodhisattva practices the ten pāramitās, the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), the four immeasurables (apramāṇa), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma), and all other dharmas of awakening.

As in the first section, the Sūtra states: "Cultivating the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, along with compassion, one does not abandon any sentient being. This clarifies that while the followers of the Two Vehicles cultivate emptiness, their own delusions have already been extinguished, and thus they lack the compassion to benefit living beings.

Bodhisattvas of the Pure Land cultivate the three gates of emptiness; once their own afflictions have been extinguished, they are born in the Pure Land according to their vows. Only after they have heard the Buddha’s teachings and achieved self-mastery do they return to the defiled lands to skillfully benefit sentient beings.
However, there are two types of obstacles regarding the coming and going between the defiled land and the pure land.
This is as described in the sūtras of the Three Vehicles: for instance, when bodhisattvas from other regions come here to this Sahā world to hear the Dharma and then return to their own native lands.

In this teaching of the One Vehicle, it is clarified that when Bodhisattvas enter the Dharma from delusion, they are said to have gathered from other Buddha-lands; yet once awakened, they do not speak of returning to their original lands, clarifying that the body and the land are non-dual in nature.
The meaning of this passage of eighteen lines of scripture is that the essence of the three emptinesses is not separate from the myriad practices.

This intends to clarify that prior to the sixth stage, the three emptinesses achieve the perfection of the supramundane; within the seventh stage, one fulfills mundane acts of compassion through the three emptinesses.

The Sūtra states: "Although one practices the equality of all Buddhas, one delights in constantly making offerings to the Buddha. This clarifies that through the equality of the natureless Dharmakāya, one performs acts of veneration that are pervasive and boundless, thereby demonstrating that quiescence and function do not obstruct one another.
"Though entering the gate of wisdom that contemplates emptiness, one diligently accumulates merit" clarifies that one practices the ten *pāramitās* by means of the wisdom that contemplates emptiness.

"Though far removed from the triple world, one adorns the triple world" clarifies that while being free from the karma of the triple world, one constantly takes birth within the triple world through wholesome conduct to teach and transform sentient beings.

"Although they have ultimately extinguished the flames of all afflictions, they are able to give rise to the extinction of the flames of the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion for all sentient beings" clarifies the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The ten messengers are: first, greed; second, hatred; third, delusion; fourth, pride; fifth, doubt; sixth, the view of a self-identity; seventh, the view of extremes; eighth, the grasping at views; ninth, the grasping at precepts and observances; and tenth, false view.

The delusions of the ten afflictions (*kleśa*) within the three realms regarding the Four Noble Truths, along with the afflictions pertaining to the path of cultivation, constitute one hundred twenty-eight types of afflictions.
Within each of the Four Noble Truths of the desire realm, there are ten types of afflictions; thus, there are forty for each of the Four Noble Truths.

In the path of cultivation, there are six root afflictions, which take as their roots: first, greed; second, hatred; third, delusion; fourth, pride; fifth, the view of a self-identity; and sixth, the view of extremes.

There are forty-six afflictions in the desire realm; the remaining four—view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), precept-and-vow grasping (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—arise from the six higher [afflictions], as they are not fundamental.
In each of the two upper realms, hatred is excluded; the remainder is as in the desire realm.
From the four truths of the form realm, there are nine for each, totaling forty-one.
From the four truths of the formless realm, there are nine for each, totaling forty-one.
In total there are one hundred twenty-eight kinds, up to eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), as will be clarified in the "Chapter on the Minor Marks" (*Anuvyañjana-parivarta*).

Regarding the abandonment of afflictions within the Three Vehicles: among the five views—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)—these five views constitute the sharp fetters (*tīkṣṇa-āsrava*). Greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt constitute the five types of dull fetters (*mṛdu-āsrava*).

The five sharp afflictions (*kleśa*) constitute the afflictions of seeing the truths (*darśana-mārga-kleśa*), while the five dull afflictions constitute the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-kleśa*).
The five sharp afflictions obstruct the path of seeing because, as long as various views have not been eliminated, the principle does not manifest before one.

The five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) obstruct the practitioner; they arise repeatedly through habitual practice in accordance with one's actions. Although one may enter the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), greed, hatred, ignorance, and so forth still persist as residual impressions (*vāsanā*). Because these habitual tendencies have not yet been fully eradicated, those who are *srotāpannas* have exhausted all afflictions pertaining to the Truths (*satya-darśana-kleśa*), while *sakṛdāgāmins* and *anāgāmins* have not yet exhausted the afflictions pertaining to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-kleśa*). Because *arhats* have exhausted both types of afflictions—those pertaining to the Truths and those pertaining to the Path of Cultivation across the three realms—they are no longer reborn within the three realms.

Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles subdue the afflictions of the ten fetters and ten entanglements of the triple world through the contemplation of emptiness, and by cultivating the six pāramitās, they are born in the Pure Lands.
It is also said that above the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there exists a separate heaven where bodhisattvas of the ten stages are born as a result of their retribution, named Maheśvara.
It is also taught that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages have not yet completely severed the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).

As for the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*): first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*); second, lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*); third, sleep (*middha*); fourth, regret (*kaukṛtya*); fifth, stinginess (*mātsarya*); sixth, envy (*īrṣyā*); seventh, resentment (*pradāśa*); eighth, drowsiness (*svapna*); ninth, anger (*krodha*); and tenth, concealment (*mrakṣa*).
These ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) arise following the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), and they also act as the generative causes for those ten proclivities.

For example, a Bodhisattva of the One Vehicle, from the stage of the Ten Faiths, believes that his own discriminative mind arises from the Tathāgata’s wisdom; at the initial moment of the Ten Abidings, he is equal to the first ground, and by reaching the sixth abiding, he is equal to the sixth ground, attaining entry into the samādhi of cessation. His supernormal powers are just like those of the sixth Bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja among the Ten Abidings.

The general meaning is that the three stages previously mentioned—ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications—are collectively identical; their essence consists in the sequential progression through the ten grounds, which in turn has as its essence the immovable wisdom of all Tathāgatas.

All afflictions, through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), give rise to the wisdom of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*), which simultaneously and universally seals them within the essence of identical wisdom.
The three periods of past, present, and future are a single boundary, devoid of any characteristics of shortness or length, or extension or contraction.
The following passage further clarifies the essential meaning:

If, within the span of a single thought-moment, one perceives that one's own mind has attained Buddhahood or has not yet attained Buddhahood, thereby establishing limitations and measures of temporal duration, it should be known that this person has not achieved right view, because the essence of the Tathāgata’s wisdom has not yet manifested before them.
The above clarifies the conclusion of the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*).

As for the scripture stating, "Although one knows that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams," this is self-evident from the text itself. Regarding the statement that "the karma produced according to the mind has immeasurable distinctions," this clarifies that through wisdom devoid of intrinsic substance, one manifests all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as an illusion, responding to the immeasurable distinctions within the minds of sentient beings.

Although one knows that all lands are like empty space, yet one is able to adorn Buddha-lands with pure and wondrous conduct; this clarifies that while karma is empty and the objective realm is quiescent, the retributive adornments arise from compassion and wisdom. Since compassion and wisdom have no dependence, the marks of retribution are like shadows.

Although one knows that the nature of the dharmakāya of all Buddhas is inherently bodiless, yet adorns their bodies with the marks and signs; this clarifies that the dharmakāya is signless, and through the purification of delusive karma, delusion perishes and karma ceases.

The realm of wisdom, with its reliance on the primary and secondary merits, is like a pure reflection of light; it does not belong to the attachments of existence or non-existence, being like the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*).

Although one follows the Buddhas in realizing that the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment, yet for those who practice various paths according to the conceptual distinctions of sentient beings' intentions—employing various forms, various times, and various kalpas—it is clarified that the essence of the Dharma-body wisdom has no time, no kalpa, and no substance of the three periods. Nevertheless, in accordance with the differences in the karma of all sentient beings, there exist the distinctions of all times and kalpas.

Yet, for the sake of sentient beings, one differentiates the distinctions of time and kalpas while practicing various deeds; this refers, as it has been taught, to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the three births, one birth, a single thought-moment, the sixty kalpas, and so forth.

When a bodhisattva thus gives rise to these ten kinds of superior practices through skillful means and wisdom, they enter the seventh stage from the sixth stage; it should be understood that the ten dharmas mentioned above constitute the approach to the seventh stage, while what follows below is called "abiding."
The seventh stage contains twenty kinds of dharma-gates for entry, as fully detailed in the text itself.
From the passage beginning "This bodhisattva forms this thought" onwards, the meaning of the preceding analytical text is presented as it appears in the sūtra itself.
The second section of the prose commentary consists of forty-four lines of sūtra, which may be divided approximately into seven subsections.

First, from "At that time, Vimukticandra... down to "...is also able to fulfill," there are two and a half lines of sūtra, clarifying the section on the fulfillment of all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) within the various stages (*bhūmi*) as requested by Vimukticandra.

2. From "Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said" onwards, up to "the tenth effortless practice," there are approximately ten lines of scripture that clarify the section on the distinctions between the practices and realizations of the various stages (bhūmis) from the first through the tenth, in response to the preceding questions.

3. From "O Son of the Buddha, it is as if there were two worlds" down to "is thus able to transcend," there are five lines and a half of scripture which clarify that the Bodhisattvas of this stage, by virtue of their power of vows, enter into both defiled and pure practices without dwelling in either extreme.

4. From "The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said" down to "surpassing the human state," there are eight and a half lines of scripture which clarify that the two types of practice—defiled and pure—performed on this stage are explained through analogies as being neither purely defiled nor purely pure.

5. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva is likewise" down to "because they have attained the complete transcendence of all," there are six lines of scripture that clarify the stage of effortful practice (*sābhoga-prayoga*) in the seventh ground and the stage of effortless practice (*anābhoga-prayoga*) in the eighth ground.

6. From "O Son of the Buddha, this seventh stage" down to "is not called 'without'"—these three and a half lines of scripture clarify that this stage is neither designated as having afflictions nor designated as being without afflictions.

7. From "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this seventh stage" down to "becoming even more excellently perfected," there are nine and a half lines of scripture that clarify the section on extracting the world from [samsara] so that he may become a Great Illuminating Teacher (Mahāvidyā-ācārya).
Within these forty-four and a half lines of scripture, from the very beginning when Vimukticandra asked Vajragarbha Bodhisattva:
"O Son of the Buddha, do Bodhisattvas fulfill all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) only within this seventh stage?"

Regarding the phrase "it is also able to bring fulfillment within all the stages": if one considers it through the perspective of common characteristics, it is, in its entirety, the single, fundamental, universally radiant great wisdom of the Tathāgata—the very essence of bodhi in which quiescence and activity are non-obstructive.

If one looks toward the progressive advancement of the practitioner, there are, within the gate of diverse characteristics (*nānātva-lakṣaṇa*), fifty kinds of distinctions in the practices that follow enlightenment (*bodhi-anuvartana*).

In terms of the general essence and common characteristics, these are based solely on the distinctions of enlightenment within these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as the fundamental framework for spiritual ascent.
Within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), enlightenment (*bodhi*) is collectively constituted by five types of enlightenment as its primary essence.

These five types of enlightenment are: first, the enlightenment of emptiness and signlessness; second, the enlightenment of universally luminous wisdom that abides nowhere; third, the enlightenment of great vows capable of giving rise to great wisdom and great compassion to extensively benefit sentient beings; fourth, the enlightenment that, through great compassion, can accord with both defilement and purity without being stained by either; and fifth, the enlightenment of non-action in which wisdom, compassion, and the myriad practices are perfected.
Now, "bodhi" is translated here as "awakening.
Awakening means that among all phenomena, there is nothing superior.
As for "unsurpassed," it refers exclusively to the One Vehicle and not to the Three Vehicles.

The bodhi that is empty, signless, and non-conceptual is attained in common by both the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle; however, they differ in that some possess the practice of great compassionate vows while others do not, and in their varying degrees of breadth, narrowness, stillness, and function. In its essential nature, it all returns to the same signlessness.
Regarding the second, the Bodhi of the Wisdom of Universal Radiance Dwelling Without Dependence: this is the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*) alone, not the Three Vehicles.

A Bodhisattva of the Single Vehicle enters this wisdom at the first stage of the ten stages of mind; this is called "dwelling where the Buddhas dwell," because one is born into the family of Tathāgata-wisdom.

By means of this ground of wisdom, one advances in the cultivation of various practices; according to the distinctions of wisdom and the distinctions of practice, through the deepening of habitual cultivation, one establishes the ten pāramitās and fifty successive stages of ascent, all without departing from the ground of wisdom—the universal radiance and non-abiding state—attained at the initial moment of resolve.

Because wisdom has no substantiality and time likewise undergoes no transition—relying on this fundamental suchness and because it does not exist as a deluded fabrication—it is said that "the two minds, the initial resolve and the ultimate, are not distinct. That "the former mind is more difficult" is because attaining this stage is difficult.
As this sutra states: "One thereby treads upon the Tathāgata’s Ground of Universal Radiance.

Because the essence of the ground for generating the mind of enlightenment and practicing within this dharma-gate of the sutra is this very wisdom, the ocean of all varieties of wisdom and the ocean of the ten thousand practices arise therein.

Regarding the statement that "the three great vows can give rise to great wisdom and great compassion to extensively benefit sentient beings and [attain] bodhi": this clarifies that because all phenomena do not arise from themselves, wisdom is produced and compassion is perfected by relying upon the great vows.
Furthermore, it does not arise from another because wisdom and aspiration lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It does not arise from both together because phenomena do not possess the quality of conjunction.
It is not without cause because wisdom must depend upon aspiration to give rise to compassionate conduct.
Therefore it is said: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions; for this reason, the One Vehicle is taught.

This is because those of the three vehicles may either stagnate in quiescence or merely be reborn in the Pure Land, lacking the great compassion that gives rise to vast vows to bring wisdom to fulfillment for the sake of sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.

Some say that those who remain in the Sahā world by intentionally retaining afflictions through their vows have merely attained the bodhi of dharma-emptiness and signlessness, but have not yet attained the wisdom of universal radiance.

Thus, although the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles possess vows and practices, they all aspire to attain buddhahood after many kalpas; they do not, on account of this teaching, realize it in a single kṣaṇa without the passage of time.

Furthermore, when the effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) manifests for the Bodhisattva of this eighth stage, he may still fear stagnation in quiescence; therefore, he employs the eighth pāramitā as a safeguard and maintains mindfulness of his original vows.
Furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions employ the three empowerments and seven exhortations to cause wisdom not to stagnate in quiescence.
Moreover, within the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), there are ten great gates of vows that give rise to wisdom.

Fourth, regarding "because of his great compassion, he is able to follow along with both defilement and purity, yet remains undefiled by purity, [attaining] bodhi": this clarifies that through the practice of the six *pāramitās* in the preceding six stages, one attains both supramundane and mundane [realizations], as well as the emergence of bodhi.

Upon reaching this seventh stage, by means of both the supramundane and the mundane, one emerges from the application of bodhi to enter the world; acting in concert with the activities of all ordinary beings, one accomplishes the practice of great compassion so that the conduct of Samantabhadra may be brought to fulfillment.

Although they are immersed in worldly defilements, because their wisdom is by nature undefiled and they remain unattached while dwelling in the world, they are like lotuses that grow perpetually in water yet remain unsullied by it.

Furthermore, because he abides in the world through his original vows to benefit sentient beings, and because he has no self-attachment to worldly pleasures within the essence of wisdom, he does not delight in love, pride, arrogance, or the opulence esteemed by the world.

Furthermore, the essence of clear wisdom is without dependence and without intrinsic nature; it can follow great vows to abide within the mundane stream, remaining sovereign because it belongs neither to defilement nor purity.

This seventh stage dharma-gate is not accessible to those of the two vehicles, nor is it known by bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās while still harboring longing for or aversion toward afflictions.

As stated in the following passage, this is something that even Bodhisattvas possessing the six supernormal powers cannot know; for the sake of realizing the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), they are unable to follow the cycle of birth and death to fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra and perfect great compassion.
This is because there is joy and aversion toward birth and death, and there is weariness, due to the desire to be born in the Pure Land.

Regarding the "spontaneous Bodhi" (anābhoga-bodhi) in which the five wisdoms, compassion, and myriad practices are perfected: if one considers this through the gate of the general and specific characteristics, since the essence of wisdom is not different and the time is not different, it is fully possessed from the very first mind of the ten stages (daśabhūmi).

If, by way of the gate of distinct characteristics (*bipakṣa-mukha*), one attains a portion of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom of identical essence (*sahaja-jñāna*) through the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), and the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*); and attains a portion of the Tathāgata’s conduct of identical essence; and attains a portion of the Tathāgata’s gate of the perfect integration of compassion and wisdom through the dedication of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna-pariṇāmana*).
From the first bhūmi through the sixth bhūmi, one relies on the dharmas of the three preceding stages of worthiness (pūrvayoga) to nurture and perfect them, thereby emerging from the entanglements.
Although there is compassion, it is the resolve that desires all sentient beings to transcend the world.

Just as the compassion of the seventh stage constantly abides in the world yet remains unsullied, like a lotus in water, it clarifies that birth and death are eternally quiescent. Since the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one has followed the teachings to give rise to faith and compliance; this is not merely due to the natural state of one's own nature. Thus, now reaching this seventh stage, one takes the previously transcendent mind of liberation and only then abides within the entanglements of the world without being defiled.

In order to establish a new dwelling and harmonize with local customs, he takes birth through the power of his compassionate vows; from the gate of the three types of emptiness and non-action, he first enters the world to practice expedient deeds that share in worldly entanglements. Thus, there still remain two kinds of habitual tendencies—those of non-action and those of action—and he continues to exert effort in the cultivation of these practices.

Therefore, Sudhana’s spiritual friend who symbolizes the Dharma is named Kapphiṇa (Kai-fu-shu-hua); he is so named because he causes the flowers of the myriad practices upon the tree of wisdom to blossom, leading them to become like the ocean of Samantabhadra’s conduct.

From this point, entering into the entanglements, the blossoms of practice unfold; reaching the eighth and tenth stages, compassion and wisdom are perfected, benefiting sentient beings according to their capacities, and only when non-action is fully realized does the process finally conclude.

Upon reaching the eleventh stage, the beings benefited are equal in extent to the Dharma-realm; according to their faculties and the timing, he manifests a form-body, benefiting all without exception. He acts without striving and responds without effort, for his wisdom of universal radiance does not belong to any specific location. It accords with the minds of sentient beings, manifesting forms as required by things, and because it is free from coming and going.

Because the wisdom of universal radiance and the deluded minds of all sentient beings share the same essential nature, it is able to know the karmic actions performed by all sentient beings and manifest accordingly.

Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "Because one aspires for all Buddha-dharmas within the first stage," this clarifies that the first stage consists in aspiring to accomplish the model of the Buddha-fruit established during the three stages of the preceding stage of worthies (pūrva-śaikṣa); it is not because one's own practice is perfected, but rather because one aspires for bodhi as the cause for its fulfillment.
The model of the Buddha-fruit in the Three Vehicles occurs after the ten stages (*bhūmi*);

the model of the Buddha-fruit practice in this sutra occurs before the ten stages, even down to the assembly of gods and spirits in the first chapter, all of whom have "left behind the stains of the mind" in the second stage. This clarifies that by means of the above-mentioned ten wholesome dharmas, which are the nature-precepts (*dharmakāya-śīla*) of the Dharma-body, one purifies all delusions.

Regarding the third stage, where the vows increase further and one attains the radiance of the Dharma: this clarifies that by cultivating the four dhyānas and eight samādhis of the two upper realms, one attains what is called the pure clarity of the wisdom-principle; because one overcomes the mental obstacles of the three realms; and because one enters the ninth concentration.
Regarding the fourth stage, "entering the path," this clarifies that by cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as aids to the contemplation of awakening, the eye of wisdom is purified.

Regarding the fifth stage, "conforming to worldly activities," this clarifies that through the meditative gate of the non-constructive nature of the dharma-realm itself, one is able to conform to and thoroughly master all worldly arts and crafts.

Regarding "the sixth stage because of entering the profound dharma-gate," this clarifies the entry into wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), for there is no phenomenon—whether mundane or supramundane—that is not illuminated.
Regarding "the seventh stage because of giving rise to all Buddha-dharmas," this clarifies that the seventh stage is able to enter worldly learning and practice the conduct of Samantabhadra.

Although the preceding stages all take universal radiance wisdom as their essence, they each involve learning, understanding, practice, and aspiration toward higher-level dharma-gates. From the eighth stage through the tenth stage, the practices of effortlessness (*anābhoga*) are fully accomplished. At the beginning of the eighth stage, one first attains the wisdom of effortlessness; at the ninth stage, one clarifies the wisdom of effortlessness and achieves mastery in teaching; and at the tenth stage, within that state of effortlessness, both wisdom and compassion are collectively perfected, thereby becoming equal to the rank of a Buddha.

Regarding why the seventh stage is the most preeminent, the subsequent text states that "the practice of effort is fulfilled. This clarifies that from the sixth stage onward, through the wisdom of non-effort (*anābhoga*), one accomplishes the myriad practices of effortful cultivation.

The fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s conduct up to the tenth stage constitutes the fruit within this position; this clarifies that while causal practice is difficult to initiate, the practice of the fruit is easy to accomplish.
Just as water entering a current flows spontaneously to the ocean, how much more so this practice, which does not fail to reach the ocean?

This seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā), is identical to the seventh dwelling within the Ten Dwellings; it is the practice of the laywoman Śreṣṭhī Bhadrā, who performed the practices of eighty-four thousand nayutas of sentient beings, all of which I have practiced in common with her.
It is also like the King who has perfected the seventh of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*), who manifests through his own transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) the act of killing;
and it is also like the seventh of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), where one beholds Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to the west of Mount Vajra.
This seventh stage consists of the gates of practice, each of which follows the pattern of the practices of understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) prior to the stages.

Within the ten stages, the practices of liberation from the three stages prior to the stages are fully completed; thus, the accumulation of merit and the perfection of virtue are exactly like the dharmas of fruition prior to the stages.

The practices of the path on the grounds (bhūmi) are causes that follow from the fruits prior to the grounds; because they emulate those prior fruits, the Buddha-fruit is not established as occurring after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* as it is in the three vehicles.
If a practitioner understands the intent of the teaching well, let them not falsely interpret the Buddha’s mind.

Just as when one correctly cultivates the causes of the ten abodes, one simultaneously traverses all five stages—the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten grounds, and the eleventh ground—all at once.
Regarding the realm of wisdom, wisdom does not differ and time does not shift; by sealing it with the single seal of the Dharma-realm wisdom, the distinction between past and present is severed.
Returning to the meaning of the six characteristics, it is simply because the perfect cause of realization is such that no fruit is not fully contained within it.

If one looks toward the arising of wisdom that penetrates the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), then the first stage, the Abiding in the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*), is of the highest merit.

If, however, one prioritizes great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), then the seventh abiding, the seventh practice (*caryā*), the seventh dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and the seventh ground (*bhūmi*) are supreme, because all others are spontaneously fulfilled therein.
As the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!

It is as if there were two worlds, one defiled and one purely pure; the space between these two is difficult to traverse. This clarifies that the sixth stage is purely pure and the seventh stage is purely defiled, and that within these two positions, one is hindered by the duality of defilement and purity, making it difficult to pass beyond.
The subsequent passage states, "Except for Bodhisattvas who possess great skillful means, supernormal powers, and the power of vows," and so forth, which is self-evident from the text itself.

The meaning clarifies that by means of great compassion and great wisdom, and never departing from these two practices, one teaches and transforms all sentient beings, causing them to ultimately attain great bodhi and be endowed with the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

By means of preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*), one brings forth fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); by the power of the contemplative illumination of fundamental wisdom, one accomplishes discriminating wisdom (*viśeṣa-jñāna*).
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!..."
"Is this Bodhisattva of the seventh stage one who practices defiled conduct,
or one who practices pure conduct?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied:
"O Son of the Buddha!

From the first stage through the seventh stage, all practices performed are relinquished; one becomes free from the portion of afflictions and karma and attains equanimity, yet this is not yet called 'transcending the practice of afflictions.'"
As in the analogy of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), he does not depart from the human state, nor is he afflicted by poverty or suffering; this is clearly explained in detail in the text.

The general meaning is that, by attaining the subtle wisdom of the three emptinesses and fundamental gnosis within the sixth stage, and further through the power of great vows and mastery over wisdom, he does not depart from the human state and remains untainted by worldly phenomena, being able to engage in mundane affairs without being defiled or purified.

Because wisdom has no basis, it is never defiled; because defilement has no basis, it cannot stain what is pure. This staining and purification are merely the skillful means of great compassion, arising through dependent origination to benefit sentient beings.

At the eighth stage, the integration of practice reaches its consummation; yet, while the practice of non-action attains a degree of mastery, it is only at the tenth stage that this is fully perfected.
Were it not for the seventh stage—characterized by both practice and effort—the inexhaustible great wisdom and the great compassion of Samantabhadra could not be accomplished.
Therefore, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, for those of the three vehicles who have emerged from the entanglements, it is said that "the density of afflictions is the seed of the Tathāgata";
it also says that "to produce a lotus flower within fire is truly a rare wonder."
This is explained for those who have already attained the sixth stage and above and have emerged from the entanglements; those still bound by all fetters cannot yet fully ascend this path.
The remaining text is as it appears in the sutra itself.
The various dhyānas are meditative concentration (samādhi).
Samāpatti is the absence of sinking and agitation.
Samāpatti is right reception (samyak-prativedha).

Regarding "the supernormal powers and liberations through association with the knowledge of all phenomena": because one correctly realizes the knowledge associated with all phenomena, one immediately attains mastery over the supernormal powers; this is termed liberation.
The third section of the prose consists of seven and a half lines of sūtra, which is divided into four parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this stage" down to "purifies this stage," there are five and a half lines of sūtra, clarifying the attainment of the ten kinds of samādhi.

Second, from the passage "This bodhisattva, having attained this samādhi" onwards, there is one and a half lines of sūtra which clarify the attainment of ten great samādhis, thereby transcending the stages of the two vehicles.

This should state that it "surpasses the stages of the three vehicles" (tri-yāna-bhūmi); however, because those who study the three vehicles translated this sutra together, they did not properly understand the intent of the teaching and merely stated that it "surpasses the two vehicles" (dvi-yāna), rather than stating that it "surpasses the three vehicles."

If it were merely to surpass the two vehicles, as this sutra says: "Among all the various classes of living beings in the world, few desire to seek the path of the śrāvaka; those who seek the path of the pratyekabuddha are even fewer still; and those who seek the Mahāyāna are exceedingly rare."
"To seek the Mahāyāna is still relatively easy; to be able to believe in this Dharma is exceedingly difficult.
If this stage merely transcends the two vehicles, how then should the meaning of these four vehicles be established?
How could it be that the meaning of a single section of a sutra lacks coherence between its preceding and succeeding passages?
This is solely because the seeds of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles are deluded, leading to a mistaken manifestation of the Sage’s intent.

In the future, there will be gentlemen of refined understanding who should not rely on these words; rather, one should say that [the Bodhisattva] "transcends the Three Vehicles," and must not say "the Two Vehicles.

As the Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva dwelling in this stage enters the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation and Discernment. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva in this stage enters into the contemplation and discernment of various samādhis, sequentially distinguishing: "This is the dhyāna of the Form Realm; this is the Formless Realm; this is the Śrāvaka; this is the Pratyekabuddha; this is the samādhi of the Three Vehicles; and this is the samādhi of the One Vehicle."

The Samādhi of Skillfully Discerning Meaning refers to clearly and skillfully discerning worldly meaning and world-transcending meaning, as well as what constitutes right meaning and what constitutes false meaning.
The Samādhi of Supreme Wisdom exists because it is the wisdom of the Buddha of the One Vehicle.
The samādhi of the treasury of analytical meaning refers to the Hīnayāna treasury, the Mahāyāna treasury, and the Ekayāna treasury.
The samādhi of analytical meaning according to reality is so called because one knows all phenomena as they truly are, without false interpretation.
The samādhi of the firmly established, solid root is so called because it is non-retrogressive.
The samādhi of the gateway of wisdom and supernormal powers is so called because, by means of this wisdom, one can give rise to various gateways of supernormal powers.
The Samādhi of the Karma of the Dharma-realm is so called because there is nothing—whether movement or stillness within the mind and its objects—that is not true.

The Tathāgata-vijaya (Victory of the Tathāgata) Samādhi is so called because it is without mind and without thought; wisdom accords with the teachings and transformations of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, yet remains free from the characteristics of coming and going.
The Samādhi of the Treasury of Various Meanings contains all phenomena in their entirety; there is nothing it does not penetrate.

The Samādhi of Birth-and-Death and Nirvāṇa clarifies that by means of the eternally quiescent dharma of nirvāṇa, one manifests birth-and-death, and by means of birth-and-death, one takes nirvāṇa as such. This is because both are devoid of intrinsic nature, because stillness and function are one true reality, and because, being without self or person, wisdom can accord with worldly conventions to benefit all sentient beings.
The following is a summary, which is fully contained within the text itself.
The fourth section consists of twelve and a half lines of scripture, which may be divided into five parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage" down to "the radiance of dharma-patience," there are two and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the portion concerning how the immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions of a Bodhisattva in this stage are all characterized by signless conduct (*animitta-caryā*).
2. From "Vimukticandra" onwards, up to "surpassing the three vehicles," there are approximately two lines of scripture; this constitutes the section where Vimukticandra raises the question.

3. From "Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" down to "that which cannot be reached by any of the three vehicles," there are two and a half lines of scripture; this is the section in which Vajragarbha Bodhisattva answers the questions posed.
4. From "For example" down to "surpassing by one's own power," there are two and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on explaining through the use of analogies.

5. From "All bodhisattvas" down to "surpassing all three vehicles," there may be approximately three lines of scripture, clarifying that the bodhisattva of this stage surpasses the three vehicles by their own power, rather than having surpassed them since the first stage by seeking the Great Dharma.

The above twelve and a half lines of scripture clarify that the immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental karma of the Bodhisattvas on this stage, through their own power, transcends the wisdom of the Three Vehicles; they cultivate emptiness and practice only the Six Perfections. Unlike Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, who suppress the active manifestations of afflictions so they do not arise, these Bodhisattvas attain the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-jarāmaraṇa*) and are born in other regions—or it is said that there exists a pure land of the Ten Stages Bodhisattvas separately in the upper direction.
Thus, these three vehicles are all provisional arrangements of the Tathāgata, established as skillful means merely to alleviate coarse suffering;

they do not accord with this teaching of generating the bodhicitta through wisdom, wherein this very Sahā world becomes a pure land, and the Flower Treasury World (Puṣpaka-raśmi-dhātu) pervades all of space, such that purity and defilement are mutually contained, and within a single atom there are many lands without any perception of coming or going between them.

The assembly of translators did not fully grasp the Buddha’s intent and erroneously manifested the Sage’s teaching as stating that [the Bodhisattva] transcends the Two Vehicles. Hereafter, students must not fall into this error.

Furthermore, it is clarified that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the sixth stage, this is due to the aspiration for the Great Dharma and the surpassing power of vows, rather than transcending the Three Vehicles through one's own power; this is self-evident in the text itself.
The fifth section consists of nine and a half lines of scripture, which may be divided approximately into five sub-sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this stage" down to "though they practice the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), they do not realize it," there are two and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the aspect of non-abiding in non-action, constantly practicing the three karmas, and not realizing nirvāṇa.
2. From "Vimukticandra" down to "is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation," there is one line of scripture; this is the section where Vimukticandra raises the question. 3.

From "The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said" down to "yet does not realize [it]," there may be two lines of scripture; this clarifies the section concerning how the bodhisattvas of this stage and the sixth bhūmi are able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation yet do not realize it.

4. From "This bodhisattva is named 'Accomplishing the Inconceivable'" down to "practicing within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without realizing it," there are two lines of scripture that clarify the inconceivability of the three karmas of the bodhisattva in this stage, specifically regarding the non-attainment of the portion of quiescent realization.
5. The two lines of scripture beginning with "For example, suppose there were a person" cite the metaphor of one who boards a ship and enters the sea without encountering maritime disaster.

Bodhisattvas from the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, as well as those in the seventh stage who enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), do not realize cessation by suppressing thought as in the four dhyānas and four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) of the higher realms; nor do they, like Arhats who weary of suffering and cultivate emptiness, follow the nature of emptiness into extinction such that compassion and wisdom cease to arise, becoming like the great void with nothing further to be done, remaining unaware even for eons, or hearing no more the drum tied to their heads, or even undergoing self-immolation through transformed fire and entering the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-vaśitā-nirvāṇa*).

Nor is it like the Pratyekabuddha’s contemplation of the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination, wherein one accords with the perception of emptiness to extinguish compassion and wisdom so that they do not arise.

Nor is it like the Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings who cultivate the six perfections; although coarse consciousness has ceased, subtle consciousness still remains, and by the power of their vows they are born in a Pure Land—or as some say, in a Reward Land situated above the realm of form, possessing a body that transcends the three realms.
Because the mind has a basis and pure karma serves as its condition, every place of birth likewise has a basis.

Thus, within this One Vehicle, in the mind of the sixth stage of the ten stages, it is like the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja, who sat cross-legged by the side of a walking path, detached from inhalation and exhalation; according to the dimensions of his body, he manifested physical forms that arose as emanations like clouds, pervading the entire ocean of lands.

This refers to the gateway of the fundamental, universal radiance wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*), whose self-substance is the infinite dharma-realm of quiescence and function; it differs from the three vehicles, all of which possess places of reliance for birth resulting from karmic retribution, and even when manifesting for the sake of transformation, they are subject to limitations.

Thus, regarding this sixth stage among the ten stages, by means of guarding all that increases power, one clearly becomes able to guard the city of the mind, such that it is no longer encompassed by either meditative absorption or distraction.
The worldly activities one engages in are those required for "sameness of purpose" (samānārthatā), as they do not arise from one's own [independent] karma.
The seventh stage possesses utility and development, because one initiates practice as in the previous three emptinesses.

Therefore, Sudhana, in this stage, the spiritual friend is named "Flowering Tree" (Kai-fu-shu-hua), signifying that he constantly causes the flowers of practice to bloom through the illumination of the three emptinesses.

Thus, from the sixth ground onward, one is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); specifically, taking the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja as the model for the sixth dwelling of the ten dwellings, this same principle applies generally to every sixth mind throughout the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten grounds, and the eleventh ground.

If one does not enter meditative absorption, then it is simply that the ocean-like Samudraketu of the ten abodes constitutes the essence, while the subsequent sections represent the great functions within that ocean-like Samudraketu.
The remaining meaning is as clarified by the sutra itself.
The preceding section clarifies the gate of not realizing *nirvāṇa*.

The sixth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva attains such samādhi," consists of eleven lines of scripture; it concerns the portion on how, through the skillful means of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), ten kinds of manifestations are produced that transcend the world, yet without abandoning the mind that delights in the Dharma.

As the sutra states: "Though they accord with the Buddha's wisdom, they manifest entry into the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. This clarifies that after those of the two vehicles have attained their respective fruits, they become weary of and afflicted by the body born of parents through the process of segmentation and gestation; they thus spontaneously produce fire to incinerate their own bodies and enter the body of transformational birth-and-death (*pariṇāmika-jarāmaraṇa*).
The remainder is self-evident from the text itself.
Regarding the "gods" mentioned below, these refer to the gods of the Desire Realm, the Form Realm, and the Formless Realm.
Regarding the "nāgas," these are the various nāgas of the world.
Yakṣa is translated here as "one who lives in suffering," or "sacrificial observer," or "the swift.
Gandharva is called "eater of fragrance," or "fragrance-seeking deity," who seeks food by providing music.
Asuras are included within the realm of the devas; this term means "those who lack the exquisite pleasures of the heavens.
Garuḍas are translated as "those with voices of sorrowful suffering," for because they consume dragons alive within their gullets, they produce sounds of piteous distress.
They are also the jewel-winged birds.
As for the *kiṃnara*, this is called the "doubt-inducing deity"; because there are horns upon their heads, when people see them they are struck with doubt:
"Is this a human, or is it a non-human?"
*Mahoraga* means "one who moves on the chest and belly"; these are among the various classes of animals and belong to the same category as the *nāgas*.
The ancients called them "Great Python Deities.
Regarding "humans and non-humans," "non-humans" refers to the class of ghosts (*preta*).
Śakra is here translated as "Capable Ruler.
Brahmā Devānām Indra is the king of the first dhyāna.
"Brahmā" means purity; because he has transcended the desire realm, he is called the King of Purity.

Because a Bodhisattva in this stage is able to universally identify with their peers, leading them to cultivate the merit and wisdom of bodhi without attachment or delight, it is said that they do not abandon the mind that delights in the Dharma.
The remainder is fully contained within the text itself.
Furthermore, it clarifies that after one has personally rejoiced, because the subsequent stages are not yet fulfilled, one must diligently apply the mind to delighting in the Dharma.
The seventh section consists of twenty-nine and a half lines of scripture, which may be divided approximately into six subsections.

First: From "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva has accomplished such [qualities]" down to "cannot be equaled by other ornaments," there are twelve lines of scripture that clarify how, upon reaching this Ground of Far-Going (Dūraṃgamā), one beholds many Buddhas and, through making offerings and hearing the Dharma, one’s excellence increases further.

Second, from "The Bodhisattva abiding in this seventh stage" down to "the mire of the afflictions of all sentient beings," there are five lines and a half of scripture, clarifying that which is beyond the reach of the three vehicles.

3. From "In these ten pāramitās of this bodhisattva" down to "the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching," there are two and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the division of the practice-gates cultivated in this stage.

4. From "The Bodhisattva abides in this stage" down to "the one who is the support for all-knowledge," there are four and a half lines of sūtra that clarify how the Bodhisattva in this stage receives his office and is capable of serving as a support for sentient beings seeking wisdom.

5. From the passage beginning with "If this bodhisattva exerts diligent vigor" below, there are four and a half lines of scripture that clarify the measure of the retinue of dharma-gates and samādhis obtained through this bodhisattva’s own power of diligence and his vows.
In the sixth section of the verses, there are forty-two lines that further clarify the preceding teachings, as detailed in the text itself.

This is illustrated by the analogy of refining pure gold until it becomes increasingly bright and clear. While the stages prior to the sixth ground involve only the refinement, smelting, and polishing of the ground of wisdom through the application of morality, concentration, wisdom, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, on this present ground, one skillfully enters the world and manifests various modes of conduct among sentient beings, being able to teach and transform them through "acting in concert" (samānārthatā).

It is illuminated by various exquisite jewels interspersed as adornments; it is illuminated by pure and wondrous wisdom that adorns various practices, thereby adorning the ground of wisdom, with each mutually manifesting and further increasing clarity and purity.

This clarifies that on this stage, one adorns the myriad practices with the function of universal radiant wisdom; because one gives rise to the practice of benefiting sentient beings in the world through the mastery of wisdom's function, wisdom becomes even more manifest and clear.
If wisdom does not act in accord with the myriad practices, that wisdom lacks great utility; this refers to the Three Vehicles.
If the myriad practices do not proceed by means of wisdom, they are subject to limitations and obstructions; this refers to the virtuous conduct of humans, devas, and non-Buddhists.
The remaining text is fully contained within the sutra itself.

Chapter Eight: The Immovable Ground (*Acālā-bhūmi*).
Regarding the explanation of this ground, there are five gates as previously stated.
First, regarding the explanation of the name of this stage: why is this stage called the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*)?

It clarifies that at this level, the Bodhisattva, with respect to worldly knowledge, does not require effortful application or deliberate mental calculation; without thinking or acting, their wisdom spontaneously adapts to all phenomena through boundless transformations. Thus, it is named the Immovable Stage.
Second, to clarify the practice-gate of this stage: the practice on this stage is the perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
Because the wisdom of this stage increases, and because the essence of wisdom is fundamentally pure, one’s practices undertaken through vows become increasingly more sovereign.

If one does not give rise to wisdom through the power of vows, there is a fear of becoming identical to those of the Two Vehicles; therefore, one uses vows to guard against this so as not to stagnate in pure tranquility.

Upon reaching this stage, it is in accordance with the Dharma that one receives the Buddhas' three empowerments and seven kinds of exhortations, which cause one to remember original vows and give rise to the functional application of wisdom, spontaneously enabling the arousal of vast compassion, thereby perfecting the effortless application of wisdom and compassion.

In the preceding seventh stage, one achieves entry into the mundane with both practice and development; in this stage, one achieves that which is without practice and without development within the state of having practice and development, because the application of wisdom is spontaneous and great compassion is fulfilled.

Nevertheless, because later on Good Intelligence (Sudhana) has not yet attained mastery, and because his spontaneous wisdom is further clarified rather than depending on deliberate mental attention, the three insights (vidyā) of Sudhana represent the Dharma.

That the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) whom Sudhana encounters during this practice are present within this dharma-assembly clarifies that the eighth stage is called "entering the truth according to principle," where wisdom is termed "effortless" (anabhisaṃskāra), as it accords with the meaning of the middle way.
It is said that within this site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), clear wisdom accords with the Middle Way; thus it is called "Middle.
Since in principle there is no distinction between self and other, person and individual, or oneself and another, it is called the "site of enlightenment."

This spiritual friend, titled "The One Who Possesses the Power of Great Vow and Diligence to Rescue and Protect All Sentient Beings," indicates that it is only at this stage that one can truly fulfill their original vow to save sentient beings who lack the eye of wisdom; this serves to demonstrate that the wisdom of acting in accordance with compassion at the seventh stage is difficult to achieve.
In this stage, one follows wisdom while practicing compassion;

because the salvation of sentient beings is vast and easily accomplished, the essence of wisdom is all-pervasive, manifesting before those in the ten directions according to the breadth or narrowness of sentient beings. It is like an echo that, though without intention, merges with all sounds.

That wisdom is without conceptual thought; it accords with the aspirations of all sentient beings throughout the realm of empty space and the dharma-realm, benefiting them through a unified mind. It has no objective locus of accomplishment and no agent; therefore, she is called by the night goddess’s name, "Great Vow and Power of Diligence Who Protects and Saves All Sentient Beings."

Regarding "sitting upon the lion throne of the treasury of the mani-jewel king that universally manifests all palaces": this clarifies that great compassion universally covering all sentient beings constitutes the palace; manifesting benefit for living beings through wisdom constitutes the hall; and wisdom being free from defilement or purity constitutes the mani-jewel. Because it dwells amidst defilement and purity without effort, yet extensively rescues sentient beings, it is called a "king."

The phrase "universally manifesting the lands of the Dharma-realm, with nets of mani jewels covering them from above" symbolizes that the realm of wisdom universally contains all things; it provides teachings according to the faculties [of beings], and is thus called a "net."
Because wisdom has no substantial body yet can manifest all phenomena without an agent, it is called "maṇi.

This clarifies that, regarding the fruition of reliance resulting from the application of wisdom to benefit sentient beings, one contemplates the cause through the fruit and exhortation toward the cause by means of the fruit.
As explained at length in the sutra, it clarifies that the teaching of this eighth stage (*bhūmi*) is the dharma to be practiced.
The night goddess named Great Vow and Power of Diligence (*Mahāpraṇidhānavīryabalā*) is the practitioner of this path.

The fourth clarification concerns what kind of liberation from the three realms is attained at this stage: it clarifies that one attains the function of wisdom, which benefits all beings universally and is characterized by liberation that is eternally effortless.
It is explained that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, there is cultivation and training in both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

In this eighth stage, these two practices have already been completed; as it is said in the *Bodhisattvacaryā*, the work of this stage is finished here, whereas the ten powers (*daśabala*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), and the masteries (*vaśitā*) of the Buddhas are only finalized at the tenth stage.
Regarding the fifth section, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, there are two points as previously stated.
First, concerning the long-term structural division of the sūtra’s intent: within this eighth stage (*bhūmi*), the text is divided into eleven sections.

First: From "At that time, the Heavenly King and the assembly" down to "with single-minded devotion they gazed up, desiring to hear the Dharma," there are twenty-two verses of verse. This section clarifies how the various devas, upon hearing the Dharma, presented offerings and praised the Buddha’s divine virtues.
2. The two lines of verse beginning with "At that time, Vimukticandra" clarify the section on requesting the exposition of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

3. The prose section from "At that time" onwards consists of ten lines of scripture, clarifying the section on cultivating the eighth stage and entering the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

4. From "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva has accomplished this patience" onwards, there are seventeen lines of scripture clarifying the stage where the Bodhisattva of this level enters the effortless (*anābhoga*) state.

5. "O Son of the Buddha, as for this stage of the Bodhisattva... and so forth; the following section of forty and a half lines of scripture clarifies that once this stage has entered the state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), the Buddhas provide encouragement and empowerment through seven kinds of divisions.

Sixth: The section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" consists of fifty-nine lines of scripture, clarifying the stage of the Bodhisattva who, through the virtue of their own wisdom, thoroughly understands the distinctions between the formation and disintegration of all phenomena; this is the stage of vast mastery in gathering and nurturing sentient beings through the practice of *samānārthatā* (common purpose).

7. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, there are ten lines of scripture that clarify the section on how the Bodhisattva of this stage is free from fault regarding the ten masteries over body, life, and wealth.

8. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, there is a passage of six and a half lines of scripture that clarifies the section on the ten names corresponding to the qualities of the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

9. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva... onwards, there is a section of ten and a half lines of scripture which clarifies that the bodhisattva of this stage enters the realm of the Buddhas and receives the protective mindfulness of the Buddhas; Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Mārutas attend upon him, universally subduing the paths of Māra and abiding in the stage of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*).

10. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the subsequent section consisting of thirty-two and a half lines of scripture clarifies the vastness of the knowledge and vision of the bodhisattvas in this stage, as well as their portion of receiving office (*abhiṣeka*).

11. From "The Skillful Means and Wisdom for Cultivating the Seventh Stage" below, up to "cannot be exhausted even after passing through hundreds of millions of kalpas," there are forty-four verses that repeat the preceding teachings; these are fully contained within the text itself.

Second, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: First, as in the initial section of the prose, ten lines of the sūtra state, "Entering into the nature of all phenomena as being like space is called attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). This clarifies that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, one is in accordance with the patience of non-arising, whereas it is only at the eighth stage that one is said to have attained the patience of non-arising.

Prior to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) involve the cultivation and study of vitarka and vicāra; it is only upon reaching this eighth stage that these two modes of activity finally come to an end.
As for the remaining textual meanings, they are self-evident from the text itself.
The second section of the *Dīrgha-caryā* consists of seventeen lines of sūtra, divided into four parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva has accomplished this patience" down to "all [conceptualizations] are completely stilled," there are five and a half lines of sūtra. This clarifies the entry into the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*), wherein one is detached from all conceptualizations and quiescence manifests before one; it is a realm that the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the two vehicles cannot reach.

2. From "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to "the two modes of activity do not manifest at all," there are eight lines of scripture that clarify the stage where, from the first bhūmi onward, the efforts of skillful means have reached their culmination, and the two modes of activity involving effort no longer manifest.

3. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "none appear before them," there are approximately two lines of scripture that clarify the section using the analogy of being born in the Brahma world where the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm do not manifest.

4. The passage from "This bodhisattva-mahāsattva" onwards, comprising one and a half lines of scripture, clarifies the stage where even the mind of a bodhisattva, the mind of a Buddha, the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and the mind of nirvāṇa do not yet manifest before him.

As for the sūtra’s statement that “this is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,” it is because the followers of the two vehicles are weary of existence and realize non-existence; they do not possess the fulfillment of both the practices of existence and non-existence, nor do they exercise the effortless function (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Having transcended all clamor and strife, quiescence manifests before them. Because their efforts in the dual practices of existence and non-existence have been fulfilled, and because they are free from strife, [the Buddha’s state] is unsurpassed by them.
On the fifth stage, one uproots all worldly things and attains perfect realization;
on the sixth stage, the wisdom of the three emptinesses reaches its consummation;
on the seventh stage, great compassion and all practices are fulfilled.
On the eighth stage, because one spontaneously and effortlessly attains mastery over wisdom for the sake of great transformative benefit for sentient beings, there is no agent.
As the Sūtra says, "For example, a bhikṣu who is fully endowed with supernatural powers and has attained mastery over the mind," this is an illustration of the great by means of the small.

Just as a bhikṣu who has attained liberation from the three realms and possesses no mind of the three realms, yet emerges from the three realms solely through the power of pure meditative concentration, manifesting supernormal powers by means of a wondrously pure mental transformation.

There are six such supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): first, the power of the body; second, the power of the divine ear; third, the power of the divine eye; fourth, the power of recollecting past lives; fifth, the power of knowing the minds of others; and sixth, the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Thus, while the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) of the two vehicles are similar in name and number to those of the bodhisattvas in the Pure Lands, they differ only in the breadth or narrowness of their application.

The supernatural transformations of the two vehicles cannot pervade the Buddha-lands of other directions; the supernatural powers of the bodhisattvas can travel to the Pure Lands of other directions; and the supernatural powers of the bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle encompass all sentient beings and lands throughout the ten directions within a single pore.

The practitioners of the Three Vehicles take the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) as their realization, whereas Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle, having departed from all desires, do not take the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows as their realization.
The six supernormal powers of the Three Vehicles are all limited, while the ten supernormal powers of the One Vehicle are limitless.
This is clearly explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers" (*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*).

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Though he practices the six supernatural powers, he does not exhaust his outflows (*āsrava*)," for his mastery of wisdom differs from that of those who have attained the lesser fruits.
The supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the three vehicles all involve coming and going, as the sūtras of the three vehicles state, “I wish to return to my native land,” and so forth.

However, the supernatural powers possessed by the bodhisattvas of the one vehicle rely on the seal of the principle of wisdom (*prajñā*), which is inherently all-pervasive; they respond to sentient beings and bestow gifts throughout the realm of empty space, for they possess no nature of coming, going, center, or periphery.

The reason why Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle do not realize the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is that they take the sphere of knowledge regarding the bases of clarity as their domain; they perceive neither the nature of outflows nor the absence of outflows, and thus have nothing to grasp or reject. This is because the nature of all phenomena is itself the Dharma-realm, because of the mastery of wisdom, and because their practices for gathering sentient beings are universal.
Because the three vehicles differ in their having preferences and aversions, as well as acceptance and rejection, this [text] now employs the small to illustrate the great by means of analogy.

As in the following case where a dream is used to illustrate the Dharma: it clarifies that from the first stage to the seventh stage there is learning and cultivation, which are like actions performed in a dream before one has awakened.
Because one has already awakened from the dream-like state of the eighth stage, all phenomena are entirely non-existent; thus, one acts according to wisdom as required.
Because wisdom is sovereign, it is termed the "King of Wisdom.
All other matters are self-evident from the text.
The third section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," consists of forty and a half lines of scripture, which can be roughly divided into twelve parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, by the power of this Bodhisattva’s original vows" down to "in this gate of patience," is the section on the manifestation of the ten directions' Buddhas as if to exhort the cultivation of the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of all Tathāgatas.

2. From "Furthermore, good son" down to "you should compassionately regard such sentient beings," this is the section on the encouragement and praise by all Buddhas for attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and on mindful deliverance of sentient beings who possess afflictions and evil perceptions.

3. Furthermore, from "Moreover, son of good family, you should recollect" down to "the gateway of wisdom," there are two lines of scripture; this is the section on how all Buddhas exhort one to recollect their original vows for the sake of universally and greatly benefiting all sentient beings.

4. From "Furthermore, good son" down to "all those of the two vehicles can also attain the non-conceptual dharma," there are two and a half lines of sūtra text, clarifying the section on the Buddhas' exhortation to abide in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

5.
