Furthermore, from "Moreover, son of good family, you should observe our physical marks" down to "you ought to accomplish this matter," there are two and a half lines of scripture; these constitute the section on the Buddhas' encouragement to cultivate merit and wisdom and to employ the voice for preaching the Dharma.

Sixth: From "Furthermore, good son" down to "you should practice to accomplish this dharma," there are three and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the Buddhas' exhortation to cultivate immeasurable dharmic illumination (*dharmāloka*).

7. Furthermore, from "Again, good son" down to "thoroughly penetrating that matter," there is one and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the section on the various Buddhas' exhortations to practice the various distinctions and the thorough penetration of those matters as they truly are.
In the above twenty and a half lines of sūtra, there are three empowerments and seven exhortations in total.

As for the three empowerments: first, the manifestation of the bodies of all Buddhas; second, the bestowing of wisdom; and third, the praise "Excellent, excellent! along with the touching of the crown of the head.
Regarding the "seven exhortations," this refers to the division of the preceding topical outline into seven sections.

Regarding the eighth, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestows upon this Bodhisattva immeasurable gateways of arising wisdom; there are approximately two lines of scripture in total that clarify how all Buddhas, through seven exhortations and three empowerments, cause the differentiation of karmic activities to arise.

9. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "not even a fraction of an upaniṣad," there are approximately seven lines of scripture which clarify the gateway for generating the arising wisdom; this arising cannot be compared to the initial generation of the mind mentioned previously.

10. From "For what reason" down to "because of the immovable nature of the Dharma," this section of approximately five lines of the sūtra clarifies the attainment of the divisions of immeasurable bodily, verbal, and mental karma.

11. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "even after a hundred years they could not equal it," there are three lines of scripture that clarify the use of a metaphor to illustrate how traveling by ship to the ocean allows for a swiftness that surpasses [the journey] by a factor of a hundred years.
12. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "cannot reach," there are four lines of scripture clarifying the section on arriving here by boat without the practice of meritorious deeds.

Thus, through this encouragement and empowerment, from the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the ten stages, at the very beginning of each stage, all Buddhas exhort, praise, and empower the speaker of the Dharma, so that they may preach the Dharma.

Regarding these three empowerments and seven exhortations at the eighth stage, which clarify the practitioner’s own cultivation: this is because one attains [realization] through self-practice without deliberate effort.

In this stage, the wisdom of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) manifests spontaneously; because one accords with the empowerment of all Buddhas and the Dharma, one is capable of receiving the vast Dharma of all Buddhas.

Just as when a worldly sovereign is fully endowed with virtue, auspicious phoenixes and majestic qilin appear in response—this being moved by his virtue—so too, when the non-effortful wisdom manifests in this eighth stage, all Buddhas of the ten directions respond; for it is the natural law that such a convergence must occur.

The Sūtra states, "Good son, this patience is foremost and accords with all Buddha-dharmas. This clarifies that at this stage one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which is not like the conforming patience (*anuloma-kṣānti*) attained prior to the sixth and seventh stages.

Regarding this patience that is foremost in accordance with all Buddha-dharmas: it clarifies that this patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the fundamental nature of the wisdom-body (*jñāna-svabhāva*) of all Buddhas.

"Good son, what we possess as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)" refers to the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*) and so forth, as well as the four fearlessnesses.

Regarding the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha that you have not yet attained, this clearly exhorts you to advance toward the sovereign mastery of a Tathāgata, rather than allowing you to remain within the state of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*).
The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are: first, no error; second, no harsh or abrupt speech;
third, no loss of mindfulness; fourth, no lack of concentration; fifth, no perception of diversity; sixth, no relinquishment that is not preceded by discernment;
seventh, no regression from diligence; eighth, no regression from mindfulness; ninth, no regression from meditative concentration.
10. Non-retrogressive wisdom; 11. Non-retrogressive understanding; 12. Non-retrogression in all activities; 13.
Acting in accordance with wisdom, with wisdom as the precursor; 14. All verbal actions preceded by wisdom and acting in accordance with wisdom;
15. All mental actions preceded by wisdom and acting in accordance with wisdom.

The four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*)—the sixteenth being unattached knowledge of the past, the seventeenth being unattached knowledge of the future, and the eighteenth being unattached knowledge of the present—are as follows:
first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); second, fearlessness regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*);
third, fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path; and fourth, fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path that leads to the end of suffering.
The Ten Powers have already been explained previously.

From the passage "Although you have attained this liberation of tranquility" onwards, he exhorts [the bodhisattva] to keep in mind those sentient beings who have not yet attained it, causing him to remember his original vow.
From "Universally and Greatly Benefiting" onwards, there are generally three additions and seven exhortations, as clarified by the text itself.
By means of these seven exhortations, one causes the arising of immeasurable varieties of wisdom-activity (*jñāna-karman*).

Regarding the term "kalābhāga," this is translated as "a single portion obtained by vertically dividing a single hair on a person's body into one hundred parts," or alternatively, "one-sixteenth part," because in the Western Regions (India), sixteen parts constitute one *śuǎng* (a measure of volume).
What is meant is that the arising of wisdom and the advancement on this stage cannot be compared even in the slightest degree to the dharmas of the preceding stages.
Regarding the term *upaniṣad-bhāga*: *upa* means "near" and *niṣad* means "to face"; this clarifies the vastness of the benefit for sentient beings through the arising of wisdom on this stage.

The benefits produced during the preceding stages, even if established for hundreds of thousands of billions of incalculable eons, cannot compare with even this small amount of benefit, as minute as a hair-tip; this is because the benefits of the preceding stages were inferior, whereas the benefits arising from this stage consist of the manifestation of infinite transformation bodies.
The remainder is fully detailed in the text itself.
The preceding section clarifies the rules for establishing the Dharma through the three empowerments and seven exhortations.

Within the eighth stage—comprising the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten grounds—the overall power is shared; it collectively elucidates how the initial mind of the first abode enters the Way in a single thought-moment, and how, at the time of being born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, all dharmas are fully present.

However, the Dharma must be established with a sequential progression so as not to stagnate in various practices, and so that those who have first resolved their minds may understand the proper measure.
This is because from the initial resolution one gives rise to great vows, causing the wisdom of great compassion and the Dharmakāya to ascend and progress together.

In establishing the teachings, the learner is led through stages; yet, within a single moment of consciousness, there are paths of delusion and awakening, as well as varying depths and shallows, for the realm of wisdom has no before or after.
The fourth section consists of fifty-nine lines of scripture, which may be divided approximately into eight subsections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this eighth stage" down to "knows them all as they truly are," there are four lines of scripture that clarify how, through skillful wisdom, one observes by what karmic causes the formation and destruction of the world occurs.

Second, from "Furthermore, knowing the small and great characteristics of the earth element" down to "differentiated characteristics," there are two lines of sūtra that clarify the division of the small, great, and differentiated characteristics of earth, water, fire, and wind.

3. From "knowing the subtle characteristics of atoms" down to "the wisdom that knows the distinctions among atoms," there are seven lines of scripture, which clarify the distinct characteristics of atoms.

Fourth, from "knowing the formation and destruction of the desire realm and the form realm" down to "the wisdom that contemplates the distinctions of the three realms," there are two and a half lines of scripture which clearly elucidate the characteristics of the formation and destruction of the three realms.

5. From "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva further gives rise to the light of wisdom" down to "manifesting his body everywhere," there are seven and a half lines of scripture, which clarify how he manifests bodies according to the needs of sentient beings by observing the distinctions among their bodies.
6. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "and manifests his body," there are twelve lines of scripture, clarifying the section on manifesting the body through shared activity (*samānārthatā*).

7. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "manifests such forms within this body," there are ten and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the Bodhisattva of this stage dwelling within the signless state of non-mind (*acittanimitta*) and exercising mastery over manifesting bodies that are both identical and distinct.

8. From "This bodhisattva knows the accumulation of sentient beings" down to "the manifestation of the marks of the form-body," there are twelve and a half lines of sūtra, which clarify the section on the distinctions between the body of karmic retribution and its marks.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: "The observer of all-knowing wisdom" refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
"The sphere of its activity" refers to discriminative wisdom (*pravicaya-jñāna*), because it is that which is differentiated from fundamental wisdom.

Regarding the observation of the world’s characteristic of formation: such as the initial formation of the world and its four seasons, as well as the characteristics of formation and destruction of humans, devas, hells, animals, and hungry ghosts—all are formed by karma and all are destroyed by karma; they are all alike in their mutual correspondence and are universally impermanent.

Within the state that is neither shifting nor changing and is devoid of time, one perceives long lifespans and short lifespans; the myriad categories of beings differ in their extension or brevity, whether they arise spontaneously or perish through external causes, or even do so simultaneously—all of which occurs according to karma, for these are not truly existent.
Thus, the duration and reduction of the periods of formation, destruction, and abiding of the kalpas—all these the Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage fully know.
Regarding the small and great characteristics of the earth element, it is clearly understood that the "small characteristic" refers to a single atom (*paramāṇu*).
In the great characteristic, even a single atom has no inherent substance; thus, the vast and the narrow are entirely equal.

Furthermore, within a single pore one may establish vast worlds and small worlds, with all their distinctions of purity and impurity dwelling therein—subtle and infinite, layer upon layer without obstruction, like the Indra’s net where the ten directions interpenetrate—all of which is seen in this manner.

Regarding the characteristics of the magnitudes of the elements of water, fire, and wind: for instance, in this world, according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it is said: "In establishing the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) dwells at the very bottom; its extent is immeasurable, and its thickness is sixteen hundred million yojanas."
Next is the water wheel (*jala-maṇḍala*), which is eleven billion two hundred and thirty-four and a half *yojanas* in thickness; its lower eight *yojanas* of water solidify and congeal to form gold.
"In this way, from above the vajra-limit, accumulated dust forms the world-system.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The moisture of false conceptualization can produce the internal and external water element."
The delusion of capability gives rise to the internal and external fire elements.
The delusion of severance gives rise to the internal and external earth elements.
The delusion of agitation gives rise to the internal and external wind elements.

That which is called craving gives rise to the water element; the sense of "mine" and capability give rise to the fire element; the dual grasping of subject and object can give rise to the earth element; and the conceptualization of self and other can give rise to the wind element.

When affection (*anunaya*) has ceased, one is not reached by the calamity of water; when "I" and "mine" (*ātma-ātmīya*) have ceased, one is not reached by the calamity of fire; and when discursive thought (*vitarka*) has ceased, one is not reached by the calamity of wind.

The second dhyāna is not reached by the calamity of water, the third dhyāna is not reached by the calamity of fire, and the fourth dhyāna is not reached by the calamity of wind, because discursive thought has been cut off.
Within, there is no inhalation or exhalation; without, there is no calamity of wind.
Within, there is no subject or object; without, there is no calamity of fire.
Within, there is no sensual craving; without, there is no calamity of water.

Just as there is a sequential order for the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), so too, through the intensification of sensual craving (*kāmarāga*), one is able to produce the fire element. This is like the Lotus-Jewel Woman Hell (*padmaratnī-strī-naraka*): because one grasps with a mind of craving, when sensual craving becomes predominant, it results in the suffering of hot copper pillars and the like. Being scorched by the heat, one faints and dies, only to be born again.
In this way, there is the suffering of being born and dying a thousand times a day for ten thousand days, which is without end; all of this arises from attachment.
It is like the blazing fires of superior karma that melt copper, or the fierce winds of karma, as described in the *Niraya-sūtra* and other scriptures concerning the hells.
A Bodhisattva in this stage is able to know and see all such destruction of karma as it truly is.

As the Sūtra says: "In whichever world-system there may be, the earth, water, fire, and wind elements each consist of a certain number of atoms. This refers to how one forms larger units from the accumulation of smaller ones: by comparing the *paramāṇu* (infinitesimal atom), the *aṇu* (dust mote passing through a lattice), the *loharajas* (dust mote of copper), the *ayorajas* (dust mote of iron), the rabbit-hair dust in a crevice, wool-dust, a nit, a louse, a grain of grass, and a wild barley grain—each seven times greater than the preceding—one establishes the measurements of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), a cubit (*hasta*), a fathom (*vyāma*), and so forth.
That which is known by them is what is known through ordinary perception, as described in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Furthermore, the dimensions of this continent of Jambudvīpa—its extent from north to south and east to west—are also as stated therein.

If one were to compare the bodies of humans and animals by their respective heights and lengths, using the principle of accumulated dust through seven-times-seven cycles, and thereby know the number of dust particles in the bodies of humans and animals—this is merely the limited perception of ordinary sentiment.
In this stage, the Bodhisattva perceives with the eye of wisdom the bodies of all beings in the world-realms, including humans and animals.

Regarding the wise one who knows the formation and destruction of the triple world: all that exists within the triple world, from its period of formation through its major and minor characteristics, is known and seen by this Bodhisattva through the power of wisdom.
The assembly of brahmins consists of those of pure lineage.
The assembly of kṣatriyas consists of those of royal lineage.
The assembly of vaiśyas consists of those of the merchant class.
The *śūdra* class refers to those who are farmers and cultivators.
When the Sūtra states, "This Bodhisattva knows the bodies of sentient beings," it refers to the body of karmic retribution (*karmavipāka-kāya*).

Regarding the "body of the land" (*deśa-kāya*), sometimes the body of a sentient being is taken as the land, such as the fact that within a human body there dwell eighty-four thousand families of worms, and so forth.
Regarding the ten bodies listed below, this bodhisattva is able to exercise mastery over both their unity and differentiation.

As for the "body of accumulated karmic action" of sentient beings, this bodhisattva knows exactly which karmic fruits have been accumulated as the dominant condition to result in such a retribution-body; he knows them all.
The body of afflictions refers to bodies throughout the three realms.
The form-body refers to bodies in the realm of form.
The formless-body refers to the formless realm.
Such characteristics as the size and form of these bodies can be known through wisdom.
The Tathāgata’s body consists of ten kinds of bodhi-bodies.
As for the *praṇidhāna-kāya* (vow-body), it is so called because it is formed by the arising of vows from the bodhicitta.
The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests in accordance with sentient beings.
The body sustained by power (*baladhārakakāya*) is so called because it is supported by the ten powers (*daśabala*).
The body of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjanakāya*) is adorned by the myriad practices of merit and wisdom.
The body of majestic power is so called because it manifests the subduing and overcoming of all forms of self-conceit.
The mind-made body is so called because it accords with the inclinations and desires of sentient beings.
The body of merit is so called because it is fully endowed with adornments.
The Dharma-body is so called because it is like space.
The Wisdom-body is so called because it knows boundless dharmas.
One who knows the Wisdom-body is one who awakens to both their own wisdom and the wisdom of others.
The characteristic of skillful deliberation is that it is known by wisdom as it is, being devoid of conceptual consciousness.
The characteristic of discerning according to reality is that, through fundamental wisdom, one gives rise to differentiated wisdom, thereby skillfully discerning the characteristics of meanings.
Regarding the characteristic of being subsumed by the fruition of practice: it is because the One Vehicle arises from the fruit of fundamental wisdom as the vows and practices of Samantabhadra.
Regarding the characteristic of the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane: it is because both the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional are manifest before one.

Regarding the characteristics of the distinctions between the three vehicles: the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) tend toward quiescence, whereas bodhisattvas are born in pure lands or, as it is said, "retain delusions to moisten their rebirths" and so forth.
As for the common characteristics, the three vehicles share the single essence of the mark of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Regarding the unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*): possessing compassion and yet being without compassion is called the unique characteristic.
Furthermore, regarding the common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-lakṇa*): ordinary beings and sages are of one essence, fully endowed with the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, regarding the "unshared characteristics" (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*), they exist because there is a distinction between delusion and awakening.
The "characteristics of transcendence" (*niḥsaraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) refer to the Three Vehicles.
The "characteristics of non-transcendence" (*aniḥsaraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) refer to all ordinary beings who possess afflictions (*kleśa*).
The One Vehicle is neither of these two matters.
Those characterized as being with training (*śaikṣa*) are bodhisattvas from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onward.
Those characterized as being beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are bodhisattvas from the eighth stage onward.
One who knows the equal characteristic of the dharmakāya does so because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; thus,
it is an indestructible characteristic.
Because it is a realm obtained as the result of what wisdom has reported;
as for the distinctions of conventional designations according to time and worldly custom,
these are the transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) that accord with the minds of those who desire [them].
Regarding the distinct characteristics of the phenomena of sentient beings and non-sentient beings:

it is because of the distinction between the animate and the inanimate. Regarding the distinct characteristics of the phenomena of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha: [it is because of their respective distinctions].

Because of the distinct characteristics of the śrāvaka saṃgha, the pratyekabuddha saṃgha, the bodhisattva saṃgha of the Pure Land, and the bodhisattva saṃgha of the One Vehicle, the Buddha likewise knows them according to their respective types.

Regarding "knowing that the locus is empty and the body possesses immeasurable marks": this is because the Dharma-body gives rise to wisdom, and according to its activity, it manifests immeasurable distinctions of form.

Regarding "the mark of pervasiveness": because the Dharma-body and the Wisdom-body are pervasive, and their activity is likewise pervasive, their formal marks are also pervasive. Regarding "having no marks of form and no marks of difference": this is because they are entirely identical in essence.
Regarding "boundless characteristics," this is because the realm of the wisdom of the Dharma-body is not limited by insentient matter.
Regarding "the manifestation of the characteristics of the form-body," this clarifies that the form-body has no substance and no support, manifesting through the sovereign power of wisdom.

The above contains eight sections of scripture as categorized in the preceding analysis; those passages where the text is profound and obscure have been explained, while those where the text is self-evident are clear according to the text itself.
The general meaning clarifies that this is because the power reached by the bodhisattva of this stage through non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) is such.
The fifth section consists of ten and a half lines of scripture, which may be divided approximately into three parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "mastery over dharmas," there are two and a half lines of scripture, clarifying that at this stage one has already perfected the aforementioned body-knowledge (*kāyajñāna*) and has attained the tenfold mastery (*vaśitā*).

2. From "Because of attaining these ten masteries" down to "one whose wisdom cannot be destroyed," there is one and a half lines of scripture; this constitutes the section on attaining the fourfold mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*).

3. From "This bodhisattva" onwards, up to "accumulating all Buddha-dharmas," there are six and a half lines of sūtra which clarify that the bodhisattva in this stage, by means of faultless actions of body, speech, and mind, follows the *prajñāpāramitā* and is able to accumulate the portions of all Buddha-dharmas.
The Sūtra says, "Mastery over life" means that upon the essence of great wisdom—which is neither born nor extinguished—one exercises mastery over birth and death in common with all sentient beings.
"Mastering the mind" means that one is able to accomplish whatever is to be done by following non-conceptual wisdom (*amanasikāra-jñāna*).
The rest is fully contained within the text itself.
The sixth section consists of nine and a half lines of scripture, forming a single unit in total.

From "The Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattvas, dwelling in this stage" down to "there is no fault or transgression in any matters," it clarifies that the Bodhisattva in this stage attains the portions of the ten powers, as detailed in the sutra itself.
Regarding the term "one who possesses all modes of omniscience": "all modes" refers to the clear cultivation of various types of wisdom through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
"Omniscience" refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
As for the statement "the one of all-knowledge and omniscience," it clarifies that the wisdom of differentiation arises from fundamental wisdom.
The intent is to clarify that by means of fundamental non-effortful wisdom, one performs various manifold efforts; yet because these wisdoms are non-dual, they are one.
"Because wisdom is manifested" clarifies that the aforementioned sovereign wisdom has become manifest.

From "this bodhisattva" onwards, it clarifies that because he has attained the power of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), he is able to manifest all activities; yet among all these activities, there is no fault or error, because his wisdom is devoid of subject and object.
The seventh section consists of six and a half lines of sūtra, clarifying that the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) possesses ten stages of the name.
The meaning of these names is self-evident from the sūtra itself.

Because it cannot be fathomed by anyone in all the worlds, it is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*). Having clarified that prior to the seventh stage there is practice and development which constitutes worldly knowledge, this eighth stage is so named because the effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) manifests before one; as it is the first entry into true wisdom for those who were previously like children, it is designated the Stage of Youthful Truth.

Because it is free from fault, it is called the "ground of birth" (*upapatti-bhūmi*). It is known as the ground of birth because, having clearly transcended both applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), one is no longer wounded by the thorns of such thoughts; for one is born within the wisdom of effortlessness (*anābhoga-jñāna*).
The remainder is fully contained within the text itself.
The eighth section consists of ten and a half lines of scripture, which may be divided into two parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva accomplishes such wisdom" down to "manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment," there are five and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies that a Bodhisattva of this stage enters the realm of the Buddhas, sustained by their own power, and thus causes the Brahma-kings, Śakra-kings, and others to constantly attend and serve them.

2. From "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva has thus entered the assembly of the One Vehicle" down to "abiding in the Immovable Ground," there are five lines of sūtra that clarify the entry into the effortless assembly of the One Vehicle, which is the section on attaining supernormal powers and mastery according to one's will.

"Constantly being protected by the mindfulness of the Tathāgata" clarifies that the Buddhas do not fail to protect and mindfully care for even those sentient beings who have severed their roots of goodness. This protective mindfulness has three meanings:
first, protecting and mindfully caring for sentient beings on the path of suffering who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment;

second, protecting and mindfully caring for those who have already resolved to attain enlightenment—both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those who have attained realization; and third, protecting and mindfully caring for Bodhisattvas who have entered the stage of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*), so as to enable them to attain the sovereign mastery of a Buddha.
Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Vajrapāṇi spirits constantly follow and attend him; this also has three meanings:

first, to attend and protect all sentient beings; second, to attend and protect those who have already resolved their minds [for enlightenment]; and third, to attend and protect those who have attained effortless wisdom (anābhoga-jñāna) as well as all Buddhas.
"Attendant" (*paricāraka*) also carries two meanings:
first, the protection and nurturing of great compassion; second, the protection through reverence for that Dharma by Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages.

Regarding those who possess the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) obtained as a karmic retribution of great power within each individual body: prior to the seventh stage, these are supernormal powers produced through cultivation and as karmic retribution, which are not yet autonomous; on this [eighth] stage, the supernormal powers of karmic retribution consisting of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) are vast and autonomous.

Prior to the seventh stage, the supernormal powers of retributive karma arise based on meditative concentration and the power of vows; at this stage, the supernormal powers of retributive karma arise from non-conceptual wisdom (*nirnimitta-jñāna*), because there is no longer any deliberate cultivation or effort.
As for "emitting great radiance," because all created obstructions have vanished, radiance manifests spontaneously.
As for "entering the unobstructed dharma-realm," because all conditioned activities have ceased, one acts according to wisdom without any hindrance.
The remainder is fully detailed in the text itself.
The ninth section consists of thirty-two lines of scripture, which may be divided into four parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "because they are well able to open and expound the gates of wisdom," there are thirteen and a half lines of scripture; this clarifies that the Bodhisattvas of this stage see the Buddhas in vast numbers, as well as the section on the analogy of refining pure gold into precious ornaments.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "cannot be exhausted," there are six and a half lines of scripture that clarify how the Bodhisattva of this stage universally radiates light, as well as the superior aspects of the perfections of conduct and vows they practice.

3. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the one who is the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge," there are seven lines of scripture that clarify the conferral of office upon the bodhisattva at this stage, as well as his practice of the various *pāramitās*, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), which do not deviate from the division of the Three Jewels.

4. From "This bodhisattva" below, there are five lines and a half of sūtra which clarify that the bodhisattvas at this stage, through the power of diligence arising from non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) and what is sought by the power of their vows, manifest a vast multitude of bodhisattva retinues.
The tenth section contains forty-two verses that repeat the preceding teachings, as is fully detailed in the text itself.
9. The Ninth Ground, *Sādhumatī*. Regarding the explanation of this ground, there are five sections as previously described.
First, regarding the explanation of the name of this stage: why is this stage called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*)?

Because the practice of this ninth stage is identical to the ninth *Dharmarāja-putra-vihāra* (Abode of the Dharma Prince) among the ten abodes; and because it corresponds to the ninth position within each of the five stages, sharing the status of a Dharma Master who possesses excellent knowledge of all dharmas, it is named the Stage of Excellent Intelligence.

Second, to clarify what gateways of practice are cultivated on this stage: on this stage, the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is cultivated as the primary practice, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.
Third, regarding Sudhana’s representation of the Dharma: in Jambudvīpa, there is a grove named Lumbinī where Sudhana beholds a deity named Sumati-paripūrṇa.

This "Jambudvīpa" is the name of a forest in this continent; because this continent is named after that forest, it clarifies that the wisdom established as teaching in this stage is like a forest, for it provides vast and abundant shade and shelter.
Furthermore, the mention of "gardens and groves" within it clarifies that wisdom is layered, profound, and inexhaustible.
It is named Lumbinī, or sometimes Rumminī;
"nī" is a feminine suffix.

"Ratnārciḥ" (Flowing Radiance) refers to the stainless, perfect radiance of the joy of the Dharma of wisdom in this Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*). It is explained that through the perfect radiance of excellent intelligence, one destroys afflictions and attains bliss.
The deity’s name is Perfectly Complete Sublime Virtue (*Sudharmaparipūrṇa*), for he possesses the rank of a Dharma teacher whose sublime wisdom is perfectly complete.
He dwells in a pavilion adorned with jewel trees; these jewel trees represent the conduct of the Dharma teacher.
The "pavilions" (lúgé) signify that wisdom is lofty and far-reaching, as it illuminates all things in successive layers without obstruction.

It signifies that one adorns wisdom with various practices and skillfully expounds the various teachings to cause sentient beings to have faith and submission; thus, this Dharma Master is fully endowed with both understanding and practice.
Fourth, regarding what kind of liberation from the three realms is attained on this stage: one attains the liberation of the perfection of wisdom.
Fifth, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the two meanings are as previously stated.
Regarding the detailed analysis of the meaning of this scripture: within this *Bhūmi of Excellent Intelligence*, it is analyzed into seven sections.

The first section, beginning with "When this eighth stage of the Bodhisattva was being taught," consists of twenty-six verses; it clarifies how the great assembly, having heard the teachings of the preceding stage, offered worship, uttered praises, and requested the teaching of the dharma-gate of the ninth stage.

The second section of the prose commentary consists of sixty-two and a half lines of sūtra text, which clarifies the stage of entering the nine grounds through cultivation; it specifically concerns the section on the mind abiding correctly in the nine grounds and knowing the distinctions among all phenomena.

The third section of the prose commentary consists of thirty-six and a half lines of scripture, clarifying that the Bodhisattva of this stage serves as a great Dharma-preacher, expounding all dharma-gates by means of the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).

The prose section of the fourth segment consists of twenty-eight and a half lines of scripture, clarifying that the Bodhisattva of this stage acts as a great Dharma teacher, attaining the division of mastery over ten million billion unspeakable dharanī-doors according to his will.

The fifth section consists of sixteen and a half lines of prose, which clarifies that the Bodhisattvas of this stage preach the Dharma and respond to inquiries for infinite sentient beings with a single voice, causing them all to rejoice according to their respective inclinations.

The sixth section of the prose consists of twenty-nine and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies that the Bodhisattvas of this stage see a vast multitude of Buddhas, as well as their making offerings and serving them, along with their receiving their own assigned duties.
The seventh section consists of forty-eight verses, which are a reiteration of the preceding *dharmaparyāya*.
Regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, within the first twenty-six verses there are two further sections:
the first twenty-five verses constitute the section on the Great Assembly’s Joyful Offerings and Praise of the Dharma upon Hearing the Previous Ground.
Second, at the very end there is one verse-line, which constitutes the request for the subsequent section on the stages (*bhūmi*).
The meaning of these two segments of verse is self-evident from the verses themselves in the Chinese text.
The second segment consists of sixty-two and a half lines of prose in the sūtra, which is divided into fourteen topical sections.
I. From "At that time" down to "the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence," there are six and a half lines of scripture; this is the section on entering the ninth stage.

II. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the practice of unconditioned dharmas," there may be four lines of scripture, clarifying the section on abiding in the ninth stage and knowing the ten kinds of practices of all sentient beings.

3. From "This bodhisattva, by means of this wisdom" down to "the dense forest of the three aggregates," there may be approximately three lines of scripture, clarifying that the bodhisattva at this stage knows the eleven types of dense forests of all sentient beings.

4. From "This bodhisattva knows as it truly is" down to "knows all as they truly are," there are four lines of scripture that clarify this stage of the bodhisattva’s penetration into the distinctions among the ten types of characteristics.

5. From "Furthermore, knowing the various characteristics of all afflictions" down to "knowing them as they truly are in eighty-four thousand ways," there are four and a half lines of sūtra. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva at this stage knows the specific characteristics of the eighty-four thousand afflictions as they truly are.

Sixth: From "Furthermore, knowing the various characteristics of all karmas" down to "knowing all eighty-four thousand [types] as they truly are," there may be five lines of sūtra text that clarify how the Bodhisattva at this stage knows the various characteristics of karma up to its eighty-four thousand divisions.

7. Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Moreover, knowing the characteristics of the faculties as weak, middling, or superior" down to "even up to eighty-four thousand [faculties], he knows them all as they truly are," there are approximately four and a half lines of scripture that clarify the stage where the Bodhisattva distinguishes the various characteristics of the faculties.

8. "Furthermore, knowing all understandings": this passage of one and a half lines clarifies that the Bodhisattva in this stage knows the distinctions among all understandings, up to eighty-four thousand divisions.

9. From "Furthermore, knowing the various characteristics of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)" down to "only by means of the Noble Path does one uproot their characteristics," there may be six lines of scripture clarifying that the Bodhisattva in this stage knows the various classifications of the characteristics of the latent tendencies.

10. From "Furthermore, knowing the various aspects of taking birth" down to "falsely claiming to have transcended the three realms while greedily seeking signs," there may be five lines of scripture that clarify the section on how Bodhisattvas at this stage know the various aspects of taking birth.

Eleventh: From "Furthermore, knowing the various characteristics of habitual tendencies" down to "the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s perfuming," there are five lines of scripture that clarify the stage where the Bodhisattva knows the various divisions of the characteristics of habitual tendencies.

12. Furthermore, from "knowing again that sentient beings are fixed in the right" down to "abandoning both as they possess the characteristic of being unfixed," there may be four lines of scripture; these clarify how the Bodhisattva at this stage knows the distinctions between those fixed in the right and those fixed in the wrong.

13. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "causing them to attain liberation," there are two lines of scripture which clarify the general conclusion of the preceding twelve sections concerning the differentiation of all dharmas.

14. From "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva" onwards, there are four and a half lines of scripture that clarify how benefit is obtained according to the faculties through the four vehicles of Dharma.
Within the sixty-two lines of scripture from the second section of the prose commentary, these are divided into fourteen segments.

Furthermore, from the first section of six and a half lines of the sūtra—beginning with the passage where the Sūtra states, "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva," and continuing for those six and a half lines—this constitutes the stage of cultivating the ninth bhūmi. By means of such immeasurable wisdom, one contemplates and observes; this clarifies that while one seeks to further attain a more supreme, tranquil liberation, the eighth bhūmi has already entered the non-effortful state of the union of principle and wisdom (*jñāna*), wherein one proceeds toward and ascends to the great functioning of the Tathāgata’s fruit—the ten powers and four fearlessnesses—which is characterized by tranquil liberation and non-effortful spontaneity (*anābhoga*).

Furthermore, "practicing the wisdom of the Tathāgata" clarifies the cultivation of the eighth and ninth stages, because one has not yet attained mastery over the Buddha’s functional powers (*karman*).

"Entering the secret dharma of the Tathāgata" refers to transcending the cultivation of the knowable through discursive thought, while not forming the notion that one universally responds to all phenomena without rest.
To observe the nature of inconceivable great wisdom is the fundamental, universally luminous great wisdom.
"Nature" refers to the essence of clear wisdom; this nature has no basis or dwelling, for it manifests great function in response to the sense organs and their objects.

Regarding the "purification of the gates of dhāraṇī-samādhi": by means of non-abiding wisdom, one universally responds to sentient beings to accomplish great function; this is because it is the meaning of correct meditative absorption (samāpatti) and total retention (dhāraṇī).
One who possesses great supernormal powers (*mahābhijñā*) is so called because their wisdom responds to the faculties [of beings], which is termed "supernormal" (*ṛddhi*);
because their essence pervades the ten directions without having to go there, it is termed "power" (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, because their wisdom is non-abiding and possesses equal knowledge and vision regarding both self and others, it is termed "power."
Furthermore, the nature of wisdom possesses great power yet is formless; this is termed "spirit" (shen).
It lacks intrinsic nature yet possesses manifold names; this is termed "penetration" (tong).
Moreover, it possesses knowledge and vision yet is free from birth and death; this is termed "spirit."
To be equal to the dharma-realm and identical in both unity and multiplicity is called "pervasion" (sāmānya).
The following is self-evident according to the text.
The six lines and a half of scripture above constitute the stage of practicing the ninth ground.
The second section, comprising four lines of scripture, pertains to the stage of abiding in the ninth bhūmi.

The sūtra states: "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this Bhūmi of Good Intelligence (Sādhumatī), he knows, as they truly are, the activities of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas. This clarifies that the Great Dharma Master of this stage thoroughly understands the mental activities of all sentient beings—whether they be wholesome, unwholesome, or those not performing wholesome or unwholesome acts, which are termed indeterminate (avyākṛta)—knowing them all completely.

Just as there are four types of unwholesome [dharmas]—namely, by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*saṃprayoga*), production (*ākṣepa*), and ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*)—there are thirteen types of wholesome [dharmas]:

by intrinsic nature, association, following (*anuvartana*), origination (*samutthāna*), ultimate meaning, innate (*upapatti-labdha*), presence through application (*prayoga-sammukhībhāva*), honoring and benefiting (*pūjā-anugraha*), attraction (*parigraha*), antidote (*pratipakṣa*), tranquility (*upaśama*), outflow (*niṣyanda*), and cessation (*praśama*).

There are two types of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): as among the eight kinds of consciousness, the five consciousnesses such as those of the eye and ear are unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); the sixth mental consciousness is obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*); the seventh grasping-consciousness is obscured-indeterminate; and the eighth, the seed-consciousness named the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), is unobscured-indeterminate. However, because it serves as the cause for future rebirth by acting as the basis for the seeds of outflowing wholesome states produced by the grasping-consciousness—just as a vessel holds seeds—it is so designated.
There are four kinds of neutral (*avyākṛta*) mental activities: deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), transformation (*nairmāṇika*), and maturation (*vipākaja*).
For example, when people are engaged in deportment, non-deportment, or craftsmanship, they all lose right mindfulness.
Just as one learns worldly transformations, so too is it inconsistent with right mindfulness.
Just as karma created in this life results in the maturation of future lives, the body is subject to death;
yet in a single moment of unawareness, one undergoes rebirth.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of indeterminate [phenomena]: those indeterminate by nature, those indeterminate through association, those indeterminate through projection, and those indeterminate in the ultimate sense.
These four types of indeterminate phenomena constitute the supramundane path.
A bodhisattva in this stage fully understands such dharmas of practice.
Regarding the dharmas that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*): the three realms are with outflows, while the dharmas that transcend the three realms are without outflows.
The dharmas for transcending the three realms within the Three Vehicles are with outflows, whereas the universal radiance wisdom of the One Buddha Vehicle is without outflows.

Regarding the practice of mundane and supramundane dharmas: the three vehicles constitute the practice of supramundane dharmas; ordinary beings constitute the practice of mundane dharmas; and the One Vehicle is neither mundane nor supramundane, for it is able to conform to the world while fully embodying the practices of Samantabhadra.
Regarding the categories of the conceivable and the inconceivable: all that pertains to the triple world is a conceivable phenomenon.
Furthermore, the supramundane paths of the three vehicles are also all conceivable, because they all involve something to be attained.
The wisdom-realm of the One Vehicle is inconceivable because it is non-apprehendable; it is the great sovereign power of boundless quiescence and function.

Regarding the dharmas of the fixed and the unfixed: the four dhyānas of the form realm and the four dhyānas of the formless realm are fixed dharmas, yet they are unfixed dharmas because they are not true concentration and because they possess arising and ceasing.

The supramundane meditative concentration of extinction (*nirvāṇa*) of the Three Vehicles is both a dharma of fixed concentration and a dharma of non-fixed concentration, because it involves the dharmas of both grasping and relinquishing.
The Chan of the Dharma-realm of the One Vehicle is both a dharma of fixed concentration and a dharma of non-fixed concentration, because it is the sovereign mastery of quiescence and function.
All dharmas of ordinary beings are indeterminate dharmas;
all Buddhas are determinate dharmas.
All ordinary beings and sages alike lack determinate dharmas, for their nature has no point of reliance.

The Dharma of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas involves revulsion toward suffering and its origin, the cultivation of cessation and the path, and the realization of dependent origination as the nature of non-arising; because they abandon compassion and wisdom, they transcend the worldly bonds of conditions.
The Bodhisattva who practices the dharma-conduct of practice performs the six pāramitās and maintains the dharma-conduct of retaining afflictions and being born in a pure land.
The dharma-conduct of the Tathāgata stage is universal radiant wisdom, for it serves as the ground by being one with all sentient beings and those of the two vehicles.

Regarding those who practice conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*): the humans and devas of the three realms, as well as those of the three vehicles who cultivate the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) through their training, all belong to the category of conditioned practice; this is because they possess mastery over both pure and impure minds.
Regarding the practice of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), it is solely the ground of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
This preceding section of four lines concludes the clear exposition of the ten types of dharma-practice.

Third, regarding this Bodhisattva’s knowledge of the ten kinds of dense forests (*gahana*) within all sentient beings, the Sūtra states: "This Bodhisattva, by means of such wisdom, knows the dense forest of the minds of sentient beings as they truly are. This refers collectively to the vast proliferation of afflictions (*kleśa*) being like a dense forest; all arise from the mind, and when there is no mind, the dense forest of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is extinguished.
Great wisdom is like a forest, for it is able to universally cover and protect all sentient beings.

Regarding the "dense forest of afflictions": this refers to being deluded regarding the self-nature of the dharma-realm and its dependent origination, thereby forming a dense forest of all afflictions as numerous as the atoms within world-systems throughout the entire expanse of space. This clarifies that the vast and manifold obscuring hindrances of afflictions are like a dense forest; yet, upon reaching the realm of singular wisdom, they immediately become a dense forest of the merits of the ten thousand practices.
The faculties (*indriya*), roots (*mūla*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), spiritual lineages (*gotra*), and inclinations (*chanda*) can all be understood [through this].
As for the dense forest of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), there are seven:

first, the tendency toward sensual desire; second, aversion; third, resentment regarding existence; fourth, craving; fifth, pride; sixth, ignorance; and seventh, views and doubt—this latter being the doubt regarding the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
These seven kinds of constant delusions and obscurations are termed *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).
Because they can delude the boundless objects and states of mind and obstruct the wisdom of *bodhi*, they are called a "dense forest.
Regarding the dense forest of rebirth, at the limit of a single moment, eight hundred births and cessations arise simultaneously.

Regarding the "dense forest of habitual tendencies," as established in the sutras through the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten stages, these are all for the purpose of manifesting a portion of the wisdom of the Tathāgata and suddenly severing the coarse delusions of the triple world.

On the stages (*bhūmi*), one gradually subdues and purifies habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): on the first stage, one clearly contemplates worldly phenomena; on the second stage, one subdues the habitual tendencies of afflictions in the desire realm through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); on the third stage, one cultivates the four dhyānas and eight samādhis to subdue the habitual tendencies of afflictions in the two higher realms; on the fourth stage, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata; on the fifth stage, one cultivates the gateways of all worldly arts and skills; on the sixth stage, wisdom emerges from the entanglements and becomes full; on the seventh stage, one enters the skillful means for benefiting sentient beings; on the eighth stage, effortless wisdom manifests before one; on the ninth stage, practice becomes spontaneous and effortless; and on the tenth stage, merit is perfected and the activity of a Buddha is realized—all of these are skillful means for subduing habitual tendencies.

Regarding the "dense forest of the distinctions among the three aggregates": from within the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*), there are sixteen kinds of dense forests; when expanded, these number eighty-four thousand, as well as the inexhaustible categories of the three unwholesome roots, the three poisons (*viṣa*), the three stumps (*skandha*), the three impurities (*mala*), the three burnings (*paridāha*), the three arrows (*śalya*), the three evil conducts (*duścarita*), the three residues (*vāsanā*), the three fetters (*bandhana*), the three possessions (*parigraha*), the two fevers (*paritāpa*), the three afflictions (*upāyāsa*), the three impurities (*aśubha*), the three inflammations (*ādīpana*), the three dense forests, and the three obstructions (*āvaraṇa*). All of these take greed, hatred, and delusion as their essence, and are given various names for the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The three lines of sūtra above clarify the section on the dense forest of afflictions (*kleśa-gahana*).
Fourth, "this bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the various characteristics of the minds of sentient beings" is a comprehensive statement of the whole.
What is called the characteristic of mixed arising refers to the mind taking various objects as its focal point.
The characteristic of rapid transformation refers to birth and cessation, impermanence, and not abiding for even a single moment before perishing.
The characteristic of non-perishing refers to the fact that worldly phenomena are impermanent; this is what is called the characteristic of perishing.
The characteristics of the world are unestablished, and thus there is no destruction; this is the mark of the equality between the mundane and the supramundane.
That which has no form or substance is like the mind’s contemplation of emptiness, perceiving emptiness as the signless.
Regarding the characteristic of being boundless: one forms the mental conception of it as boundless.

Regarding the characteristic of purity: one knows such a characteristic of purity, as well as defilement, purity, bondage, and non-bondage, all exactly as they are; even up to the immeasurable, one knows them all exactly as they are.
The above clarifies that the Bodhisattva in this stage knows, as they truly are, the various characteristics of mental conceptions, knowing them through wisdom.
The five sections and four lines and a half of the sūtra further state that he knows the various characteristics of all afflictions; this is a general summary of the matter.
Regarding what is called the "aspect of long-term accompaniment," it means that all afflictions have no beginning or end, as they constantly accompany the objects of ignorance.
Regarding the "aspect of boundless origination," it refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); because the mind takes name-and-form as its object, this is termed "formative action" (*saṃskāra*).

When the mind takes an object as its condition, sensation arises simultaneously; as thought and perception become entangled, the seeds of consciousness ripen. The five aggregates and eleven conditions surge like unceasing waves: name-and-form serves as the object, the mind acts as the sovereign, and sensation, perception, and volitional formations act as the instigators.

The manas-consciousness, grasping at objects, gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion; within the field of original karma, it plants the seeds of consciousness that produce various sprouts numbering eighty-four thousand.
Regarding "simultaneously arising and not abandoning," this has already been explained previously.
As for the single meaning of "dormant and active": dormant afflictions (*anuśaya*) are those seven types mentioned before;
active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) are the ten underlying tendencies (*daśānuśaya*), the ten envelopments (*daśaparyavasthāna*), and so forth, which manifest as active functioning.

Among the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), six—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the view of precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and [wrong] views (*dṛṣṭi*)—are obstacles to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). The four—namely, attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), delusion (*moha*), and pride (*māna*)—are obstacles to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Although these practices are seen in the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), they arise repeatedly during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The afflictions of the path of cultivation are eliminated up through the third stage; the afflictions of the path of vision are eliminated across the six stages. From the seventh stage to the tenth, one accords with the Buddha’s compassion and wisdom to perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings.

The ten wholesome actions of the first and second stages and above counteract the afflictions of the desire realm; because one cultivates the four dhyānas and eight samādhis in the third stage to counteract the afflictions of the two higher realms and attain a mind that transcends the three realms.
In the sixth stage, the three emptinesses manifest before one, and because supramundane wisdom is fully perfected, there are no afflictions of the path of seeing.
From the seventh stage onward, one dwells exclusively in the world, training in the gateway of the Buddha’s wisdom and compassion to benefit sentient beings.
Established in this manner, the dharmas of the division of illumination must likewise be practiced simultaneously by those who have first resolved their minds upon awakening.
As the Sūtra says, "Sleeping and waking share a single essential characteristic," because the essence of illumination is devoid of dual characteristics.
Those who, deluded regarding the single true wisdom, produce manifold delusions, are nevertheless subsumed within that single essence.

Regarding the characteristics of being associated with or dissociated from the mind: when the mind merges with an object, it constitutes the characteristic of association; when it does not merge with an object yet falsely takes it as an object of cognition, this is the characteristic of dissociation from the mind.
Regarding the characteristics of dwelling as one takes birth according to the various realms of existence, he fully knows how such abodes arise due to such afflictions.

Regarding the distinct characteristics of the three realms—the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm—he knows as they truly are the objects grasped upon taking birth therein, as well as the focal points of his thoughts, whether in meditative concentration or distraction.

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the faults of craving, views, delusion, and pride, which penetrate like arrows": this clarifies that taking birth within the three realms is entirely due to these four types of afflictions (*kleśa*).

As for the production of various afflictions up to eighty-four thousand: just as the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are composed of the five aggregates (*skandha*), with one hundred within each aggregate, there are five hundred within the five aggregates.

The five aggregates (skandhas) constitute the five objects (viṣayas); within these five objects there are further the five aggregates and the ten fetters (anuśaya), making one hundred, and thus there are five hundred within the five objects.
Taking the aggregates as internal and the objects as external, the mind (manas) is the sovereign of them all.

The mind (*manas*) acts as the subject that perceives, and objects (*viṣaya*) act as the perceived; since there are five hundred each for these internal and external factors, they together constitute one thousand.

When these are assigned to the seven consciousnesses, they become seven thousand. Dividing these across the three periods of time, with three times seven being twenty-one, they total twenty-one thousand. These further multiplied by nine [mental afflictions] result in eighty-four thousand gates of the Dharma.

Those with a predominance of hatred, those with a predominance of greed, those with a predominance of delusion, and those with equal proportions of the three poisons each number twenty-one thousand; together, they total eighty-four thousand.
Because the afflictions and karmas created through attachment involve only the seven consciousnesses, the others cannot act as such.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks": "Regarding form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, there are five hundred afflictions within and five hundred afflictions without."

Those with a predominance of hatred are twenty-one thousand; those with a predominance of greed are twenty-one thousand; those with a predominance of delusion are twenty-one thousand; and those with equal proportions of the three are twenty-one thousand.
"However, these words alone are not yet sufficient.
The above four and a half lines of scripture clarify that the Bodhisattva in this stage knows, as they truly are, the various characteristics of the divisions of all afflictions."
The sixth [section] may consist of five lines of scripture, clarifying that the Bodhisattvas at this stage know the various characteristics and divisions of karma.
As the sutra says, "Furthermore, they know the various characteristics of all karmas," this refers to the subject as a whole.
These are the characteristics of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
The wholesome and the unwholesome can be known.
As for the indeterminate, there are two kinds of indeterminate:
First, regarding that which is neither-defined as wholesome nor unwholesome, such as dullness and sleep, these are unwholesome or neutral.

Second, in the meditative attainment of *samādhi*, both mind and objects vanish; with right wisdom manifesting before one, one merely turns the wheel of the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Because there is no correct designation regarding the existence or non-existence of self and others, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
Its characteristics consist of both informative and non-informative aspects.
To clarify informative action (vijñapti-karman): there may be an action that has a cause and possesses an informative aspect.
Birth is itself the cause; when there are external objects that can be seen, heard, sensed, or known, the mind grasps them to form karmic seeds.

Alternatively, some karmic seeds have no external manifestation; they are formed through the mind’s arbitrary conceptualization and self-referential calculation, thereby constituting the characteristics of karma.

Regarding the characteristic of being inseparable from that which arises simultaneously with the mind: this clarifies that karma originates from the mind and that the mind itself is karma, like an image within a mirror.
The retributive fruits of karma are reflections of the mind; when the mind ceases, the objects become still.

Regarding the fact that the self-nature perishes moment by moment yet the sequential accumulation of fruits does not lose its characteristic: this clarifies that the performance of karma arises from delusion regarding self-nature.
Although one performs deluded karma, it suddenly arises and immediately vanishes.
Although they are not constantly bound before one, the retributions accumulated from them do not fail to manifest one by one.
Unless right knowledge manifests before one and all karmas are thus utilized by wisdom, liberation cannot be attained.

Regarding the characteristics of having retribution and being without retribution: sentient beings of the three realms, those of the two vehicles, and even Bodhisattvas of the Pure Lands all possess the characteristic of having retribution.

In the fruit of Buddhahood of the One Vehicle, the mind of defilement and purity has perished; one does not rely on karmic retribution, but merely manifests forms according to the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, like a wish-fulfilling mani jewel that takes on the same color as the object it encounters. It possesses neither self-nature nor other-nature, for it is fundamentally identical in its single mind with all sentient beings. For those who reach realization through whatever their own minds perceive, the Dharma is naturally thus, for it is not a matter of coming and going through active exertion.
Regarding the characteristics of receiving various retributions such as black-and-black: this clarifies that within the karma of ignorance, one repeatedly performs black karma.
Here, wisdom is taken as white, while consciousness is taken as black.
Regarding the "immeasurable characteristics of the field," this is illustrated by the analogy of various kinds of grasses and trees growing within a field.
Likewise, within the field of karma, the seeds, sprouts, and shoots of various forms of consciousness grow in great profusion, because they form a dense forest.

Regarding the characteristics that distinguish ordinary beings from sages: this Bodhisattva of this stage is fully able to discern whether it is the karma of humans, the karma of animals, that of hell-beings, that of hungry ghosts, that of devas, that of śrāvakas, that of pratyekabuddhas, that of bodhisattvas in pure lands, or the karma of the great compassionate wisdom of the fruit of Buddhahood in the One Vehicle.
The characteristics of present, future, and subsequent experiences are clearly known because one foreknows the karma for rebirth throughout the three periods of time.

Regarding the characteristics of vehicles and non-vehicles, as well as those that are fixed or unfixed: this includes the vehicles of external paths and their fixed states, as well as the supramundane [paths] of the three vehicles—yet these are falsely claimed to be supramundane because they are actually the karma of non-supramundane paths. Thus, all eighty-four thousand [teachings] are known as they truly are, and all the differentiated karmas from the fruit of Buddhahood onward are known as they truly are.
The above clearly explains the characteristics of the distinctions among karmas.

Seventh, regarding the knowledge of the superior characteristics of the various faculties—mild, medium, and sharp: "mild" refers to inferior faculties, "medium" refers to middling faculties, and "sharp" refers to superior faculties.

Regarding these distinctions and non-distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior characteristics between the prior limit and the posterior limit: it is because one knows the distinctions among the faculties and conducts of the three periods of time, knowing all their similarities and differences.
Regarding the characteristic of the co-arising and inseparable nature of afflictions: one fully knows the characteristic of the inseparability between cultivated afflictions and innate afflictions.
The characteristics of being a vehicle or non-vehicle, and being determinate or indeterminate, are as previously described.

Regarding the characteristic of the shifting and disintegration of the net of faculties according to [afflictions]: he is fully able to know the characteristic of the shifting and disintegration of the net of teachings established according to the faculties, as well as the shifting and disintegration according to the gravity of afflictions.
Regarding the characteristic of being unsurpassed and indestructible: this means that the categories of faculties are of the highest degree and are thus free from regression or fluctuation.

Regarding "following along with and arising together with distant [objects] while possessing different characteristics": it is like all sentient beings who, from beginningless time, have arisen together and are not separate from the single nature; yet, one knows all their differences according to the distinctions of their faculties and natures, even up to eighty-four thousand such distinctions, knowing them as they truly are without any error.
Eighth is the knowledge of the various faculties (*indriya*).

Within the aforementioned "knowledge of the distinctions among faculties," one knows the various understandings, as well as the lower, middle, and superior natures and inclinations, up to eighty-four thousand types, as detailed in the text itself.

The above concerns the distinctions among knowledge, understanding, disposition, and inclination. Regarding the "eighty-four thousand":
through delusion, eighty-four thousand afflictions are formed; through awakening, eighty-four thousand liberating wisdoms are formed.
"Knowing the various characteristics of all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)" refers to them collectively.

As for "latent tendencies," it clarifies that they are constantly associated with defiled afflictions such that there is not a single moment of conscious awareness; thus they are termed "latent tendencies."

Regarding what is called "arising simultaneously with a defiled mind": this clarifies that [the mind] arises together with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its cause. Being deluded regarding this name-and-form, one conceives it as arising from one's own mind yet clings to it as being externally existent; consequently, a defiled mind arises. Because it arises together with name-and-form, it is said to "arise simultaneously with the mind."

Regarding the characteristics of the distinctions between mental association and non-association: it means clearly knowing all the characteristics of the distinctions between the minds of all sentient beings and their corresponding or non-corresponding objects.

"Having long followed the characteristics of conditioned phenomena, yet never uprooting the characteristics that have no beginning" clarifies that from time immemorial one has always been accompanied by the five aggregates and the twelve links of dependent origination, never for a single moment awakening the mind to use contemplation to uproot them.

Regarding the characteristics that are contrary to all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, samāpattis, and supernormal powers: when the mind and its objects are devoid of intrinsic nature and cannot be moved or shifted, this is called *dhyāna*.
When the mind ceases, all fetters are extinguished; this is called liberation.
Samādhi is the absence of sinking and agitation. Samāpatti is right wisdom.
Regarding supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): they are associated with unconfused right concentration and possess unhindered supernormal wisdom through their own correspondence.
In contrast, the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are contrary to this; one clearly knows and sees all aspects of the continuity of birth and the bonds within the three realms.
The characteristic of causing the continuum of the boundless mind to manifest arises because of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
The characteristic of opening the gates of the various sense bases arises because of the latent dispositions, which open the gates for taking birth within the three realms and six destinies.
The characteristic of being solid and difficult to cure is due to the persistence of deep ignorance (*avidyā*).

Regarding the characteristics of attainment and non-attainment in relation to the state of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), this clarifies the characteristics of attainment and non-attainment among the ten types.

"Only by means of the Noble Path are the characteristics [of these afflictions] uprooted" clarifies that the aforementioned latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) cannot be rescued or extracted by anything other than the Noble Path.
The above has clarified that the Bodhisattva at this stage understands the characteristics of the latent proclivities.
Tenth, as for the various characteristics of taking birth according to reception, this refers to them collectively.
Specifically, these are the characteristics of taking birth according to karma; this section contains thirteen types of causal conditions for taking birth according to karma.
To clarify the distinctions among the six realms of existence refers to the distinct characteristics of devas, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings.
To clarify the distinctions between the realms with form and the formless refers to the characteristics of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

Regarding the characteristics of the distinction between those with perception and those without perception: "those with perception" refers generally to the desire realm and the form realm; "those without perception" refers collectively to the heavens of the formless realm. Within these, he fully knows and sees all the distinct characteristics of taking birth.
Karma is the field, craving is the moisture, and it is covered by ignorance; consciousness is the seed, which arises simultaneously with name-and-form, such that they are entirely inseparable.

Thus, being deluded regarding the realm of the one mind, one gives rise to bodies in future existences; these continue to serve as causes for one another without interruption. Although there is truly no inherent nature, one falsely creates manifold births—know all this thus.

Regarding the continuity of existence characterized by delusion, craving, and seeking: it is due to being deluded regarding the wisdom of one's own mind as being without intrinsic nature and without arising, that one constantly harbors seeking for both good and evil; by means of this, there is the continuity of birth.

Those who desire to receive and desire to be born always possess desire and reception toward all name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); thus, birth occurs, for craving is the root of birth. When one illuminates that the mind has no substance, then objects have nowhere to arise.

When both mind and objects are entirely absent, the substance of karma perishes. There remains only the wisdom of universal radiance, which is neither darkness nor light; thus, ignorance ceases and the twelvefold chain of false conditions is extinguished. There is only the sovereign, unimpeded wisdom and compassion of the *dharmadhātu*, spontaneously accomplished through conditions. In its nature, there is no subject or object; self and others are of one essence, appearing according to conceptualization to guide those who are deluded.
Thus, one knows these conditions of dependent origination as they truly are.

Seeing that those who have long been attached to pleasure falsely claim to have transcended the three realms—clearly because they harbor aspirations—they falsely claim to have transcended the three realms, even up to the liberation of the Three Vehicles.
However, outside the triple world, they receive a transformation body of coarse dust-like birth and death, which is like a subtle transformation body as minute as a speck of dust.
Within a single speck of dust, the entirety of the ocean of lands and all Buddha-activities are fully encompassed; this is accomplished solely by the wisdom-body of the One Vehicle.
The above constitutes the knowledge of the various characteristics of the arising of sensation.

Eleventh, regarding "furthermore knowing the various characteristics of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the distinction between their active and inactive states," this clarifies that the Bodhisattva at this stage knows the distinction between the active and inactive states of habitual tendencies.

Regarding the characteristics of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that follow the destinies: this clarifies the characteristics of the habitual tendencies that follow one’s rebirth within the six destinies, such as those of devas or humans; it means that, rather than depending on external objects, one acquires [these tendencies] in accordance with the conduct of sentient beings.

Regarding the characteristic of perfuming (*vāsanā*): it is clearly seen that the actions performed by others give rise to defilement according to the specific circumstances; good and evil are to be understood by this same principle.
Regarding the characteristic of the perfuming of afflictions (*kleśa*) according to karma: it refers to arising spontaneously without depending on external objects.
One thoroughly knows all such perfumings (*vāsanā*).

Regarding the characteristics of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral perfuming: although one practices what is wholesome or practices what is unwholesome, that which is neither recorded as wholesome nor recorded as unwholesome is the characteristic of neutral perfuming.
Regarding the characteristic of permeation that follows into subsequent existence: such neutral states likewise become seeds permeated for future births, and all of this is fully known.

Regarding the characteristic of sequential permeation: as there are karmas within the three realms, whichever karmic seed is predominant, permeation occurs sequentially based upon that predominant karma.
Furthermore, just as in the ten abodes, ten practices, ten dedications, and ten stages, because each is characterized by sequential perfuming, one does not sever the afflictions.

That which is called "the far-reaching stage where the characteristic of perfuming is not abandoned" refers precisely to the seventh stage, the Stage of Complete Skillful Means; it is so named because, while dwelling in the seventh Far-Reaching Stage, the eighty-four thousand afflictions all function in concert with that perfuming.
Regarding the characteristics of the perfuming of both the real and the unreal: one thoroughly knows and perceives whether they are real or false.

Regarding the characteristics of the perfuming of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas through seeing, hearing, and associating with them: by associating with those of the two vehicles, one becomes weary of suffering, cultivates emptiness, and abandons the habituation of great compassion.
