Sixth, "Furthermore, knowing the wisdom regarding the eons entered by all Buddhas" consists of seven lines of scripture.
From "One eon enters into incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), and incalculable eons enter into one eon" onwards, it is fully contained within the text of the sūtra itself.

Regarding the dharma of the mutual inclusion of kalpas—whether long or short, many or few—since there is no such thing as objective reality (li) or cognitive consciousness (zhi), the extension or brevity of time is merely according to the faculties of sentient beings; thus, it is the kalpas themselves that are extended or brief.

The Tathāgata, through the skillful means of wisdom, suddenly manifests all karmic realms at once. Within this single, unified wisdom, each individual perceives the duration and differences of their own karmic timing. This is not to refute deluded sentiments or the attachment to fixed durations and the length or shortness of kalpas.

If insentient matter were to conceive of cognition and so forth, there would simultaneously be no characteristics of extension or brevity, nor any limitations of kalpas, years, months, days, or hours.
This concludes the above explanation on knowing how kalpas interpenetrate.

7. Furthermore, regarding "knowing the Tathāgata’s wisdom of all entries," there are six lines and a half of scripture which clarify that the Bodhisattva at this stage knows the Tathāgata’s thirteen kinds of wisdom of entry.

That which is called "entering the wisdom of the path of hair" means entering among sentient beings of indeterminate nature, giving rise to the wisdom of skillful means, and causing them to attain the wisdom of right faith.

That which is called "entering the wisdom of subtle particles" means entering into the paths of minute sentient beings, being born together with them, inducing the arising of wisdom, and causing them to dwell in the roots of goodness of humans, devas, and Buddhas.

Regarding the knowledge of entering the bodies of buddha-lands and attaining perfect enlightenment: it is because one manifests the attainment of buddhahood and entry into parinirvāṇa within the body of a buddha and even inside its pores.

Regarding the wisdom of right awakening that enters into the conduct of sentient beings: it is the awakening of sentient beings through the skillful practice of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Regarding the wisdom of right awakening that enters into the minds of sentient beings: it is because the mind of sentient beings and the mind of the Tathāgata share the same single essence; by means of this, the Tathāgata knows all sentient beings and engages them according to their karma.
"Entering the wisdom that accords with the perfect enlightenment of all places" means that one is born throughout all six realms of existence, awakening according to the faculties [of beings].

"Entering the wisdom that manifests universal conduct" means that regarding the conduct of all sentient beings as well as the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths, one employs the wisdom of acting in common with them (*samānārthatā*).

Regarding those who enter into and manifest the wisdom of counteracting conduct: they manifest as evil Māras to afflict and delude practitioners, or they act upon non-paths; yet there is nothing that does not benefit sentient beings.
For example, by manifesting as King Ajātaśatru committing acts such as killing his father and mother, they cause others to gain faith, whereby their karmic obstacles are eliminated.

Regarding those who enter into and manifest the knowable and unknowable aspects of the conceivable and inconceivable world: they may cause the world to know that this is the inconceivable noble conduct, or they may cause the world to be unable to discern whether these are ordinary beings or noble ones.
The remainder may be understood by analogy, as fully detailed in the sūtra itself.
The above concludes the knowledge of the Tathāgata’s various modes of entry.
From the section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, this passage summarizes how the bodhisattva of this stage is able to enter the vast and immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas.

The sixth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," consists of seven and a half lines of scripture concerning the attainment of ten inconceivable and unspeakable gates of liberation (*vimokṣa*).

Within this passage, four categories are presented: first, the presentation of ten kinds of inconceivable liberations; second, the general presentation of hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* liberations; third, the presentation of the number of samādhis attained; and fourth, the presentation of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). All of these are fully detailed within the text itself.

In the seventh section, forty-five and a half lines of scripture clarify that Bodhisattvas in this stage are able, within a single thought-moment, to receive and comprehend all the Buddha-dharmas of the ten directions; this constitutes the section on illumination.
This section is further divided into eight parts.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "cannot uphold," there are eight and a half lines of scripture which clarify that the Bodhisattvas of this stage are capable of upholding the great Dharma-illumination and the great Dharma-radiance of all Buddhas, whereas other vehicles and Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage are not capable of upholding them; this part also includes the analogy of the Sāgara Dragon’s rainfall.

The second section, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "named the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud," comprises approximately six and a half lines of scripture. This passage clarifies the analogy of the great ocean being able to receive the rain poured down by the great dragon kings, and further illustrates the portion concerning how a Bodhisattva at this stage is capable of receiving all the illuminations of the Dharma and can expound them all simultaneously within a single thought-moment.

Regarding the two sūtra passages concerning the three existences (*tribhava*): in the first, Vimukticandra asks how many portions of the Tathāgata’s illumination of the Dharma (*dharmāvabhāsa*) a Bodhisattva in this stage can receive and uphold in a single thought-moment.

In the second, from the words "Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said, 'O Son of the Buddha'" onwards—comprising approximately one and a half lines of sūtra—it clarifies the extent of what is received by a Bodhisattva in this stage, describing it through the division of the immeasurability of all dharmas by means of calculation.

5. "O Son of the Buddha, it is as if in each of the ten directions there were ten unspeakable [worlds]," from here down to "even analogies cannot reach it," consists of eleven and a half lines of scripture. This is the first analogy, the section on the vastness and incomparability of the light of the Tathāgata’s Dharma that is encompassed by Bodhisattvas in this stage. It illustrates how much more vast and numerous those dharmas are.

6. From "As at the place of one Buddha" down to "is named the Dharma-Cloud Stage," there are approximately four lines of scripture that clarify how the rain of all Buddha-dharmas received by the Bodhisattva at this stage exceeds the previous metaphors.

7. From "The Bodhisattva of this stage" down to "named the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma," there are seven lines of scripture that clarify the aspect of the benefit brought about by the vast compassion and power of the vows of the bodhisattva at this stage.

8. From "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva" down to "is called the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud," there are four and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva of this ground is able to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven palace to take birth in the worlds of the ten directions, exceeding the previous dust-mote analogy by a factor of two.

Regarding the phrase "Great Dharma Illumination" (*mahā-dharmāloka*) mentioned in this first section: it refers to the supramundane dharmas of the worlds of the ten directions, for there is nothing that is not comprehensively known and comprehensively understood.

Regarding "Great Dharma Radiance" (*mahā-dharma-avabhāsa*): it clarifies that one is able to illuminate all sentient beings and their karmas throughout the ten directions with the sun of wisdom; thus, all sentient beings—whether good or evil—are always as if before one's eyes, such that there is nothing that is not seen.
The "great rain of Dharma" means that it clearly shows the ability to rain down the Dharma equally upon the faculties of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions at one and the same time.
All such vast Buddha-activities of this kind can be stabilized and received by the Bodhisattva in this stage, like the analogy of the great ocean rained upon by the Dragon King Sāgara.
Sāgara is so named because he rains upon the great ocean and is thus called "the one who can rain upon the great ocean"; the rain from this dragon can only be received by the ocean.
Likewise, the Dharma rain of the Buddhas of the ten directions can only be received in a single thought-moment by a Bodhisattva of this stage.
The following is fully detailed according to the text itself.

The eighth section consists of thirty-five lines of scripture, which clarify that for a Bodhisattva on this Stage of the Cloud of Dharma, through the power of their mental resolve, the vast and the subtle interpenetrate one another; the one and the many, the large and the small, mutually encompass each other; and their supernormal powers and virtuous functions are sovereign, all being accomplished in accordance with the thoughts of their own minds.
Just as all the spheres of activity and experience of sentient beings are produced by the retributive karma of their own minds,
so too are the retributive fruits of good and evil— whether as humans, devas, hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts— all created in reliance upon the mind alone.

Thus, by the power of the great wisdom of the unconditioned Dharma-body, these Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, according to their mental inclinations, simultaneously exercise sovereign mastery throughout the ten directions; they know and perceive all things, for they take universal radiance-wisdom as their essence.
The essence of wisdom is non-reliant; conforming to its nature, it pervades the entire dharma-realm, equal in measure to empty space, filling the worlds of the ten directions.
Through the great function of non-substantial wisdom that accords with mindfulness, and through the wisdom of non-forgetfulness, all things are accomplished in accordance with mindfulness.

By means of the wisdom that encompasses both the general and the particular, they simultaneously effect the formation and destruction, as well as the similarities and differences, of both the general and the particular; through the sovereign wisdom of the vast and the narrow, the great and the small, their transformations are universally unimpeded.
By means of the wisdom of the same essence as all sentient beings, they are able to transform the realms of all sentient beings entirely into lands of pure buddha-fields.
By means of the wisdom of the non-duality of self and others, one manifests many bodies from a single body and a single body from many bodies.
By means of the wisdom of the Dharmakāya, which is without magnitude and transcends all measure, one can cause a Buddha-field to be extensively contained within a single pore.
By means of wisdom that is equal to space—boundless and without direction—one manifests birth in a single thought-moment, filling the ten directions without coming or going.
By means of the wisdom of an echo, one is able to respond like an echo, manifesting forms according to the needs of sentient beings.
Possessing fully perfected merit and wisdom, they constantly dwell in sublime buddha-fields and always reside together with all sentient beings.
Were it not for the power of the sages' empowerment, sentient beings would not perceive such powers of knowledge and spiritual transformations of the bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
Although it is said that the nature [of wisdom] is like empty space, empty space is vast and without function.
Likewise, the wisdom of the ten stages fills empty space; this wisdom has no intrinsic nature and no creator, being in every respect identical to empty space.
Nevertheless, the power of recollection pervades the entirety of space; through a succession of fruits, it manifests transformations endlessly.

It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*): although its nature is devoid of subject or object and free from deliberate action, it assumes the same color as the objects of the mental states of all sentient beings.
The remainder is fully contained within the text itself.

The ninth section consists of eighteen and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies the portion in which, when this great assembly hears of the supernatural powers of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages and conceives doubts, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha enters the Samādhi of Essential Nature (*dharmatā-samādhi*) and manifests the supernatural powers of a Bodhisattva to eliminate the doubts of the assembly.
In this section, there are approximately ten matters: first, the great assembly harbors doubts; second, Vimukticandra makes a formal request;

third, Vajragarbha enters meditative absorption; fourth, the realm manifested within that concentration; fifth, the entire assembly perceives their own bodies within the body of Vajragarbha; sixth, the appearance of the Bodhi tree as exceptionally sublime and lofty; seventh, beneath the tree, a Buddha sits upon a lion throne named Sarvajñānābhijñārāja; eighth, the great assembly beholds the Buddha; ninth, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha withdraws his supernormal powers; tenth, the great assembly again perceives their own bodies, each in their original place, having attained what they had never experienced before.
As for the samādhi of the essential nature of all buddha-lands, it is precisely the dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya) of unconditioned activity.
As for the bodhi tree, it is established by virtue of being obtained as a karmic reward through the practice of the dharma-nature body.

The Buddha beneath the tree named Sarvajñābhijñārāja (King of All-Knowledge and Supernatural Powers) is the great wisdom of non-action within the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena); he is called "King" because of his sovereign mastery.
These three dharmas are eternally thus in the essence of all sentient beings; it is only because they do not exert their own application (*prayoga*) to manifest them.
The remainder is fully contained within the text itself.

The tenth section consists of twenty-seven lines of scripture, which clarify that the wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the bodhisattva in this stage surpass those of the lower stages; yet they cannot be compared to even a fraction of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power and wisdom.
In this section, there are approximately ten points:
first, Vimukticandra’s inquiry regarding the name of the samādhi;
second, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva’s formal response concerning the designation of the samādhi.
Third, the question regarding the realm of samādhi;
fourth, Vajragarbha’s formal response;
fifth, the formal explanation of the general characteristics of the samādhis attained on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).
Sixth, it clarifies that the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the three karmas of a Bodhisattva on the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*) surpass those of the lower grounds;
seventh, it briefly explains the sphere of the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, noting that a detailed exposition would take immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas and be difficult to fathom;
eighth, it describes how Vimukticandra asks about the Buddha’s supernatural power.

Vajragarbha raised a single clod of earth as an illustration: the quantity of soil in the four continents is difficult to compare [to the vastness of space]; yet Vajragarbha himself finds it difficult to fully proclaim the power of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), so how much more so can the spiritual power of the Tathāgata be described? These ten metaphors are employed to clarify the underlying intent within this matter.
The details are fully contained within the text itself.

The tenth section consists of thirty-five and a half lines of scripture, which elucidates the portion concerning how the Bodhisattvas of this stage are not distinct from the body, speech, and mind activities of the Tathāgatas; they do not relinquish the power of the various Bodhisattva samādhis, and for incalculable eons, they serve and make offerings to all Buddhas.
In this middle section, there are approximately twenty dharma-gates:
first, being non-different from the bodily, vocal, and mental activities of the Tathāgata;
second, not relinquishing the powers of the various samādhis of a bodhisattva.
Third, serving and making offerings to all Buddhas throughout incalculable eons;
fourth, having wisdom that is exceptionally superior through being empowered by the spiritual power of all Buddhas;
fifth, being well able to explain and resolve all questions and difficulties regarding the dharma-realm.
Sixth, it is likened to genuine gold inlaid with mani-jewels to form a celestial jewel crown;
seventh, it is worn by the Sovereign King of Gods, whom no other gods can equal;
eighth, it is correctly taught that the Bodhisattvas of this stage surpass those of the lower stages.

Ninth, it is like the deity Maheśvara, who can cause the minds of sentient beings to attain coolness; this illustrates that the Bodhisattva of this stage can cause all sentient beings to attain the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), which neither the twelve vehicles nor the Bodhisattvas of the nine stages can equal.
Eleventh, for the Bodhisattvas of this stage, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, further expound ten gates of wisdom.
Twelfth, it clarifies that on this stage, the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*) practiced by the bodhisattva is primary, while the other nine are its companions;
thirteenth, it briefly explains the general outline of this stage, noting that a detailed exposition would be difficult to exhaust;
fourteenth, it describes how the bodhisattva of this stage receives office and becomes the celestial king Maheśvara.
Fifteenth, it clarifies that the bodhisattva in this stage is well able to extensively practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);
sixteenth, they do not depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākāra-sarvajñajñāna*);
seventeenth, they reflect upon themselves as being capable of serving as a refuge for all sentient beings.
Eighteenth, he personally and diligently cultivates them;
nineteenth, in a single thought-moment, he attains ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of samādhis;
twentieth, if augmented by the power of his supreme vows, they exceed the aforementioned numbers manifold times.
The meaning of the text is fully contained within the sūtra itself.

As for Maheśvara, this is translated as "Great Sovereign" (Mahādeva); he is the ultimate pinnacle of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), who has attained great sovereignty over the trichiliocosm, and whose supernatural powers, spiritual penetrations, and wisdom are unsurpassed.

The twelfth section contains forty-two and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the ten stages of wisdom and skillful means by citing the analogy of the ten great mountain kings surrounding Lake Anavatapta.
This section consists of twelve sub-sections of scripture, as delineated by the text itself, so there is no need for further structural analysis.

At the beginning of the passage, the Anavatapta Lake is cited as a metaphor: it illustrates how the Bodhisattva, from the first thought of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and from the *bodhicitta*, flows forth the waters of roots of goodness and great vows; through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), these waters fill sentient beings without end, continuing to increase until they enter the ocean of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

It clarifies that from the initial stage of generating the mind of enlightenment, one is born within the water of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and great vows; through the practice of the four means of integration, one brings sentient beings to maturity and fulfills the ocean of all-knowledge, never departing from the essence of the water of wisdom and great vows at the first moment, yet gradually expanding and increasing in breadth.

Furthermore, the metaphor of ten mountain kings throughout the great earth is cited to clarify that ten kinds of progressive cultivation arise from the ground of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; because they do not depart from the essence of the ground of wisdom, they become increasingly lofty and superior.

Just as the ten dharmas of the five stages and five levels do not depart from the Tathāgata’s ground of universal radiance and omniscience, one initiates the fivefold, tenfold progressive cultivation.

These fivefold, five-stage, tenfold progressive cultivations are, in their entirety, a single time, a single limit, and a single thought-moment; they possess no superior advancement across the three periods of past, present, and future, because they take the wisdom of the Tathāgata as their essence.
It is just as the waters flowing from Lake Anavatapta form the great ocean;
or as the ten great mountain kings emerge from the land of Jambudvīpa, yet do not depart from the substance of the earth itself.
This can be seen by illuminating it with meditative concentration and wisdom.
That one attains Buddhahood immediately upon first generating the mind of enlightenment is intended as a symbolic representation; understand it by following this principle.

It is for this reason that the ten levels of faith are taught within the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsā*). This hall is established in accordance with the retributive birth of universal radiance-wisdom; thus, the cause is explained within the context of the fruit, because when cultivation is perfected, one does not depart from this wisdom.
Regarding the ten mountain kings: the king of snowy mountains (Himavat) is a metaphor for the first stage (*bhūmi*), as the meaning is self-evident from the scriptural text.
The subsequent ones are to be understood by analogy in order.
Next is the king of fragrant mountains (Gandhamādana).

Regarding "next, King Vaidūrya-parvata": *Vai* means "various" in this language, and *dūrya* means "to hold"; because this mountain can support various kinds of precious flowers and fruits, it serves as a metaphor for the third stage (*bhūmi*).
The meaning of the scriptural passage is self-evident.
Regarding the phrase "as in dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti," how is it that, while referring to dhyāna, it speaks only of "samādhi that accords with the essence"?

Because the characteristics of consciousness do not function, it is called "darkness" (*mai*) as if the sun has not yet risen; because the perceptions of consciousness are obscure, right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) only then manifests.
Thirdly, it is called "correct" (*zheng*): because from the eleventh month to the first month, the three yang lines arise, the number three is taken as correct.
When the three yang lines arise, wisdom is clearly manifest, for it takes wisdom as its standard.
When the five aggregates do not arise and worldly sentiments suddenly cease, this is termed "obscurity."
From this, one is able to manifest right knowledge; thus it is called samādhi.
Furthermore, "one-pointedness" (ekāgratā) constitutes the syllable *sam*.
As for *samāpatti*, because it clarifies that the obscurations of the five aggregates can be manifested as right wisdom, it is termed *samāpatti*; it is, therefore, right wisdom.

When the obscurations of the five aggregates are dispelled and right wisdom manifests, it is called the meditative concentration of liberation; this is collectively termed the Great Essential Samādhi.
To specifically illustrate its practice: the "Mountain King of Divine Transcendents" represents the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), with the textual meaning as explained in the sūtra.
Regarding Mount Gandhamādana: "Ganda" is translated here as "pair," and "mādana" is translated as "to hold"; this clarifies that the yakṣas and great deities of this mountain hold it together.

This mountain illustrates that on the fifth bhūmi, one attains the two types of wisdom—supramundane and mundane—as well as the supernormal powers and various clarities (*vidyā*), for it signifies the capacity to master and maintain them all with broad proficiency.
The Horse-Ear Mountain King represents the sixth bhūmi, as detailed in the sūtra itself.

The king of mountains, Nimiṃdhara, is named Dharanimandala; it represents the Stage of Far-reaching Practice (*dūramgamā bhūmi*), for it is able to sustain all the various practices of biased views among sentient beings, and even sustains all those within the three realms and six destinies.
Cakravāḍa Mountain—here translated as "Wheel-Encircling"—encircles the great trichiliocosm, signifying that on the eighth stage, practice becomes effortless and spontaneously perfected.
Ketumatī Mountain—"Ketū" means "banner" and "matī" means "wisdom"—signifies the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (Sādhumatī).

Mount Sumeru stands within the four continents of Jambudvīpa and is situated in the midst of the great ocean; this illustrates that the wisdom of the Middle Way within the Dharma-Cloud stage of the ten bhūmis is full, because it universally encompasses all samādhis.

The passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" and extending for one and a half lines of scripture summarizes the distinctions among the ten stages (*bhūmi*). These stages receive their names based on the distinctions within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

This clarifies that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is non-dual from the initial stage of resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*) through the ten stages up to the stage of Buddhahood; it is only by virtue of the distinctions in its manifestations that these names are assigned.
The twelve preceding sections correspond exactly to the wording of the sutra.
The sequence of the stages (*bhūmi*) they represent is clearly explained by the sutra itself.
Within the thirteenth section, there are fourteen lines of scripture that clarify ten qualities of the great ocean, using them as metaphors for the sequential progression through the ten stages.
The meaning within this is divided into two sections:
first, enumerating the ten virtues of the ocean; second, using the ten virtues of the ocean as a metaphor to represent the Dharma.
Regarding the progressive cultivation of the distinctions of wisdom across the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the textual meaning therein is complete as presented in the full text.
Each of these possesses ten dharmas in their entirety; there is no need for further sub-sectioning.

The fourteenth section contains twenty and a half lines of scripture, which cites the tenfold nature of the *maṇi* jewel as surpassing all other gems, serving as a metaphor for how the ten stages (*bhūmi*) surpass the various ranks of the sages. This section is divided, for the sake of analysis, into six subsections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "filling their vows according to the minds of sentient beings," there are six lines of scripture that clarify the presentation of the tenfold nature and divisions of the *maṇi* jewel.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "able to extensively perform the Buddha-work for sentient beings," there are seven and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on the sequential stages of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Just as in the sixth stage one thoroughly understands the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, and thoroughly understands that the root and branches, the essence and characteristics, of birth, old age, sickness, and death are all of one suchness.
What is taught in the sixth stage is that through skillful contemplation of birth and death, one reaches the bottom of dependent origination, like drilling [to find fire].
The seventh stage, by taking the wisdom of various skillful means as its thread, is able to follow the cycle of birth and death without receiving any defilements.
In the eighth stage, the myriad practices are employed throughout the realms of all sentient beings; this wisdom is eternally without substance and immovable like a banner.
The remainder is fully contained within the text itself.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "cannot be heard," there are two lines of scripture praising the difficulty of hearing this stage.
4. From "Vimukticandra" onwards, there may be one line of sūtra, in which Vimukticandra asks how much merit is obtained by hearing this Dharma.

5. Following that, there may be one and a half lines of sūtra, in which Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replies that it is like the merit accumulated by all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), clarifying that the merit of one who hears the Dharma is equal to the merit of a Buddha.
Sixth: From "For what reason" onwards, there are three and a half lines of scripture explaining the section on generating doubt regarding the vast merit obtained from hearing this Dharma.
For example, if omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the fundamental wisdom attained by the Buddha, and if one who hears the Dharma possesses merit equal to that of the Buddha, then what is the point?

This is because it clarifies that it is only through hearing this Dharma that faith and understanding arise; because it serves as the primary condition for first hearing of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); because it demonstrates that the merit of the initial cause of faith is of the same essence as the fruit, showing that there can be no fruit without a cause—just as there can be no grain without a sprout, and no fruit without a sprout; and because it clarifies that the cause is established by means of faith in the fruit.

This is as explained regarding the stage of the Ten Faiths: within the Great Wisdom Palace of the Tathāgata’s Universal Radiance Dharma-realm, ten Wisdom Buddhas are taught, with Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*Acalamati-buddha*) at their head to constitute the faith-mind. Because Immovable Wisdom Buddha and the ten Wisdom Buddhas are the fruits of wisdom of one's own mind, they are ultimately perfected and fulfilled without ever departing from this very wisdom.
The remaining meanings are fully contained within the text itself.

The intended meaning is as follows: just as a seed plants a fruit to constitute its cause for growth, fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) is likened to the seed, while discriminative wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna)—which is the preparatory application—is likened to the fruit upon the sprout; these two wisdoms each possess boundless merits.

The fifteenth section consists of twenty-two and a half lines of scripture, which clearly explains how this Dharma-gate of the ten stages causes the great earth to shake in six ways and eighteen modes.
This section is further divided into three parts.

First, from "At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power" down to "all worlds were likewise," there are eight lines of scripture explaining the section on the Dharma-majesty shaking the earth and the heavens raining down offerings.

2. From "At that time, again by the Buddha’s spiritual power" down to "all likewise come to bear witness," there are nine lines of scripture clarifying the section on how the Bodhisattvas named Vajragarbha from the ten directions all come to bear witness.

3. From "At that time, Vajragarbha" onwards, there may be six lines of scripture clarifying the section on observing sentient beings and the dharmas that serve as objects of focus, intended for the exposition of verses.

Regarding the statement that from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there come to this assembly bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields: this clarifies that the dharmas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the fundamental essence are vast and exceedingly many. It uses the atoms of ten billion fields as a measure for distance, proximity, and numerical magnitude. This is because it brings together all those bodhisattvas who have newly entered the first stage; their wisdom regarding the causal and resultant dharmas—from beginning to end—is free from doubt. It clarifies that the resultant dharmas of the original ten stages are identical to the wisdom of the bodhisattvas who have newly entered these ten stages, such that they are non-dual. Furthermore, it is because they have integrated the inferiority of the preceding nine stages into the vast wisdom of the tenth stage, and because it sets forth the distance, proximity, and the quantity of the dharmas.
This also clarifies that the Dharma taught by Vajragarbha is non-dual with the assemblies of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
"Outside the world" refers to the stages below [the eighth bhūmi].
Those who come to this assembly immediately ascend and enter this wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The exclamation "Excellent! clarifies that the Dharma being taught accords with reality and is not otherwise.
"Having the same name" clarifies that their wisdom regarding the Dharma-treasury is identical.
"The worlds are each distinct" clarifies that their wisdom of differentiation gives rise to differentiated practices.
"All are named Vajra-virtue" clarifies that their wisdom of differentiation and their practices are not separate from vajra-virtue.

The name of the Buddha is Vajradhvaja (Golden Vajra Banner), which clarifies that the wisdom of the vajra can shatter all deluded karma because it is itself devoid of a substantial essence that could be moved.
Other meanings are fully contained within the text itself.

Just as the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is the basis for all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajña-jñāna*), so too this wisdom is the wisdom of differentiation (*viśeṣa-jñāna*), which functions from within all-encompassing wisdom;

therefore, it is expressed with reduplication. The sixteenth section consists of eighty-three verses, clarifying that the entire eulogy—from the initial resolve of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) onward—pervades these ten stages. Both the sequential and simultaneous aspects of the ten stages are fully restated in verse, with the textual meaning as complete as in the sūtra itself.

The "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers," the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences," the "Chapter on the Incalculable," the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata," and the "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas."

Chapter 27: The Ten Samādhis. In this chapter, the Buddha himself speaks of the names of the ten samādhis, while Samantabhadra explains their functions. This is to clarify that the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Buddha is the essence (*tattva*), whereas the differentiated wisdom (*prabheda-jñāna*) of Samantabhadra is its function (*vṛtti*). Thus, it is shown that all activities do not depart from the great samādhi-essence of fundamental wisdom.
For this reason, he returns to the Hall of Universal Radiance within the Fundamental Wisdom to expound the gate of quiescent function.
Now, in order to explain this "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," it shall be analyzed by way of five sections.

First, explaining the purpose for which this assembly has come; second, explaining why it is necessary to restate the origins of his initial attainment of Buddhahood in the kingdom of Magadha within this assembly; third, clarifying by what causes and conditions this eleven-chapter sutra is being taught here in the Universal Radiance Hall; fourth, clarifying the sequential explanation of the general meaning of the eleven chapters; and fifth, clarifying the word-by-word commentary based on each chapter.

First, regarding the explanation of the purpose for coming to this assembly: it is because from within this Great Wisdom Palace of Universal Radiance, one gives rise to faith; by taking Immovable Wisdom as the basis for ascending practice, one proceeds through the ten stages and the path of the eleventh stage until the course of practice is perfected and the fruit of Buddhahood is attained, all the while never departing from original wisdom.

Therefore, one must come to this assembly; this clarifies that causes do not shift. This is because time does not shift, wisdom does not shift, and practice does not shift, for cause and effect are of one essence.
This is like Sudhana seeing Maitreya, and Maitreya in turn causing him to see Mañjuśrī again, as well as entering the body of Samantabhadra.

Second, regarding the second explanation which seeks to recount the origins of where the Buddha first attained enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha prior to this assembly: the Sūtra states, "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Aranya-dharma Bodhimanda in the kingdom of Magadha, having just attained perfect enlightenment; he entered the Samādhi of the Limit of Kṣaṇas in the Hall of Universal Radiance. This clarifies that from his initial attainment of Buddhahood through the turning of the Wheel of Dharma over forty years, as well as his descent from the Great [Heaven], all occurred without departing from a single kṣaṇa, for time neither shifts nor migrates.

Fearing that future sentient beings might lose their fundamental intent and give rise to false notions of transition, it is necessary to restate and clarify that from beginning to end there is never a time when [the essence] can shift.

This clarifies that the Buddhas of the three periods and all sentient beings share one and the same non-transmigrating substance; from the initial stage of faith through the progression of practice across the five positions, they never depart from the original months, years, days, and hours, nor from the Buddha’s fundamental wisdom-dharma.
Third, regarding the explanation of the causes and conditions for preaching these eleven chapters within this Hall of Universal Radiance, the commentary states:

This is to clarify that at the first assembly in the Bodhimanda, the Buddha had just attained perfect enlightenment; thus, he cites his own initial attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood to exhort others to practice.

The second assembly was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala*), which clarifies that this is the retributive dwelling where the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata naturally resides as its fruit.

Ten Wisdom Buddhas were taught, with Akṣayamati Buddha (the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom) at their head, serving as the gateway for faith, diligence, and practice. This enables those who have first resolved to attain Bodhicitta to give rise to faith, diligence, and practice from within this Great Wisdom Dwelling of Universal Radiance, so that they ultimately do not depart from the Tathāgata’s original wisdom, original conduct, and original time, thereby returning to the state of an Original Buddha; thus, all matters remain as they were.

Following these ten stages, within the locus of the original faith-mind, these eleven chapters of the sutra are taught to clarify cause and effect based on the original time, days, months, and years; because they all rely upon the original, it is here that the eleven chapters are expounded.

These eleven chapters of the sutra collectively clarify the realms of experience at the moment of attaining Buddhahood; that is to say, they clarify that one who is able to give rise to the bodhicitta naturally becomes a Buddha, and is no different from Vairocana Buddha in the first assembly.
Cultivating in accordance with this model is exactly as it was originally,

because from the standpoint of wisdom being timeless, all Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the past and present have all attained Buddhahood simultaneously with those who have first resolved to attain enlightenment in the present moment.
When illuminated by wisdom, it can be seen; yet when heard through the consciousness of emotional afflictions, one immediately becomes deluded.
Therefore, because the manifestation depends upon the fundamental reality as it is, I shall here, at this very locus, explain the gateway to the beginning and end of the Buddha-fruit.
Therefore, this is explained by means of the Dharma-realm essence, wherein the beginning and the end share the same limit.
This is a discourse based on ultimate reality; it is not a teaching that accords with the common sentiments of ordinary people which speaks of many kalpas.

Fourth, to clarify the general meaning of the eleven chapters in their sequential order: first, it is explained that the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" (*Daśadharmasamādhiparivarta*) is the great essence of all Buddhas of the past and present, in which quiescence and activity are universally pervasive and timeless.

Second, the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers" elucidates how the supernatural powers of the universal radiance wisdom of all Buddhas of the past and present—consisting of mastery over the maturation of karma and the benefit of sentient beings—are omnipresent.

Third, the "Chapter on the Ten Endurances" elucidates the gate of endurance that accords with the non-arising of all phenomena, which is the unconditioned Dharma-body of the intrinsic nature of all Buddhas of the past and present throughout the ten directions.

The fourth, the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (Asaṃkhyeya), and the fifth, the "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks," clarify the two types of delusion regarding the fruit of Buddhahood; these two chapters of the sūtra were spoken by the Tathāgata himself.

Chapter Six, "The Lifespan of the Tathāgata," concerns the various lifespans manifested by all Buddhas according to the varying capacities and natures of sentient beings; yet their own karmic reward-life is coextensive with the duration of empty space.

Seventh, the "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas" concerns the sphere of gathering sentient beings within the fruit of Buddhahood, clarifying that the gates of bodhisattva practice are never interrupted.

Eighth, the "Chapter on the Inconceivable Buddha" clarifies that the wisdom and virtue of all Buddhas of the past and present are difficult to conceive and cannot be measured by ordinary consciousness.
Chapter Nine, "The Ocean of the Ten Marks of the Tathāgata’s Body," clarifies that the two fruits of the Buddha’s recompense body—the primary and the secondary—are immeasurable.

Chapter Ten, "The Practices of Samantabhadra," clarifies that the practices for self-benefit and benefiting others, which all Buddhas of the ten directions throughout past and present have collectively performed, are universal.

Chapter Eleven, "The Appearance of the Tathāgata," clarifies that when the practitioner of the five stages has perfected their ascent through the stages and the Buddha has appeared, the two modes of practice—transcending the world and entering the entanglements—are both fulfilled.

Mañjuśrī is the master of wisdom that emerges from the entanglements, while Samantabhadra is the master of conduct that enters into the mundane world; because these two practices are perfected within this chapter, these two figures engage in mutual dialogue to explain this gateway of manifestation.
The general purport of the eleven chapters above is as follows.
While each passage will be explained individually, the main outline shall be further clarified here.

This collectively elucidates the dharmic principles practiced within the stage of Buddhahood following the eleven stages (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, it demonstrates that for all Bodhisattvas and all sentient beings, there is no departure from this very essence, and because there is no shifting or change at this time, it clarifies that time does not transmigrate.
Fifth, regarding the explanation of the text according to the "Chapter on Relying" (*yi-pin*): in order to explain this chapter, "The Ten Samādhis," it is analyzed through five sections:

first, explaining the purpose for the chapter’s appearance; second, explaining the title of the chapter; third, why there are three successive assemblies at this location; fourth, explaining why the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha is recounted three times in this single location; and fifth, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.

First, regarding the purpose of this chapter: it clarifies that these eleven stages have already explained the distinctions in the progressive practice of cultivation and the functions of wisdom; it clarifies that the stage of the Buddha-fruit’s Universal Radiance Wisdom is now fulfilled; it clarifies that the essence of the Dharma-realm consists of the mutual interpenetration and non-obstruction of quiescence and function; furthermore, it clarifies the beginning and end of the causal and resultant progression of cultivation; and because time and phenomena do not undergo transmigration, this chapter must follow.
Furthermore, this chapter must appear because it clarifies the sovereign mastery over the one and the many, the pure and the mixed, and the identical and the distinct.

Moreover, this chapter must appear because it clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages know for themselves that they have not yet perfected the practices of Samantabhadra and thus do not see the body of Samantabhadra.
This is clearly elucidated within this chapter itself.

Second, regarding the explanation of the chapter title: it is because the Tathāgata himself proclaimed ten kinds of samādhi names in this chapter that the title was established based on the teaching of the Dharma.

This samādhi is the eternal dharma of all Buddhas of the past and present, which causes the bodhisattvas of the five stages to all equally attain it, and all sentient beings likewise share this same essence.
Samantabhadra explains the function (yòng) while clarifying that the Buddha is the essence (tǐ), and Samantabhadra is the function. Why are there these successive triple assemblies in this section?

It clarifies that faith, the essence of meditative concentration, and the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Líshìjiān Pǐn*)—these three matters are constantly practiced by Samantabhadra. Altogether, they constitute the single essence of cause and effect within the Tathāgata’s Universal Radiance Wisdom (*Puguāng Zhì*). Furthermore, they represent the constant practice of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva after attaining Buddhahood; all are the singular functional manifestation of Universal Radiance Wisdom. From beginning to end, throughout the sequence of cause and effect, time, days, months, and years, there is ultimately no temporal substance.
These three assemblies are layered and simultaneous; they exist as a single moment, rather than as something that departs and returns again as perceived by worldly sentiments.

Because these three types of phenomena exist within each of these layered, simultaneous assemblies, or because the distant and near kalpas of the three periods of time are made to interpenetrate as nine periods of time, they are layered and mutually inclusive without obstruction.

This is because one does not depart from the wisdom of universal radiance; for there is nothing that is not sealed by it, being without beginning or end, and nothing that is not ultimately penetrated, as the ocean of kalpas across the three periods of time is, in its entirety, a single moment. Thus, even the causes and effects of the five stages do not transcend this essential nature of meditative concentration.

Regarding the fourfold explanation of why this single location—the first attainment of perfect enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha—is recounted three times, it clarifies that this section of the sutra contains five layers of cause and effect.
What are these five?

First, it is like when the Buddha, having first attained the Way beneath the Bodhi tree, manifested his perfect enlightenment and gathered the assembly of devas and spirits; this is the first layer of the Buddha’s cause and effect.

Second, within the Hall of Universal Radiance, he expounded upon the causes and effects of the Buddha’s own self-attainment, so as to inspire faith, diligence, and practice in all future learners; this refers precisely to the emission of light from between his brows and the assembly of beings.

By reciting these eleven chapters of the sutra, beginning with this "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," it clarifies how all bodhisattvas practice through faith and diligence, traversing the six stages of faith, abiding, practice, dedication, the ten grounds, and the eleventh ground; these eleven chapters constitute the Buddha-fruit accomplished when one's own cultivation reaches full completion.

Chapter Four, "Transcending the World" (*Lokātīta-parivarta*): This is the stage where all Buddhas have attained the fruit of Buddhahood; they constantly engage in their own enlightened activities to perpetually benefit sentient beings, and it is also called the "Chapter on Benefiting the World."
One must not conceive of detachment as a separation; otherwise, the title of this chapter would likely be erroneous.
Perhaps the translators of the scriptures may have erroneously elaborated upon the Buddha’s intent, yet within it, there is also a sense in which the meaning remains coherent.

Regarding these four sections of the sutra, the fact that each chapter begins with the words, "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment in the forest of Aranya-dharma, having just attained perfect awakening," clarifies that this single sutra is taught through the wisdom of bodhi as being without prior or posterior limits, all at once; it is not as the limited perceptions of ordinary beings see it, with a sequence of before and after.
When the ancients spoke of the "three assemblies" at the Hall of Universal Radiance, their intention was not as it might seem.
Not only did they preach this entire sutra without shifting even for a single kṣaṇa, but their descent from Tuṣita Heaven and their entry into nirvāṇa were likewise of the same nature.
Even throughout the inexhaustible kalpas of the three periods of time, the Buddhas likewise act simultaneously, for they all achieve Buddhahood within this single limit of a kṣaṇa.

This is because all sentient beings, within the time that is fundamentally non-existent, delusively give rise to the appearances of many kalpas—whether extended or abbreviated—and upon awakening, find these were originally non-existent.

The meaning of this section of the sutra is to clarify that within the wisdom of Bodhi, there are no characteristics of extension or contraction, nor of coming and going across time; therefore, it is stated generally that he attained perfect enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha.
When viewed through wisdom, it is clearly visible; yet when contemplated with ordinary sentiments, one immediately becomes deluded.

This is because even in the accounts of ascending to the heavens, it is consistently stated that one does not depart from beneath the Bodhi tree or the Hall of Universal Radiance to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa or Yāma heavens.

This is because the essential nature of the fundamental wisdom of bodhi is inherently all-pervasive, and thus there are no perceptions of interior, exterior, or middle; of long or short, extended or contracted, large or small, coming or going, and so forth.

The fifth, the "Dharmadhātu Chapter," is the common fruit of all Buddhas, shared by both ordinary beings and sages; it is the fruit of the infinite, perfect, and functional virtue of the great wisdom that does not depart from the dharmadhātu.
All Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment through this great wisdom of the Dharma-realm, which is also called the Great Wisdom Hall of Universal Radiance.

These five sections of the sutra collectively clarify the single, true, unobstructed great wisdom—an infinite scripture without beginning or end—whose magnitude equals all realms throughout the ten directions; it can be recited and upheld in its entirety within a single kṣaṇa, and is also called the Sutra of the Universal Eye.

The intent of this explanation is that this entire section of the sutra, as well as the supramundane nirvana, does not transcend the fruit of this single momentary limit of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This "Dharmadhātu Chapter" is the ultimate fruit of the sphere of bodhi-wisdom; it encompasses the entirety of the work.
Regarding the fifth section, the explanation of the meaning according to the text, it is divided into two parts:
first, the general outline of the sūtra’s intent; second, the word-by-word commentary.
As for the first, the general outline of the sūtra’s intent, this chapter is divided into eleven sections.

First, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "that which is called signlessness," there are six lines of scripture that clarify the introductory section for the eleven chapters of the sutra that follow.

The second section, from "together with bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields" down to "practicing together the various roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas," consists of thirty-six and a half lines of scripture, which clearly sets forth the assembly of the bodhisattva multitude.

The third section, from "At that time, Universal Eye" down to "Mastery over Samādhi and Liberation," consists of sixteen and a half lines of scripture. This passage clarifies how the Bodhisattva Universal Eye addressed the Buddha to inquire about the virtues and conduct of Samantabhadra; specifically, how many samādhis, supernatural powers, and transformations do the various bodhisattvas cultivate so that their virtues become sovereign, and it further details the Tathāgata’s instruction to request the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra to expound upon the section on "Mastery over Samādhi."

The fourth section, from "At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas in the gathering" down to "it was through the mastery of supernatural powers that it became so," consists of eight and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the portion concerning how the assembly of bodhisattvas, upon hearing the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, attained inconceivable and immeasurable samādhis.

The fifth section, from "At that time, Universal Eye" down to "therefore you are unable to see him," consists of eleven lines of scripture. It clarifies how the various bodhisattvas, through the power of entering samādhi, sought everywhere to see Samantabhadra but could not find him; it is the portion in which the Tathāgata explains that the resolve and virtue of Samantabhadra are so profoundly deep that you are unable to perceive them.
Why is it that Samantabhadra is not seen?

It is because it is to clarify that for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), supramundane wisdom and compassion have increased; all their samādhis are thus supramundane wisdom and compassion, and for this reason, Samantabhadra is not seen.

This gateway of practice of the eleven stages is ever-present in the world; yet because the supramundane mind has ceased and tranquil function is sovereign, it is not perceived due to its non-correspondence with supramundane samādhi.

Sixth: From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye heard the Tathāgata speak of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra" down to "he earnestly entreated to behold the Great Being Samantabhadra," there are thirty-two lines of scripture which clarify the section wherein the great assembly of bodhisattvas thrice invokes the name of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and earnestly entreats to behold him.

The seventh section, from "At that time" below until "attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," consists of nineteen and a half lines of scripture; this is the manifestation of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s own body for the sake of the assembly.
Why is it that one is able to see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva?
It is because one sees him by maintaining mental recollection; since the essence is turned toward its function, this is the body of Samantabhadra.
Because it is clarified that all mental conceptions are the functioning of the Buddha, seeing all sentient beings universally is likewise the functioning of the Buddha.

The eighth section, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye" down to "praising his inexhaustible merits," consists of nine and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies how the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, by means of ten modes of abiding, praises the ten kinds of vast dharmas upon which the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra abides.

The ninth section, from "At that time, the Tathāgata addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" down to "all of them joyfully desired to hear," consists of forty-five lines of scripture, clarifying the command for Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to expound the ten kinds of samādhi divisions.
The tenth section, from "At that time" onwards, consists of ten passages that correctly explain the functional efficacy of the ten kinds of samādhis.

The eleventh section, beginning with "At that time, Samantacakṣus Bodhisattva addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva," and continuing until the end of the forty-third fascicle, clarifies how Samantacakṣus Bodhisattva questioned Samantabhadra Bodhisattva regarding why such bodhisattvas are not called Buddhas nor called those endowed with the Ten Powers.
The first long section, within the first division, consists of six lines of scripture that clarify the introductory portion (*nidāna*) of these eleven chapters.

From the words "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha"—which here is translated as the "Innocent Kingdom" (*Ahiṃsā*) and is also called "Wise" (*Prajñā*)—the name is derived from the people, as the inhabitants of this country were wise.

Furthermore, it is said that "Mo" means "not," and "Jieti" means "to arrive. Because the generals of this country possess such strategic planning and valor that the enemy from neighboring states cannot approach, the name was established based on the chief general.
Furthermore, it is said that "Maha" means "great" and "Ceti" means "body"; this country is the greatest because it constitutes the great body of the five regions of India.
Since this country is the center of Jambudvīpa, the Tathāgata manifested the attainment of perfect enlightenment there to clarify the meaning of the Middle Way.

Furthermore, this clarifies the meaning of great compassion as being free from harm; it also signifies that great compassion universally benefits all without partiality in its transformation of beings. Both points are as explained in the discourse on the *āraṇya* dharma in the first assembly, which has already been interpreted in the first assembly.

Regarding "initially attaining perfect enlightenment," this clarifies that descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the womb, taking birth, preaching the Dharma, and entering nirvana are all, in total, not separate from the single moment of the samādhi of initially attaining perfect enlightenment.

Throughout all four chapters of this sutra, these words appear consistently, clarifying that the essence of the Great Wisdom of Universal Radiance is timeless, and clarifying that the substance of this palace is the realm of the retribution of wisdom, named after that wisdom.

Because object and wisdom are non-dual, the substance of the palaces they inhabit encompasses many kalpas of the three periods of time; they do not belong to time and are not subject to collection, possessing no substance of past or present, or coming and going.

All phenomena of the three periods of time, which are the direct perceptions resulting from the individual karma of all sentient beings, appear within it; they do not belong to the characteristics of transition or the shifting of time.

Regarding the infinite karmic retributions and mental objects of all sentient beings manifested by the Tathāgata, this Wisdom of Universal Radiance is ever-present before him, such that there is not a single minute matter throughout the worlds of the ten directions that he does not know or see.

Because the great wisdom of universal radiance shares the same single essence with all sentient beings and the infinite realms equal to space, it is able to know all things without exception, for this wisdom is pure and free from obstruction.
Furthermore, regarding the samādhi of all Buddhas at the limit of a single kṣaṇa: it clarifies that the three periods of time—past, present, and future—are identical in a single moment.
A single kṣaṇa is the realization that there is no time of arising or ceasing across the three periods.

At this moment, in order to teach and transform sentient beings, he establishes the Dharma by synthesizing the terminology of the ancient and the modern; for according to the *Jñānasiddhi-śāstra*, such a substantial entity does not exist.
Because there is no such thing as a momentary instant that does not contain all kalpas of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—as they are fundamentally one and the same.
This can be seen by observing through the gateway of the six characteristics (ṣaḷlakṣaṇa).

Regarding the samādhis of all Buddhas: it clarifies that all Tathāgatas have long since extinguished the afflictions of the mind and sensory objects, and thus their wisdom is eternally non-dual with them.

As for the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s body—pure, unimpeded, and without dependence—through the sovereign power of supernatural penetrations (abhijñā) of omniscience: this is because omniscience is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is effortless and spontaneous.

Regarding "sovereign supernormal powers" (*vaśitā-abhijñā*): it clarifies that while fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is eternally devoid of intrinsic nature, it is able to universally manifest bodies in accordance with the faculties [of beings], establishing all dharmas without missing the proper time; this is called the power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-bala*), and is also termed the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s pure body.
This is a general explanation at once, clarifying that from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one gives rise to unimpeded and vast function in accordance with all sentient beings.
"Having no basis" clarifies that fundamental wisdom has no inherent nature or substance.
Because fundamental wisdom is devoid of intrinsic nature, it is able to universally illumine the ten directions and accomplish great powers of function.
"There is no攀緣 (pān-yuán, object-dependent clinging)" clarifies that this is the quiescent function of the realm of wisdom, and not a false, object-dependent clinging.

Regarding "abiding in the most ultimate tranquility of *śamatha*": this clarifies that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) possesses mastery over tranquil function; both object and wisdom are true, and all myriad functions are tranquil. Arising is solely the arising of phenomena, and tranquility is solely the tranquility of phenomena. Since among the myriad dharmas of the ten directions there is not a single thing that is not true, it is called "the most ultimate tranquility."

*Śamatha* means "concentration" (dìng) in this context. It clarifies that this concentration is the tranquil function of the fundamental essence of the Buddhas' non-conceptualizing great body—the fundamental wisdom—and because it is the concentration of the great mastery over the essence and function of the fundamental wisdom of all Buddhas. This clarifies that the entirety of this assembly is the functioning of the fundamental wisdom within the fruition state of all Buddhas.

"One endowed with great majestic power" refers to the Buddha’s mastery over the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*). This is because all who see or hear the Tathāgata remember him with reverence, resolve their minds toward enlightenment, and submit themselves entirely to him.
The remainder is fully contained within the text itself.
"Appearing at will without missing the proper time" means that he appears when it is fit for beings to see and hear him, responding to the occasion without fail.
He dwells eternally in a single mark, which is to say, the markless.
The above six lines of scripture conclude the praise of the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue upon attaining enlightenment.
The following section on the assembly of followers will be further clarified below.
Within the second section, there are thirty-six and a half lines of scripture that clarify the division of the assembly.
Within this section, it is divided into three parts:

first, from "together with bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields" down to "abiding in the bodhisattva’s liberation of non-abiding," there are five lines of scripture that clarify the section praising the aspirations and virtues of the bodhisattvas.
Second, from "Their names were" down to "Bodhisattva Boundless Wisdom," there are nine lines of scripture; there are thirty bodhisattvas who share the same name, Wisdom-Light (Hui-ming).
The wisdom produced within the three gates of liberation through the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the three emptinesses is likewise termed the "wisdom division" (*prajñā-bhāga*).

This concludes the explanation that within the meditative concentrations of the three gates of liberation of the three emptinesses, ten kinds of wisdom arise within each single gate of liberation; thus, there are thirty distinct varieties of wisdom-knowledge within the three emptinesses.
The three emptinesses are the emptiness of signlessness (*animitta*), the emptiness of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and the emptiness of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

These three gates of emptiness spontaneously give rise to these thirty kinds of wisdom; because they manifest inexhaustibility, the thirty bodhisattvas here are all given the same name, "Wisdom" (*prajñā*).

3. From "The Bodhisattva Adorned with Mindfulness" down to "Cultivating the Various Roots of Goodness of the Bodhisattvas," there are twenty-two and a half lines of scripture. There are seventy bodhisattvas, each distinguished by their respective practices and named individually; this constitutes the section on the assembly.

The above seventy bodhisattvas have completed the clarification of the three preceding emptinesses and liberations; by means of the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, they constantly dwell within birth and death, for they are well able to awaken all sentient beings.
This clarifies that the path of the ten stages has reached its conclusion, and the skillful practices for constantly entering birth and death are complete.

Now, because one wishes to accomplish the practice-gate of Samantabhadra, the number of Buddha-lands used as a measure is set at the dust motes of ten; this clarifies that each and every bodhisattva possesses such tenfold universal pervasion. Therefore, among the previously praised virtues, there is none that does not enter the stage of empowerment, which is precisely the stage of the ten bhūmis.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "attaining the Samādhi of Universal Vision of All Bodhisattvas," this clarifies that by means of the eye of wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one universally perceives the differences in the faculties and inclinations of all sentient beings.

Regarding "great compassion bringing peace and security to all sentient beings," this means that because one has fulfilled the path of the ten stages oneself, one does not depart from the skillful means of the three gates of liberation and the seven factors of enlightenment; through these skillful practices as flowers, one guides and receives sentient beings, thereby entering the conduct of Samantabhadra.

In this chapter, the fact that Samantabhadra is not seen despite seeking him through three types of investigation by the power of samādhi clarifies that although this samādhi possesses compassion, it is predominantly a supramundane mind; therefore, it does not perceive the gateway through which Samantabhadra at the stage of the eleventh bhūmi enters into the mundane world to benefit sentient beings.

Regarding the third point, "seeking and searching until finally seeing Samantabhadra": this clarifies that one ascends from the ten stages (*bhūmi*) to enter the rank of the fruit of Samantabhadra’s practice, thereby accomplishing the gate of Samantabhadra’s sovereign mastery over quiescence and function.

Therefore, the subsequent passage uses the analogy of the sovereign wish-fulfilling maṇi-jewel, which can grant whatever is sought and assumes the same color as the object it is placed with without losing its own jewel-nature, to clarify that the Tathāgata always employs his own fruition, the sovereign of all-knowledge, to follow the various skillful means of the bodhisattvas and the diverse inclinations of sentient beings, leading them all accordingly so that they may attain happiness.

Furthermore, although it is clarified that [the practitioner] attains the stages from the eighth stage up to the tenth, eleventh, and the stage of Buddhahood thereafter, they constantly do not abandon the three emptinesses, the seven factors of enlightenment, and various skillful means prior to the seventh stage; therefore, within the listing of the assembly, they are represented by the numerical count of "bodhisattvas" to facilitate easy understanding.
The reason for taking the number of atoms in ten Buddha-fields as the measure is to clarify that each and every bodhisattva universally possesses such practices in their entirety.

Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Though one has attained perfect enlightenment and turns the wheel of Dharma, not abandoning the path of a bodhisattva—this is the practice of a bodhisattva."

Regarding the seating arrangement of the assembly in this "Ten Samādhis" chapter, these are all members of the assembly who have already perfected the supramundane wisdom and compassion of the ten stages; yet, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they do not abandon the various auxiliary paths of practice prior to the seventh stage.

Furthermore, all bodhisattvas, from their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, do not depart from the essence of this samādhi; they practice with faith and diligence until reaching the fulfillment of the fruit, for there is no lapse of time.

The beginning of this chapter describes the intent of the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment; it clarifies that the preaching of these forty chapters of the sutra and the dates of his birth and parinirvāṇa are entirely non-transient, because from beginning to end they are of one and the same limit and because the Dharma-nature is thus. This is not brought about by the supernatural powers of the Tathāgata.
According to the discourse on the reality of the realm of wisdom, the many eons spoken of do not follow deluded sentiments; when illuminated by wisdom, they can be seen as such.

The dharmas and assemblies of the five successive stages listed above are each manifested instantaneously by the Bodhisattvas according to their respective stages, clarifying that the Dharma-realm of clear wisdom has no beginning or end. In total, these ten concentrations constitute the essence.

The first section of this chapter consists of the introductory narrative and the enumeration of the assembly’s praise of virtues; it briefly sets forth the general meaning to harmonize the beginning and the end.

Within this, the names of the bodhisattvas are established according to their conduct and dharmas. Based on these names derived from dharma and conduct, they are as previously briefly enumerated as being equal to the atoms within ten buddha-fields.

To speak in terms of ultimate reality, there is no limit or exhaustion; however, taking fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) alone as the Buddha’s own fruition, all phenomena within the remaining differentiated wisdoms (*prabheda-jñāna*) constitute the practices of a bodhisattva. Therefore, they are quantified by the number of dust motes in ten Buddha-fields.
The third section contains sixteen and a half lines of scripture. Within the portion concerning the Path of Samantabhadra as inquired about by Samantanetra, it is divided into four parts.

First, from "At that time, Samantanetra" down to "I pray you will graciously grant permission," there are three lines of scripture, which clarify the section on Samantanetra Bodhisattva initiating his inquiry regarding the dharma-gate of the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s path and virtue.
2. From "The Buddha said, 'Universal Eye'" down to "'causing your heart to rejoice,'" there is one line of scripture that clarifies the section on the Buddha’s permission for the inquiry.

3. From "'Universal Eye said'" down to "'there is no rest,'" there are four and a half lines of scripture that clarify the section on the actual inquiry regarding the number of samādhi practice gates of Samantabhadra and the great assembly.

4. From the words "The Buddha said, 'Excellent! down to "he explained the liberation of mastery over samādhi," there are approximately eight lines of scripture. These clarify the Tathāgata’s praise of what Puyan asked and his indication of where Samantabhadra resides; they further praise the conduct of Samantabhadra and exhort Puyan to request that Samantabhadra explain the thirteen divisions of samādhi.

The remainder is fully contained within the text itself. The fourth section consists of eight and a half lines of scripture, which clarify that among the immeasurable samādhis obtained by the assembly upon hearing the name of Samantabhadra, there are ten points: first, the great assembly hears the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and immediately attains immeasurable samādhis;

second, having attained these samādhis, the assembly directly beholds countless Buddhas; third, the assembly acquires the ten powers of a Tathāgata and becomes identical to the nature of a Tathāgata; fourth, the assembly obtains merit; fifth, the assembly becomes fully endowed with supernatural powers; sixth, the assembly honors and reveres Samantabhadra, longing to behold him; seventh, the assembly thoroughly observes [all things] everywhere; eighth, the assembly ultimately does not see the body or seat of Samantabhadra; ninth, this is attributed to the majestic power sustained by the Buddha; tenth, this is attributed to the inherent power of Samantabhadra himself.

The general purport clarifies that from after the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) up until before the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), one accomplishes the *dharmakāya* and fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) through the practices of Samantabhadra. Having attained the differentiated wisdom (*viśeṣa-jñāna*) within the supramundane, one accomplishes the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*). Within this state where the *dharmakāya* and fundamental wisdom are purely perfected, there arises the infinite great function of the Samantabhadra-gate amidst the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Because this is equal to the deluded thoughts of all sentient beings, it employs their common mental activity to accord with their liberation. For this reason, the Tathāgata causes one to bring Samantabhadra to mind.
The Sūtra states, "All Bodhisattvas attain the powers of the Tathāgata," which refers to the ten powers (*daśabala*).
"Being of the same nature as the Tathāgata" refers to the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*).
The general meaning clarifies that the progression from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) and the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*) up to the stage of Buddhahood concludes here.

As for the profound reverence and yearning to behold Samantabhadra, this clarifies the advancement in the practices of Samantabhadra; it is because the wisdom of the ten stages is perfected as the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra, reaching its full equality only at the "Emergence" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*), as indicated by the symbolic significance of that very chapter.

This is the manner [of practice]: for example, when Sudhana beheld Maitreya Bodhisattva—who shares the same fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime—he was instead led to see Mañjuśrī; by recollecting Mañjuśrī, he heard the name of Samantabhadra and entered immeasurable samādhis, seeing his own body enter the body of Samantabhadra. Such is the pattern.

Just as the ten levels of faith were explained here in this Hall of Universal Radiance, so too does one reach the fruit of Buddhahood without shifting from the causal stage; furthermore, the fulfillment of the stages of Samantabhadra’s practice subsequent to the fruit of Buddhahood is described in the "Chapter on Leaving the World," which constitutes the practice of Samantabhadra after attaining the fruit of Buddhahood.

Regarding the statement that "one observes everywhere but does not see Samantabhadra or his seat," this clarifies that from the initial stages of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten grounds, one has personally advanced by riding upon the conduct of Samantabhadra. Having extensively sought the supramundane mind of the Tathāgata’s liberation, compassion, and wisdom while concurrently practicing them, one has perfected the effortless path of a Buddha’s mastery; because one has already personally seen [this reality] pervading everywhere.

For example, the conduct of Samantabhadra and all the samādhis following the fruit of Buddhahood on the tenth bhūmi consist purely of skillful engagement with the world, because there is no seeking of a supramundane Buddha-fruit.

Because he was about to concurrently cultivate compassion and wisdom to attain the supramundane fruit of Buddhahood through samādhi, he sought him three times and did not see him; this was because [the Buddha] was purely in a state of great compassion and had no practice for self-benefit, and thus they could not meet.

In the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one practices the conduct of Samantabhadra prior to attaining the fruit of Buddhahood; because there is still a mind seeking both self-benefit and the benefit of others, it is for the sake of seeking supramundane liberation.
In the eleventh stage, one practices the conduct of Samantabhadra without seeking one's own liberation, as it consists purely of conduct for the benefit of sentient beings.
Because that which precedes the tenth stage assists in manifesting the fundamental wisdom, and because one has already fulfilled the path of self-liberation and thus has nothing further to seek;
at the eleventh stage, one acts solely for the benefit of all sentient beings, without accumulating any merit for oneself.

Therefore, because they had sought the conduct of Samantabhadra within the eleventh stage by means of the conduct of Samantabhadra for self-benefit and benefit-of-others prior to the tenth stage, yet had not yet attained the vision of it, the great assembly, despite searching everywhere, was ultimately unable to see the body and seat of Samantabhadra.
