One may see this through careful observation and contemplation with wisdom.
The remainder is fully contained within the text itself.

The fifth section, beginning with "At that time, Universal Eye" and comprising eleven lines of scripture, clarifies the portion concerning the bodhisattvas' desire to see Samantabhadra; this is further divided into four sub-sections.

First, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye" down to "Where is the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra now?"—this remaining line of scripture clarifies the section in which Universal Eye asks about the location of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

2. From "The Buddha said" onwards, up to "originally without movement or shift," there is approximately one and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the Tathāgata’s manifestation of the location of Samantabhadra.

3. From "At that time, Samantacakṣus and the bodhisattvas" down to "their bodies and seats," there are two and a half lines of scripture which clarify that although Samantacakṣus and the other bodhisattvas observed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva once more, they were still unable to see even a portion of him.

4. From "The Buddha said, 'Thus it is, son of good family'" down to "you cannot see it," there are six lines of scripture. These clarify that the Tathāgata, for the sake of Universal Eye and the others, extols the profound resolve and virtue of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, who has entered the Lion’s Rush Samādhi, a portion of which you are unable to perceive.

The Sūtra states, "Entering the Lion’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi," which clarifies that after attaining the fruit of the ten stages, one enters the conduct of Samantabhadra; this is because it is entirely a samādhi of fearless mastery.

"Enlightenment" (*ming*) means that boundless thoughts and perceptions are identical with the conduct of sentient beings; it means that the great function arises from the truth itself and does not depend on thought.
"Lion" (*shizi*) signifies fearless sovereignty.

"Vigorous exertion" (vega) refers to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s constant practice of the Samādhi of Universal Activity throughout the ten directions. Because he universally delivers every single sentient being in the worlds of the ten directions without exception, and because he benefits those whose faculties are capable of being sharpened without missing the opportune moment, it is called the "Samādhi of Vigorous Exertion."
It is like a lion that, in a single moment of its majestic display, causes all the hairs on its body to vibrate simultaneously.

This illustrates how Samantabhadra Bodhisattva constantly dwells in the ocean-like samādhi of great function, employing wisdom universally and simultaneously in all activities. Because he acts in accordance with the conduct of sentient beings without missing the proper time and without waiting for a thought, and because his universal great function benefits sentient beings without rest—since from the beginningless past until now it is a single thought, being devoid of past and present, and because the Dharma functions in this very way.
The mind is luminous in its great functioning yet eternally quiescent; this is the meaning of "exertion" (*visphurana*).

One who has attained supreme sovereign functioning is, within that great functioning, constantly and universally benefiting sentient beings entirely through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), with no separate cessation.
This is because prior to the ten stages, there is the ascent and progress characterized by a mind that transcends the world.

Regarding "entering the realm of pure non-obstruction," this clarifies that the measure of Samantabhadra’s wisdom is equal to space; for there is no root of phenomena he does not fully know, and there is no practice that is not equally beneficial.
Regarding "giving birth to the ten powers of the Tathāgata," this clarifies that the ten powers of the Tathāgata’s wisdom are born from Samantabhadra.
Furthermore, the teaching and transformation of sentient beings so that they attain the ten powers of a Buddha all arise from the power of Samantabhadra’s vows.

Regarding "taking the Dharma-realm treasury as one's body": because the body of fundamental wisdom and the body of differentiated wisdom are by nature all-pervasive, their magnitude is equal to that of the mental activities of all sentient beings, encompassing them all without exception for the sake of the Buddha-work.

Within a single pore, the lands of the ordinary and the holy throughout the ten directions are universally contained without exception; this is because wisdom has no distinction between inner, outer, or intermediate limits, for it is fundamentally thus.
"Protected and sustained by all Tathāgatas" means that he shares the same fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as the Tathāgatas and performs great activities on their behalf.

"Able to realize and enter non-differentiated wisdom in a single thought-moment" clarifies that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva manifests the skillful means of attaining perfect enlightenment and delivering sentient beings within the realms of beings throughout the ten directions, demonstrating such matters as attaining Buddhahood in a single thought-moment.

It also elucidates the discourse on the essence of wisdom, which is without distinction between beginning and end: infinite eons are, in total, a single thought-moment, yet all sentient beings within that single thought-moment give rise to the view of infinite eons of birth and death for themselves.
If one employs the clear contemplation of the wisdom that penetrates principle, then infinite eons are made into a single thought-moment due to non-discriminative wisdom.
When one accords with this, one attains Buddhahood simultaneously with all Buddhas of the three periods of time—past, present, and future.

By means of the seal of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one seals the fact that the essence of the three periods of time is fundamentally equal, as there is no distinction between prior and subsequent limits.

To clarify that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)—because they still possess a supramundane mind—are yet deluded regarding the conduct of entering the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) on the eleventh stage and thus cannot perceive it, this is to cause advancing Bodhisattvas to maintain their own self-power so as not to stagnate within the preceding ten stages.
The remainder is fully explained in the text itself.

Regarding the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (Lion’s Sport Samādhi): it universally matures the thoughts and activities of all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions; its great function is effortless—this is the meaning of "sport" (*vijṛmbhita*) and this is the meaning of "samādhi."
Speaking in terms of the Great Function (*mahā-vṛtti*), there is no separate cessation.
*New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Scroll 29;
*New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Scroll 30.
The Venerable Li Tongxuan composed the sixth section.

Furthermore, the passage titled "When the Bodhisattva Universal Eye Heard the Tathāgata Praise the Pure Merits of Samantabhadra" consists of thirty-two lines of scripture; within this section, it is further divided into seven sub-sections.

First, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye" down to "neither could be seen," there are three lines of scripture which clarify the section wherein the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, seeking Samantabhadra through ten unspeakable samādhis, was nonetheless unable to see him.

Second, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye" down to "none of them saw anything," there are three and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva Universal Eye arose from samādhi and addressed the Buddha, stating that he did not see the body, speech, mind, or seat of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

3. From "The Buddha said, 'It is so'" down to "reaching the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm," there are twelve lines of scripture which clarify that the Buddha, for the sake of the Universal Eye, praises the profound profundity of Samantabhadra’s three karmas, stating that they cannot be distinguished by the ability to emerge from or enter into samādhi, nor by the ability to see them.

4. From "Good son" onwards, up to "none of it goes to waste," there are three and a half lines of scripture which clarify that the Buddha praises the benefits of seeing, hearing, drawing near to, and serving Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, such that none of it is in vain.

5. From "At that time, Universal Eye" down to "prostrated with his head in reverence," there are approximately three lines of scripture which clarify the section where Universal Eye and all the other bodhisattvas, filled with longing and yearning for Samantabhadra, thrice cry out "Namo" and prostrate with their heads in reverence.

Sixth: From "At that time, the Buddha addressed Samantadarśin" down to "one shall immediately behold Samantabhadra Bodhisattva," there are six and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies that the Buddha further exhorts the great assembly, including Samantadarśin, to pay further homage and to contemplate the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), seeking out Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as if he were standing before one's eyes.

7. From "At that time" below until "all saw the Great Being Samantabhadra," there is one and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies how the Universal Eye and the great assembly of bodhisattvas, following the Buddha’s exhortation, further increased their prostrations and veneration; meanwhile, Samantabhadra, knowing the proper time, desired to manifest his own body for them.

In the seven sections of the above thirty-three lines of scripture, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva does not appear; this is intended to clarify that because the various bodhisattvas such as Samantacakṣus enter and emerge from samādhi, they are unable to perceive the three karmas, the seat, or the realm of Samantabhadra.

This uses the analogy of the various illusory forms that abide within the words of a magical illusion to clarify that the essence of the words of a magical illusion has no location whatsoever; how, then, could one seek it?

One must not seek it by entering or exiting the state of samādhi; rather than suppressing that profound stillness and extinguishing thought-constructs, one should clarify that the very substance of thought-activity is omnipresent and eternally quiescent, which is not a further extinction.

By means of this, Samantabhadra enters the Dharma-realm with adamantine wisdom; throughout all worlds, he neither acts nor dwells. Just as the bodies of all sentient beings are ultimately no-bodies, having neither coming nor going, he has attained unceasing, undifferentiated, and sovereign spiritual powers.
This clarifies that allowing things to be as they are in their own suchness is termed "spirit" (shen).

Not deliberating, not thinking, not fixed, not disordered, neither coming nor going—allowing wisdom to pervade everywhere, benefiting sentient beings with sovereign mastery, and manifesting in accordance with the faculties of others is termed "penetration" (tong).
All phenomena are thus; without entering or emerging from meditative concentration or distraction, they are truly called the activity of the three karmas and the seat practiced by Samantabhadra.
As for the substance of the seat of a Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds, it is simply said to have a magnitude that fills a trichiliocosm.
This seat of Samantabhadra is equal in measure to empty space, for it is the great lotus-womb treasury of the entire dharma-realm.

It is clearly known that the scope of the wisdom of bodhisattvas on the ten stages remains still limited; thus, although they have ascended to this rank, there remain obstacles regarding the limited capacity for such entry and exit as is appropriate, as well as the limitations of such ineffable gates of samādhi. This is because they have not yet attained the ultimate fruit of the tenth stage—the great sovereign mastery of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Therefore, through threefold seeking of Samantabhadra and threefold advancement, only when conceptual thoughts are set aside does he manifest his body.

Furthermore, in explaining the matters of the thirteen samādhi-realms, his intention is to reprove those in the tenth stage who still harbor a seeking for transcendence; they remain within the worldly realm of birth and death and have not yet attained equality with the sovereign mastery and freedom throughout the ten directions.

By means of this instruction from the Tathāgata, one reverses the arising of conceptual thoughts; because one removes the defiled habitual tendencies within the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and [cultivates] the supramundane pure mind, this clarifies that the ten stages eliminate the residual habitual tendencies and delusions regarding the conventional and ultimate truths of the mundane and supramundane realms.

The above explanation clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages have not yet eliminated the dual habits of the ultimate and the conventional, nor have they exhausted the dual habits of tranquility and agitation; because they still possess the habit of entering and emerging from various samādhis, they have not yet attained the quiescent entry into saṃsāra.
Just as the nature of space is devoid of an agent yet is eternally pervasive, not contained within any limits, and takes all sentient beings and their environments as its essence.
The wisdom of Samantabhadra is like space, taking all sentient beings as its substance.

When sentient beings are deluded regarding this wisdom themselves, it is called ignorance. In accordance with those deluded states, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra manifests physical bodies throughout the worlds of the ten directions. Because wisdom has no substance and is like space—neither created by effort, without coming or going, neither arising nor ceasing—he awakens those who are deluded everywhere through an ocean of wisdom equal to space.
Wisdom has no substantial form or characteristics, for its great function conforms to the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
How could the Bodhisattvas at the stages of the ten grounds perceive it by means of entering and emerging from samādhi through some deliberate seeking?
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said to the bodhisattvas: "If one seeks the essential nature or characteristics of illusory spells and written words, can they be found?
Since even the mind that seeks the illusion cannot be found, how could those illusory forms be found?"

Therefore, when entering or emerging from samādhi and seeking the mind, one seeks the great function of Samantabhadra—the skillful wisdom-body that is without dependence—and finds that nothing at all can be apprehended.

For this reason, the Tathāgata instructs all bodhisattvas to refrain from giving rise to conceptual thoughts and to reverently perform three prostrations to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra; only then will he manifest his body according to their needs through the power of spiritual penetrations. This is because the wisdom-body cannot be sought within the locus of samādhi, for the essence of wisdom abides nowhere and depends on nothing.

If one conceives thoughts, recollections, and aspirations, they will manifest accordingly; yet because there is no fixed location or basis for them, they are like an echo—merely sounds that respond to objects—and if one seeks them, no location can be found.

The Buddha said: "When it is said that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is now present here in this assembly at the site of enlightenment, personally attending me and remaining without the slightest movement, it clarifies that because the nature of fundamental wisdom is inherently without dependence, he is said to be 'present here at this site of enlightenment.'"

Because it serves as the remedy for the aggregates of views that grasp at objective existence, and because its unimpeded wisdom—comprising both the general and the particular, as well as identity and difference—is universally luminous and identical in essence to the great functioning of all Buddhas of the ten directions, it is called the "Assembly."

The ocean of wisdom of infinite distinctions functions simultaneously and with equality; it does not shift from the essence of fundamental wisdom and is the wisdom that abides nowhere. This is called "drawing near to me," because one dwells in the initial state of being unmoving and unshakable.
The term "Namo" (Homage) signifies the clarity of taking refuge, placing faith, and following [the Dharma].

According to the principles of the *Li* trigram, the south represents *Li*; since *Li* is characterized by its central void, and because this void is non-existent [in substance], it clarifies that *Li* is the sun.

Detaching from the subjective mind, one penetrates the principle of vacuity through the mind; thus, the wisdom-mind becomes luminous. Therefore, it is called "Namo," signifying that one takes refuge in and faithfully accords with the principle of the wisdom of vacuity.
Therefore, the meaning of Sudhana’s seeking his friends in the south is likewise so;
the meaning of the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood in the south is also like this.
It is simply by realizing the principle and wisdom of emptiness that all ten directions are collectively designated as "south."
If one were to hold that all phenomena exist as substantial entities, [it would follow that they] would be collectively situated in the north throughout the ten directions.
The remainder of the text is self-evident.

The seventh section, beginning with "At that time," consists of nineteen and a half lines of scripture; within this, Samantabhadra’s desire to manifest his own body is further divided into three parts.

First: From "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" down to "manifesting all Buddhas of the three periods of time," there are seven lines of scripture clarifying how Samantabhadra Bodhisattva manifests his body according to what is appropriate.

Second, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye" down to "as if seeing all Buddhas of the ten directions," there are two and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the section on how the great assembly of bodhisattvas beholds Samantabhadra and the Bodhisattva’s joy, which is like seeing all the Buddhas of the ten directions.

3. From "At that time" onwards, there may be ten lines of scripture which clarify the power of the bodhisattvas' faith and understanding, as well as the original vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; they describe how clouds of offerings arise, how light shines everywhere to pacify the three evil destinies, and how all bodhisattvas enter the stage of Samantabhadra’s practice.

Because one sees Samantabhadra Bodhisattva manifesting his body according to what is appropriate, one seeks him while entering and emerging from samādhi but does not find him; this clarifies that there is no entering or emerging, for wisdom cannot be sought through the entering and emerging of samādhi.
Were it not for the fact that their positions are harmonized and their paths are identical, their wisdom would naturally coincide.
To perceive them through conceptual thought is merely to see them as they manifest in accordance with conditions; only thereafter does one truly encounter their original bodies.
The remaining meanings are fully contained within the text itself.
The intent clarifies that the wisdom of non-abiding is the great essence of Samantabhadra, while manifesting bodies according to need is the great function of Samantabhadra.

Eighth: The section beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye" and extending for nine and a half lines of scripture clarifies how the Bodhisattva Universal Eye praises the ten kinds of vast abodes of Samantabhadra, and how the Tathāgata praises the ten vast merits of Samantabhadra.
The meaning of this is as praised in the text.
The forty-fifth fascicle of the sutra clarifies how the Tathāgata causes Samantabhadra to expound the ten great samādhis.
This section is further divided into eight parts.

First: From "At that time, the Tathāgata" down to "shall attain liberation," there are four and a half lines of scripture, clarifying that the Buddha commanded Samantabhadra to expound the ten great samādhis.

Second, from "What are the ten? down to "the Unobstructed Wheel Samādhi," there are approximately six lines of scripture that clarify the section in which the Tathāgata himself first speaks the names of the thirteen samādhis.

3. From "These ten great samādhis" down to "shall be spoken and are now being spoken," there is approximately one and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section wherein these samādhis are taught by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Regarding the statement that "the name of this samādhi was spoken by the Tathāgata himself," the intent is to clarify that the Tathāgata is the essence (*tattva*) of this samādhi. As for the instruction to Samantabhadra to explain the functioning (*karman*) of the samādhi, it clarifies that Samantabhadra is the function of this samādhi; thus, it demonstrates that within the stage of Buddhahood, both essence and function are perfected.

This refers to the Buddha by way of his essence (*tattva*), while Samantabhadra represents his activity (*vṛtti*); this stage is so designated because it realizes the mastery of both essence and activity.

Fourth, from "If any bodhisattvas... down to "...is called mastery over all dharmas," there are approximately four and a half lines of scripture, which clarify that when the Buddha praises those who, upon hearing this samādhi, joyfully practice it, they are said to have attained the stage of mastery over the Buddha.

5. From "This bodhisattva" onwards, up to "universally understands all that is spoken by the Buddhas," there are nine lines and a half of scripture. This clarifies the section on how one who cultivates and studies these thirteen samādhis attains non-attachment toward all phenomena and gains mastery and skill in turning the wheel of the Buddha-dharma.

Sixth: From "This is the gate of the dharma-characteristics of all bodhisattvas" down to "By this, through the Buddha's spiritual power, he purifies all worlds," there are five lines and a half of scripture, clarifying the section where the Buddha praises the cultivation of these thirteen samādhis as being able to enter ten kinds of dharma-gates.

7. From "If a bodhisattva enters this samādhi" down to "manifesting various kinds of great supernatural powers," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies that the Buddha praises how, upon entering this samādhi, one attains the utility of great skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood while not abandoning the practice of the bodhisattva path.

8. From the line beginning with "Therefore" onwards, for one and a half lines of the sūtra, it clarifies that the Tathāgata exhorts Samantabhadra to explain this thirteenth section on the sovereign power and function of the samādhis.
The meaning of these passages is self-evident from the sutra itself.

Thus, the intent of the eleven chapters following the "Ten Samādhis" is that by means of the supramundane wisdom of great compassion attained within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one perfects the mundane wisdom of great compassion; only when this wisdom of differentiation is brought to full maturity and mastery does one truly fulfill the conduct of Samantabhadra.

Transcendental compassion and wisdom constitute the fruit of Buddhahood, while worldly differentiated wisdom and compassion constitute the practice of Samantabhadra and the path of the Bodhisattva; these two aspects reach their culmination only in the "Chapter on the Manifestation" (Samantabhadracaryā-prasthāna).
The tenth section, from "At that time" onwards, consists of ten passages explaining the ten types of mastery over samādhi.
Within this text, regarding the first, the Samādhi of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsa*), it is divided into four sections:

first, the explanation of the name of the samādhi; second, the elucidation of the essence and function of the samādhi; third, the presentation of the sphere of the samādhi; and fourth, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the name of the samādhi: why is it called the Samādhi of Universal Radiance?
"San" (三) means "correct" (zhèng).
"Mèi" (昧) means "concentration" (dìng); because the conscious mind does not manifest, it is termed "mèi."
Correct wisdom that is all-pervasive is called "universal" (pu).
That which illuminates delusion and shatters ignorance is called "light" (guang).
That to which no phenomenon is inaccessible is called "clarity" (ming).

Second, regarding the elucidation of the essence and function of samādhi: it is clarified that this samādhi takes the fundamental wisdom of the dharmakāya as its essence and the ten kinds of inexhaustible wisdom as its function.
For this reason, the Buddha himself speaks of the names of the samādhis, while Samantabhadra explains the functions of the samādhis.

Regarding the three instances of the "spheres of samādhi," within these first three samādhis, the spheres are briefly illustrated by taking a trichiliocosm as a single lotus flower, wherein the body manifests and sits cross-legged, pervading the entirety of this lotus.

Within his own body, he further manifested a trichiliocosm, containing ten billion sets of four continents. In each set of four continents, he manifested ten billion bodies; each body entered ten billion times ten billion trichiliocosms. In every set of four continents within those worlds, he manifested ten billion times ten billion bodhisattva practices. Each bodhisattva’s cultivation produced ten billion times ten billion resolute understandings, causing ten billion times ten billion faculties and dispositions to reach fulfillment. Within each faculty and disposition, there were formed ten billion times ten billion non-regressive karmas of the bodhisattva-dharma.

However, the bodies manifested are neither one nor many; there is no confusion regarding entering or emerging from meditative concentration. In this manner, they increase and expand twofold after twofold, as fully described in the sūtra.
This is the realm of the first three samādhis; it clarifies that the bodies and lands are layered and interpenetrating in infinite succession, pervading everywhere in vastness without limit.
Fourth, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, ten points will be briefly presented within this section.
First, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, receiving the Tathāgata’s intent, explains that this samādhi does not arise from his own merit.
"Intent" (zhì) refers to the underlying purpose.
Second, he restates the name of the samādhi.
Third, it sets forth the ten kinds of inexhaustible wisdom of bodhisattvas.
Fourth, it clarifies that such bodhisattvas are able to give rise to ten kinds of boundless minds.
Fifth, it clarifies that these bodhisattvas possess ten kinds of differentiated wisdom for entering samādhi.
Sixth, it clarifies the skillful knowledge of entering ten kinds of samādhis.
Seventh, it cites the analogy of the asura king Rāhu manifesting a transformation body without destroying his original body.
Eighth, it clarifies that bodhisattvas profoundly penetrate the dharma-gate of how the mind and dharmas are like illusions.
Ninth, it clarifies that the bhikṣu contemplates the impurity of his internal body, using the analogy of the physical body remaining as it was without decay.
Tenth, it clarifies that the bodhisattva dwelling in this samādhi contemplates the dharma-body, seeing all worlds and worldly phenomena universally enter into his own body.

As practiced above, the Samādhi of Universal Radiance takes the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body as its essence, the ten inexhaustible wisdoms as its function, the arousal of the ten boundless minds as its practice, and the ten kinds of differentiated wisdom for entering samādhi as the power of mastery over the commonalities and differences of samādhi. By means of the ten kinds of skillful wisdom for entering samādhi, it causes the body of samādhi—within which exist the sentient beings and buddha-fields of many buddha-fields—to remain within one's own present body without abandoning one's own self, which always returns to its original state; furthermore, within that body, it manifests immeasurable bodies to deliver sentient beings and make offerings to all Buddhas.
As the subsequent text states: "Abiding in this samādhi, one contemplates the Dharma-body and sees all worlds universally entering into it.

This clarifies that one clearly perceives all worlds and the phenomena of the world, yet remains entirely unattached to those worlds and their phenomena. This is because the nature of the Dharma-body itself is without internal or external, large or small, center or periphery, and without measure; because the Dharma is seen in such a way; and because the Dharma is thus without attachment.

Because the mundane world and its phenomena, which manifest from the principle of the Dharma-body’s lack of intrinsic nature and lack of marks, are all like shadows and illusions in essence; because the mundane world and its phenomena are all of one flavor with the Dharma-body and devoid of dualistic characteristics; and because all retributive objects appear like reflections, layer upon layer, without mutual obstruction.
As for Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, his brilliance is able to seize the sunlight, causing affliction to arise in the world.
"Rā" means to seize, and "hu" means affliction.
Asuras are so called because they lack the sublime play of the devas.
Regarding the transformative activities therein, they are as clearly explained in the sutra itself.
As for the second, the Samādhi of Sublime Radiance (*prabhāsvara*), within this section there are four points as previously mentioned.
The first is the explanation of the name of the samādhi.
First, the essence and function of samādhi will be clarified below;
second, the realm of samādhi; third, the explanation of the meaning according to the text.

First, regarding the explanation of the name "samādhi": it is established by virtue of clarifying that the essence of the dharmakāya’s wisdom and principle is pure and capable of manifesting wondrous light.
Second, regarding the explanation of the essence and function of samādhi: it clarifies that this samādhi takes fundamental wisdom as its essence and illusory wisdom as its function.

Regarding the realm of the samādhi of the three vidyās: by entering as many trichiliocosm world-systems as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm world-system, one further manifests within each individual world-system as many bodies as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm world-system; furthermore, from each individual body, one emits as many rays of light as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm world-system, as fully described in the sūtra.
Even to the point where all lands of both sages and ordinary beings can be manifested within the body of a bodhisattva, with each reflecting the other in a manner of infinite mutual penetration—
this is the sphere of this samādhi, as fully elucidated in the sutra.
Regarding the fourth section, the explanation of the meaning according to the text, it is further divided into two parts:
first, an extended topical outline of the sutra’s intent; second, the word-by-word explanation of the meaning.
As for the first, the extended topical outline of the sutra’s intent, this section is divided into ten subsections.
I. The single line of scripture beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" is the section in which Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addresses the assembly to once again state the name of the samādhi.

II. The eleven lines of scripture from "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva... down to "...various dharmas are likewise neither destroyed nor extinguished" clarify the entry into the realm of the samādhi; they show how the vastness and narrowness of the bodies and lands manifest and mutually interpenetrate, wherein light and shadow are layered upon one another without confusion.

3. From "O Son of the Buddha, it is as if the sun rises" down to "nor does it leave the water," there are eight lines of scripture which clarify that the seven-jeweled mountains, the great ocean waters, and the spaces between the mountains are manifested by the light of the sun; that these solar reflections mutually illuminate one another, creating layers of images in an inexhaustible succession of light and shadow—this is the section on the metaphor of the inexhaustible light and shadow.

4. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to "never abandoning or departing from it," there are five lines of scripture that clarify how such a bodhisattva dwells in the Samādhi of Wondrous Light and Vastness, neither destroying worldly appearances nor destroying true nature, remaining non-abiding in both and non-destructive toward both.

5. From "O Son of the Buddha, it is like a magician... down to "...the original day is not extinguished," there are seven lines of scripture that clarify the section on the analogy of how a magician creates illusions of days, months, years, and varying durations of time without destroying the original day.

6. From "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" down to "not destroying those many worlds," there are seventeen lines of scripture which clarify that when a bodhisattva enters this wondrous light Great Samādhi, they are able to cause one world and many worlds to arise again, mutually interpenetrating without any mutual obstruction.

7. From "For what reason" onwards, up to "this is called one who dwells in the dharma of great compassion," there are eleven lines of scripture that clarify the section on how the Bodhisattva dwells in the dharma of non-self, remaining unimpeded regarding all dharmas, the spheres of self and others, the body, and the mind.

8. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "because there is no regression," there are six and a half lines of scripture which clarify that this Bodhisattva enters one world by means of incalculable worlds; he skillfully knows the distinctions among countless sentient beings and the distinctions in the Bodhisattvas' modes of entry. Although Buddhas appear everywhere and he manifests his own body before each and every one of those Buddhas to practice all the various deeds, his body neither comes nor goes between them; he is able to exercise mastery over both identity and difference.

9. From "Just as there is a magician" down to "the latter does not disturb the former," there are five lines and a half of scripture that clarify the section on the simile of the illusory nature produced by the Bodhisattva’s true wisdom, using the magician as a metaphor.

10. From "The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands all worldly dharmas" onwards, there are twenty and a half lines of scripture clarifying the section on attaining mastery over the gateway of the wisdom-illusion (*jñāna-māyā*) by entering this wondrous *Mahāprabhāsa* Great Samādhi.

Second, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: This section explains that because the nature of fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) is inherently all-pervasive, it manifests all objects through the wisdom that is like a reflection. Through the mutual interpenetration of self and other, there is mastery over the one and the many. Because of fundamental wisdom, the many enter into the one; because of the wisdom that is like a reflection, the one manifests as many objects, due to the distinct differences in the physical forms and characteristics of each individual body.
Regarding "the causes of the world": that which is cultivated in the present life serves as the cause for the future life.
Regarding "the establishment of the world": this clarifies the principles by which each respective world is established.
Regarding "world-dwellers," there are many types of sentient beings dwelling together within a single world.
Regarding "the radiance and color of the world," it is because some sentient beings dwell within the light of the Buddha.
Thus, these suns, moons, and stars are transformations produced by the collective karma of emperors and sentient beings among humans; their refined radiance ascends upward.
Furthermore, there are devas who dwell therein because they reside within them.
As for those who travel back and forth through the world, holding and turning [their bodies] as they move through the void, this Bodhisattva knows them all.
The names of the eight classes of divine beings have already been explained in the first assembly.
The teaching on the *pudgala* refers to the person (*pudgala*), clarifying how the person pursues unwholesome dharmas and thus proceeds toward the fruit of suffering.
The teaching on the *māṇava* refers to the dharma for instructing the youth (*māṇava*).
The remainder is fully contained within the sutra itself.
Regarding the third [section], "The Samādhi of Supernatural Power that Successively Travels to All Buddha-lands," there are three gates within this passage:
first, the explanation of the name of the samādhi; second, the explanation of the essence and function of the samādhi; and third, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning.
First, regarding the explanation of the name of this samādhi: why is it called the "Samādhi of Supernatural Power that Universally Travels to All Buddha-lands"?

It is because when the rational nature (*dharmatā-svabhāva*) is all-pervasive, the essence of the function of wisdom is itself all-pervasive; and because the essence of the function of wisdom is all-pervasive, supernatural power is all-pervasive.

This clarifies that, regarding the essence of wisdom and principle which is all-pervasive, one responds to phenomena through illusion-like wisdom in both movement and stillness; yet, by relying on fundamental wisdom, there is eternally no coming or going, nor any distinction of self and other, nor any extension or contraction. Based on this, it is given the name "the Samādhi of Supernatural Power that Universally Travels to All Buddha-lands."

Regarding the second [point], the explanation of the essence and function of samādhi: this samādhi takes the Dharma-nature body as its essence and the arising of illusory-like wisdom from fundamental wisdom as its function.
This illusory-like wisdom is like an echo in an empty valley; it produces sound in response to objects, yet possesses no inherent substance of its own.
These two wisdoms take the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as their essence; they both possess virtuous functions yet have no basis for support.

This is because the minds of all sentient beings are fundamentally thus; it is only because wisdom itself lacks inherent nature and cannot self-illuminate, thereby following after objects and becoming deluded.
Illuminating this through the two gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), delusion and liberation both rely upon the fundamental source.

This explains that with respect to the *dharmakāya*, it serves as the essence of *śamatha*; and with respect to the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, it gives rise to the essence and function of wisdom (*jñāna*). Thus, it clarifies that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can give rise to insight (*prajñā*), and contemplation can initiate wisdom (*jñāna*).
Regarding the third section, the explanation of the meaning according to the text, there are two points as previously mentioned.
First, concerning the expanded structural analysis of the sūtra’s intent: within this section, it is divided into four parts.
The first part, from “O Son of the Buddha” down to “supernatural powers,” consists of one and a half lines of sūtra; this is the section where Samantabhadra reiterates the name of the samādhi.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva" down to "reaching the ultimate," there are sixteen and a half lines of scripture that clarify the entry into samādhi; it shows mastery over the extension and contraction [of time] without discrimination, and the aspect of non-forgetfulness regarding all dharmas.

3. From "For example, like the Sun Deity" down to "is also likewise," there are three and a half lines of scripture that clarify the section using the analogy of the Sun Deity shining over the four continents, where day and night neither arise nor cease.
4. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "skillful wisdom," there is one and a half lines of sūtra, which clearly summarize the divisions of this samādhi as previously mentioned.
The meaning of the preceding text is self-evident and need not be further explained.
Regarding the fourth [stage], the Samādhi of the Practice of the Deeply Purified Mind, there are three sections within this passage as previously described.
First, regarding the explanation of the name of this samādhi: why is it called the "Samādhi of the Practice of the Pure and Profound Mind"?

It is because the Bodhisattva has already cultivated the wisdom and principle of emptiness and signlessness, thereby attaining a body that pervades all things according to the wisdom of reality. Arising from this body that pervades all according to the prior wisdom and principle, he performs offerings with a profound mind through skillful means. Following his offerings of the ten items—such as incense, flowers, and canopies—to all Buddhas, his mind remains unbroken; his Dharma-body and Wisdom-body are without fabrication or conceptualization. For these reasons, this name is established.

Regarding the second explanation of the essence and function of samādhi: its essence is the fundamental wisdom of the dharmakāya; its function is to give rise to the wisdom of skillful means and to perform the ten kinds of offerings for Buddhas as numerous as all sentient beings.
Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text, there are two points as previously stated.
First, concerning the long-term structural analysis of the sūtra’s intent: within this section, it is divided into four parts.
The first, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, consists of one line of sūtra text, which clarifies that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again mentions the name of the samādhi.

2. From "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva" down to "does not discriminate between the appearance in the world and the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata," there are eighteen and a half lines of scripture which clarify the section on making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as all sentient beings through ten matters, such as incense, flowers, and canopies.

3. From "O Son of the Buddha, it is like a mirage in the midday sun" down to "all are the conceptual distinctions of the mind," there are seven lines of scripture that clarify the analogy of the midday mirage to explain how Bodhisattvas know the arising and passing away of the Tathāgata.

4. From "O Son of the Buddha, this samādhi" down to "skillful wisdom," there are ten lines of scripture that clarify the section on entering samādhi and not forgetting the perceived objects as if in a dream, thereby skillfully explaining them through analogies for others.

Regarding the fourth section, the explanation of the meaning according to the text: its significance is fully contained within the text itself; however, one who enters contemplation must skillfully attain what is appropriate. First, one must enter the concentration of no-thought and no-mind, realize the principle of the Dharmakāya, and accord with the nature of empty space. Only then may one, through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), give rise to a mind of offering, wherein both beginning and end are extinguished. One must attain such mastery as to act in accordance with the principle of reality (*li*).
If one cultivates only the dharma-body of emptiness and signlessness, one will be unable to give rise to function within wisdom.
If one gives rise only to conceptualization and fails to perceive the signless dharma-body, it is purely conditioned.
Each of these is clearly elucidated within its respective scriptural passage according to the sequential methods of these ten concentrations.
Regarding the fifth, the samādhi of knowing the treasury of past adornments, there are three sections within this passage as previously described.
First, regarding the explanation of the name of this samādhi: why is it called the "Great Samādhi of the Treasury of Adornments of Knowing the Past"?

It is because when this bodhisattva enters this meditative absorption, they are able to know the kalpas and lands in which past buddhas appeared, as well as the dharma-gates through which those buddhas appeared.

By adorning one's own mind with fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and accomplishing it through discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), this is called the arising of the first samādhi and its offering.
Within this meditative concentration, one must understand the dharma-gate of the sequential order in which the Buddhas appear throughout the kalpas and lands.

Regarding the second [point], the explanation of the essence and function of samādhi: fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) constitutes its essence, while the wisdom that knows the sequential distinctions of kalpas and lands constitutes its function.
The details below are fully contained within the text itself.

Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: as for the "three wheels," these are the three wheels of purity—supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and correct teaching (*samyagdeśanā*). This clarifies that by attaining this samādhi, one acquires supernatural powers, excels in remembering without forgetting, and skillfully expounds all dharmas.
As for "kalala," this is translated as "thin curd"; it refers to the initial stage of conception being like thin curd.
The remaining details are fully contained within the text itself.

Regarding the sixth samādhi, the "Treasury of the Radiance of Wisdom": it clarifies that this bodhisattva is able to know all Buddhas throughout all future kalpas—whether they have already taught the Dharma or have not yet taught it—and is able to know them all completely.

Regarding the "Treasury of the Radiance of Wisdom" (*jñānālokagarbha*): it is called a "treasury" because it does not depart from a single thought-moment while encompassing the wisdom of kalpas spanning the three periods of time.
Other meanings are self-evident according to the text.
Among these, the names of the eight classes of kings and others have already been explained in the first assembly.
This does not signify a formal teaching, but rather refers to the Bodhisattva’s approach to the Tathāgata solely for the purpose of making offerings and showing reverence to the Dharma.

Regarding the seventh, the Samādhi of Knowing the Buddha-Adornments of All Worlds: this clarifies that this Bodhisattva is able to enter universally into all worlds throughout the ten directions, seeing all the adornments of the teachings of every Buddha; because they are able to see them all completely, serve and make offerings to them, and because they universally enter all realms of existence and so forth to exhaustively master all the teachings they hear, it is named accordingly.
Regarding the meaning of these words, the sūtra itself provides full clarification.

As for the eighth, the Samādhi of the Differentiated Bodies of All Sentient Beings: this explains that by entering this samādhi, one can manifest the body of a Buddha and bodies equal in number to the different bodies of all sentient beings, appearing in accordance with each of their respective types; hence its name is established.
Furthermore, it is named after the ability to enter the samādhi of "conformity and difference" (*sādharmya-vaidharmya-anuloma-pratiloma*) and so forth;
the remaining meanings are fully contained within the text itself.

Regarding the ninth, the *Dharmadhātu-vaśitā-samādhi*: this clarifies that this bodhisattva enters samādhi within each and every pore of his own body, naturally able to know all worlds as well as the phenomena of those worlds. He completely knows and exhaustively understands all worldly phenomena throughout the space-realm of the ten directions, even including the assemblies of Buddhas and bodhisattvas.

Why is this? Because wisdom accords with the dharma-realm; because wisdom has no center, periphery, magnitude, or measure, being like empty space; and because the essential nature of wisdom is luminous and pure.
Within a single pore, space has no measure of large or small; it is equal to the realm of empty space.

One is able to universally know all realms throughout the worlds of the ten directions; this cannot be known through the calculations of emotional consciousness. Only after manifesting it through the skillful means of extinguishing thought can the wisdom of principle appear before one, at which point one becomes capable of it. This is because it is realized through the seal of non-active wisdom when concentration exhausts conceptualization and there is neither thinking nor mind; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma Realm.
Not abiding in emotional fabrication, one relies on wisdom for universal knowledge; therefore, it is called "sovereignty over the Dharma-realm. This sutra states:

"It is like the space within a hole bored by an insect in a mustard seed, which suffers no diminution. It can be perceived through non-conceptual wisdom; those who perceive it through conceptual thought deviate from it.

When one perceives that all things around them are exhausted [in their ultimate nature], then the ten directions and the measure of one's own body are of the same single essence, for there is no distinction between interior and exterior;
yet when the mind harbors attachments, they become separated.

As for the four rivers flowing from the palace of the Great Dragon King Anavatapta, according to the sutras: atop Mount Gandhamādana is Lake Anavatapta; from each of the four sides of this lake flows out a river. On the eastern side is the Sītā River, which flows from the mouths of lions and carries golden sand; it enters the land of China in the east and then flows into the Eastern Sea.
To the south is the Gaṅgā River, which flows from the elephant’s mouth with silver sand; it enters South India and then flows into the Southern Ocean.
To the west is the Sindhu River, which flows from the bull’s mouth with golden sand; it enters the country of Sindh and then flows into the Western Ocean.
To the north lies the Varku River, which flows from the horse’s mouth with lapis lazuli sand; it enters the kingdom of Pārasīka and then flows into the Northern Sea.
This pool measures fifty yojanas in length and breadth, and its four mouths extend one yojana each in their respective directions.
Regarding the symbolism within this, the Sūtra itself provides clear explanation:
the *utpala* flower is here called the blue lotus;
the *padma* flower is here called the red lotus.
The *kumuda* flower—here translated as the "small white flower"—is so named because when its blossoms have not yet opened, the petals are all tightly pressed together.
The *puṇḍarīka* flower—here translated as the "hundred-petaled lotus."

Regarding the dragon king Anavatapta: "An" means "non-existent," and "avatapta" means "matured affliction"; thus, it signifies that this dragon is eternally free from the feverish afflictions found among dragons.
Regarding the expression of the meaning of the text, each point is fully contained within the sutra itself.

As for the tenth, the Great Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel (*anāvaraṇa-cakra-mahā-samādhi*): "Wheel" is like the thousand-spoked adamantine wheel of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), whose hub, spokes, rim, and linchpin are all perfectly complete. This signifies that the practice of destroying birth and death is perfected; it represents how this Bodhisattva’s compassionate wisdom, myriad practices, spiritual powers, and divine faculties fill the realm of sentient beings, as they have completely severed the delusions of sentient beings and attained full perfection.

It clarifies that one’s own Buddha-fruit has already been realized, and that the Bodhisattva’s wisdom, compassion, vows, and practices continue without rest; that within a single thought-moment, one fulfills the kalpas of the three periods of time; and that without departing from a single pore, one pervades the realms of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm. The clouds of compassionate wisdom and practice simultaneously and universally cover all; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel.

Regarding the Dragon King Manas: "Manas" means mind, and "Sī" means compassion; this refers to the fact that when this dragon king raises clouds and sends down rain, it arises from a compassionate heart.

Regarding the phrase "the elephant king Ilāpatra dwelling on the flank of the Golden Mountain": *Ilāpatra* here means "fragrant leaf" (*xiāngyè*). It is so named because there are many trees with fragrant leaves near the jeweled cave, and it takes this as its name.
Furthermore, he manifested thirty-three heads; each head had six tusks, upon each tusk were manifested seven ponds, and within each pond were manifested seven lotus flowers.
Because he takes lotuses with fragrant and pure petals to transform others, he is named accordingly.

He dwells on the flank of the foremost Golden Mountain; knowing when Śakra wishes to go on a journey, he vanishes from here and appears in the heavens. When escorting Śakra to the gardens for sightseeing, he transforms his own body to resemble that of a celestial being. When Śakra returns to his palace, he again assumes the form of an elephant to escort Śakra back to the palace. Then, he vanishes from the heavens and emerges from within a precious cave.
This illustration clarifies that although this bodhisattva has already attained the rank of Buddhahood, he does not abandon his practice of skillful means (*upāya*).
It is like that elephant king who, though able to transform his body into a celestial being, never loses his fundamental status as an elephant.
The remaining extensive meanings are fully detailed in the text of the sutra.

The ten preceding sections on the "Ten Determinations" clarify the process from the initial generation of the bodhicitta through the attainment of enlightenment, from birth into the world until entry into nirvana; in sum, they take this very moment (*kṣaṇa*) as their essential substance.
This is because all Buddhas of the past and present likewise attain Buddhahood simultaneously as a whole.
Regarding the long and short lifespans of sentient beings, from the perspective of the Truth (tathatā), there is neither beginning nor end.

Furthermore, it clarifies that this single assembly and its eleven chapters of scripture collectively elucidate the attainment of the Buddha-fruit according to each stage, without undermining the path of Samantabhadra’s universal conduct through skillful means.

As from the stage of the ten faiths onward, one mounts the fundamental wisdom of the Tathāgata, gives rise to the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, and both teaches and transforms sentient beings, as well as purifying one's own wheel of self-sustaining wisdom.
As for the analogy of refining true gold through ten stages of smelting, this too does not depart from the essence of this samādhi.
Now that one has reached the eleventh stage and beyond, the refinement by one's own wisdom is complete; it is then purely the conduct of Samantabhadra for the benefit of sentient beings.

In this first assembly of the "Ten Samādhis Chapter," from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the attainment of Buddhahood by all Buddhas throughout beginningless time, the eons do not pass.

The fruit of Buddhahood and the expedient practices of Samantabhadra have no beginning or end; their temporal and karmic activities of body and mind fill the ten directions without ever emerging from a single pore and without departing for even a single moment, for they are non-transmigratory.
All ages and kalpas throughout the three periods of past, present, and future are encompassed within this "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis.
Sentient beings are deluded by them and falsely perceive them as long or short; through the dissolution of delusion, they return to the source.
This "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" constitutes the fundamental essence; the eternal Way, which neither extends nor contracts, is inherently thus.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Ten Supernatural Powers (Daśābhijñā). In explaining this chapter, there are two sections for analysis:
first, the intent behind the chapter's inclusion; second, the word-by-word commentary on the text.

First, regarding the purpose of this chapter: it is to clarify that since the preceding "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" exists, this chapter clarifies how these samādhis give rise to functional activity, which consists of the ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Second, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: this clarifies that there are ten kinds of supernormal powers (abhijñā) below.
The names of these ten powers are fully listed as follows, with each clearly explained in the text.

The first section consists of thirteen and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies the total enumeration of the ten types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and presents the great function of the first among them, the power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*).
The second section consists of eleven lines of scripture, elucidating the great function of the supernormal power of the divine eye-knowledge (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*).

The third section consists of twenty-four and a half lines of scripture, elucidating the great function of the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
The fourth section consists of eighteen lines of scripture, which clearly elucidates the supernormal power of wisdom that extends throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
The fifth section consists of thirteen and a half lines of scripture, which elucidates the great function of the supernormal power of the perfected celestial ear-wisdom.

The sixth section consists of twenty and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies abiding in the supernatural power of the absence of intrinsic nature and the arising of the thirteen kinds of great functions of supernatural power.
The seventh section consists of thirteen lines of scripture, which clarifies the great function of the wisdom-power of skillfully discerning the speech and sounds of all sentient beings.
The eighth section consists of forty-one lines of sūtra, which elucidates the great function of the supernormal power of wisdom that produces the adornments of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* form-bodies.

The ninth section consists of twenty-two and a half lines of sūtra, which elucidates the great function of the supernormal power of wisdom regarding all phenomena; this clarifies that from the fundamental wisdom of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*), all differentiated wisdoms arise.

The tenth section consists of thirty-five and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the great function of the supernormal power of wisdom (*jñāna-abhijñā*) through the samādhi of the cessation of all phenomena. This section clarifies that within the principle of the quiescent extinction of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the great functions of great wisdom and great compassion constantly arise to benefit sentient beings, remaining eternally perfect.
Yama-rāja means "The Obstructor"; it refers to obstructing and admonishing sinners so that they may be freed from suffering.

These ten aforementioned powers all arise from inconceivable, unconditioned, unimpeded, and infinite great sovereign wisdom, manifesting infinite quiescent functions and entering the realm of Indra’s net—a dharma-gate of layered sovereignty. None of these should be viewed through the limited perspectives of the three vehicles.
For example, as with Aniruddha, I see the trichiliocosm with my divine eye as clearly as one observes an *āmra* fruit in the palm of one's hand.
This is like the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings, who perceive their own and others' buddha-fields and travel between them, for all such perceptions are limited in scope.

This refers to the fact that the Dharma-body is limitless and without interior or exterior; the intermediate Wisdom-body is likewise so, because it is universally limitless and functions through the重重 (repeatedly layered) great activities within the Indra-net.

This refers generally to the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning and the Heaven of All-Knowledge; it is not like the supernormal powers of sight and hearing possessed by those in the higher realms of the mundane world, nor like the powers of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the Pure Lands belonging to the Three Vehicles.

Abiding in the supernatural power of the absence of intrinsic nature, his body never leaves its original location, yet manifests its sovereign body within all Buddha-lands and all sentient-being lands of the ten directions, even within a single pore. His eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are entirely one body and one nature, like the manifold images in Indra’s net, mutually containing one another, devoid of any nature of coming, going, self, or other.
The essence of these ten is such that they are all-pervasive and all-penetrating; thus, they are called "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*).

Because wisdom universally penetrates and knows objects by virtue of sharing the same nature as those objects, they are termed "supernormal powers"; it is not a matter of coming and going between self and others. Therefore, these ten concentrations, ten supernormal powers, ten patiences, and so forth, represent the culmination of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), serving as the skillful means for entering birth and death to benefit sentient beings. They are also cultivated throughout the five positions: the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages, and the eleventh stage.
The remaining meanings are fully contained within the text itself.
Chapter Twenty-nine: The Chapter on the Ten Patiences (Daśakṣānti-varga). In preparing to explain this chapter, it is divided into three sections:
first, an explanation of the title; second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; and third, an explanation of the meaning according to the text.

First, regarding the explanation of the title of this chapter: it clarifies that this chapter encompasses the gateway of practice for ascending through one's own stages from the very beginning of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*), as well as the skillful means for benefiting sentient beings after attaining the fruit of Buddhahood; it is named "Patience" (*kṣānti*) because it is established based on practice in accordance with these modes of conduct.

If one follows the provisional teachings for bodhisattvas, those prior to the stages (bhūmi) are considered to be in the stage of "subduing patience" (kṣānti), while upon entering the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) on the stages, they enter "patience conforming to non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

If one follows the One Vehicle (ekayāna), from the very first thought of the ten abodes (daśa-vihāra), one attains the "gate of recollecting the light of the Buddhas' wisdom," which is called being born into the family of Buddha-wisdom, attaining "patience of sound" (ghoṣānugā-kṣānti), and is also termed "patience conforming to non-arising."

However, because their names differ according to their respective practices, this refers only to the initial birth into the family of Buddha-wisdom within the ten stages; in terms of its name, it accords with the Tathāgata’s correct wisdom of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Within the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*), it is called the "patience of non-arising that accords with the Buddha’s wisdom.

Within the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), by means of the integration of principle and wisdom, one gives rise to the gate of great compassion through fearless great vows; harmonizing and fusing great compassion and great kindness within principle and wisdom so that they are brought into equilibrium is called the "patience of non-arising in the tranquil function of the great vows, great compassion, and great wisdom that harmonize and fuse."
This is the practice of conformity to the patience of non-arising prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).

From the first stage through the third stage, taking the three preceding stages as a whole, one practices them collectively as a single dharma; this is called "nurturing wisdom and compassion" so that they may become habitual and perfected.

Because at the first stage, based on the ten stages of abiding (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one fulfills great vows and arouses the resolve to remain perpetually within birth and death to protect sentient beings, it is therefore also called "conformity-patience" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
Up to the eighth stage, one is said to have attained the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of Sudhana on the first stage is named Vasundharā; this means "Mistress of the Sprouting of Crops in Spring," and is also called "Abiding in Fearlessness. This serves to clarify that she presides over the sprouts of the Bodhi-mind first generated by sentient beings.
They are also called "lords of sentient beings," for they act as a refuge and cause them to be free from fear.
This is because these bodhisattvas of the first stage, through the power of their vows prior to the stages, dwell within the realm of sentient beings.

In the second stage (*bhūmi*), one clarifies the cultivation of the ten supreme wholesome precepts (*śīla*) in order to remedy the afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the desire realm and bring about non-attachment.

In the third stage, one cultivates the eight dhyānas and nine meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the upper realms to ensure non-attachment to the dhyāna realms; this is called conforming to the benefit of conventional wisdom through the principle of reality, nourishing great compassion, and conforming to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
In the fourth stage, one illuminates that the three realms are undefiled and further clarifies being born into the family of the Buddha.
In the fifth stage, through the gateway of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one gives rise to skillful wisdom and cultivates worldly arts and crafts.

Having completed the cultivation of mundane and supramundane wisdom in the sixth stage, the three emptinesses manifest within the meditative absorption of cessation; this is termed "patience of quiescence" (*śānti-kṣānti*).
In the seventh stage, one constantly abides in birth-and-death while bringing practice to perfection.
On the eighth stage, the effortful application of practicing the bodhisattva path comes to an end, and one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
From this point downward, the characteristics of the nine minor stages conclude, and the partial manifestation of the Buddha-activity of the tenth stage finally reaches its completion.

Beyond the fulfillment of the practices of Samantabhadra on the eleventh stage, one is purely a Tathāgata of Wondrous Enlightenment; yet, without departing from the skillful means of a Bodhisattva, one continues to deliver living beings.

Regarding these ten kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) in terms of advancement through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one attains one patience per stage; the same applies to the ten concentrations (*samādhi*) and the ten penetrations (*abhijñā*).
Based on the stage of "Endurance" (*kṣānti*), this chapter is established within the context of the practices of Samantabhadra; thus, it is given its title.

Furthermore, as the stages of progressive cultivation and the merit of skillful training correspond to these practices, the chapter is named the "Chapter on the Ten Endurances" (*Daśakṣāntiparivarta*).
Second, regarding the purpose of this chapter: previously there were already the ten penetrations (*abhisamaya*), yet here we speak of patience (*kṣānti*) in relation to those penetrations.

If one lacks the penetration of spiritual wisdom, one merely achieves the patience of subduing (*vinīyakṣānti*) and the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) does not arise; for this reason, this chapter must follow.

This means that prior to the tenth stage, one accomplishes the supernormal powers (abhijñā) through patience (kṣānti), while within the eleventh stage, one accomplishes patience through the supernormal powers.
This is because these ten supernormal powers and ten patiences are the functional manifestations of a single virtue.
Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the following ten sections clarify the ten kinds of patience (*kṣānti*).
Following the tenth section, there is one verse, which serves as a recapitulation of the aforementioned ten dharmas of patience.

As for the first patience regarding sounds, it is generally assigned to the initial stage among the five stages: the beginning of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), the beginning of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the beginning of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), the beginning of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), and the beginning of the eleventh ground (*ekādaśabhūmi*).

As for the second degree of compliant patience (*kṣānti*), it refers to the second stage among the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the second practice among the ten practices (*caryā*), the second dedication among the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), the second ground among the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the second position among the eleven grounds.

In this manner, each of these stages is correspondingly assigned in successive order; however, they differ according to the degree of mastery and ripening produced through the habitual practice of progressive cultivation.

Thus, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the patience like an illusion, the patience like a mirage, the patience like a dream, the patience like an echo, the patience like a shadow, the patience like a transformation, and the patience like space—all are to be correspondingly assigned and cultivated one by one in accordance with the five stages as described above.
Furthermore, because one person possesses the ten kinds of patience (*kṣānti*),
the remaining meanings are self-evident from the text itself.
Thus ends the fulfillment of the practices of the eleven stages (*bhūmi*).
Chapter Thirty: The Chapter on *Asaṃkhyeya*. Regarding the explanation of this chapter, four sections are established:

first, explaining the purpose of the chapter’s inclusion; second, explaining the principal questioner; third, explaining the principal teacher of the Dharma; and fourth, explaining the meaning according to the text.

First, regarding the intent of this chapter: it clarifies that the preceding three chapters—“The Ten Samādhis,” “The Ten Supernatural Powers,” and “The Ten Endurances”—comprehensively encompass the beginning and end of cause and effect; that from start to finish, without shifting even for the duration of a single kṣaṇa, one has already perfected supernatural powers and the dharmas of endurance.

This clarifies that the causal and resultant teachings and practices bestowed by all Buddhas, as well as the mutual support between causal and resultant actions from beginning to end, are uninterrupted and inseparable throughout every moment (*kṣaṇa*).
As stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, ten cycles of arising and ceasing constitute one *kṣaṇa*, and ninety *kṣaṇas* comprise nine hundred cycles of arising and ceasing.

Thus, because the fruits of Buddhahood throughout the three periods of time and the skillful practices of Samantabhadra are such that time does not shift, they are measured solely by the *kṣaṇa* (instant), and the names "arising" and "ceasing" are not established.
Regarding the establishment of arising and ceasing, it is posited solely within a single *kṣaṇa* and possesses no further duration.
From this point down to the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," the text clarifies the gateways of vast and sovereign conduct of the three karmas within the state of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, this chapter, "The Incalculable" (*Asaṃkhyeya*), clarifies the vast sovereignty of the Tathāgata’s mental karma;
the second chapter, "The Lifespan of the Tathāgata," clarifies the vast sovereignty of the Tathāgata’s life-force.
Chapter Three, "The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Abodes," elucidates the Tathāgata’s practice of gathering and sustaining sentient beings, which is vast, eternally abiding, and sovereign.
Chapter Four, "The Chapter on the Inconceivable Buddha," extols the vast sovereignty of the Buddha’s divine virtues in the three karmas.
Chapter Five, "The Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata," elucidates the vast sovereignty and majestic adornment of the Buddha’s bodily karma and its retributive merit.
Chapter Six, "The Merit of the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks," elucidates the vast sovereignty and majestic merit induced by the Dharma-body in accordance with the Buddha’s three karmas.

According to the *Āṭānāṭīya-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng), this is assigned to the third dhyāna; it speaks of the Buddha-flower Samādhi (*buddhapuṣpa-samādhi*) consisting of one hundred trillion verses, of which this "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" is a summary.
The seventh assembly is collectively titled the "Chapter on the Buddha-flower Samādhi.
The seventh chapter, "The Conduct of Samantabhadra," elucidates how the fruit of the Buddha’s three karmas—body, speech, and mind—is all-pervasive, vast, and sovereign.

Chapter Eight, "The Appearance of the Tathāgata," clarifies that the Buddha’s awakening and practice are all-pervasive; he is never absent from any world at any time, manifesting vast and sovereign mastery.

These eight chapters of the sutra collectively praise the Buddha-fruit’s two types of activity—those of practice and wisdom—as well as the vast sovereignty of the marks of the reward-body (*vipākakāya*) and its adornments; for this reason, these chapters must appear here.

Second, regarding the explanation of the Dharma Master who is able to inquire: the Bodhisattva is named "Mind-King" (*Cittarāja*). This clarifies that after attaining the mind and achieving patience, the activities of the mind become sovereign; thus, it is called "King."
Regarding the third explanation of the Lord who preaches the Dharma: why does the Tathāgata himself speak this chapter?
It is to clarify that these numerical dharmas are so vast that they exceed the scope of the wisdom of those in lower stages; only a Buddha can exhaustively master them.

This is the fruit of Buddhahood; the two delusions have not yet been reached, and it is only when the wisdom of differentiation is perfected that this is fully realized. These two chapters, "The Incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) and "The Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks," were spoken by the Tathāgata himself; all other sections of the five stages were each spoken by the Bodhisattvas corresponding to their respective levels.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths preach the Dharma of the Ten Faiths; these are Mañjuśrī, Buddhamati, and others.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abidings preach the Dharma of the Ten Abidings; these are Dharmamati, Vasumati, and others.
One should understand other cases by analogy with this example.

This chapter clarifies the fulfillment of the fruit of the knowledge of non-attainment (*aprāpti-viśeṣa-jñāna*) only upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood; furthermore, it is because this was spoken by the Tathāgata himself.

The one capable of posing the questions is the Tathāgata, who possesses mastery over the mind and is thus called a "King"; it is because he has attained mastery over the mind that he is able to inquire. Since this is the sovereign mind of the Buddha, when he establishes the teachings, he causes those who study them to emulate it.
It is said that practice is presided over by Samantabhadra; when practice achieves patience (*kṣānti*), it is then presided over by the Mind-King (*citta-rāja*).

Furthermore, these sequential dharmas culminate only when wisdom is perfected at the stage of Buddhahood; because wisdom is all-pervasive, one knows spontaneously, not through the application of effortful mental attention (*prayoga-manasikāra*), as the Buddha himself has declared.

Therefore, regarding the fourfold explanation of the text according to its literal meaning: "one hundred lakṣas constitute one koṭi" means that one lakṣa is here called one hundred million (yì), and one koṭi is here called one billion (zhào). Furthermore, [the following applies].

Examining this method of the Yellow Emperor’s calculations, there are twenty-three numerical units in total: namely, one, two, three, four, five; six, seven, eight, nine, ten; hundred, thousand, ten-thousand, million, ten-million, hundred-million, billion, ten-billion, hundred-billion, trillion, ten-trillion, hundred-trillion, quadrillion, ten-quadrillion, hundred-quadrillion, quintillion, ten-quintillion, hundred-quintillion, sextillion, ten-sextillion, hundred-sextillion, septillion, ten-septillion, and hundred-septillion.

From the stage of *raṅ* (壤) onward, there are three grades of numerical calculation: the lowest increases by tens at each step; the middle increases by ten thousand times ten thousand (*wan wan*) at each step; and the highest increases by one hundred million times one hundred million (*yi yi*) at each step.
Now, this "Chapter on Incalculables" (*asaṃkhyeya*) employs the highest numerical methods; thus it speaks of "hundreds of thousands. One hundred thousand constitutes one *koṭi*.

A *koṭi* multiplied by itself is equivalent to the number here termed "continent" (*dvīpa*). A *nayuta* is equivalent to the number here termed "ravine" (*khila*), "match" (*titha*), or "coming carriage" (*āgata-vatsara*). Beyond this point, the numerical names of this region are exhausted.
Mīgha and Vigha are both pronounced with the rising tone (shǎngshēng).
Kiṅkara is pronounced with the "jūlíng" rhyme (the level tone). Masapā is pronounced with the rising tone.
Ra-laṅ (pronounced with the retroflex *ṛ* sound),
vi-kha-daṃ (pronounced with the retroflex *ḍaṃ* sound),
ṭi-ra-ṭe (pronounced with the palatal *ṭe* sound).
A-mo-mo (pronounced with the "ma" of "mo-wa" reversed);
Bo (pronounced with the "pu" of "pu-mo" reversed);
Pi (pronounced with the "pu" of "pu-ji" reversed).
Su (with the *sū* reversed),
pi (with the *pǔ* reversed),
mi (with the *mò* reversed).
The character "tu" (荼) is pronounced with the retroflex *zhai* (宅) and *jia* (加) finals.
