These aforementioned numerical meanings are vast and expansive; although they are immeasurable and difficult to fathom, their intent clarifies that the Tathāgata’s wisdom and the vows, practices, and three karmas of Samantabhadra are so immense that no worldly calculation can reach them.

As is fully explained in the verses below, these aforementioned numbers based on the great count total one hundred and twenty; reaching the point of "unspeakable-unspeakable-fold," it constitutes one completion.
A verse from the Sūtra says: "The ineffable is unspeakable, filling all that is unspeakable.
Throughout ineffable eons, one could not exhaustively speak of what is unspeakable."
All the unspeakable Buddha-fields are entirely ground into fine dust; within a single mote of dust are unspeakable fields, and as it is for one, so it is for all.
These unspeakable Buddha-fields are reduced to atoms in an unspeakable number of moments; in every thought-moment they are thus pulverized, and this continues thus throughout all unspeakable eons.

There are unspeakably many lands within this single atom; it is even more difficult to speak of these lands as atoms. Using the method of incalculable calculation, one would count in this manner for unspeakably many eons.

Using these atoms as the number of kalpas—where one atom represents one hundred thousand unspeakable numbers of kalpas—even if one were to praise a single Samantabhadra for that many kalpas, one could never exhaust the measure of his merit.
This clarifies that the merit of the Tathāgata’s Samantabhadra vows and practices transcends all measure and calculation; it is beyond the reach of numbers.

Thus, this chapter describes the Samantabhadra vows and practices within the stage of Buddhahood, which are as immeasurable as space and incomparable to the atoms of lands—limitless upon limitless, infinitely layered upon infinitely layered—as fully detailed in the sūtra itself.
Thus, many eons constitute a single momentary limit (*kṣaṇānta*), for many such practices of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra are inexhaustible within a single moment.
According to the previous questions and answers in the second assembly, the text of the "Chapter on the Ten Summits" has not yet arrived.
Chapter Thirty-one: On the Lifespan. In preparing to explain this chapter, three sections will be established:
first, explaining the purpose for which the chapter appears; second, identifying the master who proclaims the teaching; and third, explaining the meaning according to the text.

First, regarding the intent of this chapter: it clarifies that since the preceding chapter concerns *asaṃkhyeya* (incalculable), this chapter logically follows as concerning the measure of lifespan (*āyus-pramāṇa*).

Second, regarding the explanation of the teacher who expounds the doctrine: the reason the teacher of this chapter is identified as Bodhisattva Cittarāja is to clarify that the Buddha’s lifespan has the mind as its essence, and that the "King of Mind" (*cittarāja*) symbolizes mastery over life.

This clarifies that the life-span of the Tathāgata, the King of Minds, accords with the capacities of sentient beings, extending or contracting, lengthening or shortening, as he acts with sovereign mastery; yet in reality, the life of the Tathāgata is such that there is no life-span, nor is there any length or shortness.

Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: this chapter of the sutra clarifies the length of the Buddha’s lifespan. For the sake of those who have not yet attained awakening, it establishes a graduated sequence to enable them to know that the Tathāgata’s lifespan is inexhaustible, using the few to manifest the many and the short to manifest the long.
If it were not thus, how could one know the lifespan of the Buddha?
Yet, in reality, the Tathāgata has neither long nor short life, for his nature is without birth or cessation.
The lifespan of the Tathāgata is like fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), for it is without arising or cessation, and without going or coming.
It is represented by the lifespans of ten Buddhas to signify its inexhaustibility.
Chapter Thirty-Two: The Abodes of Bodhisattvas. In order to explain this chapter, three sections are established: first, the purpose for which the chapter appears;
second, the identity of the master who preaches the Dharma; and third, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.

First, regarding the intent of this chapter: whereas the preceding chapters concerned the Tathāgata’s lifespan and the duration of his abiding for kalpas, this chapter concerns how the Buddha sustains the world through the practices of a bodhisattva, pervasively gathering and transforming beings throughout the human realm and the oceans.
As it is in this region, so it is throughout the lands of the ten directions and all of Jambudvīpa.

Although these abodes have their respective bases, the manifestation of the teaching is without fixed direction or limit. In essence, every mote of dust contains Buddha-fields and every hair-pore accommodates the multitudes of the Dharma-realm; within a single kṣaṇa, they respond to the ten directions with universal pervasiveness, manifesting physical bodies that are perceived by all according to their individual faculties.
This chapter must follow because it clarifies the sphere of the Bodhisattva’s sustaining, gathering, and transforming activities.

Second, regarding the explanation of the subject who preaches the Dharma: it clarifies the Bodhisattva’s practice of gathering, transforming, and sustaining, as this is the sovereign activity of the Mind-King that accords with wisdom.

He causes the Bodhisattva Mind-King to expound this chapter on the "Abiding Place. This is to clarify, in general, that because the function of wisdom arises from one's own mind-king, once one has perfected the patience through the practices of Samantabhadra, all such states are termed the "Mind-King"; it clarifies that one thereby attains mastery over the world and does not conflict with phenomena.

Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: "Caitika Mountain" (Zhiti Shan) means "Pure Faith" (Jingxin), as those who behold this mountain are able to give rise to pure faith.
"Vaiśālī City" means "Extensive" (Guangbo), because it is the most vast among the cities of Central India; it is also called "City of Vast Splendor" (Guangyan Cheng).
The city of Mathurā is here translated as "Peacock City" (Mayūra-pura) and is also named "Dense Canopy" (Ghanavyūha); both names were established based on ancient events.
The city of Kujinana is also called Kujinana.

Regarding "Juchen" (俱陳): this is translated here as "large basin. He kept water in a large basin as if it were a pond, and constantly practiced the methods of the Immortals by its side. He regularly preached the *Hu Jing Jing* (Sūtra on Protecting Purity) and the *Yang Sheng Jing* (Sūtra on Nourishing Life) for others.
The disciples of later generations all took their teacher’s dharma-name as their surname; thus, the city is named after this [teacher].
The Mucilinda Cave—translated here as "Liberation"—is the name of a dragon.
Linta is translated here as "Place" (sthāna), so named because there was a dragon in this location who attained liberation upon hearing the Dharma.
Mālava is untranslated.
The country of Bīja (Bhīṣmaka) has not yet been translated [into Chinese].
Zhendan (China), also called Zhina, is further termed Zhendan; this is translated as "contemplation" (*sīlù*).
It is named for the fact that the people of this country are characterized by much contemplation and deliberation; it is this country of Han.
Nārāyaṇa is translated here as Jiānláo (Firm and Solid).
The kingdom of Shule is correctly called Kharaśūtra; in this region, the name is abbreviated and simply referred to as Shule.
The kingdom of Kāśmīra—formerly called Jibin—is translated here as "Whose Entry.
In ancient times, before this kingdom was established, there was a great dragon lake to which no one dared to approach.
Later, there was an Arhat who, seeing that the location was magnificent and suitable for habitation, requested from the dragon a space as large as one knee.
The dragon granted his request; the Arhat then transformed his body to become vast, and his knee gradually filled the entire pond.
The dragon, trusting his words, abandoned the place and departed.
The Arhat then used his supernatural powers to dry up the water, allowing the common people to dwell there and establish their houses and dwellings.
The multitude all said:
"Were it not for our holy teacher, who among us would have been able to enter this place?
For this reason, they established its name based on these words.
That country is situated on the northern border of North India, adjacent to the kingdom of Gandhāra.
Gandhāra is translated here as "Holder of the Earth" (Chí dì), because many sages and saints resided in this country, and it was not subject to invasion by other nations.
It is further said that *gandha* means "fragrance" and *lā* means *dhāra*, which here signifies "pervasive.
This is because fragrant scents abound and pervade this country.
It lies between the two regions of Central India to the north and North India to the south.
The Śāṃbara Cave is so named because it is situated near many trees called *śāṃbara*, which are fragrant flowering trees; it is named after them.
This section, in its general purport, clarifies the bodhisattva’s practice of sustaining and maintaining the Three Jewels through the gathering of sentient beings without interruption.
By citing this single Jambudvīpa as an illustration, it is shown that the lands of the ten directions and all other Jambudvīpas are to be understood in the same way.
To the above, the third dhyāna assembly of the Buddha’s Flower is added, making seven assemblies in total.

Including the assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance from the "Leaving the World" chapter and the assembly in the Jeta Grove from the "Dharma Realm" chapter, these constitute ten assemblies in total.

The "Chapter on the Inconceivable Buddha," the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks and Signs of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies," the "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks," the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra," the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata," and the "Chapter on Transcending the World."
Chapter Thirty-Three: The Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddha. In preparing to explain this chapter, four sections are established:

first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; third, the explanation of the speaker who expounds the Dharma; and fourth, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the title of this chapter: this chapter derives its name from the three karmas of the Tathāgata—body, speech, and mind.
Why is it called the "Inconceivable Buddha"?
Because it cannot be reached by the conceptualizations of ordinary consciousness, it is inconceivable.
Because it cannot be reached by the names of emotional consciousness, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
Since the mind of conceptualization is termed "thought" (*citta*), it is a state of grasping; therefore, it is called "meaning" (*artha*).
"Name" (*nāma*) and "discourse" (*vāda*) are worldly conventions; thus, to speak of "the measure of meaning and names" is a false calculation.
The mind cannot reach it; when emotions cease and consciousness is extinguished, one acts according to the function of wisdom.

This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s function of wisdom is not something known by the deluded thoughts and deliberations of the conscious mind. It is not that emotions have ceased while conceptualization remains; rather, only when wisdom is quiescent does it manifest. This must be manifested through the power of practicing the samādhi of skillful means.
When consciousness ceases and the delusions of the mind are stilled, correct wisdom manifests; this is termed "inconceivable.

Second, regarding the purpose of this chapter: since the preceding chapter explained the appropriateness of the Bodhisattvas' dwelling places for gathering and sustaining sentient beings, this chapter clarifies the wisdom capable of such transformation; therefore, it is titled "The Inconceivability of the Buddha."

This is not something produced by the measurement of emotional consciousness; rather, it functions through the pervasive nature of wisdom. It responds to phenomena without deliberate effort; thus, this chapter has come forth.

Regarding the third explanation, concerning the master who preaches the Dharma: the Bodhisattva who preaches the Dharma is named Padmagarbha (Blue Lotus Treasury). This clarifies that the Bodhisattvas of the preceding chapter have attained the Dharma and perfected patience, having gained mastery over the mind, and are therefore called "Mind-Kings."

This clarifies that fundamental wisdom is perfect and luminous; it is called the "blue lotus" because it is pure and unstained. Since this perfect and luminous fundamental wisdom can give rise to the various forms of differentiated wisdom, it is named the "Treasury."

The address to the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha clarifies that it is based on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to instruct through discriminative wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), thereby manifesting the perfection of signs.

While in the Three Vehicles it is said that one first attains fundamental wisdom which takes the ultimate truth as its object, and subsequently attains discriminative wisdom which takes the conventional truth as its object—in this One Vehicle, attainment is simultaneous and identical, for there is no distinction of the three periods of time or of priority and sequence.

The Bodhisattva Blue Lotus Treasury addressed the Bodhisattva Lotus Treasury, explaining this inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata, as well as the inconceivability of his body, eyes, ears, nose, and so forth, because of the mastery of wisdom over phenomena.

The intent of this chapter is to clarify that by means of the fundamental wisdom of the sovereign mind-king, one explains the wisdom of differentiation; this is because it constitutes the great sovereign function of the Buddha’s own work in teaching and transforming sentient beings.

For this reason, within this assembly, there are eight chapters of scripture from the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*Asaṃkhyeya*) to the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Abhyudgama*), as they collectively discuss the mental practices and principles pertaining to the stage of Buddhahood.

Because the distinctions of the preceding five stages share the same ultimate destination, they do not shift from the essence of the thirteen samādhis—the universal radiance wisdom—and yet there exist these eight categories of Dharma gates and this entire collection of sūtras.
All [the names] are established as Bodhisattva titles based on the Buddha’s own wisdom and virtues, so that his teachings may be easily understood.
Fourth, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning: this chapter of the sutra is divided into thirty-five sections.
The first three sections consist of the questions, the Buddha’s empowerment, and the benefits obtained by the blue lotus;
the latter thirty-two sections constitute the answers.

In the first part, from "At that time" down to "How inconceivable," there are six lines of scripture clarifying how the assembly of bodhisattvas conceived the thought to ask the Buddha about ten kinds of inconceivabilities.

The second section, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "the skillful means of the Buddha-dharma," consists of four and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies the portion in which the Tathāgata empowers the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha by means of ten dharmas.

The third section, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Blue Lotus Treasury" down to "addressing the Bodhisattva Lotus Treasury, saying: 'O Son of the Buddha,'" consists of six lines of scripture. This clarifies how the Bodhisattva Blue Lotus Treasury, having received the Buddha’s empowerment, intends to answer the tenfold dharmas previously inquired about by the assembly of bodhisattvas through ten kinds of sovereign wisdom.

The fourth section, from "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have immeasurable abodes" down to "the ultimate dharma free from all obstructions," consists of five lines of scripture. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha universally enumerates ten kinds of immeasurable abodes of all Buddhas, providing a general response to the ten types of questions posed by the great assembly.

The following section encompasses the ten kinds of infinite abodes, totaling thirty-two types of infinite, universal, all-pervasive, and unobstructed gates—both general and specific, identical and different, involving formation and disintegration, and characterized by sovereign Indra’s net—to answer the ten previous questions regarding the inconceivable dharmas of the Buddha.
Within these thirty-two kinds, they interpenetrate and pervade one another like Indra’s net.
Within these Dharma gates, there are three hundred and twenty types in terms of their numerical enumeration, which answer the ten preceding questions.
Within these three hundred and twenty methods of the Indra-net of mutual interpenetration, the inconceivable, inexhaustible, and infinitely layered infinity of the Buddhas is revealed.
The following section inherently contains ten dharmas, as is clearly evident from the sutra itself; there is no need for further detailed analysis.

The general meaning of this chapter is to clarify that through progressive cultivation, one reaches a state where the activities of one's own three karmas—body, speech, and mind—and their functional applications become vast and great, thereby realizing the vast and great functional application of the Buddha’s three karmas.

Because a single karmic action responds to ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a million, and so forth—immeasurable applications of the three types of karma; and because each of those three types of karma responds to thirty, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a million, and so forth; and because above each of these ten kinds of infinite and immeasurable threefold karma, there respond to thirty, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a million, and so forth—inexpressible and immeasurable karmic applications.

The remaining two sections each possess ten, one hundred, one thousand, ten thousand, and one million immeasurable [categories], clarifying that the karmic functions elucidated by the three karmas do not depart from the two truths.

Within each of the ten dharmas of the two gates—Ultimate and Conventional—the body, speech, and wisdom constitute the essence, while the remaining seven are the functional applications of these three karmas.
The Bodhisattva Padmagarbha answers the ten preceding questions with thirty-two types of responses; this is because within each individual response there are ten kinds of inexhaustible dharmas.

This clarifies that because the true and conventional dharmas are fully perfected within the threefold activity of the fruit of Buddhahood, the Buddha is titled the "Unsurpassed Honored One Among Two-legged Beings.
This explains that the three types of karmic activity and the two wisdoms are all-pervasive, universally encompassing all phenomena.

The blue lotus is true wisdom (*tathatājñāna*), and the lotus treasury is conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); by means of these two wisdoms—true and conventional—he himself proclaims the threefold activity of his own vast, sovereign, and inconceivable gateways.

Regarding the "capital city of a human king": the city where the king resides and the territory under his jurisdiction constitute the capital (*du*), while all other areas are considered districts (*yi*).

Regarding the "palace": the chambers where he dwells, stays, and sleeps are the palace (*gong*); the hall where he administers the state according to the Dharma and arranges the exposition of the True Dharma is the hall (*dian*).

The *piśāca* belongs to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*); here it is translated as "one who devours the vital essence of humans," and is under the jurisdiction of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the East.
*Dhṛtarāṣṭra* means "Holder of the Nation" (*chíguó*); he is so named because he protects and sustains the land.
Gandharva—here called "Seeker of Fragrance"—is a deity of music, and is likewise governed by this king.

Just as all world-systems and lands, all Buddhas, and all sentient beings appear within a single pore of the body or within a single atom, and all dwell therein performing the work of Buddhahood, so too do deluded attachments entirely cease; such is the realm of wisdom alone.
It manifests only through the power of samādhi and cannot be sought by ordinary consciousness.
The Dharma is always thus; yet, it is only because of deluded attachments that one is self-obstructed.
This is as previously explained in the "Flower Treasury" chapter regarding the seeds of worlds and so forth.
The remainder is fully contained within the text itself.

Chapter Thirty-Four: The Ocean of Marks and Signs of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the explanation of this chapter, it is divided into three sections:
First, the intent of the chapter; second, the explanation of the master who preaches the Dharma; third, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning. Regarding the first, the intent of the chapter:

it clarifies that the preceding chapter explained how the three karmas and two wisdoms of the Buddha himself enter the inconceivable limit, pervading everywhere in vastness and infinity to benefit sentient beings. This chapter follows because it concerns the body within which the three karmas enter the inconceivable wisdom; thus, this chapter appears.

Second, regarding the explanation of the Dharma-master who can preach the teaching: it clarifies that this ocean of marks is accomplished through the retribution of practice. Samantabhadra is that practice; he, in turn, causes the practitioner to personally proclaim the fruit of the merit resulting from their own practice and retribution.
Third, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning: this chapter of the sutra is divided into ninety-nine sections.

The first section, from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" down to "all the oceans of marks," consists of one and a half lines of scripture; it is the initial general presentation of the Tathāgata’s bodily marks as being as vast and numerous as the ocean.
The second section provides a brief exposition of ninety-seven kinds of marks of a Great Man, divided into ninety-seven segments.
At the very end, there is a general description of marks as numerous as the atoms within ten lotus-treasury worlds, serving as a comprehensive conclusion.

From "At that time" onwards, there are ninety-nine sections of scripture in total; because they take as their subject the adornments of the ocean of marks, numbering as many as the atoms in ten lotus-treasury worlds, this is titled the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies."

The general purport of this chapter of the sutra elucidates the three types of karmic functions—body, speech, and wisdom—which are vast and limitless, benefiting all sentient beings through the auspicious signs and practices of superior rebirth and merit.

As when first raising [the hand] to the crown of the head, there is the mark of a Great Man adorned with thirty-two jewels; among these marks of a Great Man is one named "Illuminating All Directions," which universally emits immeasurable nets of great light.

Regarding "adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels": first, thirty-two kinds of jewels are clarified; this clarifies that the three types of karmic functions constitute the general characteristic of the ten thousand virtues.

The two kinds of jewels are the two wisdoms; they clarify that the three karmas and two wisdoms of the Tathāgata are the foundation for cultivating all merits. Because there is no ocean of myriad roots of goodness that does not take these three karmas and two wisdoms as its essence, the fruits initially realized are presented with these at the forefront.
Furthermore, because it serves to adorn the head of the Tathāgata, the Sūtra states:

"Within it is a mark of greatness called 'Illuminating All Directions' (*sarvadik-prabhāsvara*). Here, "directions" (*dik*) refers to the Dharma, for it is the Dharma by which fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) becomes differentiated wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).

"Universally emitting immeasurable nets of great light" refers to the manifestation resulting from the retribution of providing teachings according to the faculties of all sentient beings within the context of differentiated wisdom; it is termed a "net of light" by way of its cause.
Regarding "adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels": all karmic fruits and the marks of merit obtained as retribution are adorned by these two types of wisdom.
The hair being "jeweled and all-pervading" clarifies that he takes birth as a reward for governing beings with wisdom and circulating everywhere to provide universal protection.
The hair being "jeweled, soft, and dense" indicates that his compassionate softness accords with the faculties of sentient beings to rescue them, thereby fulfilling his karmic reward.

The statement that "each and every one emits the light of mani-jewels, filling all boundless worlds and manifesting the Buddha-body with its perfect form and marks" clarifies that because the various differentiated wisdoms arising from fundamental wisdom give rise to differentiated practices that are purely clean and free of defilement, the pure light of mani-jewels obtained as a result of maturation manifests the Buddha-body in its entirety.

Because these two types of wisdom are purely refined and unimpeded, all objective realms of retribution collectively constitute the functional activity of wisdom; therefore, they are all identical to the body.
Regarding these three karmas, there is one [type] of retribution and ten [types] within each, making thirty [types] across the three karmas.

The two wisdoms (jñāna) have twenty [attributes] each; collectively, these thirty-two kinds of precious functions adorn the hair on the crown of the head, extending throughout both this crown and the body.

To briefly enumerate the ninety-seven marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) clarifies that, based on the two wisdoms of the ultimate and conventional truths, one purifies the three karmas and practices the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) and the ten perfections (pāramitā). These are able to purify all nine grades of afflictions within the triple world, thereby constituting the function of wisdom. Because wisdom is pure, all resultant fruits are also pure; because wisdom is unimpeded and sovereign, all resultant fruits are also sovereign.

Regarding the nine grades of afflictions: there is one grade in the desire realm; in the form realm there are four dhyānas and in the formless realm there are four dhyānas—thus there are eight grades in these two upper realms; together with the one grade in the desire realm, they constitute nine grades in total.

Those who are able to awaken to this immediately employ the two types of wisdom, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the ten pāramitās through skillful means to benefit themselves and others; by perfecting the practices of Samantabhadra, they fulfill these ninety-seven marks.

Because the skillful means of the ten pāramitās initiate the functional application of sovereign conduct within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the triple world, one accomplishes the practice-gates of the ten pāramitās upon each of the nine grades of afflictions, thereby forming the ninety kinds of marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Because the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) serve as superior aids that clarify the skillful means, they accomplish the sevenfold penetration.

By means of these seven factors of enlightenment and the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*), which are the skillful practices that aid the path, they assist in manifesting the two wisdoms—ultimate and conventional—from the nine grades of afflictions, thereby bringing great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to fulfillment.
Upon each category of affliction, ten modes of practice are established, resulting in ten kinds of manifested signs.
These nine and ten are correlated with the ten pāramitās, and the seven kinds are correlated with the seven factors of enlightenment.

Regarding the marks numbering as many as the atoms within ten lotus-treasury worlds: these are assigned to the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional, the three karmas, and the universal pervasion of the practice of Samantabhadra.
Question: From which teaching does this assignment originate?
Answer: All the dharma-gates contained in this sutra arise solely from its own teaching; no other sutras can accord with these dharma-gates.
What constitutes its own teaching?
Answer: This is because Samantabhadra represents the Buddha’s own practice; he causes that very practice to explain the marks obtained as the fruition of that practice.
As for the practitioner of Samantabhadra, they do not depart from the two wisdoms of the ultimate and conventional, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the ten pāramitās.
However, by means of names one knows the teaching; by means of the teaching one knows practice; and by means of practice one subdues delusions.
When delusions are extinguished and retribution is perfected, one realizes that what is produced through cause and effect is itself the teaching.

One must not cite the practice-gates of the three vehicles from other provisional teachings as examples for the causes, effects, and retributive attainments cultivated here; rather, one should understand their meaning by correlating them with the number of light rays emitted, the names of the bodhisattvas, and even the names of the seats mentioned in the preceding chapters.

When a Buddha practices the conduct of Samantabhadra, he does not depart from the afflictions of the three realms and nine stages to establish the gates of compassion and wisdom; rather, all the causes and fruits of his retributive birth are achieved within the nine grades of afflictions of the three realms as a superior practice of wisdom. Because he attains sovereign conduct that transcends the three realms, he acquires the superior karmic retribution that surpasses the three realms.
By this standard, one can clearly understand the Buddha’s intention, which is precisely the teaching of the sutra.

All subsequent characteristics take these three karmas, two wisdoms, seven factors of enlightenment, and ten pāramitās as their essence. Furthermore, by combining the seven factors of enlightenment with nine pāramitās to form a single wisdom-pāramitā, this wisdom-pāramitā constitutes the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because the seven factors of enlightenment and the nine pāramitās constitute their practice, they obtain as a karmic reward the ninety-seven marks of a great man.

As for the marks of a great man numbering as many as the atoms within ten lotus-treasury worlds, these are obtained as the reward for the conduct of Samantabhadra, through which their discerning wisdom and great compassion are perfected throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Regarding these two preceding and succeeding explanations, their meaning applies to either one.

From here on, the various characteristics concern the arising of the function of great compassion based on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while manifesting in accordance with the retribution-born [wisdom] of differentiated wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*); this is self-evident from the text itself.
As the Sūtra says, "the *kanapu* is accomplished," the meaning clarifies that the three folds of the neck's lines are accomplished as a decorative knot (*yingjie*).
It is said that in the Western Regions there is a fruit called the *kanapu*, which is red in color and forms three-fold lines; this is used as a comparison.

"Clouds stored within Mount Meru" clarifies the mark of the Tathāgata’s upper right canine tooth as a great person; its precious flames rise high and far, resembling the form of Mount Sumeru. Chapter Thirty-Five:
The Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks (Anuvyañjana). In order to explain this chapter, four sections are established:

first, an explanation of the title; second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; third, an explanation of the master who proclaims the teaching; and fourth, an explanation of the meaning according to the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the title of this chapter: Why is it named "The Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks"?

It clarifies that the preceding chapter already explained how the Ocean of Ten Physical Marks adorns the body with as many oceans of marks as there are atoms in ten *padma-kośa* worlds. This chapter, however, focuses on the merit of the non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) of each individual mark within that ocean of physical marks. Since these marks are achieved through the retribution of practice and constitute the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), and since they form radiance by means of the principle and wisdom of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that accords with such practice, the title of this chapter is established accordingly.
By means of the wisdom of the sublime principle that destroys afflictions through following practice, one brings to fruition the light of the marks of retribution.

Second, regarding the purpose for the arrival of this chapter on "Explanation": it clarifies that the marks of the Great Man in the preceding chapter arise as retribution obtained from the Tathāgata’s practices; therefore, it is made for Samantabhadra to speak, because the conduct of Samantabhadra is the conduct of all Buddhas.

These minor marks (*anuvyañjana*) are the radiance of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Dharma-body; they take the non-substantiality, the absence of essence, and the absence of characteristics as their merit and serve as radiance. They are able to bring great benefit to sentient beings by using formless substance and essence-less nature to illuminate those with whom they have a karmic connection. Just as the sound of the formless celestial drum preaches the Dharma to bring about liberation, this chapter must be included here.

Although principle and practice are non-dual and constitute a single essence, there must nevertheless be a sequential order based on the distinctions between the realization of fruits and the benefiting of sentient beings.

Third, regarding the explanation of the master who proclaims the teaching: it clarifies that such wondrous principle is the fruit; since the "Precious Hand" signifies the meaning of guidance and reception, it symbolizes the use of the wondrous wisdom and nature-light of the Dharma-body to guide and receive all sentient beings; therefore, this chapter is established.
For what reason does the Tathāgata himself teach this chapter?

It is to clarify two types of ignorance within the state of Buddhahood: first, ignorance regarding the vastness of the numerical categories of dharmas; second, ignorance regarding the merits of the minor marks (*anuvyañjana*) and the radiance. These two dharmas are beyond the reach of the wisdom of bodhisattvas and are only fully clarified upon the attainment of the perfection of Buddhahood.

Because the Dharma-body of principle and wisdom serves as the non-reliant essence for practice, thereby reaching the conditions of deluded sentiment, the marks of merit realized within that practice belong to the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
Thus, Samantabhadra’s own practice of retribution-birth leads him to personally explain the final fruit of his own practice of retribution.

The "Chapter on the Incalculable" concerns the vastness of numerical phenomena, while the "Chapter on the Merits of the Radiance of the Minor Marks" concerns the merits of the very nature of the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body, which are without self-nature and without dependence. These two dharmas are neither attained through conditioned practice nor reached by the scope of Samantabhadra’s conduct; rather, they serve as the basis for such conduct. Therefore, these represent the dharma at the conclusion of the stage of Buddhahood when Samantabhadra’s practices are fulfilled. For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of them himself, clarifying that he is teaching the dharma-gate of his own stage from within that very stage, so that future learners will not be confused.

This chapter clarifies that within the principle of the signless nature of the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body, the dharmas that benefit sentient beings consist of the merits of the Radiant Heaven’s celestial drum—a formless object whose resonance proclaims the teaching of the signless, wondrous principle of the Dharma-body, thereby enabling one to suddenly ascend to the ten stages and achieve the merit of being free from defilement.
This is because it is not attained by the convergence of great vows, wisdom, compassion, and the myriad practices of other lower stages; rather, it is spoken by the Tathāgata from his own station.

Although the fruit of practice and the fruit of wisdom are not distinct, the distinctions of stages are established according to the Dharma so that the principles may be clear, enabling those who resolve to practice to understand them without confusion.

This clarifies that the Dharmakāya and fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) do not belong to that which is produced through the cultivation of conditioned practices; they consist solely of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).

One must rely upon this fundamental wisdom, augmenting it with the power of Samantabhadra’s great vows and cultivating it through harmonious dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), always taking fundamental wisdom as the essence of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Although this Dharmakāya and fundamental wisdom are augmented by the ten pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four means of integration, and the four immeasurables—practices for accomplishing the benefit of sentient beings—the fundamental wisdom and Dharmakāya possess no intrinsic nature and thus cannot undergo formation or destruction; rather, they serve as the essence of liberation from all conditioned activities and vows, characterized by non-attachment, the absence of afflictions, and freedom from the karma of the three realms.

In this chapter, it is clarified that these qualities of the minor marks (*anuvyañjana*) function in accordance with practice so as not to lose their own fruit, extensively benefiting sentient beings; because these constitute the constant Buddha-fruit of all bodhisattva practices, the Tathāgata himself has spoken of them.
If this fruit of wisdom and virtue did not exist, all conditioned practices would be impermanent.
Like the essence of space, it constitutes the very substance of all sentient beings; yet, space is not produced through cultivation.
Fourth, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning: within this section, the text is divided into thirteen parts.
First, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "and [they] became his retinue," there are three lines of scripture which clarify the presentation of the essence and function of the light.

The second section, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "having passed away there, they are reborn in this heaven," consists of eight lines of scripture. It clarifies that when the Tathāgata was in Tuṣita Heaven, he emitted the wondrous light of the non-conditioned purity of the Dharma-body’s subtle principle and wisdom, whereby those in the hells obtained benefit; this is the portion concerning the cause announced by the celestial drum.

The third section, beginning from "O Son of the Buddha, beneath the Bodhisattva’s feet are wheels with a thousand spokes" and extending to "entering the Samādhi of the Seal of Non-reliant Wisdom," consists of forty-two and a half lines of scripture. This portion clarifies how sentient beings in the evil realms, upon being illuminated by the light, relinquish their retribution and are reborn in the heavens; it is the section on the Dharma Drum preaching the Dharma.

The fourth section, from "At that time, the sons of gods heard this sound" down to "yet they could not see," consists of four and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies how the sons of gods arose to make offerings and proceeded to their celestial palaces, yet were unable to see the portion concerning Vairocana Bodhisattva.

The fifth section, from "At that time, there was a son of heaven" down to "the womb of Queen Māyā," comprises approximately two lines of scripture; it clarifies the portion concerning how the son of heaven informs the assembly of devas regarding the Bodhisattva’s descent into the human realm.

The sixth section, from "At that time, the sons of the gods observed with their divine eyes" down to "repenting and eliminating all obstructive faults and evils," consists of fourteen and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the portion concerning how the sons of the gods desire to go to the human realm to make offerings, and how the sound of the celestial drum informs them that the Bodhisattva Vairocana is without coming or going, while simultaneously exhorting them to resolve upon bodhicitta and repent for their transgressions and evils.

The seventh section, beginning from "At that time, the sons of the gods" and continuing down to "all evil deeds are completely purified," consists of twenty-seven and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies how the celestial drum expounds for the sons of the gods the Bodhisattva’s repentance and removal of evil deeds, leading to the realization of the non-arising of karma.

The eighth section, from "When this Dharma was being taught" down to "has not yet manifested even a small portion of the power of the Stainless Samādhi," consists of eleven and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies the section on how the sons and daughters of the gods obtained benefits.

The ninth section, from "At that time, those devaputras" down to "roots of goodness as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River," consists of twelve lines of scripture. It clarifies how the devaputras offered incense and flowers as worship, and how sentient beings who smelled the fragrance had their eighty-four thousand afflictions completely purified, thereby accomplishing the pure roots of goodness of the Sovereign Radiance of the Fragrant Banner Cloud.
If there are sentient beings who see his canopy, they plant roots of goodness equal to a portion of the merit of a *suvarṇajāla-cakravartin* king as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River.

From the tenth section, "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this position of a *cakravartin* king," down to "teaching and transforming sentient beings," there is one and a half lines of scripture that clarify the extent of the sphere of influence and the scope of the transformative guidance of the *suvarṇajāla-cakravartin* stage.

The eleventh section, from "O Son of the Buddha, it is as if there were a bright mirror world" down to "one will certainly attain rebirth in that Buddha-land," consists of four lines of scripture that clarify the division on obtaining benefit by hearing the name, using the Tathāgata Candraprabha as an analogy.

The twelfth section, from "The Bodhisattva’s Abiding" down to "Accomplishing such a pure fleshly eye," consists of nine lines of scripture which clarify that if one encounters the light of this Golden Net Universal Monarch, one immediately attains the portion of the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages.

Thirteenth: From "O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were a person" down to "there has not yet been," these twenty-one lines of scripture clarify the immeasurable extent of the vast realm perceived by the physical eyes of this Wheel-Turning King with the Pure Golden Net.
Fourth, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning: within this chapter, the thirteen sections of text are organized according to three gates:

first, explaining the cause of the light and from where it comes; second, the causes and conditions by which those touched by the light are affected; and third, the causes and conditions by which the celestial drum is able to preach the Dharma.

Regarding the first explanation of the cause of the light and from where it comes: it arises from the self-nature of the Tathāgata’s own intrinsically pure Dharmakāya, from the fundamental wisdom that abides nowhere, and from the self-nature of pure merit; because it is able to accomplish the primary and secondary marks without depending on anything else, it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of the Light of the Anuvyañjanas."

This radiance is shared equally by all sentient beings; yet, unless it is aided, uplifted, and manifested through the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, the practices and vows of Samantabhadra will not be made manifest.

Without this essence of radiance, one could not achieve the infinite great function of the Dharma-realm; therefore, this sutra is titled the *Sutra on the Mutual Adornment of Enlightenment and Practice*.
Having thus brought these two practices to completion, each then manifests its own merit.

As for the marks of a Great Being described in the preceding chapter, because they were accomplished through the practices of Samantabhadra, it is therefore Samantabhadra who is now asked to explain them.

This chapter on the light of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) is the light of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) that is the Buddha’s own fruition—the unconditioned *dharmakāya* which abides nowhere. This was spoken by the Buddha himself.
However, in relying solely upon the Teacher to grasp the intent of the scripture, one should understand that within this manifestation of light, the lights of the secondary marks are immeasurable.
Now, based on this chapter, I shall briefly cite three points.

First, it initially mentions that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) named "Perfect King" (*Pūrṇarāja*); this collectively presents how the fundamental wisdom—which is without dependence and without intrinsic nature—is able to universally illuminate with sovereignty, and is thus named "Perfect King."

To distinguish this from the specific functions within the light, it is said that a great radiance emerges from these secondary marks (anuvyañjana), called "Blazing," and that the specific function of this light is able to destroy delusion.
Regarding the statement that seven million asaṃkhyeya rays of light constitute the retinue: this clarifies that the functions are fully equipped according to the faculties [of beings].
The total number of seven hundred approximates the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga), which bring rest to the sufferings of the six realms.
That it is "seven hundred" is because it is the greatest number; it is because they all cause the ten stages of the path within the One Vehicle to be initiated.
For this light is the light of the fruit of Buddhahood itself, and all those reached by the light rely upon the fundamental source.
Furthermore, regarding the seven hundred thousand [practices] prior to the eighth stage, which involve both practice and development:
"ten thousand" refers to the ten thousand practices;
"asamkhyeya" signifies that the luminous essence is complete and the faculties are universally pervasive.

Next, when he was a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita Heaven, he emitted a great light called King of Banners, which illuminated the hell-beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields. Their manifold sufferings were stilled, and they attained ten kinds of purity in their eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind. They cast off their bodies in the hells and were reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven; there, hearing the sound of celestial drums, they were taught the Dharma, attained the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement, and gave rise to the path of the ten stages.

This clarifies that for those whose power of cultivation during the ten stages of faith and understanding was not firm, and who fell into evil realms due to negligence, their suffering ceases upon encountering this light, and their three karmas are restored to their original state.
This clarifies the attainment of the fruit through three lifetimes.
In the first lifetime, one cultivates the ten minds of faith and understanding, yet because the mind is not focused and single-minded, one commits various evil deeds;
in the second lifetime, one is born into the evil realms and dwells within hell.

In the third birth, they receive the touch of light and their suffering ceases; they are born in Tuṣita Heaven, where the resonance of the celestial drum announces them, and they achieve the fruit of the tenth bhūmi.
These constitute the three births.

If, within this teaching, one gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment based on wisdom, seeking it with single-minded diligence and without slackening, and cultivates the concentration of skillful means with a mind free from negligence to enter the Buddha’s wisdom—thereby being born into the family of the Tathāgata as a true son of the Buddha—one is then said to have attained Buddhahood.

Just as the eldest son born of the chief queen of a wheel-turning monarch, though not yet occupying the throne, possesses the marks of a wheel-turning monarch and is the true lineage of a king, being in essence no different [from his father].

Thus, a bodhisattva at the first stage of the ten stages, having newly begun from the seed of faith to cultivate the concentration of skillful means, manifests their own correct wisdom and is born into the family of the Tathāgata.
Although they do not yet possess the supernormal powers of the divine feet, when they reach the rank of a Buddha, their true seed of wisdom will be no different from that of a Buddha.

From this point onward, through the cultivation and purification of the practices of a single lifetime, one enters into birth by transformation in accordance with right wisdom, attaining mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

It is like a person who, having cultivated the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*)—which are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)—through the actions of body, speech, and mind during a single lifetime, still attains rebirth in heaven and gains celestial supernormal powers as a result.

How much more so when right wisdom is manifest, and one realizes the Dharma-body, ceasing to commit evil and exclusively cultivating compassion—how could such a person not enter the transformation body of birth?

If one were to discuss this solely from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), then all within the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) is universally considered a transformation; awakening wisdom is itself the Buddha, as this does not depend on supernatural powers (ṛddhi), for such powers are merely provisional means (upāya) for benefiting sentient beings.

If one takes the meaning of "awakening" (*bodhi*) in its direct sense, wisdom (*jñāna*) constitutes correct awakening (*sambodhi*), while all other supernormal powers, the descent from heaven, and the attainment of Buddhahood are collectively subsumed under "practice" (*caryā*).
Now, having reached this chapter which clarifies the perfection of awakening and practice, the Buddha elucidates the two aforementioned types of light.

Regarding the one named King Light-Standard (Prabhāketu), this refers, for the time being, to the great function of the luminous penetration of delusions by means of the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya of the Buddha-fruit.
Without converging with this light of fundamental wisdom, there can be no prospect of attaining Buddhahood through any practice of the path.

Second, regarding the light of the thousand-spoked wheels beneath his feet called "Perfect Sovereignty": this clarifies that the light of the bodhisattva’s progressive preparatory practices constitutes his feet, thereby symbolizing the conduct he performs.
The constant emission of forty kinds of light signifies the accomplishment of the four stages prior to the [ten] faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, and ten dedications.

Among these, there is one light that accords with all the various desires and enjoyments of the six realms of existence, causing them all to be fulfilled. Even those in the Avīci Hell who undergo uninterrupted suffering, upon encountering this light, are all reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. There, the sound of the celestial drum preaches the Dharma; through this, they repent and eliminate their delusions, attaining the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement or the Seal of Non-reliant Wisdom.

This one light is the light that causes sentient beings in all six realms of existence to give rise to faith according to their faculties; the other three are the lights of the fulfillment of the fruits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) through the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).

The three stages of the Sages prior to the ten bhūmis represent the completion of the perfect integration of compassion, wisdom, vows, and practice; the ten bhūmis merely fulfill the merit of the ten practices preceding them and do not constitute a separate stage. For this reason, they emit only forty rays of light and do not emit fifty.
The fruit of no-effort is the Buddha’s own station, for it does not belong to the realm of conditioned practice.
The light beneath his feet signifies the stages of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten transferences of aspiration and conduct.
The ten stages (daśabhūmi) constitute the perfection of merit in terms of the Dharma, because they fulfill all prior vows.

Third, regarding the manifestation of immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers from a single minor mark (anuvyañjana) of light within the palm of the raised right hand: this symbolizes the "light of invitation," for the hand carries the meaning of beckoning and receiving.
This is because it is a skillful means that secretly accords with all the worlds of the three realms, and is not something known by worldly devas and humans or by those of the three vehicles.
Thus, these three kinds of light are cited as being sufficient to pervade all states of existence; the many other details need not be discussed.
Regarding the second point, as for the causes and conditions for being touched by the light:
the intent of the sutra clarifies that it is because one possessed faith in previous lives.
As the sutra says, "In the past, you drew near to many spiritual friends," which clarifies that the seeds of faith existed in former times.

"Although one has committed evil karma and been born in hell," because the seed of faith exists, light reaches their body; as the seed of the cessation of suffering remains, they are able to immediately resolve to cast off that body and be reborn in heaven.
If one lacks the seeds of faith from previous lives, even if light were to illuminate their body, they would neither perceive nor know it.

Regarding the third point—how the celestial drum can preach the Dharma—it is as the sutra says: "It is solely by the power of Vairocana’s samādhi and the majestic power of the Prajñāpāramitā that these sounds are produced."
"Approximately three conditions must converge for one to hear it:

first, the power of the Samādhi of the Bodhisattva Vairocana; second, the mastery of non-conceptual, wondrous wisdom within the Samādhi of Non-substantiality; and third, that sentient beings have previously planted the seeds of this great wisdom of the Dharma-body of Non-nature, thereby becoming capable of hearing such a sublime sound."

Regarding "delusion is eliminated and the Way is attained, like the stainless Samādhi": this refers to the essence of the wondrous principle of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*), which is devoid of center or periphery and possesses a nature like empty space. Its nature is inherently stainless; it is endowed with limitless wisdom and insight, and is naturally free from the notion of "mine. It must be manifested through the arousal of skillful means and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is exemplified by the Bodhisattva Dharmamati entering the "Samādhi of Immeasurable Skillful Means," as well as by Sudhana attaining the "Light of Wisdom that Recollects All Buddhas" atop Mount Śubhaśikhara. In all such cases, these are instances where the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is first revealed and manifested.

In this chapter, because the fulfillment does not depart from the initial stage, it returns to the Universal Radiance Hall to explain the ten stages of faith; by explaining these eleven chapters, the eleven stages, and the gateway to the fruit of Buddhahood, it expresses this meaning: that one achieves the fruit without departing from a single thought-moment and without being separated by even a single instant of time.

Regarding the samādhi of skillful means (*upāya-samādhi*): by resting in the nature of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one becomes naturally settled in vast openness; without gathering or grasping, the mind rests of its own accord. Thus, myriad delusions are naturally purified and the Way manifests of itself; only then can one employ various activities without losing their underlying principle.

However, it is only through the vows and practices of Samantabhadra that one can fully realize the gate of the unconditioned dharmadhātu dependent origination—the great functioning of compassion and wisdom—just as those who progress through the five stages above do.
As the Sūtra says: "Within the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch there are five hundred afflictions, and likewise five hundred afflictions without.

Those with a predominance of hatred are twenty-one thousand; those with a predominance of greed are twenty-one thousand; those with a predominance of delusion are twenty-one thousand; and those with equal proportions of these three are twenty-one thousand."
The total above amounts to eighty-four thousand.
Just as form, sound, smell, taste, and touch each have five aggregates, so too do the ten underlying afflictions (*anuśaya*) all take the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) as their primary basis.
One knows that form, sound, odor, taste, and touch are external, while feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and the mind are internal.
Just as the conditions are formed through the interaction of these internal and external mental objects, they are all capable of giving rise to the ten types of afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*).

Regarding form, sound, smell, taste, touch, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and the mind—both subject and object—they intersect with one another, resulting in ten types each for the internal and external.

Thus, these ten internal and external afflictions are each capable of giving rise to ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Consequently, there are five hundred afflictions for each of the internal and external objects of perception.

Due to the delusion regarding the mind and its objects, the internal and external mutually support one another: the internal five aggregates constitute the object, while the external five sense-objects give rise to the subjective perceiver. Through these two conditions—the internal and external, the subject and the object—the ten underlying afflictions (āśravas) continue without ceasing, extending even to eighty-four thousand varieties.
Thus, these ten proclivities (daśa-ānuśaya) are all formed based upon the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).

Within each individual proclivity there are one hundred; this is because the five aggregates within each of the ten proclivities are themselves formed by the five aggregates, resulting in one hundred within each aggregate. Thus, across the five aggregates, there are five hundred.
The five aggregates (skandhas) constitute the five sense objects (viṣayas), and within each sense object there are five hundred.

Taking the sense objects and aggregates as internal and external factors, they together total one thousand; when these are assigned to the seven consciousnesses (vijñānas), there are thus seven thousand.
Dividing these across the three periods of time, with seven times three making twenty-one, there are twenty-one thousand for each.
Thus, based on those in whom hatred, greed, or delusion predominates, as well as those in whom they are equal, there are twenty-one thousand for each category, totaling eighty-four thousand.
The remaining text is self-evident.

Just as within each of the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*) there are five internal and five external aggregates (*skandha*), when these ten afflictions intersect with one another, they total one hundred; and for each of these one hundred afflictions, there are five aggregates, resulting in five hundred.
Because the internal mind and external objects act as mutual primary and secondary factors, there are five hundred each for these internal and external aspects, totaling one thousand.

Since the *manas* and the six consciousnesses function through mutual causality, there are seven thousand afflictions; these are to be assigned according to the same principle as the dharmas mentioned previously.
Three times seven is twenty-one, which also amounts to twenty-one thousand.

If one considers this Dharma-gate, the wisdom of the principle of non-arising and the methods for repenting and eliminating transgressions taught by the Drum of Heaven are most excellent and most wondrous.

Those on the path of cultivation who have resolved their minds toward Bodhicitta may emulate this by means of recitation and mental attention; through the power of skillful means, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they should diligently contemplate and investigate, thereby attaining Buddhahood in a single kṣaṇa, just as described in this chapter.
Within this, the sequential integration of the Dharma gates is fully contained in this chapter.
For instance, all the spiritual friends encountered by the youth Sudhana declare: "I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Regarding the question, "How should I be taught to study the bodhisattva path? it clarifies that because *bodhi* (enlightenment) is without seeking, without cultivation, and without the three periods of time, one seeks only its practice.

Since *bodhi* is without cultivation, these marks of excellence (*anuvyañjana*) and the light of merit serve merely as illumination for practice, causing that practice to be without dependence, without cultivation, and without an agent. For all who resolve their minds [on enlightenment], they first cultivate the samādhi of skillful means and manifest it through this.

From within this principle, one should now apply the preparatory practice (*prayoga*); therefore, it is called "the gate of using the fruit to establish the cause" and "the gate of the cause being identical to the fruit.

Since there is no separate practice apart from the wisdom of the principle, one takes the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena as the means of cultivation; thus, one seeks only the Bodhisattva path.
This very practice is bodhi, for it is clear that following the practice involves no attainment.

Thus, because the conduct of Samantabhadra has not yet been perfected, one seeks the Bodhisattva path; yet since bodhi is without the three periods of time, all myriad practices are fully realized within a single kṣaṇa. Therefore, it is called the Buddha Vehicle (Buddhayāna).
This discourse directly addresses the realm of wisdom (*jñāna-viṣaya*), without distinguishing between the obstacles of the three periods of time, such as extension or brevity.

For both ordinary beings and those of the Three Vehicles, the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) and infinite eons are, within this teaching, the gateway to the non-transmigration of the realm of wisdom. This is because it is thus by nature, and because phenomena (*dharma*) are thus; it is not brought about by the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of a Buddha.
The mental views of those of the three vehicles perceive the supernatural powers of the Buddhas because they are deluded regarding the fact that the true Dharma is originally thus.

These eleven chapters within this Hall of Universal Radiance encompass the entirety of this section, as well as all of time—past and present without end—without shifting by even a hair’s breadth or a single thought.
One must practice with such faith and understanding, for this is called awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

It should be known that the ten stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the two positions of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimalā-bodhi*), are all collectively established based upon the principles of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences.
Chapter Thirty-Six: The Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra. In explaining this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to four sections:

first, the explanation of the chapter title; second, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; third, the explanation of the master who teaches the doctrine; and fourth, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the chapter title: why is it named "The Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra"?

It is because it clarifies that from the first assembly at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Tathāgata represents the fruit of Buddhahood, while the ten Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas and the assembly of bodhisattvas, gods, and others below them represent the Buddha’s practices of Samantabhadra.

In the second assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance, the ten Tathāgatas of the Ten Wisdoms—such as Immovable Wisdom Buddha and Unobstructed Wisdom Buddha—were taught to establish the ten stages of faith. This clarifies that one’s own mind is capable of believing that it is the Immovable Wisdom Buddha, which is the fundamental fruit of one's own mind, and that the same applies to the other nine.
Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattvas such as Awakening Head (Bodhi-mūrdhan) and Eye Head (Netra-mūrdhan), these ten "Head" Bodhisattvas, are the practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct performed by one's own body.

Through the successive stages of the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, and the eleventh ground, all the various sets of ten Buddha names and ten sets of Bodhisattva names, up to the infinite names of Buddhas and infinite names of Bodhisattvas, are all the cultivation toward the fruit of Buddhahood by means of one's own body and one's own mind.

From the "Universal Worthy Conduct" chapter up to this present "Chapter on Universal Worthy Conduct," these constitute one Buddha-fruit within one's own mind and one Universal Worthy conduct within one's own mind.
It is only upon reaching the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" that the essence and function of one's own Buddha-fruit—the wisdom and reality (*jñāna-dharmatā*)—are finally elucidated.

Within this "Appearance Chapter," the Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows to moisten the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head and emits light from his mouth to moisten Samantabhadra’s mouth; thereby, Mañjuśrī, who embodies the sublime wisdom of the *dharmakāya* of wisdom and reality, and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra engage in mutual dialogue regarding all the realms of the Tathāgata’s appearance. Only through this are one’s own sublime wisdom of wisdom and reality and the ocean-like conduct of Samantabhadra clarified, bringing the beginning and end of the cultivation toward the Buddha-fruit to ultimate perfection.
The entrustment and circulation are also contained within the "Chapter on Manifestation.
This is because the "Chapter on Transcending the World" concerns the constant path after the fruition of Buddhahood—the beginningless and endless conduct of Samantabhadra.

The "Dharmadhātu Chapter" is the Buddha’s eternal path of the *dharmadhātu*; because it constantly consists of the conduct of Samantabhadra subsequent to the fruit of Buddhahood, according to its meaning, it may also be categorized as benefiting others (*parārtha*).

The "Lokadhātu Chapter" represents the fulfillment of one's own path of practice; it consists purely of benefiting the world, for there is no world to be abandoned and no supramundane realm to be reached, as its fundamental purpose is the constant benefit of sentient beings through the conduct of Samantabhadra.
The remaining meanings will be further elucidated in subsequent chapters.

Because this chapter comprehensively covers the entire scope from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) up to the "Appearance" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*), encompassing the beginning and end of the single momentum as well as cause and effect, root and branch, it is established with this title.

Generally speaking, these eleven chapters of the sutra, beginning from this "Ten Samādhis" assembly, are collectively subsumed within the essence of the ten samādhis from beginning to end, as they do not transcend the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
This chapter is titled as such because it clarifies that within the stage of the Buddha’s fruition, one’s own practice of the conduct of Samantabhadra has been fulfilled.

Second, regarding the purpose for which this chapter appears: whereas the preceding chapter clarified that the luminosity of the nature-wisdom of the ultimate fruition benefits sentient beings, this chapter clarifies that the conduct of Samantabhadra is capable of benefiting them.
If there is wisdom-principle (prajñā) without practice, the wisdom-principle will not be perfected while remaining in the mundane world;
if there is practice without wisdom-principle, that practice has no means by which to transcend the mundane.
Therefore, only when the essence of wisdom-principle is thoroughly penetrated does one form the gate of non-dual mastery; for this reason, this chapter must follow.
Regarding the third explanation concerning the master who expounds the teaching: why is it that in this chapter, Samantabhadra is the master who expounds the teaching?

It is because the gateways of practice in this chapter represent the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s conduct; thus, Samantabhadra is made to speak for himself, clarifying the function of the wondrous principle of the fundamental wisdom of Samantabhadra’s Dharmakāya.

Because these two dharmas cannot be perfected when practiced in isolation, the light of the nature-wisdom of the *dharmakāya* is presented first, followed by the exposition of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
Fourth, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, this chapter of the sutra is divided into fifteen sections.

First, from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" down to "appeared in the world," there are five lines and a half of scripture. This clarifies that because sentient beings are far removed from the Buddha-way, the Buddha appears in the world; it is a brief exposition of a small portion of the realm described in the preceding chapter.

The second section, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "accomplishing one million gates of hindrances," consists of two and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies that although ordinary sentient beings may have great transgressions and evils, one has never seen even a single such fault; however, if one sees a single Bodhisattva harbor a mind of anger, it constitutes one million gates of hindrances.

The third section, from "What are the one million gates of hindrances? down to "accomplishing such one million gates of hindrances," consists of forty-four lines of scripture; it clarifies the initial portion of the one million gates of hindrances by citing one hundred representative gates of hindrance.

The fourth section, from "For what reason" onwards to "those who give rise to a mind of anger," consists of one and a half lines of scripture; it clearly concludes the preceding portion concerning not giving rise to a mind of anger toward other bodhisattvas.

From "Therefore, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas" down to "Sons of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should all resolve their minds to respectfully receive and uphold [this]," there are six sections of ten dharmas; their meaning is self-evident according to the scriptural text.
First, bodhisattvas who wish to swiftly fulfill all bodhisattva practices should diligently cultivate the ten factors of practice;
second, they will thereby be able to fully realize the ten factors of purity.
Third, one is able to fulfill the ten kinds of vast and great portions of wisdom.
Fourth, one attains the ten kinds of portions for universal entry.
Fifth, one abides in the ten kinds of supreme and wondrous portions of mind.
Sixth, one attains ten kinds of skillful wisdom (*kauśalya-jñāna*).
Above are ten sections of the sūtra. The eleventh section, from "For what reason?

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who upholds this Dharma" to "is entirely equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time," consists of three and a half lines of verse; it clarifies that by hearing this Dharma, one is exhorted to reverently accept and uphold it, thereby attaining the stage of swiftly becoming a Buddha through minor expedient means.

The twelfth section, from "At that time, by the Buddha's spiritual power" down to "in all worlds it was likewise," consists of eleven and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the division concerning the Dharma-offering, wherein the majestic resonance of the True Dharma causes the earth to shake in six ways and the heavens to raise clouds of offerings as an act of worship.

Thirteenth: From "At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha" to "In all worlds of the ten directions, it was likewise," there are ten and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the arrival of Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas from all places in the world of Universal Victory to serve as witnesses.

Section Fourteen: "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... and the following seven lines of scripture constitute the portion clarifying Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s observation of the assembly and his intent in reciting the verses.
Fifteenth, the section on formally presenting the meaning of the verses.

Regarding the fourth point, the explanation of the meaning according to the text: as previously stated, the preceding "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies" and the "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks" were brief expositions of only a small portion [of the teaching]. This is because those who are bound by wrong views and the fetters of afflictions (*kleśa*) are constantly associated with them; thus, they remain far removed from the path of the Tathāgata and do not know it.

The Tathāgata appears in the world to manifest for such beings; he briefly describes a small portion of the realm of merit, yet in reality, the Tathāgata neither arises nor passes away. Only those whose minds accord with the Path perceive this through their own wisdom-realm; they do not entertain views of Buddhas being born or passing into extinction. Rather, they personally employ the two gates of meditative concentration to purify the defilements of the mind, whereby the views of self and what belongs to self are extinguished, and wisdom accords with the ultimate realm.
If one possesses right view, what is there to emerge from or submerge into, what is there to be formed or destroyed, and what is there to be defiled or purified?
If one attains such equanimity of one's own mind—neither defiled nor purified—that is the arising of a Buddha;
to reckon in terms of "self" and "what belongs to self" constitutes the two views of self and extremes.
Perversion and doubt refer to the so-called four inversions: reckoning the impermanent as permanent, the selfless as having a self, the unsatisfactory as satisfying, and the impure as pure.
Wrong views consist of what are known as the eight wrongs: wrong mindfulness, wrong livelihood, wrong intention, wrong diligence, wrong concentration, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong wisdom.
Regarding "fetters and bonds," these refer to the fetters and bonds of the six sense bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Below this, one hundred gates of obstruction and a million gates of obstruction are explained as primary means to prevent practitioners on the path from giving rise to even a single thought of anger toward other bodhisattvas, as detailed in the sutra itself.
Those who cultivate the Way must exercise great caution.

When first initiating the mind to cultivate the Way as described above, one should only worry about the extinction of conceptual thoughts so that the Way may be realized; if the emotions remain and conceptual thoughts persist, seeking the Way through the view of a self will ultimately be incompatible with it.

One must rely on the wise to personally subdue arrogance and allow a spirit of reverence to penetrate to its depths; only then, through the two gates of meditative concentration and contemplation (*samādhi-vipaśyanā*), can one resolve the distinctions regarding the dhyānas of the two upper realms, as well as the meditative concentration and wisdom cultivated by śrāvakas, non-Buddhists, and bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings—each of these must be known individually. Only then will one recognize the True Dharma, and only then will the mind be free from the dualistic seeking of the "heterodox" and "orthodox," seeking instead the gate of discerning wisdom. Through the power of great vows, one expands great compassion and accomplishes the conduct of Samantabhadra.

If one seeks the Dharma with a thieving mind, fails to properly discipline the mind, and allows arrogance to increase, such that they give rise to even a single thought of anger or resentment toward another bodhisattva, they shall enter a hundred thousand gates of obstacles. As clearly explained in the sutras, they will encounter difficulties from malevolent spirits and evil ghosts; yet, because they possess a single portion of the mind seeking the Way, the power of their [karmic] retribution becomes so formidable as to be irresistible.
All who have resolved their minds [toward enlightenment] must guard themselves, practicing with humility and reverence according to the Dharma and seeking with single-minded resolve.
Furthermore, they should constantly recite and uphold this "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" to protect the three karmas, thereby enabling them to attain the state of a true sage (arhat).
As the Sūtra says, "the wisdom that knows the mental activities of all sentient beings" is called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

Because one is without a [discursive] mind of one's own, and because the obstructions between self and other are severed, one's own mind and the minds of all sentient beings are of one essence and non-dual.
