It is by means of this that one can know the minds of all sentient beings, for one's own mind and the minds of sentient beings are non-dual.

Even so is the wisdom that knows the profound and secret principles of all Buddha-dharmas; because one's own mind is devoid of the distinction between self and other minds, the sages and ordinary beings are of one principle and a single essence.
The sages and ordinary beings share the same principle and the same essence, because they fully know the mental phenomena of both sages and ordinary beings.
Since the minds of sages and ordinary beings are of one principle, the body is devoid of all views regarding internal and external.
Because there is no perception of internal or external, the boundless world and the realm of space are equal.
When one’s own mind is equal to the realm of space, there is then no distinction of large or small, far or near, nor any intermediate.
Since one's own mind has no size, distance, or intermediate space, wisdom is eternally pervasive throughout the worlds of the ten directions without coming or going.

Since wisdom is eternally pervasive throughout the worlds of the ten directions without coming or going, one is able to manifest form-bodies at will in accordance with the faculties [of sentient beings].
Since one is already able to manifest mastery over the physical body in accordance with the faculties, one should likewise possess mastery in preaching the Dharma in accordance with those faculties.

Since one is already able to possess mastery in preaching the Dharma in accordance with the faculties, one should likewise possess mastery in the mutual interpenetration of a single body and multiple bodies.

All the various dharmas of mastery described below should be cultivated in this same manner; through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, their nature is spontaneously integrated, and they are not objects known by the deluded thoughts of birth and extinction.

Thus, the nature of right wisdom—which is itself without mind, without thought, and without conceptualization—is inherently all-pervasive, yet it neither comes nor goes. In order to teach and transform all sentient beings according to the time and their faculties, it manifests the performance of all activities equal to those of sentient beings; yet these are entirely without an agent and have no location, for they function through the spontaneous employment of intrinsic wisdom.
Like an echo responding to a sound, it has no location or agent, and thus there is no coming or going.
From this point onward, all should be understood and cultivated according to this wisdom.
Regarding the three meanings of making offerings when the earth trembles:
First, the majestic resonance of the Dharma;
second, the joy and delight of all bodhisattvas upon hearing the Dharma;
third, as the sutra says: "Because the Dharma is thus."

As the Sūtra says: "One who upholds this Dharma shall swiftly attain Bodhi with little effort. This means that when the wisdom of non-thought and non-reliance manifests in a single thought-moment, that itself is Bodhi.

If, for example, from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields coming to this land and filling the ten directions, it would be because the practices of Samantabhadra have been fulfilled.
The exclamation "Excellent! Excellent! is made because the teaching of the Dharma is difficult to encounter.

That the Son of the Buddha is able to expound this most profound Dharma of the prediction of the great vows of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas clarifies that the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra are the Dharma of the perfection of wisdom, principle, and great compassion; for the culmination of the fruition marks the end of the practice, and this culmination of the fruition constitutes the most profound Dharma of the Buddhas' prediction.
This clarifies the practice of the Great Compassion of the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body, because within every atom are fully present the inexhaustible practices of the Buddhas and Samantabhadra.
As for the title "Profound Dharma-Buddha" and our all being of the same name "Samantabhadra," this clarifies that the practice of the Dharma is non-dual, and thus we share this identical name.

Those who have come from the world of Universal Excellence (Pǔshèng) under the Tathāgata Sovereign Universal Banner (Pǔcháng Zìzài) dwell in the Way with humility and harmony; thus, that world is named Universal Excellence.

Because they are able to shatter their own and others' pride as well as all afflictions, they are called "Banners" (Cháng). Since their enlightened wisdom and principle do not follow after objects to move, and their compassionate practices are layered and pervasive, it is named the Universal Excellence Banner (Pǔshèng Cháng).
Though dwelling within birth and death, one does not associate with defilement; this is called "mastery.
This name for the Buddha-world is a designation for the cause and effect of following practice.
That those who come to this land do so clarifies that they have ascended to the ultimate stage and reached this Dharma.

"By the Buddha's spiritual power, this Dharma is expounded in all places": the preceding section clarified the pervasiveness of physical action (*kāyakarma*), while this section clarifies the pervasiveness of verbal action (*vākkarma*); the details below may be understood according to the text.
As the sutra states, that which "seeks to reveal the bodhisattva practices" is the practice of Samantabhadra;
that which "seeks to explain the Tathāgata’s realm of awakening" is the fundamental wisdom of the natureless Dharmakāya.
If one wishes to speak of the realm of great vows, it is that which was initiated by Samantabhadra through the arousal of the vow of great compassion.

If one wishes to speak of the number of eons in all worlds, it is as described above: a single eon entering into all eons, all eons entering into a single eon, and a single thought-moment entering into all eons.
To clarify that the merit of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is not in vain, it is shown that he responds to the faculties [of beings] without missing the proper time.
To clarify that the roots of goodness planted will inevitably yield their fruit, it is shown that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas bring benefit to sentient beings according to their faculties.

To clarify that the Bodhisattva of Great Majestic Virtue manifests forms and preaches the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings: it is clarified that while the principle of wisdom (li-zhi) is all-pervasive and devoid of coming or going, he manifests a physical body (rūpakāya) in response to them, bestowing the Dharma according to their faculties.
The ten matters mentioned above are all fully elucidated one by one in the following verses.

This section consists of one hundred and twenty-one lines, which collectively praise the preceding ten dharmas; it clarifies the completion of Samantabhadra’s practices, as cause and effect, principle and wisdom, compassion and vows have all been perfected.

As is self-evident from the verses below. Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Appearance of the Tathāgata. In explaining this chapter, four sections are established: first, an explanation of the title of the chapter;

second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; third, an explanation of the reasons why the Tathāgata emits light and bestows empowerment upon Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; and fourth, an explanation of the meaning according to the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter: why is it called "The Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata"?

It is because, starting from the second assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*), the ten levels of faith were taught; with Buddha Immovable Wisdom (*Acala-jñāna*) as the head of the first faith, the remaining nine Buddhas—such as Buddha Unobstructed Wisdom (*Asaṅga-jñāna*) and others—represent the progressive cultivation within these ten faiths. Furthermore, since the ten kinds of wisdom are fully contained within a single wisdom, the name is established according to their respective practices.

From within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one advances in practice without departing from the essence of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*). One gives rise to the vows and practices of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), cultivates discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), and achieves great loving-kindness and compassion. When this stage is fulfilled, it is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" (*Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta*).
The manifestation of the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment within the Bodhimaṇḍa during the first assembly mentioned previously refers to the appearance of Vairocana Buddha.

The manifestation described in this chapter, however, refers to the appearance of a bodhisattva who has perfected the stages of practice, realization, wisdom, and compassion through the progressive cultivation of the five paths; therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on Manifestation" (Prādurbhāva-parivarta).
Furthermore, it is like Sudhana seeing the youth Kṣāntivādī and the maiden Śrīmatī, which signifies the fulfillment of the two practices of wisdom and compassion;
he then sees the Tathāgata Maitreya, which signifies the meaning of the appearance of a Tathāgata.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, by means of his light, empowered these two individuals in their dialogue to expound the gateway of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world: Mañjuśrī manifests fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while Samantabhadra represents discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*); together they accomplish the gateway of benefiting sentient beings.

Second, regarding the purpose of this chapter: previously, within the explanation of the five stages, the three dharmas of Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the Buddha-fruit were fully expounded; since this chapter clarifies the perfection of the practices of the Buddha-fruit, it must now follow.

Regarding the third explanation, which clarifies the reason why the Tathāgata emits light to empower Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra: it demonstrates that the light from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows is the Middle Way of the Buddha.

That the light of the resultant wisdom of the Buddha is poured upon the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head demonstrates that the wisdom and virtue of the Buddha’s fruition are supreme and eminent; it is intended to cause Mañjuśrī to initiate the inquiry into the gateway of the Buddha’s fruition.

As for the Tathāgata emitting light from his mouth to灌 (irrigate/empower) the mouth of Samantabhadra, it clarifies that Samantabhadra is one whose discriminative wisdom (*prajñā*) is perfected, and that [the Buddha] intends to have him preach the Dharma. Question:
For what reason does the Tathāgata not preach this chapter himself, but instead emits light to empower these two individuals, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra?
Answer: It is for the purpose of manifesting the Dharma and enabling later students to understand it easily; it is not because the Tathāgata himself was unable to speak it. Question:
What is the meaning of "manifesting the Dharma" (biao fa)?
The answer is:

it is to clarify that Mañjuśrī is the manifestation of the Buddha’s Dharmakāya as fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), while Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s ascending practice as discriminative wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna).

When clarity reaches this stage, both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*) are simultaneously perfected and complete; only then is it called the manifestation of the Tathāgata.

This is symbolized by the fact that within the self-nature of the Dharmakāya—which is inherently pure and stainless—the self-body of non-reliant, luminous, and pristine fundamental wisdom can manifest.

Questioning the wisdom of differentiation, he speaks for himself of the mind of his own practice and realization, showing that it accords with the wisdom and virtue of all Buddhas of the past and present; only then is he a Buddha whose own practiced awakening and conduct are perfected.
Therefore, the Tathāgata emits light and bestows empowerment upon them so that they may fulfill the Dharma-ordinance.
This clarifies that for all Bodhisattvas, when the fruit is perfected and their merit is consummated, the Dharma is always thus.
The light emitted by the Buddha grants permission to reach the rank of Buddhahood, for the Dharma is not erroneous.

This indicates that when the primordial wisdom of such a dharmakāya and its various discerning wisdoms are fully perfected and complete in all practices for benefiting sentient beings, only then does one’s own Tathāgata appear.

The text indicates that Mañjuśrī is the manifestation of fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), Samantabhadra is the one who expounds the Dharma, and the Buddha is the fruition; this can be seen through reflection.

The general meaning is clear: Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra represent the gates of wisdom and practice that accomplish the fruition of Buddhahood, and they in turn cause the Dharma of the Buddha’s appearance to be proclaimed.
The Buddha is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); his essential nature is ineffable. All that possesses speech is discriminative wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*).

Because Vairocana Buddha appeared at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) during the first assembly, it is clarified that the site of enlightenment in the first assembly is not [identical to] Vairocana himself; rather, the Tathāgata emits light to establish the Dharma as a model for those who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment and are practicing the path.

This clearly demonstrates that because their fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya and their skillful means for benefiting beings through differentiated wisdom are both fully perfected, these two individuals are made to teach that their own Buddhas and the ancient Buddhas who appeared in the world are exactly alike.

Thus, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are the common dharma of all Buddhas of the past and present; for those who have first resolved their minds, from the very moment they first give rise to the mind of faith, they have traversed these two practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, reaching fulfillment only upon arriving here.
Practicing in this manner, one never departs from the essence of the ten wisdoms of the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom within the initial faith.

This is because, as clarified in the sutra, time is immovable, wisdom is immovable, practice is immovable, the ability to travel everywhere throughout the ten directions is immovable, entering the many into the one is immovable, entering the one into the many is immovable, entering the small into the large is immovable, entering the large into the small is immovable, and so forth, as explained in the scripture.

To realize that the body, mind, phenomena, and wisdom are without intrinsic nature and without dependence, such that the fetters of emotional consciousness are extinguished and the Dharma-assembly is eternally thus—

therefore, by means of these five stages of advancement, whether ascending through the celestial realms as a symbolic method or pervading the ten directions with the body, one ultimately accomplishes non-separation from the essence of fundamental wisdom within the Hall of Universal Radiance at the very limit of a single kṣaṇa.

Therefore, this Dharma, which has already brought its own fruit to completion, is preached without departing from the place where faith was first established—the Hall of Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā).
It is just as when Sudhana, having reached the Tathāgata Maitreya, again beheld Mañjuśrī; it is similar to the initial arousal of faith upon entering the body of Samantabhadra.
Fearing that future learners might become confused regarding the Dharma, each point is illustrated by means of Sudhana’s journey so that it may be easily understood;
the general meaning can be known based on this.
Furthermore, according to this single scripture, there are three stages of cause and effect and two types of eternal paths.

From the initial *bodhimaṇḍa* up to the "Vairocana Chapter," there are six chapters of the sūtra; up to the "Vairocana Chapter," this constitutes the cause and fruit within the Buddha’s own five stages.
These consist of fifty assemblies, including the ten Bodhisattvas of Samantabhadra’s Ocean Moonlight Great Radiance and the Ten Devas of Supernatural Penetration.

Second, regarding the five stages of Bodhisattvas who have developed faith, which encompass the stage of faith itself—corresponding to the cause and fruit of the six stages—from the second assembly, the "Chapter on the Names of Buddhas" and those following, spoken in the Hall of Universal Radiance, up to the eighth assembly, the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," also in the Hall of Universal Radiance, there are thirty-two chapters of scripture that clarify the complete cycle of the causes and fruits of a Bodhisattva’s initial resolve for enlightenment.
Among these thirty-two chapters, the "Chapter on the Buddha-flower Samādhi" of the third dhyāna has not yet appeared; it constitutes the sequence of preparatory practices within this cultivation.

Third, from Mañjuśrī’s arrival at the Great Stūpa Temple until the preaching of the *Sūtra on the Gate of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*, he transformed Sudhana by causing him to seek fifty-three sublime friends to the south, thereby clarifying through practice the causes and effects of the five stages of spiritual progress from beginning to end.

To clarify that these teachings are merely for the purpose of instruction, lest one become confused regarding actual practice, Sudhana is presented as the practitioner capable of initiating and carrying out practice, while the fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are those who have already accomplished such practice. By showing him seeking instruction from each and progressing upward, this serves as a model for the five stages of advancement for those who later resolve to attain *bodhicitta*, ensuring they do not lose their way in their own practice.
The meaning therein will be explained according to the text.

Regarding the two kinds of eternal paths: as described in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" and the "Lokātīta-parivarta," one constantly benefits sentient beings through the path of renunciation; this is because the eternal true *dharmadhātu* is not false, and it is the eternal path of the Buddha-fruit.
Constantly remaining detached from worldly benefit for oneself while seeking no self-interest for one's own sake—this is the practice of Samantabhadra, the eternal path of the Buddhas.
This clarifies the two kinds of eternal paths regarding cause and effect throughout the three stages of this sutra.

As in the second through eighth assemblies, the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata" (*Tathāgatotpattisambhavanirdeśa*) elucidates the completion of the bodhisattva’s advancement through the five stages from the initial resolve; the entrustment and dissemination are all contained within this chapter, clarifying that this chapter marks the conclusion of the fruition of the advancement through the five stages.
If someone seeks at the conclusion of the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" for an entrustment and a mandate for circulation, they have not yet grasped the intended meaning of this sutra.

This is because the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" encompasses the entire body of the teaching as a whole, as well as the great essence of the quiescent function throughout the three periods of time—past, present, and future—which is devoid of beginning or end and is not something established through preparatory application or produced by causes and conditions.

It is solely for the purpose of guiding bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment and leading deluded followers by means of the Vehicle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-yāna*) that this "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" is explained; it clarifies the merit of the progressive cultivation of the five stages of practice and specifically addresses the entrustment for the circulation of the teaching.

If one discusses the fundamental dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), its nature is inherently neither deluded nor awakened; it neither emerges nor disappears, neither comes into being nor perishes, and it is neither flowing nor penetrating.

This intent of the entrustment and circulation is explained at the conclusion of the stage of preparatory application for ordinary beings who have not yet attained awakening; therefore, it does not follow after the "Dharmadhātu Chapter."
As in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," which directly discusses the ultimate fruit of the merits of all Buddhas, this is self-circulation and requires no formal entrustment.
In the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," the Tathāgata’s lion throne extends throughout the dharmadhātu without limit or boundary; this clarifies the culmination of the fruit.

Thus, in this "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," it is clarified that only when the power of the five stages of preparatory practice (*prayoga*) of those with faith has reached its consummation does [the realization] become truly pure and substantial. Once one has first ascended to the completion of these powers and the two types of practice have reached their full cycle, the entrustment and dissemination are then proclaimed.

Because the initial fulfillment of the fruit of enlightenment has been realized, one then enters the eternal Way of the Dharma-realm; it is not a matter of temporal measures such as past and present, beginning and end.
To circulate this Dharma is called "circulation" (liutong).

That is, the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" constitutes the fulfillment of one's own merit through the dharmadhātu; by constantly exhorting sentient beings with the dharmadhātu to emulate and learn it through skillful means, it is called "entrustment and circulation."

The practitioner of skillful means refers to the methods within the five stages; these include the various *pāramitās*, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), as well as the great vows, great wisdom, and great compassion.
The teachings of all Buddhas are likewise; only in this way can they be accomplished.
Regarding the fourth section, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, this chapter is divided into two parts.

First, from the initial passage "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "O Son of the Buddha, in this way immeasurable asaṃkhyeya dharma-gates are perfected in the Tathāgata," there are one hundred and three lines of scripture, including verses, which clarify how the Tathāgata emits light to empower Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, causing them to expound the section on the Appearance of the Tathāgata.

The second section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, it is as if, for example, in a trichiliocosm," consists of ten scriptural passages concerning the section on the realm of the Tathāgata’s manifestation-body and the ten dharmas of the practices he performs, as expounded by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Within these two long sections, the first section is divided into five parts.

The first part, from the initial passage "At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a light from the white tuft between his eyebrows" down to "and spoke in verse," consists of twelve and a half lines of scripture; it clarifies the stage where the Buddha emits light to anoint Mañjuśrī’s crown, thereby enabling him to inquire about the Dharma.

The second section, consisting of twenty verses, clarifies Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s praise of the Tathāgata’s virtues and the purpose of the emission of light and empowerment, as well as his inquiry as to who is capable of expounding the "Chapter on the Sphere of the Buddha."

The third section, from "At that time, the Tathāgata immediately emitted a great radiance from his mouth" down to the verse, consists of thirty-five lines of scripture. It clarifies how the Tathāgata’s light entered the mouth of Samantabhadra, enabling Mañjuśrī to know where to inquire about the Dharma, and it introduces the ten dharmas regarding the appearance of the Tathāgata as the subject of inquiry.
The fourth section, consisting of twenty verses, is the prose-poetic restatement by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, requesting the exposition of the ten dharmas concerning the appearance of the Tathāgata.

The fifth section, from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to "O Son of the Buddha, in this way, immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya dharma-gates are fully perfected in the Tathāgata," clarifies the section in which Samantabhadra informs the assembly that the appearance of the Tathāgata is accomplished through ten immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeyas of matters.
The five preceding sections constitute the "Division on the Manifestation of the Buddha," in which the Buddha’s light empowers Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra to engage in dialogue with one another.
The significance of this empowerment by light has already been explained above.

The general meaning of the "Manifestation of Dharmas" (Dai-i hyō-hō) clarifies that the culmination of the progressive cultivation of the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya*, the discriminative wisdom, and the practices of compassion throughout the ten directions is called the "Appearance of the Tathāgata."

The *Prabhāsa-uttara-sūtra* further clarifies that the mutual penetration of the essence and function of the luminous wisdom and principle of these two—Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra—is the manifestation of the Tathāgata. It explicitly states that Mañjuśrī is the gate of the fundamental wisdom manifesting the wondrous principle of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas of the ten directions, while Samantabhadra is the gate of the differentiated wisdom, myriad practices, and great compassion of all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Now, it is clarified that having progressed through the five stages, one reaches this stage where the two dharmas are perfected; thus, it is called "the appearance of one's own Buddha.
Light is emitted from between the eyebrows to consecrate the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, enabling him to inquire about the dharma gate of the ultimate summit of the fruit of one's own Buddhahood.

The light emitted from the mouth is called the light of teaching; it causes one to explain the supreme pinnacle of one's own Buddha-fruit, the dharma that perfects the myriad practices, wisdom, and compassion throughout the ten directions.
These two individuals are used as symbols for the Dharma so that students may understand it more easily; it is not that the Tathāgata himself was unable to explain it.
Furthermore, they symbolize that fundamental wisdom is beyond the reach of words.
This chapter of the sutra clarifies that the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya, along with its differentiated wisdoms, compassion, and practices, are perfected.

From the preparatory stages (prayoga) prior to the tenth and eleventh bhūmis, the cultivation of both the ultimate and conventional truths reaches completion in this stage; the meaning of this is self-evident from the text itself.

Secondly, within the second section of the long recension, among the ten gateways of the Tathāgata’s manifestation, there are ten scriptural passages which state that the manifestation of the Tathāgata involves hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya matters.

Regarding these ten: first, clarifying the ten immeasurable manifestations of the Tathāgata; second, clarifying that the manifestation of the Tathāgata possesses ten immeasurable bodies; third, clarifying that the manifestation of the Tathāgata possesses ten immeasurable voices; fourth, clarifying that the manifestation of the Tathāgata possesses ten immeasurable minds; fifth, clarifying that the manifestation of the Tathāgata possesses ten immeasurable spheres of activity; sixth, clarifying that the manifestation of the Tathāgata possesses ten immeasurable practices to be performed; seventh, clarifying that the manifestation of the Tathāgata possesses ten immeasurable attainments of perfect enlightenment; eighth, clarifying that the manifestation of the Tathāgata possesses ten immeasurable turnings of the wheel of Dharma; ninth, clarifying that the manifestation of the Tathāgata possesses ten immeasurable entries into nirvāṇa; and tenth, clarifying that the manifestation of the Tathāgata possesses ten immeasurable instances of being seen, heard, or approached.
New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll 31 and Scroll 32,
composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan.
Thus, as described above, there are ten immeasurable dharmas regarding the appearance of the Tathāgata,
each of which has ten similes, as fully elucidated in the sutra.
As for "Mount Khadiraka," this is the name of a tree.
Nimindhara is here translated as "Holding-the-Borders Mountain.
Mount Munjinaṭa is here translated as "Liberation"; this is the dwelling place of the Nāga named Liberation.
The section on the *upaniṣad* has already been explained above.
Alternatively, *mūsala* means "purple-colored jewel.

Thus, the hundred parables mentioned above illustrate, by way of metaphor, a small portion of the ten immeasurable matters and spheres of the Tathāgata’s manifestation of body, mind, and wisdom. This is because these matters transcend the path of mental cognition; they are left to the inconceivable, non-substantial, and non-active state, and are governed by the power of infinite sovereignty. Therefore, they cannot be expressed by the measure of words or represented by metaphors.

Regarding the entrustment and circulation at the end of this chapter, as for the statement that "this Dharma-gate shall not fall into the hands of other sentient beings," those who delight in studying the Lesser Vehicle or the Three Vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and those who delight in emptiness and selflessness while aspiring to be born in a Pure Land—these are "other sentient beings. This is because they have not yet turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna] and remain within the cycle of death and rebirth in the *parināmika-saṃsāra* (the transformed birth-and-death).
If there are ordinary beings of great resolve or those of the three vehicles who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment], that which the Buddha entrusts to them is called "circulation.

Even if this Dharma were expounded by a Bodhisattva of the noble stages themselves, if there were no ordinary beings who delighted in studying it, it would not be called an "entrustment," nor would it be called "circulation."

To clarify that this sutra is entrusted to ordinary beings and those of the three vehicles who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment], causing them to delight in study, and having studied, to awaken and enter [the truth]—this is called "circulation" (pravacana).

As for those who have not yet received the entrustment—bodhisattvas who have already been born into the Buddha-family and have entered the stages from the first bhūmi upward—if we speak of bodhisattvas from the tenth bhūmi onward who have entered the realm of the Buddhas, their numbers in the ten directions and in this land are difficult to measure. Why, then, would the Tathāgata need to worry that there will be no one to believe and rejoice in [this teaching], or no one to propagate it?

Therefore, one should know that entrusting [this teaching] to ordinary beings of great resolve and those of the three vehicles who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment], causing them to awaken and enter [it], is called "entrustment for circulation"; it is not entrusted to the great Bodhisattvas from the tenth stage upward.

The intent of the sutra is solely to expound this Dharma-gate for Bodhisattvas who aspire toward the Inconceivable Vehicle; it clarifies how those of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings who have turned their minds may awaken to and enter the Vehicle of the Dharma-realm, thereby enabling them to advance through the ten stages of faith and the ten abodes of the Inconceivable Vehicle.

Furthermore, it cites the analogy of the crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch who possesses all the royal marks; after the king’s death, his seven treasures do not disperse or perish because this son is capable of governing the king’s rightful position.
If this son were not present, after the King’s death, all these treasures would vanish and perish within seven days.
Son of the Buddha!

This sūtra-treasure is likewise; it does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for the true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King—those born into the family of the Tathāgata and who have planted the various roots of goodness that constitute the marks of a Tathāgata.
"If there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate would soon perish.

This is because it is clearly understood that [the teaching] is intended only to cause ordinary beings to resolve their minds and enter [the path], and is not entrusted to Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage and above.

If one were to discuss those bodhisattvas who have already entered the stages and attained the Way, their number would be like the atoms within an ocean of worlds; even this cannot yet serve as a comparison. How, then, could one worry that there are no people to propagate it?
This clarifies that even if there were sages who constantly spoke [of it], there would be no ordinary beings who could cultivate and realize entry into it; that dharma would naturally cease.
To say "there are no ordinary beings practicing" and "the dharma ceases" is to say that the dharma is without arising or cessation.

The Sūtra states: "Except for the true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, who are born into the family of the Tathāgata and plant the roots of goodness that are the marks of the Tathāgata. This clarifies that the Tathāgata takes the wisdom of liberation as his family.

Just as in a single thought-moment there is no-thought, when all views regarding body and mind have perished, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s sublime principle of non-substantiality and correct wisdom; therefore, this is called the first stage of Initial Resolve within the Ten Abodes, marking the initial birth into the Buddha-family.
In the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), one attains the exhaustion of all phenomena within the three realms; this is also called being "born for the first time into the family of the Buddha.

In the eighth stage, one attains the manifestation of a portion of effortless activity (*anābhoga*); this is also called being "born for the first time into the family of the Tathāgata’s patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
As previously stated:

those who plant the various roots of goodness that constitute the marks of a Tathāgata perceive all phenomena as having non-existence as their nature and non-characteristic as their characteristic. Because they do not destroy characteristics yet are without characteristics, and because the characteristics of the objects of clear wisdom are inherently true, this is called "planting the marks of a Tathāgata."
To understand that the realm of one’s own mental consciousness is free from arising, abiding, and ceasing is the mark of the Tathāgata.

To understand that the wisdom of one’s own mind is equal to the wisdom of all Buddhas and all sentient beings—being of a single nature yet without nature, a single characteristic yet without characteristic, devoid of interior, exterior, or middle, like the realm of empty space—and to see that it can manifest according to the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings like a shadow follows the body, such that its arising has no place of origin and its ceasing has no place of departure, and to realize that the state of mind and its objects are like illusions, is the mark of the Tathāgata.
One who attains such a Dharma as this is born into the family of the Buddha.

Regarding "planting the various roots of goodness that constitute the marks of a Tathāgata": "planting" clarifies that there is the cultivation and study of the seeds of such true wisdom of a Tathāgata.

When ordinary beings hear this Dharma and cultivate and study such seeds of the Tathāgata’s true wisdom, it is called the non-interruption of the Buddha-seed; it is termed the entrustment for circulation.
Therefore, one should know that this teaching was not entrusted to those bodhisattvas who have already entered the stages and attained the Way. As the sutra says:

"Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated and accumulated various factors conducive to enlightenment; yet, if they have not heard this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great majesty and virtue, or if having heard it at some time, they do not believe, do not understand, do not comply with, and do not enter into it, they cannot be called a true bodhisattva, because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata."

Thus, such bodhisattvas belong to the provisional teaching of the Middle Way, wherein they contemplate emptiness and non-self and take joy only in the supramundane; although they cultivate the six pāramitās, they develop the aspiration for enlightenment out of weariness with suffering and seek to attain a pure land, for they have not yet realized that their own ignorance is fundamentally the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

This bodhisattva cultivates pure conduct by contemplating emptiness and non-self, developing the resolve for awakening through weariness with suffering; yet their acceptance and rejection remain entirely dependent on external conditions, and dualistic views persist constantly. This is not like this teaching, which relies on wisdom to develop the resolve for awakening and realizes that the fundamental nature of one's own mind and境 (objects) is inconceivable, being free from a mind of longing or aversion and devoid of the obstacles of purity and impurity.
The realm of sentient beings is the realm of the Tathāgata, and the mind of sentient beings is the mind of the Tathāgata, exactly as explained in this chapter.

When this chapter was being taught, the earth shook in six ways and with eighteen signs; whereas when the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" is taught, it simply mentions a sixfold shaking, which is to clarify that the essence of conduct is straightforwardness.

This chapter elucidates the Dharmakāya, its wisdom and principle, as well as the practices of Samantabhadra; it demonstrates the perfection of both compassion and wisdom by showing the shaking of the lands of the ten directions, up to and including the perfection of the offering of worship.

It is said that beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there are likewise Tathāgatas named Samantabhadra, as numerous as the atoms in eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, all manifesting their bodies to come and bear witness, praising [the Bodhisattva] and performing such deeds; in each case, eighty is cited as the measure.

The Buddhas who bear the same name as Samantabhadra are so named because they clarify that the Noble Eightfold Path is the practice of a Buddha, and because they establish their names based on the practices they have performed.

This clarifies that because the realization and practice of the Eightfold Noble Path are perfectly complete and pervade the ten directions, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in eighty unspeakable nayutas of Buddha-lands who all share the same name, Samantabhadra.
This perfection of awakening and practice has the eightfold noble path as its essence.

Within this assembly, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions who have attained all supernatural powers and samādhis and have all received the prediction of enlightenment in one lifetime. This clarifies that while they have already realized the fruits of their own cultivation, because they are the audience being transformed, they likewise receive the prediction in one lifetime.
"One birth" (ekajāti) means that because one does not perceive births across the three periods of time, it is termed "one birth.
This fundamentally subsumes the essential identity of ordinary beings and sages as a single dharma-characteristic, devoid of any distinct natures.
One who enters this state in a single kṣaṇa is called "one-life" (ekajāti), because they no longer perceive the nature of birth across the three periods of time.
Such is the reality of dharmas; all other views are incorrect.

Furthermore, sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and I likewise grant them the prediction that in a future world, after passing through unspeakably many eons as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, they shall all attain Buddhahood under the same name, "Excellence of Realm" (*Viśeṣa-viṣaya*). This clarifies that when the ocean of true wisdom manifests through the samādhi of skillful means within a single kṣaṇa, the delusions of boundless eons are instantaneously extinguished; this liberation of mind and境 (objective realm) is called the "Excellence of Realm" of a Buddha.
It is not like the bonds of worldly emotion, which require such kalpas of successive accumulation and cultivation;
those who form such interpretations merely give rise to idle thoughts and will never have the opportunity to attain Buddhahood.
In the true Dharma, it has never been thus.
The following clarifies that the number of sentient beings saved within these four continents is vast and numerous; the conclusion states that the same applies throughout the ten directions.

The subsequent passage—describing how, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields, there are likewise ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas from each of those fields who all come to this place, filling the ten directions—clarifies that the practices of Samantabhadra are universally pervasive, and that they have come together to bear witness to the Dharma of Samantabhadra.

When it says, "We are all named Samantabhadra, each having come from the world of Universal Radiance (Samantāloka) to the presence of the Buddha Universal Banner Sovereignty (Samantadhvaja-īśvara)," this clarifies that they have all emerged from the fundamental nature of the Dharma-body, which is primordially pure universal radiant wisdom; because they give rise from this wisdom to various practices equal in number to the realms of phenomena, space, and sentient beings, and thus practice the conduct of Samantabhadra, it is said that they have come from the world of Universal Radiance to the presence of the Buddha Universal Banner.
The remaining meanings are fully elucidated in the sutra.

All of these take fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as the world and differentiated wisdom (*prabheda-jñāna*) as Samantabhadra; by synthesizing and unifying awakening, practice, compassion, and fulfillment, this dharma-gate of the present chapter is thus revealed.

This is because it clarifies that within the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata, one practices the differentiated wisdom (*viśeṣa-jñāna*) of Samantabhadra; thus, the Buddha is titled "Samantabhadra Buddha.

In sum, this signifies that all practices are performed through Buddha-wisdom. Since the Eightfold Noble Path and the Ten Perfections (*daśapāramitā*) do not depart from fundamental wisdom and pervade all practices, they are cited here as the numerical count.
The statement that there are "eighty unspeakable nayutas of Buddha-fields as numerous as atoms" is entirely a symbolic representation of the Dharma.
This teaching is expounded for those of great resolve; it is not for those of inferior understanding to engage in arbitrary and forced interpretations based on their limited knowledge.

One must thoroughly penetrate the meaning of the sutra’s text regarding its beginning and end, its preceding and succeeding sections, and the distinctions between general and specific, as well as similarities and differences, according to their respective stages.

This chapter marks the conclusion of one's own progress through the five stages, completing the perfection of wisdom, the myriad practices, and great compassion; it is the gateway of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world to benefit sentient beings without attachment.
This chapter is like the great ocean, the ultimate limit of vastness where the rivers of the five stages of preparatory practice flow in;
this chapter is like Mount Sumeru, the king of all jewel mountains, beyond which none are higher.
This chapter is like the great earth, for it nurtures and supports all sentient beings through its great compassion.
This chapter is like space, for the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body pervade the entire Dharma-realm.

Just as a perfectly pure mani-jewel mirror, in its measure encompassing all, manifests the forms and images of all worlds throughout the ten directions within it without obstruction, so too does this Dharma-door of the Tathāgata’s appearance utilize the wondrous principle of the Dharmakāya—formless and shapeless, the root-purified great perfect wisdom-mirror of universal radiance—to universally manifest the oceans of karma and the practices of Samantabhadra of all sentient beings in the ten directions; the bodies and lands of all Buddhas are all contained therein, each with sovereign mastery.

Therefore, those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta should believe that their own minds and the minds of all sentient beings collectively possess such sovereign wisdom and virtue of a Tathāgata; they should know that before long, they will become identical with the Buddha-body.

Because there is confidence [in this], as stated in this chapter: "Sutras of a volume equal to the three-thousandfold world system are contained within a single minute atom; so it is with all minute atoms. The intent is to cause one to believe and know that all minute sentient beings possess an ocean of sutra-volumes of the Tathāgata’s four wisdoms.

Regarding the statement "breaking open those atoms to reveal the sutra scrolls," this clarifies that once the Bodhisattva has personally attained this [realization], they perceive that all sentient beings equally possess it. Then, by means of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), while dwelling within the ocean of birth and death, they manifest bodies as numerous as all sentient beings to perform skillful means and lead them forth, causing their minds to open to awakening. Thus, they reach the realm of their own wisdom, which is no different from that of a Buddha; therefore, it is said that "by breaking these atoms, these sutra scrolls are revealed."

As the Sūtra says: "Just as the waters of the great ocean flow secretly beneath the lands of the four continents and the eight hundred million minor islands, there is no one who, upon digging, fails to find water.
This metaphor clarifies that all sentient beings possess the power of self-observation; thus, there is none who cannot obtain the heart-water of the Tathāgata’s ocean of wisdom.

Furthermore, a sutra states: "A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should know that within every thought-moment of his own mind, a Buddha is always attaining perfect enlightenment. This is to clarify that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not differ from this very mind in their attainment of perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, the text below states: "The minds of all sentient beings are likewise thus; all possess the Tathāgata’s realization of perfect enlightenment.

This clarifies that the intrinsic nature of the minds of both ordinary beings and sages is pure and without difference; there is only the distinction between delusion and awakening, yet they do not differ by so much as a hair's breadth.

It is simply that when not even a single thought of delusion arises, the mind and its objects become utterly vast and empty; since the nature itself is without birth, without attainment, and without realization, one immediately achieves perfect enlightenment.
Then, by means of this very dharma, one extensively benefits all sentient beings, for this is the practice of Samantabhadra.

The wondrous wisdom that discerns the principles of the non-substantial mind, distinguishing between the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles, the causes and effects for humans and devas, and the karmic retributions of the evil realms, is named Mañjuśrī.
Following this wisdom of differentiation, practicing in concert with others to know their faculties and benefit sentient beings without ceasing, is named Samantabhadra.
Because one uses great compassion to rescue and protect all sentient beings, one is named Avalokiteśvara.
Because these three minds are cultivated and studied simultaneously, one is named Vairocana.
When habitual mind is perfected, it is called mastery (*vaśitā*).
When there is no phenomenon that is not clearly known, it is called non-obstruction (*asaṅga*).
When wisdom responds to the faculties throughout the ten directions, its nature being without coming or going, it is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
If one cultivates this from the very beginning, even if delusions arise through long habituation over many kalpas, the sun of wisdom will not shift.
This totality is not difficult; why need one fail to practice it?
To study and yet not attain [realization] is still superior in merit to humans and devas.
Without faith and without cultivation, how can the exhaustion of suffering ever be reached?

This great intent—the gateway to the fruit of Buddhahood through the appearance of the Tathāgata—is such that the sublime principle of Mañjuśrī and the sublime practice of Samantabhadra are shared by all sentient beings. Neither ancient nor modern, they are by nature a single unity; thus should later students believe and cultivate them.
Your sincere devotion is not far from the goal; do not create difficulties for yourself.

As the verse in this chapter says: "Just as the ocean seal reflects the bodies of sentient beings, it is therefore called the great ocean; so too, Bodhi universally reflects all mental activities, and for this reason it is named Perfect Enlightenment."

This clarifies that bodhi is the wondrous principle of the mind's absence of nature, the absence of substantial characteristics, and the absence of attainment or realization; one who penetrates this dharma is called one of wondrous wisdom.
By means of this wondrous wisdom of bodhi, one universally seals all deviant thoughts and deluded practices so that they have no place of arising; this is called "Perfect Enlightenment.
The Master of the Treatise says in verse:
The bodhi-realm of all sentient beings Is pure, stainless, and indestructible wisdom.
The priceless jewel of wisdom lies within one's garment, yet one remains outside the gate, wishing only for perpetual poverty.
The vast and precious vehicle stands at the crossroads, guided by Mañjuśrī and supported by Samantabhadra;
its stout white oxen possess immense strength, traversing all realms in a single thought without expansion or contraction.
Thus they cannot enter this precious vehicle; They take pleasure only in standing before the gate of toil and hardship.
Unaware that their own bodies are always within it, They send others up and constantly say, "I am not yet capable."

In general, one must always have confidence that the spheres of one’s own body, speech, and mind, as well as all conceptualizations of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), arise from the spheres of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind, and from his conceptualizations of conditioned phenomena; that they all lack substance and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and that they are devoid of self (*ātman*) and person (*pudgala*). They arise solely through the non-active intrinsic nature of the *dharmadhātu* via dependent origination, and fundamentally no root, faculty, or location can be found.

The nature of phenomena is, by its very essence, the dharmadhātu, devoid of internal, external, or intermediate distinctions; one should know it thus and observe it thus. Contemplating oneself and others as being of one and the same essential nature—without self and without what belongs to a self—one should practice in this manner through the power of concentration and wisdom.
Having thus attained self-knowledge, one contemplates the suffering of sentient beings; this benefiting of both self and others is entirely like the vast vows and practices of Samantabhadra.

Just as in the five stages of the Dharma-Method of this sutra, this chapter brings them together: it clarifies that Mañjuśrī is the Dharma-gate of the essence, which is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while Samantabhadra is the myriad practices within the functioning of fundamental wisdom. Since non-conceptual fundamental wisdom is the Buddha, the essence and its function are made to question and answer one another to explain the gate of fundamental wisdom and the fruit of Buddhahood, clarifying that fundamental wisdom is accomplished through these two practices.

The fundamental wisdom is inherently devoid of arising and ceasing because it is manifested through the two dharmas of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; since these causes of manifestation are themselves explained by that very wisdom, the Buddha himself is without arising or ceasing. This clarifies that while the cause can be described, the fruit is beyond fabrication.
Because these three dharmas are sovereign and perfectly penetrating, it is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
This clarifies that there is acting without acting, and acting while not acting.
Chapter Thirty-Eight: Leaving the World. In preparing to explain this chapter, it shall be treated according to five sections:

first, explaining the title of the chapter; second, explaining the purpose for its inclusion; third, explaining the reasons for the introductory narrative concerning the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment; fourth, explaining the reason for the identity of the principal teacher of the Dharma; and fifth, explaining the meaning according to the text.

First, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter: it is named the "Chapter on Leaving the World" because, as the preceding chapter was titled "The Appearance of the Tathāgata," this chapter follows by attaining the state of leaving the world; therefore, it is called "Leaving the World."
This has two meanings:

with respect to the master who expounds the Dharma, his teaching that benefits sentient beings constitutes the "Chapter on Benefiting the World," and thus it is appropriately given the name "Benefit."
The aspiration that sentient beings hear the Dharma and remain unstained while dwelling in the world pertains to the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*).
This is explained by way of two meanings: the subject who preaches the Dharma and those who derive benefit from it.

Second, regarding the intent of this chapter: it clarifies that the preceding chapter marks the completion of the progression through the five stages, wherein one’s own realization and practice of the Buddha-fruit have reached fulfillment.

This chapter concerns the constant practice of Samantabhadra, which has been taught simultaneously since the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment; it is the common practice of all Buddhas of the past and present.

From the *Samantaprabhā Hall*, where he taught the Dharma of the Ten Faiths, up through the twelve assemblies of sutras—including the *Ten Samādhis*, *Ten Supernatural Powers*, *Ten Endurances*, *Asaṃkhyeya*, *The Lifespan of the Tathāgata*, *The Abodes of Bodhisattvas*, *The Inconceivable Buddha*, *The Ocean of Marks and Signs of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies*, *The Merit of the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks*, *The Practices of Samantabhadra*, *The Manifestation of the Tathāgata*, and *Leaving the World*—up to forty such assemblies, [the Buddha] remained within the *Single-Moment-Interval Samādhi* among gods and humans, using the wisdom of universal radiance to seal everything at once and preach it all simultaneously.

From these various assemblies up to the ascent to heaven, it is all stated that they did not depart from the Hall of Universal Radiance where he first attained perfect enlightenment; this clarifies that throughout the beginning and end of universal penetration, time and phenomena do not shift, and thus this chapter must appear here.

Regarding the third explanation, which describes the origins of the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment: for what reason does the beginning of this chapter describe the time and place of his first becoming a Buddha, and what is its intended meaning?

The Sūtra states: “At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) according to the dharma of araṇya, in the Hall of Universal Radiance, until his wondrous awakening was fully perfected. The intent is to clarify that the beginning and end of the cultivation and progress through the five stages—including this “Ten Samādhis” chapter and the “Leaving the World” chapter—are all advanced by means of this essence of Samantabhadra’s practice.

Furthermore, although the forty chapters are distinct, they collectively do not depart from the essence of the ten concentrations of universal radiant wisdom; they are expounded simultaneously without temporal sequence, and are likewise so throughout the ten directions.
By means of this, one ascends to heaven; yet it is said that one does not depart from the Bodhimaṇḍa or the Hall of Universal Radiance.

For example, when the *Daśadharmaka-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Ten Samādhis) is taught as a single assembly comprising eleven chapters, its opening is identical to the introductory narrative of this present chapter: it likewise states, "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha... until his wondrous enlightenment was fully perfected. This clarifies that the *Daśadharmaka-parivarta*, through its samādhi which is without before or after, universally encompasses the beginning and end of the entire sutra as well as the three periods of time.

This "Chapter on Leaving the World" (Lokottara-parivarta) universally encompasses the essence of Samantabhadra’s practices, the causes and conditions for attaining Buddhahood, and the eternally abiding path of the past, future, and present through two thousand dharma-gates; therefore, it is presented here as such.

This clarity refers to the moment when one first attains perfect enlightenment; at that time, by means of the wisdom of universal radiance, the human realm, the heavens, and the worlds of the ten directions are all instantaneously and simultaneously reflected without any sequence, just as a perfect mirror suddenly illuminates all objects.

This teaching is established as sudden for the sake of sentient beings of great capacity, abruptly presenting the realm of wisdom; it is not like that which is known by the conceptual consciousnesses of those with limited understanding.

Thus, the attainment of Buddhahood is accomplished in a single thought-moment, and the preaching of the teaching is also proclaimed in a single thought-moment. This is because it refers solely to the essence of wisdom, and is not encompassed by the temporal divisions of the three periods, nor by the conceptual measures of years, months, and days.
Regarding the reason why the Master of the Dharma-Preacher is explained in four ways: why is it that in this chapter, it is again Samantabhadra Bodhisattva who is made to speak?

It is to clarify that these two thousand dharma-gates are the constant practice of Samantabhadra; thus, by having Samantabhadra himself explain his own practice, it causes all who hear the Dharma to emulate and learn from him, thereby performing the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Thus, even up to the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood and entering nirvana, all of these are the practices of Samantabhadra.
From the perspective of the fundamental Dharmakāya and Jñānakāya, the Buddha has no merit of either formation or destruction;
yet from the perspective of the discourse on differentiated wisdom, they are all subsumed within the practices of Samantabhadra.

Therefore, the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" clarifies that because one's own awakening and practice are perfected, the Buddhas of the ten directions all share the same name, Samantabhadra. This is to show that within the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten transferences, one possesses only a partial aspect of the awakened mind; thus, one can remedy only a portion of the coarse afflictions among all afflictions, cultivate a portion of compassion, and follow a portion of Samantabhadra’s tracks. Nevertheless, because the practices of Samantabhadra are not yet fully complete, the Buddha-fruit attained at each respective stage is designated only by names such as Moon, Eye, or Wondrous.

Upon reaching the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," it is revealed that the practice of awakening has reached perfect completion; therefore, Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields all share the same name, Samantabhadra Buddha.

Fundamental wisdom fully becomes differentiated wisdom; because it attains its name through the fulfillment of its function, the essence subsumes the function. This is because the name is established based on the function.
Now, the reason this chapter has Samantabhadra speak is likewise because fundamental wisdom establishes its name based on its function.
If one considers the faith and understanding of the initial mind, its function immediately proceeds from the source.

Because the function of Samantabhadra proceeds from fundamental wisdom, the world is named Golden Color; the Buddha-fruit is titled Immovable Wisdom, and the person capable of awakening is named Mañjuśrī.

When this reaches the point where one's own practice has perfected the awakening and conduct of the Buddha-fruit, one immediately employs the fundamental wisdom; because the Buddha is named Samantabhadra, the conduct practiced is likewise named the conduct of the Buddha Samantabhadra.
As for the mention of Samantabhadra in this chapter, it refers to Samantabhadra in terms of function derived from the fundamental [nature].
Furthermore, the Samantabhadra mentioned in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" is also like the Samantabhadra in the first assembly; he is the Samantabhadra of Vairocana Tathāgata’s own practice.

From the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" onwards, Samantabhadra represents the ordinary person who, having ascended from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) until the path is perfected, practices the conduct of Samantabhadra.

This clarifies that from the ten faiths through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one employs these to realize fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) from the very beginning, thereby bringing it to full completion.

From the tenth stage to the eleventh stage, one takes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and, through its application, brings about the differentiated wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*), exclusively benefiting sentient beings; this refers to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra from the ten concentrations (*daśa-samādhi*) onwards.

Therefore, when the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" was being taught, those bodhisattvas who had already ascended to the ten stages and yet sought Samantabhadra repeatedly without finding him were shown to have not yet fully mastered the application of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

The Tathāgata causes the thought of Samantabhadra to arise so that one may see him as if before one's very eyes; this clarifies that because one employs this Samantabhadra purely, the essence of wisdom proceeds from its function.
Therefore, the reason Mañjuśrī is made to question Samantabhadra in the "Chapter on Manifestation" (Avatamsaka) is to clarify that the essence follows from the function.

As it is said regarding this Samantabhadra of the chapter, he is the Samantabhadra who directly embodies the essence following the function; his merit is similar to that of the Samantabhadra in the first assembly of the primordial Tathāgata.
Therefore, in the first assembly, all dharma-gates taught were caused to be expounded by Samantabhadra; this was also because the essence follows from its function.

In the second assembly, Samantabhadra’s wisdom-function follows from the essence, continuing thus through to the tenth stage, where in every case the function follows from the essence, thereby causing fundamental wisdom to be perfected and made luminously clear.

Thereafter, at the conclusion of the tenth stage, one relinquishes the bliss of samādhi and nirvāṇa because it is like a dense forest of afflictions; only then can one fully realize the great function of Samantabhadra, whereby one first attains the title of "one who has established the teaching universally" and achieves mastery within the realm of birth and death.

Establishing the practice in this manner, because the realm of wisdom is simultaneous, the "Ten Samādhis" chapter and this present chapter together provide a comprehensive account of the beginning and end of the initial attainment of perfect awakening at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Those who have resolved their minds to practice must deeply grasp the essential meaning before they are fit to cultivate the Way.
If one seeks through many previous and subsequent lifetimes without attaining correspondence with this truth, it will be of no avail.

Rather, by relying on the power of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one should contemplate the objects of focus—the internal and external states of mind regarding the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and conventional (*saṃvṛti*) truths—to identify where defilement or purity predominates. One should then apply the Dharma of the equality of the essence and function of true principle (*tattva-jñāna*) to remedy these imbalances: if distraction and agitation predominate, remedy them with concentration; if the attachment to quiescence predominates, remedy it with the Dharma-body of equality, the power of great vows and dedication, and the union of compassion and wisdom. Proceeding in this manner according to the five stages of cultivation in this sutra, one remedies these conditions until reaching the ultimate goal.
If one’s own wisdom is insufficient, one must seek out a skilled master; it is not possible to remain complacent and achieve no benefit.

One should know that this Dharma Master is Samantabhadra, who, after attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, manifests the essence through its function. He expounds the two thousand dharmas of Samantabhadra—the eternal Way from beginning to end—whose function encompasses the ten thousand practices.
In the eighth stage, one relinquishes the practices and developments of the seven stages; wisdom is pure and effortless.

In the tenth stage, one relinquishes the dense forest of meditative concentrations on nirvana, accomplishes the conduct of Samantabhadra, and enters into birth-and-death to perfect great compassion, only then attaining true mastery.
Fifth, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: this chapter consists of seven fascicles of scripture, which are divided into ten sections.

First, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "extending throughout the dharma-realm, equal to the realm of space," there are eight lines of scripture; these clarify the praise of the dharma-gate attained by the Buddha upon his enlightenment and constitute the introductory section (*nidāna*) of this chapter.

2. From "With unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions" down to "cannot be fully described," there are twenty-one lines; this is the section praising the perfection of the resolve and virtue of the great assembly of bodhisattvas.

3. From "Their names were" down to "entering the unimpeded, pure dharma-realm," there are ten lines of scripture, which clarify the section on the exemplary names and the praise of the virtues of the bodhisattvas.

4. From "At that time, Samantabhadra... down to "...thereafter he arose from that samādhi," there are three and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the section on Samantabhadra entering meditative absorption, the eighteen signs by which the great earth trembles, and the division concerning Samantabhadra’s emergence from absorption.

5. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra" down to "O Son of the Buddha, we pray that you will expound such dharmas as these," there are seventy-two lines and a half of sūtra text. This section clarifies that the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra has two hundred questions, which collectively inquire into the characteristics of the dharma-gates and practices from the initial generation of the bodhicitta up to the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood.

Sixth: From the passage "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Bodhisattvas headed by Samantamati" onwards, until the end of the two thousand answers in the fifty-ninth fascicle—specifically the section ending with "O Son of the Buddha, it is for the sake of contemplating ten meanings that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha manifests parinirvāṇa"—this entire segment contains two thousand answers from Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wherein each of the dharmas he answers possesses ten further dharmas.
Each of its passages is self-evident and need not be further explained; one should simply practice according to what is taught.
This constitutes the section on the Correct Teaching.

Seventh: from "O Sons of the Buddha, this dharma-gate is named 'The Vast and Pure Conduct of Bodhisattvas'" down to "one should know that such a person will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture. This is the section on the Entrustment and Circulation of this dharma-gate.

8. From "When this chapter was being taught" down to the verse, there are eleven lines of scripture that clarify how the Dharma’s majesty shook the earth, how the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared before him, praised the Dharma spoken by Samantabhadra, and how the Buddhas together protected this portion of the Dharma.

9. From "Having practiced asceticism for immeasurable eons" onwards, this section of sixteen verses collectively praises those who have generated the great bodhicitta and practice compassion and vows; their merit is vast and peerless.

10. From "His mind is neither high nor low" onwards, there are five-character verses extending to the end of the volume, totaling two hundred and seventy and a half verses. These employ various parables to praise the great compassion and benefits of the bodhisattvas, as well as the dharma-gates they practice.
As fully set forth in the sutra itself, each point is clearly explained therein.

Anyone who gives rise to the bodhicitta should revere this with their head bowed and recite it, using it to adorn the actions of body, speech, and mind; thereby establishing the gateway to the great wisdom, great compassion, and vows of the Dharmakāya, and accomplishing the universal wondrous activity of the Buddha-fruit Samantabhadra.
Regarding the phrase "in the midst of praising his virtues, his wondrous awakening is fully perfected": this is because the nature of the principle of effortless wisdom is inherently all-pervasive.
Regarding "the two paths are eternally severed": this refers to the severing of the two views of existence and non-existence, as well as permanence and annihilation.
Those who have realized the dharma of signlessness perceive the realm of wisdom as being like an illusion; the mind and its objects have no master.
Those who abide in the abiding of the Buddha find that the Buddha has no place of abiding.
Those who attain the equality of the Buddha possess great wisdom that pervades everywhere; they know the faculties of beings and how to benefit them, without distinction between self and other.
Regarding "reaching the state of non-obstruction": the holy and the ordinary share the same essence, such that the general and the particular are sovereignly interpenetrating.
Regarding "the unalterable Dharma": essence and function are sovereignly free, as there is no inherent nature that can be altered.
"Unimpeded in all actions" means that the function of wisdom is universally pervasive, as no object can obstruct it.
"Establishing the inconceivable" means that delusion has vanished and one acts spontaneously through wisdom.
"Universally perceiving the three periods of time" means that the seal of wisdom views past and present without extension or contraction.

As for the body constantly pervading all lands: with the disappearance of internal and external views and the exhaustion of notions of large and small, the mind is like space and the essence of wisdom naturally pervades; the manifested form-body appears in response, yet it does not come or go.

"One whose wisdom is ever-lucid and penetrates all dharmas" praises the Tathāgata’s perfection of distinctive wisdom, which fully comprehends all practices and exhausts all doubts, such that no one can fathom his person.

Regarding the wisdom sought by all Bodhisattvas and others, they extol the virtuous functions of the Tathāgata’s final body: its meaning is exhaustive, its practice is all-pervasive, its presence is omnipresent, its affairs are all-knowing, its wisdom is perfectly complete, it acts without effort, its mind neither contracts nor expands, it universally responds throughout the ten directions, and it operates without thought, intellect, or consciousness, responding to all that is sought through its inherent virtue.
By means of a voice that abides nowhere, he proclaims universally with a single sound; yet each awakens according to their own faculties, as their wisdoms differ.
What follows is self-evident from the text itself.
This "Chapter on Transcending the World" represents the perpetual conduct of Samantabhadra following the attainment of Buddhahood, universally sealing the ten directions without rest.
Just as when Sudhana saw the Tathāgata Maitreya, the Tathāgata Maitreya instead directed him to see Mañjuśrī;
and having heard the name of Samantabhadra, Sudhana gave rise to immeasurable clouds of the ten great vows before seeing his own body enter the body of Samantabhadra—this chapter is similar to that.
Chapter 39: Entering the Dharma Realm. Regarding the explanation of this chapter, there is a sixfold analysis:

first, explaining the title of the chapter; second, explaining the purpose for its inclusion; third, explaining the place where the Tathāgata resides; fourth, explaining the master who preaches the Dharma; fifth, explaining the significance of the assembled multitude; and sixth, explaining the meaning according to the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the title of this chapter: Why is this chapter named "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*dharmadhātupraveśa*)?
It is called "entering" because those who possess clear faith and joy have, for the first time, attained realization after emerging from delusion.
The nature of the realm of body and mind is inherently without dependence; this is called *dharma*.
Penetrating through unity and multiplicity, where the obstructions of true and false, right and wrong have vanished, is called *dhātu*.
Furthermore, that which is purely conjoined with wisdom (*jñāna*) and is not within the domain of emotional consciousness (*vijñāna*) is called the *dharmadhātu*.

Moreover, when one realizes that the seeds of ignorance and consciousness are purely the functioning of wisdom and are no longer subsumed under delusion, this is the sphere of non-reliant wisdom; it is called the *dharmadhātu*.

Furthermore, because the essence of wisdom has no dependence, it is without spatial direction and all-pervasive; it universally perceives both the ultimate and conventional truths as collectively inconceivable. Within a single pore or a mote of dust, myriad forms are interlaced; infinite realms and Buddha-fields are layered upon one another. Wisdom and ordinary beings share the same substance, and objective realms and their images mutually penetrate—this is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, within a single atom, all lands are universally contained; there is no void that it does not pervade and no land that it does not encompass. Without destroying the realm of retribution, its layers upon layers are inexhaustible, truly penetrating and thoroughly reaching the principle; this is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, with a single sublime voice heard throughout the ocean of lands, and with a single hair-tip equal in measure to the boundless, one transcends the perception of large and small and realizes the identity of self and other; as consciousness fades and afflictions cease, wisdom penetrates without obstruction—this is called "entering the Dharma-realm."
This is based on the universal designation of the realm of wisdom; do not rely on what is seen by the emotional consciousness of the physical eye.

Second, regarding the purpose of this chapter’s arrival: it previously clarified the manifestation of the Tathāgata within oneself and further clarified that the mind is unstained, which is termed "transcending the world."
This is purely the realm of reality (dharmadhātu) and not a realm of delusion; for this reason, this chapter must appear here.
This chapter is the self-realized wisdom of all Buddhas upon attaining enlightenment—the eternal fruit that is without beginning or end.

Furthermore, this is the essence of the cultivation undertaken throughout the preceding five stages; as one becomes fully habituated to this, one acts with spontaneous wisdom, returning to the fundamental dharma of the source.

Regarding the third point, the explanation of the place where the Tathāgata resides: for what reason do the beginnings of all preceding assemblies state that [the Buddha] does not depart from the Hall of Universal Radiance at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and furthermore, why do three assemblies share the same location in the Hall of Universal Radiance?

Regarding this single assembly of the Dharma-realm, why is it not the same as the previous assemblies which state directly, "At that time, the World-Honored One was in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park"? What is the intention behind this?

Answer: This is to clarify that following the explanation of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) in the previous Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*), the gates of progressive advancement through the five stages—the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), and so forth—and the six stages are explained in succession.
