Because this cultivation and progress do not exist apart from the essence of Bodhi, it is said that one does not depart from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimanda*), which is the essence of the Tathāgata’s perfect awakening.
Fearing that the fundamental intent of the scripture might be lost, it is necessary to provide this further explanation.

Regarding the fact that the three assemblies were together in the Hall of Universal Radiance: this clarifies that the cultivation of the five stages through faith and progress has already been completed. It indicates that one does not depart from the fundamental, immovable wisdom-body of universal radiance as the objective realm; because this is not a matter of deluded sentiment, time likewise does not shift, remaining within the interval of a single kṣaṇa.

This *Dharmadhātu-parivarta* states explicitly that it takes place in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī; this clarifies that the previous section on the progression through the stages has already concluded, whereas this assembly clarifies the practice of fulfilling one's own Buddhahood and delivering sentient beings, and thus it is located in a human realm, a city, and a grove.

Furthermore, regarding the transformation of those of the two vehicles—the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—as well as the bodhisattvas of the pure lands: these consist solely of the sovereign *dharmadhātu* as their essence. Within this state, there are no five stages of bodhi to be established nor any practices to be cultivated; likewise, there are no distinct wisdoms or the vows and practices of Samantabhadra to be studied. All are already perfected in the fruit of Buddhahood and complete in the conduct of Samantabhadra. This is the dharma that constantly and universally benefits sentient beings throughout the ten directions, requiring no further reconciliation or integration.

By this direct statement, Jetavana Forest is like the various rivers flowing into the ocean where their individual names vanish; it is designated solely by the name "Dharmadhātu," for its mode of activity through the convergence and advancement of the five preceding stages is no longer present.
Regarding "Śrāvastī," it was formerly called the Kingdom of Śā-vèi.

To say it is the Kingdom of Śrāvastī means "Good Path" (Sudatta) in this language; it is also called "Renowned for Things. This is because the people within this city were fond of studying the Way and its Virtue (moral conduct), and other countries heard that there were many such persons within the kingdom; thus, the name of the kingdom was established based on the moral virtue of its people.
Regarding "Jetavana" (Śītavana): "Śīta" means to go, to cross over, and to be swift.
Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwells in this grove, all sentient beings who go to the Buddha’s presence will swiftly attain liberation.
It is named as such because the Buddha’s deliverance of sentient beings is vast and manifold.
As for "Forest" (vana), it is because this garden contains forests.

Furthermore, because the Tathāgata’s practices are numerous, and because he universally covers and shelters all living beings throughout the Dharma-realm, his Buddha-practices are taken as the forest; by taking the forest as a covering, the sense of attaining coolness and serenity is established.
Because the Dharma-realm is cool, it shades the heat of the afflictions of sentient beings and renders them cool; therefore, it is called the Jeta Grove (*Jetavana*).
If one considers the time when the temple garden was established through its causes, it is named after the donor who bestowed it.

Because Prince Jeta planted the grove and the elder Sudatta established the park, and because the elder provided for the destitute and bestowed gifts upon the orphaned and the aged, it is also called the Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Now, because it encompasses the vast and manifold wisdom and virtue of the Tathāgata to universally save sentient beings, it is called the Jetavana Garden;
in this region it is termed a monastery (saṃghārāma), while in that region it is termed a garden (udyāna).

If the essence and function of the Dharma-realm encompass the entire sphere of wisdom, then the Jeta Grove is defined by this infinite sphere of wisdom; it is not that which is seen by the physical eye or the consciousness of ordinary beings, but rather a grove that universally contains all lands and atoms.

Regarding the fourth point, the explanation of the Lord of the Dharma: this Lord of the Dharma is also the Tathāgata Vairocana at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) mentioned previously; he is also the Buddha spontaneously realized by all Bodhisattvas within the five stages of the Dharma; he is also the Buddha to be realized by the future Tathāgata Maitreya; and he is, moreover, all Buddhas of the three periods of time—past, present, and future.

Because within the dharma-realm, the essence of wisdom is devoid of the emotional perceptions of the three periods of time, antiquity, modernity, extension, or contraction; and because within the dharma-realm, there are no Buddhas characterized by newness or antiquity, formation or decay.

By means of the wheel of the Dharma-realm, one delivers sentient beings into nirvana without displacing even a single hair’s breadth or a single mote of dust within the Dharma-realm, for its essence, function, and temporal dimensions are not distinct.

While ordinary deluded minds perceive difference, from the perspective of the Dharma-realm, one sees that the initial arousal of the bodhicitta by all sentient beings up to their attainment of Buddhahood and turning of the wheel of Dharma—the enlightenment of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and the Buddhahood of all sentient beings—all dwell together in a single kṣaṇa, a single mote of dust, a single Dharma-body, a single wisdom, a single voice, a single liberation, a single supernormal power, a single inconceivability, a single realm of retribution, and a single lotus throne; layer upon layer, they are unimpeded and without obstruction.
This refers to seeing with the eye of wisdom in reality; it cannot be known through the deluded perceptions of the fleshly eye as one might wish.

If there are those who can thus truly believe and understand, you should know that such persons have awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; they sit at the site of enlightenment and attain the Tathāgata’s wisdom, for they are able to believe that the bodies and minds of self and others are, in their entirety, the essence and function of the single Great Wisdom of the Dharma-realm.
Within this dharma-realm, the essence of the teaching that can be expounded is illustrated by ten examples.
First, the Tathāgata’s supernormal power serves as the essence of the teaching that can be expounded, because it is the Dharma perceived through the Buddha’s supernormal power.
Second, it takes the inconceivable as its teaching essence (*śāstrakāya*), because the sounds and dharma-gates manifested therein do not arise from the agency of speech, mind, or thought.
Third, it takes empty space as its teaching essence, because the realms of all dharmas manifested therein are like empty space.

Fourth, it takes light as its teaching essence, for this light from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows is named "Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm of the Three Times," because the Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows to manifest all dharmas.

Fifth, the five sense objects constitute the essence of the teaching, because each and every object is mutually fused and interpenetrating, encompassing the dharmas of the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
Sixth, the fruition of the Buddha’s recompense constitutes the essence of the teaching, as it manifests the dharma-gates practiced through past karmic actions and is adorned by them.
Seventh, it takes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as the essence of the teaching, because there is no body or mind to be realized or cultivated.
Eighth, it takes the names and titles of Bodhisattvas as the essence of the teaching, because each individual name is established based on the dharmas they practice.

Ninth, the teaching-body consists of the names and numbers of the bodhisattvas; it enumerates Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and five hundred bodhisattvas, each group consisting of ten individuals sharing the same name, which signifies that within the realm of the dharma-realm—the cause and fruit of the five stages—both the one and the many are simultaneously and perfectly complete.

Tenth, the essence of the teaching consists of the wisdom of universal radiance, because it manifests transformations throughout the worlds of the ten directions simultaneously, in accordance with the faculties of sentient beings.
Thus, the essence of this Dharma teaching is immeasurable and boundless; these ten points are cited here merely as a representative selection.

If one considers the person capable of hearing and receiving the teaching in relation to six matters—namely, that the six sense bases of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, along with their contact and sensation, attain non-attachment—then this constitutes the person who is able to hear and receive the teaching; it is not the case that one is considered a "hearer of the teaching" solely by means of the auditory faculty.

Regarding the meaning of the assembly gathered here as explained in five ways: the assembly first gathered at this convocation consisted of one hundred and forty-two bodhisattvas, with Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī as the two leaders.
As for the remaining one hundred and forty bodhisattvas, ten of whom share each name, they are collectively referred to as five hundred.
Thus the sutra says: "Five hundred bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were present together."
Furthermore, the text below states: "All these bodhisattvas have fully accomplished the practices of Samantabhadra.
Thus, these five hundred bodhisattvas all take Mañjuśrī as the essence of the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body, and Samantabhadra as the great function of the wisdom of differentiation.
Regarding these one hundred and forty-two bodhisattvas, how do they constitute the number five hundred?

From Bodhisattva Heavenly Crown downward, there are one hundred bodhisattvas; these represent the mutual fusion of the ten pāramitās within the fundamental essence of the fruit of the Dharma-realm. Within each of these ten, all ten are present; within each of the ten, there are one hundred. This is the gateway to the great function of the myriad practices of all sentient beings within the equality of the Dharma-realm.
From the Bodhisattva Dashaguna-kusuma-makuṭa (Ten-Crown) downward, these constitute the fruits of practice within the Dharma-realm.

Beginning with the ten Banner-Bodhisattvas—such as Prathama-sūrya-raśmi-jvālā-ketu (First Sun-Flame Banner) and others—as well as the Ten-Power Bodhisattvas and the Ten-Treasury Bodhisattvas, these forty individuals all rely upon the two practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. Throughout the ten abodes, ten practices, ten dedications, and ten stages, they universally cultivate the forty-two practices of the sages Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. Within each stage, they harmonize and integrate the great vows and great compassion of principle and wisdom through the ten pāramitās, thereby advancing in the various practices of the forty minds.

Within each single *pāramitā* there are ten; within those ten there are one hundred. Within the forty mental states, these become four hundred. Adding the one hundred *pāramitās* from the fundamental fruit of the subsequent *dharmadhātu*, they become five hundred. All of these take Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī as their essence and function.

Within the forty-two noble practices, by means of four hundred gates of *pāramitā*, one reaches this fundamental fruit-practice of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). From the stage of the Bodhisattva Tianguan (Crown-Jewel) downward, there are one hundred bodhisattva practices and fruits; because these are all brought together to enter the Dharma-realm, they are designated as five hundred.

This clarifies that the Buddha-fruit is the culmination of the cultivation of the forty stages of mind; for it is the fundamental fruit of practice within the *dharmadhātu*, wherein there is originally no cultivation.

From the tenth stage, the Bodhisattva is thus designated as having the "crown" (*mukuṭa*) as the fundamental fruit of practice within the *dharmadhātu*. "Crown" refers to an adornment upon the head, signifying that the *dharmadhātu* is the summit of the myriad practices of the fundamental Buddha-fruit; this is known through the meaning of the name and by what it adorns.
For this reason, the names, adornments, dwellings, and number of the assembly are all *dharmamukhas*; others should be understood accordingly.
Following this, there is an assembly of five hundred *śrāvakas*, who are the assembly that has heard this Dharma.

Below that are immeasurable hosts of World Rulers, as well as the assemblies from the ten directions who have come from other lands; all of them are the fundamental practices of cause and effect within the Dharma-realm.
The assembly of five hundred śrāvakas is a manifestation of those who neither hear nor see this inconceivable spiritual power of the dharma-realm.
These five assemblies shall be clearly elucidated through a word-by-word commentary on their meaning; for now, they have been briefly described.
Sixth, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: this chapter is divided into two sections.

The first begins from "At that time, the World-Honored One was in Śrāvastī" and extends through one and a half fascicles of scripture, ending at the sixty-first fascicle with the passage: "While teaching and transforming all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm, he did not depart from this Jeta Grove, the abode of the Tathāgata. This section clarifies the Tathāgata’s entry into the Lion-Extended-Limb Samādhi and his emission of light from between his eyebrows to manifest the gateway of the dharma-realm, thereby enabling all Bodhisattvas to ascend through the five stages toward the fruit of Buddhahood and enter the stage of the sovereign fruit of Buddhahood within the dharma-realm, free from further seeking or progress.

The second section, from "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī" down to the end of the sutra, describes how the youth Mañjuśrī proceeds eastward from the Well-Abiding Pavilion to benefit sentient beings according to their faculties, thereby manifesting the practice as a representation of the Dharma. This serves to ensure that those who subsequently resolve to attain enlightenment do not become confused regarding the path and may easily achieve understanding.
Furthermore, within the first section, the Jeta Grove, it is further divided into twenty-seven subsections.

First, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "together with five hundred bodhisattvas," there is one and a half lines of sūtra; this constitutes the introductory section (nidāna) of this chapter.

2. From "Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" down to "five hundred such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas together," there are forty-nine and a half lines of sūtra, which constitute the section on the listing of the assembly.

3. From "All these bodhisattvas have fully accomplished the practices and vows of Samantabhadra" down to "because they illuminate the dharma-realm with a great network of light," there are eight and a half lines of scripture that praise the section on the resolve and virtue of the aforementioned bodhisattvas.

4. From "Together with five hundred śrāvakas" down to "profoundly entering with faith into the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom," there are three and a half lines of scripture, which constitute the section enumerating the assembly of śrāvakas and extolling their virtues.

5. From "together with immeasurable world-rulers" down to "seeking all-knowledge," there are four lines of scripture which clarify the section on the enumeration of the assembly of world-rulers and the praise of their virtues.
The five preceding sections constitute the portion on the listing of the assembly.

Section six, from "At that time, the bodhisattvas, the great virtuous śrāvakas... down to "...the wisdom of the Tathāgata," consists of three lines of scripture; this clarifies the portion in which the great assembly, with one mind, requests the Tathāgata for the ten dharma-gates.

7. From "All the devas and humans of the entire world" down to "the vast power of the vow for omniscience," there are six and a half lines of scripture which clarify that those who can believe in, understand, and reveal this Dharma do not obtain it through their own efforts; rather, they come to know its portions through the empowerment [of others].

8. From "I only pray that the World-Honored One" down to "may you explain them all for us," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the second request for the Buddha to expound upon the dharmas that accord with bodhisattvas and sentient beings, as well as the practices performed by the Tathāgata in the past leading to his attainment of the Way; it comprises thirty questions, constituting the section on requesting the Buddha to provide these explanations.
The above three sections constitute the "Section on Requesting the Dharma.

Ninth: from "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "there were none that were not composed of mani-jewels," there are thirteen lines of scripture. These clarify how the Tathāgata, by the power of samādhi, manifests the fruits of his past deeds as adornments throughout the ten directions, as well as this section on the vast and expansive Great Adorned Pavilion.

10. From "At that time, again by the Buddha’s spiritual power" down to "arrayed and adorned throughout the ten directions," there are sixteen lines of scripture which clarify how, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, the Jeta Grove suddenly became magnificent, vast, and pervasive throughout the ten directions.

Eleventh: From "At that time, above the Jeta Grove" down to "all dwelling in the void, surrounding and pervading it, serving as a magnificent adornment," there are seven lines of scripture which clarify the section on adorning the void through the Tathāgata’s past roots of goodness and the power of his own dharma.

12. From "For what reason" onwards, up to "The Tathāgata’s body dwells in the Jeta Grove, and the assembly of bodhisattvas is completely filled," there are fourteen lines of scripture. These clarify the praise of the Tathāgata’s sovereign power and majestic adornment, as well as the perfection of the great assembly, concluding with the section on how it is likewise throughout the ten directions.

13. From "Seeing the Universal Rain of All Adornments Clouds" down to "and as clouds of adornment," there are eleven lines of scripture which clarify the section on the ten directions of space raining clouds of jewels to adorn the void and the jeweled ground.

14. From "At that time, passing from the east through unspeakable Buddha-fields" down to "together with their retinues, they sat cross-legged," there are ten sections of scripture; this is the section on the assembly of Bodhisattvas from the ten directions.
The above six sections answer the forty questions posed during the previous two occasions.

The following sections likewise consist of the first five parts, answering the previous questions regarding the Buddha’s samādhi, spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*), and the realm of his retribution (*vipāka-viṣaya*).

Next, the assembly of bodhisattvas gathering from the ten directions represents the bodies resulting from past cultivation; within the context of the *niśraya-vipāka* (recompensed environment), they answer the question of how the various stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten *pāramitās* cultivated through prior causes have been fulfilled, thereby clarifying that because their practice is perfected, their adorned bodies are likewise perfected.
There are ten Buddha-lands and ten names of Buddhas; these represent the causes and effects within the practices one performs.
All ten Buddhas are titled "Kings," which clarifies that their Buddha-fruition wisdom is sovereign.
The Bodhisattvas cover their bodies with nets, fully possessing the net of the clear teachings.

Fifteen: From "In this way, all Bodhisattvas of the ten directions" down to "all are through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata," there are twenty-five lines of scripture, praising the aspirations, virtues, and functions of the aforementioned Bodhisattvas who have come from the ten directions.

16. From the passage beginning with "At that time, the foremost great śrāvakas, Śāriputra... down to "...did not see such a vast and divine manifestation," there are fifty lines of sūtra. This clarifies that the aforementioned śrāvakas lacked the seeds of such roots of goodness; because they had no roots of goodness from previous lives, they were entirely unable to perceive the Tathāgata’s dwelling in the Jeta Grove, the magnificent adornments of the divine manifestations, and the ocean-like assembly of bodhisattvas within the vast buddha-field.

17. From the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, just as there are ten billion immeasurable hungry ghosts on the banks of the Ganges River" down to the ten similes in the following verse, it is shown by comparison that the śrāvakas lack the vast roots of goodness of bodhisattvas; thus, within this assembly, they neither know nor see the sovereign powers of the Tathāgata.
The ten similes contained therein are self-evident from the scriptural text.

In this way, the śrāvakas manifest as if they neither hear nor see the realm of the Tathāgata’s transformative spiritual powers and the ocean-like assembly of bodhisattvas, in order to cause those who are truly śrāvakas to turn their minds toward awakening, planting the seeds of the Tathāgata’s great vows, great wisdom, and great compassion, so that they may constantly dwell within birth and death to extensively benefit sentient beings.
Section Eighteen: The Exposition of Verses by the Ten Bodhisattvas, beginning with Vairocana Bodhisattva.

Below this are ten bodhisattvas, all of whom have come from the ten directions; each speaks one verse, each according to their own name, and each praises their own dharma as the practice of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
All follow the names of the Bodhisattvas as their underlying meanings are expressed; the intent of these verses can be seen therein.
For instance, the "Vairocana-vow-light" Bodhisattva represents various lights, which directly signify the fruit of Buddhahood.
The "Vow of Light" is the bodhisattva practice within the state of buddhahood.
From the initial general praise, it causes all bodhisattvas to contemplate the realm of the Tathāgata in the Jeta Grove.
The following nine items are the specific instances within the general category; each is taken according to the meaning of the name of the Bodhisattva to represent the dharma praised in the verse.
For example, "Indestructible King of Diligence" (Akṣayavīryarāja) corresponds to the meaning of "King of Indestructible Diligence," which is the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
The following sections should be understood by analogy with this.

Section Nineteen: From "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" down to "expounded this Lion-Stretching Samādhi," there are six lines of scripture clarifying how Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, through tenfold and all-encompassing doors of skillful means, intends to expound the section on the Lion-Stretching Samādhi.
20. From "What are the ten? down to "O Son of the Buddha, these ten are the foremost," this is the section on the ten kinds of ineffable dharma-words (*dharma-pada*).

21. "There are dharma-words as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields" concludes the summary; together with the following six lines of scripture, this is the section on the verses spoken by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva regarding the realm of the Buddha's contemplation.

Within these ten verses, the ten previously mentioned inexhaustible phrases are reiterated; the intent is to clarify that the essential nature of the *dharmadhātu* is unimpeded, such that the one and the many interpenetrate and the large and small enter one another, with every pore and every atom containing all the oceans of Buddha-fields, and each and every realm being mutually inclusive without obstruction.
The verse says: "Within each and every pore, there are oceans of lands as numerous as atoms; in all of them, Tathāgatas sit, each surrounded by assemblies of bodhisattvas.
This is explained in detail in the sutra.

The above twenty-one sections of scripture clarify how the Tathāgata, by means of the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*, causes those within the five stages to advance toward the dharma-gate of Samantabhadra’s ten thousand practices and enter the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The nature is spontaneously perfect and fundamentally without conjunction, because it is the practice of Samantabhadra.

From this point onward, the Tathāgata emits a light from between his eyebrows named "Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm of the Three Times," causing all bodhisattvas to dwell securely in the samādhi gate of the "Lion’s Stretch."

The above twenty-one sections briefly demonstrate the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s unimpeded conduct of differentiated wisdom within the Dharma-realm; they further cause Samantabhadra to speak in verse to praise the Dharma.

The emission of light from between the eyebrows below signifies that one’s own fundamental wisdom of universal radiance, the Dharma-body, is simultaneously and perfectly unified with the various practices of Samantabhadra—characterized by unimpeded mastery regarding the distinctions and similarities within the Dharma-realm—as well as with the essence and function of principle and wisdom.

He immediately commanded Mañjuśrī to speak verses in praise of the Dharma, [revealing] the dharma-gate of the equality of the dharmadhātu, wherein the two bodies of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra become the two wisdoms of the ultimate and conventional, eternally abiding.

Within this Dharma-realm, there are two aspects: essence and function. If Samantabhadra were absent, then the wisdom of differentiation would not function, resulting in a pursuit of quiescence devoid of compassionate activity;
if Mañjuśrī were absent, then the practices of Samantabhadra would be conditioned and thus impermanent.
By means of these two persons' dharma-gates, one realizes the essence and function of a single dharma-realm; the teachings of all Buddhas are entirely like this.
As for what is called "Buddha," it simply refers to abiding nowhere within the essence and function of these two persons—this is named "Buddha."
Regarding the statement "dwelling where the Buddha dwells," the Buddha dwells in non-dwelling.
It is precisely through this wisdom that dwells nowhere within the essence and function of Mañjuśrī’s universal wisdom and Samantabhadra’s myriad practices that one attains the name of "Buddha."
Therefore, the former section on Samantabhadra is the "Gate of Revealing Principle through Practice," while the latter section on Mañjuśrī is the "Gate of Manifesting Practice through Principle.
These names are established with a sequence for the purpose of verbal expression and the formulation of the teaching;
however, regarding the *dharmadhātu*, these two dharmas mutually support one another, as they are fundamentally one in essence—body and function.

Furthermore, as the Tathāgata cites these conditions to manifest the Dharma: the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (Lion’s Stretch Samādhi) belongs to the gate of Samantabhadra, while the light from the tuft of hair between the eyebrows belongs to the gate of Mañjuśrī. This is because that light is manifested by the wondrous wisdom of the Dharmakāya, whereas the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*, which arises from fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*), functions within the sphere of differentiated wisdom (*pravicaya-jñāna*).
When these two are of one essence, they form the gateway to mastery over the Dharma-realm.
This signifies that the self-nature of fundamental wisdom is beyond words, while its functional activity—expressed through verbal teaching—is that which Samantabhadra encompasses.
If these three dharmas are practiced separately, this is precisely the cycle of birth and death for humans and devas.

Even if one were to attain the Way, such a person would be called blind, stunted, or ugly, or would dwell in a thatched hut, for they have not entered the gate of the great mansion of the Dharma-realm.

The Lion’s Stretch Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*) refers to the state in which the cultivation of the five stages is fully perfected; where the integration of principle and wisdom has reached its consummation; where the exhaustion of preparatory effort suddenly vanishes; and where one is filled with the joy of the Dharma such that there is no further need for upward progression. In this state, one acts spontaneously through wisdom, universally manifesting transformative supernatural powers.

Without acting, the wisdom-realm functions; without creating, Buddha-lands interpenetrate one another. The infinitesimal atom does not become small, yet within it lies the entirety of the inexhaustible ocean of Buddha-lands.
Space does not become large, yet the ten directions eternally abide within the interior of a single hair-tip.
This is the spontaneous unfolding of the ocean of wisdom, wherein manifested jewel-lands interpenetrate one another; this is called "Yawning" (Binyin).
It is the state where, in accordance with principle, the single and the manifold bodies and their environments mutually contain one another; this is called "Samādhi."

"Yawning" (vinidāpana) signifies the sense of being at ease, joyful, and free from fatigue; it clarifies that the preceding five stages involve the exertion of mental attention as one integrates and cultivates conditioned and unconditioned phenomena while progressing upward.
This Dharma-realm is already perfected through advancement; it accords with wisdom and brings joy, as all phenomena are spontaneously accomplished because there is no mental effort or fatigue.
From here below, he emits light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, called "The Gate of Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm of the Three Times."
This reveals the gate of mastery in practice through the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya, which belongs to Mañjuśrī.

This is because, as explained below, Mañjuśrī speaks verses in praise of the Dharma to clarify that this Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra share the same realization of principle and wisdom, and the same practice of phenomena.

The fruit of Buddhahood is thus spontaneously perfected; it is simply a matter of the essence of principle and wisdom, the substance and function of the *dharmadhātu*. One must not chase after the names and phrases recorded and transcribed upon paper, silk, or bamboo, for such names and phrases cannot exist simultaneously. Rather, one should grasp principle and wisdom to understand their general and specific aspects, their similarities and differences, and their formation and disintegration.

However, for those whose deluded minds have first been awakened, one must first employ the skillful means of various wholesome practices to reveal the gateway of principle (*tattva*), so that through these practices, the wisdom of principle may become clear.

For example, among the ten *pāramitās*, nine are practice (*caryā*) and only the *jñāna-pāramitā* is the fruit; the other nine *pāramitās* constitute the essence and function of the skillful means that assist in revealing wisdom.

Because prior to this "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s practices is first elucidated, whereas within the "Appearance Chapter" itself, the fruition and the practice are revealed as being simultaneous.
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra: the Buddha bestowed his light upon these two persons so that they together constitute the essence and function of the myriad practices of wisdom and principle.

Herein, first, through the assembly of Samantabhadra, the essence of the great function of the Dharma-realm is manifested; this is sealed by the gateway of the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi, for samādhi is practice.

Next, regarding the light between the eyebrows named "Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm of the Three Times," which causes all bodhisattvas to dwell securely in the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*: this clarifies that the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya and the manifesting wisdom of differentiation are of one essence and function; only then is it called "entering the gate of the Dharma-realm."

Therefore, the preceding twenty-one sections of the sūtra constitute the gate of "attaining the principle through practice without attachment," in which Samantabhadra is the principal figure and Mañjuśrī is his companion.

Below, the Tathāgata emits a light from between his eyebrows named "Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm of the Three Times," which immediately corresponds to the gate of the perfect fusion and unimpeded freedom of principle and practice; herein, Mañjuśrī serves as the principal figure and Samantabhadra acts as his companion.
When the primary and the attendant are thus mutually fused, it is only then called "mastery over the Dharma-realm.

From the passage beginning with, "At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause all bodhisattvas to dwell securely in the Tathāgata’s Great Lion-Stretch Samādhi," down to "not departing from this Jeta Grove where the Tathāgata resides," is titled "The Gate of the Unobstructed Freedom and Perfect Fusion of Principle and Practice."
This section is further divided into six parts.

First, from "At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause all bodhisattvas to dwell securely in the Tathāgata’s Great Lion-Stretch Samādhi" down to "entering such oceans of Buddha-emanations as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields," there are forty-three lines of scripture, which clarify the section on how all bodhisattvas, having received the illumination of the Buddha's light, attained oceans of expedient means for immeasurable spiritual transformations.

2. From "What is the various samādhis? down to "the ocean of miraculous transformations of the samādhi of Vairocana Tathāgata’s moment-to-moment pervasion of the dharma-realm," there are sixty-six lines of scripture; this is the section that correctly explains the names of the samādhis entered.

3. From "All those bodhisattvas were fully endowed with great wisdom and supernormal powers" down to "they all saw the illumination of the Buddha’s light," there are fifty-three and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on the virtues gained by the bodhisattvas through the benefits conferred by the Buddha’s light.

4. From the passage beginning with "At that time, the bodhisattvas attained the light of the inconceivable True Dharma" down to the recitation of the verses, there are twenty and a half lines of scripture. These clarify how the samādhis and supernormal powers attained by the bodhisattvas manifest clouds of transformations, adorning the Jetavana Grove as well as the various regions of the lands in the ten directions.
The section from the fifth verse onwards consists of twenty-six stanzas, in which Mañjuśrī speaks these verses as a reiteration of the preceding *dharmaparyāya*.
This is clearly explained in the full text.

The above clarifies that the various bodhisattvas illuminated by the Buddha’s light receive this radiance and enter the samādhi of *bimbiṣa* (the yawn), which is the gateway of skillful means (*upāya*) within the realm of Samantabhadra.

However, all samādhis are in fact gateways of skillful practice within the realm of Samantabhadra, for they are all accomplished through the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) of Mañjuśrī’s Dharma-body.

Sixth: From "At that time, those bodhisattvas... down to "...not departing from this Jeta Grove where the Tathāgata resides," there are sixty-three lines of scripture. These clarify how the bodhisattvas, through the illumination of the Buddha’s samādhi-light, attain the aforementioned samādhis, as well as infinite great compassion, infinite supernormal powers, and infinite portions for benefiting sentient beings.
These twenty-seven sections of scripture collectively clarify the answers to the forty questions posed previously by the Bodhisattvas and the various lords of the world.
*New Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Scroll 32 [and] Scroll 33.
Regarding the "Exegesis of the Text Following the Six Sections" composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan: from the initial listing of the assembly, there are two meanings:
first, the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva," and second, the explanation of the name "Śrāvaka."
In the initial explanation of the name "Bodhisattva," there are six thematic intentions.

First, from the first one hundred and forty-two bodhisattvas, including the two bodhisattvas Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī as well as the Buddha, the general framework encompasses the five stages and the cause and effect of the Dharma-realm; this universally includes the general and specific, the identical and different, and the formation and disintegration of the dharmas throughout the entire scripture.

Second, the ten bodhisattvas who share the same name "Dhvaja" (Banner) from the beginning are the bodhisattvas such as Dharmamati within the stage of the Ten Abidings; upon reaching this fruit of the non-conceptual dharma-realm, they are designated as "Dhvaja."

It is because the wisdom of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) of that initial resolve destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*), and upon reaching this stage of the fruit of the *dharmadhātu*, it is designated as a "banner" (*dhvaja*).

Below these three stages, there are ten "Powerful" (*balin*) Bodhisattvas; this clarifies that from among the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the ten forest-dwelling Bodhisattvas—such as Guṇakusuma-vana and others—upon reaching this fruit of the *dharmadhātu*, are designated as "powerful. This clarifies that by means of the power of various virtuous practices, one is able to accomplish the practice of the fruit of the *dharmadhātu*.

From the fourth stage downward, there are ten bodhisattvas with the same name, "Treasury" (Kośa). These are the ten "Banner" (Dhvaja) bodhisattvas, such as Vajradhvaja and others from the Ten Dedications (Daśapariṇāmanā), who, upon reaching this fruit of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-phala), are designated as the ten Treasury bodhisattvas.

By means of those ten dedications, one uses dedication to shatter biased views; through the harmonious integration of principle and wisdom with compassion and vows, one is able to accomplish all virtues, which, upon reaching this fruit of the dharma-realm, is designated as the "Treasury."

The ten Bodhisattvas from the fifth stage downward, such as Sunetra and others, are all equally named "Eye" (Cakṣus). These are the thirty-seven "Treasury" (Garbha) Bodhisattvas, such as Vajragarbha and others, who occupy the ten stages; they are designated as "Eye" upon reaching this fruition of the Dharmadhātu.
Because those ten stages contain and preserve all virtues, the Dharma-eye becomes clear and distinct, seeing the entire Dharma-realm universally.

These aforementioned forty instances of the "ten-tens" (i.e., four hundred stages) constitute the first four positions of the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-realm fruition; these forty minds, which encompass both Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, form the path of the forty-two sages and worthies, thereby establishing the gateway to the Dharma-realm fruition, and now we have arrived at its source.

From the sixth section below, there are ten bodhisattvas all sharing the name "Crown" (Guān), continuing until the end of the listing of the bodhisattva assembly where there are one hundred bodhisattvas; these represent the practice of the ten pāramitās upon the fundamental wisdom within the Dharma-realm.
Because within a single pāramitā the mutual essences are perfectly interfused, there are ten contained within one, and a hundred contained within ten.
Thus, the hundred bodhisattvas from Tianguan (Heaven-Crown) downward clarify the practice of the hundred pāramitās.

Including the preceding forty bodhisattvas, all possess the ten pāramitās; within these forty, there are four hundred [instances], wherein they cultivate the pāramitās according to their respective stages.
When these hundred *pāramitās* within the fruit of this Dharma-realm are combined, they constitute five hundred.

Therefore, the sutra states: "Thus, accompanied by five hundred people, all these bodhisattvas have fully accomplished the practices and vows of Samantabhadra. This refers to the fact that the three—Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and the fundamental wisdom of the Buddha—pervade the dharma-practices of all.
Together with these five hundred gates of practice, they constitute the sovereign essence and function, extending even to inexhaustibility.
As with the five hundred boys, girls, upāsakas, and upāsikās listed below—totaling five hundred—the name is established based on this collective summary of the five hundred gates of practice.
The ten thousand *nāgas* represent the ten thousand practices that follow wisdom through their respective categories.
As for the six thousand *bhikṣus*, they encompass the stages of faith and the five hundred practice-gates within the five positions; thus, it is said there are "six thousand."

Second, regarding the explanation of the names of the assembly of *śrāvakas*: Śāriputra’s mother possessed eyes as clear and sharp as those of a *śāri* bird; because her eyes resembled the appearance of that bird, he was given the name [Śāriputra] after his mother’s eyes.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana is translated here as "Bean-clansman" (Caishushi); he was so named after his mother's clan name, Maudgalya, because his mother was a descendant of the Green Bean Sage (Mudgalagandha).
Mahākāśyapa possessed a golden body capable of absorbing the radiance of the sun; he is also called "Drinker of Light" (Yinguang) and is a descendant of the rishis.
*Mahā* here translates as "Great."
Revata means "offering" (pūjā).
Subhūti means "well-appeared" (suvyaktam).
Aniruddha means "unextinguished" (aniruddhaḥ).
Nanda means "Joy. Kapphiṇa means "Yellow";
he is a descendant of the ancient sage Yellow-Head (Kapiṅgala).
Kaccāyana is the clan name of a lineage; because he belongs to this progeny, "Yana" signifies "descendant."
Pūrṇa’s mother was named Māitrī; he took his mother’s name as his own.

Thus, these ten great śrāvakas manifest as if they neither hear nor see the Tathāgata’s inconceivable transformations within the dharma-realm, in order to lead those who delight in inferior teachings to seek the Great Vehicle.
The five hundred śrāvakas and the lords of the world previously possessed the seeds [of enlightenment], for they were able to follow the Buddha’s conduct.
"Lion" signifies fearlessness.
"Yawning" (*bhiṃsana*) signifies being at ease and free from fatigue.

This clarifies non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*): wisdom is exercised with sovereign mastery, responding without deliberate effort, such that the boundless, profound Dharma is spontaneously realized, for it is perfected without exertion.
As previously explained, upon entering this Samādhi of Yawning, the pavilions and towers suddenly become vast and expansive, without limit; "vast and expansive" means broad and wide.
It is said that this pavilion suddenly becomes vast and expansive because it is equal to the Dharma-realm and empty space.

This clarifies that the realm of the Tathāgata is eternally boundless; when the minds of the multitude, whether deluded or awakened, correspond with it in a single thought-moment, there is no phenomenon that is not equal to it. Since the mind is like empty space, universally encompassing the Dharma-realm, it is said to suddenly become broad and extensive, without limit or boundary.
This is intended to guide future followers, rather than the assembly present here.
Regarding "the vajra as the ground," it is because the resultant retribution is accomplished through the realization of the Dharmakāya.
As for "immeasurable jewel flowers and various maṇi gems scattered throughout, filling every place," these are produced by the collective and individual merits of various practices.
That the pillars are made of lapis lazuli is the karmic response to the maintenance of compassionate vows by means of a stainless, pure mind.

That they are composed of various jewels signifies that the adornments upon the pillars are complete with all manner of gems; it clarifies that within a single pure mind, one maintains the myriad practices without wavering.
That which is adorned with great radiant maṇi jewels arises from the evocation of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Jāmbūnada gold is a gold that is supple, luminous, and pure, far surpassing ordinary gold; it arises from the evocation of a mind characterized by gentleness, reverence, and circumspection.

The wish-fulfilling jewel king placed all around it as an adornment represents the manifestation of the arising of myriad distinct practices from fundamental wisdom, spontaneously benefiting all sentient beings with sovereign non-obstruction.
Regarding the phrase "the perilous towers extending afar": "perilous" means high; "afar" means distant; and "extending" means being adorned and reflected by a multitude of jewels.
Taken as a whole, this describes jewel towers that are lofty and far-reaching, mutually reflecting and adorning one another throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Among them, numerous jeweled towers mutually adorn and reflect one another; as the galleries extend alongside the towers, their roof structures support each other like a continuous chain.

The phrase "each filling the dharma-realm, with windows and doors reflecting one another" clarifies that the doors and windows atop the jeweled pavilions are transparent, brilliant, pure, and unobstructed.

Regarding the steps, courtyards, balconies, and railings: the tiered levels constitute the steps; the level ground beneath the steps paved with jewels constitutes the courtyard; the jeweled planks atop the steps constitute the railing; and the jeweled poles atop the railing constitute the balcony.
The "Rhapsody on Ascending the Tower" says, "Leaning against the balustrade, I gaze afar"; this is precisely what is meant here.
All things are fully provided, signifying that the myriad treasures are complete and majestic.

The pavilions are formed through the fruition of discriminative wisdom (*pravicaya-jñāna*); the towers are formed through the retribution of the function of contemplative observation arising from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which transcends all realms.
Alternatively, the human and celestial forms and images adorned with jewels are formed through the retribution of practicing for the benefit of humans and devas.
The jeweled net is the jewel of teaching; the walls and fences are the jewel of precepts.

The trees represent the practice of providing shelter for sentient beings; the jeweled banners represent the practice of dedication; the jeweled rivers represent the practice of compassion. Each and every one is thus formed as a retribution resulting from the various practices associated with wisdom.
Furthermore, based on the aforementioned report, it is further adorned with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

First, the adornments of the pavilions are described; next, the pervasive adornments of the precious ground are described; next, the adornments of space are described; and next, the bodily marks and adornments of the bodhisattvas from the ten directions who have gathered are described. Each and every adornment is mutually transparent, interpenetrating, and layered within one another.

Regarding the fact that the bodies, lands, and adornments of the oceans of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions interpenetrate one another in sovereign non-obstruction: this is because they take the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body as their essence, and it is naturally so that the myriad phenomena obtained through the retribution of the differentiated wisdoms are in accord with it.

Even if all Tathāgatas were to manifest all supernatural powers, they would not depart from this wisdom to give rise to great function; thus, there is nothing that is not sovereign, nothing that does not interpenetrate, and nothing that is not luminously pure.
Such wisdom is accomplished only through the harmonious cultivation and advancement of the aforementioned five stages; it cannot be attained by practicing a single dharma in isolation.
One may practice many without departing from the one, but one must not cling to the one as being self-sufficient.
This Jeta Grove and the adornments of all lands throughout the dharma-realm do not depart from two factors:

first, they are accomplished through the great compassion, great vows, and various practices of the wisdom and principle cultivated in the past; second, they are adorned by the inconceivable supernatural powers of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
As clarified by the sutra itself,
this answers the forty questions previously posed by the bodhisattvas.
The ten sections of the sutra beginning from "At that time, from the eastern direction" clarify the gathering of the bodhisattvas from the ten directions.

This clarifies the practices of the Buddha-fruit within the Dharma-realm, which are as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields; it answers the questions previously posed by the Bodhisattvas.
Since these are all the inexhaustible and all-pervading practices of the Buddha’s own fruit, the world is named Vajra-Lamp-Cloud-Banner.

As for "Vajra-Lamp-Cloud-Banner," it clarifies that all Buddhas arise from this vajra-wisdom to initiate the practice of great compassion, destroying the afflictions of all sentient beings; therefore, it is called a "banner."
The Buddha named Vairocana-Śrīrāja (King of Supreme Virtue) is the fruit within the practice.
The Bodhisattva, also named Vairocana-Pranidhāna-prabhāsa (Light of Vows), is so called because he manifests the fruit in accordance with his past vows and practices of great compassion.

The "King" (Rāja) signifies that the fruits of Buddhahood possess various kinds of sovereign mastery and non-obstruction according to practice; this is because they arise from adamantine wisdom (*vajrajñāna*), and thus the name of these fruits and practices is identical.

Regarding the phrase "coming together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields": this refers to the fulfillment of conduct through speech, whereby they cause all these bodhisattvas to assemble for this Dharma; thus it is said they "come together. This clarifies the fulfillment of the primary and attendant practices within the *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving).
The fact that all the bodhisattvas who have come are adorned with jeweled nets signifies that their teaching and practice are complete.

From here on, the nine directions are collectively arranged according to the sequence of the ten pāramitās; these represent, in general and specific, identical and differentiated aspects, the adamantine wisdom of a single Buddha. One should understand subsequent examples by following this model.
The following sections are self-evident according to the text; I shall merely explain the general meaning of the scripture, as the specific dharma-gates are fully contained within the sutra itself.
The preceding twenty-one segments of the sutra, which constitute the "Gate of Unifying Practice with Principle," have now been explained.
Above this, Samantabhadra is the principal figure and Mañjuśrī is his companion.

Below this, the Tathāgata emits a light from between his eyebrows named "Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm of the Three Times"; this is precisely the gate of unimpeded, free, and perfectly integrated harmony between principle and practice.
From this point onward, Mañjuśrī acts as the principal and Samantabhadra as his companion.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause all bodhisattvas to dwell securely in the Lion-Stretching Samādhi, emitted from between his eyebrows a ray of light called "The Door of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma-Dhātu Throughout the Three Times. This light is the fundamental, universal radiance of wisdom within the body of the Dharma-Dhātu. When this wisdom manifests before one, one perceives the vast duration of the three times as a single entity in the present; even the birth-and-death of inexhaustible kalpas does not shift from appearing before one, for they are collectively devoid of intrinsic nature. Thus, one becomes a great ocean of wisdom where all phenomena are cool and serene. Thereupon, through various practices, one gives rise to differentiated wisdom, knowing the faculties of beings to benefit them throughout the entire ocean of lands without rest—this is called the Practice of Samantabhadra.
This refers to the section following the sutra where one attains unspeakable gateways of various samādhis and the gateway for teaching and transforming infinite sentient beings;
this is fully explained as set forth in the sutra, and is complete according to the text itself.
The above twenty-seven sections of scripture conclude the answers to the forty dharma-gates previously inquired about by the great assembly of bodhisattvas.
This Dharma-realm dharma-gate is the essence of clear wisdom and sovereign mastery; it manifests spontaneously through the power of wisdom, without depending on the verbal teachings of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra were each commanded to proclaim the practice of their own original fruition from their respective positions, so that it might be easily understood and so that one would not become confused regarding the essence and function of the teaching.
The above constitutes the complete beginning and end of this sutra, encompassing the essence of the entire Dharma-realm.
From the section below, starting with "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī," onward, it is called the "Gate of Cultivating Practice for Benefiting Sentient Beings in Accordance with the Worldly."

In the teachings prior to this, he was simply called Mañjuśrī and not "the Youth" (kumāra). This indicates that from this point onward, he enters secular life to transform and benefit the deluded; as he establishes his name through his conduct, he is then called the Youth.

Prior to this clarification, it was generally established that the modes of transformation arise from within the Universal Radiance Wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*) of the Buddha-fruit, giving rise to the worthies and sages of the ten directions; these include the five classes of Bodhisattvas, such as Jñānacakra (Awakening Head) and Cakṣuś-cakra (Eye Head), all of whom universally transform beings without fixed direction, manifesting their presence and concealment with sovereign ease.
Mañjuśrī is the foremost of those with faith and is not called a "youth" (kumāra).

From this point onward, as he enters the mundane world from within the essence of the dharmadhātu to initiate the transformation of the ignorant, he is given a name based on his engaged practice, and is thus titled Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
This is because one transforms the ignorant through wondrous wisdom, enters the Buddha’s wisdom, and is born into the Buddha’s family.

This is the initial arising of the bodhicitta of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; it is the manifestation of the fundamental wisdom and the wondrous insight into the principle of non-substantiality of the original dharmakāya.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time are born into the Buddha-family from this, and it is from this that they accomplish the great vows and practices of Samantabhadra.
For what reason is this called the "Gate of Practicing for the Benefit of Beings by Adapting to the World"?

Hitherto, it was merely stated that they "ascended to heaven," signifying that their practice had brought them to fulfillment among the various devas, yet they had not yet gone into the midst of the mundane world to transform and benefit others.

From the beginning up to this "Dharmadhātu Chapter" (one volume and a half of the remaining sutra), there have been only bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and worldly rulers who had already attained the Way; there has not yet been a single ordinary person living in the secular world who has entered this Dharma-gate.

From the time the youth Mañjuśrī descended from the Well-Abiding Pavilion, he entered the human realm to engage with ordinary people according to their faculties and to transform and benefit them, enabling them to realize the principles of this Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, it causes the youth Sudhana to seek out fifty-two spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in order to represent the three types of cause and effect across the five stages (*pañca-vastu*). Within the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of Mañjuśrī is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); within the differentiated wisdom (*prabheda-jñāna*) of Samantabhadra is its practice; and the wisdom that abides in neither of these two is called "Buddha. When these three dharmas are fully possessed, one is named a Buddha.

By means of these three dharmas, which universally function as cause and effect throughout the beginning and end of the five stages, one is said to "ride the Tathāgata-vehicle" until reaching the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
It is also called the "Dharma-realm vehicle," because the Dharma-realm takes these three types of cause and effect as its very essence and function.
The sequence of cause and effect across the five preceding stages is likewise so; in total, these three dharmas constitute the cause and effect.

These—Buddha, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—act as cause and effect in relation to the conduct of the fifty spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), yet they themselves possess no cause and effect, because within their own state of Buddhahood there is nothing to be cultivated and nothing to be practiced.

It is only for the sake of practitioners within the five stages that we speak of "cause and effect" in reference to the point where the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles—defilement and purity—are treated and brought to maturity.

However, within the Dharma-body, the wisdom of principle, and the myriad practices, there is inherently no cause and effect; it is merely by virtue of applying preparatory practices (*prayoga*) within the five stages to treat the delusions and their latencies that such a designation of "cause and effect" is established.

Because Mañjuśrī traveled to various cities and human realms to teach according to the capacities of beings, he caused Sudhana to arise in the stage of applied practice (*prayoga-avasthā*), leading him to seek fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and accomplish one hundred and ten dharma-gates of cause and effect. This was done so that students would not become confused regarding the practices of the five stages and might find them easy to understand.

Because it serves as a model for practice for those who have subsequently generated the bodhicitta, it is called the "Gate of Conduct for Benefiting Beings through Engagement with the World," so that learners may follow this model of conduct without becoming confused.
There is further meaning that will be clarified below when reaching its proper place.

From this point onward, within the section on the "Gate of Practice for Producing Benefits and Birth according to Worldly Conventions," starting from "Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta" down to the end of the sutra, it is divided into three long sections.

First, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī [emerged] from the Well-Abiding Pavilion" down to the start of the sixty-second fascicle, "At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, having exhorted the bhikṣus to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," this section of the sūtra is titled "The Gate of Initially Entering the World by Following the Roots through Traveling."

The second section, "Gradually traveling south through the human world until reaching the east of the City of Bliss," describes Mañjuśrī’s entry into the secular human realm to expound the *Sūtra Door of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*.

The third section, from "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī knew that the people of Puṇḍravardhana had all assembled" down to the end of the sutra, constitutes the gateway of discerning the faculties and the Dharma to accomplish practice.
First, from the very beginning, regarding the section on entering the mundane world through travel, it is divided into two parts.

The first part, from "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī" down to "taking his leave and traveling south toward the human realm," consists of twenty and a half lines of scripture; this clarifies the section concerning his departure from the Buddha to travel south toward the human realm, accompanied by fellow bodhisattvas and his constant retinue.

2. From "At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra" down to "accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas," there are eighty-six lines and a half of sūtra text. This clarifies how six thousand bhikṣus, including Śāriputra, followed Mañjuśrī on his journey southward; while on the road, they resolved their minds for enlightenment and attained this portion of the Dharma-gate of the Single Vehicle.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: first, within the section beginning from "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī" and so forth, the Sūtra states, "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī emerged from the Well-Abiding Pavilion. This clarifies that he manifests fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) through his own *dharmakāya*, and gives rise to discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) within the pavilion; because he does so for the benefit of sentient beings, it is called "emerging."

The "immeasurable bodhisattvas of common practice" are those who have accomplished the auxiliary paths as their retinue, for they together teach and transform sentient beings; thus, they are the primary and secondary associates of the ten thousand practices.
The "various vajra deities who constantly follow and guard" refers collectively to all the deities who serve as attendants and guardians.
Among these deities, there are approximately two meanings:
first, the names are established based on the specific virtues practiced by each deity;
second, their virtues are designated based on the differentiated practices of Mañjuśrī’s own virtues, serving the purpose of acting as attendants and guardians.

This section, together with the thirty-two assemblies of Bodhisattvas, devas, and spirits, and including the subsequent assembly of six thousand bhikṣus, constitutes forty-two assemblies; these serve as forty-two kinds of expedient practices to bring sentient beings to the ocean of great wisdom and liberation.
The first, the Vajra Deity, is the wisdom of universal radiance within the Dharma-body; because this wisdom manifests, it is called a "deity.
That he universally serves as a deity for the assembly of Buddhas through offerings to all sentient beings signifies the meaning of reverence.

By means of clouds of vast emanation bodies, they reverently make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions and guide sentient beings, as a result of which they obtain a body that is upright, dignified, and adorned.
"Practitioner on foot" signifies the meaning of diligent exertion; it is the practice of teaching and transforming sentient beings without weariness.
"Wind Deity" wears a crown made of *maṇi* jewels, signifying the meaning of being able to establish the teachings through pure and stainless wisdom.

Because the nature of wind can blow apart and disperse all things, yet can also lift, sustain, and cause all things to grow, it nevertheless lacks any inherent essence or basis of its own; this is symbolized by the stainless jewel crown.
The wisdom of the semblance-dharmakāya is able to expound the net of teachings, dispersing and destroying the defilements of affliction and purification, such that it itself has no basis.
This is because the trigram Xùn represents the wind of teaching.
The remainder is fully contained within the sutra itself.

Just as those in the realm of hungry ghosts who have been expelled by the king of the kumbhāṇḍas carry them—using these large sacks that hang down like winter gourds—sitting upon them or placing them upon their shoulders while walking.
Taking on forms to manifest the Dharma, he descends into the mundane world through great compassion, bearing the burden of sentient beings without ever speaking of weariness or fatigue.
As for the King of the Mahoragas, these belong to the class of great pythons that travel on their bellies.
Taking up the image to represent the Dharma, walking with the chest and abdomen signifies the meaning of reverence; this refers to the protector deity of the saṃghārāma.
Other instances should be understood according to their respective names, following this same principle of symbolic representation.
As for Mañjuśrī and the various bodhisattvas emerging from their respective abodes, this signifies that they adapt to the secular world according to the capacities of beings.
As for their circumambulating the Tathāgata immeasurable times to the right, this signifies their respectful compliance with his conduct.
Regarding "circumambulating to the right," this refers to proceeding from the south, through the east, and reaching the north.
In the second section, where Śāriputra and the six thousand bhikṣus follow Mañjuśrī southward, it is further divided into seven subsections.

First: From "At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra" down to "all were accomplished through the teaching and transformation by Mañjuśrī," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on Śāriputra and six thousand bhikṣus following Mañjuśrī southward.

2. From "At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra" down to "the light from the mark of the white tuft between his brows came and illuminated his body, entering through the crown of his head," there are sixteen lines of scripture which clarify how Śāriputra exhorted the bhikṣus to observe the ten kinds of auspicious signs adorning Mañjuśrī’s body as he traveled along the road, as well as the various features of the path.

3. From "At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra" down to "these bhikṣus wish to have an audience," there are ten and a half lines of sūtra. This clarifies how Śāriputra praised Mañjuśrī’s ten immeasurable virtues, and how the assembly of bhikṣus all desired to see Mañjuśrī; thus, Śāriputra made his request to Mañjuśrī on their behalf.

4. From "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī" down to "May I fully attain all [these qualities]"—this passage of six and a half lines of scripture clarifies the section on the six thousand bhikṣus prostrating before Mañjuśrī, making their own great vows, and the Buddha’s witnessing and knowing thereof.

5. From "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the bhikṣus" down to "approaching the stage of the Tathāgata," there are eighteen lines of scripture which clarify how Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva expounded for the bhikṣus ten kinds of tireless Dharma-practices, so that they would not fall into the stages of the two vehicles and would enter the portion of the stage of the Tathāgata.

6. From "At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard this Dharma" down to "abiding in the bodhicitta, firm and immovable," there are sixteen lines of scripture. These clarify that when six thousand bhikṣus heard Mañjuśrī’s teaching, they attained the Samādhi of the Unobstructed Eye regarding the Dharma, and each obtained a portion of ten gates of liberation regarding each of all dharmas.

7. From the passage beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva exhorted the bhikṣus" down to the end of the fascicle, there are six lines of scripture clarifying that Mañjuśrī again exhorted the bhikṣus to abide in the practices of Samantabhadra; they thereby attained non-separation from the feet of Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra manifested his body before the Buddhas of the ten directions, fully possessing all the divisions of the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the six thousand bhikṣus represent those who have attained faith and have likewise entered the stages of realization.

Because they simultaneously attain the ten levels of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten grounds, and the eleventh ground all at once upon this path, it is said that "six thousand [bhikṣus] surround him from before and behind."
With Śāriputra as the leader and the others as his companions, they travel together as leader and followers because they clearly advance in their quest for the True Dharma.
"Departing from their dwelling place" means departing from the stage of the śrāvakas and various provisional views, in order to proceed toward the Great Bodhi of the Dharmadhātu.
They circumambulated the Buddha three times, as all were in accordance with the Buddha’s true teaching.
This circumambulation three times was performed by keeping the right side toward him; starting from the south, they proceeded to the east, then north, then west, and finally back to the south.
Thus, three circumambulations were performed as the ritual for right circumambulation, causing the people to walk counter-clockwise.

These six thousand bhikṣus were co-residents of Śāriputra; they had not long since left the household life and were not yet arhats, but because they possessed the seeds from previous lives, they were all easily inspired to resolve their minds [on enlightenment].

The Sūtra states: "The six thousand bhikṣus have all made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, deeply planting roots of goodness; their power of understanding is vast and their eye of faith is clear and penetrating. This clarifies that they planted the root of faith in former lives, and in this present life, the seeds of faith have already matured.

Śāriputra exhorted the bhikṣus to observe the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī’s halo of merit, which shines through with penetrating clarity; this is the constant radiance of a pure mind, capable of bringing joy to all who behold it.
The "Luminous Net" refers to the perfection of the Dharma-net; it clarifies that the light of the teaching adorns the body, so that those who see it extinguish their suffering.
As for the eight paces on either side of Mañjuśrī’s path being level and adorned, this clarifies that his body and mind are always conjoined with the Eightfold Noble Path.
The phrase "there is always a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) throughout the ten directions" means that his transformative activities constantly fill the ten directions.

As for the statement that when the Buddhas preach the Dharma they emit light from between their eyebrows to drench the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, this clarifies that Mañjuśrī is the crown of the wisdom of the formless Dharmakāya—the initial aspiration awakened by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
When all Buddhas first resolve their minds toward enlightenment, they enter this wisdom and are thereby born into the Buddha-family.
All sentient beings who first resolve their minds toward Bodhi take this very Dharma-body of signless wisdom as their essence.
All sentient beings inherently possess this, yet it can only be clearly manifested through the expedient power of samādhi.
That the trees are all adorned with jewels illustrates that these arise as the retribution for past practices.

The six thousand bhikṣus, having observed Mañjuśrī and the ten kinds of tireless dharmas they had heard, immediately attained the Samādhi of Unobstructed Vision. Within the Dharma-body, they obtained the clear and pure eye of signless wisdom; because their grasping was extinguished and their views had faded away, their eye of wisdom was perfectly penetrating—it was not the physical eye.
When the five views, such as the view of self-identity and so forth, have perished, the Dharma is naturally manifest; this is the exhaustion of all spatial obstructions.

Initially, within each of all dharmas, ten dharmas are clarified to manifest the power of samādhi at its very inception. Subsequently, one is exhorted to further advance through the vows and practices of Samantabhadra, whereby all illuminations are fully realized.
The above concludes the account of the six thousand bhikṣus who resolved their minds on enlightenment.
Following this, the account of his transformative activities for the benefit of sentient beings in the city of Vārāṇasī is presented.
As for Śāriputra, he was a manifested śrāvaka, as has already been described previously.
The remaining meanings above are self-evident according to the text.
Second, the entry into the mundane world to preach the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm* took place at the Great Stūpa in the Śāla Grove to the east of Puṇyavatī City.

Furthermore, this section—from "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva exhorted the bhikṣus" down to "at the site of the great stūpa in the Śāla grove"—consists of fifteen and a half lines of scripture, which is further divided into two parts.

First: From "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva" down to "honored by humans and non-humans," there are seven and a half lines of scripture, which clarify that Mañjuśrī traveled among human beings to reach those who were suitable vessels for his transformative teachings.

II. From "At that time, Mañjuśrī, together with his retinue" down to "the site of the great stūpa," there are eight lines of scripture which clarify the section on the benefits obtained upon hearing the Dharma, namely, Mañjuśrī’s exposition of the Sūtra-gate of the Universal Illumination of the Dharmadhātu.

At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva exhorted the bhikṣus to resolve upon bodhicitta; the entire preceding teaching concerning their gradual journey southward through the human world clarifies that the Bodhisattva leads others toward illumination, taking "leaving" (li) as the means to that illumination.
"Passing through the human realm" clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s great compassion acts as an uninvited friend, drawing beings toward transformation according to their faculties.

"City of Blessings" (Puṇyavatī) is named after the fact that many people therein cultivate merit; it also refers to the fact that wherever a noble being dwells, that place is adorned with merit and virtue.
The term "banner" (*dhvaja*) has two meanings:
first, because the Buddhas of the past were able to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish at this very spot, thereby destroying all attachments, it is called a banner;
second, because this place contains ancient Buddha-stūpas and temples, as well as groves of trees that stand tall and majestic, it is adorned with such sublime features.
As for the "Great Stūpa," it is called "great" because its fame and reputation extend throughout the ten directions and are heard afar across Buddha-lands;
it is also called "great" in that, according to the gateway of the Dharma-realm, there is no interior, exterior, or middle, and all views have ceased.
Within it, one installs an image of the Venerable One that must not be defaced; this is called a *stūpa* or temple, and is also termed a banner (*dhvaja*).
A Brahman monk said:
"As for this *stūpa* or temple, if one beats a drum on its southern side, it cannot be heard on the northern side; therefore, it is called 'Great' in the world."
"Sāla" means "loftily towering.
From the passage beginning with "devas, nāgas, and yakṣas" onwards, it clarifies that the eight classes of beings, including devas, nāgas, and humans, constantly offer worship.
“Mañjuśrī and his retinue” refers to the assembly of six thousand bodhisattvas, devas, and humans who came together with him.

“Expounding the Sūtra on the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm” means that this fundamental wisdom is luminously penetrating, all-pervasive, and conforms to the faculties of beings everywhere.

"Ten million billion nayutas" refers to this "valley"; it clarifies that the *Avyaktasūtra* (Ineffable Sūtra) serves as its retinue, illustrating how the wisdom of differentiation pervades everywhere to bestow benefit according to the faculties of beings.
*Sūtra* means "long prose discourse.

From the passage beginning with "When this sutra was being preached, within the great ocean," it clarifies that immeasurable dragons, having heard the Dharma, all cast off their dragon bodies and were reborn among devas and humans.
Ten thousand nāgas attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi, and countless sentient beings were each tamed within the three vehicles.
Each clearly understood their own faculties and, according to their distinct wisdom, attained the dharma-gates suited to their respective natures.

The above clarifies the "Gate of Saving According to Capacities" from the *Puzhao fajie xuduoluo* (Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm), as fully contained within that scripture itself.
Third is the "Gate of Discerning Capacities and Dharmas to Accomplish Practice."

From the passage "Immeasurable multitudes emerged from the city" until the end of the sutra, it consistently describes Mañjuśrī’s observation of Sudhana and his retinue, as well as their journey southward to Mount Meghadri, where they successively seek out fifty-three persons as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) by traversing the stages of the five ranks of cause and effect. This serves as a model for future generations to emulate in order to perfect their practice over aeons; this section is titled "The Section on Discerning Capacities and Accomplishing Practice through the Dharma."
Within this section, there are further two subdivisions.

The first, beginning from "A great assembly of immeasurable numbers emerged from the city" and ending with "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva turned like an elephant king," consists of ninety-four lines of scripture. This clarifies how the fourfold assembly gathered at Puṇḍravardhana, and how Mañjuśrī expounded the Dharma according to their various inclinations and requests to bring them to purity; it also describes his observation of Sudhana, the investigation of cause and effect, and his exhortation to approach spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

The second section, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī turned like an elephant king" down to the end of the sutra, is titled "The Gate of Knowing the Faculties and Bestowing the Dharma so as to Enable Practice and Generate Subsequent Learning."
Within the first section from the beginning, there are ninety-four lines of scripture, which are divided approximately into six parts.

First, from "An immeasurable great assembly came out from the city and went to where he was" down to "five hundred young maidens," there are twenty-one and a half lines of scripture; this is the Section on the Gathering of the Great Assembly.

2. From "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī" down to "dedicating [merit] toward Bodhi without any hindrance," there are twenty-five lines of scripture.
