This section clarifies how the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī observes the reasons for Sudhana’s name, as well as the portion concerning his past roots of goodness and their fruition in this present life.

3. From "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva observed Sudhana in this way" down to "he expounded the dharma of the equality and non-duality of all Buddhas," there are six and a half lines of scripture; this constitutes the section on Mañjuśrī knowing that Sudhana’s faculties were capable and thus preaching the Dharma for him.

IV. From "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī" down to "and then departed," there are four and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on Mañjuśrī preaching the Dharma for Sudhana and the great assembly before departing.

5. From "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "and spoke these verses," there are two and a half lines of scripture. This section clarifies how, having heard the Dharma and given rise to faith, Sudhana diligently sought unsurpassed bodhi; it consists of his speaking verses to Mañjuśrī to lament the suffering wheel of the three realms of existence and to request instruction on the Dharma.

In the sixth section, "The Discourse in Verse," there are thirty-four stanzas that clarify Sudhana’s lamentation over the root of his own suffering; this constitutes the portion on requesting the Dharma through verse for the sake of self-benefit and benefiting others.

Within this section of thirty-four verses, the first four verses consist of self-lamentation regarding the causes of the suffering of birth and death; the remaining thirty verses constitute the section praising the virtues of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and requesting the Dharma-gate.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: in the first section, concerning the gathering of the fourfold assembly, the sutra states, "immeasurable multitudes emerged from that city," yet when enumerating their numbers, it mentions only five hundred. This clarifies that the count is established based on those capable of generating the bodhicitta, completed through the five stages and the ten pāramitās; it is not a count based on individual persons.
Because within the ten pāramitās practiced across the five stages, there are one hundred mutual embodiments—since there are ten within each one.

For instance, when the dāna-pāramitā is primary, the other nine are its companions; when the śīla-pāramitā is primary, the other nine are its companions; when the kṣānti-pāramitā is primary, the other nine are its companions; all cases are modeled after this.

Thus, these one hundred pāramitās are established as five hundred through their differentiation according to the stages of the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and the eleventh ground; they are distinguished by the varying names of the ascending progress, the vision of the path, the remediation of afflictions, and the depth or shallowness of the residual tendencies (vāsanā) in accordance with superior practice.

If one considers the conduct of Samantabhadra, which encompasses the entirety of the infinite oceans of lands throughout the Dharma-realm, there are as many pāramitās as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
For now, let us consider only the five stages, wherein each stage contains one hundred pāramitās, totaling five hundred across the five stages.
As for the previous statement that ten thousand nāgas all resolved their minds toward bodhi, this clearly illustrates the perfection of the ten thousand practices.
Sudatta means "one who provides good gifts" to those without protection; he is also called Gṛhapati (the Solitary).
Vasudatta means "bestowing wealth"; he performs virtuous deeds daily.
Thus, the fourfold assembly together with ten thousand nāgas resolved upon bodhicitta.

The number of the assemblies was five: namely, the assembly of nāgas, five hundred upāsakas, and five hundred upāsikās; all of whom, though dwelling within the worldly stream, possessed pure and profound faith.
The boys and girls are all under twenty years of age and have not yet reached their majority; being men and women of pure faith who are untainted by worldly desires, they are called "boys and girls."
In youth, one first awakens the initial resolve, returning to the stream of the Dharma to receive instruction; these are called *kumāra* (boy) and *kumārikā* (girl).
"Child" (*tóng*) refers to the state of being newly ignorant.
One establishes the lower village as the realm of childhood.
Those whose age is not yet advanced, who establish their resolve and virtue within their local neighborhoods, are called "Childlike Disciples" (Tongzi).
Those whose age is advanced, provided they possess pure faith, are simply referred to as "Pure Faith Laymen" (Qingxin Shi) or "Pure Faith Laywomen" (Qingxin Nü).
The assembly listed above follows the meanings of their respective names; these are the virtues they have cultivated.

Some names are established based on physical appearance, such as the Great Wisdom Laywoman (Mahāprajñā Upāsikā), who was named after her father’s title. Others are established according to their specific virtues.
The rest may be understood by analogy.
When the Sūtra says, "His majestic radiance was brilliant and resplendent," it clarifies that the color of Mañjuśrī’s body was so intensely bright that it outshone the entire assembly.

As for how Mañjuśrī observed the names and causes-and-conditions of Sudhana—specifically, how a seven-jeweled pavilion spontaneously appeared within his house at the moment of his initial entry into the womb—this is a case of a result being induced by its cause; it is impossible for a retribution to arise without a cause.

To clarify the faith of previous lives: being able to believe that one's own mind is the all-pervading, luminous wisdom of the dharmakāya—complete, pure, and stainless—and taking this as the seed of faith, is called the "embryo" (garbha).
As for the "Golden World" and the "Immovable Wisdom" spoken of in the Hall of Universal Radiance within the stage of faith, the pure and stainless Dharmakāya is what is termed the "Golden World."
The wisdom of universal radiance is called the Buddha Immovable Wisdom (*Acalamati*), because its fundamental nature is inherently incapable of being moved.

That which is now termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*) was, in past lives, the very faith in this ignorance of one's own mind and the ignorance of all sentient beings; it is, in its entirety, the seed of the pure wisdom of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas.
This faith is called the "womb. Born from this womb of faith into the world, one obtains as karmic retribution a pavilion made of the seven treasures.
This faith is accomplished through the power of contemplative observation by means of wisdom.
Regarding the seven treasures and the seven hidden treasuries, these are all born as retributions for the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
The same applies to the subsequent groups of seven.
As for the ten months in the womb, this represents the fulfillment of the worldly dharmas by practicing the ten *pāramitās* within the stage of faith.
"Birth" refers to the arising of supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*).
"The physical form and its members being upright and well-proportioned" is due to accomplishment through the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

"Within the house there are spontaneously five hundred precious vessels, filled naturally with all manner of things, which shine upon one another in mutual adornment" clarifies that within the seeds of faith planted in previous lives—faith in the causes and effects of the Buddha, the practice-gates of the five stages, the ten *pāramitās*, the five hundred practice-gates, the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold path, and the myriad practices of both identity and difference, as well as the causes and effects from beginning to end—all are obtained as the retributive fruit within the sphere of faith.
In this present life, by means of this faith, one is able to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment once more, without being separated from it for even a single lifetime.
The dharma-gate of the one hundred and ten cities is, in a single moment, suddenly sealed with perfect integrity.

The hundred and ten dharma-gates established within the locus of faith do not depart from the śāla grove, yet the body travels throughout all lands; this is simply because the dust contains the nature of the dharma-realm, which is spontaneously as it is, and wisdom encompasses the three periods of time, past, present, and future, within a single thought-moment.
This is based on the reality of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), yet it does not rely on the delusions of ordinary sentiment.
Other meanings will be clarified below in accordance with the respective passages.
This concludes the analysis of names based on causes and the analysis of causes based on retribution.

The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, this youth has already made offerings to the Buddhas of the past, deeply planted roots of goodness, and possesses vast faith and understanding. This clarifies that while the seeds of faith were sown in previous lives, they have now reached full maturity in this life.

From the passage beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva" onwards, what is called "the Dharma accumulated by all Buddhas" clarifies the accumulation of the ten *pāramitās*, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the five stages, and the dharma-gates of the one hundred and ten cities.

Regarding the Dharma-gate of the one hundred and ten cities: within the five stages, there are fifty points of cause and effect for cultivation. These correspond to the ten Wisdom Bodhisattvas within the preceding Ten Abodes; these are the ten Buddha-fruits that share the common name "Moon."

Thus, within the ten practices, there are the ten forest Bodhisattvas and the ten eye Buddhas; within the ten dedications, there are the ten banner Bodhisattvas and the ten wondrous Buddhas. Likewise, the ten stages and the eleventh stage all rely upon this causal and resultant relationship of the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas within these ten dedications.

Thus, within these five stages, there are fifty layers of cause and effect, each of which possesses its own progressive cultivation of cause and effect; these are divided into one hundred. These do not depart from the ten *pāramitās* within the fundamental, eternal *dharmadhātu*-essence of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, making one hundred and ten.

From the outset, within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one manifests the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya* through the samādhi of skillful means; riding upon the vehicle of the *dharmadhātu*, one practices the conduct of Samantabhadra to treat the residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Thus, one establishes the successive gates for treating the various distinctions between delusions and habitual tendencies.
These one hundred sets of cause and effect constitute the ascending and descending stages for subduing the habitual tendencies of delusion.

The causes and effects of the ten *pāramitās*—namely, wisdom, principle, compassion, and vows—are the ever-present conduct of Samantabhadra within the essence of the *dharmadhātu*. Because they serve as the tracks for all who have awakened the bodhicitta to tread upon, they are called "riding the Tathāgata-vehicle" until reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Because the initial arousal of the mind immediately mounts upon the Dharma-realm through the gate of the essence and function, principle and wisdom, great compassion and vows and practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, it is the very essence and function of the fundamental site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
The following fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the youth Sudhana are established because they represent the modes of practice within the five stages of entering the path.

While the preceding [sections] explained only their respective teachings, there was a concern that practitioners might become confused regarding the actual conduct; therefore, this Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva now intends to provide Sudhana with a model for seeking the Dharma. By once again clarifying the rules and modes of practice within the five stages of the bodhisattvas, he enables future learners to emulate them. Thus, these fifty-three individuals are established to form a hundred and ten successive gates of cause and effect.

Within the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, Mañjuśrī is established as the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the *dharmakāya* Buddha, Samantabhadra as the wisdom of differentiation (*prabheda-jñāna*), and Maitreya Buddha as the unconditioned fruit (*anabhisamskāra-phala*) within these principles and practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. Through these three dharmas, one forms the gate of the sovereign non-obstruction of the essence and function of a single *dharmadhātu*, which universally serves as the cause and effect for the fifty bodhisattvas throughout the five stages.

It is as previously stated: taking the ten pāramitās within the essence of the dharma-dhātu as the practice to be mounted, there are causes and effects for each of the fifty successive layers of pāramitās throughout the five stages of progressive advancement.

Thus, within these fifty spiritual friends, there are two in each one; within the fifty, there are one hundred. When combined with the ten *pāramitās* that have always been practiced throughout the Dharma-realm, they total one hundred and ten.

Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya’s Buddha-fruit—these three dharmas constitute, in essence, a single gate of sovereign, effortless great function within the Dharma-realm. They serve solely as cause and effect for all Bodhisattvas of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*), thereby clarifying the merit of such progress; yet, they themselves possess no cause or effect.
It is just as a sovereign king has no fixed ranks of his own; rather, through the mastery of his majestic power, he establishes ranks for all his officials according to their respective merits.
Question: For what reason is Maitreya Buddha taken here as the fruit of Buddhahood?
Why is Vairocana Tathāgata not taken as the fruit of Buddhahood?
The answer is:
It clarifies that Vairocana is the fruit already accomplished, while Maitreya is the future Buddha-fruit.

This is because it clarifies that by now generating the initial aspiration for bodhicitta before the present Buddha Vairocana, one attains a corresponding realization in a single thought-moment that accords with the future Buddha-fruit of Maitreya.

This is because, within the pavilion of Maitreya, the time-intervals of the three periods and the days and months are all unified as one; it clarifies that by means of the seal of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna-mudrā*), the three periods of past, present, and future are marked as being without before or after.
The Sūtra states: "The accumulation of dharmas explains the continuous dharma of all Buddhas, and so forth, up to explaining the sequential dharma of all Buddhas.
This is explained in general as above.

It explains the dharma of the purity of the assemblies of all Buddhas, clarifying that the assemblies of all Buddhas are uniformly and identically pure; for body and land, as well as the assemblies, do not obstruct one another, but rather interpenetrate one another in infinite layers.
The remainder is fully contained within the text itself.

Regarding these thirty-four verses, the first four verses express self-reflection on how birth and death, headed by the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), involve the incessant suffering of saṃsāra, such as aging and birth.
The following thirty verses clarify Sudhana’s praise of Mañjuśrī’s virtues and his request for the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "the three realms of existence as a city wall," it clarifies that Sudhana praises himself for dwelling within the three realms of existence, remaining firmly entrenched within them and not departing, just as one stays within a city wall.
The three realms of existence are the existence of the desire realm, the existence of the form realm, and the existence of the formless realm.
All sentient beings are unable to escape from these three bodies of existence.
Regarding arrogance (*māna*): to act with impropriety is *māna*, while to look down upon others is called *abhimāna*.

Furthermore, there are seven types of pride: pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*adhimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), overweening pride (*abhimāna*), self-pride (*asmimāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
The various destinies (*gati*) refer to the destiny of views (*dṛṣṭigati*) and the destiny of precepts (*śīlagati*).

Furthermore, there are three destinies: the destiny of wrong determination (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), the destiny of no fixed determination (*aniyata-rāśi*), and the destiny of right determination (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).
Additionally, there are four evil destinies (*apāya*).
Furthermore, there is the realm of humans and devas through the five precepts and ten wholesome paths;

the supramundane realm of the two vehicles who are weary of suffering; the realm of the pure lands of Mahāyāna bodhisattvas; and the realm of the One Vehicle bodhisattvas where wisdom and compassion are perfectly integrated, yet they have not yet attained full mastery.
These various realms of existence, when described according to their wholesome or unwholesome nature, are all karmic activities through which one enters.
Regarding "the water of craving as a moat": because craving can moisten and nourish birth and death, it is like a moat surrounding a pond.

As for "delusion" (*moha*): that which can cause one to be confused regarding ultimate truth is called delusion. There are eighty-four thousand types of delusion in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and there are twenty-two kinds of delusions regarding non-comprehension according to their respective stages in Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
If one follows the one hundred and ten types of delusion across the five stages, one will realize one hundred and ten types of liberation.

Regarding those whose fires of greed and anger blaze fiercely: among the afflictions of the three realms, greed is the head of the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); anger is the retinue of hatred; ignorance is the universal veil; pride consists of deprecating oneself and others; and doubt, together with the five views, can obstruct the Path. Together, they constitute the causes and conditions of birth and death.
When doubt perishes and views are abandoned, wisdom then manifests before one.

Among the ten fetters (*daśa-āsrava*), doubt and the five views are both capable of obstructing the Noble Path, while greed, hatred, delusion, and pride are capable of obstructing the practice of those on the path of cultivation.
If one does not govern these formations with the Path, one will continue to wander through birth and death, driven by karma and lacking self-mastery.
Here, I shall briefly explain the two gates of greed and anger according to the scriptural text; the remaining eight [afflictions] may be understood by analogy with this principle.
Because these two obstacles of greed and hatred prevent all roots of goodness from arising, they are like a blazing fire.
As for the King Māra who acts as a sovereign, he refers to the four māras: the skandha-māra, the kleśa-māra, the devaputra-māra, and the mṛtyu-māra.
Regarding "the ignorant abide in dependence": that which obscures and veils so as to leave the mind lacking clarity is called ignorance (*bāla*).
Regarding "greed and craving as fetters": previously, anger arose because of greed; now, attachment arises because of greed, thereby binding oneself.
"Shackles and fetters" refers to the ropes used to bind and restrain criminals.
"Deceit and flattery as reins and bits" clarifies that one who delights in falsehood is brought under control.
"Doubt obscures one's clarity" means that one gives rise to doubt regarding the Right Path.
Those who enter upon various wrong paths do so because they give rise to doubt regarding the principle of non-substantiality; this is the arising of wrong paths.

Regarding "due to stinginess, envy, and arrogance": there are five kinds of stinginess: attachment to one's dwelling place, one's home, one's wealth and possessions, lack of delight in praising the virtues of others, and being parsimonious toward the Dharma and unwilling to share it with others—these are the five.
Envy (*īrṣyā*) is to harbor hatred toward others who surpass oneself.
Arrogance (*mada*) is to indulge oneself recklessly due to a lack of decorum.
Extravagance (*visama*) is a lack of frugality.

Attachment, aversion, conceit, envy, and stinginess constitute only the five fetters of the lower realm; attachment to the form realm, attachment to the formless realm, restlessness, conceit, and ignorance constitute the five fetters common to both the upper and lower realms.
"By means of these ten fetters, one is firmly bound by the four Māras and enters the three evil realms.

One who undergoes the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death and cannot transcend the world"—with this, Sudhana’s lamentation concerning the causes and conditions of the suffering of birth and death within the triple world is concluded.
The following thirty verses praise these virtues and request the Dharma, as is self-evident from the text itself.

Thus, regarding the afflictions of the three realms: the first and second stages counteract the delusions of the lower realm; the third stage counters the delusions of the two upper realms; the fourth stage transcends the three realms; the fifth stage practices worldly arts and skills; the sixth stage is fully endowed with supramundane wisdom; the seventh stage enters the cycle of birth and death within the three realms and six paths to practice great compassion; the eighth stage possesses effortless wisdom and perfected compassion; the ninth stage brings the Buddha-activity to full completion; the tenth stage completes the conduct of Samantabhadra; and at the eleventh stage, one’s merit is equal to the Dharma-realm, with the wisdom and principle remaining eternally constant.

The rules for the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*) are in part similar to the methods and applications of the practices of these Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*); however, they differ in their progressive advancement. While the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*) discuss only the practice-gate of non-defilement, the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) integrate and harmonize compassion and vows, as is fully manifested in the respective stages and clearly explained in the fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) below.

Regarding the second section, in which Mañjuśrī, knowing the faculties [of the disciples], imparts the Dharma so that they may accomplish practice and give rise to the gateway for later students, five sections are established:

first, clarifying that faith has already been generated; second, clarifying the acceptance by the Noble Ones; third, clarifying the exhortation by the Noble Ones to draw near to virtuous friends; fourth, clarifying Sudhana’s request for the Dharma; and fifth, clarifying Mañjuśrī’s instruction on the destination of practice.
First, regarding those who have already aroused the mind of faith: as the sutra says, "Good son!

You have already aroused the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This refers to the bodhi of the stage of entry through this mind of faith; it is only by means of the practice of samādhi that one can manifest the principle, whereby the characteristics of practice become apparent, karma is exhausted, and pure clarity prevails.
Second, regarding the inclusion by the Noble One: the Sūtra states, "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva turned like an elephant king," which signifies the sense of inclusion.
Just as the Great Sage’s unimpeded wisdom is perfect and its form is all-pervasive, manifesting in accordance with the faculties of beings without turning away from them;

so that for all sentient beings who are to see him according to their needs, he appears face-to-face before each, yet at that time, those beings do not know one another, each thinking only, "The Sage is speaking to me alone."

Now, regarding the statement that Mañjuśrī turned toward Sudhana like an elephant king, this was because he knew Sudhana’s faculties, looked upon him with favor, and intended to guide and sustain him with the Dharma.
Thirdly, as for the Holy One’s exhortation to draw near to spiritual friends, the Sūtra says: "Good son!..."

"Approaching and making offerings to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) is the primary causal condition for the fulfillment of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā). Therefore, do not give rise to weariness or aversion toward this.
This all-knowledge is the bodhicitta; that which manifests through non-apprehension (anupalambha) is called fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna).
Taking non-attainment as its essence, it has the manifestation of the myriad dharmas as its function.
Regarding the four clarifications and Sudhana’s request for the Dharma, the Sūtra says: "How does one study the Bodhisattva path?"
There are eleven questions concerning the path of the bodhisattva.
The question is asked:
Why is it said only that one "seeks the bodhisattva path," rather than saying one "studies the bodhicitta"?
The answer is:

Because enlightenment is without anything to be attained, nothing to be cultivated, nothing to be studied, and nothing to be practiced, one merely seeks the bodhisattva path and trains in the bodhisattva conduct; nevertheless, the bodhicitta is spontaneously and constantly manifest.
Regarding the phrase "as on Mount Wondrous Peak, attaining the gate of recollecting the light of wisdom of all Buddhas," this clarifies how phenomena are used to symbolize the Dharma.

Mount Gen (艮) represents mountain and stillness; by means of this stillness, the mind is restrained so that it is free from thought. When delusive imaginings do not arise and right wisdom manifests before one, this is called "recollecting."

Because right wisdom is in accord with the signless, wondrous principle of all Buddhas, when this signless right wisdom manifests before one, it universally illuminates the mind and its objects, causing the five views—of self, of phenomena, of permanence, of annihilation, and so forth—to vanish entirely. All myriad objects become empty and still; as views perish and karma subsides, this is called "Radiance. Therefore, it is said: "The Gate of Recollecting the Radiant Wisdom of All Buddhas."

This clarifies that samādhi and dhyāna are practices of skillful means (*upāya*) capable of manifesting the two gates of essence and function of the principle and wisdom in their perfect, all-encompassing sovereignty; furthermore, it is because even unspeakable samādhis are, in their entirety, practices of skillful means for manifesting correct gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*).
Among the ten pāramitās, only the pāramitā of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā) is the fruit of effortless mastery, while the remaining nine pāramitās are the practices that assist in its manifestation.

From the initial stage of generating the bodhicitta, each of the ten stages mutually interpenetrates one another; like refined pure gold, they become increasingly bright and pure, thereby accomplishing various forms of adornment.

When karma is extinguished, wisdom is perfected, and practice is complete, one enters the *Indra-jāla* (net of Indra) Dharma-gate, at which point one may truly be called a "Dharmadhātu" and one's merit becomes capable of spontaneous activity (*anābhoga*).

From the first stage of generating the mind of enlightenment, they take as their essence the bodhicitta that is without activity, without cultivation, and without action, while seeking to study all the inexhaustible gates of practice of Samantabhadra.

By this means, one seeks only the Bodhisattva path and trains in the Bodhisattva practices; the unconditioned awakening (*anabhisaṃskāra-bodhi*) becomes self-evident through following these practices, because within the performance of these practices, the dhyāna-pāramitā constantly assists in manifesting the essence and function, such that wisdom and principle are transformed into clarity and mastery.

The general meaning is as follows: In the initial stage of the Dwelling of the First Resolve, one uses the preparatory application of the samādhi of non-thought and non-action to assist in manifesting bodhi. Because bodhi has no substance and no intrinsic nature, it acts as the condition for non-abiding in relation to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). One seeks the various practices of a bodhisattva through this, because these practices are themselves bodhi and lack any substantial nature.

If one were to cultivate enlightenment separately from practice, that would be the enlightenment of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the contemplation of emptiness; it would not be the enlightenment of the One Vehicle, nor the enlightenment of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, which consists of the wisdom and principle of the ten thousand practices and the sovereign power of compassion and vows.

For this reason, the Tathāgata spoke to bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. This was because bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching practice the contemplation of the illumination of emptiness to shatter the existence of the triple world; thus, for them, the Tathāgata spoke of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena, as he had not yet clarified that the various existences of the triple world are themselves the functional manifestation of bodhi.

According to this One Vehicle of the True Teaching, bodhisattvas seek only the bodhisattva path and practice only the bodhisattva conduct, which is itself the function of bodhi; thus, the essence and function of the principle of clarity and wisdom encompass everything as a whole, and there is nothing to be sought separately.
If one were to seek bodhi separately, then essence and function would each be distinct, and the two views would persist; thus, it could not be called "riding the inconceivable vehicle.
Therefore, one simply seeks the Bodhisattva path; there is no separate bodhi.

This clarifies that bodhi is without seeking, without the arousal of the mind, without practice, without location, without question or answer, and without attainment or realization; yet it practices all practices and fulfills the path of Samantabhadra, for this non-practice and non-cultivation is the perfection of the great function of bodhi.

Because one seeks only the Bodhisattva path and studies the Bodhisattva practices, it is only then that one may be called "attaining perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first resolving the mind.
Regarding the fifth point, Mañjuśrī’s instruction on the destination of practice, the Sūtra says: "Good son!..."
"In this southern direction there is a land called Sukhāvatī; in that land there is a mountain named Gṛdhrakūṭa, and upon that mountain there is a bhikṣu named Meghaśrī. This is who he is.

Furthermore, within this section on the faculty of knowing (*jñānendriya*), which establishes the practice and gives rise to the subsequent gates of study, the text is divided into eight long sections from the end of the sutra.

First, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī turned like an elephant king" down to "At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had finished speaking these verses," including twenty-two lines of verse, it clearly explains how Mañjuśrī exhorted Sudhana to draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). It clarifies the entry into the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*) as the gate for stabilizing the realization of principle and acceding to truth; specifically, it concerns the "Gate of Recollecting the Wisdom-Light of All Buddhas" attained by the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Therefore, proceeding downward from there, one reaches the ten spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), beginning with the princess Maitrīcaryā; these are all the spiritual friends within the stages of the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi).
From this point, starting with Mount Wonderful Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa), seven sections are established.
First is the section on entering from faith through the Ten Abodes to settle upon the principle and accord with reality, which is the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes."
The second is the gate of initiating all practices based on the Truth; this refers to the ten spiritual friends beginning with the Bhikṣu Sudarśana, as found in the "Chapter on the Ten Practices."

The gate of the harmonious integration of the three—wisdom, principle, great compassion, vows, and practice—is comprised of the ten spiritual benefactors beginning with the incense-seller Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta and the Blue Lotus (Utpala), namely, the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications" (*Daśapraṇidhāna-parivarta*).

The fourth is the gateway of cultivating compassion and wisdom to accomplish virtue, which consists of the night goddess Vāsantī and the nine subsequent spiritual friends, totaling ten; this is the "Ten Grounds" chapter.

The fifth gate, "The Arising of Wisdom and Attainment of Buddhahood through Compassion," consists of the ten spiritual friends, including the Buddha’s mother, Lady Māyā, as well as those below her; these correspond to the ten chapters beginning with the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis."
Sixth is the gate of the fulfillment of practice and the attainment of the Buddha-fruit, which is the Tathāgata Maitreya and the *Tathāgatotpattisambhavanirdeśa-parivarta*.

Seventh is the gate of the effortless, great function of mastery over the dharma-realm, wherein all things interpenetrate and harmonize like Indra’s net; this is the "effortless great function of the dharma-realm," which is the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta*, clarifying how the universal dharma-realm encompasses and subsumes all that is gathered within it.

Thus, these fifty-three spiritual friends establish these gates of practice and skillful means so that those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta may recognize the five stages and advance through the gates of cultivation, making them easy to understand.

Although the Dharma was previously explained through principles, there is a fear of confusion regarding its actual practice; therefore, Sudhana is made to once again manifest the gates of practice, so that learners may not fall into error.

First, regarding the entry from faith into the Ten Abodes through the gate of "converging with principle and acceding to truth by means of concentration," there are twenty-two lines of verse in the sūtra, beginning from "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva turned like an elephant king" and ending with "I vow to study the vehicle of Samantabhadra."
This section is divided into four parts.

First, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva turned like an elephant king" down to "Therefore, do not give rise to weariness or aversion here," there are five lines of scripture. This constitutes the part clarifying how Mañjuśrī praises Sudhana’s aspiration for bodhicitta and exhorts him to draw near to spiritual friends without giving rise to weariness or aversion.

2. From "Sudhana said" onwards, up to "How can the conduct of Samantabhadra be swiftly brought to fulfillment," there are five and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on Sudhana’s eleven questions regarding the conduct of Bodhisattvas.
3. From "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva" onwards, there is approximately one line of scripture, which clearly indicates the section where Mañjuśrī speaks in verse to praise Sudhana.

The fourth verse states: "If there are bodhisattvas who do not weary of the suffering of birth and death, they will possess the path of Samantabhadra, which nothing can destroy. This clarifies that when one takes the suffering of birth and death as *bodhi*, there is nothing that can destroy it; however, if one practices the bodhisattva conduct and generates the *bodhicitta* while remaining detached from the suffering of birth and death, then there is something that can destroy it.

Why is this? It is because one is already impaired by the two obstacles of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, as well as by defilement and purity; it is also because one is impaired by the two views of "is" and "is not," and by annihilationism and eternalism.

Furthermore, when it says, "If one enters the ocean of skillful means and dwells securely in the Buddha’s bodhi, one can follow the Teacher’s learning and shall attain all-knowledge," it clarifies that only by taking the ocean of myriad practices—characterized by great vows and great compassion—as one's skillful means can one then dwell securely in the Buddha’s bodhi.
If, regarding all phenomena and all practices, one fails to clarify even a single phenomenon or fails to engage in even a single practice, then the bodhicitta will not be perfected.
Since bodhicitta is unobstructed and devoid of intrinsic nature, the presence of grasping or rejecting toward even a single phenomenon or a single practice constitutes an obstruction.
One simply seals it with the seal of the universally radiant wisdom of the dharma-realm, such that there is no dharma that is not penetrated.

By this, one seeks only the fulfillment of bodhisattva practices, which is the perfection of the bodhicitta; for bodhisattva practices and bodhicitta are not separate from one another, neither being joined nor dispersed, as both are ultimately ungraspable.
Because they practice the bodhisattva path in this way, and because both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are ungraspable, they abide within saṃsāra while remaining securely established in nirvāṇa.
Thus they cultivate all bodhisattva practices, increasing great loving-kindness, great compassion, and great vows, thereby fulfilling the path of Samantabhadra.
The remaining portions are self-evident according to the text.

Furthermore, within the first section—concerning the entry from faith into the Ten Abodes through the gate of uniting with principle and acceding to truth via meditative concentration—from the passage beginning "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva spoke these verses" down to "The Bhikṣu Meghaśrī shall explain it for you," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture, which are divided into five segments.
From "At that time" onwards, there are two and a half lines of scripture, which clearly describe the section on Mañjuśrī praising Sudhana’s aspiration for unsurpassed bodhicitta.
2. From "Good son" onwards, up to "is even more difficult," there are two lines of scripture that clarify the section praising Sudhana’s seeking of spiritual friends as being even more difficult.

3. From "Good son" below, up to "should resolutely seek a true spiritual friend," there is one line of scripture clarifying the section on how, in seeking omniscience, one should resolutely seek a true spiritual friend.

4. From "Good son" onwards, up to "do not look for faults," there are two and a half lines of scripture. This clearly shows the section where Mañjuśrī instructs Sudhana: that one should not become complacent upon seeing a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), and that one should not look for their faults.
5. From "Good son" onwards, up to "The bhikṣu Meghaśrī shall explain it for you," there are four and a half lines of scripture which, in brief, contain five points:

first, indicating the direction where the spiritual friend resides; second, indicating the land where the spiritual friend resides; third, indicating the specific location where the spiritual friend resides; fourth, citing the spiritual friend’s name established based on their virtues; and fifth, citing the spiritual friend’s moral capacity and what dharma they are able to expound, as explained in detail in the text.
New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-three (and Thirty-four),
composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan.
From this point downward, the seven fascicles consist entirely of Sudhana’s spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
From here on, these ten spiritual friends represent the gates of the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*).
Regarding the first point—indicating the direction in which the spiritual friends reside—why is he directed to go to the South?
By means of illumination, one entrusts [the trigrams] to the cardinal directions to manifest the Dharma.
The South is taken as the primary direction; it corresponds to Li, which represents illumination.
Because the center of Li is empty, Li is identified with illumination, the sun, and the Nine Heavens. Within the human body, it corresponds to the head, the eyes, and the heart.
When the mind reaches the state of emptiness, the sun of wisdom shines forth of its own accord; thus, the image is taken to represent the Way.
Therefore, the Sutra says: "He clearly refines all rituals throughout the ten directions and presides over the deities of those quarters."

"Method" (*fang*) means "principle" (*fa*). It simply takes its principle from the Great Image, which has no fixed direction. Just as the sun moves through the heavens and its brilliance adorns the earth, so too does wisdom move through the void and its clarity adorns all things; there is nothing it does not know, and nothing it does not illuminate.
Taking up this single dharma, the ten directions become indistinguishably one.

Second, regarding the indication of the land where the spiritual friend resides: there is a land in the south named "Supreme Bliss" (Śrīmat). It is called "Supreme Bliss" because the wisdom of principle and phenomena is void and capable of purifying afflictions.
Third, regarding the indication of the dwelling place of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*): in that land there is a mountain named *Sumeru* (Wondrous Peak).

Non-conceptual, tranquil meditation is called the "mountain"; the manifestation of wisdom from an empty mind is called "wondrous"; and the fact that the clarity of wisdom regarding the pure principle can shatter delusions is called the "peak."
Gén (艮) represents the mountain, cessation, the young and ignorant, the younger son, and the gate-towers.

Taking "correctness" (zhèng 正) as the beginning, it clarifies that the first month is so called because it marks the commencement of the three yang lines; when the one yin line below ceases [its movement], it constitutes the character zhèng (正).

Because the first yang-line arises in the eleventh month, the second yang-line arises in the twelfth month, and the third yang-line arises in the first month, this [month] is taken as the first month (*zhengyue*).
Because the three yang-lines arise therein, the number three is taken as the standard (*zheng*).
Furthermore, regarding the place where the three yang lines arise: fire is generated in the branch of Yǐn; taking fire as the sun, the sun is born in Yǐn.

Because the sun is born in Yǐn, it is the locus where light first arises; thus it is called the stage of "childish ignorance" (*tóngméng*) and the position of the "young boy. This is taken as a symbol and expressed through the dharma.
As for Mañjuśrī’s residence on Mount Qingliang in the northeast, this refers to the northeast of the Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha.
This mountain lies to the northeast of the Bodhimaṇḍa in this Jambudvīpa; it is the king of all mountains in this Jambudvīpa, as the direction Gen (艮) corresponds to the mountain.
Ten thousand bodhisattvas dwell therein; these are the companions of Mañjuśrī who have perfected the ten thousand practices as his retinue.

Thus, Mañjuśrī takes the wondrous wisdom of the fundamental gnosis of the Dharmakāya as his primary function, serving as the teacher who initiates all Buddhas; consequently, there is a Mañjuśrī present in every place.
Furthermore, all sentient beings inherently possess this; it is from this Dharma that they first enter into noble wisdom.
Having been born into the Buddha-family, they share the same wisdom, liberation, knowledge, and vision as all Buddhas.
From this point forward, one studies the wisdom of differentiation, initiates vows and practices to achieve great compassion; this is called the Samantabhadra Practice of the Dharma-realm.
For this reason, the Tathāgata adopts images from worldly phenomena to symbolize these dharmas, so that they may be easily understood.

One takes the image of Mount Miaofeng in the kingdom of Shenglè as a model; it clarifies that Gen, the place where the three Yang lines arise, represents "stopping. Because stopping clarifies the initial arising [of the line], and because this initial arising is designated as "the youthful and ignorant" (tóngméng).
Furthermore, because Mañjuśrī represents the initial stage of dispelling ignorance and entering the holy path, he is titled "The Youth.

As a Bodhisattva, he establishes his name through his transformative activity; thus, he is so named because he inspires all sentient beings to enter the wondrous wisdom that is free from marks (*animitta*).

This clarifies that by means of the samādhi of skillful means, one manifests fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); because it is the first birth into the family of the wisdom of all Buddhas, this name is established.

Thus, by using the grasping of images to symbolize the Dharma, one causes the student to first settle the mind—free from discursive thought, tranquil and unmoving like the king of mountains—whereupon the wisdom of the signless, wondrous principle will manifest. When the wisdom of one's own mind attains liberation and coolness, there is no need to physically climb a mountain.

Therefore, on the summit of Mount Sumeru, the ten stages of the *bhūmis* are taught as ten successive advancements toward the fruit of Buddhahood, all of which are designated by the name "Moon. This corresponds to how the ten spiritual friends, beginning with the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī on this Wondrous Peak Mountain, first attained the refreshing bliss of the Dharma upon emerging from the state of ordinary beings.
This clarifies that Sudhana’s practice serves to manifest the gates of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
As for the term "Mount Wonderful Peak" (*Miaofengshan*), it signifies that only by emerging from meditative concentration can one manifest the fundamental wisdom of one's own mind.

Just as all Buddhas perceive that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, all phenomena are without marks, all phenomena are without dependence, and all phenomena have no fundamental or terminal place of abiding—having realized this Dharma, they are said to "dwell where the Buddhas dwell.

Only then do they attain the vision of the extinction of karma and its cessation, entering the flow of noble wisdom; they study the wisdom of differentiation to accomplish the infinite, universal application of Samantabhadra within the Dharma-realm, extensively transforming all inexhaustible sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm, causing them all to enter the knowledge and vision of fundamental wisdom.

Furthermore, for a beginner who first enters the mountains to enjoy tranquility, training the mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to manifest right wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) is likewise a skillful means; it may also be called the "Exquisite Peak Mountain" of the Land of Supreme Bliss.
Because the mind is detached from mundane objects and delights in the tranquility of the mountains, this also carries the meaning of "supreme bliss.
While employing various skillful means to benefit sentient beings for the sake of ordinary people, one simply does not abide within them.

Fourth, regarding the designation of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) based on his virtues, he is named "Cloud of Virtue" (Guṇamegha) in the sense that this cloud of virtue can rain down the Dharma to moisten and nourish sentient beings, enabling them to attain refreshing coolness.

"Bhikṣu" is translated here as "Extinction of Strife. Because he extinguishes the strife of afflictions—namely, the strifes of existence and non-existence, right and wrong—he is called one who "extinguishes strife.

Since the five views, such as the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), and the two views of existence and non-existence can obstruct the Path, one must first still them through the samādhi of non-recollection and non-thought; only then does Right Wisdom manifest. Therefore, he is called one who "extinguishes strife."

Therefore, Mount Wonderful Peak symbolizes the bhikṣu’s practice of samādhi; when wisdom manifests and concentration dissolves, one attains mastery over both quiescence and function, thereby able to preach the teachings to nourish the ignorant—hence he is named Dechen (Cloud of Virtue).
The original residence is the position of *meng* (ignorance) in the hexagram Gen; through stillness, the moisture of awakening begins to generate the dawn of enlightenment.

The Bhikṣu De-yun resides upon the summit of the mountain to take this as a metaphor for manifesting the Dharma: it clarifies that this stage begins with an ordinary person of faithful mind, who initiates the process of enlightenment through the practice of samādhi, thereby entering the first of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) within the ranks of the sages.
Because it reaches the summit of the Dharma, the place where one meets with the wondrous wisdom of signlessness is called Wondrous Peak (Miaofeng).
Because it uses wondrous wisdom to preach the teachings and nourish all living beings, it is named Cloud of Virtue (Deyun).
By practicing such skillful means, the correct wisdom of one’s own mind manifests before one.

The meaning of the Venerable Meghaśrī on Mount Sumeru is entirely within oneself; even the fruits of Buddhahood of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are all inherently present. To practice the conduct that benefits sentient beings through the manifestation of the wisdom and principle of skillful samādhi is precisely this—just as is fully elucidated in the sutra.

This clarifies that within the "Dharmadhātu Chapter," these five stages of the practice-gate are established; it clarifies that the practice-gate of the expedient cultivation of the five stages has, as its essence, the Dharmadhātu-Buddha-fruit, because the fundamental wisdom of the universal radiance of the Dharmadhātu, endowed with the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra, constitutes its great function. Thus, from beginning to end and from root to branch, nothing deviates from this.

By means of progressive cultivation, one establishes the various stages at the points where the raw and the matured meet, giving rise to the dharma-gate of the "One Hundred and Ten Cities. Within this, there are the collective practices of the ten *pāramitās*, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharmas*), and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) along with the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*); these six gates—namely, the general and the particular, the same and the different, and formation and disintegration—are all contained therein and can be seen by illuminating them with wisdom.
The meaning of the "one hundred and ten cities" has already been explained previously at the eastern side of Puṇyavatī City.

Fifth, regarding the raising of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) as one capable of [teaching] moral conduct: this spiritual friend is capable of explaining and demonstrating the preparatory practices (prayoga) of bodhisattva conduct and possesses the gateways to the five stages of Samantabhadra’s practice; for this reason, Mañjuśrī directed Sudhana to inquire of the bhikṣu Meghaśrī:
"How does one learn the bodhisattva conduct?"
"How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path?
And how, furthermore, does one swiftly bring the practices of Samantabhadra to full completion?
The bhikṣu Meghaśrī shall explain this for you."
This is the initial mind that enters the Ten Abodes, called the "Abode of the First Aspiration.

Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana, having heard these words, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness," down to "I have only attained this Dharma-door of the Universal Vision of the Radiance of Wisdom that Recollects the Realms of All Buddhas," there are thirty-eight lines of scripture, which contain eleven thematic sections:

1. Upon hearing the name of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he rejoiced; 2. He prostrated at the feet of Mañjuśrī, circumambulated him countless times, and took his leave to travel south; 3. Upon reaching his destination, he sought out the bhikṣu Meghaśrī; 4. He searched for seven days; 5. He saw the bhikṣu walking slowly in meditation on a separate mountain peak; 6. He circumambulated him three times to the right; 7. He requested what he sought; 8. Meghaśrī praised Sudhana for being able to undertake two kinds of difficult practices; 9. He first enumerated the ten kinds of bodhisattva conduct sought by Sudhana; 10. He personally declared his own virtues and bestowed them upon Sudhana; 11. "I have attained only this Dharma-door of the Universal Vision of the Wisdom-Light of the Realm of All Buddhas through Recollection."
This concludes the summary of the dharma-gates of his own stage bestowed upon Sudhana; what follows below further extols the advancement to the preceding stage.

First, regarding "rejoicing upon hearing the name of the spiritual friend," the sutra states: "Having heard these words, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. To leap is to rise entirely off the ground; to leap repeatedly without ceasing is to bound.

Regarding the second point, "prostrating at the feet of Mañjuśrī, circumambulating him countless times, and taking leave to travel south": to prostrate with one's head at his feet means to bring one’s own supreme height down to his feet; this is the ultimate form of reverence.
Circumambulating him countless times with a mind of reverent compliance toward the Dharma, he took his leave and traveled south, ascending toward wisdom and clarity.

Upon arriving three times at the place where he sought the bhikṣu Meghaśrī, he reached Mount Wonderful Peak in the Land of Supreme Bliss; "Supreme Bliss" signifies being unstained and tranquil, while the body and mind remaining unmoving like a mountain represent the practice of meditative concentration.
"Seeking throughout the ten directions" refers to this contemplation.
This contemplation of the ten directions is the perfect fusion of mind and object, such that it is as boundless as empty space.

Regarding "seeking for seven days," this clarifies the application of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) to seek further progress and eliminate the states of mental dullness and agitation.
To remain in meditative absorption is called "sinking," and to emerge from it is called "restlessness"; these two hindrances are removed.

When the five bhikṣus were seen walking slowly along a path on a separate mountain, it signified that they shared the same essence as him, representing the meaning of having already ascended to the mountain peak.

When one clarifies the abiding essence, there still remains a mind of concentration; yet, when examined through the seven factors of enlightenment, the Dharma-body of perfect awakening is fundamentally without a nature of either concentration or distraction.
The beginner possesses meditative concentration that can be stabilized; thus it is said that he sees Meghashri dwelling upon the summit of a separate mountain.
His slow pace indicates that he does not abide in a distracted body.
"Walking" (*cankrama*) signifies not abiding in a state of pure mind; it is only when concentration and distraction are harmoniously integrated that one clearly realizes the profound accord.

Furthermore, although one has attained the same manifest presence of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment as all Buddhas of the ten directions, it is only from this point onward that one is capable of seeking the conduct of a bodhisattva to fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra. This is to clarify the function of non-abiding; therefore, it is called "walking slowly."
Because one does not abide in fixed concentration and because one cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva, it is called "walking" (*caṅkrama*).

Those who cultivate the Way must first possess faith; thereafter, they must take the gateway of concentration as their skillful means. Only after attaining concentration is one capable of giving rise to the contemplation of the ten directions and the contemplation of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), thereby unifying the mind and its objects so that they pervade everywhere, and merging stillness and distraction into a single unity. When views of self and phenomena (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) have subsided, this is termed the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); only then is one capable of cultivating the Bodhisattva Way and fulfilling the Bodhisattva practices, manifesting many births in accordance with worldly convention while remaining in a single thought-moment of truth.
Regarding "circumambulating three times to the right": this signifies superior progress, reverent compliance, and the realization of the mind’s fulfillment.
As for circumambulating to the right: the left is honored and the right is lowly; thus, by placing oneself in a lower position, one accords with the sublime teaching of the Honored One.
Regarding the three circumambulations: one, three, five, seven, and nine are the positions of Yang; two, four, six, eight, and ten are the positions of Yin.
Yang gives rise to life and Yin brings about death; this is based on the principle of the number three.

Seventh, regarding the request for what is sought, the Sūtra says: "I have already first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practices, and so on, up to: how one may swiftly bring the practices of Samantabhadra to full completion."

The bhikṣu Guṇamegha praised Sudhana for being able to practice two kinds of difficult dharmas: he praised his having already generated the bodhicitta, which is difficult to generate; and he praised his now being able to practice the bodhisattva conduct, which is difficult to cultivate.

As for those who say, "I have already resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta," they have already resolved upon bodhicitta in the presence of Mañjuśrī; because they understand that awakening is neither to be realized nor cultivated, and there is nothing therein to be sought, they seek only the preparatory practices for the bodhisattva’s skillful means and samādhi, whereby their bodhicitta becomes naturally clear and stainless.

It is like clouds in the sky: when the clouds vanish, the empty space is naturally empty, and one no longer seeks that space by means of the clouds; this illustrates that one should simply cultivate the samādhi of the Bodhisattva’s contemplative observation to remedy the obstruction of attachment.

However, the bodhicitta has no essence that can be cultivated, constructed, removed, or discarded; it does not diminish among ordinary beings, nor does it increase among sages. Therefore, now, by means of the two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā and the seven factors of enlightenment as auxiliary skillful means at the summit of Mount Sumeru, the bodhicitta will naturally become clear and manifest.
Upon reaching the clarity of Bodhi, one realizes that the bodhisattva’s practice of various samādhis is itself Bodhi; there is no longer any separate Bodhi apart from this, for it is self-evident.
This clarifies that while Bodhisattvas dwell in the world and cultivate all myriad practices, the nature of these worldly practices—even up to bodhi and nirvana—is inherently detached.

By using this Dharma to teach those wandering in delusion who do not understand this, so as to cause them to awaken to the stainless wisdom of the emptiness of nature, thereby purifying all karma and ensuring that suffering does not arise, it is called "Great Compassion."

It is like a magically conjured person teaching a phantom being; observing karma through wisdom, they benefit all beings throughout the ten directions according to the time and their faculties, yet without mind, intellect, or consciousness—using the illusion of wisdom to benefit living beings.
For this reason, one seeks only all the practices of a bodhisattva to clarify that practice itself is bodhi, because everything is without arising or ceasing.

When it says, "I have already resolved upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta," it clarifies that although the bodhicitta of faith has not yet been manifested through the application of samādhi, one knows that there is nothing to cultivate and nothing to seek.

Now, for the practitioner of the Bodhisattva path, by means of the seal of the characteristics of the samādhi of skillful means, one clearly understands that practice and bodhi are, in reality, non-dual.

Within this state, it cannot be said that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and are subject to arising and ceasing," for a sūtra states: "All dharmas are unarisen; all dharmas are unceasing."
"If one can see in this way, the Buddhas will always appear before one.

This is because, as stated in the subsequent passage, one attains the vision of the countless Buddhas of the four intermediate directions, above, below, and throughout the ten directions precisely by attaining this understanding.

When the Tathāgata teaches that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent within the context of the Three Vehicles, he does so for those who cling to these phenomena as being real; it is not for the sake of those with great faculties who can immediately receive the Buddha Vehicle, wherein the essence and function of the principle and wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* are non-obstructed.
Therefore, those who resolve to attain Bodhicitta must discern the provisional and the ultimate within the teachings; only then can they be capable of giving rise to the Great Mind.
A question is asked:
Why not seek the Dharma from a single spiritual friend such as Mañjuśrī? Would that not suffice?
Why must one pass through fifty-three stages of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to seek the bodhisattva practice?
The answer is:

to clearly discern the depth or shallowness of habitual tendencies (vāsanā), the breadth or narrowness of the cultivation of differentiated wisdom (pratisaṃvid-jñāna), the thickness or thinness of great compassion (mahākaruṇā), and the extent of the gathering and transformation of beings.

By means of this established method for practicing the five stages, one is enabled to advance in the cultivation of the *dharmadhātu* without error—through the characteristics of the fifty-three spiritual friends according to the stages, the one hundred and ten causes and effects, and their general and specific, identical and different, and perfected and disintegrated aspects—so that one’s merit does not stagnate and one’s practice does not become protracted.

From this Mount Wonderful Peak, through the causal conditions of the preparatory practice of the Samādhi of Skillful Means, one manifests the self-nature of the Dharmakāya—pure in its essence, fundamentally without dependence or dwelling, and characterized by universal radiance wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*). Together with the stages from the "Gate of Non-duality between Quiescence and Function in Bodhisattva Practice" and below, one uses the function of universal radiance wisdom to cultivate differentiated wisdom and to remedy habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, by means of great vows, one gives rise to the gate of compassion and wisdom, nurturing the practice of great compassion throughout the Dharma-realm; each of these successive stages is explained in detail below.

Regarding the ninth, "Cloud of Virtue," it first enumerates the ten kinds of bodhisattva practices sought by Sudhana. From the passage beginning with "namely, seeking the bodhisattva practice" onwards, there are ten types of bodhisattva practices in total; these collectively enumerate the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground (*ekādaśabhūmi*).
Thus, within these five stages, there are ten aspects for each, all of which are subsumed within these ten types of bodhisattva practice.

To take the first of these as an example—that which is called "seeking the bodhisattva practice"—it corresponds to the initial stage among the ten dwellings (*daśavihāra*), namely the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*). Here, the gate of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) serves as the primary element, while the remaining nine perfections act as its companions.
Taking the *upāya-samādhi* (concentration of skillful means) as the essence of the practice of *dāna* (generosity), because it is able to relinquish all dharmas.

Second, regarding the seeker of the Bodhisattva realm, this corresponds to the *śīla-bhūmi* (stage of ethical discipline); taking the *śīla-pāramitā* (perfection of morality) as its essence, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.
Taking the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya as the essence of the precepts, and great compassion along with the wisdom of differentiation as its function:

it is like the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, who, observing the great ocean and seeing the appearance of a Buddha, realized the fundamental wisdom through the twelve links of dependent origination, and then, by means of the wisdom of differentiation, preached the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra* (The Universal Eye Sūtra).
Furthermore, the ten kings represent the practice of compassion and wisdom, which will be clarified below according to their respective stages.
This corresponds to the second stage (*bhūmi*) within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which remedies the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Third, those who seek the bodhisattva path of renunciation are assigned to the stage of "Abiding in Practice" (*caryāpratipatti-vihāra*).

This corresponds to the third stage among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Because one cultivates the dhyānas of the two higher realms and transcends the fixed states of those dhyānas, one remedies the afflictions of the two higher realms.

Such practice constitutes dwelling in the third spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) among the intermediate ones: the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita in the country of Sāgaratīra. He comes and goes and performs walking meditation in mid-air; he clearly attains non-abiding in the three realms and in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because he has attained mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
Regarding "the ten kings venerate him": because he simultaneously cultivates both wisdom and compassion without partiality, his status becomes manifest only upon reaching this stage.

This has the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence, with the other nine perfections as its companions; this clarifies that the exhaustion of the afflictions of the three realms constitutes the path of renunciation.

Regarding the fourth [stage], seeking the pure path of a bodhisattva: as in the fourth dwelling, the "Noble Birth" (*janmaja-vihāra*), among the ten dwellings, and the fourth stage (*bhūmi*) among the ten stages, once the mind of the three realms has been exhausted and supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*) manifests, one then studies the knowledge of worldly letters, phrases, and meanings; it is only at the fifth dwelling and the fifth stage that this is fully perfected.

Within the sixth stage, as with the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja, one attains the cessation of inhalation and exhalation, the supernormal power of tranquility, and emanates transformation bodies throughout the ten directions.
Thus, these ten kinds of sought-after and cultivated practices of the bodhisattva path—ten within each of the one—are fully manifested across the five stages.

Correlate each point as above; therein, the underlying circumstances and the literal meaning will become vividly clear. If one does not realize this while reading, one’s empty talk will merely pass by; one must grasp the meaning of each and every point.

Just as the Dharma of the Ten Abodes serves as a model for the subsequent stages and the Ten Grounds, so too do all later stages follow this pattern; once the practice is fully mastered, one then relies upon the original Dharma.
Regarding the tenth point, the declaration of one’s own virtues and their bestowal upon Sudhana, the Sūtra says:

“Good son! I have attained the power of sovereign and decisive understanding; the eye of faith is purified and the light of wisdom shines radiantly. I universally contemplate all realms, free from all obstructions; my skillful observation is clear and penetrating through the Universal Eye. Possessing pure conduct, I travel to all lands throughout the ten directions to reverently make offerings to all Buddhas.”
This clarifies that by presenting the fundamental fruit-dharma, it causes ordinary beings to believe, delight in, and practice it.

Only after one has cultivated the practices from the initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) through to the completion of the merits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) does one finally rely upon this original, fundamental fruit-dharma.

Furthermore, this is accomplished through the non-transmigration of time within the dharma-realm, the non-differentiation of wisdom, the non-differentiation of compassion, and the non-differentiation of vows and practices; because one practices within the great wisdom of the dharma-realm where there is neither extension nor contraction, it does not accord with emotional understanding.

Practitioners should not engage in cultivation by calculating time through either protraction or abbreviation; rather, they must skillfully contemplate the essence and function of the Dharma-realm, and must not follow worldly conventions by reckoning in terms of a single *kṣaṇa* or three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Since within the Dharma-realm there is absolutely no distinction between long and short, far and near, one should practice according to this understanding and conduct, performing the Dharma-practice accordingly. Thus, one skillfully illuminates arising and ceasing within all objective realms, causing attachments to be exhausted and thereby perfecting the great function of wisdom.

Do not recklessly grasp at your own mental objects; simply know that they are expansive and spontaneous, free and easy. As you practice concentration and contemplation, grasping is exhausted and wisdom manifests. Birth and cessation naturally cease, and karmic defilements naturally purify. You will then realize the Buddha’s realm and accord with the Tathāgata’s mind; this realization of the Buddha-vision occurs through natural convergence, not by means of forceful grasping.
Do not vainly attempt separate remedies that will only cause the mind to become deranged and deluded.

Simply clarify the mind and its objects so that views and attachments dissolve; when views perish and attachments subside, all myriad phenomena are fundamentally without affliction. When the realm of wisdom is luminous and clear, this is called the Buddha-land.
To stubbornly give rise to views and attachments without cause is to sink into perpetual delusion; one creates one's own calamity, which no other can inflict.

I have only attained this Dharma-gate of the Wisdom Light that Universally Sees the Realm of All Buddhas by Recollection," there are nineteen and a half lines of scripture. These clarify the universal seeing of all Buddhas in the ten directions, as well as the unimpeded gate regarding the realms of all lands; these constitute the fruits within this stage.
This clarifies that the realm of the Buddha has been primordially pure in this way; it was only until now that delusions acted as adventitious defilements.

Now, having attained the eye of definitive faith through Mañjuśrī, one reaches this true realm by means of the two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā and the seven factors of enlightenment. In accord with non-differentiation, one universally perceives that the mental states of all sentient beings, as well as one’s own mind, have been primordially liberated as the Buddha-land.
This is called the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), because one realizes through one's own mind that which the Buddha dwells in.
With the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) as the primary factor, the other nine serve as its companions.
From this point downward, whatever Buddhas and Buddha-realms are perceived are all the fruits within this stage.
From this point onward, the merit is attributed to the preceding stage.

Within each of the stages from the "Abiding in the Cultivation of the Ground" (Caryā-bhūmi) downward, there are two gates for every spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra): the gate of the original stage and the gate of advancement.

The second stage, the Dwelling of Refining the Ground (*bhūmi-viśodhana*), consists of the Dharma-gate of the Names of Spiritual Friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). As found below in the first section, "The Gate of Initial Advancement," from the passage beginning with "How could one possibly comprehend the boundless gates of pure conduct and wisdom of the great Bodhisattvas" down to "taking leave and departing," there are thirty-eight and a half lines of scripture; this constitutes the section on "Recommending Virtue and Advancing."
This section is divided into four parts.

First, from "How could one possibly comprehend the boundless wisdom of the great bodhisattvas? down to "How could one know or speak of their meritorious conduct," there are twenty-nine and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on looking up to superior virtues to encourage Sudhana’s further cultivation.
Second, in the south there is a land named Sāgaramukha; this indicates the location of the spiritual friend.
Third, there is a bhikṣu there named Sāgaramegha; this indicates the name of the spiritual friend.
The fourth is the virtue of the feet of Cloud of Dharma (*Deva-megha*), which signifies departing from one stage to ascend and enter the preceding position.

This clarifies that within each stage, ten dharma-gates are provided for entry and ten dharma-gates are bestowed for cultivation; thus, every stage possesses both the fruit of correctly entering its own fundamental position and the cause for bestowing the preceding position.
The following sections are to be understood according to this same pattern.

The first twenty-nine and a half lines of the sūtra clarify that [the author] has not yet fully presented the names of his spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), profoundly extols their virtues, and humbly acknowledges his own lack of ability.
The subsequent nine lines and a half of the sūtra clarify the names of the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), again enumerating ten dharmas and causing them to be heard in advance.
The first point is fully explained as in the sūtra.
Regarding the second, the Stage of Preparing the Ground (*Caryāpratisthita-vihāra*), within the section on its fundamental status, it is further divided into five parts:
1. From "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, he correctly contemplates ten dharmas;
2. He travels south to the country of Samudramukha;
3. Upon arriving at the place of the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, he prostrates at his feet.
Fourth, he formally articulates his request;
fifth, the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha praises Sudhana and reveals the dharma he has contemplated.
Regarding the "Country of Sāgaramukha," it clarifies that one should contemplate the ocean of birth and death as the vast ocean of buddhas.
The bhikṣu Sāgaramegha (Ocean Cloud) was named according to the Dharma he contemplates.
His mind is like the ocean, and he moistens sentient beings with the Dharma like clouds.

Furthermore, his nature-precepts are like the ocean that does not harbor corpses; when all the corpses of arising and ceasing reach the ocean of fundamental wisdom, they all become the ocean of wisdom, for therein there is no arising or ceasing.
The bhikṣu Sāgaramegha praised Sudhana and the dharmas he had contemplated, namely, the contemplation of the great ocean.

When he said, "I have dwelt here in the country of Samudramukha for twelve years," this clarifies that he did not depart from the ocean of birth and death, which arises through the twelve links of dependent origination.

Thus, within these twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), all ordinary beings are shrouded by ignorance and constantly dwell therein; the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings and those of the two vehicles both loathe and abandon them, whereas the bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle regard these very twelve links of existence and ignorance as the ocean of the Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*).

The ocean of great wisdom is without arising or ceasing; it has been thus from the beginning. Ordinary beings do not understand this and are falsely bound by the ignorance of birth and death; therefore, I say that I have resided in this country of Samudramukha for twelve years.

The Sūtra states, “Always taking the great ocean as its realm,” and so forth. Following this, there are ten ways of contemplating the great ocean; the intent is to clarify that the ocean of birth and death of all sentient beings, produced through the twelve links of dependent origination, is vast and immeasurable, such that no center or periphery, nor any substantial nature or characteristics, can be apprehended, and thus it is itself the ocean of the Buddha.

Regarding the contemplation of the great ocean adorned with the wondrous and marvelous array of immeasurable jewels: this clarifies that when one contemplates the ocean of dependent origination within birth and death, it immediately becomes the ocean of wisdom of the Buddha of intrinsic purity, which is adorned by the merit and jewels of omniscience.
To contemplate the great ocean as it accumulates immeasurable water is to contemplate the great ocean by taking the waters of all forms of affection as the waters of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
That the colors of the water differ is because within fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), immeasurable wisdoms of discernment and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) arise.

To contemplate the great ocean as the dwelling place of immeasurable sentient beings means to clarify that within the ocean of the Buddha there are dwelling places for immeasurable sentient beings, yet they do not perceive or know them.

Regarding the contemplation of the great ocean as that which accommodates various beings of immense bodies: this clarifies that immeasurable bodhisattvas all dwell within the ocean of birth and death; each of their bodies and lands completely fills its space, like shadows or light, without obstructing one another.

Regarding the contemplation that the great ocean can receive the rain poured by the great clouds: the ocean of the Bodhisattva’s mind is capable of receiving the rain of the Buddhas’ various dharmas from the great clouds.
