Within the gateway of wisdom, all stages are universally remedied;

within the gateway of stages, this stage brings together the practice of compassion from the seventh stage and the effortless wisdom of the eighth stage, activating them through the perfection of great vows so that wisdom and compassion may function with sovereign mastery.

In the second section, "Advancing by Inquiring into Virtue," from the passage beginning with "Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "...took his leave and traveled south," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture.

Within this, the meaning is divided into six sections: first, inquiring about virtue and placing it foremost; second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); third, citing the name of the village, Iṣāna; fourth, indicating the name of the spiritual friend, Jvalanānta; fifth, exhorting him to inquire about the dharma-gate he practices; and sixth, paying respects, taking his leave, and traveling south.
The south is as explained previously.

The village named Īśāna signifies "long and straight"; it serves to represent that this spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) gathers and transforms beings, causing them to lengthen the straight path free from all guile and deception; therefore, it is called "Long and Straight."
"Brahmin" (brāhmaṇa) here means "pure," signifying that this spiritual friend is undefiled and tranquil.
He is named "Victorious Heat" (Jvalanāmukha) to signify that he has triumphed over the heat of worldly afflictions and to demonstrate his mastery over the intense heat of blazing flames.

This is the ninth stage, the Abode of the Dharma Prince, wherein one attains mastery over the Dharma; it clarifies the ninth power, the perfection of the power of mastery over the Dharma, by manifesting the practice of "scorching the body with five fires" like a non-Buddhist, thereby attracting and guiding those of heterodox views to return to right wisdom.
The wisdom attained through illumination is identical to that of the heterodox; it causes all those who hold false views and practice deluded asceticism to believe and submit.
The details are provided in the text below.

Within the first section, the Dharma-gate for entering the proper stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I have only attained this liberation of the inexhaustible wheel," this segment of the sutra is divided into twenty-five sections:
First, he attained the illumination of the Dharma-light of the Invincible Banner, which enters into the inconceivable spiritual powers of all Buddhas;
second, he recollected the instructions of his spiritual friend and proceeded gradually toward the south;
third, he arrived at the village of Long and Straight and saw that Ugra-tapas performing austerities, with fires on four sides like great mountains.
Fourth, there was a mountain of sword-blades, towering and boundless, upon which he climbed and cast himself into the fire;
fifth, Sudhana prostrated and inquired about what he sought;
sixth, the Brahmin directed Sudhana to ascend that mountain of sword-blades.
Casting oneself into fire;
seventh, Sudhana’s human body is difficult to obtain;
the mind harbors doubt.
Eighty thousand Brahmā devas were in the void, exhorting him to recollect this light of the Vajra-flame Samādhi;
ninety thousand Māras were in the void, exhorting Sudhana to praise the virtuous conduct of the Brahmin;
and furthermore, ten thousand Śakra-deva-rājas were in the void, addressing Sudhana so as not to allow him to give rise to doubt.
Eleventh, there were ten thousand kings of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven who likewise stood in the sky praising the virtues of the brahmin;
twelfth, there were ten thousand kings of the Tuṣita Heaven who praised him from the air;
thirteenth, there were ten thousand gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who rained down celestial *māndārava* flowers from the sky as an offering.

14. Ten thousand dragon kings; 15. ten thousand yakṣa kings; 16. ten thousand gandharva kings; 17. ten thousand asura kings; 18. ten thousand garuḍa kings; 19. ten thousand kiṃnara kings; 20. immeasurable devas of the desire realm—these thirteen kinds of assemblies all stood in the air praising the virtues of the brahmin and exhorting Sudhana to maintain mindfulness and not give rise to doubt;
21. Sudhana repented his transgressions;
22. the brahmin spoke verses for Sudhana.
Twenty-three: Sudhana follows the instruction, ascending the mountain of blades and entering the great mass of fire;
twenty-four: Sudhana attains benefit upon entering the mass of fire;
twenty-five: from "I have only attained this Bodhisattva’s Inexhaustible Wheel" onwards is the section on extolling virtues and advancing upward.
As the aforementioned Brahmin demonstrated this practice, all sentient beings perceived the gates of practice according to their own individual differences.
Within the symbolic dharma, the mountain of blades represents the Dharma Prince.
Abiding in the power of the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), which has wisdom as its essence, the practitioner achieves realization;

they penetrate the suffering and difficulties of birth and death, perceiving only the liberation of the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, they must attain freedom from fear and become capable of sovereign mastery over the functioning of power.
The flame is the radiance of Vajra-wisdom and is also called the Vajra-samādhi, as has already been explained by the deities above.

As for the Dragon King Ena-vara, in a former life he violated the precepts and damaged an extremely foul-smelling tree; consequently, this stinking tree grew upon his head, and thus he was named accordingly.
*Upāsaka* means "purely faithful. *Nanda* translates here as "Joy";
this clarifies that the dragon, having heard the Dharma, attained faith, delight, and joy.
Regarding the "Bodhisattva's Liberation of the Inexhaustible Wheel," the intent is to clarify that he dwells as a Dharma Prince and has attained the rank of a Dharma Master.

By means of this single practice, according to the differing inclinations and desires of sentient beings, each perceives an inexhaustible variety of methods for teaching the Dharma and practicing the gates; because it clearly accords with the perfection of the faculties of all beings, it is called the "Inexhaustible Wheel."
This is the stage of the Dharma Prince (Dharmarājaputra), in which the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is primary and the other nine perfections are its companions.
In terms of the gate of wisdom, it universally remedies the five stages;
in terms of the gate of the stages themselves, it remedies the obstacle of lacking mastery in teaching the Dharma.

Within the same ten stages, this refers to the ninth stage; from here, one practices the conduct of the fruit until the merit matures in the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*), following this pattern.
Within the ten abidings, the fundamental fruit likewise takes the Great Function of the Wisdom of Universal Radiance—the essence of the Dharma-realm—as its basis.
Within the second section, "The Gate of Advancing through the Propagation of Virtue," there are four subsections:

first, advancing through the propagation of virtue; second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend by stating that there is a city in the south named Siṃhavikrīḍita; third, mentioning the name of the spiritual friend, the maiden Maitrāyaṇī; and fourth, prostrating at the feet of the Brahmin Jvalanānta and departing.
The meaning of "southern" is as explained previously in the first section.
As for the city named Siṃhavikrīḍita, it is the city where King Siṃhadhvaja resides; that king is the father of the girl Maitrāyaṇī.
Manifesting mastery over wisdom as the king, and the pervasive practice of great compassion as the queen, clarifies that compassion arises from wisdom.
Abiding within the defilements of birth and death yet remaining equal to the undefiled, clarifies that habitual tendencies have been exhausted.

In the previous seventh stage, the laywoman Śreṣṭhadattā (Xiūshē) clarified the preservation of the habit-energy of attachment to form the gate of compassion; because she had not yet severed the attachment of using the habit-energy of love to save sentient beings, she was called a *upāsikā*. By means of this, she fulfilled the practice of great compassion, and in the eighth stage, the effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) is finally perfected; this clarifies that wisdom arises from compassion.
In this stage, because compassion arises from wisdom, she is the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja and remains a maiden.
This signifies that in this stage, one benefits sentient beings spontaneously and without defiled habituation.
Within the first dharma-gate of "Correctly Entering the Dharma of the Respective Stage," the meaning of the scriptural text is divided into twenty-two sections:
first, generating a mind of respect toward spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
second, recollecting the teachings for advancement.
Third, he gradually traveled south;
fourth, he reached the city of Siṃhavijṛmbhita;
fifth, he sought out the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
Sixth, he heard that the girl was of royal lineage;
seventh, that five hundred maidens served as her attendants;
eighth, he learned of the palace where the girl resided.
Ninth, the seat upon which the maiden sat;
tenth, Sudhana hearing this and proceeding there;
eleventh, Sudhana having entered and beholding the maiden’s adornment of both the primary body and its environment.
12. Having seen her, Sudhana formally presented his request;
13. The maiden caused Sudhana to observe the environment and the fruits of her dwelling as retribution, so that he might know the causes of her conduct;
14. Having observed this, Sudhana joined his palms and gazed up at the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
The fifteenth maiden told Sudhana that the name of her dharma-gate is the "Gate of the Universal Adornment of Prajñāpāramitā";
the sixteenth maiden told Sudhana the number of Buddhas she has seen through the practice of her dharma-gate;
the seventeenth correctly stated that the number of Buddhas she had seen was thirty-six times the sands of the Ganges, and that the names of these Buddhas were each different.
18. The Bright Maiden received this Dharma-gate, and the Buddhas each entered it through different doors;
19. The Buddhas spoke it once and did not proclaim it again;
20. Sudhana addressed them, inquiring about the scope of this Dharma-gate.

21. When correctly raising the dharma-gate of contemplation that has been cultivated, one attains the universal gate of dhāraṇī; there are one million asaṃkhyeya dhāraṇī-dharma-gates, with a grand total of one hundred and seventeen.
22. From "I know only this gate of the universal adornment of the prajñāpāramitā" onwards, it clarifies the advancement through the transfer of merit.
"Traveling south by stages" signifies progressive advancement.
"Arriving at the city of Siṃhavijṛmbhita and searching everywhere for the maiden Maitrāyaṇī" signifies the realization that wisdom and compassion are non-dual in essence.

Hearing that this young girl is the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja and is accompanied by five hundred maidens as her attendants, one clearly understands that she represents the consecration stage (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*) within these ten stages of realization. Because she universally encompasses the two gates of wisdom and compassion across all five stages, practicing them collectively throughout these ten stages without any alternative path, she is called the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja.
The five hundred attendants who have heard the Dharma represent the practice within this specific stage.

To believe in this single stage as encompassing the wisdom and compassion of all five stages—collectively following this gateway—is precisely what is called the "Ten Abodes Gateway" and is termed "dwelling where the Buddhas dwell."
One should understand it thus:

within this dwelling, the environment supported by the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is entirely identical in name and essence to the realm attained through the fruition of Buddhahood; it comprises the Buddha-realm bodies and lands that mutually interpenetrate like Indra’s net, with each layer containing all others, wherein time, eons, months, and years are neither extended nor abbreviated, and each individual gate is fully endowed with infinite dharma-gates, as detailed in the sutra itself for Sudhana to observe.

The palace where the maiden Maitreyī dwells, named the Vairocana-garbha Palace, represents the fruition of Buddhahood that encompasses all virtues; for the causal and resultant gates of the Buddha throughout the five stages of practice are all contained within this stage.

Regarding the statement that he "preaches the sublime Dharma upon a seat of celestial garments with feet of nāga-victorious sandalwood and a web of golden thread," this clarifies that he sits upon the throne of the wisdom of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) in the body of great compassion for the sake of the nāgas.

The fragrant, pure net of the white teachings—the fivefold Dharma-body consisting of all precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—is used as a seat to cover, protect, guide, and receive all sentient beings.

Having heard this, Sudhana went to the gate of the royal palace to seek an audience with the girl. Seeing the countless multitudes entering the palace, he understood that this Hall of Wisdom and Palace of Compassion is a place entered in common by all sentient beings, and the capital where Bodhisattvas of the five stages reside together.
Sudhana asked, "Where are you all going now?
They all replied to him:
"We wish to go to the maiden Maitrīyaśas to hear and receive the sublime Dharma.
This was spoken with clear faith and without doubt. Sudhana then had this thought:
Regarding the thought, "Since this palace gate is without obstruction, I too should enter," one should enter once one has conceived such faith within oneself.

Having entered, one beholds the Vairocana Treasury Hall; this is because the wisdom and compassion of one's own mind, together with the myriad practices and the wisdom and compassion of the five stages and their causes and effects, simultaneously converge and enter therein.

Regarding "the *maṇi* that constitutes the ground": this clarifies that while this jewel resembles crystal, it differs in being red, white, crimson, or azure; it is categorized simply by its clarity and purity, as it is obtained as the fruition of the *dharmakāya*.
The pillars made of lapis lazuli signify that pure conduct sustains the myriad virtues.
The walls made of vajra signify the protection afforded by pure wisdom.
The perimeter walls made of Jambūnada gold symbolize the external adornment of pure precepts.
That it has hundreds of thousands of light-rays as its windows and casements is the retributive attainment resulting from teaching the illumination of the mundane world with the light of wisdom.
That it is adorned with incalculable *maṇi* jewels is born from the retribution of the adornment of stainless conduct.

Regarding the adornment of the jewel-treasury mani-mirror on all sides: it signifies that fundamental wisdom gives rise to differentiated wisdom, which illuminates the fundamental retribution-born nature of sentient beings.
Regarding the use of the world’s supreme mani-jewels as ornaments: it signifies that pure conduct, free from defilement, gives rise to the retribution of worldly conduct.
The countless jeweled nets that cover it from above represent the establishment of the net of teachings as a retribution for birth.

The hundreds and thousands of golden bells that emit wondrous sounds clarify that these are the sounds of the preaching of the Dharma, which pervade the ten directions, produced as a retribution for birth.
The following clarifies the adornment of the primary retribution.

The skin of the maiden Maitrīcāriṇī is golden in color; this signifies that the Dharma-body is pure white and her mind is free from defilement, resulting in this birth. As for the *suvarṇavarṇa* (golden-colored) *arhat* bodhisattvas, they are all likewise golden in color.
His eyes and hair are all deep blue, for he illuminates and protects all sentient beings with the light of pure wisdom.
His Brahma-voice is clear and resonant, heard throughout the ten directions.
To cause Sudhana to contemplate their "retributive environment" (niśraya-vipāka) is to clearly understand that the fruit is identical to the recognition of the dharma-gate.
As for how all the realms of the Buddhas manifested within each individual mirror mutually contain one another, it is exactly as described in the sutra.

It is said that this is the Gate of Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā; that I sought and obtained this Dharma from Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers clarifies that the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten transferences constitute thirty stages.

Regarding those who seek and attain the Dharma under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of six Ganges Rivers, this encompasses all six stages; the practices for the ten faiths, the ten grounds, and the fruit of Buddhahood on the eleventh ground are all contained within the dharmas of the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten transferences, because these constitute the dharmas of those preceding and succeeding stages.
Previously, in the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), one possessed faith, yet this was not yet the actual entry into the stages.

Regarding the causal and resultant practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*), one merely relies upon the dharmas of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*), the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), and the ten transferences (*daśapariṇāmana*); having integrated and harmonized the gates of principle and wisdom, compassion, vow, and practice, one then prepares for the ten stages and the eleventh stage by following and emulating them until they become thoroughly familiar, as there are no further new dharmas beyond this.

From the tenth bhūmi onwards through the eleventh bhūmi, there is no longer the establishment of names for the progressive cultivation toward the fruit of Buddhahood according to each stage; nor is there the seeing of the Buddha approaching from afar, nor the ritual of welcoming the Buddha.
If one examines the text from beginning to end, the meaning will manifest of itself.

Thus, within this tenth stage of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*), the two practices of wisdom and compassion comprehensively encompass the wisdom, compassion, vows, and practices of the ten stages, the ten practices, and the ten transferences; therefore, it is said that there are "thirty."

Although the teachings contain traces of sequential arrangement in their written words, when considered in terms of wisdom, compassion, vows, and practice, years, months, days, and kalpas are all in essence a single Dharma and a single moment. This applies even to the ten levels of faith; it is likewise for the ten stages (bhūmis) and the eleventh stage. Within this single position, there is not a single phenomenon—whether universal or particular, identical or different, forming or decaying—that is not contained therein.

In the sūtra passage concerning this stage, Sudhana is led to contemplate the adorned realm; within each wall, each pillar, each mirror, each mark, each form, and even within each jewel, he beholds the entire dharma-realm.

From their initial aspiration until they cultivate the bodhisattva practices, fulfill their great vows, become endowed with all merits, attain equal and perfect enlightenment, turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and even manifest entry into nirvana—all such images appear without exception, just as all the various forms of the stars, the sun, and the moon are universally reflected in water, as extensively described in the sutras.

By means of this state, one clarifies that a single stage universally encompasses all stages; throughout all kalpas, days, months, and periods of time, nothing ever shifts or changes. Therefore, it is said: "I sought this Dharma-gate from Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers; it was taught once and never again, and I received it in its entirety."
One must immediately understand that these three kinds of tenfold dharmas—the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten transferences—collectively reside within a single abode among the ten abodes.
Furthermore, because these thirty dharma-gates exist within wisdom and likewise thirty dharma-gates exist within compassion, they also constitute sixty Ganges-sands of Buddhas.

This is because each and every stage contains practices that pervade the entire Dharma-realm; because the metaphor of the sands of the Ganges is used to briefly illustrate the meaning of this pervasiveness;
because taking even one stage encompasses all six stages; and because it signifies that all wisdom and liberation are not separate from the three emptinesses and the six pāramitās.
Because there are six stages within each stage, and because each of these six stages contains inexhaustible practices and vows.

Below, one hundred and seven *dhāraṇī* gates are cited to clarify that this single stage subsumes the causes and fruits of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and the eleventh ground; for all are contained within these one hundred and seven total-holdings (*saṃgraha*).
These one hundred and seven great *dhāraṇī* gates do not transcend the practice within the ten *pāramitās*; when they are mutually integrated, there are one hundred *pāramitās*.

These one hundred *pāramitās* do not transcend the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), which serve as their mutual integration and companions, thereby establishing the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kalyāṇa*), the ten stages of holiness (*daśāryabhūmi*), and the six levels of equality and wondrousness. Collectively, these are called the Gate of Universal Adornment of the Prajñā-pāramitā sought by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers.

Because these Ganges sands represent the smallest numerical unit within this sutra, they are cited here to clarify that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) universally encompass the sixty dharmas across all six positions; thus, the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), which do not yet enter the formal positions, are excluded.
This can be understood through deep and subtle reflection.

The general meaning is that these three stages of the virtuous—namely the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*)—each individually contain the gates of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of the ten stages, the eleventh stage, and the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), because they collectively encompass the entirety of the single dharma-realm.

One wisdom, one compassion, one liberation, and one eon, one year, one month, one day, and one moment are without before or after and have no distinct categories; yet, because various conventional distinctions are established according to the world, one must ultimately avoid the views of protraction, brevity, length, or shortness.

Just as the youth Sudhana first gave rise to a mind of supreme reverence toward his spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), generating a vast and pure understanding, constantly recollecting the Buddha-vehicle and single-mindedly seeking Buddha-wisdom; may he likewise vow to see all Buddhas, contemplate the realm of phenomena, and have unobstructed wisdom ever present before him.

It is not appropriate to say "constantly mindful of the Mahāyāna," because this sutra is the gateway to the Buddha-fruit of the Dharma-realm, and it cannot be compared or contrasted with the Two Vehicles.

Nor can it be compared with the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna which establish the Buddha-fruit only after the ten stages (bhūmis); since there is no such comparison, how can one say to be "single-mindedly mindful of the Mahāyāna"?
The "great" is described by comparison with the "small.
All instances of generating the resolve within this Dharma-gate are generated in reliance upon the fruit of Buddhahood.
All spheres of mental measure—vows, practices, wisdom, and compassion—are beyond all comparison.

One must not use this to confuse the gate of the Buddha Vehicle with the vehicles of greater or lesser capacity, thereby causing the true intent of the sutra to be lost and the teachings to be falsely transmitted.
This is merely the erroneous statement of a translator who lacked full understanding.

As stated hereafter, one should single-mindedly seek the Buddha Vehicle, the Vehicle of All-Knowledge, the Inconceivable Vehicle, and the Vehicle of the Buddha-Fruit; for by means of the Buddha-Fruit, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra’s Dharmadhātu, one enters them all collectively at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta.

Furthermore, because the distinctions between beginning and end, as well as time and eons, are not differentiated, they transcend the scope of emotional cognition and are accessible only through wisdom (*jñāna*).
The remainder is as stated in the sūtra.
In this stage of the Empowerment Abode (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine serve as its companions.

In this stage, one overcomes the obstacles of the distinctions between the preceding and succeeding phases of practice through wisdom, as well as the imbalance between wisdom and compassion; thereby, one enters the gate of non-duality, characterized by mastery over both the preceding and succeeding phases of the perfection of wisdom and compassion.
Question: Since the wisdom and compassion of this stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) are already perfected, why is it not symbolized by a Buddha?
Why, instead, is it symbolized by a king’s daughter?
The answer is:
It clarifies that within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), one stage is itself the ten stages.

It clarifies that the former bhikṣus—Meghaśrī, Sāgaramegha, Susthita, and Sāgaranābha—all represent the supramundane stage of liberation upon attaining Buddhahood; while Maitreya, the householder Vimokṣa, the upāsikā Śrīsambhava, the rishi Akṣayamati, the brahmin Jvalanāntaratas, and the princess Maitrāyaṇī, all represent the perfect realization of the Bodhisattva path within the state of fruition.
By means of the mutual interpenetration of these positions, all are fully contained within them.

Whenever one sees a bhikṣu, it signifies seeking the fruit of Buddhahood as the adornment of bodhisattva practice; whenever one sees a layperson, it clarifies that seeking bodhisattva practice is not separate from the fruit of Buddhahood.

Whether male or female, whether an elder, a non-Buddhist, a spirit, or a celestial deity, each of these manifestations of the Dharma is clarified by assigning them to their respective positions within the gates of practice.

These ten spiritual friends above illustrate, first through the bhikṣu Meghaśrī, the gate of universally beholding the radiant realm of all Buddhas by manifesting the Buddha-wisdom of one’s own mind through the contemplative observation of meditative concentration.
The second was the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, who contemplates the ocean of birth and death and the twelve links of existence as the ocean-gate of the fundamentally pure Buddha-land.
The third was the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita, who possesses mastery over the wisdom of the Dharma-body and emerges unhindered through the gate of transcendence from the mundane world.
The fourth was the Elder Miga, who clarified the gate of worldly letters through practice while remaining in the secular world.

The fifth was the Elder Vimokṣa, who clarified the gate of meditative concentration wherein the body remains in the secular world while manifesting the inexhaustible adornments of Buddha-fields as its own essence and the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

The sixth is the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja, who has mastered both the ultimate and conventional truths, and possesses the gate of unimpeded spiritual powers that manifest quiescence while transcending entanglements.
The seventh is the upāsikā Śrīmati, who dwells in the world and brings to full maturity the gate of great compassion.
The eighth is Vimuṣṭi, whose effortless manifestation of wisdom resembles the gates of heterodoxy.
The ninth is the Brahmin Ugra-tapas, who encompasses the gates of asceticism associated with various false views.
The tenth is the Princess Maitrīcaryā, the gateway of the total integration of all stages where wisdom and compassion are simultaneously perfected as cause and effect.

Thus, these ten gateways encompass the causes and effects of the six stages; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are mutually interpenetrating and perfectly fused, with the one and the many fully present, like the dharma-gate of Indra’s net.
These ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*) clarify the Buddha’s own abiding.
The following ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) clarify the conduct of benefiting oneself and others.
What follows demonstrates the advancement of virtue, entering the stage of the ten practices.

This practice of compassion by the maiden is the gate of the perfection of great compassion within the perfection of wisdom; it clearly and comprehensively subsumes all stages, as each stage is likewise thus. Therefore, it is said that this dharma-gate was sought from Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers.
The thirty [stages] refer to the ten abodes (bhūmi), the ten practices (caryā), and the ten dedications (pariṇāmanā).
The sixth [section] states that they extend to the fruit of Buddhahood, wondrous enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), and the five positions.

This collectively encompasses and manifests the perfection of the wisdom-pāramitā throughout the three stages of worthiness (trividha-śaikṣa) and the six positions, subsuming them all within a single limit.
Regarding the dharma-gate of the conditioned environment (*pratyaya-vipāka*), it is illustrated as previously described and elucidated by means of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*).

Within these ten practices, from the first, the bhikṣu Sudarśana, down to the renunciant non-Buddhist, they are named "Universal Practice" (*sarvatraga*); these constitute the ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) within these ten practices.

Within this first section on initial practice, from the passage beginning with “As all bodhisattvas” down to “took their leave and departed,” there are approximately five thematic divisions according to the text and its meaning: first, the advancement through the cultivation of virtues;

second, the indication of the location of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); third, the mention of the name of the land; fourth, the mention of the name of the spiritual friend; and fifth, the paying of respects and taking one’s leave.
The section beginning with "Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... and following is the exaltation of their superior advancement of virtue.
The meaning of the southern direction is as explained previously.
Regarding the name of the land, "Three Eyes": first, the Dharma-eye; second, the Wisdom-eye; and third, the Insight-eye.
As explained in the section on "Inference of Virtue," the eye of wisdom is free from cataracts, universally observing the dharma-realm with a vast and expansive mind of insight.

This is the land of the three eyes: the eye of clarity benefits sentient beings according to the world; the eye of wisdom observes their faculties; the eye of dharma knows all phenomena; and the eye of insight discerns between the correct and the erroneous.
These three are one; they are spoken of as three according to their respective functions.

Within the first section, the Dharma-gate of the primary entry into the state [of practice], from the words "At that time" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva’s liberation door of the lamp of conformity," the scriptural text is divided into six topical sections:

(1) Sudhana contemplates the thirteen kinds of profound depths regarding the dwelling place of the Bodhisattvas; (2) his gradual journey to the country of Trayastriṃśa; (3) his search for the monk Sudarśana; (4) seeing him walking back and forth in the grove while being honored by devas and nāgas; (5) Sudhana pays homage with his head at his feet and requests what he seeks; and (6) the monk Sudarśana bestows upon Sudhana the Bodhisattva liberation door of the lamp of conformity that pervades the ten directions through constant walking.

The bhikṣu named Sudarśana is so called because he clearly perceives all phenomena through the Dharma-eye, the wisdom-eye, and the insight-eye; because he clearly perceives the root-natures of all sentient beings and teaches them at the appropriate time to bring them to liberation, he is named Sudarśana.
"Bhikṣu" means one who extinguishes disputes; because he can transform the afflictions and views of sentient beings, he is called a bhikṣu.
For what reason, at the beginning of the ten practices, is the bhikṣu seen first?
Answer: It is to clarify that the practices performed by Bodhisattvas are all intended to cause all sentient beings to be without contention, free from defilement, and transcend the world.
Since these are the foremost of practices, they must all be undefiled and supramundane; for this reason, a bhikṣu is seen first.
Only when one has clarified the mind and transcended the mundane world is one fit to dwell among the laity, sharing their radiance and benefiting all beings.
Therefore, what follows below clarifies the conduct within secular society.
As for "practicing walking meditation in the forest," this symbolizes that one's practice is as vast and extensive as a forest providing shade and shelter.
The roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits clarify that his worldly conduct is thus.

His walking back and forth in meditation within the grove clarifies that he enters the cycle of birth and death to deliver sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to attain the bliss of supramundane nirvana.
Furthermore, it causes one not to abide in nirvana, but to give rise to the vow of great compassion and enter into saṃsāra.

Moreover, delivering sentient beings so that they reach nirvana is the meaning of "coming and going. Thus, proceeding further and further without rest is like one lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps; while the darkness is dispelled and all become bright, the light itself is never exhausted. Because this Dharma-gate of the lamp is bestowed upon Sudhana, it is symbolized by his walking back and forth in the forest.

Furthermore, regarding being in the prime of youth, possessing beauty, and being upright and pleasing: "being able to practice various deeds" clarifies what it means to be in the prime of youth; "beauty and uprightness" are so described because they arise as the retribution for such practice.
Furthermore, having an upright mind and correct conduct is what is meant by being "well-proportioned.
That his hair is deep blue-black, curling to the right and not disheveled, is the retribution born of a pure mind and correct conduct.
Moreover, that it curls to the right and is not disheveled signifies conformity with the True Dharma.
The presence of a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon the crown of the head is the retribution born of supreme wisdom and the fulfillment of virtue.
His golden-hued skin is summoned by the karmic reward of pure wisdom, a mind as tranquil and white as silk, free from defilement, and the practice of benefiting others through compassion.
The yellow complexion is the color of merit and virtue.
The three lines on the neck are produced as the retribution for never having spoken falsely.
The broad and level forehead is the retribution for wide and comprehensive wisdom.
That his eyes are long and wide like blue lotuses is obtained as a retribution for wisdom, compassion, and loving-kindness.
That his lips and mouth are crimson and pure like the *bimba* fruit clarifies their red color; this is the color of the southern direction.
It is held that the South corresponds to Li (the Trigram Fire). Li represents the sun, the void, the mind, and the gateway to the Dharma.

Taking wisdom as the sun and the mouth as the gateway for expounding the Dharma, it means that by means of the sun of wisdom, the mouth is able to express and manifest the retribution born from the True Dharma.
The *svastika* marked upon the chest is produced by the purification of karma.
Regarding the "seven places being level and full": the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the horse-king-like concealed organ constitute the seven places that are full.
That his arms are slender and long is the retributive karma produced by extending a hand to receive others and establishing them in goodness.
That his fingers are joined by a web-like membrane is the retributive karma produced by teaching sentient beings how to filter out impurities.
Within his hands and feet are vajra-wheels; this clearly indicates the karmic fruit arising from the activity of turning the wheel of Dharma to benefit sentient beings.
Thus, his blessings are extensively praised, all as fully detailed in the sutras.
All these are the internal cultivation of wisdom and the external adornment of manifold merits; because their causes were not wasted, they clearly understood that effects arise from causes.

As for the immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, humans, and non-humans who surrounded him before and behind—this clarifies that the bhikṣu’s birth was encompassed by the universal sense-bases (*indriya*), and thus he summoned this multitude of attendants to follow him.
This also represents the assembly of the Dharma.

As for the presiding deities of the directions who turn according to the quarters to lead those before them: this signifies the Dharma; the Dharma turns and guides sentient beings in accordance with their respective faculties and capacities.
Since direction has no fixed characteristic, phenomena likewise have no fixed characteristic.
The deity Foot-Walker holding a lotus flower to support his feet symbolizes that practice is non-practice.
The deity Unstained and Exhaustless Light radiating light to destroy darkness signifies using the light of the teaching to destroy delusion.

The forest deity of the Jambūdhvaja grove who rains down various kinds of flowers clarifies that one should lead sentient beings by means of abundant virtuous words and manifold practices, causing them to abide in the fragrant flowers of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
The earth goddess Akṣayakośa manifesting various treasuries of jewels represents the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), for she is able to manifest the treasury of the jewels of wisdom.

The space goddess Samantaprabhā adorning space clarifies that by means of right wisdom one contemplates all phenomena to adorn the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) and gives rise to discerning knowledge; thus, one practices diverse deeds without ever departing from the emptiness of phenomena.

The deity Cloud of Accomplished Jewels from the Ocean of Virtues signifies that through the fulfillment of the great vows of Samantabhadra, one accomplishes the virtue of great compassion and universally rains down the rain of Dharma to benefit all sentient beings.
The gods of Mount Sumeru bowing their heads in prostration, bending their bodies, and joining their palms in reverence illustrates the practice of humility, freedom from pride, and respect.

The Wind God of Unobstructed Power raining down exquisite fragrant flowers illustrates that gentle speech, respectful speech, selfless speech, harmonious and pleasant speech, speech free from coarseness and evil, timely speech, truthful speech, beneficial speech, speech in accordance with the Dharma, and speech of praise—all such virtuous forms of speech constitute unobstructed power.
The Wind Deity rains down exquisite fragrant flowers; those who hear them shall all come to possess the flowers of the fragrance of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Therefore, the *Yi Jing* says: "Xun represents speech; as the wind blows across the earth, it can be observed."
This clarifies the refined speech regarding the ceremonial rites of the noble person (*junzi*).
By having something to emulate and learn from, one brings about benevolent virtue; thus it is said that "the wind blows over the earth.
"Earth" refers to *Kun* (the Trigram of Earth).
The Kun hexagram represents the multitude; because they emulate the words and teachings of the noble person (junzi), there is something worthy of observation.

This sutra uses the wind-spirit of right wisdom; it takes the verbal sounds of correct teaching emerging from the mouth as the "wind" that issues forth, and unites these words of ritual propriety as "incense and flowers."

As for the night goddess Vasanta-samaya adorning her body and prostrating herself with her entire being: this clarifies that she dwells in constant harmony and joy amidst the night of birth and death through her compassion, causing all sentient beings who see her to rejoice and give rise to roots of goodness; thus she is named the Night Goddess Vasanta-samaya.

"Adorning one's body and casting oneself to the ground" clarifies the adornment of the vows and practices of great loving-kindness and great compassion; it signifies casting oneself into the realm of birth and death to teach, transform, and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.

The deity of the day, Constantly Awakened Lord, who dwells in the void holding a mani-banner that universally illumines all directions and radiates great light, signifies the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā) which illuminates all sentient beings, and through the wisdom of differentiation, brings them to liberation.

When the youth Sudhana arrived at the place where the bhikṣu was, he prostrated himself and presented his request. All [the teachers] replied that they had already resolved upon supreme bodhicitta; this clarifies that he had already resolved upon bodhicitta at the site of Mañjuśrī mentioned in the first chapter. Thus, he realized that the essence of bodhi is without practice, without cultivation, and without seeking; it is without attainment and without realization. To seek the path of a bodhisattva in this manner is to never depart from bodhicitta; one merely seeks the path of a bodhisattva to perfect bodhicitta, for it is fundamentally devoid of both formation and destruction.
That which was sought in the past should be sought in the present; that which was resolved upon in the past should be resolved upon in the present.
Because one possesses such mindfulness, it is said that one has already resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of perfect enlightenment.
Because one has emerged from this mind of the three periods of time, it is called "having already resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and perfect enlightenment.

The bhikṣu replied to Sudhana: "As for my being young in years and having recently left the household life, I am merely beginning to clearly understand how, starting from the first stage of the ten abodes, the wisdom of all Buddhas is born; thus, I have given rise to this practice. This is what is meant by being 'young in years and having recently left the household life.'"

Regarding these ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*), although their names are listed sequentially, the actual practice occurs simultaneously; the same applies to the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

These three sets of dharmas are practiced at one time because the realm of wisdom does not transcend the limit of a single kṣaṇa, encompassing all six stages—the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground—all at once.
Furthermore, because one who has first resolved their mind does not perceive the prior or subsequent limits of birth and old age, they are said to be "young" and "recently ordained.
The phrase "in this life of mine" clarifies that one does not perceive a beginning, an end, or a middle within birth.

Those who have purified their practice of the Brahma-faring under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-eight Ganges Rivers clarify the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications, harmonizing wisdom and compassion through these thirty dharmas. Because these thirty dharmas, which correspond to the causes and fruits of the Buddha at each stage, are mutually integrated such that wisdom and compassion are inexhaustible, they are called "thirty."
Because she did not depart from the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path, it is said that she purified her brahma-conduct under thirty-eight Ganges-sands of Buddhas.

The previous mention of the girl Maitrīcaryā as having been under thirty-seven Ganges-sands of Buddhas represents the practices of the three stages of worthiness and the seven factors of enlightenment;
this mention of being under thirty-eight Ganges-sands of Buddhas indicates her further advancement to the Eightfold Noble Path.
Regarding "the Buddhas of thirty-eight Ganges-sands," this refers collectively to the causes and fruits of Buddhahood within the Eightfold Noble Path at the stage of the Three Worthies (*śaikṣa*).

It clarifies that at the moment of generating the bodhicitta, when correct wisdom manifests and ignorance is shattered, immeasurable evil karma is extinguished and immeasurable wisdom manifests; because these are numbered as being equal to the sands of the Ganges, they are designated as "Buddhas of the Ganges-sands."

From practicing the pure conduct of the Brahma-faring for one day and night, or seven days and nights, or staying with a Buddha for half a month, a month, a year, a hundred years, even up to unspeakable years and unspeakable eons to fulfill the six *pāramitās*—this clarifies that it is the supramundane path that fulfills the six *pāramitās*. As for the other four *pāramitās* of skillful means (*upāya*), vow (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*), these are for entering *saṃsāra* to accomplish the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This refers to a bhikṣu; it mentions only the six pāramitās and does not speak of the ten pāramitās.

Furthermore, regarding those who can perceive the distinct differences between attaining enlightenment, leaving behind instructions, and entering parinirvāṇa—this is the realm of clear wisdom that accords with conventional distinctions, yet within that wisdom there is not even a hair’s breadth of temporal transition.
The above [discussion of] days, months, years, and kalpas clarifies that time does not shift.
Furthermore, it says: "Good son!

When I practice walking meditation, within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), all the ten directions appear before me; even unspeakably many Buddha-fields are all purified and adorned; even the diverse practices of unspeakably many sentient beings all appear before me; and because I have accomplished the practices of Samantabhadra and perfected the power of vows, within a single thought-moment I receive and comprehend the teachings of unspeakably unspeakable Tathāgatas."
The details are as explained at length in the sutra.
This section clarifies that the inclusion of both the distant and the near is immutable and cannot be fully described.

The statement that "in total, it does not transcend a single thought-moment" intends to clarify that the essence of the wisdom-body (*dharmakāya*), which is manifested through walking meditation, is without dependence.
Because wisdom has no dependence, wisdom has neither interior nor exterior, nor middle nor periphery.
Because wisdom has neither interior nor exterior, the ten directions are neither distant nor near.

Because wisdom has neither distance nor proximity, its essence is like space, clearly illuminating the ten directions; it gives rise to practice according to vows to benefit beings in accordance with their faculties, appearing as a physical body without going or coming, like the sun manifesting within all waters.

Because this is the realm of wisdom, the nature of time—days, months, years, and kalpas—is inherently without transition; in a single thought-moment, all is extinguished. Across many kalpas of past and present, not even a hair’s breadth shifts; whether distant or near, all realms do not transcend the dust.

Wisdom acts as the messenger for vows, and vows are the king of wisdom; the practice of compassion, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the ocean-like conduct of Samantabhadra all proceed from the messenger of wisdom through vows.

Thus, although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess supernormal powers, because they lack the great vow to benefit sentient beings, their powers compared to those of the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra are like a single firefly compared to hundreds of thousands of suns.
The remaining meanings are as clarified by the sūtra itself.

Regarding the name of this dharma-door, "The Bodhisattva’s Liberation Door of the Lamp of Accordance": it clarifies that a bodhisattva, by means of their own Tathāgata-like wisdom of universal radiance, accords with the conduct of all sentient beings and gives rise to discerning wisdom; thus they teach and transform sentient beings, constantly causing them to manifest illumination without ceasing. This is called the bodhisattva’s liberation door of the lamp of accordance.
This is the Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*), in which the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is primary and the other nine are its companions.
From the perspective of the gate of wisdom, within a single practice one universally cultivates all practices;
from the perspective of the gate of stages, one specifically cultivates the supramundane practices of the six perfections.

This first gate of the ten practices takes the gate of the *jñānapāramitā* from among the ten abodes to universally seal all realms of the Buddhas and realms of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time; for it encompasses all inexhaustible eons in a single moment and does not emerge even from within a single hair-pore.
The following cases are likewise so; from beginning to end, it is entirely thus.
*New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 35.

within the second section, "The Gate of Advancing through the Promotion of Virtue," there are twenty-one and a half lines of scripture from "All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas" down to "taking leave and departing. Regarding the textual meaning, it is roughly divided into five sections:

First, he praised his virtuous advancement; second, he pointed out the location and country of the spiritual friend; third, he indicated that the dwelling place of the spiritual friend was upon a river island; fourth, he raised the name of the spiritual friend, calling him the Lord of Sovereignty; fifth, he prostrated in reverence, took his leave, and departed.
From the passage beginning with "Just as the bodhisattvas... onwards, this section concerns the advancement of merit.
Regarding the meaning of the "South" therein, it is as explained previously.
As for the name of the land being "Renowned," this name is established based on the Teacher; it is because the Teacher possesses renown.
Dwelling upon a riverbank symbolizes that the precepts are like a river, for they must inevitably flow into the ocean of wisdom.
As for "youth," it signifies that the precepts are pure and untainted; thus, one is called a youth.

The name "Lord of Mastery" (Vasitā) is established because it clarifies that he has already entered the mundane world from the fruit of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body wisdom to benefit sentient beings; thus, he is named as such because his mastery is absolute whether he enters the world or remains within the fetters while leading all sentient beings.

Regarding the first section, the "Gate of Correct Entry into the Appropriate Stage," it extends from "At that time, the youth Sudhana... down to "...I only know this Dharma-gate of the Light of Wisdom of Great Skillful Artifice and Supernatural Power. Within this passage, it is divided into seven sections: (1) Receiving the teaching, recollecting and upholding it, and proceeding forward;

(2) Being surrounded by hosts of devas, nāgas, and yakṣas; (3) Arriving at the country of Yaśovatī and searching everywhere for the youth Indradatta; (4) The devas and nāgas indicating his location; (5) Sudhana going to that place and seeing him surrounded by ten thousand youths; (6) Seeing [Indradatta] playing with sand, Sudhana prostrating, making a request, and seeking the Dharma he desires; (7) Indradatta explaining to Sudhana the Dharma to be practiced.
Within these dharmas to be practiced, there are approximately ten categories: first, writing;
second, calculation;
third, seals—referring to hand gestures (*mudrā*), talismanic seals, and so forth.
The four elements (*dhātu*); "elements" refers to the world;
the five bases (*āyatana*) refer to locations, namely the dwelling places where sentient beings reside in the world;
and the six treatments for illness.
Seventh, the arts and crafts;
eighth, the refinement of elixirs;
ninth, agriculture and commerce.
Tenth is the knowledge of the supramundane faculties and so forth of sentient beings.
Regarding the calculations therein, the brief introduction in the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*Asaṃkhyeya-varga*) applies here as well.
This is the practice of the Bodhisattva, which is known through the calculation of dharmas.
In that "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*), the Buddha’s wisdom is perfected; he knows it naturally with the eye of wisdom, without needing the methods of calculation.
The remainder is self-evident from the text.
Here, within the practice of benefiting others (*anugrahacaryā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine serve as its companions.
If categorized according to the dharma-gates of the cognitive domain, each stage universally cultivates all ten practices.

If categorized according to the gateway of stages (*avasthā-mukha*), within this practice of benefiting others, it is only when [the practice] involves writing, arithmetic, calculation, seals, agriculture, commerce, and signs, as well as supramundane matters, that it is termed the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*).

In the first ten stages (*bhūmi*), the essence of the precepts consists solely of the Dharma-body, the Dharma-nature, and the principle of wisdom; this is equivalent to a bhikṣu contemplating the ocean of birth and death—the twelve links of dependent origination—as the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.
In the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the essence of the precepts consists of being like a master mariner who skillfully enters the ocean of birth and death.
Just as in the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), the essence of the precepts consists of fearing transgression, cultivating merit, and departing from worldly conduct.

Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one cultivates great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as the essence of the precepts; this is none other than the Night Goddess (Rātridevī) who observes sentient beings with joyful eyes.
She stands at the Buddha’s right side, for wisdom resides on the left and compassion on the right.
Furthermore, "Joyful Eye Observing Sentient Beings" is the name for compassion, which serves as the precept.

According to each of the five stages, the substance of the precepts ascends differently; yet, through the comprehensive penetration of wisdom, all five stages are fully present within each single stage.

Regarding these ten superior and inferior spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), if one discusses them in terms of the essence of their practice, matters such as worldly arts, medical prescriptions, and making offerings are explained in detail according to the sutras.

Regarding the second section, "Advancing by Inquiring into Virtue," there are seventeen lines of scripture from "Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "...took their leave and departed. In terms of textual meaning, this may be roughly divided into five sections:

first, advancing by inquiring into virtue; second, indicating the dwelling place and location of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); third, citing the name of the city where the spiritual friend resides, namely Sāgaravati; fourth, citing the name of the laywoman (*upāsikā*) who is the spiritual friend, namely Pūrṇa; and fifth, paying respects and taking one's leave to depart.

The section beginning with "Just as the bodhisattvas... and following belongs to the stage of advancing through the cultivation of virtues. As for the city named Sāgaravatī (Sea-Abiding), it symbolizes that this upāsikā can contain all virtues like the ocean.
Regarding the statement that the name of this upāsikā is "Complete," it clarifies that her name was established based on her virtues.

It signifies that because this upāsikā dwells within this perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), she is complete in all ten perfections: because she is constantly able to practice great renunciation, she is complete in the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*);
because she wears simple, clean clothing, she is said to maintain the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Tearing out one's hair and disfiguring one's appearance is called patience;
constantly keeping the mind from harmonizing with worldly concerns is called diligence;
when wisdom and compassion benefit the mundane without being joined with ordinary consciousness, it is called meditative concentration.
Having already realized the supramundane sublime wisdom of the Buddha-fruit, it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*);

constantly dwelling within birth and death to guide and receive sentient beings, yet with a mind free from feminine karma while manifesting the acceptance of a female body to clarify the practice of great compassion, this is called "expedient means" (*upāya*);
constantly following one's original vows to deliver beings throughout the six realms, this is called the "great vow."
To fearlessly turn the wheel of Dharma throughout the cycle of birth and death is called power;
to manifest throughout all oceans of lands through the illusory transformations of wisdom and constantly perform Buddha-works is called wisdom.
Because he is fully endowed with these ten pāramitās, the four means of integration, and the four immeasurables, he is called "Fully Endowed.
When Sudhana heard this, the hairs on his body stood on end; having heard the name "Fully Endowed," his heart was filled with joy and wonder.

Within the first section, the Dharma-gate of Entering Properly into the Corresponding Stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I know only this liberation-door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit," this segment is divided approximately into twenty sections:
(1) contemplating the advancement through the vastness of the spiritual friend’s teaching, which is like the ocean;
(2) proceeding gradually toward the south; [and so forth].
Third, he traveled to the city of Samudrapāla to seek out his virtuous friend;
fourth, the people informed him that [the friend] was in this city;
fifth, Sudhana went to the gate and stood with palms joined in reverence.
Sixth, the fruit of the basis upon which she is observed: her residence is vast and expansive, adorned with various kinds of ornamentation;
seventh, having entered, Sudhana beholds the upāsikā seated upon a jeweled throne; eighth, he observes her primary physical form, whose appearance and deportment are most venerable;
ninth, he sees that within her residence, ten billion exquisite seats have been spread out.
10. He saw that her small vessel was before her seat and that ten thousand young maidens served as her attendants, with no other clothing, food, or drink to be seen;
11. Having seen this, Sudhana paid his respects and made his request;
12. The upāsikā explained to Sudhana the dharma-gate she had cultivated.
Thirteenth, by raising up the name of its dharma-gate, it is called the Bodhisattva’s Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit;
fourteenth, because small vessels are fully provided with all kinds of delicious food and drink required by sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the six realms;
fifteenth, once a bodhisattva bound to only one more birth has finished eating, they shall all attain Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree.
Sixteenth, he raised up a multitude of a million asaṃkhyeyas who were his fellow practitioners, all of whom shared the same three karmas;
seventeenth, Sudhana saw immeasurable sentient beings entering through the four gates;
eighteenth, according to their prayers and whatever food they required, all were completely filled.
Nineteenth, he proclaims that he knows only this gate of the bodhisattva’s treasury of merit;
twentieth, by extolling his virtues and advancing them, he brings about the subsequent practice.
As for the ten thousand maidens, they represent the fulfillment of the ten thousand practices.
Entering through the four gates refers to the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).

As for the food and drink offered from a single small vessel that universally satisfies and fills infinite sentient beings: this clarifies that although the vessel is small in measure, by means of the wisdom of giving according to the *dharmadhātu* and entering the *Indra-gate*, the small contains the inexhaustible.

Furthermore, by adding the vast mind of the power of vows and the wisdom of the dharma-realm, one causes all sentient beings born throughout the ten directions to be fully satisfied by eating even a morsel of food the size of a single atom, yet without the food ever diminishing by so much as a hair’s breadth.
A morsel of food the size of a single atom is equal in measure to the Dharma-realm, for it is unimpeded by limits of interior, exterior, middle, or periphery.
The name of this Dharma-gate, "The Bodhisattva’s Treasury of Merit," clarifies that the aspirations of giving are vast and great.
This is the third practice of non-opposition, which takes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its primary element and the other nine perfections as its companions.
From the perspective of the gate of wisdom, all ten practices are cultivated throughout the five stages;
from the perspective of the gate of stages, however, patience constitutes its essential body.
Because patience is regarded as a small vessel, it is because practice is not yet fully perfected; thus, through humility, there is nothing that is not beneficial.

Within the second section, "Advancing by Recommending Virtue," from the passage beginning with "Just as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas" down to "took his leave and departed," there are eight and a half lines of scripture. The meaning within this is summarized into four sections: first, advancing by recommending virtue;

second, indicating the location and the city where the spiritual friend resides; third, citing the name of the city, Mahāsaṃbhava, and the name of the spiritual friend, the Householder Prajñāmati; and fourth, Sudhana prostrating himself and taking his leave to depart.
The section beginning with "As all bodhisattvas... and following is titled "Advancing through the Cultivation of Virtues.
As for the name of the city, "Great Flourishing" (Mahā-udaya), it is established based on the teaching master.
Because the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) brings about great flourishing of benefit, the name of the city is established accordingly.

The lay practitioner named Mingzhi (Wisdom-Intelligence) is so called because, by means of the fourth practice of "unyielding conduct," he perceives the faculties of beings and benefits them; looking up at the void, he bestows both material wealth and the Dharma simultaneously, and is thus named Mingzhi.
This is the "Abiding in Noble Birth" among the ten abidings.

Within the ten stages, it corresponds to the fourth stage (*caturthī bhūmi*), wherein supramundane wisdom manifests before one, karma of the three realms is exhausted, and one is destined to be born into the family of the Buddhas.
Regarding the "wise layperson" (*gṛhapati*) among these ten practices: although he dwells in the secular world, he embraces the Way to benefit sentient beings; therefore, he is called a "layperson.

Within the first section, the Dharma-gate of "Correct Entry into the Dharma of One’s Own Station," from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this liberation-door of the treasury of merit arising at will according to one's intent," the meaning is divided into ten sections:
first, contemplating and advancing according to the instructions bestowed by the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Second, he gradually traveled south to the city of Mahāsaṃbhava to seek out the wise layman;
third, he conceived a yearning of thirst for the spiritual friend;
fourth, he maintained the thought that he should serve all spiritual friends with a mind free from weariness.
Fifth, he saw the householder on a seven-jeweled terrace at the crossroads of the city market, seated upon a throne adorned with countless gems;
sixth, Sudhana requested what he sought;
seventh, the elder praised his ability to resolve for great bodhicitta and seek the path of a bodhisattva.
The eighth elder showed him the multitude who had been able to give rise to the great bodhicitta;

the ninth elder told Sudhana that the name of the dharma-gate he was to practice was the "Liberation Gate of the Treasury of Merit Born According to One’s Wishes," wherein whatever is required is entirely fulfilled;

the tenth waited for the assembly to gather and demonstrated his method of giving: looking up into the void, everything they required descended from the sky and filled them completely, after which he preached the Dharma.
From the passage "I only know this liberation door of the treasury of merit produced at will" onwards, there is the advancement through the cultivation of virtues.

The laywoman of the preceding stage, using a small vessel, demonstrated the gate of patience by abandoning arrogance, indolence, and pride, thereby filling [the vessel] with her offering of food and drink.

Within this stage, it expresses a mind of diligence that is never cowed or faltering; one constantly practices the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to eliminate afflictions, attains the mind of unsurpassed wisdom, and all roots of goodness pertaining to humans and devas—whether based on the Dharma or its retribution—are fully contained therein.

When the lay practitioner says, "I am born into the family of the Tathāgata and have attained the pure Dharma," it clarifies that this stage is the fourth *janmakula-caryā-pratipatti* (the practice of being born into the noble family), which is also the fourth of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) where karma within the three realms is exhausted and one is born into the family of the Tathāgata.

Only through the fulfillment of mundane wisdom, one trains within the fifth stage among the five stages; having completed the training in both the conventional and ultimate truths of the sixth stage and the sixth bhūmi, one attains the samādhi of cessation, the three emptinesses manifest before one, and spontaneously employs supernormal powers to teach and transform beings throughout the ten directions.

Thereafter, from the seventh dwelling and the seventh stage onward, one enters the mundane world and engages in conduct identical to that of ordinary people, practicing the gateway of great compassion and mercy.
In the eighth stage, one partially attains the state of effortlessness.
It is only at the tenth stage that the ten powers of a Buddha are fully perfected.
On the eleventh stage, one spontaneously benefits sentient beings;

therefore, one gazes upward at the void. This is the practice of diligence that has been cultivated, wherein all karmic suffering is entirely severed, and all Buddha-dharmas as well as the merits of humans and devas are fully contained therein.

However, by practicing the emptiness of phenomena and attaining the single gate of the quiescence of dependent origination, all afflictions naturally cease to appear, and all wisdom naturally manifests before one.
This is merely a summary of the essential points; the extensive meaning is self-evident in the sūtras themselves.
This fourth practice of being unyielding takes diligence as its primary factor, with the other nine as its companions.
From the perspective of the gate of wisdom, these five stages and ten practices proceed in concert;

from the perspective of the stages themselves, the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena and the realization of liberation through dependent origination are supreme. This serves to remedy the residual habits of the three realms, causing the wisdom of the Dharma-body to manifest and one to be born into the family of the Tathāgata.

At the initial mind of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), one first opens the Buddha-wisdom and is born into the family of the Tathāgata. At the fourth stage, one treats the delusions of the triple world and purifies Buddha-wisdom so that it manifests; thus one is born into the family of the Tathāgata. Within the eighth stage, non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) manifests, and one is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s non-effortful wisdom. Within the tenth stage, through wisdom and compassion universally saving others, one receives the rank of a Buddha; this too is being born into the family of the Tathāgata. Throughout the ten stages, each is established according to this same pattern.

The ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) represent the progressive advancement of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*); they differ from the provisional teachings where the fruit of Buddhahood is placed after the ten stages, and where the forty minds of the three vehicles prior to the stages are considered the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), while the ten stages constitute the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

In this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Ten Abodes constitute the Path of Seeing; the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, and the Eleven Stages constitute the Path of Application, as they involve the cultivation of practice until it becomes habitual and proficient.

The fruit of Buddhahood first manifests at the beginning, because through the compassionate vows of Samantabhadra, the great functioning of wisdom and compassion has been made habitual and mastered with ease.

Because the fundamental, universal radiance-wisdom (samantaprabhā-jñāna) of the Tathāgata itself first manifests, there is from beginning to end, from root to branch, no distinction of duration, extension, or temporal limits.

Speaking according to the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya as it truly is, this differs from what is understood through the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles; therefore, all must be viewed in relation to the source. Ultimately, the habitual tendencies for the fruit of Buddhahood have been perfected, and the practices of Samantabhadra have been fulfilled.

Generally speaking, it is simply that the constant and eternal purpose is to teach and transform all sentient beings; from beginning to end, without start or finish, and without formation or destruction, one takes it as one’s perpetual task to universally manifest wisdom throughout the six realms of existence in the ten directions to benefit living beings.

From the initial arousal of the mind, when practicing with the arising of faith, one gives rise to such faith and delight, formulates such aspirations, initiates such seeking, and perceives such a path.

From the initial stage of generating the mind of enlightenment, through the power of meditative concentration and contemplation, one accords with the Dharma-body, manifesting the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance; this wisdom illuminates and knows that the nature of the ocean of birth and death for oneself and others is inherently liberated.

It is solely for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings, enabling them to resolve their delusions and depart from the suffering of false conceptualization; furthermore, one does not perceive even oneself as attaining or not attaining Buddhahood.
If one were to give rise to a mind that seeks to achieve the thought of attaining Buddhahood, know that such a person is far removed from the Way of the Buddha.

If it is merely by the power of the natureless Dharma-body—wherein self and other are devoid of inherent nature and there is no mind of formation or destruction—that one gives rise to the power of skillful means, exerts the power of great vows, and opens the gate of great compassion; and if, through non-action, one generates limitless aspirations to teach and transform all natureless sentient beings within the entire Dharma-realm so that they may resolve their delusions, leading them back to awakening and realization of the principle of the naturelessness of their own minds, whereby the fetters of false conceptualization naturally vanish; then one neither speaks of attaining Buddhahood nor of not attaining Buddhahood, and one must not harbor such thoughts of mental scheming.

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* establishes these five stages of teaching solely to guide those who have not attained what they claim to have attained, who have not reached what they claim to have reached, and who consider what is incomplete to be complete; to prevent them from stagnating in the obstacles of defilement and purity on the path to bodhi; and to ensure that Bodhisattvas do not harbor a mind of contentment or a notion of rest in their practice. By establishing fifty layers of cause and effect and one hundred and ten layers of Dharma gates, it ensures that they do not dwell in a state of stagnation, cessation, or desistance, so that they may fulfill the vows of Samantabhadra and proceed to the ultimate limit of inexhaustibility.

Within the second section, the "Gate of Advancing through the Promotion of Virtue," there are fifteen and a half lines of scripture from the passage beginning with "Just as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas" down to "took their leave and departed. This may be divided approximately into five gates.
First, regarding the promotion of virtue through advancement, this refers to the section beginning with "Just as all bodhisattvas... and following.
Second, regarding the indication of the location of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), it is said to be in the south, as explained previously.

Third, regarding the indication of the city where the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) resides: the city is named Siṃhaguhā (Lion’s Cave). This name is established in reference to the principal teacher of transformation.
"Lion" signifies fearlessness; it clarifies that within this fifth stage, the practice free from delusion and confusion, one takes meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) as the palace.

The fourth elder, named Dharmaratna-śikhin, signifies that the meditative practice performed by this elder is the meditative concentration of the sovereign and unimpeded functioning of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which encompasses the practices of the ten pāramitās and contains the eightfold noble path within it.

The description of the elder’s residence as having ten-storied pavilions and eight gates illustrates that the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) pervades all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Its name, "Dharma-Jewel-Crest" (*Dharmaratna-śikha*), signifies that it gathers and encompasses all stages and reaches the summit of the Dharma.
Fifth, the etiquette for departing with reverence.

Within the first section, the Dharma-gate of Proper Entry into the Appropriate Position, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Sudhana" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva liberation gate of the treasury of immeasurable merit and virtue," the meaning is divided into ten sections:

1. Increasing the ocean of merit through the instruction of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in a single thought-moment; 2. Gradually traveling south toward the city of Siṃhapura; 3. Searching everywhere for the elder Ratnacūḍa; 4. Seeing him in the marketplace, paying homage, and formally stating one’s request; 5. The elder taking Sudhana by the hand and leading him to his residence; 6. Causing Sudhana to observe his dwelling, which is composed of various jewels, having ten stories and eight gates; 7. After Sudhana has observed it, he asks about the causes through which it was cultivated; 8. The elder explains the causes cultivated in the past; 9. Furthermore, setting forth the dedication [of merit] to the three spheres; 10. Recommending virtue and proceeding further.

Regarding the exegesis of the text according to its phrasing: "thoroughly investigating the Elder Ratnaśikhin" clarifies the meditative gateway of universally observing that the mind and its objects are empty, that the three realms are neither fixed nor chaotic, and that spiritual advancement is without dependence, attainment, or realization.
Those seen within the city clarify such states as tranquility and turmoil.

If one looks toward the liberation of the Elder within the Ten Abodes, he immediately enters samādhi; this clarifies the gate of the body containing Buddha-lands and represents the essence of his initial dwelling.

Within these ten practices, the essence of concentration (*samādhi*) and the nature of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) remain constant; while manifesting within the marketplace of birth and death to gather and transform sentient beings, they do not impair the essence of concentration, for both the clarity and the movement are quiescent, as their nature is inherently detached.
"To immediately go and pay homage" means to swiftly realize the essence of meditative concentration without delay.
Below this, within the actual presentation of the petition, "grasping the hand of Sudhana" refers to being guided and received.
Regarding the passage "He went to where he lived and showed him his residence, causing Sudhana to observe it," this is intended to make known the underlying cause.

As for the description that "the residence was pure, radiant, and made of true gold," this refers to the stage [of the bodhisattva path] where the *dhyāna-pāramitā* (perfection of meditation) is primary, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.
The clarity and stability of the essence are pure and stainless, resulting in the radiance of retribution.
That true gold forms the main structure of the dwelling while white silver forms the walls signifies that the essence of dhyāna perfects the precepts, serving the purpose of protection.
That the palace is made of crystal signifies that through the essence of dhyāna, wisdom is manifested and patience is perfected.
This jewel resembles water in its brilliance and purity, yet it possesses various colors that differ from one another.
