That the multi-storied pavilions are made of deep-blue lapis lazuli signifies that through the essence of dhyāna, vigor is exerted, such that contemplative observation becomes even more brilliant, pure, and clean.
The pillars made of the wondrous jewel musāragalva represent the practice of dhyāna, for they sustain and maintain all dharmas.
The remaining adornments that follow are arranged in sequence according to the order of the ten pāramitās.
The ten-story pavilion is likewise arranged according to these ten *pāramitās*, stacked from bottom to top, each having its own sequential order.
As for the house opening with eight gates—each side having two gates, totaling eight in the four directions—this clarifies the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path.

In the tenth stage, the tenth wisdom-pāramitā is elucidated: the causes and effects of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are perfectly realized and fulfilled in a single thought-moment; thus, the transformation of sentient beings and the entry into nirvana are both entirely immutable.
This is because, in terms of their objective spheres, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently such.

Within the nine successive layers below, the first is assigned to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the second to ethical discipline (*śīla*), and the third to patience (*kṣānti*); these follow a natural sequence, all of which use the retribution of practice to symbolize the Dharma.

In explaining the original causes for Sudhana, it is said: "I recall that in the past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field, there was a world named Perfectly Adorned (*Paripūrṇavyūha*). The Buddha’s name was King of Universal Adornment of the Dharma-realm of Boundless Radiance (*Anantaprabhā-dharmadhātu-samantavyūharāja*). When that Buddha entered the city, I played musical instruments and burned a single pellet of incense. By dedicating this offering toward three places, I obtained this retribution of a dwelling such as this. This clarifies the attainment of the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because within the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), one has already attained the essence of concentration.

To speak of the number of atoms within a Buddha-field as the measure is to clarify that one has definitively transcended the dust of delusion and that innate wisdom manifests; this is because one enters these ten stages of practice through the gate of dhyāna. Thus, it symbolizes the manifestation of wisdom that transcends the dust of delusion. Using skillful teaching as the sound of joy signifies that wisdom arises from meditative concentration.
If one burns but a single pellet of this incense of concentration, the fivefold Dharma-body will be fully perfected.

Regarding the dedication toward the three places: by merely entering this gate of meditative absorption where quiescence and function are unimpeded, one can forever leave behind poverty, constantly behold all Buddhas and spiritual friends, and perpetually hear the True Dharma; these are the three places, as explained in detail in the sutra.

I know only this bodhisattva liberation door of the "Inexhaustible Jewel Treasury of Immeasurable Merit," which clarifies the meditative door of unimpeded application following the practice of tranquility. It is able to encompass merit, wisdom, as well as great kindness and great compassion, the four means of integration, and the four immeasurables—all of which are contained within it. For this reason, this elder is named Ratnaśikhin (Jewel Topknot), signifying that this meditative door of following practice collectively gathers all dharmas into its topknot.
The remaining details are fully contained within the text itself.
This section constitutes the fifth practice, "Abandoning Delusion and Confusion," which takes the dhyāna-pāramitā as its primary element and the other nine perfections as its companions.
From the perspective of the gates of wisdom, all stages share the same remedy;
from the perspective of the stages themselves, this particular stage remedies both mundane and supramundane states of concentration and distraction.

Thus, this ten-story tower of the Elder encompasses in its entirety the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, the eleventh ground, and the fruit of Buddhahood. Because it takes as its essence the dhyāna of the dharma-realm—which is without support and without intrinsic nature—it adorns itself with the ten pāramitās within the very body of that self-essence of non-supportive, non-abiding dhyāna.
The Master of the Treatise explains in verse:
The garden of dhyāna has non-action as its intrinsic nature; Universal luminous wisdom serves as the great residence.
The pavilions are adorned with various modes of contemplation, And the food of Dharma is bestowed to satisfy all sentient beings.
The precious robe of pure precepts is ever universally worn; diligence and a compassionate heart serve as the court ladies.
Skillfully attaining the wisdom of the world through meditative concentration, the Bodhisattva dwells on the fifth stage of supernormal knowledge and clarity.
On the sixth level is the prajñā of quiescent extinction; on the seventh level, through skillful means, one dwells within the cycle of birth and death.
The eighth stage of No-Activity brings mastery; the ninth is where the Dharma-King dwells for one lifetime;
in the tenth stage, the fruit of Buddhahood is perfected. Practicing and studying in this successive order, one ultimately does not dwell in the beginning, middle, or end.
By means of these manifold dharmas, one benefits all living beings.
The two retributions—the primary and the secondary—are attained therein.
This is a brief explanation of the general outline; the detailed meaning is as found in the text.
The intent clarifies that within a single practice, ten practices are practiced simultaneously, without beginning or end, and this applies to all cases accordingly.

In the second section, "Encouraging Virtue and Advancing," from the passage beginning with "Just as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas... down to "...took his leave and departed," there are ten and a half lines of scripture.

This is divided into six sections: first, encouraging virtue to advance; second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend by naming the south; third, indicating the name of the spiritual friend’s land, which is Mūlavatī; fourth, indicating the name of the city where the spiritual friend resides, which is Samantamukha; fifth, stating the name of the spiritual friend, which is Samantanetra; and sixth, paying respects and departing.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the praise of his virtues is intended to cause Sudhana to advance further. This is as clearly explained in the text through eight lines of verse found within the section on praising his virtues.

As for the name of the land being "Roots of the Vine" (Vīraṇamūla), it symbolizes that the sixth perfection, Prajñā (Wisdom), is deep and firm, penetrating to the source of all sentient beings; just as the roots of a vine are deep and firm, penetrating the great earth down to the water's edge.

"Grasping the meaning of firmness and penetration" means that, by means of wisdom corresponding to this, one contemplates and penetrates both mundane and supramundane phenomena, thoroughly reaching their very source and bottom.
The city is named "Universal Gate" (Pumen) to clarify that it universally knows all phenomena through the Universal Eye; thus, the name is established based on the Lord of the Dharma.
The elder named Universal Eye possesses wisdom that surpasses that of humans and devas; thus he is called an "elder.
Because there is nothing in the mundane or supramundane realms that he does not know universally, he is named "Universal Eye."
The following section encourages one to go and visit [the teacher], as detailed in the text itself.

Within the first major section, "Entering Properly into the Dharma-gate of the Specific Stage," from the passage beginning with "At that time" down to "I only know this 'Gate of Universal Joy through Causing All Sentient Beings to See All Buddhas,'" the text is divided into eight subsections.
The first is: "Properly Recalling the Instructions of the Spiritual Friend and Contemplating Progression."
Second, he traveled to the kingdom of Vaṃśa to inquire and search for the city of Samantamukha;
third, while on the road, he saw the elder who was precisely engaged in the task he sought;
fourth, the elder bestowed upon Sudhana the matters regarding his practice.
There are four practices he performs:

first, skillfully treating all manner of illnesses; second, skillfully expounding the dharma-gates for counteracting the various faculties; third, skillfully blending various incenses as offerings to universally behold all Buddhas; and fourth, promoting virtue through advancement.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: as for the city’s battlements and parapets—being lofty, steep, and layered—the highest are called *zhì* (battlements); a layer of battlements is called *dié* (parapet); the height of the city wall is called *chóng* (lofty); and its difficulty to ascend is called *jùn* (steep). This clarifies that this spiritual friend dwells within the sixth stage, wherein wisdom is layered upon layer, inexhaustible, noble, and difficult to enter.
The broad and level roads signify that the wisdom of the three voids is vast and boundless, such that there is no worldly or world-transcending knowledge that does not pervade.
Being skilled at treating all ailments refers to the treatment of the imbalances of the four great elements in the world through medicinal decoctions and drugs.
Just as the disease of afflictions is treated with the five contemplations for settling the mind and the ten pāramitās,

so too does one who skillfully blends all fragrances— using the perfumes of the dharmakāya and jñānakāya consisting of morality, concentration, wisdom, and liberation— universally infuse all faculties according to their capacities, from the moment a Buddha appears in the world.
The matters described above all employ phenomena to symbolize principles; they involve both phenomena and principles, encompassing both mundane and supramundane meanings.

For example, in the sixth stage of the Ten Abodes, the Stage of Right Mindfulness (*samyaktva-cittasthiti*), the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja enters the samādhi of extinction while his body emanates clouds of transformations that pervade everywhere to benefit others. This symbolizes the gate of the unimpeded integration of prajñā and quiescence within the sixth abode.

Now, within these ten stages of practice, during the sixth stage, the "Excellent Manifestation of Prajñā," one employs this tranquility exclusively, thereby achieving the tranquil conduct of body, speech, and mind.
As for those who can thus cure various ailments, such practices truly exist. Regarding the manifestation of the Dharma:

for those with wind-disorders (vāta) characterized by excessive discursive thought, one employs counting the breaths as an antidote to lead them toward internal stillness. Through these skillful means, one causes the object of focus and the cessation of breath to accord with non-conceptual concentration (*anabhisamskāra-samādhi*), thereby manifesting the function of wisdom and supernatural powers to benefit and transform all beings.
Those with jaundice represent those with an abundance of greed; they are countered by the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Those with phlegm-fever represent those with an abundance of delusion; they are countered by the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*).

The "demon-possession illness" symbolizes grasping at exquisite forms and failing to leave behind demonic activities and celestial retributions; it is countered by the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

"Poisonous charms" symbolize that all minds characterized by acquisitiveness can give rise to all manner of entanglements and harmful karmas; here, the karma of craving is likened to water and the karma of hatred to fire—all such illnesses can be treated through these remedies.
As for the blending of various fragrances, there is likewise such a real activity.
That which expresses the Dharma clarifies the fragrance of wisdom and skillful teaching, so as to permeate and destroy all karmic retributions of evil.
One becomes foul-smelling in accordance with various evil karmas, and fragrant in accordance with the practice of wisdom.
As for the *siṃhupāra* incense, *siṃhu* refers to the great river that flows from the Ox-Head (*go-mukha*) on the western side of Lake Anavatapta, flowing into the kingdom of Sindhu.
"Pāra" means "bank" (in Chinese). This clarifies that this incense originates from the bank of this river.

It symbolizes this sixth stage, the Practice of Manifestation (*sudarśana-bhūmi*), wherein the wisdom of the three gates of liberation and the four unhindered analytical knowledges are like the four great rivers gushing forth from a vast lake; they moisten the great earth and further form the great ocean, such that all the fragrances of the fivefold dharma-body—precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—are produced therein.
If there are sentient beings who hear [this teaching] and enter into faith, they shall all attain liberation and transcend to the other shore.
The sutra mentions one of them; the remaining three rivers are to be understood by analogy with this.

Regarding *aruṇavarti* incense, this is translated as "vivid red-colored incense. It symbolizes that red is the primary color of the south; furthermore, it symbolizes that the *Li* trigram represents emptiness, the sun, light, and the mind, because the dharma of *Li* is the mind.

"Li" signifies "exquisite beauty. It represents the radiant light of signless wisdom—the three emptinesses and four analytical knowledges—within this stage, which adorns the mental states of all sentient beings, so that they all attain the fragrance of wisdom and liberation.
Regarding "Uragasāra sandalwood": *uraga* is the name for a snake;
*sāra* refers to the sandalwood tree.
This clarifies that this snake is most venomous and constantly afflicted by poisonous heat; when it coils its body around this sandalwood tree, its toxic vapors are immediately stilled.

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing it said that both mind and objects are empty—that fundamentally they have no essence or characteristics, no location, and not even a single dharma can be apprehended—believe and enter into this realization, then all the poisonous heat of their afflictions will naturally become purified.
The remaining fragrances can be understood according to their names.

These eight kinds of wisdom-fragrance permeate the seeds of consciousness characterized by false views in all sentient beings, causing them to rely upon the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path and enter the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

“Good son! I only know this Dharma-door of causing all sentient beings everywhere to see all Buddhas and rejoice. This clarifies the aforementioned wisdom that counteracts all dharmas, the skillful means for opening the wisdom of all Buddhas, and how it causes all sentient beings to enter the Buddha-wisdom and attain universal joy.
The following clarifies the advancement through the realization of virtue.

This is called the sixth "Good Manifestation" (Sukhāvatī) stage of spiritual friendship, in which the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is primary and the other nine perfections serve as its companions.
If categorized according to the gate of wisdom, all stages have the same remedy;

if categorized according to the gate of stages, the remedy addresses the obstacles to the mastery of tranquil activity in accordance with practice, thereby causing that practice to achieve accomplishment so that the conduct of body, speech, and mind becomes purely pure and tranquil.

Within the second section, "Advancing through the Promotion of Virtue," from the passage beginning with "Just as all bodhisattvas" down to "taking his leave and departing," there are nine and a half lines of scripture, which may be divided into four sections:

first, advancing through the promotion of virtue; second, indicating the location where the spiritual friend resides and the name of the city he inhabits, Tārādhvaja; third, citing the name of the king, Anantatṛpta; and fourth, taking one's leave and departing.
The city named Tālaketu means "Luminous Purity"; this name is established in reference to the principal teacher of transformation.

This is because, within the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-attachment (*asaṅga*), one enters the mundane world through supramundane pure wisdom to act as a lord of compassion; being skilled in knowing the faculties of beings, one manifests emanation bodies to engage in common activities with them, never failing to sustain their rebirth.
The king is named Analaṃkāra (Insatiable), so called because he never tires of benefiting sentient beings; thus his name was established based on his practice.
The remainder is fully detailed in the text itself.

Within the first section, the "Gate of Entering Properly into the Stage," from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I have only attained this illusory-like liberation," this segment of the sutra is divided into fourteen sections:
First, advancing by means of a spiritual friend of right mindfulness;
second, proceeding toward the city of Tālaketu;
third, inquiring among the multitude as to the whereabouts of the king.
1. The four groups of people replied, "He is currently in the central hall.
2. Sudhana went there and saw from afar that the king was at the Nārāyaṇa-vajra throne.
3. He saw that the king’s report and his adorned palace were all made of various jewels.
Seventh, the king saw that his punishment for evil was so severe and agonizing as to be unbearable;
eighth, Sudhana’s mind gave rise to doubt;
ninth, a deity in the sky spoke to him, and by following the words of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he caused that doubt to be removed.
10. Sudhana, his doubts dispelled, went to the king’s presence, prostrated himself, and formally presented his request;
11. The king took Sudhana by the hand and led him into the palace to observe the realms of karmic retribution;

12. The king raised up the gate of liberation of "illusory manifestation," manifesting his own body as one who had committed evil deeds and was undergoing various sufferings, causing sentient beings of true existence to feel awe and fear, thereby giving rise to roots of goodness and the aspiration for bodhicitta.

Thirteenth, the king personally applies himself to his conduct, constantly ensuring that in body, speech, and mind he does not give rise to thoughts of causing harm even to a single mosquito or ant, much less to a human being;
fourteenth, he promotes others by recommending their virtues.
King Anala means "Insatiable" in this language.
He is represented by the laywoman Śūradattā, who corresponds to the stage of compassion in the seventh dwelling of the Ten Dwellings.

This seventh of the ten practices, the practice of compassion, is represented by King Never-Weary; it serves to govern the conduct of evil people, who create evil for themselves and must be disciplined through their own suffering, thereby causing sentient beings to truly grow weary of the world, cultivate virtue, and realize the path to Bodhi.

The seventh dedication is presided over by Avalokiteśvara, and within the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā), it is presided over by the night goddess named Padminī; thus, these are all specific names for the perfection of compassion corresponding to each respective stage.
The remaining details are fully explained in the sutra.
This is the seventh excellence of practice regarding spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), in which the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) is primary and the other nine are its companions.
From the perspective of the gates of wisdom, all stages universally counteract [obstructions];

from the perspective of the gates of the stages, they counteract the obstructions regarding the lack of mastery over the two modes of defilement and purity within the cycle of birth and death, thereby enabling one to abide in birth and death with great wisdom and great compassion and attain mastery.

Within the second section, "The Gate of Advancing through the Recommendation of Virtue," there are eight and a half lines of scripture from the words "All bodhisattvas" down to "took their leave and departed. This may be divided into four sections: first, advancing through the recommendation of virtue;

second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend and the city where he dwells, named *Jyotirasa* (Wonderful Light); third, citing the name of the spiritual friend-king, *Mahāprabha* (Great Light); and fourth, prostrating and taking one's leave.

The scripture states, "The city is named Wondrous Light. This corresponds to the eighth dwelling and the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), wherein the wondrous function of effortless wisdom reaches fulfillment; it is the perfection of the differentiated wisdom within this fundamental station.
The king named Mahāprabha (Great Light) is the name for Fundamental Wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
All other details are fully contained within the text itself.

Within the first section on the Dharma-gate of entering the specific stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva samādhi-door of Great Compassion as the Foremost, which accords with the world," this segment of the sutra is divided approximately into fifteen sections:
First, contemplating the instructions of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to advance;
second, gradually traveling through human settlements and cities;
third, subsequently arriving at the great city of Wondrous Light (Prabhāsa).
1. Sudhana asked people for the location of his dwelling, and everyone replied, "This very city is it. 2.
Upon hearing where the city was situated, Sudhana leaped for joy. 3.
It is clarified that as Sudhana entered the City of Sublime Light (*Prabhāpurī*), he beheld the environment resulting from the ripening of karma, adorned with various jewels.

Seventh, it clarifies that Sudhana beheld the aforementioned sublime realms and all six sensory objects of men and women without any attachment, contemplating only the ultimate Dharma with a single-minded focus;
eighth, he gradually traveled until he saw the dwelling place of King Mahāprabha;
ninth, he beheld the adornments of the king’s two-fold retribution—the primary body and its environment—and his land.
10. Sudhana prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground to worship the king’s feet;
11. He formally set forth his request;
12. The king told Sudhana that the practice he was to perform is called the Bodhisattva Practice of the Banner of Great Compassion.
13. In the City of Sublime Light (*Prabhāpurī*), what is perceived according to one’s mind differs regarding purity or defilement; 14.

When the King enters the Samādhi Door of Following Accordance with the World, headed by Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), at that time all the retribution-adorned jewel grounds and palaces shake in six ways, the forest trees bow their heads, springs gush forth, and the waters flow toward the King; the myriad subjects, devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits pay him homage, while yakṣas and rākṣasas all give rise to a compassionate heart; none among the kings of the eight classes fail to honor him with their crowns; they all experience joy and initiate roots of goodness, for such is the nature of the Dharma through the power of this samādhi headed by Great Compassion;
15. He defers his own virtue so as to cause Sudhana to advance.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: "Traveling by stages, whether reaching human cities, towns, villages, wildernesses, or mountain valleys, and finally arriving at the Great City of Wondrous Light" clarifies that one performs a comprehensive circuit of observation and illumination. This serves to remedy the deficiencies in wisdom and the incompleteness of great compassion practiced during the preceding stages; by bringing wisdom and compassion into equilibrium and achieving mastery over them, one finally reaches the eighth stage, the city of effortless and wondrous activity.

The question, "Where is the city of Wondrous Light now? clarifies that even with the power of contemplative observation, when wisdom and compassion are equalized, one still does not recognize it oneself; therefore, it is necessary to ask those who have long resided there, signifying that in the state of non-action, the convergence of wisdom and compassion is difficult to realize.

When the multitude all replied, "The city of Wondrous Light is the dwelling place of King Mahāprabha," this clarifies that Sudhana has entered the gate of the sovereign power of wisdom and compassion, which is like that king.
"Sudhana’s joy" refers to his entry into the bliss of the Dharma.
From the passage beginning with "Having formed such a thought," it means he reflects that he will certainly hear further superior teachings regarding the conduct of Bodhisattvas.

Having performed these ten kinds of recollections, he enters the City of Sublime Light. This signifies that prior to dawn, during the seventh stage of practice, he has cultivated the worldly practices of compassion and entered the eighth city of Effortless Wisdom; thus it is called "entering the City of Sublime Light," which indicates that his penetrating wisdom is radiant and his great compassion is further expanded.

Having entered the city, all that is seen—the ground adorned with jewels, trees, palaces, towers, pavilions, ponds, and so forth—is clearly explained as entering this gate of practice through wisdom rather than as a result of karmic retribution. Not one of these comes in vain; they all consist of the palace of compassion, the hall of wisdom, the observation towers, and various halls of gnosis; the flowers of the practice of the *dharmatā*, the moats of the seven factors of enlightenment, the waters of the eightfold noble path, and the trees of practices conforming to *bodhi*. With the protection of the physical, verbal, and mental actions of all sentient beings serving as the surrounding walls, this corresponds exactly to the initial correlations in the first of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
The *pīnèi* (parapet) refers to the battlements on top of the wall; their openings for viewing above are all adorned with jewels.
These seven layers are formed as the retribution for the practice of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*); the number seven is applied in this manner throughout.
That city was ten *yojanas* in length and breadth. Regarding the *yojana*, according to the twelfth fascicle of the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*:
"Seven *paramāṇus* (atoms) form one *vātāyana-rajas* (dust mote of a window); seven *vātāyana-rajas* form one *śaśa-roma-agra-rajas* (dust mote at the tip of a rabbit's hair);
seven *śaśa-roma-agra-rajas* form one *avi-roma-agra-rajas* (dust mote at the tip of a sheep's wool)."
Seven particles of sheep’s wool-dust form one particle of cow’s hair-dust; seven particles of cow’s hair-dust form one nit;
seven nits form one louse; seven lice form one mustard seed; seven mustard seeds form one large barley grain;
seven large barley grains form one finger-joint; seven finger-joints form half a foot; two half-feet [form one foot].
One *hasta* makes one cubit; four cubits make one *dhanus*; five *dhanus* make one *daṇḍa*; twenty *daṇḍas* are called one *krośa*;
eighty *krośas* make one *krośa* (in this context, *krośa* is used as a measure); and eight *krośas* make one *yojana*.
According to this measurement of the *fangchi* (square foot), eighty paces plus two *li* constitute one *krośa*.
Eight *krośas* make one *yojana*, which equals seventeen *li*.
Regarding the city being ten *yojanas* [in extent], this corresponds to one hundred and seventy li from east to west and south to north.

If, according to the account, there are ten billion thoroughfares within that city, and between each path there dwell immeasurable tens of billions of sentient beings, then this could not possibly be contained within the small measure of a *yojana* as understood in this world. Rather, it is the City of Fundamental Wisdom that constitutes the great city; because "one is ten," its essence and function are thoroughly pervasive.
Discriminating wisdom serves as the main thoroughfare; within each of the ten wisdoms, there are one hundred million functions of both identity and difference, extending even to infinity.

The Eightfold Noble Path constitutes eight gates, totaling thirty-two (four times eight). This clarifies that the ten *pāramitās*, the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the branches of the Eightfold Noble Path together constitute the progressive cultivation of the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*). By harmonizing and integrating the two practices of wisdom and compassion, one attains mastery; this is termed "fundamental wisdom" (*mūla-jñāna*).

It is said that according to the King Mahāprabha’s perception of the various faculties, dispositions, and levels—superior, middling, and inferior—of sentient beings, there are differences in the size of the Great City of Wondrous Light and distinctions between its purity and defilement.
All the various jewels that adorn the city, the ground, the trees, and the palaces are, in brief, produced as the retribution of wisdom and compassion, as is fully detailed in the text itself.

Within this city is a multi-storied pavilion named *Saddharmakośa* (Treasury of the True Dharma), where King Mahāprabha constantly dwells; this is the objective realm of the retribution of differentiated wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), while the Sovereign King of Fundamental Wisdom (*mūlajñāna*) constantly dwells therein.

When Sudhana saw King Mahāprabha sitting upon a vast and magnificently adorned lion throne of the lotus-womb of wish-fulfilling maṇi jewels at the crossroads, not far from his residence, this clarifies that the four wisdoms, the four immeasurables, and the four means of integration serve as the crossroads for guiding and receiving sentient beings.

The great thoroughfares passing through the north, south, east, and west are called "four crossroads" (*catur-mahāpatha*); this single four-crossroad encompasses many roads, even up to hundreds of thousands, because they are all subsumed under the term "four crossroads," and because it allows for the spontaneous generation of whatever is desired while ensuring that all is free from defilement.
He takes the wish-fulfilling, stainless jewel as his seat; he is so named because his conduct is undefiled.
That the lotus and lapis lazuli form the feet of the seat signifies that his clear wisdom follows the ten thousand practices, being luminously pure and unobstructed.
The canopy made of gold and silk symbolizes that wisdom follows compassion to nurture all sentient beings.
The jeweled net represents the teaching-net of concise and wondrous explanations used to repay the kindness of living beings.
The celestial garments used as a rug signify that non-reliance through wisdom serves as the very substance of the seat.
The "mattress" refers to a mattress adorned with colorful patterns.
Because wisdom is without dependence, it possesses the literary elegance of the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), thereby attracting and guiding sentient beings.
The king sitting cross-legged upon it signifies the sovereign mastery of the two activities of wisdom and compassion, which have mutually permeated one another.

As for the twenty-eight marks of a great man, this clarifies that while wisdom and compassion have already been cultivated in the two stages of the ten abodes and the ten practices, the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are as yet incomplete; because these are not yet fully possessed, it is clarified that the thirty-two marks of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) are only perfected upon reaching the culmination of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*).

This refers to the principle of harmonizing the various stages—both their similarities and differences, as well as their general and specific aspects—within the sphere of wisdom without moving from mindfulness.

One must by no means employ subjective measures of extension or contraction; otherwise, the intent of the sutra would be entirely lost, for such was the purpose for which this scripture was established.
The Golden-Wheel-Turning King is, for instance, like the Golden-Net Wheel-Turning King described in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Radiance of the Minor Marks.

This wheel-turning king transforms sentient beings across world-systems as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields. When this king emits the pure radiance from within his maṇi-jewel topknot, any sentient being who encounters this light attains the ten stages of a bodhisattva, achieves immeasurable light of wisdom, and obtains ten kinds of pure eyes and ten kinds of pure minds.

Regarding the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*): because these secondary marks are shared even by the Brahmā kings of the upper realms, they are merely mundane excellences; thus, they are not identical to the thirty-two major marks and eighty secondary marks attained upon the fulfillment of the stage of the three worthies (*tri-śaikṣa*).
Such as King Mūrdhaja and others who were *cakravartin* kings, they surpassed Śakra and thereby lost their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), subsequently falling from their station.

These are the minor golden-wheel-turning kings of a single four-continent world-system within the Three Vehicles; they likewise possess the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all fully endowed with the marks of merit.

Among these, there are differences; for instance, within these ten practices, the "Great Radiant King" represents the realm of a human king’s transformative guidance, which fully pervades hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds throughout the ten directions, manifesting everywhere to provide universal support and lead beings forth.

Just as among the three vehicles, a Golden Wheel-Turning King transforms only the people of the four continents but does not reach the various heavens, so it is with this eighth stage of the Ten Practices, the "Difficult-to-Attain" practice.

It acts as a human king who gathers and transforms beings within the boundless realms of the ten directions, as well as the heavenly kings of the upper realms; there are none among the six paths of humans and devas who are not universally gathered, because he has attained the Buddha-wisdom.
The following praises the King’s two activities of merit and wisdom, as clearly elucidated in the full text.

The Sūtra states: “It is also like space manifesting various Dharma-gates and celestial phenomena. This clarifies that the presiding deities of the directions establish the Dharma through the quarters and corners; these are precisely the Eight Trigrams and the Nine Palaces (Bagua and Jiugong).

In the upper region, within the celestial sphere, the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the twelve double-hours and their corresponding branches, as well as the sun, moon, five planets, and all the arrayed constellations, each possess their own established laws.
In that world, the human king governed by means of the law of bestowing virtue; the Buddha took this up to manifest the teaching of self-liberation, as detailed in the text itself.
As for the various precious jewels filling the thoroughfares before his seat, these were the items bestowed by the king, as extensively explained in the sutra.
That the king’s body was like a mountain of gold was the color of an Arhat; it was the result of being moved by pure wisdom, inner illumination, and the practice of compassion to bless all beings.
As for the fact that the beautiful women were all endowed with sixty-four skills, this remains undetailed.

I, who have purely cultivated the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Banner of Great Compassion, clarify that from the first through the sixth stage of the ten stages, one practices the gateway of supramundane wisdom; from the seventh stage up to this eighth stage, one cultivates the practice of generating wisdom based on worldly compassion; upon reaching this eighth stage, non-effortful worldly wisdom manifests, and with great compassion always as its foremost priority, wisdom follows in breaking through delusions—this is what is called the "Banner."

From this point onward, up until the tenth stage of practice, he universally manifests as the bodies of the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners through the practice of great compassion; he assumes these forms to guide those with false views, thereby fulfilling the final stage of his practice.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "If you fall into the same state as those six heretical teachers, only then may you take this food.

The King said: "I have questioned, deliberated, observed, and cultivated the adornment of this Dharma in the presence of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; my intention was to resolve the doubts of Sudhana."

In the first ten stages of abiding, during the eighth stage, the Stage of the Youthful (Kumārabhūmi), one prostrates with the five limbs upon seeing the seer Vimalacitra; why is it that here, within this eighth practice, one also prostrates with the five limbs upon seeing King Mahāprabha?

This clarifies that from this stage one cultivates compassion up to wisdom; these five stages collectively encompass all [the practices] to demonstrate that wisdom and compassion are universal, and thus they are represented by these.

However, within these five stages, the eighth stage all clarifies the perfection of the Bodhisattva’s practice. From this eighth stage onward, one cultivates the ten kinds of sovereign powers and functions of the Tathāgata. This is because, among the five stages, the tenth stage takes the *prajñā-pāramitā* (perfection of wisdom) as primary, with the other nine as its companions.
From this point onward, the subsequent stages will be spontaneously accomplished.

King Mahāprabha entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Great Compassion as the Foremost, manifesting the sovereign power of the beneficial activity of his compassionate mind so that future practitioners might emulate him.

By means of the wisdom that is without dependence, he enters into the minds of all sentient beings, sharing their same essence and having no distinct nature. Because both the animate and the inanimate share this same essence through the karma evoked by entering this samādhi, he causes all sentient beings, as well as the forests and the surging springs, to flow toward him, to bend their branches, and to prostrate themselves.
The yakṣas and rākṣasas all ceased their malevolence; with clear wisdom, he accords with all sentient beings, sharing in their activities and functions, as they are of one nature without duality.

If even a worldly monarch who possesses compassion for humanity can cause dragons and spirits to submit in obedience, and phoenixes and qilin to gather in auspiciousness, how much more so should humans not look up to and revere him?

Moreover, this King Mahāprabha’s wisdom penetrates the true source and his conduct is equal to the Dharma-realm; with compassion as his primary virtue, he spiritually unites with all sentient beings. He shares the same radiance as all things and serves as the fundamental root of the myriad existences. Just as a maṇi jewel takes on the colors of objects while its own original color remains unchanged, so too does the noble wisdom remain mindless, taking the minds of objects as its own mind without any contradiction.
This is because the great compassionate mind of the same essence is used in common with all things, and it causes [the King] to manifest and clarify his physical body.

That the mountains, plains, grasses, and trees all turn toward him to pay homage, and that the ponds, pools, springs, wells, rivers, and seas all overflow and flow before him, is because such is the natural correspondence of the Great Compassion of the realm of wisdom.
If a realm is a transformation of the conscious mind of sentient beings, then sentient beings cannot produce it.
For example, within the Lotus Treasury World, all realms perform Buddha-work; this is because such a realm of wisdom is not something produced by the insentient.

The Sage returns to the realm of sentient beings through wisdom, causing all insentient things—plants, trees, mountains, springs, rivers, and oceans—which are obtained as karmic retribution by sentient beings, to follow and transform accordingly; for he employs wisdom to turn back the derivative toward the fundamental.

If even in this world, when there is supreme filial piety in the heart, fish leap from frozen ponds and bamboo shoots emerge in winter, how much more so for one who possesses true wisdom and follows compassion?

In this eighth section, because the clear wisdom proceeds from the activity of compassion, the ten thousand dragon kings are listed at the head of the assembly to signify that wisdom constantly traverses the void while extending compassionate rain of the Dharma; this is symbolized by the dragon traversing the sky to raise clouds and pour down rain.

Next, regarding the various assemblies from the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven downward, it is clearly explained in the text that they are all assemblies summoned by the power of the samādhi whose primary activity is great compassion. These details are as fully elucidated in the text.

From the passage beginning with "I pay homage to the King" below, there are four and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the breadth and narrowness of his conversion and guidance, as well as the excellence of Sudhana’s advancement.

This is the eighth spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of the practice difficult to encounter; it takes the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā) as its primary element, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.
From the perspective of the gates of wisdom, all stages universally counteract [obstructions];
from the perspective of the gates of the stages, they counteract the obstruction to the mastery of wisdom and compassion within the eighth stage, thereby enabling such mastery.

Great compassion is the primary element, and wisdom is the precursor. Having previously cultivated wisdom through compassion, one subsequently practices compassion through wisdom at the ninety-second stage.

This is likewise true for the first ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the subsequent ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) and ten grounds follow this same pattern. This clarifies that through effortless wisdom, one accomplishes the functional activities of compassion and so forth for the sake of all sentient beings; there is no self-effort by which these are achieved, yet the Tathāgata’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses arrive spontaneously of their own accord.

In the second section, "Advancing through the Promotion of Virtue," from the passage beginning with "Just as the bodhisattvas... down to "...took his leave and departed," there are sixteen lines of scripture which may be divided into five sections:

first, promoting virtue by placing it before him so that Sudhana may advance; second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend; third, citing the name of the city where the spiritual friend resides, namely, Abhirati; fourth, citing the name of the laywoman (upāsikā) who is the spiritual friend, namely, Acalā; and fifth, paying respects and taking one's leave to depart.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: "There is a royal capital" clarifies that this stage is the dwelling place of the ninth-level Dharma-Prince Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is called a "royal capital."
In all five stages, the ninth stage is exclusively the rank of a Dharma Prince (dharmaputra), who attains mastery in preaching the Dharma.
An upāsikā is a woman of pure faith.
Having reached full maturity, she remained unmarried after the age of twenty, dwelling in solitude to cultivate virtue. Free from worldly defilements and pure, she was known as an *upāsikā*.

She was named "Immovable" (*Acalā*) because, from the time she first resolved her mind [on enlightenment], throughout lives spanning as many eons as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa, she had never been moved by the five worldly desires or by anger; thus she was called Immovable.
The first section: The Dharma-gate of Correctly Entering the Stage.

Within this passage, from "At that time" down to "I have only attained this light of the Samādhi of Insatiable Seeking for All Dharmas, and preach the subtle and wonderful Dharma for all sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice," there are seventeen sections categorized therein:
(1) Contemplating advancement through the instruction of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Second, as he thus reflected upon the profound and virtuous kindness of the assembly of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), he wept with streaming tears.

Third, while the youth Sudhana was thus grieving and reflecting, a celestial messenger of the Tathāgata—the Bodhisattva Anugata-avabodha—appeared in the sky and exhorted and praised him, urging him to proceed to the royal capital of Abhyudgatarāja.
Fourth, arising from that Samādhi of the Radiance of Wisdom, he gradually traveled on until he reached the city of Pratiṣṭhāna.
Fifth, he searched everywhere for the laywoman Acalā.
6. All the people told him:
"This is a young maiden who remains within her home, protected by her parents. 7.
Having heard this, Sudhana went to the place of the laywoman Acalā; entering her residence, he beheld the environment and the dwelling she inhabited.
8. The light from the hall and pavilion illuminates his body, and he attains five hundred gates of samādhi.
9. Next, he contemplates the excellence of the primary retribution body.
10. Sudhana clearly explains his verses of praise for the virtues, formally expressing what he seeks.
11. The laywoman’s correct exposition of the method of her own practice;
12. The nature of the samādhi realm requested by Sudhana; 13.
The laywoman’s own account of the causal origin, the initial inspiration, and the temporal conditions for the commencement of her own practice.
Fourteenth, while in the midst of the samādhi of emptiness, the Buddha preached the Dharma for him.

Fifteenth, he himself spoke of how, since first generating the bodhicitta, he has passed through as many kalpas as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa; during those kalpas, he cultivated all mundane and supramundane arts and dharmas, never abandoning even a single word or a single phrase.
The sixteen laywomen asked, "Has Sudhana attained the gate of adornment called 'Seeking All Dharmas Without Weariness' from the Bodhisattva?
Sudhana replied, "I wish to see it."
When these seventeen upāsikās entered this samādhi, worlds as numerous as the atoms within unspeakable Buddha-fields shook in six ways, and all were composed of pure lapis lazuli.
"Good Wealth saw them all," and so forth, which refers to the advancement through the stages of virtue.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text:
it is asked, why is it that in this stage one recollects the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) with such weeping and shedding of tears? What is the intention behind this?
Answer: It is to clarify that by cultivating compassion through wisdom, one fulfills the ten powers of a Buddha.
Again, he asked:
Why is the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of this stage a woman?
The answer is as stated in the text below: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Dīrghabāhu."
"Culture" (*bhāvanā*) means "extension"; it clarifies the sense of leading and connecting.
This indicates that, proceeding from wisdom free of effort, one practices compassion through the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), thereby leading and connecting all sentient beings.
The king named Vidyudatta represents wisdom; because this wisdom can shatter delusion and perceive the Path with swiftness like a flash of lightning, he is so named.
His sole daughter represents compassion.
From the sixth line to the seventh line, wisdom is cultivated through compassion; from the eighth line onward, compassion is cultivated through wisdom. Therefore, she is represented by the princess.

As for this young girl, prior to the eighth dwelling and the eighth practice, the stage of compassion still possessed residual defilements; because this ninth dwelling and ninth practice gives rise to compassion from wisdom and is free from such residual defilements, she is represented by a young girl.

For those living at home, their parents and guardians take skillful means as their father and the perfection of wisdom as their mother; they take the protective mind of loving-kindness as their daughter, because it is free from the obstruction of defilement.

The purification of the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) reaches its culmination at the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*), where they no longer exist; this is illustrated by the example from the "Ten Samādhis" chapter, in which even a Bodhisattva who has received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) searches for Samantabhadra through the three types of inquiry yet does not perceive him. Such is the manner [of their non-existence].

"Good son! I have attained the bodhisattva liberation door of the treasury of invincible wisdom" means that within the ninth practice of the Dharma Master, one thoroughly refutes heterodox arguments, having already entered this stage of the wisdom of the ten powers (*daśabala*).
As the subsequent text states: "In the presence of that Buddha, I heard such a Dharma; I sought all-knowledge, I sought the ten powers of a Buddha, and I sought the eloquence of a Buddha."

Furthermore, within the rank of the Dharma Master, he is represented by a woman because she symbolizes purity, integrity, lofty refinement, compassion, kindness, harmony, joy, humility, and freedom from arrogance; yet she is not a woman in essence.

That Sudhana entered the interior of the house and saw those halls and buildings illuminated everywhere by golden light signifies that this ninth stage, the station of the Dharma Master, is a chamber of compassion, for it is illumined by the light of the teaching.
As for Sudhana’s body immediately attaining five hundred gates of samādhi upon being touched: first, realizing that the fundamental nature of marks is pure, its own essence is luminous;
second, penetrating that mind and objects have no basis, abiding neither in emptiness nor existence, their nature being inherently quiescent;
third, such samādhis are able to remain unstained by the world.

Fourth, the Samādhi of Universal Eye’s Abandonment and Attainment: the clear, wise eye that is without dependence is called "abandonment," while skillfully knowing the ten thousand names is called "attainment.

Fifth, the Samādhi-gate of the Tathāgata-garbha: this clarifies how a single wisdom internally contains all virtues. By citing these five numbers, it elucidates how the five hundred [samādhis] collectively encompass the five hundred dharma-gates of the five stages.
When Sudhana enters this samādhi, it is like being in the womb for seven days; likewise, within this stage, he enters into compassion through wisdom, becoming gentle, harmonious, and delightful.

All sentient beings who see this woman have no mind of defiled attachment, and all their afflictions naturally vanish. This is because her marks of wisdom and merit are endowed with benevolence and uprightness; she has received this body through karma free from defiled passion, and the body she was born with lacks any sign of lust. Thus, devas and humans revere her, and those who behold her lose their delusions.

With a single verse, Sudhana praised this woman for her practice of the three virtues—morality, patience, and diligence—and how she had attained a body that illuminates the world with light, as explained in detail in the sutra.
The upāsikā entered samādhi and manifested the gate of the samādhi called "Seeking All Dharmas Without Weariness," causing Sudhana to see it as clearly explained in the text.
As for the "Non-empty Wheel Samādhi," it is because one must study so that both the mundane and the supramundane are fully perfected.
The Samādhi of the Wheel of Wisdom of the Ten Powers is so called because it brings to fulfillment the wheel of the Buddha’s various forms of wisdom.
The Gate of the Samādhi of the Inexhaustible Treasury of the Buddha-seed is so called because there is nothing that wisdom does not encompass and no transformation that ever ceases.

These three samādhis are the general categories, while the ten thousand samādhis are the particulars; this clarifies the teaching of the Indra’s Net, wherein the one and the many interpenetrate with sovereign freedom.
Below this follows the progression of advancing through realized virtues.
This is the ninth spiritual friend among the practices of wholesome dharmas, which takes the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) as its primary element and the other nine as its companions.
In terms of the gateway of wisdom, it universally remedies the obstacles of all stages;
in terms of the gateway of the stages, it remedies the obstacle of lack of mastery in preaching the Dharma, thereby enabling mastery.

In the second section, "Encouraging Virtue and Advancing," from the passage beginning with "Just as the Bodhisattvas... down to "...took his leave and departed," there are fifteen and a half lines of scripture. Within this, four topical gates are distinguished:
first, encouraging virtue so that Sudhana may advance;
second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend and naming the city, Tāmraparṇī; third... [and so on].

Third, he mentions the name and conduct of his virtuous friend, who is an ordained outsider known as Viśvāmitra; fourth, he pays his respects and departs. Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the city is named Anāthapiṇḍada.

“Anātha” means joy (*nanda*), and “piṇḍada” means birth (*sara*); thus, it signifies that this city gives rise to immeasurable joys and delights. This represents that the wisdom of this spiritual friend is perfected, and his practice—equivalent to having completed the ten stages—has culminated in the fruit of Buddhahood. As one who traverses all practices, he is worthy of being seen; he universally manifests his body in accordance with their respective modes of practice, receiving and guiding sentient beings and benefiting the world so that all may rejoice.

The city is named "Birth of Immeasurable Joy, Bliss, and Other Matters. Those who have left the household life and are called non-Buddhists (tīrthika) are termed "Universal Wanderers" (sarvatraga). Their wisdom being equal to the fruit of Buddhahood is termed "leaving the household life. To transform those of heterodox currents, they manifest in conformity with false views and are thus termed "non-Buddhists. Because their practices for benefiting sentient beings and their engagement with the three vehicles are entirely identical to those [of the Buddhas], they are termed "Universal Wanderers."
To act without defilement is called "leaving home.

Within the conduct of a bodhisattva, to transform the heterodox rather than the orthodox is called being a "follower of external paths"; to abide in conduct without defilement is called "leaving home."
I have acted as such for all ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders.
The meaning of the "Southern Region" is as explained previously.

Within the first section, the Dharma-gate of the primary entry into the respective stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva practice of reaching all places," there are five general divisions:
First, the contemplation of advancing toward a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in a single thought-moment;
second, gradually traveling about to seek out a virtuous friend;

third, seeing [the friend] walking in meditation upon a mountain peak and on level ground—where the mountain peak represents wisdom and the level ground represents the Dharma-body—indicating that one does not depart from the great wisdom of the Dharma-body, even when amidst false views.
Fourth, approaching and paying respects while formally presenting one's request;
fifth, the practice of the universal friend (Samantabhadra) and the dharma practiced by Sudhana.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the term "universal traveler" (*paryāpanna*) refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Bodhisattvas transform those who are heterodox and do not transform those who are orthodox; therefore, they are called "non-Buddhists."

All that has been cultivated and advanced—yet not reaching the ultimate wondrous practice of the principle and wisdom of the Dharma-realm of the One Vehicle, wherein the one and the many, sameness and difference, are sovereign, and where bodies and lands interpenetrate throughout the worlds of the ten directions like the gates of Indra’s net—is all external vision.
Thus, including both ordinary people and sages, all are led by means of identical practices; they are therefore called "universalist non-Buddhists" (sarvagāmin-tīrthika).
Those who practice in this manner—such as the followers of Kong Qiu (Confucius), Zhuang Zhou, and Laozi—are likewise of this same class.

Like one who conceals their name and hides their appearance, moving in accordance with the various types of beings, sentient beings only receive its benefits, never knowing who is right and who is wrong.

Such conduct is constantly and universally present throughout the ten directions, manifesting at no time; it follows like a shadow follows a form and responds like an echo follows a sound. It is not a substance that comes or goes, yet through the penetration of wisdom into all phenomena, it constantly manifests a physical body in response.

As the subsequent text states: "I have already accomplished the samādhi-door of universally observing the world; I have already accomplished the power of supernatural penetrations that are without dependence or effort; I have already accomplished the universal-gate Prajñāpāramitā."

Throughout the entire world, in all various locations, with all various forms and appearances, and through all various modes of understanding and conduct, I bring benefit to sentient beings, even extending universally to all realms of existence.

Although they constantly perform acts of benefit while remaining in the world, the multitudes of people do not know from where they come; they neither know nor perceive from what stream of beings these [beings] flow, for they pervade all places where sentient beings dwell.
This is the true practice of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), which takes the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as its primary element and the other nine perfections as its companions.
This stage overcomes the obstacle of lacking mastery while acting within saṃsāra, thereby granting such mastery; the further details of its significance are as stated in the text.

The first ten abodes are the manner of entering the Dharma-gate of the Buddha’s dwelling; these ten practices are the pattern of Samantabhadra’s conduct; the ten stages follow this model, and the ten dedications are likewise formed accordingly.

Within these ten abodes and ten practices, through the harmonious integration of compassion and the power of vows, wisdom is aroused and mercy is manifested; this prevents one from becoming biased toward the transcendental nirvana or the two obstacles of affliction and knowledge. It ensures that one may constantly dwell within the ocean of all birth and death throughout the ten directions, remaining perpetually filled with the great conduct of Samantabhadra—the fruit of Buddhahood—which is the dharma-realm of one's own essence. This is established by virtue of the unimpeded gate of the realm of Indra’s net. Thus it is settled.

The ten gates of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) harmonize wisdom and compassion, and cause both mundane and supramundane realms to be thoroughly integrated, because they rely on fundamental sovereignty.

For those who exclusively cultivate meditative concentration and seek the supramundane, these gates harmonize and integrate immeasurable mental conceptions, giving rise to the function of great wisdom that is not fixed to any single benefit; thus, the ten dedications are established.
This causes Bodhisattvas who practice through skillful means not to unilaterally and falsely seek a Buddha’s Pure Land elsewhere in other directions;

rather, by establishing the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), it enables them to constantly abide in the body of tranquil concentration while pervading all of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to gather and transform sentient beings.

One gives rise to the ten transferences, causing the perceptions, thoughts, reflections, recollections, and mental streams directed toward all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to become the functioning of wisdom; thus one gives rise to the ten transferences.
To cause even a field of merit as minute as a mustard seed to pervade and fill the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm, one gives rise to the Ten Transferences.
To cause all worldly views and minor supernatural powers to become the great functioning of Samantabhadra, one gives rise to the Ten Transferences.

He causes the Bodhisattvas dwelling in the eighth stage, whose wisdom has increased, to recollect their original vows to extensively benefit sentient beings; through skillful means, they give rise to great supernormal powers to universally promote great benefit, yet do not abide within pure wisdom alone.
They give rise to the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*),
causing bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds to give rise to the great vows of a Tathāgata and to be endowed with the merits of a Buddha;
they give rise to the ten dedications as extensively explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications" (*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*).

If these ten gates of dedication did not exist, all who have resolved their minds toward awakening would collectively abide on the stages of the two vehicles; no bodhisattva would attain the equipment for buddhahood or be able to practice the conduct of Samantabhadra.

A Bodhisattva of the first stage, relying on these three dharmas, generates the mind of enlightenment through the power of a sublime vow; first, by relying on the application of the aforementioned three dharmas, they advance until their merit is perfected and the Way is fulfilled. Just as when they first generated the mind, they do not shift from clear wisdom, nor do they shift with the passage of time, days, months, or years.
This is like Maitreya pointing back to Mañjuśrī, clarifying that the fruit does not depart from the cause.
Thus, one sees oneself enter into the body of Samantabhadra, clarifying that the practice of Samantabhadra likewise does not exist apart from within the cause.
Maitreya said:
"When I descend to Jambudvīpa in the future, you and Mañjuśrī shall come back to see me.
This clarifies that the future world and the present time do not shift.
This is a discourse based on the reality of wisdom, differing from the deluded conceptualizations of ordinary consciousness that falsely perceive the passage of many kalpas.

Regarding the practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the vision of the Path (*darśanamārga*) occurs at the initial stage of the first resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*), while the stage of preparatory application (*prayogamārga*) follows after the vision of the truths within that same initial resolve.
By means of this mutual support between cause and effect, one then achieves mastery over the ten thousand functions.

Regarding the Path of the Three Vehicles: the preceding three stages involve the out-flowing (sāsrava) arousal of the mind by bodhisattvas; it is only upon reaching the Grounds (bhūmi) that one realizes the Path of Vision (darśanamārga), culminating in the stage of the Eleven Grounds as the Subtly Awakened Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is said that the trichiliocosm constitutes the retributive realm of the Buddha, yet it does not encompass the boundless realm of the Dharma-dhātu.
From the section "The Gate of Mutual Interpenetration and Non-obstruction" onwards, one dedicates merit and advances to the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
Scroll Thirty-Six (and Thirty-Seven) Compiled by the Elder Li Tongxuan.
In the section on the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) of the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) for the youth Sudhana, from the passage beginning with "Just as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas...
down to "taking his leave and departing," all are treated according to the five gates; subsequent stages follow this same model.

First, he urged Sudhana to advance; second, he pointed out the location and the name of the country, which was Vistīrṇa; third, he mentioned the name of the spiritual friend, the merchant selling incense named Utpalabhūti; fourth, he exhorted Sudhana to go and inquire; fifth, he paid his respects and departed.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: among the praises of his virtues, the statement that he dwells through all kalpas by means of unobstructed vows and attains peerless practices like those of Indra’s net refers precisely to the skillful means of vow and practice within the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-praṇidhāna*).

Furthermore, by skillfully knowing the Dharma-gate of various fragrances, one blends medicinal incenses for sale; this symbolizes the dedication toward the unification of wisdom and compassion, birth-and-death and nirvana, and the conceptual distinctions of defilement and purity, so as to consolidate them all into a single pill of the fragrance of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, thereby attaining sovereign mastery over both birth-and-death and nirvana.

When these fragrances are blended in this manner, they are combined into a single pellet; they mutually benefit one another, yet all lack inherent self-nature while not losing their own specific qualities, such that identity and difference are both freely manifest.

This Elder Blue Lotus, who was about to sell incense, symbolizes the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*); it signifies that the harmonious integration of wisdom and means, great compassion and great vows, and the myriad practices—both general and specific—are freely unified into a single pill, free from attachment to their distinctions.
The meaning of "South" is as explained previously at the beginning of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
As for the name of the land being "Vast and Great" (*Vaipulya*), it is because one extensively generates great vows and initiates boundless practices, universally embracing all classes of beings.
This vow is the wind of the ten thousand practices, for it causes those practices to become boundless.
Furthermore, the vow is the wind of wisdom, for it causes all conceptual thoughts to become the sovereign function of great wisdom and supernormal powers.

May this be the wind that causes all samādhis and meditative concentrations to blossom, drawing forth those sentient beings who are obstructed by defilements so that they become free from dependence, attain non-reliant wisdom, and achieve sovereign mastery over quiescence and activity, pervading all sentient beings.

Just as the leader of the Ten Abodes uses Mount Wondrous Peak to symbolize signless wisdom, the leader of the Ten Practices uses the bhikṣu of the Three Eyes Land to illustrate manifest practice transcending entanglement.
The first of the ten dedications uses the Elder Gandhahastin to symbolize the dedication that harmonizes wisdom and compassion, as well as the myriad practices, nirvana, and saṃsāra.
This is the underlying intention according to the respective stages; one should reflect upon it to understand its meaning in detail.
These fifty-three spiritual friends are all stages for advancing in practice; one must understand them thoroughly so as not to practice or study them erroneously.

This "Selling Incense" represents the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*); through the harmonious integration of great vows, the principles and wisdom of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) and the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), and the entry into the realm of birth-and-death through compassion and wisdom, it is named the Blue Lotus (*utpala*).

The manifest activities (vijñapti-saṃskāra) are unstained by saṃsāra and unstained by nirvāṇa; they remain undefiled in the midst of duality and non-duality. They are like the blue lotus, which must grow amidst the mud and turbid water, yet remains unstained by the nature of that mud and water, its color and fragrance being supreme.

It is because Bodhisattvas, through the power of dedicating these great vows, abide within the mire of birth and death; only then do they accomplish the fruit of Buddhahood throughout the Dharma-realm—the meritorious fruits of Samantabhadra’s myriad practices—which are supreme in color and fragrance, such that nothing else can surpass them.

Among all flowers, the blue lotus is supreme in both color and fragrance; likewise, among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) harmonize birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, unifying wisdom, compassion, and the myriad practices into a single *dharmadhātu*. By teaching and transforming all sentient beings so that they are free from suffering and manifest the fragrance of great wisdom, this becomes supreme, for no other who seeks transcendence separately can equal it. Thus, the Elder Gandhahastin (Blue Lotus Fragrance) is used as a metaphor to facilitate understanding.

Within the first dharma-gate of "Correctly Entering the Appropriate Stage," from the passage beginning with "At that time, Sudhana" down to "I know only this method of harmonizing incense," five sections are established; the subsequent stages should all follow this same model.

First, reflecting on the instructions of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) with right mindfulness and progressing upward; second, traveling by stages until reaching the abode of the elder; third, paying homage by prostrating at his feet; fourth, formally expressing one's request; and fifth, the elder explaining his own practice and bestowing it upon Sudhana.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: from the passage "At that time, the youth Sudhana" onwards, there are ten gates of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*) which clarify the entry into dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). These constitute the gates through which all true and conventional, defiled and pure, wisdom and compassion are harmonized and integrated by means of these vows, such that they are without obstruction.
"Progressively traveling" refers to ascending and advancing.
"Reaching a vast country" means that by generating wisdom through aspiration, one performs inexhaustible practices to guide and receive sentient beings.

Even unto the lands as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions, within each and every atom there are inexhaustible Buddha-dharmas and physical manifestations that guide and receive sentient beings; it is thus throughout all the lands and atoms of the ten directions, like the infinitely layered net of Indra.
Because his vows and practices are vast, the land is named "Vast.
Within the fourth section, the "Gate of Requesting What is Sought," the elder replies, "I am well-versed in distinguishing all fragrances," which carries two meanings:
first, he truly knows all worldly fragrances; second, he uses fragrance as a metaphor for the Dharma.

"First, the true knowledge of all fragrances" refers to what is taught in the Sūtra: namely, the general essence of all fragrances, while "incense for burning, for anointing, and powdered incense" are their specific enumerations.
The section beginning with "the sources of the kings of fragrance" and following describes the categories of fragrances according to their origins and types.

Regarding the various fragrances produced, as follows: there are five kinds of fragrance among humans, one kind among rākṣasas, and four kinds among devas; in total, there are ten kinds of fragrance, whose functions are fully detailed in the sūtra itself.
These aforementioned incenses represent the ten dedications; they clarify that the nature of incense has no dependence, yet can give rise to all manner of goodness and extinguish all evil.

Because it clarifies that great vows have no dependence yet can produce immeasurable roots of goodness, they give rise to clouds of immeasurable great wisdom, rain down the rain of immeasurable pure and white dharmas, and perform acts of immeasurable great compassion, transforming immeasurable sentient beings so that they may attain the extinction of suffering and resolve upon the unsurpassed mind.
If there is no great vow, one will not give rise to the mind of great bodhi; even if one practices for liberation, it will all result in the two vehicles.

Among humans there is a fragrance called Elephant-Treasury (*hastigarbha*). This fragrance is produced from the battle of dragons; when a single pellet is burned, it raises a great cloud of incense that completely covers the royal capital. For seven days, it rains a fine rain of fragrance. If this touches the body, the body becomes golden in color. This signifies that at the time of first generating the mind of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*) within the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), one raises a great cloud of vows with the fragrance of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). One extensively gives rise to compassionate conduct to universally cover all sentient beings and seeks omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Through the battle between the dragon of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* against the afflictions of the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), one penetrates the boundless void. One generates the fire of wisdom and burns the incense of Great Wisdom, raising clouds of compassion and raining down the rain of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*). Sentient beings who are touched by this attain perfect enlightenment at the very moment they first generate the mind of awakening.

If even the garments, palaces, and towers are all golden in color, this clarifies that it arises from the dedication of great vows and incense; for it is because all worldly patience, compassion, contemplative wisdom, and the unified dharmadhātu of sovereign pure dharmas have been fully assembled.

If, through the wind, [the fragrance] enters the palace and sentient beings who smell it remain free from all sorrow and suffering for seven days and seven nights—neither startled, nor terrified, nor distracted, nor angry; with hearts of loving-kindness toward one another and pure intentions—then those who hear it clearly as it spreads further will also all rejoice, giving rise to the gateway of great vows and awakening the seven factors of enlightenment.

As for my knowing this and then preaching the Dharma for them, it clarifies that those who wish to exhort sentient beings to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment must first exhort them to generate vast vows of dedication and to give rise to a heart of firm and sincere resolve; only after first spreading the flowers of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment can one then preach the path of ultimate truth.
If one practices according to these exhortations, there will not be a single failure out of ten thousand.
As for Mount Malaya, this mountain is located in the kingdom of Malayagiri within the territory of South India; the kingdom derives its name from this mountain.
This mountain produces much white sandalwood incense; it also yields sandalwood known as "ox-head" (gośīrṣa), which, if applied to the body, cannot be burned even if one enters a pit of fire.

In the Meiji Earth-Abiding [Samādhi], by means of the power of great vows and the power of dedication, one takes the principle of the non-substantiality of the dharmakāya of the ten supreme wholesome dharmas to constitute the essence of precepts; using this to anoint one’s body, one dedicates it to entering the fiery pit of birth and death, such that the fires of greed, hatred, and attachment cannot burn or harm it.

In the ocean there is a fragrance named Invincible; if it is used to anoint drums and various conch shells, when their sounds are produced, all enemy armies will naturally retreat and scatter. This illustrates that one who dwells in cultivation achieves the patience of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), and returns to the ocean of birth and death to transform sentient beings.
By means of a mind of patience, upon hearing all sounds—whether good or evil—as if they were drums, wicked and malevolent enemies will naturally disperse and retreat.

On the shores of Lake Anavatapta, there is a type of agalloch incense called Padmagarbha; if even a single pellet as small as a sesame seed is burned, its fragrance will pervade the entire Jambudvīpa realm, and those sentient beings who smell it will be freed from all transgressions, their precepts becoming pure.

The Stage of Birth in Nobility (*jāti-prabhava-vihāra*) signifies that one has attained mastery over the karma of the three realms without any obstruction, being perpetually born into the Buddha-family, stainless and pure.

This corresponds to the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), where one emerges from the karma of the three realms; yet, by means of the mind of the four great vows (*catur-mahāpraṇidhāna*), one returns to the great pool of the four currents of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to teach and transform all sentient beings submerged therein, remaining entirely free from defilement or attachment—this is called the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*).
He expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma, its fragrance pervading the ten directions; those who hear it have their transgressions extinguished and their categories of precepts purified.
On the Snowy Mountains there is a fragrance named Aruṇa, which is a red-colored incense.

It is fit to be dyed crimson; if sentient beings smell this fragrance, their minds will certainly become free from all defiled attachments. This is the gate of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) wherein one dwells by means of perfected skillful means, dedicating great vows toward the cycle of birth and death to cause all sentient beings to leave behind all defilements, practice the perfection of meditative concentration, and attain entry into the *vimala-samādhi* (stainless samādhi).
The Snowy Mountains symbolize the essence of this meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), for its nature is inherently pure and stainless.
