In the realm of the *rākṣasas*, there is a fragrance named "Ocean-Treasury" (*sāgaragarbha*); this fragrance is used exclusively by a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). If one burns a single pellet and fumigates with it, the king and his fourfold army all ascend into the air. This clearly symbolizes that, by means of the sixth stage, the "Abiding in Right Mind," one takes the wisdom of the three gates of liberation as the *rākṣasa* and enters the ocean of birth and death; then, using the wisdom of the Wheel-Turning King of Prajñā to burn the Ocean-Treasury fragrance of wisdom, one fumigates the king of the ocean of birth and death.

The passage "the four kinds of Māras all ascend into the emptiness of dharmas" and below collectively represents the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), which—through the vows and practices of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) and ten conducts (*daśa-caryā*)—harmonize and integrate saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the two wisdoms of the ultimate and conventional truths, and the two gateways of compassion and wisdom, thereby rendering them sovereign.

The ten stages (daśabhūmi) are cultivated based upon this, accomplishing the principle of non-conceptual dependent origination (*anābhoga-pratītyasamutpāda*) which is the very nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-svabhāva*). This is symbolized by means of burning incense, anointing incense, and blended incense, so that students may easily understand; all other instances should be understood by analogy with this.

If, within the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten stages, there were no power of great wisdom resulting from dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one would merely attain the path of the two vehicles and could not achieve Buddhahood.

There are practitioners who must thoroughly and skillfully grasp its meaning, clearly contemplating the six characteristics—general and particular, identical and different, formed and disintegrated—which constitute the intent of the teaching.

From the phrase "I only know this method of blending incense," it clarifies the incense of the harmonious integration of the two truths (conventional and ultimate), wisdom, compassion, vows, and practice, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana, and the freedom between defilement and purity; furthermore, it uses the name of the blue lotus flower to symbolize this.
The following section concerns the advancement through the recommendation of one's virtues.
The remaining meanings are self-evident from the text itself.

Within the second section on advancement through the recommendation of virtues, there are ten lines of scripture from "All the Bodhisattvas" down to "took their leave and departed," which are divided into five gates:

First, he encouraged him to advance toward virtue; second, he showed him the location of the spiritual friend; third, he mentioned the name of the city and the pavilion where the spiritual friend resided; fourth, he mentioned the name of the boatman, Vasiṣṭha; fifth, he prostrated and took his leave.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: "Southern" has the same meaning as explained previously.
As for the city being named "Pavilion," this region borders the South Sea; because it is low-lying and damp, many people there live in pavilions.

Furthermore, it is based on the wisdom of differentiation; within the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the myriad phenomena—whether general or particular, identical or different—are harmonized in their manifold layers, and thus the name of the city is established.
As for the boatman Vāsira, this is translated as "Sovereign" (*svatantra*); it signifies one who has attained mastery over the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

In the context of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the ability to enter the ocean of birth and death while practicing great compassion constitutes the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*).

In the context of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the contemplation of the twelvefold dependent origination within the ocean of birth and death as the inherently pure foundation, which is accessible only through Buddha-wisdom, constitutes the essence of the precepts.

Within the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), the skillful arts, the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇadharma*), mathematics, and worldly crafts that benefit sentient beings constitute the essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*).

These ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*) involve entering the conventional from the ultimate; abiding within the ocean of birth and death, they lead sentient beings to cultivate the practices of compassion and loving-kindness, which constitute the essence of the precepts.
Thus, for these three stages of practicing the precepts, there are respective rules for their commonalities, differences, and progressive advancement.

Regarding the "mariner," the Master takes great compassion as the essence of the precepts; because he constantly dwells within the ocean of birth and death to come and go and ferry sentient beings across, this is fully elucidated in the section on praising his virtues.

The general meaning is as follows: He is fully accomplished in the precept of non-attachment, like a ferryman who carries people across without dwelling on this shore and without dwelling on the far shore.

Within the section on the primary entrance into the Dharma-gate of the corresponding stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Sudhana" down to "I only know this practice of the Banner of Great Compassion; if there are those who see me, hear me, dwell with me, or remember me, all such encounters are not in vain," this portion is divided into five sections:

first, contemplating the instructions of the spiritual friend and advancing upward; second, traveling by stages to reach that city; third, seeing the ferryman staying outside the city gate on the seashore; fourth, paying homage with palms joined to express one's request; and fifth, the ferryman bestowing upon Sudhana the Dharma-gate of his own practice.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: one sees the boatman standing on the seashore outside the city gate, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of merchants and a great multitude. This has two meanings:
first, this event truly occurred, as he was the leader who guided the merchants and treasure-seekers into the sea; such maritime perils are not unknown to those with noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

Second is the Dharma of Manifestation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*): having personally attained the true gate and emerged from the entanglements to leave suffering behind, they fulfill the ocean of great compassion through their vows and practices, constantly standing upon the shore of birth and death to guide and receive sentient beings.
The hundred thousand merchants represent the perfection of the ten thousand practices within the *śīla-pāramitā*.
The immeasurable multitude represents the universal pervasiveness of these practices, fulfilling all deeds.

The Sūtra states: "Going to the great jewel-island of omniscience through the accomplishment of the indestructible cause of the Mahāyāna. Here, *mahā* means "great" and *yāna* means "vehicle"; thus, the teaching that serves as the vehicle is collectively termed the "Mahāyāna Teaching."

To remain far removed from the fear of birth and death characteristic of the two vehicles and to dwell in the revolving of the samādhi of tranquility—this clarifies the praise of Sudhana’s Dharma, demonstrating that he is able to abide in the samādhi of tranquility while within the realm of birth and death, revolving therein to benefit sentient beings without ever departing from it.

“Good son! I know all the jewel islands, all the jewel locations, all categories of jewels, all species of jewels, and all vessels for jewels within this ocean. Such jewels are the mundane phenomena known by noble wisdom.
Regarding the symbolic teaching: "I know all the jewel islands within the ocean" clarifies mastery over the island of omniscience.
"All places of jewels" refers to skillfully discerning the various faculties that are capable, sharp, and pure.
Regarding all categories of jewels, they skillfully know the categories of shared practice and distinct practice.
Regarding all lineages of jewels, they skillfully know the distinctions between the lineages of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
"I know all precious vessels" means knowing the capacities—great or small—of sentient beings, and what dharma they are capable of receiving to bring them to accomplishment.
"All precious functions" means bestowing dharmas according to their faculties, enabling them to exercise their respective functions.
"All jewel realms" refers to the realms of the Three Jewels of the three vehicles.
"All jewel radiance" refers to the great and small radiances of the wisdom of the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
I know that that which purifies all jewels consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten perfections, and the skillful means of the five contemplations for settling the mind.

The skillful means that purify the jewel of omniscience and drill through all jewels consist of the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. These are what bring forth all jewels, because they are well able to rely upon the faculties [of sentient beings] and teach them so as to manifest the jewel of wisdom.

Regarding "the creator of all jewels": by means of signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*), one gives rise to discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*); through the wind of great vows, one raises the clouds of great compassion to rain down showers of various jewels. This transforms all sentient beings so that their mental objects and states of mind are brought into harmony and rendered without dependence, for it allows the jewel of omniscience (*sarvajña-jñāna*) to manifest spontaneously.

Regarding "all dragon palaces and difficult places": the bodhisattvas in the Pure Land are like dragons; they possess a portion of compassion and have a degree of mastery over the supernormal power of traveling through space.
The yakṣas serve as a metaphor for the śrāvakas, who are able to destroy the three poisons and also attain supernatural powers.

The "place of danger from rākṣasas" is a metaphor for the pratyekabuddhas dwelling in the ocean of nirvāṇa; for they can destroy ignorance, yet the seeds of the all-knowledge of the Buddhas do not manifest before them.
Regarding such difficulties as these, they all employ the power of dedication and vows to remain together within birth and death.

Without harming ignorance or the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), they penetrate the grasping of ignorance to accomplish various forms of wisdom. Abiding in the gate of mastery over the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*, this is called "dedicating everything to avoid all such difficulties."
Furthermore, "skillfully discerning the depth and shallowness of whirlpools" refers to the depth and shallowness of craving, grasping, becoming, and karma.
"The distance of the waves and billows" refers to the extent of emotional consciousness, conceptualization, and clinging to objects.
The quality of the water's color represents the goodness or evil of one's affectionate mind.

Furthermore, being able to skillfully distinguish and know the movements, quantities, and numbers of the sun, moon, and constellations, as well as the lengthening and shortening of days and nights, morning and evening, and the *ghatikā* and *lepa* measures, means that one clearly understands worldly affairs—specifically, the profound manifestations of yin and yang, the numerical degrees of the five planets' movements, the timing of wind arising, and the lengthening and shortening of the four seasons according to the *ghatikā* and *lepa* measures; all of these are fully known.

Within this exposition of the Dharma, it clarifies the stages of progress and cultivation for the three vehicles, as well as the gateways of the various teachings; it fully enables one to know the rules for turning according to practice and faculties, the methods and timing of maturation, and the duration—whether measured in days, months, years, or kalpas—of the journey traversed.

Whether the iron and wood of the ship are strong or fragile, whether its mechanisms are stiff or smooth, the size of the waters, and the favorability or adversity of the winds—all such signs of safety and danger he understands clearly; he truly knows these matters.

Regarding the exposition of the Dharma: it clarifies the skillful knowledge of those of the three vehicles who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment], whether they are capable of entering saṃsāra or incapable of entering saṃsāra, and whether their faculties and dispositions are matured or immature.

Within the One Vehicle, the Bodhisattva’s sixth dwelling—the sixth stage—becomes manifest. Abiding within the midst of birth and death, they attain the mind that transcends birth and death, as well as the mind of the wisdom of the three emptinesses; thus, the quiescence of the wisdom of the three emptinesses becomes manifest.
Bodhisattvas of the seventh abode and seventh stage, while within the cycle of birth and death, constantly remain amidst birth and death.

Bodhisattvas of the eighth abode and eighth stage attain the realization of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); their bodiless wisdom manifests, and they spontaneously benefit sentient beings through effortless mastery.
In the ninth abiding and the ninth stage, one studies the Buddha’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses.

In the tenth abiding and the tenth stage, one’s ten parts become equal and perfect with the Tathāgata’s world-transcending wisdom and the knowledge and vision of liberation, abiding in the stage of the Buddha’s consecration.

In the eleventh chapter, "The Chapter on the Universal Worthy’s Ground," one studies the wondrous practices of Samantabhadra’s supernatural powers, which conclude only upon reaching the "Chapter on the Practices of Universal Worthy.

Within the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata," the three dharmas of the Buddha-fruit—Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and [the Tathāgata]—correspond respectively to the Dharma-body, fundamental wisdom, and differentiated wisdom; thus, the great compassion of principle and wisdom is finally brought to fulfillment, just as it was originally vowed.
Just as in the teachings of the Three Vehicles, the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) employs the conduct of Samantabhadra to transform sentient beings;
so too in this teaching of the One Vehicle, although it speaks of stages as if they were sequential, such advancement does not transcend the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
In the Three Vehicles, the cause precedes and the fruit follows, with the path being perfected over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

In the One Vehicle, the realization of the Path occurs within the stage of the Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*); the causal practices of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) occur during the ten stages of Practice (*caryā*), the ten Stages of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten Grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground.

Thus, they fully know the iron and wood of the ship, its safety and danger, its roughness and smoothness, and even know the dullness or swiftness of the faculties, stopping when it is appropriate to stop.

Within the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the human and celestial realms, up to the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vinodana*), if the faculties have matured, they proceed when it is appropriate to proceed, causing them to advance into the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This is because the nature of birth and death and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are themselves employed as the great wisdom-activity of the Dharma.
The general meaning of what follows is as such:
"O son of good family!

I shall take a fine ship to transport the multitude of merchants to a path of safety, and even lead them to the treasure island to provide them with precious jewels so that they are fully satisfied; thereafter, I will lead them back to Jambudvīpa. This refers to that matter.

In the exposition of the Dharma, it is clarified that from the initial stage of generating the bodhicitta, one attains the fundamental wisdom of a Buddha; from this point onward, throughout all subsequent stages, the sublime Dharma is continuously taught until, at the tenth stage, the treasure of omniscience is fully perfected. In the eleventh stage, one must then return to the original dwelling within the ocean of birth and death, using the treasure of omniscience thus obtained to extensively benefit inexhaustible sentient beings.

This is explained in this way in order to clarify the progression through spiritual practice and to facilitate easy understanding; yet, it does not fail to produce a great jewel island within the ocean of birth and death.
The remaining details are fully contained within the text itself.
All of these are explained in terms of concrete phenomena (*vastu*), employing phenomena to symbolize the Dharma so that sentient beings may easily understand it.

This is the second "Non-Destructible Dedication" (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*). The spiritual friend, acting as a boatman, says: "I shall navigate this great ship back and forth without allowing even a single part of it to be damaged. If there are sentient beings who see my body or hear my Dharma, I shall cause them to never again fear the ocean of birth and death, ensuring they will certainly enter the ocean of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). This is the meaning of the Non-Destructible Dedication; here, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is primary, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.
From the perspective of the gate of wisdom, all stages universally serve as remedies;

from the perspective of the gate of stages, this constitutes the precept of great compassion, because—as symbolized by the shipmaster in the ocean—it constantly comes and goes without ever being born within the sea of birth and death.
Having completed the practice of the Banner of Great Compassion, the text proceeds to extol virtues and advance further.

Within this second section on advancing by extolling virtues, there are ten lines of scripture from "As all bodhisattvas... down to "...took their leave and departed. These may be divided into five sections: first, advancing by extolling virtues;

second, indicating the direction where the spiritual friend resides; third, citing the name of the city inhabited by the spiritual friend, which is called Delightful; fourth, citing the name of the spiritual friend, which is Anuttaravijaya (Supreme Victory); and fifth, paying homage and taking one's leave.

As for the city named Sukhāvatī (Joyful), it is so called because the elder is skilled in discerning and deciding all manner of human affairs, and furthermore, he is able to preach the supramundane Dharma; because sentient beings delight in him and do not wish to leave, the city is named Sukhāvatī.

The elder is named Anuttara-jina (Unsurpassed Victor); this is the gateway of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Among all practices, patience is preeminent; furthermore, because his virtue and artistry transcend those of the world, he is called Anuttara-jina.
The remaining practices are as described in the previous section on praising virtues.

Regarding the first [section], the Dharma-gate of the primary entry into the stage itself, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "the power of the spiritual transformations of non-reliance and non-action through the pure Dharma-gate of practicing the bodhisattva path in all places," five gates are established within this section:
first, contemplating the instructions of the spiritual friend and advancing upward;...
Second, he gradually traveled by stages until he reached that city;
third, he saw the unsurpassed and eminent elder in the Aśoka Grove to the east of the city, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of merchants and hundreds of thousands of householders;
fourth, he threw himself to the ground, paid his respects, and rose.
The fifth [section] correctly sets forth the request.

Regarding the exegesis according to the text: "Gradually proceeding until reaching that city and seeing the Unsurpassed Victor within the city, ascending and entering the station is called 'internal'" (內). This means that having reached the interior of that city, one sees the Unsurpassed Victor dwelling therein; ascending and entering that position is termed "internal."

Regarding the vision of the Unsurpassed Victor to the east of the city: this clarifies that birth through the faculty of wisdom is designated as "east," signifying that one does not abide in their original station.
The eastern direction symbolizes wisdom; by engaging with the mundane world to guide sentient beings, it illuminates the stage of birth.
The west symbolizes compassion (*karuṇā*); thus, the fact that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva dwells on the western slope of Vajra Mountain represents the station of compassion.
Through the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) of all these Buddhas—“Buddha” meaning “awakened”—[this merit is directed toward enlightenment].

Since the lunar mansion of Jiao (the Horn) is among the mansions of the eastern quarter, and since Jiao presides over the gateway of the monastics—both monks and nuns—and the various virtuous practitioners of the Daoist path, the common people compose this calculation of Jiao based on its presiding domain and associations; thus it should be understood as "awakening" (jue).
Because it is the gateway to all virtues for the sovereign, the corner represents the heavenly gate of manifold goodness.
Its location to the east of the city signifies that the wise conduct of Samantabhadra is represented by the east, manifesting him as the foremost source from which all virtues arise.

The great compassionate practice of Avalokiteśvara is represented by the western direction; since the west corresponds to metal, and metal is the White Tiger, which presides over autumn and governs killing.
Thus, this scripture states: "He is clearly practiced in the rituals of the ten directions and presides over the deities of the quarters."

Furthermore, the presiding deities of the directions turn according to their respective quarters; this signifies that one turns according to the methods of those directions in order to deliver sentient beings.

Yet, in reality, the nature of the Great Vehicle is inherently formless, empty, and harmonious, leaving no trace. It manifests the Dharma according to the directions, for the Dharma follows the distinctions of conditions.
The Sages bestowed their instructions upon those entangled in the mundane world, using the very phenomena within these worldly conditions to manifest the Dharma.

For instance, the principle beyond words cannot be used to lead the ignorant, and the true source devoid of form cannot benefit the common person; therefore, they used specific analogies to manifest the Dharma.

To maintain it would not benefit the mundane world nor enlighten the deluded; yet to abolish it would likewise forfeit the present opportunity to benefit the mundane world and enlighten the deluded. By taking this eastern side of the city as the starting point for the deluded, one clarifies the meaning of generating all manner of wholesome virtues; furthermore, the chamber is regarded as the Azure Dragon, which is a position of worldly merit and fortune.
Regarding "in the Aśoka Grove": this refers to the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), for it is the place where patience is brought to fulfillment, as one practices without sorrow.

As for "grove" (*vana*): because this elder’s conduct extends throughout the ten directions, providing broad shade for all classes of beings according to their forms; and because his extensive practice provides such vast shelter, it is called a grove.
Furthermore, because he transforms others so that they are free from sorrow, it is called the Forest of No-Sorrow (*Aśoka-vana*).

As for his being surrounded by immeasurable merchants and hundreds of thousands of householders, these represent the assembly of those to be transformed, symbolizing the exchange of ignorance for wisdom, the exchange of wisdom for ignorance, and the exchange of evil for goodness.

Furthermore, he is a merchant who constantly dwells within birth and death; by practicing benevolence and virtue, he transforms and benefits all classes of beings, and is thus called a *gṛhapati* (householder).
This is an explanation based on his conduct.

When the youth Sudhana, having observed the elder preaching the Dharma to the assembly, prostrated himself upon the ground, it symbolized the essence of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), which consists in returning from the ultimate truth to the conventional world, taking great compassion and skillful patience as its foundation.
To say again, "I am Sudhana," signifies the profound depth of his quest for the Dharma.
It also clarifies that he has attained mastery over self and non-self, thereby perfecting patience (*kṣānti*).

From this point forward, the Elder describes the conduct practiced by Sudhana as the "Accomplishment" and the "Bodhisattva Practice Reaching All Places. This serves to clarify how, like all Buddhas, he dedicates his practice toward all worlds and all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, such that there is nowhere his conduct does not pervade; this will be explained in detail in the text below.
Just as in the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), from the first to the third abode one sees three bhikṣus, which symbolizes the cultivation of supramundane dharmas from within the mundane world;

so too, here, from the first stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) one sees three elders—namely, the Perfumer, the Boatman, and Anuttarajaya—who represent the pure worldly stream. This clarifies that entering the mundane from the ultimate truth is termed "dedication."

This is the spiritual friend among all the dedications of the Buddhas, which takes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its primary element and the other nine perfections as its companions.
In terms of the gateway of wisdom, it universally remedies the obstacles across all stages;

in terms of the gateway of stages, it remedies the obstacle of lacking mastery over patience when entering the ocean of birth and death, thereby enabling the attainment of mastery over the patience of the Dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*).

In the preceding ten stages of abiding (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*), one cultivates supramundane patience that is free from suffering; in this stage, it is clarified that one enters into the world to accomplish the patience of compassion and further benefits for others.

Within these ten dedications, when there are those who come to beg for his body, flesh, hands, feet, kingdom, city, wife, or children, he gives them away without a heart of weariness or resentment, but with redoubled joy.

Within the second section, "Advancing through the Deduction of Merit," from the passage beginning with "Just as all bodhisattvas... down to "...took their leave and departed," there are ten and a half lines of scripture, which are divided into five sections:

first, the deduction of merit and advancement; second, indicating the land where the spiritual friend resides; third, indicating the city where the spiritual friend dwells; fourth, citing the name of the spiritual friend; and fifth, paying respects and taking one's leave.
The city named Kaliṅga-vana is translated here as "Mutual Strife.

Because the rank of this bhikṣuṇī corresponds to the fourth dwelling among the ten dwellings and the fourth stage among the ten stages, she has emerged from the entanglements of the triple world and been born into the family of the Tathāgata. By returning to the mundane from the ultimate truth, she accomplishes undefiled compassion; this clarifies that "bhikṣu" signifies the meaning of transcending the mundane, while "ni" signifies the sound of compassion. It clarifies that the gates of the stages of dedicatory practice are neither male nor female, demonstrating the manifestation of signs to represent the Dharma.

Speaking in terms of reality, because this nun is the dharma of this stage, she enters the conventional through both expression and truth; by harmonizing the ultimate and the conventional, she reconciles the dualistic views of right and wrong, defilement and purity. Thus, she accomplishes the state of the wisdom of *dharmatā* where the conventional is eternally true and undefiled, and by extinguishing the strife of the dualistic views of the ultimate and conventional, existence and non-existence, and defilement and purity, she achieves the fourth dedication, "Reaching All Places," practicing the compassion of diligence.
This city is named "Forest of Strife" because the practice of loving-kindness is so pervasive and its protective shade so vast that it is called a "forest.
Furthermore, it is designated as a "forest" because the bhikṣuṇīs, as a result of their karmic retribution, possess a multitude of magnificent jewel-forested trees.
The name of the country is Śūna, which here translates as "the courageous one," signifying diligence.
This constitutes the fourth perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*); these teachings all rely upon locations and events to symbolize the Dharma.
The nun named Siṃha-vijṛmbhitā (Lion’s Stretch) was so named in accordance with her virtuous conduct.

Just as a lion stretches its body, she manifested compassion and joy; traveling throughout the ten directions to teach and transform sentient beings without weariness, this is the meaning of the "joy of the Dharma."
It is like a person whose body and mind are at ease and full of joy.

This signifies that although the bhikṣuṇī travels throughout the ten directions to harmonize disputes, her mind remains constantly transcendent from the mundane, because she dedicates herself to a compassion that dwells in the midst of entanglements without being stained by them.

Within the first dharma-gate of entering the actual stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this liberation-door of accomplishing all-knowledge," this section is divided into five parts:
first, his gradual journey to that city;
second, his thorough search for this bhikṣuṇī; [and so forth].
Third, the people inform the bhikṣuṇī of her location;
fourth, Sudhana goes to King Prasenajit’s Sunlight Garden (Sūryaprabha-udyāna) to observe and beholds all the secondary requisites (upabhoga-pariṣkāra) belonging to the bhikṣuṇī;
fifth, Sudhana joins his palms and requests what he seeks, and the bhikṣuṇī bestows upon Sudhana the method for his own practice.

Just as the fourth [chapter] describes Sudhana visiting King Prasenajit’s Sunlight Garden and observing, within the secondary environment (upabhoga) of the bhikṣuṇī and the adornments of the great assembly, there were thirteen kinds [of features]:

1. Adornment by a single jewel tree; 2. Adornment by flowing springs, ponds, and flowers made of the seven treasures; 3. Adornment by lion thrones beneath the jewel trees; 4. Adornment of the ground by various jewels; 5. Adornment by the rain of flowers and incense from the forest; 6. Adornment by musical trees and the harmonious resonance of various jewel bells; 7. Adornment by celestial garments; 8. Adornment by hundreds of thousands of jewel pavilions and jewel canopies; 9. Adornment by radiance like the peaks of Mount Sumeru; 10. Adornment by palaces; 11. Praising the transcendent roots of goodness and the merit of the bhikṣuṇī, which arose from making offerings to all Buddhas; 12. Praising the aspirations, virtues, and the pervasive, non-vain manifestations of the three karmas of the bhikṣuṇī as perceived by those who see them; 13. Clarifying the great assembly surrounding her.

The following thirty types of assemblies all clarify that this bhikṣuṇī’s practice of gathering and transforming living beings is universal; she bestows the Dharma according to their faculties, each case being different, until reaching the vajra-wisdom of the eleventh stage, and including all assemblies from there down to those adjacent to the rank of Buddhahood. This clarifies that a single stage encompasses the practices of all five stages.
It is thus for every single stage; each and every one universally traverses the Dharma-realm.

Through such successive refinements by means of the fifty-three dharmas and the dharmas of the one hundred and ten cities, they are then called the inexhaustible and sovereign dharmas of totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration. Within each and every stage, all stages are universally present.
This is to reveal that a single dharma pervades many dharmas, because a single stage pervades all modes of practice;
and to reveal that many dharmas enter into a single dharma, because five stages and five hundred dharma-gates enter into a single dharma.
This clarifies that the general is not different from the particular, and the particular is not different from the general, like the meshes of a net interpenetrating one another.
What was previously mentioned regarding the gifts bestowed by King Prasenajit refers to this matter.
Regarding the manifestation of the Dharma: this clarifies that the three dharmas of omniscience (*sarvajñā*), patience (*kṣānti*), and compassion (*maitrī*) are collectively unified.

The bhikṣu’s renunciation of worldly adornments represents the meaning of patience; the bhikṣuṇī represents the meaning of compassion; and King Prasenajit represents wisdom (*prajñā*). This illustrates the dedication of vows through the power of aspiration to enter the secular world, wherein the practice of vigor (*vīrya*) is harmonized with patience, wisdom, and compassion. Because the practices of the five stages are subsumed as a single essence and function of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the "lion’s stretch" (*siṃha-vijṛmbhita*) is presented as the joy of the Dharma within this gateway of the Dharma-realm.

From this point within the stage of diligent practice (*vīrya-pratipatti*), one integrates these three dharmas—patience (*kṣānti*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and compassion (*maitrī*)—until reaching the seventh and eighth stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-bhūmi*), where one first beholds Avalokiteśvara and Samantagāmin Bodhisattva, at which point they finally become equal.
The latter two positions cultivate the functioning of the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśabala*).
It is not that the first three elders lack this wisdom, patience, and compassion; rather, this is stated in terms of their relative superiority and inferiority as they progress upward.

The elder represents wisdom that is abundant in compassion yet inferior [in power]; the nun represents a compassionate mind that dwells in the world without defilement; the maiden represents being stained yet remaining untainted.

As for the *pārijātaka* tree, this is translated as "Pervasive Fragrance"; the trunk, branches, and leaves of this tree all pervasively perfume the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, which here symbolizes how practice universally perfumes the entire dharma-realm.
*Kālinī* means "fine cotton garment" in this language.
*Varuṇadeva* means "Water God" in this language.

The ten gates of *prajñā*, such as the "Universal Eye" and "Abandonment," are fully explained in the sutra; these are the teachings spoken by the bhikṣuṇī, and there are countless millions of such gates of *prajñā*.
As for the Garden of Sunlight (*Sūryaprabha-udyāna*), its essential substance consists of patience, wisdom, and loving-kindness.

When Sudhana stands with palms joined and makes his request without performing a formal prostration, yet circumambulates all the trees within the garden to the right, this indicates that the trees are born as the fruition of practice. It clarifies that because the grove of various practices is endowed with these three dharmas—patience, wisdom, and loving-kindness—it represents the perfection of the three types of conduct. He merely circumambulates them because they are the dharmas he reveres; thus, there is no separate act of prostration.

Surrounded by a multitude of trees, this signifies the meaning of diligence in this stage, because one clearly realizes the three practices of patience (*kṣānti*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and compassion (*maitrī*).

When Sudhana requests the name of the bhikṣuṇī who has accomplished all-knowledge, it refers to patience, wisdom, and compassion within fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*); all differentiated wisdoms are fully produced from these three dharmas.
This assembly gathered for conversion shall continue until they reach the vajra-wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) following the tenth stage.
Sudhana further inquired about the scope of this dharma-gate, as the sutra says: "O son of good family!..."

"Having entered this gate of the light of wisdom, I attained the King of Samādhis that gives birth to all dharmas; by means of this samādhi, I obtained the mind-made body. From here on, this describes the sphere of activity and function of this dharma-gate, as fully elucidated in the sutra.

The general meaning is that, based on fundamental wisdom, one gives rise to the various distinct dharma-gates of the great function of patient acceptance, wisdom, compassion, and the myriad practices, which are as vast as the realm of the dharmadhātu.
When one practices in accordance with this mode, one is then called Avalokiteśvara, also named Samantagāmin Bodhisattva, because his non-effortful wisdom and compassion are equal.
Therefore, in the seventh dedication, Avalokiteśvara and Samantagāmin meet in one place. [The text says:
"O son of good family!

I see all sentient beings without discriminating the marks of sentient beings, because I see clearly with the eye of wisdom; furthermore, even when hearing words and sounds, I have no attachment to the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, because I see with the eye of wisdom and know through the awakening of the Dharma. From this point onward, his virtues are extolled to encourage Sudhana to advance further.
The second section, beginning with "Just as all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas," concerns the advancement through the cultivation of virtues.
Within this section on advancement, there are twelve lines of scripture, which are divided into five gates:

first, the advancement through the cultivation of virtues; second, the indication of the location and the country where the spiritual friend resides; third, the mention of the name of the city where he dwells, namely Ratnavyūha (Jeweled Adornment); fourth, the revelation of the name of the spiritual friend; and fifth, the paying of respects and taking one's leave.
In the south, as previously explained in the case of Śakra.
The land is named "Perilous" (Kṣaṇana), which serves as the gateway for this woman’s practice of the *dhyānapāramitā*.

Among the praises of her virtue: sitting upright in a single body, she fills the entire Dharma-realm; within her own body, she manifests all lands. All realms of good and evil are universally encompassed by the essence of *dhyāna* within the Dharma-realm. She universally contains all practices, universally gathers in all sentient beings, and universally engages in shared activities, penetrating and filling all environments throughout the ten directions.
There are those among the people of the world who, seeing his conduct as defiled, find it difficult to believe; therefore, they name the country "Perilous Difficulty.
As for the city named "Jeweled Adornment," because its sight and sound are difficult to believe, it is called "Perilous Difficulty."

Through faith one awakens to the realization that both mind and objects are non-existent; as this accords with the true nature (*dharmatā*), delusions are eliminated and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) are forever ended. One then attains innate spiritual powers (*abhijñā*), which is called "Jewel Adornment.
To clearly understand that the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas who have emerged from the entanglements are free from [delusions] and do not engage in them is called "Liberation" (*vimukti*).

Within this fifth dedication among the ten dedications, regarding the practice of transcending entanglements, it is the fifth: pure and undefiled dhyāna. Entering into the world to engage in common secular affairs and practicing extensively for the benefit of sentient beings—even to the point of manifesting the performance of defiled dharmas—it has never, for even a single thought-moment, possessed a defiled mind; therefore, she is called "Woman."
Yet, within the ultimate reality, there is neither male nor female.

Because one apprehends the fundamental truth of the nature of wondrous wisdom, the essence of great compassion is like a woman; it is not that one gives rise to views of male and female based on worldly conventions.
If one harbors worldly sentiments and gives rise to views of male and female, one likewise will not perceive this Dharma-gate.

This refers to the Bodhisattva who, employing wondrous wisdom, gives rise to the practice of compassion; they should accord with worldly conduct, manifesting form-bodies throughout the ten directions to appropriately establish transformative teachings.

In this state, it is manifested that the Bodhisattva possesses such virtues: dwelling in reality without realization, remaining untainted while amidst the fetters, and with the Dharma-gate pervading the entire Dharma-realm—who is right and who is wrong?
This is not something to be conceived through worldly sentiment, nor is it a practice for those deluded by worldly ignorance.

Unless one’s wisdom penetrates the true source and one’s conduct accords with the Dharma-realm—such that one is fit for the task and possesses both knowledge of the faculties and mastery of the conventional—how could one possibly realize this Way?
Vasumitrā means "World-Friend" (Śrīmitra) in this language, or alternatively "Heavenly-Friend," because she acts as a teacher and friend to all devas and humans.
She is also called "One Who Exchanges Jewels for Wealth," or one who manifests the conduct of worldly lust and defilement.

The *Yi* [Book of Changes] deals with wealth and affairs; these are all worldly practices that are difficult to fully comprehend. Within the three realms and six paths—among humans, devas, earth-dwellers, and those in hell—there is no conduct that is not present.
This is to be unstained yet stained, accessible only through the wisdom of Samantabhadra.

Within the first dharma-gate of "Correct Entry into the Appropriate Stage," from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this bodhisattva liberation gate of the limit of freedom from desire," five sections are established:

first, reflecting upon the instructions of the spiritual friend to advance; second, traveling by stages until reaching the city of Ratnavyūha in the perilous country; third, searching for the woman Vasumitrā everywhere; fourth, seeing her within her own home to the north of the marketplace in that city; and fifth, seeing her, paying homage, and formally presenting one's request.

In the exegesis of the text, regarding Sudhana seeing [the merchant's son] dwelling in his own home to the north of the marketplace: the marketplace represents the manifold afflictions of birth and death.
The north corresponds to the position of *Kan*, which is the northern direction and presides over black; it is the station of sentient beings who are collectively deluded and ignorant.
The Bodhisattva dwells in this marketplace of the ocean of delusive flows and craving, accompanying others to bring them forth and causing them to manifest their innate brilliance.
As for those who dwell in their own home, they regard the ocean of birth and death of sentient beings as the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva himself.

Out of great compassion, the Bodhisattva dwells within the house of birth and death of all sentient beings to deliver them, accomplishing the practices of Samantabhadra and perfecting immeasurable merit.
As the sutra states: "The youth Sudhana went to his gate and saw that his residence was vast, magnificent, and beautiful," and so forth, extensively describing the adornments.
This is the first instance of seeing her *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment).

Next, the passage beginning with "At that time, Sudhana saw this woman’s countenance was upright and majestic, even to the point that her skin was golden" refers to seeing her *sabhāga-vipāka* (the primary body) as well as her various arts and skills; the details below are exactly as explained in the sutra.
From "At that time, Sudhana went before him" onwards, he requests what he seeks.
From "O son of good family" onwards, the Dharma to be practiced by Sudhana is formally bestowed.

The liberation of a bodhisattva is called "the limit of detachment from desire. By means of this liberation, he manifests his body according to their inclinations and desires; what is seen by those in the ten directions and the three realms differs, as is fully explained in the sutra.

Furthermore, a sutra states: "If there are sentient beings who even briefly behold me, they immediately become free from greed and attain the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Joy. This clarifies that those with faith cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), for they find delight in their minds through the joy of meditation (*dhyānānanda*).

If there are sentient beings who even briefly engage in conversation with me, they immediately become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Immeasurable Sound; this clarifies that wisdom arises from meditative concentration, whereby one realizes that sound has no inherent substance.

If there are sentient beings who grasp my hand, they immediately become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Universally Visiting All Buddha-fields; this is the meaning of "guiding and receiving."

From the words "In this manner" onwards: ascending the seat signifies the increase of signless wisdom; momentarily observing the self signifies the meaning of contemplative observation; and stretching the body signifies the meaning of dharma-joy.
The blinking of the eyes signifies entering the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom through the vision of the truths.
"Embracing me" signifies the meaning of gathering in and not abandoning sentient beings.
"Sucking my lips" signifies the meaning of receiving the teachings and expounding the Dharma.

All those who draw near to me shall attain liberation from the realm of desire and enter the stage of omniscience of the bodhisattvas; indeed, none of those who approach me do so in vain, for all shall obtain the gateway to omniscience.

This clarifies that those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas who have merely emerged from the entanglements seek only to leave suffering behind; they have not yet entered the great compassion that enters the ocean of birth and death to engage in "common practice" (samānārthatā) for the sake of delivering sentient beings. They have not yet reached the Sovereign Wisdom King of the Dharma-realm, which remains untainted amidst both defilement and purity; nor have they realized the perfect, universal radiance of non-reliant wisdom, wherein one spontaneously benefits beings throughout the ten directions without bondage or liberation—only then can one be said to have eternally departed from the limit of craving.

If one becomes weary and emerges from the entanglements yet lacks the practice of great compassion, if wisdom is not yet ultimate, and if there remains a basis for reliance, then one should not practice with a mind that grasps at existence; nor should one be satisfied with a partial realization of the gates of liberation—signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action—which are empty. Do not consider such [realization] sufficient.

One should cultivate wisdom and compassion, giving rise to the aspiration to vow to deliver all sentient beings; one should study the wisdom of differentiation so as to fully know all phenomena within the three realms, and by clearly employing the affairs of the three realms, they are immediately realized as the Dharma-realm.

Skillfully illuminating the twelve links of dependent origination for oneself and others, one generates all-encompassing wisdom; realizing that boundless eons and the present are non-dual, one seeks no other place for a separate supramundane liberation or nirvana.

By means of the seal of non-action and non-reliance, one realizes that the fundamental nature of the dharmas of the triple world is thus; there is no further conceptual seeking, for all is naturally and perfectly integrated through reliance upon the dharma-gates of the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications, which shall correspond to this.

The woman Vasumitrā represents the fifth gate of this assembly, the Dedication of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit. She acts so as to equalize birth-and-death, thereby eliminating the views of right and wrong.

Through the gate of Dharma-realm meditation, both the defilements of the two truths—ultimate and conventional—are exhausted; through the equality of nature, her wisdom pervades both existence and non-existence like the Dharma-realm. There is neither practice nor non-practice, neither birth nor anything not beneficial. Because she summons manifold merit and virtue, she is named the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit."
From the passage, "Sudhana said, 'Noble One, what roots of goodness have you planted and what merits have you cultivated? onwards, the girl explains her own past causes to Sudhana.

When the Tathāgata Uccagāmin appeared in the world, she was the wife of a householder; she offered precious coins as alms and, through the exhortation of Mañjuśrī, gave rise to the great bodhicitta. By these causes and conditions, she attained such a liberation.
I know only this liberation that reaches the limit of freedom from greed: clarifying past causes by relinquishing what was most cherished—money—is the departure from greed;
Mañjuśrī’s exhortation to generate the unsurpassed bodhicitta is the departure from desire.
Just as with a single precious coin, although what is given is not much, because of the value placed upon it by the mind, its ability to be relinquished is no different from giving much.
This is the dedication of inexhaustible merit-treasures, and it also takes the dhyāna-pāramitā as its essence.
To clearly realize all dharmas as being perfectly penetrating is the meaning of "precious coins.
From the perspective of the gateway of wisdom, this applies universally across all stages;

specifically, within the context of the stages, it pertains to the fifth stage, the Stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Here, one employs supramundane dhyāna to overcome the obstacle of lacking mastery over the true and conventional, the defiled and pure, and the obstacle of lacking mastery in practice regarding the pervasion of all sentient beings, thereby rendering these masteries.

In the second section, "Advancing through the Promotion of Virtue," there are six lines of scripture from "As the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "...took his leave and departed. These are divided into five sections:

first, advancing through the promotion of virtue; second, indicating the location and the name of the city, Sudarśana; third, citing the name of the layperson *kalyāṇamitra*, Vīradatta; fourth, citing the deeds performed by the *kalyāṇamitra* in making offerings at the sandalwood stūpa and pedestal; and fifth, paying respects, taking one's leave, and departing.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: "the south" is as explained previously.
The city is named Sudarśana (Good Crossing) because this householder skillfully leads sentient beings across.
The householder's name is Vaiśya; this is translated here as "Dharma."
*Ti-la* means "encompassing" in this context.

This is because the wisdom of this lay devotee is vast, encompassing all dharma-gates of the ten directions; its full name is *Siddhārtha*, which is translated as "Maitreya. This is to clarify that, by means of the sixth supramundane wisdom, he dwells in the secular world practicing compassion and employing skillful means to benefit sentient beings, thereby attaining his name through his conduct.

Within the Dharma-gate of the first correct entry into the respective stage, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva’s liberation gate of the limit of the non-extinction of all Buddhas."
In this section, five topics are established:
first, his gradual journey to the city of Supāraga;
second, his arrival at the householder’s residence and his prostration at the householder’s feet.
Third, he stood with palms joined, formally presenting his request;
fourth, the layman correctly explained to Sudhana the dharma to be practiced and the gate of liberation called "The Limit of Non-Nirvāṇa";
fifth, he raised up the sandalwood stupa-seat that had been manifested and made an offering of it.

Regarding the offering to the sandalwood pedestal of the stūpa, the Sūtra states: "When I opened the door of the Tathāgata’s sandalwood pedestal stūpa, I immediately attained a samādhi named 'The Inexhaustibility of the Buddha-seed. This clarifies that the discriminative minds of all sentient beings are all seeds of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; they are identical to the seeds of the wisdom of all Buddhas, devoid of such characteristics as arising and ceasing.

This corresponds to the sixth dwelling among the ten dwellings, the sixth practice among the ten practices, and the sixth stage among the ten stages. Because one employs the sixth supramundane gate of wisdom from among the ten dwellings and ten practices to dedicate it toward entering the midst of worldly entanglements to benefit sentient beings through the practice of wisdom, one assumes the body of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) to transform the mundane world.
A single stūpa chamber is established, within which a sandalwood throne is placed; no image is set therein, signifying the sixth gate of wisdom that penetrates the dharma of signlessness.

By making offerings with this stūpa-base, all Buddhas appear before one; it clarifies that the dharma of signlessness has no perception of the three periods of time—past, present, or future. Because the wisdom of one’s own Buddha and the wisdom of all Buddhas are identical in their signless essence and constitute a single limit (*ekānta*), and because all sentient beings are likewise fundamentally one limit with the wisdom of all Buddhas, he preaches such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, so that they may open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, the city is named "Well-Crossed" (*Sudatta*).
Householder, the names [of all Buddhas] encompass the wisdom of all Buddhas and all sentient beings as being of one essence, for it is neither born nor extinguished.
Since the wisdom of all Buddhas possesses a nature that is without birth or extinction, all sentient beings likewise are without birth or extinction; therefore, all Buddhas do not enter nirvana.
This passage clarifies that, just as there is no distinct form upon the seat, so too is the Buddha.
From the words, "Sudhana said: 'What is the sphere of this samādhi? onwards, it describes the number of times the householder has entered this samādhi and beheld the Buddhas.
All Buddhas of this realm, other directions, and the three periods of time can all be seen; the number of such Buddhas seen is fully explained in the sutra.

The intent is to clarify that both Buddhas and sentient beings possess no marks of arising or ceasing, yet through skillful means, the sandalwood throne and stupa are used as a guide and representation to lead all sentient beings to realize the wisdom of the nature and characteristics of their own mind, such that the sandalwood throne and stupa are fundamentally the Buddha.

One realizes that both characteristics and nature are entirely non-existent, and that neither arises nor perishes. Understanding that characteristics are like illusions and comprehending that nature is like space, one’s wisdom has no basis for abiding; how, then, could there be arising and ceasing?
This is the dedication that accords with all firm roots of goodness; it has the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as its essence and the other nine perfections as its companions.

It serves to counteract the obstacle of being unable to exercise mastery over great compassion while dwelling within birth and death (*saṃsāra*) despite possessing supramundane wisdom, thereby enabling the attainment of such mastery.

In the second section, "Advancing through the Promotion of Virtue," from the passage beginning with "Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... to "...took their leave and departed," there are fourteen lines of verse. This is divided into five sections: first, advancing through the promotion of virtue;

second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend; third, citing the name of the mountain, Potalaka; fourth, citing the name of the spiritual friend, Avalokiteśvara, also known as Guanshiyin; and fifth, paying respects and taking one's leave.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the name of the mountain is Potalaka, which in this language means "White Flower Tree. Because many white-flowered trees grow on the mountain, and their flowers are exceedingly fragrant, their scent reaches afar.
To clarify that this noble one practices the gateway of compassion, he takes the most humble and minute as his conduct.
"Flower" signifies the blossoming of the myriad practices.

This flower of conduct—characterized by compassion, humility, extreme gentleness, and joy—is in full bloom; the fragrance of this conduct of teaching and transforming wafts far, permeating all sentient beings so that all who hear its name may give rise to the bodhicitta.

Regarding the mention of the name "Avalokiteśvara" as a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the old translation "Guanshiyin" (Avalokitasvara) is considered correct; in Sanskrit he is called *Prabhūtaratna* or *Prabhūtarava*, meaning "Light-Sound of the World," for he illuminates the world with the light of compassion and rescues those who hear his cry of suffering.

Regarding those who must rely on recollection before they can be saved, the intent is to cause them to turn their minds toward exclusively focusing on the arousal of the virtuous resolve (bodhicitta), so that their roots of merit and virtue may become firm and deep.
Question: Avalokiteśvara may be devoid of compassion; why then is it necessary to invoke Guāngshìyīn?
Answer: Generally speaking, all bodhisattvas attain their names based on their practice, and their stages are manifested through those names and practices.

Although all bodhisattvas possess both the gates of wisdom and compassion, since one now seeks to manifest advancement through name and practice, it is necessary to employ names to represent the dharmas.

Now, this seventh dedication, which accords with all sentient beings, accomplishes the gate of compassion within the world; it uses the name "Avalokiteśvara" as the designation for this compassion, serving as a signpost for the gate of practice to cause one to advance upward.
Avalokiteśvara signifies clarity of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*), because he has attained mastery over the supramundane meaning of *prajñā*.
This represents the gate of compassion (*karuṇā*) by observing the suffering of the world; it is not like the title "Guanshiyin" (Observer of the World's Sounds).

Regarding the statement in the *Lotus Sūtra* that "Samantabhadra Bodhisattva comes from the presence of the Buddha Jewel-Resplendent Sovereign King in the East," and other sūtras stating that "Avalokiteśvara is in the presence of Amitābha Buddha in the West," these are all the Tathāgata’s skillful means of intentional expression to manifest and establish names through the Dharma.

The underlying meaning is that the east represents wisdom (*prajñā*) and the west represents compassion (*karuṇā*); while directions are used here to symbolize dharmas, in reality there are no fixed locations.

It is simply that the east is taken as the direction where spring’s warmth arises and the sun emerges to shine universally; among the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the eastern asterisms such as Aśvinī (Jiǎoxù), Rōhiṇī (Fáng), and Mṛgaśiras (Xīn), along with the other seven stars, all occupy positions of manifold goodness, thereby symbolizing the gateway of wisdom.

The seven lunar mansions of the western quarter—Mūla, Pūrva-Āṣāḍhā, Uttara-Āṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and Pūrva-Bhādrapadā—are presided over by the White Tiger and represent the principles of autumn and execution.
Mūla governs criminal courts and primarily presides over the punishment of evil; it is presided over by Avalokiteśvara.

In reality, a single direction of a Buddha-land fills the ten directions, and a single mote of dust contains the entire Dharma-realm; how could there be any spatial location where self and other exist in separation such that one might encounter a distinct Buddha?

The virtuous predecessors who translated the scriptures, regarding the teachings of the Three Vehicles, claimed that Avalokiteśvara did not exist in this land and thus used "Guansizai" (Avalokitasvāmin) as the title; however, this does not accord with the principle of the realm and wisdom of the Dharmadhātu Vairocana Tathāgata.

Within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, specifically in the section on the convergence of the three vehicles into the single gate, these three dharmas are fully present. Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva represent, respectively: the signless wisdom of the Dharmakāya and fundamental gnosis, which is presided over by Mañjuśrī;
the arising of differentiated practices from fundamental gnosis, which is presided over by Samantabhadra;
and the great compassionate mind that remains constantly within the stream of suffering without seeking personal escape, which is presided over by Avalokiteśvara.

When these three dharmas are practiced by a single person and brought to full perfection throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, teaching and transforming all beings without exception, he is named Vairocana Buddha.

This clarifies that Mañjuśrī is present in all places, Samantabhadra is present in all places, Avalokiteśvara is present in all places, and Vairocana is present in all places, pervading them in ever-deepening layers even within a single mote of dust; this is explained here by way of brief illustration.
The phrase "like a mountain upon the sea where many sages and saints dwell" refers specifically to the Southern Sea, yet it also primarily signifies the ocean of birth and death.
Other meanings are clearly explained in the full text.
Furthermore, compassion is established as a flowing spring.

Within the first section, the Dharma-gate for correctly entering the stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this gate of great compassionate practice," five gates are established:
first, contemplating the instructions of the spiritual benefactor to advance further.
Second, he traveled by stages until he reached that mountain, searching for this great bodhisattva everywhere;
third, he saw Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva sitting cross-legged upon a diamond-jewel rock within a rocky valley on its western face;
fourth, having seen him, Sudhana rejoiced, and Avalokiteśvara saw Sudhana from afar and praised him.
When Sudhana prostrated and made his request, Avalokiteśvara expounded for him the liberation door of the practice of great compassion.

Regarding the exegesis according to the text: as with the fifth [chapter], the woman Puṣpamālā, she welcomed him by means of the lion’s stretch, thereby manifesting the practice of compassion; furthermore, her reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) appearance and the environment in which she dwells are all adorned with jewels.

Upon reaching the sixth and seventh dedications, his great compassion reaches its ultimate limit; he does not seek to ripen beings or benefit them for the sake of his own karmic retribution, but instead dwells in the rugged valleys of the defiled realms of sentient beings. There, springs and streams wind and reflect one another, forests are lush and verdant, and soft fragrant grasses are spread across the ground in a clockwise spiral. The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara sits upon a diamond-jewel stone, while immeasurable bodhisattvas all sit upon jewel stones.
This is the dwelling place, representing rocky valleys and clarifying the path leading through rugged terrain.
The winding reflection of the spring waters illustrates the crystal clarity of compassion.
The lush density of the forest represents the thick, protective shade of a compassionate heart.
The fragrant herbs being soft and supple signify that his verbal teachings are aromatic and bring great joy to the hearts of people.

Their being spread across the ground in a clockwise direction signifies that sentient beings follow his transformation; it represents the spreading of the ground of compassion so that all may have a place of refuge.

That Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva sits upon a vajra-jewel stone symbolizes that, through the application of vajra-wisdom, he acts in accordance with compassionate conduct—firm, solid, profound, and heavy, such that he cannot be shaken or moved.
As for sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), it signifies the mutual penetration of wisdom and compassion.
That immeasurable bodhisattvas all sit upon jeweled stones signifies that their compassionate practice is firm and profound.

That Sudhana observes them with unblinking eyes signifies his reverence for the Dharma and his esteem for these noble beings; with a heart of loving-kindness, his vision is penetrating and free from any other thought.
Sudhana praised his virtues as fully elucidated in the sutra.
Sudhana went to the place where Avalokiteśvara was; from afar, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva saw Sudhana and said, "Welcome," along with various words of praise.

That there are these words before one has yet had the opportunity to pay respects clarifies the profundity of his great compassion; he first offers consolation and praise, and only thereafter performs prostrations, circumambulations, and presents his request.

The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara bestows upon Sudhana the liberation door of the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-caryā-vimokṣamukha*), clarifying the transition from the sixth stage (*bhūmi*)—where one cultivates supramundane compassion—to the accomplishment of compassionate conduct that enters into the mundane world.

At this stage, because the Bodhisattva has fulfilled the seventh dedication, "Equal Accordance with All Sentient Beings," and because they have also entered conventional wisdom (saṃvṛti-jñāna) to its full completion at this point, it is as indicated by the subsequent text: although there is a Bodhisattva named Samyaktva (Rightly Directed) in the eastern direction, when he arrives for an audience, he remains in the same assembly. This signifies that for a Bodhisattva at this stage, conventional engagement and the manifestation of compassion and wisdom are equal.
When we reach the subsequent passage for reconciliation, the Sūtra says: "Good son!

I constantly abide in this gateway of the practice of great compassion; I am always present before all Tathāgatas and universally appear before all sentient beings, gathering in all sentient beings through the four means of integration."
This is explained in detail as set forth in the sutra.

The intent clarifies that one does not depart from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), yet manifests form-bodies (*rūpa-kāya*) throughout the worlds of the ten directions to benefit sentient beings through compassion.
Below, there is a detailed exposition of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara’s own vows and his practices for benefiting sentient beings, which will be fully clarified as follows.
From the passage "I have only attained this gate of the Bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion" onwards is the section on the advancement of virtue through self-reflection.
This is the gate of dedication that accords with all sentient beings; herein, the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine perfections serve as its companions.
From the perspective of the gate of wisdom, all stages universally counteract [obstructions];

from the perspective of the gate of stages, they counteract the obstructions to sovereignty within the mundane world during the Great Compassion that transcends the world found in the ten abodes and ten practices, thereby enabling the attainment of such sovereignty.

Second is the advancement through the inference of virtues. From the passage beginning with "Just as all bodhisattvas... down to "...took their leave and departed," there are eighteen and a half lines of scripture, which are divided into five sections:

first, the advancement through the inference of virtues; second, the indication of the location of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); third, the citation of the spiritual friend’s name as "Rightly Directed" (*Samyakprasthita*); fourth, the repeated praise of the spiritual friend’s radiant majesty, supernatural powers, and universal transformation; and fifth, the exhortation to go and inquire.
Question: With what intention is it that he does not say "I shall take my leave and depart"? Answer:

In this assembly of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one sees the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin; because the two aspects of compassion and wisdom are both fully perfected at this stage, it signifies that when compassion reaches its consummation, the wisdom of ignorance spontaneously manifests as such. Since it is shown that compassion and wisdom are non-dual in essence, he does not depart.

Furthermore, it is clarified that from the Bhikṣuṇī Siṃhaviṣṭhita, one cultivates compassion to give rise to wisdom; from this eighth dedication onward, up to the tenth stage, the Earth Goddess (Pṛthivīdevatā) arises from wisdom to manifest as compassion. Thus, the Heavenly Goddess is wisdom and the Earth Goddess is compassion; when wisdom and compassion are realized as a unified essence, this is the sovereign practice of Samantabhadra.
This one possesses clear wisdom, compassion, and the penetrating divine nature of the true reality; thus they are named the "Spirit of Heaven and Earth," and are not a worldly ghost or spirit.

Regarding Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s statement that there is a bodhisattva in the eastern direction named "Rightly Advancing" (Zhengqu): because their clear right wisdom is free from error, they are called "Rightly Advancing."

Those who come from emptiness possess an enlightened wisdom that is essentially non-reliant, a nature devoid of form or substance, and a spirit that is omnipresent. From their own essence of true emptiness, they manifest illusory bodies that respond to conditions to benefit sentient beings; in a single kṣaṇa, their resonance reaches the ten directions, yet their nature neither comes nor goes.
Because illusory images manifest within space, it is said that they "come from space.
The east symbolizes wisdom (*jñāna*).
As for the south, it symbolizes the Dharma as being void; it is the "void within the center" of the trigram *Li*, representing illumination, rectitude, and the sun.

"Li" (離) means "to be radiant. To explain how radiance rests upon the earth: the north is associated with the trigram Kan (坎) and the color black; Zi represents the ultimate limit of Yin, while Gui represents the final end of Yin. By turning one's back to the black and following the light, by turning away from the depraved and following what is correct, one occupies the position of the initial awakening; therefore, one proceeds toward the south.

Now, arriving at the eighth dedication, the Aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*), it clarifies that the eastern direction represents wisdom, thunder, lightning, sound, the blue dragon, springtime growth, merit, and auspicious celebration.

The sun is born in Yin (寅) and emerges in Mao (卯); it determines right and wrong in Chen (辰) and Si (巳). By the time it reaches Wu (午), it has already reached the east, all of which belongs to the realm of Yang.
Wu represents the culmination of Yang, while Wei (未) represents the end of Yang.
From the sign of the sheep (mei) to the ox (chou) is the position of yin.
By means of this eighth wisdom, one illumines the characteristics of True Suchness (tathatā) through dedication; thus, the eastern direction is taken as wisdom, for it clearly illuminates all errors.
It enters into birth and death and vibrates all phenomena in order to cause clarity to arise;

it teaches and transforms sentient beings so they may realize True Suchness (*tathatā*); it illuminates the path of the foolish so as to accomplish the virtue of a gentleman; it destroys the paths of the sycophantic and the heterodox so as to perfect right wisdom; it illuminates all evils so as to give rise to all goodness; and it nurtures all roots of merit so as to accomplish pure, stainless, auspicious, and meritorious fortune.
Therefore, the east symbolizes wisdom (*prajñā*) and the west symbolizes compassion (*karuṇā*); these two directions clarify that compassion and wisdom are in perfect balance.
The Bodhisattva Saṃcodaka came from the east and was seen at a location to the west of Mount Pāṇḍava, thereby clarifying that the east represents wisdom and the west represents compassion.
This Guanyin represents one portion of the beginning and end of the two stages of compassion and wisdom in the *Zhengqu* assembly.
From this point onward, he proceeds from wisdom to practice compassion; he is thus the deity of Heaven and Earth who follows immediately thereafter.

Therefore, when wisdom follows from compassionate conduct, that conduct is narrow and does not reach its consummation; whereas when compassion follows from wisdom, that conduct is vast, limitless, and sovereign.

Thus, when the stages of the ten bhūmis are fulfilled and the merits of wisdom and compassion are perfected, in the eleventh bhūmi, compassion again serves as the essence and wisdom as the function. In this regard, Māyā is compassion, and the birth of the Buddha is wisdom.
In this way, within each stage there is a progression, all of which possesses intentional meaning.

Their general and specific, identical and differing aspects are like the directions of east, west, south, and north: they manifest one's own inclination toward the goal, dispel delusion, and bring forth illumination; thus, moving toward the south represents this.
If one possesses wisdom and compassion to benefit the mundane world, then moving toward the east or west represents this.

Regarding the fact that Avalokiteśvara is located on the west side of Mount Baihua: "white" refers to the golden image; white is the color of the West, which symbolizes the position of Metal and presides over the rank of General.
The East is the position of Wood, which presides over the green image and the rank of Minister.

The "Sign" (lakṣaṇa) presides over birth, while the "General" (senāpati) presides over killing; the Tathāgata established this gateway to the Dharma by conforming to worldly conventions so that it might be easily understood by the world.
Thus, he placed the gateway of great compassion within this place of slaughter to rescue beings from suffering.
The position of spring in the east establishes the gateway of great wisdom, symbolizing that wisdom gives rise to all virtues;
this is done so that one may easily attain these matters.
As it is said in the *Laozi*: "The Senior General resides on the right, and the Junior General resides on the left."
The enlightened superior possesses compassion and fears the risk of killing the innocent.
Yet, the Great Image is vast and indistinct; how could it have a fixed shape that can be grasped?
It is merely by means of the Dharma that names are established and its principles set forth.
However, as for the path of wisdom and compassion, it fulfills the ten directions through a single dharma and pervades all myriad practices through a single practice.

Nevertheless, while the Dharma is established according to worldly conventions, there are indeed instances that resemble worldly arrangements; this is the application [of the Dharma] according to specific circumstances.
Therefore, this sutra states that there is a bodhisattva in the east named Samantagāmin (Correctly Proceeding), who represents the eighth stage of wisdom, illuminating the great night of the world.
This is because it shares the same great function as the eighth stage of non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) within the ten abodes, ten practices, ten stages, and the eleventh stage.
While the progression through these positions is identical, there are differences in terms of the maturation of faculties and the presence of adverse or favorable conditions.

This Bodhisattva Samantagāmin came from the sky and arrived at the summit of the Cakravāḍa mountains of the Sahā world; when he pressed the earth with his toe, causing the Sahā world to quake in six ways, it signified that wisdom can shatter darkness, so that the delusions of sentient beings are extinguished and objective realms vanish and disperse.

When wisdom manifests, delusion perishes; because the realm of the great earth, which is the retribution for deluded karma, also dissolves and disperses, the earth quakes—"quaking" meaning "dispersal.
Just as when meditative concentration manifests before one, delusion perishes and wisdom responds, so too does the retributive realm utterly vanish.

Pressing the earth with his toes is the activity of wisdom; it signifies that through the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), wisdom arises and manifests, whereby all the attachments of the assembly are dispersed.
Mount Cakravāḍa is the objective realm that is the retribution for false attachments; when wisdom manifests without dependence, the objects of attachment cease to exist.
It is through meditative contemplation that clarity is attained; it cannot be measured by the conceptualizing mind.
That "all are adorned with various jewels" clarifies that delusion has vanished and objects have ceased.

In accordance with the purity of wisdom and its corresponding merit, all virtues immediately manifest as the body emits radiance, eclipsing the light of all suns, moons, stars, and lightning, as well as the light of the eight classes of beings—devas, nāgas, and so forth—and that of Śakra, Brahmā, and the four world-protecting kings; all such lights become like a mass of ink.
