As for that light universally illuminating all hells and the animal realm: just as the lights of the three realms arise from tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*) produced by the merit of a mind subject to arising and ceasing, they have not yet transcended the fruits of tainted karma belonging to a self subject to arising and ceasing; in them, there still exist karmas obtained through the duality of self and other.

The light of wisdom of great compassion—which is the true reality-wisdom, untainted, selfless, and effortless, possessing the purity of the *dharmatā* and acting according to its own nature—is beyond the reach of the mundane world; it has no obstructions, boundaries, or limits by which it can be measured, for it penetrates the ten directions and pervades the six realms of existence.
The subsequent practices of wisdom and compassion are fully elucidated in the sutra.

Within the first section on the dharma-gate of entering the specific stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this bodhisattva liberation-gate of the swift practice of the universal gate," five gates are established:
first, proceeding swiftly to the place of that bodhisattva in accordance with the instructions.
Second, he prostrates, joins his palms, and requests what he seeks;
third, the Bodhisattva Samantagambhīravikramin expounds the name of the dharma he practices, called the Liberation of Universal Gate Swift Action;
fourth, Sudhana poses a question.
Under which Buddha did you receive this Dharma-gate?
From what buddha-field have you come, and how far is it from here?
How long has it been since you arrived?
The fifth correctly explains the number of objects of focus, causes, bases, attainments, locations, and durations.
When it says, "Good son!

I have come to this land from the presence of the Buddha Universal Victorious Birth in the world-system Wondrous Treasury to the east; I received this Dharma-gate from that Buddha," this is spoken according to the actual facts.

Wisdom has no fixed location or substance of distance or proximity; yet, to illustrate this dharma through a conventional designation, it is said that the Buddha Wondrous Treasury of Universal Victory in the Eastern World attained this dharma-gate. This clarifies that the East is the locus where all virtues arise.

The World of Wondrous Treasury (Miaozang) refers to the fundamental treasury of wisdom of the Dharma-body of its own wondrous principle; because its nature is all-pervasive, perfect, and omnipresent throughout the ten directions, it is called a "world."

As for the Buddhas of Universal Victory who have attained this Dharma-gate: it clarifies that from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) arises discriminative wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), which resonates with sentient beings; its intent clarifies that while the great function of fundamental wisdom does not shift, it is nonetheless without [deliberate] effort.

"An incalculable number of kalpas, as numerous as the atoms in an unspeakable number of Buddha-fields, have passed since departing from that place," means that because fundamental wisdom transcends dust and surmounts kalpas, it is not contained within the scope of numerical calculation.

Regarding the phrase "in each and every thought-moment, taking steps as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields": this clarifies that within every thought-moment, one transcends such mundane measures and calculations; with each step, one passes through as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds, entering them all universally to reach the presence of those Buddhas and making offerings with exquisite ritual implements.

These various offerings clarify that the nature of fundamental wisdom is inherently all-pervasive; likewise, the functional activity of differentiated wisdom is also all-pervasive like that of fundamental wisdom. All offerings made to the Buddhas arise based on fundamental wisdom; by means of the seal of non-active fundamental wisdom, one gives rise to illusion-like functional activity, universally sealing all offering implements so that they are spontaneously accomplished without effort, because the function returns to its source.

Having clarified this eighth dedication, one previously employed the wisdom of the fundamental nature to practice the wisdom of differentiation, utilizing great compassion along with all worldly arts and crafts and the methods of the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) to benefit sentient beings.

Regarding the distinctions within this stage, although ultimate wisdom ultimately relies on its function, it is fundamentally such that, in its totality, there is no deliberate effort; things proceed spontaneously according to the Dharma, and the same applies to the teaching and transforming of sentient beings.
All other details are clearly explained in the sutra.
This is the dedication of the marks of *tathatā* (suchness), which takes the *pāramitā* of aspiration as its primary element and the other nine as its companions.
From the perspective of the gate of wisdom, it universally remedies all stages;

from the perspective of the gate of stages, it remedies the practice of effortful application (*sābhoga-prayoga*) upon entering the world, whereby effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) spontaneously functions with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

This stage clarifies that the various dharmas of those in training have already come to an end; because it brings about the convergence of compassion and wisdom into a single nature without duality, pervading everywhere, it is seen in one location within the assembly of Avalokiteśvara.

Within the second section, "The Gate of Advancing through the Inference of Virtue," there are eight and a half lines of sūtra text from "Just as the bodhisattvas... down to "...took his leave and departed. This is established according to five gates:

first, advancing through the inference of virtue; second, indicating the location and direction of the spiritual friend; third, citing the name of the city, Dravavatī; fourth, citing the name of the deity, Mahādeva; and fifth, paying respects and departing.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the city is named Drāvaṭī, which here means "Gate of Existence" (Yǒumén). It serves as the station for the Great Dharma Master presiding over this ninth dedication. Because it is equivalent to the "Dharma Prince's Station" within the ten abidings and the "Ninth Ground of Sublime Wisdom" within the ten grounds—both of which possess great Dharma gates that benefit sentient beings—the city is named "Gate of Existence."
Question: Why does one see a great celestial deity (*mahādeva*) at this stage? Answer:

It is to clarify that the ninth stage—characterized by liberation free from bondage and attachment, the purity of the wisdom of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-jñāna-viśuddhi*)—is the "deity. This wisdom has no dependence; it does not act through non-intentionality, yet it constantly responds to all phenomena. Therefore, it is called a "celestial deity" (*deva*).
This refers precisely to the Dry Spirit (Ganshen) of this realm; when one spontaneously attains this wisdom, it is the resonance with the Way.

All those who serve as spirits of heaven, earth, sun, moon, and the five planets; of famous mountains and great rivers, the Five Peaks and Four Tributaries; and of the rivers, seas, and the altars of land and grain—all these are the works of Bodhisattvas, for they cannot be accomplished by the power of ordinary worldly ghosts and spirits.
Qian is the Gate of Heaven, because through pure, stainless wisdom it manifests all phenomena.

Xun is the Door of Earth; as Xun represents wind, it moves to give birth to the myriad things and excels at sustaining them by bearing up the great earth. It is paired with the eldest daughter who presides over the Yin position, such as the Wind Deity of the First Assembly.
The present great celestial city is named "Possessing Gates" (Yǒumén). It manifests all existing dharma-gates like the pure body of a deity; this name is established based on its presiding lord.
Because it possesses great dharma-gates, the city is named "Possessing Gates."
Like the manifestations of the heavens, both good and evil are displayed;
like the heavens, which are without thought, rewards and punishments accord with the timing.
This celestial deity has non-action and non-activity as its essence, being pure wisdom, and all sentient beings share it equally.
From the delusion of one's own mind, ignorance and wisdom diverge into distinct categories; thus, perceptions differ and the pure and the defiled are each distinct.

If the mind is pure, it becomes a pure land, termed the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (paramārtha) or the Heaven of All-Knowledge (sarvajña); it is not like the heavens born of the five elements, which are subject to arising and ceasing.
This celestial deity is a *arhat* named Shen (Divine); he is designated as "divine" because he clarifies the progressive wisdom and spiritual penetration attained through the advancement of practice.

Within the first section on the Dharma-gate of entering the proper stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I know only this liberation-gate of the Cloud-Net," five thematic gates are established:
first, contemplating the instructions of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for the sake of advancement;...
Second, he gradually traveled to the city of Ayodhyā;
third, he inquired among the people as to the whereabouts of Mahādeva;
fourth, having learned his location, he went there to pay homage and present his request.

The Great Deity appeared during the fifth watch; with four long arms, he took the waters of the four great oceans to wash his face, held golden flowers to scatter over Sudhana, and preached the Dharma for him.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the passage stating that he extended his four long arms to take up the waters of the four great oceans to wash his own face clarifies that those who give rise to the great bodhicitta are difficult to find and difficult to encounter.
Taking the waters of the four great oceans to wash one's face clarifies that one who has resolved their mind (*cittotpāda*) must first wash their face before they may contemplate.

Holding various golden flowers to scatter over Sudhana clarifies that one must contemplate with reverence and honor those who can give rise to the great bodhicitta, for it is through such noble respect and offerings that they are honored.

Furthermore, the manifestation of the four long arms reaching out to grasp the waters of the four great oceans signifies that he gathers in sentient beings through the four immeasurable minds and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

As for using [the water] to wash his face, it clarifies that he constantly receives and sustains sentient beings by observing them through the application of wisdom with the water of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
As for the *puṇḍarīka* flower, it is the white lotus with a hundred petals; it is bright, upright, fragrant, and pure, such that all people delight in seeing it.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: with an upright mind and correct conduct, he is able to perfume and moisten the minds of others with the fragrance of the Dharma, causing them all to attain liberation, and all people delight in seeing him.

"Noble son, when I say that I have already accomplished the Dharma-gate of the Cloud-Net, it means that the clouds of great compassion universally cover all things, raining down the teachings like a net to filter and gather sentient beings."
Sudhana asked: "What is the scope of this Dharma-gate?
It is as explained below.

Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, mother-of-pearl, agate, great-flame jewels, stainless-treasury jewels, great-radiance jewels, jeweled necklaces, jeweled earrings, as well as jeweled crowns, bracelets, jeweled chains, pearl nets, various *maṇi* gems, flower garlands, incense, all kinds of clothing, musical instruments, and other requisites—all gathered like mountain peaks—and countless hundreds of thousands of billions of maidens, the Great Deva bestowed upon Sudhana, commanding him to give them away to gather and sustain sentient beings, as described at length in the sutra.
As well as the practices for teaching and benefiting sentient beings, are explained extensively in the sutra.

This is the ninth spiritual friend within the practice of the unbound, unattached dedication of liberation; here, the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is primary, with the other nine serving as its companions.
In terms of the gate of wisdom, it is identical in its treatment;

in terms of the gate of stages, it specifically treats the obstacle of lacking mastery in preaching the Dharma among the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, humans, and devas within the three realms, thereby enabling them to attain mastery, enter into spiritual wisdom and divine transformations, and freely turn the wheel of the True Dharma.

Within the second section, "Advancing through the Promotion of Virtue," there are ten lines of scripture from "As the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "...took their leave and departed. These are established according to five gates:
first, advancing through the promotion of virtue;
second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), stating that he is in the Bodhimaṇḍa within the kingdom of Magadha in Jambudvīpa.
Third, he mentions the name of the earth goddess, Good Friend, who is named Abiding;
fourth, he exhorts him to go there and inquire;
fifth, he pays homage and takes his leave.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: A question is asked:
Why does it not say "the south," but instead says "in the Bodhimaṇḍa of the kingdom of Magadha in Jambudvīpa, there is an earth goddess named Anūpaliptā"?

Answer: This is identical to the tenth stage, the Stage of Consecration (*abhiṣeka*), within the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*). It involves turning back from that liberation to enter into birth and death, so that the great compassion which accords with wisdom may bring benefit to sentient beings and achieve complete fulfillment.
It merely mentions Jambudvīpa without seeking it out in any particular or partial way; this is because it is a dedication through the dharma that is equal to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Furthermore, the Earth Goddess who presides over the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) represents the sense of universal inclusion; the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) follow this same pattern.
Regarding the kingdom of Magadha, it has already been explained previously.

As for the Earth Goddess who presides over the Bodhimaṇḍa: whereas the former [goddess] represents the celestial deity presiding over the perfection of wisdom, this one represents the Earth Goddess presiding over the perfection of compassion; this signifies that the earth is able to support all phenomena and nurture all sentient beings.

To symbolize the various Dharma-gates of manifesting compassion by taking birth in the lower realms, and to represent the nurturing, supporting, and carrying of sentient beings so that they may all be freed from the suffering of birth and death, the Earth Deity is used as the symbol.
It also clarifies that the Earth Goddess is the presiding deity for the Bodhisattva of this stage; she is the very goddess of this name, manifesting great compassion that sustains all things.
Regarding "in the field of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*): it is because at this stage, the five dharmas of awakening, wisdom, principle, compassion, and kindness are unified and fully perfected.
She is named the Goddess Anvaya-vyavasthita (Abiding in Succession) because she is perfectly complete in these five dharmas and remains unshakable.

Within the first section, "The Dharma Gate of Correct Entry into the Appropriate Stage," from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Dharma Gate of the Indestructible Treasury of Wisdom," five gates are established:
first, his gradual journeying toward the Bodhimanda in the kingdom of Magadha to visit the goddess Anvaya-vyavasthita.
Two million earth spirits were all present therein, together praising the supreme virtue of Sudhana;
three million earth spirits emitted great radiance that illuminated the great trichiliocosm, universally roaring to adorn the great earth;
fourthly, they manifested the roots of goodness from Sudhana’s past karma.
Fifth, he bestowed upon Sudhana the Dharma-door of the Bodhisattva’s Indestructible Treasury of Wisdom Liberation.
To explain the meaning according to the text: the hundred thousand earth deities represent the perfection of the practice of great compassion.
That "all emit radiance illuminating the trichiliocosm" signifies that their wisdom is full and their compassion is perfected.

Furthermore, that "the trichiliocosm simultaneously shakes and roars" signifies that when Sudhana reaches this stage, his wisdom and compassion are fully perfected; the karmic activities of birth-and-death and nirvana, as well as defilement and purity, have ceased, and because his merit has increased, its retribution manifests in such a manner.

As for the earth deity pressing the ground with her toe, causing hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* treasuries of jewels to spontaneously gush forth, this symbolizes that Sudhana’s own practice has reached its full extent; thus she presses the ground with her toe.

Furthermore, this indicates that Sudhana has begun his practice and entered this stage; once he has entered this stage, the retributive objects appear, and the manifested treasure-trove is precisely these.
First, the earth goddess’s own retributive fruit is presented, and subsequently, the sphere reached by Sudhana is presented.
I have attained the Bodhisattva liberation named "The Indestructible Treasury of Wisdom. This clarifies that compassion arises from wisdom and is therefore indestructible. As for "treasury" (garbha):

because the wisdom of the practice of the *dharmadhātu* contains all things without exception and compassion fulfills all needs without deficiency—rescuing every being who is not yet saved and saving every suffering that is not yet relieved—the pervasive presence of wisdom and compassion is termed a "treasury. To be non-attached to these practices is termed "liberation" (*vimukti*).

Regarding all such distinctions, because the great loving-kindness and great compassion practiced within wisdom are all bodhisattva practices, only the fundamental wisdom of the dharmakāya is the Buddha.

"Good son! I recall that since the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I have constantly followed the Bodhisattva with reverence and protection, observing all his mental activities. This clarifies that from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), he gives rise to discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) to practice the conduct of compassion.
It is explained in detail as follows in the subsequent text: "Good son!

In the distant past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru, there was an eon named Adorned and a world named Moon Banner. The Buddha there was named Wondrous Eye; it was from that Buddha that I obtained this Dharma-gate."

The phrase "serving all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields" clarifies that the practice of great compassion is profound and vast, such that one does not seek personal peace.
Even the manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment and entering nirvana is entirely encompassed within the bodhisattva practices;
for the Tathāgata Wondrous Eye and his world are, in their entirety, the very dharma of one's own wisdom and compassion.

Just as the *saṃbhogakāya* and *saṃbhogakṣetra* of Vairocana Tathāgata represent the fruition of the ultimate perfection of the Way, so too the practice of the Bodhisattva is without beginning or end; it is an ordinary, everyday affair that pervades the ten directions like Indra’s net.

From this point onward, regarding the discussion of the nearness and distance of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), all such instances primarily manifest the profound and vast nature of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), without being restricted by the number of lifetimes or the duration of eons (*kalpa*).
It is without beginning and without end, yet it does not transcend the limits of a single kṣaṇa; though it follows the world through many kalpas, from the perspective of wisdom there is no time.
This is the immeasurable dedication of the equal dharma-realm, which takes the perfection of wisdom as its sovereign and the other nine perfections as its companions.
From the perspective of the gates of wisdom, all stages universally counteract [afflictions];
from the perspective of the gates of the stages, they counteract supramundane wisdom and compassion by causing one to enter cyclic existence with mastery.
The following section concerns the advancement through merit to enter the first stage (*bhūmi*).
*New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll 37.
*New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll 38.
The Elder Li Tongxuan composed this account of Sudhana’s ten stages of spiritual friends; from this point onward,
his cultivation throughout the ten stages strictly follows the conduct of wisdom and compassion as established by the Earth Goddess Anala.

In the stages of the ten abidings and ten practices, the conduct of supramundane wisdom and compassion still remains largely hindered by purity. Through the ten dedications, great vows harmonize and integrate the two supramundane wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional, enabling one to constantly abide in the world while practicing great compassion; thus, this wisdom is neither pure nor defiled. Although dwelling in the world, the Bodhisattva is like a pure lotus flower that, though situated in water, remains unstained as it blooms with the finest color and fragrance; likewise, the Bodhisattva dwelling in the world has the supreme merit of the blooming flower of great compassionate conduct.

The nine lower celestial maidens and the single maiden Gopā are all of the female class; they are entirely of the mundane stream and do not belong to the monastic order. This clarifies that by means of the supramundane, one enters the mundane world—just as the method of dedication nurtures great compassion, which is symbolized by the female.

As for the Night-Spirit (*rātridevatā*): by means of illumination, she enters the great night of ignorance within the world; by means of the Dharma, she enlightens ordinary beings, causing their understanding to blossom.
Because she enters the mundane realm with wisdom that transcends all entanglements to receive and guide sentient beings, she is called a "Spirit" (*devatā*).

Furthermore, through the practice of compassion, they abide within the cycles of day and night throughout heaven and earth, establishing themselves as a divine station; because they uphold worldly laws to nourish sentient beings, they employ family precepts to transform those of initial resolve whose wisdom is not yet matured.

If, through the perfection of wisdom, they were to become identical to worldly people, they would manifest as non-Buddhists skilled in arts and crafts; yet, with wisdom increased and compassion made sublime, they enter the ranks of the spirits and deities of the various heavens and earths, taking birth to uphold worldly dharmas and protect sentient beings.

Because his numinous wisdom manifests differently throughout the ten directions, yet his essential body never departs from the assemblies of all Buddhas, nor does it destroy the Buddha-bodies manifested throughout the ten directions.
One should know that by practicing and studying in this sequence, one’s efforts will not be obstructed.

Within the second section, "Advancing by Inferring Virtue," from the passage beginning with "Just as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas" down to "took their leave and departed," there are seven and a half lines of scripture, which are established according to five gates;
the first is "Advancing by Inferring Virtue."
Second, he indicates the location of the spiritual friend, saying it is here in Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Magadha;
third, he mentions the name of the city, Kapilavastu;
fourth, he mentions the name of the night goddess, the spiritual friend, Vasantī.
Five: The words of respectful departure.

Regarding the explanation of the text: as for the name of the city, Kapilavastu, this means "yellow" (kapila). In ancient times, there was a sage with yellow hair (*kapila*) who practiced the path of immortals here; thus, the city was named after him.
Within the symbolism of the Dharma, the wisdom of the night goddess corresponds to the Middle Way; she is associated with the central palace and the color yellow.
Yellow is the color of auspicious merit. Because the *arhat* bodhisattvas harbor pure dharmas within while manifesting yellow externally—the color of merit and virtue—the city is named "Yellow."
The kingdom of Magadha is the place where the Tathāgata manifested the attainment of the path to Bodhi; this clarifies that by advancing through these stages, one reunites with the fundamental stage.

It is like the first stage among the Ten Abodes at the summit of Mount Sumeru, where, through the power of skillful means and meditative concentration, one reunites with the essence of the Buddha’s wisdom—the sublime principle that has emerged from the entanglements.

Among these ten stages, the stage of the Bodhisattva in the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) is so designated because one encounters the Tathāgata’s wisdom within great compassion that has entered the bonds [of saṃsāra], thereby attaining the fruit of enlightenment (*bodhi-phala*).
Subsequent cases are to be understood by analogy with this.
The deity named Vasanta-ādi means "Lord of Spring Growth" in this language; for this deity presides over the spring growth of all the sprouts and crops of sentient beings.
In the exposition of the dharmas, this refers primarily to the Bodhisattva of the First Ground ascending and causing the sprouts of the myriad practices to grow like those in spring.
Because they are able to constantly dispel the darkness for all sentient beings within the ocean of birth and death, they are named "Night-Goddesses" (Rātridevatā).
Furthermore, they are called "devas" (heavenly beings) because of their mastery over wisdom.

Within the section on the primary correct entry into the dharma-gate of the respective stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this liberation gate of the light of the Dharma that shatters the darkness of ignorance in all sentient beings," five gates are established:
first, reflecting upon and advancing according to the instructions of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Second, he gradually traveled on until he reached that city; having entered through the eastern gate, he stood there for no long time before seeing the sun set.
Third, he recollected the four kinds of sublime virtues of the spiritual friend.

Fourth, he saw the night goddess in the sky, seated upon a lion throne within a precious pavilion and a fragrant lotus treasury; her body was golden in color, her eyes and hair were deep blue, and her appearance was dignified and majestic.
Fifth, Sudhana saw that night goddess prostrate her body upon the ground to pay homage to her and request what he sought.
From the moment he beheld the night goddess, six further points were established:
first, he saw that the night goddess’s physical form was upright and graceful, her skin golden in color, and her eyes and hair deep blue-black.
Second, he saw that the night goddess was wearing crimson robes, a Brahma crown, and necklaces;
third, he saw that star-like images were brilliantly manifest upon her body;

fourth, he saw that from every single pore of the night goddess there emerged immeasurable sentient beings being transformed and delivered according to their faculties and given the Dharma—some born in the heavens or the human realm, some as śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—their attainments being diverse.
Fifth, the night goddess manifested various sovereign powers of the bodhisattva samādhis;
sixth, Sudhana prostrated himself on the ground to pay homage at the feet of the night goddess, joined his palms, and requested the dharma-gate he sought.

This realm, with its physical dimensions and pores, is the body of the Dharma-realm; it is the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm’s sphere of activity. It causes practitioners to emulate and study it, reaching completion throughout the ten directions.
To provide an illustration for the sake of thorough instruction, one must first grasp its general portion (*bhāga*), for this is the portion within the whole.

Since the realm of wisdom and the timing do not shift, there is a complete progression through the stages (*bhūmi*). Within this progression toward the sought-after goal, seventeen gates are further established:
first, Sudhana’s aspiration to rely upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to obtain the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha’s merits.
Second, the night goddess praised Sudhana and bestowed upon him the dharma she herself practices.
Third, she raised the name of the dharma-gate, called "The Bodhisattva’s Liberation of the Radiant Light that Shatters the Darkness of Ignorance of All Sentient Beings."
4. From "Good son, regarding sentient beings of evil wisdom" onwards, [the text] sets forth the practice of great compassion as personally undertaken by [the deity].
5. The night goddess speaks twenty-one verses, using the Dharma she herself knows to exhort Sudhana to practice and enter [the path].
Sixth, Sudhana asked the Night Goddess how long it had been since she first resolved her mind [on enlightenment].
Seventh, he further asked the Night Goddess how long it had been since she attained this Dharma-door.
Eighth, she recounted from a past world-system, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru, the duration of the eons since she herself first resolved her mind.
Ninth, he mentions the name of the kalpa as *Śāntaprabha*.
Tenth, he mentions the name of the world-system as *Utpannasudharatna*.
Eleventh, he mentions the name of the four continents as *Ratnacandrapradīpa*.
Twelfth: The city was named Lotus Light, and the king was named Good Dharma Deliverer.
Thirteenth: To the east of the city, beneath a great Bodhi tree, there was a Buddha named King of the Thunderous Sound of All Dharmas, who had attained perfect enlightenment.
Fourteenth, she mentions a night goddess named Pure Moon, who announced the appearance of a Buddha.

Fifteenth, she mentions herself as the queen consort of a king named Dharma-Wisdom Moon; because she made offerings to that Buddha, she gave rise to the bodhicitta. For as many eons as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru, she was not born in the evil realms and planted various roots of goodness. For eighty times the number of eons equal to the atoms in Mount Sumeru, she constantly experienced peace and happiness, always cultivating roots of goodness in the presence of that Buddha and his bodhisattvas, yet she had not yet fulfilled the bodhisattva roots of goodness.

Sixteen thousand kalpas further back, prior to the Bhadrakalpa, there was a kalpa named Aśoka and a world named Vimalaprabhā; five hundred Buddhas appeared therein, and I was the daughter of a householder named Prajñāprabhā.

That original night goddess was born in the city of King Wondrous Banner as a night goddess; she has now come to shake my abode, emit light, and manifest signs, praising all the merits of Tathāgata Wondrous Eye, acting as a guide to lead me to the Buddha’s presence.
As soon as I saw the Buddha, I attained a samādhi called "The Light-Wheel of Wisdom for Manifesting the Seeing of Buddhas and Taming Sentient Beings Throughout the Three Times.

Because I attained the power of this seventeenth samādhi, I was able to recollect all the Buddhas who appeared throughout kalpas as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru, and I heard the sublime Dharma from those Buddhas. By virtue of hearing that sublime Dharma, I immediately attained this liberation called "The Radiance of the Dharma that Shatters the Darkness of Ignorance of All Sentient Beings."
Having attained this liberation, he immediately saw his own body pervading worlds as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields.
The above clarifies the duration of his initial resolve: it has already passed through kalpas as numerous as the atoms in eighty-one Mount Sumerus, and furthermore, ten thousand kalpas.

After kalpas as numerous as the atoms within one Sumeru Mountain, and further ten thousand kalpas, he finally attained a samādhi through the roots of goodness cultivated in the presence of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; it is named "The Radiant Wheel of Wisdom for Seeing Buddhas, Taming Sentient Beings, and the Three Times."

Furthermore, by recollecting that throughout the kalpas of mindfulness one beheld Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within all Mount Sumerus, and by hearing the sublime Dharma practiced by those Buddhas, one finally attained this liberation door of the light of the Dharma that shatters the darkness of ignorance of all sentient beings; it was precisely during these kalpas of mindfulness that one attained this door of the light of the Dharma that shatters the darkness of ignorance of all sentient beings. This clarity regarding the duration of attaining the Dharma—totaling eighty-two kalpas as numerous as the atoms within Mount Sumerus—is the measure of how long ago this was achieved.

Furthermore, for another ten thousand kalpas, throughout those kalpas she constantly practiced the bodhisattva path in a female body, clearly cultivating a profound and deep heart of great compassion over the vast expanse of these long kalpas.
By means of the final mindfulness, the three periods of time are encompassed within a single thought-moment, such that every moment contains many kalpas.

Just as one first sets out to travel to worlds as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-fields, making offerings to and serving every Buddha in each of those worlds; then sets out to travel to worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred Buddha-fields; then a thousand, then a hundred thousand, and finally to Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields—travelling everywhere to serve them and receiving all the Dharma-gates they teach; thus gradually increasing until one fills the entire Dharma-realm of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas and teaching and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
This refers to the first stage, where "a hundred" is the primary number, thereby filling all Buddha-fields throughout the infinite dharma-realm of the ten directions.

This differs from the three vehicles, which merely speak of a hundred Buddhas, without mentioning matters such as a hundred Buddha-fields as numerous as atoms, or unspeakably many Buddha-fields as numerous as atoms.
The remaining details are fully explained in the sutra.
The intent is to clarify that one practices compassion in the world with profound depth, without seeking the mind of world-transcendence even for the exhaustion of kalpas.
This is the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), where the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is primary and the other nine are its companions.

This clarifies the gate of entering the mundane world while sharing its entanglements to nurture great compassion, thereby fulfilling the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) to the point of completion.

Because she cultivates loving-kindness (maitrī), she is frequently born without being separated from a female body; this signifies that she possesses no signs of transcendence from the world and remains constantly within the flow of the mundane.
Within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), this section generally clarifies the gate of dwelling in the world to nurture great compassion.

The ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) do not possess the appearance of renunciants; they are all goddesses. This indicates that when they originally resolved to attain *bodhicitta* over many lifetimes, they were also in female bodies. This serves to represent that the ten stages consist of entering the realm of sentient beings to nurture the practice of great compassion. Furthermore, it represents that women are capable of nurturing children and grandchildren without weariness, thereby illustrating how Bodhisattvas nourish sentient beings.

In the second section, "Advancing through the Deduction of Virtue," from the passage beginning with "Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "took their leave and departed," there are fifteen and a half lines of prose and ten lines of verse. Within this, five topical gates are established: first, advancing through the deduction of virtue; second, indicating the location where the spiritual friend resides, stating that within the Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha here in Jambudvīpa, there is a night goddess named Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā; third, [the night goddess] appearing before the bodhisattva and teaching the Dharma; fourth, the bodhisattva’s inquiry regarding the names of the night goddesses; and fifth, the night goddess’s instruction on the names of the night goddesses. Among these, the first gate—advancing through the deduction of virtue—is as follows: at that time, the bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it was wonderful how the night goddess Ratnaprabhāśrī, having been exhorted by the Buddha, rose from her seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, bowed at his feet, withdrew to one side, and sat cross-legged upon the ground. World-Honored One, what is the name of this samādhi? By means of what dharma did she attain such a state? The Buddha told Vajragarbha: "This samādhi is called the 'Unobstructed Light of All Dharmas. It is by means of this dharma that she attained such a state. Vajragarbha then asked the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what is the name of this samādhi? How many kinds of dharmas does it encompass? What is its essence? What is its function? What is its cause? What is its fruit? What is its benefit? What is its excellence? What is its purity? What is its entry? What is its practice? What is its completion? What is its power? What is its manifestation? What is its field? What is its sphere? What is its support? What is its reliance? What is its dwelling? What is its abiding? What is its departure? What is its arrival? What is its path? What is its vehicle? What is its destination? What is its fruit? What is its maturation? What is its liberation? What is its attainment? What is its realization? What is its mastery? What is its perfection? What is its fulfillment? What is its ultimate goal? What is its finality? The Buddha told Vajragarbha: "This samādhi is called the 'Unobstructed Light of All Dharmas. It encompasses immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of dharmas. Its essence is the non-arising of all dharmas. Its function is to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings. Its cause is the roots of goodness planted in past lives. Its fruit is the attainment of the stage of non-retrogression. Its benefit is the protection of all bodhisattvas. Its excellence is the transcendence of all worlds. Its purity is the purification of the three karmas. Its entry is the penetration of the nature of all dharmas. Its practice is the cultivation of the six perfections. Its completion is the fulfillment of the four immeasurables. Its power is the subduing of Māras and adversaries. Its manifestation is the display of various transformations. Its field is the realm of all Buddhas. Its sphere is the realm of empty space. Its support is the great compassion for sentient beings. Its reliance is the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Its dwelling is the concentration of the mind. Its abiding is the stability of the Dharma-body. Its departure is the relinquishing of all attachments. Its arrival is the reaching of the place of awakening. Its path is the eightfold noble path. Its vehicle is the Great Vehicle of the Mahāyāna. Its destination is the city of Nirvana. Its fruit is the attainment of the three bodies. Its maturation is the ripening of all roots of goodness. Its liberation is the freedom from all fetters. Its attainment is the realization of the truth of suffering. Its realization is the understanding of the origin of suffering. Its mastery is the cessation of suffering. Its perfection is the cultivation of the path. Its fulfillment is the completion of all virtues. Its ultimate goal is the exhaustion of all outflows. Its finality is the end of birth and death. Vajragarbha then asked the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what is the name of the night goddess who attained this samādhi? Where does she dwell? What is her practice? What is her vow? The Buddha told Vajragarbha: "The name of this night goddess is Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā. She dwells within the Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha here in Jambudvīpa. Her practice is the service of all Buddhas. Her vow is to lead all sentient beings to the path of awakening. Vajragarbha then said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I wish to see that night goddess. May the Buddha grant me permission to go and pay homage to her. The Buddha told Vajragarbha: "You may go as you please. That night goddess has already known of your coming and is waiting for you. At that time, the bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having received the Buddha’s permission, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, bowed at his feet, and took his leave. He then proceeded toward the south, passing through many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields, until he arrived at the kingdom of Magadha here in Jambudvīpa. There, he saw the night goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā dwelling within the Bodhimaṇḍa. She was surrounded by a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of night goddesses. She was seated upon a lion throne made of various jewels, adorned with a canopy of celestial flowers, and attended by celestial maidens. She was emitting a light that surpassed the radiance of the sun and moon, illuminating the entire world. Vajragarbha approached her, paid homage at her feet, and sat to one side. The night goddess then taught him the Dharma, saying: "Vajragarbha, you should know that the bodhisattva path is vast and profound, and cannot be traversed in a short time. You must cultivate it over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas. Why is this? Because the bodhisattva path is the source of all dharmas. It is the mother of all Buddhas. It is the foundation of all virtues. It is the guide for all sentient beings. It is the treasury of all wisdoms. It is the vessel for all merits. It is the bridge for crossing the river of birth and death. It is the ladder for ascending to the stage of Buddhahood. Therefore, you should diligently practice and never abandon it. Vajragarbha then asked the night goddess: "What are the names of the night goddesses who have previously served the Buddha? The night goddess replied: "There are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of night goddesses. Their names are: Moon-Light Night Goddess, Sun-Light Night Goddess, Jewel-Light Night Goddess, Lotus-Light Night Goddess, Flame-Light Night Goddess, Star-Light Night Goddess, Cloud-Light Night Goddess, Wind-Light Night Goddess, Water-Light Night Goddess, Earth-Light Night Goddess, Space-Light Night Goddess, Wisdom-Light Night Goddess, Compassion-Light Night Goddess, Joy-Light Night Goddess, Peace-Light Night Goddess, Liberation-Light Night Goddess, Awakening-Light Night Goddess, Dharma-Light Night Goddess, Truth-Light Night Goddess, Virtue-Light Night Goddess, Merit-Light Night Goddess, and so forth. These are but a few examples; there are in fact immeasurable numbers. Vajragarbha then asked the night goddess: "How should we honor these night goddesses? The night goddess replied: "You should honor them with a pure heart, respect them with reverence, serve them with devotion, and follow their instructions with diligence. You should also recite their names and contemplate their virtues. Vajragarbha then said to the night goddess: "I have now seen the night goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā and heard her teach the Dharma. I am deeply grateful for her grace. I shall now take my leave and return. Having spoken thus, he circumambulated the night goddess three times, bowed at her feet, and took his leave. He then returned to the presence of the Buddha, paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. The Buddha then praised him, saying: "Vajragarbha, it is well that you have come back safely. You have seen the night goddess and heard the Dharma. You should now propagate this teaching and do not let it be lost. Vajragarbha then said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I have now understood the depth of the night goddess’s virtue. I shall propagate this teaching throughout
Third, Sudhana spoke verses in praise of the virtues of the night goddess Praśāntaviniścayaprāptā;
fourth, having spoken the verses, Sudhana prostrated at the feet of the night goddess;
fifth, he took his leave and departed.
This night goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā was the teacher who awakened her during the night when she was the queen of King Vāsantaprabha in a past kalpa.
For eighty-two kalpas, as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru, plus another ten thousand kalpas, she constantly served as her teacher, guiding and instructing her just as described above.

The reason for not mentioning the "Southern Region" but directly stating "within the Bodhimaṇḍa of the kingdom of Magadha" is to signify that the compassion within the cycle of birth and death at the site of practice does not depart from the essence of bodhi to exist as a separate worldly compassionate activity.

Thus, the statement that Jambudvīpa and the kingdom of Magadha are within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in this world signifies that this very world is within the bodhimaṇḍa. It clarifies that the practice of compassion within the world is precisely the practice carried out within the bodhicitta, and that there is nothing separate from it; it signifies that the conduct of great loving-kindness and great compassion, though appearing amidst worldly entanglements, is one with the essence of awakening.
The fruit of clarity acts as the cause; thus, cause and effect are one.

As it is said in the verses of Sudhana’s praise to the Night Goddess: "Having remained in the evil realms for many kalpas, I have finally been able to see and hear you; you should likewise receive me with joy, for this shall extinguish my afflictions."

This clarifies that the essential practice of great compassion involves dwelling within the ocean of suffering in birth and death for many kalpas without weariness, for it is only through such compassionate conduct that it can be fully accomplished.
Clearly cultivating the supramundane path, it manifests in an instant;
practicing great kindness and great compassion, one does not limit oneself by the number of kalpas.
All other matters are as clearly explained in the text itself.

Many kalpas are defined in terms of the conventional, while a single thought-moment is defined in terms of the ultimate; these two aspects are harmoniously integrated within their own essence without obstruction. Thus, many kalpas exist within a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment exists within many kalpas, because the essences of the conventional and the ultimate do not obstruct one another.

Within the first section on the Dharma-gate of entering the specific stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I have only attained this Bodhisattva liberation gate of the Universal Gait of the Joy of Tranquil Samādhi," five topical divisions are established: first, reflecting upon and advancing according to the instructions of the spiritual friend; second, gradually traveling to the abode of the night goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā to pay respects and make a formal request; third, the night goddess expounding various teachings for Sudhana; and fourth, the night goddess describing her own practice—the Bodhisattva liberation gate of the Universal Gait of the Joy of Tranquil Samādhi—and bestowing it upon Sudhana.

The Five Night Goddesses truly spoke this Dharma-gate for the purpose of universally beholding all Buddhas of the three periods of time, their lands, and their assemblies at the sites of enlightenment, and for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: as for the name of this dharma-gate, “The Bodhisattva’s Liberation Gate of the Joyful Universal Pacing of Quiescent Samādhi,” this is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Taking the Dharma-body as the essence of discipline, all objective realms are inherently meditative (*dhyāna*) by their very nature.
The dhyāna of the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is the self-pervasion of wisdom; because wisdom pervades everywhere, one traverses all realms universally.

Constantly abiding in birth and death, one practices great compassion, nurturing within oneself the essence of great compassion, for within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one possesses the bodhisattva practices that pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*.

The Bodhisattva’s liberation door of "peaceful meditative concentration and joyful universal wandering" clarifies the joy of the Dharma of Bodhi within the midst of birth and death; it also enables the fulfillment of a Bodhisattva’s great compassion and the universal practice of the path of Samantabhadra. This clarifies the conduct of a Bodhisattva’s great compassion within the Bodhimanda of one's own mind.

As for the night goddess named Universal Virtue Pure Light (*Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā*): she is called "Pure Light" because her wisdom and compassion pervade and illuminate the long night of sentient beings;
she is called "Virtue" because she possesses the compassionate nurturing of worldly beings.
That wisdom is non-active; its nature is spontaneously pervasive and all-encompassing, and is thus termed "spirit" (*shen*).

This essence of dhyāna, because it employs the bodhisattva practice of great quiescence, the unimpeded great compassion within the dharma-realm, and its tranquil yet pervasive function, is designated by the name of the "fourth dhyāna" in accordance with its functional application.

The Sūtra states: "To clearly understand and achieve mastery, to increase contemplation and observation, to be firm and adorned, to give rise to no deluded conceptualizations, to rescue and protect all sentient beings with great compassion, and to cultivate the first dhyāna with a single unmoving mind"—this is because the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya, when correctly mindful of and directed toward the deliverance of all sentient beings, is not called a deluded conceptualization, as it does not take unwholesome dharmas as its object.

Because all objects of perception distinguished within the principle of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) take wisdom as their support, they constitute the gateway to great compassion; since they are untainted by worldly habits, they are not termed "delusive thoughts" (vikalpa).

Furthermore, it is said that one who "quiets all mental karma, encompasses all sentient beings with the power of wisdom, and cultivates the second dhyāna with courageous vigor and a joyful heart" quiets all mental karma; this refers to a partial compassion rather than a universal mind.

Regarding "the mind of joy and gladness": because one practices the conduct of a bodhisattva in these two stages, and because one finds delight in the Dharma through the compassion of the *dharmatā* of enlightenment and the methods for gathering and transforming all sentient beings, it is called the second dhyāna.

Regarding the contemplation that all sentient beings, by their very nature, are free from birth and death while practicing the third dhyāna: this clarifies that one universally perceives all sentient beings as having the same bodhi-dharmatā-nature, whose self-essence is liberation, as the substance of dhyāna; it is not because one sees only one’s own body as possessing the substance of dhyāna.

One cultivates the third dhyāna for the sake of the collective liberation of all sentient beings. Regarding the scriptural passage which states, "All sentient beings, by their very nature, weary of and seek to leave birth and death, thus cultivate the third dhyāna," the phrase "by their very nature weary of and seeking to leave birth and death" is an error of the translators; it should rather read, "Because the nature of all sentient beings is inherently free from birth and death, they cultivate the third dhyāna."

Regarding those who cultivate the fourth dhyāna to extinguish all the suffering and feverish afflictions of sentient beings: these Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle, from their first resolve, mount the vehicle of the fundamental wisdom of the Tathāgata’s bodhicitta. They cultivate the practice of great compassion within the ocean of birth and death, and through contemplation, they penetrate to the fundamental source of sentient beings, seeing that it is one with the ocean of wisdom—the essence and function of the Tathāgata’s bodhi. Thus, they constantly employ the sun of the wisdom of the dharmadhātu to dispel the darkness of delusion for all sentient beings during the night of ignorance and confusion.
Unlike those of the three preceding vehicles who separately seek the fruits of their own purity and happiness, they have never actually attained the ultimate fruit of all-encompassing bliss.
Therefore, it is said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* unifies the three vehicles into one, for they come to take refuge in this Dharma.
All subsequent gateways of practice for benefiting sentient beings are clearly elucidated in detail according to the sutra.

This constitutes the upholding of the supreme ten wholesome precepts, taking the essence of bodhi as the substance of the precepts, and is symbolized by the night goddess dwelling within the field of enlightenment.

Taking the bodhicitta that has perfected great compassion as the essence of the precepts; taking the boatman as the essence of the precepts during the ten dedications; taking the various arts and crafts of the youth Śakradevendra as the essence of the precepts during the ten practices; taking the observation of the self-nature purity of the twelve links of dependent origination by the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha as the essence of the precepts during the ten abidings; and here, in this second stage, taking the night goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā within the Bodhimaṇḍa as the essence of the precepts—this clarifies that within bodhi, wisdom abides in the world while cultivating the gateway of compassion as the essence of the precepts.

This is the second spiritual friend within the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), which takes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) as its primary focus and the other nine perfections as its companions.

It remedies the obstacle of being unable to exercise mastery while abiding in the ocean of birth and death through the cultivation of bodhicitta and the practice of compassion; it causes one to attain such mastery. This clarifies how the integration of awakening and saṃsāra—which were previously both lacking in mastery—now brings about mastery.
In this stage, one contemplates the three realms as being of the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing through the essence of bodhi;

this is the contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Second, within the section on "Advancing by Inferring Virtue," from the passage beginning with "As the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas... down to "took his leave and departed," there are twenty-five lines of scripture consisting of both prose and verse.

Within this, five topical gates are established: first, inferring virtue to cause Sudhana to advance; second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend by stating that not far from here, to the right of the Bodhimaṇḍa, there is a night goddess named Pramuditanayanajagadvirocanā; third, the celestial queen Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā again speaking verses for Sudhana; fourth, Sudhana prostrating at the feet of the goddess Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā; and fifth, taking his leave and departing.
The commentary states:

"Not far from this" clarifies that, with bodhi as the second [stage], the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is situated within the field of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); since this third perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) likewise takes bodhi as its practice of patience, it is "not far from this."

Regarding "on the right side of the site of enlightenment": the right is the position of wisdom and the left is the gate of compassion. This clarifies that one accomplishes patience and loving-kindness by initiating practice through bodhicitta; for without patience there is no compassion, thus clarifying that it is because one possesses patience that one is able to practice loving-kindness and compassion.
There is a night goddess named Joyful Eyes Who Observes Sentient Beings; her compassion within patience is called "Joyful Eyes," and her non-abandonment of sentient beings is called "Observation."

Furthermore, regarding the observation of faculties for the purpose of gathering and transforming beings, that which is called the "night goddess who observes sentient beings" takes bodhi as the essence of her precepts in the preceding stage; she completely purifies the desirous mind within the three realms, the desire for the distracted mind of the lower realm, and the desire for the joyful, meditative, pure mind of the two upper realms.

This third stage, the Radiant Ground (Prabhākari-bhūmi), is so named because by cultivating the eight dhyānas, one can accord with those dhyānas while remaining unstained by their nature, and can accord with the desire realm while remaining unstained by its nature; thus it is called the Radiant Ground and the Night Goddess (Rātridevatā).
Their wisdom accords with reality, and thus they are called "divine" (*śiva*).
Within the three realms, they teach and transform sentient beings with sovereign ease, and are therefore named "heavenly" (*deva*).

Furthermore, it clarifies that each of these positions specifically subdues the habitual tendencies of desire within the three realms, bringing them to purity; by attaining the common and distinct characteristics within the three realms, they are named the "Night-Heavenly Deity who Observes Sentient Beings."
In the fourth stage, one is born into the family of all Buddhas;
in the fifth stage, one practices worldly arts and skills;

in the sixth stage, the three gates of liberation, cessation, and the supernormal powers of meditative concentration manifest before one, whereby one attains mastery over quiescent and active supernormal powers to universally gather and transform sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Because from this point upward, one attains mastery over the mundane within the supramundane, from the seventh stage onward one enters mastery over the mundane.
This same potential is present within the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), as it is also the case for the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) and the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).

Furthermore, there are differences in their functional scope (*śakti-bhāga*). For instance, within the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*), one immediately dedicates the liberation attained through the ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) and the ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*) into the mundane world.
Upon reaching the seventh stage of Dedication, one ascends and attains penetration into the state of the Sages, whereupon one beholds Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva of Right Aspiration.
Reaching the ninth and tenth stages of Dedication, one returns once more to the mundane world, where wisdom penetrates the divine and sustains the realm of sentient beings.
Up to the ninth bhūmi, these are all divine stations;

the tenth bhūmi is represented by Gopā, the Śākya woman who was the wife of the Tathāgata when he was a prince, signifying that the joy of the Dharma born of compassion for the tenth bhūmi is already fulfilled.

After the ten dedications mentioned above, one cultivates the stage of compassion within the world; this continues until the second bhūmi, where the deity Universal Virtue Pure Light (Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā) represents the ultimate limit of a portion of the essence of bodhi within the Bodhimanda.

From this second bhūmi onwards, up to the third bhūmi, one initiates activity within the Bodhimanda, practicing both the common and distinct aspects of each dhyāna realm. It is only in the sixth bhūmi that one begins to initiate activity from within the essence of bodhi, such that quiescence and activity become sovereign.
In the seventh bhūmi, one exclusively cultivates compassion and wisdom within the midst of entanglements to bring them to full perfection.

It is only upon reaching the eighth stage that wisdom and compassion begin to function spontaneously and effortlessly; yet even then, one must still rely on mindfulness of one's original vows and the Buddha’s empowerment for them to become fully manifest.
It is only at the ninth and tenth stages that one begins to train in the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of a Buddha.

Having previously expounded the stages of the ten levels of faith from the Hall of Universal Radiance, I shall next ascend to explain the five stages of progress toward enlightenment. Yet, fearing that within the teachings expressed through words, one might fail to fully realize the meaning of the similarities and differences in the progression through these five stages, I shall now proceed.

Within this "Dharmadhātu Chapter," the names of the spiritual friends sought by Sudhana, their residences and native lands, the names of their cities, their ages, their gardens and fruits of retribution, their directions (north, south, east, and west), their distances (near and far), and their genders (male and female)—whether they be sages or ordinary beings, devas or humans, dragons or spirits—are all represented through both the Dharma and its images. This is intended to enable the assembly to comprehend the sequence of progressive practices according to the holy intent, ensuring that students may skillfully attain what is appropriate, without error or stagnation in their cultivation.
Within this section, there are thirteen verses praising the Tathāgata’s realm that the Night Goddess Pramuditanayanajagadvirocanā is able to know, as clearly elucidated in the full text.

First, regarding the primary entry into the dharma-gate of this specific stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this liberation-gate of the Banner of Universal Joy," this gate is divided into five sections:
first, contemplating the instructions of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to advance further.
First, Sudhana intended to go to the night goddess Pramuditanayanajagadvirocanā;
second, through the night goddess’s supernatural empowerment, Sudhana was made to know that approaching spiritual friends brings great benefit;

third, having received this empowerment, Sudhana quickly gave rise to this thought, realizing for himself that by approaching spiritual friends he could courageously and diligently cultivate the path to omniscience.
Fifth, Sudhana goes to the goddess Rātriṃcarā (Joyful Eye) to observe the sphere of her activity in gathering and transforming sentient beings for their benefit.

From the passage beginning with "The goddess he saw was sitting upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury in the assembly of the Tathāgata" and extending below, the text is divided into twelve sections.

First, from "At that time, after the youth Sudhana had formed this thought" up to "causing them all to rejoice and obtain benefit," there are five and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on the initial observation of the goddess Rātriṃcarā’s sphere of gathering and transforming sentient beings.

2. From "namely, emitting clouds of immeasurable transformation bodies that fill all worlds throughout the ten directions" down to "thus proclaiming the various methods of practice for all bodhisattvas for the sake of benefiting others," there are eighty-three and a half lines of scripture explaining the section on gathering and transforming sentient beings by means of the ten pāramitās.

3. From "Furthermore, from each and every pore, there emerge immeasurable clouds of bodies of various sentient beings" down to "clouds of similar bodies of the Directional Guardian Deities (*digpāla*) pervading the ten directions and filling the Dharma-realm," there are seventeen and a half lines of scripture clarifying the section on how the Bodhisattva Joyful Eye (*Nayanānanda*) manifests transformation bodies from her pores throughout the ten directions to gather in sentient beings who share their same class.

4. From the passage "manifesting various sounds before all sentient beings" down to "the merit accumulated from the first production of the thought of enlightenment," there are eight lines of scripture. These clarify how the Night Goddess Pramuditanayanajagadvirocanā manifests voices that pervade the ten directions, and they describe the portion of the goddess's merit from her initial production of the thought of enlightenment—including her attendance upon various Buddhas and her practice of the ocean of *pāramitās*.

5. From "What is called serving all spiritual friends" down to "causing immeasurable sentient beings to abide in the stage of the Tathāgata," there are forty-six and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the section on the realm of the goddess Priyadarśanā’s practice and her offerings to the Buddhas for the sake of transforming sentient beings, as spoken through the sounds manifested previously.

6. From the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana saw and heard all the aforementioned marvelous events" down to "because he was capable of practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva," there are eight and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the section on the liberation door called the "Power of Sovereign Delight in the Banner of Universal Joy of Inconceivable Great Might," which is the dharma practiced by the Night Goddess Priyadarśanā, as the youth Sudhana beheld the aforementioned realm of transformation and attained entry into it.

7. From the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" and extending for one and a half lines of scripture, there is the section clarifying Sudhana’s recitation of verses in praise of the goddess Ratnaprabhāśrī’s merits.
8. Within these verses, there are ten lines of verse which clarify the formal presentation of the intended meaning of the eulogy, praising the night goddess’s virtue and realization.
9. From "At that time, the youth Sudhana" onwards, the three lines of scripture clarify the section on Sudhana’s inquiry regarding the duration since the night goddess attained liberation.
10. From "I recall a past life" onwards, up to "his mind never forgets," there are twenty-six lines of verse clarifying the night goddess’s response regarding the duration of her abiding in this eon.

Eleventh, from the verse beginning with "From this point on, I shall make offerings to ten billion nayutas of Buddhas" down to "thoroughly knowing that all ten dharma-realms are without distinction," there are sixty-five stanzas that answer the question regarding the duration and number of Buddhas to whom Sudhana has made offerings throughout his dwelling in the kalpa.

Within this section on offerings, there are eleven segments; the first ten segments each contain the names of ten Buddhas, while the final segment contains the name of one Buddha. These are all assigned according to the progressive advancement through the eleven stages (*bhūmi*): one stage is assigned ten Buddha names, ten stages are assigned one hundred Buddha names, and the eleventh stage is assigned one Buddha name. This clarifies that the latter single [stage] subsumes the many preceding ones, demonstrates that a single stage possesses the practices of all ten stages, and shows that the ten *pāramitās* are mutually interwoven to form them.

First, regarding those who thereafter make offerings to ten billion nayutas of Buddhas: this is assigned to the first stage, the Joyous (Pramuditā), because it clarifies that the beginning subsumes the end, because the beginning contains much, and because the vows are vast.

The first stage clarifies the arousal of the mind through superior vows; because it is the very beginning and occurs most frequently, it carries the meaning of a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
This first stage is the "first stage" within the second stage, and so on, up to the tenth stage being the "tenth stage" within the third stage.

Regarding "The Ocean of the First Buddha’s Merits": this is the first stage within the third bhūmi, where the gate of *dāna-pāramitā* (the perfection of giving) is the primary factor and the other nine are its companions.

Since this position contains the ten *pāramitās* of all preceding and succeeding stages within the third bhūmi, the other positions are likewise subsumed according to this pattern. This is because they interpenetrate like the jewels of Indra’s net—one entering many; thus, it clarifies that the essence of patience (*kṣānti*) universally encompasses both cause and fruit.
This is the case for each stage within the five stages.

Regarding the second, the realm of Universal Jewel Light, whose eon is named Deva-Vijaya: this corresponds to the second stage, the Stainless (Vimalā), because the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) constitutes its essential nature.
"Devas" (deva) signifies that pure precepts are sovereign over the afflictions; they are called "divine" because they are superior.
Regarding the appearance of five hundred Buddhas in the world, the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) is the primary factor.
Within the five stages, the five hundred pāramitās are collectively subsumed within the essence of pure precepts; this is called the manifestation of five hundred Buddhas in the world.
If one perceives external, separate Buddhas while one’s own mental state and its intrinsic nature remain stainless, such a person has not yet escaped the activities of Māra.

The name of the first Buddha is Moonlight Circle (*Candramaṇḍala*), signifying the perfection of the light of ethical discipline (*śīla*). The names of the remaining nine Buddhas represent the primary and attendant aspects within this ethical discipline.
The names of the causes and effects of the *pāramitās* are as follows:

I have made offerings to all such Buddhas as these, yet I still regard that which does not exist among all phenomena as being existent; this is because my perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*) is not yet complete, my clarity of advancement is not yet mature, and the grasping at precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) still persists—this is explained by means of the discourse on the maturation and immaturity of advancement.

As for the perfection of the wisdom-paramita at the tenth stage, there are five hundred levels of ascending progress; as the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) ripen differently, this clarifies the distinctions within the general characteristic and the differences within the state of sameness.

Once the bodhicitta has been generated, one receives immeasurable peace and bliss; the ten stages of birth and maturation remain as cultivated, while the eleventh stage brings the exhaustion of the two delusions, culminating in the state of Buddhahood.
To counteract habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the positions of the various stages (*bhūmi*) are established to treat them.
When reckoned according to their fundamental wisdom and principle (*jñāna-dharmatā*), the distinctions between the ten stages are like the tracks of birds in the sky;
yet, with respect to the similarities and differences of those habitual tendencies, their phenomenal aspects (*ākāra*) are not non-existent.

In succession, following this, there is another eon named Brahma-Prabhāsa (Brahma-Light). This is the third stage, the Radiant Ground (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), wherein one cultivates the eight dhyānas and completely subdues the habitual obscurations of the three realms: the obscuration of sensual desire in the desire realm, and the obscuration of attachment to meditative bliss in the two higher realms. By manifesting the pure, unobstructed light of the heaven of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is called the eon Brahma-Prabhāsa.
"Brahma" (梵) means "purity.
It refers to the purification of the defiled habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the celestial realms; the partial purity is termed "Pure Radiance" (*Vimalaprabhā*).
The world-system is named "Lotus Lamp" (*Padmapradīpa*), which signifies the name for the practice of this stage being free from defilement.
Its adornments are supremely exquisite because it takes the perfection of patience as its ornament.
It is called "supremely exquisite" because patience is the foremost of its practices.
The phrase "therein are immeasurable Buddhas" indicates that the essence of patience clearly encompasses all practices.
Regarding the statement, "I have made offerings to all those immeasurable Buddhas," this is because he offered patience and reverence as his service to all Buddhas.

As for the first Buddha, Ratnasumeru, it is because through the patience and humility of the third stage (*bhūmi*), his practice became supreme and exalted, just as Mount Sumeru is supreme and exalted in height.

This Buddha serves as the primary figure, while the other Buddhas serve as his companions within this patience (*kṣānti*). Below this, each stage is sequentially assigned a primary and companion relationship according to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the eleventh stage, the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), and the myriad practices; for all Buddhas attain the fruit of Buddhahood by relying upon the principle (*li*), wisdom (*zhi*), and vows (*yuan*) within these five stages of practice.
It is impossible for one to see the Buddha apart from these dharmas.
Described in terms of the sphere and locus of wisdom, it is called the magnitude of a kalpa, which is the domain of great wisdom; therein, there are no days, months, years, or seasons at all.
All must be discussed in terms of one's own reality, the reality of the Buddha, the reality of wisdom, and the reality of the Dharma; one must not follow the false views of oneself or others.
If wisdom is perfected and practice is complete, all are universally Buddhas.
The fourth stage is correlated with the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

The "eighty nayutas of Buddhas" signifies that the eightfold path of right awakening constitutes the essence of the practice of diligence, whereas the remaining eight types of deviant conduct are not the Buddha.
"Nayuta" is the total number of ten thousand practices.

Next, within the Dhyāna-pāramitā of the fifth stage, the kalpa is named "Quiescent Wisdom" (Śāntamati) and the world-system is called "Vajra Jewel. This symbolizes that the Dharma-nature body is the essence of dhyāna, clarifying that both speech and silence are quiescent.
"Vajra" generally clarifies that the essence of dhyāna is indestructible.

Within this, the successive emergence of a thousand Buddhas signifies that the functions of dhyāna are subsumed and returned to their source; for within each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are one hundred *pāramitās* acting as primary and secondary factors, and thus these hundred positions within each stage are gathered into the single position of dhyāna to form the sequence of a thousand.
In the sixth stage, Prajñāpāramitā is predominant. There is an eon named "Excellent Manifestation," which symbolizes that wisdom is well able to manifest all dharmas and lands.
It is called "Cloud of Fragrant Lamps," signifying that wisdom is the fragrance, the destruction of darkness is the lamp, and the universal covering of the preaching of the Dharma is the cloud.
Regarding the appearance of one billion Buddhas therein: this is because they function through *prajñā* (wisdom), and "one billion" is used as the numerical measure.
While the preceding stage had "thousand," this stage has "billion.

As for the five hundred Buddhas who appear and arise therein during the seventh stage, this symbolizes that the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means) universally encompasses the wisdom of world-transcending liberation across all five stages; because it enters into worldly affairs in common with others to accomplish the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), five hundred Buddhas are cited as the measure of its activity.
The kalpa is named "King of Assembled Firmness" (*saṃghāta-dṛḍha-rāja*); one who dwells amidst entanglements without being defiled is truly called "firm.
"King" signifies the sense of sovereignty.

The presence of eighty *nayuta* of Buddhas in the eighth stage symbolizes the great functioning of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), having already brought to completion the total perfection of the Eightfold Noble Path.
Regarding the "sixty billion nayutas of Buddhas" in the ninth stage: one *nayuta* is equivalent to this *gōu* (a unit of measure).

This is the twentieth numerical category, representing the rank of the Dharma Master; like the universal rain of the Cloud of Dharma, his transformation of beings throughout the six realms is all-pervasive.
It also symbolizes the supreme *prajñā*, for it universally encompasses the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as the rain of Dharma falls in full measure.

Regarding the presence of thirty-six *nayuta* of Buddhas in the tenth stage: this symbolizes that wisdom is perfected throughout the three periods of time; the six positions are simultaneously illuminated, as cause and effect have reached their ultimate fulfillment.
Because wisdom increases in brilliance, the six positions across the three periods of time have neither beginning nor end, for they constitute a single, perfect wisdom.
The presence of one Buddha in the eleventh stage symbolizes the gathering of the six positions of the three periods into a single dharma-realm of unimpeded great function.

This integrates the specific with the universal based on fundamental wisdom; because it accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood through the gateway of Samantabhadra, the one and the many are thoroughly penetrated.
As the sutra states, if one examines the words and meanings closely, they all inherently contain this meaning; it is not something established by human ingenuity.
