In the twelfth section, from "Good son" down to "I only know this liberation door of the Banner of Universal Joy of Great Power," there are nine and a half lines of scripture that clarify the concluding summary of the preceding section on the causes, effects, and duration of kalpas regarding the beginning and end of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
In this passage, who else could that Universal Monarch named Lord of the Ten Directions, who was able to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas, have been? It was Mañjuśrī.
The night goddess who awakened me at that time was an emanation of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
The king’s precious daughter who was transformed by that night goddess is none other than this goddess Priyanetra.

The manifestation of the Dharma arises from the principle of the Dharmakāya of fundamental wisdom to initiate the practices of differentiated wisdom; it manifests great compassion that is not limited by time or kalpas, and thus uses the number of atoms within a Buddha-field to illustrate it.

The statement that one attains this liberation of the "Universal Joy Banner" of great power after practicing for a duration of such kalpas clarifies that in the third bhūmi, one cultivates the three realms and specifically achieves mastery over the four dhyānas and eight samādhis as their antidotes; it marks the completion of a portion of the practice of compassion, patience, and conduct within the world, and the beginning of constant joy and lack of weariness toward all sentient beings, whether virtuous or evil.
By means of these kalpas of cultivation, he answers the question previously asked by Sudhana regarding the duration since his initial resolve.
This clarifies that the nature of patience is all-pervasive and provides a comprehensive response for all time; furthermore, it demonstrates that wisdom is devoid of temporal sequence.

The Sūtra states, "All requisites for the *dhyānapāramitā*. This clarifies that giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, the four foundations of mindfulness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and so forth, are the requisites of the dhyāna family. Furthermore, the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*), the eighteen things, and secluded tranquility are also the requisites of the dhyāna family. Moreover, the authentic teachings of the master and disciple regarding the Dharma and wisdom are the requisites of the dhyāna family. Finally, the ten *pāramitās*, the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*), and the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*)—which assist in manifesting the sovereign functioning of the essence of the *dharmadhātu*—are also the requisites of the dhyāna family.
This is the third stage, the Radiant Ground (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), in which the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is primary and the other nine are its companions.

It remedies one portion of the two obstacles—namely, the afflictions associated with dwelling in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) within the three realms—and practices great compassion so that it may be unimpeded.

In this way, when one portion of both the defiled and purified habitual tendencies becomes thin and subtle, one first ceases to feel aversion or indifference toward even a single portion of sentient beings, whether good or evil, thereby attaining the liberation door of the Banner of Universal Joy with Great Power.

In the preceding five stages and ten grounds, the explanations provided through verbal discourse may not allow for a full comprehension of their intended meaning. Therefore, in these present stages, the names, locations, genders, and characteristics of the spiritual friends sought by Sudhana—such as elders, laymen, laywomen, monks, nuns, upāsikās, and bodhisattva night goddesses—are expressed by relying upon both dharmas and concrete events, so that they may be easily understood.

In the second section, "The Gate of Advancing by Inquiring into Virtue," from the passage beginning with "Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "...took his leave and departed," there are fourteen lines of scripture which may be divided approximately into five sections:

first, advancing by inquiring into virtue; second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend; third, citing the name of the night goddess, the spiritual friend, Universal Savior of Beings with Wondrous Virtue; fourth, exhorting Sudhana to go and visit her; and fifth, paying respects and taking one's leave.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: within this assembly, there is a night goddess who is clear regarding enlightenment and whose wisdom and compassion are perfected; her name is present in this assembly.
Night-Spirit, it is as previously explained.

This is the fourth stage among the ten stages, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī). Herein one is born into the family of all Buddhas, abides in the position of enlightenment, and causes the gateway of great compassion to grow.
The night goddess of the second stage, named Samantābhijñāviśuddhaprabhā, resides within the bodhimanda; here, wisdom meets with the bodhicitta.
This is because the first stage is the generation of the mind through supreme vows, whereas in the second stage, one truly encounters the essential nature and attains the Middle Way.
From this point onward until the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), one nurtures the mind of great compassion until it reaches its consummation.
The eleventh [stage] consists purely of the wondrous practices of Samantabhadra as he dwells in the world.
The first three stages conclude the purification of karma pertaining to the three realms; this stage is named the Radiant Stage (*prabhākarī-bhūmi*).

Because pure wisdom manifests as one is born into the family of the Tathāgata, it is named the Blazing Wisdom Stage (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). The remaining details are fully contained within the text itself.
Within the first dharma-gate of "Correct Entry into the Appropriate Stage," from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" onwards, the text is divided into fourteen sections.

First, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "having made this vow," there are six and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the section on correctly recollecting the instructions of the night goddess Pramuditanayanajagadvirocanā, contemplating and entering [the stage] without contravening the teachings of his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

2. From "Going to the Abode of the Night Goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā" down to "Emitting light that enters the crown of Sudhana’s head and fills his body," there are five lines of scripture clarifying how the night goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā emits from between her eyebrows a light named "Wisdom-Lamp Universally Illuminating," which enters the various parts of Sudhana’s body.

3. From "At that time, Sudhana... down to "...so that he may attain the pure radiance of all-knowledge," there are thirty-nine lines of scripture. These clarify how Sudhana, having been bathed by the light, entered it within his body and immediately beheld the sphere illuminated by the Dharma-gate of the Lamp of Wisdom Shining Everywhere, as well as an infinite portion of the ocean-like realm of the Night Goddess Samanta-rakṣitā’s practice of teaching and transforming sentient beings.

4. From "At that time, the youth Sudhana saw such supernatural power as this night goddess" down to "he praised her with verses," there are five lines of scripture which clarify Sudhana’s vision of the night goddess’s supernatural power and his subsequent section on praising her virtues with verses.
5. Sudhana’s formal exposition consists of twenty and a half verses, which further clarify the section on the phenomena previously perceived.

6. From "At that time, the youth Sudhana, having spoken these verses," down to "by practicing what conduct does one attain purity," there are three lines of scripture; this is the section where Sudhana asks what kind of practice must be cultivated to attain purity, as well as how long it has been since he attained this liberation.

7. From "O son of good family, Night Goddess... down to "...I now speak for you by the Buddha's spiritual power," there are nine lines and a half of scripture. This clarifies that the Night Goddess defers to the fact that the Dharma is difficult to know, asserting that it cannot be fathomed by devas, humans, or those of the two vehicles, and thus she defers to the Buddha's spiritual power to explain this section for him.

8. From "Good son, in ages past" down to "manifesting the inconceivable signs of the Tathāgata’s appearance," there are ninety-seven lines of scripture. These clarify how, before the Bodhi tree to the north of the wheel-turning king’s city, within a pool of jewel-flower radiance, a lotus flower emitted light ten times for the benefit of beings in different ways, as well as the universal arising of clouds of adornment throughout all realms.

9. From "Good son, this Universal Illumination of All Tathāgatas of the Three Times" down to the forty-eight and a half lines of verse, this section of the sūtra clarifies the initial appearance of the Buddha within a lotus in the city of Ratnapuṣpadīpārāja; it describes how Samantabhadra Bodhisattva informs the Wheel-Turning King and his retinue to go together to see the Buddha, as well as the section on the verses of praise for the appearance of the Tathāgata.
The ten verses spoken in praise of the Tathāgata’s virtues are explained in detail according to the sutra.

From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Cakravartin King" down to "he resolved his mind upon Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi," there are seventy-two and a half lines of scripture. These clarify the offerings made by the Cakravartin King and the woman, specifically the section concerning how the woman, Sunetra, obtained benefit and resolved her mind upon Bodhicitta.

11. "Good son, I recall that in the past, through the spiritual friend Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... from here until "...listening to the preaching of the Dharma and practicing according to the teachings," there are sixteen and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the collective conclusion regarding the causes and conditions of the aforementioned practice, the names of its associated retinues, and the section on the cultivation of roots of goodness initiated by Samantabhadra.
This is the first dharma attained by that Buddha: the liberation gate of the Bodhisattva universally manifesting in all worlds to discipline sentient beings. Twelfth:

"Good son, after the world-system of Vairocana’s Great Majestic Virtue and the eon of Perfect Purity have passed, there is a subsequent world named Jewel Wheel Sublime Adornment and an eon named Great Light, in which five hundred Buddhas appear. From this point downward, through the locations of ten Buddhas, this Night Goddess Universal Savior takes birth at the site of each and every Buddha; her various modes of making offerings and listening to the various Dharmas are fully detailed in the text itself.

13. "Good son, within this world-system there are as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field; during these, all Tathāgatas appeared, and I served, honored, and made offerings to them all, never forgetting a single word or phrase of the Dharma-gates they taught. From here until the end of the ten and a half lines of verse, the text clarifies the section on the general conclusion regarding the eons passed, the Buddhas honored, and the attainment of the Dharma-gates.

This section clarifies that the practice of fulfilling wisdom is all-pervasive; because the assembly of Buddhas constitutes a single Dharma-realm, the measure is taken as the total number of atoms within a Buddha-field, roughly because it extends throughout the fruit of Buddhahood itself.
The following verse summarizes the total number of Buddhas offered worship as described in the eleven preceding sections.
With ten as the primary unit, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru who have been worshipped.

This refers to the eleven stages (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*) as the Buddha-fruit of one's own practice; thus, the correspondence of one's own practice is the oneness of body with other Buddhas within their own assemblies. One must not seek this as a unilateral distinction between self and other.
14. From "I only know this bodhisattva liberation of universally manifesting in all worlds to discipline sentient beings" onwards, this is the section on advancing by extolling virtues.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: it is said that in the past, beyond kalpas as numerous as the atoms of Buddha-fields, there was a kalpa named "Perfectly Pure" (*pariśuddha-sampūrṇa*). This refers to the essence of the universal illumination of all-knowledge (*sarvajñāna*).
That world is named Vairocana-Tejas; this is the sovereign radiance of various differentiated wisdoms, both pure and mixed, and this is the pervasive reach of the practice of diligence.

The appearance therein of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru signifies the advancement through the stage of diligence; it is the supramundane fruit characterized by the vastness and height of differentiated wisdom.

In the preceding stage, thirty-six nayutas were mentioned; furthermore, there is one more immeasurable and another five hundred, along with yet another Buddha, for the purpose of ascending and perceiving the vast extent of the Buddha’s wisdom.
The atoms of this Mount Sumeru serve as the measure for the Buddhas, signifying the clarity of superior progress and lofty ascent.

On the side of the Cakravāḍa mountains at the eastern limit of this world-system, there is a set of four continents named Ratnapradīpapuṣpadhvaja; this signifies the eastern limit as well as the jewel-lamp-flower-banner, which collectively clarifies the cultivation of differentiated wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "there are hundreds of billions of nayutas of lands," this clarifies the realm of the sovereign wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), which encompasses the primary and secondary teachings, the retinue of the dharma-gate, the gathering of sentient beings, and the abodes of karmic retribution.
Within this Jambudvīpa of the four continents, there is a land named Ratnapuṣpadīpa; this signifies the meaning of the sovereign illumination of the wisdom of discernment.

Within that realm, sentient beings fully practice the ten wholesome actions, and a wheel-turning king appears therein named Vairocana-Maṇiratna-padma-śekhara. His sudden miraculous birth from within a lotus signifies that while the various differentiated wisdoms of omniscience arise, they are all unarisen, and though they arise, they remain unstained.
The thirty-two marks are born from the retribution of wisdom.
The possession of the seven treasures symbolizes the seven factors of enlightenment.
Ruling over the four continents signifies the universal pervasiveness of the four wisdoms.
"To constantly instruct all sentient beings with the True Dharma" means that right wisdom is manifest and no erroneous conduct exists.
"The King has a thousand sons" means that the ten thousand practices are fully perfected.
The Lord’s Jewel-Woman and his Jewel-Daughter both symbolize the dharmic joy of compassion and wisdom.

Among them, there is a daughter named Universal Wisdom Flame Wondrous Virtue Eye; she represents the conduct of wisdom and compassion realized through the assembly of the Night Goddess Universal Savior. This very world, a synthesis of purity and defilement where the ignorant and the wise dwell together, is precisely this state in which the integration of defilement and purity forms the two practices of wisdom and compassion.

To the north of that city, in front of the Bodhi tree, there is a fragrant pond named Jewel Flower Radiance (*Ratnapuṣpāvabhāsa*). This symbolizes the fragrance of the essence of the Dharma-body’s precepts and meditative concentration.

From within this fragrant pond emerges a great lotus flower named Cloud of the Adorned Realms Manifesting All Tathāgatas of the Three Times. This represents the arising of the practice of the ten *pāramitās* within the Dharma-body, for it is able to manifest the realms of all Buddhas like a cloud.

Regarding the appearance of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru within it: this collectively clarifies that all Buddhas appear by arising from the pool of the Dharma-body—which consists of the great compassion and great kindness of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) and the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*)—through the practice of vigor (*vīrya*).
Regarding the fact that the lotus flowers in the lower Fragrant Pond emit light ten times: this clarifies the successive stages of benefiting sentient beings.

Ten thousand years ago, this great lotus emitted pure radiance named "Manifesting All Spiritual Powers to Accomplish Sentient Beings. If any sentient being encounters this light, their mind naturally awakens such that there is nothing they do not understand. This corresponds to the *dāna-pāramitā* as the primary factor, with the other nine as its companions.

Regarding the statement that a Buddha shall appear ten thousand years hence, each instance of a Buddha’s appearance is through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). These mutually interpenetrating bodies constitute the ten, as well as the hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions; all are the ten Buddhas of wisdom.

Furthermore, nine thousand years ago, he emitted a pure light named "Stainless Lamp for All Sentient Beings," which was primarily associated with the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), while the other nine perfections served as its companions.
Regarding the statement that "a Buddha shall appear nine thousand years hence," this refers to the appearance of the Buddha through the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*).

Regarding the statement that "eight thousand years prior [to his appearance], he emits a great light named 'The Sound of the Karmic Results of All Sentient Beings,' and if any sentient beings encounter this light, they all come to know for themselves their own karmic retributions," this corresponds to the ten perfections within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
"After eight thousand years, a Buddha shall appear. Following this, [the numbers] seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one are assigned in this same manner.

At the end, it says "making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field" because when wisdom is perfected and conduct is universal, one's own mind is like the Buddha, one's conduct is entirely like the Buddha, and one's vision is entirely like the Buddha; thus, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is nothing that is not the Buddha.
In the following verses, the one hundred and ten Buddha names correspond to the causal and resultant stages of the Buddha-positions within these ten and eleven grounds (*bhūmi*). The verse states:

"The first Buddha is named Jñānārciṣmatī" (Flame of Wisdom), which refers to the first ground, the Joyous (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Here, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine perfections serve as its companions.

Within the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) on this first stage (*bhūmi*), the ten perfections act as both primary and secondary to one another; by carefully observing the names of the Buddhas according to each perfection, one will personally perceive the state of one's own mind.
From this sequence, there further emerge ten Buddhas.

The first is named Ākāśasthāna (Abiding in Space); this corresponds to the second stage, Vimalā (The Stainless), and the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). This is because the nature of ethical discipline is like space, and the body is taken as the essence of that discipline.
The remaining nine Buddha names are the names of the perfections (pāramitās) in which ethical discipline (*śīla*) serves as the primary factor and the others as its companions within this stage.

Following this, ten more Buddhas appear in succession. The first, Light Banner Buddha (*Prabhāketu*), corresponds to the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) in the third stage, the Radiant Ground (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*). It is called "Light" because one purifies the three types of afflictive obstacles through the cultivation of the eight dhyānas; it is called "Banner" because, once delusions have ceased, one achieves the immovability of patience.
The nine Buddha names listed below are the fruits within the practice of the primary and attendant *pāramitās*.

Thus, in each of the following stages, the ten *pāramitās* are interpenetrated and fused; all are names of the fruit of the ten Buddhas. By correlating them as above, one will naturally perceive their significance.
Regarding "raising all Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields": because wisdom is perfected and practice is pervasive, there is nothing that is not Buddha.
Regarding "serving them all": this means that the holy and the ordinary share the same essence; there is not a single dharma that is not Buddha, for emptiness leaves no interval.
Viewing them with the universal eye, one penetrates both mind and environment; there is nothing that is not Buddha.
Wisdom follows reverent practice because all things are Buddha.
For one who sees in this way, even from the perspective of conventional phenomena, it is indeed so.
Speaking in terms of the manifestation of the Dharma, all things are collectively real.
Therefore, if there were even a single dharma or a single object that was not seen as the Buddha, one should know that such a person possesses false views and not right view.
Thereupon, subject and object, right and wrong, and various views arise in competition; one cannot enter this realm of the wisdom-eye of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī.
Thus, the initial mind and the perfection of wisdom remain unmoving; this is elucidated through the meaning of the six characteristics—both general and specific—within each stage (*bhūmi*).
As the Sūtra states: "Who else could the Universal Monarch Vairocanagarbha-sarvaratna-padma-śekhara have been?

He is none other than the present Maitreya Bodhisattva. This means that the perfection of the treasury of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge constitutes the fulfillment of the Buddha-fruit, and the bodhisattva practices are likewise complete.
The queen’s "perfect face" refers to the joy of the Dharma through the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, the term "face" signifies that she is complete in the perception of all phenomena—such as forms, sounds, odors, and tastes—and thus represents the meaning of a wife who brings joy through the Dharma.

Now, the Night Goddess Silent Ocean of Sounds is assigned to the gateway of the fifth dhyāna; she represents the bliss of meditative joy (*dhyāna-prīti*), and is not like a worldly wife who merely takes on a partial likeness.
The maiden King’s Daughter Wondrous Virtue Eye represents the practice of compassion through wisdom, being free from the dual habits of defilement and purity.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "Good son!..."

"After passing through the kalpa of Perfect Purity in the world-system of Great Majestic Virtue of Vairocana, there is next a world named Jewel-Wheel Adornment, with a kalpa named Great Light, wherein five hundred Buddhas appear, all of whom I have served. This means that throughout these eleven stages, one practices each of the ten pāramitās within each of the five paths, with each path serving as the essence for the others; thus, there are one hundred [pāramitās] per stage, totaling five hundred.

Among these, the body that serves the Buddha in accordance with the Buddha’s appearance—whether as a night goddess, a universal monarch, or a king of the asuras—is the practice according to the respective stages within the state of Buddhahood.

Finally, regarding those who serve as courtesans: this symbolizes the joy of the Dharma, clarifying that within the eleventh bhūmi, the five hundred practices are fulfilled; one should understand it in this way.

Those who depart from the self-Dharma and the self-Buddha-fruit to seek the truth by exclusively focusing on external Buddhas outside themselves are, fundamentally, neither practitioners of the Path nor those who have realized the Path.
If one were to attain the fruit of the stage of self-cultivation, it would mean being in correspondence with the Buddhas' own realization.

Because it is through correspondence with their own Buddha-fruit that they see [the Buddhas], even if one were to seek it with great effort and succeed in seeing them, this would be a temporary manifestation; it is not something that can be reached through one's own cultivation.

This clarifies that within a single stage, the dharmas of all ten stages are complete; for within each stage, there are the ten essential natures of the ten stages, which are formed through the mutual interpenetration of the ten pāramitās. Thus, both the common and the specific are fully present.
In this way, all are like the Indra’s Net, wherein the one and the many mutually penetrate one another.
This is the fourth stage, the Radiant Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), in which the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) is primary and the other nine are its companions.

To remedy indolence in cultivating compassion while dwelling in the world, and to abandon the obstacle of not delighting in diligence, one causes them to apply themselves with focused vigor in order to teach and transform sentient beings.

These five stages and ten grounds are identical to the fruit of Buddhahood; each is designated by the name "Buddha" in reference to the scope of the wisdom of practice, the reach of compassion, and the extent of one's conduct. One must not follow mere sentimentality; rather, one must establish a firm resolve so that, even for a moment, one may behold the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of a Buddha.

Each must be established as a Buddha by means of its own wisdom, its own practice, and its own locus; each name and its underlying meaning must be applied according to their respective order so that one may perceive the intended significance for oneself, rather than attempting to fabricate a conceptual model outside of one's own Dharma.
“Good son! I only know this bodhisattva liberation of universally manifesting in all worlds to discipline sentient beings,” this clarifies the advancement through the recommendation of virtues.

Regarding the second section, "Inquiring into the Excellence of Virtue," from the passage beginning with "As the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "taking his leave and departing," there are eight and a half lines of scripture, which are established according to six headings:

first, inquiring into the excellence of virtue; second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend by saying "not far from here"; third, citing the name of the night goddess, Samudra-śānta-ghoṣā; fourth, citing the number of deities who lead her retinue; fifth, exhorting Sudhana to go and inquire; and sixth, hearing of the location of the spiritual friend, paying respects, and taking one's leave.
The commentary states:
What was previously called "within the assembly" is here called "not far."
The preceding represents the perfection of vigor:
it brings all practices together to converge within the essence of bodhi,
never departing from that essence of bodhi.
Therefore, it is said "in the midst of the assembly.

This clarifies that through ritual propriety one establishes oneself in a superior stage of cultivation; within this stage, one practices worldly techniques, crafts, and various other arts and skills that are superior to the preceding stage. Because one does not depart from the essence of bodhi and does not depart from diligent practice, one acquires the designation of "skillful ability."
Not far from here is the night goddess named Silent Sound Ocean (*Śāntasvaranirghoṣasāgara*).

"Silent" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while "Sound Ocean" refers to its function; thus, it clarifies that based on this fifth stage, wisdom arises from the causal concentration of the dhyāna-gate, and its function is as vast as the ocean.
"Sitting upon a lotus throne adorned with mani-jewel banners" clarifies that the essence of meditative concentration is stainless and free from defilement or attachment.
"Surrounded before and behind by ten million asaṃkhyeya night goddesses" clarifies that the essence of meditative concentration is all-pervasive, and its activity is likewise all-pervasive.
"A hundred million" is the highest of numbers.
To cite "a hundred million asaṃkhyeyas" is what this region calls "a hundred million that cannot be counted.
Since the source of such numbers is inexhaustible, it merely refers to the fact that the practices for converting and benefiting sentient beings throughout the ten directions are all-pervasive.

This Night Goddess, Sound-Ocean of Tranquility, is the mother of the Night Goddess Wondrous Virtue Who Universally Saves All Beings; she represents that meditative concentration can bring about the perfection of diligent practice.
Without meditative concentration, all spiritual practices are subject to weariness.
Within the first dharma-gate of "Correctly Entering the Dharma of the Respective Stage," the initial long outline is divided into ten sections.

First, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "having thoroughly known and attained mastery over faith and understanding, dwelling in peace," there are two and a half lines of sūtra; this is the section on recollecting the teachings of the previous spiritual friends without forgetting them.

2. From "He went to the abode of the night goddess Śāntarutasāgaravatī" down to "How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path," there are five lines of sūtra text that clarify the section on Sudhana expressing his own quest.

3. From "At that time, the night goddess said to Sudhana" down to "the liberation of Vast Joyful Adornment," there are two and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on the night goddess explaining the dharma-gate of her own practice to Sudhana.

4. From "Sudhana said, 'O Great Sage, what is the activity of this gate of liberation? down to "I have taught him the bodhisattva's straightforward mind," there are sixty-five lines of scripture that clarify the section on the activities and skillful means practiced by the night goddess as she instructs Sudhana in this dharma-gate.

5. From "Good son, by means of these immeasurable gifts of Dharma" down to "immeasurable and boundless great joy arose," there are seventeen and a half lines of scripture which clarify the Night Goddess’s answer to the previous question asked by Sudhana regarding the sphere of practice he should traverse.

Sixth: From "Good son, I observe the Tathāgata Vairocana" down to "because he is able to preach all boundless dharmas," there are thirty-two lines of scripture; this constitutes the section answering the previous question regarding what kind of observation is performed.

7. "Good son, having entered this ocean of light of liberation called 'The Vast Adornment of Great Joy Arising Moment by Moment in the Mind'... from here down to "...you should contemplate and accordingly enter into realization," consists of thirty-four lines of scripture; it answers the previous question asked by Sudhana regarding the sphere of practice he should traverse.

8. From "At that time, the youth Sudhana addressed the night goddess Samudrareṇu-vigatasaṃghāta-ghoṣā" down to "increasing, accumulating, firm, securely established, and perfected," there are sixteen lines of scripture. This section answers Sudhana’s question regarding how to practice this dharma-gate, explaining that the practice consists of the ten pāramitās.

9. "The youth Sudhana said, 'Noble One, how long has it been since you first resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? From here until the passage, 'In every thought-moment, he gives rise to the liberation of the vast adornment of great joy,' there are fifty-four and a half lines of sūtra, which answer Sudhana’s question regarding how long it has been since [the Noble One] first resolved upon the Great Bodhicitta.

10. From "Having attained this liberation, one is able to enter ten unspeakable [realms]" down to the verse, there are fifty-eight lines of scripture. This clarifies that after the Ocean of Tranquil Sound Goddess herself explained the practice she had undertaken—the liberation that gives rise in every thought-moment to the vast adornment of great joy—it further describes the Dharma-gates she has entered, the Buddhas of the three periods of time whom she has made offerings to, and the worlds in which she has resolved her mind, all of which remain as they are in the present.
This indicates that because the essence of meditative concentration does not shift throughout time, it remains thus at all times.
Below are ten verses which clarify how the Night Goddess herself recounts her past conduct and exhorts Sudhana to practice; these are self-evident according to the text.
"Good son, I only know this liberation of the 'Vast Adornment of Great Joy Arising Moment by Moment. From here on, he defers further excellence and ascends in his realization.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: as for "the liberation of the vast adornment of great joy arising moment by moment," it clarifies that the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prīti*) is all-pervasive and benefits sentient beings extensively; it is named after its correspondence with one's fundamental vows and practices.
The mutual adornment of principle and practice is called "adornment.
This night goddess is named Silent Sound Ocean (*śānta-svara-sāgara*): she is called "Silent" because she clarifies that the nature of reality is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
she is called "Sound Ocean" because her speech and resonance benefit all sentient beings equally, clarifying that sound itself is the essence and function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding how long it has been since the Night Goddess Sudhana first resolved her mind, the passage from "The Night Goddess said: 'To the east of this Flower Treasury World-Ocean, passing through ten world-oceans, there is a world-ocean named All-Pure Radiant Jewel'" down to "thereafter, at the end of her life, she was born in this Sahā world within the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean" consists of forty-eight and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the ten Buddhas whom the Night Goddess served and made offerings to during their appearance in the world; it details how she attended upon them with her own body, made offerings to them, and heard the Dharma—these being the deeds she performed.

In response to Sudhana’s question regarding the duration since he first resolved his mind [for enlightenment], if one were to explain it by means of the symbolic dharma-gate, this refers to practicing the ten stages within this stage; subsequently, he was born in the Sahā world, where he first beheld three Buddhas, and thereafter beheld Vairocana Tathāgata.

One who attains this liberation of "the adornment of vast great joy arising in every thought-moment" enters the dharma-gate of the first stage through to the tenth and eleventh stages; they receive the seal of the wisdom of the three periods of time upon the Buddhas of the three periods of time, serving them all and hearing their teachings from all, as is fully explained in the sutra.

This demonstrates that the essence of dhyāna universally encompasses the three periods of time; in a single thought-moment, it universally seals all phenomena as being without past, future, or present—this is the answer to Sudhana’s question regarding the duration since he first resolved his mind upon Bodhi.

The passage concerning "those who, after ten Buddhas, make offerings to as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a Buddha-field" symbolizes that after the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*) universally pervades. Within a single atom, one dwells throughout many Buddha-fields while remaining within that single atom; this is because wisdom is unobstructed, lacks interior or exterior, and because it is equal to the wisdom of all Buddhas and identical to the minds of sentient beings. This is discussed in terms of the essence and function of the meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The statement that one passes through ten oceans of worlds to the east of the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpakaraṇḍa*) signifies the progressive advancement through the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
"East" indicates the beginning of the sequence.
The existence of an ocean of worlds named "All-Pure Radiance Jewel" (*Sarva-vimala-prabhā-ratna*) signifies that the essence of dhyāna in the fifth stage encompasses all positions.

Within this, there is a world-system called "The Sound of the Light of the Vows of All Tathāgatas," which signifies that in this fifth ground, the initial Ground of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), the arousal of the ten indestructible minds constitutes the world-system.

This clarifies that the great wisdom and compassion of the dharmadhātu serve as the seed; because one first resolves the mind based on the supreme vows of the Buddhas of the ten directions, it is called the "Light-Sound of the Tathāgata’s Vows."
Furthermore, as the ancient masters have said:

"If one counts the number of three-thousandfold great thousand-world systems up to the sands of the Ganges, it is called one world-nature (*dhātu*); if one counts these natures up to the sands of the Ganges, it constitutes one world-lineage (*gotra*)."

Within this, there is a world named Pure Radiance Adorned with Gold (*Vimalaprabhā-svarṇavyūha*). It encompasses the essence of dhyāna universally, reaching all the way to the adamantine wisdom (*vajrajñāna*).

That which takes the fragrant *vajra-maṇi-rāja* as its essence does so because it takes the nature of the fragrant *vajra-jñāna*—which is intrinsically stainless through the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—as its essence; this constitutes the essence of the progressive advancement through the five stages and ten grounds.
The "King" symbolizes mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
His form being like a multi-storied pavilion signifies that the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is layered upon layer, inexhaustible.

That he is adorned with the various dharmas of knowledge, vision, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and bounded by clouds of various wondrous jewels, signifies that he establishes the ten stages through the great clouds of compassionate vows.

Regarding "the ocean of all jewel necklaces," this refers to the establishment of the sequence of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) by means of the ocean of necklaces of the ten thousand practices (*daśapāramitā*).

Regarding "a cloud of sublime palaces covering its summit," this refers to the palace of wisdom and the palace of vast, non-substantial compassion (*karuṇā*) which encompass and cover all sentient beings.

Regarding "the cohabitation of the pure and the defiled": this clarifies that within the gate of the great tranquil samādhi of the Dharma-realm, wisdom and compassion advance together; the Buddha-land and the realm of sentient beings are non-obstructive in their shared essence, encompassing all such that there is no distinction of interior or exterior, nor of purity or defilement.
In this world-system, in a remote past age, there was an eon named Universal Radiance Banner (*Samantābhāsa-dhvaja*), which symbolizes the light of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

There was a land named Universal Fulfillment Wondrous Treasury (*Samantapūrṇa-suvicitra-kośa*), which symbolizes that the universally radiant wisdom is common to all sentient beings; it is called a "treasury" (*kośa*) because it is their shared storehouse.

The name of the site of enlightenment, "Exquisite Moonlight of All Jewel Treasuries," symbolizes that the fifth stage’s meditative concentration of intrinsic purity is the site of enlightenment, for it is able to manifest the treasury of wisdom, as all [qualities] emerge from within it.

There is a Buddha named Non-retrogressive Sound of the Dharma-realm; having attained this aforementioned dharma-gate of skillful means for subduing delusions at the site of enlightenment, he immediately attains the sound of turning the wheel of the Dharma within the non-retrogressive dharma-realm.

Regarding the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* herein, it is by means of the aforementioned teaching that the manifestation of delusion is shown to be itself bodhi; there is no separate process of formation or destruction.

At that time, I was the Bodhi-tree deity named *Puṇyasaṃpatsamudgatajñānāvabhāsadhvaja*. The "deity" represents the wondrous wisdom of bodhi, which is the principle of essencelessness (*niḥsvabhāva*). The "endowment of merit" refers to the fruits and virtues resulting from the immeasurable practices of compassion arising from that wisdom. The "lamp-light" signifies that wisdom constantly illuminates the faculties and gathers them through transformation. The "banner" signifies that wisdom is eternally without substance such that it can never be shaken, yet it is always able to destroy the afflictions of all sentient beings.

Regarding "guarding the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*): this clarifies that the essence of concentration in this fifth stage is immovable; this is the meaning of "guarding," and it is also the "site of enlightenment. Since concentration can give rise to wisdom and cause delusions to perish, the act of guarding the site of enlightenment is entirely contained therein.

From this point onward, the general offerings to the ten Buddhas and the entry into the Dharma collectively represent the gates of progressive advancement through the ten stages (*bhūmi*); their respective sequential correspondences may be seen for oneself.

From this point on, the first Buddha is assigned to the first stage (bhūmi), followed by the second stage, and then the third stage. The bodies produced therein are the Buddhas venerated through the practices of each respective stage; they are the fruits of those practices.
Even within the context of provisional teachings, this does not contradict the principle of symbolic representation (*vyañjana-dharma*).

If one were to wish to see other Buddhas, their wisdom would not reach this Dharma-gate; their practice would be inconsistent with it, and because they lack the necessary correspondence, they would have no means to attain the vision of those Buddhas.

As for making offerings to ten Buddhas and to as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a Buddha-field, this is the mark of the culmination of the fruit of the tenth stage, observed by the eye of wisdom; this clarifies the general characteristics of the ten stages within the dhyāna of the fifth stage.
The phrase "those born later in the Sahā world who make offerings to the four Buddhas" clarifies the fruits within the first, second, third, and fourth stages prior to the fifth stage.

The phrase "making offerings at once to all Buddhas in all worlds throughout the three periods of time" clarifies that within this fifth stage, the wisdom of the eleventh stage is perfected and the practices of Samantabhadra are fulfilled; the seal of wisdom encompasses the past, present, and future of the three periods, as they are all of one single limit without any distinction of time.
In terms of ultimate reality, it is thus, for there is no element of artifice.

It also clarifies that within the central nature of the meditative body and the principle of wisdom on this stage, the three periods of time are perfectly integrated into a single nature; for the Buddhas of the three periods of time exist simultaneously, without before or after.
This is discussed directly from the perspective of the true essence—the Dharma-body and the realm of wisdom—and according to ultimate reality;
however, from the standpoint of deluded sentiment, it cannot be seen.

This is the Good Spiritual Friend of the Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*), which takes the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) as its primary focus and the other nine perfections as its companions, thereby subduing the obstacle of the lack of mastery over quiescence and activity to achieve such mastery.

The reason this stage is named the "Difficult to Conquer" (Duranjayā) is that on this stage, one skillfully trains in worldly knowledge within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), coming to know all five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) and all worldly arts; this is due to the application of effort toward concentration.
The sixth stage is the gate of the great function of prajñā that enters into quiescent extinction, as exemplified by the City-Ruling Spirit below.

It is also like the sixth abode among the ten prior stages, where the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja entered the samādhi of quiescent extinction, ceased inhalation and exhalation, manifested emanated bodies like clouds, and established teachings like the ocean.
Treatise on the New Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll 38 [and] Scroll 39,
composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan.

Within the second section, "Advancing through the Promotion of Virtue," from the passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas" down to "taking their leave and departing," there are eighteen lines of verse; these are established according to five gates:
first, advancing through the promotion of virtue.
First, he indicates the location of the spiritual friend, saying that he is here within this assembly of Tathāgatas at the site of enlightenment;
second, he mentions the name of the deity, who is named Guardian of All Cities and Increaser of Power;
third, Sudhana recites verses to praise the virtues of Śāntasvaranirghoṣa; and fourth...
Fifth, the words of respectful departure.

Regarding the exegesis according to the text: "within this Bodhimanda, in the assembly of the Tathāgata" signifies that one does not depart from the great ocean-like assembly, which is the essence of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the bodhicitta.
There is a night goddess whose spirit consists of the wisdom that illuminates the subtle principles within the *tathatā* (suchness) of the nature of bodhi.

She is able to shatter the ignorance and attachments of all sentient beings; as the presiding Night Goddess, she never departs from the great night of birth and death, for she gives rise to the great illumination that awakens all sentient beings.

The name "Guardian of All Cities and Increaser of Power" signifies that he constantly guards the city of the minds of all sentient beings, increases the power of wisdom within the sixth stage and for all sentient beings, causes the three emptinesses to manifest before him, and brings forth the power of the concentration of tranquil extinction as well as the power of both mundane and supramundane wisdom to manifest. Thus, he forever transcends the ocean of birth and death while abiding eternally in the world, attaining the power of the ocean of all supramundane wisdom, as will be clearly explained in the following text.

Just as Sudhana, with ten verses of praise, extolled the Ocean-God Śāntamati, saying that the infinite ocean of Buddhas of the Dharma-realm body and the ocean of sentient beings all reside within a single atom—this venerable one’s power of liberation clarifies that the meditative essence and the nature of the Dharma-body in the fifth stage are boundless and without measure of large or small. Thus, like water, a mirror, or the void, they universally contain all forms, which appear therein without mutual obstruction.
It manifests spontaneously through the seal of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as is clearly explained in the verses.

Within the first section, the Dharma-gate of entering the actual stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Sudhana" down to "I know only this liberation-door of the profound, sovereign, and wondrous sound," this portion is divided into ten sub-sections.

First: From "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "the night goddess who protects all cities," there are four and a half lines of sūtra text. This clarifies the section on contemplating superior progress by maintaining right mindfulness of the preceding dharmas.

Second, from "Having seen that night goddess" down to "manifesting the body that ultimately tames sentient beings," there are six lines of scripture which clarify the section on the night goddess manifesting various distinct bodies to teach and transform all sentient beings.

3. From "When Sudhana saw him, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness" down to "I only pray that you will compassionately deign to explain this for me," there are five lines of scripture clarifying the section on Sudhana’s formal request for what he seeks.

4. From "Then that night goddess said to Sudhana... down to "...inquired about the gates of practice cultivated by the bodhisattvas," there are seven lines of scripture which clarify the night goddess’s praise of Sudhana’s resolve, virtue, and the Dharma he seeks.

5. From "Good son, I have attained the Bodhisattva liberation of the profound, sovereign, and wondrous sound" down to "her mind never abandons the ground of omniscience," there are fourteen and a half lines of scripture which clarify the section on the night goddess’s own account of her practice of benefiting sentient beings.

Sixth: From "Good son, by means of such light of pure dharmas" down to "entering the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata," there are fourteen lines of scripture that clarify the Night Goddess’s exposition on the tenfold contemplation for entering the realm of the Tathāgata.

7. Furthermore, from the passage beginning with “Moreover, son of good family, having thus reflected with right mindfulness” down to “O Noble One, how long has it been since you attained this?”—a total of twenty-nine lines of scripture—this section clarifies the stage of attaining this liberation of Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣavatī-vimokṣa*), obtaining the *buddha-dhāraṇī*, and teaching the Dharma with mastery for the sake of all sentient beings.

8. From the passage beginning with "The Night Goddess said, 'Son of Good Family, in a past age... down to "the Prajñāpāramitā that universally enters the ocean of all dharma-gates," there are thirty-five lines of scripture. These clarify the portion concerning the answer regarding how long it has been since Sudhana attained this Dharma and the first Buddha he beheld.

9. Next, from "Then there appeared a Buddha named Vimaladharmaprabhāsa" down to "abiding in the unsurpassed city of the Dharma of all-knowledge," there are sixty-nine and a half lines of sūtra, which clarify the section on the duration for which Sudhana attained the Dharma and the number of Buddhas he made offerings to.

10. From "I only know this profound, sovereign, and wondrous-sound liberation that causes all worlds to always speak with purity" onwards, the section clarifies the stage of advancing by deferring one's own virtues.

The wheel of wisdom of a bodhisattva is far removed from all realms of conceptual discrimination; it cannot be displayed through the conceptualization of such eons as long or short, defiled or pure, broad or narrow, many or few, within the cycle of birth and death.
All the dharma-gates contained within the ten preceding sections are fully present according to the text itself.
From the passage where Sudhana asks, "How long has it been since you realized this dharma? onwards, the meaning is expressed through the mutual manifestation of principle and phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The hidden and difficult-to-know points are briefly explained in part to provide a general outline.

The intent is to clarify that, in terms of the retribution realm (*vipākagati*), it is identical to the Dharma; and to clarify that by means of skillful methods, the practice of the Dharma brings about its corresponding retribution.
The similarity between cause and effect represents the dharma of knowing the retribution of one's past conduct and views.

The Sūtra states: "In the remote past, beyond world-cycles as numerous as the atoms of worlds. Regarding "world-cycles," this is a numerical unit within the great numbers of the Western tradition, as is fully explained in the *Śakradevaputrabodhisattvasaṃkhyā-dharma*.

This clarifies the transformation of all worldly conventional expressions, numbering as many as the atoms within all worlds, into an ocean of the speech and sounds of great wisdom, thereby ensuring that the world is free from coarse and evil speech and free from defiled speech.

As the subsequent text states: "I have attained this liberation of the extremely profound, sovereign, and wondrous voice, which causes all worlds to abandon discursive speech, to refrain from dualistic speech, to always speak truthful words, and to constantly utter pure words. This intends to clarify that all worldly discourse is transformed and unified into the gateway of the *prajñāpāramitā*, taking as its measure the turning of the entire world into atoms as numerous as those very atoms themselves.
The eon is named "Stainless Radiance" because it symbolizes the fundamental essence of the principle of the threefold emptiness and quiescence within Prajñā.
The world is named "Clouds of Merit of the Dharma-realm" because it clarifies that wisdom is the cloud of merit from teaching the Dharma within the Dharma-realm.

That which takes as its essence the ocean of *maṇi* jewels manifesting the karma of all sentient beings symbolizes the wondrous wisdom of the three emptinesses—the cessation of inherent nature—because it skillfully knows the ocean of distinctions among the karmas of all sentient beings; therefore, it is designated as a "King."
Its shape being like a lotus flower symbolizes the wondrous function of wisdom, for it discerns essence and characteristics while remaining inwardly empty and untainted.

That this world abides within a network of fragrant *maṇi* Mount Sumerus as numerous as the atoms in the four continents clarifies that this wondrous wisdom of the three voids abides within the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and thus possesses a network of teachings as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru.

Regarding "emerging with the sounds of the original vows of all Tathāgatas": this refers to the sixth stage, because at the time of first generating the mind of awakening, one makes great vows based upon all Buddhas; since these vows give rise to the sound of turning the wheel of Dharma that pervades the ten directions and awakens all sentient beings, they emerge from these very vows.
That it is adorned with lotus flowers clarifies that the sound of the Dharma causes all sentient beings to attain non-attached wisdom.

That there are lotus flowers as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru serving as its retinue clarifies the following meanings: "Sumeru" signifies that wisdom rises loftily above the world; "atoms" signify that wisdom is vast and manifold in its significance; "lotus flowers" signify that wisdom is characterized by non-attachment; and "retinue" signifies the skillful discernment of the distinctions among karmic actions, various objective conditions, and the principles of the aggregate and the individual, the common and the different, and formation and disintegration.

The statement that it is interspersed with fragrant maṇi-jewels as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru clarifies that it is interspersed with the fragrance of immeasurable precepts, concentrations, wisdoms, and liberations—which are well-expounded by means of differentiated wisdom and are stainless, pure, and white; for "maṇi" carries the meaning of being free from defilement.
There are four-continent worlds as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru; these are composed of the four jewels, and Mount Sumeru stands high and preeminent within the great ocean.

If one were to discuss the four types of unimpeded eloquence within this wisdom of prajñā, as well as the measure of the speech, mental states, and various karmic discriminations of all sentient beings—wherein each of the four continents contains hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakably unspeakable cities—there exist such accomplished dharma-gates for nayutas of unspeakably unspeakable sentient beings.
"Nayuta" is the numerical designation for this *gavyūti*.
"Good Son" (*kulaputra*) is a title used to address the virtue of Sudhana, calling him by that name to proclaim the Dharma to him.
In that world, there is a set of four continents named *Sudhvaja*; within the context of the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), they are collectively called *Sudhvaja*.

Regarding the royal capital therein: taking fundamental wisdom as the king, the capital is named "Universal Jewel Flower Light" because the discerning wisdom arising from fundamental wisdom is called "Universal Jewel Flower Light."

Not far from here is the site of enlightenment known as the Universal Manifestation Palace of the Dharma King; it signifies that by means of fundamental wisdom one gives rise to the mind of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, thereby establishing the palace of great compassion and the hall of differentiated wisdom to govern sentient beings through the True Dharma.

Regarding the appearance of Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru within this realm: the afflictions of all sentient beings, as numerous as atoms, constitute the ocean of *prajñā*. These appear as Buddhas because they all rely upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to give rise to differentiated wisdom (*vicitra-jñāna*) at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), thereby being able to remedy the habitual tendencies of delusion.

The first of these Buddhas was named King of the Radiance of the Thunder-Sound of the Dharma-Ocean; he is called the "First Buddha" because he manifested the wisdom of differentiation from the foundation of fundamental wisdom, and his contemplation transcended the realm of emotional consciousness.
He is well-able to expound the Dharma and is thus called Thunderous Sound.
His teaching-light shatters the delusions of all sentient beings and is therefore named Radiance.
He establishes the Dharma with sovereign mastery, able to destroy all heterodoxies while remaining indestructible by them; he is thus named King.

When that Buddha appeared in the world, there was a universal monarch named Pure Sun Radiance Face; he was a wheel-turning king of clear wisdom, his solar radiance shining forth with brilliant clarity, just as the surface of a mani-jewel mirror clearly reflects and illuminates all forms.

Regarding "upholding the ocean-spiral of all dharmas under that Buddha": this clarifies that the wisdom of differentiation, within fundamental gnosis, upholds the myriad dharmas which are profoundly deep and boundless; thus it is named the "ocean-spiral."
*Sūtra* refers to the prose sūtras.

The fact that the king renounced the world after the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* symbolizes the completion of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) across the ten stages within this sixth stage. It signifies that the wisdom transcending the entanglements is already full and the discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*) transcending the entanglements have already ceased; thus, it is called the attainment of supramundane wisdom through the Buddha’s passing into extinction.

Within the eleven stages, it is only Samantabhadra who enters the gate of practice while still within the entanglements; this is not something that can be reached by the three types of wisdom regarding emptiness—such as the ten stages and so forth—which constitute the gate of transcendence from entanglements in this sixth stage.

As described in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," there were thirty bodhisattvas of the three types of emptiness and wisdom-liberation who had all attained the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Using immeasurable supramundane samādhi-gates, they sought Samantabhadra in three ways, yet ultimately could not find or see him;
it was only when the Tathāgata commanded them to seek him through mental recollection that Samantabhadra finally appeared.

This clarifies that the wisdom of the three emptinesses pertains only to the gate of emerging from entanglement at the tenth stage; therefore, from this point downward, it merely lists one hundred fruits of Buddhahood from beginning to end, without including the Dharma-gate of Samantabhadra of the subsequent eleven stages.

This sixth stage is the liberation through wisdom of the three emptinesses of quiescence; however, it is only when one reaches the tenth stage, the Buddha-stage, that contemplation and analysis have finally ceased, at which point it is termed "Buddha-nirvāṇa."

As for that king’s renunciation, this refers to the meaning of renunciation as the gate of wisdom of the sixfold ground of quiescent triple-emptiness, as exemplified in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* by the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

As for that king who left the household life to protect and uphold the True Dharma, he protected the supramundane True Dharma through the wisdom of the three gates of liberation; when the Dharma was about to perish, there arose a thousand different schools and a thousand varieties of teachings.
In the final age, when karmic obstructions and delusions are heavy, many wicked bhikṣus will engage in strife and contention.

Regarding those who do not seek merit, this clarifies that within this stage there are only the three gates of wisdom of emptiness and quiescent extinction; they lack compassion and provide no instruction. As for the King manifesting various matters such as supernatural powers and radiance to cause the True Dharma to flourish for sixty-five thousand years: "sixty" refers to the number of stages of progressive advancement.
The "five thousand years" signifies that a single position encompasses all five positions, with cause and effect advancing in unison.

By clarifying the gate of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), one gives rise to worldly-transcending compassion through wisdom; this continues until, together with those preceding and following, one hundred Buddhas appear in succession. This represents the sixth *prajñā* gate, which extends only to the culmination of the world-transcending Buddha-fruit at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), wherein a single stage embodies all ten stages.
The above collectively illustrates making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru, merely to signify that Prajñā is loftily transcendent, having emerged from the entanglements.
The aforementioned hundred Buddhas represent the fruits of progressive advancement through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), with each stage corresponding to ten.
The night goddess’s request to serve and make offerings to the Buddha-body is the practice cultivated within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
To make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
There is not a single thing that is not Buddha, because within every single atom there are infinite Buddhas.

All of the above clarifies that [enlightenment] is accomplished through practice based on the Dharma; as for the fruits of kalpas, lands, and world-systems, one is led to contemplate the fruit in relation to its cause. These are all gateways of the Dharma, wherein phenomena are identical to principle, and principle is identical to phenomena.

That the king and his daughter both became bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs was for the sake of the Prajñāpāramitā and the three gates of emptiness and cessation; it was the gateway to the wisdom and compassion that transcend birth and death.
The Universal Monarch of that time was none other than the present Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
this illustrates wisdom. The bhikṣuṇī was my own self; this illustrates compassion.

"I know only this liberation of the Profound, Sovereign, and Wondrous Sound. This clarifies that a single sound pervades the entire Dharma-realm; yet this sound is further without substance and free from discrimination, capable of turning all dharma-gates and teaching and transforming all sentient beings—therefore it is named the "Liberation of the Profound, Sovereign, and Wondrous Sound."
This is the sixth stage, the Stage of Manifestation (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), because all wisdoms manifest therein.
It takes the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as its sovereign, with the other nine perfections as its retinue.
This treats the obstacle to the sovereign mastery of the quiescent and active functions of the wisdom of the three emptinesses, thereby enabling the attainment of such mastery.

Within the second section, "Advancing by Inferring Virtue," from the passage beginning with "Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "...took their leave and departed," six gates are established:
first, advancing by inferring superior virtue;
Second, it indicates the location of the spiritual friend, stating that she is within this assembly of the Buddha;
third, it mentions the name of the presiding night goddess, Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamkusumitābhijñā;
fourth, there are twenty-two verses in which the City-Ruling Goddess (Nagaradevatā) reiterates the preceding teaching, as detailed in the text itself.
Fifth, Sudhana praised the virtues of the City-Ruling Goddess with twenty verses, as clearly explained in the full text;
sixth, he paid his respects and departed.

Regarding the phrase "within this Buddha’s assembly," it clarifies that one does not depart from the principle of this Perfect Enlightenment—its non-action, its inconceivability, its non-doing, and its lack of intrinsic nature—and thus it is called "within this Buddha’s assembly."

They cause all flowers of conditioned phenomena to bloom, thereby accomplishing the perfection of skillful means; within the state of no birth-and-death, they enter into all realms of birth-and-death to practice the four methods of attraction through shared activities and beneficial conduct.

This is identical to the case of the laywoman Śrīprabhā, for whom eighty-four thousand nayutas of all doors of affliction function in concert; thus, having concluded the sixth stage by means of liberation from the entanglements, this seventh stage enters into the mundane world to benefit sentient beings through those very doors of emerging from entanglement without fear. This is because both remaining within and emerging from entanglements are equal; because it causes all great compassion to grow and become vast; because it is without limit; because it desires to cause the practice of great compassion to pervade the evil realms; and because it gathers in sentient beings until they reach liberation.

Within the first dharma-gate of "Correct Entry into the Appropriate Stage," from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva liberation gate of the light of joy born from vastness," the text is divided into five sections.

1. From "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only pray that you will deign to show me compassion and explain this for me," there are seven lines of scripture, which clarify the section where Sudhana arrives at the abode of the Night Goddess and formally presents his request.

2. From "The Night Goddess said, 'O son of good family'" down to "the Bodhisattva liberation of the light of vast joy born from [the Dharma]," there are fifteen and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on the Night Goddess bestowing upon Sudhana the Dharma-gate of his own practice.

3. From "Sudhana said, 'O Great Sage,'" down to "causing him to dwell securely in the wisdom of a bodhisattva," there are sixty-six lines of scripture, which clarify the section on Sudhana’s entry into the sphere of this dharma-gate.

4. "The youth Sudhana said, 'O Noble One, how long has it been since you first gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta? From this point down to the verse, there are nineteen lines of scripture."

To clarify the section on the difficulty of believing in the long duration and proximity of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), there are twenty-nine verses. These restate the preceding teaching that the Dharma is extremely profound and difficult to believe, thereby distinguishing those of superior faculties who are capable of hearing it, as fully elucidated in the sutra.

5. From "Good son, in ages long past" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva liberation door of the light of the birth of vast joy," the preceding section constitutes the answer to Sudhana’s previous question regarding how long it has been since he first resolved his mind on enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: from the passage "Good son, in ages long past" onwards, there are four sections: first, citing worlds as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds to answer the previous question concerning the duration since his initial resolve; second, citing the name of the world-ocean, *Samantaprabhā-sarva-gold-maṇi-śikhara*; third, [citing] the name of the Tathāgata, *Vairocana-rāja*; and fourth, [citing] the name of the bodhisattva, *Samantabhadra*.
