Third, within this ocean of worlds, there appears a Buddha named King of the Tranquil Majesty of the Wisdom Mountain Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm;

fourth, within this ocean of worlds, there are world-systems as numerous as the atoms of a world, and within each world-system there are worlds as numerous as the atoms of a world, and in every single world, a Tathāgata has appeared.
From "up to" and below, it is listed separately.
Among them, there was a Jambudvīpa with a royal capital named *Dṛḍharatnavyūhadhvajapradīpa*, surrounded on all sides by ten thousand great cities, where the human lifespan was ten thousand years.
In that realm there was a king named Sarvadharmasvaranirghoṣaparipūrṇacchatra, who had five hundred ministers, sixty thousand court ladies, and seven hundred princes.
In this assembly there was a daughter of a householder named Ratnaprabhā, accompanied by sixty young maidens; they were all golden in complexion, with eyes and hair of deep blue.

In the following passage, the King praises the maiden Ratnaprabhā for her faith in the merit of others, and with his own hands, he bestows upon her a precious robe from which the light of all the constellations universally emanates.
At that time, the King Universal Canopy of the Perfect Sound of All Dharmas was none other than the present Tathāgata Vairocana;
the King Radiance was King Śuddhodana.
The Lady Padmaprabhā is none other than the present Lady Māyā;
the Maiden Ratnaprabhā is my own self;
and the sentient beings gathered through the four methods of attraction are all the bodhisattvas within this assembly.

This is the answer to Sudhana’s question regarding how long it has been since he first resolved upon the unsurpassed, great bodhicitta. It clarifies the cultivation of the practice of great compassion on the seventh stage; for were it not for the arousal of a vast mind that is unrestricted by the number of kalpas—extending to the very limit of birth and death, equalizing the kalpas of the three periods of time, lasting as long as the number of atoms in an ocean of worlds, taking immeasurable kalpas as its duration, and making the afflictions and sufferings of all sentient beings its boundary—one could not truly be said to possess the practice of great compassion appropriate to this stage.
The "dust motes of an ocean of worlds" serve as a metaphorical comparison.

If one employs worldly phenomena to represent the gates of practice—observing things to understand the Dharma—the mention of "as many as the dust motes of an ocean of worlds" indicates that there is no limit to the time required.
This is the cultivation of the practice of great compassion, which severs all limited conceptions of measure.

There is a world-ocean named Universal Radiance True Gold Mani Mountain, which symbolizes that the cultivation of the practice of great compassion arises from the wisdom of universal radiance; from the very beginning, it has neither beginning nor end.
"True gold" symbolizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
"Maṇi jewel" symbolizes this wisdom being stainless.

"Mountain" symbolizes this Wisdom of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*), which is pure and stainless; while abiding within the midst of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to benefit all sentient beings, it is as immovable as a mountain.
To awaken to this wisdom is called the appearance of a Buddha.

The name "King of the Tranquil Majesty of the Wisdom-Mountain Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm" indicates that his buddha-title is established in accordance with the wisdom of universal radiance.
"Universally Illuminating" refers to the wisdom that shines forth progressively and without interruption or exhaustion.
"Mountain" signifies not being moved by external objects, as well as the sense of being loftily elevated.
That its essence performs no action is the meaning of quiescent immobility.

Wisdom manifests and afflictions and karma perish; this is majestic power (*vibhūti*). The King is sovereign; therefore, he is called the Buddha "Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm, Mountain of Wisdom, Tranquil Majestic Power King."

"Good son! When that Buddha was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he purified that world-ocean" means that by initiating the bodhisattva path through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), he adorned his own retribution-body (*vipāka-kāya*) so that it became pure and immaculate.

Within all the world-systems, as numerous as atoms below this point, there are Tathāgatas appearing in the world; this clarifies that the Universal Radiant Wisdom universally seals all world-systems and their types, such that there is not a single place where a Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is not seen.
Extending downward through all the four continents, they are all universally sealed by the Seal of Universal Radiance Wisdom, such that there is no difference among them.
It even universally seals the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings, like the sun dwelling in the sky, its reflection appearing in clear water.
...down to the descent into the royal capital, taking the Dharma-realm as the capital city, governed by the King of Wisdom.

The king is named "Perfect Canopy of the Sound of All Dharmas," which clarifies that he exemplifies the simultaneous practice of both compassion and wisdom throughout the five stages; his expedient practices are termed the "five hundred great ministers."
Within the six realms of existence, practicing the dharma of compassion and sympathetic joy serves as the handmaidens; thus, it is said there are sixty thousand handmaidens.
The seven hundred princes represent the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyanga*).
From "down to" and below, this refers to the time when the evil age arises, when human life is short and suffering abounds while joy is scarce—this is the place where one practices compassion.
The sixty young maidens represent the practice of wisdom and compassion within the six realms of existence, as will be detailed in the subsequent assembly.
At that time, who could have feared anyone among the sovereigns of the Perfect Canopy of All Dharma-Sounds? It was none other than the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vairocana.
The King of Radiance was King Śuddhodana; the Lotus was Queen Māyā;
and the maiden Ratnaprabhā was my own self.
The general meaning expressed here is the cultivation of the practices of great wisdom, great kindness, and great compassion; one must be endowed with these three dharmas.
The Master of the Treatise says in verse:
"Universal Radiant Wisdom is named Buddha; In accordance with original vows, he is named Father."
The one who nurtures all living beings with compassion is named Lady; the one who benefits beings with the joy of the Dharma is named Maiden.

All the aforementioned oceans of worlds and world-systems, numbering as many as the atoms within an ocean of worlds, are entirely the spheres of conversion for these four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*); one should practice in this manner with infinite wisdom and compassion.
Within the ocean of the Dharma-realm, the measurements of distance, proximity, length, or brevity cannot be apprehended; this clarifies that this sutra is both phenomenon and principle.

To illustrate, throughout such oceans of kalpas, worlds, lands, and cities extending infinitely and pervasively across the ten directions, the Tathāgata appears within every kingdom; there, the king practices his conduct to save sentient beings, while the maiden seeks the Dharma.
Because the people of this degenerate age were suffering, they earnestly petitioned their Great King; the facts were indeed as they claimed.
Furthermore, this teaching serves as a model for the method of practicing the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*) on this seventh stage; thus, it employs this dharma as an analogy.

The general meaning of the above scriptural passages and verses is to cause practitioners to cultivate worldly great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) without establishing the characteristics of renunciation.

Taking Vairocana Buddha as the objective support (*ālambana*), this represents the gate of compassion of the seventh stage; it comprehensively encompasses all five stages up to the ultimate ocean of the Buddha’s fruition.

From beginning to end, this is no different from the universal radiance of wisdom; it unifies all Buddhas in a single assembly and does not establish the progressive advancement through the ten stages or the hundred Buddhas.
This is unlike the previous stage of the three emptinesses of transcending entanglements, where the King and his daughter manifested their renunciation by becoming a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī.

This is merely illustrated by means of a layperson; even if one were the Buddha-fruit Vairocana Buddha, he would still be a secular body, adorned with flower crowns, necklaces, bracelets, and armlets, and thus not an ordained monastic.

This seventh stage, the gate of compassion (*karuṇā-mukha*), shares its practice with the preceding and following five stages; however, because it is distinguished by its manifestation in both the supramundane and the mundane, it causes one to recognize its superior progress and its specific similarities and differences.
This is the seventh spiritual friend of the Ground of Far-Going (*dūramgamā*).
Why is it called the Ground of Far-Going?

Because on this ground one cultivates the practice of great compassion within the world, reaching far through the oceans of worlds in the ten directions, penetrating all realms—including those of humans, devas, and hell-beings—unlike the single thought-moment of seeking transcendence from the mundane world.

With the perfection of skillful means as the primary factor and the other nine perfections as its companions, it remedies the obstacle of dualistic minds regarding defilement and purity in their respective spheres, and the obstacle of lacking mastery while dwelling in saṃsāra through great compassion, thereby enabling the attainment of such mastery.

Upon reaching the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva attains a partial mastery over practice, yet still lacks mastery over the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśabala*); it is only upon the completion of the tenth stage that this is fully realized.

From the sixth stage and prior, one has not yet attained mastery within the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), because the two karmas of defilement and purity have not yet been extinguished. It is from the seventh stage onward that one attains mastery within the actual activities of the four means of attraction; for at this stage, one remedies the dual obstacles of defilement and purity by entering into compassionate conduct that is free from both defilement and purity.

I know only this Bodhisattva liberation called "The Radiance of Vast Joy Born of Arising," for it is only at this stage that the dharmas of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) are finally and thoroughly mastered.

In the second section, "Inference of the Excellence of Virtuous Progression," from the passage beginning with "Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "...took their leave and departed," three topical gates are established:

first, the inference of the ascent of virtue; second, the presence in this *bodhimaṇḍa* of a night goddess named Mahāpraṇidhānavīryaparākramasarvasattvatrāṇī; and third, the paying of homage and departure.

As for why it is called the "Site of Enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) but not "Enlightenment" (bodhi): it is because in this eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), the effortless wisdom manifests the universal assembly of all dharmas; since there is no enlightenment that has already been realized, will be realized, or is currently being realized, one does not speak of "leaving" or "not leaving."

It is stated directly that within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), wisdom devoid of effort abides in the Middle Way; for this reason, Sudhana likewise does not say, "I have already set forth the bodhicitta," and so on.

The night goddess named Great Vow and Power of Diligence Who Protects All Sentient Beings is so called because she benefits beings by being impelled by the wind of her fundamental vows, which operate spontaneously and effortlessly once the practices of wisdom and compassion are perfected; and because she benefits beings with a single stroke through the wind of the perfections of her fundamental vows, without ceasing.

All Buddhas exhort him seven times and empower him thrice, causing him to teach and transform sentient beings without ceasing; because he has established this name, he is called "The One Who Possesses the Power of Great Vow and Diligence to Rescue and Protect All Sentient Beings."

Within the first dharma-gate of "Correctly Entering the Dharma of the Specific Stage," from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this liberation of the roots of goodness for teaching and transforming sentient beings," this section is divided into six major headings.

First: From "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "manifesting his own inherently pure Dharma-nature body," there are fifteen lines of scripture. These clarify Sudhana’s journey to visit the night goddess Sarvajagadrakṣāpraṇidhānavīryaprabhā, and the distinct and diverse manifestations revealed by that night goddess.

2. From "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "these are the ten," it clarifies the section on Sudhana’s seeing of the night goddess, prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and generating the ten kinds of minds.

3. From "Having generated this mind" down to the verse, it clarifies how Sudhana attained the same practice as that night goddess and the bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms within a buddha-field; furthermore, it details Sudhana’s recitation of the ten verses on the practices to praise the virtues of the night goddess, as clearly explained in the full text.

4. From "At that time, Sudhana" down to "attaining non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," there are sixty-six lines of scripture. These clarify the names of the Dharma-gates in which the night goddess answers Sudhana, as well as the section on how this gate manifests various forms of physical bodies in an inexhaustible manner.

5. "Good son, as to your question regarding from what time you have set forth the bodhicitta and cultivated the bodhisattva practices," and so on down to "fulfilling the great vows and accomplishing all powers," there are thirty-seven lines of scripture. These clarify the night goddess’s response to Sudhana: that the wheel of wisdom of a bodhisattva is far removed from all realms of conceptual discrimination, and cannot be divided by the known distinctions of birth and death, such as long or short, defiled or pure, broad or narrow, much or little.

Sixth: From "O Son of the Buddha, in ages past, beyond oceans of worlds" down to the verse, this section clarifies the Night Goddess’s response to Sudhana regarding the duration since he first resolved his mind toward enlightenment.
The following section of verse clarifies the aforementioned teaching through a restatement by the night goddess.

To explain the meaning according to the text: when Sudhana saw that night goddess seated among the great assembly upon a lion throne—the treasury of all-manifesting palace-mani jewels—covered above by a net of mani-jewels manifesting all lands of the dharma-realm, this symbolizes that the essence of non-effortful wisdom is pure and stainless as a throne, constantly manifesting within which are the palaces of all humans, devas, and nāgas, all dwelling therein.
The mani-jewel net covering above symbolizes that wisdom free from effort constantly extends the net of teaching; this clarifies that it is accomplished through the retribution of wisdom.

Manifesting bodies as reflections of the sun, moon, and stars, and manifesting bodies that appear universally according to the minds of sentient beings, clarifies that by means of the retribution of wisdom one attains their seat, just as the essence of wisdom can manifest all phenomena, and the phenomena thus manifested are as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field.
The details below are clearly explained in the text.
Sudhana’s prostration with his five limbs touching the ground signifies the profound depth of his reverence for the Dharma.
The benefits attained by Sudhana are also clearly explained in the text below.

At that time, Sudhana asked the night goddess, "What is the name of this liberation? The night goddess replied, "It is called 'Teaching and Transforming Sentient Beings to Cause Them to Produce Roots of Goodness,' which clarifies that all sentient beings are born from non-conceptual wisdom."
For this wise one, all roots of goodness arise spontaneously, and all sufferings cease spontaneously, because the essential nature of wisdom is devoid of an agent.
Sentient beings are deluded by this; amidst the absence of suffering, they falsely create various karmas.
If one realizes this, suffering perishes and goodness arises; therefore, it is called "teaching and transforming sentient beings to cause them to produce roots of goodness and attain liberation."

Furthermore, within the formless body of liberation, by means of the wisdom that dwells in non-reliance, one universally manifests the bodies of all Buddhas and sentient beings, as will be clearly explained in the text below.

Furthermore, when Sudhana asked the goddess how long it had been since she first gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta, the night goddess replied: "The wheel of wisdom of a Bodhisattva is far removed from all realms of conceptual discrimination; it cannot be displayed through such distinctions as the length or brevity of saṃsāra, or its defilement or purity, its breadth or narrowness, its quantity or scarcity. This is because the wheel of wisdom of a Bodhisattva is by nature pure, free from the net of all conceptual discriminations, and transcends all mountains of obstacles, shining universally upon those who are to be transformed according to their needs."
From this point forward, six analogies are presented:
first, the analogy of the sun traveling through space without day or night;

second, the analogy of the solar disc abiding over Jambudvīpa, appearing within all jewels as well as in the rivers, oceans, and pure waters, such that there are no sentient beings who do not see the sun.
Third, it is like a boatman who constantly uses a large ship upon a river, serving as a metaphor for not relying on this shore, that shore, or the middle of the stream.
Fourth, it is like the great void, wherein all worlds undergo formation and destruction without discrimination; this serves as a metaphor for the purity of its intrinsic nature.
Fifth, the analogy of the great vows being like a wind-wheel that sustains the myriad phenomena;

sixth, the analogy of an illusory person who, though possessing all limbs and members, lacks inhalation and exhalation, as well as cold and heat, hunger and thirst, sorrow and joy, and birth and death.

These six similes illustrate that the nature of wisdom is like space itself: it is without intrinsic nature, without dependence, and has no location; yet it constantly appears before the assemblies of all Buddhas, teaching and transforming them without ceasing, sustained by the wind-wheel of its previously made great vows.

From the passage beginning, "O Son of the Buddha, in the past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds," and following, this is the night goddess's discourse on eons according to worldly convention; she cites the causes and conditions regarding the duration since her initial resolve, which is established within the realm of illusion.

The Sūtra states, "In the distant past, beyond kalpas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds," which clarifies that they are incalculable; this indicates that the essence of the original is incalculable, and the same applies to the duration of the kalpas.
There is an eon named "Excellent Light" (*Sūryaprabha*), which is a name established to signify the essence of non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*).
The world-system is named "Jewel Light" (*Ratnaprabhā*), which is a name for the manifestation of dharmas according to objects through non-effortful wisdom.

Regarding the appearance of ten thousand Buddhas within that kalpa: because they manifest in accordance with the faculties [of beings] through wisdom that is devoid of effort, it is called "the appearance of ten thousand Buddhas.
As for the number "ten thousand," it signifies that a single wisdom responds to ten thousand practices.

The first of those Buddhas was named Dharmacakra-ghoṣa-gaganapradīpa-rāja Tathāgata, whose ten titles were fully perfected. By means of effortless wisdom, he spontaneously benefited sentient beings; he constantly turned the sound of the Dharma wheel, which, like an echo in the void, had no point of dependence yet illuminated all sentient beings. Therefore, he was named Lamp of Wisdom.
He is called a "King" because he possesses sovereign mastery.
Regarding his being "endowed with the ten titles," these names were established according to the universal pervasiveness of his wisdom and its functions.
In that Jambudvīpa, there was a royal capital named Ratnavyūha; it was the realm transformed by this King of Wisdom, and thus it was named Ratnavyūha.
Not far to its east is a great forest named Wondrous Light (Miaoguang). The east symbolizes wisdom, representing the place where sentient beings are transformed so that clarity may arise.
As for the east symbolizing the Dharma, the character for "east" (東) is formed by piercing the sun with a wooden stake.
The forest was named Wondrous Light (Miaoguang), for its practice was as extensive and vast as the shade of a forest, illuminating and benefiting all beings; thus it was called Wondrous Light.
Within it was a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) named Jewel Flower (Baohua), signifying that through his practice of benefiting sentient beings, the flowers of his mind were in full bloom.

The name of that site of enlightenment is Jewel Flower. Within that site of enlightenment is a lion throne called the Universal Radiance Maṇi Lotus Treasury. When that Tathāgata attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment upon this throne, he did so by means of the nature of effortless wisdom, which constantly and universally illuminates the stainless self-nature of the dharma-realm as his seat.
Because the essence of this wisdom is without formation or destruction, it is called "accomplishing unsurpassed bodhi.
As for sitting in the place of enlightenment for a full hundred years: the number "hundred" symbolizes the fulfillment of the ten pāramitās within each of the ten stages (bhūmis).

Furthermore, with respect to the progression from this stage to subsequent stages, one passes through nine levels and fulfills one hundred pāramitās; because one reaches the fulfillment of the Buddha-stage at the tenth level, these are established as one hundred steps.
The following account of King Prasenajit concerns the conduct governed by wisdom, the conduct governed by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and the sphere of loving-kindness.
That the king and his crown prince meted out punishments for both good and evil was a skillful means (*upāya*) for giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness.

The king named Jyotiṣprabha represents wisdom; the crown prince Sudānta represents the practice of compassion. The subsequent subduing of the realms of suffering represents the stage of practicing compassion through wisdom, as will be explained in the following assembly.
The five hundred ministers who wished to harm me are now the five hundred followers of Devadatta.

Having received the Buddha’s transformation, these people shall become Buddhas in the future world-system called *Sūryaprabha*, after eons as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru; there will be five hundred Buddhas who attain enlightenment in succession. Furthermore, those very sinners whom I have saved are none other than Krakucchanda Buddha and the others—the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.

Krakucchanda—here translated as "One Who Has Already Cut Off What Should Be Cut Off"—along with the million *asaṃkhyeya* bodhisattvas who were universally practicing the bodhisattva path throughout the ten directions, was King Prasenajit; he is now the great master of debate, the Nirgrantha Sañjayin.
As for Satyaka the Nirgrantha, he was an outsider who went naked and practiced self-starvation, remaining unbound by the concerns of food or clothing.
The people of the royal palace and their various kinsmen were those sixty thousand disciples of that Nirgrantha.
The above summarizes the person who has accomplished the sphere of objects transformed by wisdom.

"O Son of the Buddha, at that time, when I had saved the one whose transgressions were to be expiated, my parents permitted me to leave the home life"—this signifies that the essence of the stage of wisdom is pure and untainted; this is called "leaving the home life," meaning one leaves the home of effortful application (*sābhoga*).

Having left the household life to study the Way under the Buddha King of the Lamp of Space (*Gaganapradīparāja*), he purified his Brahma-conduct for five hundred years and thereby achieved one million *dhāraṇīs*. These "five hundred years" symbolize that the essence of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) penetrates all five stages; it is simply that their degree of maturation differs. This represents the penetration of the first Buddha.

Regarding the statement that "nineteen Buddhas arise in succession after this first Buddha," this clarifies that upon reaching the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one masters the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha through the wisdom of effortlessness (*anābhoga-jñāna*) and becomes a Buddha in one's own right; thus, including this, there are twenty Buddhas in total. This is because one ascends to the fruit of Buddhahood in the ninth and tenth stages, and because these latter two stages are subsumed within the fruit of the eighth stage.

Within these eight stages, by means of non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), the ten stages and the fruit of Buddhahood are non-dual; therefore, nineteen Buddhas are established within these positions. This clarifies that the non-effortful wisdom of the eighth stage, together with [the others], constitutes twenty, because they interpenetrate one another. This signifies that the practice of the tenth stage is already present within the eighth stage, for the three periods of time are one.
Among these, those who serve the Buddhas represent the body that accords with practice.
The initial mention of ten thousand Buddhas appearing represents the fulfillment of the ten thousand practices of the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*).

Subsequently, the appearance of sixty billion Buddhas within the *Ratnaprabhāsa* eon represents the simultaneous completion of the six positions within the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), wherein cause and effect are of one essence and lack temporal sequence.

The above clarifies that by means of the practice of sovereign, effortless Great Compassionate Wisdom—which advances from the essence of universal radiance to benefit sentient beings—and the manner of benefiting them, one establishes the methods for initiating action to save sentient beings so as to enable students to emulate it as previously described.

Alternatively, one may establish one hundred Buddhas within the various stages; that one subsequently establishes one, two, three, or four Buddhas further on is to clarify generally that practice is accomplished in accordance with the stages, and that the fruit is contained within the practice.
Even if one perceives the Buddha externally apart from the fruits of one's own practice, it does not exist apart from what is seen through that very practice.
That which is perceived simultaneously with the practice itself is the True Buddha;
whereas that which is perceived only after a specific aspiration has been made is a temporary manifestation that vanishes once the transformation is over—this is the Transformation Buddha.
Speaking in terms of the identity of phenomena and principle:

as for the twenty-eight marks, they fall short of the thirty-two marks by four; this signifies that at this eighth stage, one is still deficient in the fourfold causes and effects of the ninth and tenth stages, and thus has not yet reached fulfillment.

The first stage contains two layers of cause and effect, because within each stage there is both the fruit of the established position (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and the fruit of the path leading toward it.

The fact that one approaches and makes offerings to all Buddhas appearing in the world throughout kalpas as numerous as the atoms in all oceans of worlds clarifies that non-effortful wisdom (*anabhoga-jñāna*) is all-pervasive; there is no phenomenon that is not Buddha, for the Buddha is itself the Dharma.
The empty space of the ten directions is without interval or defect; yet even the tip of a needle or the end of a hair is not all dharmas or all Buddhas.
Were there even so much as a speck of dust that was not the mind of non-defilement and purity, it would not be the Buddha—this is sealed by the eye of wisdom.
The following verse reiterates the preceding teaching, as is fully evident from the text itself:
"Good son, I know only this liberation of teaching and transforming sentient beings to cause them to produce roots of goodness. The subsequent section defers further merit to those who have advanced.

This is the eighth spiritual friend within the Immovable Bhūmi; it takes the perfection of aspiration as its primary quality, with the other nine as its companions. It remedies the obstacle of not yet possessing mastery in teaching the Dharma within non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), thereby enabling the attainment of such mastery.

In the second section, "Inference on the Excellence of Virtue," from the passage beginning with "All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas" down to "taking leave and departing," there are eleven and a half lines of scripture. Within this segment, it is divided into three sections:
first, indicating the dwelling place of the spiritual friend; second, explaining the name of the spiritual friend; and third, paying homage and taking leave.

It is said that there is a grove in this Jambudvīpa; this clarifies the ultimate limit of the dharma-gate of cultivating the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). It provides universal shade for the practices of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions. Its liberation is vast; dwelling within birth and death is like being in a garden, and the myriad practices are like a forest—hence its name.
"Āravī" is translated here as "Victorious Bliss.
"Ni" is translated here as "Garden.
It is so called because it brings sentient beings joy through the Dharma of wisdom.

This grove is also the garden where the Tathāgata manifested his descent to be born; it clarifies that the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage descended from the Tuṣita Heaven to be conceived in the womb and take birth.
Within the nine stages, one cultivates the sharpness of wisdom to benefit humans and devas, and because one fulfills the wisdom of all sentient beings, it is called "receiving birth.
One receives and studies the wisdom of all Buddhas in order to bring all sentient beings to fulfillment.
As clarified by the sutra itself:
"There is a spirit named Wondrous Virtue Perfect" (Miaode Yuanman) indicates that on the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (Sādhumatī), wondrous wisdom is perfected.
As for "spirit" (deva), it refers to one who, through compassion and wisdom, is skillfully able to expound the teachings; this is what constitutes being a spirit.
Regarding the first section, "Correct Entry into the Dharma of the Respective Stage," it is divided into ten parts.

First, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "increasing the great ocean of a bodhisattva’s merit," there are six lines of scripture, which clarify the stage of Sudhana going to visit spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

2. From "After Sudhana had seen him" down to "the great light of the world," there are three lines of scripture clarifying the section on Sudhana’s audience with the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and his request for what he seeks.

3. From "The deity replied" down to "the tenth, the treasury of taking birth upon entering the stage of the Tathāgata," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the section on Sudhana’s tenfold treasury of taking birth through correct reception.

4. From "Good son, what is called the 'Womb of Rebirth through the Vow to Constantly Make Offerings to All Buddhas'? down to "This is the tenth kind of womb of rebirth for a bodhisattva," there are ten distinct textual sections corresponding to the ten kinds of wombs of rebirth.

5. From "O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates and increases these ten dharmas" onwards, up to the twelve lines of verse, is the section clarifying the benefits gained through the exhortation to practice.
Below this are twenty verses that restate the preceding teachings and praise the dharma-gate of taking birth. Section Six:

From "Good son, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he is born into the family of the Tathāgata" down to "the gate of liberation of sovereign birth," there are two and a half lines of sūtra text, clarifying the section on how the spirit itself attains the dharma after a long duration.
7. "Sudhana said: 'Noble One, what is the scope of this liberation-gate? From here down to the verse, this section answers Sudhana's previous question regarding the realm of his birth."
The eighth [section] consists of twenty-three verses of *geya*, which restate the preceding teachings.

The ninth, beginning with "Good son, I only know this bodhisattva’s liberation of sovereign manifestation of birth throughout all places over immeasurable eons," clarifies the advancement through the recommendation of virtues.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the ten sections of the text: this bodhisattva attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and acquires effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), which first manifests before them, causing them to advance upward.

The ninth stage is the gateway of eloquence for learning from and teaching the Buddhas, which brings to fulfillment the intentions of all beings, both celestial and human; this is called the Matrix of Rebirth.

As a verse in the sutra says: "Listening to the Dharma without weariness and delighting in contemplation, universally unimpeded throughout the three periods of time; with body and mind as pure as space—this is the treasury of birth for those of noble renown."

Their minds dwell perpetually in the ocean of great compassion, as firm as adamant and precious mountains; having fully realized the gateway to all-knowledge, this is the womb of birth for the Most Victorious Ones.
This is explained in full detail as in the sutra.

In this ninth stage (*bhūmi*), one studies the Buddha’s wisdom which is universally pervasive; in the tenth stage, the great wisdom and the joy of the Dharma manifest before one, which is symbolized by Gopā.
In the eleventh stage, compassion is perfected and wisdom is all-pervasive; this is represented by Māyādevī, the Mother of Buddhas.

In benefiting sentient beings while dwelling in the world, these figures—primarily the Buddha, Māyā, and King Śuddhodana—are used to symbolize the fulfillment of the practices of wisdom and compassion.
As for the Buddha, there is no place or time where he is not manifesting birth.
When Sudhana asks about the realm of the Dharma, there are two meanings:

first, he asks about the realm of his manifestation of birth; second, he asks about the realm of how long it has been since he attained the Dharma-gate, as in the passage below which asks how long it has been since Mahādeva attained this liberation.
Regarding the manner of birth, it accords with the realms of the three vehicles.
Just as the Dharma-body was born from the body of Queen Māyā, this is seen by sentient beings of middling and inferior faculties;
for sentient beings of superior faculties, [the Buddha] appears as a lotus-transformation body or manifests from space, rather than from a mother’s womb.

Sentient beings of the highest capacity awaken to the Way with sudden clarity; their self-realized noble wisdom darkly accords with the primordial wisdom, regardless of whether a Tathāgata appears in the world.
This is illustrated by the various streams of causes and conditions regarding the initial arousal of the bodhicitta described by the spiritual friends encountered by Sudhana.

Furthermore, there were those who, while observing the stars and moon at night, saw a Buddha appear in the sky and preach the Dharma for them; some saw a Buddha descend from the sky and preach the Dharma; and others saw a sandalwood stupa and seat appear in the sky as offerings, with the Buddha preaching the Dharma therein.
For example, the upāsikā Bhadrottamā attained the bodhisattva liberation called "The Site of Enlightenment Without Dependence," which she both realized for herself and taught to others.
Furthermore, she attained the gate of the inexhaustibility of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, all of which are entirely inexhaustible; this was not learned from a teacher.

This body of Lady Māyā merely clarifies how compassion and wisdom mutually support one another to benefit sentient beings; according to their respective faculties and perceptions, what they see differs for each.
As Samantabhadra Bodhisattva said:
"For the sake of sentient beings of inferior understanding, he appears within a mother’s womb."
"For those of the highest faculties, the lotus flower emerges.

If one considers the distinctions among the various classes of beings with their manifold faculties across the six realms of existence, the Tathāgatas seen therein manifest births in ten thousand different ways.
Furthermore, according to what is perceived by the sensory faculties of human beings, as fully elucidated in the sutras,
one universally perceives within every atom of the worlds of the ten directions the realm of the Tathāgata’s taking birth, and takes this very realm as a grove and garden.

Regarding the statement that one hundred years pass from the time the Bodhisattva is conceived until his birth: this signifies that ascending from the ninth stage (*bhūmi*) to the tenth stage constitutes those "one hundred years," and reaching the eleventh stage is the time of birth; each point is explained in detail below.
Regarding the detailed explanation of the Ratnatāla trees following the ten dharmas: they are like the *tāla* trees of this region.

Concerning the passage beginning with "composed of superior jewels" and following, which asks about the duration since the arousal of the mind, the statement "Good son, in ages past beyond the number of atoms in a hundred million buddha-fields, and even further beyond that number," refers not to a calculable number based on quantitative distinctions, but is simply a total of the "innumerable."
The world is named Universal Jewel because its substance is formed by the vows and practices of Samantabhadra.
The eon is named Joyful Delight because it signifies birth into the family of Tathāgata wisdom from the ninth stage, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence.
The appearance therein of eighty nayutas of Buddhas signifies that one has been born from the eighth stage into the family of the Buddha-wisdom of the ninth stage.
The name of the first Buddha is Sovereign Banner of Merit (*Vaiśvarya-guṇa-dhvaja*), which clarifies that one has already ascended to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The world below represents the realm of those to be transformed.
The royal capital represents the persons to be transformed by wisdom.
The king and his consort represent the practices of wisdom and compassion.
The twenty billion nayutas of maidservants represent the two practices of wisdom and compassion.

The fact that the joy of the Dharma fills the gardens and pavilions represents the movement of wisdom within birth and death as if in a garden; this clarifies that while Bodhisattvas dwell within birth and death to gather and transform sentient beings so they may attain happiness, it is because these Bodhisattvas sport in the joy of the Dharma.
At its edge stands a tree named Sarvadānaprītiprabha (Joyful Light of All-Giving), which derives its name from the Dharma-joy bestowed by the Bodhisattva upon those who rely upon it.
That the Lady grasped a branch of that tree to give birth to the Bodhisattva symbolizes that Great Compassion reaches out to and benefits sentient beings.
However, how could a Bodhisattva actually undergo birth and become subject to the laws of birth?
This is entirely for the purpose of using manifested forms to represent the Dharma and guide sentient beings, making it easier for them to understand.
Even if one sees them being born, this is merely from the perspective of a certain class of sentient beings; it is not the case for all. This may be understood from what follows below.
To grasp [the Dharma] according to the place where sentient beings understand it is the birthright of a Bodhisattva;
for it is the birthright of a Bodhisattva to simply accord with what is appropriate for sentient beings to receive as benefit.
The mind clearly manifests images as wisdom arises; according to the desires of sentient beings, one attains mastery in preaching the Dharma—this is the manner in which a bodhisattva takes birth.

The tree called Piluśa (Pilu) means "lofty and manifest" in this language; it is named after the Buddha’s title "Lofty and Manifest," and its name is also established because of his manifest excellence and virtue.
From "having completely covered the ten directions" onwards, the causes, conditions, and fundamental practices are brought together, as clearly explained in detail in the sutra.
The following twenty-three lines of verse reiterate the aforementioned Dharma, as clearly explained in full in the text.

This is the ninth spiritual friend of the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). It takes the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) as its primary quality, with the other nine as its companions. It remedies the obstacle of being unable to freely teach the Dharma to those in all realms of existence, thereby granting mastery over them.

Regarding the second section, "Advancing through the Promotion of Virtue," there are nine lines of scripture from the passage beginning with "All Bodhisattvas" down to "took their leave and departed. This is divided into four sections: first, the promotion of superior virtue;

second, the indication of the city where the spiritual friend resides, namely Kapilavastu; third, the mention of the spiritual friend’s name, namely Gopā; and fourth, the paying of respects and taking one's leave.
The city of Kapilavastu is here translated as "Yellow City"; it was the place where the Sage Yellow-Head (Kapila) practiced the Way.
This accords with the realization of the Ten Stages by the Arhats and corresponds to the color of the Central Palace; thus, it symbolizes that the earth element of the Central Palace is yellow.

It is circular and without corners; the two virtues of wisdom and compassion pervade all things through their essence and function, sustaining and nurturing the myriad beings while remaining without a fixed substance.

One must give rise to vast compassionate vows to vow to deliver sentient beings, deeply contemplating that the mundane world and the true essence are one and the same, neither belonging to defilement nor purity, and abiding within the gate of illusory arising. This stage of the Dharma-gate is called the Bodhisattva’s Great Vow Wisdom-Phenomenal Illusion Liberation Gate; it clarifies that within these eleven stages, great compassion is primary, whereby the illusory manifestations of wisdom arise from the compassionate mind of original vows, demonstrating the deeds of attaining Buddhahood to benefit sentient beings and the gates of all practices throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.
The above eight sections harmonize the five stages of the cultivation of compassion, detailing the distinctions and similarities in the methods of progressive practice.
Furthermore, within these eleven stages (*bhūmi*), they are broadly divided into ten sections to provide a concise understanding of the sequence of their respective practices.
First, Queen Māyā, who clarifies the gateway of attaining Buddhahood and benefiting sentient beings through the illusory manifestation of various practices arising from wisdom born of compassion;

second, the Heavenly King of the Thirty-three Heavens named Samprajanya (Right Mindfulness), whose daughter is named Devendraprabhājñānakaruṇāvibhu (Sovereign Wisdom and Compassion of the Lord of Devas), clarifying the gateway of the manifest presence of all dharmas throughout the ten directions without error;
third, the Preceptor of the Youth, clarifying the gateway of the master of the Dharma who pervades the ten directions and serves as a model for the world.
Fourth is Suvijñapti, who possesses the gateway of wisdom regarding all arts and the knowledge of characters that clearly pervades the ten directions;

fifth is Bhadrottamā, an upāsikā, who possesses the gateway of benefiting sentient beings by clearly mastering all worldly techniques of divination, fortune-telling, and sorcery, as well as all traditions and transmissions concerning the right and wrong, auspicious and inauspicious aspects of the world;
sixth is Dṛḍhamati, a householder, who possesses the gateway of pure liberation through non-attachment to the world and firm mindfulness.
Seventh was the Elder Suvimalacandra, who illuminated the gate of the pure wisdom-light that abides in the world;
eighth was Anabhibhūsenāpati, who illuminated the gate of attaining the characteristic of exhaustion within the signless Dharma;
ninth was Arthaviniścaya, who illuminated the gate of truthful and vow-bound speech.

The youth Daśaśubha and the maiden Śubhavyūhā represent the gate of dwelling in the world through illusion, wherein wisdom and compassion are perfected; they are equal to the two positions of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra as described in the "Chapter on Manifestation," signifying that the wisdom and compassion of the Dharma-body are equally fulfilled.
The ten sections above constitute the practices of the eleven stages (*ekādaśabhūmi*).
From here below, up to the Tathāgata Maitreya, it clarifies the fulfillment of the Buddha-fruit within a single lifetime.
"A single lifetime" refers to birth within non-birth, for it is not a birth that occurs sequentially across the three periods of time.
Within the first section, the Dharma-gate of Entering the Proper Stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" onwards, the text is divided into eleven sections.

First, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "attaining the wisdom of beholding the realm of the Buddhas," there is one and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the stage of Sudhana’s superior entry into the gate of the eleven stages (*bhūmi*).

2. From "Having formed this thought" down to "formed this thought," there are eleven and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the section on Sudhana’s praise of the sovereign physical marks and characteristics of Lady Māyā.

3. From "There is a city-ruling goddess named Ratnanetra" down to "he shall certainly attain Buddhahood," there are thirty-six lines of scripture that clarify the section on the city-ruling goddess teaching Sudhana the Dharma-gate of governing the city of the mind.

4. From "At that time, there were the body-attendant spirits" down to "because they behold the appearance of Buddhas in all lands," there are fourteen and a half lines of scripture. These clarify how the body-attendant spirits praise the body of Lady Māyā, and how light is emitted from Lady Māyā’s earrings and enters the body of Sudhana.

5. From "At that time, there was a rākṣasa king named Sādhunetra who guarded the Dharma Hall of the Bodhisattvas" down to "these are the ten," this section clarifies the ten methods for approaching spiritual friends as taught by the rākṣasa king to Sudhana.

6. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "when these words were spoken," there are eleven lines of scripture which clarify how the Rākṣasa King expounds the dharma of thirteen samādhis for Sudhana, constituting the section on causing Sudhana to constantly draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

Seven: From the passage "The youth Sudhana looked up into the air" down to "the inconceivable and subtle merits of the Tathāgata," there are twenty-seven lines of scripture. These clarify how Sudhana saw the Rākṣasa King, who taught him the method for reverently seeking spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) throughout the ten directions; furthermore, he taught him the method of contemplating the body and mind as being like a dream or an illusion, leading to the section on beholding the lotus, seat, and pavilion-adornments of Lady Māyā.
The three classes of deities mentioned above are those who enter the preliminary expedients (*pūrvaprayoga*) prior to these eleven stages (*bhūmi*).
There are three such expedients:
first, skillfully guarding the city of the mind;
Second, he thoroughly knows that the nature of sound pervades the ten directions;

third, there is a rākṣasa king named Guardian of the Hall, who, by means of thirteen samādhi-gates and the contemplation that body and mind are like dreams and illusions, guards the meaning of the Dharma-realm hall.
The Rākṣasa King— here translated as "The Fearful"—
is named Īśvara. By means of samādhi,
he observes and guards the Dharma Hall of body and mind, so as to cause the sycophantic, depraved, and evil ghosts to be shattered and dispersed.
The light emitted from Māyā’s ear-ornaments entering Sudhana’s body clarifies the entry into the Samādhi of the Light of the Teaching.
The ear presides over the sounds of instruction;
by taking these three factors as the preliminary expedients for the eleven stages, one is then able to correctly enter the gates of the eleven stages.

8. From the passage beginning with "At that time, Sudhana saw such a seat" down to "having already attained the accomplishment of the body of quiescent extinction," there are thirty-one and a half lines of scripture. This clarifies the section in which Sudhana beholds Māyādevī’s illusory physical body pervading before all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

9. From the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana saw Lady Māyā" down to "How does one study the bodhisattva conduct so as to achieve its fulfillment," there are thirty-seven and a half lines of scripture. This section clarifies how Lady Māyā manifested a body that transcends all forms and appearances, pervading the entire ocean of worlds; it also shows how Sudhana likewise manifested an equal number of bodies, joined his palms in reverent salutation, requested what he sought, and attained entry into various gates of samādhi.

10. The passage beginning with “He replied: ‘O Son of the Buddha, I have already accomplished the Bodhisattva’s liberation of the wisdom-illusion of great vows’” and ending with “As for those who practice the Vows of Samantabhadra to transform all sentient beings, I manifest myself as their mother,” consists of one hundred and seven lines of scripture; it collectively clarifies Māyā’s response to Sudhana’s inquiry regarding the Dharma-gate.

11. At that time, the youth Sudhana asked Māyādevī, "How long has it been since you realized this liberation? From this point down to "I know only this bodhisattva gate of liberation of the magical illusion of the wisdom of great vows," there are twenty-seven lines of scripture, which clarify the portion concerning the duration since she attained this liberation in response to Sudhana’s question.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: as for Lady Māyā, she was formed through three dharmas in terms of her general characteristics; in terms of her specific characteristics, she acquired her name through practice-gates that equal the number of Buddhas and the number of sentient beings.
The three dharmas are: first, taking as its essence the wondrous principle of the *dharmakāya*, which is equal across all Buddhas and sentient beings, signless, and inherently pure;
second, taking as its essence the wisdom that is universally luminous, unconditioned, and non-reliant within the principle of equality shared by all Buddhas and sentient beings;

and third, taking as its essence the unconditioned nature within the unconditioned wisdom and principle that is equal across all Buddhas and sentient beings—this nature which nurtures all sentient beings, brings benefit through great kindness and compassion, shares the same original substance with all beings, transcends the distinction between self and other, and constantly acts for their benefit without seeking gratitude in return.
This is the original state of true nature, common to all sentient beings; by practicing according to these three dharmas, one will attain it.
Although it is common to all sentient beings, those who are deluded regarding it must possess the gates of expedient practice to initiate its manifestation before they can realize it.
What is skillful means?
These skillful means consist of ten great gates of vows, which one should practice and study according to those vows.

The first vow is to give rise, at the initial moment of generating the bodhicitta, to great vows of compassion equal in number to all sentient beings, vowing that all sentient beings shall be rescued and delivered from the suffering within the three realms, and that all shall attain Buddhahood.
Second, I vow that in serving, honoring, and making offerings to all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, not a single one shall pass by in vain.

Third, I vow that in whatever place within all worlds I may be born, should there be those whose virtue and arts surpass my own, I shall serve and study under them; though I master various skills and my wisdom excels that of gods and humans, I shall never give rise to arrogance, but shall always take great kindness and great compassion as my foremost priority.

Fourth, I vow to constantly observe the four foundations of mindfulness to treat illnesses according to their specific conditions, establishing the four right efforts to bring the faculties and powers to fulfillment.

Fifth, I vow to constantly maintain the seven factors of enlightenment within my mind, cultivating all-encompassing right wisdom to illuminate the twelve links of dependent origination and thereby manifest the great ocean of wisdom.
Sixth, I vow that the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path shall be ever-present, without beginning or end.

Seventh, I vow that my own realization of the Noble Path shall remain manifest in this world forever, benefiting all sentient beings of the six realms, including humans and devas, and that I myself shall take no pleasure in seeking a pure land elsewhere.

He clearly perceives the gateway to the entire dharma-realm and deeply understands that defilement and purity both originally arise from the provisional and are fundamentally non-existent within the ultimate reality.

He thoroughly knows the principles of the eight vows and the practice-gates of the five stages of a bodhisattva; regarding all the skillful means, samādhis, and dharmas for benefiting humans and devas within the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage, he comprehensively understands their courses in a single thought-moment and practices them in successive order.

Ninth, may they always maintain mindfulness of the wind-wheel of their original vow to sustain fundamental wisdom, thereby fanning and expanding the boundless practices of the *pāramitās*, manifesting form-bodies throughout the worlds of the ten directions to guide and lead all sentient beings according to their faculties.

In the tenth vow, may I always, through the body of great kindness and great compassion, give rise to all-encompassing wisdom and the great wisdom that pervades the Dharma-realm according to reality; may this universally illuminate all things without exception, so that all are equal as Samantabhadra.

This is the conduct accomplished by the body of Lady Māyā; if a practitioner is to practice, they should do so in this way, for there is not a single Buddha who has not arisen from the ocean of great vows and the wisdom of great compassion.
Therefore, the Sūtra states: "Only by practicing the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra are all [qualities] born from me.

This indicates that the wisdom of these eleven stages arises from compassion; that the practices of great kindness and great compassion prior to the tenth stage are all produced through original vows and fundamental wisdom, involving cultivation and nourishment through study; and that when all functions are perfected at the eleventh stage, it is purely great kindness and compassion that constitute the essence of the Dharma-realm.

By generating through compassion wisdom and illusory bodies equal in number to all sentient beings, constantly benefiting them without ever resting, one is called a "birth-Buddha"; it does not require the attainment of the thirty-two marks or even the ninety-seven marks.

However, at the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], there is a partial realization of reality, and wisdom and compassion arise together; although one has not yet attained the mastery of transformations and the changeless dharma of universal manifestation, this is because one’s knowledge and vision are identical with reality.
Cultivating and training in this manner, and awakening and entering in this manner, is what is called "attaining perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the resolve.
It is also called "showing and awakening sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," with the intent of causing sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

From this point on, Queen Māyā represents the initial gateway to the eleventh stage; the subsequent nine spiritual friends collectively clarify that, with great compassion as their maternal essence, they all follow the conduct of a mother, manifesting through the illusory power of wisdom so that compassionate wisdom pervades the ten directions and appears universally, without employing gradual stages or sequential antidotes.

Henceforth, although a spiritual friend may likewise say, "I know only this Dharma-gate and nothing else," this is intended to clarify that within the universal there is the particular; it expresses that the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra pervades all things in accordance with worldly convention, unlike those prior to the ten stages who remain obstructed and fail to reach realization.

These eleven stages merely manifest the practice of the conduct of the eleven stages; by fulfilling these eleven stages of Samantabhadra, one manifests the attainment of universal pervasiveness, wherein one is fully equipped for worldly existence while remaining free from seeking transcendence.

From the Lord Heavenly Light (Devaprabha) onwards, these [stages] all belong to the common stream of worldly beings; they do not exhibit divine marks or extraordinary features and are of one kind with ordinary people. However, there is the benefit of the Dharma for others: it clarifies that from the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) downwards is the gate of the supramundane holy path consisting of the cultivation of compassion and wisdom, while the eleventh stage is the gate of responding to the mundane world and saving sentient beings through the power of great compassion.

This manifests that the path of world-transcendence is fulfilled and there is no further seeking for liberation; though possessing a mind that both clings to and detaches from defilement, one merely boards the vessel of the Dharma-nature, hoists the sail of great compassion, and employs great wisdom as the helmsman. Blown by the wind of original vows, one spreads the net of the various *pāramitās* and constantly traverses the ocean of birth and death. One filters out all sentient beings who are like fish caught in the net of attachment, establishing them on the shore of non-reliant, universally radiant wisdom. One constantly gives birth within the unimpeded jeweled hall of the *dharmadhātu*, where the myriad practices and meritorious virtues dwell as illusions, just like the pavilion where Maitreya currently resides.

Just as Sudhana encountered the Rākṣasa King, who taught him the method for seeking spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), causing Sudhana to universally prostrate toward the ten directions, contemplate all objective realms with right mindfulness, and travel throughout the ten directions with courageous mastery, observing his body and mind as being like a dream, an illusion, and a shadow, while seeking spiritual friends.

At that time, Sudhana received and practiced those instructions; immediately, he beheld a great jewel lotus springing forth from the earth. Seeking a spiritual friend in the ten directions, he clearly examined his own body and mind throughout the internal and external ten directions, using the Dharma to seek with earnestness what essential nature exists, thereby causing them to accord with the Dharmakāya.

Furthermore, causing one to contemplate the body and the mind as being like a dream or a shadow is to cause them to penetrate the teaching; by penetrating both nature and characteristics as being identical and non-dual like a shadow, one enters the gate of the illusory birth of wisdom—this is the vision of Lady Māyā.

As for the initial vision of lotus flowers surging forth from the earth: the self-nature pure *dharmakāya* is taken as the substance of the earth, because all myriad practices arise as lotus flowers from this source.
That which has a vajra as its stem is the fundamental wisdom; it clarifies that all differentiated practices and differentiated wisdoms arise from the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya.

Even if there is such an adornment of this realm, it is likewise the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive support); ultimately, there is no separate retribution, nor is there any separate cause or fruit of retribution.
The "wondrous treasure-trove" is that which is born as a retribution for nurturing through compassion.
"Māṇi-jewels as petals" is that which is born as a retribution for stainless conduct.
"A king of luminous jewels as its pedestal" is that which is born as a retribution for the manifestation of fundamental wisdom and the sovereign power of illuminating function.

That its filaments consist of the colors and fragrances of various jewels is the retribution born from the perfumes of precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
That countless jewel nets completely cover its top is the retribution born from being able to bestow the net of the Dharma.
The presence of towers and pavilions above signifies the retribution-born arising from discriminative wisdom.
The universal inclusion of the Dharma-realm treasury of the ten directions signifies the retribution-born arising from the pervasive net of great wisdom that universally covers all.
"Wondrously adorned with precious ornaments" refers to the adornment resulting from the retribution of sublime conduct (*sucarita*).
"The ground is made of vajra" refers to the manifestation of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) as retribution.
"Arranged in rows of a thousand pillars" refers to the presence of thousands of millions of practices.
That everything is made of mani jewels signifies that within every practice there is no defilement.
That Jambūnada gold forms its walls signifies the rebirth resulting from the retribution of gentleness and patience.

The various jeweled necklaces hanging down on all four sides represent the retribution for practicing the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and extending compassion to receive and guide sentient beings.
All subsequent instances should be understood according to this principle; as the teachings are extensive and the text is lengthy, they cannot be described in full detail.

The subsequent passage—concerning the manifestation of a body pervading the entire Dharma-realm from Queen Māyā, a body identical to the activities of all sentient beings, and the birth of the bodies of all Tathāgatas—is self-evident according to the text.

When the youth Sudhana asked Lady Māyā how long it had been since she attained this liberation, Māyā replied: "Good son, it was in a past age beyond the reach of inconceivable eons, which cannot be known by the supernormal powers or the divine eye of bodhisattvas in their final birth, but can only be known by a Buddha."
The meaning clarifies that this cannot be known by means of temporal divisions, nor can it be measured by the calculation of kalpas.

One must rely on the seal of Buddha-wisdom to realize a dark harmony with the past and present until all measures are exhausted and both beginning and end vanish; only then can one know the duration—whether long or short—of their initial attainment of the mind and reception of the Dharma.
If one were to establish a view based on a beginning and an end, even if one were to compare it to the number of atoms in infinitely many lands, there would be no way to fully comprehend it.
Even if one were to compare it to the number of atoms in infinitely many successively multiplied lands, it still could not be fully comprehended.
When the calculations of conditioned phenomena are exhausted, it is only through the manifestation of wisdom that one truly knows.

Thus, there is no way to calculate their distance or proximity using numerical methods; even if one were to use mathematical algorithms to calculate the measure of empty space within a single pore over the course of all finite and infinite eons, one would find no limit to it, for empty space cannot be measured.
This is the time for attaining the immeasurable.

As the verse by Mañjuśrī says: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus understanding the matters of the three periods of time, one transcends all skillful means and accomplishes the ten powers."
"This is the general enumeration of Bodhisattvas in their final existence.
At that time, the kalpa was named Pure Light (Vimalaprabhā), signifying that the Dharma-body constitutes the substance of the kalpa.
The world-system was named Merit of Mount Sumeru (Sumeruguna), signifying that immovability constitutes the substance of the world-system."

Although there are various mountains where the five destinies dwell together, that land is composed of many jewels, pure and adorned, free from all impurities and evils; for when one's own mind is pure, all objective realms are pure, and all phenomena are stainless.
To produce the two views of purity and impurity is to perceive impurity within one's own mind.
Because great compassion universally encompasses the five realms of existence and great wisdom is free from such views as stained or pure, it is called "Adorned with Various Jewels."
The existence of a thousand billion sets of four continents illustrates the stage of manifesting the myriad practices to benefit sentient beings.
Within this, there is a set of four continents named Lion Banner, which illustrates that great wisdom pervades everywhere, such that the ten directions constitute a single realm.

Within it there are eight billion royal cities. There is one royal city named Sovereign Banner (*Svairadhvaja*), which elucidates the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path and the Ten Perfections (*daśapāramitā*).

Within that, the place where wisdom dwells and moves is called the Abode of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), and it is titled Sovereign Banner. The king is named Great Majestic Virtue (*Mahātejas*); he possesses mastery over wisdom and is able to govern birth and death while remaining himself indestructible.

To the north of that royal city was a place of practice called Full Moon Radiance. As for "to the north," north is the position of the pit; it is the abode of the Master, the Sovereign of Wisdom, and the station for governing delusion; therefore, it is termed a "place of practice" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Because it can cure the grasping of delusions, it is called "Full Moon Radiance.
As for the deity of that bodhimanda named Maitreyaguna, she uses wisdom to transform the deluded and takes compassion as her virtue.
There was a bodhisattva named Vimaladhvaja, whose conduct arose from the Dharma-body and whose nature was inherently stainless.
As he sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) about to achieve perfect awakening, he desired to become a general.

There was an evil māra named Golden Light who, together with his retinue and host of soldiers, came to where the Bodhisattva was. That Wheel-Turning King of Great威德 (magnificent power) had already attained the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of a Bodhisattva; he freely manifested a host of soldiers many times greater in number, surrounding the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). When all the māras were struck with terror and fled in all directions, the intent [of this passage] clarifies that for the evil māra named Golden Light, the realm of the Dharma-body wisdom (*dharmakāya-jñāna*) is characterized by the single mark of the identity between the true and the false.

The Bodhisattva Vigataraja had not yet clarified the equality of the mind and its objects; he required the aid of the King of All-Knowledge to clearly contemplate the principle that the mind and its objects are fundamentally non-dual. Realizing that the mind and its objects are like illusions—that all objective realms arise illusorily through illusory wisdom—he was no longer deluded regarding those objects.
The mind-demon of delusive appearances perceives the entire dharma-realm as mundane affairs, which is termed "dissipation.
That the deities of the bodhimanda feel compassion and joy is the delight of the Dharma.

That the deity of the site (maṇḍaladevatā) conceives the thought of being the king’s son clarifies that the destruction of views arises from wisdom (*jñāna*), while the initiation of practice to transform the world arises from compassion (*karuṇā*); it clarifies that the wisdom of this stage is born from compassion and loving-kindness, and thus regards wisdom as a son.

As for the statement that "the Universal Monarch who gathers [all beings] is Vairocana, and I myself am the deity of the site of enlightenment," this clarifies that fearing people might not understand the intended meaning, he relies on concrete phenomena and images to make it easy to comprehend.
Ultimately, one must not regard the mind as having objects that exist separately outside of it.
Rather, clarify that the mind has no interior, exterior, or middle; that all phenomena—self and other—are of the same essence; and that the one is not one, and the other is not other.
It is simply because the Dharma is profound and difficult to manifest that one borrows worldly affairs to clarify it; those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables.

Thus, all who first give rise to the unsurpassed mind of great Bodhicitta must first arouse the mind of great vows and great compassion to teach and transform sentient beings, before seeking the essential means of liberation and the practices for benefiting others.
When the practice is fulfilled, this Dharma does not shift.
All Buddhas are likewise, for they are first born from great compassion, great vows, and practice.

When the immeasurable Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions are about to attain Buddhahood, they all emit a great radiance from their navels to illuminate my body, my palace, and my residence—wherein the palace of compassion and the hall of wisdom serve as the dwelling that nurtures and sustains, and the ocean of birth and death serves as the abode.
It is clarified that within the center of the body at the location of the navel, at the moment when all sentient beings are born and grow, this place is the treasury that contains birth and growth.

It is like the root-base of a tree: from it, stems, trunks, and branches grow upward, while roots extend downward into the earth; it is situated at the midpoint between yin and yang, the primordial source of manifestation.
Furthermore, just as within the sexagenary cycle of the Jiazi decade, Gui (戌) serves as the Tiankui (Celestial Leader), generating Yang on the left and Yin on the right;

so too, the light now emitted from the navel symbolizes the primordial beginning of receiving birth. It is like the image of Tiankui, for it marks the inception of compassion and the source from which great wisdom arises.

As it is with the birth of a human being, so it is likewise for one who is born small and gradually grows large: from the navel wheel (nābhi-cakra), vital energy (prāṇa) arises, which penetrates both above and below as the nature of growth, because this place is the primary source from which the reception of vital energy first begins.
Releasing from this is also its position of dryness; it is the juncture between beginning and end, the source of growth and development, and this is precisely the center of the navel.
Furthermore, it symbolizes the central interval between wisdom and compassion, and the fulfillment of wisdom; this is the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the tuft of hair) between the eyebrows.
It is because within the midst of great compassion, it is precisely at the navel.

This is the eleventh stage, the gate of Samantabhadra abiding in the world to benefit sentient beings; it remedies the obstacle in the tenth stage where, despite the transcendental conditions for benefiting beings, one lacks mastery over such benefit and one's practice is not yet vast.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," when the bodhisattvas seek Samantabhadra through the three modes of seeking, this constitutes the primary practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) within the course of great wisdom; it presides over the gateway to the ocean of *pāramitās* throughout the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

It is universally said that all Buddhas of the three periods are born first through compassion; those who lack the compassion that benefits sentient beings and harbor weariness toward birth and death are merely followers of the Two Vehicles or Bodhisattvas of the Pure Lands, who must only later turn their minds back to return to the Truth.
Those of fixed nature find it difficult to turn back even over many kalpas.
The rest is fully contained within the sutra itself.
I know only this much: that for those who possess the liberation of the great vow-wisdom-illusion of a bodhisattva, their virtue clearly advances as they are promoted.
Regarding the advancement through the promotion of virtue, there are three sections:
First, indicating the location of the virtuous friend, it says they reside in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There is a king named Samprajanya (Right Mindfulness), whose brilliant wisdom and pure sovereignty are like those of the Heavenly King.

The term "right mindfulness" signifies that pure wisdom is free from discursive thought and acts with sovereign mastery in accordance with principle; it functions spontaneously without effort, such that all affairs are accomplished of themselves, clarifying how the pure wisdom of the eleven stages manifests through effortless spontaneity.
Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), he is merely called "Right Mindfulness" (*samyaksmṛti*).
When the Son of Heaven inquires about his holy life (*brahmacarya*), it is not yet said that he has a daughter.
Upon reaching this eleventh stage, he is called a "King," and it is further stated that he has a daughter; this clarifies that compassion arises from wisdom.

There is a daughter named Devendrābhā, who symbolizes the unconditioned wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) wherein compassion is untainted by nature and freely employed for the benefit of sentient beings.
This stage symbolizes the perfection of wisdom, whose function is without before or after.

Regarding the term "taking up the heavens," this signifies manifesting sovereign spiritual transformations within the cycle of birth and death without fixed direction, rather than being confined to a specific location.

I respectfully state my aspiration: may I attain the Bodhisattva liberation named "Unobstructed Mindfulness. By attaining unobstructed wisdom regarding the three periods of time, may I, in a single thought-moment, seal the entire duration of the births and deaths of all sentient beings throughout the past, present, and future, as well as the duration of the enlightenment of all Buddhas of the three periods. May I universally know all things in a single thought-moment with perfect clarity, as if they were presently before me.
Because the wisdom of non-delusive thought manifests before one, as all phenomena are fundamentally thus, this clarifies the correct mindfulness-wisdom that is free from delusive thought.

Regarding the number of Buddhas within all the kalpas therein—whether one makes offerings to many Buddhas during those kalpas in varying numbers—in a single moment of non-thought, the correct wisdom universally makes offerings to the number of Buddhas of the three periods of time; this is the state of "long duration" within that which is neither long nor near.
The great, perfectly round wisdom-realm of all time is such by the very nature of phenomena; it does not arise through cultivation.

Cultivation merely involves illuminating the twelve links of dependent origination for oneself, whereby one penetrates delusion and realizes wisdom. Since wisdom has nothing to cultivate, one simply liberates oneself from confusion. In truth, there is nothing to be done, nor is there a nature characterized by the three periods of time or antiquity and modernity.
This is the second stage of the eleven stages, the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Following this section on the spiritual friend of the second stage among the eleven stages, the text generally clarifies the body of practice for gathering sentient beings through shared conduct, wherein the unimpeded wisdom-function within right mindfulness is all-pervasive.

This is the case for all worlds throughout the ten directions; the six realms of existence and so forth are pervasive, all arising from the ocean of Great Compassion of Lady Māyā, having the wisdom of non-action through right mindfulness as their essence.
This is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) within the eleventh stage; because it is the gateway through which wisdom gives rise to compassion, the maiden is named Devendraprabhā.
The third [stage] is the city of Kapilavastu, the teacher of youths; this is the Yellow City.
The yellow color is the hue of the Central Palace;
